<meta>This page transitions from a simple archival reference on the previous page to a detailed biographical and bibliographic entry concerning the famous anatomist Andreas Vesalius. It evaluates the quality of his publications and lists his secondary works.</meta>

At the age of twenty-eight, Vesalius published his work **On the Structure of the Human Body** <note>original: "De humani corporis fabrica," the foundational text of modern human anatomy published in 1543</note>, a work so grand and truly royal that no other seems comparable to it. For it is written in a magnificent Latin style and displays such anatomical experience that the entire world of scholars, until its very last day, will never be able to admire it enough; notably, he reached that peak of learning with no [living] teacher <note>This refers to Vesalius’s revolutionary approach of learning from direct dissection of the human body rather than relying solely on the ancient teachings of Galen</note>. Among all the editions of this work, the best is the one that was produced in Basel through the <unclear>labor</unclear> of Oporinus <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a famous Swiss printer known for the high quality of his woodblock illustrations</note>, and especially that of the year 1555. Neither the Venetian editions, to say nothing of others, do the illustrations or the typesetting deserve to be compared with the elegance of the Oporinian edition; see Conring’s *Introduction* <note>Hermann Conring (1606–1681) was a German polymath and professor</note>, page [unspecified]. He <unclear>also</unclear> wrote on the **China Root** <term>Radix Chinae: a medicinal plant from the Smilax family used in the 16th century to treat various diseases, including syphilis</term> and the **Examination of the Observations of Falloppio** <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562) was a renowned Italian anatomist and a student of Vesalius</note>.

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the work to Emperor Charles V. It follows the title page and library markings from the previous leaf.</meta>

# TO THE DIVINE CHARLES
## THE FIFTH, THE GREATEST AND MOST INVINCIBLE EMPEROR, THE PREFACE OF ANDREAS VESALII TO HIS
### Books on the Fabric of the Human Body.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'V' depicting an anatomical scene. Several figures in 16th-century attire are gathered around a table; some appear to be students or assistants, while others are observing or performing a task. In the background, a skeleton is visible, and there is a sense of an active dissection or medical demonstration taking place within the letter's framework.</image-desc>

Although many obstacles gravely hinder the practice of arts and sciences, preventing them from being learned accurately or applied successfully, I believe, most merciful Emperor Charles, that no small loss is brought about by the too-great division of those disciplines which serve to complete any single art. This is even more true of the distribution of an art's practical exercises among different practitioners—so much so that those who have set the goal of the art for themselves embrace only one part of it, while leaving aside the other parts which most closely relate to it and cannot be separated from it. Consequently, they never achieve anything outstanding, and never reaching their proposed goal, they perpetually deviate from the true constitution of the art.

For—to pass over the other arts in silence and speak for a moment about that which is in charge of human health—certainly in this one, which is by far the most beneficial, necessary, difficult, and laborious of all that the human mind has devised, nothing more pestilential could have crept in than the fact that at some point (and especially after the deluge of the Goths <note>original: "Gotthorum illuuiem"; Vesalius refers to the Middle Ages as a period of intellectual decline following the fall of Rome.</note> and the time of Mansur, the King of Bukhara in Persia <note>original: "Manſoremq́; Bocharæ"; likely referring to Al-Mansur, the patron of the physician Rhazes, marking the era of Arabic medical dominance.</note>, under whom the Arabs still flourished in a deservedly familiar way with the Greeks), medicine began to be so torn apart that its primary instrument, the work of the hand <note>original: "manus operam"; this refers to surgery and manual dissection.</note> in healing, was so neglected that it seemed to be delegated only to commoners and those not at all trained in the disciplines subservient to the medical art.

For although three sects of physicians once existed—namely the Logical, the Empirical, and the Methodical—nevertheless, the authors of those sects directed the goal of the entire art toward the preservation of health and the driving away of diseases. Then, referring everything to this goal which they deemed necessary for the art within their respective sects, they employed a triple instrument of aids. The first was the theory of diet; the second, the entire use of medicines; the third, the work of the hand. This third part, above all others, elegantly shows that medicine is the "addition of what is lacking and the removal of what is superfluous" <note>A classical definition of the surgical aspect of medicine.</note>, and it never fails to offer its use in the treatment of afflictions whenever we engage in medical matters; time and experience have taught that this is most healthful for the human race. 

This triple method of healing was equally familiar to the physicians of every sect. Adapting their own hands to the treatment according to the nature of the afflictions, they spent no less industry in exercising them than in establishing a dietary regime or in identifying and compounding medicines. This is clearly shown, among other books by the divine Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE).</note>, by those he wrote most perfectly on the duty of the physician, on fractures of bones, on dislocations of joints, and evils of that kind. Furthermore, Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire (129 – c. 216 CE), whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note>, the prince of medicine after Hippocrates, besides frequently boasting that the care of the gladiators of Pergamum was committed to him alone, did not wish the apes he had to dissect to be skinned by the labor of assistants, even when he was advanced in age. He frequently emphasizes how much he was delighted by the skill of the hand, and how studiously...

<summary>In this opening to his preface, Vesalius addresses Emperor Charles V and laments the historical decline of medicine, specifically criticizing the separation of manual surgery and dissection from theoretical medical study.</summary>
<keywords>Charles V, Andreas Vesalius, medical history, surgery, Hippocrates, Galen, three sects of medicine, anatomical study</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Vesalius’s dedication to Emperor Charles V. He is explaining how the ancient practice of medicine—which combined theory, drugs, and manual surgery—became fractured during the Middle Ages, leading to a decline in medical knowledge.</meta>

...carefully practiced it along with the other physicians of Asia. Indeed, none of the ancients failed to hand down to posterity the treatment performed by hand as attentively as they did the treatment achieved through diet and medication.

However, especially after the devastation of the Goths, when all the sciences—previously flourishing beautifully and practiced as was fitting—went to ruin, the more elegant physicians first in Italy began to disdain manual labor, following the imitation of the ancient Romans. They began to prescribe to servants those things that had to be done by hand for the sick, standing by them only in the manner of architects. Soon, as others also gradually avoided the inconveniences of practicing true medicine—meanwhile losing nothing of their profit or honor—they quickly degenerated from the ancient physicians. They left the method of cooking and all preparation of the patients' food to the caregivers, the composition of medicines to the pharmacists <term>pharmacopolis: drug-sellers or apothecaries</term>, and the work of the hands to the barbers <term>tonsoribus: traditional barbers who, in this era, performed minor surgeries, bloodletting, and tooth extractions</term>.

And so, with the passage of time, the method of healing was so miserably torn apart that physicians, selling themselves under the name of "natural philosophers" <term>physicorum: meaning those who study the nature of the body and internal medicine, as opposed to manual surgeons</term>, arrogated to themselves only the prescription of drugs and diet for hidden ailments. The rest of medicine they relegated to those they call Surgeons—whom they hardly regard even as servants—shamefully casting off the most important and ancient branch of medicine, which relies primarily on the observation of nature. Yet today, kings among the Indians especially practice this; the Persians hand it down by hereditary right to their children (just as the whole art of the followers of Aesculapius <note>original: "Asclepiadum"; the Asclepiads were a guild of physicians in ancient Greece claiming descent from the god of healing</note> once was); and the Thracians, along with many other nations, hold it in the highest honor and venerate it.

That part of the art has been nearly neglected which many once banished from the State, as if it were devised for mocking and killing men—since it accomplishes nothing without the help of nature. Indeed, when nature is busy struggling against disease, this part, while trying to help, frequently ruins everything and draws nature away from its duty entirely. This is why we especially owe it to those who, with so many insults usually hurled at doctors, mock this most sacred art. Yet that part of it which those trained in the liberal arts shamefully allow to be torn from them actually brings it the greatest praise.

For when Homer, the fountainhead of genius, affirms that a medical man is worth more than many others <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, Book 11, where Homer praises the physician as being worth many soldiers</note>, and celebrates Podalirius and Machaon with all the poets of Greece, these sons of the divine Aesculapius are not praised for removing a slight fever (which Nature alone usually heals more easily without the doctor’s help than with it), or for serving the palate of men in hidden and hopeless ailments. Rather, they are praised because they were primarily in charge of treating dislocations, fractures, contusions, wounds, and other ruptures of the body's continuity, and the flow of blood; and because they freed the most noble soldiers of Agamemnon from spears, arrows, and other such evils (which wars especially bring, and which always require the diligent work of a doctor).

But I have by no means proposed to prefer one instrument of medicine over the others, since the mentioned triple method of aid can by no means be separated or torn apart; the whole belongs to a single practitioner. To execute this properly, all parts of medicine should be equally established and prepared, so that each part is applied more successfully the more one joins them all together in turn. Moreover, it is entirely rare for a disease to occur that does not immediately require the triple instrument of protection: thus an appropriate diet must be established, and something must be attempted with medication and, finally, by hand. Therefore, the apprentices of this art should be encouraged in every way to disregard the whispers of those (Gods help us!) "natural philosophers" and—in the manner of the Greeks and as the nature and reasoning of the art strictly dictate—apply their hands also to healing. Let them not thereafter turn a mangled medicine into the ruin of common human life.

<summary>Vesalius critiques the historical separation of surgery from internal medicine, arguing that the ancient Greek masters (and even Homeric heroes) combined manual skill with theory. He urges modern medical students to reclaim the "manual" part of medicine to prevent the art from remaining incomplete and harmful.</summary>
<keywords>surgery, history of medicine, Aesculapius, Podalirius, Machaon, physicians vs surgeons, medical education, ancient Greece, Homer</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of "De humani corporis fabrica," where Vesalius is decrying the separation of manual surgery from theoretical medicine. He argues that this division has led to a "shipwreck" of medical knowledge.</meta>

# THE PREFACE OF ANDREAS VESALIUS.

...turn back. And they should be urged toward this all the more diligently, because we see those more thoroughly learned in the art today avoiding manual work as if it were a plague. They do this especially so that they are not translated <note>or "betrayed/represented"</note> as barbers by the "Rabbis" <note>original: "Rabinis." Vesalius uses this term sarcastically to refer to dogmatic medical professors who rely on old texts rather than observation.</note> of the physicians in front of the uneducated commoners. They fear that they might not afterward receive the same profit, honor, and esteem among the unskilled commoners and even princes as is granted to those who are barely half-physicians.

Indeed, this detestable opinion of many is the primary obstacle preventing us, even in this age, from reclaiming the whole craft of healing. By claiming for ourselves only the treatment of internal ailments, we strive to be physicians only in small part—to the great harm of mortals, to speak truly for once. For since the entire composition of medicines was first relegated to the pharmacists <term>pharmacopolas: druggists or apothecaries</term>, physicians soon lost the knowledge of simple medicines <term>simplicium: basic medicinal ingredients, usually herbal, before they are mixed into compounds</term>, which is absolutely necessary for them. Thus, they were the authors of the shops being flooded with so many barbaric names and even false drugs, and of the loss of so many elegant compositions of the ancients—many of which still lie hidden. Indeed, they have prepared an inexhaustible labor for the most learned men of our time, and those who preceded us by a few years, who have applied themselves with untiring zeal to the knowledge of simple medicines; in attempting to restore it to its former luster, they seem to have contributed a great deal.

Furthermore, this most "childish" division of the instruments of healing among various craftsmen brought an even more execrable shipwreck and a far more cruel disaster upon the principal part of natural philosophy. Since natural philosophy <note>In this context, it refers to the study of the nature of the human body.</note> encompasses the history of man and must rightly be held as the firmest foundation of the whole medical art and its constitutional beginning, Hippocrates and Plato attributed so much to it that they did not hesitate to rank it among the primary parts of medicine. For while this science was previously uniquely cultivated by physicians, who applied every effort to mastering it, it finally began to collapse miserably when they, throwing the duty of the hands to others, lost Anatomy <term>Anatomen: the study of structure through dissection</term>. 

While physicians believed that only the treatment of internal ailments belonged to them, thinking that a knowledge of the viscera <note>the internal organs</note> alone was abundantly sufficient, they neglected the structure of the bones, muscles, nerves, veins, and arteries that crawl through the bones and muscles, as if these did not concern them. In addition to this, since the entire administration was committed to barbers, not only did the true knowledge of the viscera perish among physicians, but the skill of dissection also utterly fell away. This happened because the physicians did not undertake the cutting themselves, while those to whom the manual craft was delegated were too unlearned to understand the writings of the professors of dissection. 

Far from that class of men preserving for us this most difficult art handed over to their hands, this deplorable dispersal of the healing art introduced a detestable ritual into the Universities <term>Gymnasijs: centers of higher learning</term>: one person performs the dissection of the human body, while another provides the account of the parts. The latter, perched high in a chair with extraordinary arrogance, chirps like a jackdaw <note>original: "graculorum modo"</note> about things he has never performed but has merely committed to memory from the books of others, or has the description placed before his eyes. The former, however, are so ignorant of languages that they are unable to explain the dissections to the spectators, and they butcher what is to be shown according to the physician's instructions—a physician who, having never applied his hand to a dissection, haughtily acts as a pilot from a manual <note>original: "nautam... ex commentario," an idiom for someone giving directions for a task they have never actually done.</note>. 

And so, everything is taught wrongly, and days pass in ridiculous questions; thus, in that chaos, fewer things are shown to the spectators than a butcher in a meat market could teach a physician. I will pass over those schools where they hardly ever think of dissecting the structure of the human body; so far has ancient medicine fallen from its former glory many years ago. Furthermore, since it has long been in such [a state] of this age (which, by your divine power, you wisely [govern]...

He argues that this neglect of anatomy has ruined the "foundation" of medical knowledge.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Vesalius’s dedication to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. In the preceding text, Vesalius lamented how the art of medicine had been torn apart, with physicians abandoning the manual work of surgery and dissection to subordinates. He now describes his personal efforts to restore anatomy to its former glory.</meta>

# TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES V

...since (as the gods wish it to be moderated, not undeservedly, in later times) it had begun to revive with such happiness alongside all other studies, and to raise its head from the deepest darkness, it seemed that in some Universities it had almost recovered its old brilliance beyond controversy. Yet, it still lacked nothing more urgently than the knowledge of the parts of the human body, which had been almost completely dead. Provoked by the example of so many distinguished men, I decided that I should bring help to this cause to the best of my ability and by whatever means I could. And lest I alone should remain idle while everyone else was attempting something for the sake of our common studies with such success—or indeed, lest I should degenerate from my ancestors, who were certainly famous physicians—I thought that this branch of natural philosophy <term>naturalis philosophiae: the study of nature and the physical universe, the precursor to modern science</term> should be recalled from the underworld. My goal was that if dissection were not practiced more perfectly among us than ever before, it should at least reach a point where one would not be ashamed to assert that our method of dissection could be compared with that of the ancients; and that in this era, nothing has been so collapsed and then restored to its integrity as Anatomy has been.

But this study would by no means have succeeded if, while I was studying medicine at Paris, I had not applied my own hands to this business myself. I did not settle for having a few internal organs shown to me and my fellow students superficially by certain barbers <note>In medieval and early Renaissance universities, the "physician" would read from a book while a "barber-surgeon" performed the actual cutting. Vesalius found this method inadequate.</note> in one or two public dissections. For anatomy was handled so perfunctorily there—where we first saw medicine successfully reborn—that I had to practice by dissecting several animals on my own. Eventually, at the urging of my fellow students and teachers, I publicly performed a third dissection (which focused mainly on the internal organs, as was the custom there) more thoroughly than usual. When I attempted a second one, I tried to show the muscles of the hand along with a more accurate dissection of the organs. For, except for the eight muscles of the abdomen, which were shamefully mangled in the wrong order, no one had ever shown me a single muscle—just as they had never shown a single bone, much less the sequence of nerves, veins, and arteries.

Soon afterward, I had to return to Louvain <note>A city in modern-day Belgium, then part of the Habsburg Netherlands.</note> due to the disturbances of war. Because the doctors there had not even dreamed of anatomy for eighteen years, I decided to serve the students of that Academy and make myself more skilled in a matter that is hidden but absolutely necessary for all of medicine. While dissecting, I explained the human fabric <term>humanam fabricam: the structure, "workings," or "architecture" of the human body</term> a little more accurately than had been done in Paris. As a result, the younger professors of that Academy now seem to devote great and serious effort to identifying the parts of man, clearly understanding what excellent equipment for philosophizing the knowledge of these parts supplies them.

Furthermore, at Padua, in the most famous school in the entire world, the teaching of anatomy has fallen to me. This is because the profession of surgery was entrusted to me five years ago by the most illustrious Venetian Senate—a body by far the most generous toward the study of learning. I have devoted such effort to investigating the construction of man that I have now performed this very frequently and, having exploded the ridiculous custom of the schools, I have taught in such a way that we can lack nothing that has come down to us from the ancients.

Yet, the laziness of doctors has taken too much care that the writings of Eudemus, Herophilus, Marinus, Andreas, Lycus, and other leaders of dissection <note>Vesalius lists legendary Greek anatomists whose works were mostly lost to history.</note> were not preserved for us. Not even a fragment of a single page survives of so many illustrious authors, of whom Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (2nd century AD), the most influential medical writer until Vesalius's time.</note> mentions more than twenty in his second commentary on Hippocrates's book *On the Nature of Man*. Indeed, barely half of Galen’s own anatomical books have been rescued from destruction. Those who followed Galen—in whose rank I include Oribasius, Theophilus, the Arabs, and all our own writers I have happened to read—all of them (if they will pardon me for saying so) borrowed whatever they passed on that was worth reading from him. And by Jupiter! To a studious person who is actually dissecting, nothing is ever less...

<summary>Vesalius describes his education in Paris and his subsequent teaching career in Louvain and Padua, emphasizing his hands-on approach to dissection in contrast to the superficial methods of his predecessors. He laments the loss of ancient anatomical texts and critiques the total reliance of later physicians on the works of Galen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Vesalius’s critique of the contemporary medical establishment. On the previous page, he described his early studies in Paris and his realization that the current method of teaching anatomy was deeply flawed because physicians had abandoned the actual practice of dissection to uneducated assistants.</meta>

# PREFACE BY ANDREAS VESALIUS

<sig>a 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: ciantur (referring to "suffulciantur," the conclusion of the final word on this page)</meta>

...seen to have progressed, rather than in the dissection of bodies: to such an extent do the leaders of these men cling tooth and nail to some manner of speaking, and trusting the laziness of others in the task of cutting, they have shamefully reduced Galen into wasteful summaries. They never recede from him, while they follow his meanings, by even a hair’s breadth <note>original: "ne latum quidem unguem" — literally "not even a broad fingernail," a common idiom for the smallest possible distance</note>. Indeed, they add to the front of their books that their own writings are entirely stitched together from Galen’s decrees, and that all their work is his.

And thus everyone has given him such faith that no physician has been found who judged that even the slightest slip had ever been detected in Galen’s anatomical volumes, much less that one could be detected. This is despite the fact that, in the meantime (besides the fact that Galen frequently corrects himself, and in some books points out the negligence he committed in others once he became more experienced, and subsequently teaches the opposite), it is now clear to us, from the reborn art of dissection and diligent reading of Galen’s books—and in many places a not regrettable restoration of them—that he himself never dissected a recently dead human body.

Rather, having been deceived by his monkeys <note>Galen primarily dissected Barbary macaques, assuming their internal structure was identical to humans</note> (even if dried human corpses, prepared as if for the inspection of bones, occasionally came his way), he frequently and undeservedly argued against the ancient physicians who had exercised themselves in the preparation of humans. Furthermore, you may find very many things in his work which he even described incorrectly in monkeys. Not to mention that it is most wonderful how, in the manifold and infinite differences of the organs of the human body compared to the monkey, Galen noticed almost none, except in the fingers and the bend of the knee <term>poplitis flexu: the back of the knee</term>. He would undoubtedly have omitted these along with the rest, had they not been obvious to him without the dissection of a man.

But for the present, I have by no means resolved to criticize the false dogmas of Galen, easily the leader among the professors of dissection; still less would I wish to be held, right at the start, as impious toward the author of all good things, or as unobservant of his authority. For I am not ignorant of how physicians (very differently from the followers of Aristotle) are accustomed to be agitated when they observe, in the performance of a single Anatomy such as I now show in the schools, that Galen has declined from the true harmony, use, and function of the human parts more than two hundred times—all the while weighing the dissected particles grimly and with the greatest zeal for defending him.

Although even these men, led by the love of truth, gradually grow mild and place more trust in their own eyes and in effective reasoning than in the writings of Galen. These true paradoxes, not patched together from the attempts of others nor confirmed only by a heap of authorities, they have written so diligently here and there to friends, and have so happily and kindly encouraged them toward inspection and finally toward the knowledge of true Anatomy, that there is hope this study will shortly be so cultivated in all Universities as it was once accustomed to be practiced in Alexandria <note>Alexandria in Egypt was the greatest center of anatomical study in antiquity, where human dissection was first permitted</note>.

So that this may succeed under the happier auspices of the Muses, I have—to the best of my ability, beyond those things which I have published elsewhere on this subject, and which certain plagiarists, thinking me far absent from Germany, have published there as their own—now rearranged the history of the parts of the human body from scratch into seven books, in the same order in which I am accustomed to treat it in this city <note>Vesalius refers to Padua, where he held the chair of surgery and anatomy</note>, and in Bologna and Pisa, before that gathering of learned men.

For in this way, those who were present for the cutting will have commentaries on the things demonstrated, and will show Anatomy to others with less trouble. Moreover, these books will by no means be useless even to those for whom a personal inspection is denied, since they describe the number, position, shape, substance, connection to other parts, use, and function of every part of the human body, and many such things which we are accustomed to investigate while dissecting into the nature of the parts. They also include the technique of dissecting both the dead and the living, and they contain images of all the parts inserted into the context of the discourse, so that they place, as it were, a dissected body before the eyes of those who study the works of Nature.

<margin>of the first book</margin>
And indeed, in the first book I have described the nature of all the bones and cartilages, which, because the rest of the parts are supported by them...

<summary>Vesalius exposes the central flaw of traditional anatomy: Galen, the ultimate authority, never actually dissected a human, but instead relied on animal subjects like monkeys. Vesalius introduces his own work as a revolutionary, seven-book correction of these ancient errors based on his own human dissections.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface to the Emperor Charles V. Vesalius has just argued that Galen, the foundational authority of medieval medicine, relied on animal rather than human dissection. He now moves into a description of the structure of his own work, *De humani corporis fabrica* (On the Fabric of the Human Body), and defends his use of detailed anatomical illustrations.</meta>

->### TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES V<-

...are supported, and are described according to these, must first be known by students of Anatomy.
<margin>Summary of the second book</margin>The second book commemorates the ligaments, by whose benefit the bones and cartilages are connected to each other, and then the muscles, the workers of movements that depend on our will.
<margin>The third</margin>The third encompasses the very frequent series of veins—which carry the familiar blood to the muscles, bones, and other parts so they may be nourished—and then the arteries, which moderate the temperature of the innate heat and the vital spirit.
<margin>The fourth</margin>The fourth teaches not only the branches of the nerves, which carry the animal spirit <note>In Renaissance physiology, "animal spirit" (from *anima*, soul/life) was thought to travel through hollow nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> to the muscles, but also all the other branches as well.
<margin>The fifth</margin>The fifth delivers the construction of the organs serving nutrition, which is completed through food and drink; and furthermore, due to the proximity of their location, it also contains the instruments fabricated by the supreme Craftsman of things for the succession of the species <note>referring to the reproductive organs</note>.
<margin>The sixth</margin>The sixth is dedicated to the heart, the hearth of the vital faculty, and to its ministering parts.
<margin>The seventh</margin>The seventh pursues the harmony of the brain and the organs of sense in such a way that the series of nerves originating from the brain, expressed in the fourth book, is not repeated. Indeed, in arranging the order of these books, I have followed the opinion of Galen, who thought that after the history of the muscles, the anatomy of the veins, arteries, nerves, and then the viscera should be treated. Although not without reason, and especially for a beginner in this science, someone might contend that the knowledge of the viscera should be pursued along with the distribution of the vessels, just as I performed in the *Epitome* <note>The *Epitome* was a condensed, more affordable version of Vesalius's work intended for students</note>; which I prepared as a path to these books and an index of the things demonstrated in them, decorated with the splendor of the most serene Prince Philip, your Majesty’s son and a living exemplar of his father’s virtues. 

But here the judgment of some occurs to me, who sharply condemn not only the exquisite delineations of herbs, but also those of the parts of the human body being proposed to students of natural things; because they say these should be learned not by pictures, but by diligent dissection <term>refectione: literally "remaking" or "repairing," here referring to the act of dissecting to see the structure</term> and the intuition of the things themselves. This is as if I had added these most true icons of the parts to the context of the discourse—which I hope will never be corrupted by the printers—on the grounds that students, relying on them, might refrain from the sectioning of bodies; rather, I have added them so that I might encourage candidates of medicine by all possible means to undertake dissections with their own hands. Truly, if the custom of the ancients—who exercised boys at home in performing dissections just as they did in drawing the elements and in reading—had been brought down to this point, I would easily permit us to do without not only pictures but all commentaries, just like those ancients. For they first began to write about the *Procedures of Dissection* only when they judged it honorable to communicate the art not only to their own children but also to foreign men whom they respected for their virtue. For as soon as boys were no longer exercised in dissections, it necessarily followed immediately that they learned anatomy less successfully, once the practice they used to begin in childhood was abolished. So much so that when the art fell away from the family of the Asclepiads <note>The "Asclepiads" were a guild of physicians in ancient Greece claiming descent from Asclepius, the god of medicine</note> and for many centuries drifted into decline, books were needed to preserve the entire theory of the art. Truly, there is no one who does not experience in geometry and other mathematical disciplines how much pictures help in understanding them, and how they place the matter more exactly before the eyes than even the most explicit discourse. However it may be, in this whole work I have uniquely studied this: that in a business far most hidden, and no less arduous, I might benefit as many as possible, and treat the history of the human body’s fabric—constructed of not ten or twelve (as it appears to one looking in passing) but several thousand different parts—as truly and absolutely as possible, and bring no contemptible fruit to the candidates of medicine for understanding Galen’s books on this doctrine, which among his other monuments especially require the help of a teacher. But meanwhile, it does not escape me how this effort, at my age...

<meta>This page concludes Vesalius’s dedication to Emperor Charles V. After describing the seven books of his work, Vesalius now defends his youthful ambition and his decision to challenge the long-standing authority of Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose teachings had remained unquestioned for over a millennium. He appeals to the Emperor’s own interest in science and his family’s history of service to the crown.</meta>

->### PREFACE OF ANDREAS VESALIUS<-

Because I have not yet passed my twenty-eighth year, this occasion will carry little authority. Furthermore, because of my frequent indications of Galen’s untrue dogmas, it will not be safe from the habits of those who—just like us in the Italian schools—have not diligently applied themselves to Anatomy. These men, now old and wasting away with envy over the correct discoveries of younger men, will be ashamed to have been blind until now, along with the rest who followed Galen. Despite claiming a great name for themselves in the art of medicine, they will be ashamed not to have noticed the things we now propose. This work would hardly dare to come forth into the light under favorable omens unless it were commended, according to custom, by the great patronage of some divine power.

Truly, because it can be protected by no name more safely, nor adorned more splendidly, than by the never-dying name of the Divine Charles, the most invincible and greatest Emperor, I beseech your Majesty to allow this youthful study of mine—indebted to you for many reasons and causes—to pass into the hands of men for a time under your leadership, brilliance, and patronage. This shall continue until, through the use of things and the judgment and learning that grows with age, I may render this labor worthy of the highest and best Prince, or offer another gift of a different argument drawn from our art that is not to be rejected.

Yet I predict that, out of the entire discipline of Apollo <note>original: "Apollinea disciplina"; referring to the god of healing and medicine</note>, and indeed out of all natural philosophy, nothing could be produced that is more pleasing or acceptable to your Majesty than this history. Through it, we come to know the body and the soul, and furthermore a certain divine power from the harmony of both—and finally, we come to know ourselves (which is truly the task of a human being). As I gather this from many arguments, so I especially suspect it because, among that multitude of books dedicated to your grandfather, Maximilian <note>Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor (1459–1519)</note>, of happy memory, no book was ever more pleasing than one concerning the present business.

Nor shall I ever forget with what pleasure you inspected my anatomical tables, and how curiously you inquired about every detail, which my father Andreas—your Majesty’s primary and most faithful pharmacist—presented for your viewing at one time. I shall pass over for now that incredible love of yours for all disciplines, and especially for the mathematical sciences, particularly that which treats the knowledge of the world and the stars <note>referring to astronomy and astrology</note>, and your admirable skill in it for such a great hero. Thus, it could hardly be otherwise than that, just as you uniquely hold a knowledge of the world, you might also one day be delighted by the weighing of the most absolute construction of all creatures, and take pleasure in considering the lodging and instrument of the immortal soul. Because this corresponds excellently to the world in so many ways, it was called a "small world" <note>original: "paruus mundus"; the concept of the human body as a microcosm reflecting the macrocosm of the universe</note> by the ancients not without reason.

However, I have decided not to preach here about the knowledge of the structure of one’s own body—which is most worthy for a man, highly commendable in itself, and in which it has pleased the greatest men of Rome, foremost in both affairs and philosophical disciplines, to bestow such great effort. Likewise, being rightly mindful of Alexander the Great—who wished to be painted only by Apelles, cast in bronze by Lysippus, and sculpted by Pyrgoteles—I have thought even less of recounting any of your praises here. I fear that with a meager and poorly practiced speech, I might pour darkness over them instead of light. This is especially true since one must utterly disapprove of that too-common custom in Prefaces, where without any selection and almost beyond merit, as if from some template or formula and for the sake of some cheap little reward, there is usually ascribed to everyone: respected learning, singular prudence, wondrous gentleness, sharp judgment, untiring liberality, a wondrous love toward the literate and their studies, mature speed in conducting affairs, and indeed a whole choir of virtues. No one is unaware (even if I do not speak of it here) that your Majesty surpasses all mortals in these, no less than in dignity, success, and the triumphs of your deeds. Whence, even while still living, you are worshipped in the place of a supreme deity. I pray that the gods do not envy the world and these studies, but that they keep and protect you safe and perpetually happy for mortals for a very long time.

Padua, the Calends of August <note>August 1st</note>, in the year after the birth of Christ, 1542.

OPORINUS TO THE READER.

Since the Letter which we received from Italy, sent by Andreas Vesalius along with the woodcut blocks <note>original: "Tabulis"; referring here to the carved wooden blocks used for printing the illustrations</note> prepared for these books *On the Fabric of the Human Body* and their *Epitome*, seemed to us to contain many things of which the Reader should otherwise have been informed at the beginning—and which seemed necessary to point out to Printers (especially those who depend so little on the decrees of Princes and are born to corrupt those things published for the use of the literary world)—we have thought it worthwhile to communicate that letter to our fair-minded Readers, exactly as it was sent to us.
->communicated.<-

# TO JOHANNES OPORINUS, PROFESSOR OF GREEK LITERATURE
## AT BASEL,
### his dearest friend.

<margin>Greetings.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'A' with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
You will receive shortly, my Oporinus, through the Milanese merchants known as the Danoni, the engraved blocks for my books *On the Fabric of the Human Body* and for the *Epitome* of the same. I wish they may be carried to Basel as safely and intact as I have arranged them, with the diligent help of the engraver and Nicolaus Stopius (a young man remarkably well-versed in the humanities), so that they are not worn down in any part or suffer any other inconvenience during transport. Between the series of blocks, we have placed a sample copy bit by bit, together with a printed proof of each individual figure, on which I have written where each should be placed; this is so that the order and arrangement of them does not, by chance, cause trouble for you or your workmen, and so the figures are not printed out of sequence. In the sample copy, you will easily discern where the style of the typographic characters <note>original: "genus characterum"; referring to the specific fonts or typefaces</note> is to be changed. For I have distinguished with lines the part of the writing that encompasses the history of the organs—which is completed in each chapter in a continuous <margin>b.</margin> narrative context—from that part which serves to explain the characters that appear engraved in the plates. For this reason, that section is called the Index of figures and their characters. In the continuous narrative, never interrupted for the purpose of pointing out figures, you will weigh the small letters which you in the workshops call "superscripts" <note>original: "superlineares"; small letters printed above the line of text</note>; these correspond to those annotations which I have applied to the inner margin—not with as much skill as with labor and tedium—so that they might be like a commentary of the writers for the reader, expressing in which figure specifically the part under mention can be seen. Likewise, the annotations found on the outer margin propose, in a way, the sequence and argument of the things being narrated. In the inner margins, lest I be too wordy, I have observed this method: whenever a figure is indicated that is prefixed to the chapter where the annotation is seen, I indicate no chapter number; otherwise, I add it if the figure is placed before a different chapter. Again, if the figure is found in the book where the annotation occurs, I do not add the book number to the figure. Why indeed I thought the figures should be placed in this or that location, you will find explained in the titles of the books and generally in the indices of the characters. For in place of the marks with which parts were to be designated in any drawing, we have engraved in the blocks characters that are in perpetual use in the workshops: starting generally <margin>first</margin> with capitals, and then other Latin letters; furthermore, with lowercase Greek, then with the larger Greek letters which are not familiar to the Latins. When indeed all these were not enough, we adopted numbers, and whatever other small marks occurred in common type. In the description of these indices, it has been observed that a character acting as an indicator and having a single, private explanation is placed freely in the margin; but if it does not have its own index entry and is expressed, as it were, with another character, I have placed a dot beneath it in the margin, so that it might be encountered by the reader in sequence along with the others. But now, in every way I can, I exhort and likewise ask that everything be printed as neatly and as quickly as possible; and that in my endeavors you satisfy the expectation which everyone has conceived of your Printing House <note>original: "Officina"</note>, now established for the first time with great benefit to studies and under a happy omen of the Muses. The greatest effort must be spent on the printing of the blocks, because they are not expressed in a common or school-bookish way, as if with simple lines alone; nowhere has the artistic nature of the picture been neglected (except perhaps for the ground upon which the drawn things are supported). And although you are strong in judgment here, and I promise myself everything from your industry and diligence, I would greatly desire this one thing: that during the printing you should imitate as closely as possible the sample which you will find enclosed with the wooden blocks, printed by the engraver as his specimen. For in this way, no character, however much it is hidden in shadow, will escape the keen-eyed and diligent reader. And what is by far the most artistic feature in this illustration—and for me most pleasant to see—is that the thickness of the lines in certain parts will appear together with an elegant darkening of shadows. But there is no need for me to prescribe these things to you, since it depends on the smoothness and density of the paper, and especially on the diligence of your workmen, that each item is presented most neatly from your Printing House and shared with many. I will take care to travel to you not so long after, and if not for the entire time of the printing, I will at least stay in Basel for a while, bringing with me the form of the decree of the Venetian Senate, by which it is provided that no one may print any of the plates without my consent, or imitate any of my writings in any way. As for the Emperor's privilege, although you have a general one for all books that you print first, my mother will send it to you from Brussels; for she has long since...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS
## ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK
### THE FIRST, dedicated to those things which sustain and prop up the entire body, and by which all things are stabilized and attached.

->WHAT A BONE IS, AND THE USE AND VARIETY OF BONES. Chapter I.<-

*Because this first Chapter applies equally to all bones, no illustration of them is placed before it, nor does it claim any specific illustration for itself for this reason. This is unless one were to think that all the figures should be placed here which will necessarily be used for the Chapters on individual bones, and by which the entire and whole connection of the bones, with their various names, will be expressed at the end of this first book. But to put them all back here would be of little use, because then the same and similar figures would be found everywhere and would occupy the pages beyond measure; and also because we would seem to distrust too much the industry and zeal of the Reader in lightly looking over the images of the whole work right at the start, and in cursorily weighing the order of the books and chapters before serious reading.*

---

<margin>The nature of bone.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' depicting several cherub-like figures (putti) in a landscape. Some are holding and examining a human skull, while others appear to be performing a dissection or anatomical study on a body lying on a table.</image-desc>
OF ALL THE OTHER parts of man, bone is
<margin>The use of bones.</margin>
the most earthy, and therefore the driest
and hardest. God, the supreme craftsman
of the world, deservedly formed its sub-
stance to be this way, so as to be placed
beneath the entire body like a foundation.
For what walls and beams provide in
houses, and poles in tents, and keels along
with ribs in ships, that is what the sub-
stance of bones provides in the fabric of
<margin>The difference of bones by use.</margin>
man. Indeed, some bones are created for
the sake of strength, like the supports of
the body; among their number are the
bones of the shins <note>original: "tibiarum"; the tibia and fibula</note> and thighs, and the vertebrae of the back, and almost the entire connection of the bones. Others are placed by Nature before the remaining parts like ramparts, and very safe palisades and walls, besides the fact that they support them: such as the skull <note>original: "caluaria"</note>, the spines of the vertebrae and their transverse processes, the breastbone, and the ribs. Others, born with their main part in the tendons, are placed before the joints of certain bones, elegantly aiding the strength of the tendons, and in a certain way presiding over the loose movement of the joints. For this reason, the <sup>a</sup> <term>patella<note>The kneecap.</note></term> occurs in the knee, and likewise the <sup>b</sup> small <term>sesamoid bones<note>original: "oſsicula ſeſamo ſemini"; small bones named for their resemblance to sesame seeds, found in the hands and feet.</note></term> (so named by those skilled in dissection) are placed at the second joint of the thumb of the hand, and at the first joints of the four remaining fingers, and also at the first joints of the five toes of the foot. Furthermore, the teeth are specifically conducive to cutting, breaking, grinding, and wearing down food, just as the two small <sup>c</sup> bones of the hearing instrument serve a peculiar use in the office of hearing. But the primary function of each bone will be shown more fully in the Chapters in which we shall describe the individual bones, since for the present it is enough to recount their use in general: by which (to say it once) the bones sustain the entire mass of the body like supports, and to them all things are attached and fastened, and from them they are suspended, so much so that from the use or office of the bones, no other difference can be taken than that which we have just stated. In size, however, bones vary, because some are indeed large, such as the thigh, the shin bone, the humerus <note>The upper arm bone.</note>, and the bones connected to the sides of the <term>sacrum<note>original: "sacri ossis"; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note></term> on both sides: while some are small, such as the bones of the wrist, the teeth, and the small bones compared to sesame. Others again are broad, such as the bones of the sa...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Page 1 regarding the classification of bones. Having established that bones are the foundation of the body, Vesalius here begins to categorize them by their various shapes and textures, using everyday objects as analogies to help the student of anatomy visualize them.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY
### PAGE 2

...compressed at the sides of the ethmoid bone <note>original: "cri ossis", likely referring to the *os cribriforme* or ethmoid</note>, the shoulder blades, the sacred bone <note>the sacrum</note>, the bones of the crown of the head <note>the parietal bones</note>, and those of the forehead and the back of the head. Others are narrow, slender, and long, such as the calf-bone <note>the fibula</note>, the spoke-bone <note>the radius</note>, the elbow-bone <note>the ulna</note>, and the ribs. Furthermore, it will be better to reserve for the specific descriptions of the bones all the differences that could be drawn from their shape (since they occur in countless numbers). Indeed, it would be difficult, before the bones have been fully described, to grasp which of them are rough: such as those we will call "stony" <note>the petrous part of the temporal bone</note> at the base of the skull, because they seem like a jagged rock. Likewise, those which are smooth, such as the bones of the crown, the forehead, and the breastbone. 

Then there are those that resemble a triangle, like the shoulder blades; and a quadrangle, like the bones of the crown; and those that take the form of a wedge, like the seventh bone to be counted in the head <note>the sphenoid bone</note>; and those like a sieve or sponge, like the eighth bone of the head <note>the ethmoid bone</note>; and those resembling yokes, which are called the "jugal" bones <note>the zygomatic or cheekbones</note>; and those that imitate our letter 's' <note>original: "σ" (sigma). In the 16th century, the lowercase sigma was often written in a way that resembled the curve of the collarbone.</note>, like the collarbones <term>claviculae: literally 'little keys'</term>; and those that show the likeness of a sword, like the breastbone; moreover, those that resemble the letter 'u' <note>original: "υ" (upsilon)</note>, like the bone placed at the root of the tongue <note>the hyoid bone</note>; and those that express the shape of the weaver’s shuttle <note>original: "radij"</note> with which wide cords are woven, like the bone of the forearm given the name "radius"; and those we compare to a cube, a die, or a hailstone, such as the bone of the foot which takes its name from the shape of a cube <note>the cuboid bone</note>; and those that are hollow in the manner of a boat or skiff, like the foot bone to which the image of a boat gave its name <note>the navicular or scaphoid bone</note>; and those said to be similar to a millstone, a shield, or a small plate, like the bone placed before the knee joint <note>the patella</note>. 

To these we add those that in some way present the outline of all Italy, like the thigh bone <note>the femur; Vesalius famously noted its curve matches the Italian peninsula</note>; and those that represent a clasp, like the thinner bone in the leg called the "fibula" <term>fibula: Latin for a brooch or safety pin</term>; and those compared to the beak of the cuckoo bird <note>original: "coccygis, seu cuculi"</note>, such as the bone placed beneath the sacred bone which is called the "coccyx"; then those that slightly represent the likeness of an anvil or a molar tooth, like the smaller tiny bone of the organ of hearing <note>the incus</note>; and those like a hammer, like the larger tiny bone of the same organ <note>the malleus</note>. Furthermore, there are those that take their name from the shape of a spindle-whorl <note>original: "uerticuli"</note>, like the vertebrae of the back; and those that correspond to a nail or peg, like the teeth; and those that display the shape of a medium-sized pea or chickpea, such as the two tiny bones of the foot placed beneath the first joint of the great toe <note>the sesamoid bones</note>. Very many bones of this kind, which vary from one another in shape, would not be so easily understood in passing by one to whom bones are as yet unknown.

<image-desc>Woodcut anatomical illustration of a human humerus (upper arm bone). It shows three views: the full length of the bone sectioned longitudinally to reveal the internal cancellous (spongy) structure of the head (marked A) and the hollow medullary cavity (marked D); a cross-section of a smaller bone showing a similar spongy interior (marked I, K, L); and a cross-section of a very dense, solid bone (marked N). Letters A through N point to specific anatomical features described in the adjacent text.</image-desc>

*Since the variety of bones in terms of their shape is not easily grasped here—even though illustrations are provided in the individual chapters where each bone is described privately and shown unbroken—we have here painted one half of the upper arm bone [humerus] dissected lengthwise. This shows the small caverns at its head, where it joins the shoulder blade, formed in the manner of pumice stone and marked with* **A***. We also show the thin layer [the cortex] covering those little caverns, marked with* **B***.* **C** *marks the portion of the outer surface of this bone visible here and bordering the said layer. Furthermore,* **D** *shows the large hollow cavity which, surrounded by the very solid and thick part of the bone indicated by* **E** *and* **F***, extends along the length of the humerus. At the top of the cavity, where* **G** *is placed, and the bottom, where* **H** *is seen, bony lines occur, interwoven with the marrow contained in this cavity. Additionally, below the humerus, we have drawn a bone resembling a boat [the navicular], which is to be described in the eleventh figure of Chapter 33, but here dissected through the middle and marked with* **I** *and* **K***, so that the substance of the bone constructed like pumice stone might appear.* **L** *marks the cavernous or spongy substance of this bone.* **M** *marks the outer layer that constitutes the surface of the bone and wraps around that spongy substance on all sides. Moreover, to this bone, we have joined one of the tiny bones [sesamoids] which, squeezed at the first joint of the great toe, will be shown in the second figure of Chapter 33 as* **ω** *and* **ψ***. This one, marked* **N***, we have divided entirely through the middle so that a bone which is exceedingly solid and almost devoid of small caverns might come into view in some way.*

<margin>Distinction by appendages, processes, heads, etc.</margin>
By this same reasoning, the images of processes, appendages, heads, rims, cavities, and tubercles that occur in bones should by no means be reviewed at present. Likewise, no distinction of bones can be taken from these things yet, since I have not so far explained what a process, an appendage, and the rest of that order are; these will be treated in the second chapter from this one. And therefore, also the differences from the joining of bones...

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I
### PAGE 3

<margin>Regarding the joints of bones.</margin>
...derived from the types of joints, unless the joints are accurately explained, cannot be easily understood. That there are very many of them, and not at all easy to know, the fourth chapter will attest. Likewise, any differences that may depend on cartilage could not be readily grasped by anyone until the nature of cartilage has been explained. 
<margin>Regarding cartilage.</margin>
For if cartilage is unknown, it is difficult to understand which bones are entirely devoid of cartilage, such as the bones of the crown of the head <note>the parietal bones</note>; which are almost entirely covered by it, like certain bones of the wrist <note>original: "brachialis ossa", the carpal bones</note>; or which are encrusted only in part, like the thigh bone <note>the femur</note>; and also which turn into cartilage, like the nasal bones, the ribs, and the breastbone <note>the sternum</note>. Having reserved these differences for their proper place, let us add here those that are gathered from the substance and constitution of the bones.
<margin>Regarding the substance and constitution of bones.</margin>
<margin><insert>Contradicting Colombo, Chapter 1 on bones.</insert></margin>
For there are some bones that are completely solid, and if broken in any way, do not appear to be occupied by internal small hollows or boundaries. Such are, among others, the two bones of the nose, and the smallest bone in the socket of the eyes <note>likely the lacrimal bone</note>, and the one numbered second among the bones of the upper jaw; and those compared to sesame seeds <note>sesamoid bones</note>; and the two tiny bones proper to the organ of hearing <note>the ossicles of the ear, the malleus and incus</note>. All of these, unless dried out excessively over time, show no internal cavity at all. Some, however, appear solid on the outside as if covered by a continuous crust or layer, but when broken, they are seen to be filled inside with certain small boundaries and hollows very much like the holes of a very compact sponge or a very light pumice stone, resembling the appearance of a dried fungus. Among the smaller bones, these include the bones of the wrist <note>carpals</note> and the bones of the ankle <note>tarsals</note>; and among the larger ones, the sacred bone <note>the sacrum</note>, the bodies of the vertebrae, the breastbone <note>sternum</note>, the heel bone <note>calcaneus</note>, the ankle bone <note>talus</note>, and then the bones of the crown of the head <note>parietals</note>. Some bones, however, in addition to these small hollows placed without order or number, show a certain large and remarkably hollow space <note>a marrow cavity or sinus</note> which, surrounded by the most solid and strong substance of the bone, is marked at its extreme corners by bone-like lines. Almost every single bone that possesses such a space has only one. Among the smaller bones of this class are those of the instep <note>metatarsals</note>, the back of the hand <note>metacarpals</note>, and the bones of the fingers; and most especially the first and second ranks of the fingers <note>the proximal and middle phalanges</note>, however much it seemed otherwise to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the ancient authority whose anatomy Vesalius often updated through dissection</note>, the chief of the professors of anatomy, who established that the bones of the digits were solid. 
<margin>In Book 1 of *On the Use of the Parts*, and Book 2 of the *Commentary on Hippocrates' On Fractures*.</margin>
The larger bones endowed with such a space are the thigh bone <note>femur</note>, the shin bone <note>tibia</note>, the arm bone <note>humerus</note>, the lower jaw, the fourth bone of the upper jaw, the forehead bone <note>frontal bone</note>, the bones of the temples, and frequently the wedge-shaped bone itself <note>the sphenoid bone</note>. The teeth, which are easily the hardest of all bones, also possess a space of this kind; but meanwhile they are entirely devoid of the aforementioned small hollows and the tiny holes formed in the manner of pumice. These larger spaces, and that construction not unlike pumice or fungus, were granted to the bones so that when they necessarily had to be thick or otherwise large for some important use, they might be rendered lighter for the sake of movement. They were also made this way to contain the marrow, which is their proper nourishment, or to encompass air or some specific matter (as in the forehead bone and the bones of the temples) instead of marrow. Nor is marrow stored only in those larger cavities of the bones, as someone might perhaps think; 
<margin>In which part of the bones the marrow is stored.</margin>
but those small hollows constructed like a sponge are no less stuffed with marrow than those more notable spaces. 
<margin>Regarding the holes in the bones.</margin>
In addition to the small hollows and spaces with which the bones abound inside, some are also pierced by wide holes <note>foramina</note>, such as the bone of the back of the head <note>occipital bone</note> and the vertebrae, where they transmit the spinal marrow <note>the spinal cord</note>. The bones of the pubes <note>the pubis</note> also have a hole larger than all others, so that they may be burdened with less weight. Others are pierced by small little holes, such as most of the bones of the head and the jaws, providing a path for veins, nerves, and arteries. And the bone which is numbered eighth among the bones of the head <note>the ethmoid bone</note> is seen to be pierced with fine little holes for the sake of smells, in the manner of a sieve or, as some have preferred, a sponge. Others show no hole on the outside or on the surface that can be distinguished by the senses, such as the bones of the wrist...

<summary>Vesalius categorizes bones based on their internal density, distinguishing between solid bones, spongy bones (like pumice), and hollow bones that contain marrow or air. He argues that these structures provide essential lightness for movement and corrects Galen's claim that finger bones are entirely solid.</summary>

### OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I, PAGE 4

...and teeth, and many of the bones of the fingers. In not a few bones, small holes <term>foramina; small openings in the bone surface</term> occur which are visible on the outside and on the surface: however, these do not penetrate the entire bone, but are instead prepared for the thicker veins and arteries that enter the bones. Openings of this kind occur here and there in the heel bone <note>the calcaneus</note>, the ankle bone <note>the talus</note>, the thicker parts of the holy bone <note>the sacrum</note>, and in the bodies of the large vertebrae. This is clearly because these parts are too thick to comfortably receive nourishment from vessels merely creeping over their surface.

<margin>
By sensation.
</margin>
A very slight difference depends on the sensation of the bones. For we believe that only the teeth are endowed with sensation, while the rest of the bones are destitute of it: although it is not wise to rashly strip all power of feeling from the bones, since in the frequent treatments we perform by hand <note>surgical procedures</note>, even the most excellent physicians assert that bones are sometimes affected by pain. Meanwhile, they are not ignorant of the fact that a certain membrane is wrapped around the bones, which the Greeks for that reason called the *periosteon* <note>original: περιόστεον; literally "around the bone"</note>, as if you were to say "circum-ossal." It is because of this membrane that it has seemed to others that bones (if they feel anything at all) possess sensation.

<margin>
Bones <unclear>similar to a door and so on.</unclear>
</margin>
<margin>
By concealment.
</margin>
Furthermore, only the teeth are naked in the entire area where they protrude beyond the gums: meanwhile, the remaining bones are covered in every part and lie hidden before a dissection is made.

<margin>
By the membrane surrounding the bones.
</margin>
In addition to this, where the teeth protrude, they lack the common membrane that involves the bones <note>the periosteum</note>. This is also true of the interior surface of the skull where the brain is contained, which the tough membrane covering the brain <note>the dura mater</note> immediately lines. Otherwise, the previously mentioned membrane is wrapped around all other bones on every side, if you except those places where bones are either articulated with each other or otherwise constructed together.

**C**ARTILAGE is softer than bone: yet it is an earthy part of the body, and the hardest particle after bone. It is entirely solid and filled with no small holes or cavities in the manner of bones, and is almost entirely devoid of marrow and sensation. Its use is quite varied. For first, it performs the same function as bones, since it is like a certain support <term>fulcrum; a prop or point of stability</term> to which neighboring parts may grow and be stabilized.ª For the cartilages of which the larynx <note>the voice box</note> consists elegantly perform the duty of bones, because certain muscles are implanted into them, and some arise from them. Furthermore, they shape the larynx just as we see the houses of peasants constructed from beams before the straw, tiles, and mud are applied to them. Indeed, you could not compare the bones and cartilages of men, stripped of flesh and then woven together, to any image more closely than to the frames of huts just recently erected and not yet adorned with branches or earth. By a similar reasoning, other cartilages take the place of bone where, with no bone located there, muscles attempt their insertion: which happens in the eyelids. For in the extremities of these,ᵇ oblong cartilages exist, into whichᶜ the muscles moving the eyelids are inserted. To these, the wings of the noseᵈ are formed by cartilages which, receiving the insertion of muscles just like bones, together withᵉ other cartilages born from the bones of the nose,ᶠ elegantly support and lift the tip of the nose in the manner of bones. Furthermore, the bones of the ribs end in cartilages,ᵍ corresponding to those bones in the duty of supporting: but from the abundance of cartilages taking the place of bones in this part, a peculiar use arises, on account of their softer...

unlike bones. Add to this another use of cartilage, by no means the least, by which it provides the opportunity for bones to be less damaged by friction during continuous and frequent movements. For the connections <term>commissurae; the points where bones meet</term> of bones, constructed for the sake of movement, would be broken with little effort due to the dryness of the bones and their mutual contact, unless the bones—in every place where they touch one another and form a joint—were covered separately by a certain cartilaginous crust. This cartilage, by its own temperament of hardness and softness, resists the impact of the bones and, by yielding slightly, simultaneously dissolves the force of the collision. Nor is cartilage advantageous only in the clash of bones to prevent them from wearing down through mutual contact; it is also seen to be so smooth and flat that the head of a bone may roll most readily in its socket, and no roughness may hinder the promptness of movement—especially with the addition of a viscous and slippery fluid <note>original: *humore*; Vesalius is describing synovial fluid</note>, much like a kind of grease <note>original: *smegmate*; an ointment or cleansing agent</note> with which we smear wheels and hinges so that they are rendered more fit for turning. <header>ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY</header>

<margin>
There are various words by which the parts and locations of bones are named.
</margin>

<image-desc>
A large historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicts several cherubic figures or children engaged in what appears to be a dissection or an anatomical demonstration around a table.
</image-desc>

HOWEVER much the multitude of terms and their varied use, even by the same author, makes the description of things difficult, no collection of words is as varied or conflicting as the names used to indicate the parts and locations of bones. For while I shall reserve for the following Chapter the various names used to signify the types of joints connecting bones, I will here list: *growth plate* <note>original: ἐπίφυσις; epiphysis</note>, *bony outgrowth* <note>original: ἀπόφυσις; apophysis</note>, *crown-like process* <note>original: κορώνη</note>, *head* <note>original: κεφαλὴ</note>, *joint* <note>original: ἄρθρον</note>, *knuckle-knob* <note>original: κόνδυλος; condyle</note>, *neck* <note>original: τράχηλος</note>, *nape* <note>original: αὐχὴν</note>, *cup-socket* <note>original: κοτύλη</note>, *small socket* <note>original: κοτυληδὼν</note>, *vinegar-saucer* <note>original: ὀξύβαφον; a term for a deep socket</note>, *shallow socket* <note>original: γλυήνη</note>, *basin* <note>original: πύελος</note>, *eyebrow-rim* <note>original: ὄφρυς</note>, *rims* <note>original: ἄμβωνες</note>, *lips* <note>original: χείλη</note>, *steps* <note>original: βαθμίδες</note>, and many other words of this kind which are Greek names. As for the Latins, although they may possess only a few such names of their own, through the lack of restraint among translators, tens of thousands of names are so commonly encountered everywhere that it now becomes necessary for us to take up each Greek name individually. We must add what the ancients—who diligently taught the method of dissection to their children at home—understood by them, so that it may finally be decided which term we ourselves should use. Therefore, the *growth plate* <note>original: ἐπίφυσιν</note>, which the Latins render as *appendix, applantatio, adnexum, additamentum, adnascentia*, and in surely countless other ways, I shall constantly call the **appendix**.

<margin>
Epiphysis.
Appendix.
</margin>

Now, an *epiphysis* <note>growth plate</note> or **appendix** is a bone grown onto another bone and possessing its own distinct boundary; it is not a true, integrated part of the bone to which it is joined. One may learn the nature of such an appendix whenever a portion of a calf, a kid, a lamb, or any other young animal is served at the table. For if the thigh, shoulder, shin, radius, ulna, or any other bone similar to these is freed from the other bones and flesh, and the end parts are handled somewhat firmly, we see something like another bone fall away from it; this is given the name **appendix**. And this we observe only in younger animals; for in those of advanced age, the appendices grow onto their bones so persistently that they cannot be torn away from the bone, and they barely show a line of connection, appearing to be true portions of their bones. Meanwhile, in the newly born, we see a large portion of cartilage intervening between the appendix and the bone to which it is attached, which connects the appendix to the bone like glue.

<margin>
a Consider the appendices of the thigh bone in figure A.
</margin>

This union does not happen on a smooth and flat surface; rather, the bone to which the appendix is joined is usually full of certain boundaries and rough spots, to which the bumps and hollows of the appendix are strongly fitted by mutual entry.

<margin>
b Figure inserted for Chapter 1, between G and A.
</margin>

Furthermore, this connection has this particular quality: the bone to which the appendix is joined is found to be softer and weaker in hardness nowhere else than around the connection itself. For the bone there is always full of many small internal caverns, in the manner of a pumice stone or a sponge. And although the rest of its length may soon claim a single, amply hollow cavity filled only with marrow, and may be hardest and strongest along the length of that cavity, nevertheless, before the bone connects to the appendix, that cavity ceases, and the bone itself, having become softer, abounds with small caverns—just like the appendix itself, which is always seen to be softer than the rest of the bone.

<margin>
In Book 11 of *On the Use of the Parts*.
Appendices are not lids for the cavities containing marrow.
</margin>

And this is so arranged that Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose work dominated medieval medicine</note> taught that appendices were merely lids for the cavities containing marrow. As if, indeed, the small caverns of the appendices were devoid of marrow or a juice very similar to it, and as if many bones that lack the cavities where marrow is held (uninterwoven by bony fibers) did not also take on an appendix. For in the wide bones that are compressed at the sides of the sacred bone <note>the pelvis/sacrum</note>, such a cavity is by no means present; nevertheless, an appendix grows onto the entire spine of the flank bone <note>ilium</note>, just as it does onto the entire lowest part of the hip bone <note>ischium</note>.

<margin>
Appendices do not only occur on large bones.
Growth plate <note>original: ἐπίφυσις; epiphysis</note>.
As for ligaments and muscles, as in the chapter on bones, ch. 2.

Moreover, the vertebrae and the teeth of children—which are also adorned with appendices—not only indicate that bones lacking these cavities possess appendices: but they also serve as proof that Nature did not grant appendices to large bones alone; however much the most prominent of previous anatomists <note>referring primarily to Galen</note> seem to have asserted the opposite, attributing appendices only to large bones. Indeed, if we examine the reason for appendices correctly, we will not establish them merely as covers for cavities in whatever manner, but we will rightly assert that the **Architect of things** <note>a common Renaissance term for God or Nature as a craftsman</note> used them when He deemed it necessary for some part of a bone to be made softer than the rest of its site—either for the sake of a convenient and suitable articulation, which required a thick and therefore not entirely solid and compact site of the bone, or for the sake of the insertion or origin of softer bodies <note>such as tendons or ligaments</note>, or some other such occasion. This is despite Galen, in the eleventh book of *On the Use of the Parts*, having judged the substance of appendices to be more solid and harder than the rest of the site of the bones to which they are granted; he paid little attention to appendices in newborns, in whom they are largely cartilaginous, just as in the elderly they are found to be softer and more porous than the rest of the site of the bones (as I have already said before).

Appendices grow onto the bone of the tibia and the fibula at the knee and at the foot. The **radius** <note>the outer forearm bone</note> is also granted appendices near the wrist and the shoulder. To the **humerus** <note>upper arm bone</note>, however, an appendix is attached only at the top, where it faces the scapula: just as for the **ulna** <note>inner forearm bone</note> only at the wrist. Although sometimes in very young children a small attached appendix <margin>h</margin> occurs at its uppermost part, and similarly for the humerus <margin>i</margin>, the entire lower part of the elbow forming the joint has been seen by some to be formed by an appendix. And these are large bones, to which Nature grants notable cavities. But the small bones, which we also said (contrary to Galen’s opinion) are granted a cavity of that kind, by no means lack an appendix; for the bones of the **metacarpus** <note>original: postbrachialis; the bones between the wrist and fingers</note> and the <margin>a</margin> **metatarsus** <note>original: pedij; the bones between the ankle and toes</note> all obtain a most manifest appendix where they enter the cavities of the first bones of the fingers for articulation. At the top, however, where these bones face the wrist and the tarsus, they occasionally acquire an appendix, but it is always more firmly fused to the bone itself than at the bottom part. Likewise, all the bones of the fingers are generally adorned with appendices at the top and bottom, if you except the last ones, which have appendices only at the top.

Outgrowth <note>original: ἀπόφυσις; apophysis</note>. Process.
