An **outgrowth** <note>original: ἀπόφυσις; apophysis</note>, which interpreters translate as "process," "excess," "explantation," and by I know not what other words, shall be called by us a **process**: and it is a part of a bone, differing in nothing from its own bone, except that it proceeds from the bone like a tubercle or hump, just as roots and branches are seen to swell and proceed from the trunk of a tree. Of this kind of process, which are also sometimes called an **epiphysis** <note>original: ἐπίφυσις; here Vesalius notes the terms are sometimes confused by others</note>, there are very many in the bones. For there is no vertebra of the back that is not granted many. Since some <margin>b</margin> vertebrae of the neck have even more than eleven processes, the vertebrae of the chest seven, and the vertebrae of the loins nine,

As it is, the processes protrude like a mountain, from which more things can grow than from a flat plain, and others are then inserted into it and spread out over it. Indeed, the processes of the shoulder blades and the vertebrae will testify that certain processes act as a kind of bulwark <note>protection</note>.

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.
### 11

<margin>Summit, head. Head. Some heads are prominent, others are depressed. <note>original: κεφαλή (kephalē), κεφάλαιον (kephalaion)</note></margin>
...deserve to be called so. The Greek terms *kephalē* and *kephalaion* are explained by the Latin word for "head" (*caput*). Physicians use this word to describe a bony bump <term>tubercle<note>a small, rounded projection on a bone</note></term> that enters the hollow socket of another bone for the purpose of articulation and voluntary movement. Furthermore, we call a head either "prominent" or "depressed" in relation to its neck. For example, the <margin>q Compare D to B in fig. ch. 30. r 1, 2 in fig. ch. 29 e, f, g. s From m to f in fig. 1. t q, q in the foot.</margin> head of the thigh bone <note>the femur</note>, which joins into the socket of the hip bone, is called "prominent" because a long channel <note>the neck of the femur</note> extends from the neck to the summit. Likewise, we count the head of the shoulder bone <note>the humerus</note> joined to the shoulder blade <note>the scapula</note> as a prominent head, because its highest part stands far out beyond the neck or throat of the bone. However, the heads of the <term>metatarsal bones<note>original: "pedij ossium," the bones in the middle of the foot</note></term> which join with the tarsal bones are so depressed and flat that you can hardly tell whether they enter the sockets of the tarsal bones or if they receive the bumps of the tarsal bones into themselves. Furthermore, in the <margin>u Compare f, t. u 13 fig. ch. 33. with n, m, l fig 10. x 9 fig. 15 ch. d, i & figure 16 ch. X, Y.</margin> connection of the three inner tarsal bones with the "boat-shaped" bone <note>the navicular bone; original: "osse cymbam referente"</note>, it is impossible to distinguish the heads from the sockets. We shall point out in the proper place that small heads of this kind are also found in many vertebrae. For the present, it is enough to add that the Greeks, who were burning with zeal for the works of Nature, called those heads "prominent" which show a manifest bump and which (as far as the surface is concerned) project and swell more in their center than at their sides or in a small circle. "Depressed" heads, however, are those provided with such an obscure bump or hump that it is not entirely clear whether they should be called a head or a socket.

<margin>Condyles <note>original: κόνδυλοι (kondyloi)</note></margin>
It seems the Greeks called these latter [depressed] heads "condyles," while the former [prominent] ones they simply called *kephalaia*. We shall add more regarding the "condyle" shortly thereafter, since that name is used so variously by many authors.

<margin>Joint. Articulation. <note>original: ἄρθρον (arthron)</note></margin>
The Greeks first used the word *arthron*, which we call an "articulation" or "joint," for a joining of bones designed for movement. But Hippocrates frequently—and most especially in his books *On Fractures* and *On Joints*—and Galen likewise in his commentaries on those same books, used the name "joint" to refer to the round part of the bone that is inserted into the hollow or socket of the neighboring bone, which is also called the "head."

<margin>Vertebra. Vertebra. <note>original: uertebrum</note></margin>
<margin>Vertebra. <note>original: σπόνδυλος (spondylos)</note></margin>
The Latins also seem to call this kind of head a *vertebra* <margin>a. b. Insert A 1 fig. ch. 30 into c, f, g fig. 1 ch. 29. c. figures of ch. 14, 15, 16, 17. d 1 fig. ch. 27 C. e 1 fig. ch. 30 E, F, I. f 2 fig. ch. 27 G, H, L. g 1, 2 fig. ch. 10 A. h 1 fig. ch. 15 from C to D.</margin> or "turning-joint," as they use this name when the head of the thigh bone enters the socket of the hip bone. However, others have preferred to call the entire joint of the hip bone with the thigh by this name. It is better, though, to restrict the name *vertebra* only to the bones of the back, so that for us "vertebra" signifies the same thing as the Greek *spondylos*—namely, any bone of the back. Some also call this a *verticulum* <note>a spindle whorl</note>, evidently because of its similarity to the shape of the weight women use to weigh down their spindles.

<margin>Difference between heads.</margin>
Furthermore, the heads that swell out in the manner already described are simple in some bones, such as in the thigh bone where it joints with the hip, and in the metatarsals and <term>metacarpals<note>original: "postbrachialis," the bones of the palm</note></term> where they meet the first bones of the fingers and toes. In other bones, the heads are double and twin-like, separated by a certain groove, such as in the thigh bone where it joins the shin <note>the tibia</note>, and in the first and second bones of the fingers at their lower parts where they enter the sockets of the following bones. Again, some heads are seen to be round, like the upper head of the thigh bone; others are drawn out longer from the right side to the left, and thus become broad, like the heads of the lower jaw <note>the mandible</note>. Still others are carried further back from the front, like the heads of the <term>occipital bone<note>the bone at the back of the skull</note></term> which enter the sockets of the first vertebra. There are countless other differences of heads based on shape, which must be explained in the individual descriptions of the bones. Furthermore, the heads of bones are more than once called "epiphyses" <note>original: ἐπιφύσεις</note> or "appendices" by Galen, perhaps because some of them consist of an appendix—such as the heads of the thigh bone, the upper head of the shoulder bone, and the heads of the metatarsals and metacarpals by which they are joined to the first bones of the fingers. But meanwhile, many heads of bones are by no means formed by an appendix. For the ankle bone <note>the talus</note> entirely lacks an appendix, just as the lower jaw also possesses heads, but not appendices.

Furthermore, the Latins translate *kondylos* sometimes as a joint, sometimes as a knot, sometimes as a hump, sometimes as a head, sometimes as a small head, and sometimes as the bones of the fingers; they do this because they recognize that this word is used in many different ways by the Greeks. Indeed, in the speech of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), a foundational figure in Roman medicine whose works Vesalius both championed and corrected.</note> already mentioned, the heads of the limbs seem to be called by that name. However, in his books *On Anatomical Procedures*, he calls the two lower heads of the thigh bone <note>the femur</note> by this name, as well as the bumps or lower heads of the shoulder <note>the humerus</note>, as if the name indicated twin heads of the bones. Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC).</note> also suggests this in his book *On Joints*, where he teaches how to restore a dislocated shoulder with the *kondylois*, that is, with the joints of the fingers. For it is likely that the bones of the fingers were so named by some because they are gifted with twin<sup>i</sup> heads, just as the thigh bone is at its lower end. This is especially true of the first four bones of the fingers, which, when the hand is made into a fist during the restoration of a dislocation, are used primarily to lead the shoulder outward and then upward. 

Furthermore, Galen, in the first book of *On the Motion of Muscles*, calls a "depressed small head of a bone" a *kondylos*, while he compares a *kephalē* (head) to a *kotylē* (a deep socket or hollow). He uses *kondylos* to describe a depressed, minimally protruding, and flat small head, which we call a *glēnē* (socket); this is carved so lightly into the bone that you can hardly judge whether it is a socket or a small head. Undoubtedly, the name *kondylos* was established in this way by the first professors of dissection. Nevertheless, I will take care that this name produces no obscurity elsewhere in our discourse; for it is just as easy to say "an obscurely and lightly protruding small head" or the "inner or outer head of the thigh bone near the knee" as it is to introduce into the discussion ambiguous words like condyle, or knot, or anything similar.

Such a socket<sup>f</sup> is observed in the hip bone, where the head of the thigh bone is admitted; and also in the<sup>g</sup> bone resembling a skiff <note>the navicular bone</note>, into which the head of the ankle bone enters. # ON THE STRUCTURE AND CONNECTION OF BONES AND CARTILAGES TO ONE ANOTHER. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'O' depicting a group of putti (infant-like figures) engaged in anatomical study in a landscape. THE BONES of the human body could not be fashioned and constructed together like one single continuous bone, in the manner of a stone statue. For although in that case the fabric of man would be less subject to injuries, and his bones would obtain a firmer seat, and could not be dislocated or distorted; nevertheless, because man <margin>Movement</margin> <note>original: $\kappa \acute{\iota} \nu \eta \sigma \iota \varsigma$ (kinesis)</note> ought by no means to be deprived of movement (which is considered most characteristic of an animal, if anything else is), and since movement is hardly performed without
<margin>Man is composed of many bones for the sake of movement.</margin>
divisions and joints of the bones, it was very advantageous for man to be fashioned from many bones. Furthermore, bones are joined to one another not only for the sake of movement, but also for the occasion of the passage of some body, or for security, <margin>Galen 11. On the Use of the Parts. 1. 18. 564. Greek 4 45.</margin> or for the sake of better enduring harm, or in the name of the diversity of parts. Indeed, for the sake of movement, the bones of the fingers are joined to each other, then the ulna and radius with the humerus, and the humerus with the scapula <note>shoulder blade</note>, and the femur with the tibia <note>shin bone</note>, besides innumerable connections of bones of this kind. For the sake of transpiration or the passage of some <margin>For the sake of the passage of something, or respiration 114.</margin> body, I will say that the sutures of the head were formed, when I shall perhaps teach that these transmit the smoky wastes <note>original: fuliginosa recrementa; a Galenic concept of metabolic byproducts from the brain</note> of the brain, and provide a path for the fibers of the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note>, from which the membrane surrounding the skull is fashioned. Likewise, in the discussion of the sutures of the head, you will hear that the skull is formed not from one bone, but from several, <margin>For the sake of difficulty in suffering.</margin> lest perhaps, if it were injured in some part, it might break widely, and the flaw reach further than the boundary of the bone, as in an earthenware jar; but rather that the break might be terminated together with the bone at the suture. To these things, for the sake of the difference of the parts, you will understand in the discussion of the joints of those bones that the bones of the crown <note>the parietal bones</note>, however soft, are joined to the hard bones of the temples. Therefore, all bones together with the <margin>For the sake of the difference of parts.</margin> cartilages are contiguous with one another, and no bone is held separately by itself (unless some one exists in the base of the heart); but it is either part of a continuum, or it touches another bone—sometimes with cartilage mediating—and is bound to the other: so much so that Nature, the wise parent of things, [connected] the bones...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 14 regarding the structural necessity of multiple bones. It moves from the general composition of the skeleton to the specific classification of joints and the various types of movement they allow, such as flexion, extension, and rotation.</meta>

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.

...with the bones along with the cartilages themselves attached, Nature willed man to use them as if they were one continuous thing, and as if they were many for the stated purposes. Furthermore, just as the use of the composition of bones is varied, so also the reasoning behind it is manifold.

<margin>By which differences of joints the bones are joined together, and which movements they produce.</margin>
<margin>Joint <note>original: ἄρθρον. Articulus</note></margin>
<margin><unclear>Movement or the reason for movement... [illegible]</unclear></margin>
First, therefore, for the sake of voluntary movement, there is a natural composition of bones, which is called *articulation* and *joint* <note>original: ἄρθρωσις & ἄρθρον</note> by the Greeks, and by us. However, the mode of this movement is not the same in all joints: since some movements are evident and are hidden from no one. For there is no one who does not feel the head move upon the neck, the femur <note>thigh bone</note> at the hip bone, and the hand at the elbow. And this species of articulation, showing evident movement, is called *diarthrosis* <note>original: διάρθρωσις</note>, as if it were a loose jointing: just as Hippocrates called it *aparthrosis* <note>original: ἀπάρθρωσιν</note>, as if it were an "off-articulation."

<margin>Diarthrosis <note>original: διάρθρωσις</note>. Book on Joints.</margin>
<margin><unclear>2 work volume ...</unclear></margin>
In certain joints, the movement felt is neither strong nor manifest, but obscure, and indeed so difficult and hidden that it can by no means be promptly judged by everyone. For the movement of the joint connecting the bones of the metacarpus <note>the part of the hand between the wrist and fingers; original: postbrachialis</note> to the bones of the carpus <note>the wrist; original: brachialis</note> is not obvious to everyone; yet if you first extend your fingers on a flat surface, and then place the index and little fingers under the middle and ring fingers in the shape of an X, or crosswise, and try to arrange the roots of the fingers as if in a semicircle, the metacarpal bones will not appear entirely immobile.

And the same thing also happens in the connections of the wrist bones among themselves, and of the heel with the ankle, and of the ankle with the bone that resembles a boat <note>the navicular bone</note>, and again of this with the three lower bones of the tarsus <note>the cuneiform bones</note>, and of the heel with the tarsal bone representing a cube <note>the cuboid bone</note>, and in the connection of the tarsal bones with the bones of the metatarsus <note>the part of the foot between the ankle and toes</note>. For you will not notice even the greatest movements of these joints unless your mind is diligently applied.

<margin>Co-articulation <note>original: συνάρθρωσις</note>.</margin>
This species of articulation, however, has been called *synarthrosis* <note>original: συνάρθρωσις</note>, as if you were to say "co-articulation," which receives its distinction from "loose jointing" <note>diarthrosis</note> solely by the quantity of movement.

Furthermore, Nature has not bound each species of articulation by a single kind of composition, just as a similar form of movement is not attributed to all joints.

<margin>That all joints are not moved by the same motions.</margin>
For some are flexed and extended, and are brought toward <note>adduction</note> and away <note>abduction</note> from this or that side, and finally are also turned around as if in a circle <note>rotation</note>. The femur and the humerus <note>upper arm bone</note> show these movements. Indeed, you bring the arm toward the chest, and drive it backward toward the back, then move it upward toward the head, and carry it downward toward the hips; and finally you also move it in a circle, as when, with the thumb fixed on a table, you describe a circle as large as you can with the remaining fingers. So also you lead the femur forward and backward, and inward toward the other femur, and outward away from the other, and likewise turn it around, as when, with the heel fixed on the ground, as if about to make a circle, you move the toes here and there to the sides. For in this way it is proper to understand the motion of rotation: but not when you move the arm now forward, now upward, now backward, now downward, in succeeding movements as if in a circle, and as if you were about to hurl a stone from a sling.

Other joints are only flexed and extended, and moved to the sides, being devoid of all motion of rotation: such as the first joints <note>phalanges</note> of the fingers, and the wrist itself where it joins the elbow. Others indeed are flexed and extended, and at the same time rotated, while claiming no movement to the sides for themselves: as the radius is flexed and extended at the shoulder, and also rotated, or driven into a face-down <note>prone</note> and face-up <note>supine</note> position. Others are only flexed and extended: such as the ulna at the shoulder, and the tibia at the femur, and the second and third joints of the four fingers, and the third of the thumb. Others are only rotated: as the first vertebra of the neck <note>the atlas</note> revolves upon the second <note>the axis</note>, as if on an axle with the whole head: and the radius over the ulna is led by a motion of rotation only into the prone and supine positions. Therefore, since all joints do not possess similar movement, it should by no means seem surprising that they are also necessarily joined together by diverse forms or species of composition.

# ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>
Three forms of joints.
</margin>

<margin>
Ball-and-socket joint <note>original: ἐνάρθρωσις (enarthrosis)</note>.
</margin>

<margin>

This species of joint is divided into three parts, and was given a triple name by the most ancient Greeks: *enarthrosis*, *arthrodia*, and *ginglymus*. Though perhaps these names were later confused by Diocles <note>An ancient Greek physician often called "the second Hippocrates."</note> and those who first committed the methods of dissection to their commentaries. Therefore, *enarthrosis* <note>Known today as a ball-and-socket joint.</note> used to signify a type of articulation in which the cavity or pit of the receiving bone is deep, carved out in the manner of a "vinegar-cruet" <note>original: acetabulum. This is the anatomical term still used for the hip socket.</note>, while the head that fits into it is protruding. Add to this that in this variety of articulation, the socket—just like the head—is "simple," meaning there is one single socket and one head. We see this occur in the joint of the thigh bone with the hip bone,^a in the shoulder with the shoulder blade,^b and in the bones of the metacarpus <note>original: postbrachialis; the part of the hand between the wrist and fingers.</note> and metatarsus <note>original: pedij; the bones of the mid-foot.</note>^c with the first bones of the fingers and toes. The joints just mentioned are granted several distinct movements. For the thigh and the shoulder are flexed and extended, led to the sides, and then rotated. However, the first bones of the fingers do not rotate, just as the wrist does not rotate within the radius,^d even though it is flexed and extended no differently than those finger bones, and is also moved to the sides. Furthermore, although the radius is flexed and extended toward the shoulder and rotated besides, it lacks lateral movement because Nature, for the sake of some great benefit—as we shall teach in the proper places—did not construct the heads of these joints (which are also composed by "inarticulation" <note>original: inarticulatione; another term for enarthrosis.</note>) to be perfectly round. For even though Nature always devises this species of joint in simple articulations^e when she desires the bones to be moved with several movements at once, she does not immediately grant a triple kind of movement to all such "inarticulations." Instead, by a peculiar structure, she often took away the third kind of movement from those that did not need it, thereby looking out for the strength of the joint. In this way, the joint is rendered stronger and less exposed to dislocation than if it consisted of a fabric that allowed for a triple variety of movement.

Nevertheless, "inarticulation" is observed not only in joints producing the most obvious movements, but also—to offer some examples of obscure movements—a round head^f is "inarticulated" into the bone resembling a boat <note>The navicular bone in the foot.</note>,

just as certain bones of the wrist^g are joined to each other, and no less than the cartilages of the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth ribs are joined^h to the pits of the breastbone by this species of joint.

<margin>
Gliding joint <note>original: ἀρθρωδία (arthrodia)</note>.

The *arthrodia* <note>A gliding or plane joint.</note> is a species of joint which has the hollow or pit of one bone carved only slightly and, as it were, on the surface, while the head of the other bone is flat and barely protruding—almost as if flat surfaces were creating this connection. For while in *enarthrosis* it is very easy to judge which is the socket and which the head, in *arthrodia*, conversely, both are so obscure that you do not know to which bone you should appropriately assign the name of socket or head. In this species are joined^i the three inner bones of the ankle <note>The cuneiform bones.</note> to the boat-shaped bone <note>The navicular.</note>, and^k the bones of the mid-foot to the ankle bones, and several bones of the wrist to the bones of the metacarpus, then^m the fourth bone of the wrist to the third, and^n the collarbone to the upper process of the shoulder blade <note>The acromion process.</note>. In these connections, the movements are so obscure that they can only be perceived and judged with great difficulty. Indeed, it is as if Nature fabricated this difference of articulation in a simple and unique joint of two bones when she intended the bone to move only a tiny bit.

<margin>
Hinge joint <note>original: γίγγλυμος (ginglymus)</note>.
</margin>

The *ginglymus* <note>A hinge joint, like the elbow.</note> is formed with obvious ends and heads, but by no means simple ones consisting of only one surface—whether convex, concave, or flat. For a *ginglymus* occurs when bones are joined together by mutual entry, such that the convex parts of one bone enter the cavities of the other, and in turn, the pits of the first bone admit the convexities of the second. They are joined just like the hinges of doors and windows, from which this third species of joint found its name. And just as two primary types of those hinges are observed, so also there are two primary ways of mutual connection between bones. For the hinges, by which...

...by which two boards usually cling to one another; they are similarly convex and concave, so that the convex parts <note>original: gibba</note> of one iron piece are seen in the concave parts <note>original: caua</note> of the other, and the concave parts of the one admit the convex parts of the other, and then a bolt <note>original: clauis; literally 'key' or 'nail', here a hinge-pin</note> passes through all the convex parts at once. Therefore, in the likeness of those first hinges (o especially if one of their iron pieces has only one convex bump in its center and is cut away above and below, while the other shows two bumps and is hollowed out in their middle), the joints of the second and third bones <note>the phalanges</note> of the four fingers of the hand and toes of the foot are joined <margin>p In the 2nd table, the figure of chapter 27; join G, H, L to I, K, M.</margin> p as hinge-joints <note>original: ginglymus</note>. This is also true, among many others, of the joint connecting the thigh bone <note>femur</note> to the shin bone <note>tibia</note> <margin>q Compare G, E, and I in Figure 1, Chapter 31, with E, F, and I in Figure 1, Chapter 30. r Figures 1 and 2, Chapter 23, K, L, M to C, D, E in Figure 1, Chapter 24.</margin>. For one bone of these joints has two heads separated by a certain middle depression <note>original: sinus</note>, while the other bone possesses two depressions distinguished by a middle bump. Thus, the two heads of one bone enter the two depressions of the other bone, and the depression of the first bone admits the bump of the second. Furthermore, in the form of the second type of hinge, r the ulna <note>the larger forearm bone</note> is seen to be joined to the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, when the circular depression of the ulna is flexed and extended (or otherwise rolled) around the track or pulley of the humerus. However, in this joint as well, many features agree with the first type of hinge. Nature constructs these mutual connections when she wishes to prioritize the strength of the joints, and it is sufficient for them to govern only one type of motion. This is attested by the joints recently mentioned, which we can only flex and extend, requiring no other motion in the meantime.

<margin>
Why Nature sometimes joined two bones with several joints.
</margin>
Furthermore, the purposes mentioned so far in forming these three types of joints should be understood to apply to joints that occur as simple and unique connections between two bones. For occasionally, when common utility was hindered, Nature could by no means join two bones with a single joint, but instead fashioned two (and sometimes more) connections or joints that are distant from each other and not continuous.

For example, so that the radius <note>the outer forearm bone</note> would not gape away from the ulna along the middle of the forearm's length with a significant hollow, Nature joined the radius to the ulna by s a double joint, rather than a single one stretched across the whole length of the forearm. Near the bend of the elbow, the t head of the radius enters u a depression in the ulna; near the wrist <note>original: brachiale</note>, the x head of the ulna is articulated into y a depression in the radius. Through these two connections, the radius is able to rotate—that is, be moved into a palm-down <note>pronation</note> or palm-up <note>supination</note> position. Then, because of the passage of the spinal marrow, <margin>z Compare the 1st figure with the second of Chapter 15.</margin> z the occipital bone <note>the base of the skull</note> is fastened to the first vertebra by a double joint, each constructed somewhat in the manner of a shallow articulation <note>original: inarticulationis; likely referring to arthrodia</note>. Furthermore, <margin>a Compare the 4th figure with the 5th of Chapter 15.</margin> a the first vertebra is joined above the sides of the body of the second vertebra by two joints like "arthrodia" <note>gliding joints</note>, or flat connections; and the tooth <note>original: dens; the odontoid process</note> of the second vertebra is articulated into the first vertebra. Thus, by those three joints, the first vertebra (carrying the head) only rotates upon the second—as we shall teach in the proper place against the opinion of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius famously corrected</note>. In addition to these, because the other vertebrae of the back also had to be perforated for the sake of the spinal marrow, and many had to be established at once, Nature did not use simple connections and joints in the composition of two vertebrae...

<margin>i See figure, chapter 40 of Book II, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.</margin>
A <term>symphysis</term> is a natural union of bones, by which form of joint the "appendices" <note>Vesalius refers here to the <term>epiphyses</term>, the ends of long bones that are separate in children.</note> grow together with their main bones. This can also be seen in lambs, in which cartilage occupies these lines just as it does in children. In those slightly older, however, those three parts grow together so completely that not even the appearance of lines presents itself. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE HUMAN BODY]
## [BOOK I, Page 20]

<margin>Those things which especially deviate from Galen's views in this chapter.</margin>
...undergo a change, and through this process they grow together with the bones. However, once the cartilage is completely lost, they are so joined together that—as I have already said before—it is difficult to observe the region where they fused. I had intended just now to put an end to this chapter and direct my discourse to the descriptions of individual bones, were I not greatly delayed by the authority of Galen. His prestige rightly forbids me from passing over too lightly those points in the present chapter that deviate from his opinions. 

For to propose one point out of many (besides those already mentioned), I first did not subscribe to his dogma in his book *On Bones*, where he teaches that "sutures," "harmonies," and <term>gomphosis</term> <note>original: *gomphosis*; a "peg-and-socket" joint, like teeth in the jaw</note> are all species of <term>synarthrosis</term> <note>original: *synarthrosis*; a joint with little to no movement</note>. I, however, have ascribed an obscure and non-manifest motion to <term>synarthrosis</term>, and I have mentioned that it is formed by the same differences and shapes of articulation as <term>diarthrosis</term> <note>original: *diarthrosis*; a freely movable joint like the shoulder or hip</note>. Next, I have granted no motion at all to the suture, harmony, and <term>gomphosis</term>—not just an "obscure or difficult" one—and I have by no means included these types of connections under the name "joint" as Galen did. 

Indeed, he himself should not have done so, unless he wished to falsely assert—when describing the construction of the wrist, the palm, the ankle, the foot, and the connection of the cartilages of the ribs with the breastbone in their respective places—that these are joined by <term>synarthrosis</term>. For since he said in that context that these bones are truly tightened together by <term>synarthrosis</term>, should he not have noticed that these are connected neither by suture, nor harmony, nor <term>gomphosis</term>? This would certainly be the case if he had correctly established that the species of <term>synarthrosis</term> are harmony, suture, and <term>gomphosis</term>. 

However, as far as I am concerned, anyone is free to decide about <term>synarthrosis</term> according to their own judgment, provided they are aware that this term is often understood by Galen in a very different way elsewhere than at the beginning of his book *On Bones*. For in the 13th, 19th, 21st, and 24th chapters of that same book, Galen holds a different view than he did there. 

Furthermore, the author of the *Introduction, or the Physician* <note>original: *Introductorij seu Medici author*; a work formerly attributed to Galen, now often called Pseudo-Galen</note>, not acquiescing to Galen’s decree and dividing the connections of bones for himself privately, says: "These are either composed for motion, and that series of composition is called <term>arthron</term> <note>original: *ἄρθρον*; Greek for "joint"</note>, or joint; or they are for no motion, and then it is called <term>synarthrosis</term> <note>original: *συνάρθρωσιν*</note>." Among the species of the latter, he enumerates the suture, <term>gomphosis</term>, and <term>symphysis</term> <note>original: *symphysis*; a growing together of bones</note>. Yet by this reasoning, <term>synarthrosis</term> could by no means be applied to the composition of the bones of the wrist, palm, ankle, and foot, since they are connected to each other neither by suture, nor <term>gomphosis</term>, and much less by <term>symphysis</term>. 

Moreover, I have departed even further from Galen’s dogma when I proposed that all junctions of bones are joined either by the benefit of some intervening substance, or by none. This is because Galen attributed this only to <term>symphysis</term> in his books *On Bones*, and enumerated <term>synneurosis</term> (union by ligament), <term>synsarcosis</term> (union by flesh), and <term>synchondrosis</term> (union by cartilage) as species of <term>symphysis</term> only. 

The first occasion that prompted me not to follow him was his inaccurate statement in which he taught that "spongy and soft things grow together through <term>symphysis</term> with no intervening medium, while drier and denser things fuse with some intermediates." For I find that in bones that are still soft and tender, the "appendices" <note>modern: *epiphyses*; the ends of long bones</note> are united to their bones through the intervention of cartilage; but in hard and dried bones, and in the elderly, no <term>symphysis</term> <note>here meaning an intervening substance</note> comes between them at all. 

Secondly, no <term>symphysis</term> or union presents itself to me which could truly be asserted to be united by the intervention of a ligament. Thus, <term>synneurosis</term> cannot be included under <term>symphysis</term>, provided that no union is perfected by the help of a ligament; for indeed all joints without exception come together by the benefit of a ligament—sometimes (as I said before) wrapped around them in a circle, and sometimes even intervening at the mutual contact of the bones. 

Furthermore, as I weighed each point with the greatest precision, <term>symphysis</term> appeared to me even less as something one could rightly assert is joined by the intervention of flesh. For in no connection of bones does flesh intervene, except perhaps in the connection of the teeth with the jaws, which is considered <term>gomphosis</term>, not <term>symphysis</term>—even though that connection of teeth shows no motion, certainly no more than a harmony or a suture. But as for flesh, meanwhile,

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.
<header>THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>
<meta>catchword: HUMA-</meta>

...meanwhile, with the help of muscles, almost all joints are joined; a connection that no one could call a species of <term>symphysis</term> <note>original: *symphysis*; a type of joint where bones are held together so tightly by cartilage or fiber that they appear to grow together as one</note>. To this end, a passage from Aristotle’s <margin>Chapter 9.</margin> second book of *On the Parts of Animals* also warned me to disagree more readily with Galen. There, Aristotle asserts that bones are joined by nerves, flesh, and cartilage, most learnedly referring that connection universally to all <term>commissures</term> <note>original: *commissuras*; the seams or joints where two things meet</note> of the bones. Although Galen did not carelessly overlook this opinion of Aristotle, he was unmindful of what he had taught in his book *On Bones* when, toward the end of his second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, he runs through the constructions of bones perfunctorily—though certainly elegantly—and in a way recounts Aristotle’s own words. But now, at last, it is the opportune time to approach the specific histories of individual bones, and to begin them with the logic of the structure of the head and its various shapes.

<header>ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE] HUMAN BODY</header>

<margin>
The head is formed for the sake of the eyes.
Book 8 of *On the Use of the Parts* <note>A foundational anatomical work by Galen of Pergamon.</note>.
</margin>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'H' featuring an anatomical demonstration or lecture scene. Inside the frame of the letter, three figures are gathered around a table; one figure appears to be pointing toward an object or specimen while the others observe.</image-desc>

Galen taught that the HUMAN head was formed for the sake of the eyes, as is clearly demonstrated by the eyes of crabs, locusts, and certain animals that lack a head. In these creatures, the eyes are positioned on very long stalks; they are not placed low down, just as the mouth, nose, and ears are hidden in their chests. That the eyes required a high seat is attested by the incursions of enemies and by the scouts of robbers, who climb walls, mountains, and high towers for the same purpose that sailors climb the masts of ships: to see land sooner than those who remain below in the ship. Since those animals mentioned are covered with a shell-like and hard skin, it was possible for their eyes to be safely placed on long stalks, because they would be tougher and could be covered on the outside by a tunic that, originating from the skin of those animals, would be both very hard and shell-like. For man, however, because of the substance of the body and the soft, thin membrane that covers the eyes, and his more refined sense, he must necessarily have entirely soft eyes; these could not be placed on long stalks without danger.

<margin>
How Nature protected the eyes.
</margin>

Therefore, since it was not convenient for their function to place human eyes at the bottom, and it was by no means fitting to attach them to bare necks, Nature—wishing neither to hinder the use of the eyes nor to compromise their safety—constructed a high part that elegantly protects the eyes from injury. Above, she placed the eyelids, the eyebrows, and the frontal bone; below, besides the eyelids, the jaw and cheeks also protect the eyes. In the internal parts, the nose is placed between the eyes like a wall; then, on the outside, a very strong external bone occupies the corner of the eye sockets, so that the eyes are hedged in on all sides by prominent and protruding parts, and they lurk usefully as if in a winding valley. However, this accumulation and collection of things that protect the eyes is by no means the head itself, although those things cannot exist without a head.

<margin>
The brain is placed in the head for the sake of the eyes, and then the rest of the senses for the sake of the brain.
</margin>

What necessity was there, then, for other parts to be composed here as well, whose structure deserves the name of "head"? Each of the sense organs—namely sight, smell, taste, and hearing—requires a soft nerve. A nerve is required because it is the vehicle of the animal spirit <note>original: *animalis spiritus*; in Galenic medicine, these were subtle vapors that carried sensation and motion through the nerves</note> and faculty; it must be soft because it must be affected and disposed in some way by the sensible object striking from without. Therefore, since the eyes required the soft nerves of the brain, and all soft things would be easily torn and broken, damaged, or even hardened more than is proper by the length of the path if they proceeded further, the brain rightly had to be placed not far from the eyes. And so it is concluded that the brain is located in the head for the sake of the eyes, while the organs of smell, hearing, and taste are located there because of the brain. Although these organs also otherwise obtain a very high seat quite opportunely. For the ears, since they must perceive sound, which by nature is carried upward, are rightly placed in the high parts of bodies. Likewise the nostrils, because every odor is drawn toward the upper parts, are deservedly placed above; and because a great judgment of food and drink also pertains to the nostrils, it is not without cause that they follow the proximity of the mouth. Now taste, which must sense the types of things on which we feed, conveniently resides in that part of the mouth where Nature opened a path for food and drink. Touch, however, is spread equally through the whole body, so that we can feel all blows and all excessive approaches of both cold and heat.

Furthermore, everyone defines the most natural and fitting shape of the skull as looking like a sphere slightly compressed on both sides toward the front; and by occasion of this compression, it is made much narrower in the front part than in the back. Galen refers the reason for this shape to the brain, asserting that since the skull is the receptacle of the brain, and like a helmet and bulwark, it must express its shape; and adding likewise, that those who poste-

<summary>Vesalius explains the teleological design of the human head, arguing that it exists primarily to elevate the eyes and house the brain near the sensory organs. He describes the skull's natural shape as a sphere slightly compressed at the sides, designed to protect the soft matter of the brain and sensory nerves.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the skull's formation. Having established that the head exists primarily to protect the eyes and house the brain, Vesalius now addresses why the human skull is not a perfect sphere and how cultural practices and pathologies alter its "natural" shape.</meta>

<header>### ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>

<margin>c in figures 1 & 2, chapter 2, book 4.</margin>
...the cerebellum is positioned in the rear part of the brain, and the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsalis medulla"</note> emerges from there. In the front part, the processes for the organs of smell and for the eyes are led out from the brain. Meanwhile, as we shall easily demonstrate in the seventh book, the brain itself required no specific shape, and its posterior part protrudes further back than the cerebellum<gloss>c</gloss> itself. Furthermore, those processes serving the sense of smell and the visual nerves take their origin from approximately the middle of the base of the brain, rather than from its forward-most seat. Thus, as far as the brain's requirements are concerned, nothing would have prevented us from seeing a skull <note>original: "caluaria"</note> formed like an exact globe or sphere—a shape most suited for repelling injuries. However, account had to be taken of the upper jaw, the nose, the seats of the eyes, and the temporal muscles; moreover, for the sake of the skull's connection with the vertebrae of the back, it was fitting for the rear part of the head to be wider and more capacious, provided there was a necessary reason for its proper weight.

<margin>In the book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*.</margin>
Furthermore, Hippocrates seems to have assigned the cause of what we call the "natural" form to midwives and nurses. He asserts that some people considered oblong heads to be beautiful, and therefore they compressed the heads of young children, and thus eventually nature produced this oblong form—in nearly the same way that it is known most nations claim something peculiar in the shape of their heads. For the heads of the Genoese, and even more so those of the Greeks and Turks, express almost the image of a globe. To this shape (which many of them judge elegant and convenient for the various head-coverings they use), midwives sometimes lend their aid, much to the concern of the mothers. The Germans, however, are mostly seen with a compressed occiput <note>the back of the head</note> and a wide head, because babies always lie on their backs in their cradles, and are tied to the sides of the cradle on both sides with their hands almost without the use of swaddling bands. The Belgians preserve or maintain heads that are more oblong than others, because mothers allow their little children, wrapped in swaddling, to sleep mostly on their sides and temples. However that may be, anatomists call that head shape "natural" which is constructed primarily in the form of an oblong sphere, having a more elongated front and back. All other shapes varying from this are considered non-natural.

<margin>d Figure 4.</margin>
<margin>e Figure 5.</margin>
<margin>The first non-natural shape of the head.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
Such as the one<gloss>d</gloss> in which the forward prominence produced from the bregma <note>the top of the head</note> or the higher seat of the forehead is lost, but the rear prominence, which belongs to the occiput, is preserved. Likewise,<gloss>e</gloss> the one seen to be clearly contrary to this, which has lost the rear prominence (the occiput, naturally) while the forward one remains. Then

<margin>f Figure 4.</margin>
<margin>g Figure 5.</margin>
<margin>Third.</margin>
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
<margin>Book 9, *On the Use of the Parts*. Various other shapes of the head.</margin>
there is the third, which is even more opposed to the natural form, in which both prominences of the head are abolished,<gloss>f</gloss> and the head is observed to be perfectly round, like an exact sphere or like a squill <note>a sea-onion bulb; original: "scilla"</note>. Thersites <note>A character in Homer's *Iliad* described as the ugliest of the Greeks.</note> is handed down by Homer as having had this shape. Some assert that he called this "warped" <note>original: φοξὸν (*phoxon*)</note>, although many prefer to call all pointed head shapes by that name and "sharp-headed" <note>original: οξυκεφάλους (*oxykephalous*)</note>.<gloss>g</gloss> A fourth species of non-natural shape is also enumerated by Hippocrates, in which the head protrudes more significantly at the sides toward each ear than in the front or back seats. This is entirely unlike the natural shape of the head, just as if you were to imagine the face at one ear and the back of the neck at the other ear in a natural figure. Indeed, Galen affirms elsewhere that this shape can be imagined but cannot exist in the nature of things. Yet, meanwhile, a boy deformed in many parts and quite mindless is seen today in Venice with this shape. Indeed, a beggar wanders among the Bolognese who happens to have a square head, but a little wider than it is long. Furthermore, in Genoa, a boy perhaps three years old was carried from door to door by a beggar woman, and a little later was exhibited by actors in the most noble Brabant <note>A region in the Low Countries, modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands.</note> of the Belgians; his head, protruding on each side, was larger than two men's heads. But I believe that boy was suffering from a similar affliction...

<summary>Vesalius discusses how the "natural" oblong shape of the human skull is determined by both anatomical necessity and cultural practices, such as how different nations cradle their infants. He also categorizes four "non-natural" or deformed head shapes, citing historical descriptions and his own contemporary observations of people with cranial deformities.</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

<margin>Regarding a girl whose head had increased beyond measure over several months.</margin>
...had suffered, which I observed in a two-year-old girl at Augsburg <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum"</note>. In about seven months, her head had increased so much that I have never seen a man's head that did not yield to it in size. This was the affliction that the ancients called *hydrocephalus* <note>original: "hydrocephalum"; literally "water-head"</note>, named for the water that is preserved and gradually collected in the head. However, this water had not collected between the skull <note>original: "caluariam"</note> and the outer membrane or skin surrounding it (where medical books otherwise teach that the water is stored). Instead, it was within the very cavity of the brain, specifically in its right and left <margin>h Figure 6, Book 7, D, D and E, E.</margin> ventricles<gloss>h</gloss>. The cavity and size of these had increased so much, and the brain itself had been so extended, that they contained nearly nine pounds of water, or three Augsburg wine measures (so help me Heaven!). Furthermore, while the brain at the top of the head was thin, like a membrane, and its substance was somehow continuous with its thin membrane, the skull itself was also entirely membranous. It remained bony only in a space as large as the girl’s skull had been before the head began to grow beyond measure. This is much like the way we see the forehead bone and the bones of the crown in newborn children, where they otherwise meet one another; in very young children, they are seen to be membranous across a notable interval and width. Meanwhile, the cerebellum <note>the "little brain" at the back of the head</note> and the entire base of the brain were natural in their formation, as were the origins of the nerves. Furthermore, I found water in no other places at all except in the brain's ventricles, which, as I said, were so enlarged. The girl enjoyed the full use of all her senses until her death. However, when I observed her a few days before she died, whenever her head was moved by those standing by or was raised even slightly, she was immediately troubled by a heavy cough, difficult breathing, a strange redness of the whole face, a suffusion of blood, and a flow of tears. In the rest of her body, she was moderately well, though her joints were loose and weak (but not paralyzed); nor was there any notable wasting, any serous swelling in the limbs, or any signs of epilepsy <note>original: "morbi comitialis"; literally "the assembly sickness"</note> or tremors. When her liver was examined shortly after death, it appeared quite pale and somewhat more shrunken and harder than a natural liver. The spleen, meanwhile, was conspicuously large and soft, as if it had taken over the liver's duties for some time. Thus, along with the doctors who were present, I marveled at nothing so much as that such a great force of water had been collected in the brain's ventricles for so long without more severe symptoms. <margin>A case history.</margin> At nearly the same time, we were forced to marvel in no common way at the heart of a most noble and learned man. In its left ventricle, we found nearly two pounds of glandular (yet blackish) flesh. The heart, like a womb or like that girl’s brain, had been stretched to accommodate the mass of that flesh. Before death, the man had a somewhat melancholy habit; he was very wakeful and possessed a pulse that was truly unequal and varied in strange ways, clearly showing a contraction of the artery. For many months before death (though he otherwise walked about as if healthy), the pulse—or rather the artery—seemed to contract and stay contracted for the interval of three or four beats, as if it were struggling to expel something. Indeed, in the final weeks of life, out of an interval of nine beats, only three or two dilations of the artery could be felt by touch. His animal faculty, along with the functions of the "governing soul" <note>referring to higher cognitive functions</note>, remained sufficiently intact until death. Death itself did not occur so much from the heart defect directly as from gangrene in the left leg. This gangrene took its opportunity from the impeded pulse of the artery, just as if those intermittent pulses caused by the heart defect had failed to properly "fan" <note>original: "euentillassent"; a reference to the Galenic idea that the pulse cools the innate heat</note> the native heat of that leg. This was especially the case because several years earlier, the artery that seeks the <margin>i Figure, Chapter 12, Book 3.</margin> fibula<gloss>i</gloss> had been damaged by a gunshot wound <note>original: "sclopeti ictu"</note>. However, we shall pursue countless instances of this kind more extensively in another work, in which I will arrange the histories of my dissections for the understanding of diseases and the whole [art]...

<meta>catchword: art (artis)</meta>

<summary>Vesalius describes two remarkable pathological cases: a toddler with extreme internal hydrocephalus and a nobleman with a massive tumor in his heart. He uses these examples to show how the body's structures can stretch and adapt to extreme internal pressure while maintaining basic functions for a surprising amount of time.</summary>
<keywords>hydrocephalus, brain ventricles, pathology, heart tumor, Augsburg, pulse, gangrene, clinical observation</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory discussion on head shapes, transitioning from pathological deformities (like the hydrocephalus described on the previous page) to the standard anatomical study of the skull's bones and sutures. ...we shall describe those shapes most suitable for the practice of the medical art. Meanwhile, in the present Work, we intend to recount only the history <note>original: "historiam"; here meaning a systematic description based on observation</note> of the skillfully composed human body, passing over in silence all monstrous things and those that occur only in the unhealthy and the sick. However, we mention non-natural shapes of the head here because they are also commonly discussed by professors of dissection; and because these shapes called "non-natural" are sometimes observed even in remarkably wise men (since, as we have already hinted, the brain requires no very specific shape of its own). This is true even if such skulls—and especially those differing from the natural form in the appearance of their sutures <note>the zig-zagging seams where the bones of the skull meet</note>, as will be discussed in the next Chapter—very rarely present themselves to us in cemeteries. Indeed, they might perhaps occur more frequently if we were to examine the cemeteries of the inhabitants of the Alps that look toward Styria <note>original: "Stiriam"; a region in modern-day Austria</note>, as I hear those people are deformed not only by the aforementioned head shapes, but by even much greater discrepancies.

The present index of characters will be common to the third and fourth figures, because nearly the same characters are placed in both. Even if by chance something appears peculiar to only the third or fourth figure, I will add either a 3 or a 4 to it, according to the nature of the figure.

**A, B** The coronal or anterior suture of those which are drawn transversely. Its right part is seen in the third figure, while its left part is seen in the fourth. <note>The coronal suture separates the forehead bone from the top of the head.</note>
**C, D** The posterior of the transverse sutures, which resembles the Greek capital letter $\Lambda$ <note>original: "$\Lambda$ Græcorum maiuſculæ literæ"; this is the lambdoid suture</note>. In the third figure, the left part of this suture is visible, and in the fourth, the right part.
**E 3** The suture led from the middle of the suture resembling the $\Lambda$ to the middle of the coronal suture, or from D to B. <note>This is the sagittal suture, running down the center of the top of the head.</note>
**F** The squamous <note>scale-like</note> conglutination; in the third figure the left side is seen, in the fourth the right. Then in both:
**G** the interval from C to G is marked, which shows the construction of a true suture <note>a "true" suture has interlocking jagged edges like a zipper, rather than the overlapping "scale-like" edges mentioned below</note>, not of scales resting upon each other.
**H** That which extends from G to H through F is a true scale-like conglutination, common to the bone of the crown <note>original: "uerticis oſſis"; the parietal bone</note> and the bone of the temple <note>original: "temporis oſſis"; the temporal bone</note>. From H to A, a scale-like bonding is indicated, common to the bone of the crown and the bone of the forehead <note>original: "frontis oſſi"; the frontal bone</note>.

**K** The right bone of the crown.
**L** The bone of the forehead, which is singular <note>meaning there is only one frontal bone, unlike the paired parietal bones</note>.

However, from **n** to **o** it is not strictly a suture, just as it is not from the forward **m** to **n**; rather, it is a fissure <note>original: "rima"</note> and a notable gap between the bones, occurring quite differently than in other sutures or simple joints <note>harmonies</note>.*
*q, q The interval of the suture surrounding the wedge-shaped bone, common to it and the sixth bones of the upper jaw marked with Π. Indeed, to trace the wedge-shaped bone with sutures, look at this fifth figure along with the third and fourth, noting the characters of each. Proceed from **n** to **o**, then to **p**, **a**, **ω**, **H**, **b**, **d**, **e**, and **q**, and thus imagine the wedge-shaped bone bounded by sutures on both sides. But this is best done by inspecting a human skull, which can be easily turned in every direction; meanwhile, here three plates must be viewed at once to outline that bone even on the outer surface of the skull. To make this easier, I have drawn the lambda-like suture with its additions here, and the line common to the occipital and wedge-shaped bones, and finally the suture surrounding the wedge-shaped bone, adding the same characters in this figure as in the third, fourth, and fifth throughout.*
*r In this fifth figure, as in the fourth, a line on the temporal bone is marked; there, a suture-like line contains the bone in which the beginning of the auditory canal is carved, and separates it, as it were, from the rest of the bone.*
*s The roughness and projection <term>process</term> of the temporal bone, where it faces the transverse line common to the wedge-shaped and occipital bones, marked with **n**.*
*ζ The projection of the eighth bone of the head, or the partition <term>septum</term> coming between the cavities of the nostrils <note>the vomer bone</note>. The remaining characters contribute specifically to showing the bones of the upper jaw individually.*

*ALTHOUGH I have no wish to trouble the reader with a great frequency of plates, and for that reason I generally do not express the individual bones of the head in private figures; nevertheless, because the boundaries of the bone compared to a wedge <term>the sphenoid bone</term> and then the eighth bone of the head <term>the ethmoid bone</term> are not as readily understood as the other bones of the head, the present figure expresses the wedge-shaped bone along with the eighth bone of the head, free from all others, showing that face which looks toward the internal surface of the skull <note>original: "caluariae"</note>. We have provided this specifically so that the caverns <term>sinuses</term> usually occurring in the wedge-shaped bone might be in view, as the index of characters will show.*

*A, B, A The eighth bone of the head <note>The ethmoid bone, which Vesalius counted as the eighth bone of the cranium</note>. Specifically, B marks the septum <note>the crista galli</note> distinguishing the seat of the organs of smell.*
*C, D The two primary caverns <term>sphenoid sinuses</term> of the wedge-shaped bone.*

*F The opening of the other cavern or cave, leading into the wide space of the nostrils.*
*G A cavity placed in a lower position of the septum, which separates the two caves from each other.*
*H The processes of the wedge-shaped bone, similar to bat wings <note>the pterygoid processes or the greater wings of the sphenoid</note>.*

<margin>
Why the entire brain is surrounded by bones, and for what reason they are various, and for the most part joined by sutures.
</margin>
<margin>
a We will note those when they are described in order in the context of the head.
b We will describe the sutures, as well as other connections, in their proper place.
</margin>
It is greatly advantageous that the BRAIN, the seat of reason (which, situated in the highest part of the body like a king, rules and presides over the two concupiscible souls <note>Referring to the Platonic/Galenic division of the soul into rational, irascible, and concupiscible parts; the latter two were thought to reside in the heart and liver</note>), be guarded by a safe defense. For this reason, even the provident Craftsman of things <note>A reference to God or Nature as the "Opifex"</note> did not commit the protection of the brain to skin alone and fleshy parts, as in the abdomen; nor to bones removed from one another by intervals, as in the chest; but he placed bone around it on all sides like a helmet. However, although there was no occasion for this helmet—which constitutes the entire cavity in which the brain is contained—to be built of various bones that, articulated with one another, might possess voluntary motion; nevertheless, it consists of eight specific ^a bones. These are joined to one another by ^b sutures, or by some other entirely immovable and tenacious connection, and then further joined to the twelve other bones of the upper jaw; together with these, they constitute the skull <note>original: "caluariam"</note> as it is encountered in cemeteries. Since that helmet is necessarily formed with very different seats, and since it was therefore necessary for its bony substance and nature to vary remarkably in hardness, thickness, in its boundaries and processes, and in the fashioning of great cavities within, it could not be fashioned from a single bone. This is not even to mention that we commonly judge it to be less exposed to injuries if it is built of many parts: namely, so that fractures of the bones, and certain other of their defects, might be limited to the bones themselves, and not proceed through the entire helmet, just like cracks in earthen vessels. Furthermore, this frequent connection of the bones—

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY]

<margin>c Figure 2, letter o, shows the substance of the base of a skull stripped of flesh.</margin>
<margin>d Book 7, figure 1, letters G, H, I.</margin>
<margin>e The same figure, letter F.</margin>
<margin>f Seek these out, if you please, in order from figures 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, and 11 of Book 7.</margin>
The context [of the skull's structure] also serves the purging of vaporous and smoky waste products <note>In the 16th century, "excrements" referred to any metabolic byproducts, including "sooty vapors" thought to rise from the body's heat and escape through the skull.</note>. Indeed, since the head represents a kind of roof for a warm house, receiving those wastes that ascend upwards and therefore requiring more frequent evacuation, it was necessary for the bone<gloss>c</gloss> substance to be hard and solid, rather than being cavernous inside and out and filled with small holes like a sponge or pumice stone (which would make it entirely weak and too rough and hostile to the neighboring parts), yet still provide an exit for that waste in certain places, which is the function of the various sutures of the bones. However, this helmet or skullcap did not obtain sutures only for the reasons mentioned, but primarily so that fibers of the membranes<gloss>d</gloss> might pass through them. These fibers, besides the ends of certain vessels, join the hard membrane of the brain <term>the dura mater</term> to the skullcap<gloss>e</gloss> itself. Through the intervention and benefit of this connection, they support the brain—which<gloss>f</gloss> would otherwise easily collapse because of its softness and compress its own ventricles and cavities—and keep it as if suspended, quite elegantly, as we shall teach in the seventh book. Thus, we believe that the sutures are prepared primarily for the sake of the hard membrane of the brain and the fibers that cross the sutures to form the membrane covering the outside of the skull <term>the pericranium</term>, and that they are arranged according to the shape of the brain, which the cavity of the head bones mimics.

<margin>The natural shape of the head suture.</margin>
<margin>Coronal suture.</margin>
<margin>Resembling the letter Λ [Lambda].</margin>
<margin>Sagittal, and its various paths.</margin>
<margin>g Figures 3 and 4, letters A, B, and in figure 7, Γ Γ.</margin>
<margin>h Figures 3 and 4, letters C, D, and in figure 6 and 7, Δ Δ.</margin>
<margin>i Figure 3, from D through E to B, and in figure 7, Θ Θ.</margin>
Therefore, since an oblong body is conveniently lifted and held as if suspended by bindings and grips along its length and then across its width, the so-called "natural" shape of the head primarily possesses three sutures: two indeed are transverse, of which<gloss>g</gloss> one is in the forehead <term>sinciput</term>, and the other in the back of the head <term>occiput</term><gloss>h</gloss>. The third extends from the middle of the posterior one (the one in the back of the head), through the length of the head to the middle of the anterior one. They call the anterior one the **coronal** suture, since crowns are primarily placed on that part of the head. The posterior one they name **lambdoid** <note>original: "$\lambda \alpha \mu \beta \delta o \epsilon \iota \delta \tilde{\eta}$"</note> from its likeness to the letter Λ. The third, proceeding through the length of the crown of the head<gloss>i</gloss>, was called **rhabdoid** <note>original: "$\dot{\rho} \alpha \beta \delta o \epsilon \iota \delta \dot{\eta} \varsigma$" meaning rod-like</note>. This one proceeds straight like a rod; hence it is also called **obelaia** by the Greeks from the path of a rod, because like a spit or an arrow it sometimes creeps through the middle of the forehead<gloss>k</gloss> <margin>k Figures 2 and 4, letters S, c, d show something of this kind.</margin> all the way to the top of the nose—especially in those who happen to have a very broad and angular forehead—though not with such a notable connection or such a perfect suture joint as on the crown itself. 

And some falsely contend that this <note>the metopic suture, which sometimes divides the frontal bone</note> is peculiar to all men, and others to women; however, we have observed more than in passing that it happens very rarely in men, and even more rarely, or hardly ever, in women. 

<margin>Heads of men do not always differ from those of women.</margin>
<margin>History of Animals Book 3, Chapter 7, and On the Parts of Animals, Book 2.</margin>
You might even gather this from the fact that out of twenty skulls you find in cemeteries, you will hardly find two in which the frontal bone is divided. Nor is there any general difference between men and women in this regard, even though Aristotle <note>Vesalius frequently corrects the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, whose anatomical observations were often based on animals rather than humans.</note> taught otherwise, wandering completely from the truth in his description of the sutures. Furthermore, in quadrupeds, the **sagittal** suture extends from the posterior lambda-shaped suture all the way to the middle of the eyebrows<gloss>l</gloss>, as is clearly shown by the skulls of dogs, horses, oxen, and animals of that kind, in whom the jaw extends quite a bit with the forehead. 

<margin>l Dog's skull, figure 1, chapter 9.</margin>
For Aristotle is not to be listened to when he ascribes to dogs a continuous skullcap distinguished by no sutures; for the skulls of dogs elegantly display the sutures mentioned so far, and almost all that will be enumerated in this whole chapter. There are even those who assert that in infants this suture descends through the middle of the occipital bone to the opening <term>foramen magnum</term> providing a path for the spinal marrow<gloss>m</gloss>, dividing the entire occipital bone. 

<margin>History of Animals, Book 2, chapter 7.</margin>
<margin>m Figure 6, ε.</margin>
Truly, we have also observed this. But that division should be attributed to a union and growth together <note>the process of ossification where separate bone plates fuse as a child grows</note> rather than to the appearance of a suture, since in children this is completed by the benefit of cartilage, and in those of more advanced age no trace of that division occurs. For this reason, the explanation for such a division belongs not here in the discussion of sutures, but rather in the description of the occipital bone...

He defines the primary sutures (coronal, lambdoid, and sagittal) and corrects Aristotle's errors regarding gender differences and animal anatomy.</summary>

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.

<margin>
Herodotus, Book 3.
Skulls lacking sutures.
</margin>
...comes to be explained in the description of the bone. However, I am by no means surprised that Herodotus, and many others besides him, write that skulls are found in Persia distinguished by no sutures at all, or that Aristotle himself records a male skull found in his time without sutures. In the very old, the skulls often show us only the mere site of the sutures, and even then quite obscurely, with no visible image of a suture remaining. Indeed, it is not at all strange that sutures grow together in the elderly, since we see that in them <margin>vertebrae fuse in the elderly</margin> the vertebrae unite and grow together; it is also well known that the ridges and processes of the bones grow out in such a way that their bones cannot be moved in their accustomed motions. Furthermore, the three sutures already described, when the skull is lying on its side, express the letter H, or rather the Greek $\chi$ <note>The letter Chi</note> (because of its columns being slanted outward at their tips).

<margin>
Sutures of non-natural head shapes.
a Book 1, Fig. 5, Chap. 5.
</margin>
In head shapes that vary from the natural structure, the sutures <margin>a</margin> behave in this manner. When the anterior prominence of the head is lost, the coronal suture <term>the horizontal seam across the forehead</term> is abolished, while the one expressing the Greek $\lambda$ <note>The lambdoid suture at the back of the head</note> is preserved along with the sagittal suture <term>the seam running down the middle</term>, which then extends all the way to the middle of the <margin>b Fig. 5, Chap. 5.</margin> eyebrows. <margin>b</margin> But when the posterior prominence is lacking, the suture resembling the $\lambda$ is lost, while the coronal remains, and the sagittal is meanwhile drawn through the middle of the occiput <term>the back of the head</term> to the very base of the skull. Therefore, if you imagine this head shape resting on the occiput, the image of both remaining sutures will be similar to the letter T: just as in the first non-natural shape, when it rests on the forehead, the sutures resemble a T, or <margin>c Fig. 5, Chap. 5.</margin> perhaps more likely a Y. <margin>c</margin> Truly, when the anterior and posterior prominences collapse at the same time, the two sutures then seen, intersecting each other at right angles, represent the letter X. For one is drawn transversely from the region of one ear through the middle of the head to the <margin>d Fig. 1.</margin> region of the other ear; <margin>d</margin> the other, however, reaches from the hole in the occipital bone (carved out for the sake of the spinal cord) through the length of the head to the very top of the nose, in the manner of that which we commonly call the sagittal suture. Indeed, this one is always preserved in the first three head shapes that differ from the natural; <margin>e Fig. 5, Chap. 5.</margin> but the two transverse sutures fall away variously according to the shape of the whole head. <margin>e</margin> The fifth head shape, as it is entirely contrary to the natural one, also acquires sutures that are completely at odds with it. For the coronal, and that which resembles the $\lambda$, proceed according to the length of the head, while the straight or sagittal suture is carried transversely.

<margin>
Squamous joints of the temples.
f Figs. 3, 4.
F Fig. 6.
</margin>
But now let us direct our discourse to the remaining joints of the head. First, <margin>f</margin> there is on both sides a line roughly equidistant from the sagittal suture, stretched through the <margin>g Figs. 3, 4.
d, e at G.</margin> length of the head above the ear. The <margin>g</margin> beginning of this hangs from the lowest seat of the suture imitating the $\lambda$, where, because of the lower parts of the occiput, it hardly reflects the complete image of a suture anymore. From here, the present line is carried somewhat straight; and <margin>h</margin> soon ascending upward, it creeps <margin>h Figs. 3, 4.
G through F, H to A.</margin> like a semicircle to the end of the coronal suture. This consists for the most part of two bones, resting upon each other and connected: not indeed by a suture, but gradually <margin>i</margin> the <margin>i Fig. 5, I.
Fig. 4, K.</margin> parietal bone <term>the bone at the top/side of the head</term> descending, is thinned out like a scale, and enters <margin>k</margin> into the bone <term>the temporal bone</term> ascending from below the ears, which is similarly <margin>k Figs. 4, 1, N.</margin> thinned into a scale, with both bones possessing a certain mutual roughness where they are joined together. <margin>The sutures of the head are also visible on the internal surface of the skull.</margin> For this reason, neither Hippocrates nor any of those who accurately weighed the fabric of the body deemed these lines worthy of the name of sutures: but from their resemblance to a scale, they called them <margin>l Fig. 6, $\Lambda, \Lambda$.</margin> squamous conglutinations <note>original: "lepidoeidē proskollēmata"</note>. For <margin>m Fig. 7, $\Gamma, \Gamma, \Delta, \Delta, \epsilon, \Theta$.</margin> one must not think, as many do, that <margin>l</margin> these conglutinations appear <margin>m</margin> less than the three <margin>n Figs. 3, 4.
from H to A.</margin> sutures previously described in the cavity of the skull where the brain is placed, and for that reason are by no means gifted with the name of sutures. <margin>n</margin> Although meanwhile the three sutures, and most especially the coronal, express to me the image <margin>o Fig. 1.</margin> not so much of a suture as of a harmony <term>a smooth anatomical joint</term>. <margin>o</margin> Furthermore, of the squamous conglutinations being discussed here, <margin>p Figs. 3, 4, o.</margin> the part <margin>p</margin> nearest to the coronal suture also joins to the parietal bone and to that bone which we shall compare to a wedge <term>the sphenoid bone</term>...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>
Why scale-like joins rather than sutures occur in the temples.
</margin>
<margin>
q 3, 4 fig. b under A.

...we shall compare, should be considered common. Just as the most forward-facing site of the joins is referred to the frontal and sphenoid <term>wedge-shaped</term> bones: exactly as if Nature had established joins <note>original: "conglutinationes" — these are the overlapping, scale-like joints of the skull</note> here rather than sutures <note>original: "suturas" — the interlocking, saw-toothed seams</note>, because the area of the skull covered by the temporal muscle—acting as a sort of layer or cushion—should not be as thick as the fleshless regions of the skull. This was done so as not to be burdened by excessive weight in vain. The base of the skull itself, however, which is marked by many cavities and holes, had to be remarkably and variously thick. These parts are seen to be thick so that they do not provide too short a path for those wounding or otherwise harming the head; yet they are not entirely hard and solid, but are cavernous between two dense layers <term>the diploë, or spongy bone between the inner and outer tables of the skull</term>, primarily to avoid excessive weight. Therefore, since that entire part of the skull through which those joins run could be made thin, the composition of sutures—which requires wider and thicker bone sites—would have been weak here. Furthermore, the bones rising from the base are harder than those descending from the top; for this reason, the joins are formed so that the scales of the harder bones rightly overlap on the outside, while those of the softer bones are tucked inside, covered by the more solid ones on an otherwise flat surface.

<margin>
a 3, 4 fig. d at G.
b 3, 4 fig. b toward g.
c 3, 4 fig. Q at L.
</margin>
The fact that the temporal muscle is the primary cause of these joins is shown by their location, adjacent to the suture resembling the letter $\Lambda$ <note>The lambdoid suture at the back of the head</note>. This join reflects the image of a suture at the same interval as the portion of the skull that is fleshless, and according to the thickness of the bones themselves. Furthermore, at the forward site of the joins, we see a type of suture where the bones forming the upper jaw <note>maxilla</note> become thick along with the bones of the head, so that throughout their course, these joins do not appear entirely scale-like.

<margin>
Suture surrounding the eighth bone of the head.
</margin>
