</margin>
Besides the sutures and structures mentioned so far, another is seen in the cavity of the head surrounding the brain, common to the frontal bone and that bone which forms the seat of the organs of smell and is seen to be pierced like a sieve <note>The ethmoid bone, from the Greek "ethmos" for sieve</note>. For that bone is inserted, as it were, into the base of the frontal bone, and is obscurely bounded within the cavity of the head by this suture surrounding it. It also possesses another suture common to it and the bones of the upper jaw. This bone produces the bony septum that divides the openings of the nostrils; it is separated by a certain suture along its lower part, and along its length, from the largest bones of the upper jaw which contain the teeth, and * from those which are found at the end of the palate toward the throat, which will be counted as the sixth bones of the upper jaw. It is also separated there from the wedge-shaped bone <note>the sphenoid</note> where the openings of the nostrils lead into the throat. What sort of bone this is, perforated in the manner of a sieve, I shall pursue in the description of the other bones of the head after I have described the other remaining sutures.

<margin>
Sutures common to the bones of the head and others.
</margin>
<margin>
n 3, 4, 5 fig. O. P, and almost the whole 8 fig.
</margin>
For there are still other sutures common to the head and other bones, namely with the upper jaw and that bone which, from its resemblance to a wedge, they call the *sphenoid* <note>Greek: $\sigma\phi\eta\nu\omega\iota\delta\acute{\epsilon}\varsigma$ (sphenoides)</note>. Like many bones of the body, this bone is unique and lacks a pair. It is counted by some among the bones of the head, and by others among the bones of the upper jaw. However, it is far more correctly ascribed to the bones of the head, since it forms a significant part of the skull cavity where the brain is placed, along with the other bones that all anatomists attribute to the head.

<margin>
Additions to the sutures imitating the $\Lambda$.
</margin>
<margin>
Description of the sphenoid bone.
</margin>
<margin>

p 5 fig. n. 6 fig. P.

But we will deal with the bones and sutures of the upper jaw in the ninth chapter, where we will necessarily take up the discussion of this suture again. Now, however, the eight bones of the head, circumscribed by the sutures mentioned so far, must be approached individually.

Of these, two are of the crown <term>parietal bones</term>, one on each side; likewise two below these, one at each ear, which are called the bones of the temples <term>temporal bones</term>. The fifth is the bone of the forehead <term>frontal bone</term>, which, as is often the case, is a single bone. The sixth is the bone of the back of the head <term>occipital bone</term>, likewise single. The seventh is the wedge-shaped bone <term>sphenoid bone</term>, also single. The eighth is that which is likened to the image of a sieve or a sponge <term>ethmoid bone</term>.ᵃ

For this bone is formed, as it were, of two thin scales <term>squamae</term>, which are hollow in the middle and filled with air, just like the <margin>f Something of this sort is shown in figures 12 and 13 of Book 7.</margin> cavity which you will hear is located between its scales at the top of the eyebrows and the nose <note>The frontal sinuses</note>. Where this cavity exists, the bone is thicker than in its other parts and even protuberates. However, one of these scales, which faces the eye socket and is the outer one, appears smooth; but the one that faces the internal <margin>g Figure 8, at side 3.</margin> space of the head stands out with uneven swellings, almost like the shape of clouds, which correspond to the convolutions of the brain. In the temples, where the temporal muscles are located, the frontal bone is also thin and solid, and not at all cavernous inside, <margin>h Figure 3, B.</margin> except where it joins with the parietal bone <term>os uerticis</term> <note>Literally "bone of the crown"</note> in that area. For Nature has specifically made both bones thicker toward the interior at that interval, lest perhaps the excessive thinness of the bones should make the skull weaker than is right in that spot. Furthermore, the frontal bone shows no notable cavity between its scales in the forehead just above the eyebrows, nor in the rest of its area which is free of flesh; there, it is felt to be much thicker and denser than the parietal bones. Yet where it <margin>The softest and most porous part of the skull.</margin> joins these, and where the sagittal suture falls into the coronal suture, the frontal bone is thinner and weaker than in the forehead itself. This area, where the aforementioned sutures join together, occurs as the softest and most porous part of the entire skull; for it is that part which, in newborn infants, is still membranous and feels like fresh cheese to those who touch it, and which moves in young children when they eat or breathe. Because this area, called <term>Zeudech</term> <note>An Arabic anatomical term for the bregma or fontanelle</note> by the Arabs, is the thinnest among the fleshless parts of the head, and the sutures there are nowhere more loosely attached, doctors commonly apply to it what are called "cauteries"—either with glowing gold, or iron, or some burning medicine, according to the nature of the ailment (though often with little safety and very little benefit). This location in us is easily found with the tip of the middle finger if one places the base of the palm over the middle of the eyebrows and extends the middle finger straight down toward the crown of the head.

This bone is quite unequal in thickness and does not correspond to itself in every part. For whatever part of it in the back of the head is free of flesh and from the origins and insertions of muscles is seen to be remarkably thick—specifically, as much thicker than the frontal bone as that bone surpasses the thickness of the parietal bones. For Nature seems to have provided for this meeting of the sinuses with the thickness of the bone, both because extreme danger would hang over a person from an injury to it, and because she was not unaware that this area of the back of the head, being deprived of eyes, would frequently be struck or often dashed against the ground in various accidents. The occipital bone is smooth on the inside and not at all rough; just as on the outside, in its entire fleshless area, it is also seen to be smooth. However, in the area subject to this, where the occipital bone constitutes a significant portion of the base of the head, it presents itself as remarkably rough and uneven, so that ligaments and certain muscles might more conveniently take their origin from it, and again, so that certain others might be inserted into it more safely and firmly.

<margin>
The wedge-shaped [sphenoid] bone.
</margin>

Furthermore, we have spoken abundantly above about which sutures^u circumscribe the wedge-shaped bone. This bone, if any other, is remarkably varied; hence, not without reason, the Greeks also called it *polymorphon* <margin>πολύμορφον</margin> <note>original: "πολύμορφον", meaning many-formed</note> because of its manifold shape. At the sides, and in the hollows of the temples, it is thin, very solid, and dense. However, in its middle, at the very base of the head, it is seen to be by far the thickest of all the bones of the entire head, although it is certainly not the densest or hardest at the same time. For in the middle of its thickness—namely between its surface bordering the brain or the hard membrane of the brain <term>dura mater</term>, and that which faces the cavity of the mouth—it exists as a kind of empty or hollow space,^b somewhat in the manner of hollow images we see cast from wax.

For it is then fashioned as cavernous inside, in the form of a more solid and compact pumice or sponge, and the surfaces of that composition are lined with continuous, though not thick, scales. Whether the thickness of the wedge-shaped bone consists of this arrangement or of those caverns, its internal surface^k which faces the brain—at least in whole bones not spoiled by decay—never appears rough, cavernous, or full of small holes to me, but smooth, just like the rest of the skull's surface bordering it. From this cavity, two oblong channels^p are drawn out on both sides, upon which the carotid [soporific] arteries^q rest, and through which the phlegm seems to flow down toward the openings^r primarily carved out for the transmission of specific veins, arteries, or nerves, and toward certain fissures^s shared by the wedge-shaped bone <note>The sphenoid bone</note> and the temporal bones.

But I shall deal with the holes and boundaries of the entire skull in the twelfth Chapter; here, however, for the sake of the description of the wedge-shaped bone, this brief mention of certain things necessarily occurs. I wish to make it clear that this bone, on its surface facing the brain, does not appear to me to be covered with little caverns, nor does it—without the stripping away of the smooth scale or bone—refer to the kind of appearance of a pumice stone or sponge that a broken-off appendix^t <margin>t as the [Greek] alpha in the earth etc.</margin> or the bone of the crown [parietal bone] displays between its layers. Meanwhile, some authors, devoted to the opinions of authorities rather than to the truth, trifle with the idea that I simply do not wish to see such small holes, believing that the phlegm must be filtered through little caverns and holes corresponding to the structure of a sponge (as Galen taught). Furthermore, some, while considering my opinion on the purging of phlegm, think Galen did not feel this way, persuading themselves that in the ninth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, the word *ethmo* <note>original: "ἠθμῶ"; meaning a sieve or strainer</note> was placed there by librarians or scribes instead of *olmo* <note>original: "ολμω"; meaning a wedge or mortar</note>. In that passage, Galen, teaching the exit of phlegm to the palate, says the gland into which the brain's phlegm is distilled is received by a bone resembling a sieve. It is as if Galen had not even thought in a dream (as they say) that phlegm is filtered through winding and non-straight passages and little caverns in the wedge-shaped bone, even if one were to read that the gland is received by a bone resembling a wedge. But here in the description of the wedge-shaped bone, as never elsewhere, I do not disagree with Galen merely because of one or two words that might have been corrupted. For however much that recently mentioned word is changed, the sequence of the entire book cannot be so corrupted that we do not still grasp Galen's meaning in some way.

[The phlegm] then flows down into a certain gland <note>The pituitary gland</note>. Galen, in mentioning these things, leads the phlegm as far as that bony structure, which he concluded from his own arguments must be cavernous and full of holes on account of the phlegm. Then, he again discusses the method of straining <note>original: "tranſcolandi"</note> in such a way that he makes the discourse of the eighth book common with the ninth, and he describes no other reason for the descent of phlegm to the palate than through the little holes carved out in the name of odors. Since, therefore, the substance of the little caverns which Galen proposes in this whole context corresponds to the image of pumice or a sponge, and since he so studiously distinguishes the method of straining through a spongy body (which we see happening in what the Venetians call "cisterns" <note>A reference to the sand-filtration systems used in Venice to provide fresh water</note>) from that which occurs through a sieve, he argues against the ancients as if they had been ignorant of its use. It ought to have been clear to everyone what Galen's opinion was: he did not believe that the phlegm could be led down through the large, straight, or through-and-through holes which we encounter in the wedge-shaped bone <note>The sphenoid bone</note> without a ridiculous and entirely unskillful delay, however that passage I mentioned earlier might be read. 

However, in the eleventh book of *On the Use of the Parts*, Galen treats the wedge-shaped bone—which elsewhere in those books he called the palate bone on all sides (even though it hardly touches the palate), and which according to his opinion the common crowd of doctors calls the "strainer bone" <note>original: "os colatorij"</note>—likening it to a wedge, and stating that it is dense and hard. This grows out from the occipital bone and is spread over the entire upper seat of the **cerebellum**<sup>p</sup>, just as in humans we see the process of the thick membrane of the brain<sup>q</sup> <note>The *tentorium cerebelli*</note> drawn over the cerebellum. This separates and divides the cerebellum from the part of the brain upon which it rests. It is thickest and hardest in that part<sup>r</sup> where it leads the vessels<sup>t</sup> out from its own sinus into the anterior ventricles of the brain<sup>s</sup> near the aforementioned gland. The hardness of this part appeared so great to some in certain animals that they called it cartilaginous or even bony. Unless, perhaps, those disputing about a "brain cartilage" or "bone" were referring to that thin, wide bone of the dog, even though it never occurs in man. Indeed, it should be hidden from no one that many of the ancients, including Galen, proposed an anatomy that was a confused mixture of many animals.

## Likened to a Steep Cliff.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'I' depicting three cherubs or putti working with various tools in a workshop setting.</image-desc>

AMONG the bones of the body, certain ones lack their own distinct boundaries and limits, yet they are described by professors of dissection as if they were specific bones and are included in the number of bones along with the rest. Of this kind is the bone called **jugal** <note>The zygomatic bone or cheekbone</note> by the Latins, but **zygoma** <note>ζύγωμα</note> by the Greeks, because both bones (for there is one on each side) are compared to the **yokes** <note>A "jugum" or "zygoma" is a yoke for oxen</note> of oxen or horses. This jugal bone—or rather, the region of the skull called by this name—consists of the processes of two bones meeting together<sup>a</sup> at an oblique suture. Its posterior part is a process of the **temporal bone**<sup>b</sup>; the anterior part, however, is a process of that bone which forms the entire external corner of the eye socket and is counted as the first of the bones of the **upper jaw**<sup>c</sup>. Both processes, or the region we call the jugal bone, lack marrow and are solid. By their hardness, they are suited to warding off injuries, so that<sup>d</sup> a fit bulwark might be created for the **temporal muscle**, being convex on the outside but hollow on the inside. Meanwhile, Nature did not only protect the temporal muscle in this way, but also hid it for the most part within the bones of the head, carving out a cavity in the bones ideally suited to receive it, and hedging it in on all sides with the swellings and "promontories" of the neighboring parts. Nature struggles for this most deservedly, since when the temporal muscles are badly affected, they bring on convulsions, fevers, lethargy, and madness, because they sit so closely to the source of the nerves...

...and only bone separates them from the brain and its membranes. Add to this that five branches of the brain’s nerves (for I have discovered two in addition to the three known to other anatomists) are distributed to each muscle; for this reason, the divine Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) was an ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> did not speak without cause when he declared that temporal wounds are particularly significant and induce stupor. But we shall follow up on the excellence of these muscles abundantly, along with all the others to the last one, in the second book. There it will also be taught that the **zygomatic bone** <note>original: "iugale os"; the cheekbone</note> was formed primarily for this purpose: so that from it the **masseter**, or chewing muscle (which we will describe as the second of those moving the lower jaw), might conveniently take its origin. The ancients used the term **rock-like** <note>original: "λιθοειδῆ" (*lithoeidē*)</note> for bones which resemble a stone or a broken crag, not only in hardness but also in appearance. Such is the lower part of the head where the **spinal cord** <note>original: "dorsalis medulla"; here referring to the brainstem as it exits the skull</note> descends from the cranium, and where the breast-shaped <note>the mastoid processes</note> and **stylus-shaped** <term>stylū <gloss>the styloid process, a thin, pointed piece of bone just below the ear</gloss></term> processes of the temporal bones arise. For the bones of that region are the hardest and most solid of the entire body (on account of the organ of hearing, as I believe), appearing very much like a steep and rugged cliff for the sake of the convenient origin and insertion of muscles. Hence, I believe this part is rightly so named, and I do not think any bone in the body bounded by its own distinct border was called "petrous" or "stony" by the ancients. However, I am not unaware that many have specifically designated the temporal bones by this name alone—not indeed the whole bone, but that portion of them which brings forth the aforementioned processes. Therefore, I will allow the temporal bones to be named in this way, provided that no one is unaware that the region of the base of the skull we have mentioned is very frequently called the **petrous bone** <note>original: "petrosum os"</note>. Furthermore, certain bones are sometimes mentioned as if they were granted their own distinct borders, when in truth they should be considered nothing other than the ends of two bones meeting one another (as we have already said), and sometimes <margin>i Three figures of chapter 29.</margin> a single site of one particular bone. You will hear of this happening, for example, in the bones which, being pressed together at the sides of the **sacrum** <note>original: "sacri ossis"</note>, take on a triple name according to their specific areas.

<margin>The cavity prepared for the organ of hearing, and the openings leading from it: and finally the course of the fifth pair of cranial nerves into it.</margin>
ALTHOUGH we shall treat the structure of the instrument of hearing in the seventh book along with the organs of the other senses, nevertheless, because of the occasion of certain small bones <term>ossicula</term> entering into it, it must now be described in passing. This is so that we do not seem to have skipped them in the general history of the bones by saving those small bones all the way for the seventh book. Furthermore, it is conjectured that neither Galen, nor anyone else before him, observed these—as well as many other things—from the fact that no mention of them occurs anywhere in their writings. The part of this small bone <note>The incus, or "anvil" bone.</note> projecting outside the membrane is seen to be partly flat and partly round on top: in the same way that some smaller *anvils* <note>original: "incudes"</note> are usually fashioned, the larger part of which is flat, while the other, which ends in a sort of point, is round like a cone. For larger anvils are made entirely flat or depressed and quadrangular. However, if it is less pleasing to compare this small bone to an anvil—since it is provided with only two legs—nothing indeed shall stand in the way of comparing it to a molar tooth <term>molar tooth</term> <note>Vesalius uses this comparison because the incus has two "roots" or processes that resemble the roots of a tooth.</note> provided with only two roots.

A small bone not at all unlike a little hammer.

The other small bone <term>malleus</term> <note>From the Latin for "little hammer."</note> differs greatly from the one just mentioned and is attached to a different membrane. For the opening of the cavity, or the cavern carved into the temporal bone which faces the ear, is covered by a very thin and entirely transparent little membrane in that part where it is near the breadth of the cavity, in the same way we say a vessel is plugged at its bottom. Therefore, this small bone is attached crosswise to this little membrane, and is thus laid across it internally, just as we see one or two thicker strings stretched across the membrane or donkey-skin of drums. And so that the small bone might be more strongly secured, it has a long and thin process by which it is attached to the membrane along its width.

<margin>
r figures of chapter 30.
Comparison of the second small bone to the thigh bone.
</margin>
One might compare this process to that part of the thigh bone <term>femur</term> which extends from its processes, which we call "rotators" <note>The trochanters of the femur, which facilitate rotation.</note>, down to the lower heads of the femur. Indeed, if you imagine these lower heads cut off from the rest of the femur, the entire small bone will be aptly likened to a thigh bone. For just as the femur takes on two processes near its neck, so also this small bone claims several little processes in the same seat, by the benefit of which it is more firmly attached to its membrane. Then, just as the neck of the thigh bone recedes obliquely toward the interior of the body, tending toward the hollow of the hip bone, and ends in a perfectly round head: so also the small bone recedes inward from the membrane, ending in a round head which is smooth and not at all rough. It is joined to the upper part of the other small bone—which we likened to a molar tooth or an anvil—by the intervention of very thin membranes,
<margin>
s P, Q.
</margin>
just as if a hammer were loosely bound to an anvil: not otherwise than if the small bone last described performed the duty of a hammer, while the other took the place of an anvil, though it is far too small for the mass of the hammer.

<margin>
The use of the small bones of the organ of hearing.
</margin>
Whether these small bones truly fulfill the office of anvil and hammer just as they reflect their form—and the second small bone is moved during dissection along with the membrane to which it is attached by even the slightest breath, while the first bone remains somewhat at rest—I would by no means wish to assert, since I do not yet perceive the logic of hearing to my satisfaction. It is not that it has escaped my mind—that common refuge of doctors concerning the "temperament" of parts and their essential form, or the circles of air which we commonly persuade ourselves are carried into the ear by a strike and hit a certain membrane (like the ripples from throwing pebbles into water), while we remain entirely ignorant of the construction of this organ. For the Architect of things <note>God or Nature</note> machines far more divine things here with most clever craftsmanship, the structure of which I demonstrate clearly enough in the schools, but the use and mode of operation I do not grasp any more than I do that of the eye itself. But because the organ of hearing will be treated later, let it suffice here to have reviewed the small bones. If you have not grasped these through this discourse, then with the head of a calf, or a lamb, or another animal placed on the table, you may divide the temporal bone now in this way, now in that. Although it is much better to approach these things in a raw head than a cooked one; and in a human rather than any other animal. Not only will you find the construction of these small bones most pleasant to behold by this management, but furthermore, you will admire the logic of the construction of almost all musical instruments as being taken from the framework of the organ of hearing, and for this reason especially, the harmony of the organ of hearing...

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.
f
<meta>Catchword: hollows</meta>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'S' featuring several cherubs (putti) in a landscape setting. One figure in the foreground appears to be interacting with a skull or bone on the ground.</image-desc>

<margin>
What part of the upper skull is called the jaw.
</margin>

In our account of the bones, we give the name "upper jaw" <note>original: "superiorem maxillam"; in Renaissance anatomy, the term 'maxilla' referred to the entire upper facial skeleton, including the nose and cheekbones, not just the tooth-bearing bone.</note> to that part of the skull which remains after accounting for the eight bones of the head—which together form the seat containing the brain—and the two small bones of the hearing organ on each side, which we have yet to mention. This jaw encompasses the lower part of the eye sockets, the sides and the great cavity of the nostrils, and the upper row of teeth.

<margin>
Why it consists of many bones, and why they are hollow and light.
</margin>

We believe this structure is built not from a single bone, but from many, so that it may be more ready to repel injuries and endure damage with less disadvantage. This is because a defect in one part is confined within its own boundaries, rather than spreading through the entire jaw as it might through a ceramic vessel. However, there is another reason for this abundance of bones: namely, the variety of regions within the jaw, which do not require bones of equal density, hardness, thickness, or softness everywhere. Nevertheless, for the most part, it consists of hard but remarkably light bones. For besides the nasal cavity which they form, the bones are exceedingly hollow inside the sides of that cavity, containing notable "caves" <note>original: "antra"; these are the maxillary sinuses.</note>. Thus, you might beautifully compare the composition of the upper jaw to those images we cast from wax that are hollow inside. This is done so that a unique and rare lightness is added to its necessary bulk, which, while not burdening the head with weight, is also wonderfully suited for producing the voice.

<margin>
Book 11, *On the Use of the Parts*.
</margin>

In no way should we agree with Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose anatomical works were the undisputed authority for over a millennium before Vesalius.</note>, who teaches that the upper jaw is devoid of marrow and formed of hard bones that do not require lightness, because it does not move like the lower jaw. Yet, in truth, the upper jaw is much stronger than the lower, and consists of bone far more ready to repel injury.

<margin>
A brief enumeration of the bones of the jaw.
</margin>

Aside from the upper teeth and certain thin, spongy, and somewhat membrane-like or cartilaginous little bones found at the top of the nasal cavity, there are twelve bones of the upper jaw, six on each side. Of

<margin>
a Figures 1, 2: Γ, Γ.
b Figure 1: Δ.
c Figure 1: Θ.
d Figures 1, 2: Λ, Λ.
e Figure 1: Ξ.
f Figure 2: Π.
g Figure 2: chapter 12, n, o.
</margin>

these, <term>a</term> the first constitutes the outer corner of the eye socket. <term>b</term> The second and <term>c</term> third relate to the inner corner of the eye socket. <term>d</term> The fourth supports all the teeth on its side. <term>e</term> The fifth is considered one of the two bones we ascribe to the nose. <term>f</term> The sixth, with its partner, is placed at the end of the palate, where <term>g</term> the openings of the nostrils reach into the space of the mouth. These bones are joined to each other and to the neighboring bones of the head by sutures and "harmonies" <note>original: "harmonias"; a type of joint where the bone edges meet in a simple line without the jagged, interlocking teeth of a true suture.</note>. But since these harmonies, if they are ever broken apart, often show a mutual textured weave inside that you might compare to a suture, they are also gifted with the name "sutures" in the description of the upper jaw by those skilled in dissection. So that you may properly weigh all these bones and the boundaries they define—and observe how Galen’s descriptions here, which are otherwise obscure and inconsistent, fit dogs and monkeys rather than humans—I have been accustomed to do as follows in the schools: take all the sutures of a human skull that you encounter, however faintly visible or appearing as a "harmony," and darken them on one side with ink. Thus, once thickened and tinted, they will be more readily apparent, and you will grasp the entire boundary of the bones with less effort using the specialized description I will now provide, before you go on to consider the structure of the dog and the monkey.

</margin>

<term>a</term> The first bone of the upper jaw, then, constitutes one part of the yoke-bone <note>original: "os iugale"; the zygomatic or cheekbone.</note>. It encompasses a bit of the temple, the eyebrow, and the eye socket—specifically the entire outer corner—forming a significant portion of the cheek. This <term>b</term> bone is joined to the temporal bone by the intervention of a suture that joins the two processes forming the yoke-bone. Then it is joined to the wedge-shaped bone <note>original: "ossi cuneiformi"; the sphenoid bone.</note> by means of that suture which...

<summary>Vesalius defines the upper jaw as a complex structure of twelve bones, explaining that its multi-part, hollow design provides strength and lightness while aiding the voice. He famously critiques Galen's anatomical accuracy, urging students to ink human skull sutures to see the truth of human anatomy over animal models.</summary>

### The Fifth Bone of the Upper Jaw
<margin>

The **fifth bone of the upper jaw** is one of the two **nasal bones**. It is a small bone that is hard, solid, wide, thin, oblong, and more like a quadrangle than a triangle. a In its upper part, it does not end in a sharp angle; rather, it is so blunt b that it is granted two angles there, where it is bounded by the suture that terminates the **frontal bone** <note>the forehead</note> from the upper jaw. The outer side of the bone finds a common suture with the fourth bone of the jaw, which c slopes down along the side of the nose for as long as the length of this fifth bone, which is seen to be far shorter in humans than in dogs and monkeys. The inner side of the bone, where it joins its partner, possesses a suture not unlike a "harmony" <note>original: *harmonia*; a type of joint where flat edges meet without interlocking</note>, d common to both bones of the nose. This starts from the middle of the eyebrows at the suture common to the frontal bone and the upper jaw, and extends downward along the length of the nasal bones. e In the lower part, however, the fifth bone is not intercepted by a suture, nor is it joined to another bone; instead, this bone, along with its partner, is rough and uneven, and terminates in f **cartilage** that proceeds downward, becoming softer the further it is carried toward the tip of the nose. We shall follow up on this cartilage, along with the other cartilages of the nose and the entire body, separately after the account of the bones.

The **sixth bone**, with its partner, constitutes a significant portion of the breadth of the palate and the nostrils. Where it joins the cuneiform bone, it is c circumscribed by a suture that is carried near the rear seat of the innermost tooth and separates the upper jaw from the cuneiform bone, especially in that part where the cuneiform bone brings forth its processes d resembling **bats' wings** <note>the pterygoid processes</note>. On the front part and the outer side, the sixth bone is bounded by a suture common to itself and the fourth bone of the jaw, drawn transversely across the palate. ...about to describe, he begins their sequence from the lowest and outermost part of the cheekbone <note>the malar or zygomatic bone</note>, which I have described as being rough and uneven, because the <insert>a</insert> masseter muscle <note>the primary muscle used for chewing</note> draws its very strong and fibrous origin from there. Here, therefore, Galen describes a suture <note>original: "sutura"; the joint where two bones of the skull meet</note> separating the first bone of the jaw from the fourth. He calls the first part of this suture that which <insert>b</insert> is visible in the cavity of the temple. The second part he counts as occurring in the front part of the jaw, which <insert>c</insert> reaches upward from that roughness of the cheek to the middle of the lower rim of the eye socket <note>the orbit</note>. He later says this is split into three parts, and that the <insert>d</insert> first part of this second suture proceeds near the large or internal corner of the eye socket on the outer side toward the middle of the eyebrows, and to the common suture of the forehead and the jaw. Humans lack this part of the suture, but in dogs and long-tailed monkeys it is very obvious; <insert>e</insert> although, in the meantime, it is not carried exactly to the middle of the eyebrows, but only to that place where the fourth bone of the jaw is separated from the second. Thus, to follow Galen’s meaning, you must seek this part from the skull of a dog.

<margin>f Imagine in Figure 1 a continuous suture drawn from a to b through c and d to T, as is visible in the dog.</margin>
Furthermore, Galen says the second part of the second suture <insert>f</insert> reaches through the hollow of the eye socket under the large corner to the common suture of the head and the jaw, and that it encompasses this same corner. This part would be that suture which we taught separates the second and third jaw bones from the fourth in their lower seat. However, in humans, this is by no means joined to Galen's "second suture"; much less does it touch the first part of the second suture, since that is seen only in dogs and monkeys, but not in humans.

For it is Galen's opinion that under the two said sutures (which are the first two parts of his second suture), a third lower part of the same climbs the rim in the eye socket, striving inward toward the bottom, and is joined there to the common suture of the head and upper jaw. When you have inspected this in a dog or a monkey, consider accurately how impossible it is for this suture to extend between the teeth of a human, who possesses a very short jaw and is endowed with altogether tiny canine teeth. Furthermore, notice what Galen intended in his books *On the Use of the Parts* when he wrote in passing that there are twelve bones of the upper jaw: just as the author of the *Introduction* or *The Physician* <note>A text traditionally attributed to Galen, but often considered pseudo-Galenic in the Renaissance</note> enumerates only twelve bones of the jaw, undoubtedly following the opinion of the Ancients; or when <margin>Book 11.</margin> Galen, mentioning these bones more at length, recounts only nine, and attributes no bone specifically to the incisor teeth, not even including the wedge-shaped bone <note>original: "cuneiforme os"; the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull</note> in that number.

<margin>Man was granted the shortest lower jaw.</margin>
<margin>Table 6 of the muscles proposes the jaw cut through the middle.</margin>
Of all animals, man possesses the shortest lower jaw in proportion to the mass of his whole body. For he was granted a round face, not a long one like other animals that bend down to take food. Indeed, it was fitting for the jaw to be hard in humans because it alone is mobile and sustains various and very strong movements in biting and chewing. However, lest it be so hard and solid that its excessive weight would be a disadvantage to the muscles moving it, it shows noteworthy hollows and cavities filled with marrow, while remaining entirely free of any separate additions <note>original: "appendicis"; referring to an epiphysis or distinct secondary bone growth.</note>. These hollows are not carved out as much in the back part of the jaw in humans as in quadrupeds, but more toward the front, near the region of the chin, and at the sides of the jaw. <margin>The human jaw is constructed of almost a single bone.</margin> In most animals, the jaw consists of two bones at the tip of the chin, joined together by a union. In man, however, it is formed of a single bone, and is wide and thick at the tip of the chin,

...is seen to be thick, but not, as in other animals, sharp. Indeed, no part of the jaw is harder to split than here. I have not yet observed it to dissolve through boiling or through decay <term>carie</term> in the earth. In contrast, the jaws of dogs, oxen, and donkeys are sometimes pulled apart with little effort, even without the benefit of boiling. Meanwhile, Galen and many others after Hippocrates who were skilled in dissection asserted that the jaw was not a single bone, but that it loosened at the very tip of the chin when boiled—and that this was clear evidence it had once grown together from two parts. Be that as it may, so far no jaw constructed of a double bone has ever occurred to me. And even if perhaps among so many thousands of men, I might have once observed such a jaw in some dog-like little man <note>original: "canino aliquo homuncione"; a sarcastic reference to those whose anatomy resembles a dog's more than a human's</note> or a small child, I would not therefore immediately assert that the human jaw consists of a double bone. Rather, I would agree with Celsus—or that Greek author from whom Celsus borrowed whatever he published concerning the bones—who, caring little for Galen’s dogs (for Galen eventually held a different opinion regarding monkeys in the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*), taught that the jaw is composed of a single bone. And although in children this may be formed by two bones joined through a union, we would not for that reason say simply that the jaw consists of a double bone, unless we were also to grant that the occipital bone, the vertebrae, and the bones which are squeezed together at the sides of the sacred bone <note>The sacrum</note> are formed of many bones; for no one would deny that in children these are built from several bones coming together through a mutual union.

<margin>
a Plate 1, 2 fig. C. 6 of the muscles, table A, B.
b Plate 1, 2 fig. A. B.
c Plate 5 fig. 6 chap. h.
</margin>
<margin>Two processes of the jaw on each side.</margin>
The lower jaw <term>maxilla inferior</term> ends on both sides in two processes. One of these, ^a extended into a point <note>The coronoid process</note>, receives the insertion of the temporal muscle and is entirely surrounded by its tendon. ^b The other, which is further back, ends in a transversely oblong little head <note>The condyle</note>, articulated into a corresponding cavity which is carved into the temporal bone at the root of the yoke-shaped bone <note>The zygomatic arch</note> and the front seat of the organ of hearing. ^c A cartilage is spread over this cavity, as well as over the head of the jaw, like a crust.

But in addition to this cartilage, which is common to all joints alike, another smooth, thin, and soft cartilage <note>The articular disc or meniscus</note> is placed between the cavity and the head. It is somewhat composite in nature, like a ligament, as far as its substance is concerned. This cartilage is joined to the ligaments that hold the joint in a circle, rather than to the bones themselves. It cushions the impact of the hard bones of the present joint and, together with the cartilages grown onto the cavity and the head, skillfully ensures that the bones are not broken by mutual friction during the powerful and constant movements of the jaw.

<margin>The appearance of the unique cartilage in the joint of the jaws.</margin>

d Plate 2 fig. F.
e Plate 1 fig. G.

<margin>The foramina of the jaw.</margin>
Next, the jaw is gifted with two holes <term>foramina</term> on each side. ^d One of these is seen in its interior region, not far from the processes just mentioned; ^e the other is found in the exterior part, at the root and side of the lower lip. The internal one, which is both larger and uneven or rough, provides a path for ^f a portion of the nerve of the third pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "tertij paris neruorum cerebri"; in modern anatomy, this is the mandibular branch of the 5th cranial nerve (trigeminal)</note> which is dispersed to the roots of the teeth, together with a small vein and artery that enter this hole to nourish the teeth and the jaw.

<margin>
f Plate 2 fig. of those that are placed before chap. 2 book 4, T.
g V of the said figure &
h G of the table of muscles.
</margin>
On the outside, ^g a branch of that nerve is seen to emerge from the jaw into the lower lip, and it is much smaller than the internal one. Furthermore, if you insert a bristle into the internal hole of a dried jaw, ^h you will push it through from this hole to the external one with little effort. And if you break the jaw open, you will observe a continuous path carved like a canal from one hole to the other. Besides these holes, you will find absolutely no others on the outer surface of the jaw—unless perhaps you also wish to count the sockets <term>alveoli</term> and little partitions among them, in which the teeth are fixed like nails, as we shall soon describe.

<margin>The tooth sockets.</margin>
That the lower jaw also becomes thicker for the sake of these cavities and sockets is most clearly established by the fact that in the elderly, and in those whose teeth have been pulled out and in whom the sockets of the teeth themselves have grown over, the jaw becomes much thinner and narrower from the bottom up.

<margin>The breadth, thinness, cavities, and roughness in the posterior part of the jaw.</margin>
The jaw is broadest where the teeth themselves are not fixed, in that area from which it sends out the processes recently mentioned,

...is seen to be very broad and, if you look at the sides, very thin. On both the internal and external surfaces, it appears carved with a wide and shallow hollow <term>sinus</term>, so that the muscles lifting the jaw (besides the temporal muscle) might better manage their attachment <term>insertion</term>. This ensures that the muscle hidden within the mouth does not, by its own thickness and bulk, overcrowd the narrow passage of the throat. Indeed, the jaw is deservedly more recessed on the inside than on the outside. Furthermore, it happens that this broader part of the jaw is uniquely rough and uneven, especially near the lower and posterior region of that area. The Creator of things <note>original: "rerum Opifex"; Vesalius frequently refers to God as a master craftsman or engineer of the body</note> engineered this by design, knowing that something adheres and grows more readily to rough, uneven places than to flat, smooth ones. For the same reason, the inner side of the jaw near the chin swells with several small bumps <term>tubercles</term> or rough spots, so that the muscles by which the jaw is pulled downward might make their attachment more firmly, and finally, so that certain muscles peculiar to the tongue might better arise from here. Something similar also occurs on the outer side of the lower jaw, near the top of the chin, so that the muscles of the lower lip might more conveniently originate there.

-># ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.<-

<margin>
a Figure 2, Chapter 2, Book 4, Section 20.
</margin>
<margin>
Teeth have sensation. From the fifth book of Galen's *On the Composition of Medicaments according to the Places*.
</margin>

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'O' depicting a medical or anatomical scene with several figures gathered around a subject, possibly a dissection or a demonstration.</image-desc>

**O**F THE BONES, Galen attests with no small emphasis <note>original: "non perfunctoriè"; meaning thoroughly or seriously</note> that the teeth alone possess the power of sensation. He asserts that when he was once tormented by a toothache, he carefully weighed whether it was the teeth themselves that hurt. He clearly perceived that the tooth not only pained him but even throbbed, much like flesh besieged by inflammation. For certain soft little nerves are attached to the roots of the teeth<sup>a</sup>, originating from the third pair of cranial nerves <note>In modern anatomy, the nerves supplying the teeth are branches of the fifth cranial nerve (trigeminal), but Vesalius follows an older numbering system</note>. It is because of these nerves that we believe the teeth alone among the bones are granted a manifest faculty of feeling. For the Creator of things knew that these would frequently encounter objects that cut, break, gnaw, or are intensely hot or cold, or are altered by any other occasion; to all of these, the teeth are exposed naked, quite differently from the rest of the bones.

<margin>
The difference between teeth and other bones.
</margin>

However, they are distinguished from other bones not only by sensation and because they are exposed, but also because we believe they are nourished more than other bones and receive growth over a longer period of life. We primarily judge this because when teeth are opposite those we have lost, they subsequently grow out into the place of the extracted tooth, beyond the rest of the row of teeth. This occurs, evidently, because they are no longer worn down by the opposing teeth. For the rest of the teeth only grow as much as they are worn away by the grinding of food.

<margin>
The number of teeth.
</margin>

The teeth are usually thirty-two in number, with sixteen in a single row in each jaw, arranged like a most orderly dance <note>original: "choreae"; suggesting a harmonious or choreographed line</note>.

<margin>
b Figures 1, 2, D.
</margin>
<margin>
Incisors.
</margin>

<sup>b</sup>The front four, which face forward, are called incisors because they cut. They are broad and sharp so that they may promptly cut and divide the food offered to them by biting, in the manner of a knife.

<margin>
c Character 3.
</margin>
<margin>
Canines.
</margin>

Next<sup>c</sup>, a single canine is positioned on each side. These are broad at their base near the gums but sharp at the end furthest from the gums, so that if anything cannot be cut by the incisors due to its hardness, these may break it apart. Furthermore, this name was given to them because they correspond to the prominent teeth of dogs (who have many of these, notably in this position).

<margin>
d 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
</margin>
<margin>
Molars.
</margin>
<margin>
The molar tooth is described.
</margin>

<sup>d</sup>After these, five maxillary or molar teeth are found on each side. These are rough, broad, hard, and large, so that they can grind the food cut by the incisors and broken by the canines into a perfect smoothness. For if they were created entirely smooth, they would be least fit for their proper duty, since all things are better ground by uneven and rough surfaces. For this reason, we see that millstones <note>original: "molas"</note>, with which grain is ground, become smoothed over time and long use, and must be cut and roughened again. Nor would they be of more use if they were rough but not the hardest of all bones, as they would be worn away themselves before they could grind food into smoothness. Moreover, even if they were made rough and hard, they would not be suited to their entrusted task if they were not also broad, since those things which must be ground most finely must be braced upon broad bases. Indeed, because of their cramped and narrow edge, the incisors and canines can grind nothing without a very long delay.

<margin>
How the teeth are fixed in the jaws.
</margin>

The teeth, every single one of them, are fixed into the cavities of the jaws like nails. Because of the likeness they have to the mangers <term>stalls for feeding animals</term> of beasts, these cavities are called *phatnia* <note>original Greek: φάτνια</note> by the Greeks and *praesepiola* <note>original Latin: "little mangers"</note> by the Latins. Just as from the appearance of pits they are called *bothria* <note>original Greek: βόθρια</note>, so they are seen by some to be called *alveoli* <term>little troughs</term> and *fossulae* <term>little ditches</term>. Indeed, the teeth are inserted into these, which grip and contain them so precisely that they are not easily moved, even slightly.

<margin>
At the start of the chapter, we have depicted that series of roots which occurs most often.
</margin>
<margin>
The roots of the teeth.
</margin>

Furthermore, not all teeth are fixed into the aforementioned cavities with equal roots. For the small teeth have one root, the larger have two, and the largest have three or four. The incisors are each set with a single root. The canines also have single roots, which are inserted much deeper than the roots of the incisors; they are larger in proportion to how much the strength of the canines exceeds the others. Hence, among the incisors, the two in the middle are held by deeper roots than the two lateral ones next to the canines—doubtless because the middle ones are broader...

Vesalius also explains how teeth are anchored into the jaw's sockets, which he compares to animal mangers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed anatomical study of human dentition from page 57. ->## ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.<-

...are wider and larger. Molars vary among themselves in their roots. Those fixed in the lower jaw usually have two roots, while those in the upper jaw are often fixed with three. However, even these differ sometimes; for those above are occasionally found with four roots, and those below with three, especially the two teeth closest to the innermost tooth. Furthermore, you will very often see that the two upper molars following the canine tooth are attached with only two roots, and the remaining three with three roots; similarly, the two lower molars nearest the canine have one root, and the remaining three have two. You will also observe that the innermost teeth of all are fixed with smaller roots than those adjacent to them.

<margin>The number of teeth sometimes varies.</margin>
The number of incisors and canines rarely changes in humans, unlike that of the molars. For sometimes five molars occur on each side, sometimes four; occasionally there are four on the left and five on the right, or vice versa; or four below and five above.

<margin>Wisdom teeth <note>original: "genuini dentes"</note>.</margin>
This difference is mainly caused by the last teeth, which many call the "wisdom teeth," even though Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note> called all molars by that name. These are the ones that first emerge in humans after puberty and the experience of love <note>original: "uenerisq́; usum"; Vesalius associates the eruption of wisdom teeth with sexual maturity</note>, often with the greatest torment. Physicians, not observing this enough, either pull out other teeth or, convincing themselves that the teeth are infested by a defect of humors <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids believed to cause disease when out of balance</note>, overwhelm their patients with pills and similar drugs. Yet, for those suffering this pain, no more immediate remedy can be offered than a light scarification of the gums at the last tooth, and sometimes a piercing of the bone. I am currently experiencing this myself; as I write this, my thirty-second tooth is growing in during my twenty-sixth year. This is also proven by many skulls found in cemeteries, in which those back teeth are still stored and hidden as if in a cage, with the tips of their bases piercing the thinnest bone. A skull of this kind was recently shown to me by Giovanni Paolo Guiducci of Urbino, a young man most studious and skilled in the human structure and a very dear friend of mine. Furthermore, Aristotle and several others attribute more teeth to men than to women. It is just as easy for anyone to test whether this matches the truth as it is for me to say it is false, since anyone can count their teeth. From the frequency <note>meaning the number or health</note> of these, many even argue for the length or shortness of life. Teeth do not only serve the uses already mentioned but also help in modulating the voice,

<margin>The cavity of the teeth.</margin>
<margin>tooth marked "e".</margin>
since they are formed of a hard and stony substance containing small but noteworthy cavities inside. These provide the opportunity for the teeth to be lighter and more easily nourished. Because of this cavity, if holes ever arise in the teeth from the influx of sharp and corrosive humors reaching that cavity, the teeth are very quickly eaten away right down to the ends of the root.

<margin>The tooth attachments <note>original: "appendices"</note>.</margin>
Next, it must not be overlooked that children’s teeth consist of imperfect, soft, and almost marrow-like roots. In children, the part of the tooth visible outside the gums is joined to the tooth's root like an <term>appendix</term> <note>Vesalius uses "appendix" to describe the crown of a deciduous (baby) tooth as distinct from its root structure</note>. We learned this even as seven-year-olds when we used to pull out our own and our playmates' wobbling teeth—especially the incisors—with our fingernails or with a thread tied around the tooth. Moreover, in mules and many dogs, we observe every day that while the roots are retained, their "attachments" fall out. This must be weighed very carefully so that we never pull out the remaining portion of a child's tooth broken by an accident, but only the attachment, in whose place another will readily grow (provided the root is preserved). Furthermore, it is very helpful to have noticed this in children whose molars often begin to rot and spoil from an early age. In these cases, it is worthwhile to remove the molar attachments (which do not usually fall out on their own as the incisors do), so that...

## ON THE HOLES <term>foramina|Small openings or passageways through bone that allow nerves, veins, and arteries to pass through</term> OF THE BONES OF THE HEAD AND THE UPPER JAW,
### and on the many cavities of the bones occurring in the internal seat of the skull.
### Chapter XII.

<margin>Why a description of the holes is undertaken.</margin>
SINCE IN THE DESCRIPTIONS of veins, nerves, and arteries, an ignorance of the holes <term>foramina</term> of the skull would bring no small amount of obscurity, and since in describing them (as they are very difficult to obtain knowledge of), the foremost anatomists have strayed much, I have thought it worth the effort to dedicate this Chapter to all those holes. To do this more concisely, I will place here four figures serving the present task, intending to describe each hole individually with its assigned character <note>Vesalius refers here to the letters and numbers used to label his illustrations</note> so that the text of the characters may conveniently serve both as an Index and the context of the Chapter. Then, if by chance or diligence any cavity <term>sinus|A pocket or hollow space within a bone</term> or process of those bones described so far has been omitted, I shall describe it now.

### THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.

In this location, in the <term>eighth bone of the head|The ethmoid bone, which separates the nasal cavity from the brain</term>, many small openings are seen, carved for the purpose of odors and air entering the brain during inhalation. These are not straight in their path or passage like those mentioned thus far, nor are they open directly from one side to the other; rather, they are oblique and winding, similar to the holes in sponges. Among the rest, however, there is one on each side that is straight and quite large; it is, in a sense, the first, and is closest to the front part of the frontal bone. It transmits a vein extending from the expanse of the nostrils to the <term>dura mater|The "hard mother," the outermost and toughest membrane surrounding the brain</term>. Yet the other openings in this area might also appear straight and pierced through on both sides if only the tiny bones inside the nostrils—which are always found in equal number at the top, are remarkably spongy, and are somewhat covered by membrane and cartilage—were removed. Whether these small holes are formed secondarily for purging the brain's phlegm is a matter we shall discuss in the seventh book. For the present, however, I thought it necessary to add that phlegm is never filtered through here unless the brain is congested or unnaturally affected; when even a slight amount of phlegm flows down through here, those openings become blocked, and other symptoms of "heaviness" <note>congestion or a head cold</note> are induced. Furthermore, you should be advised that these openings do not appear with equal frequency in all skulls; likewise, the areas where the organs of smell are placed are not equally large in every individual. Moreover, the dog—an animal that produces very little phlegm but is endowed with an extremely sharp sense of smell—has these areas very large, and many wide-open holes are seen in them, facing forward rather than downward as in humans.

<margin>
K 3,4
e Book 6, Ch. 8, Fig. C, D.
</margin>
The cavity between the two <term>scales|The plates or layers of bone</term> that make up the frontal bone—located in the region of the eyebrows on the forehead and in the upper part of the eye sockets—reaches into the expanse of the nostrils through certain hidden openings. Some assert this cavity is the organ of smell because of the air trapped within it, which we do not doubt is wonderfully necessary for smelling. You will readily observe how spacious this cavity is if you break the frontal bone in the region of the eyebrows; it is very large and contains a somewhat soft body covered by a thin membrane, which in some way corresponds to marrow. However, the whole thing is such that you will find nothing like it in the entire body, except in the caverns or hollows visible in the sphenoid bone. Furthermore, in those whose outer layer of the frontal bone is eroded by the <term>French disease|Syphilis, which in its advanced stages often caused the decay of facial and cranial bones</term> or shattered by a wound, we see air propelled from that cavity with such force during exhalation that it very easily blows out the flame of a candle.

The part of the bone passable by this opening, where it looks downward toward the throat (marked **œ** in the second figure), appears rough and uneven like a pumice stone. Nature perhaps fashioned this oblique path, proceeding through a long track in the bone, for the sake of a longer and more winding passage for the carotid artery: namely, so that the <term>vital spirit|In Galenic physiology, a substance refined from blood and air in the heart, then sent to the brain to be converted into "animal spirit"</term>, led through this wandering journey, might be more exquisitely prepared for the brain. For this reason, I particularly marvel at <term>Galen|A 2nd-century Greek physician whose anatomical teachings were considered infallible for over 1,000 years until Vesalius corrected them</term>, who was unaware of this great opening (as he was of many others). In his book on the dissection of the veins and arteries of the monkey, he wrote that the carotid arteries enter the skull through the opening marked **Q** (the opening for the third and fourth pairs of cerebral nerves). And just as he handed down false information to posterity regarding this opening—having looked at neither dogs nor monkeys here—it is no wonder that he also fabricated that <term>miraculous reticular plexus|The *rete mirabile*, a network of blood vessels found in some animals like sheep, but not humans</term> in humans in his imagination, and passed down to posterity a sequence of brain vessels that was not entirely true.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE [HUMAN] BODY
<meta>catchword: nitur (is positioned)</meta>

<margin>I have placed this rough figure here so that the path of the passage is in view, which we mark with V, $\alpha$, and $\beta$. Let it represent, by "crude Minerva" <note>An idiom meaning a rough or unpolished sketch</note>, both auditory passages. V is the opening noted above with V. But b is that which will soon be explained under the letter b.</margin>
<image-desc>A small woodcut anatomical diagram of the temporal bone region showing the auditory canal, with labels alpha, beta, and V pointing to specific structures.</image-desc>

<margin>Book 1. History of Animals. chapter 11.</margin>
...is positioned <note>Completing the word "ponitur" from the previous page's catchword</note> so that only very rarely, and by great chance, can a bristle be pushed through it. Although the twists and turns of the passage itself are not the only reason a bristle is prevented from passing through, it is also because the passage becomes narrower as it faces the ear and then the brain than it was in <margin>b fig. 8 ch. book 1.</margin> the middle, where it is found to be quite large, wide, and remarkably varied. But meanwhile, Aristotle is by no means to be listened to when he asserts that no passage hangs from the ear to the brain. Instead, he says a path reaches as far as the <margin>a</margin> palate of the mouth, and a vein descends from the <margin>b</margin> brain to that same place. For the auditory passage <margin>c</margin> actually reaches into the cavity of the skull and also admits a vein; not indeed taking that vein from the <margin>c fig. ch. 14 book 3 n.</margin> brain, but from the internal jugular vein entering the skull, from which a branch is extended to the organ of hearing through the opening already expressed as V, also providing a path for a small shoot of the fifth pair of cerebral nerves. Furthermore, if you insert a bristle into the auditory passage from the outside and push it moderately forward and inward at an angle, you will see it carried into the opening marked V much more easily than into the main cavity of the skull.

### b 2
An opening from the middle of the cavity of the auditory organ carved into the temporal bone, reaching backward to this external region of the skull base next to the <margin>a 3, 4, 5 fig. ch. 6 k.</margin> mastoid process, and nowhere reaching the internal surface of the skull. Because this opening, by reason of its twists and the labyrinthine nature of its path, does not readily allow a bristle or a lead wire pushed into it to pass through to the cavity of the auditory organ, it is called <term>typhlon|Greek: τυφλὸν, meaning blind</term> in Greek and "blind" in Latin. <margin>Blind opening <note>original: "Foramen caecum"</note></margin> <margin>b 2 fig. ch. 2 book 4 c.</margin> It is prepared for a small branch of the <term>fifth pair of cerebral nerves|In Vesalius's system, this includes the modern facial nerve</term>; which, since Nature wished it to harden, she very skillfully led through the winding opening of this hardest and driest bone.

### c 2, 3
An opening common to the occipital bone and the temporal bone, prepared for the <margin>a 9 fig. 7 book N.</margin> sixth pair of cerebral nerves, the <margin>b</margin> larger branch of the internal jugular vein, and the <margin>c</margin> smaller <margin>b fig. ch. 14 book 3 C.</margin> offshoot of the <term>soporal artery|The internal carotid artery</term>. This opening is seen to be large because the organs passing through it are thick, <margin>c same fig. 1.</margin> corresponding to the shape of the bodies passing through. For it is not perfectly circular, but in a way double and twisted; one part (the inner one) is prepared for the nerve slipping out from the skull somewhat forward; the other (the outer one) serves the vein and artery entering the skull toward the back.

<margin>Here we have separately represented the opening just described, assigning alpha to its inner part and beta to its outer part.</margin>

### d 2, 3

<margin>The site and names of the U-shaped bone.</margin>
PLACED BEFORE the most prominent part of the larynx is a bone comprised under the name of "unity," but constructed from various and manifold little bones. Some call it <term>hypsiloeides|upsilon-shaped</term> <note>Greek: υψιλοειδὲς</note> from the shape of the letter U [upsilon], others more concisely <term>hyoides</term> <note>Greek: ὑοειδὲς</note>. Those unskilled in dissection, being deceived by this word, translated it in Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> as the "bone resembling a pig" <note>Mistaking the Greek 'hys' (pig) for the letter Upsilon</note>. By others again, this bone is named <term>lambdoeides</term> <note>Greek: λαμβδοειδὲς</note> from the image of the letter Lambda ($\Lambda$); 
<margin>a Figures 3 and 4 of chapter 6, C, D; and 3 of the internal parts, B.</margin> translators deceived by this name<sup>a</sup> were also accustomed to translate the suture of the head [the lambdoid suture] as being like the letter Lambda. Nevertheless, we have recently removed such errors as best we could from the Latin edition of Galen published in Italy and Germany. Herophylus <note>An ancient Greek physician often called the father of anatomy</note> is also said to have called this bone <term>parastates|the assistant</term> <note>Greek: παραστάτης</note>, perhaps because it is placed near or stands by the tongue, the larynx, or the throat; just as in the organs serving generation, certain parts<sup>b</sup> are called <term>parastates kirsoeides|the varicose assistant</term> <note>Greek: παραστάτης κιρσοειδὴς; likely the epididymis</note> and <term>parastates adenoeides|the glandular assistant</term> <note>Greek: παραστάτης ἀδενοειδὴς; the prostate</note>. There are also those who, since it sits in the throat, have called it <term>pharyngetron</term> <note>Greek: φάρυγγετρον</note>. 
<margin>b Book 5, figures 22 and 23, from A to I, and also ξ.</margin> 
<margin>c The same figures ξ; and Book 2, chapter 49, figure 4, R.</margin> 
We, however, have decided to call it everywhere the "U-shaped bone," or by the more contracted word, the **hyoid**. In humans, therefore, this bone is constructed far differently than in the quadrupeds we have examined thus far. The largest bone<sup>d</sup> of the hyoid is somewhat broad, 
<margin>d Figure 1, A, B; asterisk, C; Figure 2, D.</margin> 
<margin>The middle bone of the hyoid.</margin> 
rounded [convex] on the outside, and protruding with its own bump; but on the inside, or the rear side, it is...

seat, it is hollow. In the front part, higher up, it is depressed as if into an oblong sinus <note>a "sinus" here refers to a curved cavity or depression</note>, undoubtedly according to a shape suitable for itself and for the nature of the muscles and ligaments attached to it. For the third and fourth muscles peculiar to this bone are implanted in the upper sinus. However, at the sides of the tubercle <note>a small rounded projection</note> visible in this area—which are curved somewhat into a humped seat—the first two muscles peculiar to this bone attempt their insertion. From the hollow of the rear seat, the first two muscles moving the tongue mainly arise. Furthermore, the humped parts are conveniently placed facing outward, while the hollows face inward, positioned further away from injuries occurring from the outside. That larger little bone, sitting a little above the larynx <note>the voice box</note>, is encountered by those who touch it, while its sides meanwhile remain hidden further within.

<margin>
The lower sides of the U-shaped bone.
h One in figures 1, 2, E, F. The other at I, K.
i Figures 1, 2, G.
k Figures 1, 2, H.
l Book 1, chapter 38, figures 3, 4, A, B.

For to this wider little bone, two others are united on each side<sup>h</sup>, which we, following Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and influential physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note> in his *Chapter on the Throat*, call the "sides of the U-shaped bone." One of these is lower, the other higher. The lower little bone is somewhat shorter and wider than the upper one, and it is joined to no other bone<sup>i</sup> except the side of the middle and somewhat wide U-shaped bone, to which it is strongly tied by the intervention of cartilage and a cartilaginous ligament at a width worthy of note. Indeed,<sup>k</sup> its end is bound to the process of the upper side of the larynx's cartilage, which expresses the image of a shield <note>original: "scuti"; referring to the thyroid cartilage</note>.<sup>l</sup> These lower sides of the U-shaped bone, being suitable for receiving and giving rise to several muscles, together with the larger middle little bone, beautifully express the image of the letter U <note>original: "v"; the Greek letter upsilon</note>.

<margin>
The upper sides and the little bones joined to them.
m Figure 1, L, M, N.
n Chapter 6, figure 1; chapter 1, figures 3, 4.
</margin>
Furthermore, to the upper little bone or side—which is seen to be more rounded—and to the higher seat of the middle U-shaped bone, other oblong and rounded little bones are united as if from a point in a continuous series<sup>m</sup> until their end strikes the process of the temporal bone<sup>n</sup> that presents the image of a writing stylus <note>the styloid process of the skull</note>. These little bones are not always observed in equal number, but for the most part, three or four are seen on each side. Sometimes, however, and especially in women, we have seen them to be entirely absent along with the upper sides of the U-shaped bone; in their place, a certain rounded, strong, and oblong ligament performed their role, which reached from the middle bone of the U-shaped bone all the way to the process mimicking a stylus. Therefore, the upper sides of the bone connected to the temporal bones and the lower ones joined to the processes of the shield-like cartilage indicate that the U-shaped bone is rarely free and is not contiguous to no bone. For the cartilages of the larynx, like the cartilages of the ribs, provide the use of bones, and as far as contiguity is concerned, they are also counted in the class of bones.

<margin>
How the hyoid bone is secured.
</margin>
But since the U-shaped bone does not rest on a base as firm as the rest of the bones, we shall relate in the second book how it is pulled by its own muscles into every difference of position, so that it cannot be moved from its seat—neither to the sides, nor upward or downward, nor forward or backward—otherwise than is useful to man. 

<margin>
Its use.
o Book 2, chapter 19, figures 1, 2, D, D & E.
p Book 2, chapter 21, figures 1, 2, F. Then figures 2, 3, K.
</margin>
Indeed, it provides many very great uses, even if it is very small. We shall list these then, when we show<sup>o</sup> that several muscles of the tongue arise from it, and that it is placed beneath the tongue in the manner of a foundation and a most safe base, and that it offers certain origins<sup>p</sup> for the muscles of the larynx.

<margin>The Body</margin>

M, M *The letter M is seen on the same vertebrae where L occurs, marking the **processes** <note>bony projections</note> of the vertebrae that extend toward the sides, which are therefore called the **transverse** or **lateral** processes by us.*

N, N *You will observe the letter N on the eighth vertebra of the entire structure of the back, then on the seventeenth and twenty-third. These Ns mark certain processes of the vertebrae that point downward, by which the upper or overlying vertebrae are articulated <note>joined</note> with the vertebrae placed beneath them. We shall call these **descending processes**, following the direction of their path.*

O, O *The letter O is seen on the vertebrae placed beneath those just mentioned; it indicates the processes of the vertebrae looking upward, by which the vertebrae placed above are joined to those lying below. These we shall rightly call the **ascending processes**.*

P, P *The letter P is inscribed on those vertebrae which we previously marked with L, M, and O. These mark the processes of the vertebrae that thrust out toward the rear of the body, which are compared to a sting or a spine <note>the spinous processes, which form the "bumps" felt along the center of the back</note>.*

Q, Q *Near those same vertebrae, you will find the letter Q, where we have inscribed the characters last described. This Q does not mark a part of the vertebra itself, but rather the **foramen** <note>a hole or opening</note> located at the sides of the vertebrae, through which the nerves originating from the spinal marrow <note>the spinal cord</note> are transmitted.*

R, R *The **cartilaginous ligament** <note>the intervertebral disc</note> that comes between the bodies of the vertebrae. Furthermore, since three figures (and especially the third one) placed at the end of this book also demonstrate the back, you might also look at them in passing here, along with the figures of the third book, which show the sequence of nerves taking their origin from the spinal marrow, placed at the beginning of the eleventh chapter of that book.*

<margin>The back is constructed so that it may properly support the common use of the bones.</margin>
Nature, the parent of all things, engineered for man the **back**—which is called *rhachis* and *noton* <note>original Greek: ῥάχις and νῶτον</note> by the Greeks—after the fashion of a kind of keel and support. For by its help we walk upright and stand erect.
But Nature did not fashion the back solely for this purpose; rather, just as she occasionally renders some other limb suitable for various uses at once, she has not forgotten her industriousness here either. For, so that the bones of the back would not only support...

Vesalius describes the spine as the "keel" of the human body, enabling upright posture.</summary>

<margin>
So that a suitable path is prepared for the spinal cord.
</margin>
<margin>
a This is encountered in the figures of the four subsequent chapters.
</margin>
<margin>
b Three figures proposed for chapter 11 of book 4.
</margin>
...they might support, and stabilize the body solely by the common use of the bones, [Nature] carved out<sup>a</sup> a large hole <note>foramen</note>, by which a suitable<sup>b</sup> path might be adapted for the **spinal cord** <note>original: "dorsali medulla"</note> about to descend through the back, acting as a kind of **sacred pipe** <term>sacra fistula</term>, called *hiera syrinx* <note>original Greek: ἱερὰ σύριγξ</note> by the Greeks. And this hole is so fashioned that, for its sake, those skilled in dissection have called the bones of the back **vertebrae**, from the likeness of the little wheels <note>original: "verticuli"</note> used to weight spinning-spindles. Furthermore, Nature did not construct the back from one single, simple bone, even though that would have been better for stability and a safer seat for the spinal cord against dislocations and distortions. However, on account of the various movements by which it was necessary for man to be driven, she built the back from many bones, even though this makes it more exposed to dislocations.

<margin>
The reason for the abundance of bones in the back.
</margin>
<margin>
c Marked numbers occur in sequence in the figure of this chapter.
</margin>
<margin>
d These are to be seen in the three figures of chapter 11, book 4.
</margin>
Truly, the reason why the spine is not formed from two or three bones as long as the humerus is in the arm, or the ulna and radius, or the femur and tibia in the leg, but is instead formed of nearly thirty-four<sup>c</sup> bones (of which we count seven in the neck, twelve in the chest <note>thorax</note>, five in the loins <note>lumbar</note>, six in the **sacred bone** <note>os sacrum</note>, and four in the **cuckoo-bone** <note>os coccyx</note>), is chiefly because of the spinal cord itself. Since it<sup>d</sup> had to be the origin of thirty pairs of nerves, and since, like the brain, it was to serve the parts located below the head, it was fitting that it be fortified against every compression and kept free from distortion, lest the parts lower than such a defect in the cord lose sensation and be deprived of voluntary movement. How easily the spinal cord would be crushed, or otherwise exposed to the gravest injuries if the back consisted of only two or three bones, we learn from the sharp angular bending of the elbow and knee, and the shifting of bones in any joint capable of large and loose movement. Thus, it was necessary for the back to be constructed of so many small bones which, following one after another and gradually contributing together to movement, would permit the back to move, yet meanwhile create no movement into a sharp angle, which would be quite harmful to the spinal cord due to compression.

Hence, skillful Nature in all animals—birds, fish, reptiles, and quadrupeds alike—always established such a series of small bones, corresponding to the length of the neck and the rest of the body which, embracing the spinal cord, had to move. For she is sparing with the number of bones, and even more with their loose arrangement, when the cord is contained in a place where movement is not necessary. The **tortoises** <note>original: "testudines"</note> show this beautifully: possessing vertebrae only in the neck and near the tail, they have a long path within their immobile shell which, though it embraces the spinal cord, consists of no vertebrae at all. Birds also attest to this (to say nothing of the human sacred bone), since their thorax, unlike the neck, consists of few vertebrae; and the sacred bone in them appears to be of great length, made of almost a single, simple bone.

<margin>
The unequal size of the bones of the back.
</margin>
<margin>
e G, H. and figure of chapter 18 A, B, C, D, E, F. and M of the complete figures, to which θ is joined, and to that again Λ.
</margin>
For it is wonderful how Nature established the bones of the back for all animals according to their needs. This we learn further from the arrangement and size of the bones: we see that the bones of swimming animals and serpents gradually diminish starting from the head as a base. In walking animals, we observe that they have their largest bone at that part of the trunk which is braced by the thighs; from this bone, acting as a base and the widest support, the remaining bones ascending to the head are gradually made smaller. Likewise, those bones which reach downward toward the tail (or whatever is proportionate to a tail) from that widest base are made narrower. Thus in man, the largest of the bones of the back<sup>e</sup> is the **sacred bone** <note>os sacrum</note>, which is joined at its sides to those bones that together with it stabilize the body and receive the joints of the thighs at the hip. Nor indeed...
