<summary>Vesalius explains the mechanical design of the spine, arguing that its multi-segmented structure allows for flexibility while protecting the spinal cord from the "sharp angles" of movement that occur in simpler joints like the elbow. He compares human spinal anatomy with that of tortoises and birds to illustrate how Nature adapts bone structure to the necessity of movement.</summary>

### ON THE BONES OF THE BACK

We call the **sacrum** <note>original: "sacrum os," literally "the sacred bone"</note> large, not only because it is built from what are essentially six distinct bones or vertebrae and is named as if it were one single, simple bone, but also because the highest of its six bones, and the one placed immediately below it, each exceed the individual bones of the back in size. The vertebrae are articulated at this posterior site, though not with equal boundaries and protuberances on all sides, nor with the same method of entry, as will be taught in the following chapters. <image-desc>A large decorative initial letter P, intricately carved. It shows several cherub-like figures or anatomical assistants in a workshop or dissection setting, engaged in a task involving a large object on a table, possibly preparing a specimen.</image-desc>

# Because of the LUNGS, which are housed within the cavity of the chest, man is granted a neck; this is primarily established by the fact that the neck is always lost when the lungs are absent.

Since it was necessary for the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "asperam arteriam"; literally 'the rough artery,' the historical term for the trachea</note>—through which we draw in air when inhaling and blow it back out when exhaling—to be carried from the mouth into the lungs, a certain space also necessarily had to intervene between the lungs and the throat. Indeed, man was to be gifted with the ability to exhale (which is the material of the voice) through a convenient long channel, or rather a pipe; he thus obtains a neck of such length as is useful for the generation of the voice through the windpipe. Furthermore, since the parts neighboring the shoulder blades, the arms, and finally the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septum transversum"</note> needed to receive nerves from the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>original: "dorsali medulla"</note> traveling through the neck, it was necessary for the sake of their distribution that vertebrae be placed in the middle space between the head and the chest, from which the neck or nape of man might be woven. It is not my purpose here to review the use of the neck in birds and quadrupeds that have been granted long legs; though in the meantime it is easy to gather that Nature, because they lack hands, provided for their taking of food by the length of their necks and jaws, and for this reason their necks are constructed with more vertebrae than those of man.

<margin>
Seven cervical vertebrae.
The condyles of the occipital bone, which articulate with the first vertebra.

The human neck consists of seven vertebrae. In their description, I shall also include that part of the <term>occipital bone</term> <note>original: "occipitis ossis"; the bone at the base of the skull</note> which articulates with the first vertebra. On both sides of its opening—through which the spinal cord descends into the back—this bone possesses a <term>condyle</term> <note>original: "capitulum"; a rounded articular surface</note> leaning more toward the front of the opening than the back. These condyles, if you look at their front and back sides, are oblong and narrow, and are constructed exactly as if you were to cut a round bone head (such as the head of the thigh bone articulated with the hip bone) into two parts, and place one part of that head on each side of the opening carved in the occipital bone. For if you were to imagine both condyles of the occipital bone joined by their inner sides, a somewhat round head would arise from the two of them. Thus, it is clear that each condyle is oblong and protrudes more on the inner side than the outer, in the same way that the middle and most prominent part of any round head stands out more than the parts positioned at the edges.

<margin>
The opening of the first vertebra, transmitting the spinal cord.
Why its body is hollowed out to receive the "tooth" of the second vertebra.

These condyles, as we shall soon say, are articulated to the first vertebra, which is everywhere more solid and dense than all the other bones of the back, and differs greatly from all the others in shape. For it possesses a very wide opening carved for the sake of the spinal cord, because the cord is found to be thickest in that place. Then, its body is significantly hollowed out at its posterior side where the spinal cord passes, so that a remarkable process of the second vertebra—which we shall call the <term>tooth</term> <note>original: "dentem"; the odontoid process or dens</note>—may be placed in the body of the first vertebra like an axle, and so that the first vertebra (as we shall later teach more clearly) may rotate around it along with the head. So that this might be done more conveniently, the anterior part of the hollowed region in the body of the first vertebra possesses a lightly carved sinus, and is covered with cartilag—

...encrusted with cartilage, which you will hear matches the anterior seat of that protruding <term>tooth</term> <note>original: "dentis"; referring to the dens or odontoid process of the second vertebra</note> which is also covered in cartilage.<sup>s</sup> Furthermore, lest the first vertebra, being so hollowed out in its body and almost deprived of a body by this circumstance, should be rendered weaker and more invalid than is proper,<sup>t</sup> it is increased by a certain process and <term>tubercle</term> <note>a small, rounded projection on a bone</note> on the front side. By the benefit of this, it grows thicker than the rest of the anterior part of the vertebrae and is made stronger: besides the fact that it is well-suited for receiving the insertion<sup>u</sup> of the first pair of muscles that move the back. Galen, however, in the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de Administrandis dissectionibus"</note>, teaches that this tubercle was raised for the purpose of preventing the head from bending too far, and to support the head during flexion: or that it was the reason why the bent head could be more nimbly reflected back and up again. Meanwhile, in truth, the head cannot be inclined so loosely in any of its motions as to touch that tubercle: it is so far from the case that the tubercle performs the use ascribed to it by Galen. However, to what extent that motion of the head is achieved, I shall suggest at the end of the section on the Head for no small reasons, though otherwise I would not disturb the context of my discourse on the rest of the Head with my disagreements with Galen's opinions. Therefore, the first vertebra at the sides<sup>x</sup> of the cavity, where it admits the tooth of the second, is very strong and, in its proportion, very thick; and on both sides<sup>y</sup> it shows one <term>sinus</term> <note>original: "sinum"; here meaning a socket or articular cavity</note> by which the little head <note>condyle</note> of the occipital bone on its side is received. In order that the sinuses might respond exquisitely to the little heads, they are (if<sup>z</sup> you look at the front and back parts)<sup>a</sup> oblong, and<sup>b</sup> they rise up at the outer sides,<sup>c</sup> while at the inner sides they are hollowed out, exactly as if both sinuses had been split from one round and deep cavity. For if you were to divide the sinus of the<sup>d</sup> <term>hip bone</term> <note>the acetabulum or hip socket</note> and place one part of it on each side of the first cervical vertebra, these sinuses of the first vertebra would be established for you, in which the little heads of the occipital bone are flexed and extended, or are moved forward and backward in a very straight motion, inclining to the side in no way at all. To the outer sides of these sinuses, the first cervical vertebra<sup>e</sup> extends its <term>transverse processes</term> <note>projections extending sideways from the vertebra</note>: one of which is on each side, much more prominent and somewhat thicker than the other transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae; yet not as large in men as in dogs and long-tailed monkeys, where they are like a kind of wing. Moreover, the transverse processes of the first vertebra are extended more significantly, as if in abundance and beyond the other transverse processes of the neck, so that each might receive the convenient insertion of two muscles. For into those specifically are inserted the<sup>f</sup> fifth and<sup>g</sup> sixth pairs of muscles moving the head; and a significant portion of the<sup>h</sup> muscles that are counted as the second pair of those lifting the shoulder blades <note>the levator scapulae</note> arises from them. These processes are perforated by a large<sup>i</sup> <term>foramen</term> <note>a hole or opening in a bone</note> through which the artery and vein seeking the skull are carried. At the posterior seat of the sinuses with which the head articulates,<sup>k</sup> a sinus is also carved out on both sides of the first vertebra, to which<sup>m</sup> another corresponds in the occipital bone, engraved at the posterior seat of each little head, and together with the sinus of the first vertebra providing a path<sup>n</sup> for the<sup>l</sup> first pair of nerves of the spinal medulla. In dogs, however, there is not just a sinus in the first cervical vertebra yielding to the nerve, but a whole foramen is cut into both sides; in them, since the first vertebra is remarkably large and high, it can be conveniently perforated. Nevertheless, in man, a larger portion of the path transmitting the nerve is carved into the vertebra than into the occipital bone. This portion of the path occurring in the vertebra also belongs to the posterior seat of the<sup>o</sup> foramen through which the transverse process is passable: so that it offers a path not only for the nerve, but<sup>p</sup> also for the vein and artery entering the skull through the<sup>q</sup> foramen carved at the root of the little head of the occipital bone in the posterior seat. The first cervical vertebra is the only one among the other vertebrae to be<sup>r</sup> deprived of a posterior process <note>the spinous process</note> for this reason: because, since it would be far from the occasion of any muscle...

These are shallow and only hollowed on the surface, and for that reason are called <term>glenoid</term> <note>original: "γληνοειδεῖς"; meaning socket-like</note>. <margin>x: Figure 4, right Y, left a, b.</margin> Their circumference is circular, having in the middle scarcely any detectable hollowness, but the outer "eyebrows" <note>the rims or edges</note> of the sinuses descend much further down than the <margin>y: Figure 4, between a and b.</margin> inner ones. In these sinuses, which are encrusted with cartilage, the <margin>The small heads of the second.</margin> two small heads of the second cervical vertebra are received; these are <margin>z: Figure 4, b.</margin> found at the side of the body of that vertebra and protrude very little. The circumference of these sinuses is also <margin>a: Figure 4, a.</margin> circular in a way, although at times the posterior part seems to be drawn out somewhat beyond the curve of the <margin>b: Figure 5, 6; c on the right, f on the left; d, e, f.</margin> circle. Additionally, the inner side of the small heads rises higher than the outer side. However, this height and depth of the sides is not as <margin>c: Figure 5, 6, f.</margin> remarkable as that of the rims of the sinuses of the first cervical vertebra. Furthermore, the small heads <margin>d: Figure 5, 6, d.</margin> do not protrude as much in their center as the sinuses of the first vertebra are hollowed between their rims; it is exactly as if the sides of the small heads rose up <margin>e: Figure 5, 6, c.</margin> taller than the middle itself. Thus it happens that in bare bones fitted together, the sinuses do not match the small heads perfectly, and in the middle of those sinuses a space remains that is not entirely filled. This occurs specifically in humans; however, in dogs, horses, and other animals that rotate their heads a great deal, the two sides of the second vertebra form one continuous head, and the sinus in the first cervical vertebra also appears continuous, matching that head perfectly. In humans, Nature repeatedly corrects this inequality with a <margin>Here we have depicted the peculiar cartilage of each side which we have occasionally observed.</margin> peculiar cartilage which, besides the cartilages that grow on the bones like a crust, comes between the sinus and the small head. It is attached only to the ligaments that hold the joint in a circle, and is smeared above and below with a very viscous humor, like an <term>ointment</term> <note>original: "smegmate"; referring to a lubricating fluid</note>. In the middle of the two small heads of the second vertebra, from the upper region of its body, a certain remarkable, high, and very solid process grows out. <margin>The tooth of the second vertebra.</margin> Because it resembles a tooth, and especially a human canine tooth, the Greeks called it <term>odontoid</term> <note>original: "ὀδοντοειδῆ" and "ὀδόντα"</note>. By this name Hippocrates also <margin>f: Figure 5, g, h; Fig 6, h, i, k, l, n; Fig 10, 11, r.</margin> designated the second vertebra, though not the first (as Julius Pollux and Celius, who were entirely unskilled in dissection, <margin>In the book On the Joints.</margin> wrongly record). Others have called this process "lamp-shaped" <note>original: "λυχνωειδῆ"; perhaps referring to a spinning top or a wick-holder</note> from the image of a top or a pine nut; others, because it protrudes like a point, a pyramid, or even an olive kernel, have called it "kernel-like" <note>original: "πυρῆνα" and "πυρηνοειδῆ"</note>. This process enters the cavity of the first <margin>g: Figure 3, K.</margin> vertebra, which we wrote was located where the body of the first vertebra ought to stand. For here, <margin>l: Figure 5, 6, k, l.</margin> on both sides, it possesses individual sinuses and a third in the posterior seat. Furthermore, the muscles situated in the posterior seat of the neck are considered the most powerful reason for the division into small processes. For so that these might more readily take their origin and also manage a stronger insertion into the spines of the vertebrae, the spines are divided into small processes. And Nature specifically contrives this in these vertebrae of the neck because it was not safe to produce such long spines from those small vertebrae as from the vertebrae of the chest and loins. The second vertebra is larger than several of those placed beneath it.

...and it is seen to be wider and thicker than the others, clearly because it specifically provides an origin for the <gloss>f</gloss> third pair of muscles moving the head, and also the <gloss>g</gloss> sixth pair. Lest Nature should unfairly produce a longer and wider spine <note>In this context, Vesalius refers to the spinous process, the "bump" felt on the back of the neck.</note> from a slender vertebra, she made the second vertebra itself larger than several of those placed beneath it. However, this was done not so much for the sake of producing the spine, as to be abundantly sufficient for the second articulation which it manages with the first vertebra. And this is what we hinted at before: that Nature, once and again, created a superior vertebra larger than an inferior one. For the second is thicker, larger, and stronger than the third; then, we taught above that the first is wider than all the vertebrae of the neck due to the occasion of its transverse processes.

<margin>
h: Figures 5, 6, 7, u.
The nature of the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae.
</margin>
Furthermore, the transverse processes in the remaining vertebrae of the neck are not very far extended, <gloss>h</gloss> especially in the second vertebra, which was granted a short and simple transverse process on both sides. It seems, however, that this process in the second vertebra protrudes less than in the others and is shorter because of the amplitude and thickness of the "little heads" <note>The superior articular processes.</note> of this vertebra, which enter the cavities of the first.

<margin>
i: Figures 5, 7, 11, x.
k: Figure 8, a.
The hole of the transverse processes.
</margin>
Moreover, that amplitude of the "little heads" is also the reason why the <gloss>i</gloss> hole by which the transverse process of the second vertebra is pierced appears to be carved out obliquely, rather than straight—quite different from the first vertebra of the neck, <gloss>k</gloss> and the five situated below the second, whose transverse process is passable by a straight and ample hole. Only the cervical vertebrae are adorned with this hole, so that <gloss>l</gloss> they may lead the vein and artery upward, which derive blood and spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; referring to the "vital spirits" believed to be carried in the blood to the brain.</note> to the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsali medullæ"; literally the "marrow of the back."</note> and finally to the brain itself.

<margin>
l: Last figure of Book 3, f.
m: Figures 8, 10, y, z; and Figure 9, numbers 7, 8, 9, 10.
</margin>
Besides this, the four vertebrae that immediately follow the second also claim this peculiarity for themselves: that their <gloss>m</gloss> transverse processes are wide and bifid <note>split into two parts or "forked."</note>; yet they are not, like the spines of the same vertebrae, rough and unequal. For the transverse processes correspond to each other in form, and their inner part is always wider and is raised higher than the posterior part. The form of the parts of the spine, however, is unequal in almost all vertebrae, and they continually protrude and are roughened in various ways.

<margin>
n: Muscle Table 8, the other C is noted. Table 14, the other N.
</margin>
Although, meanwhile, this width and bipartition of the transverse processes happens for the same reason that we previously reported for the spines being bifid: namely, for the sake of the origins and insertions of the muscles. For, to pass over other muscles of this region, we shall write in the second book that <gloss>n</gloss> two muscles are specifically joined to the transverse processes of the vertebrae on both sides, by whose benefit the neck, and then by a secondary motion the head, are drawn to the sides. These muscles are so placed on each side that one is assigned to the anterior seat of the transverse processes, and the other to the posterior.

Meanwhile, the seventh cervical vertebra possesses wide transverse processes (which are rarely pierced in dogs and monkeys), but they are quite obscurely split in two. For since they are wide and long, no necessity is incumbent for them also to become bifid, especially since the muscles drawing the neck to the side are not so strongly attached to the seventh as to the others; because this one is moved to the side obscurely, no differently than the vertebrae of the chest <note>the thoracic vertebrae.</note>.

<margin>
o: Figures 9, 11, d, e; Figure numbers 3, 4.
p: Figures 6, 7, 9, 11, y.
The nature of the ascending and descending processes.
Measure the oblique path from a to b.
</margin>
The ascending <gloss>o</gloss> and descending processes, by which the vertebrae are mutually articulated, are similar to each other in all the cervical vertebrae situated below the second; and the second also possesses descending processes <gloss>p</gloss> not unlike the processes of the others. Those, therefore, which look downward and admit the vertebra placed below, are adorned with a circular cavity <note>an articular facet.</note> marked significantly by an oblique path from the anterior seat downward into the posterior parts, and carved and incised no less than deeply. But the ascending processes, which are sent into the overhanging vertebra, have a circular "little head" which protuberates so lightly and superficially that you might not know whether to assign it to the number of cavities or heads. This head of the ascending processes fits the cavity; and, encrusted with cartilage just like the cavity, it extends from the anterior seat downward into the posterior parts.

<margin>
*The structure of the bodies of the cervical vertebrae.*

it is also carried quite obliquely. This is a point that should not be considered in passing. For that oblique path in the cervical vertebrae which are closer to the thorax <note>The part of the spine associated with the ribs.</note> always becomes smaller and straighter along the length of the body, because those vertebrae do not need to move as loosely as the upper ones, and for that reason, they do not need to be so loosely articulated. Indeed, Nature has not only granted these vertebrae looser joints, but so that the neck might be moved more promptly than any other part of the back—for its remarkable use—she has bestowed something else privately upon the vertebrae of the neck.

<margin>
*Here compare the cervical vertebrae with the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae in chapter 14, figures 8, 9, and the characters l, s, p, r, η, θ, ι. Note also the numbers 1 and 2 in the figures.*
</margin>

For while the bodies of the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae are joined to one another by flat and minimally protruding surfaces, in the same way that two large planks rest upon each other, Nature willed that the <gloss>r</gloss> lower part of the body of the cervical vertebrae should be oblong and protrude, in the manner of a head of some joint made for evident movement. Furthermore, she excavated the <gloss>s</gloss> upper part of the vertebral body with a wide sinus <note>A hollow or cavity.</note> so that the oblong body of the superior vertebra might enter into this sinus of the vertebra placed beneath it. Thus, the connection of the vertebrae rises up more ready for movement, especially lateral movement and that which occurs toward the shoulders. And this connection—which is also perfected, as in the thorax and loins, <margin>* Chapter 14, figures R, R.</margin> by the intervention of a <gloss>*</gloss> cartilaginous and exceedingly thick ligament that beautifully yields and rises in turn—is more conspicuous in the connection of the second vertebra with the third, and then in several of the bodies of the underlying vertebrae. However, the seventh vertebra of the neck rests upon the first of the thorax with an almost entirely flat surface, and its upper seat is not as excavated as that of the superior vertebrae; this occurs chiefly because it is useful for the upper vertebrae to move more loosely than the lower ones.

<margin>
s 1, 10 figures λ, μ, ν.
</margin>

But because the body of the second vertebra is seen on its <gloss>s</gloss> anterior seat not to be flat in the manner of the bodies of the rest of the cervical vertebrae, but stands out with a ridge led along its length in the form of a wider line, and is depressed on both sides of that ridge, <margin>t Table 8 of the muscles, A, B.</margin> <gloss>t</gloss> those muscles which flex the neck and join at this site must be considered the cause, as they are more strongly inserted into that form of the vertebral body. Truly, since the third cervical vertebra lies beneath the second, and the muscle flexing the neck on both sides is also inserted above this one, it is no wonder that the anterior face of the body of the third vertebra is somewhat similar to the second. Indeed, by the occasion of the said muscles, the anterior seat of all the cervical vertebrae appears as if compressed, rather than protruding in a semicircle or like our letter 'C', as the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae do.

<margin>
*The number of processes.*
</margin>

Since these things are so, it is hidden from no one that the same number of processes <note>Bony outgrowths or projections from the bone.</note> has not fallen to all the cervical vertebrae. But lest I seem to have omitted anything here, it is necessary, even in Galen’s name, to recount the processes of some cervical vertebra in such a way that you find eleven processes in them; for that many <margin>Book 13, *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin> are ascribed to these vertebrae by Galen. Take, therefore, the third, or fourth, or fifth, or sixth vertebra of the neck, and first count two processes in the upper seat of the body, namely one on each side of the cavity in which the oblong body of the overlying vertebra sits. <margin>*Observe here figure 8, the numbers of which denote the processes in order.*</margin> Second, count the third and fourth as the two ascending processes which go under the overlying vertebra. Third, count the fifth and sixth as the two descending processes by which the ascending processes of the underlying vertebra are received. Furthermore, you will count the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth as the transverse processes; since there is one on each side, and these are again seen to be twin and bifid <note>Split into two parts.</note>, they constitute four processes. The eleventh will be the spine itself. But since the vertebrae which happen to have a twin transverse process on each side also bear a <gloss>u</gloss> bipartite <margin>u Figure 8, ψ, ω.</margin> spine, nothing prevents you from inventing a twelfth process here as well, to increase Galen’s number. Likewise, because the <gloss>x</gloss> oblong body of the vertebra is also drawn out from the lower seat in the manner of a process, <margin>x Figure 8, ρ; figure 9, ζ.</margin> what will forbid it from being placed in the thirteenth position as a process?

[bones] which are normally separated by a great distance due to the intervention of cartilaginous ligaments, sometimes fuse together so thoroughly that you may see three or even four vertebrae grown together in such a way—as is often seen in those dug up from cemeteries—that they cannot be pulled apart. This fusion occurs through the intervention of certain processes that emerge during growth, which the body of one vertebra produces from its external surface into another. Furthermore, I believe no one can doubt that this fusion is the reason why the elderly move their backs less, cannot extend their backs at all, and are themselves more hunched; this is especially clear if one has ever inspected the vertebrae of a hunchback <note>original: "gibbosi"</note>, which are curved, in a way dislocated, and most stubbornly united in their bodies. For, to say nothing of the many points where I could easily show that Galen—judging by the size of the <term>transverse processes<note>Bony protrusions on the sides of each vertebra.</note></term> of the first vertebra, by the pathways transmitting the branches of the first and second pairs of spinal nerves, by the perforation of the transverse process of the seventh vertebra, and not a few other such things—described monkeys and dogs rather than man in those vertebrae, I must by no means pass over the fact that Galen’s views on the movements of the head upon the first vertebra, and the first vertebra upon the second, and then the movements of the remaining vertebrae of the neck, are far different from my own. Indeed, this must be weighed all the more carefully because Galen, with great zeal, requires a diligent, learned, clever, and industrious listener who can grasp those things which he treats in the twelfth book of *On the Use of the Parts* concerning the movements of the head. Why say more? He contends that so few will achieve what is taught there, and he so terrifies the reader with the difficulty of the matter—especially one who is little practiced in mathematics and the method of demonstration—that everyone ought to try to unearth his meaning, and finally observe with me whether I decline from his views with good reason.

<margin>
Galen's opinion on the movements of the head.
</margin>
Galen, ascribing two movements to the head, teaches that one occurs in nodding and refusing <note>original: "annuendo renuendoque"; nodding 'yes' and shaking 'no'</note>, and the other to the sides. And in the first category, he includes that motion by which we flex the head forward, incline it, and nod; and then that by which we reflect the head backward and recline it—precisely that function by which the Thracians and most of the Cretans even in this age "refuse" <note>original: "abnuunt"; to signal 'no'</note>. For when they refuse, they move the head straight back or lift it slightly; they do not, as we do, turn it around or lead it in a circle. Furthermore, by the other movement, Galen understands that by which we incline the head to the side and, as it were, move it toward the shoulders or shoulder blades. That this was his opinion regarding lateral movement, and indeed regarding refusing and nodding, you will be taught by the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, provided you carefully weigh in what position Galen asserts the small heads <term>condyles<note>The rounded structures at the base of the skull (occipital bone) that join with the first vertebra.</note></term> of the occipital bone (which are articulated to the first vertebra) are located, rise up, and rest, when the head is moved to this or that side, and when, according to Galen's pleasure, we refuse or nod. For he affirms that the first movement, which occurs in nodding and refusing, is performed by the benefit of the second cervical vertebra, or upon the second; but the latter movement, by which the head is led to the sides, he says occurs upon the first cervical vertebra. This is very easy to gather both from many of his passages and especially from the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*. For as he wrote those books last of all, so he also explained his opinion in them more briefly and openly than elsewhere. But whether this view of his is consistent with the truth, you yourself shall now inquire with me; for I establish the movements of the head quite differently than Galen. # THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I

<margin>An opinion regarding the movements of the head differing from that of Galen.</margin>...or secondarily, as when the head follows the movement of the neck, even if you attempt to lead it in a different direction than the neck is moving. There are two proper movements of the head: in the first, we bend it forward and tilt or extend it backward; you perform this movement either with a rigid and unmoved neck, or with the neck also moving at the same time, whether you do this with a movement equal to the head or contrary to it. For although you may lead the neck forward, and the head necessarily follows the neck, you can nevertheless tilt the head backward by its own proper movement, and at the same time readily observe that the neck and the head possess their own distinct and private movements in bending and tilting back. The second proper movement of the head is to be considered that by which we turn the head around in a certain way, or drive it in a circle, as a wheel revolves on an axle; you will perform this even while the neck is at rest, if only you strive to look alternately now to the right, now to the left, or turn the head around. This present movement is entirely proper to the head, and the neck is deprived of it. Hence, in whatever way you move the neck, this rotation of the head is conveniently completed. For when the neck is bent and the head tilted with it, you easily lead it in a circle; so also, if the neck is extended or moved to the side toward the shoulder, you promptly turn the head around. But just as the head is granted one movement—that of rotation—which is its own, so the neck also claims for itself a peculiar movement by which it is led to the side, as if toward the shoulders. For the head possesses no proper movement by which it is tilted to the side, but is carried there only by the benefit of the neck and by a secondary movement. It is denied to us to move the head toward this or that shoulder blade even the slightest bit, unless the neck is led there. Therefore, the head is granted two proper movements: the first of which, performed by bending and tilting back, we have said is celebrated by the benefit of the joints of the head with the first vertebra of the neck; just as it was reported that the latter movement, by which the head is driven in a circle, is completed upon the second vertebra of the neck, as if upon an axle. It is therefore my opinion that by the double

<margin>The head is bent and tilted back upon the first vertebra, but not moved to the sides or otherwise.</margin>joints of the head with the first vertebra, the head is bent and extended, or led forward and backward in a very straight movement. By no reasoning, however, is it carried to the sides by the work of those joints, although this has been handed down by <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories Vesalius is here challenging based on direct dissection.</note> in so many places. For with the neck unmoved, we cannot move the head even the least bit to the sides. And, if the head were moved to the side upon the first vertebra, who doubts that in that movement the first vertebra ought to be kept unmoved? If indeed in movement one bone of a joint ought to remain at rest, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC).</note> in his book on the <term>Common Movement of Animals</term> <note>original: "Communi animalium gressu"</note> rightly demonstrated. Furthermore, since the articulations of the first vertebra with the head are of such a kind that they cannot sustain even for the smallest moment of time a slight dislocation or luxation without the man being immediately rendered devoid of breath, mute, and without movement and sense—as if the root of the nerves were affected—how can we, with <term>Galen</term>, impose such drowsiness upon <term>Nature</term> as to admit that she slept so in the most worthy joints of the whole body? Is it necessary that the bone of the head which is moved must be so lifted out of the cavity in which it is otherwise articulated that it no longer touches the cavity, and is not in some part so strengthened and fixed upon it, as we know all other bones by no means depart or gape from their cavity in the movements entrusted to them? For <term>Galen</term>, thinking that the head is led to the side upon the first vertebra, was forced to assert in the fourth book of <term>On Anatomical Procedures</term> <note>original: "Administrádis dissectionibus"</note> that when the head is led to the right side, the right condyle of the occipital bone is then pressed into the right cavity of the first vertebra, but the left condyle rises out of the left cavity; and conversely, if ever the head is tilted to the left side. Therefore, let us not attribute movement to the side to this twin joint of the head with the first vertebra, but rather simple bending and tilting back; and let us by no means strive here to devise an excuse for <term>Galen</term>, that by him movement to the sides...

<margin>He differs from himself more than once in the book *On Bones* and book 4 of *Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>
understanding, which I say occurs in a circle and by rotation: nor indeed do we concede with Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist whose "Onomasticon" contained anatomical terms.</note> that such motion occurs above the first vertebra. For besides the fact that Galen by no means considered that motion to be in the place of lateral motion, who is so stupid as to think that the two oblong little heads <term>condyles</term> of the occipital bone, distant from one another, and entering the two high or deep and similarly oblong cavities of the first vertebra <term>the atlas</term>—which are separated from each other by a wide interval—could be rotated? For who has ever noticed a pair of compasses, with both legs fixed into a beam, being turned around? Nor is there any reason for someone wishing to defend Galen to imagine that the little heads of the occipital bone are flat, and to contend by this reasoning that the head can be rotated above the first vertebra. Since Galen, among the other little heads of the bones, hardly ever deigned to use the name *koryphe* <note>original: κορυφῆς, meaning "summit" or "peak"</note> except for these little heads of the occipital bone, which he everywhere calls *koryphas* <note>original: κορυφὰς</note> (though not very correctly), using that name for the rare points of the occipital bone's heads which occur in dogs rather than in humans. But as far as the connection of the first vertebra with the second is concerned, I can by no means agree with Galen that the head is flexed or tilted backwards by its help in any way whatsoever. Since if you examine every detail in the fabric of these bones,
<margin>The head is rotated with the *first* vertebra above the *second* vertebra, but is by no means flexed or extended there.</margin>
the second vertebra of the neck <term>the axis</term> will represent to you a post driven into the earth, with a dense axle on top; while the first vertebra (which is joined in this rotational movement as if it were one and the same body with the head) will be likened to a beam revolved around that axle. Furthermore, the ligament drawn transversely across the tooth <term>the dens or odontoid process</term> demonstrates abundantly that the first vertebra is by no means flexed upon the second, even if the tooth were still, and the first vertebra were moved forward and backward on the right side. For who doubts that this ligament contains the tooth in the cavity of the first vertebra?
<margin>*Book 12 of On the Use of the Parts.*</margin>
And such laxity cannot be ascribed to it (even if Galen attributes it to him) as to allow the first vertebra to be carried so far forward from contact with the tooth that the head experiences a proper flexion. Furthermore, two names now occur to me in Julius Pollux, one of which he calls the first vertebra, and the other the second. Indeed, he calls the first *strophos* <note>original: ὠροφῶς, likely a corruption of στρόφος, "the turner"</note> and the second *axon* <note>original: ἄξωψ, likely ἄξων, "the axle"</note>. These names undoubtedly flowed down from the ancients who exercised boys in Anatomy <term>dissection</term>, wishing by this name to indicate the vertebra toward which another is turned as if toward an axle: and by that name the vertebra which is turned as if upon an axle. That I think these names were used by the ancients before Galen, besides the poets, Celsus is my witness; although his book, where he explains the vertebrae of the neck, is corrupted, and he himself translated things he least understood, yet he seems to have assumed that opinion from one of the ancients which is closest to my own and finally to the truth itself. But as to why Nature willed that only flexion and extension—and not the other two motions, one of which is to the sides and the other in a circle and rotation—be performed above the first vertebra (just as the arm and thigh are moved by a triple difference of motions), you may consider it done chiefly for this reason: that it was necessary for the first vertebra to be perforated more largely and amply than all the others for the sake of the spinal cord, and because of this, a single round and ample cavity could not be formed in it, nor could the occipital bone, by reason of its opening, bulge out into only one large head, which would be moved with every kind of motion in that cavity of the first vertebra, just as the thigh is in the cavity of the hip bone <term>the acetabulum</term>. Since therefore the head had to be joined by a double joint, namely right and left, and almost every double joint serves only a single motion (when that motion is significant), Nature rightly willed the head to be flexed and extended above the first vertebra. For above this,
<margin>The head could not be moved to the side, nor rotated, above the *first* vertebra.</margin>
it could not be moved to the side: unless Nature had here forgotten herself, [and made] one little head of the occipital bone...

<summary>Vesalius argues against Galen's view of spinal mechanics, asserting that the head rotates on the first two vertebrae (atlas and axis) like a beam on an axle, rather than flexing at that specific junction. He uses mechanical analogies, such as compasses and axles, to prove that the shape of the occipital bone allows only for nodding (flexion/extension) at the topmost joint.</summary>

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.</header>

<margin>Book 4 of *On Anatomical Procedures*</margin>
...had [Nature] desired that one small head <note>original: *capitulum*; referring to the articular processes of the vertebrae</note> be squeezed into a single vertebral cavity, while the other head be raised up significantly and entirely separated from the first vertebra. Nature otherwise always strives to ensure that the bones of a joint are contiguous with one another, and do not pull apart or create some sort of empty space as imagined by Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories Vesalius often challenged through direct dissection.</note>. Furthermore, the head could have moved even less in a circular motion upon the first vertebra, unless Nature had produced a sharp process from the first vertebra into the expanse of the head where the brain is contained, around which the head might turn as if on an axis; otherwise, she would have set out to ruin many other things now so elegantly formed.

<margin>The head could not be bent forward or backward, nor tilted to the side, upon the second vertebra.</margin>
Therefore, it is with the highest craftsmanship that the head is moved in a circle upon the second vertebra. For if it were bent forward, the "tooth" <note>The *dens* or odontoid process of the second vertebra (the axis).</note> would break the spinal medulla <note>The spinal cord.</note>. Since, while the tooth remained stationary, the first vertebra would be drawn downward and its posterior part raised upward; then the spinal cord, being utterly constricted and compressed within the opening of the first vertebra, would be snapped. Furthermore, the first vertebra could in no way be bent backward over the second, unless the first were entirely hollowed out in its anterior part where it contains the tooth; only then, not being hindered by the tooth, could the vertebra be drawn freely backward. Add to this that the head could by no means be moved to the side upon the second vertebra, for the same reason we proved that lateral motion could not occur upon the first. Otherwise, it would be necessary for the first vertebra to be greatly lifted from the second on one side, a danger that does not loom during rotation.

<margin>To which vertebrae lateral motion is entrusted.</margin>
Nature, therefore, with no common industry, has entrusted lateral motion to all the vertebrae of the neck. These cannot move sideways individually; rather, all of them together, through successive movements, incline so harmoniously that the head is conveniently carried to the side by this secondary motion with their help, without any harm.

Indeed, the upper vertebrae would have resisted that movement no less than the lower ones. For just as the part of the back which is placed below—being received by the vertebrae above and below—is led along in that motion, so too it is necessary for the part lying above to be carried along with the back, provided that the back must be drawn to the side as if into a semicircle. The midpoint of the circumference of that semicircle is rightly considered to be that vertebra which (whichever one it may finally be) is supported from above and below. But what need is there to dwell longer on this discourse, which is still difficult to understand because of the vertebra being supported on both sides? Especially since the tenth thoracic vertebra, and the two vertebrae lying below it, have transverse processes <note>The bony projections on the sides of each vertebra where muscles and ribs attach.</note> as prominent as is necessary for their use in the origin and insertion of the muscles.

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BY ANDREAS VESALIUS

<margin>Why it was necessary for one vertebra in the middle of the back to be supported on both sides.</margin>...can be gathered, than that it should be received above and below the twelfth? However, in the meantime, it does not matter much whether this one, or the eleventh, or any other is supported on both sides: provided that the singular industry of Nature does not escape us here. She fashioned a stable vertebra in the middle of the back, supported on both sides in the same way we see architects place a single stone between the stones of both sides in vaulted and arched buildings <note>Vesalius is describing the "keystone" of an arch</note>, which is supported on both sides while it supports nothing itself: just as all the other stones support one stone and are received and sustained by another. For in order for the back to be moved in its dedicated motions, it was uniquely necessary for this one vertebra to be supported on both sides and, in a way, to be made firm, while all the others meanwhile recede slightly from this one and from each other. For while that one remains at rest, when we bend the back, we lead the upper ones downward, but we curve the lower ones upward in some manner. In extension, however, we move the vertebrae again with the opposite motion: since these motions of the back—and we have previously mentioned others, lateral and circular—are not performed in a strictly angular shape. How little these things agree with the decrees of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius frequently challenged</note> in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts* <note>original: "de Partium usu"</note>, you will readily notice if you compare the passages. Here, however, in the vertebrae of the chest <term>thoracic vertebrae: the twelve vertebrae of the middle back to which ribs attach</term>, at the root of the ascending and descending processes, and even at the origin of their posterior process or spine, remarkable roughnesses and irregularly protruding small processes are still to be observed. These are prepared so that strong ligaments might arise from here, binding the thoracic vertebrae together all the more robustly and firmly, as it was useful for the thoracic vertebrae to be moved with more obscure motion than those of the neck. 

<margin>The number of processes of the thoracic vertebrae.</margin>Since things are so, all the thoracic vertebrae are endowed with seven processes <term>process: a protruding part of a bone</term>: namely, two transverse, two ascending, and as many descending, and one posterior, or spine. How the holes transmitting the nerves are situated in the thoracic vertebrae, we have expressed in the previous Chapter.

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.

<page-num>97</page-num>

Indeed, this muscle <note>likely referring to a portion of the spinal erectors or psoas complex described in the preceding text</note> takes its origin from a nervous and somewhat broad beginning at the seat of the **hip bone** <note>original: "coxendicis ossis"</note>, where the primary muscles that flex the thigh roll downward. From here, ascending obliquely and first becoming fleshy in the region of the loins <note>the lumbar region</note>, it is inserted into all the sharp processes <note>the spinous or transverse processes</note> of the vertebrae on its side; at its upper end, it terminates in the vertebra just below the one that is "received on both sides" <note>a reference to the transitional vertebra between the mid-back and lower back</note>. At its lower end, it does not descend in the same way in dogs and apes, since it is inserted into more lumbar vertebrae in those animals than in humans. Likewise, more lumbar vertebrae in apes possess this process: which is always more evident and projects further from the vertebrae the closer those vertebrae are to the one "received on both sides," and the more strongly this muscle exerts its insertion upon them. So much so that even the vertebrae of the chest <note>the thoracic vertebrae</note> located lower than the "received" one—which in those animals is usually the tenth—claim this process for themselves just like the upper lumbar vertebrae; for those closest to the neck <note>original: "feruoris," likely a misprint for "ceruicis" or referring to the heat of the upper torso</note>, not fully receiving the insertion of this muscle, are deprived of that process.

<margin>Book 13, *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin> This was to be observed from **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose work dominated anatomy until Vesalius</note>, when he writes that this process first became known to him, and when elsewhere <margin>Book 5, *On Anatomical Procedures*.</margin> he boasts that the muscles placed in the loins, serving the movements of the back there, were poorly understood by the ancients; he presents his apes to us everywhere when he pursues something more accurately and, as it were, with zeal.

<margin>Apes and dogs have more than five vertebrae in the loins.</margin> But meanwhile, all the apes dissected by me so far—which were mostly the tailed variety—possessed more than five vertebrae in the loins, just like dogs. Nor do I know for certain whether any kinds of apes might be found by chance endowed with a shorter trunk of the body than ours, which have only five vertebrae in the loins, just as in humans. For Galen everywhere counts only five, nevertheless adapting the rest of his discourse to apes (as we have already shown) rather than to man. Unless perhaps, having settled on the number provided here by all the ancients together, he rested satisfied and passed down to posterity fewer vertebrae than were actually presented to him in apes. Perhaps in human skeletons offered to him in the countryside—but certainly, as is likely, not brought home—he observed the number five; and meanwhile, in the rest of the structure and the fuller history of the bones, he persuaded himself (as he often did elsewhere) without a more diligent examination that the vertebrae of a man were similar and equal to the vertebrae of apes.

## Index of the three figures of the eighteenth chapter, and of their characters.

The present figures express the entire structure of the bones of the back which are placed beneath the lumbar <term>vertebrae</term><note>The bones of the spine</note>. Indeed, the first figure, which occupies the right side, shows the anterior face of these bones; the second, however, standing on the left side, shows the posterior face, drawn slightly to the side for the sake of demonstrating the <term>sinus</term><note>A cavity or depression in the bone</note> to which the right <term>ilium</term><note>The large, wing-like bone of the pelvis</note> is joined. For P marks the upper cavity of the posterior part, while Q marks the lower. <margin>What the sacred,</margin>

BELOW the lumbar<gloss>a</gloss> vertebrae<gloss>b</gloss> ten bones are placed, by which the remaining part of the back, reaching from the loins all the way to the anus, is constituted. And the six upper ones of these grow together in such a way that they are usually all dug out of graves together like a single bone, which is called *makros* <note>original: "μαρῦ" (likely a typesetter's error for μακρός - long/large)</note> by the Greeks, but in Latin is called the *broad* and ample bone in man. In humans, this bone has happened to be the broadest in proportion to other animals—just as the rest of the back is—and it easily surpasses the size of the other vertebrae in its higher position, and is placed beneath them as a very safe support like a pedestal. For I do not truly think it was granted such breadth compared to all the bones of the body, since the bones of the ilium<gloss>c</gloss> <note>The hip bones</note> are far larger than it. Why they also called it *ischion* <note>Greek for hip/pelvis</note>, or the *sacrum* <note>Sacred bone</note>, is not quite clear to me, unless it happened from some rare appearance and form, or because it is so excellent and presents a great image of a bulwark in various ways to those who look at it leaning on its base: or because it is believed by many (though falsely) that it is mild and yields to the will of women in childbirth, being released from its connection with the bones and then joined again: or perhaps because it is seen to be large and great. Just as among the Poets we believe that *Troy <note>original: "ilium"</note>, the sea, hunger, and certain other things are called sacred.* But even then (as was said of its size) the sacred bone...

And so that the lowest region of the back flows together with the coccyx bone placed beneath it in a semicircular, rather than straight, pelvic curve. Sometimes—and this is not infrequent—the <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> is constructed of only five bones, showing nothing else peculiar in its entire fabric except in the series of the more numerous <term>foramina</term> <note>Natural openings or passages through bone</note> passing through it, as I shall say shortly. For from the part of the spinal marrow <note>The spinal cord</note> stored in the sacrum, six pairs of nerves usually sprout; **a** the first of these emerges between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the first bone of the sacrum, just as the nerves in the loins and thorax leap out from the **b** sides of the vertebrae. For at the back of the body of the first bone, and in front of the seat of the first ascending process of that same bone, **c** a **d** sinus <note>A cavity or hollow</note> is hollowed out on both sides, which constitutes a common opening with the sinus of the fifth lumbar vertebra, through which the nerve of its own side glides out, **e** and the vein and artery seeking the spinal marrow enter here. Furthermore, for the remaining pairs of nerves, openings are not prepared in the sides of the sacrum, which are occupied above by the connection of the hip bones <note>The ilium</note>, and below are so thin across that they could not be perforated by too long a duct into the sides. So much so, that when the sacrum is composed of six bones, ten circular **d** openings are seen on its anterior and posterior surfaces; namely, five on each side of those surfaces, which, carved into the inner bones where they grow together, are rendered narrower the **e** lower a seat they occupy in the sacrum. Just as the nerves to which they provide a path do not consist of equal mass below and above. By the same occasion, the openings carved in the **f** posterior seat are smaller than those seen in the anterior; because thicker nerves glide out from this seat than that one, and because more and more significant veins and arteries enter the sacrum through the anterior openings than the posterior. With the openings being in this manner, the second pair of nerves of the sacrum leads out two branches forward and as many backward, through the four openings prepared for them between the first and second bone. Then other pairs besides leap forth in that manner, so that the falling pair is referred to the bone placed beneath it, just as in the number of vertebrae. Besides these openings, however, carved on account of the nerves in the posterior seat of the sacrum, **g** others occur from time to time between the spines of the bones, pertaining to the way by which the spinal marrow is led, and filled with ligaments just like the intervals or openings visible between the spines of the remaining vertebrae. Moreover, if ever the sacrum consists of only five bones, then in its anterior seat two openings are missing, and for the sixth pair a path is carved only in the posterior seat (but more toward the sides), another then also being obvious in the lower seat of the sacrum with the coccyx bone in the form of a joint. For the highest small bone of the **coccyx**, with a higher sinus carved into its seat, not only receives the body of the fifth bone of the sacrum, but also puts forth two small processes besides, which, led upward, grow together with the downward-looking processes of the fifth bone of the sacrum; and a very small portion of cartilaginous ligament intervenes in the rest of the connection, almost responding to the mutual structure of the bones of the sacrum. Whereas, meanwhile, when six bones of the sacrum present themselves, the highest small bone of the coccyx **h** raises no processes in the posterior seat, and is loosely committed only to the body of the sixth sacral bone, and that by **i** means of a cartilaginous ligament. This small bone at the sides of its sinus **k** swells out on both sides transversely and upward, and from here is gradually rendered **l** narrow toward the lower parts, and is fastened to the second small bone of the coccyx just as to the sixth bone of the sacrum. After the second small bone, the **m** third and **n** fourth succeed, joined together in entirely the same way, and so much narrower and shorter as each one in the series occupies a lower place. The **o** fourth small bone, with its point, by which it touches the back and lowest **p** seat of the rectum, [ends] in cartilage...

Moreover, their entire structure tapers from a wider base into a point, and is remarkably curved inward with an oblique bend: and by occasion of its loose connection, it is mobile during childbirth, and sometimes during a great opening of the anus. Therefore, since the structure of those four small bones gradually ceases from a certain base into a narrow point, and is curved, and in a way—like the breastbone <note>The sternum.</note>—is obscurely red before it dries out, the ancients, who taught the art of dissecting bodies to boys, compared this to the appearance of a cuckoo's beak: and hence they especially called it the *cuckoo-bone* <note>original: "ῥόκκυγα" (rhokkyga); the Greek root for coccyx.</note>, as we said before, as well as the *loin-support* <note>original: "ὀσφύογύον" (osphyogyon).</note>, because that structure for the most part matches the mobile small bones in the tails of birds, but truly not the beginning of the tail of quadrupeds.

<margin>That Galen confuses the sacred bone <note>The sacrum.</note> and the cuckoo-bone <note>The coccyx.</note>.</margin> How truly this history of ours of the sacred bone and the cuckoo-bone agrees with the descriptions of Galen, you will readily weigh if you first compare those descriptions with each other (since they certainly do not correspond to themselves in all respects) and then with ours.

<margin>Books 12, 13, 15, and elsewhere.</margin> For in the books on the <term>Use of the Parts</term>, mention of the sacred bone occurs more than once: and it is taught therein to be built of four bones, with not even a little word meanwhile ascribed concerning the cuckoo-bone. And besides the fact that Galen did not remember the cuckoo-bone in those books, it must not be doubted that this was unknown to him when he was writing those books and by no means handing down the correct number of nerves. For teaching that there are four bones of the sacred bone, he adds that such a cartilage grows at their extremity as we said covers the point of the cuckoo-bone, and into which the ends of bones not joined to another bone almost perpetually degenerate. Furthermore, in the twelfth book of the <term>Use of the Parts</term>, he asserts that the transverse processes of the sacred bone are thin and subtle: whereas in the book on <term>Bones</term> <margin>Chapters 11 and 12.</margin> he teaches that they are (as by Hercules they truly are) thick and large. Then in this book, he reckons the sacred bone to be formed of only three bones, writing that three others are placed beneath them, which he gifted with the name of the cuckoo-bone.

<margin>Books 2 and 6 especially.</margin> Also in the books on the <term>Procedures of Dissection</term>, he mentions the sacred bone and the cuckoo-bone from time to time, just as sometimes in the <term>Commentaries on Hippocrates' book on Joints</term>: but (as far as I follow his opinion) entirely by that reasoning by which they are described more fully in the book on <term>Bones</term> than elsewhere. <margin>Book 3 of the Commentaries.</margin> However, so that you may now judge more accurately whether the constitution of the bones of an ape rather than a man is handed down there, I will now gladly relate which bones, placed under the vertebrae of the loins, occur in apes and dogs. Although even in puppies, the union of those three bones is filled with some cartilage, just like the connection of the epiphyses. First, at its upper seat, the bone possesses a circular body—not unlike the vertebrae of the loins <note>the lumbar vertebrae</note>—joined to the lowest lumbar vertebra in the same way that the lumbar vertebrae are compacted together. In these three bones, a continuous foramen <note>a hole or opening</note> is carved through which the spinal marrow <note>the spinal cord</note> creeps forward; and at their posterior seat, each bone leads out a posterior spine or process, looking upward rather than downward (though not remarkably so), and it is smaller in proportion to the size of the bone from which it arises in the series. <margin>The sacred bone and the bone of the coccyx in the ape are described by Galen.</margin> <margin>*a* Figure 4, characters rad. 4, 5, 6. and the figure of the chapter which compare with the characters 1, 2, 3 of the same figure.</margin> Likewise, because in apes and dogs at least three bones follow below that one, which also transmit the spinal marrow and, in the connection of their bodies, acquire a cartilaginous ligament unlike the three bones of the sacred bone of those animals; and since they are therefore easily pulled apart from one another like the lumbar vertebrae without much or long boiling or other great force; and since these bones emit nerves only from the back of their bodies, and not truly toward the front as well, I am persuaded that Galen gave them the name of the "coccyx bone" <note>Latin: *coccygis ossis*</note>. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

structure, and provide such great utility along with the rest, that they ought not to be easily overlooked by one dissecting the human body. But those subverters of Galen's <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the ancient authority whose anatomical teachings Vesalius famously challenged.</note> books say that our coccyx bone <note>The tailbone.</note> was intentionally omitted by him because it is not dug up from tombs <note>original: "monumentis"</note> along with the sacred bone <note>The sacrum.</note>; or because Galen did not wish to present it to beginners in his book *On Bones*, just as he omitted the hyoid bone <note>original: "os urens" (u-shaped bone)</note>, the heart bone, and the small bones compared to sesame seeds <note>Sesamoid bones.</note>. Or perhaps he considered all four bones as a single cartilage. This last point they especially approve of, so that Galen's *On the Use of the Parts* might not seem inconsistent with his other writings: namely, so that the three bones of his "sacrum" would be counted in place of three, and the three bones of our coccyx would count as only one; and that our coccyx would be that cartilage which he claimed in those books grows out from the end of the sacrum.

When these things are reported and I feel them being thrown against my opinion, I seem to hear those who try—quite ridiculously and with great arrogance—to show that Galen and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD), the influential Persian physician.</note>, or some other physicians and philosophers, or even the conflicting writings of the same author, do not disagree with one another. They attribute things to the authors themselves which they never even dreamed of in their sleep, and which are entirely foreign to their actual opinions. For if Galen had omitted our coccyx bone in the eleventh and twelfth chapters of his book *On Bones* because its discussion did not pertain to those being introduced to the subject, he would undoubtedly have mentioned our coccyx at the end of *On Bones*, just as he did other small bones which he described more fully elsewhere. Yet, in none of Galen's books does a mention of our coccyx occur.

However, the fact that it is found separated from the sacrum in tombs or graves, and its small bones are seen disconnected in the manner of vertebrae, is proof that Galen adapted the descriptions of the ancients to his apes <note>Vesalius frequently points out that Galen's "human" anatomy was actually based on the dissection of Barbary macaques.</note>. This is because the bones following their sacrum are dissolved one by one as the ligaments rot away, unlike the three lower bones of our human sacrum. For it is necessary, when dealing with these men, to hold no discussion of the human sacrum other than that it is constructed of six bones. For when only five or four bones are found in a man constituting our sacrum, then they can in no way be reconciled with Galen's six bones, since not even the number of bones providing a path for the spinal marrow <note>The spinal cord.</note> would correspond.

Furthermore, if we had to take account of bones found separated from one another in cemeteries, what should be thought of the vertebrae, ribs, and the bones of the hand, foot, chest, and almost all parts? For these present themselves torn apart and separated quite differently than the bones of our sacrum. Moreover, when they pretend that Galen rightly held our coccyx to be a cartilage because its bones appear soft and cartilaginous in children—and as they say, only four cartilages appear—it is as if Galen had woven a history of children rather than of middle-aged men or animals.

But these men weigh too cursorily how this substance in many bones, in the whole system of appendages, and especially in number, in the cartilages of the ribs, and elsewhere nearly a hundred times, fits more elegantly with apes and dogs (as they are very dry and, so to speak, "bony" animals) than with man, who is almost the most moist and soft of all. But as far as I am concerned, they are free to devise whatever they like and impose their corrupted version of Galen's opinion on their students, provided that I, to the best of my ability, show the true fabric of man to those eager to learn. I would not think Galen's books, as if they were sacred, should be left unchanged when, in the great and infinite difference between man and the apes and those beasts which Galen primarily tackled, Galen's description is more conformable to them than to man—especially if that difference, however remarkable, does not seem to have been noticed or otherwise expressed by Galen. Indeed, he himself should be heard at the beginning of the third book of his *Commentaries*...

<header>ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>
<margin>Above all other anatomical books by Galen, this one on Bones, as it seems, is the one to be used here.</margin>
In his commentaries on Hippocrates' <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) is often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> book *On Joints*, when he says he wrote a book on Bones, he had diligently inspected exactly what kind of thing each individual bone was—primarily indeed in the dried cadavers of men themselves, but if not those, then certainly in apes; thus beautifully indicating that he had described apes with all his zeal, and that these are most similar to man in the construction of the bones. Whence also, none of all the anatomical books of Galen seems to me more rightly ascribed to him than this one *On Bones*; and it is surely the one which he so often praises and considers deeply worthy to be read repeatedly and, since it is so succinct, to be committed entirely to memory. And although that work corresponds more exactly to apes than to men, it nevertheless teems with fewer false descriptions and errors than all the others: as I have been accustomed to show openly in the schools, and indeed (so may the Gods above favor my efforts) candidly and without any bias in the presence of the actual subjects. Meanwhile, I am unable to escape the calumnies and most false detractions of certain idle old men who are wasting away with envy because these things, of course, are hidden from them.

THE THORAX we shall appropriately call whatever is intercepted and circumscribed by the ribs: but not, with Aristotle, the entire trunk of the body, which we measure from the throat all the way to the pubes. Truly, the anterior seat of the thorax <margin>b figure 3</margin> we shall rightly name the Breast: and the broad bone ^b^ consisting in that seat, to which the ribs are articulated, the Breastbone <note>original: "Pectoris os"</note>. Thus we may not seem to carelessly confuse the three terms of the Greeks, and especially of Galen: *thorax, stethos, and sphondylon* <note>original: "θώρακα, στῆθος, & σφόνδυλον" — referring to the chest, breast, and vertebrae respectively</note>. Therefore, the breastbone and the ribs, and likewise the twelve vertebrae of the back, which I have hitherto assigned to the thorax, are the bones of the thorax. Moreover, there is <margin>The industry of the Creator of things in creating the thorax.</margin> <margin>These bones are given in muscle plates 7 & 8.</margin> an admirable industry of the highest Creator of things, by which the whole thorax is made neither entirely of bone nor entirely of flesh, but rather bone is changed with muscles in turn and alternately. Although, meanwhile, the skull <note>original: "caluaria"</note> is indeed constructed entirely of bone, and the abdomen is for the most part muscular. Furthermore, it is fitting to weigh these things accurately and with special zeal. For since there are three principles dispensing man, the first principle is surrounded by bone, which is immobile and interspersed with no muscles; the muscles indeed by the third; but by the second, a certain medium is woven together from bones and muscles. For the brain required muscles for no uses, since no part of the skull requires either dilation or compression. Wherefore also the skull is deservedly placed around it like a helmet and an immobile wall. Furthermore, if such a septum were placed around the organs serving the liver—namely the stomach, the intestines, and the bladder, and finally the uterus itself, <margin>The first 5 figures of the book demonstrate these.</margin> surely no small instrument of generation—where would the stomach receive food and drink? To what end would the swelling of those carrying a child in the womb project? By what way would the excrements be led out, or how would the birth be propelled by a happy effort, with no muscle here bringing aid? Moreover, the movement of the thorax, which we require most of all for the inspiration of air, would be entirely abolished if the thorax consisted only of bones. If, however, it consisted only of muscles, the makers of movement, they would collapse upon the lungs and heart, even with no external thing pressing them. Therefore, so that some capacity of the thorax may be made within, and the thorax may also be driven by voluntary motion, muscles are interposed alternately with the bones. <margin>c 6th muscle plate S, T, V, X & 11th plate T, V.</margin> Soon, however, this also contributes not a little to the security of the heart and lung: for they are now better fortified than if the thorax had been fabricated of muscles alone. Furthermore, the mass of the bones of the thorax wonderfully contributes to strengthening and sustaining the shoulder blades <margin>This whole figure Q, R, S, T, V, Z & Δ.</margin> (to which the arms are then joined). For we shall teach that these, leaning only on the ribs and collarbones, are strengthened by no bone other than the shoulder blades and the breastbone. Besides, if the thorax consisted of no bones, there would be no place from which the muscles for the shoulder blades, arms, abdomen, and certain other members might take their origin; nor would the muscles cling to or stand upon any foundations. And truly, the tortoises most beautifully teach this necessity of the bone of the thorax, if anything else does: which, although they are hedged in by so safe a dwelling, nevertheless demonstrate in the seats of the breast and the sides of the thorax a most elegant fabric of bones, very pleasant to behold, created in this incredible artifice for this purpose alone: that the forelegs may lean upon it, and that the muscles of the tortoise moving the shoulder may conveniently take their origin. Since therefore neither respiration...

Reason, nor can the voice be produced without the thorax; and since the heart, and moreover with it the lung, is given to the thorax for its duty, it was necessary for the Artisan of things <note>The "Artisan" or "Opifex" refers to God or Nature as the divine creator in Vesalius's teleological view.</note> to attend especially to four goals in the fabric of the thorax: namely, the voice, respiration, and the size of the heart and lung. For the thorax, which in a way follows the shape of the lung, is as large as the mass of the lung needed to be. Yet meanwhile the lung follows the form of the thorax, but the thorax does not follow the lung. For in the history of the lung you will learn that it required no peculiar shape of its own, just as neither the liver, nor the spleen, nor in a certain way the brain. Furthermore, it will now be the proper time to describe the bones of the thorax in order: and since we have previously described its twelve vertebrae, we shall begin the discourse with the ribs, which in men and women consist of twelve in number on each side. If they ever vary from this, thirteen occur more often than only eleven: just as we reported above that among thirteen thoraxes, only eleven such cases occur. Since there are twelve thoracic vertebrae, a single rib is articulated on both sides of each. 

The common opinion that men are destitute of a certain rib on one side, and are thus surpassed in number by women, is plainly ridiculous; even though Moses, the producer of Eve from Adam's rib, has transmitted this. For although perhaps Adam's bones, if someone had assembled them into a skeleton, might have lacked one on one side, it does not follow that all men should be so. Aristotle, in his *History of Animals*, wrote that humans have eight ribs on each side, though he also noted that some say they have seven. It is as if Aristotle were confirming his dogma only by the testimony of others. However, while I was once explaining this passage of Aristotle at Padua, I learned from young men of the highest promise (on account of their singular knowledge of letters and civil law), Jacobus Niger and Joannes Centurio, Genoese patricians, that the noble Ligurians were called <term>inflammatores</term> <note>original: "inflammatores"; likely a reference to a local historical epithet or a specific anatomical variation noted in that population.</note> in ancient monuments: yet that people, as they are strenuous in naval and land battles, are also most remarkable for the excellent symmetry and number of their members. 

There are, therefore, usually twelve ribs on each side: and the seven superior ones are articulated to the breastbone <note>The sternum.</note> and the vertebrae, as we shall say later; but the five lower ones are joined only to the vertebrae, and do not reach as far as the breastbone, but ending in the sides of the thorax, they are joined to each other by the ends of their cartilages: the twelfth only excepted, which gapes further <gloss>h</gloss> from the eleventh, nor does it touch it in any part. This <gloss>i</gloss> not infrequently happens to the eleventh as well, when it does not then reach the cartilage of the tenth. These five lower ones, because they are not articulated to the breastbone, are called <term>nothai</term> <note>original: "vóθαι"; Greek for "bastard" or "false" ribs.</note> by the Greeks, as if you were to say spurious and illegitimate. It is common to all ribs that they consist of both a bony <gloss>k</gloss> and a cartilaginous <gloss>l</gloss> substance, and they claim an appendix for themselves in that seat. The bony substance is not similar to itself in every part: for where the ribs are articulated with the vertebrae, and where they constitute the back, they are much more solid and harder than in the sides of the thorax, and near the region of the breast, where they are constructed of a more spongy substance, which is covered by a thin scale or plate: and this is finally thinnest there, where it degenerates into cartilage. The cartilage also does not show the same appearance everywhere: for the cartilage of the lower ribs is softer. Whence perhaps some report that the illegitimate ribs are specifically called <term>chondrous</term> <note>original: "χόνδρους"; Greek for "cartilages".</note>, as if you were to say "the cartilages." But the cartilage of the superior ribs is harder, more solid, and in the elderly...

Therefore, the first rib is articulated by a round head to the body of the first thoracic vertebra: and then it ascends for a little while to the transverse process of the same vertebra, so that it may be articulated to its tip by another head. But the second rib, and the seven following, are always articulated to a common cavity of two vertebral bodies, not by a round head, but by one protruding like an obtuse angle: they are secured to the transverse processes just like the first rib, although here too some difference arises in the joints, because the cavities are not carved in the same place in the transverse processes. For the transverse processes of the superior vertebrae bear their cavities carved in the lower part of their internal seat, but those of the inferior (as we also advised above against the opinion of Galen) in the upper part: while the cavities of the middle vertebrae hold themselves in a middle fashion. Furthermore, because the articulation of the ribs which is made at the body of the vertebra is so much higher than that which the ribs manage at the transverse processes, it is sometimes completed only at the body of the vertebrae, <margin>h 8 *fig. N.*</margin> and is performed with cavities and heads that do not protrude very deeply. And in this manner the ribs are joined to the vertebrae. For in these animals (as can be seen even while eating) the breastbone consists of seven bones, not differing much from each other in form.
