# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE] BODY
<page-num>116</page-num>

<margin>The use of the pointed cartilage.</margin>
I believe it is hidden from no one that the bones of the chest were created for the purpose of forming and stabilizing the thorax; just as I rendered at the beginning of this chapter that they also serve secondarily as a bulwark, and that these uses provide practical protection for a man carrying the chest. The cartilage into which the breastbone <note>the sternum</note> is sharpened is also a bulwark for the parts placed beneath it, and is commonly called the "pomegranate" <note>the xiphoid process, from the Latin *malum granatum*</note>, because (as I believe) it approaches the likeness of the tip of a single pomegranate flower. From which form also, the common people call it the "epiglottal" cartilage, evidently from the likeness of the lid of the larynx <margin>m. 12, 13. & 14. f. cap. 5. & 8.</margin> <note>the epiglottis</note>, which is not very dissimilar in appearance to the cartilage of the breastbone. But we shall add an abundance of names of this sort at the end of the present book, together with the names of the other bones. For now, nothing remains to be added to the history of the bones of the thorax, except perhaps the course of the ribs, which is far different in the bony parts of the ribs than in the cartilages.

<margin>The course of the ribs.</margin>
For the bones of the ribs <margin>n. 5 fig. from A through c. to f.</margin> when they first depart from the vertebrae, are remarkably slanted downwards toward the back, and from here they always decline obliquely toward the front at the sides of the thorax, <margin>o. 3 fig. from f to A. p. same fig. q. B to E.</margin> until they end in the cartilage, which climbs obliquely and circularly upward toward the front: so much so that the ribs, where they first lead out the cartilage, are reflected upward in an arch and in a certain manner into an angle. This course of the ribs is evident not only in those which are joined to the breastbone: but also in all the rest, if perhaps you except the twelfth, whose cartilage looks upward quite obscurely. Although this bending is seen most especially in the middle ones, namely the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth. <margin>q. These are whole, and especially the second.</margin>

LEST PERHAPS we should seem to have passed over anything in this book, mention must now be made of the bony substance of the heart. For Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> recorded that a bone of extraordinary size was cut out from the heart of an elephant by one of his friends: and he ascribes a bone to the hearts of large animals, but cartilage to smaller ones. I, however, thus far, as in no other heart, so neither in the human (which is of a very moist constitution if compared to other animals) have I found <margin>The human heart truly lacks a bone.</margin> a distinct bone: and that <margin>The cartilaginous substance of the heart.</margin> in my opinion is nothing other than the roots of the great artery and the arterial vein, leading first from the heart. Indeed these roots, in which the bases of the membranes <note>the heart valves</note> consist—which are put in charge of the reflux of materials from those two vessels into the heart—are much harder than the rest of the substance of those vessels, so that the roots seem to participate somewhat in the nature of cartilage: which in oxen, and even more in stags (endowed with a very dry temperament), so hardens over time that we have written that the cartilages of the ribs of quadrupeds degenerate into a white and brittle bone, covered on the outside by cartilage as if by a membrane. These roots of the vessels are therefore adjacent to each other, just as if you were to join two circles together at a point, and continue them so that the right circle of the arterial vein... <margin>d. 10 fi lib. 6 fi B, C, D. b. 8 fig. lib. 6 under E, F. G. by which characters the membranes are noted. c. c. d. A, B.</margin>

is the root, while the left (which is larger) belongs to the great artery <note>The aorta</note>. Where they meet in a mutual circuit, that is the place where these vessels are born together from their circles and united, and where the principal portion of the bony cartilage resides. This part is oblong and somewhat rounded; it occupies the entire seat where those roots are joined together, while the remaining portions of the circles are cut away. And therefore, I will allow these roots to be called either the "cartilage of the heart" or "bone," depending on the temperament of the animal you happen upon, and even more so its age—provided that one looks accurately at their nature. One should not be so dull-witted as to be persuaded, along with the followers of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> who extract his meanings quite drowsily, that the bone of the heart is formed like the letter Λ <note>Greek letter Lambda</note> or υ <note>Greek letter Upsilon</note>. For those who set out to write the history of the human body after Galen recount that in the base of the human heart, something is constructed which they liken to the bone placed before the larynx, named from the image of the voice <note>The hyoid bone, which supports the tongue and larynx.</note>. Nor was it enough for these men to fabricate a bone in the base of the human heart in this manner; they even added to the discourse that the base of the heart, and thus the entire heart itself, is supported by it, just as the root of the tongue is supported by that bone placed before the larynx. For they think the heart, supported by such a bone, is moved; they do not consider that even if the heart were gifted with such a bone, it could no more be supported by it than an iron pole could hold up a bed in mid-air if the pole were tied to the bed and thrown down from a height along with it. Meanwhile, we cannot deny that the connection of the four vessels of the heart at their adjoining seats does provide some support to the heart. Yet, from the entire history given by Galen regarding the bone of the heart—in which he undeservedly rebukes the ancients and the physicians of his own time who denied its presence in man—we must also confess that Galen never actually handled that bone he discusses in a human heart, which is, as we have warned, moist and soft compared to others.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'S' depicting a landscape with a river, trees, and a small figure in the foreground.</image-desc>The <term>SHOULDER BLADES</term> <note>original: "CAPVLARVM"</note>, one on each side, rest upon the posterior region of the chest <note>the thorax</note> toward the upper parts. They are joined to the occipital bone <note>the bone at the back of the skull</note>, the vertebrae of the neck and chest, the ribs, and the bone resembling the letter U <note>the hyoid bone</note>, solely through the intervention of muscles. Indeed, they are joined to the occipital bone by the benefit of the second of the muscles moving the scapula, which also connects it to the spines of many vertebrae of the neck and chest, just as the third muscle binds it to the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae. To the ribs, however, the shoulder blades are bound by the first muscle that moves them and the second of those moving the chest. Furthermore, the shoulder blade adheres to the U-shaped bone by the help of the seventh of that bone's particular muscles. In humans, moreover, and in apes, squirrels, and whatever other animals are endowed with collarbones <note>clavicles</note>, the shoulder blade is joined to the collarbone by the aid of ligaments and is contiguous with it. In all animals, however, the bone of the arm or humerus is articulated into the shoulder blade. And therefore, if you were to imagine a man destitute of a shoulder blade, you would nowhere find a suitable place for the so-called shoulder joint. For its construction, it is necessary that the head of the humerus enter the cavity of some bone, and so that it may move, it must rest in some bone as if on a stable base; so much so that this must be considered the primary use of the shoulder blade. Another use follows closely after this, by no means to be regretted: namely, the protection of the parts contained within the chest. For Nature has placed the shoulder blades against the back of the chest like two bucklers or shields. From this, she was not ignorant that another use would accrue to man, whereby many muscles—the authors of the movements of the arm, chest, and elbow—might conveniently obtain a seat by which they are supported and from which they take their origin.

<margin>The position and connection of the shoulder blades.</margin>
<margin>The use of the shoulder blades.</margin>

It is, therefore, a matter of great and singular industry to adapt the shoulder blades to such various and entirely necessary uses, and to build them in every part just as if they were fashioned privately for each individual use, as we shall now describe. For the shoulder blade is quite unequal and unlike itself in every part. For besides its various processes, cavities, swellings, appendages, and other things of that kind from which we seek the distinctions of bones, the shoulder blade expresses in a certain way the image of a triangle formed with differing sides or edges.

<margin>The triangular shape of the shoulder blade.</margin>

For its first side, which we shall perpetually call the **base of the shoulder blade**, is that part of the shoulder blade which is extended along the length of the back, closest to the spines of the chest vertebrae. It consists of an oblique line, inclined above and below toward the outer sides of the body as if into the convexity of a circle, but in the middle, it is slightly crescent-shaped and hollow. Yet meanwhile, the base of the shoulder blade sometimes has a continuous curve, almost in this manner **(**, and in man, just as in other living creatures, it is convex.

<margin>The base of the shoulder blade.</margin>

Next, this base appears somewhat thicker in the middle—though perhaps more so in the lower and upper parts than in the center—and the thickness of the lower part still exceeds the thickness of the upper part. To this base, two appendages are usually attached: one, which is larger, thicker, and longer, stands at the lower angle of the base, which is remarkably obtuse and almost circular; the other appendage is found somewhat below the upper angle and grows together with that part of the base from which you will hear us say the **spine of the shoulder blade** takes its beginning.

<margin>The appendages of the base.</margin>

In addition to these appendages, a certain soft cartilage is attached to the base, of that kind of cartilage by which the ends of bones not joined to any other bone are accustomed to grow. But in humans, this cartilage is far shorter and smaller than in sheep and oxen and other quadrupeds, whose shoulder blades lie upon the sides of the chest rather than, as in man, near the vertebrae at the back of the chest. And so stands the first side of the shoulder blade; the remaining two, however, vary between themselves. For the lower one, from the lower...

-># THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.<-

It is bound together by very strong ligaments. A unique cartilage intervenes here, exactly similar to those observed in the joints of the lower jaw with the head <note>Vesalius refers to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint</note>, which is smooth and slippery on both sides where it faces the bones, and is continuous only with the ligaments encompassing the joint. That part of the aforementioned process which is closest to the back of the shoulder blade is appropriately named the **Spine**, as I have already written; this is also seen in *dogs, sheep, and other animals*. But the part of the process which departs from the shoulder blade forward toward the outer side, and gradually widens—and which can be observed only in humans and animals endowed with a collarbone—we call the **summit of the shoulder** <note>original: "summum humerum"</note>. We borrow this name from the Greeks, who undoubtedly called the joint of the arm bone with the shoulder blade the <term>acromion</term> <note>Greek: ἀκρώμιον; the "topmost point of the shoulder"</note>. And accordingly, they called this part of the process so because it constitutes the superior, outermost seat of the joint, and is held as its safest bulwark. And indeed, it is always understood this way by Hippocrates, both in many other places and especially when he teaches that the shoulder (which he himself calls the <term>brachion</term> <note>Greek: βραχίονα; the upper arm</note>) can by no means be dislocated upwards (the summit of the shoulder surely preventing it), and when he treats a fracture of the summit of the shoulder.

<margin>e Figure 2, c.</margin>
<margin>d Figure 4, c.</margin>
<margin>e From Huer. fig. K. fig. 2.</margin>

Although here Galen must also be heard in his book *On Bones*, who asserts that the connection of the present process with the collarbone is called the <term>acromion</term> by some professors of dissection. Where he also adds that some people place a third bone here, besides this process and the collarbone, in humans alone, and call it the <term>acromion</term> and the <term>acromioclavicular bone</term> <note>Greek: ἀκρωμιοκλεῖδα</note>. Galen lists this third bone in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts* in humans, and deprives monkeys of it; just as he does in his books *On Anatomical Procedures* and in his commentaries on Hippocrates' book *On Joints*. For he writes that, besides this superior process of the shoulder blade and the collarbone, there is a certain third cartilaginous bone which is spread over the connection of the collarbone to that process of the shoulder blade, and from which membranes and ligaments arise, by whose benefit that connection is more strongly established.

<margin>f The whole of Q. to 4.</margin>

Galen, in the fifth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, says such a bone is called the <term>acromion</term> by Hippocrates, and he himself calls it by that name in the same place; just as he testified in the book *On Bones* that some people place a third bone here, and that it is called the <term>acromion</term> by them. Meanwhile, Galen repeatedly in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, and in the books *On Anatomical Procedures*, and in almost all his commentaries on Hippocrates, has called this process of the shoulder blade—or at least the connection of this shoulder blade process with the collarbone—the <term>acromion</term>. So much so, that I wonder not a little at Galen's inconsistency here, and I would wonder much more if that third cartilaginous bone ever occurred to me in a human. For I by no means think that Galen considers the unique cartilage of this joint mentioned above to be a bone, since cartilages of that kind depart greatly from the nature of true cartilage toward the nature of a ligament, and are much less bony in any way; besides the fact that it is found in the monkey just as in the human. And if by chance it were to be considered a bone—besides the fact that Galen would have mentioned it differently and written that it intervenes in the joint, not that it is spread over it—he would also not lack blame for not having established a unique bone in the joint of the collarbone with the breastbone, and again in the joints of the lower jaw to the temple bones, and in the knee, since meanwhile cartilages of this kind appear more clearly there than here in the summit of the shoulder, however much they seem to have been entirely unknown and overlooked by Galen. Thus far, therefore, I have never been able to notice a third bone here, however diligently I have looked. And I am well enough aware that Galen never saw it either: and if I dared to go so far as to be impious toward him, I would affirm that he...

<margin>Among which [animals], besides man, the monkey, and the squirrel, and if I remember correctly, the dormouse, I have encountered none possessing this upper process of the shoulder blade; so much so that I wonder whether he who first wrote that only man is gifted with an acromion <note>original: "ἀκρωμίῳ" - the bony point of the shoulder</note> meant that only man possesses this process.</margin>

...to have devised a bone of this sort from a certain similarity with the bones that resemble sesame seeds <note>sesamoid bones</note>, which you will hear are fixed to certain bare heads of muscles and placed before the joints and connections of other bones. Furthermore, no animal has ever occurred to me, besides man, the monkey, the squirrel, and if I remember correctly, the dormouse, that possesses this upper process of the shoulder blade <note>the acromion</note>. Thus, I am uncertain whether he who first wrote that man alone is gifted with an *acromion* understood that only man possesses this process: since in dogs, sheep, goats, hares (which often also lack the inner process of the shoulder blade), and other quadrupeds usually served at the table, he would see no upper process of the shoulder blade (but only the spine), being little concerned with monkeys, unlike Galen <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose anatomical findings were often based on animal dissection</note>. Furthermore, for what purpose this was described for man and other animals born with clavicles, we shall then explain better when we undertake the history of the clavicles. For besides the fact that this process prevents the dislocation of the humerus <note>upper arm bone</note> upwards, and is a very safe bulwark for the shoulder joint, and that it elegantly serves the insertion and origin of muscles, it is most helpful in this: that by the addition of the clavicle, it removes the shoulder joint as far as possible from the sides of the chest and the ribs, and preserves it in that position in which it is most *suitably* disposed for its movements. However, in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, [Galen] gifted the upper process with that name: just as it is also sometimes called by him *loxakophysis* <note>original: "λωξακοφύσης" - an oblique process</note>, as we see Galen is not entirely consistent with himself. But now it would be appropriate to set a limit to the discourse on the shoulder blades: especially since nothing remains to be told except that the base of the shoulder blade, where it is adorned with appendices, appears somewhat spongy and full of small tubes, and that several holes are seen in the shoulder blade. One is seen now and then in that wide space which the upper rib of the shoulder blade forms with its spine: and also in the internal surface of the shoulder blade, where it is more deeply hollowed out. Then, in the circuit of the neck, for the sake of the same use and for the ligaments that must be produced, holes of this kind also occur.

<gloss>Number of the clavicles.</gloss> ON BOTH sides of the body there is a single clavicle (which are called <term>kleitòn</term> <note>original Greek: λειτὸν; likely a variant or error for 'kleis'</note> by the Greeks), joined to the breastbone and the upper process of the shoulder blade. <gloss>The articulation of the same.</gloss> They articulate with the breastbone at those ends which we said were carved into all the sides of its first part. And just as those cavities are oblong, led from the front parts downward toward the back, and are seen to be wider at the front than the back, and wider internally than externally: so also are the heads of the clavicles that are connected to the breastbone. For these are oblong and flattened in the manner of the cavities (in which they roll primarily upward and downward); and if anyone were to observe their outline more accurately, he would judge it to be somewhat triangular. For one angle is situated in the front part of the head toward the lower side, being somewhat obtuse. The second is also obtuse, visible in the upper part of the head slightly toward the back. The third is sharper and longer, placed in the posterior position and sloping downward. Furthermore, as these angles are obtuse, so also the lines of the triangle occur unequal and slanted outward. For the line drawn from the first angle to the second is the shortest; but that proceeding from the second angle to the third is seen to be much longer; while that which is carried from the first angle to the third is the longest of all and the most curved. This head of the clavicle is encrusted with much cartilage and is smooth; however, if the cartilage is broken away along with the very thin <term>appendix</term> <note>epiphysis</note>, the head is seen to be rough and uneven. But although the clavicle here abounds in cartilage no less than the cavity of the breastbone does, Nature has nevertheless placed a cartilage between this joint, unlike...

## ON THE CLAVICLE <note>original: "DE CLAVICULA"</note>

<margin>The clavicle at the upper process of the shoulder blade.</margin>
...standing above the upper process of the shoulder blade <note>the acromion</note>, which is extended in such a way that, by the benefit of the clavicle, it is supported and stabilized while being pushed away from the chest; by this means, the joint itself is moved far 
<margin>The joint of the outer process of the shoulder blade.</margin>
away from the thorax. Indeed, the clavicle is articulated to this process by a very small protruding head, which is wider than it is long. Such an articulation arises here that you can hardly judge which bone receives or is received; there is also a peculiar cartilage intervening here, which we described in the previous chapter for the sake of those who incorrectly ascribe a certain third bone to this joint, besides the upper process of the shoulder blade 
<margin>The substance of the clavicle, its swellings, roughnesses, ligaments, and openings.</margin>
and the clavicle. That part of the clavicle which is connected to the upper process of the shoulder blade is somewhat wide, just as the process itself is also seen to be wide and ample. Furthermore, this part of the clavicle, and that which is joined to the bone of the chest <note>the sternum</note>, is hollow and more porous inside than the rest of the clavicle, which is most solid in the middle of its length, because it also becomes very thin and somewhat rounded. For it is not entirely rounded, since in its lower part it protrudes as if into a line, which begins not far from the head of the clavicle articulated to the chest—specifically near the middle of the angles of its posterior and anterior head. This line reaches a little beyond the middle of the length of the clavicle, prepared for this purpose: so that the first of the muscles moving the thorax might take its origin from it. Near the beginning of this line, by the head of the clavicle, a sinuous roughness is seen, from which a strong ligament arises, binding the clavicle 
<margin>The tubercle of the root of the clavicle.</margin>
to the cartilage of the first rib of the thorax. Moreover, at the other end of this line, another roughness occurs, and 
<margin>The seat of the clavicle.</margin>
as if a certain rough end, where the clavicle almost rests upon the <term>tubercle</term> <note>a small rounded projection on a bone</note> and root of the inner process of the shoulder blade <note>the coracoid process</note>, and from which a ligament is produced, stubbornly binding the clavicle to that tubercle. Furthermore, this lower seat of the clavicle, where that line 
<margin>The seat of the clavicle.</margin>
ends and the width of the clavicle is seen, becomes sinuous and rough, especially near the connection of the clavicle to the upper process of the shoulder blade, where the ligaments containing this joint arise stronger than at the upper seat. The upper 
<margin>The seat of the clavicle.</margin>
region of the clavicle, however, is entirely smooth, except near its joints, where it is somewhat roughened for the sake of producing ligaments, as well as for the sake of the muscles. For from the upper part of the clavicle, near the chest bone, that muscle arises which, also originating from the chest bone, is implanted into the <term>mammillary process</term> <note>the mastoid process behind the ear</note> of the head; it is counted as one of the two parts of the seventh pair of muscles moving the head <note>the sternocleidomastoid</note>. To the upper part of the clavicle joined to the upper process of the shoulder blade, that muscle is inserted which is reckoned the first of those leading the shoulder blade upward <note>the trapezius</note>. Also in the anterior part of the clavicle, at the root of the angle of its head, a line also protrudes, ending before the middle of the length of the clavicle, from which a significant part of the muscle bringing the arm to the chest <note>the pectoralis major</note> takes its origin. In addition, in the anterior seat of the clavicle, where it bends backward and where a hollow is seen not far from its articulation with the upper process of the shoulder blade, there stands a roughness worthy of note, prepared for the muscle lifting the arm <note>the deltoid</note>, a large part of whose origin arises from here. In the posterior seat of the clavicle, nothing uneven occurs that has not been mentioned, except for a certain tubercle protruding here where the clavicle is most convex; that tubercle constitutes, as it were, the angle of that convex seat, and leads a ligament to the inner process of the shoulder blade. Furthermore, in the most solid part of the clavicle, and especially in its posterior region, two and sometimes three <term>foramina</term> <note>small holes or openings in bone</note> are seen, which are not passages through the bone but are carved for this purpose: to admit the small veins that nourish the clavicle.

One figure is seated, holding a tool, while the other stands over a table.</image-desc> **The Humerus** <margin>Humerus.</margin> is the name given by Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work 'De Medicina'</note> and many others to that bone <margin>d entire. r to R, and to T, V.</margin> which articulates with the scapula <note>shoulder blade</note> and the cubitus <note>forearm</note>; it is called *brachion* <note>original Greek: βραχίω</note> by the Greeks (as well as by <margin>Brachium.</margin> not a few of the Latins). However, so that we may distinguish the entire mass of bone and muscles—along with the nerves, veins, arteries, skin, and other things that perhaps enter into the construction of the arm—from the bone itself in the context of our discourse, when mention of the bone alone occurs, it shall be called the **Humerus**, or sometimes the **bone of the Arm** <margin>compare here the entire S with A, and 4. above with e.</margin>; but when we indicate the remaining parts of the limb together with the bone itself, we shall use the word **Arm** (*Brachium*) for the sake of clearer teaching.

The Humerus, <margin>The humerus is not the largest of all bones after the femur.</margin> in the opinion of Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in his book *On Bones*, is the largest of all the bones of the entire body, with the exception only of the femur <note>thigh bone</note>; nevertheless, in man, the fibula and the bones of the tibia <note>shin bones</note> significantly surpass the humerus in length. Furthermore, the bone of the tibia in thickness and weight, as well as the bones articulated to the sides of the sacrum <note>the pelvic bones</note>, far exceed the humerus in weight: so much so that we encounter many bones besides the femur to which the humerus yields in size. But we shall grant this to the authority of Galen along with many other things, since by the grace of some we are not permitted to go against his decrees, and because of the difference seen between man and the ape in the length of the femur, tibia, humerus, and cubitus.

Therefore, the uppermost part of the humerus, by which <margin>Description of the upper part of the humerus.</margin> <margin>b 1 Fig. a. Furthermore, there is a part not indeed raised for any articulation, but <margin>e 1 Fig. D. 1, 2 Fig. E.</margin> merely protruding like a neck, into which many strong ligaments <gloss>and</gloss> binding the humerus to the scapula are conveniently implanted. For into this sinus—which is wider or more spacious and deep on the anterior surface of the humerus than on the posterior—many ligaments are inserted, just as I said those others were implanted into the outer head, as if into a hill or some promontory. And just as the sites of all bones in which something is inserted, or takes its origin, are rough <gloss>and</gloss> unequal; so also the present sinus, together with the outer head, is deservedly seen to be rough <gloss>and</gloss> unequal. is seen to be perfectly smooth, just as the body is smooth according to its convex shape, for the sake of which it is carved out; this is the external head of the muscle with the <term>tefterium</term><note>Vesalius likely refers to a specific muscular attachment or "shuttle-like" structure here</note> <margin>h. 6th muscle table, the muscle is marked with the symbol ☉, the head however is m. Furthermore, this groove does not only belong to the <term>appendix</term><note>The epiphysis or bony outgrowth</note>, but also extends through that seat of the humerus bone to which the appendix grows, and which constitutes a very short and exceedingly thick neck for the humerus.

<margin>Description of the lower part of the humerus.</margin>
The lower part of the humerus, which consists of two bones existing in the forearm—namely the <term>ulna</term> and the <term>radius</term>—is articular, and in certain children consists of an obscure appendix; it is far more varied still, both in the abundance and appearance of its grooves, heads, and protuberances.

<margin>The pulley of the humerus, to which the ulna is articulated.</margin>
For in the middle of the lower seat of the humerus, a groove with its own protuberances is first observed, exactly such as is seen in the wheel of a pulley <note>original: "trochleæ rotula"</note> around which ropes are wound. For just as this wheel is round and circular in its circumference, but flat and wide on its sides, so also in that seat of the humerus a circular and round part is seen, which you could liken to no image more closely than a pulley-wheel. Then, just as the wheel is carved out in its circumference (where the cord is wound) with a certain smooth, polished, and slippery groove, and the sides of this groove protrude on both sides and equally embrace the rope within themselves so that it does not wander; so also this part of the humerus is grooved in the middle and protrudes on both sides. In this one respect, however, it differs from the protuberances of a perfect pulley-wheel: the sides of a pulley's groove are extended almost equally, but this part of the humerus <margin>o 1,2 fi.L. p 1,2 fi.M. q 1,2 fi.P.</margin> on the inner side indeed prominently projects and corresponds perfectly to a pulley, while on the outer side it is drawn out much less. This occurs because of the head of the humerus, to which you will hear the radius is articulated, and which is placed at the external side of the humeral pulley; without a greatly prominent production of its own, it elegantly stands in the way along with the radius, so that the ulna is not easily dislocated outward. Furthermore, in the upper part of the pulley or wheel at this seat, Nature has carved out two remarkable grooves: one indeed in the anterior part, the <margin>r 1 fig.N. s 2 fig.O. t 1,5 fig. 24. cap. C,D.</margin> other truly in the posterior, which is much larger, deeper, and in every way more remarkable than the anterior. These grooves, separated only by a thin layer of bone like a scale, receive the processes of the ulna visible in its upper part. And the anterior of these, when the elbow is bent, the anterior groove admits; but when the elbow is extended, the posterior groove receives the posterior process of the ulna. For these grooves are the boundaries of extreme flexion and extension, made with such providence that they allow the elbow to be bent into a very acute angle, and permit the same to be extended beyond a straight line; because we certainly have no need for extension into an angle, just as we surely need flexion, especially since the humerus can be turned quite loosely at the shoulder blade and led significantly toward the rear. Because these present grooves are like bases and obstacles in the movements of the elbow, which do not allow the ulna to be carried further, Hippocrates called them <term>bathmidas</term><note>original: "βαθμίδας" - meaning "steps" or "bases"</note>. To this also the pulley of the humerus, encrusted with a certain cartilage and smooth, [receives] the upper radius, which as we first briefly advised, has a head that is round and somewhat oblong; this, similarly to the <margin>u first figure cap. 4 lower cap. 24 O. x 1 fig.P.</margin> pulley, is encrusted with cartilage and smooth, and enters the upper groove of the radius, and the radius (as I shall discuss more fully elsewhere) moves upon that head into pronation and supination. Next, the length of the head, which I measure from its upper part to the lower according to the length of the humerus, is also the reason why, in the flexion and extension of the elbow, that head does not slip or wander from the groove of the radius (which is round, but not oblong). And on this occasion also, the entire part of the head covered with cartilage faces only the anterior seat of the humerus, because in no extension of the elbow does the radius approach the posterior seat of the humerus. Nevertheless, at the external <margin>External protuberance of the humerus, to which the radius is articulated.</margin> side of this head, the humerus protrudes significantly, showing the image of a mountain or a rock, prepared for this purpose, so that as many muscles as possible may conveniently [originate] from here...

->THE ENTIRE<- part positioned between the upper arm and the wrist is called *olecranon* <note>original: ὠλέκρανoν</note> by the Greeks, but the Cubitus <note>the forearm</note> by the Latins. This consists of two bones, resting upon one another and joined by an articulation: of which the ᵇ lower one, which is also the longer, is also called the *pechys* <note>original: πῆχυς; the forearm or cubit</note>. However, lest a similarity of names <term>homonymia: the use of one name for multiple things</term> should produce any obscurity in our discourse, we have decided that whenever mention occurs of the entire part constructed from those two bones, we shall use the word "Forearm" <note>Cubitus</note>; calling the lower bone the **Ulna**, ᶜ and the upper one the **Radius** <note>original: πῆχυς; though Vesalius notes the Greek term was used for both, he clarifies the distinction here</note>. These two bones are long, and differ from one another in almost every part. For the Ulna, at the seat of the ᵈ track and pulley <note>trochlea</note> of the humerus, is quite thick and solid, ᵉ and acquires two remarkable processes <term>processus: a bony projection</term>.
<margin>c Figures 3 and 4 in their entirety, or Figure 2 in its entirety. X.</margin>
<margin>d Chapter 23, Figures 1 and 2, K, L, M.</margin>
<margin>e The whole figure; Figure 5, C is anterior, D is posterior.</margin>
Since one of these is in front of the other, we shall call this one the anterior, and that one—perhaps inconveniently—the posterior. The anterior process ᶠ looks toward the higher region of the pulley itself at the front of the humerus and is perfectly fitted to it; it is wide, resembles an obtuse angle, and is exceedingly hard and solid.
<margin>f Figure 1 of this chapter.</margin>
<margin>g Figure 2 of this chapter.</margin>
The posterior process, however, corresponding in some way to the shape of the anterior, is carved into a ᵍ cavity in the back of the humerus at the higher region of the pulley. Since, however, it is much deeper and wider, the posterior process has rightly turned out thicker and larger than the anterior, and reflects the appearance of an even more obtuse angle. The Athenians called this process the *olecranon*, the Dorians *ankones*, Hippocrates *ankona*, and Galen sometimes *olecranon* and sometimes *ankona*. These terms are confused by translators to the great disadvantage of those who read Latin; they frequently translate these not only by the single name of "cubitus," but also use it for the ulna, the entire part located between the arm and the wrist, the joint of the humerus with the ulna and radius, the internal seat of that same joint, and its bend. Furthermore, ʰ in the middle of these processes of the ulna, where they face each other from opposite sides, a large cavity is carved out, receiving the pulley of the humerus and corresponding to it in every way.
<margin>h Figures 1, 2, 5, C, D, then E.</margin>
First, it is carved in the likeness of a semicircle, or even a little deeper than a semicircle; it approaches the image of our letter C, and the Greek letter Sigma <note>original: C; the lunate sigma</note>. Hence, from the shape of that character, the Ancients called this cavity the *sigmoidal* <note>original: σιγμοειδῆ</note>. Then, ⁱ so that it might fit the pulley of the humerus exactly, a blunt and ample bump protrudes in its middle, which runs along the length of that cavity; it can be compared to a rope or cord wound around the wheel of a pulley.
<margin>i Figure 5, F, F, F.</margin>
For just as the rounded part of a cord is wound into the rounded hollow of a pulley wheel, so also this bump of the cavity of the ulna is matched by the protruding sides. So that this may be done more precisely, the inner side of the cavity of the ulna is hollowed out deeper than the outer side; since the inner side of the pulley [of the humerus] projects and bulges much more prominently than the outer. This entire cavity of the ulna is smooth and encrusted with cartilage, and together with its processes, it grips the pulley of the humerus so that it may be extended and flexed.
<margin>k The same figure, G, G, then H, H; compare these with K, L, M in Figure 2 of Chapter 23.</margin>
To this end, not only does that most pleasant-to-behold structure of the bones—perfected by their mutual entry into one another—provide help, but also the strength of the ligaments tightening the joint. For so that strong ligaments might surround the joint, ˡ the surfaces of the processes not facing the cavity are rough and uneven.

This lower seat of the ulnar appendage facing the wrist, at the inner side of that sharp process, acquires an **a** unequal sinus, in which a **b** cartilage is fixed, which is of such a kind that it is born neither to the wrist nor to the ulna, and is of that type of cartilage which we recently reported was held by a connection to the neighboring bones. Furthermore, if you except this sinus of the ulnar appendage and its sharp process, the whole of its seat looking toward the wrist represents a **c** blunt and depressed surface, and is encrusted with cartilage in that manner by which the sinuses and heads of joints are usually covered and smoothed. To these things, the appendage of the ulna on its external seat also bears a **l** sinus carved into itself, which is oblong and rounded according to its cavity, and [contains] the tendon of that **m** muscle which, being the posterior [extensor] of the wrist, is inserted before the little finger...

it was necessary for it to occupy the external regions of the elbow. Although the fact that the radius is slanted is due more to the occasion of its oblique movement than for the sake of the muscles, and that the two bones of the forearm <note>original: "cubiti offa," referring here to the radius and ulna</note> depart from one another most in the middle of their course, we are taught this by those animals in which neither the radius, nor the hand by benefit of the radius, is led into pronation and supination <note>Pronation is turning the palm downward; supination is turning it upward.</note>. For the horse, the sheep, and animals of that kind, gifted with solid or cloven hooves, possess a radius so grown together and stabilized with the ulna along the entire length of the forearm that the radius cannot be moved even the slightest bit apart from the ulna. In dogs, however, and cats, and those animals whose feet are divided into digits, the radius does move indeed, but so much more obscurely and with more difficulty than we, who perform the movements of the hands more perfectly. Therefore, in these animals also, the radius stands apart from the ulna, but by far less than in man: and the structure of the articulation is not nearly so loose

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.
<page-num>139</page-num>

<margin>b, 1,2, fi.R.</margin>
<margin>c 9. fig.x.</margin>
<margin>d 1,2,3,4, 7,8 of the figures in T.</margin>
it would be impossible for the radius and the hand to be carried together into pronation <note>turning the palm downward</note> and supination <note>turning the palm upward</note> if the ulna remained stationary at the humerus as if it were the base and support of this motion. For that part of the wrist which would then be articulated into the cavity of the ulna would stand in the way like a bolt, so that the radius could not be moved even the slightest bit while the ulna remained unmoved. It was therefore a worthwhile work of Nature that the lower part of the radius should thicken considerably because of the cavity into which the wrist is articulated. But because it was by no means expedient for a thin bone to be increased too much, Nature also willed that a portion of the wrist be supported by the ulna: but in such a way that the ulna, by its pointed process <note>the styloid process</note>, would scarcely touch the wrist. For lest the ulna, by the rest of its appendage, be joined to the wrist without the intervention of another body, Nature led down a cartilage from the lower seat of the cavity carved into the appendage of the radius for the sake of the wrist. This cartilage, ascending the appendage of the ulna, separates it from the wrist, and thus fits this joint so that the ulna indeed supports the wrist, but does not touch it directly, and the entire cavity (as was indeed proper) belongs to the radius.

And I would wish these matters to be investigated all the more diligently, the more they conflict with the dogmas of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose authority Vesalius often challenged</note>. For in this business, which is otherwise tedious enough, I do not care to stitch in Galen's passages everywhere from which I prudently dissent, nor to subjoin the reason why I feel otherwise, since the diligent reader will notice these things abundantly even without being warned. But lest I seem to have bypassed his favorite views in the meantime—especially those which I usually require to be weighed by students in public dissections—I will now take up a portion and small detail in Galen's history of the radius and ulna, which he hammered home quite at length and quite often. This is the sharp process of the ulna, which we compare to a stylus <note>the styloid process</note>. To pass over the fact that he ascribes a large and (as far as I can gather from his writings) half the portion of the cavity in which the wrist is articulated to the ulna, he grants less of a private connection to the wrist for this sharp process where he treats the ulna and radius in his book *On Bones*. But where he reviews the bones of the wrist a little later, he expresses the appearance of that connection: namely, when he mentions that the <margin>e 1,2,3,4,5, fig. ch. 25.</margin> third bone of the upper row of the wrist <note>the triquetrum</note>, which faces the little finger, is hollowed out, and that the sharp process of the ulna enters into it. He proposes, as it were, two joints of the wrist with the ulna and radius: one of which he refers to the radius and ulna together, and the other to the sharp process of the ulna. And he asserts that it belongs to this [latter] joint to lead the wrist into an oblique motion, but to the former, into a straight motion, by the work of which we extend and flex the hand.

I think, however, that Galen understands by "oblique motion" that other motion by which the hand is led toward either side, by a motion exactly like that by which we bring the fingers together and move them apart: for Galen almost always understands "oblique" or "lateral" motion in this way elsewhere. If this is so, what could be said more absurdly than that this motion is celebrated by the service of that sharp process? Since, if it entered deeper into the wrist, it would hinder that motion no differently than a long stick tied along the ulna to the elbow, reaching with its tip to the outer side of the back of the hand, would beautifully obstruct the hand from being drawn away toward the outer side. Furthermore, if you wish to examine the passage of Galen in the second book of *On the Use of the Parts*, you will notice there that he also reviews a double joint, and says that the one made by the sharp process was made for this purpose: so that by its help the hand might be led into pronation and supination, and then also to the side. You will confess that this opinion, once noticed, is no less repugnant to the truth than the former one. This is especially true when you learn that almost the entire articulation of the wrist is referred to the radius primarily for this reason: so that the hand might secondarily follow the motion of the radius, which occurs in supination and pronation. And you will further conclude that those motions would have to be hindered if that sharp process, according to Galen's opinion, were articulated to the wrist. Which...

For their wrist-to-elbow articulation <note>original: *brachialis ad cubitum articulatio*; Vesalius uses *brachialis* to refer to the carpus/wrist bones</note> corresponds more to the descriptions of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose animal-based anatomy Vesalius frequently corrects</note> than to their own true structure, and meanwhile, they cannot be moved aptly into a face-down <term>pronation|turning the palm downward</term> or face-up <term>supination|turning the palm upward</term> position. Since, however, not just a single wrist bone refers to this cavity of the radius, but rather among the three wrist bones—which we shall teach look toward the radius and ulna—two are referred to the cavity of the radius alone, and the third looks toward that cartilage uniquely produced from the radius and the sharp process of the ulna's appendage. The cavity of the radius appears to be double, because the cavity protrudes slightly there where the second bone of the wrist is first joined, as we shall say in the chapter that follows. Now, moreover, it must further be considered that the part of the radius where its appendage fuses here, and the appendage itself, appears sinuous and slightly hollow on the internal side; this is to give way to the muscle of those lower parts leading the radius into a face-down position <note>the pronator quadratus</note>, so that it might be exactly adapted for the series of tendons which, extended from the elbow, serve the flexing of the fingers. However, the external part of this seat of the radius, just like the external region of the wrist, is convex <note>original: *gibba*</note>, so that (since it is placed on the outside) it is rendered more persistent in enduring injuries. Lest, however, the tendons of the muscles seeking the hand and led down from that convex seat should wander here and there, many channels <note>original: *sinus*</note> are carved into this seat, through which the tendons, covered by transverse ligaments as if passed through rings, will be described in the second book. There are four such channels in number.

And the first is indeed wide, prepared for the tendons which extend the index, middle, and ring fingers. The second transmits the tendon that leads the index and middle fingers sideways away from the thumb. The third is in a way double, transmitting the two-pronged tendon of the other muscle extending the wrist, together with the tendon of the muscle turning the thumb toward the index finger, or extending it. The fourth channel is carved very lightly and hardly deserves the name of a channel; yet it is rough for [the attachment of ligaments], of which one is inserted into the wrist bone supporting the thumb, the second into the first bone of the thumb, and the third into the second and third bones of the thumb. Indeed, the seat of the fourth channel is not only rough and protruding for the sake of that ligament, but also so that the tendon of the longest of the muscles driving the radius into a face-up position <note>the brachioradialis</note> may be more strongly implanted there. Besides these channels, there also exists a channel on the external side of the joint where the appendage of the radius is articulated to the appendage of the ulna near the wrist; this channel, common to both the ulna and radius, carries the tendon of the muscle by whose benefit especially the little finger is extended. No noteworthy small holes <note>foramina</note>, besides those which serve the origins of nerves and muscles, have fallen to the lot of either the ulna or the radius; and everywhere, except where they claim their appendages, they consist of a solid and exceedingly hard substance. Although, meanwhile, just like the humerus, femur, and the bones of the shins <note>tibia and fibula</note>, they possess a cavity carved out inside along their length, prepared for storing marrow and suited for the lightness of the bones.

**1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8** With these eight numerical characters, the eight bones of the wrist <note>original: *brachialis*; the carpal bones</note> are marked in all six figures, provided that they all come into view on that surface in which the wrist presents itself.
**II, III, IIII** In the first and second figures, the four bones of the back of the hand <note>original: *postbrachialis*; the metacarpal bones</note> are noted.

**D, E, F, I** The three bones of the index finger; and the same logic applies to the rest of the fingers.
**G, 3, 6** The cavity and seat of the fifth wrist bone, to which the first bone of the thumb is articulated. We measure the length of this cavity transversely in the sixth figure from **a** to **b**. It marks the internal seat **c**, and the external **d**. And **d** indeed leads into the fourth.
**H, 3, 4, 6** The seat of the sixth wrist bone, to which the metacarpal bone supporting the index finger is joined. **h** truly marks the seat of the index finger on the fifth bone, where the metacarpal bone touches the sixth bone of the wrist.

BY HIPPOCRATES, as also occasionally by Galen, the "hand" (or rather *akrocheir* <note>Greek: ἀκροχειρ, meaning the extremity of the hand</note>) was the name given to what we commonly call the arm, when we say a man is endowed with legs and arms—namely, that whole part which extends from the shoulder blade to the very tips of the fingers and nails. But what is called the "hand" by almost all Latins, which we measure from the lowest part of the forearm and that loose joint joining the hand to the forearm, was called by Hippocrates the "highest hand" <note>original: *summam manum*</note>. This distinction, although perhaps convenient for the Greeks, cannot be of use everywhere for those writing in Latin. Therefore, dividing the hand only into the wrist <note>original: *brachiale*; carpus</note>, the back of the hand <note>original: *postbrachiale*; metacarpus</note>, and the fingers, we shall assign to each of its parts its own chapters, being about to describe in the present one that part which is joined to the forearm.

<margin>The wrist bone, and its bones differing in form among themselves.</margin>
It is constructed of eight bones distinguished in a double row: which in those of older age are hard and small, and slightly spongy inside, filled with a moderate amount of marrow in the manner of attachments; but they are not entirely devoid of marrow, as it has seemed to some, especially those larger ones which occur among them. For they do not all obtain an equal size, nor shape, nor position; since among them all there is none which corresponds entirely to another, and each individually acquires something by which they can be discerned from one another. Furthermore, however varied they may be, they are nevertheless mutually adapted so neatly, and approach such a harmony of composition, that their number is not very easy to find. For unless the strongest cartilaginous ligaments with which they are covered, together with the membranes...

If you were to cut away the membranes and accurately scrape them away, all these parts would appear to you as one, or you might think, along with Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman medical writer</note>, that they consist of a smaller number and are born together as one.

Furthermore, all these parts, bound together by these sinewy and cartilaginous connections, form two complete surfaces: on the outer region, as much as is useful for the hand, it is convex; but on the inner region, it is hollowed out.

<margin>g figure.</margin>

<margin>Why there are two rows of wrist bones.</margin>
The surfaces are bound by ligaments. For above, where the bones are joined to the forearm <term>cubito</term> <note>Vesalius uses 'cubitus' to refer generally to the forearm or the ulna specifically depending on context; here it refers to the forearm joint</note>, they are smooth and encrusted with cartilage, just as they are below, where they are articulated with the bones of the back of the hand <term>postbrachialis</term> <note>the metacarpals</note> and the first bone of the thumb. Moreover, where the bones touch each other, they are provided with smooth ends and small heads encrusted with slippery cartilage, by which they are articulated in turn. Indeed, in the mutual contact of none of the wrist bones do membranes or ligaments intervene, except in the connection of the bones of the lower row among themselves, where something—though hardly worthy of notice—of a cartilaginous ligament intervenes like a small point. Thus, the lower bones are not as closely bound together as the upper ones. Nature has achieved this with good reason, fashioning two rows of wrist bones primarily because the upper row had to be joined to the forearm, while the lower row had to be joined to the metacarpals and the first bone of the thumb in an entirely different manner. For it articulates with these as distinct and separate bones, whereas with the forearm, it meets the difficulty of a single bone. Some believe the wrist is composed of many bones to endure injuries, so that by yielding, they dissipate the force of impacts on the joints—in the same way we see that a loose spear or arrow is harder to penetrate than one held tense. However, we also observe that this strength and abundance of bones was constructed by Nature not least for the innumerable differences in the movements of the hand.

<margin>Names of the wrist bones.</margin>
<margin>The joint of the wrist to the forearm.</margin>
There are four bones in the upper row of the wrist which we have examined toward the forearm. We shall assign names to them not without reason, based on the sequence in which they are arranged: always calling the "first" that which occupies the inner side of the upper row; the "second" that which follows it; the "third" that which is next to the second toward the outer side; and the "fourth" that which occupies the outer side entirely. Likewise, in the [lower row], we shall name them the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth, and in this manner, we shall begin the history of each. Thus, the first row, joined together, forms the upper seat of the wrist so that, like a single wide bone with a transversely oblong head, they are neatly articulated into the cavity of the radius. And indeed, the first and second are placed in the cavity carved into the appendage of the radius; but the third rests on the cartilage which, as we have written, arises from the radius and for the most part separates the ulna from the wrist. Although the outer side of the third bone also touches the sharp process of the appendage of the ulna <note>the styloid process</note> when we tilt the hand toward the outer side. But meanwhile, that third bone, covered in cartilage, can be distinguished in man; it does not possess that process for itself, since even that process—unless it bulges out along the side of the cavity where the wrist is constricted—can be lightly discerned if one attempts to insert the tip of the thumb of the other hand between the wrist and the ulna while the hand is drawn toward the inner side.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>To which bone it is joined.</margin> Next, a tendon of the muscle that is the lower of those flexing the wrist <gloss>x 4th muscle, table 4.</gloss> is inserted into the upper seat of the fourth bone <note>The pisiform bone</note>. From its lower seat, however, a muscle arises <gloss>y 3rd muscle, table 7.</gloss> whose origin takes a portion from here, which is considered the outer of the two muscles flexing the first bone of the little finger <gloss>z 4th, table 1.</gloss>. Thus, this fourth bone is joined to no other bone at its lower or upper seat, nor even on its outer side; but only on its inner side, by a very depressed small head, is it articulated to the outer side of the third bone (larger than the palm) in that manner by which we said bones are constructed through entirely flat surfaces, smeared meanwhile with slippery cartilage. Therefore, this fourth bone of the wrist claims this as its own peculiarity: that it is joined to only one bone of the wrist, and that it is the smallest of all the wrist bones, and protrudes and curves less than the others. For it is somewhat spherical, but a little longer than it is thick: namely because it receives the insertion of a muscle below and a very strong tendon above, as we said, and for that reason it had to protrude more upward and downward than to the sides. Whence also the ancient professors of dissection (as I conjecture) called it the *Rectum* <note>Latin: "Straight"</note>, being uncertain into which row they should refer it.

<margin>To which row it should be assigned.</margin> Now, we have assigned it to the upper row, because the anatomists also assigned this present bone to the third row; <margin>Marinus* <gloss>a 1, 2 fig. chapter 36.</gloss></margin> not otherwise than Marinus gave that name to the bone placed before the knee joint, which we call the *mola* or *patella* <note>The kneecap</note>. Certainly not (as far as I think) because they thought that bone was soft or entirely cartilaginous, since it is easily the hardest and most solid of all the wrist bones; but because when cooked, it is seen to be covered on the outside with cartilage, on account of the beginnings of the envelopes and the ends of the tendons, which after boiling take on the appearance of a somewhat soft cartilage. <gloss>explanation 12. and of the whole</gloss>

<margin>Book 2, On the Use of the Parts.</margin> Galen seems to have counted this bone as the eighth bone of the wrist, attributing to it the specific property of being a bulwark for a certain nerve, which is reflected from the inner seat of the hand to the outer according to that wrist bone. This nerve is not hidden from me, but in humans it is not revolved around this little bone. For that is the nerve which you will hear of in the fourth book, which seeks the arm from the fifth pair <gloss>b 2 book 4 chapter on the radius 46.</gloss>, a little after the middle of the length of the ulna, extending from the inner seat of the ulna into the posterior part, and deriving two small forks to the little finger, the same number to the ring finger, and one to the middle finger. Furthermore, besides the fourth bone of the wrist, there is none entirely hidden or annexed and contiguous to many bones.

<margin>How many bones the first bone borders.</margin> For the first bone <note>The scaphoid</note>, besides the fact that it is articulated with the radius, is also joined to the second bone of the wrist, entering into a sinus <note>A cavity or depression</note> of the second bone with a somewhat large head. Then, by another much larger head produced from its lower seat, it enters a common sinus which the fifth bone of the wrist forms with the sixth. But Nature, taking care lest the first bone should enter the various sinuses of other bones while it itself, like a tyrant, received none, carved a remarkable sinus in it, by which (together with the second wrist bone, to which this sinus is also common) it might admit the large and round head of the seventh bone, easily the largest of all. And so the first bone is joined to the radius, and to the second, fifth, sixth, and seventh bones of the wrist.

<margin>How many the second.</margin> The second bone <note>The lunate</note> (which is as much smaller than the first as it is larger than the third) is connected to the first bone and the seventh, as we have already said. To the third, however, it is bound by a large connection with flat surfaces: so that the second bone is joined to the radius and to three bones of the wrist: namely the first, seventh, and third; nor is it moved far from the eighth.

<margin>How many the third.</margin> The third bone <note>The triquetrum</note>, to which we have already said the fourth is articulated, enters the sinus of the eighth bone with a moderately protruding but large head; and from this it is easily established that this bone is joined to the ulna, and even more to the peculiar cartilage of this joint, then also to the second bone of the wrist, <gloss>c 2, 24 Table and the fourth</gloss>

The post-brachial bones are therefore longer than the remaining bones of the fingers, and for the most part are rounded. The longest and thickest is placed before the index finger, and thus they gradually become shorter and thinner, so that the shortest of all is easily the one placed before the little finger. But because the bone supporting the index finger is articulated more superiorly to the brachial, or by its connection there approaches closer to the cubit <note>ulna/forearm</note> than the bone placed before the middle finger, this appears deservedly longer in the intact hand, and is led further downward toward the digits.
<margin>In the appendices <note>epiphyses</note>.</margin>

<margin>In mutual connection.</margin>
Moreover, the appendices touch each other at the sides, and are bound together by the intervention of a cartilaginous ligament. The inferior appendices serve the bones with a conspicuous connection, and are quite large and round, and they end in an oblong head from the external side of the hand to the internal: which, covered with cartilage, enters the hollow of the first bone of the fingers. These also touch at the sides, but not as closely as the superior ones. # THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.

<image-desc>An initial capital 'M' depicting a man working at a table or workbench, possibly dissecting or studying, with tools and objects around him. Another figure is partially visible behind him.</image-desc>

<margin>a In figures 1 and 2 of chapter 25, the bones of the thumb are marked A, B, C; those of the index finger are D, E, F. The pattern is the same for the rest.</margin>
<margin>b This appearance, where all the bones occur together in their proper series.</margin>
<margin>c That the individual fingers are rightly formed of three bones.</margin>
<margin>d Their appropriate size.</margin>

**W**e reviewed in the previous chapter that all the fingers of the hand<gloss>a</gloss> consist of three bones, arranged in an excellent series like<gloss>c</gloss> a line of battle or a rank of soldiers. That they ought to have been constructed with neither more nor fewer bones is readily gathered from this: if the bones exceeded that number, they would impair that perfect and powerful extension by which we use the hand as a single unit, making it less firm than it is now. Conversely, if the fingers were formed of fewer bones, we would be unable to move them into such varied and opposing shapes. Because the bone placed before <note>the metacarpal</note> is primarily responsible for tapering the fingers from a wider base gradually into a point. Nature had no less regard for the number and size of the finger bones than for the fingers as a whole, which we see are rightly constructed as five because of the duties they perform: four of these are placed in one row, while one large one is positioned somewhat opposite them, acting as a sort of "fore-hand" (hence it is called *anticheir* <note>original: ἀντίχειρ</note> by the Greeks, just as it is called *pollex* by us from its power <note>Vesalius links "pollex" (thumb) to "pollere" (to be powerful)</note>). Likewise, we see the fingers differ from one another in mass and strength just as their duties mutually vary. We observe why they are unequal in length whenever we grasp a round body, or when we hold something in the hand with the fingers interlaced, or when we thrust the fingers joined and extended into something. 

Furthermore, the more diligently we express the use of the hands along with their description, the more it will be established that the finger bones do not possess the exact same form as the whole fingers do when covered by skin and nails and possessing a somewhat hard fat. This fat, filled with nerves, is placed beneath the skin on the sides of the fingers and in even greater abundance on their inner surfaces. 

<margin>e These things are proposed by a healthy and dim hand.</margin>
<margin>f What the form of the whole fingers is.</margin>
<margin>g How the bones of the fingers vary in form from the whole fingers above and below, and what the substance of the bones is like.</margin>

For the whole fingers are formed to be almost entirely cylindrical, because such a shape is least liable to injuries. However, they are not so accurately and precisely cylindrical on their inner side as on the outer, because regard for warding off injuries had to be held only for the outer side. The inner side, however, softens, handles, rubs, and grasps; all of which would be performed less effectively if they were made cylindrical here. Additionally, since the fingers are less exposed to harm on their sides, and since they must be drawn together and constricted on various occasions without leaving any empty space in their middle, it was by no means useful for them to be cylindrical on the sides. Hence the thumb acquires a cylindrical shape on both sides (but more on the inner), the little finger only on the outer, and the index finger, by contrast, on the inner; because in these places those fingers do not touch others, and they correspond almost to the outer part of the fingers as far as warding off injuries is concerned. Furthermore, no finger bone presents itself that is not thicker and wider at the top and bottom than along its length; this is seen to be common to almost all long bones, which perpetually thicken and increase toward the articulation <term>articulation: the joint where two bones meet</term>. For if they were of equal thickness everywhere as they are at the joints, they would greatly inconvenience a man with their weight and bulk. And the joints themselves, unless they were neatly adapted to wider bases and were no larger than the rest of the bones...

<margin>Nature's purpose in the finger joints.</margin>
However, on the upper surface of the first of the four finger bones <note>the proximal phalanges</note>, the carving is somewhat circular, and it is first flexed and extended over that head <note>the metacarpal head</note>; movements to the sides are not as notable as flexion, nor are they performed at such acute angles, because the head of the post-brachial bone <note>the metacarpal</note> is only slightly depressed on the outside and at the sides. Yet, the more that head is covered with cartilage on the outside than the heads of the second and third joints, the more the first joints can be extended beyond a straight line compared to the second and third. Just as the index finger is inclined more toward the inner side, and the little finger toward the outer side than the other fingers: because the heads of their first joints are extended toward those sides and dilated as if into a circle. Thus, the industry of Nature is singular wherever it is encountered, so solicitously providing for the strength of the parts that she did not wish the first joints to be rotated, since the movements of the hand or the radius into pronation and supination <note>turning the palm down or up</note> accommodate the rotation of the fingers without needing them to circle on their own. Furthermore, just as those movements, together with the rotation of the shoulder at the scapula, ensure that we have less need for equal extension and flexion of the fingers: so, since we can move the first joints of the fingers to the sides, there is no need for the second and third joints to be so loosely composed that they possess the same movement. And so, the more diligently I weigh these things—which indeed propose one craftsmanship of Nature after another—the more I wonder at Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius often challenged</note> in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, for having compared all the joints of the fingers to a nearly mutual entry: and in his book *On Bones* for attributing the same species of joint to all the bones, when he says the head of the upper bone enters the cavity of the following one, just as if he had thought all the joints were joined together in the same way in their articulation. Then, in his books *On Anatomical Procedures*, he sets forth the history of the muscles everywhere so contrary to the decrees of the ancients, that he attributes the tendons leading the fingers to the sides no less to the second and third bones of the fingers than to the first. However it may be, either by reason of the joints, the bones of the fingers vary greatly from the image of the whole fingers. And

Meanwhile, although the bones of the fingers are rounded on their outer surface, they are drawn from the joint where they meet the second bones toward their very tips. They do not occupy the surface of the nail in the same way, specifically so that the entire finger does not protrude further at the third bone than at the others; rather, yielding to the nails, they protrude less in proportion to the space the nails occupy, so that the entire finger does not rise higher at the third bone than at the remaining bones.

<margin>What kind of sides they have.</margin>
The sides of the first bone of the thumb, as well as the sides of the third bones, are somewhat rounded. However, the sides of the first bones, which are in the four fingers, correspond to the side of a half-part that would be cut through the middle of a rounded body: because surely those bones ought to be flat on the internal surface and convex on the external. Nor do the sides of the bones of the thumb, index, and little finger claim anything for themselves privately here (as the whole fingers otherwise do): so much so that Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the ancient Greek physician whose anatomical theories Vesalius often corrected.</note> seems to propose the form of the whole fingers and of these same bones less than correctly.

### ON THE TINY BONES WHICH ARE COMPARED TO SESAME SEEDS. Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>What sort of things the sesame-like bones are.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorated initial 'P' depicting a scene with several figures, possibly mythological or allegorical, surrounding a central figure or object.</image-desc> **B**EYOND the bones explained in the three immediately preceding Chapters, certain other tiny ones occur in the hand, <gloss>a *See figure of chapter 25, T, V, and X, X.*</gloss> compared by those skilled in dissection to the sesame seed <note>The term "sesamoid" comes from the Greek 'sesame' and 'eidos' (form/shape).</note>. However, what sort of things they are, and in what locations, and in what number they are placed in man, or even in the ape, I know of no one who has observed or described. And even less has the use of those tiny bones been treated exactly and truly by anyone. Opportunely, therefore, I shall here follow up on how many bones of this kind I have found so far by a diligent examination of the muscles and tendons. For by the inspection of the muscles more than the bones, I have discovered a not-regrettable number of the present tiny bones, as much in the foot as in the hand: since for the most part, and almost entirely, they are born in the tendons, and with only one surface, encrusted with smooth and slippery cartilage, they touch the slippery and smooth seat of some other bone, being nowhere joined to that bone by peculiar ligaments. Just as we see the bone of the knee,

<margin>The structure of the kneecap. ...polished, and called the patella by us, seen born in certain tendons extending the shin. Indeed, one could not more readily derive the constitution of the sesamoid bones from elsewhere.</margin>
<margin>b figure of chapter 12 on muscles, table * and 8th muscle table, h.</margin>
polished in its joint and called the <term>patella</term> <note>The kneecap.</note> by us, born in certain tendons that extend the shin. Indeed, you could not more readily seek the constitution of the sesamoid bones from anywhere else than from the structure of the patella. For these tiny bones seem immersed and born in the tendons, so that by their hardness they may sustain and receive the impact of the bone in certain movements, for which a tendon of this kind, increased and fortified by the tiny bone, is placed in front. Since they repress that impact of the bone, one might also not undeservedly think that they contribute to this very thing: that the bone they are placed before does not easily leap out of its joint: so much so that the patella, being a bone far larger than the sesamoids, skillfully shows their nature. Moreover, these are seen to be more significant, and in a way more numerous, the older and more exhausted the human body you employ for dissection. For in children they are still cartilaginous, and not very much in their own tendons, by which they are contained...

However, of all these, none is as large and hard as the inner little bone of the two seen at the first joint of the big toe. For this reason, I suspect that the magi and followers of occult philosophy <note>Vesalius is likely referring to practitioners of the Kabbalah or medieval alchemy</note> were mindful of this bone when they taught that there is a certain hard bone in man, subject to no corruption, and resembling a chickpea in appearance. For that little bone of the foot is located in the lowest seat of man and is remarkably hard; although it yields in hardness to the teeth, it is no less subject to corruption than the teeth themselves. Furthermore, the eighth bone of the wrist <note>The pisiform bone</note> expresses the likeness of a chickpea better than this little bone of the foot does. Whether, however, the Arabs and those truly occult and shadowy philosophers claim that man is propagated again from this little bone—called by them the *Albadaran* <note>original: "Albadaran"; likely a reference to the 'Luz' bone of Jewish and Islamic tradition</note>—is a matter for their own discussion and opinion regarding the resurrection, the immortality of souls, and the final outcome.

For in the higher seat of the hip bone, a wide notch is cut, which in a cleaned bone is seen to be filled with certain holes so that it may bring forth a ligament; by its benefit, the bone there is seen to be smooth, slippery, and as if anointed with oil, so that the seventh muscle of the thigh, together with the tendon of the sixth muscle, can be reflected and rolled around this notch correctly.

<margin>q 4th muscle table o.</margin>
<margin>r S is placed in the first six figures of the notch.</margin>
<margin>The protuberances of this notch.</margin>
On both sides of the lateral parts of that notch, a notable <term>tuber</term><note>A rounded swelling or protuberance on a bone.</note> stands out, enlarging the notch and preventing these descending muscles from declining out of it, which is convenient. Then, the tuber standing at the external side of the notch, common to both the ilium and the hip bone, specifically produces the ninth muscle of those moving the <term>tibia</term><note>The shin bone.</note>; for the sake of its use, it appears somewhat wide and unequal, claiming for itself a small notch like a slit. From this, that muscle—which necessarily had to be thick and strong, both for the sake of the joint's strength and because it had to be carved from the deepest notch of the whole body (as we shall soon say) where the femur is articulated—takes its origin.

<margin>S 3rd figure M, N, O.</margin>
<margin>t 6th muscle table F, G, H; 13th table r.</margin>
<margin>How the strength of the hip bone is provided for.</margin>
And on the occasion of this use, the ilium bone is rendered thick and strong in its internal seat at the higher region of its connection with the <term>sacrum</term><note>The triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>, and it is extended like a continuous protuberance to the internal notch of the internal tuber. This not only increases the strength of the hip bone but also offers a beginning for the tenth muscle of those moving the thigh, which, occupying the internal seat of the bone there and also arising from the entire internal seat of the hip bone, turns the femur outward.

<margin>u 1, 2 figures g. c, f, g.</margin>
<margin>x 1, 2 figures g.</margin>
