<margin>a 1, 2 figures b.</margin>
<margin>b figure of chapter 6, book 5, placed at n.</margin>
<margin>The acetabulum prepared for articulating the femur.</margin>
Therefore, in the external seat of the hip bone (whose strength Nature has so solicitously provided for), a wide and round notch is carved, the deepest of all the notches in the body to which bones are articulated. It is called the <term>acetabulum</term><note>Literally "vinegar cup"; the socket of the hip bone.</note>. It is not smooth in every part nor encrusted with slippery cartilage. For in the anterior seat, a significant portion of it is cut deeper than the rest of its circumference and is seen to be rough and filled with certain small cut holes for the sake of producing a ligament, which, being round, is inserted into the summit of the head of the femur. Furthermore, the "eyebrows" <note>The rim or margin of the socket.</note> of the present notch, which we have seen formed as an <term>appendage</term><note>An epiphysis or separate bone growth in children.</note> in some young children, protrude more lightly in the anterior seat than in the posterior, because the thigh must be bent more into an angle when sitting than extended or drawn backward when standing or doing something else. Moreover, in the lower seat of the hip notch or the eyebrows of the acetabulum, it must also be noticed that the eyebrows are not carried in a continuous circular path, but are cut and interrupted, as if to prepare a way for a small vein extended here into the rough seat of the acetabulum (which is not covered by cartilage). This vein supplies nourishment to the joint, from which a viscous humor <note>Synovial fluid, which lubricates the joints.</note> is adapted, by whose help the joint becomes readily mobile. Lest the joint be rendered too subject to dislocation by reason of this cut in the eyebrow of the notch, Nature has attached a strong and cartilaginous ligament in a circle to the eyebrows. This appears nowhere interrupted and increases the acetabulum even more than the eyebrows do, and provides a path for that small vein creeping safely between the bone and the posterior seat of the ligament itself. Furthermore, one must now also weigh the "blind" small holes prepared everywhere in the external seat of the eyebrows of the hip bone's acetabulum for this purpose, that they may bring forth <insert>the strongest [ligaments]</insert>.

<margin>Why the pubic bone is pierced by the largest opening, and regarding its cavity and protuberances.</margin>
To put it briefly, these structures form a convenient seat for carrying the fetus. However, I do not believe that the pubic bones of newborn girls are separated for the sake of an easier birth among any race of people <note>Vesalius is debunking a contemporary myth that certain ethnicities had different pelvic bone structures to facilitate childbirth</note>, despite how persistently the common folk affirm this now of these nations, now of those. Now, as to why the pubic bone is pierced by the largest opening of all the bones in the body (which, because of its size, is called *thyroeides* <note>original: "βυγοειδὴς" (likely a typesetter's error for θυρεοειδής), meaning "shield-shaped" or "door-like"</note> from its appearance), those finally understand who have learned with precision during dissection which muscles take their origin from the bones of the hip <term>coxendix: the ischium or hip bone</term> and the pubis.

The process of the femur <note>The greater trochanter</note>, on its inner side where it faces the head of the femur, shows a rough and uneven cavity, into which the ninth and tenth muscles moving the femur are inserted. Its outer side, however, is convex, and in bony men <note>Those with little body fat</note> and those advanced in age, it presents four impressions or seats, prepared to receive the insertions of four muscles. And indeed, the **first** is large and appears convex on the posterior side of the process, where the insertion of the first muscle moving the femur is implanted. From the root of this compression, a certain rough *line* is drawn downwards somewhat obliquely through the back of the femur, into which that first muscle moving the femur is also very strongly inserted. The **second** compression consists on the anterior side of the process, more unequal and rough than the first, and somewhat curved, and finally receives the insertion of the second muscle responsible for the movements of the femur. The **third** is seen at the upper region of the process, standing between the higher seats of the first and second. This is convex and admits the insertion of the third muscle moving the femur. The **fourth** presents itself at the apex of the process, far narrower than the other three, and receiving the tendon of the fourth muscle moving the femur. The exterior process takes the insertion of these muscles, but from its very root on its anterior and external side, it provides the origin for a muscle which will be reviewed as the seventh of the movers of the <term>tibia</term> <note>The shin bone</note>.

As for what pertains to the rest of the form of the femur, the whole femur on its anterior side and on its sides is rounded and somewhat smooth, surrounded on all sides by the eighth muscle moving the tibia: for the sake of which the anterior side of the femur near the root of its neck is somewhat large and rough, so that that muscle might arise more strongly and from a larger beginning. On the posterior side, however, the femur is brought to a sort of sharp edge, and shows a remarkably protruding line, rough and uneven, which creeps from the root of the femoral processes to some distance beyond the middle of the length of the femur. Into this line the fifth muscle moving the femur is tenaciously inserted: and it is only this part, out of the rest of the breadth of the femur, that is not surrounded by the eighth muscle moving the tibia. Furthermore, at the lower part of this line, and near the root of the lower heads of the femur, the femur is seen to be broad and flattened, not rounded, so that the very large vein seeking the tibia, along with the artery and nerve, may be carried more safely: and lest, if the femur were convex here, they might wander and decline from the femur. 

Although also for the sake of lightness, Nature did not want this part of the femur—which necessarily had to broaden at the sides for the sake of bringing out its lower heads—to be rounded and prominent on the posterior side, since it serves the extension or insertion of no muscles there, and is not exposed to injuries, and is in a way hedged in by the lower heads of the femur being led backwards. Indeed, it is most pleasant to see how Nature, besides the function and chief use of the parts, has everywhere taken account of strength and lightness at the same time; she also communicated to the femur a long and large cavity along its length, which, filled with marrow, makes this largest bone of the body quite light for its mass. 

Furthermore, the path of the femur is not directed downward in a straight line from the <term>acetabulum</term> <note>The hip socket</note> of the hip bone: but the neck of the femur is carried from its head very far outward obliquely, and as if transversely, and from here the femur again proceeds with the rest of its body descending obliquely toward the interior to the knee. Nature did not devise this shape by chance: since all those to whom it happens from their first formation that the femur is straighter than is useful for a man, are rendered knock-kneed and lame in the knee. How harmful this is, not only for running but for walking and standing firmly, we learn by seeing it daily. Then, if the neck of each femur did not immediately from the hip joint...

<summary>Vesalius describes the specific muscle attachment points on the greater trochanter and the shaft of the femur, noting how the bone's shape accommodates blood vessels and nerves. He emphasizes Nature's design in balancing strength with lightness and the necessity of the femur's oblique angle for proper human gait.</summary>

joint, as we have said, were it to project outward, what place would remain for the internal muscles embracing the thigh? What space would be left for the nerves, veins, and arteries distributed throughout the whole leg? What, likewise, for the glands <note>The author likely refers to lymph nodes or protective fatty tissues</note> appointed for the protection of these vessels? For it was not fitting for them to descend through the external regions, since they would be exposed to injury from every slight occurrence in all outward encounters. Furthermore, the posterior part of the thigh is seen to be flat and hollow; the anterior part, however, is rounded <note>original: "gibba," meaning convex or hunched</note>, because this shape of the thigh is very suitable for sitting, as well as for the many tasks we perform while seated—namely, when we cross one thigh over the other. I shall remain silent for now on how elegantly the thigh yields to the muscles occupying its posterior region.

### Index of the Figures and their Characters for the Thirty-First Chapter.

The eleven figures of this chapter represent the right leg. The first figure expresses both bones located in the leg from the anterior <note>front</note> view: namely the thicker, inner one which we shall call the **tibia** <note>the shinbone</note>; and the more slender one, placed on the outside, which we shall call the **fibula** <note>the calf bone</note> rather than the *sura*. The second figure shows the tibia together with the fibula from the posterior <note>back</note> view. In the third, the anterior surface of the tibia alone is demonstrated. The fourth subjects the posterior surface of the tibia to view. The fifth expresses the fibula from the anterior view. The sixth shows the fibula drawn from the posterior side. The seventh shows the upper surface of the tibia, with which the **femur** <note>thigh bone</note> is articulated. The eighth contains the two **cartilages** <note>the menisci</note> which enlarge the cavities in which the heads of the femur are received at the ends of the tibia. The ninth presents the lowest part of the tibia from the anterior side, so that the cavity prepared for the articulation of the **talus** <note>ankle bone</note> with the tibia might come into view. The tenth offers only the lowest surface of the tibia drawn from the posterior part, by which the talus is received. The eleventh demonstrates the inner side of the lower part of the fibula, which articulates with the talus. The index of characters shall be of this sort:

<margin>The appendages of the tibia and fibula.</margin>
The tibia and fibula, which contain long cavities for the preservation of marrow, each have an appendix <note>An "appendix" here refers to the epiphysis or the distinct bony ends of a long bone</note> fused to them above and below. The upper appendix of the tibia <margin>The appendages of the tibia first, A, B</margin> is quite thick and wide, and is drawn further downward on its anterior side than on its posterior side. <margin>1, 3 fig.</margin> <margin>The surface where the femur articulates.</margin> Into this [appendix], * two oblong cavities are carved, <margin>D 1, 3 fig.</margin> separated from each other by a sort of hump and encrusted with slippery cartilage, in which the lower heads of the femur are received. This hump, which separates the cavities, [corresponds to the space] dividing the lower and posterior heads of the femur. <margin>C 1, 5 fig.</margin> Furthermore, from the upper and middle part of this hump—which is seen to be rough and pitted, and not coated with any cartilage—a very strong ligament <note>The cruciate ligaments of the knee</note> is sent forth; <margin>furthermore E</margin> it is inserted into the interval or cavity between the aforementioned heads of the femur, primarily at its posterior side. <margin>1, 3 fig. B.</margin> Indeed, the middle part of this hump is rough and pitted for this reason: so that the ligaments may more successfully reach into the femur, <margin>* 2, 4, 7 fig. F, G.</margin> leading out from its most protruding part and then from its posterior region. <margin>7 fig. H.</margin> For from the anterior region of the hump, which protrudes the least, <margin>I, K.</margin> even though it is similarly rough and widely pitted, no ligament is inserted into the femur; instead, ligaments are produced there which bind the cartilages to the anterior part of this hump, <margin>chap. 1, 2 fig. E, F.</margin> which I shall now say increase the cavities of the tibia. <margin>Cartilages by which the cavities of the tibia are enlarged.</margin> For since the two cavities of the tibia that admit the heads of the femur are carved out somewhat superficially, and do not exactly match the humps of the femoral heads, [Nature] has increased the depth of the cavities. <margin>1 fig. 10 chap. 1.</margin> <margin>Book 3 on the Use of the Parts & in the commentaries on Hippocrates' book on fractures.</margin> Indeed, besides the slippery cartilages spread like a crust over the cavities of the tibia and the heads of the femur, she <note>Nature</note> applied one cartilage to each cavity, <margin>2, 3, 4, 7 fig. 1.</margin> connected neither to the femur nor to the tibia except by a ligamentous connection. <margin>fig. 1, chap. lib. 3 X.</margin> For these [cartilages] <note>The menisci</note> grow only to the ligaments encircling the knee joint in a ring, and furthermore, by the intervention of a ligament, they are connected to the anterior and posterior parts of the hump that divides the cavities of the tibia receiving the femoral heads. <margin>2, 4, 7 fig. K.</margin> These cartilages are exactly softer than simple cartilage, and participate as it were in the nature of a ligament. <margin>7 fig. H.</margin> Then, because they are applied to themselves, they are seen to be exceedingly equal, slippery, smooth, and finally smeared with an oily humor. <margin>all S</margin> To this end, they are thick at the circuit of the joint, and end much thinned out before the center of the cavities. <margin>8 fig.</margin> Their shape is indeed lunar <note>Crescent-shaped</note>, just like the inner side of the internal cavity and the outer side of the external cavity. <margin>8 fig. O.</margin> Furthermore, they are nowhere thicker than at the center of the side; where they approach the parts distinguishing the anterior and posterior hump of the tibial cavities, they are very thin and end in sharp points. <margin>1 fig. 8 Q</margin> Those points which are joined to the anterior part of that hump are close to each other, and the right cartilage is bound to the left there. But the points approaching the posterior part of the hump are more distant from each other, nor are they joined together like the anterior ones. For a very thick ligament, inserted from the hump into the femur, separates the posterior points of the cartilages. Since these things are so, it is easily gathered how neatly, by the help of these cartilages, the hollowness of the tibial cavities is increased, not only in humans, but in all quadrupeds and birds I have seen so far. For in these, similar cartilages are also placed in the knee joint. Whence it is very easy for anyone to be acquainted with their nature even at the dinner table, provided they inspect the knee joint exactly; <margin>Book on the common gait of animals.</margin> and not [err] everywhere with Aristotle, and Galen in the third book of *On the Use of the Parts*, regarding the knee of quadrupeds, or the end of the fibula where the lower part of the tibia is joined to their talus <note>Ankle bone</note>. <margin>The connection of the fibula to the tibia.</margin> And in this way indeed the tibia is articulated to the femur. But the fibula does not climb so high as to touch the femur; rather, its upper appendix bears on its inner side a large and very slightly indented cavity, to which a very small protruding...

For the fibula, a little below the middle of the length of the tibia, is curved somewhat inward and toward the tibia, and on its outer side is rendered <term>sima</term><note>Flat-nosed or concave.</note> or hollow. However, I shall describe the course of the tibia and fibula, and the lines and impressions protruding through their length, more opportunely only when I have fully explained their upper and lower parts by which they are joined to other bones. Therefore, the upper appendix of the tibia is joined to the femur and fibula in the manner I have described. And its front and long part, together with the front part of the tibia nearest the appendix—called by many of the Greeks *sphurokneme* <note>original: "σφυροκνημη" - literally "ankle-leg," referring here to the shin or the region of the tibial tuberosity.</note>—is seen to be rough and rather prominent, so that it might receive the strongest tendons of the muscles moving the leg. For the sake of these tendons, the upper appendix of the fibula also protrudes remarkably on its outer side and upper part, to receive the very robust tendon of the fourth muscle moving the tibia; besides the fact that this part of the fibula gives rise to the head of the seventh muscle moving the foot. 

The lower appendices of the tibia and fibula together form a cavity and seat into which the <term>talus</term><note>The ankle bone.</note> is articulated as if by a mutual entry. For in the lowest part of the appendix of the tibia, a wide and in a certain way double cavity is carved. For in its middle part, it is divided by a wide but moderately prominent bump, and is hollowed out more deeply at the sides of that bump. At the inner side of this cavity, the lower appendix of the tibia is carried downward by a strong and large process, which on its outer side (where it faces the cavity) is hollow, and like the cavity itself is smooth and encrusted with cartilage. On the inner side, however, facing the other leg, it is convex, and since it is without flesh and covered by no muscular parts, it is easily perceived in us by touch, and is the **inner malleolus** <note>The inner ankle bone.</note>. This process, in its lowest part toward the rear, possesses a rough cavity from which it produces a cartilaginous ligament, binding the tibia to the talus. And for the sake of producing such a ligament, the front part of the lower appendix of the tibia, in its human part, also presents a transverse, oblong, rough, and unequal cavity, from which a ligament comes forth, connecting the neck of the tibia to the talus. The rear part of this appendix, where it first gives rise to the inner malleolus, is depressed and shows channels which, covered by transverse ligaments, allow the tendons of the muscles approaching the foot here to be carried safely, lest they wander from their paths. These are three in number: namely, the fifth of those moving the foot, and two serving the flexion of the toes. Furthermore, the outer side of the lower appendix of the tibia gives rise to no process corresponding to the inner malleolus; but rather

The appendix <note>The epiphysis or bony outgrowth</note> of the fibula <note>The outer, thinner bone of the lower leg</note> attached to the outer side of the tibia bone <note>The shinbone</note> becomes significantly thicker here, and the malleolus <note>The bony prominence of the ankle</note> is carried further down than the internal one. This is the reason why the talus <note>The ankle bone</note> is more rarely dislocated toward the outer side of the foot than toward the inner side. For the fibula descends here as much lower than the tibia itself as the tibia reaches higher toward the femur <note>The thigh bone</note> above; so much so that the fibula is not surpassed by the tibia in length by even the smallest amount. This lower appendix of the fibula constitutes the outer side of the cavity that receives the talus. However, the appendix protrudes so much on its inner side and is encrusted with cartilage that one might rightly say it is supported by the talus rather than receiving it. Even if it appropriately covers the outer side of the talus and in that manner, together with the inner malleolus, grips the talus so that in healthy men the talus can nowhere be touched.

<margin>The talus does not occur alone before itself.</margin>
<margin>Compare the figure of the whole bone expressing the structure of the bone in the muscle tables of the foot.</margin>
For the appendix of the tibia bone, embracing its upper internal surface, also covers its outer side. The fibula, moreover, by its lower appendix, occupies the outer side of the talus: the front seat of the talus, which is visible in a bare skeleton, is hidden by tendons led through the upper parts of the foot to the toes. So also its posterior seat, which is no less conspicuous in bare skeletons, is covered by tendons inserted into the heel and by certain others passing under the lower parts of the foot. This lowest part of the fibula, joined to the talus and convex on its outer side, and covered by no part of a muscle at all, constitutes the outer malleolus, which Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> testifies was wrongly called the "talus" by some. And indeed, that error has flowed down even to us. For, to say nothing of others, our Erasmus of Rotterdam, in his dialogue *On the Game of Dice* <note>original: "de talorum lusu Dialogo"</note>, suggests that the malleoli in men are called "tali" along with Pliny. This so pleased some interpreters of Galen that they interpret <term>σφυρὰ</term> <note>sphura: Greek for the ankles or malleoli</note> as such. Therefore, the posterior seat of the outer malleolus shows a wide cavity which, covered by a transverse ligament, leads down the tendons of the sixth and seventh muscles moving the foot, holding them so they do not slip from their place. The inner side of the same malleolus, at its lowest seat toward the back, shows a deep and rough cavity from which a cartilaginous ligament emerges, here connecting the fibula most strongly to the talus.

<margin>The fleshless part of the fibula.</margin>
<margin>f. chapter 1. book 2. figure 8. 9. 15 figure.</margin>
<margin>h 1. 5. figure f. 1. 2. 5. 6. figure. second line 1. 2. is noted. the third however 4. 1. k first side 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. table 4. m 3 muscle table 4. n muscle table 4. o 4 table 4. p 5 table 4. q 1. 5. figure. r 6 muscle table 4. s 6 table 4.</margin>
Furthermore, out of the entire breadth of the fibula, no part of it is bare or fleshless except for the outer side of its lowest part, which is seen to be fleshless for some distance above the lower appendix of the fibula. Meanwhile, the rest of its breadth is covered by muscles, embracing the fibula in such a way that it seems to yield to them everywhere, as if toward the middle of its length. For on the front seat of the fibula, a sharp and notably protruding line appears, forming the first angle of the fibula. On the posterior seat, however, the fibula is depressed and flat, and on both sides possesses one remarkably protruding line: the internal one of which forms the second angle of the fibula, and the external one the third. By these three angles or lines, the three sides of the fibula are contained. And one side provides a suitable seat for those muscles which are carried from the front seat of the tibia into the upper parts of the foot. These are the sixth muscle of those moving the foot, then the one extending the four toes of the foot, together with the ninth of those moving the foot, and that which extends the big toe. And specifically on this first side of the fibula, it is seen to be somewhat rough, so that the eighth muscle takes its whole origin from here...

On this part, the lower surface of the kneecap faces the bone of the shin <note>the tibia</note>, and it leads out a sort of process which, like its entire anterior surface, is embedded within the tendons that extend the shin. This is beautifully shown in the table of the muscles of the bones, at the character **k**, which is embedded at characters **g, h, i**. Indeed, the small holes in this part, as are visible on the anterior surface of the kneecap, are easily observed even without the help of those characters.

<margin>The position and shape of the kneecap.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate initial capital 'A' depicting a pastoral scene with figures, possibly satyrs or putti, among foliage.</image-desc>
**A**t the front of the knee <gloss>d the whole, 1, 3 figures; of the complete figures.</gloss> a certain orbicular bone is placed, not unlike a small shield. Because of the roundness of a millstone, it is called *myle* <note>original Greek: μύλη</note> by the Greeks, and from its position, *epigonatis* <note>original Greek: ἐπιγονατὶς; literally "upon the knee"</note>. On its posterior side, where it faces the thigh bone <note>the femur</note>, it is seen to be covered for the most part with smooth and slippery cartilage, elegantly fitting the suitable swelling and borders at the front of the lower heads of the thigh bone <gloss>b 2nd figure, chapter 30 H. c 2nd figure A, B.</gloss>. For along its length <gloss>c</gloss> it bulges with a wide and moderately prominent swelling, which enters the wide groove carved into the front of the heads of the thigh bone. <term>On both sides</term> of this central swelling, a single groove <gloss>d 2nd figure C, D.</gloss> is found, receiving the prominent and cartilage-encrusted surfaces of the heads of the thigh bone. But just as the outer head of the thigh bone extends further forward than the inner head, and is covered with smooth cartilage over a larger area, so indeed the outer groove of the kneecap meets the inner one. Therefore, that part of the kneecap which touches the thigh bone is seen to be smooth and slippery throughout that space. However, on its anterior surface and at the sides, it is seen to be rough and beset with certain hidden small holes. Likewise, on its posterior surface <gloss>e the whole of the 1st figure.</gloss>, where at its lowest part it is drawn downward like a sharp process <gloss>f 2nd figure e.</gloss> and looks toward the higher surface of the shin bone, it is also rough and adorned with those small holes, so that it may be more aptly and firmly embedded in the tendons extending the shin.

<margin>How the kneecap is connected to the thigh bone.</margin>
For the entire kneecap, across its whole breadth and in every place <gloss>g 2nd muscle table k.</gloss> where it is not covered by slippery cartilage, is embedded in those tendons. It is joined to neither the thigh nor the shin in any way other than by the benefit of the tendons. For the kneecap claims this uniquely for itself: it is not bound to another bone by the work of ligaments, but is born within those tendons crossing the knee joint. Emerging from them with only a single surface, it is most strongly constrained against the thigh bone.

<margin>The substance of the kneecap.</margin>
The substance of the kneecap in those of older age is exceedingly hard and solid, even though Galen <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius often challenges.</note> asserts it to be cartilaginous on the outside. Marinus also, along with other principal anatomists, asserts it to be separately cartilaginous; he even titled the chapter he dedicated to the kneecaps "On Cartilaginous Bones." And perhaps these men turned their minds to the substance of the tendons in which the kneecap is born, which, when boiled, takes on the appearance of a softish cartilage, in the manner of those parts from which the nervous heads of muscles or ligaments take their origin, or into which they are inserted. But when the kneecap is properly cleaned of the tendons, or is found alone in cemeteries, it is seen to be by no means cartilaginous, but thoroughly solid and strong. This is true not only in humans, but also in oxen, sheep, and other quadrupeds; for these also the Creator of things <note>the "Opifex" or Divine Craftsman</note> provided a kneecap at the knee joint, much longer and narrower than in humans, just as in most birds it is wider and shorter due to the shape of the lower heads of the thigh bone.

<margin>The use of the kneecap.</margin>
The kneecap is created so that the thigh bone is less easily dislocated forward during the bending of the knee or shin. But this use of the kneecap, which those skilled in dissection alone seem to have attributed to it, anyone will rightly judge to be secondary if they diligently weigh how it provides for the strength of the very powerful tendon into which it is inserted, whenever the knee is bent deeply, and the tendon itself is thereby [pushed] by the thigh bone protruding forward...

<summary>Vesalius describes the anatomy, composition, and function of the patella (kneecap), arguing against ancient authorities like Galen by asserting that the bone is solid rather than cartilaginous. He explains its role in the mechanics of the knee joint and its placement within the tendons.</summary>

<image-desc>A large ornate initial 'Q' depicts several figures, possibly engaged in an anatomical study or dissection. One figure points to a foot, while others observe or interact.</image-desc>

<margin>The similarity of quadrupeds with the legs and feet of man.</margin>

JUST AS dogs, weasels, cats, rabbits, hares, bears, monkeys, squirrels, and all quadrupeds whose feet are split into toes, obtain the same type of joint of the thigh to the hip bone, and of the thigh to the shin, as humans do: so indeed a similar connection is also discerned in the bones of the hind feet. For if you understand that the construction of the "thumb" <note>the big toe</note> of those animals differs from ours, and approaches it more or less, and that sometimes more or fewer toes fall to those animals, you will see that the human foot (to which we ascribe the ankle, the heel bone, the boat-shaped bone, four of the tarsus, five of the metatarsus, and fourteen bones of the toes, besides not a few sesamoid bones) is gifted with no bone at all which you would not find in their feet: where the foot begins in those places where Aristotle established a joint proportional to our knee in all quadrupeds. From which it is also clear how much this paradox of mine concerning the bones of quadrupeds disturbs the dogmas of Aristotle and of everyone (as is the custom of philosophers, and easily of Galen, the prince among Anatomists) concerning the common gait of animals, in the flexion, extension, and sitting of the legs, and the movement of the thighs with the back, and the erection of the body. Furthermore, I have approached the discourse on the bones of the foot from this similarity of bones in those animals with man, so that no one might immediately require of me here at the beginning what I have written on so many pages...

<margin>*Book 3 of Galen's On the Usefulness of the Parts.*</margin>

...which Galen pursues in the third book of *On the Usefulness of the Parts*, when he writes that the human foot (which is otherwise very short) is longer than the foot of quadrupeds <note>four-footed animals</note>; he is so occupied with the scattered sole, and not with the upright posture or the animals themselves, that he seems more intent on mocking Pindar <note>The Greek lyric poet</note> than on actually observing the bones. I believe, therefore, that students will hereafter compare the bones of humans, quadrupeds, and even birds with one another, investigating in what way we walk supported as if on four legs, and by what logic a cat or a dog (to say nothing of monkeys, squirrels, and running hares) sits or leans upright against a wall; and finally, they will investigate each part individually to see where they agree or differ. Thus, they may more correctly evaluate the long-discussed decrees of such great men, and, having been warned, finally recognize how manifest the similarity of these bones refutes those claims.

<margin>*The position of the TALUS, and the nature of its articulation with the tibia and fibula.*</margin>
<margin>l 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>m 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>n 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>o 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>p 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>q 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>r 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
<margin>s 1,2,3,4,5,6.</margin>
The human **talus** <note>the ankle bone</note> (which corresponds in form to the talus of dogs, bears, and similar animals endowed with paws, and is called *astragalos* or *astragalon* by the Greeks) is contained beneath the bone of the **tibia** <note>shin bone</note> and the **fibula** <note>calf bone</note>, held in a large seat by the appendages of those bones, as I reported above. For the higher part of the talus, which looks upward whenever the whole foot rests on the ground, projects as a very notable protuberance, encrusted with slippery cartilage. In the manner of that part of the nut in a reversed <term>ballista</term> <note>a Roman siege engine; Vesalius compares the joint to its mechanical trigger mechanism</note>, as we call it, it is circular and smooth, and bounded by four sides or ribs. The first and second of these run along the sides of the protuberance according to its length, as if in a circle; the third follows the front boundary of the protuberance, and the fourth follows the rear. Thus, this protuberance of the talus is in a way quadrangular, and for that reason it is called *tetroron* <note>original Greek: τέτρωρον, meaning four-sided</note> by the Greeks, and *quatrio* by the Latins. Nor does this present protuberance correspond to that fourth part of the little wheel <note>the pulley</note> only by those ribs; but like a pulley around which a rope is turned, it is gifted in its middle with a certain groove, which is very lightly carved and bulges more at the sides on both ends, fitting exactly into that seat which we described as prepared for receiving the talus at the lowest part of the tibia's appendage. Furthermore, this protuberance of the talus is assimilated to that pulley-part not only in its upper seat, but just as the sides of a pulley (by which it is supported as if in a fork or, as others prefer, in a <term>trochlea</term> <note>a mechanical pulley system</note>) are seen to be worn, smooth, and united, so also the protuberance of the talus is compressed at the sides where it touches the **malleoli** <note>the bony bumps on either side of the ankle</note>, and is seen to be encrusted with smooth cartilage, though not in the same way on both sides. On the inner side, it is compressed only with small breadth and superficially, because the process of the lower tibia bone, which forms the inner malleolus and grips this side of the talus, is encrusted with smooth cartilage over a not very large space. But the outer side of the talus's protuberance appears widely hollowed and encrusted with cartilage over a greater interval, so that it may constitute a fit seat with which the inner side of the outer malleolus <note>the end of the fibula</note> may neatly agree, which extends further downward than the inner malleolus. Therefore, by this whole joint of the talus with the tibia and fibula, and by their mutual entry into one another, the talus is flexed and extended almost without any lateral motion. Dogs are even more deprived of this lateral motion, as the protuberance of their talus is carved with a deeper groove along its length than in man, and is more tightly constrained by the mutual entry of the tibia. Just as we said the outer side of the inner malleolus possesses a rough <margin>*Cavities of the talus, from which the ligaments attach to the tibia and fibula.*</margin> cavity from which the cartilaginous ligament binding the talus to the tibia arises, so also, for the sake of receiving that ligament, the inner side of the talus is carved with a rough cavity...

<summary>Vesalius describes the anatomy of the talus (ankle bone) and its articulation with the tibia and fibula, comparing human ankle structure to that of quadrupeds. He emphasizes the pulley-like mechanical nature of the joint which allows for flexion and extension while limiting side-to-side movement.</summary>

quite far beyond the straight line of the shin bone <note>Latin: *tibia*</note>, it is drawn backward in this area so that the shin may be conveniently supported like a perpendicular line upon the foot, as if upon another line drawn transversely; and also so that the most robust tendon <note>The Achilles tendon</note> of the whole body may be inserted into the posterior part of the heel. For into this depressed and somewhat rough part (which in children is the "appendix" or growth plate of the heel) is implanted the tendon formed from the first, second, and fourth muscles moving the feet. However, in quadrupeds—such as dogs, sheep, and horses—this posterior part of the heel bone claims for itself an abundantly long groove in which that tendon is safely carried; in those animals, unlike in man, it produces a broad tendon <note>The plantaris tendon</note> situated beneath the skin of the sole. 

<margin>The nature of the inner side of the heel.</margin>
Furthermore, of the sides of the heel, which are amply depressed and broad, the inner side is seen to be smooth and remarkably curved <note>Latin: *sinuatum*, referring to the tarsal tunnel</note>, so that it may constitute a fit seat for the tendons of the muscles seeking the lower parts of the foot.

The Greeks call the four series of the bones of the foot the <term>tarsus</term> <note>original: "πτερνὸς" (pternos), though Vesalius here uses it to discuss the tarsal region</note>: three of which are joined to the navicular bone, and the fourth indeed to the heel. Although meanwhile the Greeks occasionally express [this], they do not accommodate these names to these bones alone, but they often understand the entire upper part of the foot by that name: as Galen constantly does in his books *On Anatomical Procedures*, writing that the tendons, veins, arteries, and nerves are carried along the tarsus, which are extended through the upper parts of the foot and approach the toes. Very many of the Latins [call] this pile of bones the <term>planta</term> <note>The sole or flat of the foot</note>.

<margin>The tarsus compared to the bones and cartilage of the wrist.</margin>

The tarsus, therefore, is more properly compared to the bones and cartilage of the wrist, along with the arm, radius, ulna, carpus, and fingers. For it is from more numerous and smaller parts, which are in the upper part of the foot, and which are more properly compared to the bones and cartilages of the wrist, with the arm, radius, ulna, carpus, and fingers. # ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE] BODY
<page-num>180</page-num>

the big toe <note>original: *pollicem*</note> stands out much more than the others. Of the middle bones, that which is joined to the innermost bone is short and does not extend as far forward as the one joined to the cube-shaped bone <note>The cuboid bone</note>. All of these joined together form a convex and arched upper surface, but a concave or hollow lower surface; everyone knows this is useful for the foot. The two middle wedge-shaped bones <note>The cuneiform bones</note> resemble their name; where they face the upper part of the foot, they are somewhat wide and arched, but where they form the sole, they are seen to be sharp, just as if they were driven like wedges between the innermost and outermost bones of the tarsus. Then the tarsal bone joined to the cube-like bone is particularly sharp and extends lower into the bottom of the foot <margin>page 5, figure</margin> than the second tarsal bone (joined to the innermost one), because the tendon of the fifth muscle moving the foot <margin>q. 15th muscle</margin> is very strongly inserted into the process brought down here. <margin>Tables D, E, then c, d.</margin> Where the tarsal bones are joined to one another at the sides, they are not covered with smooth, slippery cartilage across the whole width of the connection, but only at the back part of the sides, nearest to the boat-shaped bone <note>The navicular bone; original: *cymbami*</note>; for in the remaining part they stand somewhat apart from each other, coupled together by the intervention of cartilaginous ligaments. All these lack "appendages" <note>epiphyses</note> and, just like the boat-shaped bone, are constructed of such substance.

<margin>History of the FOOT.</margin> The part of the foot follows the tarsus which Hippocrates, perhaps from the series of ribs in the chest, called *stethos* <note>original: *sui* (likely a typo for Greek *stethos* - chest/breast)</note>; <margin>r. 1. fig. II, IIII, IIIII. V. complete.</margin> other Greeks call it the *pedion*, while the Latins call it the *planta* [sole], and some call it the *pecten* [comb] or the *vestigium* [track/footprint]. However, since those Latin terms would bring much obscurity to the narration of the muscles and the description of the vessels and nerves (if we were to use them), it is certainly better to borrow the name from the Greeks here as well. <margin>but of the figures h. b. d. d. e. f. g. and l. l.</margin> For "plain" <note>original: *planum*</note> (the name by which others translate *pedion*) is almost unheard of in this sense where it signifies a part of the foot.

<margin>The metatarsus consists of five bones.</margin> The metatarsus <note>original: *pedium*</note>, therefore, corresponds to the post-brachial <note>metacarpus</note> of the hand; <margin>s. 1. 2. fig. II, IIII, IIIII. s. 1. 2. fig.</margin> but it is formed of five bones, not four like the metacarpus. For in the hand it was fitting for the thumb to be placed opposite the other fingers, and for this reason its first bone is bound to the wrist by a looser joint than the four bones of the metacarpus. Therefore, following Galen, we have assigned the first bone of the thumb to the fingers rather than the metacarpus, attributing three bones to the thumb just as to the other fingers. <margin>The seats in the tarsus are noted in order, etc. a. b.</margin> But the five bones of the metatarsus, which in their entire substance and the long cavity containing marrow correspond to the bones of the metacarpus, are joined to the flat bones of the tarsus and their smooth surfaces in a single row. For since the foot is the organ for walking, stability and security are most suitable for it, which requires bones—not only of the metatarsus but also of the toes—to be placed in a single rank.

<margin>The articulation of the metatarsus to the tarsus.</margin> Thus the metatarsal bone placed before the big toe supports the innermost bone of the tarsus; <margin>s. 2. f. chapter 25 character II, IIII, IIIII. at s. s. 1. 2. fig. chapter 25 N. s. 1. 2. fig. y. 2. f. i. m.</margin> the second, which supports the middle, is articulated to the third bone. The remaining two are attached to the cube-shaped bone; just as it was stated that those bones of the metacarpus are joined to the eighth bone of the wrist, to which the ring and middle fingers are attached. We said that a certain small bone is placed on the outer side of the wrist bone; so also, not infrequently in the foot, a small bone is seen placed at the outer side of the joint where the fifth metatarsal bone articulates with the cuboid bone. Furthermore, just as the tarsal bones do not end in the same line at the front, so also among the metatarsal bones, one extends further back than another.

<margin>The intervals of the metatarsal bones.</margin> The metatarsal bones, where they are joined to the tarsus, are thick at their adjacent sides <margin>z. 1. 2. fig. p. p. a. 15th muscle table L.</margin> and are pressed together by surfaces that are partly flat and smooth. But where they move away from the tarsus toward the toes, they become thinner and form intervals in their middle, in which is placed the muscular substance by whose help the first joints of the toes are flexed. And so that the metatarsal bones may provide a more suitable seat for that substance, they are not so sharp and thin on their upper [surface]...

## ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK I.

<margin>The articulation of the foot to the toes.</margin>
The connection of the metatarsal bones with the first bones of the toes is formed by a hinge-like joint <note>original: "ginglymus"</note>, allowing for the flexion and extension necessary for walking. Each head of the metatarsal bone is received into the shallow cavity of the first phalanx of the toe.

<margin>b See figure 1, chapter 27, C. Then follow the remaining articulation of the toes through that part.</margin>
<column-break/>
<margin>d See figure 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and 15 of the muscle tables, specifically at b.</margin>
The structure of these joints is reinforced by strong ligaments on either side, ensuring that the toes do not displace during the heavy pressure of movement. The great toe, being the primary support for the weight of the body during the stride, possesses a much larger and more robust articulation than the smaller toes.

<margin>a See figures 1 through 22, which illustrate the various views of the bones of the foot and their connections.</margin>
As we examine the subsequent joints of the toes—those between the first, second, and third phalanges—we observe that they are simpler in design, primarily allowing for bending inward toward the sole of the foot. These joints are essential for maintaining balance and providing the final push-off from the ground.

### ON THE CARTILAGE OF THE EAR.
Chapter XXXVI.

<margin>Since the cartilage of the ear is so perfectly free from the skin which covers it, and expresses the shape of the entire ear (if the earlobe is meanwhile removed), we have not illustrated it here.</margin>
<note>The "earlobe" is referred to here as the "pinnula" or little wing.</note>
The primary power of the ear is considered to be its use in receiving the coils and windings of the air; by these names, the cartilage of the ear comes to be enriched. This cartilage, reflecting the shape of the ear, is formed for this purpose: so that when clothed in skin, it constitutes the body of the ear like a winnowing fan <note>A "vannus" or winnowing fan was a shallow basket used to toss grain into the air to separate the chaff; Vesalius uses this to describe the ear's concave, air-catching shape.</note>, supporting it conveniently and keeping it upright.
This cartilage is soft and thin, always becoming softer from the bone of the head toward the extremities of the ear, as it approaches the curve of the ear and where it has less to support. Accordingly, in the lobe of the ear, no portion of this cartilage is extended, because this hanging part needs neither to be raised nor supported. Therefore, near the temporal bone, this cartilage is felt to be harder and, so that it may cling with a firmer root, thicker. For it arises in the ring of the auditory passage <note>The external acoustic meatus.</note> carved into the temporal bone; the circumference of which is made rough for this reason, so that it may more readily bring forth the ear's cartilage. Why Nature constructed the ear from this kind of cartilage, rather than bestowing some bony substance upon it, I explained in the second Chapter: when I said that Nature, with such providence, fashioned the temperament of the cartilage so that it might conveniently support some things like bone, and yet meanwhile be so soft that it is not broken by the impact of things striking it, but by yielding slightly, it escapes the force; and thus it renders the outermost parts less exposed to injuries than if they were made of bone. <margin>a Figure 2, chapters 13 and 4.</margin>

### ON THE CARTILAGES OF THE NOSE.
Chapter XXXVII.

<margin>Although the cartilages of the nose can be properly distinguished by touch almost before dissection, nevertheless the fourth plate of the muscles shows these marked with the letters K and L.</margin>
The Creator of the world built the boundary and extremity of the nose with cartilages for the same reason that we just mentioned regarding the cartilage of the ear. The tip of the nose in quadrupeds almost proves this: it exists as a cartilaginous structure with less width than the tip of a human nose, because it does not protrude from the rest of the face's surface as much as a human nose does. From the lower part of the nasal bones <margin>a Figure 1, chapter 9. b to the same figure. c to the same figure. d 4 Z to Y.</margin>, where they are rougher and wider than at the upper part, two cartilages arise. These extend downward toward the front and, joined together, gradually become softer; and at the tip of the nose, degenerating as if into a cartilaginous ligament, they constitute the entire front region of the nose, which extends from the lower part of the nasal bones to the end and apex of the nose. From the bony septum <margin>e Figure 15. f Figure 6 A, B, and A.</margin> dividing the nostrils—which, as we mentioned above, is a part of the bone of the head—another cartilage arises. This proceeds forward from the entire front part of that septum and is attached to the inner region of the first two cartilages along their length, being more soft and possessing the nature of a ligament the closer it is to the tip of the nose. This, in like manner, in that part of the nose which [protrudes] from the face...

extends from the flat surface of the face and divides the openings of the nose, where that bony septum <note>The nasal septum, which separates the nostrils.</note> separates the openings themselves in the same place where they are led above the region of the palate from the nose all the way to the throat. To these three cartilages of the nose, two others are added—one on each side—which participate even more in the nature of ligaments than the other cartilages do; each of these individually forms one circular nasal opening. These cartilages are bound together at their inner sides, and the ends of the other nasal cartilages cover them. These alone possess voluntary movement, by the help of which they are pulled upward and downward, and inward and outward, being gifted with their own <gloss>muscles</gloss> for this purpose. The wider and softer parts of these cartilages consist in the sides of the nose toward the back and are called the wings of the nose <note>original: "nasae alae"; today known as the ala nasi.</note>, because they enclose the nostrils like wings, providing no common use to man during respiration.

# THE THIRD AND THE REMAINING TWELVE
## figures placed here in succession, and the
### Index of their characters.

THE first of these figures, which is labeled as the third, shows the first cartilage of the <term>larynx</term><note>The thyroid cartilage, often called the "Adam’s apple."</note> viewed from the right side. The fourth figure in the sequence presents the internal or posterior face of the same cartilage. The fifth shows the same cartilage drawn from its front face. The sixth demonstrates the front face of the second cartilage of the larynx <note>The cricoid cartilage, which is shaped like a signet ring.</note>. The seventh contains the second cartilage of the larynx shown from the right side. The eighth offers the second cartilage of the larynx depicted from its posterior face. In the ninth, the third cartilage of the larynx <note>The arytenoid cartilages, which help move the vocal cords.</note> is drawn from the right side. In the tenth, the front part of the third cartilage appears. The eleventh subjects the same cartilage to our eyes from the posterior face. The twelfth shows the lower part of the <term>lid of the larynx</term><note>The epiglottis, which prevents food from entering the windpipe.</note>, where it looks toward the cavity of the larynx. The thirteenth contains the upper part of the lid of the larynx, which faces the palate. The fourteenth presents a single cartilage of the trunk of the <term>rough artery</term><note>The trachea or windpipe.</note>, constructed in the manner of the letter C, to be seen from its front or outer face. The fifteenth presents the same cartilage from its posterior face, which looks toward the internal width of the rough artery.

<margin>The whole of figures 1 & 2 of chapter 9, book 4; H, I, K, L, M, N.</margin>
<margin>Where the nature of the rough artery will be treated in detail.</margin>
ALTHOUGH the sixth book, dedicated to the heart and the organs of respiration, will treat the nature of the rough artery <note>trachea</note> at length, nevertheless its cartilages must be explained at present, so that nothing bony or cartilaginous left unexpressed here may delay us in the description of the muscles. In the sixth book, therefore, we shall teach that the rough artery is led down from the throat into the cavity of the chest and is spread into the lungs by a manifold offspring of branches, so that it may deliver air to them and lead it out from them again. Nor shall we only designate this as the instrument of respiration, but we shall also attest that it is the most principal organ of the voice, at which time we shall treat the logic of its substance exactly. For it consists partly of cartilages, and partly of membranous bonds, of a simple—

...and its simple membranes, or tunics, and finally the muscles peculiar to its head. This head of the windpipe <note>original: *asperæ arterię* (rough artery). In early anatomy, the trachea was called the 'rough artery' to distinguish it from 'smooth' blood vessels.</note> (which I thought should be called the **larynx** <note>original: *laryngé*</note> rather than the **throat** <note>original: *guttur*</note>) is primarily composed of three cartilages:

<margin>FIRST cartilage of the larynx.</margin>
<margin>
b total figs 4, 3, 4, 5 & figs of ch. 21 book 2 g & h.
c figs 3, 4, 5 A, B.
d same figs C, D.
e figs 1, 2 cd. 13 E, F.
f figs 2, 3 cd. 21 book 2 C.
g fig 8 E, F.
h fig 7 E.
h figs 1, 2, 3 G, H.

The $^{b}$ first of these is the largest and most spacious and is located at the front. It is convex on the outside and hollow within, somewhat resembling a shield <note>original: *scuto*</note>—not a round one, but the elongated type which we see the ancients used in battle and some Turks still use today, especially on ships. For this reason, those skilled in dissection called it **shield-shaped** <note>original Greek: θυρεοειδῆ (*thyreoeidē*); this is the thyroid cartilage.</note>. In humans, this is seen to be broader at the $^{c}$ top than at the bottom; however, as far as its appearance goes, it corresponds to itself in both areas. At the $^{d}$ top and bottom, it puts forth two processes <note>In modern anatomy, these are the superior and inferior horns (cornua) of the thyroid cartilage.</note>, one on each side. The two superior ones are longer than the inferior ones and are bound by membranes and ligaments to the lower $^{e}$ sides of the bone that resembles the letter *u* <note>The hyoid bone, which is shaped like the Greek letter upsilon (υ).</note>. The inferior processes are joined to the $^{f}$ sides of the second cartilage toward its posterior part. This shield-shaped cartilage, which in men protrudes $^{g}$ forward more than in women and is more exposed to the touch <note>The laryngeal prominence, or "Adam’s apple."</note>, is sometimes seen to be double, especially in men. For in its $^{h}$ middle, where it is shortest and bulges most toward the front, a line is often drawn along its length; when the membranes are carefully cleaned away, this line proves that the two parts of the cartilage were joined together even before dissection. Indeed, this is peculiar to humans. For in cattle, the cartilage is simple, and its form varies greatly from that of the human cartilage. I wish architects would carefully observe this: for it is wonderful how skillfully the shield-shaped cartilage of cattle approaches the form of a bulwark, and how cleverly it is adapted for scouts at its higher part (because of the specific notches cut into it), and how aptly it is suited for repelling the strikes of catapults <note>original: *bombardarum*</note>. It is exactly as if it were a portable machine which could be fixed into the earth by its two lower processes, like two stakes, and placed in front of an army.

<margin>SECOND cartilage of the larynx.</margin>
<margin>
i total figs 6, 7, 8 & figs of ch. 21 book 2 i, then k.
k figs 2, 3, 5 ch. 21 book 2 H. & figs 14, 15 book 5 A, B, C, D.
l figs 6, 7 K, L.
m fig 6 I.
n fig 5 L.

The $^{i}$ second cartilage is smaller than the first and larger than the third; its greatest portion is located at the back of the larynx, where the **esophagus** <note>original: *stomachus*. Historically, this term often referred to the gullet/esophagus.</note> is carried down from the throat. For as much as the shield-shaped cartilage lacks a perfect circular shape, this one supplies it at its upper and posterior part. At its $^{l}$ lowest part, it forms a perfect circle, the front of which we can feel by touch in the forward region of the larynx, beneath the base of the shield-shaped cartilage. The internal $^{m}$ space of this cartilage is perfectly smooth, but its posterior side, facing the esophagus, has a long $^{n}$ ridge protruding along its length, extended like a spine. This ridge separates and largely constitutes the two $^{o}$ hollows of this cartilage in which two $^{p}$ muscles are fixed, inserted in a straight line from the second cartilage into the third. The upper part of this cartilage, where it forms the back region of the larynx, ends in two $^{q}$ oblong tubercles, one on each side, which you will soon hear are articulated with the $^{r}$ ends of the third cartilage. The second cartilage is joined to the first in the manner I explained above, when I said the lower processes of the first cartilage were united to it. To make the connection of those processes firmer, the second cartilage bulges slightly $^{s}$ and is thicker where the processes themselves coalesce; in this protruding area on both sides, a hollow is seen that very strongly receives the process of its side. The $^{t}$ lower part of the second cartilage, where it forms the back of the larynx, is seen to be somewhat thin, reaching further down than the rest of its lower part; this is so that the $^{u}$ muscles might take their origin from a more distant place, which, extending straight through the length of the second cartilage, are inserted into the third. No name has been given to this cartilage, and therefore, in a certain sense, it is called by the specific name **Unnamed**... <note>This is the cricoid cartilage. Vesalius notes it had no common name in his time, though "cricoid" (ring-like) eventually became standard.</note>

...can be called by [the name mentioned before]. <margin>
The THIRD cartilage of the larynx.
</margin>
The Greeks called the third cartilage of the larynx the **arytainan** <term>ἀρύταιναν; a ladle or pitcher</term> and **arytainoeidē** <term>ἀρυταινοειδῆ; ladle-shaped</term> because, when it is still whole and covered by the membrane lining the inside of the windpipe <note>original: *asperam arteriam*</note>, it is very similar to that part of the pots from which we pour water for those about to wash their hands, which the Greeks called an *arytaina* and some of the Latins called a **gutturnium** <note>A narrow-necked ewer or water pitcher.</note>. For it fits that part of the mouth of the pots more aptly than those long wooden shells <note>Vesalius refers to large scoops or ladles.</note> which we see sailors use to bail water or gardeners use to water their gardens. Indeed, the Greeks seem to have compared this cartilage to such slanted vessels—not to the whole vessel, but to its spout. However that may be, all have described the third cartilage of the larynx as a single and simple unit; meanwhile, when freed from its membranes, it is always found to consist of $^{a}$ two cartilages, joined together quite loosely only by the benefit of their ligaments and the membrane lining the larynx. And indeed, one of these rests on the right side of the second cartilage, and the other on the left, possessing a smooth and quite deeply carved $^{z}$ groove by which it receives the $^{y}$ tubercle of the second cartilage. Thus, it is articulated so that it can move toward the inner space of the larynx and back out again, and this cartilage is the most mobile of all the laryngeal cartilages.

<margin>
b figs. 9, 10 Y.
c figs. 9, 10, 11 Z.
d figs. 10, 11 T.
e figs. 3, 9, 10, 11, ch. 21, book 2.
</margin>
The $^{b}$ base of each cartilage is broad, and at the front, it ends in a long $^{c}$ process extending into the interior of the larynx. The upper parts of these cartilages, however, gradually gaping away from each other from the base and then becoming thinner, softer, and fatty, are joined together. The upper part of the $^{d}$ right cartilage, joined to the part of the left cartilage, builds that seat of the larynx which corresponds to that part of the vessels from which water is poured onto the hands, as we mentioned just before. This area of the larynx is so soft and flexible that, in those who are vomiting, it leans forward into the inner space of the larynx and covers the windpipe so perfectly that not even the slightest bit of vomit slips into the airway itself. Furthermore, although this $^{e}$ third cartilage is double and is rightly constructed of two cartilages for the sake of its function, we shall not, for that reason, count it as two cartilages. Instead, following the custom of other anatomists, it will be held by us as only one, lest I seem to disturb their established views more than is fair (even if they have, in the meantime, numbered the cartilages rather than described them).

<margin>
f all of figs. 12, 13 & figs. 3, 4, 5, 6, 11, ch. 21, book 2.
g figs. 12, 13 a.
h same figs. b.
</margin>
<margin>
LID of the larynx.
</margin>
<margin>
Book 4, On Diseases.
</margin>
To these three cartilages of the larynx, $^{f}$ another is added, which serves as a very elegant **lid** <note>original: *operculum*; the epiglottis.</note> for the larynx, accurately preventing any food or drink from flowing into it. This lid of the larynx arises from a broad and forward-curving $^{g}$ base, from the inner region of the shield-shaped <note>The thyroid cartilage.</note> cartilage near its higher part. Proceeding inward from here, it expresses the image of a triangle or, as Hippocrates beautifully taught, an **ivy leaf**. Its base is formed by the origin of the lid from the shield-shaped cartilage, or rather its connection with that cartilage. The $^{h}$ peak is formed by that part which extends inward, as if toward the region of the stomach <note>Vesalius uses "stomach" here to refer to the esophagus or the general direction of the digestive tract.</note>. This body, where it faces the palate, is convex and softer; where it rests on the larynx, it is hollow, curved, and much harder than the upper part. At its very end, where it looks toward the stomach, it is remarkably soft; covered by a fatty membrane, it reflects in a way the nature of a ligament and matches the substance of the upper part of the third cartilage. Where it is joined to the shield-shaped cartilage, it also abounds in much fat; there it is so hard...

<summary>Vesalius describes the third laryngeal cartilage (the arytenoid), comparing its shape to a water pitcher and identifying it as two distinct pieces despite traditional views. He then introduces the epiglottis, describing it as an "ivy-leaf" shaped lid that protects the airway during swallowing.</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY
<page-num>188</page-num>

<margin>The little tongue or slit of the larynx, and the principal organ of voice.</margin>
...is seen to be hard and in its middle. Many have thought that this body is the principal organ of the voice, recklessly calling it the **glottis** <note>original: γλωττίδα</note> and **epiglottis** <note>original: ἐπιγλωττίδα</note>; yet these names signify completely different and even conflicting parts to the ancients.

<margin>
i. Figure 11 at the end of chapter 21, book 2.
k. Figures 9 and 10, Y, Y.
l. Compare L with figure 11, chapter 21, book 2.
</margin>
For the **glottis** <term>glottis; from the Greek for "tongue"</term> indicates the slit of the larynx, which is formed by two processes of the third cartilage, covered by a fatty membrane in the middle of the laryngeal cavity; we shall demonstrate in its proper place that this is the principal organ of voice. For the ancients called such a slit the *glottis*, or "little tongue," from its resemblance to those little tongues made from two reeds joined together that we fit into flutes <note>Vesalius refers to the "tibiae," ancient double-reed instruments similar to an oboe.</note>. However, the lid of the larynx is called the **epiglottis** <term>epiglottis; "upon the glottis"</term>, which is placed over the aforementioned "little tongue" of the larynx to prevent anything from falling into it while eating. That these things are hidden from the physicians of our age is not only their own fault—for they follow nothing but the opinions of authors without any practical use of dissection—but even **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – c. 50 AD), a Roman medical encyclopedist.</note> misunderstood these things poorly (as he did many things pertaining to Anatomy). He called the lid of the larynx the "little tongue" <note>original: lingula</note>, not considering that the Greeks called it the *epiglottis* because it rests upon the slit of the larynx, which we compare to the little tongue of flutes. Furthermore, **Theodore Gaza** <note>A 15th-century Greek humanist who translated Aristotle into Latin.</note>, deceived by Celsus's error (who perhaps compared the laryngeal lid to the image of the human tongue), translated *epiglottis* as "little tongue" in Aristotle, even though Aristotle actually meant the lid of the larynx.

<margin>
Aristotle, Book 2 on the Parts of Animals, chapter 3.
Galen, especially in Book 8 on the Use of the Parts.
</margin>
I shall for now pass over how often in **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of antiquity, whose works Vesalius was both correcting and clarifying.</note>, through the fault of both translators and the scribes of the Greek manuscripts, *glottis* is read for *epiglottis*, and vice versa. But I shall follow up on these things more extensively in their proper place. For here it is enough to have established the discourse on the cartilages of the larynx insofar as we require it for the treatment of the muscles in the Second Book.

<margin>
The remaining cartilages of the windpipe are shaped like the letter C.
</margin>
And therefore, the cartilages which for the most part match the shape of our letter **C**, and which occur in series just below the larynx throughout the entire trunk of the **windpipe** <term>aspera arteria; literally "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea</term> and all its branches distributed through the substance of the lungs, will be treated together with the rest of the history of the windpipe in the Sixth Book.

### ON THE NUMBER OF BONES AND CARTILAGES.
### Chapter XXXIX.

<margin>The number of bones.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' set in a square frame, depicting several figures (likely scholars or anatomists) in a landscape with architectural ruins.</image-desc>SINCE I have little doubt that many, now that the history of the individual bones and cartilages is finished, will desire from me a count of their number—just as students in our schools are accustomed to do—I will now briefly review the bones and cartilages so that anyone may readily perceive which ones can be included in a certain number. In a human of advanced age, whose **appendices** <note>epiphyses; the ends of long bones that fuse to the main shaft as a person matures</note> have already fully fused with their bones, one may count the bones in roughly this manner. There are twenty bones of the **skull** <term>calvaria; the braincase and upper face</term>: namely, eight called the bones of the head, and twelve of the upper jaw. However, we establish here only a single bone for the forehead <note>the frontal bone</note>, and we do not separately enumerate the cheekbones <note>zygomatic</note> and the "stony" bones <note>petrous part of the temporal bone</note>, since parts or sites of those twenty bones lack their own circumscription <note>i.e., they are fused parts of larger structures</note>. There are four tiny bones of the organ of hearing, two in each ear. The teeth are usually counted as thirty-two. There is one bone of the lower jaw. The tiny bones of the **v-shaped bone** <term>hyoid bone; situated in the neck</term> are roughly eleven; there are seven vertebrae of the neck, twelve of the chest, five bones of the loins, six of the **sacred bone** <note>sacrum</note>, and four tiny bones of the **cuckoo bone** <note>coccyx</note>. There are twenty-four ribs. We have counted three bones of the breastbone <note>sternum</note>, though others count seven; but let there be only three in this catalog, or as many as you wish according to your judgment. There are two shoulder blades, an equal number of collarbones, two humeri, two ulnae, and two radii. The bones of the wrists...

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.
<page-num>189</page-num>

<header>THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>

...sixteen bones, namely eight for each hand <note>original: "octo": the carpal bones</note>; likewise eight bones of the post-brachial region <note>original: "postbrachialium": the metacarpals</note>, being four in each hand. There are thirty bones of the fingers, fifteen for each hand. At the very least, twelve sesamoid bones <term>sesamamina ossicula; small, seed-like bones embedded in tendons</term> occur in each hand, and therefore we shall set that number at twenty-four for the hands. There are two bones joined to the sides of the sacrum <note>original: "sacri ossis": the pelvic or hip bones</note>, one on each side. Two thigh bones <note>original: "femora"</note>. Two sesamoid bones in each popliteal space <note>the area behind the knee</note>. Two shin bones <note>original: "tibiae"</note>, two fibulae, two kneecaps <note>original: "patellae"</note>, two heel bones <note>original: "calces"</note>, two ankle bones <note>original: "tali"</note>, and two navicular bones. There are four bones of the tarsus <note>the mid-foot</note> in each foot, and five bones of the metatarsus <note>original: "pedij"</note> in each foot. There are fourteen bones of the toes in each foot. The sesamoid bones of a single foot are, at the minimum, twelve in number. Therefore, if you gather these bones into one sum, the total will be (if I add correctly) three hundred and seven. If you wished to add to these the four bones of the breastbone <note>original: "pectoris ossa": the segments of the sternum</note>, and established two bones for the lower jaw, and finally considered the cartilaginous substance of the heart as one bone in the class of bones, the count would rise to three hundred and thirteen. Furthermore, if one were to list separately all the appendages <term>appendices; known today as epiphyses, the ends of bones that fuse to the main shaft as a person matures</term>—on the grounds that they are bones, each defined by its own boundary at least in children—you could easily double that previous number, and then increase it again by half. You may gather this from remembering the vertebrae, the shoulder blades <note>original: "scapulas"</note>, the thigh bones, the shin bones, and others which are gifted with many appendages; and then also remember that a single appendage is occasionally formed from several parts, as happens with that process which falls to the upper shoulder blade. Again, if you subtract the bones as they are seen in children—good gods!—what a heap of bones you will pile up? Since the bone of the back of the head <note>original: "occipitis os"</note> consists of nearly three parts, and many vertebrae (without considering the appendages) consist of two, and most of three bones; and since the breastbone is composed of more bones in children than in those who have reached full growth; and the bones which are squeezed together at the sacrum are each fashioned from three bones. Thus, anyone may fashion a number of bones according to their own whim.

<margin>The number of cartilages.</margin>
However, in defining a certain number of cartilages, there is even more work, since they are found to be so varied and are not the same at all ages. Nevertheless, so that you may weigh whether they can be reduced to a number by any means at all, let those first be recounted which are entirely continuous with bones: such as the cartilage of each ear, born from the temporal bone; two of the nose, arising from the two nasal bones; that which, springing from the septum of the nostrils, is also referred to the nose; the twenty-four cartilages of the ribs; those in which the spines of all the bones of the back and many of their transverse processes terminate; that into which the breastbone is sharpened <note>the xiphoid process</note>; the cartilage at the base of each shoulder blade; that which belongs to the tip of the coccyx; and the tiny ones which belong to the final bones of the fingers and toes. Then there are all the smooth and slippery cartilages with which bones are encrusted for the construction of joints; these, no different than the surfaces of the joints, are very numerous and far exceed the number of three hundred and five bones. Furthermore, there are those seen in the connection of appendages with their bones, which also exceed the stated number of bones, besides those which privately join the parts of certain bones in children. Added to these are those which intervene in the mutual weaving of the bones of the sacrum, and that which knits the pubic bones together. Likewise, those which, sharing in the nature of a ligament, are also continuous with bones: such as those by which the small bones of the bone resembling the letter $v$ <note>the hyoid bone, shaped like the Greek letter upsilon</note> are joined, those which intervene between the bodies of the vertebrae, those between the three bones of the breastbone, those occurring between the sacrum and the bones joined to it, and those which join the little bones of the coccyx to one another. As for those which are not continuous with bones, two are established for each eye: one of which resides in the upper eyelid and the other in the lower. There are two for the wings of the nose. In the larynx <note>the voice box</note> there are three principal ones, the first of which is occasionally found to be double, while the third is always found to be so.

<summary>Vesalius provides a detailed census of the bones and cartilages in the human body, noting how the total count varies significantly between children and adults due to the fusion of appendages (epiphyses).</summary>

the lid of the larynx <note>original: "laryngis operculum"; the epiglottis</note>; the C-shaped cartilages which are found in the trunk of the rough artery <term>aspera arteria: the classical term for the trachea or windpipe</term> and its innumerable branches distributed into the lungs; and the cartilaginous substance at the base of the heart <note>Vesalius refers to the "cordis os" or cardiac skeleton, which he believed to be cartilaginous in humans</note>. Lastly, there are those cartilages which are free within the joints and not entirely continuous with the bones: such as the two that sometimes occur in the two lower connections of the first vertebra to the second, and occasionally one in the joint of the shoulder to the scapula on either side. There are always two in the joints of the lower jaw to the temple bones <note>the temporomandibular joint discs</note>; four in the joints of the collarbones with the breastbone and then with the upper processes of the shoulder blades; and two in each knee <note>the menisci</note>. The one seen as somewhat free between the ulna and the wrist is actually continuous with the radius. Since, therefore, the account of the cartilages is so complex, I could not easily define their number to everyone's satisfaction. Accordingly, it is now the proper time to set down the method by which bones and cartilages are prepared for instruction, or learned through anatomy; I shall follow that method by which I always subjoin the practical art of dissecting the parts after their description (as I deem it can be most aptly done in its proper place).
