# BY WHAT ARTIFICE THE BONES AND CARTILAGES
## of the human body are made visible for inspection.
### Chapter XL.

<margin>The method of macerating bones in lime and then cleaning them in a river.</margin>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a group of several men gathered around a large wooden chest or vat. They are performing the process of macerating a human body in lime (calx) to clean the bones, as described in the text. One figure leans over the chest while others observe and assist.</image-desc>

Physicians who are worthily devoted to the Hippocratic art are accustomed to prepare the bones preserved for instruction with no small labor, whether they intend to inspect them joined together or each one separately. For they usually first free a hanging or otherwise dead corpse of its flesh for the most part, and cut out the viscera without loosening any joint of the body. Afterward, they would place the body, thus dissected, into a long box, filling it with lime and then sprinkling a little water over it. Then, when they had kept the box in this manner for eight days, they would tie it, perforated everywhere with narrow holes, in a fast-flowing river, so that the lime, together with the now-rotting remains of the flesh, might flow away over time and recede from the bones on all sides. After a few days, the retrieved corpse was cleaned everywhere by the use of knives, with care taken so that no connection of the bones was dissolved in that work, and the ligaments binding the bones together (by whose intervention they would remain attached thereafter) were kept intact; and finally, everything except the joints of the bones would shine. They would expose the cleaned corpse to the sun in whatever position they wished it to be seen—either seated or upright, and arranged in this or 그 form—so that the ligaments, dried out by the heat of the sun, might hold the joints of the bones in that position. But this method of preparation, besides being troublesome, filthy, and difficult, shows almost none of the processes, appendices, heads, cavities, and other such features of the bones that truly ought to be studied with the greatest care: because, of course, all these things are still covered by ligaments that have turned significantly black. Thus, this way of cleaning or scouring the bones provides almost nothing for learning. Just as the ridiculous method of viewing muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves, veins, and arteries, with which the professors of our art have hitherto deceived candidates of medicine, brings no benefit; instead, it merely restrains the minds of students, lest they demand a demonstration of those organs I just mentioned from those "Rabbis" <note>original: "Rabinis"; Vesalius's mocking term for traditional academic authorities who preferred old texts to hands-on dissection</note>. For these men used to claim that such things were to be learned only from bodies emaciated (heaven help us!) in whirlpools of water, and not from those recently dead: as if, indeed, anything worthy of education could be learned in bodies prepared in that way, or rather, utterly corrupted by this method. Moreover, in what way the other small parts of the body...

<margin>
The method of preparing bones by boiling.
</margin>
...how they are to be approached, I shall follow up in their proper places with abundance. However, you will prepare the bones—as I will now subjoin—with little trouble, provided you are at least eager to learn, and (as Galen <note>original: "Galenus"</note> especially requires in a student of dissection) patient in labor and industrious. Therefore, having obtained a cadaver from somewhere, of whatever kind it may be (although you will judge one emaciated by disease to be far more suitable), you will take care to have at hand one vessel for storing the flesh, viscera, and skin, and for receiving the blood, together with a great and large cauldron or pot <term>cacabus: a large cooking pot</term>, of the sort women use for heating lye <note>original: "lixiuium"; a solution used for washing or making soap</note> on the fire. For that is most suitable for boiling the bones, and you will conveniently cast the bones into it. Furthermore, a large sheet of paper or parchment shall be stretched out on some board so that the cartilages, which are not to be boiled, can be applied to it and placed in order. Soon, with a sharper knife, you will attempt a circular incision through the forehead, the temples, and the back of the head, penetrating all the way to the skull <term>calvaria: the upper part of the skull</term>. Next, along the circle of this incision, you will divide the skull with a saw, being little concerned even if you damage the brain, or if you divide the skull a little lower or higher; for since the purpose now is only to inspect and preserve the bones and cartilages.

<margin>
a You will divide it so that the seventh figure of chapter 6 is seen freed from the sixth figure. Truly, there is no need for me to note anything else in this chapter for you, who are now well-instructed in the bones and cartilages, especially since otherwise, for almost every single word, paper would have to be applied to the rest.
</margin>

Once the skull is dissected, the brain—torn out from it with the hands alone—must be cast into the vessel. The part of the skull taken away from the rest of the head is put into the pot, though first freed from the skin of the crown. Now, having cut off each ear very close to the temporal bone, place them separately on the paper to which the cartilages are applied, along with the eyelids and the tip of the nose, which consists of cartilages; these are to be cut away very closely from the bones to which they are joined, together with the skin. Next, you will free the lower jaw from its connection with the bones of the head; and you will cut away the cartilages (which we said are held privately in its joints with the head) from the ligaments containing the joint with a small knife, applying them in order to that paper, where they will readily stick. When you remove the lower jaw, and in passing free it from the skin and tongue (leaving, if you wish, the attachments of the muscles), and finally cast it into the pot, you will also take from the throat the entire larynx, with the bone resembling the letter U <note>original: "υ referente"; the hyoid bone, which is shaped like the Greek letter upsilon</note>, and the tongue, and a portion of the esophagus <note>original: "stomachi"</note> and the rough artery <term>aspera arteria: the trachea</term>, and place them on that paper, cleaned in no other way. Now you will perform an incision from the tip of the breastbone <note>the xiphoid process</note> down to the pubic bone, penetrating as far as the caul <note>original: "omentum"; the fatty membrane covering the intestines</note>. To this you will then add another incision reaching across from the right hip-bone to the left, and without selection you will tear out everything contained by the peritoneum in the manner of butchers <note>original: "laniorū more"</note>, and cast them into the vessel. You will briefly dissect the skin of the abdomen together with its muscles from the bones; and catching the blood with sponges, you will squeeze it into the vessel. Then, from the throat down to the tip of the breastbone, you will lead an incision so deep that, as it penetrates to the breastbone itself, you can remove the muscles spread over the chest together with the skin, from the bones of the ribs and their cartilages, so that the collarbones <note>original: "clauiculæ"</note> appear at once naked and free of flesh. Indeed, these are to be freed from the breastbone with a sharper knife, and the cartilages proper to these joints (just as you approached the cartilages of the lower jaw) must be accurately removed and then applied in order to the paper. The breastbone, together with the cartilages of the ribs, will be studiously freed from the bones of the ribs, with incisions led through the cartilages there with a sharper and not very thick knife, where the bones of the ribs degenerate into these <note>the costochondral junction</note>. And this is quickly accomplished, if only it has not escaped memory that the cartilage of the first rib is carried more to the side from the middle of the breastbone than the cartilage of the second rib. Nor are only the cartilages joined to the breastbone to be separated from the ribs; but also all the cartilages of the false ribs, which will be sticking to the upper cartilages by the intervention of the intercostal muscles. The cartilages being disjoined in this manner, you will lift the breastbone from the throat, and it with the veins and arteries reaching from the throat to it, and the membranes also...

you will also clear away the membranes <note>original: "quæ... intersepient"; likely referring to the pleura</note> that partition the thoracic cavity. Then, being about to dissect the **shoulder blade** <note>original: "scapulam"</note> together with the **collarbone** <note>original: "clavicula"</note> from the thorax, you will make a long incision from the top of the shoulder through the arm and forearm all the way to the thumb. You will strip the shoulder blade, upper arm, forearm, and hand of their skin and flesh, not being overly anxious even if some portion of the tendons and flesh remains attached to the bones. Indeed, it will even suffice to leave the skin of the hand, simply cutting it here and there with a few incisions so that the hand may be boiled more easily later. Now, the collarbone shall be cut from the upper process of the shoulder blade <note>the acromion</note>, keeping in mind whether, besides that process which we call the "summit of the shoulder" and the collarbone, any other third bone occurs there. Once you have performed this, and applied the unique cartilage of that joint to the paper, you will cast the collarbone into the **pot** <term>cacabum: a large boiling vessel</term>, and you will separate the shoulder blade from the upper arm, and then the upper arm from the bones of the forearm. Leaving the forearm connected to the hand, you will also place them all together into the pot. However, before the shoulder blade is put into the pot, you would do well to remove the cartilage that sometimes increases the size of the socket of the shoulder blade <note>the glenoid labrum</note> which receives the head of the humerus, and attach it to the paper with the other cartilages. 

This must be performed similarly on the other side, and then you must immediately return to the thorax. From here, you will first cut out the **lung** with the **heart** and the **diaphragm**. Before you throw the heart into a vessel, you will divide the base of the heart transversely from the rest of the heart’s body. Then, you will remove the base again from the vessels that proceed from it, in such a way that you keep the orifices of the **pulmonary artery** <note>original: "venæ arterialis"</note> and the **aorta** <note>original: "magnæ arteriæ"</note> unharmed. Afterwards (if it seems right), you may attach them to the paper to be preserved among the number of cartilages; or you might even weigh whether the shared root of those two vessels is also a bone in man <note>Vesalius is investigating a common belief of the time that the heart contained a "bone," which is actually only found in certain large animals like oxen</note>. 

Therefore, when you have thrown the rest of what is found in the thorax into a vessel, you will turn the cadaver onto its front <note>original: "in pronum"</note>. As far as is possible, you will clean the flesh from the neck and the rest of the back, together with the entire width of the thorax. Be carefully on guard lest you break any **rib** (since they are fragile), or, by cutting the flesh too closely, you damage any process <note>bony projection</note> of the bone. This must be guarded against even more when you are about to free the individual ribs separately from the vertebrae of the thorax. For with the cadaver turned on its back, the head of each rib must be separated from the socket of the vertebral body with a sharper knife. Then, after gradually dividing the ligaments, the ribs are to be removed from the transverse processes of the vertebrae as well; after a cursory cleaning, they should be sent into the pot. 

You will handle the legs in the same manner as you approached the arms and hands, cleaning the entire **thigh bone** <note>original: "femur"</note> of flesh, and then the **shin bone** <note>original: "tibia"</note> and the foot. When, however, you strip the knee, and consider whether any **sesamoid bones** <note>original: "sesamina... ossicula"; small, seed-like bones found in tendons</note> exist there at the back of the root of the lower heads of the femur, you will cut the **kneecap** <note>original: "patellam"</note> out of the tendons occupying the front of the knee. You will cast it into the pot just like the femur as soon as you have freed it from the **hip bone** <note>original: "coxendicis osse"</note> and the shin bone, and have cut away the cartilages that enlarge the sockets of the shin bone which receive the heads of the femur. Indeed, you will not inopportunely glue those also to the paper. Next, you will put the shin bone, together with the **calf bone** <note>original: "fibula"</note> and the foot, into the pot. 

When this has been performed on both legs, and the bones pressed together at the sides of the **sacrum** <note>original: "ossis sacri"</note> have been somewhat cleaned, the cartilaginous ligaments coming between the bodies of the vertebrae <note>intervertebral discs</note> must be cut out with great precision and arranged in order on the paper. ...region of the cartilaginous ligament, you will perform a similar incision, and by this means you will remove the ligament whole. When you have placed this on the paper, you will cut out the following ones one by one until you reach the second vertebra of the neck. Therefore, once twenty-three cartilaginous ligaments <note>original: "ligamenta cartilaginea"; these are the intervertebral discs</note> have been applied to the paper in this way, the back must be cautiously and gently separated into three or four parts, lest by attempting it with too much force you accidentally break some process of the vertebrae. For this reason, care must also be taken that you do not strive to free the first vertebra from the head too negligently. For it is permissible to place the neck vertebrae into the **pot** <term>cacabum: a large bronze cooking vessel or cauldron used for boiling</term> along with the head, just as you may do with the thoracic vertebrae and the lumbar vertebrae: provided you have first separated them from the **sacrum** <note>original: "sacro osse"</note>. 

However, there is nothing to prevent putting the **sacrum**, together with the bones joined to it on both sides—which constitute the **ilium**, the **ischium** <note>original: "coxendicis"</note>, and the **pubis**—and then the **coccyx** <note>original: "coccyge osse"; the tailbone</note>, into the pot. This is because the iliac bones, when still "raw" <note>fresh and unboiled</note>, are separated from the sacrum with great difficulty and effort, and the cartilage of the pubic bones might be damaged at that stage. You will otherwise preserve that cartilage whole if you cast the pubic bones into the pot without having first pulled them apart. 

Once the bones have been placed in the pot in this manner, it should be filled entirely with water so that, as the bones sink deep into the liquid, no part of a bone protrudes. This must be observed above all else during the entire time of cooking: that no bone remains uncovered by water, and much more so, that no bone sticking out of the pot catches the smoke. For this reason, it is appropriate that the pot be large. 

No peculiar artistry is required for the overall boiling; but as in other types of stewing, the scum must be diligently removed so that you render the broth clearer and extract the bones themselves less grimy. In the same way, all the fat (which often tends to float on the surface in great quantities from those who were not emaciated by disease) must be skimmed off and put aside under its common name. The common people attribute much to this fat for the fading of scars and for the "extending" of nerves and tendons <note>Vesalius refers here to the use of human fat as a folk remedy for joint stiffness or skin healing</note>. 

No fixed time is prescribed for the boiling, since it varies greatly according to age. For two or three hours may be more than enough when the bones of young children are being cooked, especially since in their case one must take care that the **epiphyses** <note>original: "appendices"; the ends of long bones that have not yet fused in youth</note> do not fall off while you are cleaning the bones. Meanwhile, the fusion of these parts in men of more advanced age is hardly ever dissolved, no matter how long you boil them. 

The goal of the boiling is this: that the bones may be properly cleaned with the help of knives, just as is done while eating. To do this more conveniently, you will gradually remove some bones from the boiling broth with forceps and clean them by yourself—unless perhaps a studious companion is present to lend a hand to the work. For the greatest care must be taken lest some unskilled person damage the **ridges** <note>original: "supercilia"; the rims of joint sockets</note>, processes, heads, and cavities of the bones by scraping, or imprudently remove the smooth cartilage that covers the bones like a crust. For these must be preserved with the utmost accuracy when you remove the flesh, ligaments, tendons, and membranes surrounding the bones. 

Truly, I would not wish this duty to be entrusted to someone inept or little interested in Anatomy for this reason alone: but so that, by cleaning each bone privately, you may diligently contemplate its cavities and heads, and most especially the nature of the ligaments, the insertion of the tendons, and the origin of the muscles. For I could not easily say how much knowledge of the parts you will acquire for yourself through that labor. 

Therefore, when you extract the bones from the boiling broth in order in this fashion, and place them when cleaned upon the ground or into some small basket, do not be overly anxious about which bone you happen upon first. However, when extracting the hand with the bones of the forearm <note>original: "cubiti ossibus"</note>, you will observe that you do not violently separate the **wrist** <note>original: "brachiale"; the carpus</note> from the forearm bones; rather, by gradually dividing the ligaments of the joint with a knife, you will accurately free the wrist from the forearm, as also in the separation of the **metacarpus** <note>original: "postbrachialis"</note> from the wrist. For I would desire care to be taken lest the bones of the wrist be separated from one another. Hence, as soon as you have disjoined it whole from the forearm, the first bone of the thumb, and the metacarpus, you should briefly remove the tendons and ligaments...

...and you will tear away the ligaments growing onto the bones themselves, striving to ensure that the bones are not cleaned entirely of their ligaments on their internal and external surfaces, but rather that they still cling to each other by means of the ligaments. For when the **wrist** <note>original: "Brachiale"; the carpus</note> is subjected to fire in this way, the ligaments are gradually dried out and hold the bones of the wrist firmly together. Consequently, the wrist is joined with less trouble to the bones of the **forearm** <note>original: "cubiti"; the ulna and radius</note> and the **metacarpus** <note>original: "postbrachialis"</note>—unless perhaps, being more skilled in joining bones, you dare to separate the bones of the wrist from each other and clean them of their ligaments, later intending to join them back together with **bronze wires** <note>original: "aeneis filis"</note>, or even wish to keep them separated. Soon, when you have placed the wrist near the fire in that manner, take a sheet of paper and place upon it the bones of the metacarpus and the fingers, thoroughly cleaned, not overlooking the **sesamoid bones** <note>original: "sesaminis ossiculis"; small, seed-like bones found in tendons</note> from all sides. This prevents these bones, when wrapped in that paper, from being confused with the bones of the other hand and increasing the labor of joining the bones later. It is beneficial, therefore, to enclose the bones of the hands and feet separately in four sheets of paper. However, before you wrap the bones of this or that hand or foot in paper, you must always investigate whether any uncleaned bone remains, lest while you are seeing to the disposal of the scraps and the broth, you carelessly hand over some bones to be thrown away. If by chance you wish to preserve the **nail** <note>original: "unguem"</note> as well, you will pull it off while you are cleaning the bones of the fingers of the hand and foot. For we see that human nails, no less than the claws of birds and the hooves of quadrupeds, come away by boiling or by the force of hot water. 

Furthermore, when you clean the **ulna** and the **radius**, the **cartilage** <note>the triangular fibrocartilage complex</note> should not be neglected; it originates from the radius and for the most part separates the ulna from the wrist. This cartilage is freed from the ulna so that, still attached to the radius, it may again sit between the ulna and the wrist when the bones are reconnected. Moreover, when you clean the head, take the utmost care that you do not carelessly remove those **tiny bones** <note>the ossicles: malleus, incus, and stapes</note> which are part of the structure of the organ of hearing while pulling away the membrane that lines the opening of the ear canal. Indeed, those must be carefully pulled out and shaken out together by sending a **stylus** <note>a pointed tool</note> into the opening. You will store these tiny bones somewhere for the rest of the bone assembly. 

Finally, you will remove the vertebrae from the broth last of all, as well as the **sacrum** <note>original: "sacrum os"</note>—unless perhaps, after a little boiling, you choose to free the **tailbone** <note>original: "coccyx os"</note> from the sacrum. This is because the small bones of the tailbone, due to the cartilaginous ligaments that connect them, tend to separate from each other if they are cooked for too long. If, however, you have first removed the sacrum for the sake of detaching the tailbone, the sacrum must be put back into the **cauldron** <term>cacabo: a large bronze cooking pot</term>, and the tailbone should be placed separately in a paper or a small basket in which you will place the minute bones, such as the teeth (if any of them have fallen out) or any portion of a bone that was carelessly broken off. 

However, to preserve the cartilage of the **pubic bones** <note>the pubic symphysis</note>, before you free the **hip bones** <note>original: "ilium ossa"</note> from the sacrum, the pubic bones must be lightly cleaned of their ligaments and surrounding membranes at their front and back surfaces. Then they should be separated from each other using only your hands, so that the intervening cartilage comes away from one bone and remains attached to only one; it can then be joined with the other pubic bone with little trouble during the assembly of the skeleton. Once the bones have been cleaned in this manner, you will count them again—not indeed the bones of the hands and feet, which you have already wrapped separately in papers—but you will recount the part of the **skull** <note>original: "caluariae"</note> which you removed from the rest of the head with a saw. In this, you will consider whether the small portions of the **temporal bones** <note>original: "temporum ossium"</note>, which are applied like scales to the bones of the crown and are usually removed by the saw from the rest of the temporal portion, have fallen off during boiling, lest you accidentally throw them away with the bone scraps or the broth. Then, you will weigh whether any tooth has fallen out of the upper or lower jaw. # THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I

...two, and likewise two **kneecaps** <note>original: "patellas"</note>. When you have counted everything, it will be greatly beneficial to place the bones again into clean and boiling water; and as soon as they are removed, wipe them separately with a rough and coarse linen cloth. If any remnants of the ligaments, membranes, or muscle attachments remain, rub and wipe them away, while taking care meanwhile that the slippery **cartilage** <note>cartilage at the joints (articular cartilage)</note>, which is applied to the bones like a crust, is not removed at the same time. While these things are placed around the fire to dry lightly, the cartilages of the ears should be stripped of skin and placed on paper with the rest of the cartilages. The same must be done with the cartilages of the eyelids and the nose; and then, with sharp knives, you shall clean the **hyoid bone** <note>original: "os υ referens"; the bone at the base of the tongue, which Vesalius notes is shaped like the Greek letter upsilon (υ)</note> from the muscles attached to it as accurately as possible while it is still raw. Once that bone is cleaned, you will accurately free the cartilages of the **larynx** <note>the voice box</note>, likewise raw, from the flesh and membranes, together with one or two cartilages of the trunk of the **trachea** <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"; literally 'the rough artery,' the standard term for the windpipe at this time</note>, which are shaped like the letter C. Now you will diligently clean the **breastbone** <note>original: "pectoris os"; the sternum</note> and the cartilages connected to it. This you will accomplish with less ease because it is covered by many membranes and is fatty; meanwhile, it should not be boiled at all, and should scarcely be sprinkled with warm water. When you strip the flesh from the cartilages, you must beware not to remove the membrane most closely covering the cartilages and corresponding to them, which we call the **periosteum** <note>original: "circumossale"; the 'around-the-bone' membrane</note>. Indeed, if this membrane is torn from the cartilages, they are more weakly joined to the breastbone, and they become shrunken, short, and twisted. Furthermore, to prevent these cartilages from shrinking, the breastbone must not be dried by the fire; rather, until you intend to connect the bones, it should be put away in a place that is not too damp, lest the cartilages again become excessively flabby and later create a deformed structure of the **thoracic** <note>chest</note> bones. For nothing so ruins an elegant construction of a **skeleton** <note>original: "sceleti"</note> as the breastbone and its cartilages, if they are handled carelessly or allowed to dry out before the bones are already joined together. However, the rest of the cartilages, placed on paper, may be moved somewhat near the fire, but in such a way that they do not warp too much; though it is better for these also to be dried after the assembly. Now you are free to join the bones and cartilages in the manner I shall soon describe, or to keep them disassembled—which would be far better, if one had to choose between joined or loose bones.

<margin>Which bones are most useful for teaching.</margin>
For bones that are disconnected and placed in order in a long box can be inspected separately at any time and can teach everything that pertains to the **knowledge of bones** <note>original: "ossium cognitionem"</note>. However, those that are standing upright and joined together do not show the sockets and heads of the bones very accurately; to tell the truth, they serve for display rather than for instruction. On the other hand, those bones are most suitable for study which are taken from Italian **tombs** <note>original: "monumentis"</note>—which are built like storehouses (as almost everything is here) and are so exposed to the air under some courtyard roof or otherwise that they occasionally receive rainwater. For besides the fact that such monuments are damp, water also gets in from time to time, by the benefit of which everything that grows onto the bones decays very quickly. Thus, after some time, those bones are removed and then washed; they are perfectly intact, and show everything to be seen in bones, provided they are placed in a box in order without being joined. Indeed, they are somewhat useless for joining because the cartilages of the ribs and the entire body are lost; for if any of them happen to be found, they are brittle due to rot and are free from the bones on all sides. Again, bones are unfit for this use which are dug up from the earth in other nations and kept in piles in **cemeteries** <note>original: "cœmiterijs"</note>. For besides the fact that they are affected by decay due to the dryness of the earth, you never find all the bones of the same person together as in the aforementioned monuments, or even in the **Cemetery of the Innocents** <note>original: "Innocentū cœmiterio"; a famous, massive central cemetery in Paris used until the 18th century</note> in Paris, where, if anywhere, by Hercules, I have seen a great many...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for preparing a human skeleton. The previous page detailed the cleaning of the cartilages and the sternum. # THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I

You have heaps of bones dug from the earth; these supplied such a rich abundance to me when I was first applying myself to the study of bones that, through long and tireless practice in observation, I even dared to bet with my companions, with my eyes blindfolded, that within the space of half an hour no bone could be handed to me from those heaps that I could not identify by touch. This had to be done all the more diligently because, as a student eager to learn, I was abandoned (I may truly say) by the efforts of teachers in this part of medicine.

<margin>How cleaned bones should be joined.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the connection and erection of the gathered bones, they must be joined soon after cleaning (lest they become too hard). For immediately after boiling, the bones may be perforated without trouble using only the **awls** <note>original: "subulis"</note> with which shoes are cobbled, and they are bound together with **brass wires** <note>original: "æneis filis"</note>. Everyone will accomplish this by their own effort, according to the manual skill they have acquired and the extent to which they have followed what we have described so far in this whole book. However, if someone should happen upon bones that are too dry and hard to be pierced as easily as those who puncture leather with awls, it will by no means be out of place to employ the instrument I once prepared for this purpose when I encountered certain very hard bones (which were most pleasant to look at due to the dry temperament of a middle-aged man). This was made by taking two wooden blocks, nearly three palms in length and almost three fingers in thickness; these were then perforated on one side, not far from the rounded end, with a hole large enough to admit a thumb, so that an axle could be rotated within them. This axle was nearly three palms long, the thickness of a thumb at its ends, but doubled in thickness and rounded in the middle, so that the ends would fit the holes in the blocks and rotate easily within them. This middle thickness would restrain the axle so that, once the blocks were firmly wedged into the corner of a table or bench according to the length of that thicker section and secured with the axle placed in them, the axle itself could only be rotated within the blocks and could not move forward or backward.

->[Image of a bow-drill apparatus]<--
<margin>In this figure, we have depicted the instrument with which harder bones are easily perforated. A and B indicate the two blocks which can be fixed into the corner of a table or bench. C, C the axle. D the part of the axle where the iron bit, like an awl, is inserted. E the bow by which the axle is rotated.</margin>

And so, one end of the axle, for the width of about three fingers, was as round as a thumb; for the width of four or five fingers, it was twice as thick; and the rest of the axle matched the thickness of a thumb so that it projected some distance beyond the other block and the edge of the table or bench. Into this end, I would insert the iron bit with which I perforated the bones—sometimes thinner, sometimes thicker, according to the need, following the method of those who daily prepare the small **beads** <note>original: "sphærulas"</note> suitable for piously counting the **Lord's Prayers** and the **salutations to the Divine Virgin** <note>This refers to the making of rosary beads (Pater Nosters and Ave Marias).</note>. Moreover, that middle thickness of the axle, sitting between the secured blocks, was perfectly rounded so that a thin leather strap could be more easily wrapped around it. This strap, once wound around the axle, was tied to the ends of a long rod like a **bow** <note>original: "arcui"</note>. Thus, by moving the rod up and down with the left hand, as if **playing a lyre** <note>original: "tanquam lyra ludente"</note>, the axle with the iron bit fixed in it would be rotated in the blocks and would perforate the bone which I held with my right hand. Therefore, bones will be perforated either with this instrument or with the aid of shoemaker's awls. You should have brass wire at hand, some thicker and some thinner; afterward, to make it more pliable and so that it breaks less often no matter how much it is twisted, it should be placed in the fire until it glows for a while.

<margin>Instruments of this kind are presented in order in the table of Chapter 41 at characters S, T, V, X, Y.</margin>
To these will be added two pairs of **pincers** <note>original: "tenaculæ, seu forcipes"</note>: one to twist the wire, the other to cut it once it is twisted. You will begin the joining of the bones from the feet, and first...

<meta>This page continues the specific technical instructions for articulating (assembling) a human skeleton. While the previous page discussed the cleaning and early preparation of the bones, here Vesalius provides a step-by-step guide on how to drill and wire the bones of the feet and legs, and how to construct the mounting base and central iron support rod that holds the entire structure upright.</meta>

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.

And first, you shall join the <term>talus</term> <note>The ankle bone.</note> to the <term>calcaneus</term> <note>The heel bone; Latin: "calx".</note>, and then the <term>cuboid bone</term> to the heel, and the bone <term>resembling a boat</term> <note>The navicular bone; Latin: "cymba".</note> to the talus, and the three internal bones of the <term>tarsus</term> <note>The cuneiform bones.</note> to the boat-shaped bone. Next, you will attach the bones of the <term>metatarsus</term> <note>Latin: "pedium".</note> to these, and then the bones of the fingers <note>The toes.</note> in order, along with the small bones compared to <term>sesame seeds</term> <note>Sesamoid bones, small rounded bones found near joints.</note>. You should perforate these more cautiously with a thinner <term>awl</term> <note>A small pointed tool for piercing holes.</note> because they are harder and more solid, and they may split apart quite easily under the force of the tool. When you have joined both feet, the tubercle of the <term>tibia</term> <note>The shin bone.</note>—which separates the cavities that receive the heads of the femur—must be bored with a hole large enough to reach the cavity of the tibia where the <term>marrow</term> <note>Latin: "medulla".</note> is stored, so that it is sufficient to receive a quite hard wooden rod. This rod, being also thrust into the <term>femur</term> <note>The thigh bone.</note>, joins the tibia to the femur in the manner of a nail, just as we see the planks of the bottom of a vessel joined together without glue.

For another hole must be fashioned in the lower part of the femur, positioned directly opposite the one I wanted made in the tibia, so that the same rod may be inserted into both the femur and the tibia; by its help, the knee joint may remain in a flexed position. Besides this rod, however, the femur must be joined to the tibia on both sides with a thicker wire, without neglecting the <term>cartilages</term> <note>The menisci.</note> which deepen the sockets of the tibia. When these bones are joined, the cartilages will be secured along with them and preserved in the knee joint. Soon, the <term>fibula</term> <note>The smaller, outer bone of the lower leg.</note> will be bound to the tibia above and below, and the <term>patella</term> <note>The kneecap.</note> will be fixed to the femur and tibia at the same time. When this has been accomplished in both legs, the bones of the <term>ilium</term> <note>The large wings of the hip bone.</note> are to be bound to the sides of the <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note> with a thicker wire; and then the bones of the <term>pubis</term> are to be joined, with their cartilage also intervening.

Now you will have at hand a <term>circular board</term> <note>A wooden base for the skeleton.</note> upon which the bones will be erected. It is appropriate that the circle of this board be large enough so that the feet can be fitly secured in the position in which you intend to raise the bones. In the middle of this board, a hole is prepared, so that when you store the bones in an upright case, the bottom of the case may have an axis which, when inserted into that hole, allows the circle to be rotated. Besides this hole, another will be fitted near the circumference of the circle, in which a wooden support can be fixed; this support, prepared in the likeness of a spear, a pike, or a scythe (whichever you prefer), will prop up the hand of the skeleton. Once the base is constructed in this manner, you will place the feet upon it, and with the help of someone standing by, you will ensure that the remaining bones of the legs rest upon the feet. Then, insert the heads of the femurs into the <term>acetabula</term> <note>The hip sockets; literally "vinegar cups" in Latin.</note> of the hip bones, so that you may correctly measure with a wire or a small rod the distance from the base to the lower part of the opening carved in the sacrum for the <term>spinal cord</term> <note>Latin: "dorsalis medulla".</note>.

This distance will teach you what the measurement of the iron support should be. This iron, fixed firmly to the center of the base and inserted into the opening of the sacrum and the rest of the vertebrae that transmits the spinal cord, will beautifully support the entire assembly of bones. The iron must be fitted so that it is strongly fixed to the middle of the base with nails, and it should be round or square from the base up to the very lowest part of the aforementioned opening. From that point upward, however, it is fitting for it to be wider than it is thick, so that it may later be slanted to the curve of the back, and adapted to the vertebrae themselves with lateral supports and small rods inserted so that they remain unmoved and do not rotate around the iron.

And therefore, the iron will first be made thinner at the point where the sacrum must be propped up so that it does not sink downward. For unless this bone is fixed and supported, it and the rest of the vertebrae will gradually descend, and with the passage of time, the legs of the skeleton will become shamefully crooked.

<margin>
a As if you were leading the hole through the middle of the body of the second bone of the sacrum from above.
b Of the first figure of chapter 18.
c Of the second figure of the same chapter.
</margin>
But because the sacrum (no matter how much you drive a straight hole through it with a knife for the sake of the spinal cord to pass the iron through) is not angled far enough back in this structure of bones we are now preparing, nor does it look upward enough when compared to the pubic bone: I am sometimes accustomed to carve a hole straight upward from the ^a middle of the body of the second bone of the sacrum in the proper position, as far as the opening for the spinal cord, where it ^c consists ^b in the highest seat of the first bone of the sacrum. Therefore, the length of the iron to be prepared must be measured accurately from the base to the opening of the sacrum, whether that be the end of the one prepared for the spinal cord, or a completely new one carved into the bone itself, as I was just saying. Concerning the rest...

<meta>This page continues the technical guide for assembling a human skeleton. Having previously discussed the feet and lower leg bones, Vesalius now moves upward to the mounting of the pelvis, the alignment of the thighs, and the systematic reassembly of the spinal column onto a central iron support rod.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

However, one does not need to worry much about the length of the iron rod; since, if it happens to be too long, it is easily cut back after the assembly of the bones. And even if you decide the bones should be placed in a case, it will be of great help if the iron is made roughly two palms longer than the entire skeleton, so that the portion of it protruding beyond the crown of the head can be inserted into a hole in the top of the case and allowed to rotate within it. Furthermore, once the <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large, triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note> is fixed to the iron disc along with the <term>ilium bones</term> <note>The large, flaring bones of the pelvis.</note> connected on both sides (as we have already described), you shall bind the heads of the <term>femurs</term> <note>The thigh bones.</note> into the <term>acetabula</term> <note>The "vinegar cups" or hip sockets.</note> of the hip bones with a thicker wire. You must carefully weigh how much you rotate these either outward or inward, lest you accidentally create a shameful twist in the legs, or cause the <term>patellae</term> <note>The kneecaps.</note> to face the inner sides of the legs rather than the front. This will surely happen unless you join the heads of the femurs to their boundaries precisely according to the position of the entire leg. However you do it, the wire in this connection must not be fully twisted tight until you have committed the feet to the base and the shins in the position that appears most elegant to you. You should seek this position primarily from the shape of the staff by which the hands will be stabilized; for a reaping scythe requires one position, a spear another, or Neptune’s trident, or any other tool you might choose. <note>Vesalius refers here to the common practice of posing skeletons holding symbolic objects, a hallmark of Renaissance anatomical illustration.</note> Now all the <term>vertebrae</term> <note>The individual bones of the spine.</note> must be fitted in sequence, and it is not difficult to observe the position and order of each, for the shape of the vertebrae and the nature of their articulation show this readily. Therefore, as soon as you have laid them all out in order on a table, you shall join the five <term>lumbar</term> <note>Lower back.</note> vertebrae to one another with two bindings made at the sides of their bodies, which together contain the cartilaginous ligament that comes between the bodies of the vertebrae. These types of ligaments are to be taken in order from the paper to which you attached them, always leaving behind the one that comes between the vertebrae you are not currently binding. For instance, at this moment, there is the ligament (or cartilage) coming between the sacrum and the lowest lumbar vertebra, and that which comes between the highest lumbar and the lowest <term>thoracic</term> <note>Chest/mid-back.</note> vertebrae. For once the lumbar vertebrae are joined, the six lower thoracic vertebrae are connected to each other, and afterwards the six upper ones together with the lower <term>cervical</term> <note>Neck.</note> vertebra. The remaining vertebrae of the neck, however, are not to be bound to each other; instead, the cartilaginous ligament coming between them is merely to be glued to the body of the lower vertebra. This is because the neck vertebrae, being simply threaded onto the iron rod, keep their place and do not have to support ribs in the manner of the thoracic vertebrae. Therefore, as soon as you have joined the vertebrae according to the method I prescribed, and before the iron is passed through them, you shall place the connected lumbar vertebrae onto the iron, diligently bending the rod to match their curvature. Then you shall join the lowest vertebra together with the sacrum, just as you previously bound the lumbar vertebrae to each other. Soon after, you shall add the lower thoracic vertebrae to these, constantly bending the iron as accurately as possible according to the path of the entire back, and binding the lowest thoracic vertebra to the highest lumbar. In the same way, the upper thoracic vertebrae are added; and when the lowest of these has been bound to the highest of those already placed on the iron, you shall adapt a somewhat wide and long stick, dyed black, which is placed against the back part of the iron and thrust down as far as possible between the iron and the vertebrae. By the benefit of this stick, the vertebrae are held more firmly against the iron and are not able to rotate in any way, so that later the entire thorax cannot shamefully wobble toward one side or the other. Moreover, for the <term>calvaria</term> <note>The skull cap or the skull as a whole.</note> to be attached to the iron, it is necessary that the crown of the head be pierced with a hole exactly corresponding to the width and thickness of the iron. This is so that if you ever pass the iron through a circular hole in the crown, the skull does not rotate in every direction upon any occasion; for depending on whether you want the face to look exactly forward or toward the sides, the hole in the crown must be carved either transversely or obliquely. Now the skull must also be perforated...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for assembling a human skeleton. Having previously discussed the mounting of the pelvis, the spine, and the orientation of the legs, Vesalius now explains how to articulate the skull and mandible, the ribcage, the shoulder girdle, and the intricate bones of the arms and hands.</meta>

# THE FIRST BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

It is best that the section you have worked with the saw in the skullcap <note>The upper part of the skull, often removed during dissection to examine the brain.</note> be joined with small hinges, so that when it seems appropriate, the skullcap removed by the saw can be taken off and put back again. For it will be of the greatest benefit to be able to look into the internal cavity of the skull, which contains the brain, as often as you like. To make this possible, both parts of the skull will be drilled with three holes that correspond to each other. One hole should be conveniently made in the <term>occiput</term> <note>The back of the head.</note> and one in each temple. As for the lower jaw, you shall attach it to the ends of the temporal bones with a bronze wire, not neglecting the unique cartilages found here. But since this connection is not firm enough to accurately bring the teeth together, and the lower jaw would simply hang down, it is more elegant for it to be joined to or separated from the upper jaw at will. Therefore, besides the mentioned connection, the sharp <term>processes</term> <note>Specifically the coronoid processes of the mandible.</note> of the lower jaw must also be drilled, and a small cord tied to them; this cord, passed under the <term>zygomatic arches</term> <note>The cheekbones.</note> and resting upon the bones and the crown of the head, can be pulled toward the forehead or toward the back of the head, allowing the teeth to be brought together.

Furthermore, it will now be the proper time to bind the ribs to the vertebrae and to their own cartilages. To do this accurately and diligently, you must first distinguish all the right ribs from the left, making a judgment either from the groove where the vein, nerve, and artery run along the ribs, or from the upper edge of the ribs, which is wider and thicker than the lower edge. Next, you should lay the ribs out in order on a table in this manner ((( ))) <note>The triple parentheses likely represent the curved arrangement of the ribs on the assembly table.</note> so that the right ribs correspond to the left, taking care in the process. It will be easy to place each in its own seat, provided you have not forgotten what we mentioned above regarding the identification of the ribs. From this series of ribs, you shall connect the first rib of each side to its cartilage at the <term>sternum</term> <note>The breastbone.</note>, and then you should have an assistant hold the sternum with its attached cartilages in its proper place. Next, you will bind the first ribs to the <term>transverse processes</term> <note>The bony projections on the sides of the vertebrae.</note> of the first thoracic vertebra. After that, you will join the second ribs to their vertebra, and then to their cartilages, and so on with all of them in order. Meanwhile, observe that you allow those ribs to gape open across their entire interval, just as they were separated by their cartilages before the dissection.

Now you will bind the <term>humeri</term> <note>The upper arm bones.</note> to the <term>scapulae</term> <note>The shoulder blades.</note> with a thicker wire, and then the <term>clavicles</term> <note>The collarbones.</note> to the upper processes of the scapulae with a thinner wire; then attach the scapulae to the ribs and the clavicles to the sternum. However, when you bind the humeri to the scapulae, you must consider what position you have decided the hands should be placed in. For here it matters much how the head of the humerus is joined to the socket of the scapula. In this connection, the cartilage must by no means be overlooked, by whose help the socket of the scapula is sometimes enlarged; likewise, the cartilages peculiar to the joints of the clavicles should not be neglected and should be bound to their joints. Furthermore, the bones of the forearm <note>The radius and ulna.</note> are not to be bound to the humerus before the entire hand has been joined to them. Thus the <term>radius</term> <note>The outer bone of the forearm.</note> is to be bound to the <term>ulna</term> <note>The inner bone of the forearm.</note> at the top and bottom, taking into account the future position of the hand. Next, if the bones of the <term>brachiale</term> <note>The carpus or wrist bones.</note> are separated and free from their ligaments, they must be joined to each other; otherwise, they are held together sufficiently by their own ligaments. To their lower part, you will first attach the bone of the thumb and the four bones of the <term>post-brachiale</term> <note>The metacarpals.</note>, and then to these the bones of the fingers, together with the <term>sesamoid bones</term> <note>Small, seed-like bones found in the joints.</note>. Finally, you will join the wrist to the radius, and then the ulna to the humerus. And when this has been performed on both sides, you will bind the hands to that staff which I said should be firmly fixed to the base, constructed like a scythe or in some other fashion.

Now that the bones are erected, you may fashion a "necklace" out of the bone resembling the letter <term>upsilon</term> <note>The hyoid bone in the neck, named for its U-shape.</note>, the tiny bones of the organ of hearing <note>The ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes) of the middle ear.</note>, the cartilages of the <term>rough artery</term> <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note>, the cartilages of the ears and eyelids, the <term>unguis</term> <note>The lacrimal bone of the eye socket, so named because it is thin like a fingernail.</note>, and the cartilaginous portion of the heart <note>The "bone of the heart," a calcified cartilage found in the hearts of some large animals (like oxen), which Vesalius sometimes included in human anatomical study.</note>. You can attach all of these to a small chain or a dried tendon from the leg or hand.

# ILLUSTRATION OF ANATOMICAL INSTRUMENTS.

## Index of the figures and their labels for the forty-first chapter.

In the present figure, we have depicted a board resting upon a table, which we use in the dissection of living animals <note>Vesalius refers here to vivisection, often performed on pigs or dogs to demonstrate functions like breathing or the heartbeat.</note>: then, to this board, we have adapted nearly all the things that one might use in the performance of dissections, and indeed throughout the whole study of Anatomy.

**A, A** The Table, upon which all the other items to be indicated in order are spread.

**B, B** The Board, suitable for performing dissections on living subjects.

**C, C** Various holes, in which we use loops according to the size of the animal, for when we bind the thighs and arms.

**D, D** Rings of this sort are adapted for binding the hands and feet.

**E** To this ring the upper jaw (free from the lower) is bound with a small chain, so that the head is kept unmoved; meanwhile, neither the voice nor the breathing is obstructed by the bindings, as might otherwise happen. <note>In the 16th century, vocalization and breathing were key areas of study in live subjects; Vesalius designed his table to ensure the animal could still breathe and "cry out" so the effects of nerve manipulation could be observed.</note>

**F, F** Different kinds of razors, near which a sponge lies.

**G** Knives, shaped like those used for sharpening quill pens.

**H** A common knife such as is used at the [dining] table.

**I** A large and strong knife.

**K** Knives made of boxwood. <note>original: "e buxo parati." These were likely used for blunt dissection to separate delicate tissues without cutting them.</note>

**L** Hooks. <term>Hamuli</term> <note>Small surgical hooks used to retract skin or hold vessels out of the way.</note>

**M** Various styles <note>Probes or blunt-ended needles.</note> together with a syringe.

**N, N** Curved needles with thicker thread, with which we bind together bundles of notes. <note>original: "literarum fasciculos colligamus." While literally "bundles of letters," this may refer to organizing anatomical labels or specimens during a long demonstration.</note>

**n** Smaller needles, which we adapt for sewing up wounds.

**O** A saw.

**P** Small scissors.

**Q** A wooden mallet.

**R** Reeds, suitable for inflating the lungs and certain other parts. <note>Arundines; these were used like straws to blow air into the lungs or vessels to make them visible and demonstrate their capacity.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' containing a scene of several nude children (putti) performing an anatomical dissection or demonstration around a table. One child points to an organ or tissue, while others assist or observe closely.</image-desc>Since in the previous chapter we happened to mention some of the instruments we use for Anatomy, and because talk of these and similar things will occur frequently in the subsequent books, I thought it would not be out of place to review them all in passing, just as they are depicted in the illustration of this chapter and as they ought to be at hand for students of dissection. First, therefore, many 
<margin>*a* F. Razorsᵃ</margin> 
knives must be obtained of the sort that barbers use for shaving hair, which we commonly call **razors**. It is fitting that some of these be sharp, while others should be rather dull—though you will always have a greater supply of the latter than you might wish. One should choose the smaller and lighter ones, although nothing prevents having a few large ones present as well. Indeed, many must be purchased, because they are ruined on every slight occasion when cutting through membranes, tendons, or ligaments; and since they are made of quite brittle iron, they chip easily, especially if you use new ones that have not yet been worn down by sharpening. From some of these, especially the smaller ones, the small iron "bump" <note>Original: *tuberculum*. This refers to the stop-pin or shoulder on a folding razor that prevents the blade from swinging too far.</note> is usefully removed, as it prevents the knife from extending beyond the straightness of the handle. This should be attempted primarily when no razors can be found constructed with an angled handle, such as those used by our own countrymen and French barbers. For the Italians, as well as the English for the most part, use crude razors equipped with large, upright grips or handles; these handles often prove to be an obstacle in diagonal incisions, preventing you from bending your hand exactly as you intended. To these 
<margin>*b* G. Small knives, used for trimming pens.</margin> 
one should add the small knives with which we trim <term>quills</term> <note>Original: *calamos*. These were reed or feather pens; the knives used to sharpen them are the ancestors of the modern 'pen-knife'.</note>. It is appropriate that some of these have a rounded point, while others have an oblong and sharp one. Those made entirely of iron are preferable; for in others, 
<margin>*c* 1st muscle table, characters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. A, ζ, Ξ.</margin> 
the handle breaks easily when we attempt to cut through transverse ligaments, and the iron itself, being fixed into the handles with resin that has been softened by washing in hot water, becomes loose. Those that are curved and resemble sickles should be utterly rejected, since we use almost only the tip during dissection; in those curved knives, the tip is bent inward and is only with difficulty placed beneath transverse ligaments, especially throughout the entire inner surface of the fingers. Furthermore, 
<margin>*d* H, I. Common knives.</margin> 
some of those knives we place on the table for dining are usefully employed. It is fitting that one or two of these be larger, but dull and thick, and made of iron rather than steel—or at least not excessively brittle. If it seems good, you may 
<margin>*e* K. Wooden knives.</margin> 
add to these two fashioned from <term>boxwood</term> or <term>guaiac wood</term> <note>Guaiac is a very hard, dense wood from the Americas, often called 'lignum vitae' or wood of life.</note>; let one of these be thin with an oblong point for cutting, and the other broad with a rounded point. Truly, I use those very rarely in dissections, since duller razors are always at hand. It will also be permitted 
<margin>*f* L. Hooks.</margin> 
to fashion two small **hooks**, similar to those we illustrated at the beginning of the Chapter. I have been accustomed to prepare these from the small forks <note>Original: *furculis*. Vesalius is describing the early two-pronged table forks, which were still a relatively new novelty in 16th-century Europe, especially outside Italy.</note> which are placed daily on Italian tables and claim the name "pyramids" for themselves. For if you thin both legs of such a fork with a file, and then bend their tips slightly into a semicircle, you will have prepared an elegant hook for yourself, the points of which you are free to sharpen with a file as you see fit. Thus, it will be helpful to prepare one hook that is blunter and another that is sharper. Although, in the meantime, setting the hooks aside, the fingernails are sometimes used in the work of lifting certain...

<meta>catchword: ...certain (busdam)</meta>

<term>syringe</term> <note>original: "syphonem"</note> at hand, if perhaps you should wish to insert it through the penis into the bladder at some point, so that you might be more diligent in that work. <margin>Various needles. 
h N.</margin>

<margin>i n.</margin>

<margin>Thread. 
k the needles are fixed to the thread itself.</margin> 
Silk **thread** is fitted to these needles, with which wounds are joined, or some other special kind if you fear that any sewn parts might be loosened or disturbed by others while you are away. For the rest, for tying off vessels, you will use that common thread with which we tie up bundles of letters, which is brought from Germany into Italy as the finest; among other nations, however, it is found to be weaker, thicker, less twisted, and less smooth.

l P.</margin>

# THE HUMAN BO-
## OF THEM JOINED TO-
### FRONT VIEW.

<column-break/>

# DY’S BONES
## GETHER FROM THE FRONT

<image-desc>
A full-page anatomical woodcut from Andreas Vesalius's "De humani corporis fabrica," showing a human skeleton in a frontal (anterior) view. The skeleton is posed naturalistically in a hilly landscape; it leans its right elbow on the handle of a spade that is stuck into the earth, while its left arm is extended downwards. The bones are meticulously detailed and labeled with small letters and numbers for anatomical reference:
- The ribs are numbered 1 through 7.
- The skull is marked with letters such as A, B, C, and G.
- The pelvis and limbs feature letters including O, P, Q, S, T, V, and n.
- The hands and feet are labeled with various characters including Greek letters like Δ <note>The Greek letter Delta.</note>.
The background depicts a detailed landscape with rolling hills, distant mountains, and sparse tufts of grass and shrubs.
</image-desc>

<note>This illustration is one of the most famous in the history of science. Vesalius broke with the tradition of showing "dry" diagrams, instead posing his skeletons in lifelike, dramatic stances. The presence of the spade is a "memento mori"—a reminder of death—suggesting that the skeleton has just dug its own grave or is contemplating its mortal remains.</note>

<summary>This page features the iconic frontal view of the human skeleton from Vesalius's masterwork, marking the beginning of his detailed study of the skeletal system. It combines unprecedented anatomical accuracy with artistic Renaissance landscape elements.</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS’S DELINEATION
## OF THE BONES OF THE HUMAN BODY
### FROM THE SIDE.

<image-desc>A celebrated anatomical woodcut from Andreas Vesalius's "De humani corporis fabrica" (1543), depicting a human skeleton in a melancholic or "Thinking" pose. The skeleton is viewed from a posterior-lateral perspective, leaning its right elbow on a high, classically styled stone pedestal. Its skull is bowed, resting against the right hand, while the left hand lies atop another human skull placed on the pedestal's surface. A hyoid bone, labeled "H" <note>The hyoid is a U-shaped bone in the neck that supports the tongue; it is often lost in skeletal preparations, so Vesalius highlights it here.</note>, sits nearby on the pedestal. The skeleton's bones are extensively marked with Greek and Roman letters (including A, B, Γ, Δ, k, K, R, m, M, T, l, Π, Σ, χ, φ) for anatomical identification. The pedestal is decorated with a frieze of rosettes and features a central plaque with an inscription. The scene is set on a patch of rocky earth with minimal vegetation.</image-desc>

->LIVES ON,<-
->ALL ELSE SHALL<-
->BELONG TO DEATH.<-
<note>original: "VIVITVR INGENIO, CAETERA MORTIS ERVNT." This famous Latin motto suggests that while the physical body is temporary and subject to decay, the products of the mind and the spirit are immortal.</note>

<note>This pose is a masterpiece of Renaissance art and science. By placing the skeleton in the "Philosopher" or "Melancholy" pose—contemplating a detached skull—Vesalius uses the <term>memento mori<note>Latin for "remember you must die"; an artistic or symbolic reminder of the inevitability of death.</note></term> tradition to make the study of dry bones a profound meditation on the human condition. The anatomical precision remains high, with the Greek and Roman letters serving as a key to the detailed descriptive text that accompanies these plates in the original volume.</note>

<header>ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY</header>

# AN INDEX OF THE CHARACTERS, WHICH are used in the three figures representing the entire
# skeleton, together with the various names of the bones.

In the three figures by which the entire structure of the bones is expressed—which I usually call the "complete figures"—almost the same characters are inscribed. However, if any character is unique to just one of them, it will be easily identified by the number I will now place after each character in the Index. My primary goal here is to list the names of the bones (though without explaining their anatomical function at this moment). I will first list those terms which I primarily use throughout the text; then the Greek names; and soon after (if there are others) the Latin names accepted by the most respected authors. I have arranged them this way so that the order itself carries a certain authority. These will be followed by the Hebrew names, though they are still partly Arabic in nature, since almost all of them were transcribed for me from the Hebrew translator of Avicenna by my close friend Lazarus the Hebrew de Frigeis <note>Lazarus de Frigeis was a Jewish physician and friend who assisted Vesalius with Semitic terminology</note> (with whom I am accustomed to study the works of Avicenna). I decided that Latin letters should be added to those names because many of them still appear in the Latin-translated books of the Arabs; therefore, it is right that other terms commonly found in the Latin translations of Arabic authors will also be included here, along with those read in the handbooks of doctors in our own time.

A bone, therefore, is called *osteon* <note>original: ὀστέον</note> in Greek, and *etzem* <note>original: עצם</note> in Hebrew. Cartilage is *chondros* <note>original: χόνδρος</note>, or *hash-hushim* <note>original: החשוחים</note> in Hebrew. We shall begin the names of the bones, as is convenient, with the skull, which is called in Greek *kephalaie*, *nyche*, *lyto*, *lodeia*, and *skaphion* <note>original: κεφαλαιοη, νύχη, λύτω, λωδεία, σκαφίον</note>. It is also called the "dome of the head" or the "helmet of the brain." Some have used these names to refer to the entire mass of the head, as it is found in cemeteries or commonly depicted; others use them only for the part covered by hair, the circle of which is called *stephane* <note>original: στεφάνη</note> and *peridromos* <note>original: περιδρόμῳ</note>. In Hebrew, it is *thik hamoah* <note>original: תיק המוח</note> or *kederath hamoah* <note>original: קדרות המוח</note>: the case and the pot of the head, the shell of the head, the bowl of the head, or the *asoan*.

The sutures, by which the bones of the head are joined together, are generally called *rhaphai* <note>original: ῥαφαὶ, meaning 'seams'</note>, or in Hebrew *shelavim* <note>original: שלבים</note>. Other terms include *fenan*, *direzan*, *adoren*, or "the clasped."

<margin>A 2,3</margin>
The coronal suture <note>The seam across the top of the skull</note>, called *stephanaia* <note>original: στεφαναία</note>. In Hebrew *hachlily* <note>original: חכלילי</note> or *chascthy* <note>original: משחתי</note>. Also called the "arc-like" or "the suture of the stern."

<margin>B 2,3</margin>
The suture resembling the Greek capital letter Lambda (Λ) <note>original: λαμβδοειδής, the lambdoid suture at the back of the head</note>, and from its likeness to the letter U, it is called *hyiloides* <note>original: υιλοειδής</note>. In Hebrew, *lamdy* <note>original: למדי</note>. Also called the *laude*, the *hypsili*, or the "suture of the prow."

<margin>C 3</margin>
The sagittal suture <note>The seam running front-to-back along the top of the head</note>, called *oboliaia* <note>original: ὀβολιαία</note> or *rhabdoides* <note>original: ῥαβδοειδής</note>. It creeps along the length of the head like a missile, a spit, or a rod. In Hebrew *checy* <note>original: החיי</note> or *scefody* <note>original: שפופירי</note>. It is also called "nerve-like," especially where it meets the coronal suture; this spot is called *zeudech*, particularly in the works of Mesue <note>A famous medieval Persian Christian physician</note>.

<margin>D 2,3</margin>
This joint, which does not look like a true suture, is called with its partner "the arrangement joined in the manner of scales" <note>The squamous suture</note>, or in Greek *lepidodeieis* or *lepismatai* <note>original: λεπιδωδείεις, λεπισμαται</note>; also the temporal or scale-like sutures. In Hebrew *chelaphym* <note>original: חלאפים</note>. Also called cortical or "false" sutures. The remaining sutures of the skull and its other connections lack specific names.

<margin>α 2,3</margin>
This bone, along with its mate, is called the bone of the vertex <note>The parietal bones</note>, or in Greek *bregmatos* or *koryphes* <note>original: βρέγματος, κορυφῆς</note>. Some call both the "sinciput bones." In Hebrew *hezem hachodchod* <note>original: עצם הקדקד</note>. Also called the "nerve-like," "paired," or "arc-like" bones (though others give the latter name to the zygomatic bones). Also called "wall bones" [parietal], a name some use for the temporal bones. They are also known as the "bones of reason" or "of thought."

<margin>β 1,2,3</margin>
The bone of the forehead [frontal bone], called *metopo* <note>original: μετώπῳ</note> in Greek; some call it the bone of the sinciput. In Hebrew *hezem hametzeach* <note>original: עצם המצח</note>. Also called the coronal bone, the "stern bone" of the head, the "shameless bone," and the "bone of common sense."

<margin>γ 2,3</margin>
The bone of the back of the head [occipital bone], called *iniou* <note>original: ἰνίου</note> in Greek. In Hebrew *hezem hahoreph* <note>original: עצם העורף</note>. Also called the *laude* bone, the box bone, the "prow bone," and the "bone of memory." There are some who also call it the "basilar bone" (because it forms a large part of the base of the head), although that name is specifically given to the wedge-shaped [sphenoid] bone.

<margin>δ 2,3</margin>
The temporal bones, one on each side, called *leptophon*, *korson*, *korrhon*, *lepidodo* <note>original: λεπτοφῶν, κορσῶν, κορῤῥῶν, λεπιδωδῶ</note>, and by some *lithoeide* <note>original: λιθοειδῆ</note>, meaning stony or rock-like. In Hebrew *hazemoth haabnim* <note>original: חזמות האבנים</note>. They are called the bones of the ears, even though that name could be applied to the two tiny bones that form the organ of hearing. These are shown in the bench where the second figure 
<margin>q, *</margin>
rests its elbows, marked with **q**, **☉**, and *****. The bone marked **q** denotes the one shaped like an anvil or a molar tooth <note>The incus</note>; the one marked ***** is the one we compare to a little hammer or the thigh bone <note>The malleus</note>. Since these little bones were unknown to the ancient professors of anatomy, it is no wonder they lack ancient names. Otherwise, the temporal bones are called by some the "drum bones," the "false," the "wall," the "hard," or the "arm bone."

<margin>ε 2</margin>
The process on the temporal bone resembling a stylus or a needle <note>The styloid process</note>, called in Greek *styloides*, *graphoides*, *belonoides*, or *plektron* <note>original: συλοειδὴς, γραφοειδὴς, βελονοειδὴς, πλῆκτρον</note>. Also called the "spur of the head." In Hebrew *chemo marhetz* <note>original: כמו מרחץ</note>. Also called the reed-like, sagittal, nail-like, or needle-like bone.

<margin>ζ 1,2,3</margin>
The process of the temporal bone resembling a nipple <note>The mastoid process</note>, called *mastoides* <note>original: μασοειδής</note> in Greek, or the mammillary process. In Hebrew *hezem potmy* <note>original: עצם פטמוי</note>.

<margin>E 2,3</margin>
The bone compared to a wedge <note>The sphenoid bone</note>, called *sphenoides* <note>original: σφηνοειδές</note>. Galen called it "the bone toward the exit" <note>original: πρὸς τὴν ἐκφόραν ὀστοῦν</note> (though it hardly touches the palate). Also called the *circūmoscau hamoach*. Also called the basilar bone, the stake, the "strainer bone," the "sieve-like bone," or the *cavilla*—though they also call the ankle bone by that name. In Hebrew *etz hamoach* <note>original: עץ המוח</note> or *moschab hamoach* <note>original: מושב המוח</note>.

<margin>η 2</margin>
The base of the skull, which we call the "stony part" <note>The petrous portion of the temporal bone</note>.

<margin>θ 2</margin>
The processes of the wedge-shaped bone that are compared to the wings of bats <note>The pterygoid processes</note>, called *pterygoides* <note>original: πτερυγοειδείς</note> in Greek. In Hebrew *hezzem chenaphy* <note>original: עצם כנפיי</note>.

<margin>F 1,2,3</margin>
This area, along with its mate on the other side, is called the zygomatic or "yoke" bones. In Greek *zygomata*, *zygoeide*, *zygode*, *syzygode*, or *magyros* <note>original: ζυγώματα, ζυγοειδὴ, ζυ- γώδη, συζυγωδή, μαγυρός</note>. In Hebrew *hazamoth hazogh* <note>original: חזמות הזוג</note>. Also called the "bones of the pair" or "paired bones," names which some also attribute to the temporal...
