<header>ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>
<page-num>207</page-num>

<margin>A.</margin>
...they ascribe to the bones, the handles of the temporal bones, the bow-like bones. The eighth bone of the head enumerated by us, which is compared to a sieve or a strainer, and by some to a sponge, is for that reason named the <term>ethmoid <note>original: ἠθμοειδές; meaning "sieve-like"</note></term> and <term>spongioid <note>original: σπογγοειδές; meaning "sponge-like"</note></term>. As it is also commonly called the "crested" bone, it presents itself nowhere in these three plates expressing the complete framework of the bones, since it occurs only in the internal cavity of the skull, just as the eighth figure of Chapter Six shows at A, B, A. Unless, perhaps, because it constitutes the septum of the nostrils outside the said cavity, someone might contend that it is visible in some part.

<margin>G.</margin>
On the twelve bones of the upper jaw, we have inscribed no character because they lack individual names. Otherwise, the upper jaw is called the <term>jaw <note>original: σιαγὼν</note></term>, the <term>cheek <note>original: γένυς</note></term>, the <term>smile-bone <note>original: γέλιον</note></term>, or the "mandible." In Hebrew, it is called <term>the upper jaw <note>original: חלהי העליון / halechi hahelioi</note></term>. These names are also applied to the lower jaw, marked G in the three figures, which the translator of Haly Abbas <note>A famous Persian physician</note> specifically calls the "Throat."

The teeth—<term>teeth <note>original: ὀδόντες</note></term>, or in Hebrew <term>teeth <note>original: שיניים / scinaijm</note></term>—are most often fixed sixteen in each jaw. Of these, the four middle and forward ones are called "incisors." They are also known as the <term>cutters <note>original: τομεῖς</note></term>, the <term>sharpeners <note>original: ἀκτῆρες</note></term>, the <term>combs <note>original: κτεῖνες</note></term>, or the <term>laughing teeth <note>original: γελασίνοι</note></term>. They are also called "teeth of laughter," or "four-of-a-kind." In Hebrew, they are <term>the cutters <note>original: המתחבים / hamechatechim</note></term>, or the "quadruple" teeth. However, the two middle ones are specifically called "duals" by the Barbarians <note>Vesalius often uses "Barbarians" to refer to medieval Arabic or Scholastic authors</note>. The tooth next to the incisors on each side is called "canine"; thus there are two canines in each jaw. They are the <term>dog-teeth <note>original: κυνόδοντες</note></term>, or in Hebrew <term>the dog-like ones <note>original: כלביים / chelauym</note></term>, or the <term>eaters <note>original: מתלעה / metalehoth</note></term>. Some also called these "laughing teeth." The five following teeth on each side are called "molars." They are the <term>millstones <note>original: μυλῖται</note></term>, or <term>bolts <note>original: γόμφοι</note></term>. They are also known as mill-teeth, jaw-teeth, peg-teeth, table-teeth, or what Cicero calls the "genuine" teeth. Others use that name for those that grow mostly after puberty, called by the Greeks the <term>wisdom-bringers <note>original: σωφρονιστῆρες</note></term>, the <term>completers <note>original: κραντῆρες</note></term>, or the <term>late-born <note>original: ὀψίγονοι</note></term>. In our language, they are "teeth of sense and wisdom and intellect," the "late teeth," "completers of age," and then "helmet-teeth." In Hebrew/Arabic, they are called <term>the grinders <note>original: נגחייר / naghuidi, negueguidi, nanged, alhalm</note></term>. The molars are called <term>the grinders <note>original: טוחנות / tochanoh</note></term> by the Hebrews.

<margin>H 2</margin>
The bone resembling the letter U (which lies depicted on the table in the second figure) is called the <term>hyoid <note>original: ὑοειδές</note></term>, the <term>lambda-shaped <note>original: λαμβδοειδές</note></term>, the <term>supporter <note>original: παραστάτη</note></term>, or the <term>throat-bone <note>original: φαρύγγετρον</note></term>. It is the bone expressing the image of the letter U or Λ. In Hebrew, it is the <term>L-shaped or L-like bone <note>original: עצם לאמדי או למדי / hezem lhami aut lamdy</note></term>. It is also called the bone of the tongue, the fulcrum, the throat bone, the bone of praise, or "Adam’s bite." In Arabic, *Alfaic*.

<margin>I, K, L, M, N</margin>
By these characters, visible in almost all three figures, the back is marked. It is called the <term>spine <note>original: ῥάχις</note></term>, the <term>thorn <note>original: ἄκανθα</note></term>, the <term>back <note>original: νῶτον</note></term>, or the <term>sacred pipe <note>original: ἱερὰ σύριγξ</note></term>. It is also known as the spine, the ridge, or the "keel of the human." In Hebrew, it is <term>the row <note>original: שדרה / scidra</note></term>. It is constructed of many vertebrae, <term>vertebrae <note>original: σπονδύλοις</note></term>, or "cubes." In Hebrew, <term>the links <note>original: חולייך / chulioth</note></term>. They are called "whirls" or bones of the spindle, which in their posterior part lead out to a sharp process called the spine, the <term>thorn <note>original: ἄκανθα</note></term>, the "Siminea," the "adsenascem," or "senasem." Furthermore, from I to K, the neck is indicated: <term>the neck <note>original: τράχηλος</note></term>, the <term>nape <note>original: αὐχήν</note></term>, or the throat. In Hebrew, <term>the neck <note>original: צואר / char gharaon</note></term>. It is also called the "Tenon" or "Atlas," which name some grant only to the seventh cervical vertebra. Further, from K to L, the vertebrae of the thorax are marked: <term>of the thorax <note>original: θώρακος</note></term>, sometimes the <term>back <note>original: νῶτος</note></term>, or the <term>mid-back <note>original: μετάφρενον</note></term>. They are the vertebrae of the breast, or sometimes simply the back. In Hebrew, <term>the chest <note>original: חזה / chaze</note></term>. Also called the "interscapulars." From L to M are the vertebrae of the loins: <term>of the loins <note>original: ὀσφύος</note></term>, the <term>flanks <note>original: ἰξύος</note></term>, or the <term>psoas muscles <note>original: ψοῶν</note></term>. These are the vertebrae of the kidneys. In Hebrew, <term>the loins <note>original: מותניים / mothnaim</note></term>. Also called the "Alchatin." From M to N, the sacrum is presented: <term>the sacred bone <note>original: ἱερόν</note></term>, or the <term>broad bone <note>original: πλατύ</note></term>. In Hebrew, <term>the bone of the anus opening <note>original: עצם פי הטבעת / hezem pi hatabahath</note></term>. It is also called the lumbar bone, the bones of the buttocks, the bones of the keys, the "alagas," "agit," "abhans," "abhaum," the "old woman," the "bone of the anuses," or the "bone of the anus"—names which are now attributed by some to the bone that follows. Therefore, N is marked as the coccyx bone: <term>the coccyx <note>original: κόκκυξ</note></term>, the <term>little vertebra <note>original: σπονδύλιον</note></term>, or the <term>rump-bone <note>original: ὀρροπύγιον</note></term>. In Hebrew, <term>the tail-end <note>original: עצה / haaze</note></term>. It is the bone of the tail, the "alhosos," and then the remaining names which we have assigned to the sacrum according to the opinion of certain translators.

<margin>O 1, 2, 3</margin>
The bone of the breast: <term>the sternum <note>original: στέרνον</note></term>. Some call the upper part of the bone by this name, while calling the lower part the <term>stake <note>original: σῦρον</note></term>. In Hebrew, <term>the bone of the chest <note>original: עצם החזה / hezem hehace</note></term>. It is also called the thorax, the plank, the "cassos," or the "shield of the heart." The upper part of this bone, which constitutes the collarbone area, they call the "upper little fork," and the lower part they call the "lower little fork."

<margin>P 1, 2, 3</margin>
The pointed cartilage of the breast, compared to a sword: <term>the xiphoid <note>original: ξιφοειδής</note></term>, or sword-shaped. In Hebrew, <term>the broad bone of the breast <note>original: עצם בדליי רחב / hezem bedely rachauch</note></term>. Also called the <term>throat-bone <note>original: גרוני / gheroni</note></term> or the "alchangri"—names by which the entire breastbone is occasionally gifted. It is also called the pomegranate, the "ensifoidis," the "knife-like," the "epiglottal cartilage," the "shield," the "buckler of the mouth of the stomach," or the middle of the lower fork.

<margin>1, 2, 3, etc. up to 12.</margin>
In the three figures, the twelve ribs of the thorax are indicated, both the true and legitimate ones, as well as the "nothae" <note>spurious or false ribs</note>, the illegitimate, or the faulty ones. They are called <term>ribs <note>original: πλευραὶ</note></term>. In Hebrew, <term>ribs <note>original: צלעות / zelahoth</note></term>. The false ribs are also called <term>false <note>original: ψευδῆ</note></term>.

<margin>Q 1, 2, 3</margin>
The clavicle: <term>the key <note>original: κλεῖς</note></term>. They are the keys or the "throat-bones." There are those who have also called these "shoulders." In Hebrew, <term>the shoulder-neck <note>original: שכם / scechem</note></term>. Also called the "little fork."

<margin>R 1, 2, 3</margin>
The scapula: <term>the shoulder-blade <note>original: ὠμοπλάτη</note></term>, the <term>back-plate <note>original: ἐπινώτιον</note></term>, the <term>flat bone <note>original: πλάτη</note></term>, or the <term>shoulder <note>original: ὦμος</note></term>. To the Latins, this is also very often called the "humerus." It is also called the "covered little shovel" or "scoptula." In Hebrew, <term>the shoulder <note>original: כתף / chatheph</note></term>. Also known as the "spatula," the "buckler," and the "shield of the thorax." Furthermore, in the three figures, λ marks the upper 
<margin>λ.</margin>
process of the scapula, which we generally call the "top of the shoulder," <term>the acromion <note>original: ἀκρώμιον</note></term>. Sometimes, however, it is called by Hippocrates <term>the acromid bone <note>original: τὸ ἀκρωμὶς ὀστέον</note></term>, and by Galen it is also sometimes called the <term>anchor-shaped <note>original: ἀγκυροειδής</note></term>, the <term>crow-beak <note>original: κορακοειδής</note></term>, the <term>closing-key <note>original: κατακλείς</note></term>, or the <term>shoulder-top <note>original: ἐπωμίς</note></term>. It is the "highest arm," and in Hebrew/Arabic <term>the beak-like process <note>original: אגרו חרטום / agrasso chartom</note></term>, or <term>the crow’s mouth <note>original: פי העורב / pi hahoreub</note></term>. It is also called the "pig’s snout," the "head of the scapula," the "alacharam," "manchar," "algorab," or "the destroyed." However, the inner or lower process of the scapula, marked in the first figure by 
<margin>μ.</margin>
μ, is called <term>anchor-shaped <note>original: ἀγκυροειδής</note></term>, and by Galen sometimes <term>crow-beak <note>original: κορακοειδής</note></term> or <term>sigma-shaped <note>original: σιγμοειδής</note></term>. It is the "anchor-form" process, or the process resembling the letter C. In Hebrew, <term>the eye of the shoulder <note>original: עין חבתה / hayn hacateph</note></term>. It is the "eye of the scapula," by which name the spine of the scapula is also called.

<margin>S 1, 2, 3</margin>
The humerus, or the bone of the arm: <term>the arm <note>original: βραχίων</note></term>. There are some to whom it is called the "ulna." In Hebrew, <term>the shaft of the arm <note>original: קת הזרוע / chane hazeroha</note></term>, or <term>the arm <note>original: עצר / hazad</note></term>. It is the "little arm," the "helper of the arm," the "reed of the arm," or "aseth."

<margin>T, U 1, 2, 3</margin>
This entire region is called the elbow-region: <term>the cubit <note>original: πῆχυς</note></term>, the <term>ulna <note>original: ὠλένη</note></term>, the <term>elbow <note>original: ὤλψος</note></term>, or the <term>short-arm <note>original: πυγὼν</note></term>. These are the "cubit" or "ulna"—names which are also granted to the lower bone of this region. In Hebrew, <term>the forearm <note>original: זדין / zadin</note></term>, or <term>the arm <note>original: זרוע / zeroha</note></term>. Also called <term>the two pillars <note>original: שתי עמודים / scete hamudim</note></term>, the "asaid," "aseid," or "alfahad."

<margin>X 1, 2, 3</margin>
The upper bone in the cubit, called by us the "radius." It is the <term>shuttle <note>original: κερκίς</note></term>, or the <term>near-cubit <note>original: παραπήχιον</note></term>. In Hebrew, <term>the upper pillar <note>original: עמוד העליון / hamud haelion</note></term>. Also called the "focile"...

<meta>This page concludes the detailed anatomical index for the skeletal illustrations of Book I. It covers the remaining bones of the arm (ulna and hand), the pelvis, the leg (femur, patella, tibia, fibula), and the foot. The translator notes that Vesalius continues to reconcile classical Greek and Latin terms with the "Barbaric" (medieval Arabic-derived) and Hebrew terminology common in the medical schools of his time.</meta>

<header>ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK I.</header>
<page-num>208</page-num>

*smaller [bone] of the arm, the reed, the lesser pipe of the arm.*

$\Upsilon$ 1, 2, 3 The lower bone of the forearm, called the <term>ulna</term> by us, and given the same names as the whole forearm. <note>Greek: πῆχυς / pēchys</note>. In Hebrew it is called <term>the lower pillar</term> <note>original: עמוד התחתון / hamud hatachthon</note>. It is also known as the "greater focal bone" of the arm, the "reed," and the "larger and lower pipe" of the arm. The process of this bone, marked 
<margin>$\nu$</margin> $\nu$ in the second figure, is called the <term>olecranon</term> <note>the point of the elbow</note>, the "mouse-tail," or the "elbow-tip" by the Greeks; some Latins call it the "hump" or "protuberance." It is an attached growth. However, the process marked 
<margin>$\xi$</margin> $\xi$, which resembles a writing stylus, is called the <term>styloid process</term> <note>original: στυλοειδής / styloeidēs</note>.

$Z, Z 1, 2, 3$ The <term>carpus</term> or wrist. <note>Greek: καρπός / karpos</note>. Some call it the "palm." In Hebrew and Arabic it is known as <term>rafegh</term>, <term>rafcha</term>, <term>rafeta</term>, <term>ascam</term>, or the <term>bones of the rafete</term>.

$\Gamma$ 1, 2 The <term>metacarpus</term> <note>the bones between the wrist and fingers</note>. <note>Greek synonyms: metakarpion, anthrōpos, stēthos ("chest"), kleis ("key"), ktenion ("little comb")</note>. By many it is called the "palm," the "chest of the hand," or the "comb." In Hebrew: <term>the comb of the palm of the hand</term> <note>original: מסרק כף היד / mafrech chaph haiad</note>; also called <term>alfelanuat</term>.

$\Delta, \Delta 1, 2, 3$ The <term>fingers</term>. <note>Greek: δάκτυλοι / daktyloi</note>. In Hebrew: <term>etzbaoth</term> <note>original: אצבעות</note>. The bones of these are called <term>phalanges</term>, "rods," "knuckles," "ranks," "battle-lines," "joints," or "internodes." Furthermore, private names are assigned to each individual finger. The thumb, or first, is called <term>the great finger</term> <note>original: μέγας / megas</note>, the "hand-opposer," or the "fore-hand." The second is the <term>index</term> <note>original: λίχανος / lichanos</note>. The third is the <term>middle</term> <note>original: μέσος / mesos</note>, also called the "lewd," "infamous," or "shameless" finger. The fourth is the <term>ring finger</term> <note>original: παραμέσος / paramesos</note>, also called the "medical finger," the "physician's finger," or the "finger of the heart" (especially on the left hand). The fifth is the <term>little finger</term> <note>original: μικρός / mikros</note>, the "smallest," or the "ear-finger" <note>the auricularis, used to scratch the ear</note>.

$\Theta$ 1, 2, 3 The bones joined to the sides of the <term>sacrum</term> <note>the base of the spine</note>, of which there is one on each side. These are distinguished into three regions (even if they are continuous) by professors of dissection. The first part, marked 
<margin>$o$</margin> $o$, is called the <term>ilium</term>. <note>Greek: λαγόνων / lagonōn</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the flank bone</term> <note>original: עצם הכסל / hezem hachefel</note>. Also known as the <term>alharia</term>, the "hips," and sometimes the "lumbar bone." The second region, in the middle and marked 
<margin>$w$</margin> $w$, is called the <term>ischium</term> or hip-bone. <note>Greek: ἰσχίον / ischion</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the thigh bone</term> <note>original: עצם הירך / hezem haiarech</note>. These names are often used for the whole [pelvic] bone, as is the term 
<margin>$\rho$</margin> <term>innominate bone</term> <note>the "nameless" bone</note>. It is also called the <term>althauorat</term>, the "box-bone," or the "bone of the femur," though very incorrectly. The third region, toward the front and marked $\rho$, is called the <term>pubis</term>. <note>Greek: ἥβης / hēbēs; also pektinis</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the mound of the genitals</term> <note>original: גבי הערות / gabe haherua</note>; in Arabic <term>helhaua</term>. Also called the "penis bone," the "shameful bone," and the "perforated bone." The barbarians <note>medieval authors</note> sometimes call this the "femur bone." However, the entire bone is called by the Hebrews <term>the bones of the mound of the genitals</term> <note>original: עצמות גב הערוה / hazamoth ghau haherua</note>.

$\varsigma$ 1, 2, 3 The joining of the pubic bones. Specifically, the <term>cartilage</term> is marked here, which comes between the union of those bones <note>the pubic symphysis</note>.

$\Lambda$ 1, 2, 3 The <term>femur</term>, or thigh bone. <note>Greek: μηρός / mēros</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the terror of the thigh</term> <note>original: פחד הירך / pachad haiarech</note>. Also called the "hip bone," the "hip," the "agis," or the "bone of the haunches." By some it is called the "leg."

$\tau$ 1, 2, 3 The outer process of the femur, which is called the <term>greater trochanter</term> <note>original: τροχαντὴρ μέγας</note> and usually the "rotator" or the "buttock-point." Also called the "pomegranate of the testicles," the 
<margin>$u$</margin> <term>tharuca</term>, or the "greater trochametra." The smaller and inner process is marked with $u$ <note>the lesser trochanter</note>.

$\Xi$ 1, 2, 3 The <term>patella</term> or kneecap. <note>Greek synonyms: mylē ("millstone"), ōpilis, hōlmakrys, konchē ("shell"), konchos, epigonatis</note>. Also called the "mill," the "shield-shaped bone," or the "little wheel of the knee." In Hebrew: <term>the eye or shield of the knee-joint</term> <note>original: עין או מגן הארכובה / hayn au maghen haharcuba</note>. Also: "eye of the knee," "pole," "adaicon," "rasca," "alrasa," "atrasafe," "aresfatu."

$\Pi, \Sigma$ 1, 2, 3 This entire part is called the "leg" <note>crus</note> by Celsus. However, according to Galen, the "leg" <note>skelos</note> refers to everything from the hip bone or the groin down to the very tips of the toes: namely the thigh, the lower leg, and the foot itself. This part between the knee and ankle is marked $\Pi$ and $\Sigma$. Within this region, the larger and 
<margin>$\Phi$</margin> inner bone, which we have marked $\Phi$, is what we usually call the <term>tibia</term>. <note>Greek: proknēmion and sometimes antiknēmion</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the great reed</term> <note>original: קנה הגדול / chane hagadol</note>. Also called the "greater focal bone," the "reed," and the "greater or domestic pipe of the leg." 
<margin>$Y$</margin> Furthermore, the outer and slenderer bone, marked $Y$ and called the <term>fibula</term> <note>clasp</note> by us, is named <term>peronē</term> or <term>paraknēmion</term> in Greek. It is also the "calf" <note>sura</note>. In Hebrew: <term>the small reed</term> <note>original: קנה הקטן / chane hachaton</note>. Also: "lesser focal bone," "reed," and "lesser pipe of the leg."

$\Phi, X$ 1, 2, 3 The lower parts of the tibia and fibula, called the <term>malleoli</term> <note>ankles</note>. <note>Greek: σφυρά / sphyra; aisa</note>. By some Latins it is incorrectly called the "talus." In Hebrew: <term>the two protruding ends of the two pipes</term> <note>original: שתי קצות הבולטים משני חקנים</note>. Also: "little key," "peg," "cahabin." $\Phi$ indicates the internal malleolus, while $X$ indicates the external.

$\Omega$ 1, 2, 3 The <term>talus</term> <note>ankle bone</note>. <note>Greek: ἀστράγαλος / astragalos; asris</note>. By some Latin translators it is incorrectly called the "malleolus," perhaps led here by an opinion not held by anatomists, who contend that <term>sphūra</term> signifies a "mallet" or "hammer," while in the neuter gender <term>sphūra</term> signifies the tali. In Hebrew: <term>hacharsul</term> <note>original: החקרסל</note> or <term>haarcchom</term> <note>original: ערכום</note>. Also called the "ballista bone," "ballista nut," "peg," "chahab," or "alfochi."

$a$ 2, 3 The <term>heel</term>. <note>Greek: πτέρνα / pterna; lakanen</note>. The heel bone <note>calcaneus</note>. In Hebrew: <term>haacheu</term> <note>original: עקב</note>. Also: "alrip," "spur of the foot."

$b$ 1, 2 The bone resembling a small boat or skiff. <note>Greek: σκαφοειδής / skaphoeidēs</note>. The <term>navicular</term> or "boat-shaped" bone. In Hebrew: <term>the equal bone or little ship</term> <note>original: עצם השוה או ספינה קטנה / hezem hafcane, aut sephinachotena</note>.

$c, c$ 1, 2, 3 This part of the foot, formed of four bones, is called the <term>tarsus</term> by us and the Greeks. In Hebrew: <term>rafegh</term>. Also: 
$d, e, f.$ "rafeta of the foot," and "bones of the rafeta." The three internal ones, marked $d, e, f$, are specifically called 
<margin>$g$</margin> <term>chalkoeidē</term> <note>bronze-like</note> by some. The outermost one, marked $g$, we call the <term>cuboid</term>, as it resembles a cube or a die. <note>Greek: κυβοειδές / kyboeidēs; polymorphon</note>. "Square-shaped." In Hebrew: <term>chardy</term> or <term>the separate bone</term> <note>original: עצם נפרד / hezem nipirat</note>. Also: "hailstone-like," "varied," "nerdi."

$h, h$ 1, 2, 3 The <term>metatarsus</term>. <note>Greek: πεδίον / pedion; metatarsos; stēthos</note>. Also: "sole," "flat of the foot," "footprint," "ground," "chest of the foot," or "comb." In Hebrew: <term>the comb of the foot</term> <note>original: מסרק הרגל / mafrech hareghel</note>. Also: "alfelameet."

$i, i$ 1, 2, 3 The <term>toes</term> of the foot.

$k$ 1, 2, 3 With the character $k$, the <term>sesamoid bones</term> are marked. <note>Greek: σησαμοειδῆ / sēsamoeidē</note>. In Hebrew: <term>helthesaminiath</term>; in Arabic: <term>alsemsemina</term>.

<meta>The previous page concluded Book I of *De Humani Corporis Fabrica*, which focused on the skeletal system (the "foundation" of the body). This page marks the beginning of Book II, shifting the focus to the "instruments of movement": the ligaments and muscles. The translator notes that this page serves as a technical preface to Vesalius's famous "muscle men" illustrations, explaining how the reader should navigate the visual and textual data.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS
## ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK TWO
### Dedicated to the ligaments joining the bones and cartilages 
### to one another, and to the muscles, the instruments of voluntary 
### movement: and presenting their own figures, as will now be 
### described.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'T' depicting several putti or cherubs performing an anatomical dissection of a human cadaver on a table in an indoor setting.</image-desc>

The tables <note>These are the famous anatomical "plates" or illustrations.</note> following in order here will be common to almost all the chapters of the second book. For the first fourteen show whole men: and the first of these in order contains a drawing of the front aspect of the man; the second shows the side; the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth also present the front aspect, but shown deeper or from the side according to the nature and position of the muscles being indicated. The six plates following the eighth, however, refer to the posterior <note>back</note> aspect of the body. Almost all are depicted in such a way that the muscles which were fully visible in the preceding plate are cut away in the following one and hang from their insertion points <note>The points where a muscle attaches to a bone.</note>. Furthermore, all the tables correspond with each other so that one showing the front aspect can be followed by another showing the back. For it was perfectly feasible to follow the third plate with the ninth, then the fourth with the tenth; next the fifth followed by the eleventh; then the sixth followed by the twelfth; then the seventh followed by the thirteenth; and finally the eighth followed by the fourteenth. 

Thus, you would not find it inconvenient if you viewed these muscle tables in both series and quickly looked up what each primarily represents from the indices of the plates and their <term>characters</term> <note>Vesalius uses the word "characters" to refer to the letters and symbols used as labels on his diagrams.</note>, so that you may more readily refer back to them during the text of the chapters. For very few chapters of the second book are preceded by their own specific figures—only those whose muscles could not be skillfully expressed in the general figures. Among these are the muscles moving the eye, the muscles of the <term>larynx</term> <note>the voice box</note>, those specific to the <term>penis</term>, and those proper to the <term>rectum</term> and the neck of the <term>bladder</term>. Additionally, a small table will be used at the beginning of the first chapter, primarily suited for showing the different types of ligaments; and the start of the second chapter will show those figures which are appropriate for understanding the composition of muscles.

Furthermore, it will not be enough to look at a certain muscle in just one table, even if I have marked it with a label; rather, so that you may see exactly where each one stands out or lies beneath another, you must seek it out in various places, especially where it offers itself to view in its entirety. This generally occurs where several labels are applied specifically to a single muscle, particularly when it is marked outside the usual order with a large Greek character. 

As for why I have arranged the images of the muscles into these full-body tables, rather than attaching individual joints with their specific muscles to each chapter, you should know this was done primarily because if the joints were illustrated in isolation, they could be distinguished by no one except the most expert in anatomy. Now, however, since everything is shown connected, it is obvious to anyone where each muscle is located—so much so, indeed, that it was entirely worthwhile to draw the whole tables in this manner, even if the joints had also been illustrated separately. Moreover, if I had thought it necessary for any reason to provide each chapter with its own muscles, students would not have lacked for them; since, apart from the expense, no extra labor would have been required of me. Because these full tables had to be engraved anyway, it would be no more work for me to order individual parts or joints to be cut out separately than it would be to take the printed sheets and cut out a head, an arm, a leg, or a chest as I saw fit and give them to the engraver. To this, the reader would always have spent the same labor in turning pages, since a single page cannot contain the image of the muscles, the index of labels, and the description and history of those muscles.

<summary>In this preface to Book II, Vesalius explains the pedagogical logic behind his famous sequential muscle plates, arguing that showing the body in full, layer by layer, is superior to showing isolated parts for the student's understanding.</summary>
<keywords>muscles, ligaments, anatomical plates, dissection method, Book II, anatomical labels, pedagogy</keywords>

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

## INDEX of characters for the FIRST MUSCLE PLATE.

The FIRST plate expresses the anterior face <note>The front view</note> of the body, from which the skin, along with the fat and all nerves, veins, and arteries standing out on the surface, have been cut away. No portion of the membrane we call "fleshy" <note>The platysma or panniculus carnosus, a thin layer of muscle just under the skin</note> has been left, even in those places where it becomes muscular. We have depicted all of those parts in the third plate—already dissected in many places—rather than in this one, so that this plate, along with the second and ninth, would not be obscured by those areas of the fleshy membrane. In this way, they may conveniently present the whole of what painters and sculptors almost exclusively consider in the study of muscles. Truly, the index of characters for the plates themselves will teach what the others specifically demonstrate. The characters of the present plate are as follows.

**A** Many glands are marked which are located under the root of the ears at the back of the lower jaw; they fill the cavity here and are positioned for the safe distribution of vessels. In this place where the glands are located, even without the help of a character mark, the opening of the ear (which has been cut away here) is very easy to observe.

**B** The muscle of the left side, inserted from the lower jaw into the bone resembling the Greek letter upsilon <note>original: "os $υ$ referens." This is the hyoid bone, named for its shape.</note>.

**C** The muscle originating from the breastbone <term>sternum</term>, which, together with its partner, is inserted into the upsilon-shaped bone.

**D** A very slender muscle, inserted from the upper rib <note>superior border</note> of the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term> into the upsilon-shaped bone: it is marked as $υ$ and $υ$ in the fourth figure of muscles, and as R and S in the fifth. The space seen on both sides of the letter D is hollow and contains the nerves of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>In Vesalius's system, the 6th pair includes the vagus nerve</note>, accompanied by the internal jugular veins and the "sleep-inducing" arteries <note>original: "arterijs soporalibus." These are the carotid arteries, so named because pressing them was thought to cause deep sleep or stupor.</note>.

**F** The muscle implanted by a fleshy insertion from the breastbone and collarbone <term>clavicula</term> into the mammillary process <note>mastoid process</note> of the temple bone; it is one of the seventh pair of muscles moving the head.

**G** A portion of the second of the muscles moving the shoulder blade. Nothing else of the present muscle is visible here except that it is inserted into the collarbone and the part of the top of the shoulder connected to the collarbone. However, in the ninth figure, the whole muscle appears, marked with $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$.

**H** This site transmits the external jugular veins. For this reason, even without any muscle distinction, it appears only as a hollow in living people (except perhaps in those who hold their breath more forcefully and make the jugulars bulge). However, once the vein is cut away here and certain mucous membranes are removed, that muscle I marked with D is encountered, as well as one which, inserted from the first rib of the chest into the site of the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae, is marked C in the eighth muscle plate.

**I** The anterior part of the collarbone, which appears bare of flesh.

**K** The muscle that lifts the arm <note>the deltoid</note>, whose origin arises from the collarbone, the top of the shoulder, and the spine of the shoulder blade; here the part of it originating from the collarbone and the top of the shoulder is seen.

**L** The muscle bringing the arm toward the chest <note>pectoralis major</note>.

**M** The breastbone, appearing bare of flesh. For the muscle bringing the arm to the chest only begins to be fleshy at the side of the bone. And although the right muscle touches the left by a nervous and thin membrane-like origin, the breastbone is nonetheless not entirely hidden in living men.

**N** N lurks under the armpit, marking part of the muscle that pulls the arm downward toward the back, which is to be indicated by $\Gamma$ in the following plate.

**O,O** This finger-like image indicates several insertions of the muscle which, inserted into the eight upper ribs of the chest, serves inspiration <note>breathing in</note>; it is marked F and F in the eighth muscle plate.

**P,P** This finger-like appearance is the origin of the muscle of the abdomen descending obliquely <note>external oblique</note>, which I did not wish to mark with more characters here. Likewise, I have not applied a mark to the straight muscle of the abdomen <note>rectus abdominis</note>, because it is still entirely hidden under the nervous thinness of the oblique muscles and the muscle bringing the arm to the chest. Nevertheless, the swellings which you see stretched along the length of the abdomen belong to the straight muscle of the abdomen. The thinness of the tendons of the oblique muscles does not prevent them from bulging out, just as the thickness of the skin in people who are not very fat does not prevent them from being seen before dissection.

**Q** The anterior muscle of those flexing the elbow <note>biceps brachii</note>.

**R** R is hidden under the armpit, marking the fleshy part of the inner head of the aforementioned muscle, bulging out here like a peculiar muscle.

<margin>Z</margin> *On the right elbow, this indicates the muscle taking its origin from the inner tubercle of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle</note>, which, being inserted into the straight bone of the wrist <term>brachiale</term>, flexes the wrist.*

<margin>a</margin> *On both elbows, a muscle is noted that leads the radius into a supine position <note>palm up</note>: it arises from the humerus bone and is implanted into the lower attachment of the radius.* <note>The brachioradialis.</note>

<margin>b</margin> *On both elbows, a muscle is shown that extends the wrist with a two-pronged <term>bicorni</term> tendon.*

<margin>d</margin> *On the left hand, there occurs here the tendon of the muscle that turns the thumb toward the index finger.*

<margin>e</margin> *On the left hand, the tendons are seen which are stretched out toward the outer part of the index finger.*

<margin>3, 4, 5, 6</margin> *On the left hand, the transverse ligament <note>the extensor retinaculum</note> is noted, visible on the outer side of the elbow/wrist. Truly, the number characters indicate separately how many channels and rings can appear to those dissecting this surface of the hand. There are four in total belonging to the radius, and they are adapted to those tendons in whose region you see the number. On the right elbow, **6** is also seen, indicating the same thing as on the left.*

<margin>f</margin> *A muscle is seen on the right hand, occupying the outer side of the palm and leading the little finger away from the others.* <note>The abductor digiti minimi.</note>

<margin>g</margin> *To the inner side of the muscle marked **f**, there appears a portion of the outer of the two muscles flexing the first bone of the little finger, or rather the muscle that bends that bone more toward the outer side.*

<margin>h</margin> *On the left hand, the site of the muscle is indicated that draws the thumb closest to the index finger.* <note>The adductor pollicis.</note>

<margin>i</margin> *On the right hand, a muscle occurs that draws the thumb furthest away from the index finger; and at its lower side, a portion of that muscle is seen which is the superior of those flexing the first bone of the thumb.*

<margin>k</margin> *The sheath <term>tunica</term> enveloping the testis and its seminal vessels, which emerge here in men. For in women, these vessels, along with the remaining organs serving generation, are hidden deep within the body.* <note>Vesalius is describing the structures of the inguinal canal.</note>

<margin>l</margin> *Beside the left testis, the character **l** is hidden, marking the glands that fill the cavity here in the groin, where a significant vein and artery enter the leg. Indeed, if the glands were removed, a large hollow space would appear here.* <note>Lymph nodes in the femoral triangle.</note>

<margin>m</margin> *The muscle proceeding from the pubic bone into the femur, noted as Σ in the eighth plate, and the eighth of those moving the femur.* <note>The pectineus or adductor longus.</note>

<margin>n</margin> *Two muscles emerge here, of which one will be considered the sixth of the movers of the femur (to be marked with Θ in the eighth plate), while the other is the seventh (to be indicated by Λ in the same plate).*

<margin>p</margin> *The muscle arising from the junction of the pubic bones <note>the pubic symphysis</note>, and the second of those moving the shin bone.* <note>The gracilis muscle.</note>

<margin>q</margin> *The sixth muscle among those moving the shin bone, whose fleshy substance is seen here: its tendon, however, is so thin that it does not obscure the outline of the muscles lying beneath it. For this reason, it does not show itself separately here, just as it does not in the second muscle figure. However, in the third and fourth, by using a certain method of dissection, it is somehow subjected to the eyes, marked in the former with the character **3**, and in the latter with Φ.* <note>The plantaris muscle.</note>

<margin>r</margin> *The present muscle, although it is covered—along with others placed there on the surface—by the recently mentioned membrane-like tendon of the sixth muscle moving the shin bone, nevertheless shows itself: just as it does not escape notice in muscular men even when the skin is still intact. Moreover, **r** specifically marks the seventh muscle of those moving the shin bone.*

<margin>s</margin> *The muscle taking its origin above the joint of the hip bone <term>coxendicis</term>, and the ninth among the movers of the shin bone. However, this one too is covered by the membrane-like tendon of the sixth muscle moving the shin bone.*

**t** This muscle almost entirely surrounds the thigh bone <term>femur</term> <note>original: "femoris os"</note>. It is the eighth of the muscles that move the lower leg <term>tibia</term>, and it is covered here by the tendon of the sixth muscle.

**ι** The slimmest tendon in the entire body <note>The plantaris tendon</note>. It arises from that muscle which begins at the outer head of the thigh bone and is described as the third of the muscles moving the foot.

**κ** The largest muscle of the calf <term>sura</term>, arising from the connection of the calf bone <term>fibula</term> to the shin bone <term>tibia</term>; it is easily the most powerful of the foot-movers and is the fourth. <note>The soleus muscle.</note>

**λ** The muscle that flexes the bones of the four toes; a small part of it is visible here. <note>The flexor digitorum longus.</note>

**ν** The transverse ligament extending from the shin bone <term>tibia</term> to the heel <term>calcaneus</term>. <note>The flexor retinaculum.</note>

**ξ** The muscle that moves the big toe toward the inner side; it is stretched out entirely along the inner side of the foot. <note>The abductor hallucis.</note>

BOOK II ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY.

# INDEX OF THE CHARACTERS
## FOR THE SECOND TABLE OF MUSCLES.

*The second table corresponds entirely to the first in terms of the dissection shown, but it is turned to the side. It displays the same muscles as the first, along with the sites of the bones that protrude on the surface and are, in a sense, stripped of flesh. Because almost the entire face and head are bony—with very little flesh covering them—they are marked with only a few letters in the following manner:*

**A** *The <term>temporal muscle</term> <note>original: "Temporalis musculus"</note>. Everything that stands above this semicircle, which marks the origin of the temporal muscle, is entirely without flesh.*
**B** *The <term>zygomatic bone</term> <note>original: "Os iugale"; commonly known as the cheekbone</note>. The opening appearing at the end of this bone is the ear canal.*
**C** *The muscle primarily called the <term>masseter</term> <note>original: "mansorius"</note> because of its role in chewing; it is the second of the muscles described that move the lower jaw.*
**D** *The muscle serving the movements of the cheeks <note>the buccinator</note>, which arises from one jaw and extends into the other.*
**E** *The left muscle <note>likely the digastric or mylohyoid</note> extending from the lower jaw to the <term>hyoid bone</term> <note>Vesalius refers to this as the "os υ," or U-shaped bone, following the Greek name for the hyoid</note>.*
**F** *The muscle inserted from the breastbone into the hyoid bone <note>the sternohyoid</note>.*
**G** *The left muscle <note>the sternothyroid</note> taking its beginning from the upper part of the breastbone and inserted into the lower region of the <term>thyroid cartilage</term> <note>original: "cartilaginis scuti," meaning shield-shaped cartilage</note>. Because it lies hidden beneath the muscle marked F, it does not entirely escape view here on the side.*
**H, H** *The muscle <note>the omohyoid</note> hastening from the upper edge of the shoulder blade to the hyoid bone. When the fat is removed and the external jugular vein is carefully cut away, it is visible near the lower H. Additionally, the upper H indicates the glands <note>the parotid and submandibular glands</note> placed here at the root of the ear and the inner part of the lower jaw.*
**I** *The muscle <note>the sternocleidomastoid</note> taking its beginning from the breastbone and the collarbone, and inserted into the <term>mastoid process</term> <note>original: "mammillare processum"; the bony bump behind the ear</note> of the temporal bone.*
**K, L** *The second of the muscles moving the shoulder blade <note>the trapezius</note>. K marks its upper part, which pulls the shoulder blade upward, while L marks the lower part, by which the shoulder blade is driven downward. On the right side, a portion of the right muscle also presents itself, just as we see the right buttock on this figure to the left. However, in the ninth table of muscles, the muscle of both sides is most clearly seen marked with the letters Γ and Δ.*
**M** *The muscle that lifts the arm <note>the deltoid</note>, which will be indicated far more accurately in the fourth figure by Ξ and in the tenth by Δ. I wanted to add this so that no one, seeing this muscle provided with many impressions, might persuade themselves from this single drawing that there are several muscles; especially since these impressions often trick skilled sculptors and painters. I would wish them to be most attentive not only here, but also on the entire outer side of the upper arm, because they often wrongly drag the muscle we will now mark as N out toward the exterior of the elbow. Although it is truly difficult to beautifully express in the dead the origins of the muscles that arise in sequence from the outer bump of the humerus and the line drawn upward from it; this is because during the process of skinning, due to the flexing and extending of the elbow, the muscles leading from those heads become flaccid in the region of the elbow fold, and they show a different curvature in the dead than in the living. Hence, when I explain some of the subsequent muscles, I would wish you to also look at the right arm of the ninth table, as well as the arms of the tenth table and the second figure of the second chapter of this book; for in those, we have imitated Nature more successfully than in the origins of the muscles of the present arm marked S, T, U, and X.*
**N** *Although you see several characters placed on both arms, pay attention only to the left for a while until I mention the right. N marks the posterior of the muscles that flex the elbow <note>the brachialis</note>. In living people, it seems to arise higher above the insertion of the muscle that lifts the arm than it actually does; although here it does not begin too low, it is perhaps (as painters should note) even higher than is proper.*
**O** *The muscle extending the elbow <note>the long head of the triceps brachii</note>, which takes its beginning from the neck of the shoulder blade where it meets the head of the humerus.*
**P** *The muscle also extending the elbow <note>the lateral head of the triceps</note>, whose origin hangs from the lower edge of the shoulder blade.*
**Q** *At this site, the two mentioned muscles extending the elbow join into one, no longer representing the appearance of a double muscle. The reason they bulge more noticeably here than in the rest of their course is due to another of the elbow extensors <note>the medial head of the triceps</note> which, hidden beneath them here, arises from the humerus; it is to be indicated in the twelfth figure by X and in the thirteenth by d.*
**R** *At this part, the authors of the elbow’s extension are implanted into the posterior process of the <term>ulna</term> <note>the olecranon, or "funny bone" point</note> and the ligaments of the joint, extending the sinewy part of their insertion into this triangular site, which is the fleshless portion of the ulna.*
**S** *The muscle arising from the humerus <note>the brachioradialis</note>, which is inserted into the lower attachment of the <term>radius</term> and brings the radius into a face-up position <note>supination</note>.*
**T** *The muscle extending the wrist <note>the extensor carpi radialis</note> with a two-pronged tendon.*
**U** *The muscle chiefly extending the index, middle, and ring fingers <note>the extensor digitorum</note>.*
**X** *The muscle that is the primary author of the extension of the little finger <note>the extensor digiti minimi</note>.*
**Y** *The lower of the muscles extending the wrist <note>the extensor carpi ulnaris</note>.*

## MUSCLE PLATE.

<image-desc>
A full-page woodcut illustration from Andreas Vesalius's *On the Fabric of the Human Body* (1543). The image depicts a flayed human male in an anatomical study of the superficial muscles <note>the muscles closest to the skin</note>, viewed from the front. The figure is posed dynamically, standing in a *contrapposto* position <note>a classical pose where the weight is shifted onto one leg</note> with the head turned to his right and arms extended outwards.

**Anatomical details:**
The musculature of the entire body is revealed with fine lines indicating muscle fibers. The figure is annotated with numerous small Roman and Greek letters acting as keys for anatomical identification.
- **Head and Neck:** Labeled with **A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I**, and the Greek letter **$\Gamma$** <note>gamma</note>. These point to the muscles of facial expression, the jaw, and the large "fleshy membrane" (platysma) of the neck.
- **Torso:** Labeled with **R** on the chest <note>the pectoralis major</note>; **S, T, V,** and **X** on the abdomen <note>the rectus abdominis and external obliques</note>; and the Greek letter **$\Delta$** <note>delta</note> on the right shoulder area.
- **Arms:** The left arm (viewer's left) is labeled **L**. The right arm (viewer's right) is more extensively labeled with **N, O,** and **P** at the shoulder, and a series of lowercase letters (**a** through **q**) on the forearm and hand, showing the complex layering of the muscles that move the fingers.
- **Legs:** The left thigh is marked **M**. The right leg features lowercase letters (**r** through **z**) and several Greek letters including **$\Phi$** <note>phi</note>, **$\Lambda$** <note>lambda</note>, **$\Xi$** <note>xi</note>, **$\Psi$** <note>psi</note>, and **$\Omega$** <note>omega</note>.

**Background:**
The figure stands in a detailed Italianate landscape. To the left is a hilly terrain with clusters of deciduous trees. To the right, in the distance across a body of water, is a cityscape featuring walls, towers, and a prominent dome. 
<note>This landscape is widely believed to depict the Euganean Hills and the countryside around Padua, Italy, where Vesalius conducted his dissections. The woodcuts are often attributed to the workshop of the artist Titian.</note>

### THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

O. *Although the part of the **muscle** that resides in the back of the neck <note>likely referring to the trapezius or splenius</note> does not offer itself to be seen, nevertheless the O placed at the root of the ear shows the transverse fibers creeping forth from there in some way. Therefore, in describing the sides of the muscle, you must first imagine the side from N to O; the second from O to H. K through L to N will indicate the third side. From K to M, you have the fourth side. For the more intensely dark line, drawn from K to M, is to be considered the location of the gap <term>interstitium</term> between the right and left muscles.*

P. Q. *The **muscle lifting the arm** <note>the deltoid</note>, which is here circumscribed on the anterior face of the body by L, N, and Q, although it creeps forward with its insertion lower than where Q stands.*

$\Delta$ *The **muscle bringing the arm to the chest** <note>the pectoralis major</note>, which is to be inspected simultaneously in the following table. For in that place, having been freed from its origins, $\Delta$ is noted just as it is here, and is circumscribed there and here by nearly the same characters. From K to L is that part of its beginning taking its origin from the clavicle <note>collarbone</note>. From K to R is the part of the beginning born from the middle width of the breastbone <note>sternum</note>. Furthermore,* R. *notes the membranous part of the muscle, which is stretched out toward the side of the mucronate cartilage <note>the xiphoid process at the base of the sternum</note> and the nervous thinness of the obliquely descending muscle of the abdomen.* S. *moreover signifies the fleshy part of the muscle, specifically arisen from the cartilages of the sixth and seventh ribs on account of the obliquely descending muscle of the abdomen.* Q. *is the index of the insertion of the present muscle, which is inserted into the humerus <note>upper arm bone</note> between the one lifting the arm (noted as P) and the first of those flexing the elbow, indicated by Z. Furthermore, if the mind is set on observing its sides and the insertion of the fibers,* T. *behold also the following table, which shows the insertion of the present muscle noted by Q and T (which character is peculiar to that table). By this means, with the characters of both tables joined together, you may measure the five sides of the muscle. The first from K to L. The second from K to R. The third from L to Q. The fourth from R to T. But in the present table, the broad insertion of the muscle is hidden; whence it also happens that the fifth side, reaching from Q to T, is visible only in the fourth table.*

U *The **fourth of the muscles** moving the arm, which draws it downward <note>the latissimus dorsi</note>.*

5, 6, 7, 8 *By these numbers, several insertions of the **second of the muscles moving the thorax** <note>the serratus anterior</note> are noted. And the individual numbers denote the positions of those ribs into which these visible insertions are made.*

$\Theta$ *The **obliquely descending muscle of the abdomen** <note>external oblique</note>, which with its mate covers the entire region of the abdomen and also covers a large part of the thorax. The origin of the present muscle, which hangs from the ribs, is also indicated in a way by the numbers by which the insertions of the second muscle moving the thorax are signified, since that origin corresponds mutually to these insertions. Furthermore, from R to X shows the white and fleshless line of the abdomen <note>original: "lineam albam"; the linea alba</note>, which cannot otherwise be expressed in a simple color. And although perhaps it would have been worth the effort to distinguish the tables of all copies with their own colors, the expense would have been not at all moderate for some.*

X *The **penis**, freed from its skin, which they call the prepuce <note>foreskin</note>.*

Y *The **seminal vessels** <note>spermatic cords</note>, still covered by their own tunic, which the peritoneum brings forth.*

Z *The **anterior muscle** of those flexing the elbow <note>the biceps brachii</note>.*

a, a *The **posterior muscle** of those flexing the elbow <note>likely referring to the brachialis or the triceps from a specific angle</note>.*

b *The **muscle extending the elbow**, which takes its beginning from the lower rib of the scapula <note>shoulder blade; this is the long head of the triceps</note>.*

c *The **muscle extending the wrist** <term>brachiale</term> with a two-horned tendon <note>extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis</note>.*

d *The **muscle leading the radius** into a supine position <note>brachioradialis</note>, which is implanted into the lower appendage of the radius.*

e *The **superior muscle** of those moving the radius into a prone position <note>pronator teres</note>.*

$\Lambda$ f, g, h. *The **muscle of those flexing the wrist** which is inserted after the wrist before the index finger <note>flexor carpi radialis</note>. And f marks its beginning; g the origin of the tendon from the belly of the muscle; h the place where the tendon would be thought to end by those who flex too negligently.*

$\Pi$ i, k, l. *The **muscle producing the broad tendon of the hand** <note>palmaris longus</note>, whose head is indicated by i, the beginning of the tendon itself by k, while l suggests the place where the tendon first begins to broaden out.*

m *The **other and lower muscle** of those flexing the wrist, which is chiefly implanted into the fourth bone of the wrist <note>the pisiform bone</note>.*

n *Here is obscurely seen a portion of the muscles, one of which offers tendons to the wrist, the other indeed to the thumb; on which $\Xi$, and then k and l, are inscribed in the tenth table.*

o *The **fleshless position** of the first internode of the thumb.*

p *The **muscle leading the thumb** furthest away from the index finger <note>abductor pollicis longus</note>.*

q *The **more significant of the two** flexing the first bone of the thumb.*

r *The **muscle moving the little finger** furthest to the side from the others <note>abductor digiti minimi</note>.*

$\Sigma$ s, t, u. *On the right leg <term>crure</term> is noted the **first worker of the motions of the tibia** <note>the sartorius</note>, whose beginning is marked s, the beginning of its tendon t, and its insertion u. Furthermore, the character 2 notes the insertion of the **second muscle** moving the tibia; 3 indeed, the insertion of the **third**.*

$\Phi$ x, y. *The **sixth muscle** of those moving the tibia <note>tensor fasciae latae</note>, whose beginning x marks; y indeed the place where it ceases to be fleshy and is drawn over the entire breadth of the femur in the manner of a membrane <note>the fascia lata</note>. It was not possible to express its tendon or membrane otherwise than is observed here in both thighs: in which we have dissected its thinnest part, drawn over the inner side of the femur, like a torn membrane, so that the section might show the nature of the membrane for a little while.*

For whatever is held toward the outside of that unequal line of section or side, it is still the membrane or tendon of the sixth muscle.

$\alpha$ Ninth muscle of those moving the shin <note>tibia</note>.
$\beta$ Eighth muscle of those moving the shin, seen more clearly on the left leg than the right, revealed by the sixth muscle, which is the author of the shin's movement. I have not applied a character to the seventh muscle moving the shin; for although it seems to bulge out in some way under the tendon or membrane of the sixth muscle (just as it does under the skin in muscular men), in this figure no portion of it is revealed.
$\gamma$ In the region of the groin <note>inguinum</note>, the muscles are indicated which we shall review as the sixth and seventh of those moving the thigh <note>femur</note>. Furthermore, $\gamma$ also suggests the glands of the groin, together with the cavity from which I have cut away the vessels seeking the leg.
$\delta$ Eighth muscle of those moving the thigh.
$\epsilon$ Second muscle of the makers of movement for the shin, whose tendon is shown by the character 2.
$\zeta, \eta$ The part of the shin bone <note>tibia</note> devoid of flesh; however, $\eta$ specifically marks the inner ankle <term>malleolus</term>.
$\theta$ Sixth muscle of those moving the foot. Its origin is indicated by $\theta$, while $u$ indicates the beginning of its tendon, the path of which 
$\iota, \kappa$ is manifest without the placement of characters, although $\xi$ shows the seat, as it were, of its insertion.
$\lambda$ Seventh muscle of those moving the foot.
$\mu$ The tendon of the muscle extending the big toe <note>pollicem</note>.
$\nu$ The muscle extending the four toes.
$\xi$ The muscle leading the big toe away <note>abductor</note> from the other toes toward the inner side.
$o$ The transverse ligament, placed in the anterior seat of the shin, and here reflected to the sides after a section was made.
$\pi$ The tendon of the two-headed muscle, the ninth of those moving the foot.
$\rho$ First muscle of those moving the foot.
$\sigma$ Fourth muscle of those moving the foot.
$\tau$ The longest and most slender tendon, produced by the third muscle of those moving the foot.
$\upsilon$ The muscle flexing the third bone of the four toes.
$\phi$ Fifth muscle of those moving the foot.

## Index of the Characters of the FOURTH PLATE of Muscles, which the following page will present.

The FOURTH plate shows a great many muscles of the preceding plate removed in the series of dissection: and then offers for viewing most of those which have not yet come into sight in the previous figures. All the subsequent plates up to the eighth plate of muscles will continue this until the bones occur naked in their anterior face.

$\Gamma$ The temporal muscle, whose beginning, not unlike a semicircle, is circumscribed by A, B, and C.
$D$ The external seat of the yoke-bone <note>the zygomatic or cheekbone</note>, which is devoid of flesh.
$\Delta$ The chewer <term>masseter</term>, which will be described as the second among the muscles moving the lower jaw. 
$E, F$ The beginning of this muscle is indicated, arising from the cheek. F is the portion of the beginning itself nearest the ear. And thus from E to F, the entire path of its 
$G$ beginning is measured according to the length of the yoke-bone. G marks the lowest seat of the muscle's insertion. Furthermore, if you wish to liken this muscle to a triangle, you will imagine E, F, and G as three angles; the third of which, marked G, is so obtuse that it might even be called a side.
$H$ A small nerve of the smaller root of the third pair of brain nerves <note>the trigeminal nerve</note>, seeking the muscular structure of the forehead and the higher eyelid.
$I$ A small nerve of the root just mentioned, propagated to the upper lip and the external seat of the wing of the nose.
$K$ The cartilage in which the left bone of the nose ends.
$L$ The left wing <term>ala</term> of the nose, bound to and leaning upon the end of the said cartilage. Between K and L, the skin of the nostrils having now been removed with certain membranous ligaments, the anterior muscle of the wing of the nose comes into view, which is exceedingly thin.
$M$ The muscle inserted from the upper jaw into the lower, and the second of those moving the cheeks on the other side <note>the buccinator</note>.
$N$ The left muscle peculiar to the lower lip, whose body can certainly be delineated with less trouble than its manifold intersection of fibers; this also occurs in the muscle marked M. Moreover, the opening of the ear shows itself without the placement of an O, as does the gland placed under the root of the ear, which in some way expresses that character.
$O$ Hardly visible is the portion of that muscle which pulls the lower jaw downward <note>likely the platysma or digastric</note>.
$P$ In this seat is placed the bone resembling the letter upsilon <note>the hyoid bone, named for its U-shape</note>.
$Q$ The muscle arising from the process of the temple bone that imitates the shape of a stylus <note>the styloid process</note>, and inserted into the bone resembling the upsilon.
$R$ The left muscle, attempting an insertion from the lower jaw into the bone resembling the upsilon, whose partner also offers itself to be seen here.
$S, T$ The right and left muscles of the bone resembling the upsilon, arising from the top of the breastbone <note>sternum</note>.

## INDEX TO THE CHARACTERS OF THE FIFTH PLATE OF MUSCLES, WHICH THE FOLLOWING PAGE CONTAINS.

*JUST AS the fourth plate showed many muscles dissected and removed that were visible in their entirety in the third plate, so this fifth plate, in the sequence of dissection, has many removed which the fourth had completely uncovered. For this reason, I present many here that the sixth plate will show as cut away. Meanwhile, it should not be neglected—as we warned at the very beginning of this book—that the plates expressing the front view of the body correspond in their order of dissection with those showing the rear view; just as if this plate followed the tenth. For the muscles which the tenth plate contains in a dissected state are nowhere encountered in this one.*

<margin>A</margin> *The opening <note>The supraorbital foramen</note> through which a small nerve of the third pair of brain nerves <note>In Vesalius's system, the "third pair" corresponds to parts of the modern trigeminal and facial nerves</note> seeks the muscular substance of the forehead and upper eyelid.*
<margin>B</margin> *The temporal muscle.*
<margin>C</margin> *Here a large portion of the cheekbone <note>The zygomatic or jugal bone</note> has been cut away so that the meeting of the temporal muscle with the muscle now marked D might come into view.*
<margin>D</margin> *The second muscle moving the lower jaw, which we generally call the "chewer" <note>The masseter muscle; original: "mansorium"</note>.*
<margin>E</margin> *The opening <note>The infraorbital foramen</note> through which a branch of the third pair of brain nerves is led to the upper lip and the wing of the nose.*
<margin>F</margin> *The wide muscle leading from the upper jaw to the lower, being the second of those serving the movements of the cheeks on either side <note>The buccinator muscle</note>.*
<margin>G</margin> *Nerves meeting on both sides at this character are spread out to the lower lip. Furthermore, the upper part of the character suggests the spongy substance of the lips, visible at both lips.*
<margin>H, I</margin> *The muscle pulling the lower jaw downward <note>The digastric muscle</note>. Each character marks one of the two bellies of the muscle, in the middle of which consists a fleshless, rounded part of the muscle.*
<margin>K</margin> *A portion of the muscle moving the head <note>The sternocleidomastoid</note>, which, arising from the breastbone and collarbone, is inserted into the entire mastoid process.*

<margin>L</margin> The bone resembling the letter upsilon <note>the hyoid bone, named for the Greek letter 'Y'</note>, from which we have cut away the first, second, and third pairs of muscles that move it.
<margin>M</margin> The first and second muscles of the tongue, arising from the bone resembling the letter upsilon.
<margin>N</margin> The cartilage of the larynx, resembling a shield <note>the thyroid cartilage</note>, which is still covered by the muscles yet to be described.
<margin>O</margin> The right of the two muscles which are inserted into the shield-like cartilage from the bone resembling the letter upsilon <note>the thyrohyoid muscle</note>.
<margin>P</margin> The right of the two muscles inserted from the breastbone <note>sternum</note> into the shield-like cartilage of the larynx <note>the sternothyroid muscle</note>. To the outer side of this muscle, one can see the cluster of the "soporary" artery <note>the carotid artery, so named because pressure on it was thought to induce sleep</note>, the internal jugular vein, and the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "sexti cerebri neruorum paris"; in Vesalius’s classification, this refers to the vagus nerve</note>.
<margin>Q</margin> The front part of the "rough artery" <note>the trachea</note>.
<margin>R, S</margin> The muscle proper to the bone resembling the letter upsilon, which originates from the upper edge of the shoulder blade <note>the omohyoid muscle</note>. Each letter indicates its individual bellies. The part consisting in the middle of these is the site of that muscle’s substance, which is not unlike a tendon.
<margin>T</margin> A portion of the second pair of muscles that move the head.
<margin>U</margin> The third muscle moving the shoulder blade, taking its origin from the transverse processes of the upper neck vertebrae <note>the levator scapulae</note>.
<margin>X</margin> Since this area showed nothing else specifically in a human than the seventh table; and because, having "sworn by the words of Galen" <note>original: "in Galeni uerba iurati"; a reference to the intellectual authority Galen held over anatomy</note>, we favored his opinions more than was right when these were being drawn: you see here a muscle depicted from a dog, which humans completely lack. Galen considers this the third of the muscles moving the thorax; it will be marked in its entirety as Γ in the following table.
<margin>Y</margin> Here we have torn the collarbone of the right side from the breastbone, though it is still connected to the top of the shoulder, and it still keeps its muscle,
<margin>Z.</margin> which will be numbered as the first of the thorax movers, and is marked here with Z.
<margin>a</margin> The top of the shoulder, or the higher process of the shoulder blade <note>the acromion</note>.
<margin>b</margin> The inner or lower process of the shoulder blade <note>the coracoid process</note>.
<margin>c</margin> The fourth of the special ligaments of the arm-bone <note>humerus</note> joint to the shoulder blade, reaching the top of the shoulder from the inner process of the shoulder blade.
<margin>d</margin> A round ligament <note>original: "ligamentum teres"</note>, inserted from the tip of the inner process of the shoulder blade into the front part of the outer head of the humerus; this is the first ligament of this joint after the membrane common to all joints.
<margin>e</margin> Another round ligament, proceeding from the highest part of the socket of the shoulder blade <note>the glenoid cavity</note> to the outer head of the humerus; it is the second of the special ligaments of this joint.
<margin>f</margin> In this place, the two ligaments marked d and e are joined at their sides and form a kind of transverse ligament, which lets through the outer head of the muscle that flexes the elbow <note>the biceps brachii</note>, soon to be marked ζ.
<margin>g</margin> The breastbone <note>sternum</note>, to which the cartilages of the seven upper ribs are connected on both sides.
<margin>h</margin> The first rib of the thorax; the others are also visible without the help of labels, along with the spaces between them.
<margin>Γ</margin> The first of the muscles moving the shoulder blade <note>the serratus anterior</note>. *i* and *k* mark the beginning of this muscle,
<margin>i, k, l.</margin> which represents a kind of hand-like shape at its origin, just as the muscle lying beneath it, marked *m*, does at its insertion. *l* indicates the tendon of the current muscle. Furthermore, *i*, *k*, and *l* together show the triangular appearance of this muscle to some extent.
<margin>m</margin> The muscle which, arising from the base of the shoulder blade, is inserted into the eight upper ribs of the thorax.
<margin>Δ</margin> The right of the straight muscles of the abdomen <note>rectus abdominis</note>. And *n* marks the fleshy beginning of the straight abdominal muscle,
<margin>n, o.</margin> not unlike a triangle. *o* marks the nervous origin of the same muscle, which forms almost the entire muscle.
<margin>p, q.</margin> In the whole interval from *p* to *q*, the straight muscles of the abdomen touch each other at their inner sides. In the entire area
above *q*, or just above the navel, the muscles are separated from each other the higher they climb. Moreover, *q* will also mark the thin, nervous part of the oblique abdominal muscles where they connect to the transverse abdominal muscle in this part up to the breastbone.
<margin>r.</margin> Furthermore, the line marked *r* ends the fleshy part of the straight muscle, which is the last part of its insertion in humans, as can be seen at the character *n* in the fourth table.
<margin>s.</margin> In the space from *r* to *s*, the tendon or membrane of the straight abdominal muscle of a monkey <note>simia</note> presents itself, or the non-fleshy part of the muscle.
<margin>t.</margin> *t* indicates the fleshy part of the muscle inserted into the first and second ribs of the thorax; this broad tendon and fleshy part is the muscle that Galen lists as the fifth mover of the thorax, which is not at all visible in humans as it is in long-tailed monkeys and dogs. We have drawn it here for the sake of understanding Galen, because otherwise this part of the chest would not correspond to the chests of the next two tables without these muscles.
<margin>u, u, u.</margin> Finally, *u, u, u* mark the inscriptions or nervous outlines impressed transversely on the straight muscle, to which the thin nervous part of the obliquely ascending muscle is very firmly attached.
<margin>x</margin> This line marks a small portion of the obliquely ascending muscle of the abdomen, where it is so strongly joined to the transverse abdominal muscle that during dissection it cannot be freed from the transverse muscle unless this mark is left.
<margin>y</margin> The transverse muscle of the abdomen <note>transversus abdominis</note>.
<margin>α</margin> The obliquely ascending muscle of the abdomen, here reflected back from the abdomen.

<margin>7.</margin> You see its tendon marked with **7**.

<margin>8</margin> The seventh muscle of those moving the foot <note>the fibularis or peroneus longus</note>.

<margin>9</margin> The eighth muscle of those moving the foot <note>the fibularis or peroneus brevis</note>, offering itself only slightly for inspection as it is hidden by the seventh.

<margin>Y</margin> A fleshy mass placed in the upper part of the foot <note>the extensor digitorum brevis</note>, which, divided into four fleshy parts, brings forth four tendons and moves the big toe and the three fingers nearest to it toward the outer side.

<margin>Ω</margin> Here is laid out the muscle extending the four toes, along with that portion of it which we counted in place of the ninth muscle moving the foot, and which you now see marked with the character (**σ**).
<margin>σ.</margin> I have applied no characters to the muscles occupying the posterior part of the tibia, because their series and abundance are the same as in the preceding tables.

# INDEX OF THE CHARACTERS FOR THE SIXTH TABLE OF MUSCLES,

### PRESENTS.

The head of the sixth table is tilted backwards, and it shows the lower jaw divided at the tip of the chin and pulled apart to the sides.

<margin>A</margin> Here, the same portion of the zygomatic bone <note>original: *iugalis ossis*; the cheekbone</note> has been cut away as we also removed in the fifth table. However, **A** specifically marks the temporal muscle, now that the <term>masseter muscle</term> <note>original: *mansorio musculo*; the primary muscle used for chewing</note> has been removed.
<margin>B</margin> The sharp process of the lower jaw <note>the coronoid process</note>, into which the temporal muscle is very strongly inserted.
<margin>C</margin> The left part of the lower jaw.
<margin>D</margin> A muscle hiding within the mouth <note>the medial pterygoid muscle</note>, which is inserted into the inner seat of the lower jaw where it is widest; it is considered the third of those moving the jaw.
<margin>E</margin> The <term>uvula</term> <note>original: *gurgulio*</note>, hanging down from the end of the palate.
<margin>F</margin> The left gland, not unlike an almond <note>the tonsil</note>, placed at the most prominent seat of the <term>larynx</term> <note>the voice box</note>; though it sits a little higher in the throat than the larynx.
<margin>G</margin> The tongue; however, the upper part of the character is adjacent to the lid of the larynx <note>the epiglottis</note>.
<margin>H</margin> In this seat, many muscles serving the movements of the head and neck are blended together.
<margin>I</margin> The muscle pulling the lower jaw downward <note>the digastric muscle</note>; here it hangs from its origin.
<margin>K</margin> The third of the muscles moving the human <term>scapula</term> <note>the shoulder blade; likely the levator scapulae</note>.
<margin>L</margin> A remarkably fleshy gland <note>the thyroid gland</note>, which grows onto the left side of the root of the larynx, and has a partner on the other side.
<margin>M</margin> The <term>trachea</term> <note>original: *aspera arteria*; literally 'rough artery', the standard Renaissance term for the windpipe</note>, now free from the muscles lying upon it.
<margin>N</margin> This mass consists of the vessels and nerves stretched out along the sides of the trachea, although the first of the muscles moving the back also show themselves here to some extent.
<margin>Γ</margin> Since it would have been necessary to draw this region of the chest and neck similar to what the following table shows, I thought it would not be out of place to represent this <term>muscle of Galen</term> from a dog. <note>Vesalius frequently points out where the ancient physician Galen described animal anatomy as if it were human; this refers to the serratus posterior superior</note> It takes its origin marked **O** from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and is carried as a fleshy mass as far as the fourth rib. There, marked **P**, it ends in a membranous tendon marked **Q**, which extends downward to several more ribs.
<margin>O, P, Q</margin> <note>These letters refer to the origin, body, and tendon of the canine muscle described in Γ</note>.
<margin>R</margin> A muscle taking its beginning from the base of the scapula, the second of those moving the <term>thorax</term> <note>the chest; the serratus anterior muscle</note>.

->The bone of the chest <note>the sternum</note> is visible without the placement of characters, just as are the ribs and their intervals, together with the external intercostal muscles. However, so that you may better weigh each part, let **S** signify the bone of the third rib; **T** the cartilage of the third rib; **U** the external intercostal muscle placed in the interval between the bones of the second and third ribs, whose fibers are carried downward and forward. **X** will denote the external intercostal muscle visible between the cartilages of the second and third ribs, whose fibers creep upward and forward.<-

<margin>S, T, U, X</margin> <note>Refer to the rib bone, cartilage, and intercostal fibers described above</note>.
<margin>a</margin> An artery and vein <note>the internal thoracic/epigastric vessels</note> propagated downward beneath the chest bone to the upper parts of the abdomen, here cut away from the <term>rectus muscles</term> of the abdomen.
<margin>Δ</margin> The <term>transversus abdominis</term> muscle, which the path or ends of the ribs and the region of the <term>sacrum</term> joined to the left side of the hip bone abundantly circumscribe here.
<margin>b</margin> This marks the place where the tendon of the <term>internal oblique</term> muscle <note>original: *obliquè ascendentis*</note> is very tenaciously attached to the transverse muscle of the abdomen before it climbs over the rectus muscle.
<margin>c</margin> This indicates the roughness produced by the connection of the oblique muscles with the transverse muscles at the point where the rectus muscles gap away from each other above the navel toward the chest bone.
<margin>d</margin> A hole <note>the inguinal ring</note> providing a path for the seminal vessels in men.
<margin>e</margin> A vein and artery running upward into the rectus muscles of the abdomen and neighboring areas, from the great distribution of vessels going to the legs.
<margin>f</margin> Here the rectus abdominis muscle of the left side hangs from the pubic bone, also showing the series of vessels joined to its posterior side.
<margin>g</margin> The spine of the <term>ilium</term> <note>the hip bone</note>, cleared of the fleshy parts of the two oblique muscles of the abdomen.
<margin>h</margin> Direct your attention to the shoulder blades and the left arm. There, **h** marks the superior angle of the scapula, into which the third of the muscles moving the scapula, marked **K**, is inserted.
<margin>i</margin> The top of the shoulder <note>the acromion</note>, or the higher process of the scapula.
<margin>k</margin> The fifth of the muscles moving the arm <note>the supraspinatus</note>, occupying the hollow of the scapula which lies between its higher rib and the root of the superior process, or the spine of the scapula.
<margin>l</margin> The inner process of the scapula, resembling the shape of an anchor <note>the coracoid process</note>.
<margin>☉</margin> The anterior muscle of those flexing the elbow <note>the biceps brachii</note>, whose outer head, arising from the rim of the socket of the scapula, is marked **m**.
<margin>m, n</margin> **n** indicates the inner head, born from the inner process of the scapula. To more accurately distinguish the tendinous part of this head from the fleshy part, look at the right arm of this table, in which **n** denotes the tendinous part and **o** the fleshy.
<margin>o, p, q</margin> Furthermore, **p** indicates the union of the two heads, and **q** the beginning of the tendon which this muscle leads out.
