# Index of Characters for the SEVENTH Table of Muscles.

The body in the *SEVENTH* muscle table, having had the cord by which it hung during the painting loosened at the end, has fallen backward just enough to allow the <term>transverse septum<note>The diaphragm.</note></term> to be seen, now that the <term>peritoneum<note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note></term> and all the organs it encloses have been removed. You can see this septum depicted on the left side of the present table in the same shape in which it appeared to us when it was upright and clinging to the wall by its own moisture. To prevent the right <term>scapula<note>Shoulder blade.</note></term> from drooping downward like a broken wing, we have suspended it with a small cord so that its entire cavity is in view.

**A** The <term>uvula<note>original: "Gurgulio"; the small fleshy part hanging at the back of the throat.</note></term>, hanging from the edge of the palate, with the lower jaw entirely removed.
**B** Several bodies of the cervical vertebrae are shown here in their anterior position, where they are not covered by muscles.
**C, D** The first pair of muscles that move the back.
**E** Part of the <term>stomach<note>Here referring to the esophagus or "gullet".</note></term>, or gullet, cut away here.
**F** The part of the <term>rough artery<note>The trachea or windpipe.</note></term> laid over the esophagus; here also it is freed from the rest of its trunk near the throat. Furthermore, the vessels occurring on both sides of the rough artery are the <term>carotid arteries<note>original: "soporales"; literally "sleep-inducing" arteries, as pressure on them was thought to cause sleep.</note></term>, along with the internal jugular veins and the sixth pair of cerebral nerves <note>In modern anatomy, the vagus nerve is the tenth cranial nerve (CN X), but was classified as the sixth pair in Vesalius's time.</note>.
**G** The other muscle of the second pair that moves the back.
**H** The third muscle moving the scapula, which has been cut through on the right side.
**I** The fifth muscle moving the arm, situated between the higher ridge of the scapula and the root of its superior process <note>The supraspinatus muscle.</note>.
**Γ** <note>Greek letter Gamma</note> The sixth muscle moving the arm, occupying the entire anterior cavity of the scapula <note>The subscapularis muscle.</note>. Its insertion is marked with 
**K, K**, and its remaining form is understood from the image of the scapula. However, if you wish to establish the triangular shape of this muscle, you may consider **K**, **L**, and **$\mathcal{L}$** together.
**L, L** The second muscle moving the <term>thorax<note>The chest.</note></term>, inserted into the eight upper ribs in the manner of a hand <note>The serratus anterior muscle.</note>.
**M** The third muscle acting on the arm, arising from the lower rib of the scapula near the inferior angle of the scapula's base <note>The teres major muscle.</note>.
**N, N** The muscle that extends the elbow, whose beginning, marked by the upper **N**, is drawn from the scapula <note>The triceps brachii.</note>.
**O** A portion of the tendon of the fourth muscle moving the arm.
**P** The posterior muscle flexing the elbow, which is almost entirely visible here <note>The brachialis muscle.</note>.
**Q** The superior muscle that places the <term>radius<note>One of the two bones of the forearm.</note></term> in a <term>prone<note>Palm down.</note></term> position <note>The pronator teres.</note>.
**R, R** The anterior muscle flexing the elbow, which has been freed from the bones where it took its origin and torn away from the arm, hanging now from its insertion <note>The biceps brachii.</note>.
**S** The radius.
**T** The <term>ulna<note>The other bone of the forearm.</note></term>.
**U** The ligament passing between the radius and ulna where they gape apart from one another <note>The interosseous membrane.</note>.
**X** The inferior muscle moving the radius into a prone position, which is nearly square in shape <note>The pronator quadratus.</note>.
**Y, Y** Hanging from its insertion on the right radius (which is lifted higher than the left along with the whole hand) is the longer muscle that leads the radius into a <term>supine<note>Palm up.</note></term> position <note>The brachioradialis.</note>.
**a** The smaller muscle flexing the first bone of the thumb, freed from its origin and hanging only from the bone into which it is inserted.
**1, 2, 3** These three characters mark the muscles flexing the second bone of the thumb.
**b** The muscle flexing the third <term>internode<note>The joint or segment of a finger.</note></term> of the thumb hangs from its insertion.
**c** The muscle responsible for the flexion of the third bone of the four fingers, cut from the elbow and reflected downward. You should observe this carefully, because the muscles that bring the four fingers toward the thumb attend its tendons; the one that moves the index finger is marked with 
**d.** or **d**, hanging from its insertion just like the other three. Furthermore, portions of the muscle flexing the second bone of the four fingers are still preserved here; the portion proper to the index finger is marked with **e**; the tendon flexing the third bone of the index finger is marked with **f**. Moreover, in the right hand, only the insertions of these muscles are visible:
**g, h** mark the insertions; **g** on the index finger indicates the insertion of the muscle bringing the index finger toward the thumb; **h** the insertion of the tendon flexing the second bone of the index finger.
**i.** marks the insertion of the tendon that governs the flexion of the third bone of that finger.

-># ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY: EIGHTH TABLE OF MUSCLES.<-

This illustration presents a full-length anatomical figure viewed from behind. In a characteristic blend of science and art, the figure is placed within a landscape, leaning against a tall, ruined stone pillar. This pose is not merely for dramatic effect; by leaning the body and tilting the head sharply backward, the <term>musculature<note>The arrangement or system of muscles in the body.</note></term> is stretched and positioned to reveal the deep layers of the back, the spinal column, and the internal anatomy of the throat.

The body has been partially <term>flayed<note>The process of removing skin and superficial tissue to expose the structures beneath.</note></term> to expose the layers beneath the surface. You can see the intricate muscles of the neck and the sturdy bones of the <term>pelvis<note>The large bony structure at the base of the spine.</note></term>. 

### Anatomical Labels

The figure is extensively labeled to guide the student of anatomy. These markers include:

*   **Latin Letters:** Both uppercase (**A** through **Z**) and lowercase (**a** through **z**) are used to identify specific muscles and bony landmarks.
*   **Greek Letters:** Vesalius employs characters such as **Θ** (Theta), **Λ** (Lambda), **Π** (Pi), **Σ** (Sigma), **Φ** (Phi), and **Ψ** (Psi) to denote deeper structures.
*   **Special Symbols:** The symbol **⊙** is used to pinpoint exact locations of muscle attachments.

### The Larynx Inset

In the lower-left corner of the page, there is a separate, detailed diagram. This inset focuses exclusively on the <term>larynx<note>The voice box, located in the throat.</note></term> and its associated muscles. 

**1, 2, 3...** These Arabic numerals mark the various cartilages and muscles that facilitate breathing and speech.
**α, β, γ, δ** These Greek letters <note>original: alpha, beta, gamma, delta</note> identify the smaller, delicate muscles that control the tension of the vocal cords.

The background, featuring a crumbling wall and rolling hills, serves to remind the viewer of the transience of life—a common theme in Renaissance anatomical art—while the figure itself provides an enduring map of human construction.

## INDEX OF CHARACTERS
->For the Ninth Muscle Plate<-

The NINTH plate is the first to show the entire back view of the body. It has no muscles cut away except for those formed by the "fleshy membrane" <note>original: *carnea membrana*; a layer of tissue under the skin</note>, which were shown in the third plate. However, we have here dissected the transverse ligaments located on the outer part of the forearm near the wrist <note>original: *brachiale*</note>, as they were clearly visible and marked with numbers in the first and second plates.

<margin>A</margin> The temporal muscle.
<margin>B</margin> The cheekbone <note>original: *os iugale*; the zygomatic bone</note>.
<margin>C</margin> The muscle specifically called the masseter <note>the primary muscle for chewing</note>, or the second to be described among the muscles moving the lower jaw. The opening of the ear, with the glands situated below it, is visible just past this character.
<margin>D</margin> The muscle that moves the head which, arising from the breastbone and the collarbone <term>clavicle</term>, is inserted into the mastoid process of the temporal bone. <note>This is the sternocleidomastoid muscle.</note>
<margin>Γ, Δ</margin> The muscle to be listed second among those moving the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term>. The origin of this muscle, springing from the bone at the back of the head <term>occiput</term>, is marked with E and F. The area from E to G marks the origin of the muscle from the back of the head down to the spine of the eighth vertebra of the chest, arising in a certain way from the tips of the middle vertebrae. H and I indicate the insertion which the muscle makes into the spine of the shoulder blade, the top of the shoulder, and the broad part of the collarbone. In this area marked with *, the present muscle possesses a sort of membranous semicircle, or rather, its fleshy fibers end here at the circumference of a semicircle. At the part marked K, the neck is joined to the highest part of the chest. The two lines circumscribing the sides of the muscle are gathered in this manner: the first extends from E to F, drawn across the back of the head. As for the fact that the end marked F does not seem as far from the root of the ear as E is from F, the cause lies in the illustration, which eludes the eye: the left arm, stretched forward, clearly demonstrates this. Perhaps someone ignorant of optics <note>original Greek: *optikes* (ὀπτικῆς); the science of perspective and sight</note> would think the arm is shorter than it should be. Furthermore, the second line of the present muscle is measured from E through K to G. The third from F to H. The fourth from H to G. The muscle is bounded by these lines. However, the line of insertion extending from H to I, and that path which could be measured from I to K, are by no means marks of separation or division of the muscle into parts. <note>Vesalius is describing the trapezius muscle here.</note>
<margin>L</margin> The muscle lifting the arm <note>the deltoid</note>, and the second of its movers.
<margin>M</margin> The muscle occupying the convex part of the shoulder blade, and the seventh of those moving the arm.
<margin>N</margin> The muscle arising from the lower edge of the shoulder blade, and the third of those moving the arm.
<margin>O</margin> The fourth muscle of those driving the arm, to be marked with the symbol ☉ in the following plate.
<margin>P</margin> On the right side of the present plate, P indicates a portion of the abdominal muscle which we call the "obliquely descending" <note>the external oblique</note>.
<margin>Q</margin> On the right arm, there appears something of the front muscle that flexes the arm <note>the biceps</note>.
<margin>R</margin> The rear muscle of those flexing the elbow.
<margin>S</margin> The muscle of those extending the elbow <note>the triceps</note>, whose origin hangs from the neck of the humerus <note>upper arm bone</note>.
<margin>T</margin> The muscle of those extending the elbow, whose origin springs from the lower edge of the shoulder blade.
<margin>U</margin> The triangular area of the ulna <note>forearm bone</note>, covered by no muscles, or "fleshless," which specifically receives the tendinous <note>original: *neruofae*; literally 'nervous', but referring to the tough, white texture of tendons</note> insertion of the muscles extending the elbow.
<margin>X</margin> The muscle driving the radius <note>the other forearm bone</note> into a supine <note>palm up</note> position, which is inserted into the lower attachment of the radius.
<margin>Y</margin> The muscle extending the wrist with a two-pronged tendon.

<meta>Catchword: TENTH</meta>

**Z** We shall now review the muscle marked **Z**, which is the primary agent for extending the index, middle, and ring fingers; its starting point is indicated by **a**. The place where it ceases to be fleshy and sends out tendons is marked **b**.

**$\odot$** This is the muscle which we identify as the agent for extending the little finger. Although we have attempted to depict it on the outer side of the metacarpus <term>postbrachialis</term> <note>the bones between the wrist and fingers</note> and at the base of the fingers, the tendons of the two muscles marked **Z** and **$\odot$** are intertwined; they spread out in various hidden ways and then rejoin their own portions. Nevertheless, since this intertwining is not the same in everyone, I would prefer that you seek a true understanding of this from various dissections rather than from this single illustration alone.

**$\Lambda$** This is a muscle that extends the wrist <term>brachiale</term>. Its beginning, marked **c**, hangs from the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, while its insertion, indicated by **d**, is completed in the metacarpal bone that supports the little finger.

**$\Xi$** On both elbows, the muscle that flexes the wrist is marked **$\Xi$**; it is inserted into the fourth bone of the wrist and is nowhere as visible in the muscle plates as it is here. Just as the beginning of the muscle **$\Xi$** (which produces the broad tendon of the hand) is visible here at the character **q**, so too is the origin of the muscle that flexes the wrist, which is inserted into the metacarpus and is marked **$\Lambda$** in the third muscle plate.

**e** These muscles creeping forth obliquely are those of which one inserts a single tendon into the wrist bone supporting the thumb; the other offers one tendon to the first bone of the thumb and inserts another into the second and third bones of the thumb.

**f** This muscle is inserted into the three bones of the thumb on the outer side; it turns the thumb outward toward the index finger.

**g** The muscle that brings the thumb closest to the index finger <note>an adductor muscle</note>.

**h** The muscle responsible for drawing the little finger away from the others <note>the abductor of the little finger</note>.

**$\Pi$** The first of the muscles moving the thigh <term>femur</term> <note>the gluteus maximus</note>, circumscribed by **i, k, l, m**, and **n**. <margin>i, k, l, m, n.</margin> The area from **i** to **k** marks the part of its origin that arises from the spine of the ilium <note>the hip bone</note>. From **k** to **l** indicates the part of the origin hanging from the coccyx <note>the tailbone</note> and the lowest part of the sacrum, where the left muscle is adjacent to the right. **m** indicates the higher part of its insertion, while **n** marks the lowest part of the insertion; because this part winds itself deeper here among the muscles moving the leg <term>tibia</term>, it is tucked away and not visible from every side.

**o** The second of the muscles moving the thigh <note>likely the gluteus medius</note>, which is still largely covered by the first.

**p** The sixth of the muscles moving the lower leg <term>tibia</term>, which turns into that broad tendon that wraps around the muscles embracing the thigh; however, it does not reach such a thickness that it can obscure the muscles lying beneath it, so much so that I am now able to mark those muscles with characters as well. <margin>q.</margin> Furthermore, **q** marks the end of the fleshy part of this sixth muscle.

**r** The seventh muscle moving the lower leg, covered by the membrane-like tendon of the sixth muscle.

**s** The fourth muscle moving the lower leg, stretched toward the back part of the seventh muscle.

**t** The third muscle moving the lower leg, marked on both legs (as are several that follow).

**u** The muscle which we consider the fifth of those moving the lower leg.

**x** A portion of the fifth muscle moving the thigh also appears here.

**y** The second muscle moving the lower leg.

**$\alpha$** The first muscle moving the lower leg.

**$\beta$** The eighth muscle moving the lower leg.

**$\gamma$** The ninth muscle moving the lower leg, which is visible only in small part, as are the two muscles immediately preceding it.

**$\delta$** In this hollow, the artery reaching the lower leg travels along with the largest vein of the leg and the thickest nerve in the entire body <note>the sciatic nerve</note>.

**$\epsilon$** The first muscle moving the foot.

**$\zeta$** The second muscle moving the foot.

**$\eta$** The seventh muscle moving the foot.

**$\theta$** The eighth muscle moving the foot, hidden under the seventh, offers itself only slightly to be seen here.

**$\iota$** The part of the fibula <note>the outer leg bone</note> devoid of flesh, and thus the outer ankle bone <term>malleolus</term>.

**$\kappa$** A small portion of the ninth muscle moving the foot occurs here; for its tendon presents itself here at its insertion.

**$\lambda$** The muscle that draws the little toe away from the others.

**$\mu$** On the left calf, the tendon of the third muscle moving the foot is marked <note>the Achilles tendon</note>.

**$\nu$** The inner ankle bone <term>malleolus</term>.

### [Description of the Illustration]

The accompanying woodcut depicts a flayed male figure standing in a vast, serene Renaissance landscape. The figure is viewed from the back, displaying the second layer of musculature. To demonstrate the depth of the anatomy, Vesalius has his "muscle man" hold strips of his own dissected flesh; notably, the large muscle of the buttocks <note>the gluteus maximus</note> is peeled back on the left side to reveal the deeper structures of the hip. The figure points toward the horizon with his right hand, a pose that serves both to display the muscles of the arm and to add a sense of life and "memento mori" (a reminder of mortality) to the scientific study.

For the ulcer that is burned is near this branch of the nerve marked θ; and since it is made a little lower than where the upper appendix of the fibula stands, that branch in its principal portion cannot be touched. And indeed I would add many such things to my frequent discourse, were I not to think it ridiculous to mix other parts of medicine with this anatomical study, or were I not myself to have written such things separately in their own time, as I have already begun to do.

Γ The left muscle of the first pair of muscles moving the head, the beginning of which is marked by *A*: *B* and *C* indeed mark the insertion <note>original: "A, B, & C"</note> which it effects into the occipital bone. *D* moreover indicates the place where the right muscle first departs from the left. Finally, *E* indicates the inner side of the insertion of the right muscle. Therefore, if you wish to see that muscle acting in the form of a triangle, you will circumscribe it with the lines *A, B; A, C; B, C*. Furthermore, if you also wish to view the interval standing between the right and left muscle in the manner of a triangle, you will appropriately circumscribe it from *B* to *E*, then from *B* to *D*, and from *E* to *D*. <note>Vesalius is describing the geometric relationships of the suboccipital muscles.</note>

Several tendons of the present muscle are indicated by *M, M*.

*m* The bone of the post-wrist <term>postbrachialis</term> <note>The metacarpal bone</note> supporting the ring finger: which we have noted separately so that you might distinguish the bones of the post-wrist from their intervals and the muscles occupying them.

<image-desc>This iconic anatomical woodcut from Andreas Vesalius's *On the Fabric of the Human Body* <note>original: "De humani corporis fabrica"</note> depicts a human figure viewed from behind (a posterior view). The figure is "flayed" to show the second layer of muscles in the neck, back, arms, and legs. The figure stands in a naturalistic landscape; the foreground is composed of rocks, while the background depicts a distant Italianate cityscape with a prominent tower and rolling hills.

The entire figure is annotated with numerous labels for anatomical reference, including Roman letters (A, B, C, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S, T, V, X, Y, Z), Greek letters (Gamma Γ, Delta Δ, Theta Θ, Sigma Σ, Phi Φ, Psi Ψ, etc.), and small-case letters and numbers. These labels correspond to the muscles described in the preceding index, such as the muscles moving the head and the thorax. The figure's right hand (to the viewer's left) holds a long, dissected muscle or tendon that hangs down toward the ground. The detail captures the complex interplay of the trapezius <note>the large muscle of the upper back and neck</note>, the deltoids <note>shoulder muscles</note>, the latissimus dorsi <note>the "broadest muscle of the back"</note>, and the deep structures of the gluteal and leg regions.</image-desc>

ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE BODY <note>original: "And. Vesalii de corporis"; this is the running header of the book, which translates fully as "Andreas Vesalius on the Fabric of the Human Body."</note>

## THE FOURTEENTH TABLE OF MUSCLES. <note>original: "Decimaquarta musculorum tabula"</note>

<note>This page features a famous full-page anatomical woodcut, the final illustration in the series of muscle tables. It shows the human figure from a posterior (rear) view in a state of advanced dissection. The "fourteenth table" focuses on the deepest layers of the musculature, particularly the muscles of the spine, the deep neck, and the hip, which were hidden by the layers shown in the preceding plates. 

The figure is shown in a dramatic, expressive pose, leaning forward over a large stone block with its head bowed toward a detached skull. This artistic choice—common in the Renaissance—serves both a scientific purpose (by stretching the muscles for better visibility) and a philosophical one, acting as a "memento mori," a reminder of mortality. The landscape in the background, featuring a winding path and a distant Italian town, is characteristic of the studio of Titian, where these woodcuts are believed to have been designed.</note>

<summary>This page presents the fourteenth and final anatomical plate of the muscle series, illustrating the deepest posterior muscles of the human body.</summary>

## INDEX OF CHARACTERS
### for the Fourteenth Plate of Muscles.

**THE PRINCIPAL** *image of this plate, now in the series of dissection, lacks the shoulder blades <note>scapulae</note> and arms, and bends the knees so that it might propose the sole of the foot to be viewed on the other leg. Truly at the knees, lest any other entire plate had to be drawn, the head is replaced along with the first two vertebrae of the neck <note>cervix</note>, to show the fourth pair of muscles moving the head. I have applied no characters <note>reference letters/labels</note> to the ribs and the intercostal muscles, because these are common to the preceding three plates. And for the same reason, the bones already stripped bare by the order of dissection are not explained, because these should be sought from the complete figures of the bones. It would be useful, however, to compare the form and the path of the ribs of this thorax <note>chest cavity</note>, as well as that of the eighth plate, with those others, because everything is expressed here more in its natural position than can be delineated from bones reassembled by our industry. For in whatever way I connect the bones, there always arises a greater interval between the tip of the lowest rib and the hip bone <note>ilium</note> than occurs in all parts placed in their natural position in a man.

<header>THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.</header>

*I would certainly have also included here the table to be presented in the thirtieth chapter of this present book, which depicts the connection of the first cervical vertebra to the second, and of the first and second to the head, were it not that the one I have just shown demonstrates every variety and use of ligament reasonably well.*

<image-desc>A circular woodcut portrait in the upper left corner, depicting a bearded man in profile facing right, wearing a garment with a high collar. He is framed within a square border featuring decorative line work.</image-desc>

<margin>a. Ligaments appear everywhere in the figure placed at the beginning of this chapter.</margin>
<margin>What a ligament is.</margin>
SINCE the first book reviewed everything we deemed to belong to the history of bones and cartilages, the present book will most opportunely follow up with their <term>ligaments<note>from the Latin 'ligamentum', meaning a binding or tie</note></term> and the muscles by which they are moved. A ligament, therefore—which we also include under the name of "nerve" in a general sense, and which is called <term>syndesmos<note>original Greek: σύνδεσμος, meaning 'that which binds together'</note></term> by the Greeks—is a <term>homogeneous body<note>original: 'corpus similare'; a tissue where the parts are like the whole, a foundational concept in Galenic medicine</note></term>, taking its origin primarily from a bone or cartilage. It is hard, yet softer than cartilage; it is white, and provides various uses in binding, containing, covering, separating, and establishing muscles. For if the joints of bones and cartilages—which were certainly not constructed by slight chance—<margin>b. O, P, S, T, V</margin><margin>The use of ligaments in binding.</margin> were not held together by ligaments, nothing would prevent them from being dislocated by almost any movement and departing from their natural seat. Wherefore one must also marvel at the industry of God, the Architect of all things, who willed that from these mutually articulated parts a certain substance should arise, <margin>The substance of a ligament.</margin> so hard that it binds them together precisely and safely; and it beautifully ensures that they are not broken or pulled apart from one another by violent, continuous, and nearly tireless movements. And meanwhile, it is so tempered in its softness that it can be stretched and relaxed just enough so as not to hinder the movement of the joints (which each must perform according to the logic of its construction) or stand in the way of their graceful action. Thus, this is considered the chief and primary use of the ligament, from which it also primarily derives its name. <margin>c. b, c.</margin> In its second use, the ligament contains the <term>tendons<note>tough cords of fibrous tissue connecting muscle to bone</note></term> within the channels through which they are carried, and <margin>The use of ligaments in containing tendons.</margin> it prevents them from wandering from these channels or being lifted away from them. Six ligaments of this kind are seen on the outer side of the elbow, where the <term>brachiale<note>the carpus or wrist bones</note></term> is articulated with it; <margin>d. 1st muscle table, characters 3, 4, 5, 6; or 2nd table, characters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.</margin> while on the internal region of the wrist, there is one notably strong one. Then, on the internal side of the fingers of the hand and toes of the foot, a single one likewise exists along almost their entire length. Furthermore, on the front side where it joins the foot, <margin>e. 4th table, 8.</margin> another one occurs, wide and strong. Finally, <margin>f. 1st table A, 2nd table λ.</margin> others are observed between the <term>tibia<note>the shin bone</note></term> and the heel, and between the <term>fibula<note>the smaller outer bone of the lower leg</note></term> and the heel, all created primarily for this: that the tendon does not rise out of its own channel during the contraction of the muscle. For that cord, pulled toward the knee, would pull very far away from the joint where the foot meets the tibia. But if you bind another cord transversely across the lowest part of the tibia, and pass the cord with which you wanted to extend the toe under it, that cord, even if pulled, will no longer pull away straight from the tibia; rather, held out along its whole course by the occasion of that transverse bond against the tibia and foot, it will lift the toe. This ingenuity of Nature...

<header>### ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE BODY</header>

We see charioteers imitate this third use with the rings they attach to the yokes of their horses. By passing a long rein through the ring, they can more easily turn the horses they are not sitting upon. Because these ligaments—just like the ring for the reins—are spread across the tendons, or rather embrace them in a circle, they were called <term>transverse<note>original Greek: *ἐγκαρσία* (*enkarsia*)</note></term> by the Greeks. We, however, call them sometimes "transverse" and sometimes "annular" (ring-shaped). The interior surface of these ligaments perfectly corresponds to the rings through which ropes are drawn; while the tendon is convex, the ligament's cavity is circular and smooth, bathed in a viscous fluid like oil <note>Vesalius is describing what we now call synovial fluid, which lubricates the movement of tendons</note>. Indeed, these ligaments are not only wrapped around the outside of the tendons where they face the skin, but they even form a sort of bedding for them. To prevent the hardness of the bone from causing damage, they slip between the bone and the tendons, embracing them on all sides in a circle without any direct connection—just as a ring allows a rein to pass through. To this class of ligaments we should also assign the membranes spread transversely over an entire mass of muscles, which beautifully assist them by preventing them from becoming entangled with one another or wandering from their proper place. We shall observe such membranes presiding over the muscles throughout the entire length of the forearm, thigh, and leg.

<margin>*What a muscle is, and the logic of its composition, according to the opinion of other Anatomists.*</margin>
**I**t seems to be granted by all professors of dissection that the muscle is the proper instrument of voluntary motion—movement that depends upon our own will. Likewise, the method of a muscle's construction is described by all in the same way. This description certainly appears plausible and demonstrates the great craftsmanship of Nature; nevertheless, since I observe it in very few muscles, or rather in none at all, I am forced to feel differently about the construction of muscles than they do. However, I will now set down the opinion held by nearly everyone as briefly and clearly as possible, gathering their doctrines into a continuous narrative that is most consistent with the truth. They define a muscle, therefore, as an instrumental part fabricated from nerve, ligament, flesh, veins, and arteries, and the peculiar organ of voluntary motion. In its manufacture, they recount the work of Nature in roughly this manner:

<margin>*The necessity of the ligament and nerve in the muscle.*</margin>
Since there are two bodies which we require for the present discourse (which concerns the constitution of the muscle)—namely the ligament and the nerve, properly so called—and since the ligament is hard while the nerve is soft, the industry of the Creator is marvelous. In every part presided over by voluntary motion, He uses both, never putting a nerve in the place of a ligament, nor a ligament in the region of a nerve. For it is granted by all that neither the hard is suitable for sensation (inasmuch as it is not easily affected), nor is the soft suitable for motion (since it is too weak). Therefore, no part is moved by nerves alone, nor by ligaments alone. For a nerve is indeed sensitive insofar as it is soft, but it is too weak to move and transport an entire limb. A ligament, on the other hand, could certainly bind things together safely and meanwhile not obstruct the movements of the limbs; yet it could not by itself be produced as the organ of voluntary motion, since it takes its origin from bone or cartilage, and not from the brain—the source of voluntary motion—in the manner of a nerve. For no one doubts that the body of such a source or principle ought to be made soft, since it is impossible for anything perfectly hard to be born from the soft, or anything soft from the hard. For these reasons, Nature could not use ligaments alone for voluntary movements, because they are endowed with neither sense nor motion, as they are not continuous with the seat of the soul’s sovereignty. Nor should nerves alone have been used, since these, on account of their softness and thinness, were by no means strong enough to move such great weights.

<margin>*Nature placed the muscle as a medium between ligament and nerve.*</margin>
Therefore, it was necessary that some organ of motion be created as a mixture of both, which would be harder than a nerve in every way and softer than a ligament. For that reason, it would also participate in sensation—less so than a nerve, certainly, but more than a ligament. Furthermore, it was fitting that it also exist in a middle state between strength and weakness, and other contraries found in ligaments and nerves. On this occasion, the instrument of motion communicates with both substances that compose it; yet it is not exactly either one of them, neither alone nor...

Furthermore, the distribution of the nerve and ligament into fibers is accomplished in this manner: the nerve approaches the ligament, and together they are sorted, as it were, into two fibers; these are again divided into others, and these again into many more, until they proceed into the thinnest, membrane-like fibers. After these have reached the furthest extent of their diffusion, they gather back together, coalescing by a mutual meeting just as they had been divided. And just as

Moreover, if Nature had only divided the nerve <margin>The use of flesh in the muscle.</margin> and ligament in this way, and had not stuffed the middle regions and the gaps between the fibers with a soft substance—which serves as a bed or cushion for the fibers and provides a firm seat for their texture—the muscle could not preserve those fibers unbroken and uncorrupted for even a tiny space of time. That seat or bed is simple flesh covering the fibers, which is joined to the fibers much like milk is joined to baskets and other wicker strainers when those skilled in such matters curdle it within them. Imagine, then, that the fibers diffused from the nerve and ligament correspond to the rushes of the basket, while blood is proportional to the milk itself, and the flesh to the cheese; for just as the latter is prepared from milk, so the former is prepared from blood. Though you will imagine a truer image the more you visualize many frequent rushes or cords stretched through the cheese, and not merely attached to the sides of the cheese. Lest this flesh and the rest of the muscle substance be <margin>The necessity of veins and arteries in the muscle.</margin> left lacking blood and nourishment, and its own innate heat not be refreshed, it was necessary for veins and arteries to be mixed into the muscles like certain small streams. Then also a <margin>The membrane of the muscle.</margin> membrane, covering the entire body of the muscle, had to be produced from the ligaments that commit the head and end of the muscle to the bones. <margin>A nerve is not mixed into every muscle, as it has seemed to other professors of dissection.</margin>
<margin>Nerves are not inserted into the heads of all muscles, or are otherwise not observed there, even if a nerve is inserted into their substance elsewhere.</margin>

...who arise from a very broad beginning and gradually taper into a narrow point toward their insertion? Of this sort, besides the temporal muscle <note>The muscle on the side of the head used for chewing</note>, is the one among the rest that raises the arm $^k$ <note>The deltoid muscle of the shoulder</note>: then $^l$ the one that moves the arm toward the chest <note>The pectoralis major</note>, and nearly all those serving the movements of the thigh: in whose origins we cannot imagine a nerve which, as Galen believes, can be spread out with the ligament. For immediately at the origin of such muscles, there is a much greater abundance of fibers than in the rest of the muscle: indeed, in those muscles, and especially those which govern the movements of the thigh, the fibers are not divided into many more from the origin itself; rather, as they hasten gradually toward the insertion, they are gathered together, forming a muscle of triangular shape. 

From this it also becomes clear that, if indeed that division and mixing of nerve and ligament—which is proposed to students of anatomy—ought to occur in muscles, then a tiny nerve would have to be mixed with every single fiber at the origin. The sequence of the nerves themselves shows that this happens in no way at all. For in most muscles, you will see only a very thin little nerve, divided no more than a vein is, extending toward either the inner or outer surface of the muscle in the manner of a vein or artery, adhering to the membrane of the muscle, but by no means spreading into the fibers through the substance of the muscle. This you will learn clearly among many muscles of the body, particularly in $^m$ those which approach the thigh bone from the hip bone <note>original: "ab ilium osse," the ilium</note>. Among these you may even find some where a nerve is scarcely observed to be in contact with even the surface, just as neither a vein nor an artery is. 

Nor will you observe this only here, but also in the square $^n$ muscle that moves the radius into a prone position <note>The pronator quadratus muscle of the forearm</note>, in which I have never seen a nerve, vein, or artery extended—except for those nerves, veins, and arteries that creep forward to the hand with the tendons that flex the fingers. Although these are not far distant from that muscle, they nonetheless do not touch it, and even less do they grow into it or are they inserted there. Add to this that no little nerve is observed inserted into the slender $^o$ muscles that bring the four fingers toward the thumb <note>The lumbricals or interossei</note>, nor into $^p$ those which govern the flexions of the first bone of the four fingers. 

Join to these, moreover, the muscles of the abdomen $^q$ (which it would have been proper to review first, as they seem better known to everyone), which show no proportion of nerve with ligament: since in none of these muscles, which extend their fibers obliquely and transversely, is a nerve implanted at the sites of their origins; and since their "enervation" <note>Vesalius uses "eneruatio" here to mean the aponeurosis or tendinous part, literally "becoming nerve-like" in the old terminology</note> or tendon is much broader than the origin of the same, a feature they have in common with most muscles. A muscle is not, therefore, a "middle nature" between a ligament and a nerve; nor does that mixing of ligament and nerve, which they commonly imagine, actually take place. For even if you happen to notice a nerve inserted into the head of some muscle, you will certainly never find the offspring of the nerve spreading out to the very beginning of the tendon in the manner of ligamentous fibers, or in any way united and truly mixed with the fibers of the ligament. 

This, indeed, you will weigh more easily in no muscle than in those $^r$ which take their beginning from the inner tuberosity of the humerus <note>The medial epicondyle of the upper arm bone</note>: for their heads are pointed, and the insertions of the nerves reach into their substance, and not only upon the surface. And you will also notice this in $^s$ that muscle which, taking its beginning from the upper appendage of the fibula <note>The calf bone</note>, creeps forward to the foot: so also in $^t$ those which are carried from the roots of the lower heads of the femur to the heel. For not all muscles receive the implantation of a nerve at the emergence of the head (even if a nerve is sometimes extended into their substance), but repeatedly much lower than where the head is held, and somewhat in the middle of its path and length. This is shown, besides the temporal muscle, by $^u$ the anterior muscle of those that flex the elbow <note>The brachialis</note>, which first receives a $^x$ branch of the nerve where its two heads come together as one. The same is observed in several muscles clasping the thigh bone,

<margin>A tendon corresponds to a ligament, not to a nerve.</margin>
<margin>z Compare the abdomen in Table 6 and the abdomen in Figure 11, book 5.</margin>
...and in the muscles of the abdomen, and in most of those found in the neck, and in almost all those spread over the ribs. However, in whatever way nerves weave themselves into the substance of a muscle, or if they only attend to its surface, they are almost always extended in their own sequence and offshoots according to the path of the muscle (which the <term>recurrent nerves</term><note>The laryngeal nerves, which loop back upward toward the larynx</note> also prove). Furthermore, a **boiled tendon** differs from a **ligament** neither in taste, color, nor substance—unless perhaps someone would argue that the tendon is softer, not indeed than all ligaments, but only certain ones. However that may be, the tendon does not yield at all to the softness of the muscle’s head; although no one can deny that at its very origin, a ligament is pure and not mixed with a nerve at all. Nor should it be wondered at that a tendon is usually softer and less cartilaginous than a ligament that binds bones together, since the ratio of hardness is not the same even among the substances of ligaments that bind bones to one another. Add also that a boiled tendon is not proportional to a nerve: for a nerve, whether boiled or raw, if it is cut crosswise, will appear constructed of many little cords, just as if you had divided a thicker rope. A <term>tendon</term>, however, will be seen as more solid, more like a <term>similar part</term><note>A "similar part" in Galenic anatomy is a tissue that is uniform throughout, like bone or fat, rather than an "organic" part made of multiple tissues</note> such as a ligament, and continuous; especially if you apply your examination to some thick tendon from those that go to the foot, the shin, or the hand. For in broad and somewhat membranous tendons, the series of fibers is somewhat more manifest; for which reason they are distinguished from true membranes during dissection, just as can be seen in a comparison of the <term>peritoneum</term><note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note> with the nervous thinnings of the oblique and transverse muscles of the abdomen. And although this may be observed intact in any animal while eating, you will do it most aptly in **beef**, when some part is served at the table through which a notable nerve wanders, which is usually seen with a vein and artery among the glands. Once the nerve is found, a tendon can never be lacking to teach the points just proposed.

<margin>The head of a muscle without flesh is not always thinner than the tendon.</margin>
<margin>a Gather this from Table 14, n, o, q.</margin>
<margin>b Compare A, B, C with D in the figure added to Table 11.</margin>
Next, regarding that point by which others strive to prove that a tendon is mixed with a nerve, and is made of ligament and nerve equally (or more or less confused together), one ought first to have weighed whether the matter truly stands as they propose before they inferred anything. For they say that a tendon is thicker than the head of the muscle for the reason that it consists not only of the muscle's substance but also of the nerve. As if indeed anyone could rightly assert that the origins of the calf muscles, collected together, were smaller (in terms of what is generally called nervous substance) than the tendon of those muscles which is inserted into the heel <note>The Achilles tendon</note>. It is just as if the muscle raising the arm <note>The deltoid</note> had fewer fibers at its origin than the collection of them shows at the insertion. Therefore, that point had to be proved before a false conclusion was drawn.

<margin>The heads of muscles, especially those lacking flesh, feel no less than the tendon. What nerves truly provide in sensation.</margin>
Just as this too is an ineffective assumption: "A tendon participates in very exact sensation, therefore it consists of nerve and ligament." As if the heads of muscles—especially the ligamentous ones and those entirely lacking flesh—possessed less power of sensation than the tendons themselves, or if injured, brought less danger of **convulsion** <note>Tetanus or muscle spasms</note> than tendons do, even if a nerve is not inserted into the heads immediately at their origin, but only happens to be stretched near them, and even then often removed from the head by a notable interval.

<margin>c Observe Table 6, f, d. d Table 3, r.</margin>
By this occasion, therefore, and many others of this kind which would be tedious to review, I am forced to confess that there is absolutely no other distribution of a nerve into muscles than that of a vein and artery; and by the same logic, a nerve approaches a muscle just as a vein and artery do. Nor do I establish any other difference between a vein and artery and a nerve, except that at the end or insertion of a muscle, a nerve is never implanted as those vessels sometimes are, although I could enumerate very few muscles of that kind. There are, however, among others, the **straight muscles of the abdomen** <note>The rectus abdominis</note>, which take branches both from veins and arteries creeping downward under the breastbone, and...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE [HUMAN] BODY

<margin>See figure, chapter 6, book 2.</margin>
<margin>See figure, chapter 12, g.</margin>
The temporal muscle also admits vessels from its lower seats, even though it derives its origin from higher ones. Thus, just as the vein serves in nourishing the muscle, and the artery refreshes its <term>innate heat</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, "innate heat" was the vital warmth believed to be essential to life, distributed throughout the body by the arteries.</note>: so too I believe that the nerve continuously carries the <term>animal spirit</term><note>Derived from the Latin "anima" (soul/life-force), the "animal spirit" was considered a subtle substance produced in the brain and transmitted through the nerves to enable sensation and voluntary movement.</note> to it, and that the nerve never leaves the muscle lacking in that spirit, just as the vein does not deprive the muscle of nourishment.

<margin>How muscles perform their function.</margin>
Furthermore, through the power of the animal spirit, and by the benefit of the muscle's proper and peculiar construction and its essential form, I perceive that the muscle is contracted and relaxed. It performs its duty in no other way than the eye or the other organs of the senses; each of these possesses a unique and particular structure, and being imbued with the animal spirit (which the brain extends to them through the nerves), they perform their functions. For it is not one kind of animal spirit that is spread to the eye, or the tongue, or the organ of hearing, and another to the muscles; rather, by reason of its own construction and the addition of the spirit, the eye sees, the tongue tastes, the organ of hearing perceives sounds, and indeed the muscle itself governs voluntary movements. In this same way, all parts to which a nerve is stretched possess the power of sensation, unless their own substance prevents it. 

Furthermore, while the artery does not touch a great many muscles, and in others it only reaches the surface or is occasionally attached to it—though sometimes it extends its branches more deeply into the substance of the muscles—it meanwhile tempers the heat of all of them. This includes those it does not touch directly, those to whose surface it is attached, and those in whose substance it is more deeply spread. So indeed it happens with the nerves, which extend their faculty both to those muscles which they barely touch, as well as those to whose surface they are attached and into whose substance they are distributed through some series of branches. Nevertheless, you might more closely liken nerves to veins than to arteries. For fewer muscles are deprived of the touch and insertion of a vein than of the arteries; although I previously reviewed certain ones which you will observe are touched directly by neither nerve nor vein, which nevertheless are not meanwhile deprived of nourishment, vital faculty, or animal spirit.

<margin>What a muscle truly is.</margin>
A muscle, therefore, is the instrument of voluntary motion, just as the eye is of sight and the tongue of taste. It is constructed from the nature of a ligament divided into many fibers, and the flesh containing and strengthening these, occasionally taking into itself the small branches of veins, arteries, and nerves; and by the benefit of the nerves, it is never deprived of animal spirit as long as the animal is healthy.

<margin>Flesh: the primary substance of a muscle.</margin>
And I consider this flesh not merely to be some layer, or a kind of bedding and support by which the fibers of the muscles (or the divisions generally called "nervous") are contained. Nor do I, with **Plato** and **Aristotle** (to whom the true nature of muscles was entirely hidden), attribute to flesh such a trivial use as to concede that, in the manner of fat and grease or some kind of garment, it only stands against heat in the summer and wards off cold in the winter. Rather, I am persuaded that the flesh of muscles, to which no other in the entire body is similar, is the *primary agent* through whose benefit the muscle is made thicker, shortens and collects itself, and thus draws and moves the part into which it is inserted. This occurs provided the nerves—the messengers of the animal faculties—are not failing. By this same occasion, the muscle then relaxes and extends itself again, releasing the part it had drawn. This is exactly how we know that the proper substance of the brain, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, kidneys, stomach, and testes is the primary author of their respective functions.

<margin>That fat is also present everywhere in the flesh.</margin>
As for the fact that all writers hitherto have falsely claimed that no fat is interwoven with the flesh of muscles (or flesh simply), the **obese oxen** which the people of **Brabant**<note>A region in the Low Countries, encompassing parts of modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands; Vesalius's home region.</note> preserve with salt bear witness to the contrary; in their muscle fibers, fat is seen throughout the flesh. Add also that during dissection, the muscles of obese women which extend the thigh appear so filled with fat that you would doubt whether the flesh is mixed into the fat, or the fat into the flesh. Nor do I speak here of...

Regarding their insertion, it is right to say that some muscles are inserted into bone, such as those moving the thigh, the lower leg, and the head. Others are inserted into cartilage: such as all those of the <term>larynx</term><note>Voice box.</note>, those responsible for the movements of the eyelids, and those assigned to the <term>wings of the nose</term><note>The nostrils.</note>. Others are inserted into the skin, like the muscles of the lips. Others into something else entirely: like the muscles of the eyes into the <term>hard coat of the eye</term><note>The sclera.</note>; the four muscles of the penis into the bodies of the penis and the urinary passage; and the muscle of the testicle into the vessel carrying semen upward from the testicle. In addition, we see the muscles proper to the <term>straight intestine</term><note>The rectum.</note> implanted into its external coat, and the circular muscle of the neck of the bladder implanted into the body of the urinary passage. Furthermore, muscles also differ by insertion in this way: some, arising from several parts, are inserted into only one: as the muscle moving the arm to the chest and the one that raises the arm, having arisen from several places, are inserted only into the humerus. Thus also the one <insert>^f</insert> that pulls the arm downward arises from the spines of several vertebrae, yet ends only in the humerus. For the same reason, all the muscles responsible for the movements of the shoulder blade take their start from several bones and are implanted into only one shoulder blade. Some, however, arising from one bone, are inserted into many. For the muscle <insert>^g</insert> that comes forward from the base of the shoulder blade <insert>^h</insert> and serves respiration is inserted into the eight upper ribs of the chest. Of this kind also are those that extend the four toes of the foot and fingers of the hand.

Corresponding to these are those which, extended along the length of the forearm [cubitus] or leg [tibia], go to the fingers or toes.

<margin>From the shape.</margin>
The shape of all muscles is also not the same. A muscle of a wondrous shape existsᶜ that extends tendons to the individual roots of the ribs, which you might not ineptly compare to a vine shoot: just as the woody part of the vine shoot would be the fleshy portion of the muscle, the leaves emerging from only one side are the tendons themselves. <note>Vesalius is likely describing the Serratus Posterior or a similar multi-fingered muscle.</note> Furthermore, the longest muscle of those moving the backᵈ also belongs to this order; it is primarily inserted into the tips of the transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae.ᵉ The shape of the transverse septum <note>The diaphragm.</note> is also quite rare: it approaches the likeness of the ray fish (which the Greeks call <term>baton</term>), if only you first imagine its tail divided lengthwise. Those muscles which are put in charge of the excretion of feces correspond to rings: both the oneᶠ that regards the anus, and the oneᵍ that circularly surrounds the neck of the bladder. The seventh muscle in the order of the eye musclesʰ resembles a pyramid or a spinning top. The muscle which we believe moves the eyelid downward appears similar to our letter C. Also, in the posterior part of the human leg, near the heel,ⁱ images of muscles occur that are somewhat similar to a butcher's axe: such as the muscle flexing the bone of the big toe, the one that flexes the third bone of the four toes,ᵏ and one which, extending a tendon under the sole, aids in the backward reflection of the foot. For the belly of these muscles corresponds vaguely to the iron of the axe, while the tendon corresponds to the handle. 

Now, if you consider the muscle on both sides which is held to be the second among the movers of the shoulder blade [scapula],ˡ you might contend—not with certain irreverent people that it came from the Devil who tempted Jesus in the desert—but rather that the Franciscans, Jacobites, <note>Jacobins: a common name for the Dominican Order in France, named after their first house, Saint-Jacques.</note> and especially the Benedictines, borrowed the likeness of their cowls <note>The "cuculla" or monastic hood.</note> from the shape of these muscles, at least as much of it as covers the back and shoulders. But lest, in reviewing the shapes of the muscles (and especially those belonging to the thigh and leg), I should stumble upon monks elsewhere, I shall simply add to the differences already mentioned that some muscles have a much wider insertion than origin. Suchᵐ is the one which, born from the shoulder blade, is inserted into eight ribs of the thorax; thenⁿ the transverse muscle of the abdomen, as well asᵒ the one descending obliquely. Others possess a broad beginning and, gradually narrowed, are carried to a sharp point: such asᵖ the muscle moving the arm upward <note>The deltoid.</note>, andᵠ another which draws it downward toward the back <note>The latissimus dorsi.</note>, and furthermore all those inserted into the femur from the hip bone [ilium]. Others obtain an origin equal to their insertion: such asʳ the one inserted into the base of the shoulder blade that draws it to the back, and thenˢ all the intercostals; furthermore the squareᵗ muscle in the forearm, hidden near the wrist, which turns the radius into a prone position. 

From the described differences of muscles, it is clearly established that some are long and slender: such as the oneᵘ which is carried from the anterior part of the appendix of the hip bone into the leg, which is the longest of the whole body and also slender.ˣ The muscle led down from the shoulder blade to the bone resembling the letter <term>upsilon</term> <note>The hyoid bone, which is U-shaped.</note> is similarly long and slender in its proportion, as are the muscles of the testes.ʸ Others, however, are quite broad: such as the muscles of the abdomenᶻ descending obliquely, and the transverse septum [diaphragm]. To this could also be referred the shapes of the insertion and origin. For one origin occurs as if from a single point: such asᵃ the origin of the muscle producing the broad tendon in the hand, and the origins of thoseᵇ muscles which, born from the appendix of the ischium [coxendix], are inserted into the leg bone and the fibula. Some, however, obtain an origin in the likeness of a simple line: such asᶜ that by which the arm is drawn downward toward the back; andᵈ that one also which, inserted into the base of the shoulder blade, draws it to the back; then with many others,ᵉ that which will be reviewed as the first and larger among those drawing the shoulder blade upward. Other muscles again arise not just in the manner of a simple line, but in the style of a broad surface: such asᶠ the three which go to the femur from the back of the hip bone, andᵍ the muscles occupying the hollow and convex parts of the shoulder blade, by whose help the arm is rotated. ...sometimes it is so thick that it does not appear transparent at all. Since it is thick and <term>fibrous<note>original: *nervea*. In 16th-century anatomy, "nerve" (nerveus) often referred generally to white, tough connective tissues like tendons and ligaments, rather than just the nerves that carry signals.</note></term>, and the flesh beneath is red, or rather blackish, a color composed of mixed black and white easily arises. However, the same redness of flesh does not occur in all humans: just as the nature of the blood, by which the flesh is nourished, is surely not the same for everyone.

<margin>The fibrous part of the muscles.</margin>
Furthermore, we shall call this white substance of the muscle, which is as yet without flesh, "fibrous" in the context of our discussion—as if we were saying "ligamentous"—distinguishing it by this word from the <margin>Fleshy.</margin> fleshy part. However, that which is in the middle of these parts may not inappropriately be called <margin>Livid.</margin> "livid" [bluish-gray] by us. <margin>Difference based on position.</margin> Not all muscles share the same position: for some are located at the surface of the body and lie against the skin, such as all those formed from the fleshy membrane; and countless others, which I will almost always list among the primary movers of the joints. Others lie hidden, deeply concealed: <margin>f Table 14, r.</margin> such as the muscle<sup>f</sup> hiding in the <term>ham<note>The popliteal space behind the knee.</note></term>, <margin>g Table 16, F, G. Indeed, the muscles of the abdomen elegantly show the diverse positions of muscles, or rather the path of their fibers: since <margin>l Table 3, Θ.</margin> some<sup>l</sup> are carried obliquely downward toward the front, <margin>m Table 4, Π.</margin> others<sup>m</sup> <margin>n Table 5, Δ.</margin> obliquely upward toward the front, others<sup>n</sup> <margin>o Table 6, Δ.</margin> straight upward, and others<sup>o</sup> entirely in a circular and transverse manner. <margin>Based on the type of fibers.</margin> For almost all muscles, the type of fiber is only one and simple: unless we assign a double type of fiber to the muscle<sup>p</sup> bringing the arm to the chest <margin>p Tables 3, 4, 14, Δ.</margin> and also to that one<sup>q</sup> <margin>q Table 9, Γ, Δ.</margin> which is the second among those moving the shoulder blade, and a still more manifold type of fiber to the muscles of the <margin>r Table 3, r, H, F. Table 4, M, N.</margin> cheeks and lips<sup>r</sup>. To every other muscle, a single type of fiber is assigned, corresponding for the most part to the path and shape of the muscles.

The muscles that we seemed to exclude from the number of others are as follows. The muscle bringing the arm to the chest acquires certain fibers led from the upper parts downward toward the outside, and some from the lower parts upward, also toward the outside. The one that is second among those moving the shoulder blade also possesses some fibers extended from the upper parts downward toward the front or outward; others, however, from the lower parts upward similarly toward the front or outward. Thus, a double type of fibers occurs in those two muscles; in the one by whose help we bring the arm to the chest, they intersect each other in the shape of an **X** at some point (and especially near the insertion), or are carried in a cross-wise manner.

Again, if we inspect the fibers of the muscles moving the jaw—those that take their origin from the lower jaw and the cheekbones—we will certainly behold a varied difference of fibers near the insertion. Just as we see the broad muscle, which consists of a fleshy membrane, possess straight, oblique, and transverse fibers. And just as diverse fibers belong to these muscles, so also they serve diverse movements, according to the logic of the tension and relaxation of these or those fibers. <margin>s Figure 3, chapter 19.</margin> Furthermore, what shall we say of the tongue<sup>s</sup>, interwoven with every kind of fiber? Surely nothing else than that diverse fibers are present in the muscles, and these serve their movements separately. <margin>Galen, while often elsewhere and especially where he strives to prove the heart is not a muscle, nevertheless argues otherwise in Book 1 of *On Anatomical Procedures*.</margin> For we can by no means entirely deny this contrary series of fibers in the same muscle, and especially in those muscles where a mutual intersection of fibers is performed, or where the fibers are driven cross-wise: so much so, indeed, that I am utterly unable to acquiesce to the opinion of other anatomists (who assign a simple and single type of fiber to all muscles). Furthermore, one will learn that fibers are not gathered equally or equally thin in all parts of a muscle. For in muscles that arise from a sharp head and end in a thick tendon, the fibers are thinnest in the middle of the muscle belly where it is thickest; there, they are more distant from each other due to the intervention of the flesh than they are at the beginning of the head and the tendon. The differences taken from the bellies of the muscles were nearly all explained in the preceding distinctions when I reviewed the shapes and fibers of muscles. Nothing more needs to be added here, except that the belly of the muscle is properly situated where the fibers of the muscle are less packed together and are contained by more abundant flesh. And thus, in some muscles, the bellies are found primarily at the origin itself, such as those inserted from the <term>ilium<note>The uppermost and largest part of the hip bone.</note></term> into the femur. <margin>Different numbers of muscles are established by different people because of the fibers and motions.</margin>

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap letter 'A' depicting two putti performing a dissection on a human leg, which is propped up on a wooden block. One putto is using a surgical tool to dissect the muscles while the other putto looks on closely.</image-desc> I believe the preceding chapter has clearly enough demonstrated that it is an arduous and difficult task to pursue the number of muscles and to recount, all at once, how many there are in the entire body. This is not because it is entirely impossible to describe them, but because everyone may hold a different, and not altogether absurd, opinion regarding the number of muscles. For someone might say that the muscle ^a which brings the arm to the breast is one, because in no part of itself is it not continuous and contiguous with itself. But another will perhaps contend that it should be considered in the place of two muscles, because all its fibers do not observe an equal path, and the muscle itself performs somewhat contrary motions. For that part of it, to which the clavicle and the middle part of the breastbone closest to the clavicle provide a beginning, extends its fibers obliquely downward toward the insertion of the muscle into the arm, and draws the arm higher toward the breast, as if toward the throat and clavicle. But the lower part, which arises from the remaining seat of the breastbone and certain cartilages of the ribs, directs its fibers obliquely upward to the arm, and brings the arm to a lower position on the breast. However, when the parts of both muscles are gathered together, the arm is moved toward the middle of the breast. Furthermore, in addition to this continuity of muscles and the circumscription like a single part—with no division as there is between two fingers of the hand—someone could refer not only to the muscle we have just recounted because of its different path of fibers, broad origin, and varied duty, but also to that one ^b which I shall recount as the second among those moving the <term>scapula</term> <note>The shoulder blade; he is describing the trapezius muscle.</note>. This muscle is indeed continuous, yet with its upper part it pulls the scapula upward toward the back of the head; with its lower part, downward toward the back; but in its middle seat, or with both its parts, it moves the scapula straight backward. In the class just mentioned, there is also found—besides several other muscles—the one <margin>s Table 9, Z.</margin> which clearly extends the index, middle, and ring fingers. But if tendons are inserted into bones of a different kind, those skilled in dissection count the muscle that leads out the tendons as several muscles. <margin>t Tables 10, 11, Ξ.</margin> Just so, some have counted the muscle that extends two tendons to the thumb and one to the <term>brachial bone</term> <note>Here referring to the metacarpal bone of the thumb.</note> supporting the thumb as two muscles, even if all these tendons contribute to turning the hand outward: the tendons of the thumb for the movement of the thumb, and that of the brachial bone for the movement of the brachial bone. Indeed, such a thing is still more <margin>u Table 4, ψ, Ω.</margin> conspicuous on the front side of the tibia: for at the middle of the length of the tibia, from the muscle extending the four toes, a fleshy muscle is led out which is inserted into the bone of the foot placed before the little toe, and it helps in lifting the foot forward, while meanwhile the tendons of the toes extend the toes. So it may seem to some that two muscles should be counted here, but to another only one: depending on whether the latter has turned his mind to the continuity of the origin, or the former to the different tendons, their insertions into various bones, and their differing functions. Nor does the mutual connection of muscles produce less <margin>A' By mutual connection.</margin> <margin>x Table 4, S, T.</margin> obscurity in number. For those which, arising from the top of the breastbones, are inserted into the <term>U-shaped bone</term> <note>The hyoid bone in the neck, which Vesalius calls the "os υ" or upsilon-shaped bone.</note>, are so joined to one another at their internal sides that one person might not ineptly call these two, while another calls them a single muscle. This is also demonstrated by those <margin>y Figures 1, 2, Chapter 49, Book 1, from M.</margin> which, arising from the circular muscle of the anus, embrace the passage of the bladder where it first begins to extend under the bodies of the penis, just like two fingers. The obscurity of the number of muscles is also increased by their <margin>A' By concurrence.</margin> <margin>z Table 10, Ψ. Table 11, ω, ξ.</margin> concurrence <note>The merging or joining of muscles.</note>. From this list, if any other, surely it is the fourth of those moving the tibia, which, arising from the <term>appendix of the hip bone</term> <note>The ischial tuberosity, or the "sit bone" of the pelvis.</note>, is carried strongly downward; and having become <term>sinewy</term> <note>Vesalius uses "nerueus" (nervous/sinewy) to describe the tough, white appearance of a tendon.</note> at the middle of the length of the femur, it is joined to another fleshy part to which the femur bone provides an origin. ## ON THE SKIN, THE CUTICLE, AND THE MEMBRANE
## covering the entire body beneath the skin, and furthermore on
## the fat placed between that skin and membrane. Chapter V.

*The parts to be described in this Chapter are expressed in some way in the figure of the twenty-fifth book <note>The Latin reads 'uigeſimaquinti libri' (25th book), though the 'Fabrica' has only seven books; he likely refers to the 25th figure of this second book.</note> at the letters r, s, t: and then in the twenty-fifth figure of the same book, near the right nipple.*

<margin>What SKIN is.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate historiated drop-cap initial letter 'C'. Within the frame of the letter, a group of anatomical students or observers are gathered around a table where a limb or body part is being dissected or examined. One figure points toward the anatomical subject while others look on intently.</image-desc>SKIN is the covering of all the parts of the body, drawn over the body like a natural garment, not only for all the parts of a man, but for the entire substance which we know to be subject to generation and corruption; it is of a medium hardness and softness. 
<margin>The substance of the skin.</margin>
For the skin is like a <term>nerve</term> <note>In the 16th century, 'nerve' often referred to any white, fibrous tissue, including tendons and ligaments.</note> endowed with blood, and a thing plainly halfway between a nerve and the flesh of the muscles, just as if it were constituted from a mixture of both. 
<margin>The difference of skin.</margin>
In man, this is called <term>human</term> <note>original: ἀνθρωπινὴ or ἀνθρώπειος</note> by Herodotus, and it corresponds to the hides of oxen and horses from which leather is prepared, though it does not adhere to or connect with all the parts lying beneath it in the same way. 
<margin>From its connection.</margin>
For it grows to the underlying parts in the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot in one way; in another way again on the forehead to the muscular substance lying beneath it; and otherwise on the lips, eyelids, ears, nose, anus, and genitals; and otherwise throughout the entire body, the skin is joined to the underlying parts, and during dissection, it is removed from the underlying parts in different manners. 
<margin>From the abundance of nerves.</margin>
Furthermore, there is not an equal distribution of nerves to all regions of the skin, nor is the thickness of the skin the same everywhere: for very many nerve fibers are extended to the internal skin of the hands, but very few to the skin of the crown of the head. 
<margin>From its softness.</margin>
Moreover, the skin of the face is seen to be softer and thinner, while that of the crown and the sole of the feet is harder. That which invests the internal seat of the hand (unless it has become more calloused through labor) is most exquisitely halfway between the remaining skin and all other bodies in hardness and softness, approaching as nearly as possible a temperament equal in weight. However it may be, the skin in man is thinner in proportion to the size of his body than that which has fallen to the lot of four-footed animals: although indeed in man it is quite thick on the crown, back, legs, and the sole of the foot, but not equally in everyone. 
<margin>From its movement.</margin>
Furthermore, some parts of the skin are altogether immobile and difficult to move around: such as the skin of the palm and the sole. Others are indeed versatile but are moved by no voluntary motion: such as the skin of the entire body, except that which is moved, such as all the skin of the forehead and face, and that which embraces the front and sides of the neck. And these participate in motion either by their own muscles serving this purpose, like the skin of the forehead, neck, cheeks, and lips: or for the sake of the neighboring skin itself, like the skin of the cheekbones, which, being destitute of muscles, is moved together with the skin closest to it (though obscurely in the meantime). 
<margin>From the hair.</margin>
That indeed some areas of the skin are hairy, such as the crown, the armpits, the genitals, and in men the chin; while others are entirely deprived of hair, such as the skin of the palm and the sole, I believe is conspicuous to everyone. 
<margin>From the openings.</margin>
Just as I know it escapes no one that the skin is the largest part of the whole body, formed in a continuous texture: except that it is perforated by thin little holes, for the soot-like...
