<meta>This page continues Chapter 5 of Book II, following the introductory remarks on the skin and its underlying layers. Vesalius is moving from a general definition of the skin's purpose to a detailed refutation of Aristotle’s views on skin sensitivity.</meta>

->ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE BODY<-

...is permeable, being prepared for the expulsion of waste <note>Vesalius refers here to "excrementorum," which in a 16th-century medical context includes sweat, oils, and other "sooty" vapors the body releases.</note> and the generation of hairs. In the eyelids, nose, ears, mouth, anus, and genitals, and where it provides a path for the nails, it is interrupted and can be seen to be perforated. Furthermore, compared to the rest of the skin, the skin of the inner hand (as well as that covering the sole of the foot) is seen to be the most continuous and the least perforated; some have been inclined to attribute this also to the skin of newborns.

<margin>What the CUTICLE is.</margin>
The skin is covered by another thin and entirely bloodless layer called the cuticle <note>The epidermis.</note>, which corresponds almost to the thin and transparent layers of an onion—except that in some places, and especially in the palm and the sole of the foot, it is found to be thicker and harder. Since this layer is a kind of outgrowth of the skin (which the Greeks call *derma* <note>original: δέρμα</note>), they call it the *epidermis* <note>original: ἐπιδερμίδα</note>. If it is sometimes removed by friction in cases of scabies, or in wounds, or by the application of ointments, or the application of fire, or the pouring of boiling water, or from a long journey, and occasionally separates from the skin like a blister or a pimple, it grows back very readily—and quite differently than the true skin. Only the true skin contains blood and vital spirit.

<margin>That veins, arteries, and nerves extend to the skin, and that it possesses sensation.</margin>
For this reason, the ends of very thin veins, arteries, and the finest parts of nerves converge upon the true skin. These are believed to form the skin itself as they grow together. One should certainly not listen to Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational but often challenged by Vesalius’s direct observations.</margin>, who deprives the skin of sensation, as if the sense of touch were only achieved through the benefit of the flesh situated beneath the skin. We learn from dissection that specific nerves are distributed to the skin in a definite sequence, especially in the face, the arm, the elbow and hand, and then also the legs and feet.

<margin>Book 2 of "On the Soul," chapter 11.</margin>
Throughout the rest of the body, even if nerves are not led to the skin in an ordered series, many still end there. They are spread out beneath the skin, especially at the sides of the chest, supported by the membrane situated under the skin (as are the veins themselves), just as I shall explain more fully in the fourth book, which will be dedicated to the nerves. And so, the skin does not feel by virtue of the muscles (which Aristotle called "flesh"), but rather, as we said, by the presence of its own nerves. Even though the skin of the crown of the head is endowed with a duller sensation, it still feels, however inconvenient it was for Nature to distribute nerves upward to the crown, and even though the skin here does not greatly lack sensation.

Furthermore, who has not learned from daily experience that skin torn from the underlying muscles or bones—and later struck by a scalpel or squeezed by fingernails—still feels? There is no reason for any of Aristotle's followers to claim some sort of "earthiness" <note>original: "Terrestritatem." In Aristotelian physics, "earth" was an insensitive element; his followers argued skin was too "earthy" to have its own sense of touch.</note> here, since the nerves arising from the spinal cord (especially from its lower seat) are harder than the skin itself; and harder still are the tendons, which no one denies are easily affected. Indeed, if we must trust reason as much as experience, I would dare to assert that many muscle bellies (such as those surrounding the thigh) are less sensitive than the skin of the face and hand.

They also seem ridiculous to me who deny the skin can feel because there is no "medium" <note>Aristotelian theory suggested that every sense required a medium between the object and the organ (like air for sight). Critics argued the skin couldn't be the organ of touch because nothing sat between it and the object.</note> here; as if we did not see a nerve, even when stripped of its own membranes or divided in the middle, suffer the most severe pain whenever sharp powders are sprinkled on its bare substance. And if we ridiculously desired a "medium" for the sense of touch beyond reason, is the cuticle itself not right there, growing on the skin and meanwhile (as we think) devoid of sensation?

<margin>The FLESHY membrane.</margin>
But now let us approach the membrane situated beneath the skin throughout the entire body. It is much stronger and thicker than the cuticle and adheres to the underlying muscles with sparse fibers, but it is more firmly attached to the skin. Indeed, many veins and a very few thin arteries (which nourish the skin) and nerve branches (which communicate sensation to the skin) pass through this membrane. Creeping between the skin and this membrane, they are supported by it...

Why the present membrane is called "fleshy."

...they couple the membrane to the skin, except for a certain continuous and very close series of fibers, by the benefit of which the membrane is very strongly grown together with the skin. This membrane does not maintain the same thickness throughout the entire body; rather, in certain parts of the body, it is increased with fleshy fibers, and having been made thicker, it becomes so fleshy that it is granted the name of a muscle. This type of region is found in the entire breadth of the neck, in the forehead, and in almost the rest of the face. In certain animals, however, it is filled with fleshy fibers almost everywhere, and especially in those animals that move the skin of their whole body (just as we move our forehead). I have even heard that there were men who were able to move the skin in the region of the chest and elsewhere in the body; for these people, this membrane undoubtedly happened to be similar to the fleshy membranes of horses and donkeys.

<margin>
The fleshy layer.
</margin>
Furthermore, I do not think the word "Fleshy" is wrongly added to this membrane, which the Greeks call *muscle* <note>original: "μυΐα" (myia), literally "mouse," used for muscle</note> among the names of other membranes, since among the remaining membranes of the body, this one alone appears almost fleshy and should truly be considered such. The Arabs, weighing this a little more precisely, seem to have been the first of all, as far as I know, to have called this the Fleshy membrane. And certainly, this should have been investigated more deeply by the leading physicians of our age, who contend that the "fleshy layer" <note>term: *panniculus carnosus*; a layer of tissue beneath the skin that in many animals allows for skin movement, but in humans is mostly reduced to specific areas like the neck and face.</note>—which was not badly named by certain "Barbarians" <note>Vesalius often uses "Barbarians" to refer to Medieval or non-Greek authors, though here he admits they got the name right.</note>—consists of the eight muscles of the abdomen. Contrary to Galen’s opinion and the truth of the matter, they deny that a membrane is stretched under the skin in the whole body and finally in the abdomen itself (about which they seem to have at least some knowledge). Others, even if they have seen me demonstrate this membrane throughout the entire body, are so foolish that they do not admit this is the one Galen mentions frequently elsewhere and in the third book of *On Anatomical Procedures*. They do this because I show fat between the skin and this membrane, often even three fingers thick, and because a person's membrane is always separated from the skin by as much as the thickness of the fat. Truly, such enemies of Nature and truth ought to have considered that Galen was speaking of his apes, not of humans; in apes, no fat intervenes between the membrane and the skin, and the membrane itself is not only continued to the skin by fibers but is directly contiguous to it everywhere without the intervention of another body. For this reason, it is not so difficult in a human to divide the skin alone while leaving the membrane unharmed, as it is in the apes, dogs, and those animals from which Galen described anatomy.

To this membrane, in that part where it covers the proper membranes of the muscles, is spread that mucous stickiness which Aristotle attributed to the skin—perhaps for this reason, so that the membrane itself does not hinder the movement of the underlying muscles. For it is common for all membranes that contain or surround a body which sometimes changes its position and place, to be smeared with a certain mucous and sticky humor on the side facing that body.

<margin>
FAT, or grease.
</margin>
<margin>
Where fat may be more abundant.
</margin>
There are, therefore, three things constantly encircling the entire human body: namely the cuticle, the skin, and this fleshy membrane. To these a fourth is added, namely the grease itself, or fat, called *pimele* <note>original: "πιμελὴ"</note> by the Greeks. Unless a person is extremely emaciated, this is contained most abundantly everywhere between the skin and the membrane we just mentioned. For from many veins and arteries (if any are found) creeping through the membrane and propagated between it and the skin, a great deal of blood sweats out; due to the coldness of the membrane and the lack of heat, it degenerates into grease or fat—or as others call it in horned animals, *axungia* <note>term: *axungia*; literally "axle-grease," used here for animal lard or tallow.</note>. For this is the method of generation for fat in the membranes of the entire body, the ligaments, and (to say it once) in all cold bodies unworthy of blood: namely, that the blood emanating from the veins is congealed by the force of the cold and adheres to those bodies. But in the meantime, Nature has most accurately provided that...

<header>ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY</header>

...extremely well, lest fat <term>adeps; the fatty tissue beneath the skin</term> be produced where it might be harmful or useless. For Nature has not covered the membranes of the brain with fat, nor the coverings of the testes, nor the inner surface of the heart’s covering <note>the pericardium</note>, even though the heart itself is not without it. Nor did she place fat on the inner site of the ligaments which are wrapped transversely around the tendons; nor under the skin of the eyelids, the forehead, or the penis; nor even very much on the outer surface of the hand and foot.

<margin>Which animals have an abundance of fat.</margin>
She has, however, certainly covered the buttocks most copiously, so that they might use that fat in place of a cushion. A great deal of fat is collected in "moist and cold" animals (among whose number are humans and pigs); but in "dry and hot" animals, there is none, or very little, as in lions, hunting dogs, and even the monkey itself. Although, besides the human, the pig, and the hedgehog <note>original: "ericium"</note>, I have never encountered another terrestrial quadruped that possesses fat between the skin and the fleshy membrane, however much sheep and dormice are occasionally found to be very plump. Furthermore, fat is white, although not equally so in all animals, and in humans even less so than in all others, because the membranes, the skin, and other bodies to which it adheres are white, and not merely red like flesh. For all things in our body that are transformed by something else also take on a color as close as possible to that of the thing transforming or altering them. It is utterly ridiculous to believe that fat is white because it possesses an "airy substance," when one finds hardly anything whiter than bone, cartilage, ligament, and tendons, yet you will find nothing in the body so "earthy" <note>Vesalius is refuting ancient Greek theories that linked the color white to the element of Air and hardness to the element of Earth</note>.

<margin>The use of fat.</margin>
To the fat collected between the skin and the membrane, we can ascribe the same use that we grant to clothing: namely, that it may warm the body in time of cold, and if a man is exposed to the Sun, it may also cool him in some way by preventing the heat from penetrating. And yet, the use of fat is so slight that we do not think a person lacks a necessary part or substance of the body if they happen to be deprived of fat. Thus, it is not surprising that newborn children and the fetuses of other animals show no fat attached or grown onto any of their membranes.

### CHAPTER VI. How the nature of the cuticle, the skin, the fat, and the fleshy membrane should be observed through dissection.

<margin>The method of cutting the muscles will be interspersed with their description.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter V, featuring several cherub-like children (putti) in a landscape. Some appear to be playing or working with tools, a common motif in this book representing the "labor" of anatomy.</image-desc>JUST as in the preceding book, after I completed the description of the bones and cartilages, I handed down the reasoning and method by which someone might conveniently prepare these for their own instruction; so also in this book, I shall subjoin the craftsmanship of cutting for all things that will be presented in order, following each description. In this way, someone who is about to correctly undertake and complete the dissection of every muscle and ligament in a single body may do so in order. From this, a different sequence for describing or teaching the muscles will sometimes occur here than in my *Epitome* <note>the "Epitome" was a shorter, simplified version of this book intended for students</note> of these books, in which I followed the logic of proximity rather than the logic of dissection when arranging the order; thus, different orders are set for different purposes. Although I might perhaps have followed the logic of proximity here as well, and relegated the method of cutting the muscles to the end of the book in a single chapter and a single sequence, it would have been entirely too long, and would have occasionally contained something pertaining to the history of the muscles that would otherwise have had to be included in their descriptions—not to mention that we must occasionally accommodate ourselves to understanding Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose authority Vesalius was both following and challenging</note> (who is more prolific and diligent in the description of the muscles than in other parts of the body). Thus, a varying order in the same book would not only be awkward and inconvenient, but furthermore, it would lead to proli—

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

...lest I should increase the volume in vain. In the meantime, however, I will allow anyone to rearrange my Chapters in their reading according to their own judgment. I am forced to endure those who have never even in their dreams practiced dissection, yet are dedicated to claiming the labors of others as their own under any pretext. Finally, thinking they have achieved some "golden mean," they will disgracefully concoct my efforts and long nights of work into an epitome—or rather, a reduction—imposing a poisonous deception upon students. Indeed, they are the reason I am now forced to occasionally strive for brevity against my own feelings, and to restrain myself more than once from things that would otherwise be most useful.

Therefore, following the method we now consider superior, and about to begin the anatomy of the parts described in the preceding Chapter, you will take a sharper razor. In the abdomen, or in whatever part of the body you choose that is not lacking in fat <term>adeps; the fatty tissue beneath the skin</term>, you will make a straight incision through the skin down to the fat, and then a transverse one (so that you create at least one or more corners).

<margin>Management of the skin.</margin>
Apply the razor to the skin so lightly and moderately that you divide only the skin itself, leaving the fleshy membrane <note>The *panniculus carnosus*, a layer of tissue that in some animals allows the skin to twitch, which Vesalius correctly identifies in humans as well</note> uninjured. You will do this without trouble in a human, especially a fatter one. Frequently, and especially in women, the thickness of the fat exceeds the width of two fingers on the chest and abdomen; whereas on the hips and buttocks, we have seen in public dissections that it exceeds the width of a palm, even in women who are not extremely obese. Consequently, the incisions must be made more accurately the leaner the body happens to be.

Next, you must also strive to become accustomed to performing this incision without difficulty, both because of the muscles formed from the fleshy membrane and to learn the pathways of the nerves and veins scattered between the skin and this membrane. Therefore, after you have dissected the skin down to the fat (leaving the fleshy membrane untouched), you will lift the skin at one of the corners of the incisions with a hook or your nails. Then, carefully making transverse strokes with a sharper razor toward the skin, you will separate the skin from the fat as far as you wish. 

<margin>The cuticle and the fat.</margin>
Next, you will apply a burning candle to the folded-back skin so that the cuticle <note>The epidermis, or the very outermost layer of skin</note> comes away like a blister by the force of the fire, allowing you to view the skin and the cuticle separately. While you are freeing the skin from the fat, it is proper to track the small nerves and the veins which, creeping over the membrane within the fat, approach the skin. 

<margin>The fleshy membrane.</margin>
Then, the membrane itself must be diligently inspected, joined as it is to the skin by those frequent fibers. Now, if a fat corpse is at hand, strive to free the fat from the membrane; this must be performed in exactly the same way as you separated the skin from the fat. Care must be taken lest the membrane be carelessly removed along with the fat. 

In this, the anatomists following Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (2nd century AD), whose anatomical writings were considered absolute authority until Vesalius challenged them</note> have erred, denying that this membrane is found in humans. By this occasion, they were necessarily ignorant of the muscles constituted from the fleshy membrane, and the veins and nerves extended through it. 

Once the fat is removed, you will make a light incision through the fleshy membrane down to the muscles lying beneath it. With little effort—driven almost by the fingers alone moved across here and there, or with a boxwood knife, or if you wish, a razor—you will separate it from the underlying parts. You will learn that the separation of the membrane from the skin is one thing, and the pulling away of the membrane from those bodies upon which it rests is another—a process which Herophilus <note>An ancient Greek physician (3rd century BC) often called the "father of anatomy"</note> called flaying <note>original Greek: δάρσιν (darsin)</note>. 

<margin>The difference in dissection between the skin and the fleshy membrane, and then between the fleshy membrane and the muscles beneath it.</margin>
For this latter task is easy to do and is completed quickly, corresponding exactly to the operation by which we see the skin removed without trouble from oxen, calves, sheep, and hares. Indeed, this pulling away is so prompt that we see daily, using only breath <note>Vesalius refers to the practice of blowing air under the skin to help separate it during butchery</note>, this membrane separated with the skin from the underlying bodies in kids, lambs, and even younger calves. However, the separation of the skin from the fat or from the membrane is not completed except by very frequent incisions, very sharp razors, and a long space of time. This is also what butchers teach us whenever they try to remove the skin from under the armpits, where they are careful not to take away too much flesh with the fleshy membrane attached to the body of the ox...

<summary>Vesalius provides practical instructions for dissecting the skin and subcutaneous layers, emphasizing the distinction between the skin, fat, and fleshy membrane. He critiques earlier anatomists like Galen for failing to recognize the presence of the fleshy membrane in humans and uses analogies to butchery to explain the ease of certain anatomical separations.</summary>

## ON THE MUSCULAR SUBSTANCE
## moving the skin of the forehead. Chapter VII.

<margin>Muscular substance of the forehead.</margin>
<image-desc>Historiated initial letter 'C' depicting several cherubs or children in an outdoor setting; some appear to be examining or interacting with a figure seated on a stone plinth.</image-desc>I have previously mentioned that the fleshy membrane <note>The *panniculus carnosus*, a layer of tissue beneath the skin that Vesalius identifies as being particularly muscular in the face</note>, which is placed beneath the entire skin, is reinforced in certain parts of the body with fleshy fibers and in some places takes on the nature of a muscle. Now, however, we will treat why and in what way this happens under the skin of the forehead, which the Greeks call the <term>metopidion <note>Greek: μετωπίδιον; the forehead or the area between the eyes</note></term>, just as they call the lines impressed upon it <term>liparas <note>Greek: λιπαρὰς; smooth or shining lines</note></term> and <term>asarkas <note>Greek: ἀσαρκὰς; lean or fleshless lines</note></term>. So that the eyebrows may be raised, and sometimes lowered to narrow the seat of the eyes and protect them by wrinkling, the entire skin of the forehead (which is hairless), along with the skin of the nose, is moved by voluntary motion as needed. This occurs thanks to the fleshy membrane stretched beneath the skin of the whole forehead and nose. For this membrane is reinforced with very many fleshy fibers, and having been made muscular, <margin>a This could not be drawn on the forehead in any way other than in the 3rd Plate, at A.</margin> it receives many branches of nerves. Furthermore, this membrane grows into the skin of the forehead and nose more tenaciously, and without the intervention of any fat (or with very little), than it is usually attached to the skin throughout the rest of the body. This has deceived other anatomists into thinking that the skin of the forehead is itself a fleshy and muscular substance; for the skin here is no more endowed with a flesh-like substance than elsewhere, but only the present membrane is made fleshier and joined to the skin itself (as we have said) more stubbornly than in the abdomen, back, or legs—just as if the membrane and the skin were forming a single body. In this way, the same movement is correctly performed by both the membrane and the skin.

<margin>The arrangement of fibers in the forehead.</margin>
Furthermore, the fibers of this muscular structure, lying side-by-side, are seen to be fleshier from the top of the nose to the middle of the forehead (which lies between the first roots of the hair and the eyebrows) and also at the sides of this area. All of them run upward in a straight path, unless you count the very rare fibers stretched in an oblique direction.

<margin>Transverse incisions must not be attempted in the forehead.</margin>
And surely this straight arrangement of fibers must not be considered lightly by physicians, lest they perform transverse <note>horizontal</note> rather than straight <note>vertical</note> incisions in the forehead. For it happens that when someone attempts a transverse incision there—and especially near the eyebrows, where I said the fibers are fleshier—both the eyebrows and the skin contiguous to them are rolled downward toward the roots of the eyelids and weigh upon the eyes over which they lie, so that they can neither be opened as desired nor freely perform their function.

...then manage another cut on the head, following the path of the coronal suture <note>The joint where the frontal and parietal bones of the skull meet</note>, all the way to the temples and the roots of the ears. Nor is this as difficult to do as other leading figures of dissection seem to imply; for, as I have testified before, the membrane is not grown into the skin in such a way that a single body arises from the confusion of both.

## ON THE MUSCLES OF THE EYELIDS.
### Chapter IX.

<image-desc>Woodcut anatomical diagram of the human eye showing the muscles and tissues involved in the movement of the eyelids. Labels A through F indicate specific components such as the primary eyelid muscle, its origin points, and the secondary muscle.</image-desc>

> *ALTHOUGH the third plate of muscles <note>Vesalius refers to the large, full-page anatomical illustrations found earlier in Book II</note>, at the characters C, D, and E, expresses these muscles in some way, we have nevertheless placed this specific figure here. In it, A indicates the first muscle of the eyelid; b and C, however, show the beginning of that muscle. D indicates the second muscle, whose origin is marked by e. The mutual connection of the two muscles is marked by F.*

<margin>a Figure 18, chapter 14, book 7; b Figure in chapter 35, book 1.</margin>
<margin>The structure of the eyelids.</margin>
Each eyelid, the lower as well as the upper, is formed by a membrane that takes its origin from the membrane surrounding the skull <note>The pericranium</note> and exists as a single continuous body with the adherent or "white" tunic of the eye <note>The conjunctiva and sclera</note>; then there is also the skin along with the fleshy membrane. These are joined together very firmly at the edges of the eyelids, where the cartilage that keeps the eyelashes upright—called the <term>tarsus <note>A plate of dense connective tissue that gives the eyelid its shape and firmness</note></term>—is located. Throughout the rest of the eyelid region, the skin is joined to the fleshy membrane just as it is in almost all other parts of the body regarding their connection; however, no fat lies between the skin and the membrane, but only a certain oily moisture.

<margin>Two eyelid muscles.</margin>
In the upper eyelid as well, across its entire width, the fleshy membrane is abundantly reinforced with muscular fibers, and it creates, as it were, two muscles placed in the middle, between the skin and that membrane which we said was continuous with the adherent tunic of the eye.

<margin>Why the upper eyelid must move.</margin>
For it was necessary for the upper eyelid to be moved according to our will, otherwise it would serve no use to us. Indeed, Nature would have bestowed eyelids in vain if we could not close them at our will when something was brought from the outside toward a person's eyes—which are far softer than the eyes of beetles and crabs—that might strike or injure them. Nature therefore produced two thin, broad, membranous muscles, almost entirely similar to each other in substance, placing one in the larger angle of the eye <note>The medial canthus, near the nose</note> and the other in the smaller angle <note>The lateral canthus, near the temple</note>.

<margin>o A. then C, b. and Plate 3, C.</margin>
<margin>One muscle.</margin>
The one that occupies the portion of the larger angle begins from the middle of the angle’s seat at the side of the nose, its beginning even touching the part of the eyebrows nearest the nose. The end of this muscle is broad, just as the entire muscle is, and is flattened against the cartilage in which the hairs are fixed, occupying the entire middle seat that faces the larger angle.

<margin>d D. then e. and Plate 3, D.</margin>
<margin>The other.</margin>
The other muscle embraces the entire smaller angle, following a somewhat semicircular path. For arising from the middle of the lower eyelid, it is led around through the smaller angle and, ascending into the upper eyelid, inserts itself into the remaining half of the cartilage’s seat; and [it connects] to the first muscle, not at the car-

...not only to the cartilage, but it is also joined along the rest of the upper eyelid's length in such a way that unless you distinguish the two by their fibers, both will appear to be one. For the fibers of the second muscle, marked with our **C**, correspond to the eyelid when it is drawn upward; however, when the eye is blinking, they form a more acute angle. But the fibers of the first muscle are seen to be less oblique and are drawn from a twofold origin: specifically from the larger angle <note>The inner corner of the eye near the nose</note> **f b**, and from the part of the eyebrow adjacent to the nose. This muscle **g c** raises the upper eyelid, while the second one moves it downward. For both the part of the tarsus <note>The firm, plate-like structure that gives the eyelid its shape</note> where the contracted muscle is not implanted and the rest of it are always drawn together simultaneously; and this is by the benefit of the cartilaginous constitution of the tarsus, into which the muscles are inserted.

<margin>
Why the tarsus is not soft like the rest of the eyelid.
</margin>

For if it were membranous, or fleshy, or in any way soft (like the rest of the eyelid's base), then besides the fact that it would not keep the eyelashes upright, the part drawn by the muscle's contraction would not be followed by the rest. Just as if you pull any crooked or twisted stick by whichever part you wish, the whole thing follows; in the same way, the entire tarsus now follows each muscle alternately. That the movements of the eyelid are celebrated in the same manner as the other movements of the entire body—which are performed by opposing muscles—ought to be clear to everyone: namely, with one muscle contracted into itself, while the other rests from its own function and is rendered longer and relaxed. For if both muscles were convulsed and each drew the part of the tarsus continuous with it toward itself, the part facing the large angle would be pulled upward, while the part nearer the small angle would be pulled downward; thus the eye would no more be opened than closed. Such an eyelid would look like what Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> called "retorted" in his books of *Prognostics* <note>original: "Prælagiorum"</note>.

<margin>
Knowledge of the muscles moving the eyelids is difficult.
</margin>

For the sake of this oracle <note>referring to Hippocrates's authoritative observation</note>, I would certainly wish that the muscles of the eyelids be observed by students with great care; for, like almost all movements in the face, the study of these is also arduous. Galen <note>A 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius frequently corrects</note> easily attests to this, for in his books *On the Knowledge of Affected Parts*, he recounted three muscles of the eyelid differently than elsewhere. He suggested that those two I have already enumerated draw the eyelid downward, and he proposed a third, originating from the forehead, as the author of the eyelid's upward movement. Nor is the movement of our eyelids yet as marvelous as that of the little membrane which we see drawn over the entire eye from the larger corner of the eye in birds, turtles, and many other animals whenever the eye blinks; when the eye is opened, it is collected back to the larger corner, appearing somewhat similar to our caruncle <note>The small, pink, fleshy nodule at the inner corner of the eye; original: "carunculæ"</note> located in the large corner of the eye.

<margin>
The lower eyelid is immobile.
</margin>

Thus, the matters pertaining to the movement of the upper eyelid are so arranged; meanwhile, for the best of reasons, the lower eyelid is both smaller and immobile.

**T**HE dissection <note>original: "administratio"; here referring to the manual procedure of anatomical preparation</note> of the muscles moving the eyelids should correspond to that by which you approached the muscular substance of the forehead: namely, that on the eyelids of one side, you remove the muscles together with the skin all the way to their insertion; and then you separate the muscles from the skin as whole as you are permitted. But on the eyelids of the other side, the skin must be removed from the muscles all the way to the tarsi themselves, keeping the muscles entirely preserved against that membrane which arises from the adherent "white tunic" <note>The conjunctiva or sclera; original: "alba'ue oculi tunica"</note> of the eye and constitutes the internal seat of the eyelids. This membrane encloses between itself and the skin the muscles moving the upper eyelid, without any intervention of fat (just as is nearly the case in the forehead). Where

The third is found above and moves the eye upward; just as the fourth, which is located below, moves it downward. These four muscles, as they preside over the straight movements of the eye, also maintain a straight position and are similar to one another in every respect. For their "heads" <note>the origin or starting point of the muscle</note> take their beginning from the dura mater <note>the "tough mother," the outermost membrane of the brain</note> which covers the optic nerve <note>original: "neruum uisorium"</note>, and from the nerve of the second pair of cranial nerves, just as the optic nerve emerges from the cavity of the skull. Then their "belly" <note>the thick, central part of the muscle</note> is seen to be wider than it is deep, yet almost round; and when that belly reaches the region of the eye that is halfway between the back and the front, it ends in a broad, membranous tendon. This tendon extends beyond the middle region of the eye toward the front and is inserted into the hard tunic of the eye <note>the sclera, or the white of the eye</note>, as if into a bone that is to be moved, not far from the iris and the greater circle of the eye, following a straight line according to the width of the eye. Furthermore, the fifth and sixth muscles are the workers of circular movement <note>circumduction</note>; they correspond to the four previously mentioned in both shape and origin, but they are smaller and differ from them in their path and insertion. For one takes its origin from the dura mater surrounding the optic nerve, in the region of the smaller corner of the eye <note>the outer canthus</note>, and is implanted into the lower part of the eye with its thin, nervous tendon along an oblique line near the iris. The other, however, arises from the membrane of the optic nerve in the region of the larger corner <note>the inner canthus, near the nose</note> and inserts its thin, nervous tendon into the hard tunic of the eye, also along an oblique line, at the upper part of the eye. Although both of these contribute especially to the turning of the eye, they also move the eye upward and downward to some extent.

<margin>*Fat placed between the eye muscles.*</margin>
<margin>m * Figures F, G.</margin>

<margin>*The seventh muscle.*</margin>
These six muscles, when they all still preserve their position and are joined together, constitute a cone-like shape <note>original: "turbinatam," like a spinning top or cone</note>; the cone's point is their origin, while the base is their insertion. For they are connected to the optic nerve by a very short path. In the space they collectively form, much fat is contained, which is somewhat hard and very white; this fat, in turn, is wrapped around another certain muscle. For besides the mentioned muscles of the eye, there is still another large one, surrounded on all sides by them and by the fat we described; it alone forms a shape similar to that which the first six formed together. For this muscle begins a little further forward than those six, also taking a fleshy beginning from the dura mater involving the optic nerve; it encircles that nerve in a ring and, stretching forward, widens like a cone until the muscle touches the back part of the eye. There it is implanted in a fleshy, circular manner—not right next to the optic nerve, but nearly where the eye begins to be widest at this posterior seat.

Just as I said there was fat placed between this muscle and the first six, so also fat is collected between the nerve itself and this present muscle in that interval where the muscle recedes from the nerve. This muscle has no divisions <note>original: "inscriptionem"</note> at all, except perhaps one in the lower part, extending along its length. For this reason, I wonder why this has not been counted as a single muscle by anatomists, but by some as two, and by others as three; meanwhile, they have all described this muscle only in passing.

<margin>*The function of the seventh.*</margin>
And therefore, I also fear that they have not very aptly expressed its use when they assert that it is specifically the author of "retaining" the eye in its place, ascribing no other use to it besides that.

<margin>This first figure shows [this].</margin>
Since, however, the first six muscles could more aptly claim that duty—because their outer surface is somewhat joined by fibers to the membrane lining the eye's socket in the skull—they hide the seventh muscle within themselves on all sides, preventing it from touching the skull anywhere. Indeed, perhaps there will not be wanting those who [claim] the six...

# THE DISSECTION OF THE EYE MUSCLES
## Chapter XII.

<margin>Dissection of an eye removed from the skull, and the method of removing it.</margin>
<margin>a Figure 1, Chapter 9, Book 1; T, V, $\Theta$, and many other characters.</margin>
<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'R'. The scene depicts several putti (cherubic infants) in a landscape with classical architectural ruins. One putto in the foreground uses a large pair of dividers to measure a human skull resting on the ground, while another watches. In the background, other putti appear to be engaged in scholarly or investigative activities.</image-desc>
You will perform the dissection <note>original: "administrationem"</note> of the muscles moving the eye more correctly if the eye is plucked out from the cavity of the skull <note>original: "caluariae"</note>. It is quickly removed in its entirety while the skull is still intact if you free it from its cavity on all sides with a long knife, always leading the cuts in a circle against the bone, and finally cut the optic nerve <note>original: "neruum uisorium"</note> where it first emerges from the skull. But if the skull has perhaps already been dissected for the inspection of the brain, and the brain itself has been removed, it will be helpful to divide the skull with a saw along two lines: one line made from the region of the larger angle <note>the inner corner of the eye near the nose</note> toward the hole for the optic nerve; the other from the smaller angle <note>the outer corner</note> to the end of the first section near that hole. For if you force the saw to penetrate into the seat of the eye in this manner, you will remove the entire upper part of the socket like a triangle; and thereafter, having freed the eye from fat on all sides, you will take it out. Or, if it seems better, you will allow the eye, freed from the bone everywhere, to hang from the skull only by the connection of the optic nerve. You will hand the plucked-out eye to a companion to hold, so that with the tips of his right hand's fingers he holds the end of the optic nerve (which he will also lift), while with his left hand closed as if in a fist, he grasps the front part of the eye between his index finger and thumb. Then, remove the fat placed around the eye and the glands that come between the divisions of the veins and arteries.

<margin>Figures 1 and 2 of Chapter 11 show these things.</margin>
Next, having considered the paths of the muscles and the shape they all form together, free the six "heads" <note>the points of origin</note> of the first muscles from the optic nerve with a sharper knife. Then, by lightly cutting each muscle, lead them to the middle region of the eye, extending each one over your companion's left hand as if you were going to form the shape of a star. In this way, you will learn the attachment, shape, and use of each muscle with little effort. Furthermore, nothing should be guarded against as diligently as accidentally scraping the adherent or "white" tunic <note>the conjunctiva or sclera</note> of the eye away from the cornea <note>the clear front window of the eye</note>, or cleaning the eye too much before you have seen the insertion of the six muscles. Otherwise (unless you are perhaps more experienced), you will ruin it, carelessly cutting away the thin, tendon-like portion of a muscle along with the adherent membrane.

<margin>b Figure 18, Chapter 14, Book 7; u, u.</margin>
<margin>c Figure 17, Chapter 14, Book 7; x.</margin>
Now, when you have removed the fat heaped in the middle cavity of these muscles with your fingernails or a knife from the seventh muscle of the eye, it is time to approach that muscle while it is still intact. Examine how it surrounds the nerve and is implanted circularly into the root of the eye, by scraping it from the nerve all the way to the hard tunic <note>the sclera</note> of the eye.

<margin>Dissection of the eye muscles while the eye still adheres to the skull.</margin>
However, if your intention is to dissect the eye while it still adheres to the skull, you will handle the muscles by first freeing their heads in the manner I have already described, leading the heads from the nerve (which is still fixed) all the way to their insertion. Yet, you will perform the first method of sectioning more conveniently and with less trouble.

<margin>d Figure 19, Chapter 14, Book 7; $\lambda$.</margin>
In either method of dissection, however, the position of the eye must always be carefully weighed, which the caruncle <note>the small, pinkish nodule at the inner corner of the eye; original: "caruncula"</note> will indicate, as it occupies the larger angle in humans, and (as it is believed)...

The fourth side, which extends from the top of the chin to the upper part of the breastbone, can hardly be distinguished because in humans the muscles of both sides meet here so closely that the two muscles seem to be one; and also because in this part they are far more fleshy than in the rest of their extent. These muscles pull the cheeks and the entire lower lip downward, and draw them to the sides together with the upper lip. This muscle is similarly membrane-like and interwoven with various types of fibers, encompassing that entire region of the cheeks which we are able to puff out. Indeed, that whole body which is puffed out should be considered as nothing other than the skin, beneath which the first muscle already mentioned immediately lies; then, depending on how fat a person is, a greater or lesser amount of fat; and then a certain muscle of the upper lip, and another common to that same lip and the wing <note>nostril</note> of the nose, which we shall describe later. Furthermore, there is the wide, circular muscle whose nature we are now striving to explain, and whose internal surface is lined by the membrane <note>the mucous membrane</note> that clothes the mouth. This membrane is so closely joined to the muscle that it cannot be removed from it without tearing. Indeed, this second muscle of the cheeks is little more than a very thin and somewhat membrane-like entanglement of fleshy fibers. You will most readily recognize the function of both mentioned cheek muscles, and especially the first one, if you move your lips and cheeks as much as possible in any direction while the lower jaw is drawn up against the upper jaw and held still; you will also observe how you can pull the skin of the front of the neck downward along with the cheeks by the action of that first muscle. Again, if the skin of the neck is held still and you move the entire area of the cheeks—which is free to be puffed out—now into the fullness of the mouth, now outward, now upward, now downward, now forward, and now backward, you will greatly admire the function of the second muscle and the movements we perform by its power and the air in the mouth. 

However, Galen was so partial to the first muscle on each side—which was hidden from him when he wrote his books *On the Usefulness of the Parts* <note>Latin: "De Usu partium"</note>, but which he claims to have finally discovered himself in his books *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>Latin: "De Adminitrandis sectionibus"</note>—that, in order to further prove the sluggishness of the ancients, he handed down that it was of such great importance that in the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, he seems to establish it as the sole author of all the functions we perform with the lips and mouth while eating, drinking, or speaking. He specifically attributes the duty of movement to the nerves that converge here, making almost no mention (as he should have) of the other muscles in addition. ### THE PROCEDURE FOR THE MUSCLES MOVING THE CHEEKS, LIPS, AND
### THE WINGS OF THE NOSE. CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>d 3rd plate, r.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'H' depicting several cherubs or putti engaged in an anatomical dissection of a human figure in an outdoor landscape setting.</image-desc>
<margin>Procedure for the first and second of the twelve muscles from the preceding chapter.</margin>
YOU will most opportunely begin the procedure for these muscles from the <gloss>d</gloss> broad muscles consisting of a fleshy membrane <note>Vesalius refers to the platysma, the thin sheet of muscle just under the skin of the neck.</note>. First, with a very sharp razor, you will lead a straight incision in the skin from the top of the chin and the middle of the lower lip (where the skin ends in redness) down to the chest, following the length of the neck. Do this so precisely that only the skin is divided down to the underlying muscle or fleshy membrane. Then another incision must be led to the edge of each lip, following the limit of the redness, so that the entire mouth is encircled by a circular cut. To these, another incision along the length of the nose shall be added. If you have already tackled the muscular structure of the forehead and the muscles of the eyelid, no other incisions besides these (except under the ear to the middle of the back of the head) need be made in the face. Otherwise, you would have to manage a transverse incision from the top of the nostrils, under the lower eyelid and the ear, toward the back of the head. Furthermore, from the end of the incision led to the bone of the chest, one transverse cut shall be completed under the collarbone, the top of the shoulder, and the spine of the shoulder blade all the way to the back. It will also be permissible to add to these a transverse cut from the throat, or the region of the windpipe, to the spine. Once these incisions have been attempted, the skin shall be lifted with a small hook; and on one side, with a sharper razor, the skin shall be freed with all diligence from the underlying membranous muscle. You will find this more troublesome nowhere than where a noose has compressed the neck <note>Vesalius likely refers to the bodies of executed criminals, a common source for dissection.</note>; for here, by occasion of the noose, the skin is found most stubbornly grown together with the membranous muscle, and the skin there soon hardens like horn, so that <margin>The type of body suitable for the dissection of muscles.</margin> it hardly admits the razor. Although a body will be more suitably employed for the dissection of muscles from which the veins, having been previously cut, have poured out all the blood into warm water; since then the veins, emptied of blood while you divide the muscles, will not have to be tied off so often, nor so frequently wiped clean with sponges. From the other side of the corpse, however, you will remove the broad and thin muscle along with the skin (which is very easy to do); and on both sides, you will observe the nature of the muscle, the fibers, the nerves, and their functions (if you pull toward yourself the parts we previously described). You should by no means lazily pass over the series of fibers of this muscle in the whole lower seat of the inferior jaw, but rather examine them carefully for the sake of <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "strumarum, uel... scrophularum"; scrofula is a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, often caused by tuberculosis.</note>, so that in that kind of abscess, when the need arises, you may more successfully and skillfully cut out the swelling glands. For attempting the procedure of incision in this condition outside the path of the fibers quite unsightly stretches or wrinkles the skin of the neck on either side. When, therefore, you have carefully observed these things, the muscle of that side, which you left attached under the skin removed from the aforementioned bodies...

### ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE LOWER JAW. Chapter XV.

<margin>The lower jaw moves while the upper remains at rest.</margin>
<margin>a Figures of Chapter 10, Book 1.</margin>

<margin>
The movements of the lower jaw, which are accomplished by eight muscles.

...the crocodile is seen to be similar to a lizard in appearance (though not in size, nor in the jointed bumps of its tail). <note>Vesalius is likely finishing a comparison between human and animal jaw mechanics from the previous page.</note> The human lower jaw is drawn upward toward the upper jaw with a remarkably strong movement when we close the mouth, and then, while chewing, it is moved forward, backward, and to the sides; and finally, when we open the mouth, it is driven downward, sometimes straight, sometimes deviating slightly to one side or the other.

The first muscle of the side, or the temporal muscle.
</margin>
We complete these movements of the jaw with four muscles on each side. One of these, occupying the temple of its side and therefore called the "temporal" <term>temporal muscle</term><note>The large, fan-shaped muscle on the side of the skull used for closing the jaw.</note> by everyone, takes its origin from the bones of the crown <note>parietal bone</note>, the temple, and the forehead, as well as from the bone that imitates a wedge <note>sphenoid bone</note> and that bone which embraces the outer or smaller corner of the eye socket, which I consider the first of the bones of the upper jaw. For like a third part of a circle, this muscle arises from the parietal to the frontal bone much higher up than the scale-like suture <note>the squamous suture of the skull</note> is located. From here, gradually thickening and becoming fleshier and more constricted, it descends into a cavity carved into the bones of the head for the sake of the whole muscle—with the great industry of Nature—surrounded and fenced in by a beautiful ridge. It arises throughout its entire course from the temporal bone, the wedge-shaped bone, the frontal bone, and that bone which forms the outer corner of the eye socket. When it reaches as far as the yoke-bone <term>zygomatic arch</term> and has become very thick (though narrow), it also attaches to the upper part of the yoke-bone, continuous with that muscle which we will list in the second place and which we will show arises primarily from the yoke-bone. The entire body of the temporal muscle, as far as the yoke-bone, is fleshy, and on its outer surface, because of the thickness of its own membrane, it is quite bluish-gray—especially at the start of its origin and where it connects to the yoke-bone.

<margin>
l Book 1, Chap. 10, Figures 1 and 2, C; Plate 6, B.
m Plate 6, A.
n Plate 11, Γ; Plate 7, Γ; Plate 9, P; Plate 10, Σ; Plate 11, Σ; Plate 8, Δ.
</margin>
Where it touches the sharp process of the lower jaw <term>coronoid process</term>, it ends in a short, though remarkably strong and sinewy tendon, which embraces the process with its breadth and is very firmly inserted into it. All the fibers of the temporal muscle run toward this tendon as if from three parts of a circle toward their center. They form this tendon in the manner of those muscles which you will hear fill the convex and concave parts of the shoulder blade, and those which arise from the hip bone and serve the movements of the thigh. Truly, I cannot wonder enough what that "peculiar" thing might be that was so celebrated by Galen regarding the temporal muscle.

<margin>
*On the Use of the Parts*, Book 11.
</margin>
Nor do I quite understand why he <note>Galen, the 2nd-century authority whom Vesalius often corrected.</note> extols Nature with so many praises, as if she had deviated here from the form of other muscles with a great and singular artifice by bringing forth a tendon not from the end of the muscle, as is otherwise always the case, but from the middle. For I find nothing rare in the production of the tendon here, nor anything different from many of the aforementioned muscles. So much so, that I do not wonder that Galen spoke differently about the temporal muscle in the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures* (when he was already more skilled in dissections) than he did in the eleventh book of *On the Use of the Parts*. However, what the function of the temporal muscle actually is will be opportunely explained once I have added two more muscles to the discussion.

The second [muscle], or the masseter.
</margin>
The second of those to be mentioned in this chapter is that muscle which we can feel with our hand at the rear part of the lower jaw, below the yoke-bone. For while you place your thumb between the root of the ear and the lower jaw, and place your middle finger against the cheek, and try to push it, as it were, into the fullness of the mouth, you hold the entire outer surface of this muscle. You will recognize it again by touch if, having first brought the jaws together, you strive to compress them even more strongly: for then that muscle, gathered more into itself, will strike the thumb and index finger as it dilates and contracts.

...observing whether a fleshy or sinewy <note>Latin: *nerueus*. This second muscle <note>The masseter muscle.</note> arises from a sinewy, broad, and very strong origin at that part of the cheeks where the lowest part of that suture <note>The zygomaticomaxillary suture.</note> sits, which joins the bone of the upper jaw—occupying the entire smaller corner of the eye socket and leading out the middle portion of the <term>jugal bone</term><note>The zygomatic bone or cheekbone.</note>—to the largest bone of the same jaw. Next, the origin of this muscle is led from the cheeks toward the rear, extending from the entire lower and inner seat of the jugal bone all the way to the ear. While I said its origin at the cheeks was exceedingly sinewy, it is also seen to be sinewy and livid where it emerges from the lower part of the outer surface of the jugal bone; however, where it takes its origin from the inner seat of the jugal bone, it is fleshy, existing there in great width and growing alongside the temporal muscle which produces its own tendon.

This muscle, arising from this origin, tends downward and embraces the entire width of the lower jaw, visible on its external and posterior seat; it is implanted there most strongly, partly fleshy and partly sinewy, with a very wide insertion. 

<margin>
b Plate 4, G.
c Book 1, Ch. 10, Fig. 1, E.
d Plate 4, G, where you will circumscribe the whole muscle [at] E, F, G.

Of the whole width of the insertion, however, none is more notable or stronger than that which the muscle works into the roughness <note>The masseteric tuberosity of the mandible.</note> that swells out like several processes on the lowest seat of the lower jaw. At this point, the muscle is at its narrowest and expresses, in a way, the obtuse angle of a triangle. For the whole muscle is to some extent triangular. One of its lines is stretched along the entire width of its origin; the second is led backward from the cheeks (or the anterior part of the origin) to the lowest seat of the lower jaw, touching that roughness of the jaw we just mentioned; the third line is carried from the ear (or the posterior part of the origin) forward and downward to the lower point of the second line, forming an angle with that line so obtuse that one might almost assign a fourth side to this muscle. However that may be, this obtuse angle—or, if you prefer, this fourth side of the muscle—is much narrower than its broad origin. For this reason, it is also necessary that the course of its fibers varies.

<margin>
e Plate 4, from E to G.
f Plate 4, from F to G.
</margin>
For the fibers taking their origin from the front part of the origin are carried downward and backward; those, however, which emerge from the rear part of the origin creep obliquely downward and forward. All of them extend from the broad origin to the obtuse angle I described, and are inserted into the width of the lower jaw without the formation of a [distinct] tendon. Galen called this muscle, which alone moves the jaw, the <term>masseter</term> <note>From the Greek *masasthai*, "to chew."</note> or "chewing muscle" from its function. When he describes it in the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, he seems to suggest clearly enough that there were some anatomists who counted two masseters on one side, turning their attention to the course of the fibers and the broad origin of the present muscle (as he himself judges). And then he hints that others existed who recorded three masseters on each side, attending to the origins and insertions of this muscle; just as if they had enumerated the individual angles of the muscle in place of a single muscle, quite contrary to all reason.

But for me, this muscle is considered as only one, by whatever means it is held. I believe that those who established two masseters—

And since others

The third muscle, which hides in the mouth.

...even though I have meanwhile, to avoid ambiguity of speech, everywhere followed Galen in calling the second muscle moving the jaw the **masseter**. The third muscle, therefore, takes a very sinewy <note>Latin: *neruosum*. Vesalius often uses this to describe tendinous or fibrous tissues.</note> beginning from the entire cavity 
<margin>
m Figure 5, Chapter 6, Book 1. P then characters 2, 3, 4, 5.
</margin>
or hollow of the processes of the bone resembling a wedge <note>The sphenoid bone, located at the base of the skull.</note>, which are compared to the **wings of bats**; these processes, along with their hollow, are constructed in this way so that they may neatly surround the beginning of this muscle, allowing it to arise opportunely from them. Furthermore, as soon as that sinewy beginning leaves the cavity or hollow of the aforementioned processes, the muscle itself becomes fleshy, large, and thick. It is closely joined to the internal part of the temporal muscle near the extension and insertion of its tendon. In many respects, it is similar to the masseter—the second muscle moving the jaw—and thus it is implanted into the internal and rear seat of the jaw by a large, wide, and exceedingly sinewy insertion, just as the masseter is fixed into the external seat of the jaw.

<margin>
n Figure 2, Chapter 10, Book 1. D.
</margin>
To ensure that this third muscle, by its thickness, would not overly occupy the space of the mouth and throat, a large and open hollow is carved into the jaw (as we also explained in the first book), into which the muscle may be conveniently placed and a large portion of it may remain hidden.

<margin>
The function of the muscles described so far.
</margin>
To these three muscles, along with their pairs on the other side, is primarily entrusted the task of drawing the lower jaw upward and pulling it together when we bite. I do not believe this duty is committed to any one of them privately, although perhaps the temporal and the masseter, being larger and more expansive, perform it more powerfully than the third. How eagerly and strongly these muscles complete this task is obvious in almost all men; however, many performers <note>Latin: *histriones*. These were often traveling strongmen or acrobats.</note> clearly attest to this. Some of them handle certain iron bars with their teeth almost as if with their hands; others support the greatest beams with marvelous strength, relying only on their lower teeth. We saw at **Padua** a performer from **Trent**, who was endowed with a wonderful looseness of joints, who lifted an iron bar of twenty-five pounds from the earth with his teeth, and after holding it upright in his mouth for some time, threw it backward over his head to strike a wall. I myself measured the distance, and the wall stood thirty feet away from the performer. Moreover, I have often seen a certain Turk, as well as a performer from **Mantua** of not very tall stature, support a beam—which had been brought and held upright by two men—using only his lower teeth, and carry it for some time, while many of the bystanders could scarcely lift the beam from the ground.

Furthermore, the movement of the jaw toward the front and the back, which we especially perform when chewing, is achieved chiefly by the second muscles, or **masseters**, thanks to their wide origins and the direction of their fibers. For when the front parts of the origins are contracted, the lower jaw is drawn forward, and the chin projects toward the front. But when the rear seats of the origins are gathered together, the jaw is retracted backward, as if toward the ears. Although the temporal muscles, arising from broad origins and ending in a point toward their insertions, also seem to offer some help to this movement, depending on how they contract or relax these or those fibers of their bodies. Moreover, primarily by the work of the masseters and the muscles hiding in the mouth, the lower jaw is moved in a circle toward the sides. For when the right masseter and the left muscle hiding in the mouth are contracted together, the jaw is driven toward the right side; however, when the masseter of the left side and the muscle hiding in the mouth on the right side work together in contraction, the lower jaw is moved around toward the left side by those who are biting and chewing.

<margin>

...firstly the chin is held; running obliquely, they are inserted into its inner part. The right muscle is united with the left at that seat of the lower jaw where, perhaps because of these muscles, the bone is roughened and bears unevenly protruding processes. These muscles, when both are contracted together, open the mouth and pull the lower jaw straight downward. Furthermore, thanks to their oblique position and path, when only one of them acts, it is the cause of the jaw being drawn obliquely toward its own side. 

However, something unique has happened to both these muscles—something shared by no other muscle in the whole body except for one, which, contrary to Galen's opinion, I shall attribute to the bone resembling the letter U <note>The hyoid bone (ossis u referenti). Galen and Vesalius often used the shape of Greek or Latin letters to describe bones.</note>. For in the middle of the journey that these muscles travel from their origin to their insertion, the fleshy part completely vanishes and becomes bloodless and sinewy <note>Latin: *neruosa*. In this period, this often refers to tendinous or ligamentous tissue rather than nerves in the modern sense.</note>, like a tendon or some kind of ligament, not at all nourished by flesh-like fibers. Indeed, it is as if one were to say each muscle is composed of two "bellies" of muscle, in the middle of which a species of rounded tendon is seen. 

But here, the Craftsman of things <note>Vesalius refers to the "Opifex," the divine or natural creator, highlighting the purposeful design of the body.</note> did not deviate from the usual construction of muscles by mistake or pointlessly. I will not, as Galen did, attribute this to their origin (which he asserts should have been directly opposite their insertion if the layout of the area had allowed it). Because of the oblique movement over which they must preside, the origin they currently hold is extremely necessary for them; meanwhile, it in no way hinders the straight movement of the jaw when both work together. 

Nor would I think that this craftsmanship of the Creator should be attributed so much to the crowdedness of the organs in the throat and the space of the lower jaw (as if this had forbidden these muscles from being fleshy in their middle), as to that reflection or "bending" which the muscles perform along the lower angle of the jaw, where the lowest part of the third muscle moving the jaw is located. For since the muscles pulling down the jaw had to be contracted remarkably strongly at this angle during their gathering, and since they are quite slender, they could not have safely sustained the force of their own tension unless they had become sinewy, fleshless, and hard at that point. They have, in effect, assumed the nature of muscles that become sinewy at least in those places where they are bent back against a bone as if against a pulley—as can be seen in the sixth and seventh, and even more so in the tenth muscles moving the thigh. Furthermore, for the sake of strength, that slender and very long muscle which is inserted from the shoulder blade into the U-shaped bone <note>The omohyoid muscle, which connects the scapula to the hyoid.</note> will be shown to become entirely sinewy in the middle of its path. This is surely so that it may more readily repel and sustain the force of that very strong muscle lying near it, which we shall establish as the second of the seventh pair of muscles moving the head.

Ligaments of the jaw joints.
</margin>
The ligaments binding the lower jaw to the temporal bones correspond to the membrane-like ligaments surrounding other joints, claiming nothing peculiar to themselves.

Now you are free to scrape the masseter from the lower jaw with a knife, after it has been freed from the yoke-bone <note>The zygomatic bone.</note> and the cheekbones, and to weigh its insertion and function with careful attention. You can only manage the muscle hidden in the mouth with precision if the lower jaw is dissected through the middle in the region of the chin. Therefore, applying a larger knife to the work, beginning at the top of the chin, you will divide it through the middle of the incisor teeth; then, taking it in your hands, you will forcefully reflect both parts of it to the sides and luxate it from the cavity carved into the temporal bone. Soon, around the ends of the jaw, you will separate the tunic of the mouth from the bodies lying beneath it, like skin, until the muscle hidden in the mouth presents itself from every side. If it seems best, you may either leave it attached to the bones or throw it away after scraping it from them, likewise weighing its function with care. You will now find the muscle that pulls the jaw downward <note>The digastric muscle.</note> stretched out along the length of the lower seat of the jaw and inserted into the jaw on the internal seat of the top of the chin. This muscle requires no special management now that the masseter muscle has been removed along with the glands, veins, and arteries located under the ears. However, you will more opportunely undertake the sectioning of this fourth muscle and its partner, just like the third pair (the muscles hidden in the mouth), and the examination of their duty or function, when you examine the muscles of the tongue, the bone resembling the letter U <note>The hyoid bone; Vesalius refers to the Greek letter upsilon (υ).</note>, and the larynx.

# ON THE MUSCLES ATTACHED TO THE BONE RESEMBLING THE LETTER U <note>The hyoid bone.</note>
# Chapter XVII.

<margin>
a Figures 1 and 2, chapter 13, book 1; and Figure 1, chapter 21, book 2, A.
b Plate 4, S, T; Plate 1, C.
z Plate F.
c Consult the figure of the head in chapter 13, book 1 at *, A, B, C, etc.
The muscles attached to the bone resembling the letter U partly serve the bone itself and partly serve other parts.
The first pair proper to the bone itself, or the first of the other side.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' showing several figures in a room with a bed, possibly performing a medical or anatomical preparation.</image-desc>
**S** We have already said that the bone resembling the letter U <note>The hyoid bone (ossis υ referentis).</note> is placed in the throat at the upper part of the larynx, serving as a foundation for the root of the tongue upon which it must move, and acting as an anchor for many muscles. Of the muscles attached to this bone, some are proper to it, constructed solely for its sake, all of which take their origin from other bones and are inserted into the U-shaped bone. Others, however, proceed from this bone to serve other organs. Those which are peculiar and proper to the bone itself are believed to primarily ensure that the bone—not being fixed on a very stable base—is not pulled out of place to the sides, or up or down, or forward or backward. Furthermore, these are reduced to a minimum number of seven, or a maximum of eight; that is, four on each side, so that together they constitute four pairs. The first, stronger and thicker than the others, is bifid or twin, stretched out toward the shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx <note>The thyroid cartilage.</note> and the rough artery in the neck <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note>. For it arises with a broad and fleshy beginning from the higher seat of the breastbone <note>The sternum.</note> at its more internal part; and stretched straight upward, always keeping a width equal to its origin, it is inserted into the anterior seat of the bone resembling the letter U, gripping with a fleshy connection the whole breadth of the middle bonelet to which the sides of the U-shaped bone are fastened. A line is incised in the middle of this muscle along its length, on which account it is not ineptly said to consist of two muscles, namely a right and a left one.

...is said: and it is counted as two muscles, or as a single pair, which—when the bone resembling the Greek letter upsilon <note>original: *os $\upsilon$ referens*; the hyoid bone</note> is pulled upward more violently by the superior muscles—pull it back down; they can be considered a bulwark for the shield-shaped cartilage <note>original: *scutiformi cartilagini*; the thyroid cartilage</note> and the rough artery <note>original: *asperæ arteriæ*; the trachea</note>. The third and fourth muscles (namely one on each side) are opposed to these two: they are wide, short, and fleshy in every part, arising from the inner side of the lower jaw under the very top of the chin. From here they descend, becoming only slightly narrower, and are inserted into the upsilon-shaped bone adjacent to the first two, occupying exactly the same width of insertion on the front of the bone as those others do. Consequently, these muscles pull the bone upward—a motion opposite to the two inferior muscles—and then slightly outward, just as those lower ones also move the bone outward, though quite obscurely.

<margin>
Third pair.

The fifth and sixth muscles—one on each side—are quite slender and round. They originate from the roots of the processes that resemble a stylus or a cock's spur <note>The styloid processes of the temporal bone.</note> and are inserted into the upsilon-shaped bone at the side of the area occupied by the first four muscles. This is the region where the sides of the bone meet the middle small bone. Throughout their entire course, these muscles are joined externally to those I reported pull the lower jaw downward <note>The digastric muscles</note>; these also arise from the same stylus-like processes, but slightly lower than these muscles of the upsilon-shaped bone. A duty is entrusted to them to prevent the bone from being pulled away either to the right or the left, and furthermore, they pull it

somewhat upward and inward. But the seventh and eighth muscles of the present bone, again one on each side, are seen to be slender and long; indeed, no other muscle in the entire body is found to be both more slender and longer than these. Furthermore, each claims for itself a certain "enervation" <note>A loss of fleshy fiber, becoming tendinous.</note>, just like the muscles pulling the jaw downward. For in the middle of its course, it ceases to be fleshy, showing for some distance the nature of a tendon, from which it becomes fleshy again; thus it acquires, as it were, two bellies. It takes its fleshy beginning from the higher rib of the shoulder blade <note>The superior border of the scapula</note>, near its neck and the root of the process that resembles an anchor <note>The coracoid process</note>. Hidden under the first of the muscles that lift the shoulder blade, it extends upward obliquely under the muscle that runs from the breastbone and collarbone into the mammillary process of the head <note>The sternocleidomastoid muscle</note>. This muscle compresses the muscle of the upsilon-shaped bone so much that it ceases to be fleshy beneath it and shows the appearance of a tendon—as if it were giving way to that worthier muscle moving the head, or perhaps because it has become harder so that it might more easily withstand the pressure of the overlying muscle during contraction. For as soon as it has passed beyond that muscle, it appears fleshy again, until it is implanted into that region of the upsilon-shaped bone where the fifth and sixth were said to make their insertion.

<margin>
The fourth pair does not serve the movements of the shoulder blades.
</margin>
In the fourth book of *On the Procedures of Anatomy*, Galen thinks these muscles of the fourth pair belong to the shoulder blades <note>The scapulae</note>, asserting that by their help the blades are driven upward toward the throat. However, I would very much wish it to be observed how consistent this is with the truth; for to me they seem to belong to the upsilon-shaped bone and not to the shoulder blades, and I do not think they have anything in common with the movement of the shoulder blades. Indeed, they are smaller and are fixed upon a less firm base (since they are attached to the upsilon-shaped bone) than would be required to lift the shoulder blades (from which the arms, elbows, and hands hang) with an oblique motion. Furthermore, in substance and form they correspond to the other muscles of the upsilon-shaped bone, and in no way to the authors of the shoulder blades' movements. The ancients knew this well, and following their opinion, Galen in the eleventh book of *On the Use of the Parts* ascribes these muscles to the upsilon-shaped bone—though he forgot himself again in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts* and listed them among the movers of the shoulder blade, erring easily in these as he did in many other muscles of the shoulder blade. Moreover, the upsilon-shaped bone absolutely requires these muscles if it is to be moved in a direction opposite to that achieved by the fifth and sixth muscles.

<margin>q d v, 2nd branch marked with i, fig. 2, ch. 11, book 4.</margin>

It seems to me, therefore, that the muscles listed in the last place pull the U-shaped bone <note>original: *os υ referens*; the hyoid bone, so named for its resemblance to the Greek letter upsilon</note> downward and to the sides on both parts. Unless that action were entrusted to them, the position of the U-shaped bone would be entirely unstable. Add to this that a small nerve is attached to these muscles where they are joined to the shoulder blade <note>original: *scapulæ*</note>, but not at all where they are inserted into the U-shaped bone. Therefore, in my opinion, there are eight muscles formed solely for the purpose of the U-shaped bone—specifically so that it is not disturbed from its seat on either side, lest too weak a foundation be created for the tongue and for the larynx itself. Furthermore, the muscles which I said are *not* proper to this bone borrow their origin from it: of these, four extend to the larynx, and others to the tongue. The first two reaching the larynx are wide and fleshy; they arise from the lower seat of the U-shaped bone, and afterwards, being stretched toward the front part of the shield-shaped cartilage <note>original: *scutiformis cartilaginis*; the thyroid cartilage</note>, they are finally inserted across the lower seat of that cartilage. The other two are a little less than completely round and are slender; leading their beginning from the middle of the inner seat of the U-shaped bone, they are implanted into the root of the lid of the larynx <note>original: *laryngis operculi*; the epiglottis</note>. What the function of these four might be, and which of them Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the ancient authority whose anatomical works Vesalius frequently corrected through direct observation.</note> overlooked, will be taught in the description of the muscles of the larynx. The discussion of the muscles of the tongue, however, will be established shortly after the following chapter.

### U-SHAPED BONE. Chapter XVIII.
