<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C depicting a scholar in a room with a celestial globe and a window showing a landscape.</image-desc>
To conveniently manage the dissection of these muscles, you shall place a small block or an oblong stone under the neck (so that it is stretched out with the head hanging backward). Once the veins, arteries, and glands located in these distributions have been cut away as much as possible, you will begin the dissection with smaller knives. First, from the lower jaw—which is still intact (unless you have broken it for the sake of the muscle that pulls it down or the one that, hidden in the mouth, raises the jaw)—you will scrape away the oblique and wide muscles which were considered the third and fourth pairs, dissecting them down to the region where they are implanted into the U-shaped bone. Next, once the head of the first and second pairs has been freed from the breastbone <note>original: *pectoris osse*; the sternum</note>, lead both toward the bone, separating them from the muscles lying beneath them that extend from the breastbone into the shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx. For when you approach the origin of the first muscles of the U-shaped bone, you must take care not to damage the beginnings of the muscles that ascend from the breastbone and collarbone <note>original: *clauicula*</note> to the mammillary process <note>original: *mamillarem processum*; the mastoid process of the temporal bone</note> of the head; and do not accidentally remove the recently mentioned muscles of the shield-shaped cartilage <note>The thyrohyoid muscles.</note> which arise from that same seat. You will draw out the fifth and sixth pairs with your fingertips or a small knife from the neighboring parts, up to the stylus-like processes <note>original: *stylu referentes*; the styloid processes</note> of the head, and free their beginnings from there. It is hardly easy to approach the seventh and eighth pairs unless the second muscle of those moving the shoulder blade <note>The omohyoid muscle.</note> and the muscle seeking the mammillary process from the breastbone and collarbone have been cut away. Nevertheless, nothing prevents you from freeing them from the neighboring parts with a small, long wooden knife or with only your fingers; once their head is grasped, divide it from the shoulder blade with a knife. Although I believe these should sometimes be preserved until you approach the muscles moving the shoulder blade, so that—as I myself have tried more than once—you too may experience whether those muscles can drive the shoulder blade upward when it is entirely free of flesh; you may observe how beautifully they will be broken at the very first impulse of tension. The dissection of the muscles *not* proper to the U-shaped bone will be reserved for that place which deals with the anatomy of the parts into which they are inserted.

### Index of the three figures of the nineteenth chapter, and their characters.

*The FIRST figure shows the tongue, together with its own muscles, freed from the rest of the body, from the right side; it expresses, as closely as possible, the nature and position of the muscles of the right side.*

*The second figure presents the same things to the eyes as the first: but so that the nature of the first muscles of the tongue, and likewise the ninth, might be seen here in some way more clearly than in the first, we have reflected <note>turned back or folded</note> the third and seventh muscles of the tongue upward, while the fifth meanwhile hangs downward from its insertion.*

<margin>The size of the tongue is exactly right, and it requires muscles whose understanding is difficult.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'L' depicting several individuals engaged in an anatomical or scholarly activity, possibly a dissection or measurement.</image-desc>
THE MASS OF THE TONGUE fits the mouth exquisitely, for it reaches conveniently into every part of it; which would certainly be denied to it if it were smaller. Nor, on the other hand, is it hindered by the narrowness of the mouth—although this can easily happen if it ever grows to an unnatural size. Since, indeed, the Supreme <term>Artisan of things</term><note>original: "summus rerū Opifex"; a common Renaissance reference to God as the master creator.</note> willed that the tongue be moved promptly at our will wherever necessary, He chose for it to be muscular. It was worthwhile to grant it many muscles to serve as the authors of its various movements. However, it is extremely difficult to know which, what kind, and how many muscles move it; for they are so connected to one another, and their fibers join together so variously, that it is considered a hard task to know the correct number and shape of the muscles, and the different movements of the tongue. Indeed, I fear that the construction of the tongue has not yet been perfectly understood by anyone, nor will it be soon. Thus, we are forced to admit that our Creator's skill and industry in shaping Adam from the earth went so far that this whole structure cannot be fully discovered, no matter how long a time it is investigated, even by illustrious men. To what extent <term>Galen</term><note>A 2nd-century physician whose anatomical texts were the standard for over a millennium.</note> perceived the exceptional miracle and craftsmanship of Nature in the tongue's construction is not at all clear. For that part of his book *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de Administrandis sectionibus"</note>, in which he undoubtedly reviewed the muscles of the tongue, has been lost to us along with his books *On the Dissection of Muscles*. In his books *On the Use of the Parts*, he mentions the movement of the tongue only in passing and lightly, without a specific description of any muscle.

<margin>What rare thing occurs in the muscles of the tongue.</margin>
As far as I have been able to grasp, I observe that the tongue possesses something rare and peculiar compared to other muscles. At its root, where it is wide and broad and sits as if firmly fixed (so that it might be more ready for movement, ending in a blunt point where it appears thin), it possesses certain proper muscles that are somewhat distinct in their fibers. The ends of some of these terminate where the tongue begins to extend in length, <margin>Table 2, Figure, Chapter 21, L.</margin> forming a kind of angle with its root where the body of the tongue presents itself to block the <term>larynx</term><note>The structure at the top of the windpipe.</note> during the swallowing of food.

<margin>The third figure presents these almost in sequence with the letters K, K, L, L, I, I.</margin>
<margin>The part of the tongue visible before dissection, and what parts it consists of.</margin>
Others of these muscles do not stop here at all: but mixed together, they form a rare part of the body, namely the meeting of two oblong muscles, which for the most part acquire a very thin, membranous ligament in their middle, as wide as the thickness of the tongue. Thus, the entire body of the tongue as it appears to us before dissection is formed from those two muscular bodies, this ligament, the occurring veins, arteries, and nerves, and the two membranes covering all these. One membrane is common to all the muscles, which is the inner one; the other is considered part of that <term>tunic</term><note>A lining or covering layer.</note> which lines the entire cavity of the mouth and is the same and continuous with the inner tunic of the <term>rough artery</term><note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"; the trachea or windpipe.</note> and the <margin>Table 2, Figure, Chapter 2, Book 4, Y, Y.</margin> <term>stomach</term><note>In this context, referring to the esophagus or "gullet."</note>. Specifically, it claims for itself the primary portions of the third pair of cranial nerves, by whose benefit the tongue is made an organ of taste. Indeed, it is a rare and peculiar thing that these two muscular bodies possess...

### ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE] BODY

<margin>Chapter 11, Book 6, l, I.</margin>
...As we have said, the matter stands roughly in this manner. While the other muscles of the body possess almost a single type of fiber—either straight, oblique, or transverse—these bodies <note>The "bodies" of the tongue.</note> seem to me to have obtained oblique, transverse, and straight fibers all at once. These are so joined and mixed with one another that it is nearly impossible to follow any one type of fiber through dissection. Indeed, these muscular bodies acquire something not unlike the substance of the heart in that mixture of opposing fibers, although they do not consist of a substance as solid as the heart. In fatter and older animals, the fleshy fibers possess a certain amount of fat grown into the tongue, which expresses something spongy and fungous; furthermore, the fibers in the tongue are much less densely packed than in the very compact substance of the heart. These facts become clear to anyone even while eating: namely, how much the part of the tongue which we consider a delicacy differs in nature, form, and taste from the flesh of common muscles. But from which muscles it is formed, and where the muscles of the tongue—which I have observed during dissection—take their origin, will now be opportunely set forth.

<margin>
The first two among the obvious muscles of the tongue.
d 1, 2 figure D, D.
e figure of chapter 13, book 1; but especially figure D and figure C.
</margin>
There are two straight and immensely thick muscles, which are indistinctly separated from each other in several places as if there were more than two. These take their beginning from the middle and upper seat of the **bone resembling the letter $v$** <term>hyoid bone</term><note>The hyoid bone at the base of the tongue is often described by early anatomists as being shaped like the Greek letter upsilon (υ).</note>. They are fleshy, yet somewhat spongy, and extended along the length of the tongue, they are inserted into its middle; when contracted, they pull the tongue straight inward and toward the back.

<margin>
The third and fourth.
f 1, 2 figure E.
g 1, 2 figure chapter 13, book 1, K.
h of the same figures E, F.
</margin>
The third and fourth muscles arise from the two upper small bones of the $v$-shaped bone, which we said are found at its sides, and whose ends terminate at the processes of the head that imitate **styli** <term>styloid processes</term><note>Pointed projections of bone, named after the 'stylus' or writing needle.</note>. However, these muscles sometimes take their beginning from the lower sides of that bone, which is bound to the upper processes of the **shield-shaped cartilage** <term>thyroid cartilage</term>. This occurs specifically when the upper sides of the bone are not entirely bony but share something in common with the nature of ligaments, which is observed most often in women. These muscles, having taken their origin from there and proceeding somewhat obliquely, are implanted into the sides of the tongue. If one of these is contracted while the other is relaxed and loosened, the tongue (especially at its root) is pulled downward to the side; but if both act together, the tongue—inclining to neither side—is also moved downward toward the interior.

<margin>
The fifth and sixth.
i 1, 2 figure F.
k 3, 4, 5 figure chapter 6, book 1.
l 1, 2 figure E.
The seventh and eighth.
m 1, 2 figure G.
n 1, 2 figure D, D.
</margin>
The fifth and sixth muscles, similarly fleshy and quite thick, are positioned opposite the two just mentioned. Having branched off from the processes of the temporal bones—which resemble the image of a **stylus and a needle** <note>The styloid processes.</note>—they grow into the tongue at the ends of the muscles just described. Whenever both are pulled together, they move the tongue upward toward the interior; but if only one is contracted, the tongue is drawn upward and inclined to the other side. There are also two others, drawing the tongue to the lower parts and involving the sides. These arise from the sides of the lower jaw, inside at the root of the molar teeth on both sides, with a wide and somewhat mucous beginning. They insert themselves into the tongue along its length, up to the end of the ligament by which the tongue is bound to the throat—not exactly into the middle of the tongue, but into the sides of the two muscles we listed first. When only one of these contracts its fibers, the part of the tongue visible before dissection collapses toward the side of the contracted muscle; but when both are working, the tongue is persistently driven toward the throat in a straight motion.

<margin>
The ninth.
o 1, 2 figure H.
p 2 figure chapter 10, book 1 H.
</margin>
After these, a certain fleshy mass arises from the inner seat of the lower jaw in the region of the chin, especially from those small processes and their sides which protrude unevenly in the internal seat of the lower jaw at the top of the chin. The present mass, drawn upward and backward toward the throat, effects a wide insertion into the root of the tongue, just as it also takes its origin from a broad beginning. This mass seems to contract the tongue toward the chin—now precisely toward the middle of the lips, now toward the side, depending on whether it [moves] these...

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

<margin>
q 1. figure K, L, L, L.
r 1. figure I, I.
The muscular substance of the part of the tongue visible before dissection.
</margin>
...or loosens and tightens those fibers: for its fibers, along its entire breadth, are led straight backward from the front seat. Next, this muscle, besides fibers, also possesses certain straight-running inscriptions <note original="inscriptiones">These are tendinous intersections or lines of connective tissue within the muscle that Vesalius suggests might make one muscle appear to be several.</note>, as if on their account it should be considered multiple muscles in number. We see the muscles already described—which have fat spread around them everywhere—reaching toward the tongue during dissection, and many of these are confused with one another near their ends, forming two muscular "bodies" of the tongue. These bodies possess three types of fibers so confused and mixed together that it is extremely difficult to distinguish between them. Nevertheless, many oblique and transverse fibers of all the others are found in the middle of these bodies. These fibers seem to me to terminate on both sides into the tongue's own ligament <note>The septum of the tongue.</note>, which is very thin and not unlike a membrane. This acts as their support; in humans, dogs, and apes, it is arranged differently than in oxen and sheep. Fewer straight fibers present themselves, almost all of them running along the outer surface of those muscular bodies. By the benefit of the transverse fibers, I believe the body of the tongue visible before dissection can contract, thicken, and again extend and thin itself: for the insertion of the fibers into the ligament will demonstrate this to you as you dissect. With the straight fibers, however, the tongue is seen to roll into a semicircle toward the palate and the throat <note original="fauces">The opening at the back of the mouth leading to the throat.</note>, depending on whether the upper or lower fibers have been gathered. Furthermore, I conjecture that the tongue is moved to the sides by the oblique fibers—in such a way, certainly, that some muscles move the root of the tongue, while others move the body of the tongue visible in the gaping mouth before preparation. The ligament, truly, to which the fibers are fastened, is given in place of a bone for the tongue. For it would not have been fitting for a bone or cartilage to grow within the tongue along its length—even if divided into small vertebrae—since the tongue must be moved with such various and diverse motions during chewing and speaking, and meanwhile it supports no other body, and must be more agile and fluid than any serpent.

<margin>
s 2. chapter 2. book 7, then g.
The ligament binding the tongue to the throat.
</margin>
And these things I hand down just as they occurred to me; I would gladly share anything more well-known or truer if it offered itself to me. Furthermore, I purposefully defer the nerves—principally from the seventh pair of cranial nerves and from the sixth <note>In Vesalius's system, the "seventh pair" included the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, while the "sixth" referred to the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves. Modern anatomy uses a different numbering system.</note>, which provide the source of motion to the muscles of the tongue—to the fourth book, just as I do with the other nerves. Therefore, very few things remain to be reviewed here, except for the ligament binding the tongue to the throat. This is what is seen under the tongue when it is folded back toward the palate with the mouth open; it was formed for the sake of great utility. For if that ligament were not there, the tongue might sometimes be gathered too far back into itself, and once thrust out, it would not be easily drawn back in. Moreover, it would not possess a stable and safe seat, as it would be detached on all sides. We experience from the works of the [medical] art that the ligament performs both duties, whenever we cut it <note>Vesalius refers to "tongue-tie" surgery (frenotomy).</note> or dry it out when it is loose due to excessive moisture.

THE dissection of the MUSCLES of the tongue will be shared with the dissection of the muscles in the mouth mentioned so far. Therefore, after drawing down both jaws as much as possible, and after the tunic of the mouth <note>The mucous membrane.</note> has been pulled away from the underlying organs with a scalpel as precisely as possible (in the manner of skin), the oblique muscles will be dissected first. The beginning of these, which comes from the processes imitating a stylus <term>styloid processes</term>, must be freed. Now, having zealously followed these to the root of the tongue, you will free that fleshy mass, which I reviewed in the ninth place, from the lower jaw: and as accurately as you can, you will observe its inscriptions and the things mixed into it...

<margin>
The dissection of the rest of the body of the tongue.
</margin>
<margin>
g Figure 8, chapter 19, letters l, l.
</margin>
For the rest, I advise approaching the remaining body of the tongue in this manner. Before all else, the thicker membrane surrounding it, which is common to the whole mouth, should be scraped off: for it is more firmly grown together than can be removed from the tongue like skin <note original="citra coctionem">without boiling</note> <note>Vesalius suggests the tongue's surface is so tough that, unlike skin, it cannot be easily peeled off unless it were cooked.</note>. Then, leaving aside that membrane which is common to all muscles—and which you would strive in vain to separate—a cut should be led to the middle of the tongue, over the <margin>g</margin> ligament we mentioned, and along the length of the tongue. This cut should not be merely superficial, but should penetrate all the way to the middle of the tongue, or even divide the whole. Soon, with hooks and knives, you will diligently investigate the nature of the fibers of the tongue’s body; and you will perceive how the fibers are joined to the ligament, and how they in turn vary and mix together.

# INDEX OF THE THIRTEEN FIGURES 
## of the Twenty-First Chapter, and of the Labels for the Same.

Since in the complete plates of the muscles, which were placed in order at the beginning of this book, all the muscles of the larynx could not be placed before the eyes, I thought it would not be out of place to exhibit the muscles of the larynx separately here at the start of this chapter with this abundance of figures.

The *first* figure expresses the front face of the <term>upsilon-shaped bone</term> <note>The hyoid bone, named for its resemblance to the Greek letter upsilon (υ).</note>, here stripped of all its own proper muscles, together with the front of the larynx and the trunk of the <term>rough artery</term> <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note> (which is located in the neck), with no muscle of the larynx yet cut away. Which muscles are visible here, the index of labels will clearly explain.

The second figure shows the same things as the first from the right side, although here we have not preserved such a large portion of the tracheal trunk (as doing so would have been useless); furthermore, we have also cut away the upper sides of the hyoid bone from this view.

The third figure corresponds entirely to the second, except that it shows from the posterior face the same things that the second shows from the side. However, here too, the upper sides of the hyoid bone are intentionally drawn, just as in the first figure.

The fourth presents the front seat of the larynx, with a portion of the trunk of the trachea, the hyoid bone now having been cut away, along with the muscles offered to the larynx by that bone and by the breastbone. Thus, of the common muscles of the larynx, the fifth and sixth are still preserved, as well as the muscles proper to the <term>lid of the larynx</term> <note>The epiglottis.</note>.

The fifth figure does not vary at all from the fourth in the order of the dissection, but offers the same things as the fourth, to be viewed elegantly from the left side.

The sixth expresses the larynx, freed from the rest of the tracheal trunk, from the posterior face, such that I have left behind no portion of the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: "stomachus." In this period, "stomachus" often referred to the esophagus or gullet leading to the stomach.</note> nor of any common muscle; meanwhile, however, none of the cartilages of the larynx have been moved from their place.

The seventh contains the larynx expressed from the right side, so that its lid is now cut away, along with the muscles connecting the second cartilage to the first. Then, the lower process of the first cartilage on this side has been freed from the second; and the first itself occurs bent forward and away from the second in such a way that the middle seat of the first cartilage is offered to be viewed bare in the posterior region.

The eighth differs from the seventh in this: that here we have cut away the straight muscles of those four which connect the third cartilage to the second, and the second cartilage itself appears more uncovered.

The ninth varies from the eighth because, besides the muscles recently mentioned, we have also removed the four oblique muscles of the four joining the third to the second, and then the two positioned at the base of the third cartilage, with only those muscles that tie the third to the first being preserved with those three cartilages.

The tenth provides a view from the front seat of the larynx, with the first cartilage now removed, and with only the muscles joining the third to the first appearing with the second and third.

We have drawn the eleventh, as well as the two following, for the sake of showing the <term>tongue or slit of the larynx</term> <note>The glottis.</note>. Thus the larynx is expressed here, free from the rest of the tracheal trunk and its common muscles; and this, with its lid still preserved, lies upon its posterior seat, showing the upper face.

The twelfth differs from the eleventh in that it contains the lower seat of the larynx drawn.

The thirteenth has this variation from the twelfth: it represents the slit, or <term>little tongue</term> <note>original: "lingulam." A reference to the glottis or the structures of the vocal apparatus.</note>, of the larynx as more constricted or closed. Otherwise, the index of labels will be as follows.

<margin>A</margin> In the first, second, and third figures, the hyoid bone, not yet entirely free from its membranes.

I described the three cartilages<gloss>a</gloss> of the larynx in the previous book, counting the third cartilage as one—even if<gloss>b</gloss> it is actually a pair—so that the established opinions of other professors of dissection would not be too much disturbed. Furthermore, I reported that upon these cartilages<gloss>c</gloss> rests a body similarly cartilaginous, but also possessing a fatty and membranous substance, which is called the *glottis* <note>original: γλωττίς</note>.<gloss>d</gloss> For I categorized the glottis as a certain body, or rather a seat of the larynx located in its middle, very similar to the reed or slit of the little tongues with which pipes are blown <note>Vesalius compares the glottis to the reed of a woodwind instrument like an oboe or flute</note>. Now, therefore, I shall follow with the muscles of the larynx. Since this organ is constructed from several cartilages so that it might be aptly closed and opened, and since it must be moved by voluntary motion for the sake of holding the breath and likewise for the voice, Nature rightly shared with it muscles as movers of the cartilages. Some of these are committed to the cartilages alone in both their origins and insertions, and for that reason are called the "proper" muscles of the larynx. Others, however, arising from other parts, are inserted into the cartilages of the larynx and into its lid <note>The epiglottis</note>, and are therefore generally called "common" muscles. <margin>There are twelve proper muscles of the larynx, and eight common ones.</margin> <margin>e A little later each will be noted separately.</margin> <gloss>e</gloss> The human larynx possesses twelve proper muscles; of these, four join the first cartilage to the second, four connect the third to the second, two couple the third to the first, and two have their seat at the base of the third cartilage. We count eight common muscles: six inserted into the first cartilage, and two into the lid of the larynx. Of what sort all these may be, I shall now follow in order, beginning my discourse with the proper ones. <margin>Proper muscles 1, 2, 3, 4.</margin> <margin>f Figures 1 and 4 show one marked N, the 5th figure shows the other marked O.</margin> Thus, of the four<gloss>f</gloss> joining the first to the second, two are held on each side at the lower parts of the larynx, in the front...

These four muscles turn the third cartilage backward toward the outside of the larynx, opening the little tongue <note>original: *lingulam*; refers here to the glottis or the opening of the airway.</note>, or, if you prefer, the larynx itself. And the first two, occupying the posterior seat of the second cartilage (which for their sake is hollowed out on both sides according to its length, and in the middle stands out like a sharp line or a kind of spine of the back), perform this with a straight motion. The remaining ones, however, as they are endowed with an oblique position, so too they pull the third cartilage backward obliquely. The ninth and tenth muscles, which couple the third cartilage to the first, are also broad and fleshy on both sides: they arise, continuous with each other, from the middle seat of the first cartilage, according to the entire length of its internal seat. The right one (understand the same for the left) shows a sort of triple origin, because of certain inscriptions so impressed upon it that by this occasion it seems to be a triple muscle, ascending obliquely upward from its beginning, and implanted into the front seat of the right part of the third cartilage. By these two very strong muscles, the third cartilage is drawn to the first, and by their benefit, the two parts of the third cartilage—with the muscles contracted—certainly draw together <note>original: *conniuent*; to blink or close together.</note>, and the little tongue itself is compressed chiefly by their help.

...is compressed. The eleventh and twelfth muscles consist in the base of the third cartilage <note>The arytenoid cartilages, which sit atop the back of the cricoid.</note>, in that region where<sup>y</sup> the larynx is joined to the esophagus <note>original: *stomachus*; in this period, the term often referred to the esophagus or gullet</note>, and the third cartilage is articulated with the second <note>The cricoid cartilage</note>. There is one of these on each side, taking their beginning from the root of the third cartilage where it is closest to the first <note>The thyroid cartilage</note>; stretching slightly upward along the base of the third cartilage, they finish at the middle of the third cartilage (where its two parts are bound together), meeting each other there. These muscles are short and appear somewhat round on the outside like a pear, but inside they are grown onto the third cartilage at every part. Where they meet each other, they are wider and thicker than at their origin. Both muscles, by constricting the base of the third cartilage and compressing the two parts of that cartilage together, close and narrow the little tongue <note>original: *lingulam*; referring here to the glottis or the opening of the airway</note>. Together, they serve as proof that the third cartilage is necessarily double; for if it were a single piece, it could not be constricted by those muscles, nor could it have been closed by the<sup>z</sup> two muscles joining the third cartilage to the first, nor opened by the<sup>a</sup> four muscles connecting the third to the second.

Therefore, out of the twelve proper muscles of the larynx, eight narrow the larynx—namely, the four connecting the first cartilage to the second, the two joining the third to the first, and finally the two placed at the base of the third cartilage. Four, however, unseal or open it: specifically, those which join the third cartilage to the second. Other muscles as well, which we call "common," are in a way the leaders of both movements, through which the respiratory passage or "little tongue" is widened and compressed.

The first two of these,<sup>b</sup> one on each side, take their beginning from almost the entire lower seat of the U-shaped bone <note>original: *ossis υ referentis*; the hyoid bone, named for its resemblance to the Greek letter upsilon</note>. They are seen to be broad and fleshy, and close and contiguous to each other at their inner sides. Stretching downward from here and moving away from each other at their inner sides, they are each implanted into the lower seat of the first cartilage <note>the thyroid</note> on their respective sides, with a width equal to the width of their origins. In their entire descent, where they extend over the front part of the first cartilage, they are attached only by fibrous connections, in the same way that muscles resting upon one another are usually joined.

These take their origin from the inner region of the breastbone <note>the sternum</note> at the throat with fleshy but narrow beginnings. Stretching upward along the front of the rough artery <note>original: *asperæ arteriæ*; the trachea</note> and gradually becoming wider, they are inserted into that seat of the first cartilage we mentioned.<sup>f</sup>

The fifth and sixth common muscles of the larynx are transverse, and there is one<sup>g</sup> on each side embracing the esophagus. They take their beginning from the back part of the esophagus facing the vertebrae of the neck, along the length of the esophagus, so continuous with each other that the origin of both muscles appears to be one and the same. From there, being large and fleshy, they stretch transversely toward the front and are implanted into the sides of the first cartilage along the length of those sides; they are heavily grown onto and continuous with the esophagus for the entire breadth where they touch it.

These pull the sides of the first cartilage toward the back, applying it to the second cartilage in such a way that they also narrow the larynx or "little tongue." Those, however, which proceed from the U-shaped bone [hyoid], by pulling the first cartilage upward and away from the back parts, dilate the larynx. But the muscles inserted into the first cartilage from the breastbone [sternum] achieve the opposite function: for they contract the lower parts of the first cartilage and pull them downward, at the same time<sup>h</sup> somewhat contracting and tightening the rough artery [trachea], so that when a person produces a voice, the artery is not doubled back on itself nor dilated too excessively.

# BOOK II ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>k Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, letter L.</margin> ...planted at the base of the bone shaped like the letter U <note>the hyoid bone; original: *os υ referens*</note> and inserted into the root of the lid of the larynx <note>the epiglottis; original: *operculum*</note><sup>k</sup>. I believe these were unknown to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose work Vesalius was often correcting through direct observation</note>, as he does not mention them in any of his surviving works. They should not be dismissed (as someone might perhaps think) as part of Galen's count of the common muscles of the larynx. Although he said <margin>Book 7, On the Use of the Parts.</margin> there were eight of these, he only described six, and later added in his discussion that all eight are attached to the first cartilage <note>the thyroid cartilage</note>. These two muscles are entrusted with the task of raising the lid of the larynx again after it has been pressed down by food and drink. For when their origins are pulled toward <margin>Figures 1, 2, 3, letter A.</margin> the hyoid bone, that lid is raised. However, I have observed no muscles that perform the opposite task. Nor is this surprising, since food and drink easily compress the lid of the larynx when it has been turned over and raised, and the lid itself, being heavy by its own mass, is promptly applied to the larynx. It is not only these muscles that lack opposites, but also<sup>m</sup> those <margin>m In figure B and C of chapter 51, the muscles of the intestine are noted; in figure 5, the testes.</margin> by whose benefit we pull the rectum and the testes upward. For bodies that by their own nature tend downward more than enough do not require a specific movement for the downward path; they have the least need for their own muscles for that action. The larynx possesses no rare or peculiar ligament at all <margin>Ligaments of the larynx.</margin> except for the membranes that surround the joints in a circular fashion; thus, there is no reason for us to describe them separately. And if the larynx happens to claim anything of its own because of the membrane with which it is lined or girded, that belongs to the <margin>n Seen in figures 11, 12, 13.</margin> history of the tongue.

### THE PROCEDURE FOR DISSECTING THE MUSCLES OF THE LARYNX. Chapter XXII.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'F' depicting two putti in a landscape; one is seated on the ground while the other stands nearby, amidst grass and distant trees.</image-desc>

<margin>a Table 4, letters S, T, R, Q, V, V. b Table 5, letter O.</margin> YOU SHOULD approach the structure of the larynx first in an ox, if it seems right, and then, having been restored by the exercise, in a human. Therefore, once the muscles proper to the hyoid bone<sup>a</sup> have been managed in the sequence of the dissection, two muscles will immediately appear<sup>b</sup> <margin>Procedure for the first and second common muscles.</margin> proceeding from that bone to the first cartilage <note>the thyroid cartilage</note>. Freeing their origins from the bone with a small knife, and gradually scraping the muscles away from the cartilage, you will lead them all the way to their insertion. By the same method,<sup>c</sup> you will first separate the muscles led from the breastbone <note>the sternum</note> to the first cartilage <margin>c Table 5, letter P.</margin> <margin>Third and fourth common muscles.</margin> from the bone; and afterward, lightly pulling them away from the windpipe <note>original: *aspersa arteria*; literally 'rough artery'</note>, you will follow them to the first cartilage where they are inserted. Having carefully inspected these four, you will lead the cut through the membrane of the palate and the inner parts of the throat, and you will remove the larynx with the gullet <note>original: *stomachus*; in this period, the term usually refers to the esophagus</note> from the throat, in exactly the same way that butchers are accustomed to cut out the larynges of oxen. Once the larynx is freed and cut away from the body along with a portion of the windpipe and the gullet, hand it to a companion to hold; and <margin>d Figures 2, 3, 5 of chapter 21, letter I.</margin> soon you will inspect<sup>d</sup> the muscles <margin>Fifth and sixth common muscles.</margin> led from the back part of the gullet to the sides of the first cartilage. To do this more quickly, divide them with a long cut where their heads touch each other; and having grasped the head of one with a hook or the tips of your fingers, carefully separate the whole thing from the gullet all the way to the sides of the first cartilage. You may now learn the action of these six muscles common to the larynx, provided you pull their heads back and forth toward their origins. Once this is done, <margin>e Figures 2, 3, 4 of chapter 21, letter K.</margin> you will immediately free them all from the first cartilage and turn the dissection to<sup>e</sup> the two which were said to be implanted at the root <margin>The two muscles of the larynx lid.</margin> <margin>f Figure 1 of chapter 19, letter C.</margin> of the larynx lid. For soon the ends of those muscles will be ready...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

Once you have drawn the muscles away by separating them, you will dissect them from the bone. To learn their function, you should press down the lid of the larynx <note>the epiglottis; original: *laryngis operculum*</note> with your finger: as their heads are pulled back toward the <margin>u</margin> U-shaped bone <note>the hyoid bone; original: *os υ referens*</note>, you will see the lid flip back, stretch forward, and be raised. Now, you may also entirely remove these muscles, the esophagus <note>original: *stomachum*; in this period, this often refers to the gullet/esophagus leading to the stomach</note>, and even the lid itself from the larynx, so that the three cartilages of the larynx are left alone with their twelve intrinsic muscles. However, when you cut away the remaining part of the windpipe <note>original: *asperae arteriae*</note> from the second cartilage <note>the cricoid cartilage</note>, examine the <margin>Human glands, in whose place there are muscles in oxen.</margin> glands <margin>g 27 p, 4, 5 fig. cap. 21 M.</margin> attached to the human larynx, which are somewhat fleshy, as I shall describe in the sixth book. In the ox, however, you will find a completely fleshy substance in place of these, located at the sides of the second cartilage; it resembles a muscle, and in the ox, it could be considered the seventh and eighth of the common muscles of the larynx. Meanwhile, in place of that substance or those muscles, the human possesses large and prominent glands, as I have just mentioned.

Furthermore, it is now time for you to look precisely <margin>h as can be seen in the 11th, 12th, and 13th figures of chapter 21.</margin> at the shape of the "little tongue" <note>the glottis/vocal folds; original: *linguula*</note> or <margin>How the little slit or tongue of the larynx is to be viewed.</margin> slit <note>original: *rimae*</note>. You will see that the larynx is wide in its upper and lower parts, but in the middle, it has an oblong slit, formed from the substance we explained in the first book. To stretch and open this with your own hands before you begin the dissection of the muscles, grasp the sides of the larynx with the thumb and middle finger of your right hand, while your index finger is inserted into the inner space of the third cartilage <note>the arytenoid cartilages</note>. Then, place the thumb and index finger of your left hand into the lower opening of the larynx, and with those two fingers of the left hand, try to pull the second cartilage <note>cricoid</note> away from the first <note>the thyroid cartilage, or "shield-shaped" cartilage</note>, while with the index finger of the right hand, you turn the third cartilage outward. In this way, you will see most clearly how the "little tongue" <note>glottis</note> is opened. If, however, you pull the second toward the first with your left hand, and with the thumb and index finger of your right hand you push the third cartilage toward the interior and make its two parts blink together <note>close against each other</note>, you will see the little tongue closed perfectly.

I write these things at some length so that Galen <note>The Greek physician whose 1,300-year-old authority Vesalius was challenging through direct observation</note> may finally be understood. Let those who profess themselves "Galenists" today no longer contend that the lid of the larynx <note>epiglottis</note> is the primary organ of the voice. Nor should they believe that the same body is both the glottis <note>original: *γλωττίδα*</note> (or little tongue) and the epiglottis <note>original: *ἐπιγλωττίδα*</note> (which we call the lid of the larynx). They are truly ignorant of the fact that the little tongue is in the middle of the larynx, and is very much like the reeds of the pipes <note>original: *tibiarum linguis*; referring to the vibrating reeds of woodwind instruments like the aulos</note> through which they are blown.

Therefore, when you have closed and opened the little tongue with your hands as you see fit, you will dissect the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, <margin>The management of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th intrinsic muscles.</margin> starting with the <margin>i Ch. 21, fig. 4 N, then fig. 5 o.</margin> four that connect the second cartilage to the first. With a light and transverse cut, you will free the outer muscle from the first cartilage, taking care not to wound the inner one at the same time. Once this is removed, scrape the inner one similarly from the second cartilage, paying attention to that intersection of fibers I mentioned. You should not only investigate precisely whether there are one or two muscles here, but also, while you free the esophagus from the larynx, you should carefully consider whether <margin>k Fig. of chapter 21 inserted at C, D.</margin> you will find those muscles which I said are sometimes observed, which are inserted from the spine of the second cartilage into the lower processes of the first cartilage. 

When the four muscles joining the second cartilage to the first have been cut away from the larynx, you will free the lower process of the first cartilage from the second <margin>l as in Table 8, figures 8 and 9 of chapter 21.</margin> on one side of the larynx. In this way, you will reflect the first cartilage forward away from the second, <margin>m 7, 8, 9, 11 fig. ch. 21 a, b.</margin> in order to inspect the <margin>Intrinsic muscles 9 and 10.</margin> two muscles that bind the third cartilage to the first. When you have examined these, you will be free to remove the first cartilage from the other two with a sharper knife—or, if you prefer, keep it hanging by the two muscles that connect the third to it—and <margin>Intrinsic muscles 5, 6, 7 and 8.</margin> afterwards turn your attention to the <margin>n 7 fig. ch. 21 P, R.</margin> four muscles connecting the third to the second. You may free these from their origins on the second cartilage and trace them to the third, where they are <margin>Intrinsic muscles 11 and 12.</margin> inserted. Finally, <margin>o 7, 8 fig. ch. 21 V.</margin> you will remove those which are at the base of the third cartilage, si-

## ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE ARM.
### Chapter XXIII.

<margin>A different order for proximity than for dissection.</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'V' featuring two children (putti) in an outdoor setting; one child is seated and holding a staff, while the other stands nearby amidst foliage and trees.</image-desc>
The order of proximity indeed would indicate that, before the muscles moving the arm, those leading the movements of the head, the back, and the scapula <note>the shoulder blade</note> ought to have been described—if, that is, the intent were to proceed to the parts nearest to those already narrated. However, since the muscles moving the scapula cannot be managed while the muscles moving the arm are still intact, and since it is even less possible to dissect the head or back if those have not yet been removed, I decided it would be worthwhile to follow the muscles of the arm and then those of the scapula before the muscles moving the head. I do this for the sake of the dissection itself, following the occasion of Galen's order in the fourth and fifth books of *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: *de Administrandis sectionibus*</note>. <margin>How many movements of the arm.</margin> The arm is moved forward toward the breast, backward toward the back, upward toward the neck and head, and downward toward the sides of the thorax. In addition to these movements, in whatever position the arm is placed, it is also driven in a sort of circle, turning around as if you were to take a staff in both hands—not bent, but placed against each other along their length—and then, by moving your hands alternately forward and backward, you rolled the staff. Thus, it is established that the arm is driven by three kinds of movements.

<margin>The first of those moving the arm.</margin> <margin>d 2,3,4 td. Δ, 1 tab. L. b 3 tab. d K to R. c 3 ta. from R toward s. d 3 tab. d K to L.</margin> A single muscle brings the arm toward the breast <note>the pectoralis major</note>, taking its origin from the middle of the width of the breastbone <note>the sternum; original: *pectoris ossis*</note> and the cartilages inserted into it. Then, it also originates specifically from the cartilages of the seventh and eighth ribs, and from the middle of the collarbone <note>the clavicle; original: *clauiculæ*</note> where it faces the breastbone. The part of the origin proceeding from the collarbone appears entirely fleshy; however, the part that arises from the middle of the breastbone along the right and left sides—and is contiguous with the beginning of the muscle on the other side—is seen to be more nervous, more membranous, and less thick. Yet, the portion that arises from the side of the breastbone and the cartilages articulated to it is already quite fleshy. The part which arises specifically from the cartilages of the seventh and eighth ribs, near the pointed cartilage <note>the xiphoid process; original: *mucronatam cartilaginem*</note>, is seen to be a membrane and thin for some distance. 

The muscle proceeding from these sites becomes gradually thicker and fleshier, and is slowly narrowed. It proceeds to a point <margin>e 3 ta. Q. 4 tab. Q. Γ in the arm. f next to f, e fig. 1 ch. 2, book 1. g Here are the ribs 3rd table muscle Δ with 4th table.</margin> until it is implanted into the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, or the bone of the arm, along its length by a broad, nervous, and very robust but short tendon. This insertion is below the neck of the head of the humerus, in its inner region, though turning somewhat toward the front. The fibers of this muscle vary among themselves: and a little before the production of the tendon—while still in the fleshy part of the muscle—and then along the entire width of the tendon, they cross one another in a decussation <note>an X-shaped crossing</note>. For those fibers which arise from the collarbone and the middle of the length of the breastbone adjacent to the collarbone, proceeding obliquely from the upper parts downward and outward, form the upper part of the tendon along its entire width; they remain fleshy throughout their course, except at the insertion of the muscle into the humerus. But those fibers which borrow their origin from the rest of the breastbone, and specifically from the cartilages of the seventh and eighth ribs, stretched obliquely upward, constitute the lower part of the tendon according to its width; and they lose the flesh by which they are filled and supported sooner than the upper ones do.

For higher up, toward the insertion point, the muscle retains its fleshy nature; lower down, however, long before the insertion, it appears leaden and sinewy <note>original: *nerveus*, often used by Vesalius to describe the appearance of tendons</note>. This is undoubtedly because the upper fibers have a shorter path. Indeed, we have said it is common to all muscles that they are granted a shorter tendon when they are carried along a more direct path, according to the reason for their motion. Furthermore, when I speak of "upper" and "lower" in the tendon, I do not mean those that approach closer to the head of the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note> or recline further from it; rather, I am referring these differences of position to the insertion of the tendon, which is completed along its width, just as if you were to call this piece of paper "higher" or "anterior" than the one placed beneath it. Thus, this muscle is in a way five-sided, but formed with unequal edges.

For if its upper fibers, drawn from the clavicle and the upper part of the chest, are contracted, the arm is pulled toward the upper chest and the clavicle. But if the lower fibers are strained, this muscle becomes the agent of pulling the arm lower toward the chest, since it is then carried toward the ^k sword-shaped cartilage of the chest and the false ribs. But if both sets of fibers, and especially the middle ones, are at work, they will drive the arm toward the chest without inclining it to either side. Since this muscle obtains an ample origin arising from various bones, and has fibers that cross each other and are drawn in opposite series, and even achieves different movements, there might perhaps be nothing to stop one from declaring it a double muscle and counting it as two muscles, as some leaders of dissection <note>previous anatomical authorities</note> do—though it will be treated by me as only one throughout the context of this discourse. Since the lower part of the muscle, which produces the lower fibers, brings the arm to the chest toward the lower parts, it has also deservedly become smaller and thinner in its deep section than the upper part, which acts upward and to which a more vigorous and powerful function is entrusted.

Consequently, neither the insertion of this muscle nor its path comes into view unless that great muscle is completely lifted away; this is a point that must be observed with care so that you may understand Galen. For unless you recognize that this muscle of Galen's is so hidden in its progress, and stands out only slightly at its membranous beginning, the fifth book of his *On Anatomical Procedures* will immediately seem entirely erroneous and very difficult at the very outset, since he incorrectly reported that it was stretched out beneath the skin across the surface of other muscles, and even across the surface of the one we said draws the arm to the chest.

Besides this one, Galen describes^q another muscle, which he believes is the author of the higher movement of the arm toward the chest. This one certainly did not escape my notice in humans: yet it by no means moves the arm toward the higher parts of the chest as Galen asserts. Rather, it was created for the sake of the scapula <note>the shoulder blade</note>, namely so that it might draw it toward the chest; both its origin and path, and the^r insertion of its tendon, demonstrate this clearer than light. For it takes its beginning beneath the muscle that I reported brings the arm to the chest, and is entirely spread out under it. It arises with a fleshy beginning^s from the second, third, fourth, and fifth—and sometimes (though very rarely) the sixth—upper ribs^t of the thorax. It does not arise (even though Galen more than once affirms otherwise) where the ribs are joined to the breastbone <note>the sternum</note> or from the breastbone itself, but rather before the bones of the ribs begin to end in the cartilage that articulates with the breastbone. Nor does it arise in a perfectly straight path or a straight line, but proceeds as if with certain fingers arising further out from the bones of the ribs. From here, stretched toward the outer parts, it is made narrower and thicker until^u it ends at the joint of the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note> with the scapula in a broad and sinewy tendon mixed with flesh. By this, it is implanted into the inner side of the process that resembles an anchor <note>the coracoid process of the shoulder blade</note>, becoming more sinewy there, where that process sends out a more sinewy part of the inner head from its own attachment^x—that is, the part of the muscle which we shall count among the anterior flexors of the elbow^y <note>referring to the coracobrachialis or the short head of the biceps</note>. However, in humans, this tendon by no means touches the ligament of the joint, as it certainly does (though still somewhat obscurely) in tailed apes, in whom the anchor-like process protrudes only slightly. Furthermore, you will find no region of the scapula vacant, besides this process, to which that tendon could be conveniently implanted. In addition, if you weigh the fabric of this muscle with precision, you will undoubtedly maintain that it was brought forth chiefly for the sake of its own insertion.

Therefore, I consider there to be <sup>d</sup> one muscle that is the author of all adductions of the arm toward the chest: and I also <sup>e</sup> establish that there is one that raises the arm toward the upper parts. Furthermore, this muscle is fleshy, having various but continuous origins, and formed as if from different muscles (if you observe its broad origin and various inscriptions). <sup>f</sup> For it takes its origin from the middle part of the clavicle along its length facing the scapula, adjacent to the muscle that brings the arm to the chest; then it proceeds from the upper process of the scapula, or the top of the shoulder <note>the acromion</note>, where it joins the clavicle, and also from the entire spine of the scapula. It emerges in a continuous line <sup>g</sup> and with a nervous <note>In 16th-century anatomy, "nervous" often refers to sinewy or tendinous tissue</note> beginning, which, barely having emerged, immediately becomes fleshy, quite thick, and bulging. Soon, remaining fleshy from its beginning, <sup>h</sup> it stretches into a narrow point, like the vertex of a triangle, until it is <sup>m</sup> inserted into the width of the humerus bone by a broad tendon, composed of a mixture of flesh and nervous substance, and strong, not far below the neck of the bone. Its insertion, <sup>i</sup> which is more sinewy on the inside than the outside, is not performed exactly transversely; rather, it is slightly oblique from the front, turning somewhat downward toward the back. It is anything but sloping or straight (although Galen <sup>k</sup> attests otherwise), who attributes to it the same form of insertion as the <sup>l</sup> muscle that brings the arm to the chest, which we said is performed straight and along the length of the humerus. Thus, the whole muscle, if one looks at it in passing, presents the image of a triangle: and therefore, from its similarity [to the letter Delta], the Greeks called it <term>Deltoid</term> <note>original: Δελτοειδῆ; meaning triangle-shaped</note>. Likewise, because it is spread over the joint of the shoulder at the scapula, which they called <term>Omos</term> <note>original: ὤμον</note>, and covers it in a certain way, they named the same muscle <term>Epomis</term> <note>original: ἐπωμίδα; meaning "upon the shoulder"</note>. I, however, throughout the context of my discourse, shall call it the muscle raising the arm, or the <sup>n</sup> second of the muscles <sup>p</sup> moving the arm. Moreover, the sides describing this muscle are as follows. <sup>o</sup>

The first side extends from the middle length of the clavicle to the top of the shoulder, and from here along the spine of the scapula, all the way to its base. The second side is drawn from the clavicle obliquely downward to the internal side of the insertion. The third side extends from the base of the scapula, where its spine begins to protrude, to the external side of the insertion, obliquely downward and forward. Furthermore, the ancient Greeks seem to have likened the origin of the present muscle to the vertex of a triangle, which the muscle hardly shows until it is freed from its origin on all sides and placed on a flat surface. For then the part of the origin which is closest to the muscle bringing the arm to the chest, and then that which is held at the base of the scapula, both project and rise more than that part of the origin which hangs from the top of the shoulder, expressing as it were a very obtuse vertex of a triangle. Its fibers vary among themselves in no other way than that the anterior ones, belonging to the clavicle, are carried obliquely downward toward the back; while the posterior ones, hanging from the spine of the scapula, descend obliquely toward the front. ...in the manner of one bringing the arm toward the chest, they intersect in a cross-shape; although, because of certain lines drawn obliquely, the fibers appear to be slightly intertwined. If, therefore, that part of the muscle taking its origin from the collarbone <note>the clavicle</note> is contracted, the arm is lifted upward toward the front of the neck and the face. But if the fibers originating from the top of the shoulder <note>the acromion</note> and the seat where it joins the collarbone are contracted, the arm rises straight up, leaning to neither side. Yet if the rear part of the muscle, proceeding from the spine of the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note>, is bunched together, the arm turns toward the back of the neck and the back of the head itself. The beginnings of this muscle do not arise from the entire breadth of those bones we have mentioned, but only along a thicker line from their most prominent parts, so that the starting point appears quite thin. Nor should this be entirely overlooked: for besides this muscle, which lifts the arm by its own motion, there is no other, nor does the arm require another to perform the same duty. Although I am not unaware that <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the ancient authority whose anatomical works Vesalius frequently corrected</note> describes certain others here, he does so with such little truth that he is inconsistent with himself in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of Parts* and the fifth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*; if I were to follow all his points, the present chapter would grow to excessive length. I will add, however, that the form of the muscle lifting the arm in <term>monkeys</term> <note>Latin: *cercopithecis*; Vesalius often points out that Galen's errors stemmed from dissecting monkeys rather than humans</note> is exactly the same as in humans. But dogs, horses, and oxen vary from the human construction in this joint, not only in the bones but especially in the muscles and ligaments.

<sup>p</sup> The muscle driving the arm straight toward the back <note>the teres major</note> is fleshy and thick, and compared to the other muscles of this joint, it is somewhat rounded. It arises with a fleshy beginning from the lower angle of the <sup>q</sup> base of the shoulder blade, taking a small part of its origin from the base, but a significant portion from the lower border <note>Latin: *costa*, literally "rib," but here referring to the lateral border of the scapula</note> of the shoulder blade. Indeed, it grows from a continuous and fleshy origin from the middle of the length of that border near the base, and from the outer <sup>r</sup> rounded part of the lower angle of the base. Near the middle of the length of the lower border, this muscle departs from the bone of the shoulder blade: and being stretched slightly upward toward the front and approaching the upper arm bone <note>humerus</note>, it ends in a strong and short, but wide tendon. This tendon corresponds in its form (referring to its width, thickness, and insertion) <sup>s</sup> to that of the muscle which moves the arm toward the chest <note>the pectoralis major</note>; indeed, these two muscles are implanted in almost the same region, leaving a space between them into which the <sup>t</sup> tendon of the muscle is inserted which moves the arm backward toward the flanks, as I shall describe shortly. However, the tendon of the muscle arising from the lower border of the shoulder blade is implanted slightly closer to the head of the upper arm bone than the tendon of the muscle reported to drive the arm to the chest. Here again, it does not escape me that the present muscle is wrongly listed by Galen among those that rotate the arm, and that he <sup>u</sup> identifies the triangular muscle occupying the hump of the shoulder blade—which I must place in the class of those rotating the arm—as the author of the movement of the arm toward the back.

The arm is pulled downward by a <sup>x</sup> certain large and very broad muscle <note>the latissimus dorsi</note>, which takes its <sup>y</sup> beginning from the tips of the spines found from the spine of the sixth thoracic vertebra all the way to the middle of the sacrum; it is thin like a wide membrane, continuous, and directed in a straight line. But once it has passed over the muscles moving the back and reaches that region of the ribs which bulges most toward the rear, it becomes fleshy and dense. The entire muscle, increased in this way, proceeds into a <sup>z</sup> narrow shape until it inserts a broad and strong tendon into the upper arm bone, beneath its neck and along its length, in the middle between the <sup>a</sup> tendon of the muscle moving the arm to the chest and the <sup>b</sup> tendon which drives the arm backward toward the back. Thus, this muscle is also triangular, but it is formed with clearly unequal sides.

...edges <note>original: "costis"; here referring to the sides or borders of the muscle's triangular shape</note>. For it possesses two very long sides: one that extends along the length of the back; the other, which climbs upward from the sacred bone <note>the sacrum</note>, through the flanks <note>the ilia</note> and the lower part of the chest <note>the thorax</note>, to the insertion of the tendon, and constitutes the other wall of the hollow of the armpit <note>the axilla</note>. But the third side, much shorter than the others, is carried transversely from the spine of the sixth thoracic vertebra, over the angle of the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note> (which the lower part of its base reveals), to the insertion of the tendon. Due to the inequality of this triangle of sides, the fibers of the muscle also differ: those that stretch upward through the flanks and the ends of the false ribs <note>the ribs not attached to the breastbone</note> are the longest and least slanted; but those that arise from the spines of the lower vertebrae are shorter and creep forward more transversely. This muscle is the worker of the arm's downward motion; it performs this not by a single motion, but in various ways, according to the difference of the fibers. Since as the upper or lower fibers are gathered or contracted into themselves, the arm is depressed toward the back, moving downward, sometimes toward the higher parts and sometimes toward the lower. Furthermore, Galen left it written that this muscle, while it crosses the lower angle of the shoulder blade, 
<margin>
e: at the position Y in Table 10.
</margin>
is joined to the shoulder blade by certain fibers and grows onto it by some significant attachment. He then asserted not only that the arm is moved by this muscle, but even records that, by the benefit of this insertion, it is the author of the downward pulling of the shoulder blade. 

Truly, although I am very much afraid to go against the opinions of <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose anatomical errors Vesalius sought to correct through direct dissection</note>, and would gladly wish in this chapter to describe at least one muscle fully without controversy, I can by no means remain silent here, as the matter stands. For the present muscle, while it covers the lower angle of the base of the shoulder blade, is seen to be touching the bone of the shoulder blade only by the intervention of the muscles that arise from it. It is in no way grown onto the bone, nor is it joined or grown by any special insertion to the region of the muscles upon which it lies there. For it is connected to the muscles lying beneath it there in no different a way than it is to the muscles moving the back, the chest, and the abdomen, which lie under this muscle no less than those occupying the shoulder blade. Therefore, since this muscle effects no insertion into the shoulder blade, it by no means pulls it downward by its own motion along with the arm, as Galen supposed. And even if I were to grant him that in that entire area where it passes over the angle of the shoulder blade, it grows into it or is more strongly attached or bound in some way, that would be achieved only by the transverse fibers—those, I mean, which are held in the highest seat of its origin and depend from the spines of the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth thoracic vertebrae. These would certainly not move the shoulder blade downward, but straight toward the back. This Galen would easily have noticed if he had diligently observed the beginning of the present muscle. For although in the fifth book of *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "De Administrandis sectionibus"</note> he wrote in passing that this muscle takes its beginning from the spines of the vertebrae, especially where the false ribs

Galen enumerates another muscle, formed for nearly the same function as the one just mentioned—specifically, to draw the arm downward. He records that this muscle is indeed wide and broad, yet thin. He relates that the membrane which we call "fleshy" <note>original: "membranam... carnosam"; this refers to the *panniculus carnosus*, a layer of muscle attached to the skin that is prominent in many mammals but largely absent in humans</note> is increased by fleshy fibers as soon as it reaches the flanks. He teaches that these fibers, stretched upward, become fleshier until 
<margin>Table 3, figure g, f.</margin>
the membrane corresponds to the nature of a broad and thin muscle (similar to the one we said moves the cheeks <note>the buccinator muscle</note>) and is implanted into the shoulder <note>humerus</note>. Furthermore, Galen never stops boasting that this muscle remained hidden from all who preceded him and was discovered by him in monkeys. I have certainly observed it in monkeys, dogs, and many quadrupeds, though it is not equally broad or fleshy in all of them. But in the monkey (to speak of it specifically), it appeared to me in this manner: the fleshy membrane is born more firmly attached to the underlying organs along the entire length of the spine than elsewhere, just as if it drew a portion of its origin from the tips of the vertebrae—as if from bones or cartilages—in the manner of other ligaments. But in that area where the membrane sits opposite the five lumbar vertebrae and touches the hip bone <note>ilium</note>, it is augmented with fleshy but thin and sparse fibers. These fibers creep upward obliquely toward the armpit <note>axilla</note> and, being gradually gathered from a wide base into a narrow space, they form a broad but thin muscle which, ending in a point, 
<margin>Table 3 and 4, figure h, d.</margin>
is obscurely and with great difficulty implanted into the shoulder, continuous with the tendon of that muscle which we mentioned brings the arm to the chest <note>the pectoralis major</note>. In dogs, it shows no manifest insertion into the shoulder, and it seems to be mixed in some way with the tendon of the muscle bringing the arm to the chest, or rather it grows into the proper membrane of that muscle. In horses, oxen, sheep, and animals of that kind, it also becomes quite conspicuous. Therefore, I even advise that it be examined especially in the ox; this will be done most readily if you inspect the armpit of a skinned ox. For it will appear broad and redder in the neighboring areas. You will find that the largest portion of it has been removed, as butchers <note>original: "lanij"</note> leave it attached to the skin because they are accustomed to removing the fleshy membrane together with the skin during the skinning process. Because of this, they also remove as much of the present muscle as does not yet appear completely and notably fleshy. For this reason, it will also be helpful to watch the butchers at work; they use a much sharper knife and take more time in removing the skin in the armpits than in the rest of the body, where they separate the membrane together with the skin from the underlying structures. It will also not be useless to ask for the removed skin to be stretched out for you, so that you may contemplate the portion of those muscles still attached to the skin. You may observe that this muscular flesh has fibers interwoven somewhat more straightly

than that broad muscle <note>the latissimus dorsi</note> which we testify moves the arm downward toward the spine. ### The seventh muscle.
<margin>septimus.</margin>
The seventh muscle moving the arm is the one which Galen, in the thirteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts* (for in the fifth book of *Anatomical Procedures*, all the muscles stretched from the shoulder blade to the humerus are strangely confused, and the present muscle seems to be recounted there almost among those lifting the arm), believed moved the arm backward toward the back <gloss>u</gloss>: <margin>u 13 tab. ### THE PREPARATION OF THE MUSCLES MOVING THE ARM. Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'S' depicting a group of several anatomists in Renaissance attire performing a dissection or anatomical demonstration on a human cadaver positioned on a table.</image-desc>

If until now you have managed the other muscles in the series of our dissection up to the muscles moving the arm—and primarily <gloss>a</gloss> <margin>a 3 tab. from the skin, you should draw another line from the middle region of the chest all the way to the pubic bone, within the fleshy membrane <note>original: "membrana carnosa"; in humans, this is largely represented by the platysma and the fascia, though in many animals it is a distinct muscular layer used to twitch the skin.</note>; and then another line transversely from the pubic bone, following the hip joint, to the spine of the sacrum; and a third from the top of the shoulder, all the way to the middle region of the arm. Once these incisions have been made, you will grasp the fleshy membrane with a hook or your fingernails and strip it away from the entire thorax and abdomen, while in the meantime leaving it still connected to the glands found in the armpits <note>the axillary lymph nodes</note>. Thus, once the membrane has been pulled away as far as the cavity of the armpit, it must be stretched out toward the light: and you must carefully observe whether, under the armpits, it transforms into a fleshy muscle beginning from the loins and the false ribs (as Galen taught). But meanwhile, you will be diligently on guard lest you fall into such a state of ignorance that the fat, which occurs on the sides of the chest and across the entire back, deceives you by appearing to be flesh. For I have seen some so unskilled, and so negligently practiced in distinguishing between similar parts, that at first glance they thought the fat of the back was flesh, because they saw it reddening much more here than elsewhere due to the body's position. For when a corpse that has not been thinned by long illness has lain on its back for a day or two, the entire site of the pressure reddens as if occupied by inflammation, and therefore the fat of that area does as well.

...along the length of the back, having made an incision that only wounds that muscle <note>The trapezius muscle</note> as far as the underlying parts; then another incision is to be drawn along the back of the head <note>original: "occipitiū"</note>, which also frees the beginning of the muscle there from the occipital bone. But if perhaps you fear that some underlying muscle might be damaged by those incisions, you shall place a boxwood knife <note>A blunt wooden tool used for "blunt dissection" to separate tissues without cutting them</note> under the outer sides of the muscle—specifically that side which is carried from the back of the head to the collarbone <note>original: "clauiculam"</note>, and then to that side which descends from the top of the shoulder, or collarbone, to the spine of the eighth thoracic vertebra. For with the knife placed under the sides and moved up and down, you will force that muscle of the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note> to pull away from the underlying muscles; then you will easily estimate the thickness of its nerve-like origin. Once the muscle is freed from the underlying structures, you will lead it with little effort toward its insertion point. 

But again, as you will hear in the specific description of this muscle, care must be taken under this layer so that the muscle proceeding from the back of the head into the shoulder blade is not removed along with it—the one which Galen claimed also pulls the shoulder blade upward. I do not say this because humans have this muscle in common with apes <note>original: "simijs"</note>; rather, I say it so that you may observe, not cursorily, whether humans are also endowed with it. By using an ape in the procedure at the same time, you may compare these findings of ours with Galen (if you are a diligent admirer of Nature). Nor should you trust dogs in this matter, who—just like horses, oxen, and other animals that lack collarbones—vary greatly from apes in the muscles moving the arm and shoulder blade. 

<margin>Preparation of the second [muscle] moving the arm.</margin>

These animals have yet another muscle in addition, arising from the outer side of the transverse processes <note>the bony projections on the side of the vertebrae</note> of the first four vertebrae of the neck, and inserted into the spine of the shoulder blade, which humans also lack. Yet, that muscle would also have to be dissected now in humans, if it were found. 

<margin>h 4 tab. Ξ. 10 tab. Δ.</margin> 

In apes, therefore, after the origins of these three muscles that lift the shoulder blade have been freed and led to their insertions, but in humans only the single one <note>the trapezius</note>—which is the only one of those three ape muscles that the human possesses—having been led toward its insertion, you will then approach the ^h^ muscle <note>the deltoid</note> by whose benefit we raise the arm. You will cut away its head from the entire spine of the shoulder blade, the top of the shoulder, and the middle part of the collarbone, using a razor or a knife held very close to the bone, until you see it forming its transverse insertion into the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>. 

After you have weighed the triangular shape of this muscle and the form of its head (which will now show the blunt peak of a triangle), it must be looked at from all sides, not just on the surface. With the greatest diligence, one must inquire whether that whole mass covering the outside of the joint—which we consider a single muscle—consists of several muscles lying upon one another. Galen seems to suggest this in the fifth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, undeservedly (as he often does elsewhere) accusing the ancient professors of dissection (who practiced on human cadavers) of some sort of drowsiness or negligence. 

<margin>i 9 tab. Π. 10 tab. Σ. 11 tab. Σ.</margin> 

Therefore, you will examine the entire origin of the muscle and consider how it thickens and gradually becomes a fleshy muscle. Furthermore, after examining the tendon (which is simple), you will divide this muscle everywhere crosswise, so that you may eventually admit that it is nothing less than doubled, nor does it resemble that appearance which the ^i^ first three muscles arising from the hip bone <note>original: "ilium oſſe"</note> and serving the movements of the thigh beautifully express when they lie upon one another.
