<margin>Figure 10, Table Y, l.</margin> You will observe how this muscle <note>The latissimus dorsi</note> crosses the lower angle of the shoulder blade and adheres to it; and then, if you stretch its starting point in various ways toward its place of origin, you will clearly learn how this muscle draws the arm down, and that it primarily moves the arm rather than the shoulder blade. Furthermore, when you work on <margin>Figure 11, Table a, b, m.</margin> that line **m** which frees the beginning of that muscle from the tips of the spinal processes <note>The bony ridges of the backbone</note>, you must <margin>Figure 11, Table Δ, n.</margin> certainly take care not to cut through the beginning of the abdominal muscle that ascends obliquely, nor the one which, arising transversely from the spinal processes of the vertebrae, is said to be inserted into the tenth and eleventh ribs of the chest <note>thorax</note>. Therefore, if you do not trust your hands enough, you shall try the same method on this muscle that we proved <margin>Figure 9, Table Γ, Δ, o.</margin> successful in the muscle we numbered as the second of those moving the shoulder blade. Specifically, you should place an outstretched hand or a boxwood knife <note>A blunt wooden tool used to separate tissues without cutting them</note> under the outer side of the muscle, and move it transversely up and down until you judge the muscle to be divided from the underlying organs all the way to the tips of the spinal processes. By this method, you will readily recognize the thickness of the membrane at its origin, and you will understand precisely how deep the knife or razor must be inserted to separate it. Indeed, you will act quite opportunely if you extend a longer stylus <note>A probe or surgical pointer</note>, decorated with a round little knob, directly under the beginning of the muscle, and gradually divide the origin with a knife lowered under the muscle to the side of the stylus. The edge of the knife should always be led outward and slightly slanted, and always pushed upward with the stylus, in much the same way as we divide paper. You might even wish to use the technique we employ for extracting stones <note>calculi</note> from the bladder, when we insert a tube <note>original: "siphonen"</note> shaped like a half-channel into the neck of the bladder so that the incision can then be made into its cavity. This is exactly the way that weavers of hairy silk <note>original: "pilosi serici textores" — velvet makers who cut the loops of the fabric to create the pile</note> divide the silk into hairs. By these methods, all things are beautifully divided which you will later hear must be <margin>Figure 10, Table Θ, p.</margin> dissected along the length of a stylus. When, therefore, <margin>Third procedure.</margin> you have brought the muscle that drives the arm downward to the shoulder <note>humerus</note>, you will free its tendon from the shoulder; <margin>Figure 13, Table S, q.</margin> and finally, you will prepare yourself for the muscle that pulls the arm backward. You will likewise cut its origin from the lower rib of the shoulder blade, and you will accurately investigate <margin>Figure 11, Table Γ, r.</margin> whether Galen more truly attributed the duty of rotation to this muscle than we do to the muscle occupying the convex seat of the shoulder blade. <margin>The seventh [muscle].</margin> You may thus leave the third worker of the arm's movements hanging from the shoulder until you have scraped away the muscle which fills the convex part of the shoulder blade—which we number as the seventh—from the shoulder blade all the way to the <margin>Figure 12, Table H, H, s.</margin> ligament of the joint, so that you may weigh each detail more truly. <margin>The fifth [muscle].</margin> The muscle that lies in the cavity of the shoulder blade, seen between the spine and its upper rib <note>The supraspinatus muscle</note>, you shall scrape from the shoulder blade to its insertion with two lines: one drawn through the upper side of the spine of the shoulder blade, the other along its higher rib. The muscle <margin>Figure 7, Table Γ, t.</margin> that rotates the arm <margin>The sixth [muscle].</margin> and claims the internal seat of the shoulder blade <note>The subscapularis muscle</note> does not offer itself conveniently for viewing unless you have first freed the shoulder blade from the collarbones <note>clauiculis</note> by a series of cuts. But because it would be inopportune to separate the shoulder blade from the collarbone while the muscles moving the shoulder blade are still intact, or even to separate it from the chest along with the collarbone now against reason, you shall refrain for a while from the management of that muscle which I have recorded as the sixth in the order of those moving the arm, until in the sequence of the dissection the hollow of the shoulder blade meets you, and you can <margin>Figure 7, Table I, u.</margin> promptly scrape this muscle from it. It will also be useful sometimes to reserve even the fifth muscle of those moving the arm until this point, so that, as it is continuous with the sixth, it may be perceived beautifully and conveniently.

In the **first book**<sup>a</sup>, I reported that the large, round head of the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note> and the socket of the scapula<sup>b</sup> <note>original: "acetabulum scapulae"; the shallow cup of the shoulder blade</note>, which is neither very wide nor remarkably deep, were rightly constructed for the various movements we perform with the arm. However, lest such a loose joint be poorly secured and the humerus fall out of its seat with almost any movement, I added that Nature produced certain processes<sup>c</sup> <note>bony outgrowths</note> of the scapula and then various ligaments to bind the bones together. But since I have now finished describing the processes that somewhat protect the joint and most of the muscles that tighten it,<sup>d</sup> time surely demands that I now treat the ligaments of the joint one by one in order.

<margin>Ligaments connecting the humerus to the scapula.</margin>
Therefore, three robust ligaments connect the humerus into the socket of the scapula, in addition to the common one that surrounds all joints like a membrane—sometimes thinner, sometimes thicker.<sup>e</sup>

# ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE SCAPULA. Chapter XXVI.

<margin>a Table 5, r. b 3, 4, 14. Δ. The first of the muscles moving the scapula. c Table 5, from i to k. d Table 5, l in b. e compare R, R, Table 3 with i, k Table 5. f Table 9, r, Δ, Table 1 G. 2 K, L, 4 b. g Table 9, from E to F. The second of the muscles moving the scapula. h Table 9, from E through K to G. i Figure 6, Chapter 15, Book 1 from f to u, and Figure 9, d t to z. k Table 9, *. l Table 9, from F to H. m Figures 1, 2, Chapter 22, Book 1 from I to Q with L, Figure 1, Chapter 21, Book 1. n from H to G, Table 9.</margin>
The **SCAPULA** <note>shoulder blade</note> is moved by the same motions as the arm, if you except only that rotation which we said the arm performs. A **triangular muscle**<sup>a</sup> <note>the pectoralis minor</note> moves the scapula toward the chest; it is positioned beneath that muscle<sup>b</sup> <note>the pectoralis major</note> by whose benefit we pull the arm to the breast. For this is the **first muscle of the scapula**, which I taught in the twenty-third chapter takes its origin<sup>c</sup> from the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sometimes sixth upper ribs of the thorax <note>chest</note>, just before they end in cartilages. I noted then that it varies greatly from the descriptions given by Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius frequently challenged</note>. Indeed, its substance is entirely fleshy except near its very short tendon; its **insertion**<sup>d</sup> is fixed into the inner side of the process that resembles an anchor <note>original: "anchoram imitantis proceffus"; the coracoid process</note>; and the path of its fibers, which are carried from a broad origin to a blunt apex without being intersected anywhere, need not be reviewed here at length. Therefore, if the higher fibers of this muscle are contracted, they pull the scapula upward toward the chest; but when the lower fibers contract, the scapula is driven lower toward the chest. When the fibers of the entire muscle, or rather the middle ones, are working, the scapula is drawn to the chest without tilting in either direction. However, the scapula is not drawn toward the top of the breastbone <note>sternum</note> or the pointed cartilage <note>the xiphoid process</note> in the same way the arm is, because it is moved to higher or lower positions on the chest with significant differences in motion, just as its muscle takes its origin higher or lower than the scapula muscle itself. Furthermore, strong muscles lift the scapula upward toward the head, since the scapula consists of a large mass and supports a great deal of flesh attached to it.<sup>f</sup> The **first** of these <note>the trapezius</note> is the one we said should be dissected before several of the muscles that move the arm; it originates from the **transverse line**<sup>g</sup> of the occipital bone <note>the bone at the back of the skull</note>, extending from the middle of that bone toward the root of the ear. Its outer side is as far removed from the earlobe as the length of the muscle's origin is from the middle of the occiput. For if you divide the interval of the occiput that extends from its middle to the ear into two equal regions, you will see that the origin of this muscle (which is fleshy, though thin) occupies the one closer to the middle of the occiput. In the middle of the occiput, the right muscle touches the left; and both joined together, as if taking their origin from the **tips of the spinal vertebrae**<sup>h</sup> <note>the spinous processes</note>, extend through the spine of the neck and thorax down to the eighth thoracic vertebra. The right muscle (and you shall understand the same for the left) appears membranous where it arises from the tips of the spines, and is roughly as wide as the width of the vertebrae on its side. In the rest of its region, it is seen to be entirely fleshy (if you except only one single spot<sup>k</sup> which we will explain shortly). Thus, two lines of this muscle have now been described: one follows the occiput, the other follows the spines. Besides these, however, there are two other diagonal lines: one<sup>l</sup> extends from the end of the transverse line where it faces the ear, stretching obliquely downward toward the front until it touches the broader part of the **clavicle**<sup>m</sup> <note>collarbone</note> where it joins the top of the shoulder. Another<sup>n</sup> line extends from the end of the line just mentioned, where it touches the clavicle...

Thus, the transverse line from A to B extends along the occiput <note>the back of the head</note>. From A to C, a straight line is drawn from the occiput down to the eighth spine of the thoracic vertebrae. From B to D, a line pertains obliquely from the occiput to the clavicle <note>collarbone</note>. From D to C, a line proceeds obliquely from the clavicle to the spine of the eighth thoracic vertebra. <sup>u</sup>It does not have all its fibers stretched in only one way. For those which are extended from the occiput and the spines of the cervical vertebrae descend obliquely (just like the outer line of that part of the muscle) forward to the spine of the scapula, the top of the humerus, and the broader part of the clavicle; they are always more oblique or more transverse the further they take their origin from the cervical spines closer to the thorax, so that those which the root of the neck sends out are now only slightly less than completely transverse. But those which truly arise from the spines of the thoracic vertebrae, being stretched upward toward the front, are seen to be straighter and less transverse the closer they are to the eighth thoracic vertebra. This series of fibers demonstrates that by the benefit of this muscle, the entire scapula is not only pulled upward but also dragged downward and moved directly toward the back.

For if the upper part<sup>x</sup> of the muscle is drawn toward its origin, you see the whole scapula lifted upward. But if the lower part<sup>y</sup> of the muscle, which stands between the spine of the scapula and the eighth thoracic vertebra, is contracted, the scapula is pulled downward. Finally,<sup>z</sup> when the middle part of the muscle is pulled during dissection, we see the mass of the scapula drawn directly backward. And hence it happens that the present muscle is put in charge of movements that are entirely conflicting, and possesses fibers drawn in opposite series; although meanwhile, no one could truly say that this muscle is disconnected or unjoined in any part of itself. Therefore, by reason of its unity, this muscle will be held by me as one; however, I will not object if someone, for the sake of its function, should count it as two or more. But I marvel at Galen, who, dividing this muscle, makes mention of the upper part of the muscle more prolifically than almost any other in the whole body near the middle of the fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*—disputing, surely too enviously, against Lycus <note>Lycus of Macedon, an earlier anatomist whom Galen frequently criticized</note>—yet at the end of that same book, he barely named the lower part of the muscle in passing, namely when he says the scapula is moved toward the back by two of its own muscles...

<margin>The muscle lifting the scapula, which the monkey possesses.</margin>

First, if you believe Galen, you will find yourself accused of ignorance and sluggishness during dissection when you subsequently try to diligently track down other muscles lifting the scapula in a human. To this muscle was assigned the task of lifting the base of the scapula toward the occiput. But you will search for this in vain with me in a human (as the human lacks it), while meanwhile it occurs most readily in tailed monkeys <note>likely referring to the Barbary macaque, Galen's primary subject</note>, preserving exactly that structure which Galen attributed to it and which I have just described. 

<margin>The third muscle of the monkey among those lifting the scapula.</margin>

This muscle, after it first emerges from the remaining muscles attached to the cervical vertebrae, appears rounded yet wider than it is deep; it is inserted downward and toward the rear, where it becomes wider.

In a human, this strong muscle originates from the <gloss>g</gloss> <term>transverse process</term> <note>the bony projections on the sides of the vertebrae</note> of the first cervical <note>neck</note> vertebra. To all his muscles that lift the scapula, Galen added a long and slender <gloss>l</gloss> muscle. He left it written that this muscle proceeds from the sides of the <term>U-shaped bone</term> <note>original: "ossis υ referentis"; the hyoid bone in the throat</note> and is inserted into the inner part of the scapula near its neck; he believed that by the benefit of this muscle, the scapula is lifted toward the front of the neck. However, in the chapter on the muscles of the U-shaped bone, I have asserted that this muscle was formed for the sake of that bone, and not for the scapula. Consequently, the movement of which it should be considered the author must be investigated by careful dissection. In this matter, there is no difference between monkeys and humans, except that in monkeys it appears fleshy throughout its entire course, while in humans it becomes slender in the middle of its path, showing the appearance of a tendon and being gifted with two "bellies" as it were. Surely, if Galen had ever dissected a human, he would have noticed this no less than he observed that the <gloss>m</gloss> muscles that draw the lower jaw downward <gloss>n</gloss> <note>the digastric muscles</note> are gifted with two bellies. <note>Vesalius is referring to the omohyoid muscle, arguing it moves the hyoid bone rather than the shoulder blade.</note>

One muscle for moving the scapula still remains, which drives it backward toward the spine of the back and somewhat toward the upper parts. # THE PROCEDURE FOR DISSECTING THE MUSCLES MOVING THE SCAPULA <note>shoulder blade</note>. Chapter XXVII.

<margin>a Plate 5, Gamma. Procedure for the first.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'H' featuring an anatomical dissection scene where several individuals are gathered around a cadaver placed on a table or bench.</image-desc>
YOU SHALL APPROACH the dissection of these muscles with the same method as all the others. <gloss>a</gloss> For the first muscle, by which the <term>scapula</term> <note>shoulder blade</note> is drawn toward the chest, its origin must be freed with a scalpel from the ribs where it emerges. Then, once the entire muscle has been separated from the <term>thorax</term> <note>chest cavity</note> all the way to the internal process of the scapula <note>the coracoid process</note>, and its origins have been pulled back, you shall investigate of which movement it is primarily the author: namely, whether it moves the arm, as Galen used to teach, or the scapula, as I was saying. <gloss>b</gloss>

<margin>b Plate 9, Gamma, Delta. Of the second.</margin>
You have already previously undertaken the dissection of the second muscle—which I said both raises the scapula and pulls it downward—during the dissection of the muscles moving the arm. Therefore, there is no need to repeat its sectioning here, just as there is no need to repeat the observation of those muscles which are attributed specifically to the necks of monkeys, and are described by Galen as if they belonged to humans.

<margin>c Plate 7, H. Plate 13, Q. Of the third.</margin>
<gloss>c</gloss> But the third of the muscles moving the scapula, which is led from the <term>cervical vertebrae</term> <note>neck bones</note> to the superior angle of the scapula’s base, must not be entirely freed from its origin unless some of the neck muscles have been cut away beforehand. And therefore, it will be worthwhile to cut it transversely where it first emerges from the neck muscles; and, leaving its origin at the vertebrae, you should free it from the scapula, though only after its function has been first weighed. <gloss>d</gloss>

<margin>d Plate 10, Gamma. * Plate 10, E. † Plate 10, F. Of the fourth.</margin>
You shall cut the fourth muscle <note>the rhomboids</note> with a light and long incision from the tips of the <term>spines</term> <note>the bony ridges of the backbone</note>; and when you have observed its insertion with precision, you shall move it away from the scapula, taking diligent care lest you cut the * third muscle moving the human thorax <note>the serratus posterior superior</note> at the † same time, or at least imprudently free it from its origin.

<margin>e Plate 5, R, S.</margin>
Then, if <gloss>e</gloss> that long muscle—which, contrary to Galen's opinion, I reported as being proper to the <term>U-shaped bone</term> <note>original: "ossi υ referenti," the hyoid bone in the throat</note>—is still preserved, observe carefully whether the Creator of things produced this for the sake of the scapula or for the sake of that bone.

<margin>f Chapter 22 of Book 1, Figure 4, R. g In the margin of Chapter 10, Book 1. h Chapter 22 of Book 1, Figure 4, S. Freeing the clavicle from the scapula.</margin>
Now with a knife, as close as possible, you shall cut the ligaments from the <term>acromion</term> <note>original: "summo humero," the highest point of the shoulder</note> and the <term>clavicles</term> <note>collarbones</note> where they are joined together, freeing the acromion from the clavicles, and <gloss>f</gloss> observing the unique cartilage of this joint, which is similar to that <gloss>g</gloss> found in the joints of the lower jaw at the temple bones, and <gloss>h</gloss> again in the connection of the clavicle with the breastbone. Then you shall accurately weigh whether any third bone exists here besides the clavicle and the acromion with its <term>appendix</term> <note>outgrowth</note> and the aforementioned cartilage; Galen teaches that Hippocrates remembered such a bone in his book *On Joints* when discussing dislocations of the arm. But what I feel regarding that bone, I have followed through in the first book.

<margin>i Plate 7, Gamma. k Plate 8, Gamma.</margin>
When, therefore, you have separated the clavicle from the scapula, the latter must be carefully kept in its place. But once the vessels creeping out from the thorax into the arm have been intercepted by two cords and then cut in the middle of the cords, you shall turn the scapula away from the thorax, so that you may now inspect the nature of the <gloss>i</gloss> muscle rotating the arm, which occupies the hollow seat of the scapula <note>the subscapularis muscle</note>. This muscle, therefore, having been scraped away from the bone on all sides and led down to the ligament of the joint, and its function weighed, you shall also cast it aside, so that now the scapula, fixed to no part, hangs from the thorax by the intervention of the <gloss>k</gloss> greatest muscle, which will be numbered as the second of those moving the thorax <note>the serratus anterior</note>.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE HEAD. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>A large woodcut historiated initial 'S' depicting several putti or small children performing an anatomical dissection on a cadaver's head and neck on a table.</image-desc>

<margin>Movements of the head.</margin>
In the previous book, while describing the structure of the neck vertebrae and—rightly so—finding ourselves in little agreement with the opinions of Galen, we reported that the head is moved by its own primary movements and by secondary ones. For by however many primary movements the neck is driven, by just as many secondary movements is the head also moved. Indeed, the neck is extended, or drawn backward toward the back, and is flexed forward; then it is also tilted to both sides toward the shoulders. The head, however, is flexed and extended by one primary movement of its own—even while the neck remains still—being moved forward and backward upon the first cervical vertebra <note>the atlas</note>. Then, by another movement entirely peculiar to itself, it is rotated upon the second vertebra <note>the axis</note> as if around an axle, whether it be flexed or extended with the neck, or positioned independently of the neck. To the sides, however, or toward the shoulders, the head does not tilt except by the benefit of the neck, and as if secondarily; for when the neck is unmoved and rigid, we cannot move the head toward the shoulders by any primary movement of its own. It is timely, therefore, now that those muscles which preside over the movements of the neck have been set aside in their proper place, to approach those which serve the primary movements of the head. These are comprised of seven pairs, moving partly the head and partly the first cervical vertebra; six of these pairs are located in the back of the neck, where our discussion must now begin.

<margin>In the 4th book of Galen’s *Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>
But before Galen approached the description of these, he placed two other pairs of muscles in the sequence of dissection which serve the movements of the <term>scapula</term> <note>shoulder blade</note>. Of these, <margin>a Plate 9, P.</margin> one is found in humans and is common to monkeys; specifically, that muscle on either side which was said to be inserted into the spine of the scapula, the top of the shoulder <note>the acromion</note>, and the broader part of the <term>clavicle</term> <note>collarbone</note>. However, humans lack the other pair, the muscle of which (on either side) was noted in monkeys to arise from the <term>occiput</term> <note>the back of the skull</note> and extend to the higher angle of the base of the scapula.

<margin>The first pair of muscles moving either the head or the first vertebra.</margin>
And from this it follows <margin>b Plate 12, F; Plate 10, 11, A.</margin> that the first pair of those moving the head is enumerated by Galen in the third series among the muscles occupying the neck. <margin>c Plate 12, A.</margin> This pair consists of two muscles <note>the splenius capitis muscles</note>, taking their origin from the tip of the spine of the fifth thoracic vertebra; then also from the tips of the spines of the fourth, third, second, and first thoracic vertebrae. This origin, where it first emerges from the fifth thoracic vertebra, forms an acute angle which, stretching upward, gradually widens so that by the time it reaches the third and second thoracic vertebrae, it is so enlarged that its outer side stands in line with the transverse processes of those same vertebrae. Both muscles, maintaining this width, are carried upward, also assuming an origin (though quite lightly) from the spines of the five lower vertebrae of the neck. <margin>d Plate 12, D.</margin> When, however, they have climbed as far as the spine of the third cervical vertebra—whereas up to this point in their progress the right muscle has been joined to the left—they both gradually move further and further away from each other until they are implanted into the <term>occipital bone</term> <note>the bone at the back of the head</note> by a broad and fleshy insertion along a transverse line. <margin>e Plate 12, B, C.</margin> Indeed, the breadth of this insertion is as great as the distance the inner side of each muscle is removed from the center of the occiput, and the outer side from the root of the ear. Thus, the breadth of the insertion of both muscles is as great as the interval of the occiput from one ear to the other that is not occupied by the insertion of the muscles. Furthermore, the shape of this recession of the muscles from one another <margin>f Plate 12, B, E, D.</note> is seen to be exactly triangular, if you draw one line transversely at the occiput from the inner side of one muscle to the inner side of the other, and then extend two other lines from the ends of that line along the inner side of each muscle to the spine of the third cervical vertebra, as if to the apex of a triangle.

<summary>Vesalius describes the mechanics of head and neck movement, distinguishing between the primary motions of the head (flexion, extension, and rotation) and the secondary motions facilitated by the neck, while introducing the first pair of muscles (the splenius capitis) that control these actions.</summary>

### THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II. 329

<margin>g Table 12, B, A, C, A. C, B.</margin>
Furthermore, each of these muscles <note>marked 'g' in the referenced illustrations</note> is triangular in shape, if you imagine one side as a line drawn along the length of the spine up to the occiput <note>the back of the skull</note>; the second side as a line extending along the outer edge of the muscle; and the third side as the line describing the muscle’s insertion across the occiput. The fibers of these muscles are directed obliquely upward from the spines of the vertebrae, almost toward the transverse processes <note>the bony projections on the sides of the vertebrae</note> of the higher vertebrae, until they all eventually end at the occiput. Indeed, these muscles effect only a very slight and small connection to the transverse processes of the vertebrae.

<margin>h Table 13, A. B through G; Table 5, T. 10, 11 B. 12 F, F.</margin> <margin>The second pair is exceedingly variable.</margin>
We observe that the h **second pair of muscles** is quite varied, and is much different in humans than it is in dogs and monkeys. In those animals, these muscles of the second pair arise from the transverse processes of the third or fourth thoracic vertebrae <note>the vertebrae of the chest</note>, and additionally from the transverse processes of the second and first thoracic, as well as the five lower cervical <note>neck</note> vertebrae. Proceeding toward the spines of these same vertebrae, they are attached by several insertions. Furthermore, the right muscle never moves away from the left throughout its entire course, and both are joined together at the middle of the occiput with a broad insertion. They show nothing tendon-like that is worthy of note, although they may occasionally show some oblique impressions running from the transverse processes of the lower vertebrae toward the spines of the upper ones. However, these should be considered quite light and do not penetrate deeply enough for anyone to say the muscle is divided into parts. 

Nevertheless, Galen seems to testify that some professors of dissection did not count only two muscles in this pair, but rather some counted four, and others six, as they approached human subjects differently than Galen did. In monkeys and dogs (about which I have spoken so far regarding this second pair), I would count only one muscle on each side; for if one had to pay attention to those "impressions," each would have to be considered as many muscles as there are origins from the transverse processes and insertions into the spines. In humans, therefore, I have observed this pairing to be much different than the way Galen described it, or rather, the way he categorized it. For many muscles appear on both sides, mixed together in multiple series, having origins in quite varied ways, and achieving their insertions into the occiput by entirely different means. 

<margin>i Table 13, A.</margin>
For as soon as the first pair of muscles <note>marked 'i'</note> is pulled back, a muscle appears that takes its sharp origin from the middle of the transverse processes of the fifth and fourth thoracic vertebrae. Appearing fleshy immediately from its origin, it takes on the shape of a mouse or a lizard <note>original: "muris & lacertæ formam"; the word 'musculus' literally means 'little mouse'</note>. 

<margin>k 13, 14. B.</margin>
When it creeps upward to the beginning of the neck k, it ceases to be fleshy and ends in the nature of a rounded tendon, l imitating that muscle <note>the digastric muscle</note> which draws the lower jaw downward and is provided with two bellies. 

<margin>l 14. H, l.</margin> <margin>m 13, 14. C.</margin>
Indeed, m there, where this muscle of the second pair moving the head has passed the root of the neck, it begins to be fleshy again until it is inserted into the middle of the occipital bone n. 

<margin>n Table 13, D. o Table 13, 4 C to D.</margin>
But before its insertion, another muscle o joins it, which arises from the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra with a tendon-like and rounded origin. Ascending upward, it also becomes fleshy and is inserted into the occiput along with the aforementioned muscle. Here, the muscles of the right side are touching those of the left side, and are not separated from each other (as the first pair is). 

<margin>p Table 13, E to F.</margin>

It arises partly fleshy and partly tendon-like from the tips of the transverse processes of the second and first thoracic vertebrae. Thus, this is the second pair of muscles in man: in which it is up to the observer whether to place four muscles on each side: namely, the first, second, and third—those three described before the fleshy mass—and the fourth, the fleshy mass itself. Unless perhaps someone proposed to subdivide that flesh again into as many muscles as there are impressions, or origins and insertions, seen within it. But I think it wiser to establish only a single pair from all these, and only one muscle on each side in number, since the other pairs are formed of only two muscles, and all the muscles of this second pair were created for the sake of the same function. For this pair (like the first pair) achieves the extension of the head and, quite obscurely, the extension of the neck as well, or its movement toward the rear. If, therefore, the muscles of both sides are contracted, they will extend the head very straight; but if they work alternately, they will serve the motion of turning the head.

Indeed, I have found only a single muscle on each side in humans, located immediately beneath the <margin>i Table 3, r.</margin> wide, membrane-like muscle encountered in the neck <note>the platysma muscle</note>, and it is visible in almost all men even without dissection. 

However, in certain four-footed animals, I have observed this muscle divided or bipartite in the middle of its path as it is carried upward, with one part inserted into the mastoid process and the other into the skull at the root of the ear. Truly, I have so far found three ends and insertions of this muscle in no living creature; much less has a beginning proceeding from the breastbone and collarbone, clearly dissected into two or three parts, occurred to me—although I am not unaware that these muscles on both sides have been counted as three, and sometimes two, by some Anatomists. But this number varies among those skilled in dissection according to the proportion of the muscle's ends in monkeys and dogs; although most have contended that these muscles arise from the head and are inserted into the breastbone and collarbones, and thus oversee the movements of the chest <term>thorax</term>. Yet meanwhile, I read no one who has granted them a description worthy of mention, far less has anyone truly expressed their function and nature to us. 

<margin>The duty of the 13th and 14th muscles.</margin> For the muscle of either side is appointed to duties entirely contrary to those of the first four pairs: for when both are contracted, the head is bent forward, whether the neck is held stiff or inclined. If only the right one is contracted, the head is turned forward to the left; but with the left alone working, the head is driven forward to the right. 

<margin>Muscles appointed to the movements of the neck alone.</margin> Furthermore, besides these <margin>k Table 8, A, B.</margin>, other muscles are seen which the ancients seem to have called those "hiding under the <margin>l Table 7, E. or Book 5, Fig 14, A, B.</margin> gullet" <note>original: *stomachon*; in the 16th century, this often referred to the esophagus or throat rather than the modern stomach</note>. These are born with the bodies of the first four thoracic vertebrae and all the cervical <note>neck</note> vertebrae, and partly take their origin from them, and are partly inserted into them; they are no less clearly inserted afterward into the occipital bone <note>the bone at the back of the skull</note>, near the <margin>m Book 1, Chapter 15, Figure 1, G.</margin> anterior seat of the opening through which the spinal cord passes. 

But we shall review these more exactly among the muscles moving the back; for they bend the upper part of the back, while the head itself is hardly flexed by its own motion with their help. For this reason, they should hardly even be enumerated among the muscles of the head; just as <margin>n Table 8, C; Table 13, H.</margin> another four (namely, two pairs on each side) placed at the sides of the neck, which move the neck by its own motion to the side but not the head, [should not be listed]. And again, <margin>o Table 14, o.</margin> another pair extending the neck must be passed over here and reserved for the remaining discussion of the muscles moving the back; since that also moves the head only secondarily, in the same way that the muscles moving the arm lead the elbow and hand.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE DISSECTION <note>original: *administratio*; in this context, it refers to the systematic procedure or manual demonstration of a dissection</note> OF THE MUSCLES MOVING THE HEAD. Chapter XXIX.

<margin>Dissection of the first pair.</margin>
<margin>a Table 11, A; Table 12, Γ <note>the Greek letter Gamma</note>.</margin>
<margin>b 11. 14. F.</margin>
You will begin the dissection of those muscles which govern the movements of the head with the <sup>a</sup> **first pair**. You should carefully examine the <sup>b</sup> membrane-like beginning of a certain muscle which, arising from the spines of the lower cervical vertebrae <term>neck bones</term>, is spread over the first pair of head muscles and the other muscles here that move the back. Eventually, it is inserted into several of the upper ribs of the chest, acting as an instrument of respiration <note>Vesalius is likely describing the serratus posterior superior muscle here</note>. It will therefore be permissible to free the beginning of this muscle (which will be the third of those moving the human chest) from the spines of the vertebrae with a knife. Once the muscle is torn away from the underlying parts all the way to its insertion, leave it hanging there from the ribs for a while until you approach the muscles of the chest. For the present, you will place a blunter knife, or one made of boxwood, under the outer side of the muscle of the first pair and attempt to free it from the parts beneath. Then, having made a cut along the length of the spine, you will lead the muscle up to its insertion in the back of the head <term>occiput</term>. When you have performed this on both sides, reflect these muscles of this pair away from the back of the head—without cutting them off—to one side, so that <margin>The second pair.</margin> they do not impede the rest of the dissection. Next, you will consider the various <sup>c</sup> muscles of the **second pair**, <margin>c Table 13, A, B through G.</margin> cutting them away from the vertebrae in the order I have listed them and tracing them to the back of the head. By pulling on their origins, you may rightly perceive which functions they are primarily responsible for. This is best seen only when the brain has been removed from the skull and the lower jaw itself has been cut away, so that the head is lighter and more easily moved. <margin>The third.</margin> You will afterward free the <sup>d</sup> **third pair** from the spine of the second cervical vertebra, <margin>d Table 14, A, B.</margin> <margin>The fourth.</margin> gradually lifting it toward the back of the head away from the <sup>e</sup> **fourth pair**, <margin>e Table 14, G, F.</margin> taking care that you do not accidentally remove that one as well. For the fourth pair must now be separated from the first vertebra and, like the others, led to its own insertion which it serves. <margin>The fifth.</margin> Furthermore, the <sup>f</sup> **fifth pair**, having been freed from the back of the head, <margin>f Table 14, H, I.</margin> <margin>The sixth.</margin> shall be led to the transverse processes of the first vertebra, just as the <sup>g</sup> **sixth** is led from the spine of the second vertebra to those same <margin>g Table 14, L, K.</margin> processes. Now, having turned the cadaver over, the origins of the <sup>h</sup> **anterior muscles** <margin>The thirteenth and fourteenth muscles.</margin> <margin>h Table 4, θ <note>the Greek letter theta</note>.</margin> must be cut away from the breastbone <term>sternum</term> and the collarbones <term>clavicles</term> with a sharp knife. Meanwhile, keep in mind whether several origins of muscles run together at once, or whether several muscles can be observed on both sides. Once you have traced these also to the mammillary processes <note>original: *mamillares processus*; the mastoid processes behind the ears</note> and have scrutinized their insertion, cut them away from the head. Leaving the specific muscles of the neck aside for the present, turn the dissection toward the ligaments peculiar to the head and the first two cervical vertebrae, to which we shall now dedicate a separate chapter.

*THIS figure represents the first and second vertebrae of the neck, drawn from the posterior side, together with their ligaments, which are to be described in this Chapter.*

<margin>A, B, C</margin> *The first vertebra of the neck <term>the atlas</term>, connected to the second. Specifically, A indicates the right socket of the first vertebra, which receives the right condyle <note>original: "caput" (head); in modern anatomy, these are the occipital condyles</note> of the occipital bone. B is the left socket, in which the left condyle of the occipital bone sits. C is the posterior part of the first vertebra, where other vertebrae end in a spine <note>The atlas lacks a true spinous process, ending instead in a small posterior tubercle</note>.*

<margin>D, D, G, H</margin> *The second vertebra of the neck <term>the axis</term>.*

<margin>E, E, E</margin> *The membranous ligament connecting the first cervical vertebra to the occipital bone; it is seen here still attached in part to the first vertebra.*

<margin>F, F</margin> *The membranous ligament binding the first cervical vertebra to the second.*

<margin>G</margin> *The body of the second vertebra, producing the tooth <term>the dens or odontoid process</term>.*

<margin>H</margin> *The tooth, or the sharp process of the second cervical vertebra.*

<margin>I</margin> *The round ligament, inserted from the tooth into the occipital bone; it is shown here cut across.*

<margin>K</margin> *The transverse ligament, which holds the tooth in the socket carved for it in the first cervical vertebra.*

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'C' depicting a group of figures in a scholarly or clinical setting, some seated and some standing around a table.</image-desc>
The fifteenth chapter of the previous book explained that the articulation of the head with the first cervical vertebra, and likewise the connection of the second vertebra with the first, and again the second with the head, are worthy of all admiration. The present text will briefly touch upon the ligaments containing these joints. Since it was necessary for the first cervical vertebra to be joined to the head, <margin>Ligament joining the first vertebra to the head.</margin> Nature rightly created a robust and strong ligament <margin>a E, E, E.</margin> surrounding the entire joint (which is considered common to other joints as well). However, this ligament possesses nothing unusual or unique beyond its strength and thickness. But that which joins the <margin>b I.</margin> second cervical vertebra to the head <margin>The second vertebra to the head.</margin> is round and very strong, participating in the nature of cartilage; arising from the peak of the tooth <margin>c H.</margin>, it is inserted into the occipital bone <margin>d Figure 1, chapter 15, book 1, G.</margin> where it forms the anterior region of the opening <term>the foramen magnum</term> through which the spinal medulla <term>spinal cord</term> descends. This ligament, very firmly binding the second vertebra to the occipital bone, forms a kind of axis along with the tooth, according to which the head—by the intervention of the first vertebra (which then acts as if it were a continuous bone with the head)—is driven in a circle. But lest that <margin>Ligament drawn across the tooth.</margin> <margin>e Figure 3, chapter 15, book 1, K.</margin> tooth, occupying the internal seat of the first vertebra and positioned in front of the spinal cord there, should ever slip out or be dislocated from its socket during more violent movements of the head <margin>f K.</margin>, and then compress or break the spinal cord, the Creator <note>original: "Opifex"; Vesalius frequently uses this term for Nature or God as the master craftsman of the body</note> produced another ligament. This arises from one side of the inner region of the first vertebra and is inserted into the other side, drawn across the posterior side of the tooth; it is remarkably robust and composed of the nature of cartilage. There remains <margin>g F, F.</margin> another ligament, binding the first vertebra to the second <margin>Binding the first to the second.</margin>, which is considered to have the same structure and use as other membranous ligaments containing joints. To perform the demonstration <note>original: "administres"; refers to the manual act of dissection</note> of these ligaments precisely, it is helpful if the muscles moving the neck have first been dissected. <margin>Procedure for the ligaments.</margin> Then, with a sharp knife, the membranous ligament connecting the first vertebra to the head will be conveniently divided. With the head bent forward, you will also cut the spinal cord transversely so that the round ligament connecting the tooth to the head comes into view. When you have seen this, you will divide it with a transverse stroke; then you will carefully observe the ligament wrapped across the tooth, holding the tooth in its cavity. By moving the first vertebra in every direction, you will learn which movements are completed above the second and first vertebrae. Finally, you will approach the membranous ligament joining the first vertebra to the second with a sharp knife all around; and with the first vertebra torn away, you will again consider the socket of the tooth, the ligament embracing the tooth, and that which proceeds from its peak.

->ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE MUSCLES OF THE ABDOMEN<-

### Chapter 31.

<margin>A brief enumeration of the eight abdominal muscles.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'V' featuring two figures in an architectural setting, possibly representing anatomical study or a classical scene.</image-desc>
I FEAR that here, too, someone who is perhaps over-critical of the order of instruction will blame me because I am not first approaching the muscles that move the elbow, the chest, or the back before those that constitute the abdomen. Indeed, nothing prevents me from treating the muscles that move the elbow right now. However, since the muscles that move the back precede those of the elbow by reason of proximity, and since those that move the chest must be dissected before the back muscles (according to the sequence of dissection), and since those we call the abdominal muscles must be dissected even before those of the chest, it is most appropriate to follow with the abdominal muscles. We name these based on the direction of their fibers, and we count them as eight: four oblique, two straight <term>the rectus abdominis</term>, and two transverse.

<margin>a Table 3, Θ.
b Table 4, P.
c Table 5, Δ.
d Table 6, Δ.</margin>
Of the oblique muscles, therefore, there are two on each side; they lie upon one another and possess fibers that run in contrary directions, crossing each other like an X <note>original: "decussatim"</note>.^a For the fibers of the upper one proceed obliquely downward and forward;^b while those of the lower one tend obliquely upward and toward the front. Of the straight muscles,^c there is only one on each side, which has its fibers extended according to the length of the body.^d Similarly, one transverse muscle is found on each side, whose fibers are carried crosswise according to the width of the body, or from right to left with no oblique path.

<margin>The descending oblique muscle.
e Table 3, Θ; Table 4, O, P, Q.
f Table 3, characters 6, 7, 8 & Table 1, O, O, P, P, Q.
g Table 2, O, O, P, P, P.
h Chapter 29, Figure 2, H, R, R, P.
i Table 8, Θ.
k Table 8, Λ.</margin>
The descending oblique <note>The External Oblique</note>,^e is spread over the other muscles of the abdomen. It takes its fleshy beginning from the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth ribs, before they end in cartilage. This is because of the muscle <term>the serratus anterior</term> which, as we shall say, arises from the base of the^f shoulder blade <note>scapula</note> and is inserted into the eight higher ribs of the chest, truly moving the chest. This wide beginning does not emerge in a straight line, but rather like a hand. For that chest muscle is inserted into the ribs as if stretching out fingers; from the intervals between these fingers, the more prominent parts of the descending oblique muscle arise like fingers of their own, just as if you were to insert the fingers of your right hand into the gaps between the fingers of your left. Then, after the ninth rib, this muscle also arises from the three lower ribs, always imitating that origin which it acquires at the intervals of the great chest muscle. However, it is no longer joined in that mutual interlocking with that chest muscle, but rather with^g another one <note>The latissimus dorsi</note>, which arises from the spines of the lower chest vertebrae and one or two of those placed in the loins, and is inserted chiefly into the tenth and eleventh ribs of the chest, as will be told in the description of the chest muscles. For that muscle is also implanted into the ribs like a hand, before they begin to turn into cartilage; and the beginning of the descending oblique muscle also proceeds alternately from the ribs themselves out of the gaps of that muscle, in the manner of a hand. This beginning of the oblique muscle is fleshy everywhere, though thin. But the muscle itself gradually becomes fleshier and thicker as it is carried downward and forward, embracing the flanks (which the Greeks call <note>original: "κενεῶνας" (keneōnas) and "λαγόνας" (lagōnas)</note> "the empty spaces" between the hip bone and the lowest rib) with its fleshy part, until it creeps to the hip bone^h <note>ilium</note>. It is inserted fleshily into the top of that bone along the entire path of its appendage <note>the iliac crest</note>. But when the fleshy part of the muscle hastens from the regions of the hips toward the front and middle of the body along the whole length of the abdomen, it thins out into a tendon-like <note>original: "nervosam," referring here to the aponeurosis</note> substance, very much like a membrane. This is spread over the cartilages of the sixth and seventh ribs, the point of the breastbone <term>the xiphoid process</term>, and the straight muscles. It is most firmly implanted into the upper region of the hip bone and the pubic bone, where it becomes devoid of flesh. For where the^i sixth and^k seventh muscles that move the femur descend over the hip and pubic bones, this oblique muscle is not attached directly to the bone.

<margin>Table 4, π, ς, τ, υ. and now especially Table 5, a, b.</margin>
<margin>Obliquely ascending.</margin>
Along the length of the body, in the middle of the abdomen, the right muscle joins with the membranous thinness <term>aponeurosis; a flat, sheet-like tendon</term> of the left, so that as they both descend together, they form a kind of tunic drawn over the entire abdomen.<sup>m</sup> The oblique muscle lying beneath this one arises as fleshy from the upper region of the iliac bone <note>The hip bone</note>, which is circumscribed by its spine and appendix; at the same time, it takes a very thin and membranous origin from the spines of the lumbar vertebrae and the sacrum. As the muscle progresses, it is eventually increased and nourished by fleshy fibers. This muscle, tending upward, covers the fleshy part of the flanks and is inserted fleshily into the ends of the four lowest ribs.

<margin>Here carefully compare Tables 3 & 4 with 5 & 6.</margin>
Where it ascends to the front and middle of the abdomen, it ends in a thin, nervous <note>In Vesalius’s time, "nervous" often referred to the white, tough texture of tendons rather than nerves that carry sensation</note> substance. This sits between the rectus muscle, which lies beneath it, and the membranous tendon of the muscle that descends obliquely. It is inserted into the pubic bone and the sword-pointed cartilage of the breastbone <term>the xiphoid process</term>. Through the rest of the length of the abdomen, it is joined with the tendon of the obliquely ascending muscle of the other side, so that from the muscles of both sides, a covering is created for the whole abdomen at once. The membranous tendons of these muscles claim for themselves almost the same direction of fibers as the rest of the muscles.

<margin>n Table 5, a, q, upward.</margin>
<margin>o Table 5, c. p Table 5, x. Table 6, b.</margin>
Furthermore, in that place where the tendons are spread over one another at the middle of the abdomen, they both meet, having grown together most firmly with a width as great as the average width of the rectus muscle. This is completed so strongly along the entire length of the abdomen that one might think the tendons of the four oblique muscles here in the middle of the abdomen produce a single structure, were it not for the fact that a most accurate dissection and the direction of the fibers show that two are held on each side. Where the right ones are joined to the left, they express no line of separation or union at all; instead, having become a little thicker and pressing themselves between the rectus muscles,<sup>n</sup> where those muscles stand apart from each other, they are most robustly grown together with the nervous thinness of the transverse muscles and even with the peritoneum<sup>o</sup> itself.<sup>p</sup> This also happens with the nervous thinness of the obliquely ascending muscles along the outer sides of the rectus muscles before they climb over them; for along the length of the abdomen, like a line, they effect a strong insertion into the nervous thinness of the transverse muscles, and also into certain "impressions" of the rectus muscles<sup>q</sup> now to be mentioned.

<margin>q Table 5, u, u. r Table 5, ∆. Table 4, n. Table 6, f.</margin>
<margin>s Table 5, n. The upper origin is marked above, the lower below.</margin>
<margin>The Rectus muscles.</margin>
Under the nervous thinness of the oblique muscles,<sup>r</sup> therefore, the rectus muscles of the abdomen are hidden. Each takes its origin from the middle region of the pubic bone<sup>s</sup> by a twofold beginning, as it were: one superior and internal, the other inferior and external. This is not because these beginnings are separate or discontinuous for each muscle, but because the origin of the muscle itself expresses a different substance in this manner. The superior part of the origin, or the superior beginning (so to speak), turning somewhat inward, is perfectly fleshy; ending from wide to narrow, before it reaches the middle region of the top, it terminates in what is almost an acute angle. The lower part, however, which also projects a little more outward, is nervous <term>tendinous</term> and entirely devoid of flesh; but reaching upward, it gradually becomes wider as it takes on flesh and seems to produce the entire rectus muscle.

<margin>t Table 5, p to q.</margin>
<margin>u Table 5, a, q, upward.</margin>
<margin>x Table 5, r. Table 4, n.</margin>
<margin>y Table 5, u, u, u.</margin>
Thus the rectus muscles, each born from the pubic bone by two such beginnings,<sup>t</sup> are contiguous to each other, reaching straight upward until they reach the navel.<sup>u</sup> There, being somewhat distant from one another and having become slightly wider, they are carried all the way to the chest, where they are implanted, wide and fleshy,<sup>x</sup> above the sword-pointed cartilage to the sides of the breastbone and the cartilages connected to it. These muscles do not seem to be carried along their whole length by a single course of fibers; instead, each expresses different markings in the region of the abdomen,<sup>y</sup> or "inscriptions" <term>tendinous intersections</term> drawn across them in a curved white line, exactly as if each of the rectus muscles were composed of several

...ought to be counted by number. For the fibers do not run straight from the pubic bone to the chest without leaning anywhere; instead, they are somewhat intertwined and slanted toward the aforementioned boundaries or impressions <note>Vesalius refers here to the tendinous intersections of the rectus abdominis, commonly known today as the "six-pack" lines</note>, and some appear to be produced from others in a certain way. Furthermore, the nerves are not only inserted into the rectus muscles near the pubic bone, but also on the inner side, where the muscles are provided with these impressions. Two of these impressions usually sit above the navel, and sometimes one below the navel in a woman, and occasionally even three above the navel. I do not believe Nature granted these to the muscles in vain, but rather so that they might be extended more conveniently upward and somewhat toward the front; and being slanted according to the circular region of the abdomen, they might press the peritoneum <term>the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity</term> appropriately, and perform more opportunely the duty we are about to describe when we follow the muscles that move the thorax <note>the chest</note>.

<margin>
The part of the rectus muscle which is abundant in monkeys.
Table 5, from r through s to t.
</margin>
We shall enumerate <sup>z</sup> one muscle in monkeys and dogs—which would be the fifth in order among them—which we will show is stretched along the side of the breastbone by the cartilages of the true ribs. We will teach that this is entirely membranous, except at the interval of the first and second ribs, where it becomes more fleshy and ends at the first rib. Certainly, this muscle, in all animals in which I have detected it through dissection, seems to me to be a part of the rectus abdominis muscle; and I flatly assert that the rectus muscle in those animals ascends all the way to the first rib of the thorax. This is most conspicuous in dogs and tailed monkeys; however, in humans (to tell the truth), I have never observed this muscle. Humans, being endowed with a very short chest, easily lack it.

<margin>
The transverse muscles.
Table 6, Δ; Table 5, y; Table 12, p.
</margin>
Beneath all the muscles just mentioned lie the <sup>a</sup> transverse muscles, one on each side. They arise from the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae by a thin and membranous beginning. Then, emerging in their progress from the muscles that move the back and increased by fleshy fibers, they are joined fleshily to the upper region of the ilium <note>the hip bone</note> and the ends of the false ribs, with their entire fleshy part covering the flanks.

<margin>Table 6, b.</margin>
But where it has crept toward the middle of the abdomen <sup>b</sup> as far as the outer side of the rectus muscle, it ends in a thin, nervous <term>aponeurosis; a flat, white, sheet-like tendon</term> which is implanted into the pubic bone and the sword-pointed cartilage <note>the xiphoid process at the base of the sternum</note>. Throughout the rest of the length between these extremes, this membranous tendon is continuous with the nervous thinness of the transverse muscle of the other side. Together, they encircle the entire abdomen like a tunic, imitating the oblique muscles in this regard. However, the nervous thinness of these muscles is not as wide as that of the oblique ones; for the transverse muscles are seen to be fleshy for some distance under the rectus muscles, especially near the region of the chest.

<margin>Book 5, first figure.</margin>
The <sup>c</sup> peritoneum, or the membrane wrapped around the organs serving nutrition, is so strongly attached to the transverse muscles that it is difficult to free them from it without tearing, especially in humans. Nevertheless, the fleshy parts of the muscles are joined to the peritoneum in hardly any other way than muscles lying upon one another are usually stuck together. For the transverse muscles, in the place where they are covered by the peritoneum, are by no means (even if many think otherwise) found by the dissector to lack their own proper muscle membrane. Nor is any other arrangement of the abdominal muscles ever seen than what we have now described—though perhaps someone, acting as a "sailor by the help of books only" <note>original: "librorum duntaxat ope nautam agens"; a metaphor for an armchair expert who has never actually performed a dissection</note>, might readily conclude otherwise, being surely deceived by the conflicting passages of Galen. For Galen reviews these muscles one way in his books *On the Knowledge of Affected Sites*, again differently in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, and quite differently in his books *On Anatomic Procedures*, where he enumerates them in such a way that he correctly describes their site in the sixth book of the *Method of Healing*.

<margin>The use of the abdominal muscles.</margin>
The eight muscles of the abdomen, besides the common use of all muscles by which they assist in warming and cooling the body and are considered a kind of bulwark <note>protective barrier</note>, primarily preside over the movements of the thorax, as we shall discuss in the specific chapter...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the abdominal muscles, specifically their role in bodily functions like excretion and childbirth, before transitioning into the practical dissection instructions for these muscles. It maintains continuity with the previous page's focus on the rectus and oblique muscles.</meta>

ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

<margin>d Table 7, Δ.</margin>
We shall speak more at length in the chapter concerning the muscles that move the thorax <note>the chest</note>. Next, these muscles serve man most aptly for the expulsion of solid waste: for when all of them work together, drawn in and contracted, while the diaphragm <term>septum transversum</term> is meanwhile depressed by the holding of breath, they compress the intestines so that they push out and expel feces from a narrow place into a larger one (which is lower down). At the same time, they prevent those materials from being carried back up to the stomach, just as if you were to place a soaking sponge between two hands joined at the wrist, with the hands spread further and further apart toward the tips of the fingers, and then tried to squeeze out the water by gradually bringing the hands together. Truly, this function of the abdominal muscles cannot be clearly perceived unless the function and position of the diaphragm are known. In the same way, it is not properly understood how the abdominal muscles assist women in labor (so that the fetus may be more conveniently propelled forward). And this is even less understood by those who think the diaphragm is pushed downward while it contracts and opens the thorax; they do not notice that when we draw air in and continually distend the thorax—without holding the breath or compressing the filled chest—the diaphragm exerts no force in excretion, because, being drawn perpetually upward, it is not depressed. However, in those holding their breath and meanwhile forcibly compressing the thorax, it remains in a firm position. Furthermore, the physicians of our age, who seem to recount only these muscles as if there were no others in the body, must be considered entirely delirious. They contend that food is drawn into the stomach by the rectus muscles, expelled by the transverse, and retained by the oblique, attributing to these present muscles what truly ought to have been ascribed to the fibers of the stomach and intestines. But these ideas are too absurd to be brought forward for discussion, since some fibers serve voluntary motion, while others serve natural motion, which does not depend on our own impulse. Certainly, they should never have fabricated these things; instead, they should have praised the Creator of things, who, when He willed the abdomen to be created necessarily without bone, prepared such skillfully made tunics and coverings for it. These, besides being coverings and most suitable defenses, also serve the movements of the thorax most usefully, as we have advised.

But where the membranous tendon of the ascending [internal] oblique muscle faces the outer side of the rectus muscle, it must be separated from the underlying parts with a sharper razor. So great a connection occurs here between this tendon and the nervous <note>tendinous</note> thinness of the transverse muscle next to the outer side of the rectus muscle, that I once thought the tendon of the ascending oblique was divided: I believed one part of it, fused with the transverse muscle, proceeded under the rectus muscle, while the other expanded over the rectus. This is especially obvious above the region of the navel. However, if you free the tendon of the ascending oblique from the transverse with absolute precision, you will find that it is spread over the rectus muscle, from which it must be accurately separated all the way to the white line of the abdomen. This is very easily done in the fleshy parts of the rectus muscle, but you will observe that it is difficult at those <gloss>m</gloss> nervous <note>tendinous</note> intersections of the rectus muscle.

Now, when you have brought this muscle also to the middle of the abdomen and have freed it from the peritoneum as best as possible, you will put the four muscles of this side back into their place. I prescribe making this incision at the midpoint of the rectus muscle’s width because I would not want the cut to be made fruitlessly through the <term>white line</term><note>The *linea alba*, the fibrous structure running down the midline of the abdomen.</note> which occurs in the middle of the belly. Indeed, I judge it impossible for the tendon of the descending muscle to be freed separately from here without wounding or damaging the tendon of the ascending muscle. However, I would not entirely discourage trying to start the cut from the white line sometimes, even if you were to separate the torn tendons from one another. Therefore, once this or that cut has been made, you will strive to lift the tendon of the descending muscle with a hook and cut it away from the muscle lying beneath it with a razor, until you have drawn the entire muscle—now freed from the ribs and the iliac bone—toward the spine of the back.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY
## ON THE MUSCLES OF THE MALE TESTES AND THE FEMALE UTERUS. Chapter XXXIII.

<meta>catchword: with vi-</meta>

It would have been possible to place several figures from the fifth book here, from which the nature of the muscles of the testes and the uterus could be sought; however, lest we present the same figures in different places, only a note will be added here as to which figures these present muscles appear in. Thus, the muscle of the testis is seen somewhat in the third table of muscles at **f**, and in the twenty-second figure of the fifth book $\dagger$. The muscular substance of the uterus, however, is expressed as far as was possible in the twenty-fourth figure of that same book at the character **O**.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'I'. The scene inside the letter depicts several infants (putti or cherubs) in a room with a window, gathered around a table conducting an anatomical dissection or demonstration. One child points to an internal organ while others assist with instruments.</image-desc>

It is now the right time, for the inspection of the muscles moving the thorax, the back, and the thigh, to manage the <term>peritoneum</term><note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>, and with it also to approach the muscles of the testes.
<margin>a Figure 22 of Book 5 $\gamma$. And from that figure, seeking those that follow here in order from 20.</margin>
<margin>The muscle of the male testis.</margin>
Thus, to each testis <gloss>a</gloss> reach individual muscles that are quite slender, formed from that tunic <note>The <term>tunica vaginalis</term>.</note> of the seminal vessels and the testis which, taking its origin from the peritoneum, contains the vessels together with the testis. For this tunic, in its posterior seat, soon at its very emergence from the peritoneum, is so augmented by long, fleshy fibers close to one another that those fibers express the nature of a slender and oblong muscle. This muscle is always innate to that tunic of the testis, stretching downward, and finally near the lowest seat of the testis, it is implanted together with that tunic <gloss>b</gloss> into the seminal vessel <note>The <term>vas deferens</term>.</note> which, having been prepared by the testis,
<margin>b Figure 22 of Book 5 $\kappa, 1$; Figure 23 of Book 5 $\nu, \delta, \epsilon.$</margin>
now receives the semen and, leading it upward into the cavity of the peritoneum, pours it into the neck of the bladder <gloss>c</gloss>. Nor does that tunic attach itself stubbornly to the testis or the seminal vessel in any part
<margin>c Figure 23 of Book 5 $\delta, o.$</margin>
except where, together with its muscular substance, it attempts an insertion at the bend of the vessel which is completed at the lowest seat of the testis; hence, the muscle itself never touches the testis. Thus, the muscle of the testis corresponds to those formed from the <term>fleshy membrane</term><note>The <term>tunica dartos</term>.</note>; since it is nothing other than fleshy fibers innate to the wrapping of the seminal vessels and the testis—just as the muscles of the fleshy membrane <gloss>d</gloss> are also constituted by fleshy fibers distributed through the membrane. By the benefit of the muscles of the testes, men may, by voluntary motion, draw the testes slightly
<margin>d Table 3, A. C, E, Γ.</margin>
upward (just as the muscles themselves are slender and thin), lest the testes, perhaps loosened more than is right and hanging downward, be too great a burden <gloss>e</gloss> to the seminal vessels. The muscles perform this use most especially when somewhat contracted during intercourse; for if
<margin>e Figure 22 of Book 5 $\delta, \mu.$</margin>
the testes were always a burden to the seminal vessels, and these were pulled toward the lower parts and perpetually constricted, they would not transmit the semen as conveniently as they do now, when they open more widely, being relieved of the weight of the testes already drawn up by the muscles. However it may be, it is certain that these muscles (which are called *kremastēres* by the Greeks <note>original: "κρεμαστῆρες"; literally "hangers" or "suspenders."</note>) are to be counted among that class which lack any muscle assigned to provide a contrary motion. For no muscles are constructed to pull the testes back to the lower parts; since the testes, which ought to fall in no direction except straight down, are let down abundantly by the natural weight implanted in them. Indeed, this occurs so much that they cannot be drawn upward even in the slightest degree in the sick and the elderly by the benefit of these muscles. Truly, I do not know what came into the minds of the Arabs <note>Vesalius refers here to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna, whose works dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>, who left it written that two muscles are held for each testis in men, but only one in women; for I have always observed only one to be extended to each testis in males.

# OF THE TESTES. Chapter XXXIIII.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting several figures in a classical landscape setting with architectural ruins.</image-desc>
JUST AS in the fifth book it will be necessary to mention the muscles I have attributed to the testes, so too I will treat their procedure along with the dissection of the other parts to be described in that book. However, as far as the procedure to be pursued in this book is concerned, you shall divide the peritoneum with a razor from the <term>xiphoid</term><note>The pointed cartilage at the base of the breastbone.</note> cartilage of the breastbone down to the pubic bone, and again with another section drawn transversely on both sides from the region of the navel. Soon, without selection, you will remove everything in men that is enclosed by the peritoneum, except for the end of the rectum and the bladder. Once these are removed, and the scrotum has been freed from the testes along with the fleshy membrane <note>The <term>dartos</term> tunic.</note> lying beneath it, you will insert a small probe from the inner part of the peritoneum into the passage which provides a way for the seminal vessels in the lower region of the peritoneum toward the groin. After you have pushed the probe as far as the testis, and have inserted a small knife at its side, or (if such a probe is at hand) into its own groove or channel, making a long incision from the peritoneum to the testis according to the length of the probe, you will divide the membrane or tunic covering the vessels along with the testis. Once this is drawn out and extended, you will see the slender muscle of the testis <note>The <term>cremaster</term> muscle.</note>, by which that tunic is as if nourished. Once this muscle is freed from the lowest bend of the vessel carrying the semen from the testis <note>The <term>vas deferens</term>.</note>, you will most readily learn its nature and see how it draws the testis upward. It would be permissible now, once the testes with their vessels and muscles have been cut away, to approach the muscles of the penis and the neck of the bladder; but since before this is complete, one must dissect the muscles of the thorax, back, arm, forearm, and hand, the discourse will now turn to the muscles of the thorax. <margin>Procedure for the female muscle.</margin> Otherwise, the muscles of women, once the peritoneum is opened and the intestines reduced to the sides and upwards, and the woman's testes <note>Vesalius refers to the ovaries as "female testes," following the terminology of the time.</note> also raised, come into view without another incision, provided that one does not mind turning one's attention to the sides of the uterus and the membranes binding it to the peritoneum.

IN THE PREVIOUS book it was declared that the thorax—for the sake of that motion which we require when breathing—was not formed of a single bone, nor was it entirely bony. ANDREAS VESALII ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY.

...it is provided: <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the heart's requirements.</note> that the heart itself indeed requires the substance of air, and that the heat burning within it greatly desires to be cooled. Inspiration indeed cools the heart by supplying it with a cold quality; expiration, however, by the discharge and expulsion of the burning and, as it were, charred and <term>sooty waste</term><note>Latin: *fuliginosi recrementi*. In ancient medicine, it was believed the heart acted like a furnace, producing "smoke" or "soot" that had to be exhaled.</note> in the heart, also contributes to its cooling. And so, primarily for the sake of the heart, respiration is achieved by two contrary movements: for it draws in during distension and dilation, and it empties during constriction—by the same movements, clearly, by which the heart itself is perpetually driven. 

However, the movements of respiration and the heart otherwise vary greatly in kind. For the heart moves by a natural <note>involuntary</note> motion, whether we wish it or not; respiration, on the other hand, depends so much on our will that we read of certain people who killed themselves by holding their breath (though I wonder from where they finally supplied themselves the strength for such a thing). And this [voluntary control] is considered greatly useful to man, not only for living well, but for life itself. For if the same rhythm and harmony of respiration were necessarily tied to the movement of the heart, and respiration itself did not depend on our own impulse and will, we would be unable to speak for long, to say nothing of diving into water or passing through smoke or other corrupt air. Furthermore, since the lung follows the movement of the chest whenever it is compressed or dilated (primarily by the force of a vacuum), it is most certain that muscles had to be constructed to dilate and narrow the chest. 

<margin>*The number of muscles moving the chest.*</margin>
<margin>b We will note each one individually as we go.</margin>
In total, including the eight muscles of the abdomen in man,^b there will be eighty-nine: specifically, forty-four on each side, and finally one common to both sides. However, dogs and monkeys have two more on each side, so that they have ninety-three in total; these I shall not be burdened to enumerate in their proper order, taking the opportunity to understand Galen.

<margin>c Table 4, d; Table 5, Z.</margin>
<margin>*The first muscle moving the chest on either side.*</margin>
^c Therefore, the first muscle of either side arises from the lower and inner region of the <term>clavicle</term><note>The collarbone.</note>, along its length where it faces the first rib, possessing a fleshy origin throughout. It is inserted by a fleshy end into the first rib where it joins the breastbone (sternum), and also into the breastbone itself where it receives the cartilage of that rib. This muscle is short but wide and thin, and it is allotted remarkably oblique and almost transverse fibers. By the benefit of this muscle, the first rib is drawn upward and outward, and in this way the chest is dilated in that area.

<margin>*The second [muscle].*</margin>
^d The second muscle is large: for it originates with a fleshy beginning from the entire inner base of the <term>scapula</term><note>The shoulder blade.</note>, and proceeding from there always fleshy and stretched over the ribs, it becomes very wide and inserts itself into the eight (or sometimes nine) upper ribs, primarily at the middle of their length. As for the remaining part where the muscle is extended over the ribs, it merely rests upon them and is joined to them only by small fibers (as muscles laid upon one another usually are). Furthermore, its insertion is not implanted into the ribs in a straight or simple line; rather, the muscle here is divided as if into fingers, which proceed further forward through the bones of the ribs than that part which is born in the intervals between the ribs. 

<margin>e This is observed in Table 1, O, O, O, P, P, P and Table 2, o, o, o, p, p, p.</margin>
^e This occurs in a manner quite opposite to the way the obliquely descending muscle of the abdomen takes its origin from the lower six ribs. This refers to the saw-like appearance of the Serratus anterior muscle.</note> with the second muscle of respiration. If the fibers of this second muscle are ever contracted, they pull all the ribs into which the muscle is inserted toward the outside, dilating the chest. This muscle behaves almost exactly like this in humans, but in dogs and long-tailed monkeys it is different: for it is not only inserted into eight ribs in them, but is also very strongly implanted into the transverse processes of the seventh, sixth, fifth, and fourth cervical <note>neck</note> vertebrae—or rather (as someone might perhaps argue not entirely absurdly) it takes a portion of its origin from those processes.

The fourth in the series of muscles described in this chapter is found in humans as well as in monkeys and dogs, but it is somewhat different. In humans, a broad and membranous beginning arises from the spines of the three lower cervical vertebrae and the first thoracic vertebra. This <gloss>l</gloss> lies over the first pair of muscles that move the head and the muscles placed here that move the back and chest; it <gloss>n</gloss> extends forward—or, if you are looking at the right muscle, it slopes toward the right—becoming fleshy and showing the nature of a broad muscle as soon as it passes the outer side of that first pair.
