Being implanted into the third rib and the three succeeding it in order downward, it always descends obliquely forward or toward the side until it ends, hidden for some distance under the <gloss>o</gloss> origin of the second muscle moving the chest and divided into fingers. This muscle, whenever it is contracted, pulls the ribs into which it is implanted upward, visibly dilating the chest. It should be considered the third of the muscles moving the chest in humans, but the fourth in monkeys.

...appearing like a tendon in the middle, it is gifted with two bellies. Or, if this portion stretched out to the ribs should not be considered part of the **rectus muscle** <note>the rectus abdominis</note>, no one will deny that it is most firmly joined to its end, or rather born from it. However the matter stands, whether it is a unique muscle or a portion of the rectus, it will always perform the same function: namely, to compress and constrict the ends of the true ribs articulated with the **breastbone** <note>original: "pectoris ossi", the sternum</note>, and by doing so, to narrow the chest. Furthermore, since it has never been seen by me in humans (nor was it seen by those anatomists who preceded Galen, who practiced on human bodies), I have so far enumerated only three muscles of the human thorax, but five in long-tailed monkeys and dogs; and even then, I did so on the condition that, though our eyes might protest, we would set aside a fifth muscle as distinct from the rectus abdominis for the sake of Galen.

From here, along with the eleventh muscle moving the back, resting upon the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, it is led upward; it is so stubbornly mixed and joined with that muscle throughout its entire path through the loins <note>the lumbar region</note> that it might deservedly be considered a part of it, and cannot easily be separated from it by dissection. However, as soon as both reach the twelfth thoracic vertebra, this sixth muscle departs from the eleventh back-moving muscle by a noteworthy interval: so much so that to those dissecting carefully there, it would seem to take its beginning from it. From this point, it climbs upward slightly obliquely toward the side, and from its fleshy substance, it sends out tendons (which are a little less than perfectly round) to the ten upper ribs. It is not made of fleshy parts throughout its length, even though Galen, in his fourth book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, claimed that this muscle consists of fleshy parts on all sides. These tendons are inserted into the tubercles of the ribs <note>small rounded projections</note>, which, as was reported, bulge out from them a little after they have departed from the transverse processes of the vertebrae. This muscle ends at the first thoracic vertebra; sometimes, however, it climbs so high that it also offers a tendon to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra, no less than to the ribs. Into the eleventh and twelfth ribs, it is inserted only fleshily: for the higher the muscle ascends, the more conspicuous the aforementioned tendons become. The muscle itself, as if consumed by the generation of the tendons, gradually becomes more slender, pulling the ribs of the thorax downward, compressing them, and finally narrowing the chest.

The seventh of dogs, and the fifth of humans, is located in the posterior part of the thorax, following the lower parts. it takes a broad and membranous origin from the spines of the eleventh and twelfth (sometimes tenth) thoracic vertebrae, and also from the spines of some of the first lumbar vertebrae. This beginning is spread over the muscles that move the back and the fourth muscle of the human thorax, stretched transversely straight toward the front. When this muscle passes over these and is joined to the bones of the ribs, it is immediately increased by fleshy fibers: and finally, as if divided into several fingers, it inserts itself into the intervals of the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth ribs, and into the ribs themselves, long before they turn into cartilage. This muscle is far wider in humans than in monkeys and dogs; although even in dogs it is seen more significantly than in monkeys, and in all of them it forms a **saw-like joint** <note>the serratus posterior inferior</note> with the muscle of the abdomen that descends obliquely. Since it is the agent of retraction for those ribs into which it is inserted, it is also appropriately counted among those muscles that distend the chest.

**external**, and others **internal**. i The external ones in each of the rib intervals have their beginning just as the ribs k depart from the **transverse processes** <term>transverse process: the bony projections on the side of a vertebra</term> of the vertebrae, and consist of fibers creeping from the upper rib into the lower one, obliquely downward and forward. The external muscles maintain this course of fibers through all the intervals of the **false ribs** <note>the lower ribs that do not attach directly to the sternum</note>, both those consisting between bones and those between cartilages; and the muscles of the true ribs also retain that course up to the part of the ribs where they end in cartilage.

</margin>
l However, where the bones of the true ribs degenerate into cartilage, the course of the fibers immediately varies. For there, fibers proceed from the cartilage of the lower rib, obliquely upward and forward toward the cartilage of the upper rib, until in this part also the external muscle is joined to the breastbone. It happens uniquely to these external intercostal muscles that they appear far more nervous and lacking in flesh in that part of the ribs which first departs from the vertebrae than through the rest of the length of the interval; furthermore, they are not only led from the lower site of the upper rib into the upper site of the lower rib, but they also begin from the outer surface of the upper rib and are inserted into the outer surface of the lower one.

Internal intercostals.
</margin>
m The fibers of the **internal intercostal muscles** hold a position contrary to those mentioned above: for where they are closest to the bodies of the vertebrae, they send fibers stretched obliquely upward and forward from the upper site of the lower rib into the lower site of the higher rib. The internal muscles retain this series of fibers through all the intervals of the false ribs, as also in the intervals of the true ribs, up to that part of the ribs where they degenerate into cartilage; for there, as soon as the internal muscles reach that point, they change the course of their fibers. For from the cartilage of the upper rib into the cartilage of the lower rib, the fibers are stretched obliquely downward and forward. And to say it once and for all, in the intervals of the true ribs, the muscles situated between the bones of the ribs are gifted with an entirely opposite fiber arrangement to those existing between the cartilages. # OF ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY, BOOK II.

...intervals there are not two, but four muscles, as some of the ancient anatomists have taught: although they truly asserted this only regarding the intervals of the six **true ribs** <note>The first seven pairs of ribs that attach directly to the sternum; Vesalius refers to the six spaces between them</note> (which are counted as seven in number). For in the **false ribs** <note>The lower five pairs of ribs that do not connect directly to the breastbone</note>, only two muscles can be counted. Thus, since there are six intervals between the true ribs, nothing in the arrangement of the fibers prevents one from counting thirty-four intercostal muscles on each side—just as I noted a little earlier, when I mentioned that twenty-two on each side, and then twelve more, <margin>n 7 tab. Δ.</margin> were missing from the description, in addition to the muscle common to both sides.

<margin>The function of the intercostal muscles.</margin>
<margin>In the fragment *On the Causes of Respiration*.</margin>
<margin>At the end of the book *On the Motion of Muscles*.</margin>
By the benefit of the intercostal muscles, **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years until Vesalius challenged them</note> believes in many places that the chest is tightened and loosened. Since these muscles are double-layered, he taught that the outer ones manage **expiration** <note>breathing out</note>, which is to pull the ribs together and compress the chest; to the inner ones, however, he assigned the task of **inspiration** <note>breathing in</note>, which is to lead the ribs away from each other and create a wider cavity in the chest. Yet at other times, being inconsistent with himself, he wished the outer muscles to oversee inspiration and the inner ones expiration. Whether either of these opinions—whichever appeals to you more—is consistent with the truth, I would like you to weigh carefully (setting aside bias for the moment). For I, however much I am devoted to the teachings of Galen, cannot agree with his conclusions here. Thus far, I have by no means discovered how the intercostal muscles, whether internal or external, could pull the ribs apart or lead them away from each other. I have observed this even during Galen's own methods of **vivisection** <note>dissection performed on living animals to observe functions like breathing</note>, which I first performed alone and later attempted in the schools; these actually prove the opposite of Galen’s dogmas rather than supporting them. Furthermore, the position, shape, and fibers of the intercostal muscles, and everything else regarding their construction, more clearly suggest that these muscles pull the ribs toward one each other rather than loosening them. The outer ones, located between the bones of the true ribs and throughout the intervals of the false ribs, appear to pull the lower rib toward the upper one; the inner ones, however, pull the upper toward the lower. Furthermore, I believe the outer muscles placed between the cartilages of the true ribs pull the upper cartilage toward the lower, and the inner ones pull the lower cartilage toward the upper. If this is so, what else is it but for all of them to tighten the chest together and make it narrower? By Hercules, it is not inconsistent with reason that Nature produced all intercostal muscles for expiration or the narrowing of the chest, since we require a stronger motion and force for blowing out, for the voice, coughing, sneezing, the excretion of waste, and for more easily excluding the fetus during childbirth—briefly, for the compression of the chest—than we do for inspiration or the dilation of the chest. Thus, the muscles responsible for inspiration are deservedly few and weak, the chief of which will now be described.

<margin>The transverse septum, or the muscle common to both sides.</margin>
<margin>o 7 tab. Δ. 1 fig. lib. 6 1, 1, 2 fi. R, R. 3 fig. H. 4 Q, 5 E 6 n, o, 12 I.</margin>
Since we have so far explained all the muscles of one side (which have matching pairs on the other), it will now be appropriate to turn the discussion to the muscle common to both sides. This is the one which the Greeks called *phrenas* <note>original: φρένας</note>, *diaphragma* <note>original: διάφραγμα</note>, *ano koilian* <note>original: ἄνω κοιλίαν, literally 'upper cavity'</note>, and *parapidia* <note>original: παραπίδια</note>; the Latins called it the **transverse septum** <note>original: septum transversum; today known simply as the diaphragm</note>, and sometimes the *praecordia*. This muscle corresponds in neither position nor shape to any other muscle in the whole body; for it is wide and circular, and <margin>p 7 tab. between k, l, m, n.</margin> carries its "head" or origin in its very center. There, in its great width, it is exactly like a membrane, from which fibers run out like lines drawn from the center to the circumference of a circle, extending to the parts where the diaphragm is inserted. These, augmented by the specific flesh of muscles, make the rest of the muscle fleshy; this part gradually becomes thicker and meatier as the fibers progress in length. The fibers proceed from the membranous <margin>q Table 7 shows the lower viscera.</margin> circle to the lower region of the breastbone, near the root of the **pointed cartilage** <note>original: mucronata cartilago; the xiphoid process at the base of the sternum</note>.

<summary>Vesalius challenges Galen’s theory on how intercostal muscles function, arguing that they all serve to compress the chest for expiration rather than expansion. He then begins a detailed anatomical description of the diaphragm, noting its unique circular structure and central membrane.</summary>

# BOOK II ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...process, and then the others following in order, are inserted into the ends of the **false ribs** <note>The lower ribs that do not connect directly to the breastbone</note>. This occurs not on the outer side of the cartilages, but on the inner side, so that the rib cartilages, together with the **xiphoid process** <note>original: "mucronata pectoris ossis cartilagine"; the pointed cartilage at the base of the breastbone</note>, form a very secure defense for the **diaphragm** <note>original: "septi transversi"</note>. Furthermore, it is not only inserted into the cartilage of the twelfth rib, but grows fleshily along the entire length of that rib, and is joined to the ends of the lower ribs by the **internal oblique muscle** <note>original: "oblique ascendente abdominis musculo"</note> and even more so by the **transverse muscle** of the abdomen. Moreover, the fibers of the diaphragm that creep toward the vertebrae of the back do not attempt an insertion into the eleventh thoracic vertebra which they face; this is because the **aorta** <note>original: "magnae arteriae"</note> creeping under the diaphragm and the **psoas major** <note>original: "sextus femur movens musculus"; literally "the sixth muscle moving the thigh"</note> cover the eleventh vertebra so completely that the diaphragm cannot grow into it. Consequently, the fibers of the diaphragm which ought to have been connected here to the eleventh thoracic vertebra end in two membranous but extremely powerful tendons. These stretch downward at the sides of the aorta and adhere there to the muscles of the loins; becoming gradually narrower and passing somewhat beneath the artery, they extend until they find the bare lumbar vertebrae, to which they are most robustly attached over a long stretch. Thus, the whole diaphragm is slightly less than a complete circle and shows an oblique position. For it extends from the breastbone, through the ends of the false ribs, to that region we mentioned in the lumbar vertebrae; it therefore holds a position sloping downward from the front toward the back. Furthermore, it possesses two circles: one membranous, which is considered its head, and another surrounding this, which is fleshy.

<margin>
y Plate 7, u—one between k, l, m, n; the other outside.
</margin>
However, just as this fleshy part becomes gradually more muscular as it approaches the ribs, so the other part becomes more membranous as it nears the center of the diaphragm. Yet both do not represent the image of a perfect circle, but rather, so to speak, are wide and terminate at one part in an acute angle. For the membranous part extends an acute angle upward and toward the front, while the fleshy part extends one downward and toward the lower regions, appearing very similar to those **rackets** <note>original: "reticulis"</note> which we use in the game of **tennis** <note>original: "parvae pilae ludo"; literally "the game of the small ball"</note>—especially if the handle of that racket were loosened and slightly gaping, and the wood itself had been beaten against walls to make it shorter and wider.

The **peritoneum** <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note> encircles its entire lower breadth where it faces the organs of nutrition; however, the entire upper breadth, facing the heart and lungs, is covered by the **pleura** <note>original: "membrana costas succingente"; the membrane lining the ribs</note>.

If anyone wishes to count the vertebrae among these along with Galen, I certainly permit it, although it seems quite improper to say the diaphragm provides a path for the vertebrae. Indeed, we barely give the name "opening" appropriately to the path where the artery travels, since this represents a semicircle carved into the circumference of the diaphragm rather than a hole, and the diaphragm is joined to the upper or anterior part of the vertebral bodies, but not to the sides.

is joined together by the benefit of the membranes growing upon it: just as these membranes are also stubbornly committed to the remaining parts to which the diaphragm <note>original: "septum"</note> provides a path. A third opening is found, lower than the middle seat of the diaphragm and veering slightly toward the left side, through which the **esophagus** <note>original: "stomachus"; in Vesalius’s time, this term often referred to the gullet or esophagus leading to the stomach</note> and the branches of the **sixth pair of nerves** <note>The vagus nerves, which Vesalius classified as the sixth pair; modern anatomy classifies them as the tenth cranial nerve (CN X)</note> are sent down to the orifice of the stomach <note>original: "ventriculi"</note>. This is certainly far different from what Hippocrates, Galen, and the other leaders of the anatomists believed. Not only dissection, but reason itself supports my view on this matter. For the winding path of the esophagus would have been arduous if, leaning on the back near the twelfth thoracic vertebra in the first opening, it were twisted upward toward the front into the upper orifice of the stomach. For the first opening is a little lower than the middle region of the stomach measured according to the length of the body: and the stomach itself is rounded in that part where the esophagus enters it, and the esophagus does not form a continuous body with it more toward the front than the back. However, since it is enough to have spoken of the structure of the diaphragm, we shall now rightly describe its function.

<margin>The function of the diaphragm.</margin>
**Plato** thought that it was merely a transverse fence between the desiring (or natural) soul and the spirited soul. **Aristotle**, however, since he believed these "souls" were only parts of a single soul located in the heart, asserted that this diaphragm was created by Nature to separate the seat of the heart from the belly, so that the origin of the soul might be kept unharmed by the exhalations of food and the abundance of external heat. In truth, it not only performs such a role, but among the muscles moving the chest, it is primary in conducive power for **respiration** <note>breathing</note> and for expelling the waste of the belly. Yet its duty, by which it moves the chest, is obscure; nor do I know for certain if anyone has truly left an account of it for posterity, or even attempted to hand it down worthily.

<margin>
m Plate 2, 3 of chapter 11, book 4, n, o, o. Plate 1 of book 6, P, P.
</margin>
Indeed, it is peculiar to **Galen** (if I dare say so) that, although he is otherwise extremely wordy, he sometimes passes over in silence that which most needs explanation—not as if by design, but by stealing away into some fable or some insult against others. Furthermore, as far as I have grasped it thus far, the **diaphragm** <note>original: "septum transversum"</note> by its own motion draws the lower end of the breastbone and the ends of the false ribs inward toward its own head, as if toward a center, also pulling them somewhat upward. For the head of the diaphragm is placed in the middle of the parts to be moved: and the nerves running down from the neck <note>the phrenic nerves</note> are inserted into the higher seat of its head, which faces the amplitude of the chest. Therefore, when the diaphragm is drawn together into itself and collects the ends of the false ribs toward the center in a certain way, it narrows only the lower and anterior part of the chest, which the cartilages of the false ribs constitute. But it dilates the posterior part, which is held from these cartilages all the way to the vertebrae, and in turn separates the five lower ribs, together with the sixth and seventh ribs of the chest, by whose cartilages the diaphragm is also flattened. By this reasoning, therefore, the diaphragm dilates and extends the lower part of the chest.

Indeed, so that you may more clearly grasp what I am saying, first fit both hands to the cartilages of your **false ribs** <note>original: "notharum costarum"</note>: and with a breath forcefully drawn in, feel how the ends of the cartilages are pulled inward and upward. Then, leaving one hand here, place the other extended over the posterior region of the ribs: and again, having taken a breath, examine how the ribs are separated near the back, and how the cartilages conversely blink together <note>i.e., move closer or contract</note>; unless perhaps a dog or another animal is at hand, whose **living dissection** <note>vivisection</note> may teach the function of the diaphragm. And in this procedure, care must be taken lest, while the animal draws breath in, you think it is breathing out; which you would certainly do most readily if you only paid attention to the ends of the false ribs and those seats where the diaphragm is implanted. Nor does it escape me even now that certain leading men of our age, who were occasionally present while I was performing...

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II

...persisted in their presence, contending that the proper motion of the diaphragm <note>original: "septi"</note> is directed downward. These people, besides the evidence of live dissection—which is by far the most obvious proof—ought to be taught by the fact that when we are emptying our bowels, we hold our breath by strongly compressing the chest <note>original: "thorace"</note>, rather than immediately breathing in and expanding the chest. Surely, that expansion would have to be done if, during the dilation of the chest, the diaphragm were drawn downward, so that it might then assist the abdominal muscles in excretion. This is also shown by the strongest inspiration, whenever you attempt to exert yourself so that you do not allow the cartilages of the false ribs to move upward and inward; for when you restrain them by force, after one or two breaths are taken, the area of the cartilages suffers no less than if you had struck it forcefully with your fists. But I believe you also experience these things in various ways, just as I am now so intent on various types of breathing that, out of weariness, the pen <note>original: "calamus"</note> must be laid down as it falls from my hands. I will add, however, that those who have been suffocated, or have died by some other means while taking a final breath and not letting it out (which is indeed a wondrous thing), clearly subscribe to my opinion. For in these cases, the diaphragm <note>original: "septum transversum"</note>, drawn upward and so severely convulsed, appears during dissection to have been brought into the cavity of the chest, pulling the liver and stomach into the chest with it. This presents us with a difficult dissection of those organs; however, it becomes easy at once if the chest is perforated somewhere between the ribs or through the diaphragm itself. For then it immediately becomes flaccid and falls downward like a wet cloth <note>original: "instar madidi panni"</note>, allowing the liver and stomach to hang down further than you might wish. How this happens is well known to those who have observed the nature of muscle contraction and relaxation.

<margin>Enumeration of the muscles moving the chest, and when they perform their duty.</margin>
Thus far we have explained all the muscles serving the movements of the ribs alone, which all together number eighty-five in monkeys, but eighty-one in humans. However, when we also add the eight abdominal muscles to these, which must be placed entirely in the class of those compressing the chest, there are eighty-nine in humans<sup>n</sup>, <margin>n Plate 3, Θ.</margin> but ninety-three in monkeys. For the <sup>o</sup>obliquely descending muscles of the abdomen, if they are stretched, compress the much lower seat of the chest and narrow the chest cavity. The <sup>p</sup>rectus <note>straight</note> muscles, when they draw the ribs downward together with the <margin>o Plate 3, Δ. p Plate 4, Π. q Plate 6, Δ.</margin> obliquely ascending muscles, also constrict the chest significantly. The <sup>q</sup>transverse muscles also contribute to narrowing the chest by drawing the ribs inward. Furthermore, one might think that those muscles which move the arm and shoulder blade <note>original: "scapulam"</note> also assist slightly in the movements of the chest, if they were to constrict the chest more forcefully at some point. But in that case, the number of respiratory muscles would increase even further; however, not all of these are believed to operate simultaneously in every type of breathing. There are, first of all, two kinds of respiration: namely, inspiration and expiration. Each of these, in turn, has two parts. For one type of expiration is natural and not violent, occurring only by natural necessity; the other is vehement and violent, which we call "blowing out" <note>original: "efflationem"</note>. Likewise, one type of inspiration is natural, while another is violent, used for generating the voice or for some other purpose; and these differences vary greatly among themselves by reason of being greater or lesser. The <sup>r</sup>diaphragm <margin>r Plate 7, Δ.</margin> alone is considered the manifest author of natural inspiration and expiration; for physicians believe that when it is contracted or tensed, the chest is sufficiently dilated and that inspiration is completed. Then, when the diaphragm is relaxed again, they affirm that the chest promptly collapses by its own weight and produces expiration. And this is why Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose anatomical theories Vesalius often challenged</note> left it written that natural expiration is performed without the <sup>t</sup>help of muscles. <margin>s Plate 4, d. t Plate 7, L. u Plate 11, F. x Plate 4, Δ. y Plate 6, Γ. z Plate 8, E. α Plate 8, D.</margin> But if either the quality of the heart's heat increases, or if you need more air for the voice or some other duty, then <sup>s</sup>the first, second, and in humans<sup>u</sup> the third and <sup>x</sup>fifth, and in monkeys and dogs<sup>y</sup> the third muscles, will work together on both sides with the diaphragm for inspiration; and according to Galen's vote, <sup>z</sup>the internal <sup>α</sup>intercostal muscles will also act. Although I do not know whether it is to the external or...

Galen, however, assigned the function of inspiration to the inner intercostal muscles <note>The muscles between the ribs</note>, since he was so inconsistent. But if a need for greater expiration or blowing out arises—for the voice, shouts, or for blowing into flutes, trumpets, and similar instruments—the outer intercostal muscles will set to work along with the inner ones. <image-desc>Ornamental initial 'O' depicting a group of students or surgeons in a 16th-century anatomical theater, observing a dissection on a central table.</image-desc>
ONCE ALL THE MUSCLES which we have taught to be dissected up to this point have been laid back, you will begin the procedure <note>original: "administrationem"</note> for the muscles moving the chest with the<sup>a</sup> first one. By no means should you omit—for the sake of Galen’s teaching—to have a monkey, or if a supply of those is not available, a dog, to use alongside your work. Therefore, with a sharp scalpel, you will first cut through the membranous but exceedingly strong ligament by which the collarbone <note>original: "clavicula"</note> is joined to the breastbone <note>original: "pectoris ossi"</note>, examining the soft and gristly<sup>b</sup> cartilage which, in addition to the cartilage naturally grown onto the bones, comes between the breastbone and the collarbone. In addition to this, among the remaining ligaments of this joint, you will look for a certain strong ligament which, arising from the lower part of the collarbone, is inserted into the breastbone at the point where the cartilage of the first rib grows onto the breastbone. Next, you will bend the collarbone now upward, now downward, away from the first rib of the chest, and you will consider the origin and insertion of the first muscle, together with the path of its fibers. Then, once the muscle is freed from the collarbone, you will allow it to remain attached to the chest.

The<sup>c</sup> second muscle, since the shoulder blade <note>original: "scapula"</note> is now hanging away from the chest, offers itself entirely to view; hence, to ensure a successful job, it must be dissected from the base of the shoulder blade and traced all the way to the insertions it makes into the ribs. In this procedure, you will carefully observe whether the second muscle, stretched from the base of the shoulder blade to the ribs, provides help for the movements of the chest, or whether, taking its beginning from the ribs, it is inserted into the shoulder blade and moves it. To this investigation, it contributes in no small measure that in dogs you will see it either inserted into, or arising from, so many transverse processes of the neck vertebrae. 

Now, having removed the shoulder blade together with the arm, you will set it aside somewhere, so that it may later serve for the dissection of the muscles occupying the arm, elbow, and hand. But now you will proceed to the<sup>d</sup> third muscle of the canine chest; once it has been freed from the vertebrae and pulled away at its insertion, you will examine the nature of its<sup>e</sup> tendon with great precision. When you have observed this muscle in the dog, it must also be sought in the human. When you have done this in vain for some time, you will turn your dissection to the<sup>f</sup> fourth muscle of the dog, which is the third muscle in man. Once its membranous beginning has been freed by a long cut from the spines of the vertebrae from which it comes, you will pull the muscle away from its underlying sites toward the ribs into which it is inserted—unless perhaps you already severed the beginning of this muscle when you were attacking the muscles of the head, and tore it away from the<sup>g</sup> first pair of those muscles.<sup>h</sup> Similarly, you will remove the seventh muscle of the dog (which is the fifth in man) from its own spines where it arises; then you will free it from the muscles moving the back and from the dog’s<sup>i</sup> sixth muscle (man’s fourth) all the way to the end where it is implanted into the ribs, leaving it hanging from the chest.

<margin>Look for these in the 8th table.</margin>
To see the inner ones as well, you should attempt to divide the outer muscle with a very light cut in one of the spaces between the ribs, along the lower edge of the rib. Gradually lifting it with a hook, separate it from the inner one. Immediately, the nature and fibers of the intercostals will appear, lying in a position contrary to each other <note>The fibers of the outer and inner intercostals run at roughly right angles to one another</note>. However, you will also be able to examine the inner ones once the chest is opened. In the meantime, however you track them down, I urge you to investigate most diligently whether the inner ones perform a different duty than the outer ones—whether the former serve inspiration and the latter expiration (or vice versa)—or if, in my opinion, they are all assigned the same task, and all of them narrow the chest.

<margin>The transverse septum <note>The diaphragm</note>.</margin>

There you will soon see two circles, one membranous and the other fleshy. Additionally, you will see the three openings I mentioned, and the tendons attached to the lumbar vertebrae. To see the fibers precisely and the rest of the lower surface of the diaphragm more exactly, the peritoneum must be pulled away from the diaphragm with your hands. In pigs, this is done without any trouble, but it is not the same in humans or dogs.

To bring the upper part of the diaphragm into view (the side facing the cavity of the chest), you should make a cut with a medium-sized knife <margin>p as was done in the 8th table.</margin> from the cartilage of the first rib where it joins the bone of the rib itself, down to the lowest rib, working through the cartilages on both sides. Then, lifting the pointed cartilage <note>The xiphoid process at the bottom of the breastbone</note> with your left hand, scrape the diaphragm away from the lower region of the breastbone and the cartilages of this area.

Next, with the cartilages and the breastbone <margin>q Look for these in the 2nd figure of Book 6.</margin> held upright, you will cut away the membranes attached to the inner side of the bone which partition the chest cavity <note>The mediastinum</note>, as well as the veins and arteries extended from the throat to the chest, until the breastbone is freed from everything and you can conveniently remove it with the cartilages from the chest.

After setting the breastbone aside for a little while, you will cut away the membranes partitioning the chest cavity from the diaphragm, and also the envelope of the heart <note>The pericardium</note>. <margin>r View in order the 3rd and 4th figures of Book 6.</margin> This envelope, contrary to what Galen everywhere believes, is attached to the diaphragm over a large part of its surface in humans. This is quite different from dogs and the monkeys Galen studied. Furthermore, you will cut away the nerves inserted into the diaphragm, the hollow vein <note>The vena cava</note>, and the esophagus <note>original: "stomachum"</note>, gradually scraping the diaphragm away from the loins along with its tendons. Once freed and laid out on the table, you may examine it again if you wish.

## ON THE LIGAMENTS OF THE THORAX.
### Chapter XXXVII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial T. It depicts several small figures (cherub-like putti) in a study or workroom; one is seated at a desk while others stand in a group, appearing to be in deep discussion or study of a text.</image-desc>

<margin>d, g, f, i, chapter 19, book 1, from a to c; in this way, seek the nature of the ligaments from the locations of the bones. Since these are membranes, they cannot be shown in our illustrations.</margin>
The ligaments of the chest most worthy of note—besides those we described in the previous chapter regarding the connection of the collarbone <note>The clavicle</note> to the breastbone and dissected together—pertain to the twelve thoracic vertebrae. For this reason, these must be examined along with the remaining ligaments of the spine. However, no unique ligament is wrapped around the ribs at the vertebrae, except for the membranous one common to all joints. Here, that membrane is very hard and shares the nature of cartilage; this occurs most notably between the root of the transverse process (or the first joint of the rib to the vertebra) and the tip of the transverse process (or the second joint). Furthermore, because the first rib sustains a nearly greater burden than the others, it is bound to the body of the first vertebra with a stronger and almost specialized ligament than the ten following ribs. As for the twelfth rib, since it gapes away from the eleventh on all sides and is in no way joined to the transverse process of its own vertebra, it is also bound by a remarkably strong and specialized ligament. It is for this reason that we said the twelfth vertebra possesses a private cavity (as does the first, also by occasion of its own ligament). The cartilages of the ribs are not bound to their own bones, as the bones themselves transform <note>original: "degenerent," in the sense of one tissue type transitioning into another</note> into the cartilages. Moreover, where they are articulated into the breastbone by their oblong heads, they claim no specialized ligaments for themselves either, except for the membranous ones common to other joints. The breastbone also possesses nothing unique in its ligaments. Just as a certain membrane—which the Greeks call the *periosteum* <note>original: περιόστεον, meaning "around the bone"</note> because it surrounds the bone—is drawn over other bones, so it is over the breastbone. This membrane is strong and almost doubled, and the rib cartilages themselves possess this in common with the rib bones. <margin>Management of the ligaments.</margin> Thus, you may observe these types of membranes and ligaments with small knives on the breastbone and cartilages. However, those ligaments which join the ribs to the vertebrae cannot be conveniently approached until the muscles moving the back have been removed.

<margin>By how many movements the back is moved.</margin>
Let us now review by how many movements the back is moved. The whole back, from the head down to the <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>, is bent into something of a semicircle, inclining to neither side; then it is raised into a straight line, verging toward neither part; afterwards, it is also rolled into a semicircle toward the side, extended neither forward nor backward. Thus, there are now four simple movements of the entire back: namely, flexion, extension, and inclination to the right and left sides. And these movements (if any others of the body are) are also performed obliquely, or verging toward another part. For we bend the back not only straight, but also more inclined to the right or left. Likewise, when we roll it to the side as if into a semicircle, we are able to lead it toward the front and back, and not just straight to the side; so much so, that even a certain obscure rotation is present in the whole back at once. Again, as we have already said, the vertebrae perform all these movements together; or, while the part of the back under the neck is resting, the neck alone is capable of the exact same movements we have already attributed to the whole back. The neck performs these movements not only while the rest of the back is at rest, but also while the rest of the back is bent, extended, or inclined to the side. Indeed, it was most useful for a human that the neck be moved quite loosely and independently, especially when the neck is driven in opposite or contrary movements to the other parts of the back. For however much you bend the <term>lumbar vertebrae</term> <note>The vertebrae of the lower back</note> forward along with the <term>thorax</term> <note>The chest/ribcage area</note> and keep them in flexion, nothing prevents the neck from being able to be strongly reclined and extended backward. However, the movement of the lumbar vertebrae is not very distinct from the movement of the thoracic vertebrae: for they move almost as one, except that a looser movement in every direction is entrusted to the lumbar vertebrae. This happens both because of the attachment of the ribs to the thoracic vertebrae and because of the muscles presiding over these movements. For the whole thorax is inclined to the side in a certain way together, although the individual lumbar vertebrae can do this more independently. But as the articulation of the bones demonstrates all these things, the dorsal muscles themselves teach these movements most of all—muscles which were described by <term>Galen</term> <note>A Greek physician whose anatomical theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years until Vesalius challenged them</note> too superficially, and by no means in their entirety.

This origin appears fleshy, thin, and like an acute angle. Climbing obliquely upward, it proceeds more toward the middle of the body of the fourth thoracic vertebra with an oblique path of fibers. For those fibers creep from the outer parts obliquely upward into the inner parts, so that by the time they reach the body of the third thoracic vertebra, the muscles on both sides, having become larger, become somewhat adjacent to each other. At their origin, however, they are as far apart from each other as the width of the vertebral body. They preserve this sequence (namely, that they take their origin or expansion from the side of the body of the lower vertebra and strive for insertion more toward the middle of the body of the upper vertebra) continuously, until, gradually approaching each other, they climb all the way to the anterior site of the first cervical vertebra <note>The atlas, or top vertebra of the neck</note>. There, narrowed and stripped of its flesh, it ends in a round tendon: which finally is inserted <margin>T.</margin> <gloss>t</gloss> into the smaller or inner process of the femur <gloss>u</gloss> <note>the lesser trochanter</note> and aids in the flexion of the femur <gloss>x</gloss> <note>moving the thigh toward the belly</note>. This muscle <gloss>y</gloss> <note>the psoas major</note> in the loins appears sometimes more and sometimes less livid <note>original: "liuidus"; a bluish-gray or bruised color often seen in cadaveric muscle</note>, especially near the extension of its tendon. And this is one of the internal muscles of the loins: not because it governs the movements of the lumbar vertebrae, but because it is located here. <gloss>z</gloss> However, as for the muscle which arises from the cavity of the ilium bone and effects the same insertion into the femur as the aforementioned one <note>the iliacus muscle</note>, I do not include it in the count of the lumbar muscles—something which, as far as I know, no one has done until now.

The fibers themselves ascend from the exterior parts obliquely inward and upward: and those which take their beginning from the sacrum are inserted into the fifth and lowest lumbar vertebra; those which follow these in order toward the ilium bone and the outer side gradually end in the superior vertebrae. To this muscle—which is enumerated by me as the ninth among those moving the back—and to the tenth, which is the partner of the ninth muscle, is entrusted the duty of flexing the lumbar vertebrae, and they alone are the authors of that movement. But since one of these exists on each side and is endowed with oblique fibers, these muscles also effect an oblique flexion, according as this or that one is contracted alone. Therefore, only <gloss>f</gloss> the lower and upper parts of the back possess their own muscles born to be the workers of flexion; by their benefit, the middle part of the back—namely the thoracic vertebrae themselves, whose bodies are without muscle <note>original: "excarnea"</note>—is inclined somewhat, specifically the upper ones together with the neck, and the lower ones together with the flexed lumbar vertebrae. Then, this entirely fleshy origin is also drawn from the entire internal seat of the <term>ilium</term> <note>the hip bone</note>, <gloss>m</gloss> which projects backward outside the transverse region of the sacrum. This is in the same manner as the fourth muscle moving the human thorax, which also offered a tendon to each rib. However, that thoracic muscle spreads such tendons from its outer side further away from itself; but this muscle of the back emits tendons not from the other side, but rather from its internal or anterior seat, expanded upward not in a straight path, but obliquely toward the outside, just as all the fibers of the muscle are oblique. From this it also happens that the thorax and the loins, by the help of these muscles—namely the eleventh and twelfth—are extended straight and also to the sides. For when both are equally contracted, that entire part of the back into which these muscles are inserted is extended without leaning to either side; but when only one is contracted, the spine, having experienced extension, is turned toward that side.

The intervals between the spinal processes are also filled by these muscles, and they are contiguous <note>touching</note> with one another there; for nothing lies between them except a membranous ligament stretched from a higher spine to a lower one. The primary function of these muscles is to pull together the spinal processes to which they are inserted, and thus, together with the other muscles, to extend that part of the back to which they are attached. But just as these present muscles, among the other authors of the movements of the back, are mostly endowed with straight fibers, so too they are responsible for only very slight oblique movements.

If you wish to learn their origin and insertion more precisely, you should scrape them away from their vertebrae with a small, sharp knife. ...[you will see] no difference in those muscles either, which you should examine for the sake of understanding Galen. With the cadaver now turned over <note>original: "resupinato," usually meaning lying on the back, but here implying the body is prone to access the spine</note>, you will immediately scrape away the fifth muscle from the thoracic vertebrae with a small knife, until you have seen it in all its insertions. The seventh will follow this one, similarly to be scraped away from the vertebrae. But in this operation, care must be taken lest you cut away a portion of the fifteenth muscle in place of the seventh: for they cling to each other tenaciously, and the fifteenth goes under the origin of the seventh muscle to some extent. Now with a razor or a sharper knife, following the line of the spines in the loins <term>the lumbar region</term> and in the sacred bone <term>the sacrum</term>, a section must be attempted which frees the origin of the eleventh muscle from the spines. Lest you inadvertently remove the thirteenth at the same time (as Galen undoubtedly did in monkeys, which are otherwise most suitable for dissection) and think it part of the eleventh, that cut should not be made deeper than just to divide the origin of the eleventh. You will easily guess its thickness if you dissect the muscle from the transverse processes <note>the bony projections on the sides of the vertebrae</note> of the lumbar vertebrae with a small knife, and having raised it from the thirteenth, you also turn it back toward the spines of the vertebrae. Therefore, once this muscle is freed from the spines of the loins and the sacred bone, care must be taken lest you think it so conjoined with the spines of the thoracic vertebrae that you remove the fifteenth muscle along with the eleventh itself, and wander in error <note>original: "hallucineris"</note> along with all the other anatomists. After you have seen the inner side of the muscle also separated in some way from the parts underlying and conjoined to it, it shall also be scraped from the bone of the ilia <term>the pelvis or hip bones</term>, and having grasped its origin, it will be raised gradually. Thus, by freeing it from those parts into which it is inserted, you finally see those tendons which it distributes in a most elegant series, like palm branches <note>original: "palmitis instar"</note>, into the tips of the transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae. Once this is removed, without further cutting, the thirteenth and fifteenth are in view. Yet, to investigate their nature precisely <note>original: "ad amussim," literally "by the carpenter's rule"</note>, it is necessary to diligently scrape these too from the vertebrae; you will perform this all the more laboriously in the muscles of the spine, as they are both born in and take their origin from more bones. On account of which the Creator of things <note>referring to God or Nature</note> also comes to be praised, who so fashioned these muscles that we can move each part of the back separately with successive motions: lest we be forced to move the whole always at once, which would hinder many actions. Furthermore, when you have removed these as well, you will make a transverse cut which penetrates the sacred bone and the lowest lumbar vertebra, from the front all the way to the spinal cord. Then, with the thorax bent together with the ribs, you can divide the back from the sacred bone, as you are now about to investigate the ligaments of the vertebrae.

## ON THE LIGAMENTS OF THE VERTEBRAE. Chapter XL.

<margin>Figure for chapter 30.</margin>
<margin>Nor was it permitted to us to present these ligaments otherwise than one might imagine for the description of the bones; therefore you will also refer yourself to the bones.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'L' featuring two putti (cherubs) in a classical landscape with architectural ruins. One putto is seated on a stone block, while the other stands nearby. The entire scene is enclosed within a square decorative border.</image-desc>
I have described above the ligaments binding the first vertebra to the head, and the second to the first, and the second again to the head. Now I will treat those which join the remaining vertebrae together, beginning my discourse with those which join the bodies of the vertebrae. Thus, between the bodies of the second and third cervical vertebrae <note>neck bones</note>, and thereafter between the bodies of all the remaining vertebrae, a certain substance is placed which Galen calls cartilage. He asserts that the vertebrae are not bound together by this, contrary to the opinion of the leaders of dissection who preceded him. For he does not wish them to be joined by the benefit of this cartilage, but rather by the third tunic <note>membrane</note> of the spinal cord, which inserts itself between the bodies of the vertebrae. Of what sort this actually is, I will follow up in the discourse on the spinal cord, namely at that time when

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spinal column's structure, moving from the muscles of the back to the specific nature of the ligaments and cartilages that bind the vertebrae together. Vesalius is here contrasting his own observations (and those of ancient authorities like Hippocrates) with the widely accepted teachings of Galen.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS: ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE BODY

...besides the two membranes of the brain <note>the meninges, specifically the dura mater and pia mater</note>, which are closely attached to the spinal cord, you will hear that the openings of the vertebrae, or the cavity (which provides a path for the spine), is lined on all sides by a certain membrane fused to the bones. This membrane differs in no way—except perhaps in thickness—from that which we commonly call the periosteum <note>original: "circumossalem," referring to the membrane that wraps around bones</note>. Whether you should agree with Galen's opinion, or with those of the Ancients <note>the "Veteres" often refers to pre-Galenic anatomists</note> who were quite diligent in dissections (as Galen's own writings show), let the judgment be yours. For even if a human cadaver is not at hand, it will nonetheless be possible, as you rise from your reading, to have the back of some animal brought to the table, or even if you are to eat a fish.

<margin>
To help you follow the matters I am treating here with less effort, you have two vertebrae from the thorax, depicted from the front view of a child's body. In these:
**1** marks the cartilage of the upper vertebra, its lower appendage, and the intervening body itself.
**2** marks the lower appendage <term>the epiphysis, or growth plate</term> of the same vertebra.
**3** marks the cartilaginous ligament <term>the intervertebral disc</term> coming between the appendages of the upper and lower vertebrae.
**4** marks the upper appendage of the lower vertebra.
**5** marks the cartilage joining the said appendage to its own vertebra.
</margin>

<image-desc>
Anatomical woodcut illustration of two juvenile thoracic vertebrae shown from an anterior (front) perspective, stacked to show their articulation. Five numerical labels (1-5) refer to the structural components described in the marginal note, highlighting the growth plates (epiphyseal cartilages) and the intervertebral ligament/disc.
</image-desc>

And so, even if just for the sake of sport (provided you do not despise those divine oracles of Hippocrates in his book *On Joints*), separate one vertebra from another. Comparing it with any other cartilage of the body, consider within yourself whether that cartilage of the vertebrae possesses the nature of a true cartilage, or rather that of a cartilaginous ligament. For by this reasoning, you will go over to the opinion of the Ancients with "hands and feet" <note>A Latin idiom meaning with total commitment or wholeheartedly</note>, leaving Galen's decree far behind. Nor will you allow yourself to be persuaded that some membrane, by whose benefit the vertebrae are connected to each other, is drawn between the bone of the vertebra and this ligamentous, fibrous, soft, and mucous cartilage—which is not solid or continuous in the manner of true cartilage (lest perhaps we seem to speak only of hardness). 

However, when you weigh these matters, you must take diligent care that, if you happen upon the spine of a lamb, kid, or calf, the cartilage occurring between the appendage <term>epiphysis</term> of the vertebral body and the body itself does not deceive you, leading you to think that cartilage is the one we are discussing here. Rather, in those vertebrae, consider three "ranks" of cartilages, so to speak, separated by two bones between two vertebrae. After observing those ranks, notice the natures of the cartilages, and subscribe even more firmly to the dogma of the Ancients. For you will see two cartilages placed between the bodies of both vertebrae and their appendages; these are strictly cartilages, and differ in no way from those that come between the other appendages and bones. 

But the middle cartilage between the appendages, you will surely say (unless you trust your eyes too little because of Galen's name) is nothing other than a ligament. The family of the Asclepiads <note>ancient Greek physicians</note>, who trained their sons in the dissection of cadavers with such care, called these **fibro-cartilaginous ligaments** <note>original Greek: "νευροχονδρώδη σύνδεσμα"</note>. You will maintain that it is by the intervention of this ligament, and not by a third tunic of the spinal cord, that the bodies of the vertebrae are bound together, with no membrane intervening. 

Therefore, if you agree with the Ancients, count these vertebral cartilages among the ligaments that possess the nature of cartilage. Consider likewise the great industry of Nature, which adapted this cartilaginous ligament so that it might assist the movements of the back by yielding and rising (as I have already understood previously). Furthermore, the bodies of the vertebrae are bound together by still other ligaments; for throughout the entire length of the back, very strong ligaments are wrapped around the entire circumference of the vertebral bodies. Although these are thick, dense, and robust on all sides, they are nonetheless smeared with a mucous humor <note>a lubricating fluid</note>; yet in the front part of the body, on either side, they become more visible because of their thickness. Thus, when these ligaments—or, if you wish to encompass them all under one name, this ligament—have perhaps become hard and are drawn equally over all the vertebrae, it certainly acts as an obstacle, lest...

<meta>catchword: est, ne (it is, lest)</meta>

<summary>Vesalius argues that the material between vertebrae is actually a "cartilaginous ligament" (intervertebral disc) rather than true cartilage, correcting Galen's views by citing Hippocrates and providing evidence from juvenile bone growth and comparative anatomy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed anatomical description of the spinal column's connective tissues. Having previously discussed the membranes lining the vertebral canal, Vesalius now turns to the ligaments that connect the various processes of the vertebrae and compares human anatomy with that of quadrupeds.</meta>

### THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

<margin>Ligaments located in places other than the vertebral bodies.</margin>
...this is to prevent the back from being stretched or curved too much during extension. For if the back were to bend back excessively, it would have been extremely harmful to the stomach, the great artery <term>the aorta</term>, and the hollow vein <term>the vena cava</term>. Furthermore, from each of the transverse processes to the neighboring transverse processes, a membranous ligament is stretched across the entire width of the interval; and in the spaces between the spines, from one spine to the next, membranous ligaments are contained, binding the spines to one another like the partitions between muscles. These membranes become so thick at the tips of the spines that, as they come together at the apexes, they constitute a ligament for the entire spine of the back, also possessing the nature of cartilage. Then, where the ascending processes of the vertebrae are articulated with the descending ones, membranous ligaments (but very strong ones) surround the joint on all sides. Moreover, there is a certain private, yellowish ligament <note>original: "subflavum ligamentum," known today as the *ligamentum flavum*</note> that arises from the internal side of the vertebral opening (which is carved out for the spinal cord), at the root of the spine or the process of the posterior vertebra, between the two ascending or descending processes, and is always inserted into the same spot of the subsequent vertebra.

<margin>Ligaments unique to dogs.</margin>
In dogs, and in those animals that can easily touch their muzzles to their backs, and which possess much looser joints in the neck vertebrae, and also longer neck vertebrae than man, we observe a certain ligament whose nature I shall not be burdened to add here for Galen's <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated anatomy for over a thousand years</note> sake. In dogs, therefore, as soon as you have approached the second pair of muscles serving the movements of the head, a rare ligament presents itself in the neck, corresponding to nothing else in the entire body, unless perhaps to those ligaments of the vertebrae we reviewed in the last place: for it is stronger than the others, yellow in color, and can be dissolved into many fibers. It arises from the sides of the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra's apex; and ascending upwards, it is joined to no vertebra until it reaches the second of the neck <term>the axis</term>, into whose spine it is inserted at the very tip. In some animals, such as sheep, it is inserted into the occipital bone. This ligament is wrapped in a special membrane and appears double because of an impression stretched along its length. Furthermore, one may learn the nature of this ligament whenever the neck of a calf, pig, kid, or even an older ox is served at the table. For this ligament is that yellow body which, when freed from the meat, we are accustomed to offer to the dogs; for among the rest of the body’s ligaments, it alone is rejected as unfit for eating. For this reason, because of its strength, it is called *Vaſt* <note>Vesalius uses the local Brussels/Flemish word *vast*, meaning "tough" or "firm"</note> by the people of Brussels, who recommend the eating of it to girls to obtain longer hair; laughing at them for this, I suppose, because it is easily separated into what looks like pale yellow hair. It is especially suited for the purpose of preventing the neck vertebrae from easily jumping out of place, since they are articulated quite loosely and are moved much more obliquely than the other vertebrae. And so also in certain quadrupeds, we see one large ligament of this nature carried along the spines on both sides, hidden among the muscles moving the back, nearly for the entire length of the whole back—the sort of ligament Galen attributed to humans in almost all his books *On the Use of the Parts*.

<margin>The preparation of the ligaments.</margin>
The preparation <note>original: "administratio," referring to the method of dissection</note> of the ligaments of the back possesses nothing peculiar. For when all the dorsal muscles have been removed, in the front part of the back, along the entire circumference of the bodies of the vertebrae, those membranes—tough and soaked in a certain moisture—are in view. You can free these from the bodies of the vertebrae with small knives placed crosswise under them; noting that there does not appear to be just one simple ligament here, but as if many small membranes were lying upon and growing into one another. Afterward, once the ribs have been disconnected from the vertebrae, you will also inspect their ligaments, just as you will those membranes in the intervals of the transverse processes and the spines...

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'Q' depicting several figures gathered in a room, with one figure seated at a table pointing towards a demonstration or dissection subject, typical of 16th-century anatomical textbook illustrations.</image-desc>SINCE I have resolved to follow the muscles in the same order of teaching as I am accustomed to demonstrate them in a single body, I thought it would be convenient to now approach the muscles situated in the arm, elbow, and hand in individual Chapters, and afterward subjoin their preparation in a general chapter for all. Thus, so that I may accommodate myself to Galen’s order regarding these muscles (which he described more extensively than all others), I shall begin with the <term>muscle</term> <note>The *palmaris longus*, a muscle often absent in some humans but prominent in the monkeys Galen dissected</note> which is stretched under the internal region of the hand by its spreading, slender tendinous nature. It arises from a tendinous and rounded <sup>b</sup> beginning at the apex of the internal tubercle of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle</note>, lying upon and attached to the middle <sup>d</sup> of the two muscles that flex the wrist (which come forth from the same tubercle), though it is <sup>c</sup> not placed exactly in the middle of their heads as others have written. This beginning immediately becomes more fleshy and thick, forming a muscle belly of moderate thickness. Before it has crawled halfway down the length of the elbow, being led somewhat obliquely toward the middle of the inner side of the forearm, it becomes thin and slender again, ending in a narrow tendon—though it is wider than it is deep, and by no means entirely round. From here, reaching as far as the root of the wrist, it begins to gradually <sup>e</sup> broaden in the inner part of the wrist and is born beneath the skin of the hand, extending almost to the very <sup>f</sup> tips of the fingers. This is accomplished with fibrous connections so strong and continuous that it is difficult to free the internal skin of the hand from the tendinous thinness, even with a very sharp razor. But in the meantime, one should by no means agree with Galen’s opinion if he believed that this muscle is born under the entire hairless skin of the hand in humans (as he teaches regarding his monkeys). Indeed, the tendon is born under the skin of the middle of the palm only, but it does not touch the skin <sup>g</sup> covering the muscle which we shall teach leads the little finger away from the others at an angle; nor is it stretched under the skin <sup>h</sup> covering the muscular flesh which, lying upon the first joint of the thumb, is composed of several muscles. Furthermore, no portions of this tendon run out to the sides of the fingers; on the contrary, the present tendon is seen to be born quite obscurely even in the internal region of the fingers. The muscle producing this tendon is slender and, as we have advised, is stretched out in the middle of the elbow above the rest of the muscles in this region; for it would not have been fitting for this to be built large, since we do not believe it is set in charge of moving any bone.

...scarcely mobile, partly due to certain other reasons, but primarily for a more exact and safer grasping of objects; however, this skin is also endowed with a finer sense of touch than the skin on the rest of the body. Yet, it is not by the benefit of this <term>broad tendon</term> <note>the palmar aponeurosis</note> that the hand attains its accurate sense of touch, but rather through the assistance of many nerves. We shall teach in the appropriate place that four branches are propagated from these to each individual finger: two for the outer side of the fingers and just as many for the inner side. It also contributes not a little to this exquisite touch that the inner skin of the hand is hairless, which Galen affirms is primarily due to the tendon dilated beneath it. For if it were very hairy, it would by no means be able to touch objects approaching it, because the hairs would encounter the object before the skin could, and would thus hinder its contact. Furthermore, because this tendon also makes the skin of this region somewhat hard, it is obvious to anyone that this serves many useful purposes for us. Therefore, for the sake of these benefits, the tendon is believed to originate beneath the inner skin of the hand. 

Indeed, I have shown more than once in my public dissections that this muscle we are describing was certainly absent, and that a portion of the tendons that flex the wrist, before they ascend the wrist, ended in a broad tendon. Sometimes, however, we have seen that the part performing the role of the broad tendon was not provided by those tendons, but rather by the <term>transverse ligament</term> <note>the flexor retinaculum</note> stretched over the tendons in the inner part of the wrist. Similarly, in humans—unlike in apes—no tendon widens out under the foot; for you will hear that in man, a membrane arises from the heel bone which most aptly expresses the nature of a broad tendon. 

Otherwise, however, despite certain passages in Galen, one should not conclude that these tendons, or their nervous nature, are attached to the skin without any intervening substance, or that the skin is separated from the tendon by no interval. For between the tendon and the skin in both the hand and the foot, a great deal of fat is contained, the nature of which I shall now explain. Not only do humans have this, but dogs also possess a great deal of it. Indeed, the entire tubercle that protrudes at the root of their four toes, and by which they primarily fix their foot, swells with the presence of that fatty substance, even though otherwise apes and dogs may be entirely destitute of fat between the fleshy membrane and the skin.

# ANDREAS VESALII ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II

...substance differs from fat, but also by the frequent intertwining of nervous fibers and thin veins. Furthermore, in extremely emaciated individuals, a certain portion of this substance is always found, as if it were a distinct and peculiar part of the body, quite unlike fat, which in very young children, and those who are completely wasted away and died of marasmus <note>original: "marasmode mortuis," referring to death from severe malnutrition or wasting</note>, is hardly detected during dissection. But the Arabs <note>Vesalius refers here to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna, whose anatomical works he often critiqued for inaccuracies</note> seem to me to be hallucinating when they affirm that this substance outside the muscle body is simple and unmixed flesh, in the manner of those who place some unknown simple flesh in the gums and the penis. For they by no means considered the innumerable nerve fibers and thin veins, like hairs, running through this substance, and that it resembles muscle flesh neither in color (since it tends toward white rather than red) nor in substance, nor in the equality or continuity of the muscles (which otherwise is entwined with so many fibers and is almost nothing but a kind of fiber). Nature has prepared this kind of substance—which you could only accurately compare to a somewhat hard and clustered fat—as a kind of layer or soil, into which the infinite forks of small nerves are aptly implanted. These needed to be spread everywhere from the larger nerve branches entering the inner part of the hand because of the exquisite sense of touch. Moreover, although this fat is harder and quite fibrous, it is nonetheless soft in its overall substance; and thus it yields to things it encounters, and it serves the fingers for something else—and that not the least important. For it is placed between the tendons that flex the fingers and the hard bodies we grasp; it most aptly protects the tendons so they are neither pressed nor bruised. For this reason, quite rightly, a great deal of this substance is placed beneath the skin of the sole of the foot. Furthermore, it corrects the alignment of the bones when the hand is about to grasp something in a circle. Accordingly, the Creator <term>Opifex</term> <note>Latin for "The Craftsman" or "Artisan," a term Vesalius frequently uses to describe the intelligent design of Nature</note> did not grant this to the outer region of the fingers at all, as it would bring useless weight to the fingers there; since this region neither requires that most perfect sense of touch, nor does it grasp anything obliquely, nor does it so often push forward awls, scalpels, or tools of that kind, nor soften and rub many things. Furthermore, in the inner part of the hand, the industrious Creator of things <note>original: "Conditor," another term for the divine architect of the body</note> produced the least amount of this substance at the joints themselves, but the most in the parts midway between the joints. For the sites of the bones where they are articulated with each other did not need this kind of substance, since they must be flexed and thus move away from the object being grasped. And that substance, besides providing no benefit in those places, would become an obstacle to movement, both as a burden (being superfluous) and by preventing the joints from being flexed into acute angles. Nature has nourished the sides of the fingers with just enough of this substance to fill the middle regions there, which would have remained empty because of the protrusions of the joints. Thus, the hand could perform its duty not only as an organ divided into many parts, but also as if it were variously undivided. For when the fingers are brought together, their middle region is so filled by this substance that if one wishes to hold even a liquid in the upturned palm, it does not leak out. Indeed, it is most obvious to everyone how much help this substance provides for grasping objects with the fingertips; it is no secret that if nothing that could yield had been placed

->at the ends of the bones, they would easily have been broken, nor could many bodies<-
->be lifted by them: which we now through the work of this substance, and<-
->the fingernails resisting it, accomplish most successfully.<-

## ON THE MUSCLES Moving the Fingers of the Hand. Chapter 43.

Movements of the fingers.

<image-desc>A large historiated initial letter 'C' depicting a group of several men gathered around a table, performing or observing a medical demonstration or dissection of a limb.</image-desc>
WHEN I pursued the construction of the bones of the five fingers in the previous book, I wrote that a far<sup>a</sup> different type of joint is found in the first segments <note>original: "internodiis," the phalanges of the fingers</note> of the five fingers and in the second segment of the thumb, than in the second and third segments of the four fingers and the third segment of the thumb. For the latter enter into one another with that kind of joint which the Greeks call a <term>ginglymus</term> <note>original: "γίγγλυμον," a hinge joint</note>. In this arrangement, the upper bone receives the protrusion of the lower bone into its own cavity, while the lower bone itself receives the small heads of the upper bone within its boundaries. Consequently, these segments possess only a simple movement, which is performed through extension and flexion, never turning even slightly to the side. However, the first bones of the four fingers are joined in articulation with those bones by which they are supported <note>the metacarpals</note> in a tighter fashion: for a single cavity in the finger bone receives a single head of the <term>postbrachial</term> <note>original: "postbrachialis," referring to the metacarpal bones</note> bone. For this reason, those first bones of the fingers, as well as the first joint of the thumb, can be moved with a double motion, by which they are flexed and extended, and moreover are inclined to the sides, or—as we have established our way of speaking—are <term>adducted</term> toward these or those fingers, or <term>abducted</term> from them. Furthermore, we shall teach that all movements of the fingers are completed by twenty-eight muscles; but since in the discussion of them<sup>b</sup> a certain muscle inserted into the wrist must also necessarily be treated, twenty-nine will be described in this chapter.

As soon as the tendons have passed that ligament, they spread apart from each other, forming three sharp angles equal in their intervals; each one approaches the one of the four fingers positioned before it, and having been made broader and membrane-like, they are inserted into the base of the second bone of the fingers, and then into the whole length of the bone.

^z^ Furthermore, so that the tendons of the second muscle might elegantly reach the third internode <note>The distal phalanx, or fingertip bone</note> of the finger, since the tendons of the first muscle are already necessarily seeking their insertion into the second bone, it was necessary for either the tendons of the second muscle to be extended to the sides of the first muscle's tendons, or—since they are placed directly beneath them—for the tendon resting upon them to be perforated, and in this way for the underlying tendon of the second muscle to be passed through. But since the width of the bones does not allow the tendons of the second muscle to turn to the side, and since, if they were led to the side, they would surely hold an oblique position and thus lead to an oblique movement, it remained for the upper tendon to be split by a long section with wondrous industry. Through this section, the tendon of the second muscle is carried to reach the base of the third bone, acting as the author of its flexion, as I shall say later.
