...it was formerly <note>The text begins mid-word with "tiquum," likely completing "antiquum" from the previous page.</note> believed that these tendons are inserted into the sides of the second bone of the fingers. In truth, they are implanted most strongly into the internal surface of those bones. After they have been perforated <note>Vesalius is describing the "chiasm," where the superficial tendon splits to let the deep tendon pass through it.</note>, their tips are gathered together under the tendons of the second muscle. As if they had not been perforated at all, but only made wider, they effect their insertion. In old men, or those with particularly bony frames, a small bone <term>sesamoid bone</term><note>Small, seed-like bones embedded in tendons to reduce friction, named after sesame seeds.</note> often grows within the tendon just before this insertion. This bone is classified among those compared to sesame seeds; in both use and form, it somewhat resembles the kneecap <note>original: *patella*</note>, as do the other sesamoid bones. With its smooth surface (which protrudes from the substance of the tendon), it is placed before the groove that occurs between the two heads where the first bone of the four fingers meets the socket of the second bone. And just as such little bones grow in the tendons of the first muscle, others also occur in the tendons of the second muscle before they are inserted into the third bones of the fingers. This little bone of the tendons is placed before the groove and corresponds to the heads of the second bone of the fingers, which are articulated into the sockets of the third bone. However, among all the sesamoid bones visible elsewhere in the hand, these which grow in the tendons of the two muscles just mentioned are the smallest and most difficult to observe. Furthermore, just as the tendons of the first and second muscles are bound by a **transverse ligament** <note>The flexor retinaculum at the wrist.</note> at the wrist and along the entire length of the first finger bone, so too, along the whole length of the second bone, another ligament wraps around the tendon of the second muscle as it extends here. To put it simply, a ligament of this sort is stretched over the entire internal surface of the fingers. It is attached to the tendons by no membrane, no other bond, and not even a fiber; nor does any membrane intervene there between the two tendons where they support each other. However, in the palm of the hand <note>original: *vola*</note>, before the tendons enter the ligaments of the fingers, each is covered by its own small membrane, which is attached to the tendons by certain fibrous connections.

The **third muscle** <note>The *flexor pollicis longus*, which moves the thumb.</note> is entirely distinguished by me from the second muscle. I am not particularly concerned whether you count it with the second (and then claim the second is divided into five fleshy parts and as many tendons), provided that the true description of this third muscle is not suppressed. It extends along the whole length of the forearm <note>original: *cubiti*</note> along the upper side of the second muscle. It is nowhere continuous with that muscle, except perhaps at the joint where the forearm meets the upper arm <note>original: *humerum*</note>; rather, just as other muscles lying against each other usually do, it merely adheres to it throughout its course. It arises from a fleshy and rounded beginning on the ulna, at the spot where the ulna receives the head of the radius into its own socket. From here, it stretches along the radius, being attached to it for almost its entire length and continually drawing its origin from it—especially from that place where the membranous ligament <note>The interosseous membrane between the radius and ulna.</note> arises, which stretches along the length of the forearm and also offers a portion of origin to this muscle. When the muscle, thus spread out over the radius, hastens toward the wrist, it ends in a rounded tendon covered by a specific membrane moistened with fluid. It is not covered by the common membrane that invests the tendons of the second muscle in the space of the wrist. Furthermore, the tendon of the third muscle is placed under none of the four tendons of the second muscle, although it is carried through the transverse ligament of the wrist, held against the side that stands at the base of the thumb. There, the wrist bone that supports the thumb <note>The trapezium.</note> has a groove carved out specifically for this tendon. Once the tendon has turned back and been hidden between the muscles that flex the first and second bones of the thumb, it creeps to the second joint <note>original: *internodium*</note> of the thumb. Caught there by a transverse ligament along the entire length of the second bone, it reaches the third bone, into which it is strongly and broadly inserted. It is the architect of the flexion of that bone, as I shall soon describe. However, before the tendon [reaches] the third joint of the thumb...

...this tendon <note>original: "tendo iste"; referring to the tendon of the flexor pollicis longus</note> completely surpasses [the others] right up to its insertion. In this tendon, a tiny **sesamoid bone** <term>sesamoid bone: small, seed-like bones embedded in tendons to reduce friction</term> is born, which—with its smooth and slippery surface protruding outside the tendon—is placed before the front seat of the cavity, visible between the two "heads" <note>the condyles of the bone</note> where the second bone of the thumb enters the cavity of the third bone. <margin>q. As if a portion were led from the tendon marked "q" in the 6th table to the 8th.</margin> In **tailed monkeys**, you will not find this third muscle; rather, in the middle of the palm, a small portion arises from the tendon of the second muscle <note>the flexor digitorum profundus</note> as it seeks the middle finger. This portion is led transversely to the thumb and is implanted into its last bone. Thus, this small part of the tendon does not acquire a unique fleshy portion like the other four tendons of the second muscle do, nor is it even tied to the tendon approaching the middle finger; instead, it arises directly from it, carried transversely across the tendon of the index finger.

<margin>r. 6th table, u. s. 6th table, z.</margin>
On the other hand, **tailless monkeys** <note>apes</note>, which approach the human construction more closely, do possess a third muscle similar in shape and path to the human muscle (except that it is even more notably continuous with the second muscle). However, just as the thumb in those monkeys is much smaller and weaker than the thumb given to man, so too their third muscle is seen to be proportionately smaller and more slender than the human muscle.

Indeed, since the thumb of those monkeys is built with even shorter and more slender bones than their other fingers, the third muscle deservedly produces a more slender tendon in them than the tendons of the second muscle are. Meanwhile, in man, the tendon of the third muscle significantly exceeds the tendons of the second muscle in thickness, just as the human thumb surpasses the other fingers in size and strength.

<margin>Book 1 of *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin>
Thus, it is hardly surprising that Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius is correcting</note>, when approaching his dissections more precisely, wrote in the first book of *Anatomical Procedures* that the tendon of this muscle (which we call the "third") is more slender than those tendons produced by the second muscle. He surely would not have done this if he had been eager to hand down the description of humans rather than monkeys to posterity, or if he had otherwise adapted humans for his dissection—especially then, when he so extensively mocked the Epicurean philosophers and the physicians of Asclepiades regarding the difference in size and strength between a human thumb and a monkey's thumb. By rebuking them, he easily showed how he himself never actually dissected a human thumb.

<margin>Many things are proposed here contrary to Galen's views.</margin>
Furthermore, if you consider that our discourse on the true fabric of the human body has thus far brought forward many things that conflict with Galen’s opinions in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*—and especially that fiction where he, still quite unskilled in anatomy, invents the idea that the thumb is not flexed toward the middle of the wrist like the other fingers, but over the others toward the middle of the palm—

<margin>At the end of Book 1 of *Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>
do not accuse me of ignorance, or of "impiety" toward Galen, our common teacher, until you have performed a dissection with your own hands (to use his own words), or until you have watched someone else handle a dissection accurately, now that you have been warned, observing the whole matter diligently in both monkeys and humans.

For you will find that not only the things just mentioned rightly conflict with Galen’s opinion and teaching, but also this especially: what I have added regarding the function of the second and third muscles. Galen thinks—and with him the entire chorus of professors of dissection—that the second muscle <note>flexor digitorum profundus</note> flexes the first and third bones of the four fingers, and that what we have listed as the "third" muscle manages the flexion of the second and third bones of the thumb. However, both are in truth the workers of the flexion of only the *third* bone of their respective fingers, just as the first muscle [is for] the second bone. For it is held as a most firm axiom by Galen and other anatomists that no muscle primarily moves a bone unless it is inserted into it. But the tendons of the second muscle are not inserted or even attached to the first four bones of the fingers, nor is the tendon of the third [muscle] inserted into the second bone of the thumb, even in the slightest way. Therefore, these muscles do none of those things. For I believe there will be no one (even if Galen asserts it in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*) who [would say] the tendon of the second muscle...

## ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

...he [Galen] was about to say that the tendon is implanted into the first bone as it spreads out. Although Galen, having become more practiced in dissection over time, attempted to restore an entire page in that same place—with three phrases concerning the transverse ligament thrown in—he was nevertheless poorly mindful of his own words when he later collected the count of the insertions of the tendons into the fingers. Therefore, if by the benefit of the transverse ligament <term>transverse ligament: referring here to the annular ligaments or "pulleys" of the finger</term>—which exists on the first bones of the four fingers and the second bone of the thumb—these bones were flexed by the tendons of the second and third muscles, let any man who fights for Galen (and who thinks his later views are truer and more sensible) answer this: why would the **tendons of the first muscle not also flex the first four bones of the digits?** <margin>t. 5th table, e.</margin> Since these, too, are contained by the same ligament. For there is absolutely nothing by which one could demonstrate why the first segments <note>original: "internodia"; the phalanges</note> should be flexed by the tendons of the second muscle rather than those of the first. Furthermore, let him bring forward, I pray, why Galen did not perceive that the tendons of the second muscle are entirely responsible for the flexion of the second bone of the four fingers? Even though at the base of the second bone, and along its entire length, these tendons are covered by a transverse ligament. In addition to this, I should like him to teach me why the first, second, and third muscles moving the digits do not also flex the wrist <note>original: "brachiale"; the carpus</note>, since even in the inner seat of the wrist they are contained by a **strong and substantial transverse ligament of no small length.** <margin>u. 4th table, θ.</margin>

<margin>x. 1st table of muscles, Σ, s.</margin> Similarly, I would like someone to devise a reason why the many muscles occupying the shin <note>original: "tibia"</note>—which, as they approach the foot, **are wrapped in transverse ligaments between the end of the shin bone and the heel, and again between the tip of the fibula (or the outer ankle) and the heel**—do not also move the foot with the help of those ligaments, even though the logic is the same in all these cases: as it is indeed in all other muscles which are clothed in a transverse ligament on a bone other than the one from which they took their origin. And therefore, to gain support for this paradox of mine, I do not bring forward the many tendons in the **outer seat of the forearm and in the anterior region of the shin**, which are surrounded by ligaments in those same places.

Therefore, just as it is more certain than certainty itself that the three muscles of the fingers described so far do not flex the wrist, so too must they not be considered the agents of flexion for any bones except those into which they are actually inserted. If anyone, nevertheless, should think that the first bone of the four fingers is flexed by the first and second muscles, and the second bone of the thumb by the third muscle, through the intervention of the transverse ligament (even though we shall soon show that Nature has bestowed **two peculiar muscles on each of the first bones of the four fingers, and three on the second bone of the thumb, as the authors of the flexion of those bones**), <margin>a. 7th table, characters 1, 2, 3; 8th table, Δ.</margin> let him not carelessly weigh the power of flexion of each segment. For the first segment <note>the proximal phalanx</note>—which, in his opinion, would be bent by the tendons of the first and second muscles, and then by two other muscles to be explained shortly—shows a strength of flexion hardly firmer than that of the third segment <note>the distal phalanx</note>, even though only a single tendon is considered the leader of that motion. Furthermore, if anyone contends that flexion is performed by the benefit of the transverse ligaments, he must surely provide a reason why it happens that the third and second bones of the fingers can be flexed while the first bones remain extended and unmoved. For if, by the help of the transverse ligaments, the tendons of the second muscle bent the first bones, it would follow that whenever the third bones were flexed, the first would always experience the same, since a contracted tendon must necessarily exert force and resistance against the ligament in which it is wrapped. <margin>b. 6th table, ε, ζ, η.</margin> **Nature, therefore, produced the three muscles now mentioned from distant regions—namely, through the entire length of the forearm**—lest, if they took their origin in the hand, they would overwhelm it with flesh and make it large and heavy. Considering the various tasks performed by the hand, how much inconvenience this would have caused anyone...

<summary>Vesalius critiques Galen's understanding of finger flexion, arguing that tendons only flex the specific bones they insert into, despite passing through various "pulleys" or transverse ligaments. He explains that Nature placed the bulky parts of these muscles in the forearm to keep the hand light and agile for delicate tasks.</summary>

anyone can very readily gather. Furthermore, a greater strength was required for flexion than could be provided by short muscles that took their origin from the bones nearest to those that were to be moved. And for this same reason—namely, so that the fingers might be capable of powerful flexion—the three joints of the fingers are not flexed by the help of only one muscle, but each joint requires its own specific muscles. Those joints, indeed, which needed to be moved only in a straight line, without inclining to either side, were satisfied with a single, strong tendon. Those, however, which by their flexion also needed to be inclined to the sides, required several tendons and muscles, and those not particularly strong (just as their lateral flexion is also weak).

<margin>Use of the transverse ligaments.</margin>
Furthermore, transverse ligaments <term>transverse ligaments: these are the fibrous sheaths or "pulleys" that hold tendons against the bone</term> are drawn over the tendons along the bones of the fingers (as is sufficiently clear by now). This is done so that whenever we bend the second or third bone of the fingers, the tendons—instead of being like straight, stretched cords or rods that do not curve according to the flexion of the bones—do not rise up from the bent bone toward the elbow, lifting the skin to a strange height and filling the palm of the hand in an ugly way. For these ligaments, even if the tendons are contracted, force them to lie against the bones into which they are not inserted.

<margin>Use of the mucous membranes.</margin>
In the palm and the seat of the wrist <note>original: "brachialis"; the carpus</note>, the tendons are clothed in mucous membranes <term>mucous membranes: here referring to synovial sheaths</term>, so that they might proceed more safely, having obtained these membranes as if they were bulwarks and walls. But another use for the membranes of the second muscle <note>the flexor digitorum superficialis</note> also exists: for you will hear that the oblong and small muscles <margin>c, 6th table; f to y, 7th table.</margin> <note>These are the lumbrical muscles</note> by whose work we bring the four fingers toward the thumb, take their origin from that membrane.

<margin>Thirteen muscles following the third in number, succeeding in order.</margin>
However, it will now be appropriate to approach the muscles that flex the first four bones of the digits, and the first and second bones of the thumb. These are thirteen in number: specifically, two for each of the first joints of the five fingers, and three for the second joint of the thumb. <margin>d to f, 7th table.</margin> Those that serve the four fingers all go straight along the length of the metacarpus <margin>Those eight which serve the four fingers.</margin> <note>original: "postbrachialis"</note> to the fingers. Of the two muscles flexing the little finger <margin>f, 4th table, 7.</margin>, one arises from a fleshy beginning on the outer side of the upper part of the metacarpal bone positioned before the little finger, being also somewhat attached there to the wrist. From here, ascending straight, it remains fleshy as far as the first bone of the finger; but where it touches the bone, it is inserted into the side of the outer bone toward the interior by a somewhat broad tendon. The other muscle takes its origin from the inner side of that same metacarpal bone, near its end by the wrist; and extending toward the finger between that bone and the one next to it, it also remains fleshy until it is implanted into the inner side of the first bone of the little finger by a broad and, as it were, membranous tendon. When both muscles are contracted together, the first bone of the finger is flexed without leaning to either side. If, however, the outer one acts while the inner is at rest, the finger is flexed while inclining slightly toward the outer part; but with only the inner one working, the finger experiences flexion while drawing toward the interior.

The muscles of the other three fingers behave in exactly this way, so that two are placed in each of the intervals of the metacarpal bones (of which there are three). <margin>g, 8th table, X.</margin> The one which is inserted into the inner side of the index finger is attached to the internal side of the metacarpal bone supporting the index, protruding more into the palm than into the external region of the hand, like the other muscles flexing the first joints. Furthermore, those which flex the second bone of the thumb are reckoned as three in number, occupying a position more different from those that flex the first bones of the four fingers than do the two workers of the first thumb bone's flexion. For those serving the four fingers proceed straight along the length of the hand; however, those which flex the first bone of the thumb are led somewhat obliquely; but the muscles that are the authors of the flexion of the second thumb joint are seen to be somewhat transverse. For it was worthwhile for the four fingers to be inclined toward the wrist, but for the thumb, opposed to them in function, to be bent toward them. Rightly, therefore, the three muscles flexing the second thumb bone take their origins from the palm, as if from a quarter-circle: specifically at the circumscription of that line which is customarily called the **line of life** and the **line of the heart** by palm-readers. Although they take their beginning from the palm a little further out than where that line stays, specifically at the upper and outer side of that **triangle** which palm-readers place in the middle of the palm. Thus, the first muscle takes an oblique and broad origin from the metacarpal bone on which the middle finger rests, slightly below its small head articulated to the finger. Creeping forward from here as a fleshy mass, it is rendered somewhat narrower and inserts itself with a membranous tendon into the side of the second thumb bone that faces the index finger, toward the interior. The second muscle, contiguous on its lower side to the muscle just mentioned, takes its origin from the middle seat of the metacarpal bone which is placed before the middle finger, also touching somewhat the bone by which the ring finger is supported. The origin of this one is also thin and broad, and it is seen to be fleshy immediately up to its insertion, which it attempts in the middle of the inner part of the second thumb joint. The third muscle, closest to this one, takes an equally broad origin from the root of the metacarpal bone supporting the ring finger, which is narrowed at the wrist; and approaching the thumb obliquely, it is implanted into the inner side of the second thumb joint toward the front, also with a broad and short tendon, in which the principal or largest of the <note>original: "sesaminorũ ossiculorũ"</note> sesamoid bones found around the fingers of the hand is born: just as it is in the tendon of the first of the muscles flexing the second thumb bone.

### ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY]

...to the tendon, another small bone <note>original: "ossiculum"</note> fell to its lot, but a slightly smaller one. <margin>z Figure 2, Chapter 25, Book 1, T.</margin> These two small bones <note>These are sesamoid bones, small seed-like structures that function like pulleys to improve mechanical advantage.</note> meet, or rather are positioned with their smooth and slippery surface—where they protrude from the tendons—at the anterior seat of the first bone of the thumb, which is articulated into the socket of the second bone. Thus, <margin>a Table 6 of muscles, d; the marked muscles.</margin> these small bones face the sides of that seat, so that they allow the tendon of the muscle moving the third [set of] fingers to be carried safely and without compression, or otherwise a deceptive seat, to the third bone of the thumb. Furthermore, when these three muscles are contracted and gathered together, they most strongly flex the intermediate [second] bone of the thumb. However, when only the first acts, the thumb is directed upward toward the index finger. When only the second is contracted, the thumb is flexed toward the middle fingers, just as when the lowest one is contracted toward its origin, the flexion of the thumb downward and more toward the little finger is accomplished. <margin>Three muscles flexing the second bone of the thumb, unknown to Galen.</margin> Although these three are also observed in apes, <term>Galen: A 2nd-century Greek physician whose work was the undisputed authority for over a millennium</term> was not only ignorant of them but even constructed false reasons in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*. An inexperienced person paying attention to these reasons would not even attempt to approach these [muscles] among the second [group]. Nor is it likely that when he issued his *Anatomical Procedures* for the second time, and inserted one line in the second book of *On the Use of the Parts* about the muscles flexing the first joints of the fingers, that these muscles were known to him—undoubtedly after the publication of those books and not from the general opinion of the description occurring elsewhere in them—since he described them nowhere. This is unlike what the <term>Arabs: Referring to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna or Rhazes, whose Latin translations were standard medical textbooks</term> did, who, as far as I can guess, knew these and yet neglected the two that preside over the flexion of the first bone of the thumb. For they enumerated eleven muscles constructed for flexing the fingers in the hand: eight referring to the four fingers, and three to the thumb. Though again I may doubt whether they themselves wrote "eleven" instead of "ten" by chance following Galen, since without any other description, they merely list the muscles in the manner of <term>Oribasius: A 4th-century Greek medical compiler</term>. Furthermore, in the first book of Galen’s *Anatomical Procedures*, all the codices I have seen so far have three errors in the numbers. For "eight" is read there instead of "two" where the muscles of the hand serving the lateral movements of the thumb are described. And again, almost at the end of the book where the muscles moving the elbow are listed, "three" is written where "two" should be, and "two" where "three" should have been written. This is just as "First Use" is badly read there for "Second," where Galen in the same book commemorates the uses of the ligaments. But these things, along with truly innumerable others, have been honestly restored in Galen by my own effort, which Italy and Germany have recently given in Latin.

Thus far, I have commemorated sixteen muscles by which the fingers are flexed; and therefore, <margin>The seventeenth of those moving the fingers.</margin> now <margin>b Table 9, Z; Table 2, V; Table 10, f.</margin> the seventeenth, which will be the first of those extending the fingers, will be described at an opportune time. It <margin>c Table 9, 4.</margin> arises from a principle mixed of fleshy and nervous substance, and somewhat broad, from the more prominent part of the outer <margin>d Figure 2, Chapter 23, Book 1, P.</margin> tubercle of the <term>humerus: the upper arm bone</term>. It extends through the middle of the forearm, large and fleshy, and slightly less than entirely round, having no connection to any other bone nor drawing its origin from anywhere other than the humerus. But when <margin>e Table 9, b.</margin> it reaches the end of the <term>radius: the outer and shorter of the two bones of the forearm</term>, where the <term>brachiale: the wrist or carpus</term> is articulated, having become narrower, it is split into three fleshy portions. These, being clothed together by a common membrane and clinging to each other by thin fibers, degenerate immediately into a tendon from their separation from the belly of the muscle. Together, they hasten toward the wrist through <margin>f Figures 2 and 4, Chapter 24, Book 1, y.</margin> a groove carved in the outer side of the radius. That groove is the one, out of four excavated in the outer side of the appendix of the radius, closest to the <margin>g Figure 1, Chapter 24, Book 1, i; or rather Figure 2, d.</margin> joint of the radius with the <term>ulna: the thinner and longer bone of the forearm</term>. Therefore, these three tendons lie in this groove—which is quite ample and corresponds exactly to the size of the bodies it must admit—and are wrapped <margin>h Tables 1 and 2, character s.</margin> by a transverse ligament peculiar to them, lest they should at any time slip out of the groove, and lest they should rise up high when their muscle is contracted. But when they have crept through the ligament and are already in the wrist...

The nineteenth muscle, lying beneath the two most recently described in the forearm <note>original: "cubito"</note>, is granted an oblique course. For from the <gloss>p</gloss> posterior process of the ulna, down to the seat of the ulna where it becomes exactly rounded not long before the wrist, certain muscles arise in a continuous series as if from a straight line, all endowed with an oblique position. And these possess three roots or beginnings: the first, which is the highest and closer to the arm, refers to the <gloss>r</gloss> muscle peculiar to the radius. The second, following in the next order, looks toward the thumb and the wrist; the description of the muscles extending the thumb will teach its course and its distribution into several muscles, as it were. But the third root—which we most need at present and which follows the second beginning in order—arises from the bone of the ulna beyond the middle of its length toward the wrist. Leading its origin as a purely fleshy and oblong line, it is rendered slightly narrower from its start; ascending obliquely downward toward the appendix of the radius, it is split into <gloss>u</gloss> two fleshy portions. The lower of these forms the nineteenth muscle, distinct from the upper part of that origin, which for the sake of teaching I shall call the twenty-first muscle, the one turning the thumb toward the other fingers. Therefore, I shall distinguish this third beginning into two muscles, although in the meantime, by reason of their origin, I do not object if anyone wishes to count both parts as a single muscle. The nineteenth, then, having arisen from the ulna in the manner I have described, seeks the appendix of the radius obliquely. Before it reaches this, it ends in two tendons joined to each other, which, resting in their own <gloss>x</gloss> groove in the appendix of the radius and bound across by a <gloss>y</gloss> peculiar ligament, expand over the wrist. This groove, carved in the end of the radius for these tendons, stands between the <gloss>z</gloss> groove cut for the seventeenth muscle and that in which the two-pronged tendon of the <gloss>a</gloss> muscle (by whose benefit the wrist is extended) is carried. This groove for the two-pronged tendon also transmits <gloss>b</gloss> another portion of that third beginning arising from the ulna, which you will hear serves the motions of the thumb. For it should by no means be thought that both portions of the third beginning use a single groove and ligament, or that a peculiar ligament is not drawn over this nineteenth muscle. Furthermore, when the tendons of the nineteenth muscle have passed the wrist and are quite compressed, they seek the root of the index and middle fingers, being inserted so that they are the authors of the abduction of those fingers—and especially the index finger—away from the thumb.

For the oblique course of the entire muscle testifies abundantly that it could not have been set in charge of anything but an oblique [motion]...

...to motion: as on the contrary, the eighteenth [muscle] rather works for the extension of the little finger than its abduction <note>moving away from the midline</note> from the other fingers, as is proven by its straight path through the forearm <note>original: "cubitum"</note>, and even more so by its position, which is seen under the little finger and not at all slanting toward the lower parts. Nor should one apply only a common level of attention to the varied mixing of tendons—which is not equal in all men—that occurs at the roots of the fingers, produced by the three muscles last mentioned: so that you may carefully weigh how many things I have necessarily written in the history of those muscles that conflict with Galen's teachings. For he handed down that the seventeenth muscle, before it reaches the wrist <note>original: "brachiale"</note>, is split into four tendons, assigning one of these to the little finger as well; although I have noted that this muscle is dissected into only three tendons. Furthermore, Galen wrote that these tendons are born together with the bones of the fingers only where they approach the joint connection, even though they are actually attached equally to the entire length of the bones. To this, he says that the muscle extending the fingers is carried through a sinus <note>a cavity or channel</note> and a transverse ligament that is common to the radius and ulna: whereas that ligament serves the eighteenth muscle, and the seventeenth claims its own ligament and sinus in the appendage of the radius. Next, when he describes the structure of the nineteenth muscle, much differently than the reality of the matter, he mentions that its origin hangs from the entire ulna, or the upper part of the ulna near the arm: though I have described the nineteenth muscle as being the lower portion, closer to the wrist (as it truly is), of the three origins or roots that come forth in a series from the ulna. Moreover, he assigns two tendons to the eighteenth muscle, and establishes it as the author of the abduction of the ring and little fingers from the thumb, with no account taken of that rare mixing of tendons mentioned by us: while I, meanwhile, contend that the eighteenth muscle primarily extends the little finger, for the reasons previously stated.

And now I shall describe the two following muscles. Of the<sup>t</sup> three origins of the muscles that were reported to arise from the ulna <note>The inner and longer of the two bones of the human forearm</note> along its length, the<sup>u</sup> middle origin is seen to be quite large and born from a sufficiently long line. Ascending obliquely over the radius, it is spread over that<sup>x</sup> muscle which I shall teach is extended into the wrist by a two-pronged tendon. As soon as this origin covers that muscle, it is<sup>y</sup> divided into two unequal portions, separated by no interval, but clinging to one another in the manner of muscles lying side by side. The upper portion, remaining fleshy for some time, ends in a somewhat round tendon inserted into the outer side of the wrist<sup>z</sup> bone that supports the thumb <note>This refers to the trapezium bone</note>. However, the lower portion of the origin, as soon as it has crept forward some distance, is<sup>a</sup> divided again into two fleshy parts. Each of these ends in a tendon, and together with the tendon of the upper portion, they sit in a<sup>b</sup> specific groove on the appendage of the radius <note>original: "radij appendice," referring to the styloid process of the radius</note> which is lightly but broadly incised. These three tendons, lying against one another, are covered by a<sup>c</sup> special ligament, although we have occasionally seen individual tendons provided with their own individual rings or transverse ligaments.

After the tendons of the lower portion have passed the wrist, one is implanted into the root of the first bone of the thumb, ending there on its external region near the internal side. The other tendon, adhering to the length of the first thumb bone only by a membranous connection, is inserted into the root of the second bone on its outer side toward the inner side. It does not entirely end there, but remains attached to the very tip of the thumb, clinging persistently to the second and third bones <note>Vesalius counts the metacarpal as the first bone of the thumb, followed by the two phalanges</note> like a membrane. Thus, it is<sup>d</sup> within our discretion, based on the second origin produced by the ulna, to establish one muscle here; or, for the sake of the<sup>e</sup> division of the tendons and the fleshy origin, to count three muscles, so that we assign one muscle to each tendon. Alternatively, because of the<sup>f</sup> continuity of the fleshy lower portion and the<sup>g</sup> insertion of its tendons into the same finger, it would be permitted to count only two muscles: so that the<sup>h</sup> upper portion looking toward the wrist is considered as one, and the<sup>i</sup> lower portion, divided in its course into two fleshy parts and as many tendons, is commemorated as one muscle.

<margin>
In the book *On Anatomical Procedures*.
</margin>

This latter view will be more accommodating to the opinion of Galen, since in any enumeration he counted the lower portion as only one muscle, as one who recognized and described its<sup>k</sup> single tendon as common to the three bones of the thumb. However, even tailless<sup>l</sup> apes lack that tendon which we said is inserted in humans only into the first bone of the thumb. Indeed, in tailed monkeys—which vary from the human fabric even more than the tailless ones—the entire second or middle<sup>m</sup> origin proceeding from the ulna produces only a single tendon. This tendon, first divided by a small interval in the region of the wrist, is inserted by a small portion into the wrist bone supporting the thumb, and by a larger portion it reaches the thumb as appears in other apes.

...muscles subservient to the movements of the thumb; and <sup>q</sup> four others besides, by which the four fingers are drawn toward the thumb. For the <term>thumb</term> <note>original: "pollex"</note>, since it must be opposed to the remaining fingers like a second hand, rightly claims for itself muscles by whose benefit it is mostly led away from them, and again, for the sake of various actions, is moved closest to the index finger. <sup>r</sup> The muscle which therefore abducts the thumb the most arises with a nervous principle—which immediately becomes fleshy—from the anterior seat of the <term>wrist bone</term> <note>original: "ossis brachialis"; Vesalius uses "brachiale" to refer to the carpus or wrist</note> upon which the thumb rests. Stretching downward, it is inserted by a membranous tendon into the second joint of the thumb. This muscle, together with <sup>s</sup> two others that flex the first <term>internode</term> <note>The space between joints; a phalanx</note> of the thumb and upon which this muscle is spread, forms the fleshy part of the palm that sits at the base of the thumb. 

Now, Galen, in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, left it written—not very truly—that this present muscle is inserted into the first bone of the thumb; yet it does not grow into it by any notable or true insertion, but merely clings weakly by fibrous connections. But it is no wonder that Galen taught us such an insertion, since when writing that, he was ignorant of the two muscles flexing the first bone of the thumb and thought them to be parts of the present muscle. This muscle <sup>t</sup> takes up the action of the inner muscle among those turning the thumb outward (which was the twenty-second in our order); and thus it removes the thumb as far as possible from the index finger. It is unique among the muscles occupying the hand and the forearm in that it appears somewhat leaden or bluish <note>original: "liueat"</note>, owing to its own proper membrane, which is thicker than others. 

<sup>u</sup> Another muscle, serving the lateral movements of the thumb, takes its fleshy beginning from the inner side (though toward the back) of the <sup>x</sup> <term>metacarpal bone</term> <note>original: "ossis postbrachialis"</note> which is placed before the index finger, and it arises along the entire length of that bone. This muscle is inserted by a fleshy implantation into the entire outer side of the first thumb bone, extending a membranous tendon also to the base of the second bone. Hence, its fibers are also somewhat transverse, led from the metacarpal to the thumb, and accordingly they also bring the thumb closest to the index finger, taking up the action of the <sup>y</sup> muscle that <sup>z</sup> turns the thumb outward (which is the twenty-first in our series). 

Furthermore, the <sup>a</sup> muscles that draw the four fingers toward the thumb are slender and round, each one extended from the four tendons of the second muscle (those which flex the third bone of the four fingers) <note>These are the lumbrical muscles</note>. For they arise from the membranous sheath that covers those tendons as they pass through the hollow of the wrist and its <sup>a</sup> transverse ligament. Moving from here together with the tendons to the fingers, and stretched along the inner side of the tendons, they are inserted into the base of the fingers, effecting a membranous insertion toward the inner side. Indeed, it was fitting for them to be inserted in that place, as they were intended to incline the four fingers sideways toward the thumb. It is certainly a rare thing in these present muscles, just as occurs in the <sup>b</sup> muscles of the eye, that they take their origin not from bone or cartilage, but from the membranous sheath of tendons.

<margin>
Out of the twenty-nine described muscles, twenty-eight serve the movements of the fingers.
Some remarks on the insertions of tendons.

Now, if for the sake of instruction you add these muscles to your count, a total of twenty-nine described in this chapter will emerge: twenty-eight of these are the leaders of the fingers, while the <sup>c</sup> twenty-third is meanwhile referred to the wrist. Furthermore, someone may perhaps wonder why I said the <sup>d</sup> muscles drawing the four fingers to the thumb and <sup>e</sup> the one that abducts the little finger from the rest are inserted into the first bone of the four fingers, making no mention of the succeeding internodes or bones. This is because Galen, in the first study of *On Anatomical Procedures*, left it written in a serious manner that the tendons of those muscles are inserted into all the bones of the fingers along their entire length like a membrane, and grow into them—differing from what he wrote in the book *On the Use of the Parts*, and what even earlier anatomists wrote. I do not at all deny that the bones of the fingers, along their length, are covered by membranes from the region of the insertion of those muscles, but they are not of such a kind...

...of the sort that the muscles just mentioned ought to extend. Since those membranes show no kind of fiber running lengthwise, they do not even maintain a similar path to the <sup>f 9 table Z, g 10 table f, r, p, o.</sup> tendons of the muscles that are inserted from the forearm into the outer surface of the fingers. Furthermore, it is only by the benefit of the first joint in the four fingers—and in a certain way the first and second joints in the thumb—that the fingers are moved sideways or at an angle. I previously mentioned the reason for this when I was tracing the bones of the fingers: it is due to the difference in the way the joints are formed. Therefore, if anyone should contend, along with Galen (to whom the differences and distinctions of the joints in the fingers were hidden), that such membranes are the tendons of the muscles acting on the sides, they must admit that these membranes are attached in vain, serving only as a ligament to the second and third bones of the fingers.

<margin>
A collection of muscle insertions.
</margin>

Again, a more diligent student well-versed in Galen’s books, noticing that he teaches very contradictory things about the insertion of tendons, will wait until I have reduced all the insertions of the muscles moving the fingers into a single total. In this, I shall imitate Galen in the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*, though he follows these details incorrectly. For, omitting <sup>g 6 table u, λ. 7 table characters 1, 2, 3. table 8 under Δ. h 6 table Ξ, i 9 table Z. k 9 table Θ. l 10 table p. 11 table t.</sup> thirteen muscles located in the hand that are the authors of finger flexion <note>The action of bending the fingers toward the palm.</note>, he falsely recorded there that the tendons of the muscle are implanted in the first bone of the four fingers. Furthermore, Galen attributes tendons to the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth muscles other than those he actually describes, and consequently, he attributes different insertions than those they actually achieve. 

And indeed, I would list the insertions of all the muscles moving the fingers in a catalog for the sake of understanding Galen, were it not for that varied mixing of tendons at the roots of the fingers—which the three mentioned muscles put forth—and their series divided as if into many forks through the outer surface of the fingers, which prevent me from stating the certain number of all those insertions in a brief discourse. 

However, if you were to ascribe to each of the four finger bones a double implantation on their back surface (in Galen's name and for the sake of concise speech), even though I meanwhile ascribe a nearly simple one to some of them (and especially to the bones of the little finger), and if you thereafter understood everything according to our opinion, there will be sixty true insertions in all (I do not mean mere "resting-places" or slight attachments). Specifically: five into the first joint of the thumb, seven into the second, and three into the third; six into the first <term>internode</term> <note>original: "internodium"; the bone between two joints, i.e., a phalanx bone.</note> of the little finger; but only five into the first internodes of the other three fingers; and three into the second and third internodes of the four fingers. 

Repeat to yourself what these insertions are, so that you may contract the muscles again in your memory as if in a summary. And then consider again how many there would be in total if the <sup>m 3 table r, p. 6 table f. f. 11 table f. n 10 table l, then m, n. o 3 table p.</sup> muscles presiding over lateral movements, which are placed in the hand, also achieved insertions into the succeeding bones—which do not move to the side (except secondarily)—according to Galen's opinion. And then also, if you admitted both tendons of the twenty-second muscle to be inserted into the first bone of the thumb by a true <term>insertion</term> <note>The point where a muscle's tendon attaches to the bone it moves.</note>, so that now the first internode of the thumb would admit six insertions (for the muscle that abducts the thumb the most is not truly inserted into its first bone), while the third bone of the thumb would have five, and the second and third internodes of the index, middle, and ring finger would also have four, while the second and third internodes of the little finger would obtain five insertions—then the total rises to seventy-three. 

If you then also numbered the applications made to the bones by the benefit of the <sup>p 6 table n, then θ. q muscle i" table 3, where the tendon is marked.</sup> transverse ligaments, and increased the second internode of the five fingers by one application, and the first of the four fingers by two, you will find (unless the addition has escaped me) eighty-six. For you cannot attribute the tendon of the third muscle to the first internode of the thumb, although this number could still claim for itself the applications of the broad tendon, so that the three of the four fingers...

## ON THE MUSCLES that produce the movements of the WRIST. Chapter XLIIII.

<margin>*The first of those moving the wrist.*</margin>

WHEN the remaining part of the hand is flexed or extended with the wrist, and then also moved to either side, it is done chiefly by the benefit of four muscles. Of these, the <sup>a</sup> first takes its <sup>c</sup> beginning, mixed from fleshy and nervous substance, from the <sup>b</sup> inner tuberosity of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle of the upper arm bone at the elbow</note>; from here it is attached to the whole length of the ulna, taking its strength from its origin along its progress from that bone. Moreover, this muscle is extended along the lower side of the muscles which, <sup>c</sup> creeping through the forearm, are in charge of flexing the fingers; hence it also embraces a <sup>e</sup> large part of the inner seat of the ulna, just as it also occupies the middle of the lower seat of the forearm, <sup>f</sup> upon which we lean when writing. <sup>g</sup> Another muscle claims for itself the remainder of that lower seat of the forearm, which is on the outside; you will hear that this muscle is inserted into the <term>postbrachiale</term> <note>the metacarpus, or the bones of the palm</note> before the little finger, and manages its extension. For those two muscles, sticking strongly together with fibrous connections, form a kind of layer and cushion upon which we allow the whole forearm to rest comfortably. Furthermore, when this first muscle has crept along to the end of the ulna, a little before the joint of the forearm with the wrist, it <sup>h</sup> terminates in a strong and somewhat rounded tendon, its inner seat always increased by fleshy substance up to the wrist. But where it transcends that point, it is entirely without flesh, being implanted by a very strong insertion into the upper <sup>i</sup> seat of the fourth bone of the wrist <note>the pisiform bone</note>, which we said in the first book is called the "straight and cartilaginous" bone, and is <sup>k</sup> connected to only a single bone. This present tendon, where it is supported by the appendage of the ulna and the joint of the wrist, possesses no specific ligament to be drawn across it; rather, it is surrounded by the common membrane of all the muscles (which acts in place of a ligament, and which we shall also review among the ligaments of the hand), and is very strongly connected to the ligaments of the wrist's joint with the forearm.

This muscle also takes its origin in part from the posterior process of the ulna <note>the olecranon, or the bony point of the elbow</note> which articulates with the humerus. It lies over that muscle which, also beginning there, goes to the radius and acts to turn it upward <note>the supinator muscle</note>. From here, the third wrist muscle emerges, embracing the lower and outer region of the ulna, stretched between the first of the wrist-movers and the muscle that extends the little finger. As it approaches the wrist, it ends in a round tendon that rests in a groove carved into the end of the ulna <note>the ulnar styloid process</note>, covered by a transverse ligament that is unique to the ulna. As soon as it passes over this ligament and reaches the wrist, it becomes wider and is inserted into the base of the <term>metacarpal bone</term> <note>original: "postbrachialis ossis"; the bones forming the palm of the hand</note> that supports the little finger. <margin>*The fourth muscle.*</margin>
The other of the outer muscles, which is fourth in order, arises with a somewhat broad beginning far above the outer bump of the humerus <note>the lateral epicondyle</note>, where the arm bone protrudes into an oblong sharpness and line. From here, emerging as a fleshy mass along a long line, it lies upon the radius; a little below the middle of its length, it terminates in a robust tendon. This tendon is seen to be "two-horned" or split into two parts right from its start, with each part being almost entirely round, though slightly wider than it is deep. These parts, or tendons, even if they are separated from one another, are not set apart by any noteworthy distance. They stretch in a straight path along the radius toward its end near the wrist. When they reach there, they rest in a groove carved for them and are surrounded by a ligament shared by them and the muscle that turns the thumb toward the index finger. Passing beyond this, they diverge from each other more than before and are implanted into the metacarpus with wide insertions (lest these thick, round tendons should bulge out beyond the rest of the surface of the hand). One attempts an insertion into the base of the bone supporting the index finger, while the other goes to the base of the bone upon which the middle finger rests.

<margin>*The function of the muscles.*</margin>
This fourth muscle, together with the third, reflects the wrist outward and extends it if both are contracted together. They are assisted by the muscle that we taught is inserted into the wrist bone where the thumb is supported, which we named the twenty-third in the entire series of muscles described in the previous chapter. And just as the wrist is extended by these two, so it is beautifully flexed by the two inner or first muscles. Furthermore, by these same muscles to which the flexion and extension of the wrist are entrusted, we also move the wrist to the sides. For if the inner and outer muscles facing the index finger are contracted while the other two are relaxed, the wrist is moved inward and toward the inner side. But if these are relaxed and the other two, which face the little finger, are contracted, the wrist moves toward the outer side.

<margin>
*t 1, 2, 4, 5, figures of chapter 25, book 1 characters 1, 2, 3 in x, y, z ft. 8 chapter 24, book 1.*
</margin>
<margin>*The wrist does not move into pronation or supination by its own motion.*</margin>
Furthermore, besides these movements that we attribute to the wrist, Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius often challenged</note> ascribed to it a specific version into <term>pronation and supination</term> <note>palms-down and palms-up positions</note>, distinct from the motion the hand secondary acquires by the benefit of the radius. To me, however, it has not yet been possible to perceive any movement of the hand or wrist into pronation or supination while the radius remains still. Moreover, the cavity of the radius where the wrist articulates is oblong; the wrist itself, where it meets this cavity, is also oblong, and is not seen to be round like the head of the humerus or the femur. Thus, the joint formed here by the bones is utterly unsuited for rotation. <margin>*Book 2, On the Use of the Parts.*</margin> But just as Galen ascribes specific pronation and supination movements to the wrist, so he also contends that the four muscles described are the authors of those movements, depending on which one contracts or rests. If you weigh his opinion carefully, you will notice that he made these things up—imagining them rather than seeing them in <term>dissection</term> <note>original: "resectione"</note>—as he did with many other things (by Jupiter!) in his books *On the Use of the Parts*.

-> ## Chapter XLV: On the muscles moving the radius in pronation and supination. <-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' showing several young children (putti) in a classical setting. One child appears to be leaning against a stone block while others play or work nearby, set against a backdrop of ancient ruins and a small tree.</image-desc>

<margin>
a Book 1, chapter 24, figure 9, from O to P; and book 1, chapter 21, figure 1.

Four muscles specifically for moving the radius.
</margin>
Provided that you remember what we handed down in the previous book concerning the joint of the radius at the rounded head of the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, the joints of the wrist with the radius, and the connections of the radius and ulna <note>the two bones of the forearm</note> to one another: you will now perceive with moderate effort the manner in which the radius is pulled by its own muscles. While the ulna remains at rest against the humerus, the radius is led around into <term>pronation</term> <note>turning the palm downward</note> and <term>supination</term> <note>turning the palm upward</note>, and you will see how the hand, by the benefit of the radius, obtains these same movements secondarily. Therefore, since the radius is articulated with the ulna at both its upper and lower ends, and since those two bones are distant from each other through the rest of their length, it was worthwhile for muscles to be constructed above and below to move it. There are four of these: two serving the upper end of the radius, and the remaining two the lower. Of these, two occupy the internal side of the elbow, while the other two occupy the external side. The inner ones move the radius into pronation; the outer ones pull it back into supination.

<margin>
The first.

The interior muscle, which moves the part of the radius closest to the wrist <note>the pronator quadratus</note>, arises along the length of the ulna from the entire breadth of its inner side where it is nearest the wrist. From here, being fleshy, it proceeds transversely to the inner region of the radius, and is inserted into it while still fleshy. Thus, if this muscle is compared with the others stretched along the length of the forearm, it has transverse fibers, climbing across from the ulna into the radius. This muscle does not, as it seemed to the professors of dissection <note>a reference to earlier anatomists who followed Galen's animal-based descriptions</note>, lie between the radius and the ulna; rather, along the breadth of the forearm, it encompasses the entire inner side of the radius and ulna, and is perfectly square <note>original: "quadratus est"</note>. Indeed, it possesses a length equal to the width of the inner region of the forearm formed by the radius and ulna together; and it is seen to be as wide as it is long. In addition, it is fleshy in every part, and in its middle it is observed to be thick and bulging, like a cushion <note>original: "instar puluinaris"</note> placed under the tendons passing over it to the fingers. The fibers of this muscle, by pulling the part of the radius that faces the wrist inward, drive the radius into pronation.

For otherwise, Galen would have wrongly said that it was the longest of all, since many of those extending to the fingers are simply much longer. Therefore, from the outer region of the humerus, higher up than the head of the muscle that extends the wrist with a double tendon, the origin of this radial muscle is brought forth. Because it is born wide along the length of the humerus and is fleshy, its higher seat is placed far above the outer tubercle of the humerus. From here the muscle expands downward, appearing wide and strong, and rests upon the radius, lying next to the upper side of the muscle that extends the wrist with a double tendon. But when it reaches the end of the radius where the wrist is joined, its process ends in a precise tendon which, broadening like a membrane, is inserted into the upper region of the radial appendage <note>the styloid process</note>, insofar as it is extended into the inner parts...

# ON THE MUSCLES FLEXING
### and extending the elbow. Chapter XLVI.

<margin>
a Book 1, ch. 24, fig. 9 with P; book 1, ch. 23, fig. 1.
b Book 1, ch. 23, fig. 1, 2, K, L, M with C, D, E; book 1, ch. 24, fig. 1, 5, 11.
</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'Q' depicting several infants (putti) in a clinical or workshop setting. One child is seated on a low stool while others assist in what appears to be an anatomical preparation or surgery involving a limb and surgical tools.</image-desc>
<margin>Muscles moving the elbow: either 5, 4, or 3.</margin>
JUST AS the radius is placed in a prone or supine position by the benefit of its joint with the ^a humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, so also the joint of the ^b ulna with the humerus most fitly serves the flexion and extension of the entire elbow: and meanwhile the radius is articulated to the humerus in such a way that it can be flexed and extended toward the humerus together with the ulna. Now the muscles that lead these movements, if reduced to their maximum number, are two for flexion and three for extension. If, however, they are referred to a smaller number, there will be either two or one for extension; yet, however you count them, there are two for flexion. In dogs and monkeys with tails, three extending muscles are necessarily and always counted; I will subjoin a description of these as soon as I have described the muscles of man, so that you may more accurately follow the end of the first book of Galen's *On Anatomical Procedures*. I will hand these down according to the rule that I shall not be forced to review all the fictions concerning the muscles moving the elbow from the second book of *On the Use of the Parts*. For once you have learned the true nature of those muscles, you will abundantly refute those ideas by your own ^r effort <note>original: "Marte"</note>; you will surely wonder why Galen handed down such contradictions to the senses to posterity, and why later, having become more skilled in dissection, he did not revise them along with certain other things in his books *On the Use of the Parts*. <margin>c Table 6. We mentioned at the beginning that it was divided at its origin. Such a connection has sometimes appeared so strong to me, and I have seen that fleshy part of the inner origin so long, that I thought it was its own muscle leading from the inner process of the scapula <note>the coracoid process of the shoulder blade</note> into the humerus <note>the upper arm bone</note>, which would also raise the arm. But after this anterior muscle that flexes the elbow, formed from those two origins, has established this connection to the humerus, it then departs from the humerus. Presenting the likeness of a perfectly round and fleshy muscle—extraordinarily visible in muscular subjects before dissection—
<margin>q Table 5, O.</margin>
it climbs over another muscle that is stretched beneath it throughout its entire course; for it no longer touches the humerus or the arm bone, not even by a point. 
<margin>r Table 6, r, r; Table 5, r.</margin>
Furthermore, a little above the elbow joint, having become more sinewy and devoid of flesh, it ends in a sturdy, thick, and perfectly round tendon. 
<margin>s Table 6, q.</margin>
This tendon, spread over the joint and supported by the muscle placed beneath it,
<margin>t Table 8, Q.</margin>

We have already said that, so that the insertion of the tendon into the radius might be made more conveniently, a wide, moderately prominent, and quite uneven process <note>the radial tuberosity</note> was constructed at the upper end of the radius. And this is the sequence of the first muscle <note>the biceps brachii</note>, which claims this unique characteristic among certain others: that it is found to be "livid" <note>leaden or bluish in color</note>.

<margin>The second muscle, or the posterior of the flexors.</margin>
<margin>x Table 8, r; 1 S, S; 2 N, 3, 11 d, d; 4 x, x; 5 q; 6 r, r; 7 P; 9 R; 10 d; 11 & 12 Y.</margin>
**The second muscle** <note>the brachialis</note> lies beneath this one; it is entirely fleshy and nowhere shows a notably sinewy substance. Moreover, it is much shorter than the first muscle and much wider near its lower position. 
<margin>y Table 8, between r and N.</margin>
For it begins to take its origin from the humerus at that place where the lowest insertion occurs of the muscles moving the arm—
<margin>z Table 4, g, h; Table 11, P.</margin>

<margin>a Table 8, L.</margin>
From the outer side of the insertion of the muscle that raises the arm, this second muscle takes a fleshy origin from the humerus. This origin is pointed and, gradually tending downward obliquely toward the front of the humerus, it widens according to the shape of the insertion of the muscle that raises the arm (which is transverse), and it declines slightly inward from the outer parts toward the lower regions. When that origin has crept to the lowest seat of the insertion of the muscle that raises the arm, 
<margin>b Draw an angle in Table 8 from L to M.</margin>
it is carried back again slightly toward the inner side of the insertion, not climbing quite as high as it did when it arose near the outer side. 
<margin>c Table 8, L, M.</margin>
Near the middle of the length of the humerus, therefore, the second muscle moving the elbow arises with a fleshy and wide origin that is "two-horned" <note>bifurcated</note> and expresses an obtuse angle in its middle. Since the line of the origin’s start creeps from the outer side of the humerus downward obliquely toward the front, and from here is led from the front part upward obliquely toward the inner side of the humerus, one "horn" of the origin is held on the outer side of the humerus, while the other is in a way on the inner side, and the angle sits in the anterior seat of the humerus. Furthermore, if you value the present path of this oblique line and those two horns of the origin so much that you say, with some anatomists, that this posterior muscle arises from a double origin, then consider that I have now described the beginnings of this muscle most truly and much differently than they have. Let the two origins you propose be considered by me as one single origin, lest I be forced to ascribe multiple origins to all broad muscle starts, contrary to custom. For unless you granted me this, all broad origins of muscles would have to be doubled, or, if compared with this origin of the second muscle, most origins would even have to be tenfold, contrary to all reason. Therefore, this present muscle, having arisen from this origin, gradually becomes thicker and fleshier, extended straight downward and very strongly attached to the humerus. From its very start, it assumes strength throughout its entire descent until it reaches the elbow joint. 
<margin>d Table 8, N.</margin>
Covering the joint with its width and fleshy substance across the entire anterior seat, it forms a wide attachment <note>the catchword "tione" suggests "implantatione" or "attachment"</note> to the ligament of the joint and to the anterior seat of the ulna and radius...

### THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.
### Page 383

<margin>The function of the first and second muscles.</margin>
...is inserted <note>original: "tione inseritur", continuing from the previous page's "mod..."</note>, and at that part where it crosses the joint, it most fittingly represents the appearance of a mound. Furthermore, just as the path of this muscle is completed in a straight track, it also possesses entirely straight fibers, exactly like the first muscle; I would not dare to assert that it lies upon the fibers of the second muscle in the shape of the letter X or in a cross-wise manner for any reason. And however accurately I look into the function of these muscles, I gather nothing else than that both are the authors of a very straight flexion <note>bending</note> of the elbow, whether we assume both are contracted together or each one individually. And why, I ask, for the sake of Galen—the prince of the professors of dissection—should we invent flexions of the elbow which we never actually see? Should we say, for instance, that the elbow is flexed first straight, and then inclining toward one side or the other, and then attribute a straight flexion to both muscles together, and additionally a private lateral flexion to each individual muscle? Especially since, in the meantime, Galen is inconsistent with himself as to which muscle he should assign the duty of flexing toward the internal side or toward the external side. For he feels quite differently about the importance and use of these muscles in his books *On the Usefulness of the Parts* than he does in his books *On Anatomical Procedures*. In the latter, he judges the posterior muscle to be the author of the flexion of the elbow inclining toward the outside; but he teaches that the anterior muscle manages a flexion verging inward. In the former, however, he left it written that the anterior muscle flexes more toward the outside, while the posterior muscle flexes more toward the inside. Indeed, I am not unaware that when you weigh these matters, you busily attempt the flexion of the elbow, and when you bring your fingers to the top of the humerus <note>upper arm bone</note>, you think a straight flexion is achieved; but when you lead your hand toward the clavicle <note>collarbone</note> and the top of the breastbone, you think a flexion toward the inner side occurs; while when you move your fingers toward the scapula <note>shoulder blade</note>, a flexion of the elbow inclining toward the outer side is celebrated. And therefore, just as I used to do formerly, trusting Galen too much, you neatly conclude that he proposed these types of flexions most correctly—even if, in describing the function of the muscles, he does not agree with himself at all in the aforementioned books. But a little later you will think otherwise, once you have weighed the movement of the humerus in the socket of the scapula as well. Try, therefore, with some bare bones <note>skeletal remains</note> which you may use for examining the business together, to keep your own arm unmoved from all rotation, and only then study to attempt a different flexion of the elbow in that same position of the arm. If you observe it then, it will be time to devise, along with Galen, a crossing or intersection of fibers and a different path for the muscles that produce the flexion of the elbow (even if no such thing exists). Furthermore, when you see that no other flexion occurs besides a very straight one, you will celebrate the skill of the supreme Creator of things with a song of praise, because He placed two very strong muscles in charge of this movement, because He knew it would be powerful and useful to man for many things—not to mention other reasons here. What I have just said about flexion, I also propose regarding extension; although you can test this in various ways, you will notice no better way that the elbow is moved even the slightest bit to the side than if, when it is exactly stretched out, you were to attempt in vain to move it even a hair's breadth to either side while the arm remains at rest.

<margin>The fleshy part by which the first of the extensors is increased, which may be established as the second muscle.</margin>
<margin>i 1, 5, 11 f, chapter 24 book 1 D.</margin>

It is therefore possible in humans either to call this entire muscle a single unit, or to say there are two: so that <margin>k 13 table b.</margin> one arises from the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term>, while the <margin>l 13 table d.</margin> other arises from the humerus and is fused with the one to which the scapula provides a beginning. 

<margin>Book 1 of *On Anatomical Procedures*, section.</margin>
<margin>The third of the extensors.</margin>

But in Galen’s name, let us now review them as two, while we enumerate a third extensor <margin>m 11 table Θ, 2 table O, 9 S, 10 b, 12 V, 13 c.</margin> which arises tendinous from the posterior side of the neck of the humerus. Descending gradually and directly downward and occupying the outer side of the posterior region of the humerus, it <margin>n 11 table d.</margin> becomes fleshy and, being very firmly attached to the humerus, borrows the vigor of its origin from it. <margin>o 11 table e, 2 table Q.</margin> Before it has passed the middle of the length of the arm, it is so mixed with the two previously mentioned muscles, and so unites with them, that in humans it can in no way be distinguished as a whole from them all the way to the insertion. It appears as nothing other than a single body constituted from three muscles. Nevertheless, this third muscle, maintaining its own course, is inserted very strongly into the external side of the <margin>p 2 table R.</margin> posterior process of the ulna, partly as flesh and partly as tendon. 

Thus, as these three muscles unite with one another, the entire posterior process of the ulna is embraced. In the lower part of its surface, <margin>q 6 figure chapter 24 book 1, the triangle enclosed in X, Y, Z.</margin> upon which we lean, it receives a more tendinous portion of the insertion than it does on the sides or above. That mutual meeting of the muscles is seen to be quite dark in color on the posterior side, becoming more tendinous the closer it approaches the process of the ulna. However these muscles may run together, none loses the path of the fibers it began with: all are carried straight downward, never intertwined or crossing each other in an X-shape, and they all perform the same function, by which they extend the elbow without inclining it to either side. 

It is clear, therefore, that these three muscles can be counted as one, formed from three origins; or as two, if you consider the first and second as one. <margin>How the muscles acting on the elbow are arranged in dogs.</margin> But in tailed monkeys <note>likely Barbary macaques, which Galen dissected</note> and dogs, this is not possible. For in these animals, just as in the horse, the ox, and most others that lean on their forelegs and require a powerful extension of the elbow for walking, there are three remarkably distinct muscles—not counting a very slender one in tailed monkeys that extends from the scapula to the ulna, which was entirely overlooked by Galen. 

Furthermore, while dogs have only a single author of flexion <note>the brachialis/biceps complex</note>, monkeys indeed have two, very similar to those seen in humans. The only difference is that the posterior one in monkeys proceeds somewhat further back from the humerus and appears more tendinous at the insertion itself; thus, the descriptions in the first book of Galen’s *On Anatomical Procedures* match these animals in all respects better than they do the human muscle. 

Among tailed monkeys, the first of the muscles extending the elbow arises from the lower rib of the scapula, as in humans; but it soon possesses two origins that merge together. Stretched downward and rendered quite fleshy, it is born attached to no other muscle; but a little above the elbow joint, having become thin and tendinous, it is inserted into the inner side of the posterior process of the ulna. The second lies beneath this one and arises where the second was said to arise in humans, remaining attached to the whole length of the humerus until it is inserted with a strong attachment into the middle and back of the ulnar process. The third, as in humans, takes its origin from the neck of the humerus; from there it becomes fleshy and, adhering to no muscle except by fibrous connections, is implanted into the outer side of the posterior process of the ulna. 

And these are the muscles which Galen, after writing his books *On the Use of the Parts*, diligently dissected and obscurely described in his books *On Anatomical Procedures*, even if in the meantime absolutely nothing from the first edition... <note>original: "editione", the catchword for the next page</note>

<summary>Vesalius describes the triceps brachii muscle group, arguing that while it appears as a single fused muscle in humans, it consists of three distinct heads that Galen described more accurately for monkeys than for humans. He emphasizes the functional role of these muscles in extending the elbow and critiques Galen's reliance on animal anatomy.</summary>

<margin>Annotations on Galen’s anatomical works.</margin>
...in the edition of his books *On the Use of the Parts*, he seems to have added to the history of the muscles moving the elbow, just as he often elsewhere mixed certain lines into his own copy—which was preserved for posterity—that served as notes for him. In his leisure time and according to the circumstances of the day, he would have used these to make the books *On the Use of the Parts*, as well as the books *On Anatomical Procedures*, more consistent with the truth.
