### ON THE LIGAMENTS, EXTENDING FROM THE SHOULDER JOINT WITH THE
-> scapula to the very tips of the fingers. Chapter 47. <-

<margin>d in 3 table note.</margin>
<margin>The ligaments occurring in the arm, elbow, and hand, which may be considered as coverings.</margin>
<margin>Ligaments containing the tendons in the manner of rings.</margin>
<margin>b 4 tables of the hand. e 5 table. $\alpha, \beta$ table $\delta, \gamma, \theta$. d 4 table $\theta, \eta, \zeta$. e 5 table character. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, $\varpi$ table 4 character. 3, 4, 5, 6. f 2 table character. 1. g chapter 21 book 24 1. $\theta$. h 2 table muscle $\Psi$ or $\vartheta$, table Z, then b. i 1 table X, $\theta, \Theta$. k 2 table character. 2. l 2 table $\Upsilon, \Lambda$. m 1, 2 table charact. 3. n 2 table muscle $\nu$. o 1, 2 table charact. 4. p 10 table p.</margin>
<margin>Book 1 of *On Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>
Among the ligaments occurring in the arm, elbow, and hand, examples of nearly every type and use of ligament are found. We have previously described those which are in this number as coverings, when we said that membranes—moistened with a certain slippery fluid <note>synovial fluid</note> and surrounding the tendons in the manner of ligaments—envelop the individual tendons as they creep through the wrist <term>carpus</term> and the palm to the fingers. However, those which are considered protections for the underlying structures—and prevent them from slipping out of their cavities while also serving as bonds—are the transverse <note>cross-wise</note> ligaments, which contain the tendons in their own channels so they do not rise up or wander from them. One of these is stretched across nearly the entire inner surface of the four fingers, and one of this kind is also expanded over the second and, as it were, third joint <term>internode</term> of the thumb; in those places, the tendons that flex the fingers are embraced by those ligaments and held as if by rings <note>original: "anulis," referring to the annular ligaments or "pulleys" of the fingers</note>. In the internal region of the wrist <term>carpus</term>, one such ligament is visible, binding all the tendons of the fingers that crawl forward here. This one is broad and more robust than all others of its kind, but it is shared neither with the back of the hand <term>metacarpus</term> nor the forearm <term>cubitus</term>. Furthermore, as on the outer parts of the forearm where it joins the wrist, six transverse ligaments present themselves, by whose benefit the tendons are kept within the boundaries of the bones. Yet these, if viewed only on the surface, will seem to be a single ligament expanded across the width of the entire forearm; when dissected, it offers six visible rings for the passing tendons to be covered. For this reason, we distinguish it into six ligaments, just as other anatomists do—not indeed because all were known to them (for Galen was unaware of at least two) but because they counted as many ligaments here as they found rings. The **first** proceeds from the ulna into the radius and refers to the common cavity of the ulna and radius, but it does not wrap around the tendons of the seventeenth muscle moving the fingers (as Galen thought); rather, it is peculiar to that muscle which we asserted extends the little finger, numbering it as the eighteenth of those moving the digits. The **second**, placed at the outer side of the first ligament, belongs to the ulna alone and is specific to that muscle which, inserted into the back of the hand before the little finger, is considered the performer of wrist extension <term>extensor carpi ulnaris</term>. The **third** is held at the inner side of the first ligament and belongs to the radius alone, embracing those tendons that oversee the extensions of the index, middle, and ring fingers <term>extensor digitorum</term>. The **fourth**, positioned at the inner side of the third, forms a very narrow ring, just as the tendon it transmits is slender; for that tendon proceeds from the muscle which ought to lead the index and middle fingers away from the thumb <term>likely the abductor pollicis longus or extensor pollicis brevis</term>.

Besides these ligaments, along the entire length of the forearm, a strong ^x membrane <term>fascia</term> grows over all the muscles, joining the muscles together and holding them—after the manner of some transverse ligament—so that they are not moved from their place or entangled with each other; you will hear that a similar one is found in the leg, elegantly covering all the muscles located there. Ligaments that bind the bones together are found in all joints, having almost no peculiar nature different from the other ligaments surrounding the joints. For the internodes of the fingers are bound by ^y membranous ligaments that only surround the joint. The metacarpus <term>postbrachiale</term> is also bound to the wrist by strong ligaments guided through the outer parts. But the bones of the metacarpus, where they face each other at their base near the wrist, are joined together by ligaments resembling the nature of cartilage; these not only surround the bones in a circle but are also found in their middle, where, as we said, the bones face each other. The bones of the wrist are held united together by very strong ligaments resembling the nature of cartilage; and these ligaments cover them on all sides, and in certain places they even come between them: and this especially in the intervals of those bones which are placed in the second row, by which the metacarpus is narrowed. Those which bind the forearm—that is, the radius and ulna—to the wrist correspond to the membranous ligaments of the rest of the joints.

[The radius] is bound to the head <note>The "head" here refers to the distal end of the humerus forming the elbow joint.</note> by strong but membranous ligaments, just like the other joints. And although the joint of the ulna with the humerus <note>The elbow joint proper.</note> is very secure, Nature nonetheless committed the humerus to the ulna with robust ligaments as well, which similarly embrace the joint in its circumference. Beyond these ligaments, there are none in the hand or forearm <term>cubito; the region of the ulna and radius</term>, unless you decide to include those white (b) ligaments which enter into the constitution of the muscles and form their own membranes. These sometimes reach such thickness that, because the muscle flesh lies beneath them, they impart a certain livid <note>original: "liuorem"; a dark or bluish-gray appearance common in dense connective tissue.</note> hue to the muscles. And a thicker ligament of this kind is drawn over the belly (i) of the muscle that most abducts the thumb from the other fingers. Besides this one, (k) the anterior muscle of those flexing the forearm <note>The biceps brachii.</note> also acquires a livid belly due to the thickness of the membrane; just as do those (and quite clearly so) that extend the forearm (l), long before their insertion, which they effect into the posterior process of the ulna <term>the olecranon, or "funny bone" area</term>.

NOW that arm with the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term> must be brought out, which I previously instructed should be set aside when you approached the muscles of the chest, for the dissection of the muscles moving the forearm, radius, wrist <term>brachiale; the carpus</term>, and fingers. But before you begin the dissection, recall to memory how many muscles are placed in each part. To do this more readily, I will now arrange them all in a summary for you. Thus in the hand we have counted twenty: ten (a), naturally, by which the first five joints of the fingers are flexed, of which two are assigned to each finger; three (b), by which the second joint of the thumb is flexed; one (c), which abducts the thumb furthest from the other fingers; one (d), which brings it closest to the other fingers; one (e), which most strongly moves the little finger to the side; and finally, those four (f) slender muscles <note>The lumbricals.</note> by whose benefit the four fingers are moved laterally toward the thumb. Eight muscles occupy the inner side of the forearm: of which the first (g) leads out a broad tendon <term>the palmaris longus</term>; the second (h) and third (i), by which the wrist is flexed; the fourth (k), flexing the second bone of the four fingers; the fifth (l), which flexes the third bone of the four fingers; the sixth (m), which is the cause of the flexing of the third bone of the thumb; the seventh (n) and eighth (o) lead the radius into pronation <note>Turning the palm downward.</note>. If indeed you think the muscle flexing the third bone of the four fingers is one with that which serves the third bone of the thumb, the inner side of the forearm will have only seven muscles. In the outer region of the forearm we described ten: of which the first (p) is the seventeenth (q) of those moving the fingers; the second (r), the eighteenth; the third (s), the nineteenth similarly moving the fingers. Then we have counted here one (t), which turns the thumb more toward the index finger; another (u), which, turning the thumb, removes it further from the index finger; another (v) next to that one, contributing something to the extension of the wrist; two (x) notable ones extending the wrist; and two (y), by whose help the radius is led into supination <note>Turning the palm upward.</note>. If however you wish the third origin (z), which we said arises from the ulna and spreads into two fleshy parts (a) (one of which sought the index and middle fingers, the other the thumb), to be counted as one muscle, then nine will be placed here; then if you join the second origin (b) and hold it as a single muscle, there will be eight. For you would be counting as one twice where we have established two. In the anterior part of the upper arm, there are two (d) flexing the forearm: in the posterior part, however, either three, two, or one (e) extending it, depending on the reasoning...

<margin>Skinning of the arm, forearm, and hand.</margin>
Whether you choose to group these structures into fewer categories or distribute them into many is of no concern, provided that you have learned through the act of dissecting their exact position, connections, size, composition, function, and other such details. Therefore, as I have already mentioned, once you have taken up the arm along with the hand, you will first remove the skin together with the fat and the membrane that some have chosen to call the <term>fleshy membrane; membrana carnosa, a thin layer of muscle or dense tissue just beneath the skin</term>. You will accomplish this most conveniently if you make an incision from the outer side of the arm, following the line of the radius and the outer part of the thumb, which should divide the skin and the fleshy membrane at the same time. Then, another incision should be made along the side of each finger to separate the hairless skin of the hand from the outer side, so that it can be pulled away along with the skin of the arm and forearm, while leaving behind the skin that covers the palm of the hand. In removing the skin, you now need no more skill than what butchers use when skinning cattle. However, when you reach the base of the wrist <note>original: "brachialis radicem"</note> on the inner side of the hand, you will cut away the skin now freed by a transverse incision from that which still remains on the palm. This palm skin must be preserved for the sake of the expanding tendon <note>The palmar aponeurosis</note> lying hidden beneath it.

<margin>Management of the membrane grown over the muscles in the forearm, besides the fleshy one.</margin>
<margin>f 3rd table of muscles, v.</margin>
But before you approach that tendon, consider carefully that the entire area of the forearm appears somewhat dark or livid ^f because of a membrane which, being closely attached to the muscles, binds them together so they do not shift from their places. The muscles occupying the forearm now come into view, but they are so joined together that you can only see the lines that separate them; however, they will appear completely separated from one another if you make only light cuts along those aforementioned lines. You should observe the nature of this membrane all the more diligently because other anatomists have mentioned it only superficially, or rather, not at all.

<margin>Of the muscle producing the expanding tendon.</margin>
<margin>g toward i in the 3rd table.</margin>
<margin>Book 1 of On Anatomical Procedures.</margin>
Furthermore, so that you may see the expanding tendon, direct your attention to the inner side of the forearm, along the length of which its muscle and tendon (while it is still slender) extend. Therefore, with a small knife, make a light incision from the base of the wrist along both sides of the tendon and its muscle, ^g toward the inner bony prominence of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle of the arm bone</note>. Afterward, near the wrist, you will free the tendon from the underlying organs. With a knife placed crosswise under it, and the tendon lifted with the fingers of your left hand, you will separate the entire muscle all the way to its head from the muscles joined to it. Next, with a sharper razor, attempt to cut away the remaining skin of the hand from the palm and fingers, always making transverse incisions starting from the wrist, in the same manner you have long been accustomed to using when dividing the skin from the fleshy membrane. For just as in that dissection you kept the membrane attached to the body, so also you now allow the expanding tendon to remain attached to the hand. When you attempt this, a somewhat hard fat will present itself, coming between the skin and that tendon. This must be noticed all the more accurately because it separates the tendon from the skin, showing that the tendon is not closely attached to all the skin, but is only very firmly joined to it by the intervention of fibrous connections, in the manner of the fleshy membrane. Once the skin has been examined, you will allow the head of the muscle, now freed from the humerus, to hang from the wrist, as you are about to pull the expanding tendon away from the underlying structures using either a razor or a small, sharp knife. If it should ever seem preferable, it is permissible to remove the tendon along with the skin before you separate the skin. But then it will be difficult to free the tendon from the skin intact—though not so much as <term>Galen; the 2nd-century Greek physician whose work Vesalius frequently corrected</term> thought, when he judged there to be nothing between the skin and the tendon.

Furthermore, if this muscle does not present itself on the inner side of the forearm, ^h and you see no muscle lying upon the heads of the two muscles that flex the wrist at the inner prominence of the humerus, conclude that the present muscle, from which the expanding tendon is produced, is missing. I know that this will occur to you not infrequently. It is not that you will skip over it through negligence, but that it will be entirely absent, its place then being supplied by the lower muscle ^i or sometimes even the upper muscle ^k of those that flex the wrist, or by the transverse [ligament] in the wrist...

### The first and second muscles moving the wrist.
<margin>or 4, s, v.</margin> But you will do more conveniently if you preserve these until you can remove all the muscles of the hand together, and return again to the inner seat of the <margin>p 4th table, ∫.</margin> wrist, in which there now come to be processed the two <term>wrist flexors; brachiale flectentes</term>, which you will first <margin>q 3rd table, a, m.</margin> conveniently approach from their tendons near the base of the wrist. For if you lift these up, having been torn away for a short distance from the muscles lying beneath them, and then free them from those underlying structures with transverse incisions all the way to the inner <term>bony projection of the humerus; internum humeri tuber</term> <note>the medial epicondyle of the elbow</note>, you will observe almost their entire nature with moderate effort. For once the head of the lower one <note>flexor carpi ulnaris</note> is cut away, and the muscle is then freed from the <term>ulna; the inner bone of the forearm</term> so that it hangs only by its insertion, you may either remove it from there or leave it still hanging, as it seems fit. 

The tendon of the upper one <note>flexor carpi radialis</note>, however, must not be cut away from the wrist; <margin>r 11 12 t, χ, κ.</margin> rather, either the muscle, freed from its head, must be laid to the side, or the tendon must be cut back a little before it reaches the wrist, so that in the sequence of the <margin>s as in the 4th table, left hand.</margin> dissection, the insertion of that tendon may be made visible. 

### The first muscle moving the fingers.
Otherwise, the whole of the <term>first of the muscles moving the fingers; primus digitos mouentium</term> <note>the flexor digitorum superficialis</note> now offers itself, which you will separate from the one lying beneath it with your fingers alone: just as you would all those whose sides are not joined by that <margin>t 5th table, o, d, g, and so on, noted in order in the margin of the table, and both the preceding and following ones together, as I observe in the other dissections.</margin> nervous membrane which performs the duty of a common ligament. Therefore, when you have inspected its four fleshy portions in front of the wrist while its head is still joined to its origin, a sturdy knife must be thrust straight across the <term>wrist ligament; brachialis ligamentum</term> <note>the flexor retinaculum</note> so that by drawing the blade forward, that ligament is divided. Then, in the same manner along the length of the index finger, you will divide the transverse ligament of its inner seat, taking care lest you injure the tendons creeping forth here. You will best avoid this as long as the back of the knife always faces the tendons and the knife itself is straight. 

At present, you could attempt the same incision on the three remaining fingers, unless your purpose were to gradually learn the nature of these ligaments more and more, or to show them to others. Therefore, in the index finger only—or any other finger—once this incision has been made, free the head of the first muscle moving the fingers. Having grasped it and pulled it upward toward you, set the muscle aside out of the hollow of the wrist for a while, until you see its four tendons extended to the four fingers, and then separately observe the insertion of that tendon which is extended to the index finger. 

For once this is inspected and the muscle is replaced in its seat, its head must be pulled so that its function becomes known, and you may observe in what way that tendon refuses to press down <margin>u 4th table, θ.</margin> upon the first joint of the index finger during the flexing of the second; whereas the remaining tendons, still wrapped in their transverse ligaments, press upon the bones on which they lie and are held very closely. Now, having noted the ligaments of the three remaining fingers, and the insertion and perforation of each tendon through which it transmits the underlying tendon, you will extend the muscle, reflected forward from the hand, upon the table. Or, if you have the hand in a basin, you will let it hang from the fingers, and you will free the head of the muscle <margin>x 6th table, Ξ.</margin> which flexes the third joint <note>internode</note> of the four fingers <note>flexor digitorum profundus</note>. 

### The second muscle.
Its head is somewhat hidden <margin>y 6th table, χ, z 7th table, Q</margin> beneath the muscle that brings the upper part of the radius into a prone position <note>pronator teres</note>. However, before you scrape it away from the ulna, it will be useful to lift its four tendons out of the hollow of the wrist, and to pay attention so that the muscle producing these tendons is pulled away without any effort from the one lying against its upper side, which is considered the author of the flexion of the third bone of the thumb <note>flexor pollicis longus</note>, so much so that you cannot consider both as a single muscle in a human. Therefore, having freed the head of the second muscle, and also its origin...

</margin>
There remain still on the outer side of the forearm two muscles that move the radius into supination. These appear even without dissection, as do the inner muscles that guide the radius. They are the longest, except for the head, which lies hidden somewhat deeper between the posterior muscle flexing the elbow and the outer extensor; however, it is not so deeply hidden that it may not be cut from the humerus <note>The upper arm bone.</note> at its head and traced, along with the other muscles moving the radius, all the way to its insertion.

If you now observe the ligament occurring between the bones along the length of the forearm, it will be the right time to approach the muscles situated in the hand in order. From these, four slender ones [the lumbricals] immediately become visible, which Nature has extended with the tendons that flex the third bone of the four fingers. Next, the muscle is freed that most removes the thumb from the index finger, then the two muscles that flex the first joint of the thumb. Then, the three that flex the second bone of the thumb; these must be observed all the more carefully because they were previously unknown to professors of dissection, and because the principal <term>sesamoid</term> <note>Small, seed-like bones embedded in tendons, like the kneecap but smaller.</note> bones of the hand are born within their tendons. These will be followed by the muscle that brings the thumb closest to the index finger, then the one that most strongly leads the little finger away. Thus, only eight muscles remain, by whose help we flex the first joints of the four fingers [the interossei]; in their tendons, those tiny bones are born which we compare to sesame seeds, and which must be primarily investigated here.

Furthermore, now dividing the joints of the fingers, you will investigate the nature of the ligaments themselves and their specific appearance. With the hand now cast aside, free the first of the muscles flexing the elbow [the biceps] from its origins. ALTHOUGH the explanation of the construction of the penis should properly be reserved for the fifth book, where the organs of generation will be discussed, it is nevertheless useful to make such mention of it now as is necessary for the description of the muscles of the penis. Therefore, besides the <gloss>a</gloss> skin by which it is wrapped, <gloss>b</gloss> two large and fibrous bodies form the penis, which are <gloss>c</gloss> hollow inside like a sponge. The right one of these takes its rise from the <gloss>d</gloss> seat of the right <term>pubic bone</term>, a little lower than where the pubic bones begin to gape apart from each other. This, extending slightly toward the left side, joins with the left body, which takes its beginning from the left pubic bone. The principal mass of the penis consists of these bodies. At the lower part of these where they meet, they have the <gloss>e</gloss> duct of the bladder attached beneath them throughout their entire length as far as the <gloss>f</gloss> root of the glans. There, those bodies—fused together into a single body—embrace this duct, which is common to both urine and seed, as you will hear more at length in the fifth book. For the description of the four muscles of the penis, what has just been said is quite sufficient. Therefore, from the front part of the ring-shaped <gloss>g</gloss> muscle, which we shall teach is attached to the rectum to oversee the discharge of waste, <gloss>h</gloss> two fleshy muscles arise. These are entirely similar to those which extend from the breastbone to the <gloss>i</gloss> <term>U-shaped bone</term> <note>original: "υ referens", the hyoid bone.</note>. For both are close to each other and are joined by their internal sides. They ascend straight upward and forward to the sides of the <gloss>k</gloss> urinary duct, which is reflected upward beneath those bodies, and are inserted into it; and being separated from each other, they embrace the bodies of the penis somewhat like fingers.

There are two other muscles, one on each side, which take their origin from the <gloss>m</gloss> appendix of the hip bone <note>The ischial tuberosity, the "sit bone."</note>, a little lower than the bodies of the penis. This origin is fleshy and slender, forming a muscle that proceeds obliquely upward. It remains fleshy throughout its length and is inserted into the body of the penis on its own side, not far from its starting point. By the voluntary impulse of these four muscles, the 
<margin>m 2 fi. cap. 29 l, m, n, o, p, q. & the muscle is considered to be around q.</margin>
root of the penis is drawn, thereby obtaining a certain power of 
<margin>The function of the muscles.</margin>
erection or <term>tentigo</term> <note>A Latin term for tension or the state of being stretched; here referring to the physiological process of erection.</note> beyond the natural faculty inherent in the organ itself. Furthermore, the first two muscles seem to act like fingers opening that common duct for urine and semen during the excretion of these fluids, so that the duct, constricted in this oblique bend, does not prevent the expulsion of such humors. This is especially true for semen, which Nature intended to be discharged with force, even though it is much thicker than urine. Indeed, unless these muscles pulled the lower part of the duct downward at this reflex curve, the entire duct would be closed off during the erection of the penis, because its upper part would be drawn so stubbornly this way and that by the distended bodies of the penis.

<margin>METHOD of dissection.</margin>
Furthermore, to approach these muscles conveniently, you should resume with the remaining part of the cadaver left over from Chapter 40. With the thighs spread as wide as possible, you will make a circular incision around the anus, dividing the skin down to the fat (which you will find very abundant and quite moist here). Then, you will make a long incision through the skin along the <term>suture</term> <note>The raphe, the visible line or ridge on the underside of the penis and scrotum.</note> visible on the lower side of the penis and scrotum, through the <term>perineum</term> (which others call the *interfemineum*), reaching all the way to the front of the circular line. Afterward, lifting the skin with hooks or your fingers, you will use a razor to separate it from the underlying organs on both sides. You will then trace the muscles that present themselves after the skin is removed from their origins to their insertions, freeing them with a small knife. One should not examine these individually in a cursory manner, both for the sake of extracting <term>calculi</term> <note>Bladder stones, a common and painful affliction in the Renaissance requiring surgical removal.</note> and because of the <term>fistulas</term> <note>Abnormal passages or tunnels in the tissue.</note> and ulcers that not infrequently plague men in this area. These muscles must also be observed more precisely because we have almost nothing handed down about them by Galen. Indeed, the place where he followed them in his work *On Anatomical Procedures* perished through the neglect of time, along with five and a half books of that work and his specific book *On the Muscles*. However, as far as 
<margin>Book 15 on the Use of the Parts.</margin>
we can guess from his books *On the Use of the Parts*, it seems the <gloss>n</gloss> muscles described by me in this chapter were little noticed by Galen. In that work, he refers to no muscles for the 
<margin>n 1, 2, fig. H, I, K, L. o 1, 2, fi. G.</margin>
penis other than two arranged along the <gloss>o</gloss> length of the urinary duct through the whole penis—muscles which I, until now (as I willingly admit), have not found. Not to mention that Galen did not correctly understand the origin of the <gloss>p</gloss> bodies of the penis. He proposed only one body, and that entirely hollow and 
<margin>p 1, 2, 3, fig. A, B. then c, c. q as if it arose at q 4 mus. tab. r 1, fig. last of book 15. s 2 fi. C, C are next to M. t where G stands in figure 1.</margin>
filled with no humor, and <gloss>q</gloss> taught that it originates from the upper parts of the pubic bones. He did not consider that the main bulk of the penis arises much lower than where the lowest <gloss>r</gloss> joint of the pubic bones consists, and that the penis is just as thick and fleshy <gloss>s</gloss> near the anus and through the region of the scrotum as it is in that part which hangs or rises from the upper part of the pubic bones. Thus, since the origin of the penis was hidden from Galen, and he thought of it no differently than someone unskilled in anatomy, it is likely that he also did not investigate those muscles which do not extend much beyond the beginning of the penis.

### BOOK II ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

Towards the end of the male <gloss>a</gloss> bladder, where it terminates into the neck or cervix, <gloss>b</gloss> a certain glandular body <note>Original: "glandofum quoddam corpus." This refers to the prostate gland, which Vesalius describes in more detail in Book V.</note> grows upon it, as the fifth book will declare. However, the muscle now proposed for our consideration is situated chiefly between that glandular body and the <gloss>c</gloss> reflex curve, which the neck of the bladder <gloss>d</gloss> forms as it is drawn upward under the pubic bone after descending slightly. This muscle encompasses the entire seat of this passage; it is circular, mirroring the shape of a long ring or an oblong round duct, and is interwoven with transverse circular fibers. It is thicker at the top, near the glandular body, than it is at the bottom. In women, however, on whose <gloss>e</gloss> bladder <gloss>f</gloss> neck no such glandular body grows, the <gloss>g</gloss> muscle encompasses the entire passage which <gloss>h</gloss> enters from the body of the bladder into the upper part of the neck of the womb, not far from the external genitalia.

<margin>
i Table 3, Θ.
Table 4, Γ; 5, Δ; 6, Δ.
k Table 7, Δ.
l Figure 25, book 5, γ, d, ε.
*The use of the muscle.*
*Book 15, On the Use of the Parts.*
</margin>

This muscle performs the same function in both women and men, and for this reason, it was primarily established by Nature: to be set in charge of the bladder’s passage as an obstacle. It prevents the transverse fibers of the bladder, through their natural motion, from excreting urine against our will and impulse whenever its quantity or poor quality becomes troublesome, or whenever the urine might otherwise flow out due to any compression of the abdomen or the strong holding of the breath. For it was worthwhile that voluntary movements should preside over the removal of wastes from the body. Indeed, if the propulsion of excrement were committed solely to a natural, involuntary motion, waste would flow out continuously; this would not only be most foul but would also cause significant harm to the many duties we perform throughout our lives. Therefore, to prevent urine from flowing out except at our own discretion, Nature surrounded the passage of the bladder with this muscle and appointed it like a faithful gatekeeper <note>Original: "fidi ianitoris." Vesalius uses this metaphor to describe the sphincter's role in guarding the exit.</note>. It is able to gather and tighten itself when we do not wish to emit urine, which is otherwise being pressed upon by the bladder, the <gloss>i</gloss> abdominal muscles, and the <gloss>k</gloss> diaphragm <note>Original: "septo tranfuerfo." The historical term for the diaphragm.</note>. When this muscle does not contract according to the common manner of muscles but is held in its middle state (if I may call it that), it yields to the urine pressed by the organs above it, allowing itself to be drawn out and relaxed from its usual shape and habit. When the compression from the upper parts ceases, or once all the urine has flowed out, the muscle, gathering and constricting itself, protrudes whatever remains of the urine still clinging to the passage. Usually, three or four small drops are left behind, which tend to flow out after the urine has been emitted in a continuous stream and the passage is wide open. And this compression of the urine that might still happen to cling to the passage or only flow out gradually is considered the second use of the present muscle.

However, I cannot sufficiently grasp how this muscle otherwise aids in the promptness and speed of excretion (as <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose anatomical theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years until Vesalius challenged them.</note> asserts), or how that could be its primary use. For the more it is relaxed and the more it lets go of its power of compression—allowing itself to be drawn out and dilated just like muscles that are resting or being pulled by opposing ones—the freer it makes the passage. Being open and wide, it transmits a greater volume of urine pressed from the upper regions than if the muscle were not entirely relaxed or loosened, but rather strained its fibers somewhat during the flow of urine for the sake of expulsion. I do not know by what reasoning it would perform the function of muscles (which occurs through contraction) throughout the entire time of voiding, as this would necessarily make the passage narrower and spoil a more successful or thicker excretion of urine. This is regardless of what we might imagine here about the sharpness or poor quality of urine requiring an otherwise looser and more relaxed muscle. Furthermore, as for Galen's testimony that the length and curvature of the passage contribute to the retention of urine in addition to this muscle, this perhaps holds true in men; for the <gloss>l</gloss> passage of women is altogether short, proceeding straight downward...

# ON THE MUSCLES OF THE RECTUM.
## Chapter LI.

### FIGURE OF THE FIFTY-FIRST CHAPTER.

<image-desc>An anatomical woodcut illustrating the distal part of the human rectum (labeled A) and its associated muscles. B and C indicate the levator ani muscles, D shows the muscles near the pelvic floor and genitals, and E marks the circular sphincter ani muscle.</image-desc>

### Index of the Figure of the Fifty-First Chapter and its characters.

*A portion of the **rectum** is delineated here, with its muscles dissected from the body; usually, when we remove the rest of the intestines, we are accustomed to leave this part still in the body.*
*A The **rectum**, which will become visible in the figures of the fifth book, especially in the eighth and twentieth figures.*
*B, C Two muscles that pull the intestine upward after defecation.* <note>These are the levator ani muscles.</note>
*D A muscular substance attached to the root of the penis; in women, it is further joined to the lowest part of the vulva. Additionally, at **D**, the site is noted from which two muscles for the penis arise.*
*E A circular muscle which prevents the waste from being discharged against one's will.* <note>This is the external sphincter ani.</note>

---

<margin>
a See the figures of Book 5 from Y to d; and Figure 20 of Book 5, O and 22.
b B, C; and Figure 8 of Book 5, b, c.
c Figure 9 of Book 5, L.
d D.
*Muscles that lift the seat.*
</margin>
Nature, who can never be praised enough, <gloss>a</gloss> bestows muscles upon the end of the rectum which, during the excretion of feces, briskly pull the protruding end of the rectum back upward. Next, she gave it another muscle <gloss>b</gloss> which prevents the untimely and involuntary discharge of waste. The muscles that pull the seat <note>The "seat" (sedes) is Vesalius's common term for the anus.</note> upward are broad and thin, and are neither particularly fleshy nor red, hardly taking their origin from any bones. For from <gloss>c</gloss> the ligaments arising from the pubic bones, the hip bone <note>Original: "coxendicis osse."</note>, and the sacrum—which cover the muscles of this region—and finally from the lowest part of the peritoneum itself, a single muscle arises on each side. These, extending downward, embrace the rectum and are inserted into its outermost coat. Since these present muscles are quite broad and surround the entire width of the intestine with their edges, a <gloss>d</gloss> portion of them is also attached to the root of the penis, or in women, to the neck of the uterus <note>In this context, "neck of the uterus" often refers to the vaginal canal or its opening.</note>. Considering this, some writers have counted three muscles that move the seat upward. However that may be, all parts of these muscles are assigned to the same duty, by which they immediately draw the seat upward after excretion, which had been pushed downward by the force of the abdominal muscles and the diaphragm <note>Original: "septi transversi."</note>, and even occasionally with the help of all the muscles that constrict the chest and hold the breath. Furthermore, for these muscles that lead the anus upward, no muscle of a contrary function is placed opposite them, as is usually the case in almost all other parts of the body where muscles are paired in opposition. Nor did Nature here carelessly [depart] from the construction of other muscles...

...erred in dissection: since the seat <note>The anus or rectal opening.</note> is sometimes propelled forward so much by the eight muscles of the abdomen, together with the transverse septum <note>The diaphragm.</note>, that it cannot be readily retracted even by the muscles mentioned. Besides this, another muscle surrounds the end of the rectum, **e** which, similar to those previously described, is not particularly fleshy but exists smeared with a certain mucus; it possesses circular or transverse fibers, **f** and is thicker at its higher position than its lower. Where it is mixed with the skin (like the muscles of the lips), **f** it forms a common body with it. Furthermore, it is attached by fibrous connections **g** to the duct of the bladder in men, but in women **h** to the beginning of the neck of the womb <note>The cervix or vaginal opening.</note>; although it is also joined to the penis in men **i** through the intervention of two muscles for which it provides a starting point. Moreover, in its posterior region, **k** it is attached to the four small bones located at the end of the sacrum (which we call the **coccyx** bone). It is connected from the sides **i** by rounded ligaments arising from the sacrum and extending into the hip bone. This present muscle is not as short as the common sort of physicians believe; rather, it is seen **l** to be long and stretched out according to a great interval of the rectum's length, remarkably mixed with the insertion of the muscles that lift the seat. This should be weighed carefully by those who fear cutting into fistulas and growths of the seat for fear of destroying the function of this muscle. For even if a portion of the muscle is divided by the blade, or torn apart by some other occasion, yet since it is quite wide along the length of the intestine, its use is not lost as readily as is commonly believed in such surgical procedures.

<margin>
m 3rd table Θ, 4th table Γ, 5th table Δ, 6th table Δ.
n 7th table Δ.
</margin>
This muscle, encircling the intestine, when it remains in its middle shape and, as it were, at rest, keeps the end of the rectum so gathered and collapsed into itself that it by no means transmits excrements flowing down merely by their own weight and not attempting a great effort at excretion. Then, if ever these are compressed by the intestines, or even by the abdominal muscles **m** and the transverse septum, and attempt an exit by force, the muscle, by its own function, is gathered and constricted outside its middle shape and habit, so that it effectively prohibits the involuntary passage of excrement. **n** If, by chance, the time is right and we do not wish the muscle to perform its own duty, it allows itself to be relaxed and drawn out by the force of the exiting matter beyond its middle shape, so that a passage is opened for the excrements. After this, the muscle, along with the skin and the substance of the intestine, returns again to its middle shape, responding **o** to the muscle of the bladder neck in appearance, substance, and conformation, as well as in function, performing the duties of a diligent gatekeeper; and just like that one, it is called a *sphincter* <note>original: "σφιγκτὴρ"</note> by the Greeks, but by the Latins the *constrictor* and the *annulus* <note>The "ring".</note>.

The dissection procedure for the muscles of the bladder neck and the anus will begin from the bladder itself; **a** for it is appropriate to free this from the peritoneum where it is stretched over the internal region of the pubic bone with a knife or razor, so that it is no longer continuous with the peritoneum in any of its parts. Then the penis must be separated from the pubic bones: which you will accomplish with moderate effort where these bones meet, since the penis adheres there only by nervous and fibrous connections. But where the bones move away from each other and the bodies of the penis **b** take their origin, the beginnings of these bodies must be scraped away with a sharper knife very close to their source, so that the penis hangs free from the bones. Presently, you will separate the pubic bones from each other with a knife, the section being led through their **c** cartilage. You will perform this with lighter labor than most believe, provided you aim for the middle of the bones...

After the uterus has been removed, the specific muscles of the rectum are to be examined just as in men. It would now be worthwhile, with the pubic bones even more forcefully wrenched apart, to use a sharper knife to divide the ligament connecting the sacrum to the ilium on the left side, so that each leg, along with the bone joined to the sacrum, can be handled separately, and the sacrum remains attached to either the right leg <margin>h Such is nearly the case in Table 16.</margin> or the left, depending on which leg you decide to approach to study the remaining muscles.

# ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE TIBIA. Chapter LIII.

<margin>Galen's opinion on the muscles moving the tibia in Book 3 of *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin>
The next task would have been to describe the muscles moving the femur <note>The thigh bone.</note>, if I had intended to approach those nearest in position after the muscles previously explained. However, since I have proposed to follow the sequence of dissection rather than the sequence of proximity, the movers of the **tibia** <note>The shinbone or lower leg.</note> must be dealt with at present before the muscles that perform the movements of the femur. For as long as you keep these intact, you cannot conveniently manage the others. Furthermore, the more notable, longer, and more visible the muscles moving the tibia are, the less I am able to agree everywhere with Galen’s opinion, although he himself is not entirely consistent in all parts. ...in the part already mentioned, one is indeed external and the other internal, and they are inserted into the sides of the **tibia** <note>The shin bone, or the lower leg in general</note>; both are agents of oblique motion. For the one that is internal draws the leg inward <term>adduction</term>, while the other draws it outward <term>abduction</term>. The former arises from the suture of the **pubic bones** <note>The front part of the pelvis</note>, while the latter comes from the outer parts of the **ischium** <note>The "sit-bone" or lower back part of the hip</note>: for in this way, both were best positioned to pull the leg into oblique movements. For the one that is continuous with the inner parts flexes the knee and draws the tibia inward; however, the one touching the external parts abducts it outward while simultaneously flexing it, as if rolling it. <margin>
Movements of the tibia.
</margin>

Before I approach the muscles, however, I earnestly urge you to examine accurately how many movements you can perform with the tibia. For Galen, in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, as the preceding speech testifies, said the tibia is simply extended; he did not add whether it is extended more inward, or outward, or straight forward in the middle. But he seems to enumerate a triple flexion: one by which he suggests the tibia is pulled backward, or upward toward the outside; a second, by which he says it is drawn upward and inward; and a third, by which we flex the tibia straight back, inclining to neither side. Although he seems to grant this third movement only the name of "flexion," especially in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*. Then, in the aforementioned speech—unlike in the books *On Anatomical Procedures*—he affirms that the tibia is moved to the sides, since he writes that one muscle abducts it outward and another adducts it inward. Nevertheless, in both books, he assigns a movement to the tibia by which it is drawn upward obliquely, as if toward the thigh of the other leg; and by which we see the tibia moved by those who soften hides on wooden floors, or when bakers in many nations tread the dough. All these movements Galen recounts in such a way that he believes them to be entirely proper to the tibia, and he assigns specific muscles to them; while meanwhile, the tibia, with the femur remaining still, is flexed most straightly...

<margin>*The Third.*</margin>
<margin>*Book 2 of On Anatomical Procedures*</margin>
The °third [muscle], along with at least three other muscles, arises from the lowest seat of the **coxendix** <note>the hip bone, specifically the ischium or "sitting bone"</note>. Indeed, from the appendix<sup>p</sup> of that bone (which in us, when standing, is located at the lowest part of that bone; but in monkeys and dogs, when they lean on their forefeet, is considered the outermost and most posterior part), a series of heads for many muscles take their beginning. Of these, this third muscle occupies the very last<sup>q</sup> position. For from the higher and most posterior part of that appendix,<sup>r</sup> a slender and nervous <note>tendinous or sinewy</note> beginning is drawn out. Descending downward, it becomes fleshy a little below its origin, forming a somewhat rounded muscle, now much thicker than its beginning. It creeps downward through the posterior parts of the femur, led somewhat obliquely for a time, until it reaches the posterior seat of the inner head of the femur near the knee.<sup>s</sup> There, having become thin and degenerating into a rounded tendon<sup>t</sup> (not indeed a wide one, as Galen teaches and as usually occurs in monkeys), it is reflected toward the front parts of the tibia, seeking an insertion in the same region as the muscles mentioned just before. But the tendon of this muscle claims this for itself privately: that, adhering to the anterior part of the tibia at the inner side of that sharp line <note>the tibial crest</note>, it hastens down as far as the middle of the length of the tibia, while the other tendons inserted into the tibia do not descend as far. Galen assigns to no muscle moving the tibia so oblique a path as he does to this third one, failing to notice that the first<sup>u</sup> muscle is led in a much more oblique path, since it descends from the **ilium** <note>the upper part of the hip bone</note> toward the front, and from there into the inner parts of the femur almost to the back, and then again is carried by an oblique path into the front parts of the tibia. Furthermore, the<sup>x</sup> muscle which will be fourth in order is seen to be more oblique than the third. For you will hear that it, born from the hip bone similarly to this one, creeps toward the front of the tibia along the outer head of the femur. Hence, this fourth muscle also obtains a position as much more oblique than the third itself, as the seat of the hip bone from which both take their beginning looks more toward the inner parts of the femur. The third muscle is the sixth in the prescribed discourse of Galen, which he says in that place flexes the tibia by inclining it toward the inner side. But in his books *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de Administrandis sectionibus"</note>, just as he assigns to it a most oblique path, so also he establishes it as the author of a most oblique movement. For it is necessary (he says) that the tibia, pulled by this handle, be carried backward and upward, and be rolled around in a circle. And indeed we perform this movement, but not with the femur remaining still; for it is necessary that the tibia be flexed by this motion, and the femur be turned outward in no slight degree.

...descending gradually toward the rear, downwards and outwards. When the muscle has passed the midpoint of the length of the **femur** <note>the thigh bone</note>, it becomes thinner, and on its outer side, <margin>c 11 tab. g.</margin> another fleshy part, originating from the femur, is joined to it at the point where it appears ready to produce a tendon. It is as if another muscle arises here to augment the fourth; and together, one muscle is formed from both. This muscle, becoming thick again, takes on the appearance of a fleshy muscle and, extending downwards, becomes quite **nervous** <note>in the sense of "tendinous" or "fibrous"</note> on its outer part. It is implanted into the **fibula** <note>the smaller, outer bone of the lower leg</note> by a prominent tendon, having worked its way firmly into <margin>d 5, 6 fig. ch. 31 book 1 C.</margin> the process of the upper appendage of that bone. Indeed, because of this tendon, the fibula puts forth a sharp process of this kind where it is joined to the **tibia** <note>the shin bone</note>. Furthermore, the outer head of the femur bears an oblong <margin>e 1, 2 fig. ch. 30 book 1 N.</margin> groove on its outer side, specifically carved out so that this tendon might be carried fitly and safely, and it is encrusted with a smooth and slippery ligament. However, whether you count this fourth muscle as one or as two makes no difference; though for the sake of Galen, so as not to disturb the order, it is more convenient to establish it as one. For Galen, since he did not see this muscle in a human, describes it only as a single unit, just as I have found it in tailed monkeys. In monkeys, no portion arising from the femur bone is mixed with the fourth muscle; rather, it is a single, very prominent, and wide muscle. For this reason, Galen constantly calls it "the wide one" in his books *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de Adminiſtrandis ſectionibus"</note>. Following the descriptions in the third book of his discourse *On the Use of the Parts* <note>original: "de Partium uſu"</note>, we shall rank this as the seventh muscle, by which Galen asserts the tibia is drawn outward simultaneously with flexion and is, in a way, rolled inward. But in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, he testifies that the entire tibia is moved by a simple motion toward the outer part by the help of this muscle—having forgotten those things he had handed down in the books *On the Use of the Parts*. Doubtless, he thought he knew the nature of this muscle most exactly because of that runner whom he believed had this muscle torn away during a contest. For it is likely <margin>Book 2 of On Anatomical Procedures</margin> that Galen, attracted by the symptoms of that runner (whose other muscles flexing the tibia were still functioning), diligently weighed the nature of this muscle in monkeys. He then learned (as he surely ought to have done in all cases) that this muscle was assigned by Nature for a simple motion as far as the knee joint is concerned, and that it effects a flexion that does not incline to either side, even though this fourth muscle creeps toward the tibia in an oblique path. Indeed, it maintains this path by reason of the position and composition of the bones and for the sake of the femur's shape, rather than to lead a non-straight motion. But in the meantime, I interpret Galen's discourse, in which he writes that the tibia is led into the outer parts by a simple motion by this fourth muscle, as if he had understood "posterior parts" by "outer parts," and thus he was indicating flexion, and not truly a drawing toward the outer side. For otherwise, Galen's opinion would deviate too much from the truth, since it is more certain than certainty itself that the tibia is by no means moved toward the outer side by a simple motion.

<margin>The fifth [muscle] of those moving the tibia. f 11 tab. γ, 2 tab. d, d. 9 tab. u. 10 tab. π, π, 12 ξ.</margin> The fifth muscle also <margin>g 2 fig. ch. 29 book 1 n.</margin> arises from the appendage of the **coxendix** <note>the hip bone, specifically the ischium</note>, taking its beginning between <margin>h 11 tab. ω, ω, under which is ν.</margin> the heads of the third and fourth muscles moving the tibia, and <margin>i 12 tab. d muscles Ξ, Σ, Ρ.</margin> the head of that muscle which we shall number as the fifth of those moving the femur, and to which we shall ascribe the fourth head of those for which the appendage of the hip bone provides the beginning. Just as we rightly attribute to this fifth muscle of those assigned to the movements of the tibia a third <margin>k 11 tab. φ. χ is placed in the groove itself in 12 tab.</margin> head, which is entirely **nervous** <note>tendinous</note> and does not become fleshy or thicken until far below its origin. It claims this rare and peculiar trait for itself above all other muscles of the body. For no other muscle is seen to be nervous for such a long stretch from its beginning—except for the fact that on its posterior side, even beyond the middle of the length of the femur, it appears intensely bluish-gray, <margin>m 10 ι α placed in 27, 28,</margin> and has a groove elegantly and neatly carved for itself, smooth along the length of the muscle, in which the anterior part of the third muscle moving the tibia...

...this part leans so beautifully that I truly think the third muscle, along with the fifth, was removed and dissected by many **anatomists** <note>original: "Anatomicis"</note> as a single muscle. Just as the third muscle is thick and fleshy at its origin and eventually becomes round, tapering off far above the knee joint to end in a tendon, so conversely the fifth muscle remains **tendinous** <note>original: "nerueus" (nervous), meaning fibrous or sinewy in the 16th century</note> for a long time in its upper part, but becomes thick in its lower part, appearing fleshy and round. Near the knee, at the rear region of the inner head of the **femur** <note>the thigh bone</note>, it produces a round tendon <margin>o</margin> which, bent back toward that head of the femur along with the tendon of the third muscle, is inserted into the inner side of the front of the **tibia** <note>the shin bone</note>. It does not descend so far down the tibia, nor does it creep forward as much as the tendons of the first three muscles moving the tibia, which we wrote <margin>p</margin> effect their insertion in this place. Although the tendon of the fifth muscle does not attempt as low an insertion as those just mentioned, it is nevertheless not inserted into the inner head of the femur near the beginning of the muscle <margin>q</margin> which we shall testify takes its origin from that inner head of the femur when we come to list the first of the muscles moving the foot. 

And just as the tendon of the fifth muscle is not implanted into that head of the femur, so it is not secured or inserted with any special connection to the **ligaments** <margin>r</margin> joining the tibia to the femur. This should certainly be observed with care for the sake of **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon, the ancient Greek physician whose authority Vesalius frequently challenged</note>, who in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures* attributes the insertion of his fifth muscle to the head of the femur and the ligaments of the knee joint. Being anxious in strange ways about the office and duty of this muscle, he is inconsistent with himself. 

First, he says that the muscle listed by him in the fifth place gradually turns the tibia outward and performs the movement of the third muscle, though not as greatly. Secondly, however, he says that if you stretch this muscle toward its head, the tibia also seems to be carried backward and inward with the femur. Thirdly, he writes that he is almost ready to say that the fifth muscle he described is the sole cause of the flexion of the tibia; adding that it seems no more to flex the tibia than to draw it toward the internal region. Fourthly, he adds that this muscle moves or flexes the knee joint lightly and in a somewhat obscure <margin>s</margin> manner, and that there is another certain muscle hidden away in the **popliteal joint** <note>the area behind the knee</note> which can either flex it alone or is endowed with the greatest power. He is referring to that muscle which we call "the one lying hidden in the popliteal region," <margin>t</margin> and which we shall describe in a separate chapter after the account of the nine muscles moving the tibia; a most worthy duty which Galen undeservedly claims for himself, boasting that he was the first to observe it. 

Furthermore, in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, Galen more than once mocks the ancients (who <margin>u</margin> perhaps removed our fifth muscle along with the third as a single muscle during dissection, since they cling to each other so closely and seem to form one muscle) because they wrote that a certain muscle moving the femur flexed the tibia. He is suggesting that muscle which is the thickest of all the muscles in the body, and will be listed by me as the fifth of those moving the femur, just as it was by Galen in his books *On the Use of the Parts*; yet in his books *On Anatomical Procedures* he lists it as the first of those moving the femur and asserts quite truly that it does not pertain to the tibia at all. 

Whence I also wonder why he did not then correct the third book of *On the Use of the Parts* in the aforementioned discourse, since he made mention of the muscle <margin>x</margin> lying hidden in the popliteal region after those books had undoubtedly been published earlier. For in the aforementioned discourse, in place of the eighth muscle, he describes one—just as he hints the ancients used to do—which I entirely think is the posterior portion of the fifth muscle <margin>y</margin> moving the femur, inserted by its own tendon into the inner head of the femur, near the origin of the first muscle moving the foot; although in the meantime he confused that portion of his fifth muscle moving the femur with the movements of the tibia...

...nothing at all in common: <margin>z 11th table, Υ.</margin> just as the fifth muscle of those moving the **tibia** <note>the shin bone</note> described by me serves only the flexion of the tibia, and truly not the movements of the **femur** <note>the thigh bone</note>. <margin>The Sixth.</margin> <margin>a 3rd table Φ. q. r. s. character 3. 9th table p.</margin> Therefore the **sixth muscle** <note>modern: the *tensor fasciae latae* and the *fascia lata* or *iliotibial tract*</note> (which I would have described in the first place, had I not taken Galen's account into consideration) must be inspected the more accurately because it <margin>b 3rd table Σ.</margin> possesses a nature more unusual than the remaining muscles. For it arises from the outer side of the first muscle, from the spine of the **ilium** <note>the upper, broad part of the hip bone</note>, <margin>c 3rd table from x to y.</margin> possessing a sharp and fleshy head inside which, tapering in the manner of a mouse or a lizard <note>original: "muris lacertæ ue modo"; an allusion to the tapering shape of these animals’ tails, or perhaps a play on the word "musculus" meaning "little mouse"</note>, is carried downward to the region of the hip joint. There that head, or muscle, is again rendered narrower, and before it creeps over the **great and outer process** <note>the greater trochanter of the femur</note> <margin>d 1st, 2nd fig. cap. 30 book 1 Υ, Q.</margin> of the femur, it is no <margin>e under y, table.</margin> longer seen to be fleshy. This is so much the case that the sixth muscle is finally nothing else than a very long and very wide **membrane** <note>here referring to the *fascia lata*, the deep connective tissue of the thigh</note>, reflecting the nature of a tendon, into which the fleshy part just described is joined. 

For immediately from the beginning on the outer part, it comes into view like a wide membrane, covered for some distance by the muscles embracing the hip joint. But when the membrane has passed the great process of the femur, it covers the whole anterior seat of the muscles embracing the femur, and then both the posterior and outer seats, just like skin, until it descends to the knee joint. When the membrane has similarly wrapped this also, it is inserted into the anterior seat of the tibia and its outer side. Furthermore, the thickness of this membrane, or **tendon** <note>original: "tendinis"</note>, however you please to call it, is not the same everywhere. For the whole part which is drawn over the anterior and posterior seats of the femur is very thin; and this is seen to be even thinner the closer it approaches the inner region of the femur. But that part of the membrane which is extended to the outer side of the femur is strong and thick, and accurately expresses the appearance of a wide tendon. Its fibers descend in a straight, sloping path until they are inserted into the anterior part of the tibia, more toward the outer side and toward the **fibula** <note>the smaller calf bone</note>. 

Moreover, this tendon at the site of insertion is mixed with those tendons which will also be said to extend the tibia along with it. For the present muscle should be reckoned among the number of extensors, although it also provides a remarkable use to the muscles surrounding the femur: it acts like a certain **transverse ligament** <note>original: "transuersi ligamenti"</note>, containing all the muscles it embraces in their proper place so they do not shift. In this way, it performs the same office as the membrane which we previously suggested originates around the muscles of the elbow. 

Truly, how superficially Galen describes this muscle is shown by the three words with which he dignifies it in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*. For I think this muscle was hidden from Galen in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, since he did not place it in the class of the three extensors of the tibia which he reviews there, and since he added the origin of the fourth muscle to his discussion. For if he had simply (as he speaks of the other muscles) expressed only the insertion and movement of the fourth, I would have thought that this <margin>f 3rd table Θ.</margin> sixth muscle was held by him to occupy the place of that muscle which he claimed leads the tibia away to the outer side. Indeed, this muscle would perform that action, if you looked at its position and path, provided the tibia were moved <margin>g 2nd fig. cap. 29 book 1 from l to q.</margin> even the least bit to the side. But when he spoke more explicitly about the fourth muscle and added its <margin>h 11th table λ, μ, ν, ξ character Cr.</margin> origin to his text, Galen clearly demonstrates that he is not <margin>i</margin> proposing this sixth one; since this one does not [arise] from the appendix of the hip bone, with the third, fourth...

### Chapter LIIII.

...on that part, the membrane ^d of the **seventh muscle** <note>Vesalius is referring to the *fascia lata*, the tough connective tissue on the outer thigh</note>, or its tendon, will be observed; it is appropriate to free this from the underlying parts just as one does with the skin. Therefore, once the part that encircles the front of the thigh has been drawn toward the outer side of the femur, it is also necessary to separate the part covering the back of the thigh from the underlying structures toward the outer side. By inserting your hand crosswise between its tendon and the **seventh muscle** ^b and moving it up and down, you may examine the insertion of the tendon and the origin of the muscle itself. When you have found the site of its origin, you shall cut it away from the **spine of the hip bone** <note>original: "ilium ossis spina"</note> with a razor or scalpel; lifting it with your fingers, you will pull the entire muscle away as far as the **shin bone** <note>tibia</note>, accurately inspecting the nature of that very broad tendon and the fleshy part of this muscle. You should leave the muscle hanging from its insertion so that its function may later be better understood ^c, in addition to the remarkable use it provides to the other muscles. After this, you will free the head of the **first muscle** <note>modern: *sartorius*</note> from the upper front part of the hip bone with a scalpel; and, grasping its head with your fingers, you will pull it away from the underlying parts without difficulty as far as its insertion. Next, with a razor, you will separate the beginning of the **second muscle** <note>modern: *gracilis* or *pectineus*</note> from the **pubic bone** ^d, at the point where it was joined to the pubic bone of the other side by the intervention of cartilage ^e. Grasping that muscle similarly with your fingers, you will draw the entire muscle down to its insertion. Now it would be permissible to approach the **ninth muscle**; but you will do so more conveniently if, after turning the leg over, you first manage those ^g which arise from the **hip bone** <note>original: "coxendicis osse," specifically the ischium</note> ^h.

<margin>b 9 table 5.</margin>
<margin>Those [muscles] which arise from the process of the hip bone.</margin> <note>original: "coxendicis ossis appendice," referring to the ischial tuberosity</note>
In order for this to proceed correctly, it is necessary to remove the remarkable muscle that constitutes the **buttock** <note>modern: *gluteus maximus*</note>. This muscle arises from the spine of the **tailbone** <note>coccyx</note> and the posterior part of the spine of the **hip bone** <note>ilium</note> and the back, and is inserted chiefly into the **great process of the thigh bone** <note>the greater trochanter of the femur</note>, intended to move the thigh, as you will hear in its proper place. Therefore, the fleshy origin of this muscle must be scraped away with a razor from those parts of the bones from which it emerges, so that once it has been lifted from the underlying muscles, it can be conveniently reflected to the side toward its insertion. Otherwise, the muscles arising from the **process of the hip bone** <note>ischial tuberosity</note> would not show themselves at their heads, which must now be separated according to their sequence of origin. Furthermore, so that you may more exactly achieve your wish, you will separate the muscles in the posterior region of the thigh from one another with your fingers, so that you may estimate the thickness of the heads resting upon one another ^i with slight care.

You will therefore apply your mind here to see whether the head of the **third muscle** ^k is laid over the head of the **fourth**, as I have said ^l; or whether indeed the head of the third muscle lies beneath the head of the fourth, as it seemed to **Galen**, and in what manner they are situated and arise together for the most part in that region. When you have performed this, you will cut both away from the hip bone. Taking the head of the third in your hand, you will pull it away from the underlying parts as far as its insertion, considering only how it rests in the hollow of the **fifth muscle** ^m mentioned by me. ^n When you likewise pull away the head of the **fourth muscle**, you must pay diligent attention ^o to that fleshy part which, arising from the thigh bone, increases the fourth muscle.

But here your consideration of the movements of the shin bone <note>tibia</note>, because of the frequent wounds in the knee and thigh, ought to be so great that, having cut the foot from the shin, and having removed the flesh of the shin as accurately as possible without damaging the insertions of the muscles moving the shin, you should sometimes approach them so that you may learn whether I have undeservedly felt differently about the movements of the shin than all others. Nor indeed would it then be enough for the foot to have been removed with the flesh of the shin: rather, nothing would be as beneficial as taking away all the flesh lying upon the hip joint together, lest the movement of the thigh deceive you in this work as it does other anatomists. For with the joint bare, you will always observe whether the head of the thigh bone changes even a little in its socket. And as you will see that the shin bone, while the thigh remains unmoved, performs no other action besides straight flexion and extension, consider how much less the shin bone does this in us, since the thigh is clothed on all sides with so much flesh. Furthermore, the mixing of the tendons of those extending the shin bone <margin>e 8th table, Ω. then g, h, i, and also k.</margin> must be investigated with a razor: so that you may see which of the muscles has contributed a more significant portion of the combined tendon. Moreover, attention must be paid to what kind of connection the kneecap has in that tendon: and finally, how the kneecap rests upon the thigh bone by the favor of no ligament, indeed with no intervening body at all.

### ON THE MUSCLE HIDDEN IN THE HAM,
->which is incorrectly held by Galen to be the primary author of the flexion of the shin.<-
->Chapter LV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'I' showing two scholars or anatomists in Renaissance dress engaged in observation or discussion in an outdoor setting.</image-desc>
<margin>Book 2 of Anatomical Procedures, section [X].</margin>

AMONG the leaders of the movements of the shin bone <note>tibia</note>, we said before that Galen counted a certain muscle lurking in the ham <note>poples; the space behind the knee</note>: now, however, we shall describe in what place it is contained, and of what form, path, and size it is. Therefore, among the ligaments connecting the thigh bone to the shin bone (the nature of which I shall follow in a special Chapter, together with the ligaments of the hip joint and the bones of the foot <margin>b figure for chapter 1, V.</margin>), one is found on the outer side of the knee joint, <margin>c 14th table, h.</margin> very strong and thick, from the back part of which the tendinous <note>original: "nerveum", referring to the tough, sinewy nature of tendons</note> origin of the muscle arises; by its breadth, it touches the back part of the knee joint on the outer side, while in the meantime it is nowhere firmly attached to the thigh bone. From here, increased by fleshy fibers, it descends very obliquely downward toward the inner parts, forming a muscle slightly longer than it is wide. <margin>d 14th table, i.</margin> For the end of this, or its insertion, near the root of the <margin>e 2nd figure of chapter 13, book 1, A, B.</margin> attachment <term>appendix: here used to mean a bony process or epiphysis</term> of the shin bone, on the inner side of its back part, is as wide as the breadth of the whole muscle is seen to be. Then, as this muscle is oblique, it also produces an oblique insertion: for from the outer side of the back part of the shin bone, this muscle descends obliquely downward toward the inner side, so that the smallest part of it is joined to the ligaments of the knee, but the greatest part to the shin bone. No other muscle is placed under the present one, either at its origin or its insertion: but it is closest to the ligaments and bones of the joint

...stretched out, it is hidden under those <gloss>f</gloss> muscles which, arising from the lower heads of the thigh bone <term>femur</term>, primarily form the calf along with <gloss>g</gloss> the fourth muscle moving the foot: so much so, that it was not without reason that Galen called this muscle "the one hiding in the hollow of the knee" <note>Latin: *poples*</note>. But whether he correctly assigned to it the task of flexing the shin <note>tibia</note>, you may judge for yourself. For he favored that muscle to such an extent (perhaps because he was the first to discover it, or because other dissectors had not listed it as an agent of flexion) that in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>Latin: *De Adminiſtrandis ſectionibus*</note>, he wrote that this muscle alone is able to flex the knee, or is endowed with the greatest power to do so. To me, however, it seems not only to lack the greatest power for flexing the shin, but to have none at all. Since this muscle is entirely oblique and almost transverse, it cannot be in charge of a straight movement; furthermore, it is so weak that it cannot pull the shin upward even the slightest bit. To this is added that it has no proportion to the other muscles acting on the shin, since it is very short and thin <margin>h Figures 1, 2, 3, Chapter 29, Book 1.</margin> and does not originate from the thigh bone, and much less <gloss>h</gloss> from that bone which we see joined to the side of the sacrum <note>the ilium</note>. But you will observe these things much more exactly during the act of cutting, since this muscle is easy to find. For as soon as the calf muscles, born from the heads of the thigh bone, are freed from the thigh and hang reflected downward, this muscle is quite conspicuous. Before it is uncovered in the order of dissection, however, we shall describe the muscles moving the thigh; once the management of these is finished, we will gird ourselves for the movers of the foot and then the toes, in whose anatomy the muscle hiding in the hollow of the knee offers itself to be seen; and it likewise shows whether it performs any <margin>i Table 11, Q.</margin> common task with <gloss>i</gloss> the upper muscle moving the radius into a prone position <note>the pronator teres in the forearm, which Vesalius often compares to leg muscles</note>.

### ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE THIGH. Chapter LVI.

<image-desc>An ornamental historiated woodcut initial 'F'. The scene within the letter depicts several figures, likely cherubic children or putti, gathered around a low anatomical table, appearing to perform a dissection or study a body in a classical setting.</image-desc>

<margin>Movers of the thigh.</margin> THE THIGH is moved by ten muscles, or if they are reduced to the maximum number, fourteen, which extend it, flex it, lead it inward toward the other leg <term>adduction</term>, move it outward to the side <term>abduction</term>, and turn it around <term>rotation</term>. Thus the thigh is flexed when we carry it upward and forward; it is extended, however, when we are standing and leading it downward toward the ground and toward the rear. Whence Nature also rightly entrusted extension to large, strong, and many muscles, which I will now strive to follow, observing that order of Galen which he followed at the end of the fifteenth book of *On the Use of the Parts*. For that order appears to me far better and more accurately described by the consensus of other masters of dissection than the one in which he treats the muscles of the hip joint in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, which is excessively obscure and shows the <margin>
