<sup>f</sup>From this location, the **fifth muscle** <note>The adductor magnus, the largest of the muscles that pull the thighs together.</note>—which is the thickest of all the muscles in the entire body and, to put it simply, the largest in mass—takes its origin. This origin, emerging according to the breadth of that process <note>The ischial tuberosity, the "sit-bone" of the pelvis.</note>, is seen to be entirely fleshy, except for that part which immediately follows the three mentioned heads of the leg muscles, which is tendon-like and remarkably strong. This muscle, <sup>g</sup>arising from such a beginning, <sup>h</sup>immediately encompasses the root of the small process of the femur <note>The lesser trochanter.</note> at its rear region, and then continues from there to be inserted into the sharp and <sup>i</sup>rough line of the thigh bone <note>The *linea aspera*, a ridge on the back of the femur where many muscles attach.</note>. We stated in the first book that this line extends downward along the length of the posterior part of the femur from the root of the small process. However, just as the origin of the beginning of this muscle is continuous, so too its insertion is seen as continuous—provided <sup>k</sup>you understand that the posterior part of the muscle is distinguished from the anterior part, as if by a certain marking, <sup>l</sup>which inserts a tendon into the root of the internal head of the femur. For this part, born from a tendon-like and then <sup>m</sup>fleshy origin at the process of the hip bone, forms the muscle in its own right to some extent. Dilated into a wonderful breadth of "belly" <note>The "belly" is the thick, fleshy middle part of a muscle.</note>, it is carried straight down through the back of the thigh until, becoming slender again, it <sup>n</sup>leads out into a rounded tendon inserted into the inner head of the femur. And if the rest of the muscle <sup>o</sup>were not grown onto this part of the fifth muscle that moves the femur, it would rightly be considered by everyone as a distinct and peculiar muscle. But now, since this posterior part has another continuous part of the same muscle grown onto it, nothing prevents us, in different modes of teaching, from either calling this whole muscle one (as we have done so far), or <sup>p</sup>first distinguishing it into two: namely, so that one would be the part that extends a tendon to the inner head of the femur, and the <sup>q</sup>other would be the part implanted into the small process of the femur and then into the sharp line of the femur. And this is the one <sup>q</sup>marking that distinguishes that posterior part from the anterior. Furthermore, <sup>r</sup>the anterior part also possesses its own private marking, though not as manifest as the one just described; but it is such that, for its sake, one is free to subdivide this part into two portions or, if anyone wishes, into two muscles. For that portion of this anterior fifth muscle which arises from the forward seat of the process of the hip bone—which pertains from the joint of the pubic bones <note>The pubic symphysis.</note> down to the lowest part of the hip—is separated by a certain marking from that portion of the anterior muscle part which arises from the rest of the process's seat up to the forward region of the posterior part of the whole muscle. Then, these two portions of the anterior part are distinguished not only by a marking or impression, but also by the course of the fibers and likewise by the insertion—just as the posterior part of the whole muscle varies from the anterior by the occasion of the fibers and the insertion. For the portion of the anterior part which is <sup>s</sup>nearest to the joint of the pubic bones has very oblique and almost transverse fibers, which strive from their origin backward toward the root of the small process of the femur and are inserted into the upper part of the sharp line of the femur. The remaining portion of the anterior part, which takes its beginning more toward the lowest seat of the hip, acquires oblique fibers indeed, but they are nearly straight and are continuously implanted into the lower seat of the rough and prominent line; and then the posterior part claims for itself fibers that are in some way completely straight. And therefore, either establish with me one muscle in one thigh, or if it seems better, count both parts as two muscles; or if you are already more skilled in dissection and are captivated by a still greater number, subdivide the anterior part into two muscles, then describing three. This should be done, however, in such a way that you remember that I am speaking about the muscles of **humans**, not of **apes**, unlike Galen <note>Galen (129–216 AD) was the Roman-era authority on medicine whose anatomical works were based on animal dissection; Vesalius famously corrected Galen by performing human dissections.</note>; lest perhaps at some time while reading him, you [me po-] <note>Catchword for the next page, likely "me po-nite" or similar.</note>

<summary>Vesalius describes the fifth muscle of the thigh (the adductor magnus), detailing its origins on the pelvis and its complex insertions on the femur. He notes that while it can be viewed as one massive muscle, its different fiber directions and attachments allow it to be subdivided into two or three distinct parts, while specifically noting his focus on human rather than ape anatomy.</summary>

This muscle <note>The **eighth** muscle in Vesalius’s system, likely the **pectineus**</note>, is considered by those who dissect the muscles moving the thigh <note>original: "femur"</note> carelessly <note>original: "oscitanter"</note> to be a portion of the **fifth** muscle ^n, appearing in humans to arise from a broad and fleshy beginning on the pubic bone. In humans, this muscle presents a leaden-colored <note>original: "liuidum," likely referring to the dark or grayish appearance of the muscle fibers in a cadaver</note> appearance; but it is not quite the same as in tailed monkeys, in whom this muscle is seen to be smaller and not arising from a similarly broad beginning. ^q Nature entrusted to these **three muscles** <note>The 6th, 7th, and 8th</note> the task of flexing the thigh and moving it inward toward the other leg. <margin>The function of the 6th, 7th, and 8th.</margin> The **sixth**, which we reviewed as the first of the flexors <note>The **psoas major** and **iliacus**</note>, powerfully draws the thigh upward and flexes it, driving it toward the interior. The **seventh** <note>The **adductor longus**</note> similarly flexes the thigh by lifting it upward, but moves it much less toward the interior than the sixth. The **eighth** <note>The **pectineus**</note> contracts the thigh upward moderately and is considered the author of a weak flexion; however, it pulls the thigh powerfully inward. Thus, Nature has set muscles for flexion and extension, and also for those remaining two lateral movements toward the interior and exterior. When Galen, in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, reviews the function of the flexors of the thigh, <margin>Whether some muscles flex the thigh secondarily. Book 15.</margin> <margin>r Table 4, ψ.</margin> he makes one of the muscles moving the shin <note>original: "tibia"</note> also a performer of the thigh's flexion ^r; namely, that which we have listed as the **ninth** <note>The **sartorius**</note>, which takes its origin higher than the hip joint (which does not happen ^s with the **seventh** and ^t **eighth** <margin>s Table 5, Λ. t Table 5, Γ.</margin> muscles moving the shin). He claims this not because the muscle achieves it by its own proper motion, but by a **secondary** one. Whether this truly conforms to the truth, consider for yourself, while also noting whether you wish to assign some duty in the movements of the thigh to the other muscles moving the shin which originate higher than the femur or do not take their beginning from the femur itself. As for me, I refrain from doing so for the reason that many muscles do not take their origin from the bone they move, or from the bone nearest to the one into which they are inserted. Many such muscles occur in the shin, the forearm, and the upper arm, to which a secondary function (as Galen has done here) is attributed by no one, and rightly so. Not to mention that if Galen’s opinion were true, the flexion of the thigh would always have to occur with the extension of the shin, or at least the extension of the thigh would be troublesome to a man when the shin is extended. In the same way, if our fingers were flexed toward the palm, we would bear the extension of the wrist <note>original: "brachialis"</note> with difficulty; or with the arm driven backward, we would not willingly flex the elbow. Therefore, having set aside those secondary or accidental functions of the muscles described by Galen, let us add to the discourse the two muscles that still remain and which twist <note>rotate</note> the thigh, numbering them as the **ninth** and **tenth**. <margin>The ninth. u Table 8, γ. # ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE STRUCTURE
->414<-

...is marked by [descriptions], is fleshy: and occupying the entire internal seat of the pubic bone and the ischium <note>original: "ossis coxendicis," the lower and back part of the hip bone</note>, and appearing leaden-colored, it is gradually so <margin>e Table 16, f, g G; they are narrowed at H.</margin> narrowed that its width does not exceed the interval of the ischium <margin>f Book 1, chapter 29, figure 2.</margin> which is found between its sharp process <note>The **ischial spine**</note> and the posterior seat of its appendix <note>The **ischial tuberosity**</note>. For at this interval, which bears a wide groove <note>The **lesser sciatic notch**</note> carved into it, the **tenth muscle** <margin>g Table 12, a, h 1, 2, 3; book 1, chapter 29, figure k; table 13, γ, i 13, f, s, u.</margin> is bent outward, approaching the great process of the femur <note>The **greater trochanter**, the large bony prominence at the top of the thigh bone</note>.

The muscle achieves this turn through the great industry of the Creator: for where it winds around this <margin>h</margin> groove, it is fleshy on the outer part; but on the part where it touches the groove, it is seen to be entirely sinewy, and shows as if it were <margin>i Table 13, f, s, u.</margin> three rounded tendons, bent toward the groove in a certain sequence. These tendons exist broadly within the substance of the muscle shortly before the muscle touches the groove; but where they wrap around the groove, they become narrower, each claiming a particular small groove for itself within this large one.

For the wide groove shows two slightly raised lines which, drawn across, divide it as if into three parts, carved for the three tendons of that muscle. When the tendons have passed the groove, they are gathered together and end in a single tendon <margin>k Book 1, chapter 30, figure 1, R.</margin> implanted into the cavity of the great process of the femur <note>The **trochanteric fossa**</note> along with the ninth muscle <note>The **obturator externus**</note>.

Therefore, when you look at these three tendons, which have flesh growing on their outer part, you will easily conclude that here Nature wanted strength added to the tenth muscle; lest, if it were entirely fleshy (as we also warned above regarding the seventh muscle moving the femur), it might be torn in its turning and movement, compressed by the hardness of the bone. Hence also a ligament, or a thick and strong membrane, grows over the groove, so that contact with the bone might not damage the muscle during its turn.

In addition, this ligament is very smooth and smeared with a viscous and oily fluid <note>Synovial fluid, which acts as a lubricant in joints and tendon sheaths</note>, by which the turning of the muscle at the groove is made easier. We diligently imitate this craftsmanship of Nature in pulleys <term>rotulae: pulley wheels</term> and hinges, not only to accelerate movement, but also striving so that the rope being bent is not destroyed by friction too quickly. Furthermore, just as we do not trust a rope to the groove of a pulley-wheel alone, but secure the wheel in a block <term>trochlea: a pulley system or block</term> or a fork (lest the rope slip from the groove); so also Nature, not content with the groove of the bones, has brought forth one muscle from the upper part of the groove <margin>Fleshy portions belonging to the tenth muscle.</margin> and another from the lower part. These two, extended together with the tenth <margin>l One is Table 11, l; 12, β; 13, χ; 14, f. The other is in the same tables at ω, γ, ζ, g.</margin>, protect it in a way so that it does not slip from its seat.

For from the sharp process <margin>m Book 1, chapter 29, figure 2, d.</margin> of the ischium <note>The **ischial spine**</note>, a fleshy muscle is born <note>The **superior gemellus**</note>, attached to the upper part of the tenth muscle right up to its insertion. Then from the appendix <margin>n Book 1, chapter 29, figure 2, l.</margin> of the ischium <note>The **ischial tuberosity**</note>, another similarly fleshy and slender muscle comes forth <note>The **inferior gemellus**</note>, extended to the lower seat of the tenth muscle up to its insertion. Both achieve their insertion with the tenth muscle into the cavity of the great process of the femur, and with it, they assist in the rotation of the femur.

Furthermore, you will occasionally observe not only muscles of this kind produced at the higher and lower seat of the turn or track <margin>o Table 13, γ.</margin>, but also that a fleshy substance is born from the ischium in the internal region where the turn and track are no longer oblique. It is as if those <margin>p Table 13, f, s, u. q Table 13, χ, γ, ζ.</margin> three tendons were sent into a fleshy substance born from the ischium after they had made their turn, and thus enveloped, they head toward the great process of the femur.

It is, therefore, in your judgment <margin>How many muscles moving the femur can be established.</margin> whether to join these muscles, or the fleshy mass receiving the tendons, to the tenth, and thus enumerate ten proper muscles of the femur; or if you prefer, you will distinguish both and count twelve. Again, if you divide the fifth muscle into three, there will be fourteen in all. In our count, therefore, the tenth along with those two slender ones rotates the femur backward, while the ninth rotates it forward, just as if you were to rotate a stick placed between two extended hands by moving the hands alternately forward and backward. Thus far, I have reviewed the muscles moving the femur as accurately as I could.

However, so that you may be better guided through these texts as they currently stand—as if by a guiding thread—I will add that I interpret his opinion as follows: I believe Galen describes first that muscle which we have called the **r** fifth; then he briefly describes that which we have designated as the **s** ninth, which Galen later approaches more fully. After this, he treats the **t** eighth, which appears differently in apes than in humans; and furthermore, he proposes the **u** sixth and **x** seventh, but quite inconsistently, and very obscurely because of the difference here between man and apes. These are followed by the **y** first, **z** second, **a** third, and **b** fourth, which also present themselves differently in apes than in humans; then again the **c** ninth, and finally the **d** tenth. How truly the history and function of these muscles are commemorated by Galen in that work, you will readily judge if—as I warned before—you diligently compare my writings with Galen's opinion (whatever may be imagined of it, and however his books may be further corrupted day by day), while also applying a direct inspection of the things themselves.

OF THOSE muscles which preside over the movements of the thigh, you will rightly begin the <term>dissection</term> <note>original: "administrationem," referring to the practical management or execution of an anatomical procedure</note> with the extensors, on that leg where you began the muscles that move the lower leg. The **second muscle** must then likewise be separated from the ilium with the razor, taking care that the origin of the third is not taken away with it. For the continuity of their origins, which is distinguished only by a line, easily allows both muscles to be removed together. Therefore, when you have gradually reached the origin of the third muscle by reflecting the beginning of the second and making transverse cuts always following the back of the ilium, the second must now be reflected in its entirety, pulled by the hands, and torn away from the third all the way to its insertion. Once its head is grasped, the whole muscle should be separated from the underlying structures all the way to the small process of the femur; if you wish, you can do this with the help of your hand alone—unless perhaps you have already inspected this muscle long ago when you were managing the muscles that move the back. After you have tracked its tendon and the **k** cavity through which it is carried over the pubic bone, the seventh muscle will be conveniently approached. You will scrape this **l** seventh muscle <note>The *iliacus*</note> away with the scalpel using transverse strokes from the inner surface of the <term>ilium</term> <note>The large, upper part of the pelvic bone</note> to the hip bone where it descends; and with the muscle lifted by your hands, you will pull it down to the smaller process of the femur to consider its insertion, without neglecting meanwhile the inspection of the cavity through which it is led. Soon, you will tear away the **m** eighth muscle <note>The *gracilis*</note>, cut by a transverse line from the pubic bone, as far as its insertion, which is similarly as wide as its beginning; taking care meanwhile that you do not imprudently remove the **n** ninth as well. The two muscles that still remain, since the pubic bones were pulled apart while you were looking at the muscles of the bladder and the <term>seat</term> <note>The rectum and anus</note>, and you now have only one leg at hand in which you were managing the muscles moving the shin, will be easily cut. Therefore, you will scrape the **o** ninth and tenth from the pubic bone and the hip bone, and you will examine their connection and their implantation into the cavity of the larger femur process. Do not by any means pass over the reflection of the tenth or the **p** muscular substance which arises everywhere at its sides and is extended with the tenth muscle all the way to its insertion. Once these muscles that rotate the femur are cut away, a **q** membrane <note>The *obturator membrane*</note> offers itself for inspection, occupying the whole hole of the pubic bone and separating the muscles resting on it on both sides. Similarly, you will observe a **r** tough ligament extending from the sharp process of the hip bone to the side of the fifth bone of the <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>, upon which the **s** fourth muscle moving the femur rested, and which joins these bones more firmly. Then **t** another has long since presented itself, arising from the same side of the sacrum where the one just mentioned is inserted, and inserted into the posterior and higher **u** seat of the hip bone's appendix; this provides a **x** support for the rectum as well as for the muscles mentioned just before in the narration. The ligaments of the hip joint, however, along with the ligaments of the knee and foot, I shall relegate to a single Chapter, to be subjoined to the discussion of the muscles moving the foot and its toes.

### ON THE HIDDEN TENDON, BORN BENEATH THE SKIN
### of the sole. Chapter LVIII.

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.
->417<-

<margin>
The great difference between the ape and the man. Book 2 of *On Anatomical Procedures*, section 15; muscle table 5, then 10 and 11.
</margin>
...and since he <note>Referring to Galen</note> responds in his own way to the opinions in the third book of *On the Use of the Parts*, we must undertake a more diligent discussion of these types of muscles. Certainly, it is not fitting to agree with Galen that an ape differs from a man only in the spreading of the toes—namely, that the ape has longer and more separate toes than humans. Furthermore, Galen teaches that the ape surpasses the man by having **a** only a single tendon, which he says is reflected at the tarsus <note>The cluster of bones in the ankle and upper foot</note>, becomes cartilaginous there, and is inserted into the bone of the metatarsus <note>Original: *pedij os*; the bones between the ankle and toes</note> placed before the big toe. He is referring to the tendon of the muscle that we shall establish as the seventh of those moving the foot. This muscle in humans produces such a tendon as Galen attributed specifically to the ape, and of which he deprives the human, proposing a false difference. This easily proves how he never approached the human foot with a dissection. Truly, there is otherwise a great difference between man and ape in the muscles and their tendons. If I do not explain all of these (lest I become too wordy), I will nonetheless gladly relate what comes to mind as the sequence of the discourse supplies it, in the history of those muscles that still remain to be mentioned. I kindly warn students here that they should not be content only with the true description and inspection of human muscles, but should also approach the ape, so that they may more successfully understand Galen (who is nowhere as difficult as in Anatomy). Thus, when they undertake to profess his teachings (as indeed we all ought to do), they should not follow the example of their teachers and neglect the most elegant and vast abundance of his books which embrace anatomical matters. Nor should they devote themselves entirely to those works which anyone moderately educated in liberal studies achieves without any effort from a teacher. They should remember how shamefully those who call themselves "Galenists" today are forced to step back in minor works of Galen whenever he happens upon a mention of dissection and the parts of the body. And he happens upon it very frequently, both because he was wonderfully delighted by dissections, and because a doctor must frequently mention the body he proposes to cure.

<margin>
**b** 13th table, m; 14th, f.
Difference between the ape and man in the tendon arising under the foot.
**c** 12th table, phi (φ), psi (ψ).
**d** 5th table, n.

</margin>
But come, let us approach the **b** tendon stretched under the skin of the sole <note>The plantar fascia or the tendon of the plantaris muscle</note>, in which man differs remarkably from the ape. For the ape possesses a proper muscle that produces this tendon, which arises from the root of the outer head of the femur <note>The thigh bone</note> at the back, starting from a **c** fleshy beginning and hidden under two muscles **d** which, arising from the lower heads of the femur, are said to form the prominent part of the calf and be inserted into the heel bone <note>The *calcaneus*</note>. Thus, covered by these muscles, this muscle of the ape is carried downward as a fleshy mass, **d** very similar in form to the one that produces the broad tendon in the hand <note>The *palmaris longus*</note>. After it descends to the middle of the length of the tibia <note>The shin bone</note>, it ends in a slender tendon which, no longer covered by those two muscles, is extended toward the inner side of the tendon they produce, descending slantwise to the back of the heel. Specifically in tailed apes, as in dogs, the heel has a carved-out groove in which this tendon is safely carried in a non-wandering path. Meanwhile, it is not attached to the bone of the heel, except perhaps by the intervention of some transverse ligament by which it is covered. In this, it varies from Galen's description in the first book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, because it is not split into two parts, one inserted into the heel and the other spread out into a broad tendon. For it entirely passes over the **e** heel and is dilated into the sole of the foot, attached to the muscle that you will hear flexes the second joint of the four toes; it is more clearly extended into the lower seat of the five toes of the foot than the broad tendon of the hand reaches the fingers. Furthermore, just as the broad tendon of the hand is not attached to the skin without the medium of some body <note>i.e., some intervening tissue</note>, so it is in the foot; for much fat comes between the tendon and the skin, and this is especially true in humans, in whom no muscle at all leads out a broad tendon. But from the lowest part of the heel, where we rest on the ground...

...on which we lean,<sup>f</sup> a strong ligament <note>The plantar aponeurosis, a thick layer of connective tissue that supports the arch of the foot</note> comes forth, covering the entire lower breadth of the foot, except for one muscle on each side which it does not wrap. On the inner side of the foot, this muscle<sup>g</sup> is the one said to pull the big toe away from the others; on the outer side,<sup>h</sup> it is the one that moves the little toe away from the rest. This ligament is born far thicker and more robust than the tendon in the hand, and it covers the entire lower surface of that<sup>i</sup> muscle which we shall teach flexes the second joints of the four toes. Indeed, it is formed in such a way that one might call this ligament the muscle's own membrane, were it not for the fact that near the roots of the toes—where the muscle's tendons pass under the transverse ligament of the four toes—it separates from the muscle. Then, covering the transverse ligaments of the toes and dividing into five parts, it is attached to the lower surface of the five toes. Furthermore (as we warned a little earlier), a great abundance of somewhat hard fat lies between this ligament (or whatever you wish to call it) and the skin, though it is joined to the skin by very frequent fibrous connections. Humans alone are endowed with this kind of ligament in place of a broad tendon; if it had been derived from a tendon, that tendon would have had to be created exceedingly strong and thick. For if you compare the tendon of the hand with this ligamentous body, a thickness four times that of the tendon stretched through the forearm would by no means suffice in the leg. Nevertheless, you will hear that in the back part of the human leg<sup>k</sup> a muscle is placed which, arising with a fleshy beginning from the outer head of the <term>femur</term> <note>The thigh bone</note>, ceases to be fleshy before it has even passed the back of the knee and produces a tendon far thinner than the one that sends out the broad tendon of the hand. But this tendon <note>The plantaris tendon</note>, so far as I have seen, never enters the sole of the foot; rather, it is implanted into the inner side of the heel at its rear part. It does not at all reach the very back of the heel, as does the tendon of that muscle in "tailed monkeys" <note>original: *caudatarum simiarum*; Vesalius often uses this term to highlight that Galen's descriptions were based on macaques rather than humans</note>, and even less does it claim for itself a groove in this part of the heel bone in which to be carried without wandering. The similarity of its shape is proof that the ligament I mentioned in the human foot, and the broad tendon in the ape, serve the same purpose as the broad tendon that enters the hand. This is even more firmly persuaded by the frequent absence of the broad tendon in the hand. For more than once I have found it missing in the hand, and the<sup>l</sup> transverse ligament placed in the inner part of the wrist extending a portion of itself to supply the place of the broad tendon—very differently in humans than in apes. It has also been observed at times that this tendon is produced by the<sup>m</sup> tendons that flex the wrist, sometimes from the one inserted into the fourth bone of the wrist, and sometimes from the one which, led through the transverse ligament of the inner wrist, was said to be inserted much earlier into the <term>postbrachial</term> <note>metacarpal</note> bone supporting the index finger.

...where we reported the straight muscle of the abdomen <term>rectus abdominis</term> arises. <note>Vesalius is likely making a comparison to the fleshy origin of the rectus abdominis described earlier in the book.</note> For the upper part of the beginning of this muscle is fleshy and broad: and extending downward, a little below the knee joint, it merges with the rest of the starting portion, which was precisely tendinous and livid at its origin. Indeed, as both tend downward from the heads of the femur, they touch each other<term>h</term> not far from their origin, clinging to one another with fibrous connections; and the further they creep downward, the more strongly they grow together: so that now the tendon, which both produce,<term>i</term> exists as one entirely. <note>This "single tendon" is what we now call the Achilles tendon, or calcaneal tendon.</note> However, the inner, or first muscle, is drawn downward somewhat more extensively fleshy than the second: which is most evident in muscles before they are dissected. For the two protruding bellies of the muscles in the calf <term>sura</term> are the fleshy parts of the present muscles, forming the great mass of the calf. Now, the tendon arising from both muscles, having become a little narrower, is very strongly inserted into the posterior seat of the heel in tailed monkeys. In humans, however, not much below the fleshy seat of the muscles, it grows onto a certain underlying<term>k</term> muscle,<term>l</term> which we shall count as the fourth among the movers of the foot. And this connection is so persistent that you could by no means separate this tendon all the way to the heel from the underlying muscle, and you are forced to assert that from this tendon and the tendon of the fourth muscle<term>m</term> one single tendon is formed, inserted into the posterior seat of the heel.

This fact uniquely distinguishes these two muscles among almost all others of the entire body: that in their heads, not far from the origin, individual little bones compared to sesame seeds <note>original: "sesamo comparata ossicula"</note> are born. <note>These are the fabellae, small sesamoid bones often found in the tendons of the gastrocnemius muscle.</note> With their smooth and slippery surface, where they stand out from the substance of the muscles, they face the smooth surface of the lower heads of the femur on which they rest, and whose force and impact they receive, thus contributing in no small way to the strength of the muscles by the common use of sesamoid bones. <term>n</term> The third muscle is that which we said in the previous chapter produces a remarkably slender tendon. He is certainly worthy of being noted by us sometimes (were it not for his authority and the faith we place in him), and then most especially when he thrusts upon us the history of his apes instead of human anatomy, unlike those ancient writers.

...[the fifth] muscle $^g$ is one of those that, not being restricted by their flesh-like substance, emit a rounded tendon from only one side. Therefore, where the tendon is entirely free of the flesh, it is carried downward, $^h$ resting in a groove carved into the posterior seat of the process of the tibial appendix, which forms the inner ankle bone <term>medial malleolus</term>. In this groove, a transverse $^i$ ligament is drawn over the tendon, as it moves obliquely from here toward the lower parts $^i$ of the foot. For it creeps beneath all $^k$ the muscles occupying the lower surface of the foot until it is strongly inserted into the lower $^l$ surface of the tarsal bone, which is nearest to the bone imitating a cube or a die <note>The cuboid bone</note>: and which, as we said in the first book, when joined with the other, most aptly expresses the shape of a wedge <term>cuneiform</term>, and is granted a private $^m$ process for the sake of the present muscle. For the tendon of the fifth muscle does not attempt an $^n$ insertion into the first tarsal bone, as Galen wrote.

<margin>
seventh.
</margin>

*The sixth of those moving the foot is located in the anterior region of the tibia, the most forward of all in this region, representing the shape of a perfect muscle.* $^p$ It arises, however, from the anterior region of the articulation of the fibula with the bone of the tibia, assuming a portion of its origin from both bones and their common $^q$ ligament; it begins at an acute angle and, immediately widening, forms a muscle belly somewhat wider than it is deep. But before the muscle passes the middle of the length of the tibia, it gradually narrows, and far above the foot, ends in a rounded $^r$ tendon, which creeps downward through the anterior parts of the tibia bone and passes under the transverse $^s$ ligament stretched from the tibia bone to the fibula: $^t$ and as soon as it has passed that, descending downward into the inner parts of the foot, it is carried in a moderately open groove impressed into the ligament of the innermost bone of the tarsal $^u$ with the bone resembling a boat <term>navicular</term>, until it reaches the inner side of the metatarsal bone $^x$ which is placed before the big toe. For it is inserted into a peculiar $^y$ process of that bone, catching the joint of the metatarsal bone with the tarsus with a truly strong $^z$ flattening. Thus, no other muscle is stretched over the anterior seat of the sixth muscle: but on its posterior side, it rests upon those $^a$ muscles which are said to be contained under the same transverse ligament of the tibia and to serve chiefly the extensions of the toes. But the sixth muscle is joined on its inner side to the outer side of the sharp $^b$ line of the tibia bone, which constitutes the outer side of the fleshy seat of the tibia, which is also slanted inward along the side of the sixth muscle, both to give way to this muscle and to provide a seat for others which will be mentioned as being placed under the sixth. 

The outer side of the sixth muscle, at its very origin and throughout its progress where it widens, is joined to the muscle which I shall now describe and call the $^b$ seventh of those moving the foot: which, like $^d$ the eighth, takes its beginning from the fibula and is attached to almost the entire outer side of the fibula: so much so, that it ought to be reviewed neither among the anterior nor the posterior muscles of the tibia, but would be aptly said to be placed privately on the outer side of the tibia. The seventh muscle, therefore, takes a sinewy and strong $^e$ beginning around the knee, from the outer $^c$ side of the appendix of the fibula and the ligaments connecting the bones there, where $^f$ we said the fourth muscle moving the tibia strives for its insertion. This beginning, joined to the fibula for no long distance, departs from it, having the head $^g$ of the eighth muscle moving the foot spread beneath it. When, therefore, the seventh muscle departs from the fibula, it always appears leaden <note>original: "liuidus", referring to a bluish-grey or bruised color</note> in its outer part: but in its inner part, where it rests upon other muscles, it is seen to be reddish and exactly like flesh. For having become fleshy not so far from its origin, it widens, expressing the appearance of a mouse <note>A common metaphor for the shape of a muscle belly</note>. Fleshy in this manner, it is carried straight down a little beyond the middle of the length of the fibula, not being perfectly fleshy in its outer part. Since this muscle claims this for itself privately: that in its outer part, even above the middle of the length of the tibia, $^h$ it is fleshy on both sides, and between those two sides it shows a very strong $^i$ tendon on the inner part, nourished by flesh from the sides. Furthermore, once this muscle has passed the midpoint of the length of the <term>fibula</term><note>The outer, thinner bone of the lower leg.</note> by a noteworthy distance, it becomes entirely devoid of flesh, producing a rounded tendon that gradually stretches obliquely backward toward the rear parts of the fibula. For the tendon no longer covers the entire outer side of the fibula as the fleshy part of the muscle did; instead, now reflected toward the back, <margin>k Plate 6, table u.</margin> it leaves the outer ankle bone <term>external malleolus</term> bare of flesh and exposed in a somewhat triangular shape. Reaching the posterior seat of the lower attachment <margin>l Figure 6, chapter 31, book 1, q.</margin> of the fibula, it occupies its own groove here, as well as a transverse <margin>m Plate 2, table z.</margin> ligament. Thus the tendon, <margin>n Figure 15, table 4, X, Y.</margin> wrapped in this ligament which proceeds from the fibula into the heel and ankle, is led downward toward the front, toward the sole <margin>o Figure 2, chapter 33, book 1, u.</margin> of the foot. It is indeed so bent that it is inserted into the base of the metatarsal bone that lies before the big toe, which puts out a process on its outer side <margin>o Figure 2, chapter 33, book 1, u.</margin> to which the tendon of this seventh muscle is aptly implanted. Sometimes, however, this seventh muscle is seen to attempt an insertion not into this metatarsal bone, but into the base of the metatarsal <margin>p Figure 2, chapter 33, book 1, m.</margin> bone supporting the middle toe. Moreover, Nature does not devise the oblique path of this tendon casually or negligently, but has led the tendon through the middle <margin>q The left figure 15 of the table shows this at X, Y.</margin> between the bones and the muscles occupying the lower parts of the foot. This was done lest, if she had perhaps led it between the skin and the muscles, it might compress the muscles located in the sole when contracted upward, and be an obstacle to them in performing their duty. Furthermore, since it was necessary for this tendon to be reflected not only to the posterior seat of the outer ankle bone, but also to another bone located on the outer side of the foot <margin>r Figures 1, 2, 12, 13, chapter 33, book 1, character 2.</margin> <note>The cuboid bone.</note>, Nature provided for this reflection with incredible craftsmanship. For in the lower seat of the "die-like" bone <note>original: "ossis tesseram imitantis"; referring to the cuboid bone.</note>, which faces the sole and the outer side <margin>s Figure 2, chapter 33, book 1, o.</margin> of the foot, she carved out a somewhat wide and not very deep groove, which she smeared with a viscous fluid and surrounded with a very smooth and slippery ligament. Then Nature led the tendon around this groove—not indeed rounded as in its other regions, but <margin>t Plate 15, table 4, X.</margin> where the tendon is reflected at the groove, she dilated it, so that it might be turned back more firmly against the moderately open groove; and lest, if it had remained rounded, it might slip away from there. Finally, by no means content with this width, she also wished the tendon to harden there by a peculiar artifice to the point that it expresses the appearance of cartilage. Indeed, sometimes surpassing the hardness of cartilage, the tendon is seen to be bony in that same place, as if gifted with a small <term>sesamoid bone</term><note>A small bone embedded within a tendon, like a sesame seed, used to provide a mechanical advantage.</note>, by which it may more readily discharge the force of the bend at an acute angle. Moreover, the more diligently I behold this craftsmanship of Nature, the more I also admire Galen; for although <margin>Book 2 of *Anatomical Procedures*, section [6].</margin> he had proposed the difference between the toes of a human foot and those of an ape in the history of the present muscles, he quite clearly added that, by occasion of that difference, humans are deprived of that tendon which we said is so elegantly and industriously reflected toward the tarsus. For by this reasoning, since humans present that tendon so elegantly, Galen easily bears witness to how little he dissected the human foot; and how disgracefully we err when we wish Galen's account (who also poorly understood the function of the present muscle) to conform to humans. And some of our contemporaries are so insane that they refer Galen's teaching to humans rather than to apes even where a signal difference occurs between apes and humans, while in the meantime Galen’s discourse fits the fabric of apes to a hair. <margin>The Eighth.</margin> The eighth <margin>u Plate 2, table y; Plate 4, character 15; Plate 5, character 9; Plate 6, table γ, 8, 13, v. 14 l, m, 15 d under v, at b.</margin> muscle, which is hidden entirely under the seventh (if you except the anterior seat of the tendon itself), also comes forth from the fibula. For a little below the upper attachment of the fibula, it arises from the outer side of the fibula, somewhat toward the front; and being perfectly fleshy and always clinging to the fibula, it creeps downward under the seventh. When, however, it has passed the middle of the length of the fibula by some distance, it also ends in a rounded tendon, which is reflected downward toward the posterior parts of the fibula just like the tendon of the seventh. -># ANDREAS VESALIUS OF BRUSSELS ON THE MUSCLES MOVING THE TOES OF THE FOOT. Chapter LX.<-

<margin>Movement of the toes of the foot.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a scene with several human figures in a landscape with a building and a tree, possibly representing an outdoor anatomical lesson or a classical scene.</image-desc>**THE TOES** of the foot are moved by exactly the same motions as those reported for the four fingers of the hand. For the first <term>internode</term><note>Latin: "internodium," referring to the segment of a limb between joints; here, the proximal phalanx.</note> of the big toe (which is endowed with only two bones) is flexed in entirely the same manner as the first internodes of the remaining toes; however, it is not, as in the hand, drawn across the other fingers in an opposite flexion <note>Vesalius is noting that the big toe is not opposable like the thumb.</note>. And here the flexion of the first joints is either straight or slightly inclining to one side, just as we said the first joints of the four fingers of the hand are moved. The second internode of the big toe, and also the second and third internodes of the remaining toes, are granted only a simple flexion and extension that does not veer toward either side; they are endowed with no proper movement of their own to the side, while the first internodes additionally obtain the motion of both <term>adduction</term><note>Movement toward the midline of the body.</note> and <term>abduction</term><note>Movement away from the midline.</note>. Moreover, just as the ratio of movement for the fingers of the hand and the toes of the foot is somewhat equal, so also the series of muscles in both is almost similar. Wherefore, in describing them, we shall not inappropriately follow the same order which we observed in the muscles of the hand.

P.</margin> descends to the lowest part of the tibia <note>The larger shin bone.</note>, it gives off a rounded tendon <margin>u 14 tab. n.</margin> from its inner side, which previously <margin>x 14 tab. r.</margin> seemed to originate for some time within the muscle's flesh. For the sake of this tendon, a groove <margin>y 15 tab. G, & charact. 3.</margin> is carved into the inner side of the heel bone where it receives the ankle bone; this groove is covered by a transverse ligament <margin>z 14 tab. λ & 15 tab. td.</margin> <note>A band of tough tissue that holds tendons in place like a strap.</note>, which safely guides the tendon of the present muscle. After the tendon has passed over that ligament, it enters the lower parts of the foot obliquely. It creeps forward between those muscles <margin>α 15 tab. L.</margin> which are said to draw the four toes toward the big toe, and those <margin>a 15 tab. Q.</margin> to which the task of flexing the first <term>internode</term> <note>The segment of the toe between joints; a phalanx.</note> of the toes is assigned, heading almost entirely toward the big toe.

For from the present tendon <margin>b 15 tab. Q.</margin>, around the middle of the sole, a small portion <margin>c 14 tab. θ.</margin> branches out, which mingles with some of the tendons of that muscle which I shall number as the third of those moving the toes; together with them, it assists in flexing the joint of the second toe <note>Latin: "indicis," literally the "index" toe, referring to the toe next to the big toe.</note> and, as it were, the middle toe as well. The remaining part of the tendon of the second muscle moving the toes (which is certainly the strongest) is carried obliquely to the big toe, as we have said. Passing along the length of the first bone of the big toe, it is received by a transverse ligament and is implanted with a broad insertion into the length of the second bone of the big toe, being the primary agent of that bone's flexion. To this tendon, before it is inserted into the second bone of the big toe, there is added a <term>sesamoid</term> bone <margin>d 2. fi. cap. 33; lib. 1.</margin> <note>Small, seed-like bones found within tendons to reduce friction.</note> of some size; with its slippery and smooth surface, it is positioned over the groove which the heads of the first bone of the big toe have in their middle, where they meet the hollow of the second bone.

The third muscle <margin>e 14 ta. Ξ. 15 tab. P, λ, 2, u; 3, v, 8 u, 16 c.</margin>, which is spread over the fifth of the muscles moving the foot, is extended in the back part of the tibia in exactly the same manner as the second muscle of the toes, but looking more toward the inner side than the second muscle does. For it rests far more <margin>f 15 tab. m a G, 15 u à quàm B.</margin> on the bone of the tibia than on the fibula. When it has descended almost to the heel, while still appearing broad, it brings forth a rounded tendon <margin>g 14 tab. n.</margin> from its inner side. Nature has crafted a specific groove <margin>h 15 tab. F, & charact. 2.</margin> and a transverse ligament for this tendon, situated in the middle of the two grooves that are also found here.

Thus the tendon of the third muscle, guided by this groove, enters the lower parts of the foot while still rounded, lying beneath the tendon <margin>i 14 tab. θ, κ.</margin> of the second muscle toward the skin of the sole, forming the image of the letter X <note>This refers to the "chiasma plantare," where the Flexor Digitorum Longus and Flexor Hallucis Longus tendons cross each other.</note>. For the tendon of the second muscle is carried obliquely from the outer parts inward toward the front; however, the tendon of the third muscle tends from the inner parts outward, and for that reason, they are positioned crosswise in the middle of the sole with the second tendon. The tendon of the third muscle, entering the sole of the foot in this way and already positioned almost in the middle of the foot’s length, widens slightly <margin>k 14 tab. θ.</margin> and is divided into four other tendons. These run out to the four toes, corresponding to those tendons of the hand <margin>l 6 tab. γ, musculi sci licet 1. insigniti.</margin> which flex the third joint of the four fingers.

Hidden beneath the tendons of the first muscle, they approach the roots of the toes together with the tendons <margin>m 14 tab. θ.</margin> of the first muscle, covered by a transverse ligament, just as in the hand. To creep forward as far as the third bone, they pass through the tendons of the first muscle, which are divided by a longitudinal slit; having been made broader, they are implanted into the length of the third bone. Moreover, it specifically happens to the tendon approaching the second toe, and sometimes equally to the one extending to the middle toe, that in the middle of the sole they receive a small portion <margin>n 15 ta. Q.</margin> of the tendon of the second muscle proceeding to the big toe, which joins and mingles entirely with those tendons of the toes. Sometimes, however, no matter how accurately you observe each detail, you will see that nothing is extended from the second tendon, but that it is entirely consumed in the big toe. And so, indeed, the toes have three primary muscles: the first of which flexes the second internode of the four toes; the remaining two are the workers of the flexion of the last internode of all five toes. # ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE HUMAN BODY BY AND. VESALIUS

...has long since examined these passages and understands that Galen contradicts himself, and that his books are also corrupted in this section; such a reader eagerly waits to hear why I disagree with Galen. To this, for the present, I wish to add nothing other than that I have so far described the most true account of the muscles of the toes in humans, and Galen’s passages (as you will soon hear, once I have added something regarding the function of the muscles) hardly even apply to <note>Galen's anatomical work was famously based on Barbary macaques and other primates, which led to errors when applied to human medicine.</note> apes. I have judged the function of the three aforementioned muscles to be common with the muscles of the fingers of the hand. While the <margin>o 14 tab. A</margin> second muscle was considered the author of the flexion of the second <term>internode</term> <note>The segment of a finger or toe between joints; a phalanx.</note> of the big toe, no mention was made of the first joint as far as flexion is concerned. In the same way, I wrote previously that the third internode of the remaining toes is moved by the benefit of the <margin>p 14 tab. Ξ</margin> third muscle. Meanwhile, according to Galen’s opinion, it ought to have been said that the first joints are also flexed by the two posterior muscles. For Galen believes that the function of these muscles is the same here as it is in the hand. Indeed, in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, specifically weighing his own decree—in which he had suggested that the first joints of the fingers are flexed by the help of the transverse ligaments—he said that from those muscles which are inserted into the third internode of the toes, not only the third and first joints are led into flexion, but the first, second, and third internodes are flexed by their help. This would certainly be necessary if we were to grant that, by the power of the transverse ligament, the tendons could move those bones upon which they merely rest, but into which they are not <margin>q 14 tab. d, d, u, d.</margin> inserted. But even so, it would not have been enough for those <margin>r 14 tab. Θ</margin> tendons (which we said flex the third internode) to be assigned that notable duty of flexing by Galen; rather, it would also have to be added to the discourse that the <margin>r</margin> first muscle, which is inserted into the second internodes of the four toes, also flexes the first internodes, since the tendons of that muscle are also covered by the same ligament on the first bone of the toes as the other tendons. Therefore, because we do not at all concede that motion must be ascribed to the bones by grace of the transverse ligaments, it should also not be surprising that our judgment disagrees with Galen’s decree. 

<margin>
How the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd muscles appear in apes.
</margin>
However, setting function aside, I will not be burdened to describe how these muscles appear in <note>Literally "tailed apes," referring to monkeys like macaques.</note> tailed apes—not being unmindful, meanwhile, of Galen’s passage where he taught that tendons do not always mix in the same way, lest anyone think I weigh his dogmas too superficially. The apes, then, have the first muscle (by which the second internodes of the toes are flexed) in common with humans; but it is gifted with tendons that are longer in proportion to how much the ape’s foot exceeds the human foot and toes in length. The <margin>These details are obvious from the human fabric.</margin> second and third muscles are also located in the tibia of apes in the same way as in humans. However, when they lead out a tendon, they do not bring it forth from one side; rather, being constricted in the manner of other muscles, they send it out. This also occurs in the fifth muscle of the apes which moves the foot. Whence it should not seem strange to us if Galen made no mention at all of that rare and peculiar sideways extraction of the tendons <note>Vesalius refers to the way human tendons often emerge from the side of the muscle belly, a detail Galen missed.</note>. But meanwhile, the tendons of tailed apes enter the sole of the foot as in humans; and where they manage an intersection in the shape of the <note>original: "X literæ instar"</note> letter X, the tendon of the second muscle is thoroughly mixed with the tendon of the third muscle. From both, one tendon as it were arises, from which a small portion is carried transversely to the big toe, exactly like that which we reported being carried to the thumb from the middle of the palm, from the tendon approaching the index finger in the hand of tailed apes. The remaining part of this mixture of tendons is divided into four tendons, surpassing in mass the portion extended to the big toe. These, drawn out under the tendons of the first muscle as in humans, and passing through them, and finally being rendered wider, are <margin>s 15 tab. L, then o.</margin> inserted into the third internode. The <margin>s</margin> muscles flexing the first five joints of the toes...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

consisting in the anterior region of the <term>tibia</term> <note>The shin bone; original: "tibiæ"</note>, it is led forth: then creeping through the upper parts of the foot toward the <term>big toe</term> <note>original: "pollicem"</note>, it is inserted into its entire length. By the benefit of this muscle, the big toe is extended without turning significantly to either side. No other muscle from the shin bone is inserted into the upper part of the big toe in humans; however, <gloss>q</gloss> a certain muscle, stretched along the entire upper region of the foot according to its length, inserts a tendon into the outer side of the upper part of the big toe, by whose help the big toe is drawn toward the other toes. For next to the side of the <term>talus</term> <note>The ankle bone</note>, <gloss>r</gloss> where the bone resembling a die <note>The cuboid bone; original: "os tesseram referens"</note> is articulated with the heel bone, a large fleshy mass arises from the ligaments of that area. This mass, extended forward obliquely toward the toes, is divided into four fleshy parts, each of which forms a rounded tendon. The innermost and largest of these four tendons is inserted into the outer side of the big toe toward the upper part; the second is implanted into the outer side of the second toe; the third into the middle toe; and the fourth into the fourth toe. Thus, the little toe alone is destitute of such a tendon; although once, and quite indistinctly, I observed a tiny tendon extended to it as well. By the benefit of these tendons, the four toes provided with them are drawn to the outer side. Whether this fleshy body, divided into these tendons, should be counted as one or several muscles, I do not think should be strongly insisted upon; since at its origin it appears to be a single muscle, and afterward, as we have said, it is divided into four tendons. But according to Galen's opinion <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose work was the standard for over a millennium before Vesalius.</note>, there would be two muscles here: one of which would draw the second and middle toes away from the big toe, and the other would move the fourth and little toes outward to the side. Then, another muscle would be inserted from the shin bone into the big toe, taking the place of that tendon which we mentioned is inserted into the big toe from this fleshy body located in the upper part of the foot. But it is no wonder that Galen’s description here varies greatly from ours and contradicts the views of the ancients, since apes differ significantly from humans in this area. For in apes, two muscles are extended from the shin bone to the upper parts of the big toe, just as happens in the hand; then two muscles are seen situated in the upper part of the foot, drawing the four toes away from the big toe, which, just like the muscular body occupying the upper part of the human foot, are covered by a very oblique placement. Come then, for the sake of instruction, let the muscular body already described by us in humans be held as one, and let it be the sixteenth of those moving the toes of the foot.

In apes there is yet another muscle, arising from the <term>metatarsal</term> bone placed before the second toe and going into the big toe, moving it as close as possible to the second toe; humans are rightly destitute of this muscle, which Galen meanwhile (even if he recognized the difference between the toes in humans and apes) lists in the second book of *On Anatomical Procedures* <note>original: "de Administrandis fectionibus"</note> along with the other muscles placed in the foot, clearly and deliberately showing that he is presenting a description of apes everywhere rather than of humans.

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

<margin>* 14th table, lambda, mu; 15th table N.</margin>
<margin>y 14th table delta, then pi.</margin>
<margin>Four muscles, drawing the four toes toward the big toe <note>original: "pollicem"</note>, following 19, 20, 21, 22.</margin>
<margin>z 6th table Omega.</margin>
Therefore, after the eighteenth muscle, there remain in man* only four muscles yet to be described, which draw the four toes toward the internal side. These are extended in a similar way to those in the hand, by those <sup>y</sup> tendons which flex the third joint of the toes. However, the muscles of the foot vary from those of the hand in this respect: they do not arise from the sheaths of the tendons in this manner, but from the <term>calcaneus</term> <note>the heel bone; original: "calcis osse"</note>. For from the ligaments of the <term>tarsus</term> <note>the group of bones forming the ankle and upper foot</note> bones, which bind the posterior bones of the foot together in the sole, a muscular body arises. This is later divided into four slender muscles and is inserted into the internal side of the four toes. If, therefore, you consider this fleshy mass as four muscles, all the muscles of the toes of the foot in man will be twenty-two; if, however, you count that body as one, there will only be nineteen. Furthermore, depending on how many parts you dissect that <sup>z</sup> body into (which draws the big toe and the three toes nearest to it toward the external side), you will also increase the number.

### CONCERNING THE LIGAMENTS BINDING THE ILIUM BONES TO THE SACRUM,
#### and those of the hip and knee joints, and concerning all the remaining ligaments found in the leg and foot. Chapter LXI.

<margin>We have depicted very few ligaments: since they are membranes, they depend on the descriptions of the surrounding bones and must be reached by touch.</margin>
<margin>Ligaments of the sacrum bone, and of the bones attached to it.</margin>
<margin>a 13th table O.</margin>
<margin>b 10th table d.</margin>
<margin>c 14th table h.</margin>
<margin>d 7th table V between S, T.</margin>
<margin>e figure of chapter 1, P, P.</margin>
<margin>The membrane occupying the opening of the pubic bone.</margin>
<margin>Ligaments of the femur to the hip bone <note>original: "coxendicis os"</note>.</margin>
The ligament surrounding the connection of the <term>ilium</term> <note>the large, broad bone forming the upper part of each half of the pelvis</note> to the <term>sacrum</term> <note>the triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> is indeed membrane-like, but quite robust. However, the portion of the ligament that inserts itself where the bones meet becomes so strong and thick that it entirely represents the nature of a cartilaginous ligament. By its benefit, and finally through the intervention of cartilage as well, the ilium is most powerfully bound to the sacrum. For just as the <term>pubic bones</term> <note>original: "pubis ossa"</note> are joined together by the mediation of cartilage and a ligament surrounding the joint in a circular fashion, so too is the ilium tightened to the sacrum. Besides these ligaments of the sacrum, <sup>a</sup> another somewhat rounded one arises from the side of the connection of the fifth bone of the sacrum with the sixth, inserted into the sharp process of the <term>ischium</term> <note>the lower and back part of the hip bone; original: "coxendicis ossis"</note>. Furthermore, from the same seat of the sacrum, another <sup>b</sup> ligament is carried to the appendix of the hip bone, which, together with the aforementioned, connects these bones more firmly, and moreover serves as a support for the rectum and its muscles. Finally, in the opening of the pubic bone <sup>c</sup> a membrane is seen, entirely similar to that <sup>d</sup> ligament which binds the <term>radius</term> to the <term>ulna</term> along the length of the forearm; for its substance corresponds exactly to it, consisting of fibers running obliquely downward to the side. The ligaments connecting the <term>femur</term> <note>thigh bone</note> to the hip bone are considered the two most principal: <sup>e</sup> one surrounding the joint in a circular fashion, a type common to other joints as well. However, lest the head of the femur should ever be dislocated whenever the femur, sustaining the great mass of the body, is moved in various motions, this ligament we mentioned has become very thick and robust, second in thickness to none of those which surround the joints. And the Greeks thought this ligament was of such moment and use that they did not hesitate to call it *ischion* <note>Greek: ἰσχίον; here referring to the hip joint or its specific ligament</note> after the name of the whole joint itself. Indeed, not only has a particular thickness and hardness been added to this ligament surrounding the joint, but it also uniquely claims for itself that it is inserted into neither the head of the femur nor the brow of the <term>acetabulum</term> <note>the cup-shaped socket of the hip bone</note> of the hip bone, nor does it proceed from them: for it surrounds the entire neck of the femur, having grown around it in a circle nowhere but at the root of the great process of the femur <note>the greater trochanter</note>; but as for the rest of the part, it merely rests upon it without any connection. Then, it does not grow onto the brow of the acetabulum, but a little above the root of the brow on the hip bone. And here Nature has providently turned away from the structure of other ligaments surrounding joints. For if this hip ligament had been grown to the brows in the manner of other ligaments, the oblong head of the femur would by no means...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY.

...allowed the head [of the thigh bone] to be moved appropriately. You will observe this precisely <note>original: "ad amussim"</note> when you attempt to draw the thighs together and then spread them apart again. For it is remarkable to say how far the head of the femur is carried forward out of its socket when we place the heel of one foot like a plumb line against the middle of the inner side of the other foot. We see this happen in that position of the feet when, standing upright, we perform the step in dances which they call the "double simple," indicated by this sign: **ff**. To these features, in addition to the fact that the socket of the hip bone is quite deep, another ligament—though it does not bind the bones together—is attached in a circle around the rim of the socket. This increases the depth of the socket and shares the nature of those ligaments that are cartilaginous.

Indeed, it not only increases the cavity but is also the reason why the rim of the bone—since it is fragile—is less likely to be broken off during violent movements of the femur; for the ligament resists the impact with its hardness and, yielding with its softness, dissipates the force.

<margin>f figure chapter 30 or 2nd figure chapter 49 P.</margin>
Furthermore, another ligament peculiar to the hip joint is the <term>round ligament</term> <note>the ligamentum teres; original: "ligamentum teres"</note>, which is so hard that it has been rightly called a "cartilaginous nerve" by others. This arises from the middle of the head of the femur and is inserted not into the center of the <term>acetabulum</term> <note>the hip socket, named for its resemblance to a small vinegar cup</note>, but into its lowest seat, where fat rather than cartilage lines the socket and where the rim of the hip bone socket is absent.

<margin>g 1, 2 figures chapter 29 book 1 g.</margin>
<margin>h 1, 2 figures chapter 29 book 1 h.</margin>
<margin>i Seen from figure 1 chapter X, S, V, T, etc.</margin>

In the knee joint, however, besides the common ligament covering all joints, the Artisan of things <note>original: "rerum Opifex," referring to Nature or God as a divine craftsman</note> fashioned certain other strong and robust ones, especially since a single one could not surround the entire joint for certain reasons. Since there are five regions of the knee joint—anterior, posterior, interior, exterior, and middle—Nature has assigned something peculiar to each. To the anterior region, which is entirely lacking a membranous ligament and yet is a very deceptive area subject to the greatest labor, the <term>patella</term> <note>the kneecap; original: "mola patella"</note> is placed in front along with the tendons containing it. Since these bind the joint abundantly, there was no need for a ligament here, nor (as I said) for the membranous one surrounding all joints, which would have been poorly placed between the femur and the kneecap.

<margin>l 1st figure chapter 30 book 1 E, F.</margin>
Similarly, for the posterior region which is also subject to labor, a robust and nervous ligament is provided. Arising from the middle posterior region of the <term>tibia</term> <note>the shin bone</note>, it is carried straight upward and is implanted as a bifid [two-pronged] structure into the posterior seat of both heads of the femur, where they are most widely separated.

<margin>m 1st figure chapter 3 book 1 between F, G.</margin>
Furthermore, for the middle region, which is more worthy and in need of greater support than the two just mentioned, Nature grants a very strong and cartilaginous ligament <note>this refers to the cruciate ligaments</note>. This arises from the entire prominent part between the two sockets of the tibia and is inserted into the posterior part of the femur, where its heads are most distant from each other, along with the one mentioned shortly before. But besides this ligament, you may sometimes still find a certain mucous and slender one located in the middle of the knee joint, in the anterior region of the ligament already mentioned, which likewise grows forward from the tibia into the femur.

<margin>n 6th table n.</margin>
The exterior region of the knee, which is more exposed to injuries than the interior, is also covered by a thick and somewhat round ligament, binding the bones of the femur, <term>fibula</term> <note>the smaller calf bone</note>, and tibia together. The lower end of this ligament is spread beneath the head of the muscle whose tendon, creeping toward the back of the lower appendage of the fibula, was reported to extend toward the bone of the foot <note>the metatarsal</note> placed before the big toe.

Moreover, the interior region of the knee—which should gap less than the others during movements of the tibia and encounter fewer obstacles—receives a ligament that is both more slender and softer than the one just mentioned. Although it arises from the inner side of the femur, it is not inserted into the side of the tibia but, as if striving toward another exterior ligament, it extends with its greater portion toward the front parts of the tibia.

<margin>o 1st figure chapter 31 book 1.</margin>
Finally, besides all these, a peculiar cartilage is inserted into this joint, as I wrote in the previous book. In hardness, it yields somewhat to exquisite cartilage and possesses something in common with a ligament <note>this refers to the meniscus</note>. As for the joint...

Where the tibia and fibula gap apart from each other, a membranous ligament is found throughout the length of the bones,<sup>q</sup> 
<margin>q fig. cap. 1 d. 15 tab. T between S, R. r 7 tab. v between S, T.</margin>
similar to the one we mentioned was placed in the forearm <note>original: "cubito"</note>. This ligament extends from the tibia to the fibula, woven with fibers that run obliquely downward from the tibia into the fibula. Just as this ligament of the tibia corresponds in shape to the ligament of the forearm, it also performs a similar use: for it binds the fibula to the tibia and, acting as a partition, separates the muscles occupying the front of the tibia from those at the back, and provides strength for the origins of the muscles that grow from it.

<margin>Transverse ligaments of the foot.</margin>
Some of the ligaments of the foot have been described previously,<sup>s</sup> 
<margin>s 11 tab. d, v. z 14, A, Σ, r.</margin>
namely the transverse ones which are spread over the tendons. Some of these simultaneously assist the joint of the bones, while others exist merely as protections for the tendons—bonds and rings <note>these are the retinacula, which act like pulleys to keep tendons from "bowstringing"</note>—to prevent them from rising out of their channels. If considered cursorily, there are three transverse ligaments of the foot.<sup>t</sup> 
<margin>t 14 tab. d, A.</margin>
The first<sup>u</sup> consists in the front part of the tibia, at its joint with the foot, and is attached to the tibia and the fibula;
<margin>u 1 tab. v. 2 tab. S</margin>
for this connects the bones and transmits several tendons. No matter how you weigh it, it is simply one structure. The second is inserted from the internal <term>malleolus</term> <note>the bony bump on the inner ankle</note> into the <term>calcaneus</term> <note>the heel bone; original: "calcis os"</note>, and also aids in the binding together of the bones. If it is accurately divided, it is seen to form three rings, and as it were, three ligaments, which look specifically to their own channels, carved out for the three tendons (as they themselves are also three).
<margin>x 15 ta. ch 4 y 14 ta. Δ.</margin>
The one closest to the heel<sup>y</sup> admits the tendon of the muscle that flexes the second joint of the big toe. 
<margin>z 14 tab. θ & 8 musculi f.</margin>
The second channel<sup>z</sup> lying next to this provides a path for the tendon flexing the third joints of the four toes. The third channel, placed with its ligament in the back part of the inner ankle,<sup>a</sup> 
<margin>a 15 tab. D, E. b 2 tab. Σ.</margin>
was prepared by Nature for that tendon which is formed by the fifth muscle among the movers of the foot.<sup>b</sup> Furthermore, a third transverse ligament of the foot is carried from the fibula into the heel, and thus helps in the binding of the bones; where it covers the two channels common to it (since those channels are hollowed out in only one bone), it serves only the tendons<sup>c, d</sup> 
<margin>c 2 tab. χ. d 2 tab. ψ.</margin>
of the seventh and eighth muscles moving the foot. In addition to these, in the lower region of the toes, transverse ligaments exist just as they do in the hand.

<margin>Other ligaments of the foot, joining bones only.</margin>
But besides the transverse ligaments, which we also expressed earlier, many others are held in the foot. The first, proceeding from the tibia into the fibula, binds the fibula to the tibia lower down, being a membrane similar to the ligaments of other joints. Then another also corresponds to the ligaments of the remaining joints, which embraces the entire joint of the tibia with the <term>talus</term> <note>the ankle bone; original: "talo"</note>. After these, there are four cartilaginous ligaments, some of which are hidden deep within, while others surround the bones on the outside;
<margin>We have not shown these in pictures anywhere, but they are sought from the drawings of the bones, namely from the figures of chapters 32 and 33 of Book 1.</margin>
all of these together connect the talus to the four bones by which it is supported. The first takes its origin from the inner parts of the talus, where it is received by the inner ankle, and is joined into the part of the tibia that faces the talus, binding that bone to the talus. The second is on the outside and corresponds to the inner one, knitting the fibula to the talus. The third, stronger than the rest and remarkably cartilaginous, takes its beginning from the lower seat of the talus, near the root of its neck—namely where it is joined to the heel—and is attached to the heel between the two joints by which it articulates with the talus. The fourth connects the head of the talus to the <term>navicular</term> bone <note>the boat-shaped bone of the foot; original: "ossi nauiformi"</note>; for taking its origin from the end of the neck of the talus, it is inserted into the said bone and surrounds the entire joint. But besides these cartilaginous [ligaments]...
