ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

Another membranous ligament is wrapped on all sides around the connection of the heel bone <note>original: "calcis"; the calcaneus</note> with the ankle bone <note>original: "talo"; the talus</note>, and another strong one is also implanted from the neck of the ankle bone into the bone imitating a die <note>original: "tesseram"; the cuboid bone</note>. Furthermore, the ligament joining the heel bone to this die-like bone is also robust and cartilaginous, but it only surrounds the joint. Just as in the hand the bones of the wrist are bound together by very hard and cartilaginous ligaments, so too the bones of the <term>tarsus</term> <note>the cluster of seven bones in the ankle and upper foot</note> are joined both to each other and to the bone imitating a boat <note>original: "cymbam"; the navicular bone</note>. However, the bones of the tarsus possess a very strong and unique bond in the lower part, which not only binds the outer parts but, being inserted deeper into each one, also constricts the middle of the bones together. The ligaments of the <term>pedium</term> <note>the metatarsus or the middle part of the foot</note> and the toes correspond to the ligaments of the hand. For they are all membranous, except for those that are sent into the upper part of the intervals between the metatarsal bones; for these are cartilaginous, and lying in the depth or middle of the joint, they resemble the nature of the ligament <margin>figure chapter 1 x.</margin> placed in the knee.

# THE LOCATION OF THE MUSCLES IN THE SHIN AND FOOT,
## and the method of preparing all the ligaments which have not yet been cut away. Chapter LXII.

<margin>How many muscles consist in the posterior part of the shin.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative capital 'S' showing a cherub or "putto" playing among vines and leaves.</image-desc>
If you now review in order all the muscles serving the movements of the foot and toes in their proper places for the sake of confirming your memory, in the posterior part of the shin <note>original: "tibiæ"</note> you will first <margin>a 12th table 9 y.</margin> encounter two *a*, taking their origin from the root of the lower heads of the femur and forming no small portion of the calf. After these, one presents itself <margin>b 13th table 8.</margin> *b* which brings forth the longest tendon <margin>c 13th table 7.</margin> *c* of the entire body <note>the plantaris muscle</note>. Beneath this lies the largest muscle of the calf, or the fourth of those moving the foot <note>the soleus</note>, inserted into the heel along with those just mentioned. Beneath this lies *d*, <margin>d 14th table Λ.</margin> which flexes the second joint of the big toe; then *e*, <margin>e 14th table Ξ.</margin> which is the chief author of the flexion of the third joint of the four toes. The deepest of all is held to be *f*, <margin>f 15th table D, E.</margin> which was enumerated as the fifth of those moving the foot, and is implanted into one of the bones of the tarsus. Thus, all the muscles of the posterior shin now constitute a group of seven, besides the muscle *g* <margin>g 14th table Γ.</margin> hiding in the hollow of the knee <note>the popliteus</note>. For if it seems fit to count that one also among the muscles embracing the shin from behind, you will then establish eight in the posterior part of the shin. 

<margin>How many in the anterior part of the shin.</margin>
In the anterior part of the shin, together with those *h* <margin>h 2nd table ϑ ψ.</margin> which properly occupy its outer side, we have described six in number: first *i*, <margin>i 3rd table γ.</margin> which is inserted into the metatarsal bone supporting the big toe, and was counted as the sixth <margin>k 4th table ν.</margin> of those moving the foot; second, *k* which extends the four toes. A portion of this muscle *l*, <margin>l 4th table q.</margin> which is inserted into the metatarsal bone placed before the little toe, will be the third. Or if you do not distinguish this portion from the second, then you have only two so far in the anterior part of the shin. But come, grant that there are three, and count a fourth *m*, <margin>m 5th table φ.</margin> by whose help the big toe is extended; then a fifth *n*, <margin>n 6th table ψ.</margin> which, stretched out along the fibula and passing under the lower parts of the foot, is inserted into the metatarsal bone supporting the big toe; and a sixth *o*, <margin>o 6th table ϑ.</margin> which, lying beneath the one just mentioned, is implanted into the metatarsal bone placed before the little toe. 

<margin>How many in the foot.</margin>
In the lower part of the foot, a ligament *p* <margin>p 13th table π.</margin> first presents itself, acting in the stead of a wide tendon <note>the plantar fascia</note>; afterward a muscle *q*, <margin>q 14th table ϑ.</margin> flexing the second bone of the four toes; then one on each side of this *r*, <margin>r 13th table φ, γ.</margin> this one indeed drawing the big toe inward to the side, and that one drawing the little toe outward. After these, the tendons *s* come into view, <margin>s 14th table A, β.</margin> flexing the third joints of the four toes; to which are extended four muscles *t*, <margin>t 14th table μ, 15th table N.</margin> moving the four toes toward the big toe. Of all of them, however, those *u* <margin>u 15th table L, c.</margin> consist as the deepest which flex the first joints of the toes. # THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK II.

<margin>The procedure for the remaining ligaments.</margin>
<margin>d Chapter 4, figure 1, P, P.</margin>
<margin>e Chapter 49, figure 2, P.</margin>
<margin>f Chapter 5, figure 1, S, T, V, X.</margin>
<margin>g Plate 8, h.</margin>
<margin>h Book 1, chapter 31, figure 8.</margin>
<margin>i Chapter 1, figure 1, γ.</margin>
<margin>k Chapter 1, figure 1, α.</margin>
There remain still on the shin bone <margin>y</margin> two muscles serving the movements of the foot, which are stretched out along the fibula <note>the smaller outer bone of the lower leg</note>. The management of these will begin with the dissection of the <margin>z</margin> transverse ligaments located between the heel and the fibula. Then, once their tendons have been lifted, the entire body of the muscles should be separated from the fibula, so that you may afterwards clearly see their insertion. Finally, you should lead the <margin>a</margin> muscular body that occupies the upper surface of the foot, having freed it from its origins, to the insertion of its tendons. In this way, you may now join me in putting the finishing touches on the entire fabric of the muscles, and look upon the nature of the ligaments which still remain, the management of which requires nothing private or peculiar. For if you now inspect the <margin>b</margin> ligaments proceeding from the side of the sacrum <note>the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> where the fifth bone is joined to the sixth, together with the <margin>c</margin> membrane occupying the opening of the pubic bone, it will be proper to break the hip bone <note>original: "ilium os"</note> away from the sacrum with force, and to view the ligament surrounding the joint together with the cartilaginous ligaments. 

Next, approaching the <margin>d</margin> hip joint <note>original: "coxendicis articulum"</note>, divide the ligament that surrounds it in a circle crosswise with a very sharp knife, and inspect its thickness, origin, and insertion. If you then move the thigh bone <note>original: "femur"</note> slightly outward, its head will slip out of the socket <margin>e</margin> <note>original: "acetabulo"</note>, and the round ligament will offer itself for inspection. Once this is cut across, the socket must be accurately observed because of the insertion of the ligament just mentioned, and that ligament which we said increases the depth of the cavity. 

But before the <margin>f</margin> knee ligaments are managed, it is opportunistic to consider that on the front of the joint, besides the <margin>g</margin> kneecap <note>original: "patellam"</note> and the tendons extending the shin, no ligament is placed in front. Once this is established, you will lead the outer ligament, freed from the head of the thigh bone, down to the fibula. After this, you will likewise dissect the internal ligament, freed from the internal head of the thigh bone, toward the front of the shin bone. Then you will lead the ligament of the posterior region, opportunely dissected from the shin bone, to its <gloss>own</gloss> insertion. After the ligament surrounding the joint has been divided on every side, then bend the shin bone to the side and observe the cartilaginous ligament of this joint to a hair’s breadth, separating the <margin>h</margin> cartilages that increase the cavity of the shin bone <note>the menisci</note> from the joint with a very sharp knife. 

The nature of the ligament that <margin>i</margin> binds the fibula to the shin bone is easily seen if it is divided at the joint. The <margin>k</margin> membrane also coming between these bones where they are distant from each other now offers itself without any cutting. All the transverse ones have now been dissected; and therefore it only remains to break the fibula away from the shin bone and to search for the ligament binding both bones together in this lower position. Then, with a very sharp knife, free the fibula from the ankle bone <note>original: "talo"</note>, and afterwards free the ankle bone from the shin bone. In this way, two ligaments of the ankle bone present themselves, endowed with the appearance of cartilage. You will learn of the remaining two if you divide the ankle bone from the bone imitating a boat <note>the navicular bone; original: "osse cymbam imitante"</note> with a knife, and scrape the ankle bone away from the heel. This is difficult to do, and you will not accomplish it except with a sharp knife. In this manner you will approach the remaining ligaments of the foot, namely by cutting around them according to the joints of the bones. 

I believe it is known to anyone how harmoniously all these things are formed, based on the use of each bone and the general function of the ligaments. For this reason, neither here nor elsewhere have I more often digressed into praises of the Supreme Craftsman of the world <note>original: "summi rerum Opificis"; referring to God or Nature as the divine architect</note>, lest these things grow into too vast a mass for one repeating the same points about muscles or ligaments. Especially since nothing is easier than to run on at length in a description of their uses, provided that the task and duty of the parts, which I have always described, are not hidden.

-> THE END OF THE SECOND BOOK. <-

ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE HUMAN BODY

# ANDREAS VESALIUS,
# THE THIRD BOOK OF THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, in which the distribution of veins and arteries throughout the entire body is described, and the unique figures particularly suited to them are placed before the chapters.

## WHAT A VEIN IS, AND WHAT ITS SUBSTANCE AND USE ARE. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'O' depicting a group of putti or infants engaged in an anatomical dissection of a small animal or cadaver on a table, surrounded by various tools.</image-desc>

<margin>
*What is to be taught in the third book. The reason for the order.*
</margin>

Now that the account of the bones and muscles has been related in the previous books, it seems most appropriate to proceed to the distribution of the veins and arteries through the whole body; for Galen, in the first book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, rightly taught that this order should be observed in learning anatomy. For <margin>*a The figures of books 5, 6, and 7 show these.*</margin> perhaps someone else might not foolishly judge that a description of those ᵃ parts contained within the peritoneum, the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note>, and the skull, ought necessarily to precede the description of not only the veins and arteries, but the nerves as well. This is because, without a knowledge of those parts, all discussion of the veins, arteries, and nerves would be so difficult that I would by no means disapprove if this book and the fourth (which will be dedicated to the nerves) were placed after the fifth, sixth, and seventh books, and those followed the present ones. This would be especially true for someone entirely unskilled in dissection who might come upon these books for the first time without having practiced even briefly with our *Epitome* <note>Vesalius's condensed "companion" manual for students</note>. However, lest I deviate too far for the moment from the opinion of Galen and the other professors of dissection who preceded him, I shall consecrate this book to the vessels, beginning my discourse with the veins—since they are more numerous and for the most part lie over the arteries—while leaving the reader free to rearrange our books as they see fit.

<margin>
*What a vein is. b figure of chapter 5; figure of chapter 6.*
</margin>

ᵇ A vein, therefore, is an instrumentary part <note>meaning a functional organ or "instrument" of the body</note>, round, and hollowed out like a pipe; it carries blood, which is intended to nourish the parts of the body, together with the natural spirit <note>in Galenic physiology, the 'natural spirit' was a vaporous substance formed in the liver that governed nutrition and growth</note>, which is notably dark (if indeed it exists at all).

<margin>
*Natural spirit. In what way the body of a vein differs from a membrane.*
</margin>

This vessel consists of a single, unique, and proper tunic <note>a layer or "coat" of tissue</note>, which corresponds to membranes in color and, in a way, in thickness and shape, but otherwise differs greatly from their nature. For a membrane is considered a simple and "similar" body <note>a tissue that is the same throughout, like fat or bone</note>; no matter how it is torn apart, it always retains the name of a membrane. However, the tunic of a vein is an instrumentary body, formed from similar parts—namely, fibers. Just as the membranous tendons of muscles are woven almost entirely from a single kind of fiber and are thus placed in the class of instrumentary rather than similar parts, so the tunic of a vein is constituted from a triple kind of fiber.

<margin>
*The difference between fibers that preside over natural motion and those that serve voluntary motion.*
</margin>

Fibers of this kind are called fibers <note>original: "ἰνες" (ines)</note> by the Greeks. In their substance, shape, and color they correspond to the fibers of muscles, but they vary greatly from them in their action. For muscle fibers are mostly covered by fleshy substance and are subject to the will <note>voluntary motion</note>, while these vessel fibers are entwined with no such flesh and are set over natural motion <note>involuntary motion</note>. Indeed, just as we perform movements depending on our own choice with the help of fibers in the muscles, so the natural movements that serve the whole body are carried out by certain fibers interwoven into the organs that serve the entire body.

# BOOK III OF THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY.

Although not all natural motions, but only the attraction, retention, and expulsion of some substance, are fulfilled by fibers of this kind. I am calling "attractive, retentive, and expulsive power" <note>original: *uim attractricem, retentricem & expultricem*</note> in this context not that which is innate by Nature in individual parts for their own nutrition, but that by which certain parts of the body perform some common duty for the whole body. For I consider the attraction of food through the gullet into the stomach, and of blood from the hollow vein <note>original: *cava vena*, the vena cava</note> into the right chamber <note>original: *sinum*</note> of the heart, and of air from the venous artery <note>original: *arteria venalis*, the pulmonary vein</note> into the left chamber of the heart, and of seed into the uterus, and of blood into the veins, and of spirit into the arteries, to be entirely different from the attraction by whose benefit those parts entice to themselves the familiar nourishment by which they are privately nourished. Again, the excretory faculty is far different by which the stomach drives the food it has prepared into the intestines, and by which the upper intestines in turn thrust it into the lower, and by which the heart sends blood into the lungs and the vital spirit along with the blood (rushing with force through the body) into the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, and by which one part of a vein derives blood continuously into the next, and by which the uterus excretes the fetus and the bladder the urine—different, I say, than the power by which the aforementioned parts drive away from themselves the waste products of their own nourishment. To these may be added that the retention of food and drink in the stomach, of the fetus in the uterus, of urine in the bladder, and of blood in the veins, and of spirit and blood together in the heart, is thought to be entirely different from that benefit by which the heart, stomach, bladder, and uterus keep and retain familiar nourishment for themselves. Therefore, those motions proper to all parts alike, and not serving others, are performed entirely by the power implanted in the parts themselves, without the help of fibers. But those parts which must perform an attraction, retention, or expulsion that is subservient and useful to other parts or even to the entire body, claim for themselves certain fibers for that function, by whose help they complete it.

<margin>Types and function of fibers.</margin>
And just as there are three types of motion, so too we believe a triple kind of fibers has been constructed by Nature: namely, straight, oblique, and transverse. And indeed, straight fibers lead to attraction, oblique to retention, and transverse to expulsion. For straight fibers are those which are expanded according to the length of the organ. Oblique fibers are those which are drawn over the organ at an angle. These are circular, but since they are of a twofold difference, they oppose each other and cross one another in the manner of the letter X, or rather like two circles intertwined with each other,

<margin>
A rough sketch of the fibers, in which A indicates the transverse, while B and C indicate the differences of each kind of oblique, and D the straight. But E expresses in a certain way the weaving together of the triple kind of fibers, which the depiction of a vein to be placed below soon will present more accurately.
</margin>

appropriately retaining whatever is contained within the cavity of the organ. Transverse fibers are placed exactly crosswise according to the width of the body, and they surround the body in a ring, just as the oblique ones do; although the transverse ones are sometimes specifically called circular and orbicular. Furthermore, anyone will learn the nature of the fibers if, when the stomach or intestines of some animal are placed on the table <note>likely a dining table, as anatomy was often observed during butchery or meals</note>, he will not find it troublesome to pull their fibers apart from one another with his nails, and to consider that those bodies are nothing but certain fibers interwoven among themselves in order, and according to what was useful for the part. He will observe the same thing while watching the bladder of a recently slaughtered ox or the crop <note>original: *ingluniem*</note> of geese being inflated; for that triple kind of fibers will clearly offer itself to be seen in a moderately distended bladder. On the other hand, if someone takes into his hands any membrane, such as that which lines the ribs <note>the pleura</note> or the peritoneum, he will learn with little effort that this is a simple and uniform body

# ANDREAS VESALII ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

<margin>The use of the vein's composition.</margin>
[The vein] is not the same in every part, nor is it formed without such fibers. Therefore, since the vein is an organ that usefully serves the whole body in the distribution of blood, Nature established its body as membranous and hollow like a pipe, and interwoven with certain specific fibers—not by chance, but with those she knew would be useful for the administration of blood. For this reason, since she knew the vein must necessarily admit blood into itself, she provided it with **straight fibers**, by which the vein might entice blood into its cavity. Then, because there was a need to propel the blood to the subsequent part of the vein, as if through a stream, she also gifted it with **transverse fibers**. Yet, so that the entire mass of blood would not immediately flow or be propelled from one part into the next without delay, she also entwined **oblique fibers** into the body of the vein. Thus, from these three types of fibers, the body of the vein is fashioned like a white membrane or a nerve-like tunic <note>Vesalius uses "nerve-like" (*nerveæ*) to describe the tough, fibrous texture, not necessarily its neurological function</note>, suited to be distended and to collapse back upon itself (so that it may appropriately fit the material contained within).

<margin>A portion of the hollow vein <note>original: *Vene cauæ*, the vena cava</note>, ascending from the right chamber of the heart all the way to the throat, in which we have carefully depicted the nature of the fibers in the body of the veins for the sake of instruction. If by chance you seek the reason for the branches cut off here and there, compare this portion of the vein to the full illustration of the hollow vein placed at the end of the fifth Chapter, weighing carefully what D, F, G, H, I, K, N, S, T, and *d* indicate there.</margin>
<image-desc>Anatomical woodcut illustrating a segment of the vena cava and its branches (jugular and subclavian veins), with internal textures depicted to show the arrangement of vertical, transverse, and oblique fibers discussed in the text.</image-desc>

<margin>The acquired and non-specific tunic of the vein.</margin>
Besides this specific tunic, the vein occasionally acquires another, which is also common to many parts of the body. Whenever veins are led a long way through some path, or lie upon a bone or some harder body, or are suspended from something, then another covering, like a thin membrane, is wrapped around them from the neighboring membranes, both for the sake of a safer passage and for a firmer connection to the adjacent parts. However, veins inserted into an organ <note>original: *uisceri*, viscera</note>, or distributed through the body of a muscle, lack this kind of tunic throughout the progress of their insertion; they have no need for it because they are abundantly secured within those bodies. Furthermore, such a tunic would be an obstacle, preventing the blood from "sweating" <note>original: *sudaret*, referring to the movement of nutrients through vessel walls</note> readily out of the veins, or delaying the blood collected in the veins from experiencing the power of the organ's substance.

<margin>The use of veins.</margin>
The Creator of things produced all veins for the primary purpose of carrying blood to the individual parts of the body, acting as channels and ducts from which all parts might suck their nourishment. However, He also uses certain branches of them—such as the <margin>See Figure in Chapter 5, and Figure 1 and 2 of Book 5.</margin> offshoots of the portal vein—to attract the juice <note>original: *succi*, the chyle or digested food</note> prepared in the stomach to the liver. Others He uses for the <margin>See figure in Chapter 6, and Figure 22 of Book 1.</margin> purging of waste, such as those which carry the serous blood <note>The watery component of blood that becomes urine</note> to the kidneys; all of these we shall mention in their proper place. Whether, however, the Creator (lest the blood flow through the veins without experiencing any refinement from the body of the vein) implanted a certain <margin>Book 4 of *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin> **blood-making power** <note>original: *sanguificationis uim*</note> in the veins, I would not wish to assert too readily, even though this is admitted by all professors of dissection. And if perhaps this power is attributed to the veins, it will not prepare red blood, but rather blood that is white like the body of the vein; for in every natural "concoction" <note>The physiological process of "cooking" or transforming nutrients</note> of the parts of our body, the thing cooked necessarily adopts the color of the thing cooking it. But now it is the right time to investigate from what parts the artery is fashioned.

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK III.

### WHAT AN ARTERY IS, AND WHAT IS ITS
### substance and use. Chapter II.

<margin>
a Figure 1, Chapter 12.
</margin>
<margin>
What an artery is, and what is its use.
</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap initial 'A' decorated with foliage and a small figure.</image-desc>
AN ARTERY is a vessel, just like a vein, membranous, rounded, and hollow in the manner of a pipe, through which the vital spirit <note>original: *uitalis spiritus*; in Galenic physiology, this was a refined substance responsible for life and heat</note> and the hot blood rushing with force are diffused throughout the entire body. By their benefit, aided by the movement of the artery itself (which occurs through dilation and contraction), the natural heat of each individual part and the vital spirit are refreshed. Furthermore, in the time of Hippocrates, and still in that of Plato and Aristotle, the term "artery" was

<margin>
b Figure 38, Book 1.
</margin>
used for that [vessel] through which we draw air from the nose or mouth into the lungs when inhaling, and through which we lead it out again from the lungs when exhaling. Those which we call arteries, they called "veins"; and some in that age distinguished arteries from veins by calling the latter non-pulsating and the former pulsating. Indeed, in this manner, in Hippocrates’ second book *On Epidemics* <note>original: *de Vulgaribus morbis*</note>, the name "vein" is given to an artery; its movement, when found to be swift, large, and strong during a child’s birth, testifies that there is a strong irascible power in the heart, endowed with vigorous and glowing heat. However, in the sixth book, he sufficiently implies that arteries were subsequently called "hot veins," just as some also named those vessels "veins" which lead the yellow and spiritual blood—diffused through the body with force and possessing a thin and subtle substance—to the whole body. For thus it pleased Plato to call the arteries "veins," when he attests in the *Timaeus* that the heart is simultaneously the source of the veins and of the blood that is vehemently poured around through all the limbs. Aristotle, moreover, in his books *On the Parts of Animals* and his *History of Animals*, frequently bestows the name of "veins" upon the arteries. For, to pass over other places, when comparing the great artery <note>the aorta</note> to the hollow vein <note>the vena cava</note> in the third book of the *History of Animals*, he frequently calls it the "lesser vein." But with the passage of time, the ancients began to call that [vessel] which reaches from the mouth into the lungs

<margin>
We have fashioned here a portion of the great artery, which arises from the heart, dissected and opened so that the tunics of the artery may be seen. **A** indicates the place where that tunic most specifically occurs which we liken to a spider's web. **B** and **B** mark the inner tunic of the artery. That number **1, 2, 3** suggests the three membranes set over the orifice of the great artery, to be noted as B, C, D in the sixteenth figure of the sixth book. Here indeed, **E** and **D** show the origin of the two coronary arteries. Moreover, the openings visible in the trunk of the artery as it turns downward toward the vertebrae are the mouths of those offshoots which are distributed to the ribs, then to the diaphragm, and to other organs as far as the kidneys. But these things will be clearer in their proper place; in the present figure, it seemed sufficient to note the tunics of the artery in passing.
</margin>
<margin>
The nature of the body of the artery, and its two specific tunics.
</margin>
<image-desc>An anatomical diagram of a longitudinal section of a large artery (the aorta), showing various internal layers and features labeled with letters (A, B, C, D, E) and numbers (1, 2, 3). The artery is depicted with several branching vessels (intercostal arteries) emerging from its lower portion. The texture of the layers is detailed with fine cross-hatching.</image-desc>
the "rough" [artery] <note>original: *asperam*; the trachea</note>. However, they named the pulsating vessels, which refresh the natural heat, "smooth arteries." But now, only the one which is diffused from the mouth into the lungs has kept its name, and it is called the *arteria aspera* <note>the trachea</note>. Therefore, the artery, the account of which we have just begun, consists of a membranous body similar to a vein, suited to be compressed, to collapse into itself, and to be distended again; but it is far more solid, harder, and formed from more tunics <note>layers</note>. For the artery claims two tunics peculiar to itself: the outer one certainly corresponds in strength and thickness to the specific tunic of the veins; the inner one, however, by the consensus of many masters of dissection, is thought to be nearly five times thicker than the outer tunic itself. Consequently, the whole body of the artery, when compared to a vein, is judged to be six times [thicker]. The inner tunic is called "cartilaginous" <note>original: *χονδρώδης* (chondrōdēs)</note> by some, because it is harder and far thicker than any [ordinary] membrane. Hence, perhaps, the Arabs also called the artery a "pulsating nerve." The tunics of the artery, similarly...

<margin>
The added tunic of the arteries.
The reason for the construction of the artery.
c This is evident in figures 9 and 10 of Book 6.
</margin>

...in a manner similar to veins, arteries are formed of fibers. The interior layer is interwoven with transverse <note>fibers running across the width of the vessel</note> fibers only, while the exterior layer consists of straight fibers and some that are moderately oblique, but no transverse ones. The interior tunic of the artery contains something like a skin, much like the internal surface of the intestines and the stomach, which is clearly very similar to a wide and continuous spider's web; this is especially visible in the larger arteries and has been described by some as a third arterial tunic. There is no other distinct fourth tunic; however, just as with certain veins, a thin membrane clings to and is stretched around the arteries in some places, covering them, stabilizing them, or connecting them to nearby parts, as we reported regarding the second tunic of the veins.

And all these things were most justly constructed by the supreme Craftsman of things <note>Vesalius frequently refers to God or Nature as the "Opifex" or "Artifex" (Craftsman)</note>. For the body of the artery is allotted fibers for the same purpose as the veins; it possesses many transverse fibers so that it may more swiftly dispense the blood and vital spirit sent into it from the left chamber <note>ventricle</note> of the heart to the whole body, and so that it produces no other rhythm in transmitting and receiving than the heart itself. Indeed, the transverse fibers contribute greatly to this task, as we asserted long ago that Nature placed them in charge of expulsion. However, because oblique fibers are quite a hindrance to expulsion—since they retain and keep back materials—Nature bestows very few oblique fibers upon the arteries. Since the arteries were to embrace a substance that is thinner, more rare, and flows with a swifter impetus than that in the veins, and were to be perpetually dilated and constricted while the animal lives, they are rightly constructed with a body that is harder, thicker, and formed of more tunics.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' containing a woodcut scene with three naked putti. One stands on the left holding a vessel, another sits in the center holding an anatomical object over a wooden block, and a third stands on the right.</image-desc>
HOW MANY veins and likewise arteries are distributed throughout the entire body—if every single offshoot and all the distributions of the vessels were to be enumerated—is difficult to indicate and almost impossible. But if the veins and arteries that possess their own circumscription and are limited by their own boundaries are to be grasped together in a certain number, that number is readily available. In born and fully-formed humans, all veins are for the most part comprised within a fourfold number, which are considered the roots of all the others.

And so, ^a^ one, emerging from the hollow seat of the liver, runs out into the gallbladder, stomach, spleen, intestines, mesentery <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, and omentum <note>a fatty layer of tissue hanging over the intestines</note>. A second, taking its origin from the convex parts of the liver or, as it has seemed to some, from the right chamber ^b^ of the heart, is dispensed into the rest of the body in an innumerable series of branches, with the sole exception of the lungs. However, the branches of this vein are so distributed within the substance of the liver alongside the offshoots of the first vein we listed, and they seem to meet and unite in certain places at their tips ^c^ and boundaries, that some have not hesitated to assert that the first vein is continuous with the second, even though they are reviewed by us here as two separate veins.

Therefore, the ^d^ third vein, also born from the right chamber of the heart, is distributed into the lungs by very frequent offshoots. But you will hear that this vein claims this for itself privately: it consists of the ^e^ body of an artery, and hence it is also called the "arterial vein" <note>original: *arterialis uena*; modern: Pulmonary Artery</note>. Although it is not continuous with the body of the vena cava without the medium of another substance (since some substance of the heart intervenes between both veins where they are close to each other), both nevertheless look toward a common cavity,

Because this second one consists of the "body" <note>the thickness or structure</note> of a vein, it has obtained the name "venous artery" <note>original: "venalis arteria"; this refers to the pulmonary vein, which Vesalius, following Galenic tradition, describes as having a thin, vein-like wall despite its connection to the left side of the heart</note>. Furthermore, if the arteries and veins of the fetus happen to possess any peculiar features, that will be made clear in its proper place when the history of the fetal vessels is delivered. For now, it is worthwhile to begin our discourse with the veins of mature subjects. Once the series of each has been described, I will subjoin their use and the logic of their distribution, as soon as I have added something about the glands which Nature willed to preside over the strength of the division or branching of the vessels.

# ON THE GLANDS, Inserted and Attached for the Sake of Strengthening the Branchings of the Vessels. Chapter IV.

*I have decided that no figure should be placed before the present chapter, because it would require many figures from the fifth, sixth, and seventh books to be located here at once, in addition to several tables of the muscles, to which you will be conveniently referred by the inner margin.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'H' showing several small winged children (putti). One appears to be using a bellows on a small fire, while others are gathered around a block, perhaps preparing tools or materials for an anatomical demonstration.</image-desc>

<margin>
Why and when glands are inserted into the distributions of the vessels.
</margin>
In the same way that Nature, on account of their own proper tunics, has occasionally wrapped another membrane around the veins and arteries—by whose benefit they may be aptly tied to neighboring parts and creep along safely—so too did she act because she was not at all ignorant that every vessel is more conveniently exposed to harm in that place where it is split into branches. For the sake of safe branching, she created a certain substance that is somewhat soft and yielding, with which she filled the forkings of the vessels everywhere, in the manner of knots in trees <note>Vesalius compares the reinforcing tissue at a blood vessel's fork to the hard "knots" where a branch meets a tree trunk</note>. She placed this substance beneath and around the divisions of the branches so that none of them could easily be split or become weak. Because the forkings of the vessels are most exposed to injury from violent movement, the vessels rest more gently upon a soft and moderately yielding substance. Finally, by its help, even if they are moved quite vehemently, they are kept un-struck and intact. However, Nature did not interpose this kind of substance—which is called by the common name among the Greeks <term>aden</term> <note>original: "αδην"; a gland</note> and <term>sarcoma</term> <note>original: "σαρχωμα"; a fleshy mass</note>, but among the Latins <term>glans</term>, <term>glandula</term>, or <term>glandium</term>, and sometimes "flesh"—at every single distribution of the vessels as if by chance. Indeed, she granted very little or almost none of it to divisions that are neither carried in suspension nor rest upon joints endowed with varied and very loose motion, because it was clear to her that those partitions of the vessels would suffer nothing from violent movement. <margin>a See this in Figure 3 of Book 5, and in Figure 4 at u, x, etc., then in Figure 10, Book 5, at L, L, M, M.</margin> But where divisions are suspended by some membrane, or are stretched further over joints that move into acute angles, and where these are <gloss>a</gloss> found in great number in such places: there Nature has surrounded those divisions of the vessels with a significant abundance of this substance we are discussing. This is evident throughout the entire distribution of the portal vein, because all of these branches are [suspended] by membranes...

...supported only by membranes, it extends to the stomach, spleen, and intestines. In the same manner <gloss>b</gloss> in the membranes that partition the chest cavity <note>The mediastinum and pleura</note>, and in <gloss>c</gloss> the brain, above <gloss>d</gloss> the "testes" of the brain <note>The corpora quadrigemina, four rounded bumps in the midbrain</note>, and <gloss>e</gloss> in the anterior ventricles of the brain (because in those places the vessels are carried suspended in membranes), you will learn from dissection that this substance, which provides strength for the distribution of vessels, is produced. Just as <gloss>f</gloss> you will hear that another substance, not very different from this one, is contained between the surface of the uterus and the outer covering of the fetus <note>the placenta</note>; this is involved and woven into the manifold and varied distribution and path of the vessels newly generated for the production of the fetus. Finally, it helps in marvelous ways to strengthen those vessels which had to be supported by membranes. Likewise, such substance is useful for the <gloss>g</gloss> umbilical vessels which reach from the inner covering of the fetus into its navel. Furthermore, <gloss>h</gloss> under the upper end of the breastbone <note>the sternum</note>, <gloss>i</gloss> under the ears, in the armpits, in the bend of the elbow, <gloss>k</gloss> in the groin, in the back of the knee, and in several other locations of the body, we see this glandular substance woven in and applied to the numerous distributions of vessels because of the movement of the adjacent parts; even if it also serves to fill and pack certain cavities in the region where it is placed. Just as we know that certain glands, while also helping the security and strength of the vessels, were created by Nature for some greater use than merely protecting the vessels.

Not all glands suited for the distribution of vessels serve this duty alone.

For the <gloss>l</gloss> gland of the brain <note>the pineal gland</note>, compared to the image of a pine nut or a cone, and resting upon the "testes" of the brain, contributes to the strength of the division of the vessels resting upon it. It also ensures that those vessels, hanging down, do not block the <gloss>n</gloss> beginning of the passage which leads from the anterior ventricles of the brain to the fourth ventricle through the "testes" and "buttocks" <note>the superior and inferior colliculi</note> of the brain. Then <gloss>s</gloss> the glands placed in the throat near the upper part of the rough artery <note>the trachea</note> or the larynx, and compared to almonds <note>the tonsils</note>, and furthermore <gloss>t</gloss> those which lie at the root of the larynx, being almost entirely fleshy, although they contribute to the distribution of vessels, were nevertheless created more to prepare saliva and moisten the throat with fluid; just as the <gloss>u</gloss> proper substance of the breasts, being in a way glandular, presides over the generation of milk. Indeed, a certain power is attributed by professors of dissection to the <gloss>x</gloss> glandular substance occurring here and there in the omentum and mesentery, by which they produce a certain fluid suitable for sprinkling the intestines; not unlike how the <gloss>y</gloss> glandular body, occurring now and then to dissectors in the middle of the stomach's path at the seat of the heart, moistens the stomach. Again, the <gloss>z</gloss> "testes" of women <note>the ovaries</note>, although they seem to significantly consult the distribution of the vessels approaching the uterus, nevertheless contribute primarily to the generation of offspring. But the <gloss>a</gloss> "testes" of men, however much they might perhaps be counted in the class of glands, contribute little to the distribution of vessels; even if Aristotle meanwhile attests that these were created primarily so that, like the weights <note>original: "textricum planulae" — small flat weights used by weavers</note> used by weavers, they might keep the vessels upright and hanging down. The <gloss>b</gloss> glandular body placed at the neck of the bladder in men <note>the prostate</note>, although it brings help to the various partitions of the vessels there, serves most especially to receive the seminal vessels and to produce a peculiar fluid. Since we shall thoroughly treat the form, substance, and proper private use of each gland in its own place, a longer discussion of them should not be established here, as the discourse must now be turned to the series of veins; as soon as I have added that for the already mentioned glands, not only has the strength of their distribution been provided for, but also the body of the veins is seen to be <gloss>c</gloss> thicker and more compactly joined there, where some branch, as if...

...is led away from the trunk, or some trunk is divided into branches: so much so, that something protruding occurs in the very openings of the branches, <margin>d</margin> not unlike the thicker substance of the stomach, which you will hear was created with no small industry for the sake of strength, like a certain circle in both its openings. Indeed, this thicker substance of the veins—when the veins are seen emptied of blood and hang down flaccidly, having been cut along their length—closes up toward the width of the veins <margin>e</margin> in such a way that some of those standing by have sometimes contended that it was created like a <margin>f</margin> membranous body <note>Vesalius is describing venous valves, though he is skeptical of their function as one-way gates at this point in his career.</note>, which prevents urine from flowing back or being pushed back into the <margin>f</margin> passages <note>the ureters</note> carrying it from the kidneys into the bladder. Likewise, they have sometimes sought to compare that protruding substance of the body of the veins to the <margin>g</margin> membranes <note>the heart valves</note> which are seen at the openings of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> and the vein <note>the pulmonary artery</note> where they emerge from the heart. It would surely be impossible for blood to return or flow back—otherwise than I much believe—from the "vein without a pair" <note>original: "viana sine pari"; the azygos vein</note>, and from the veins going to the arms, head, kidneys, and legs, and many such veins, into the trunk of the vena cava, either during bloodletting, or during various movements of the mind and similar occasions. I am accustomed to contend in the schools that this thicker substance of the vein's body, occurring at the very division of the branches, was created by Nature for the sake of a certain strength; I am not unaware of the poor judgment of those who shamefully concoct the idea that in intact veins, not even a breath can be drawn from the azygos vein into the trunk of the vena cava.

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial "I" depicts several men in a landscape setting, appearing to be observing or participating in a medical or anatomical demonstration.</image-desc>IN the substance of the **liver** <note>Latin: iecur</note>, from all the lower parts and those that stand in a circle at its extremities, very small and numerous offshoots of veins begin. These, stretching toward the middle of the liver, gradually come together into larger branches, and from there into even greater ones, until all (which are indeed as frequent as possible) are united in the hollow region of the liver, toward its middle—yet more toward the interior and posterior parts, near the back. Having met in larger branches, they constitute one large and exceedingly wide vein, which shall be called by us the **portal vein** <note>Latin: vena portae</note>. This vein, having arisen in this manner from the hollow of the liver, or (if you wish to speak no less truly than clearly) dispersing all the recently mentioned branches, offspring, and offshoots into the substance of the liver, descends obliquely to the left. It divides into many forks of veins to be distributed to the **gallbladder** <note>Latin: bilis uesicula</note>, stomach, intestines, spleen, **omentum** <note>A fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines.</note>, and **mesentery** <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, in the series now to be narrated. 

First, it distributes two very small branches from the upper or anterior part of its body to the neck of the gallbladder. These, embracing that neck and being divided into hair-thin forks, run out into the whole body of the bladder in the same way that we see small veins stretched in the white or adhering coat of the eye <note>Original: "alba adhærente'ue oculi tunica", referring to the conjunctiva or sclera.</note>. After these, somewhat lower down from the higher and anterior seat of the body of the vein, yet more toward the right side, another branch is put forth, more notable than those recently mentioned. This approaches the lower orifice of the **stomach** <note>Latin: ventriculus</note> and a portion of the stomach nearest the back with several small branches, creeping through the anterior seat of the stomach with no branches at all. 

The trunk of the portal vein, after it has diffused these branches, extending further downward, is split into two very large trunks. The higher of these (which we will conveniently name the "left" for the sake of teaching) is almost entirely consumed by the stomach, the omentum, and a certain region of the **colon** <note>Latin: coli intestinum</note> which is carried along the lower seat of the stomach, and then also by the spleen. The other, which is both lower and larger and will rightly be called the "right," is entirely exhausted into the mesentery and intestines, except for one or two offspring. For from its right side, near the very distribution of the portal trunk into two trunks, a notable offshoot or vein is extended to the stomach. This is supported by the upper membrane of the omentum and produced transversely under the right side of the base of the stomach; it divides small and frequent veins in a certain order and somewhat joint-like manner into the stomach. These interweave both the anterior and posterior regions of the stomach's base with many forks to some extent. This vein, when it has proceeded to the middle of the stomach's base, ends in certain small branches contiguous to that vein which you will soon hear occupies the rest of the stomach's base. Furthermore, just as this vein offers many small veins in a row from its higher seat to the stomach, so also it diffuses innumerable small veins through the whole right region of the upper membrane of the omentum, corresponding in number (though not in length or various entanglement through the omentum) to those which I said a little before were scattered into the base of the stomach.

And encircling the entire anterior seat, it is twisted back again through its left side toward the rear, and (to put it simply) it creeps around the upper orifice of the stomach precisely in the manner of a **crown**<sup>h</sup> <note>Vesalius refers to the "coronary vein" of the stomach.</note> (which is a most delightful sight to see in dogs), in its progress offering branches straight down into the body of the stomach step by step, which occupy a large part of the stomach.

From its<sup>i</sup> upper part, however, this vein also spreads little branches, but truly tiny ones, running out into the end of the **esophagus** <term>stomachus: In this context, Vesalius refers to the gullet or esophagus entering the stomach.</term> where it is continued with the stomach. 
<margin>i R from P. Figure 14, book 5. e extending to H.</margin>
Furthermore, among the other offshoots arising from this vein girding the upper orifice of the stomach like a crown, a notable vein is born from it where it strives forward from the posterior region of the stomach along the right side of the orifice. And this offshoot, born from the right side of that vein, approaches the lower orifice of the stomach along the upper part of the stomach, embracing it with rather frequent little forks, and in its progress scattering branches step by step into the front and back parts of the stomach. Now, to the vein already mentioned as belonging to the stomach with so many offshoots,<sup>k</sup> another corresponds, coming forth from a lower position of the left trunk of the portal vein and entwined in the lower membrane of the omentum; not far from its beginning, it is split into two branches departing greatly from each other, from which again very many little forks...

For the more the intestines are continuous with the stomach, the more they are entwined with the shoots of these veins; this is because more juice must be sucked out from them than from those located closer to the "seat" <note>original: "sedem," a euphemism for the anus or rectum</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The portal vein is therefore divided into these offshoots, all of which are considered to be propagated either for **nutrition**, or for the **purging** of some waste, or for the **conveyance** of food cooked in the stomach into the "gates" of the **liver**. Indeed, I have said that those branches offered to the **gallbladder** [i] run out to it to supply it with nourishment. In the same way, ^k offshoots derived from the portal vein are diffused in a numerous series into the **omentum** <term>omentum: the fatty "apron" hanging over the intestines</term> solely to nourish it and imbue it with much fat. ^l Also, the shoots that are as thin as hairs and distributed into the glands are useful only for bringing blood for their nutrition.

For since the thicker waste of blood-making is carried by these offshoots into the spleen, and since they offer this to the spleen, they necessarily offer nourishment to the spleen at the same time. Indeed—as I shall write in the fifth book, though not without a certain religious awe and fear (since I doubt these matters greatly)—the spleen processes that black waste of blood-making for its own nutrition, and the spleen, through the ^n veins poured out into the stomach from those which are brought into it, "belches" into the stomach whatever remains of that feculent blood which it cannot digest or adapt for itself. It does not pour this (as professors of dissection wrongly believe) into the upper orifice of the stomach, but primarily to the **bottom** [o], because a larger vein, arising from the veins approaching the spleen, reaches the stomach here.

### BOOK III OF THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

The offshoots of the portal vein, distributed into the stomach and intestines, are constructed for a dual purpose: partly to provide them with nourishment, and partly so that by their ends and openings <note>original: "osculis"</note>, which gape into the stomach and intestines, they may suck up the food prepared by the stomach from itself and the intestines, and transfer it to the liver as if to a common workshop of concoction for the whole human body. The entrance and ascent into this 

<margin>Names of the Portal Vein.</margin>
region is prepared from the many narrow paths we have just described into one trunk <note>original: "caudex"</note>. This is indeed the trunk of the portal vein, which some expert in Nature's works before Hippocrates called the <term>pylas</term> <note>Greek: πύλας; meaning "gates"</note>. From him, the name of the "portal vein" <note>the "vein of the gates"</note> has flowed down to us to this day. It is also called the "gate of the liver" by some (as Galen also testifies) and the "doorkeeper" <note>original: "ianitrix"</note> by others. 

<margin>q B. Lib. 6 on the Opinions [of Hippocrates and Plato].</margin>
However, some do not wish the entire vein to be given this name, but only that part of it which is first seen free from the substance of the liver. It is also called by the name <term>stelechiaia</term> <note>Greek: σελεχιαῖα; meaning "stem-like"</note>, a name which Galen sometimes seems to have attributed to the **vena cava** 

<margin>r fig. cap. 6 B, 1.</margin>
where it is closest to the liver, and furthermore to the **great artery** <note>the aorta</note> 

<margin>s fi. 12 cap. A, C.</margin>
where it arises from the heart. Likewise, in the fifth book of *Anatomical Procedures* and the fifth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, he called the portal vein "Great." Furthermore, the portal vein is called the "hand," because the liver uses it like a hand to attract the food prepared in the stomach. There are those who call it "milky," because the juice which it carries from the intestines to the liver is milky <note>Vesalius refers here to chyle, the milky fluid of digested fats</note>.

<margin>The portal vein does not produce blood.</margin>
Furthermore, I would not easily concede that the portal vein concocts the juice it draws to itself from the stomach and especially from the intestines, preparing it for the liver and changing it into crude blood during that transport—regardless of how weightily Galen asserts this in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*. For I can assign no power of blood-making <note>original: "sanguificationis"</note> to the membranous and leathery body of a vein. If there were any such power, it would surely prepare white blood, just as the materials changed by the stomach reflect a milky color; we clearly see that the substance of the stomach is white, and not red like the liver, which resembles clotted blood. I would refute this opinion of Galen’s—repeated by him more than once—even more deeply, were it not that Galen himself, in the sixth book of *On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato*, changed his mind, forgetting his own words in his eagerness to oppose Aristotle.

<margin>t d, d. Melancholic juice is purged through the branches of the portal vein.</margin>
I believe that the ^t branch of the portal vein, which we wrote is stretched out sloping under the rectum and supported by the mesentery, contributes greatly at times to the purging of feculent blood through the small veins of the anus <note>hemorrhoidal veins</note>, which sometimes flow with blood. Whenever, either due to an obstruction of the **spleen** or any other defect of it, the feculent blood <note>referring to "black bile" or thick, waste-filled blood in the humoral system</note> is not entirely absorbed into the spleen, or the spleen cannot discharge it into the stomach, I believe it is excreted through the anus at certain intervals, just as women’s menstrual purgings are accustomed to be, by the benefit of this branch. 

<margin>fig. cap. 6 at ψ.</margin>
For it seems unlikely to us, when we have the true distribution of the portal vein in view, that such muddy blood regurgitates from the whole body toward the ^u small branches of the **vena cava** reaching into the seat in those suffering from the malady of hemorrhoids. Indeed, from this it is very easy to conjecture that this blood—not attracted by the spleen or not admitted due to an obstruction of the passages—regurgitates back from where it was flowing. By its own weight, it falls downward through the branch belonging to the rectum; there it is reserved and collected for a time, until the veins, swelling too much and their openings being unsealed, allow it to flow through the anus. 

<margin>Observation.</margin>
Great strength was added to my opinion by a man whom we recently dissected, who suffered from this periodic flow of blood. This man had a smaller but harder spleen, and the vein running under the rectum exceeded the thickness of a thumb; it was swollen with blood in the same way as those in women about to give birth.

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK III.

We see the veins of animals, which embrace the uterus, to be remarkably large and distended. However, I have reported on these matters a bit more extensively in the letter <note>Vesalius refers to his "Venesection Letter" of 1539, a famous publication on bloodletting.</note> in which I taught that the right axillary vein should be opened in cases of lateral disease <note>original: "laterali morbo"; likely referring to pleurisy, an inflammation of the chest lining.</note> (if indeed it mattered at all whether the right or left side was used). And therefore, we must now approach the sequence of the **vena cava** <term>vena cava: the large vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the body back to the heart</term>; for I have decided that the method of dissecting the portal vein <note>The vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver.</note> should be deferred to the end of the fifth book, in which I will pursue the management of all the organs of nutrition and generation together.

### INDEX OF CHARACTERS FOR THE ENTIRE DELINEATION OF THE VENA CAVA, and likewise for the four figures following in order.

*A, A, A* *These three characters, found in the region where the liver would sit in proportion to this figure, mark the offspring distributed to the left from the vena cava into the liver in a very numerous series of branches. However, we have not marked the other offspring, similarly spread into the right seat of the liver, with characters: just as we have marked no right-hand branches of the vena cava (which are held equally on both sides and claim nothing unique for themselves on either side), lest perhaps we obscure the drawing with an abundance of characters.*

*a* *A slender branch, directed from the vena cava to the liver beneath those large offspring indicated by A.*

*B* *The position of the vena cava, consisting between the hump of the liver and the transverse septum.* <note>The diaphragm.</note>

*D* *The orifice of the vena cava, pertaining to the right sinus <note>The right atrium.</note> of the heart, or perhaps the very beginning of the cava itself.*

*F, F* *The vein lacking a partner, which, emerging from the right side of the cava above the heart, descends sloping along the right side of the vertebrae almost to the second vertebra of the loins.* <gloss>azygos</gloss> <note>Vesalius uses the Latin "coniugis expers" for the Greek "azygos," meaning "unpaired."</note>

*H* *The bipartition of the cava under the higher seat of the breastbone near the throat.*

*I* *A vein resting on the first rib of the chest, and led across to the armpit, forming the axillary vein of the arm after it has spread several branches.*

*K* *A thin vein, deriving branches into the membrane surrounding the ribs <note>The pleura.</note> on its own side, at the intervals of roughly the three upper ribs.*

*L* *A vein descending under the left side of the breastbone to the upper parts of the abdomen, showing branches to the intervals of the cartilages of the true ribs, and finally to the membrane of its own side partitioning the chest, and also to the muscles spread over the chest and the skin of the abdomen. It spreads its principal branch under the straight muscle of the abdomen <note>The rectus abdominis.</note>, which, ending in several shoots above the navel, looks toward the ends of another vein ascending upward from the bottom (to be marked with Γ), specifically in that seat where we have written M.*

*N, N* *The vein hastening to the skull through the holes carved in the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae <note>The vertebral vein.</note>, offering branches to the spinal marrow at each joint: just as it also dispenses offspring into the muscles attached there to the vertebrae of the neck.*

*O* *A vein stretched out by a manifold offspring to the muscles occupying the lower part of the neck and the upper seat of the chest near the vertebrae.*

*P* *A vein running out to the muscles spread over the chest, and the skin of this region, and the nipple.*

*Q* *A vein proceeding into the back parts of the chest, and derived into the hollow seat of the shoulder blade and the neighboring muscles. Very close to this are the small veins running out into the glands of the armpit, one of which is expressed here between P and R.*

*R* *An offspring led downward along the sides of the chest, and distributed especially into the muscle by which the posterior seat of the armpit cavity is formed, and by which the arm is pulled downward toward the back.*

*S* *The internal jugular, which scatters slender shoots to the side of the windpipe and to the nerves led down this way. What remains of it, besides a few branches, creeps into the skull and is divided there in various ways, as I shall pursue in the description of the vessels of the brain.*

*T* *The external or superficial jugular.*

*U* *The distribution of the external jugular vein into two branches near the jaws.*

*X* *A branch of the external jugular, entering the interior parts of the mouth, and distributed variously into the larynx and the muscles of the bone resembling the letter U <note>The hyoid bone.</note>, the tongue, the palate, the cavity of the nose, and finally into the skull by three branches, and also into the eyes by several shoots.*

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK III.

<margin>$\gamma$</margin> The outer branch of the external jugular division, made near the throat, which is distributed by a numerous series of veins into the muscles and skin of the face, then to the temples, and behind the ears, and throughout the entire skin of the head. <margin>Z</margin> And indeed, **Z** indicates the portion of this branch marked **$\gamma$** which extends into the face. <margin>9.a.</margin> The character **9** indicates the vein of the forehead. **a** indicates the portion creeping upward along the temples. <margin>*</margin> And **\*** marks that which is carried behind the ears and to the skin of the back of the head. The remaining series of veins here in the head relates to the vessels of the brain; for that reason, I have not marked them with characters, because they will be explained in a specific figure to be placed before the fourteenth chapter. However, if anyone should wish to occupy this figure of the **vena cava** <term>vena cava: the primary large vein returning blood to the heart</term> with characters in the same manner as we fashioned the one added to the end of this book—which shows the veins together with the arteries—it would first be permitted to place a character opposite the right side. This would indicate the right, or first (as I must call it), **sinus** <term>sinus: a channel for venous blood, specifically the dural venous sinuses in the brain</term> of the **dura mater** <term>dura mater: the tough, outermost membrane protecting the brain</term>, stretched out here like a semicircle. A second character would be inscribed for the left, or second, sinus of that membrane, which is also carried in a semicircular fashion on the left side. A third character would be applied to the third sinus of the dura mater, which begins where the first and second end—or where those two semicircles meet one another—and where another semicircle extends upward from them. The posterior part of this, closer to the back of the head, is seen in shadow; however, the anterior part, which goes toward the forehead, is clear. But the fourth sinus of the dura mater—which you will hear in its proper place arises from the anterior seat where the three aforementioned sinuses meet and is led straight forward—is not drawn here. In the figure sewn into the end of this book, however, it is marked with **y**. Furthermore, a fourth character would follow those three, which, placed at the root of the first sinus of the dura mater, would indicate the entrance of the vein marked **N**. Then it would also suggest the entrance of the inner branch of the jugular, which enters the skull through the opening carved out chiefly for the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "sexto neruorum cerebri pari"; in Vesalius’s classification, this refers to the nerves now known as the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves</note>. With a fifth character, the branch of the internal jugular running through its own opening into the sides of the dura mater of the brain would be marked. A sixth would note the branch of the external jugular, which enters the skull through its own opening carved at the posterior root of the **mastoid process** <note>original: "processūs mamillaris"</note> of the temporal bone. In addition to these, another character could be inscribed for those small veins which are carried here in shadow under the forehead vein marked **9**, so that the veins would also be indicated which creep into the skull through the seat where the organs of smell rest <note>the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone</note>, and through the opening carved for the sake of the second pair of cranial nerves <note>the optic nerves</note>.

<margin>a,a</margin> Each **a** indicates the **humeraria vein** <note>original: "uenam humerariam"; now known as the cephalic vein</note>. However, by the upper **a**, its origin from the external jugular marked **T** is signified. The lower **a** marks the seat of the humeraria where it emerges from the depths into the surface and skin of the arm. But when I drew this table, truly distrusting my own eyes and believing **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century Greek physician whose authority Vesalius frequently challenged</note> too much, I assigned this origin to the humeraria vein; whereas otherwise, I ought to have derived it from the vein marked **I**, at the outer side of the character **N**. You see this done on the left side of that figure which, placed at the end of this book, was illustrated after the present one, for I am now bolder in my own opinion through experience. Thus, you may attribute this error of mine to my devotion toward Galen.

<margin>b</margin> An offshoot of the humeraria, from its higher seat not far from its origin, scattered into the posterior muscles occupying the neck and the skin of this region itself.

<margin>c</margin> An offshoot of the humeraria, running out with a frequent lineage into the convex seat of the **scapula** <term>scapula: the shoulder blade</term>.

<margin>d,d</margin> Veins born from the humeraria before it is twisted deeper under the top of the shoulder, distributed into the skin of the shoulder’s summit and the surface of the muscle that lifts the arm <note>the deltoid muscle</note>, and sometimes also to the breast.

<margin>e,e,e</margin> Thin little veins, propagated from the humeraria into the skin of the outer part of the arm and the anterior region of the muscle that first flexes the elbow <note>the biceps brachii</note>.

<margin>f</margin> The division of the humeraria near the outer bump of the humerus into branches, which are seen to be unequal in size to one another.

<margin>g</margin> A branch of the said humeraria division, not always conspicuous, which dives into the depths near the muscles occupying the inner side of the elbow joint toward the lower parts, and is soon consumed.

Another branch of the recently mentioned division, which, led downward under the skin obliquely to the middle seat of the elbow’s bend, joins with the branch of the **axillary vein** <note>original: "axillaris uenæ"</note> to be marked **t**, and together with it constitutes the common vein to which **$\alpha$** is assigned <note>the median cubital vein, commonly used for drawing blood</note>.

<margin>i,i</margin> A branch of the humeraria, stretching obliquely through the radius into the outer region of the elbow, and dispersing small veins everywhere into the skin near it. 

<margin>k.</margin> Among these, the most prominent is marked with an upper **k**, which it distributes toward the outer seat of the elbow joint to the posterior parts. When the present branch, creeping obliquely in this manner, reaches the root of the wrist 

<margin>l.</margin> opposite the appendage of the **ulna** <note>the styloid process of the ulna bone</note> (exactly where **l** is seen here), the offspring of the axillary vein's branch marked **x** is mixed with it. From this axillary offshoot and the humeraria branch, one vein arises, approaching the seat of the wrist and the back of the hand under the little finger, and indeed the little finger itself and in a way the ring finger, in a series of various muscles on the outer seat of the hand.

<margin>m</margin> The axillary vein, whose names will be reviewed shortly, just like those of the humeraria.

<margin>n</margin> A branch of the axillary vein, derived into the heads of the muscles that extend the elbow <note>the triceps</note>.

<margin>o</margin> A branch extended to the recently mentioned muscles and the skin of the back of the arm.

<margin>p</margin> A notable offshoot, led obliquely downward under the shoulder, or rather the bone of the arm, toward its outer bump; it provides branches to the muscles taking their origin from here and is carried for some distance into the outer seat of the elbow with the fourth nerve seeking the arm.
