### BOOK III OF THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

**q, r** The distribution of the axillary vein <term>axillary vein: the major vein of the armpit and upper arm</term> into two trunks: one of which is marked with a double **q**, and is always located deep, hidden throughout its entire course; it is distributed in exactly the same way as the artery of the hand, which can be seen in the figure of the great artery preceding the twelfth chapter. The other axillary trunk (marked with **r**, which we shall call the "axillary" throughout the rest of our discourse) runs everywhere just beneath the skin and is divided into various offshoots. Furthermore, you will observe that this distribution of the axillary vein occurs even higher up than we have depicted here.

**s** A vein branching from the axillary into the skin of the front of the upper arm, and also somewhat into the skin of the back of the arm.

**t** The anterior branch of the axillary vein, from that division which is visible here near the skin of the inner bump of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle of the upper arm bone</note>. The present branch, marked **t**, is carried obliquely beneath the skin to the middle of the bend of the elbow joint; and by joining with the branch of the humeral vein marked **h**, it forms the **common vein**, to be indicated by **$\alpha$**.

**u** The posterior vein of the two-part division of the axillary near the inner bump of the humerus, which spreads many various offshoots from itself.

**x, x** A branch of the posterior vein marked **u**, which reaches downward under the ulna <note>the inner forearm bone</note> to the wrist, and being distributed everywhere into the neighboring skin, it offers an offshoot to the branch of the humeral vein that climbs the wrist near the pinky finger.

**y** A vein running into the skin of the back of the elbow joint.

**z, z** Indicates a multiple series of veins spread into the skin of the inner part of the elbow, and then running into the skin of the inner part of the hand. Above, **z** marks a vein taking its origin from the branch of the axillary marked **t**. Below, **z** indicates the offshoots which the axillary vein branch (marked **x** and **x**) offers to the internal region of the elbow.

**$\zeta$** The junction of the small veins entwining the **mound of Venus** <note>original: "Veneris monticulum"; the thenar eminence or fleshy base of the thumb</note> with the branch to be marked **$\lambda$**. For the branch **$\zeta$** is an offshoot of those veins that creep through the outer part of the hand between the thumb and the index finger.

**$\alpha$** The **common vein** <note>the median cubital vein, often used for bloodletting</note>, formed from the axillary branch marked **t** and the humeral branch which we marked **h**: this extends through the inner part of the elbow, climbing obliquely downward over the radius <note>the outer forearm bone</note>; and finally, having passed the radius, it runs into the outer part of the elbow near its lower region, dispersing some small branches during its progress to the nearby skin.

**$\beta$** The division of the common vein near the lower part of the radius where it faces the wrist, not unlike **$\gamma$**, **$\gamma$**, or **$\lambda$**: <margin>$\gamma, \lambda$</margin> one leg of which, marked **$\gamma$**, approaches the outer part of the hand situated below the thumb and index finger, as well as the thumb and index finger themselves, and it distributes the small branch marked **$\delta$** into the inner part of the hand. <margin>$\delta$</margin> However, the other leg, marked **$\varepsilon$**, is mostly consumed toward the middle and ring fingers. <margin>$\varepsilon$</margin>

<margin>Various names of the veins creeping through the skin of the upper arm, elbow, and hand.</margin>
Various names are assigned by our physicians to the branches reaching the outer part of the hand; since these names conflict considerably with one another and are encountered everywhere, I think something should be said about them now. I would rather fill this index of characters with these "barbarous" names <note>Vesalius often refers to non-Greek/Latin medieval or Arabic terms as "barbarous"</note> than the actual narrative in which I describe these veins. The Greeks and more refined Latin physicians called few veins in the elbow and hand by their own proper names. For the vein running through the inner upper arm and armpit, marked **r** or even **m**, they called "axillary" <note>from *axilla*, armpit</note> in both arms because it creeps through the armpit; just as they also called the inner vein of the elbow by that name because it is mostly extended through the inner parts of the elbow. 

However, they specifically called the axillary of the right arm the **liver vein** <note>original: "iecorariam"</note>, because they were accustomed to cut it in ailments of the liver. The axillary of the left arm was called the **spleen vein** <note>original: "lienaria"</note> by them, because they usually opened this one in diseases of the spleen. So again, the **$\omega\mu\iota\alpha\tilde{\iota}\alpha$** <note>Greek: *omiaia*</note>, or **humeralis** (marked **a**), obtained its name simply because it is carried through the shoulder (*humerus*) into the hand, and it was also called the "outer vein of the elbow" since it creeps along the outer side of the elbow. Hippocrates, in his books *On the Joints*, seems to have called this the **thick vein**. Because it is believed to heal diseases of the head, it is also commonly called the **cephalic vein** <note>original: "capitis uena"</note>. 

The branches marked **h** and **t**, which constitute the **common vein** (which we marked **$\alpha$**), they called the **median veins**, either because they were led to the middle of the bend of the elbow, or because they were halfway between the outer and inner veins of the elbow. Because of their slanted path, they also called them the **oblique veins**. They called the one marked **$\alpha$** the **common vein**, which rises from those branches marked **h** and **t**, and is common to the inner and outer veins of the elbow. Beyond these names, you will hardly find others among them. 

But if you read the books of the Arabs, heaps of names occur everywhere, hardly ever consistently applied to the same vein. To bring forth something more certain about these names for the sake of students—who often stall me with these names during dissection—I will not find it troublesome to list here the names used by the translator of **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text</note>, which are read in the First *Fen* of the First Book, Fifth Doctrine, Chapter Four. In that chapter, Avicenna purposefully describes the veins of the arm, seeking their sequence from **Galen’s** <note>Aelius Galenus (129–210 AD), the dominant medical authority of antiquity</note> third book *On Anatomical Procedures*, or rather from **Oribasius** <note>Greek medical writer (c. 320–403 AD)</note>. 

Avicenna, or his translator, calls the part of the humeral vein stretching from the external jugular to the place where it first goes under the skin of the arm the **spatular** vein; this part is encompassed by the two **a**'s in our drawing. Where the humeral vein extends along the arm, he calls it the **Cephalic**, as if it were the "head vein." This is contained between the lower **a** and **f**. The branch of the humeral vein which we marked **i**, he calls the **rope of the arm** <note>original: "Funem brachy"</note>. The axillary is called the **Asellaris** <note>a corruption of *axillaris*</note> by him. The common vein, marked **$\alpha$**, he calls the **Black vein** <note>original: "Nigra"</note>; but where it contends obliquely toward the radius, it is called the **Basilica** <note>royal vein</note> by him. One leg of the division of the common vein, which we marked **$\beta$** and compared to **$\gamma$** or **$\lambda$**, namely the branch marked **$\varepsilon$** which seeks the ring and middle fingers, is called the **Syelen** of Avicenna in the region of the back of the hand. But truly, other names are found from time to time among the Arabs and barbarians...

...you will observe that this is called the *Syelem* <note>original: "Syelem", a Latinized form of an Arabic term for the cephalic vein</note>, which is formed near the wrist from the branch of the humeral vein marked **i** and the offshoot of the axillary vein marked **x**, and is marked **l**. To this vein, the common crowd of physicians gives the same names as the axillary, calling it also the *Salvatella* <term>Salvatella: traditionally the vein on the back of the hand between the ring and little finger, thought to "save" health</term> and the *Salubris* <note>meaning "health-giving"</note>. In addition to these, the axillary vein is called by physicians most especially the *Basilica* <term>Basilica: the "royal" vein of the inner arm</term>, sometimes also the *Nigra* <note>"Black vein"</note>, and occasionally the *Funis brachii* <note>"Cord of the arm"</note>. The humeral vein is also called the *Ocularis* <note>"Eye-vein"</note> and *Auris* <note>"Ear-vein"</note>, for the reason that it supposedly cures inflammations of those parts. Unless, perhaps, the givers of these names were so foolish that, along with Aristotle and those who today have disgracefully published under their own names the veins correctly drawn by me before, they believed that the origin of the humeral vein was primarily under the ear. I would have to deal at great length with the <gloss>a</gloss> origin of the vena cava if anyone thought the controversy of the authors should be brought into the open; as many passages of Galen, interspersed throughout his works, and especially the sixth book *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato* attest, which he dedicated entirely to this question: from which organ the origin of the veins is derived. For if I were to undertake that same dispute by design, I could by no means carelessly pass over Galen's arguments; rather, each one would have to be examined separately with the most accurate study, and I would have to relate what I consider true and what I consider false. For we must not so give in to Galen's words that we consider everything he heaps upon Aristotle there to be true and indubitable: as will now be made obvious to anyone in the progress of the femur, which is about to relate the true series of the vena cava. # ANDREAS VESALII ON THE [FABRIC OF THE] BODY

<margin>
From figure e, chapter 12, C is divided into i and V with D.
</margin>
<margin>
f Here compare Book 6, Figure 5, C, D, and F, with O, P, and R of Figure 6. Then look at this location in the last figure of Book 3.
</margin>

...at its origin, it splits into two trunks,<sup>e</sup> in the manner of the great artery <note>original: "arteriæ magnæ", referring to the aorta</note>, and one seeks the upper parts, while the other unfolds downward; and he [Galen] teaches that of those trunks, the one carried downward along the lumbar vertebrae is the larger. From this, Galen’s own arguments—which he wove so industriously and cleverly from the flow of springs and rivers and the roots of trees—must immediately be rejected. In the same way, Galen’s dogma must be utterly rejected where he denies that the vena cava comes forth from the heart:<sup>f</sup> because it does not arise there in a similar way as the great artery; that is, it does not divide into two trunks immediately from its origin, but is led straight along the side of the heart. For first of all, Galen’s axiom is false and most unworthy of a professor of dissection, in which he asserts that the vein born from the convexity <term>gibbus: the rounded, upper surface of the liver</term> of the liver divides into two trunks just like the great artery. Furthermore, his demonstrative method fails to conclude that the vena cava does not arise from the heart simply because it extends straight along the side of the heart. For if anyone examines the origin of the artery attentively, they will surely notice that it arises from the middle of the heart’s base, as if from its very center. Therefore, if any part of the artery had to be led downward, it is visibly necessary that the artery be divided not long after its origin. However, the vein, which arises from the side of the heart’s base (being a softer vessel than an artery) according to Aristotle’s opinion, did not need to be split into two trunks immediately from its very origin. Since it can very conveniently creep upward and downward without division, such a division would be useless, besides being entirely lacking in structural logic. For if the vein coming forth from here were bifurcated in the manner of the artery, its origin and main stem would first have to creep entirely into the right side of the thoracic cavity for some distance, and then

"If the heart were the principle of the veins, all veins would necessarily have to reach the heart, just as they surely reach the liver." As if indeed<sup>g</sup> the arterial vein <term>arterial vein: the pulmonary artery; Galen called it a "vein" because it carried "nutritive" blood, but "arterial" because of its thick walls</term> did not go to the liver any less than<sup>h</sup> the portal vein goes to the heart; although in the meantime we see not a few branches of the portal vein so united with the offshoots of the vena cava in the liver, as if one might not undeservedly assert that the vena cava is continuous with the portal vein, and by this reasoning, the portal vein is also communicated to the heart—quite differently, of course, from how the arterial vein reaches the liver. But if perhaps, in support of Galen's opinion, we contend that the arterial vein does not belong to the liver because it consists of the body of an artery, we must again concede that<sup>i</sup> the venous artery <term>venous artery: the pulmonary vein; so called by Galenists because it carries "vital" air/blood but has thin, vein-like walls</term> is formed from the body of a vein,<sup>k</sup> and seeks its origin from that site of the left heart's chamber <note>original: "sinus"</note> from which the vena cava arises in the right heart's chamber. Add also that this vessel is led to the right and left sides of the lung without the production and progress of a single main stem for any distance, just as the vena cava is carried upward and downward from the heart. And then add that the arterial vein maintains one stem for some time after its origin and is afterward divided into two trunks, exactly like the great artery, which similarly arises from the middle of the heart’s base, like that arterial vein. This indeed shows the strength of Galen’s anatomical argument, by which he tries to teach that the vena cava ought to have been divided in the manner of the great artery if it took its beginning from the heart and not from the liver. As for what pertains to Galen's reasoning, that all veins [reach] the heart, just as...

...asserting that it does not pertain to the heart any more than to the liver, I would certainly bring the umbilical vein <note>The vein that carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.</note> into the discussion, if I had examined that vein in the human fetus as I have in the fetuses of dogs. In dogs, the umbilical vein—the greater part of which seeks the liver—is directed toward the mesentery and the loins. This would teach us that the umbilical vein should not have been inserted into the heart, even if the heart were established as the starting point of the veins, especially since the umbilical arteries do not end in the heart. Instead, it is enough for them to have emerged as continuous with the great artery <note>original: "magnae arteriae"; the aorta.</note> at the point where it is led down into the legs. On the same occasion, I shall say nothing of the first organ formed in the generation of the fetus; for although I could easily disprove and refute the decrees of other anatomists (who fight amongst themselves and even against their own positions), I would nevertheless offer nothing that seemed to me entirely sound and beyond doubt. Indeed, certain matters regarding the formation of the fetus and the actual use of the heart are, by Hercules, obscure to me and full of doubt.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But that "irrefutable" demonstration (as Galen calls it) which he wove against Aristotle—concerning animals that lack a right chamber of the heart—is not at all effective. In those animals, the vena cava <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart.</note> is joined to the single chamber of the heart in the same way it is joined to the right chamber in other animals, since in these animals too, the blood is spread from the liver to the heart, at least in the name of the "arteries" (even if not by way of the lungs). And who, I pray, has reached such a depth of stupidity that they would say Aristotle wished the vena cava in such animals to arise from a right ventricle which they do not possess? This is what Galen claims; yet does he not recognize that Aristotle’s style of discourse regarding animals lacking lungs was different from that regarding those which are not deprived of them?

<margin>
Book 6, Figure 7, K, L, M.
Book 6, Figure 9, E, F.
</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, who even slightly practiced in dissection doubts that the argument drawn from the little membranes <note>Valves.</note> stationed at the opening of the vena cava can be dismissed by looking at the membranes of the venous artery <note>original: "venalis arteriae"; the modern pulmonary vein, which Galen believed carried "pneuma" or air-like spirit.</note>? Nor do I know well enough what Galen is dreaming up concerning the distribution of the vena cava in birds, since I observe nothing peculiar in the sequence of the vena cava in them—except that the liver is uniquely constituted of two fibers or lobes. If the cava takes its beginning from these, it certainly does not divide into two trunks from its origin in the manner of the great artery. Moreover, when Galen asserts that the cava does not arise from the heart because it does not pulse in the manner of an artery, he should have considered the nature of the "arterial vein" <note>original: "arterialis uenae"; the modern pulmonary artery.</note> and likewise the "venous artery." Similarly, when he objects that the heart does not offer the power of blood-making <term>sanguificatio: the historical belief that food was turned into blood within the body</term> to the liver through the cava because that vessel is "leathery," he should have weighed how short a distance exists between the heart and the liver. He should also recall how he himself, in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, attributed a blood-making faculty to the entire portal vein <note>The vein moving blood from the digestive organs to the liver.</note> very similar to the power of the liver. Anatomists began to describe the sequence of the distribution of this vein from the liver, rather than from the intestines and stomach (from which it leads the juice prepared from food and drink into the liver). Since blood, urine, and bile—as well as the waste seeking the spleen—arise from this juice, it in no way corresponds in proportion to that blood which, returning through the portal vein, supplies nourishment to those parts to which it is committed. Thus, the argument Galen collects against Aristotle from the descriptions of certain anatomists regarding the sequence of the veins is clearly just a rhetorical one.

<margin>
The description of the distribution of the vena cava must begin from the liver.
</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But lest I seem here to disparage the views of Galen—the prince of dissection and indeed of all medicine—and merely refute his arguments one by one, I shall now begin the sequence of the vena cava from the liver. I do this because I still believe that blood is derived from the liver into the cava, or at least is taken up into the branches of the cava from the offshoots of the portal vein. However, I do not so strongly maintain that the "origin" of the cava is here, nor would I wish anything to be asserted by me regarding its origin—whatever might accidentally slip out from me while writing—lest I myself suggest an opportunity for calumny to certain "goatish" <note>original: "hircosis"; a common insult used by Vesalius for old-fashioned, smelly, or stubborn physicians who followed Galen blindly.</note> physicians. Such men care only for trifles of this sort, while they neglect the knowledge of bones and muscles, and...

# BOOK III ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...the more significant branches, because of the higher parts of the liver, enter into the anterior <note>front</note> seat of the cava, but not into the sides or the posterior seat, and they are in no way to be compared with the great size of the vena cava <term>vena cava</term><note>The large vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the body back to the heart.</note>. Indeed, unless you have sworn too anxiously to Galen’s <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the undisputed medical authority for over a millennium before Vesalius.</note> words along with me, you will undoubtedly assert that the vena cava is carried down from the heart through the posterior parts of the liver, and that from its anterior seat two remarkable veins sprout, diffused in a numerous series into the substance of the liver, and are continued by the small branches of the portal vein. In addition to these veins which are offered to the liver by the cava, in the remainder of its descent through the posterior parts of the organ (which is certainly very short), <margin>x d.</margin> you will also observe * tiny branches running out from the anterior seat of the cava into the substance of the liver, which are by no means equal in number in all humans. And all these things are so obvious to one accurately dissecting a human, that no one now looking at the series of the vena cava would not much more greatly approve that this, as far as the series is concerned, ought first to be described from the heart, and finally its path to the upper and lower parts be narrated. But since we still think, along with Galen, that the blood contained everywhere in the cava is produced by the liver, we have begun the distribution of the branches of the vena cava from the liver in a certain way with him, intending next to describe that part of the vein which stays above the liver.

## THE SERIES OF THE DISTRIBUTION OF THAT PART OF THE VENA CAVA WHICH
## stays above the liver. Chapter VII.

<margin>That the part of the cava passing through the diaphragm is not narrower than that which stays below the liver.</margin>

IT WAS BY NO MEANS enough for Galen to devise some sort of true origin for the vena cava from the liver; and, so that he might seem to deviate more truly and more deservedly from the opinion of Aristotle <note>Aristotle believed the heart was the origin of the veins, while Galen insisted it was the liver.</note>, he imagined that the vena cava, soon after its progress from its hump on the liver, is divided into two trunks in the manner of the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, and that one is led to the upper parts of the body, while the other is led to the lower parts. Furthermore, so that he might even prove that blood is not generated in the heart, he did not fear to add that the trunk which seeks the upper parts is much narrower and less ample than that which is extended downward. But we have already asserted <margin>
a corresponds to B, 7.
b book 6, figure 5.
6 B.
</margin>
that the cava is not divided into such trunks. And it is also by no means consistent with the truth that the part of the vena cava seen between the liver and the right ear <note>the right atrium</note> of the heart appears narrower than that which is unfolded under the liver along the lumbar vertebrae. I would wish this to be observed not cursorily during dissection. For if someone should devote study to a dissection in passing, and while moving the liver, or the heart, or another member during the cutting, should propel more blood into the part of the vein stretched out along the lumbar vertebrae than into that which is held above the liver, he will surely subscribe to Galen’s opinion. But if, in turn, he should lead the blood squeezed from this part of the vein upward into that part, with little effort he will no longer agree with Galen. When, however, these things are established by dissection, it will be profitable to weigh more closely Galen’s reasoning, by which he concludes that the ascending part of the vein must be much smaller than the descending part, because the latter, forsooth, nourishes more parts than the former. For if that reasoning of Galen is true, his fiction will be known to everyone even without dissection: since the ascending part requires more blood, contrary to Galen’s dogma, than the inferior part which is stretched out along the lumbar vertebrae. Whence it must also soon be inferred that this part ought deservedly to have been made narrower than that one. For first, neither the gallbladder, nor the stomach, nor the intestines, nor the omentum <note>the fatty tissue draping over the intestines</note>, nor the mesentery, nor the spleen, take any small branch from the cava, and these are placed below the liver. Indeed, only the kidneys, the other bladder <note>the urinary bladder</note>, the testes and legs, and the inferior part of the abdomen, obtain blood from that part of the cava which descends. But from the ascending part, the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note>, and the whole...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...the entire thorax and the upper part of the abdomen as far as the navel are nourished. For you will hear that the part of the thorax closest to the liver, reaching as far as the second lumbar vertebra, obtains its nourishment from the <margin>c F, F.</margin> vein lacking a pair <note>original: "uena coniugis experte"; this is the azygos vein, so named because it has no symmetrical "partner" on the other side of the body</note>. Then the arms, the neck, and the entire head take their nourishment from the ascending portion of the vena cava. I shall say nothing for now of the abundance of blood gushing into the brain through so many veins, and that which is carried to the heart—not only in the name of the heart and the lung, the greatest of all the viscera, but also for all the arteries, which we believe are filled by the blood brought to the heart. But to what purpose does it serve to collect such reasons to subvert Galen’s <note>Galen was the ancient Roman physician whose theories Vesalius often challenged</note> decree? Since dissection, as students have already been warned, abundantly weakens not only this point, but very many others read in his books concerning the decrees of Hippocrates and Plato. These points are willingly granted by doctors—due to their lack of skill in dissecting and the excessive faith we give to ancient authors—as if they were the oracles of Apollo. However, it would now finally be the proper time to follow the true sequence of the part of the vena cava <margin>d B.</margin> sitting above the liver to some extent; and afterwards, where the discourse differs from Galen’s opinion (lest we seem to despise his authority more than is fair), I shall add further notes.

<margin>The passage of the cava through the transverse septum, and its branches in the septum.</margin>

<margin>The opening of the cava into the right chamber of the heart.</margin>
As soon as the cava has surpassed the septum <margin>h</margin>, proceeding slightly to the left toward the right side of the base of the heart <margin>i</margin>, it is opened on its left side <margin>f 3rd fig. book 6 C, D, E. F, G. 4th fig. B, B.</margin> <margin>k</margin> and reaches into the right chamber <note>original: "sinum"</note> of the heart. This is not, as the sect of Anatomists writes, by some offshoot or any branch, but only by a certain opening or a passage so wide as would arise if the widths of the part of the vena cava sitting below the heart and the part just above the heart were brought together into a single circle <margin>g another is noted. h 5th fig. book 6 D. i 4th fig. book 6 C, D.</margin>.

### ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK III

<margin>

...produced from the side, it turns downward toward the body of nearly the fourth thoracic vertebra. Descending along the right side of the vertebrae, it extends to its end along with the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, passing under the diaphragm <note>original: "septum transversum"</note> to reach as far as some of the lumbar vertebrae. This vein performs the role of the vena cava throughout its entire course, as the trunk of the vena cava itself was unable to touch the vertebrae in the lumbar region in such a way, and thus could not provide branches to the vertebrae and the parts of the back in a joint-by-joint fashion. Rightly, therefore, the vena cava produced this great vein from itself so that, in the manner of the great artery, it could sprout branches on both sides into the intervals between the ribs. It does not spread these branches from its sides, but from the middle region of its posterior surface, which rests upon the vertebrae.

Because it lacks a partner and does not receive a similar offshoot from the vena cava on the other side, the Greeks call it **azygos** <note>original: "ἄζυγος"; meaning "unpaired" or "unwedded"</note>, and we call it the vein without a pair, or the "unmatched" vein. It arises from the right side of the vena cava rather than the left because it must be deployed along the right side of the back; the left side and the middle are occupied by the great artery, a most noble organ. It does not arise from the front of the vena cava, lest it should have to reflect toward the right by a longer path than it does now to reach the spine. Nor could it take its beginning from the back, because that area rests upon other organs, and it would have been necessary for the unpaired vein to be led further to the right than it is now. From this vein, therefore, offshoots sprout like joints on both sides, each creeping to one of the intervals between the nine lower ribs. In the intervals of the "true" ribs <note>the upper ribs that connect directly to the breastbone</note>, they extend to the point where the ribs turn into cartilage; but in the intervals of the "false" ribs <note>original: "spuriarum costarum"; the lower ribs that do not reach the breastbone</note>, these offshoots reach even further into the front parts of the abdomen, entwining themselves within the abdominal muscles. In their progress through the spaces between the ribs, they give off small branches that disperse into the muscles resting upon that part of the chest through which they creep. Furthermore, from this unpaired vein, certain offshoots reach all the vertebrae along which it is led; these run into the bodies of the vertebrae, the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsalem medullam"</note>, and the muscles lying near these areas.

<margin>
b 1st, 2nd, 3rd figures, chapter 19, book 1, A, B.
c 1st figure, book 5, E.
d 1st figure, book 6, H, H. or 2nd figure, G, G. I, I.
</margin>
In addition, small branches are offered from this vein to the membranes that divide the chest <note>the mediastinum and pleura</note> where they are continuous with the back. Furthermore, one should not overlook that as soon as this vein touches the vertebrae after its origin, a branch is sometimes drawn out from it. This branch, divided into thin offshoots, goes to the upper ribs of its side, where it is distributed into the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note> in very numerous but slender twigs. These are not carried in an orderly or straight line according to the path of the rib, as are the offshoots arranged for the lower ribs, but rather they run out in a wandering path.

<margin>
Various arrangements of the vein lacking a pair.
</margin>
And this occurs so frequently in humans (because Nature has given them a much shorter thorax than quadrupeds) that this present year in a public dissection here in Padua, we saw all the ribs of the thorax nourished by the offshoots of the unpaired vein in both a man and a woman. And in Bologna also (to say nothing of private dissections), when I first presided over the dissection there and a quite stubborn dispute was being waged concerning bloodletting in "the side disease" <note>original: "laterali morbo"; pleurisy</note>, we happened upon three human cadavers in a single lecture. In these, no one from such a great gathering of learned men could deny that all the ribs of the thorax were nourished by the branches of this vein.

<margin>
e 5th figure of chapter 5, & 4th figure of book 5, γ.
</margin>
And just as that is observed from time to time, so indeed you will sometimes see this unpaired vein, when it reaches roughly the ninth thoracic vertebra, divide into two trunks. One of these is extended to the roots of the ribs on the right side, while the other is extended to the left, offering branches to the ribs of its side as it creeps along. Sometimes, however, you will observe a large vein arise from the left side of the unpaired vein in almost that same region, exactly similar to that branch...

### ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE BODY

<margin>
In these two figures, we have represented twin sequences of the vein lacking a pair <note>the azygos vein</note>: by which it varies from that which the complete drawing of the vena cava indicated. Here **A** marks the trunk of the vein without a pair. **B** is its branch, which, being led into the left side, is divided into many offshoots. **C**, however, specifically in the lower figure, introduces a portion of the trunk of the vena cava.

<image-desc>Two anatomical diagrams of the human spine and the azygos vein (vena sine pari). The upper illustration shows the vein ascending and descending along the vertebrae, giving off paired intercostal branches. The lower illustration shows an anatomical variation where the branching is more pronounced on the left side.</image-desc>

...similar to that branch which is easily the largest of those approaching the lower membrane of the omentum from the portal vein. For as soon as this vein crosses transversely over the body of the vertebra to which it is extended, it spreads out into two branches: one of which is carried upward, the other downward along the roots of the ribs, and it derives offshoots into the intervals of its own ribs. This occurs just as if Nature had occasionally preferred one large branch to be extended here from the right side to the left, rather than one thin and slender little branch being carried over each individual vertebra. So much so, that I am even persuaded (although I have never seen it) that sometimes from the left side of the trunk of the vena cava, where it touches the throat, a vein is drawn out which, led downward along the left side of the vertebrae, offers branches to the left ribs, while that which we call the vein "without a pair" <note>original: "sine pari"; the azygos vein</note> nourishes only the right ribs. And a lamb bears witness that the origin of this kind of vein can happen not only from the throat first, but also a little lower down, in which I once observed such a thing. Truly, I should think that such sequences of veins, occurring only very rarely, ought to be weighed by a student of Anatomy no differently than if occasionally a sixth finger on a hand, or some other monstrous thing, offered itself to be seen. So much so, that if ever I observe these things in public dissections, I silently pass over them as if they did not exist, lest candidates of the art think these things are to be observed in all bodies.

<margin>
Book 7 of *Anatomical Procedures*, section 2.
</margin>
<margin>
It will be permitted here to look at figures 3, 4, 5, and 6 of Book 6, and the last figure of this book.
</margin>
And I have considered this to be done more studiously, not only in dissections but just now in pursuing the history of the "absolute" <note>ideal or standard</note> human, because I have learned more than once from experience that students admire those monstrous things more. Furthermore, it must now be added to the discourse that so far nothing in the human has been overlooked by me: as indeed he might think, who, diligently unrolling the teachings of Galen, first seeks from me the fifth fiber or lobe of the lung, by which the vena cava in the interval between the diaphragm <note>original: "septum transversum"</note> and the transverse wrapping of the heart <note>the pericardium</note> would be supported, according to Galen's opinion. To be sure, since Galen had found this lobe in monkeys, he accused other leaders of dissection of drowsiness, as if they had been ignorant of it: just as indeed it would have remained hidden from Galen too, if he had set about dissecting the corpses of humans with them, rather than those of monkeys. For since in humans there is no interval in the passage of the vena cava from the diaphragm into the wrapping of the heart, but these two are born together and are perforated at one and the same time, no lobe of the lung can truly stand here to support the vein in that interval. But in tailed monkeys, and even more so in dogs, an ample interval occurs between the diaphragm and the point of the heart's wrapping: and here, between the membranes partitioning the chest <note>the mediastinum</note>, there is an empty or vacant space through which the vena cava creeps, having beneath it a lobe of the lung, by which that trunk of the vena cava is grasped and supported as if by a hand, by a wonderful blessing of Nature.

<margin>
Book 6 of *On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Galen*; book *On the Dissection of Veins*; Book 7 of *Anatomical Procedures*; and the *Commentaries on Hippocrates' On Regimen in Acute Diseases*.
</margin>
Therefore, when you compare Galen’s description to dogs, and ours to humans, you will confess both to be true. But Galen’s opinion, teaching that veins are everywhere led out and distributed from the vena cava into the membranes partitioning the chest before it reaches the heart, spares the truth: since these membranes receive veins partly from those branches which you will hear are carried to them from the throat, and partly from the vein without a pair.

<margin>
f L. 1 fig. lib. 6 M, N, Q
</margin>
The vena cava, however, when it is carried to the heart, does not even touch the membranes partitioning the chest cavity: it is so far from offering specifically to them little branches so thin that they ought to be distributed into them.

# THE THIRD BOOK ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>
g 6th figure of book 6; also book 8, figure C, D.
h 1st figure of chapter 15, B, C.
</margin>
...may offer. Moreover, another reader, well-disposed toward Galen's book *On the Dissection of Veins*, will wonder why—before I reached the progress of the vena cava above the heart—I did not immediately ascribe the <gloss>g</gloss> arterial vein <note>original: "uenam arterialé"; this is the pulmonary artery, which Vesalius’s contemporaries called a "vein" because it carried blood, though they noted its arterial thickness.</note> as extending into the lung from the vena cava as soon as it reaches the heart. This is, after all, a dogma of Galen. Yet, how much this agrees with the truth is proven by the very proximity of the vessels. Indeed, since we say nothing truly arises from another unless it is contiguous or at least adjacent, no one should assert that the arterial vein takes its beginning from the vena cava. For besides the fact that the arterial vein <gloss>h</gloss> consists of a body six times thicker than the vena cava, the former does not touch the latter, and no small portion of the heart's substance intervenes between the higher seat of the vena cava’s orifice and the right side of the arterial vein's orifice. Furthermore, the orifice of the arterial vein reaches into the right chamber of the heart no less circularly and freely than the orifice of the vena cava; and nothing appears less likely than that it is some "offspring" produced from the cava to the arterial vein. Hence, because this vessel possesses its own distinct boundary, it must be treated privately and separately, no less than the vena cava. Next, perhaps someone will blame me because I called the coronary vein "distinguished" (as it indeed truly is), whereas in his book *On the Dissection of Veins and Arteries*, Galen wrote that it was "tiny"—just as, by contrast, in the seventh book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, he recorded that this vein is always found as a twin.

<margin>Galen's opinion on the origin of the vein lacking a pair.</margin>
To this is added Galen’s inconsistent opinion regarding the origin of the vein lacking a pair <note>original: "uenæ pari carétis"; the azygos vein.</note>. First, in his tenth commentary on the second book of Hippocrates’s *On the Diet in Acute Diseases*, he contradicts himself three times. For at the beginning of his discourse on the distribution of the vena cava through the thorax, he says in general that the vein nourishing the eight lower ribs arises from the cava before it reaches the heart. Soon after, he adds that in certain animals, this is drawn from the cava above the heart; but in man, it emerges from that seat of the cava where it touches the right auricle <note>original: "aurem"; literally "ear," referring to the atrial appendage.</note> of the heart. Again, forgetting himself, he adds a little further down that the lower ribs of a man are nourished by a vein that starts from the cava below the heart. Almost conforming to this opinion is what is read in the sixth book of *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*, when he writes that the heart's envelope <note>The pericardium.</note>, together with all the membranes that partition the cavity of the chest and those that surround the lung, takes nourishment from the cava before it is carried to the heart. In his book *On the Dissection of Veins*, he attests that in certain animals, the vein without a pair proceeds from the right side of the auricle to the left parts of the thorax and is carried to the fifth thoracic vertebra. In monkeys, however, he teaches that this is placed a little above the auricle on the right side; and he admits here that more intervals between the ribs are nourished by this vein than he stated in the book *On the Diet*. He embraces the same opinion in the seventh book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, except that here he simply records that it arises from the vein that stands next to the right chamber of the heart—whereas in the former work, he wrongly added that it proceeds to the left parts of the thorax.

<margin>i E.</margin>
Furthermore, in another place in that seventh book, he teaches that this vein without a pair arises from the right <gloss>i</gloss> chamber of the heart, just like the coronary vein—even though this does not happen even in monkeys. But there is no reason for me to bring forth at greater length other passages of this sort from the book *On the Formation of the Fetus* and elsewhere, since Galen's opinion on the origin and progress of the vein lacking a pair is established as inconsistent by these examples. How much his view agrees with the truth may be sought from our own narration, which follows the true sequence of that vein. For in man, no less than in monkeys, dogs, pigs, oxen, and as many quadrupeds as I have seen, the vein lacking a pair proceeds from the cava after it has passed the heart's envelope and reaches the point where no further connection of the lungs (which is achieved by the intervention of vessels) appears. And if anyone, disparaging the faith placed in dissection, should seek the reason for the origin of this vein...

-># ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY<-

<margin>Why it was necessary for the vein lacking a pair to be born from there.</margin>
Anyone will certainly discover this from our discourse, which has previously described Nature's skill in the propagation of that vein. For this vein lacking a pair <note>original: "uena pari carentem"; now known as the azygos vein.</note> could by no means have been born from the trunk of the vena cava below the heart: first, because it would have been suspended far too dangerously, due to the immense gap visible from that seat of the vena cava all the way to the vertebrae; and then also because if the vein lacking a pair arose from there, the entire part of the back below the heart, and that seat where the beginning of this vein is now extended, would be left in need of veins; or Nature would have had to produce another vein again from the place where this one now originates, to provide nourishment to that seat of the back. Moreover, it could in no way have been born from opposite <gloss>k</gloss> the right auricle <note>The right atrium of the heart.</note>: because the vessels approaching the lung—namely, the venous artery <note>The pulmonary vein.</note>, the arterial vein <note>The pulmonary artery.</note>, and also the rough artery <note>The trachea.</note>—would have prevented it from being carried toward the back, unless it first crept either downward or upward for some distance and cleverly found a suitable place for its descent. Furthermore, if the vein lacking a partner were spread out from opposite the right auricle of the heart, it would also pass through the heart's covering <note>The pericardium.</note> by a unique opening, different than it does now. Thus, even from this, it shows abundantly how far from the heart it takes its beginning. Nor is there any reason to bring up the slant of the human back where it faces the heart to strengthen this opinion; although this slant is much greater in man than in quadrupeds or birds, it would be easy to conclude that the vein without a pair in man ought to be born from the cava even higher than in those animals, because in them a shorter duct is seen from opposite the right ear <note>atrium</note> to the back than in man—as is certainly not only pleasant to consider during dissection, but also obvious. However, as to why Galen felt so variously, and even more incorrectly, about the human vein lacking a pair (which he never saw beyond doubt) than about the vein of apes, I have touched upon it in that Letter where I taught that the axillary vein of the right elbow should be cut in a disease of the side <note>Pleurisy; Vesalius refers to his 1539 "Venesection Letter" regarding the controversy over which side to bleed.</note> (if indeed it matters from which side you divide the vein). For Galen studied how to devise some reason from somewhere to make Hippocrates' opinion more probable, in which he teaches that blood should not be let when the pain seeks the lower parts and those below the septum. As if Hippocrates had truly thought that nothing could be drawn out from the vein without a spouse <gloss>l</gloss> through phlebotomy <note>Bloodletting.</note>, or that it stood further away from the axillary vein <gloss>m</gloss> than that this or any other vein could be opened for its sake. Meanwhile, in afflictions of the lungs, heart, liver, stomach, spleen, and kidneys, not only Hippocrates but the entire chorus of physicians cuts the vein in the elbow. But since the recently mentioned Letter pursues these matters more at length with several other paradoxes, I shall next proceed to the distribution of the vena cava, but with the sequence of my discourse interrupted as little as possible.

<margin>The path of the cava to the throat, and its division there.</margin>
The vena cava, therefore, after it has separated the vein without a pair from itself, ascends straight toward the throat under the breastbone <gloss>n</gloss>, elegantly supported by the membranes that partition the thorax <note>The mediastinum.</note>, and possessing here in the throat a soft and glandular body spread about, which the Greeks call *thymon* <note>original: "θuμὸν"; the thymus gland.</note> and the Latins call by the common name of glands, *glandium* <gloss>o</gloss>. Moreover, that mass of glands is constructed in the highest seat of the thorax so that it might keep the very frequent distributions of vessels suspended here immune from all harm. For there the vena cava <gloss>p</gloss> is first split entirely into two remarkable trunks: and from the left trunk, just as from the right, a <gloss>q</gloss> large vein is brought forth, which, resting on the first rib of the thorax, after it has scattered several branches from itself, hastens under the collarbone into the armpit <gloss>r</gloss>.

# BOOK III OF THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>† These are marked with H and another L. Then both in figure 2 of book 6, B and C. x G, G.</margin>
<margin>The veins creeping downward under the bone of the chest.</margin>
Occasionally, you will observe this [branch] to be entirely absent, or to exist as thin as a spider's web; since the shorter intervals of those ribs receive enough nourishment from the vein itself which seeks the armpit <note>The axillary vein.</note> as it rests upon them, or sometimes from the offshoots of the vein lacking a pair <note>original: "uena pari carentis"; the azygos vein.</note> (and this is seen especially on the right side). From the front seat of that great division in the throat <note>The bifurcation of the superior vena cava into the brachiocephalic veins.</note>, two veins come forth; directed forward, they strive toward the higher part of the chest bone <note>original: "pectoris ossis"; the sternum.</note>. Following its sides, where the cartilages of the ribs are joined, they creep downward all the way to the upper parts of the abdomen, spreading out numerous offshoots. For in their progress, they distribute individual branches to the six or seven intervals of the upper ribs on each side, which terminate at the end of the bone of the ribs <note>The costochondral junction.</note>, where we said the branches of the vein lacking a pair cease.

Just as it was reported that offshoots from the branches of the vein lacking a pair fall outside the cavity of the chest to the muscles spread over the ribs, so also from the veins scattered at the intervals of the cartilages, noteworthy small branches are spread into the muscles resting upon the chest, and even into the breasts <note>original: "mamillas". Vesalius is describing the internal mammary or internal thoracic veins.</note> themselves—provided that these small shoots are derived from the veins extended along the chest bone.

<margin>y Figure 1 of book 5, k. Table 6 of the muscles, a. Where you will also see the straight muscle marked with f. z M. r.</margin>
Furthermore, what remains of the veins drawn down under the chest bone is distributed to the side of the sword-shaped cartilage <note>original: "mucronatæ cartilaginis"; the xiphoid process.</note> downward into the fleshy part of the straight muscles of the abdomen <note>original: "rectorum abdominis musculorū"; the rectus abdominis.</note>. For the veins, having slipped out of the cavity of the chest, are carried under the straight muscles all the way to the middle part of the abdomen, sending across certain small branches into the neighboring parts on both sides. The most prominent of these reaches the skin of the abdomen and, spread out obliquely according to the ends of the rib cartilages, ends in very slender veinlets as fine as hairs. Moreover, the more significant branches of the veins, extended under the straight muscles, terminate in several small shoots above the site of the navel; these, entwined in the substance of the straight muscles of the abdomen, face the ends and boundaries of those veins which, in the progress of this discourse, you will hear ascend from the bottom upward under the straight muscles <note>Vesalius is describing the anastomosis (joining) of the superior and inferior epigastric veins.</note>.

<margin>b from I.</margin>
I have observed the origin of these veins creeping under the chest bone to be most often led out from the front and middle part of the bifurcation in the throat. Sometimes, however, I have observed them born from the roots of the axillary veins, after those had receded somewhat from the middle of the throat toward the sides. Occasionally, I have seen one of them (especially the left) born from the axillary, and the other from the bifurcation itself; just as it also not infrequently happens that from the front seat of the vena cava, where it is divided into two notable trunks, a single vein is born which, led upward to the chest bone, is split into two veins, and extends one to the right side of the chest bone and the other to the left.

From these veins also, drawn down along the chest bone, the membranes dividing the cavity of the chest <note>The mediastinum.</note> receive their first small shoots. And then also from the [vena] cava, where it produces the veins just mentioned, they claim for themselves certain slender offshoots, extended along the entire length of the membranes, together with the nerves of the transverse septum <note>original: "septi transuersi"; the diaphragm. The "nerves" are the phrenic nerves.</note>. Furthermore, as I warned before, small branches come from the vein lacking a pair into the membranes partitioning the cavity of the chest, very much like the veins which entwine the adhering tunic of the eye <note>The conjunctiva.</note>.

Then, from the veins interwoven in these chest membranes, offshoots also reach into the envelope of the heart <note>The pericardium.</note>, where the membranes contain it.

<margin>Several branches scattered from the vein seeking the armpit, before it enters the arm.</margin>
Moreover, the <gloss>h</gloss> vein approaching the armpit <note>The axillary vein.</note>, before it proceeds out of the chest, not so far from its beginning, from its higher seat, produces a <gloss>i</gloss> somewhat large vein which, tending obliquely upward toward the back, is led to the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae. Ascending through the <gloss>k</gloss> holes specifically carved for them <note>The transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae.</note>, it scatters offshoots into the muscles attached nearest to the vertebrae. But besides those, in a certain order and as if joint by joint, it derives individual offshoots to each hole carved for the emergence of the nerves in the vertebrae of the neck, and to the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsaliq; medullæ". What remains of this vein proceeds into the skull <note>original: "caluariam"</note>, having its own opening for itself and its companion artery <note>The vertebral artery and vein complex.</note>, which is hollowed out at the back of the base of the occipital bone. However, when the vein reaches the expanse of the skull, it is emptied into the second or left sinus of the hard membrane of the brain <note>The dura mater; the "sinus" refers to the venous channels that drain blood from the brain.</note>, as you will hear more fully later. Besides this vein, another takes its origin from the one heading toward the armpit <note>The axillary vein.</note>, before it entirely leaves the cavity of the chest from its posterior region; this is distributed to the muscles attached to the lower vertebrae of the neck and the higher vertebrae of the chest, which serve the movements of the head, back, and chest.

As soon as the vein seeking the armpit has left the chest cavity between the first rib and the collarbone <note>The clavicle.</note>, and has pierced the muscle that is one of the second pair of muscles moving the back, it brings forth that vein which we shall call the humeral vein <note>Modern cephalic or brachial vein.</note>. Immediately, as it is led downward, it reaches the glands in the armpit <note>Axillary lymph nodes.</note> created by Nature for the firm distribution of vessels; it separates off branches from itself which I will now describe. First, it sends out single veins on each side: one to the front of the chest and the other to the back. The one extended forward is spread into the muscles belonging to the breastbone <note>The sternum.</note> and ribs, reaching the bone of the arm and the shoulder blade <note>The scapula.</note>; it also reaches the skin of the chest and the breasts in women with a very frequent series of branches. However, the vein proceeding backward is distributed in a manifold offspring into the muscles occupying the hollow seat of the shoulder blade and neighboring areas. Sometimes a large vein arises from the former vein approaching the chest, or sometimes from the trunk itself located in the armpit; this vein, extended downward along the side of the chest, is mostly consumed in the muscle <note>Likely the latissimus dorsi or serratus anterior.</note> by whose benefit we move the arm downward and toward the back. Besides these branches, the larger vein held in the armpit sends away small forks to the glands and membranes which preside over the distributions and bindings of the vessels there. In what order the remainder of the axillary vein runs out into the whole arm, I shall explain in a special chapter as soon as I have finished with the other offspring of the ascending part of the vena cava. Therefore, turning my discourse back to the throat, I shall approach the other branches of the trunks of that great division in the throat.

Thus the vena cava, in the manner I have described, is divided into two trunks before it transcends the top of the breastbone; and immediately after the division, the previously mentioned vein seeking the armpit obtains its beginning. What remains of that other trunk of the division, receding slightly from the middle of the throat where it previously rested, extends upward outside the chest; and as soon as it has surpassed the collarbone and the top of the breastbone, it is split into two unequal branches. For the internal one is thinner than the external one, and ascending along the side of the rough artery <note>original: "asperae arteriae"; the trachea.</note>, it shares several veinlets, as thin as hairs, with the rough artery and neighboring membranes. This internal one is considered the jugular; it is carried toward the brain with the carotid artery <note>original: "soporali arteria"; literally the "sleep-inducing artery," because ancient physicians noted that pressure on it caused unconsciousness.</note> of its side, and in its ascent, it distributes slender branches to the membranes binding the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>In Vesalius's system, the "sixth pair" corresponds to parts of the modern vagus, glossopharyngeal, and accessory nerves.</note> in the neck, and also the seventh pair of nerves in the throat, being joined with the carotid artery through its entire course all the way to the base of the skull. When it arrives there, it is split into two branches of unequal size; the larger one, led obliquely backward along the base of the skull, enters the skull together with a certain branch of the carotid artery, using a hole carved for the sake of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>The jugular foramen.</note>. In what order this branch is distributed in the cavity of the skull, I shall follow sufficiently in the description of the vessels of the brain; for now, it will be enough to lead the veins that reach there in discourse up to the cavity of the skull. When the branch, as we have said, extends toward the posterior parts along the base of the skull <note>original: "caluariæ basim"</note>,<sup>m</sup> an offshoot is led away reaching the higher position<sup>n</sup> of the muscles that occupy the anterior region of the cervical vertebrae and lie beneath the gullet <note>original: "stomachoq;"; in 16th-century anatomy, "stomachus" often referred to the esophagus or throat.</note>. But the more slender branch of the internal jugular, having completely left the "soporal" artery <note>The carotid artery, so named because pressure on it was thought to induce sleep or stupor.</note>,<sup>o</sup> enters the skull through its own private opening <note>foramen</note>, which is carved next to the opening common to the third and fourth pairs of cranial nerves. Before that branch reaches the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note> and is entirely submerged into the skull,<sup>p</sup> it gives off a not very significant offshoot to the organ of hearing, sending it through a certain transverse opening that is considered common to this offshoot and a small nerve of the fifth pair of cranial nerves. Furthermore,<sup>q</sup> the external and larger branch of the division made above the throat <note>iugulum</note>, from its outer side—after it has pierced one of the second pair of muscles moving the back<sup>r</sup> <sup>s</sup>—brings forth a significant vein according to Galen's opinion. This vein, turned downward toward the collarbone <note>clavicle</note>, stretches toward the top of the shoulder and the arm itself, and forms the vein named by us the humeral vein <note>The cephalic vein</note>.<sup>t</sup> However, because Aristotle had falsely taught that the origin of the humeral vein was under the ear, and because of the obscurity of the passages where Galen follows the course of the veins in the throat and neck, I have investigated the origin of the humeral vein more carefully than usual.<sup>u</sup> I have seen that this vein does not arise, as Galen believes, from the external jugular (or the larger branch I just began to describe), but rather from that vein which we wrote tends transversely above the first rib into the armpit <note>the axillary vein</note>. Indeed, this seemed consistent with reason, which testifies that it is more common for one trunk to proceed together for a distance than for two branches to run parallel and equidistant from each other. Now, the humeral vein arises from almost the middle of that vessel's course, which could be measured from the throat to the armpit. From here, the humeral vein seeks the arm transversely under the top of the shoulder,<sup>x</sup> while the other vein descends more obliquely into the armpit under the shoulder joint. Moreover, before the humeral vein enters the arm, not far from its origin,<sup>z</sup> it gives off a branch that is distributed in a numerous series of small veins into the skin covering the back of the neck and the external muscles of that area. In addition to this,<sup>a</sup> it produces another larger branch dispersed in frequent offshoots into the convex <note>gibbam</note> part of the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note>. Then, when it reaches the top of the shoulder<sup>b</sup> and creeps under it into the arm, before it is completely submerged, it derives offshoots into the skin of the top of the shoulder,<sup>c</sup> the most prominent of which are distributed into the skin<sup>d</sup> covering the muscle that lifts the arm <note>the deltoid</note>. Such offshoots sometimes, and especially in women, run out even to the skin of the breasts,<sup>e</sup> led downward in a wandering progress toward the front along the collarbone; before dissection, they are visible in many women with a somewhat greenish or blue color. By what course the rest of this vein approaching the arm is distributed, I shall say later, when I follow the distribution of it and the axillary vein in a specific chapter. Furthermore,<sup>f</sup> the larger branch, which we said is found above the collarbone and from whose outer side, according to Galen's view, the humeral vein buds,

We see a third way in which the exterior jugular, near the <term>clavicle</term><note>The collarbone</note>, is spread into two offshoots which are carried upward under the skin at a distance from one another. A fourth way is prepared from the third: for sometimes those offshoots remain permanently distant and nowhere touch each other; but occasionally they merge again at the lower part of the <term>fauces</term><note>The back of the throat or the "jaws" of the throat</note>, and one vein is formed from both, which soon splits into two, as I will describe below. However, another variation sometimes arises from the third series. For occasionally one of the offshoots—and not a small one—is not placed just under the skin, but is hidden <margin>h 4th muscle table. θ</margin> by the muscle that arises from the top of the breastbone and the collarbone and is inserted into the <term>mastoid process</term><note>original: "mamillari temporis ossis processui"; the bony bump behind the ear</note> of the temporal bone <note>This is the sternocleidomastoid muscle</note>. This offshoot, submerged in this manner, often appears so prominent that even some professors of dissection seem to have called it the "internal jugular," meanwhile neglecting <margin>i s.</margin> the one that extends along the side of the <term>trachea</term><note>original: "asperae arteriae"; literally the "rough artery," the standard Renaissance term for the windpipe</note>. However the exterior jugular ascends—whether as a single vessel on each side, or through a single path in the middle of the neck, or doubled immediately from the collarbones—it always offers notable and noteworthy small forks to the skin where it creeps forward. When it reaches the throat, near the lower seat of the mandible <margin>k v.</margin> beneath the region of the ears, <margin>l x.</margin> it transmits a <margin>m y.</margin> portion of itself to the interior of the mouth and the <term>dura mater</term><note>original: "duram cerebri membranam"; the tough outer membrane of the brain</note>. The rest of it is distributed into the skin of the face, its muscles, the temples, behind the ears, and briefly, into the entire skin of the head.

<margin>n x.</margin> The portion entering the interior of the mouth contains <margin>o 1st muscle table. A.</margin> glands <note>likely lymph nodes</note> placed between its first divisions; we shall number these as the third kind of glands residing in the throat in the sixth book. To these glands, which preside over the distributions of the vessels here, small branches are dispensed from the internal portion of the external jugular. Soon, noteworthy small forks are derived to the <term>larynx</term><note>The voice box</note>, and to the <margin>p 6th muscle table. L.</margin> glands attached closely to it, and to the muscles of the <term>hyoid bone</term><note>original: "ossis υ referetis"; the bone resembling the Greek letter upsilon (υ)</note>, and to the tongue, and generally to all parts of the throat. A prominent one of these creeps under the tongue along its length, split into <margin>q These are seen when the tongue is lifted.</margin> multiple branches that creep in a wandering series. Furthermore, from this portion of the jugular, besides the large branch that enters the skull through the <margin>r fig. ch. 14 E. & last fig. a. 5, 2, 3 fi. ch. 12 book 1. g.</margin> opening <note>foramen</note> hidden at the posterior part of the mastoid process, branches are also distributed to the palate and the membrane lining the cavity of the nostrils; from these, significant <margin>s under g, & last fig. u.</margin> offshoots later seek the skull. One indeed, entering the skull through the <margin>t fig. ch. 14 G, H.</margin> opening carved for the second pair of cranial nerves <note>The optic nerves in modern medicine, though Vesalius used a different numbering system</note>, runs out into the dura mater with several forks. Likewise, another offshoot is offered to the dura mater, entering the skull through a larger opening <margin>u 1, 3 fig. ch. 12 book 1 G.</margin> among those carved in the <term>eighth bone of the head</term><note>The ethmoid bone, associated with the sense of smell</note> for the sake of odors. These offshoots, when they enter the skull, grant certain small forks to the eye, which are sometimes disseminated into the skin of the forehead. <margin>x 3 fi. ch. 12 book 1. I.</margin> The exterior portion of the external jugular, creeping everywhere through the outer parts of the head, soon possesses glands presiding over its distributions as well; these are placed there beneath the ear, where the lower jaw articulates with the upper. <image-desc>Decorative initial V showing two cherubic figures or children playing with a large classical urn or vase.</image-desc>THAT TWO VEINS are propagated from the <term>cava</term><note>The vena cava, the primary large vein returning blood to the heart</note> into the arm was related previously, for which one and the same root existed from the throat all the way outside the thorax. ...the dissection of the branches ceases; nor, as Galen writes, is it so combined with any branch of the axillary vein <term>axillary vein</term><note>In Vesalius's terminology, the *axillaris* refers to the vein we now call the basilic vein in the arm, which becomes the axillary vein in the shoulder</note> that <gloss>h.</gloss> the principal branch of the humeral vein <term>humeral vein</term><note>The *humeraria*, known today as the cephalic vein</note>—which will be second in our description—is united with <gloss>p</gloss> a certain offshoot of the axillary vein under the skin at the bend of the elbow, as you will soon hear. For you will observe from diligent dissection that Galen described <gloss>q</gloss> the principal portion of the axillary vein, which is hidden deep between the muscles, with less than total accuracy. Likewise, he did not follow the course of this first branch of the humeral vein (if indeed it is ever seen, and if Nature, contrary to her usual craftsmanship, wished the veins to be extended from the skin to the deeper parts of the body, rather than from those deeper parts—as they are safer seats for the protection of vessels—toward the surface of the body and the skin), or in his imagination he fashioned a very unskillful arrangement for himself. Nevertheless, in the meantime, Galen described those veins quite elegantly and truly which frequently occurred to him in the bare arm without dissection (as happens in <term>venesection</term><note>The practice of bloodletting</note>). When he saw that these veins in the arm agreed with those in apes, he attempted to show with a long discourse how similar their bodies are to the human body, having no knowledge of any difference except what was obvious to everyone before dissection. Yet in the meantime, I have thus far proposed so many varied and innumerable differences in the bones, muscles, and also the veins, that I have persuaded myself in no common way that the human body was never actually attempted <note>i.e., dissected</note> by Galen.

From the external side of the axillary vein, <gloss>l</gloss> another offshoot of noteworthy size is spread out, descending obliquely downward under the humerus (or bone of the arm) all the way to <gloss>m</gloss> the external tuberosity of this bone, and hidden under <gloss>n</gloss> the muscles extending the elbow: providing certain small branches to the heads of the muscles arising from the external tuberosity of the humerus: and finally <gloss>o</gloss> for some distance...

<summary>Vesalius describes the branching of the humeral (cephalic) and axillary (basilic) veins in the arm, while providing a sharp critique of Galen for relying on ape anatomy rather than human dissection. He details the specific paths these veins take toward the elbow, wrist, and fingers, noting their relationship to the underlying musculature.</summary>

### THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK III.

<margin>p. 1, 3. fig. chapter 11, book 4. <note>original: "φ. q i n g e r." - likely a citation to Galen or an earlier figure.</note></margin>
...always hidden deeply for some distance, it creeps out to the external side of the elbow, together with the nerve which will be conveniently listed as the fourth among those traveling to the arm.

<margin>Book 3 of *Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>
The axillary vein <term>axillary vein</term><note>In Vesalius's time, the *vena axillaris* referred to what we now call the basilic vein as it travels through the arm.</note> gives off these branches while still lying hidden deep in the armpit, and is itself split into two trunks. I truly wish these to be examined most accurately, not only for the sake of Galen—whom this division of the axillary vein escaped, or who wrote that it occurred near the elbow and even at the end of the arm—but also because of those who think they have achieved something worthwhile in anatomy when, having attempted a dissection once or twice, they write that they noticed the humeral vein <term>humeral vein</term><note>The *vena humeraria*, known today as the cephalic vein.</note> being extended along with the axillary vein. In their drowsiness, they remove the humeral vein (which should have been well known even before dissection) from the arm along with the fleshy membrane, and later describe the other part of the axillary vein (which I will now follow) in place of the humeral vein.

<margin>r q. q. last figure f. f.</margin>

Thus, the human axillary vein, not far from its exit from the chest cavity into the armpit, is split into two roughly equal trunks. One of these, which is usually seen to be thicker, stays hidden deep throughout its entire course. It is constantly stretched alongside the artery extended into the arm, and is distributed in almost the same sequence of branching as that artery; it is also accompanied by the third of the nerves traveling to the arm <term>third nerve</term><note>In Vesalius's classification, this is the median nerve.</note>. For it is extended downward between the two muscles that flex the elbow toward the middle of the elbow joint's fold, spreading small branches to those muscles and then to the membranes with which the nerves are clothed.

When it has passed the elbow joint and begins to be carried between the muscles responsible for flexing the fingers, it is divided into two branches. These recede slightly from one another, entangling the muscles they creep through with offshoots, and seek the inner side of the hand together with the tendons. They are extended through the ligament <term>annular ligament</term><note>The flexor retinaculum at the wrist.</note> which is visible in the inner region of the wrist like a ring. There, the branches are divided into other offshoots and carried under the tendon which, spreading out, originates under the skin of the palm. From here, they are distributed into the inner side of the fingers such that two offshoots are offered to the thumb, two to the index finger, and one to the middle finger, coming from the branch extended through the forearm along the radius. From the other branch, however, which stays close to the ulna, two offshoots are provided to the ring finger and the pinky, and one to the middle finger. From that same branch, an offshoot goes to the muscles occupying the outer part of the palm, and likewise from the other branch, an offshoot reaches deeper into the muscles that originate at the first bone of the thumb.

The other axillary trunk emerges gradually from the depths to the skin of the inner side of the arm, hurrying toward the inner bump of the humerus <term>medial epicondyle</term><note>The bony protrusion on the inside of the elbow.</note>. Before dissection, it is visible below the middle of the arm's length, no less than the humeral vein is visible above the elbow. Where it rests almost upon the inner bump of the humerus, at the higher part of that bump, it is divided into two veins of almost equal size. The anterior one, situated under the skin (as are all the offshoots of this present trunk), creeps obliquely downward to the middle of the elbow joint's fold. It joins with the second branch of the humeral vein at the lower and middle part of that fold, and there a vein arises from both together, which we rightly call the "common vein" because it is constituted from the axillary and humeral veins. The common people, however, call it the "median vein" <term>median vein</term><note>original: "medianam". This is the median cubital vein, the most common site for drawing blood.</note>, even if the Greeks and the most prominent Latins called the branches that form this common vein "middle" as well as "oblique." Meanwhile, Galen, in the first book of *The Method of Healing, to Glaucon*, seems to call "middle" the one he elsewhere names "common."
