# ANDREAS VESALII ON THE FABRIC [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

That branch, just as was described before, is directed toward the outer part of the hand. Sometimes, however, when that branch of the <term>humeral vein</term><note>The *vena humeraria*, known today as the cephalic vein.</note> is missing, the offspring of the <margin>n</margin> <term>axillary vein</term><note>The *vena axillaris*, known today as the basilic vein.</note> abundantly takes the place of that branch in the hand. Furthermore, of the branches of that posterior trunk of the axillary vein which lies under the skin, another not to be neglected <margin>o y.</margin> goes to the skin where the posterior part of the elbow joint is covered; although it does not crawl very far into the external part of the forearm. In addition, other branches worthy of note are distributed from this posterior vein into the skin of the <margin>p lower z.</margin> internal part of the forearm; these, by a varied and quite uncertain entanglement, are sometimes mixed and joined together, and sometimes again led away from each other, <margin>q x, x.</margin> taking offshoots from that primary branch which I said was extended to the ulna, and in turn sharing other offshoots with it. With these offshoots and branches crawling through the inner parts of the forearm in this manner, another <margin>r upper z.</margin> very frequent and not to be despised addition occurs, which the <margin>s t.</margin> branch of the axillary vein—forming the <term>common vein</term><note>The *vena communis*, known today as the median cubital vein, a primary site for drawing blood.</note> with the branch of the humeral vein—sends out from a lower position and from the middle of its progress. This branch sometimes heads straight, and sometimes by a wandering path, toward the <term>brachiale</term><note>The wrist or carpus.</note>, and is mixed with other offshoots of this region. These are so slender and so variously entangled with one another that the internal region of the forearm is no less frequently troubled by <term>varices</term><note>Varicose veins.</note> than the calf of the leg (the *sura*), and here it displays something not unlike the image of a net. These branches are by no means terminated at the wrist: but partly obliquely, partly straight, and partly transversely—sometimes mixed together and sometimes separated again—they crawl through the entire internal skin of the hand, being joined to the skin itself everywhere. Furthermore, of these branches which approach the root of the thumb, or the <margin>t d, u g.</margin> **Mount of Venus**, or as it has seemed to others, the **Mount of Mars** <note>Vesalius refers to the fleshy pads of the palm using the names of planets/gods from chiromancy (palmistry) to help readers identify the locations.</note>, they specifically claim for themselves that a branch is mixed into them from those veins which I am about to say spread from the common vein into the external region of the thumb.

<margin>The path of the common vein.</margin> <margin>x u. y t, h.</margin> For the **common vein**, as soon as it is formed from those two branches of the axillary and humeral veins, is led obliquely downward, gradually heading toward the higher part of the forearm, until it crosses the radius a little beyond the middle of its length on both sides. It does not always do this in the same way, spreading small branches in its progress, and sometimes taking others from the offshoots crawling under the skin of the internal part of the forearm which join with it, until it finally reaches the external part of the forearm. <margin>z l. a n.</margin> Therefore, where the common vein reaches that place, above the radius and a little before its joint with the wrist, it is split into two branches and shows a division which you might not inaptly compare to the Greek letters <term>γ</term> (gamma), or **Y**, or <term>Λ</term> (lambda), but not to <term>Γ</term> (capital gamma). <margin>b y. c d. d g.</margin> One branch of this division, which is higher, distributes a small portion to the internal side of the wrist toward the root of the thumb, which is mixed with the offshoots recently said to crawl through this place. What remains of the higher branch creeps upward externally between the thumb and the index finger; and here it is dispersed into various offspring, now united together, now separated again. <margin>e u.</margin> The other branch, which constitutes the lower head of the **γ** or **Y**, seeking the area of the index finger, middle finger, and to some extent the ring finger, is also exhausted into various offspring.

<margin>The series of veins entangling the varied skin of the hand.</margin> Indeed, this series of veins in the skin of the hand is so varied and conflicting that it is altogether difficult to explain, especially since among very many men, you will scarcely find two with an equal and corresponding distribution of veins into branches. Add to this that the right hand of the same man very rarely agrees with the left. It would be worthwhile, therefore, to learn the branches of the veins in the hand not from here, but from dissection, and before the preparation, in arms intercepted by a bandage when we divide the vein. One should consider with precision how much our—if it please the gods—**Aesculapians** <note>A sarcastic reference to physicians of his time, named after Aesculapius, the god of medicine.</note> hallucinate in the cutting of veins, ridiculously contending whether the humeral, the common, or the axillary vein is to be divided in the hand, thinking that they are opening the humeral vein whenever they cut the vein between the thumb and index...

As soon as the cava descends to the top of the <term>sacrum</term><note>Latin: "os sacrum" or "holy bone," the large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>, it yields to the large artery (which was previously positioned to its left) as if to a more noble organ, and places itself underneath the artery. For the left trunk, just like the right, right at the point of division—or rather where the cava splits into two trunks above the sacrum—sends out from its outer side a vein larger than those we described as being distributed to the lumbar vertebrae, the abdominal muscles, and others connected there to the back.

This vein sometimes takes its origin even higher up, before the division of the cava above the sacrum; it is laid across the flesh of the loins, dispersing small branches to them and to the <term>peritoneum</term><note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note> and abdominal muscles. This is much more visible in dogs than in humans. After the left trunk has branched off this vein, it is carried obliquely downward toward the outer parts, forming with the right trunk a shape not unlike the Greek letter Lambda (Λ) or an inverted Y in this manner ⅄, and offering several small forks to the upper openings of the sacrum. Then, shortly in its progress, it splits into two unequal branches: for the inner one is more slender than the outer. Soon it produces two offshoots, which I have been accustomed to call the "inner" and the "outer" for the sake of clearer instruction. Thus, the entire outer offshoot creeps transversely outward between the sacrum and the hip bone, where the largest of the nerves heading for the leg <note>the sciatic nerve</note> is led. It is distributed in a numerous series of branches into all the muscles arising from the outer surface of the ilium <note>the flank bone</note> that serve the movements of the thigh, also spreading small forks downward into the muscles that take their origin from the lower part of the hip bone. In this way, the posterior part of the hip joint where it meets the femur, and the skin of the buttocks, borrow their veins from this outer offshoot.

The inner offshoot, however, distributes small branches from its inner side to the openings of the sacrum as well; it also directs larger branches into the muscles of the rectum and the skin of the anus, which purge foul blood through here, if ever it should flow down here through the vena cava and collect there. Next, this inner offshoot sends out a noteworthy branch, which in men embraces the right side of the bladder; split into many small forks, it reaches the neck of the bladder or the penis, and is distributed into it in great number, always in such a pattern that thicker and larger forks are extended to the neck of the bladder than to its base. In women, however, the present branch, led down from the inner offshoot, is supported by a fatty membrane. With some small branches it reaches the bladder, but more frequently it runs through the lower part of the base of the uterus, also dispersing visible branches into the neck of the uterus <note>the cervix</note>. Through these, physicians have hitherto believed that the menstrual purgings of virgins flow down; they imagine for themselves a certain body in young girls—the <term>hymen</term><note>Vesalius is critiquing the traditional medical view of the hymen as a solid, impermeable barrier that necessitates menstruation through specific veins rather than through the cervical canal.</note>—which is not permeable and stands in the way, so that nothing can flow from the base of the uterus through its neck. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

...looking toward the mouth of the uterus <note>the cervix</note> or the vulva <note>original: "pudendum"</note>. Otherwise, in women who have a torn or destroyed hymen through sexual intercourse or other rough contact, the blood would trickle down from the base <note>fundus</note> of the uterus or from the veins located above the hymen. Indeed, if doctors were acquainted with the structure or nature of the hymen—which we shall rightfully examine in the fifth book along with the description of the uterus—they would by no means contend that virgins emit menstrual blood from different veins than other women. Since the hymen, resembling a fleshy membrane placed crosswise in the neck of the uterus, is pierced by a long-shaped opening, it allows that blood to pass through easily. This is just as with that "white discharge," not unlike an involuntary flow of seed <note>semen</note>, which Aristotle most truly taught sometimes occurs even in very young girls. However, just as doctors have not grasped the construction of the hymen, so too some of the Arabs <margin>The veins from which it is falsely believed menstrual purgings flow in virgins.</margin> have written incorrectly that five small veins in number are spread into the middle of the length of the uterine neck, and that the mouths of the right veins join and combine with the mouths of the left, and that the hymen of girls is formed by them; they call this abundance of veins reaching this area the *centone* <note>original: "centonem"; a Latin term for a patchwork garment, here used to describe a "patchwork" of vessels.</note>.

Regarding what remains of the inner left branch of the trunk (the division made above the <term>sacrum</term><note>The large, triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>) after the two offshoots already mentioned, it hurries toward the pubic bone. It receives a descendant from the external branch of the <term>vena cava</term><note>The "hollow vein," the body's largest vein returning blood to the heart.</note> trunk, which, joining with that remainder of the internal branch, forms a single vein with it. This vein first perforates the <term>peritoneum</term><note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note> and then the tenth muscle of those moving the thigh <note>the femur</note>. Passing through the opening <note>foramen</note> of the pubic bone, it claims for itself a particular hollow in the higher part of that opening, where it travels together with its "spouse" artery and likewise a nerve. Passing through the membrane of that opening and the ninth muscle of those moving the thigh, it offers branches to those muscles through which it creeps. When it extends into the leg, it is distributed in several branches into the higher part of the second muscle moving the shin <note>tibia</note>, and into the part of the fifth muscle moving the thigh that arises from the pubic bone, and later into the eighth muscle acting on the thigh and the muscles of the penis. From these, offshoots—too thin to name—emerge into the skin of the inner part of the thigh in the region of the groin. In addition to these branches, one also reaches the hip joint, specifically entering the socket <note>acetabulum</note> of the hip bone through its own hollow. However manifold this vein is distributed as it slips down into the leg, it only slightly passes the middle of the length of the thigh; sometimes its principal branch, dispensed to the fifth muscle moving the thigh, is mixed with the offshoot belonging here that is led down into the leg from the larger vein.

The external branch of the trunk of the vena cava (from the division made above the sacrum), as it approaches the leg obliquely and before it perforates the peritoneum, brings forth from its higher side a vein of moderate size. This is led upward to the front parts of the abdomen through the peritoneum and communicates certain small branches to it on both sides. Where it is connected to the peritoneum in this manner, it climbs to the <term>rectus abdominis</term><note>The "six-pack" muscle running vertically at the front of the abdomen.</note> muscle, passing through the peritoneum. It is inserted into the internal or posterior part of the rectus muscle and distributes various offshoots on both sides into the transverse abdominal muscle, the oblique muscles resting upon it, and the other nearby areas, extending in a straight path upward under the rectus muscle. When it has crept to the middle of the abdomen, a little above the region of the navel <note>umbilicus</note>, its end is spread into many small forks. These look toward the small branches which we mentioned are spread from the vein brought down under the breastbone <note>sternum</note> from the higher part of the chest <note>thorax</note>. Through the intervention of this vein, it is commonly believed that a "communion and fellowship" exists between the breasts <note>mamillae</note> and the uterus. Indeed, it is equally accepted by doctors that by its benefit, a retraction of blood occurs from the veins of the breasts into the uterus when the fetus is being nourished; and when the woman is nursing, a "revulsion" <note>a pulling back or redirection</note> of menstrual blood occurs from the veins of the uterus into the veins of the breasts.

For the outer branch of the left trunk of the vena cava <note>the "hollow vein," the body's largest vein</note>, which we are now describing, when it passes through the peritoneum and falls forward over the hip bone into the thigh, it puts forth another vein from its inner region. This vein approaches the middle of the pubic bones, where they are joined together by the intervention of cartilage; in men, it is distributed into the covering of the penis and the scrotum, while in women, it is spread through a numerous series of branches into the "little hills" of the genitals <note>referring to the labia majora or mons pubis</note>, and into the leathery fleshy bits (which they call *nymphae* <note>Greek original: νυμϕὰς; refers to the labia minora</note>) and the neighboring seats. Furthermore, the remainder of that branch of the left trunk, which is distributed into the leg by a copious series of layers, we shall now pursue in a specific Chapter, thereby completing the entire distribution of the vena cava.

<margin>How many roots of the veins seek the thigh.</margin>
<margin>The path of the larger vein of the thigh.</margin>

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'P' depicting two figures, possibly surgeons or anatomists, in a landscape setting with one attending to the leg of another who is seated.</image-desc>

Besides the branch of the vena cava that extends for some distance into the thigh along the back part of the hip bone, two veins descend to the leg. One is indeed more slender; we have already recounted how it creeps through the opening <note>the obturator foramen</note> of the pubic bone to certain muscles embracing the inner parts of the thigh, and ceases at the middle of the thigh's length. The other, however, is thicker and is the trunk of the other veins running out into the leg. It hangs from the external branch of the other trunk of the vena cava, where the division is made above the sacrum <note>the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>. As soon as it slips out from the peritoneum, it is carried into the groin through the upper region of the hip bone, toward the inner side of the place where the sixth and seventh muscles moving the thigh descend. It enters the front region of the thigh (though more toward the inner side) and, hidden by no muscle, it sits in a hollow or cavity formed in the groin by the long and slender muscle (the first of those moving the lower leg) and the eighth muscle responsible for the movements of the thigh.

Therefore, the vein lying in this cavity is split into several branches. So that it might be rendered less liable to injuries, Nature placed frequent glands here around its first distributions (just as in the armpits and under the ears). These glands provide a firm and stable propagation for the vein, filling the cavity we mentioned along with the vein, artery, and nerve descending here, and acting as a sort of bulwark for these vessels. The first notable offspring of this vein takes its beginning from its inner side and hastens to the skin covering the inner parts of the thigh. It is extended downward under the skin through the inner parts of the knee, and from there again through the internal region of the tibia toward the inner ankle <term>malleolus<gloss>the bony prominence on either side of the human ankle</gloss></term>. Finally, descending into the upper parts of the foot, it is variously distributed there, mixed with other small forks of veins belonging to this area. This branch, where it is stretched out at the inner ankle, does not always keep the same path; for sometimes it runs from the inner side of the tibia along the front region of the ankle to the upper parts of the foot. Sometimes, however (though more rarely), it is twisted under the ankle, climbing from there to the upper parts of the foot. Furthermore, it varies greatly in the series of branches to the toes and above the metatarsus <note>original: "pedion"</note>. For sometimes, being mixed here with certain other branches, it is led especially to the little toe and the one next to it; but sometimes it runs toward the big toe and the second toe. Briefly, in the same man, you will hardly ever find an equal series of the branches of this offspring in both feet. The branches which it produces in its descent...

A branch arises from the posterior, almost inner side of the trunk. As soon as it begins to be hidden between the muscles that move the <note>original: "x"</note> fourth and fifth toes, and those that move the <note>original: "y, z"</note> second and third toes, it reaches that region <note>original: "a"</note> where the <term>fibula|the smaller, outer bone of the lower leg</term> first separates from the <term>tibia|the shin bone</term>. It offers small branches to the <note>original: "g"</note> muscular substance to which we assign the task of moving the big toe and the three closest toes toward the outer side. In this part, it is attached to the ligaments of the bones and nowhere goes beneath the skin. As for what remains <note>original: "i"</note> of the inner trunk descending behind the tibia, it is distributed among the muscles in this area. Along with their tendons, it passes between the heel and the inner <term>malleolus|the bony protrusion of the ankle</term> toward the lower parts of the foot. It distributes small offshoots into the neighboring areas, creeping between the <note>original: "k"</note> muscle that flexes the second joints of the four toes and the <note>original: "l"</note> tendons by which the final joints of the toes are flexed. Thus, the remainder of the trunk belonging here is consumed in many small branches in a series, of which nearly two creep along the underside of each toe.

<margin>
Galen's descriptions of the path of the vena cava through the leg are varied and not very true.
</margin>
We have learned through diligent dissection that the <term>vena cava|the great hollow vein</term> is distributed into the leg in roughly this sequence. However, those who compare our history with the third book of Galen's *On Anatomical Procedures* and his book *On the Dissection of Veins and Arteries* will understand how much our account agrees with his—provided they do not read carelessly. They will see how beautifully Galen agrees with himself in those two books, wandering significantly and in more than one place from the true description of the veins of the human body. It would be a long task to recount those conflicting passages here, especially since the physicians of our age read hardly anything except summaries. Meanwhile, they argue at length about the superficial veins reaching the foot—if they ever think one of them should be opened <note>for bloodletting</note>—as if those veins did not eventually derive from a single trunk entering the groin, but were instead unique, disconnected streams led from private organs or specific areas of the body's trunk.

<margin>
At the end of the treatise on veins, in the book on the dissection of veins and arteries.
</margin>
<margin>
m Since physicians are so inconsistent, I can hardly indicate the veins they proposed in the figure.
</margin>
For when they read in Galen <note>original: "m"</note> that four veins belong to the upper part of the foot, they attribute the same number of veins to the foot, assigning to each a unique and proper duty for drawing out blood. They establish the first as the one that creeps along the inner ankle, which they call the *Saphena*, the "womb vein," or the "virginal vein." They assign the second to the outer ankle, calling it the *Schiatica*. They count a third in the upper part of the foot, drawn from some small branch of the veins extending to the big toe, and they give it the name *Popletica* vein. They call the fourth the *Renalis* <note>kidney vein</note>, fashioning it from certain small branches closest to the little toe. Yet, in the meantime, they neglect the veins in the <term>popliteal|the area behind the knee</term> and under the knee, which are more suitable for bloodletting than the veins of the foot, just as they neglect all those hidden deep in the body. I will carefully recount how the series of the vena cava is to be learned through dissection at the end of the fifth, sixth, and seventh books, where the management of those parts which the offshoots of the vena cava entwine and creep through will be described.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring cherubs/putti performing an anatomical dissection or related medical task.</image-desc>
In the history of the veins, professors of dissection give the name "umbilical vein" to that which is gathered from various veins seeking the base of the uterus; <note>original: "fundum uteri"</note> eventually entering through the <term>umbilicus|the navel or belly button</term> of the fetus, it extends primarily into the liver, carrying blood for the nourishment of the fetus just as the mother's other veins communicate blood to the parts they creep through. Since this vein is thought to be a peculiar thing, and in some way distinct from the bodies of the <margin>b ch. 6, f.</margin> <margin>c ch. 5, fi.</margin> **vena cava** <note>the main vein returning blood to the heart</note> and the **portal vein**; <note>the vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note> and since after birth, whatever remains of it in the body becomes dry, bloodless, and like a solid <margin>d ch. 12, fig.; and Book 5, fig. 2, K, L.</margin> little cord: <note>original: "funiculi"</note> I believe I will not act out of place if I pursue its history in a private chapter, even if only in passing. Because it must have something in common with the <margin>e ch. 15, fig. 1.</margin> umbilical arteries—which are only useful to the fetus while it is carried in the womb—I would have surely <margin>f ch. 15, fig. 2.</margin> saved this for the end of the present book and added it to the chapter dedicated to the <margin>g Book 5, fig. 27, A, A, B, B.</margin> arterial vein and the venal artery, <note>Vesalius uses these terms for the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, following the nomenclature of his time</note> were it not easier to describe the umbilical arteries alongside the branches of the **great artery** <note>the aorta</note>, since they can be considered entirely as its offshoots. Wherever you may transpose this chapter, it was <margin>Where the beginning of the umbilical vein arises, and its sequence.</margin> <margin>h Book 5, fig. 30 panels, E, E. and panel 2, K, K.</margin> certainly necessary for the fetus, so long as it remains in the womb, to be nourished by the mother's veins and tempered by the heat of her arteries, just as we know a leg or an arm of the mother enjoys its own veins and arteries. Therefore, when the seed of both male and female <margin>i Book 5, fig. 30 panel 1, E, E. and panel 2, I, I, I, I.</margin> is received into the <margin>k Book 5, fig. 31, A, A, and fig. 32, A, A, A.</margin> chamber of the uterus and first assumes a complete formation within itself, a <margin>l Book 5, fig. 30 panel 1, E, E, E. and panel 2, 1, 1, 1, 1.</margin> small membrane <note>original: "membranula", referring here to the chorion</note> is generated by it. This membrane surrounds the seed like a thickening and cooling broth and grows more firmly to some part of the uterus through a new intervention of <margin>m Book 5, fig. 31, A, A, and fig. 32, B, B, B.</margin> vessels. For the veins and arteries of the uterus open themselves in the region of this connection, and immediately become one with the vessels assuming form in that membrane. At first, these are as many in number as the mouths of the vessels then opening into the uterus and are continued with those new vessels; so much so, that here we must almost establish the beginning of what we call the <margin>n Book 5, fig. 25, I & Y.</margin> umbilical vein. From many more slender offshoots, thicker and fewer branches always arise in such a way that finally they are all heaped together into two veins, as it were, which, proceeding from the outer covering of the fetus, <margin>p Book 5, fig. 30 panel 3, O, O. and panel 4, V, V, X, X.</margin> penetrate the inner covering. After they have offered small branches scattered through its breadth (whatever <margin>q Book 5, fig. 30 panel 4, Y, Y.</margin> Galen may incorrectly think about this matter), they soon unite in a human being into one vein. This vein finally hastens to the umbilicus of the fetus in a long <margin>r Book 5, fig. 12, G between H, H.</margin> course, like a rope or cord, accompanied by two arteries and a <margin>s Book 5, fig. 12, N; fig. 20, G.</margin> passage <note>the urachus</note> by which the urine of the fetus is purged, and strengthened as if by a common body. After entering through the umbilicus, the vein departs from the arteries and that passage; and being attached to the front part of the <term>peritoneum|the lining of the abdominal cavity</term> on its internal surface, it stretches toward the liver. It is carried into the liver, in <margin>t Book 5, fig. 20, I.</margin> humans, through its own peculiar cleft and then a hole, reaching all the way to its hollow part where the trunk of the **portal vein** <note>original: "portæ uenæ"</note> falls out of the liver. ## WHERE THE GREAT ARTERY TAKES
### its beginning, and into which branches its ascending part is distributed. Chapter XII.

*Whenever it is written anywhere in the inner margin "figure of chapter 12," it should be understood as the one in which we proposed the complete series of the great artery before the present Chapter.*

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'L' showing several figures in classical attire, possibly medical students or philosophers, gathered in discussion or observation.</image-desc>
<margin>
$\Delta$ The entire figure placed before this chapter.
</margin>
<margin>
That the dispute over the origin of the great artery is not lengthy.
</margin>
There is far less disagreement among the leading physicians and philosophers regarding the origin of the $^a$ great artery <note>the aorta</note> than there is about the origins of the veins and nerves. For Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, and Galen alike establish the heart as the fount and origin of the arteries (as it truly is). And the opinion of Pelops, Galen’s teacher, is entirely false, teaching that the arteries and veins, together with the nerves, are born from the brain—a view he almost passed down from that author.
<margin>
Arteries are born neither from the brain nor from the outermost parts of the body.
</margin>
Since, to remain silent on other matters, the brain is not the principle of the vital spirit and of the fervent blood rushing with force through the body, as the heart is;
<margin>
b A and figure 10 of book 6, A.
</margin>
and the artery is nowhere found to be larger than $^b$ where it first arises from the heart. Furthermore, this also disproves the dogma of those who think that arteries arise everywhere from the outermost and highest parts of the body, just as if someone were to reckon the beginning of trees from the tips of their smallest twigs. However, even if the leaders of philosophy and medicine have established the heart as the fount of the arteries, they nevertheless disagree somewhat among themselves concerning the cavity <note>original: "sinu"; meaning the ventricle</note> of the heart from which the great artery arises; for some contend it arises from the middle cavity of the heart, while others say it arises from the left.

...membrane, placed over the orifice of the venous artery <note>The "venous artery" refers to the pulmonary vein</note>, Aristotle placed a third sinus or "ventricle" of the heart, as if it were a peculiar cavity distinct from the rest of the volume of the left chamber. For I can by no means agree with Galen in his book *On the Dissection of Veins and Arteries*, when he refers this third sinus of the heart (to which Aristotle attributed the origin of the arteries) to the right ventricle of the heart, and asserts it to be a portion of that, and not—as I do now—a portion of the left. Therefore, the great artery—which Aristotle called the <term>aorta</term> <note>original: "ἀορτὴν"</note>, perhaps because the Macedonians called a certain scabbard or sheath by that name, and he said its fibrous part could be seen even in the dead— <margin>f A. at figure 10, book 6, S, S.</margin> ᶠ is circular at this origin; and here its seat is at its widest, and is composed of a substance that is harder and <margin>Coronary arteries.</margin> more like cartilage. This is primarily in that part of the heart which contains the left chamber, and where the septum <note>The dividing wall between the heart's chambers</note> common to both chambers extends. The origin of the coronary arteries is located behind the membranes <note>the heart valves</note> which we believe prevent the return of spirit and blood from the artery itself back into the left chamber of the heart. However, although the size of both coronary arteries is somewhat equal, the one that takes its origin from the right side of the orifice of the great artery is seen to be larger and longer. For one arises here from the back of the right membrane, while the other claims its beginning from the posterior seat of the artery, namely from the back of the posterior membrane; <margin>i figure 10, book 6, D.</margin> ⁱ meanwhile, no coronary artery arises from the back of the left membrane (if I may call it that), or from the left side of the arterial orifice.

This offshoot runs under the <margin>k</margin> tendons that extend the thumb toward the outer side of the hand, and is distributed into the <margin>l</margin> muscles located between the first bone of the thumb and the bone of the <term>post-brachial</term> <note>The metacarpal</note> supporting the index finger. However, in the meantime, it dispenses no offshoot to the outer side of the hand, although <margin>s</margin> it provides one to those muscles occupying the outer side of the metacarpal bone that supports the little finger. We do not clearly perceive the movement of the branch extended to the ulna <note>The ulnar artery</note> unless the person is very thin and lean, or endowed with a strong pulse. Indeed, Nature—as she does with almost all arteries—keeps this branch deep, more hidden by tendons than the one extended along the radius. Thus, Nature nowhere sends a portion of them conspicuously into the skin, just as it was previously mentioned that offshoots from the veins are carried everywhere and frequently. Rightly, therefore, you will find no other artery on the outer side of the hand than the one <margin>u</margin> recently mentioned, which we assigned to the thumb and index finger. is so named <note>The text here concludes the naming of the carotid artery, or "arteria soporalis," so called because ancient physicians believed compressing it caused sleep or stupor</note>. When the artery of the left side (just like the right) reaches as far as the throat, it is split into two branches. The larger and lower of these enters the throat; soon, after deriving offshoots for the larynx and the tongue, it hastens to the base of the skull. But before it is immersed into the skull, it is divided into two unequal offshoots. <margin>The path of the carotid arteries to the skull.</margin> The larger one enters the skull through its own particular hole <note>The carotid canal</note>, unaccompanied by any vein, at the point where the gland that receives the brain's phlegm <note>The pituitary gland</note> is placed in a certain cavity of the bone that resembles a wedge <note>The sphenoid bone</note>. This offshoot, immediately at its entry, sends out individual shoots on both sides: it dispenses one through its own hole to the cavity of the nostrils, which, at its far end among the cartilages of the nose—and indeed even to the very tip of the nose—is lost among several small arteries of the face, such that by touch we can perceive its motion there. 

The other offshoot of that larger branch is divided many times into the left side of the <term>dura mater</term> <note>The tough outer membrane surrounding the brain</note>. The main offshoot itself, having now entered the cavity of the skull, divides in two; supported by the base of the skull, it creeps forward slightly for a time until it is gathered together again. From then on, it is carried along, no longer divided or gathered, but entirely simple. However it may be—whether it reaches this point simple or previously divided into two parts and here gathered again—it distributes a notable branch through the hole of the second pair of brain nerves <note>The optic canal</note> to the eye and the inner seat of the temporal muscle. What remains of it perforates the dura mater; it ascends partly into the thin membrane of the brain <note>The pia mater</note> and partly to the left ventricle of the brain, forming a plexus there. We shall compare this plexus to the <term>secundines</term> <note>The afterbirth or placental membranes</note>, and especially to the outer covering of the fetus, when we follow the series of the brain's vessels in the second chapter after this one; there we shall also explain what we have just mentioned a little more diffusely. 

The other offshoot of the thicker internal branch of that division, which the carotid artery <note>original: "soporalis arteria"</note> produces in the throat, is carried toward the back along the base of the skull with a companion vein. it offers a small branch to the muscles of the neck occupying the front seat of the vertebrae, near the interval between the first and second vertebrae, and then enters the skull. Having found a common hole with the sixth pair of brain nerves, it is exhausted along with the vein into the left, or second, sinus of the dura mater. Furthermore, the outer and thinner branch of the aforementioned division in the throat offers an offshoot to the cheeks, hiding deep within. Moreover, having been cut into two offshoots, it distributes one to the left temple and the other along the back of the left ear; these also produce a sensible pulse. And in this very manner, the ascending part of the artery ends in branches.

...carved into the vertebrae for the sake of the nerves, and then they are scattered to the muscles attached to the vertebrae and the thorax, in exactly the same order in which I previously explained the "vein without a partner" <note>original: "uenam coniugis expertem"; refers to the azygos vein</note> is distributed. The trunk of the great artery <note>The aorta</note> itself, leaning somewhat against the left side of the bodies of the vertebrae,^e^ slips down under the diaphragm^f^ <note>original: "septum transuersum"</note> at the point where it faces the body of the eleventh thoracic vertebra, passing out of the cavity of the thorax. Immediately on both sides, it offers one offshoot^g^ to the diaphragm, which, divided into many small twigs, is primarily consumed in the lower part of the diaphragm near the vertebrae, while it scatters small offspring upward to the higher parts of the diaphragm and even to the heart’s own envelope <note>The pericardium</note>,^h^ where it is attached to the diaphragm. 

After these mentioned offshoots, the great artery brings forth one trunk from the higher part of its body, which offers branches to the stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, omentum, and the duodenum, and also the colon where it is extended toward the stomach, in the following manner.^i^ As soon as this present trunk emerges, it is supported by the higher part of the lower membrane of the omentum. It is divided into two branches nearly equal in size; it sends the one which is a little thinner to the right,^k^ and that which is seen to be moderately larger to the left.^l^ The right branch is attached to the glandular body <note>The pancreas</note> which is seen interwoven in this membrane of the omentum under the back part of the stomach; it hastens upward toward the hollow of the liver <note>The porta hepatis</note>, offering in the middle of its path a twig from its lower part to the lower membrane of the omentum and to the colon itself here. 

After this, it extends an offspring to the stomach from its higher part, which is distributed into its posterior side where it faces the back in a few small branches.^m^ From the lower side again,^n^ the right branch of the artery, tending toward the hollow of the liver, produces two more offspring.^o^ One it distributes with the branch of the portal vein to the intestine which we call the duodenum,^p^ along the middle length of which it is extended even to the beginning of the fasting intestine <note>The jejunum</note>.^q^ The other offspring, slightly larger than the one just mentioned,^r^ is turned back toward the right side of the bottom of the stomach; being attached to the upper membrane of the omentum, it scatters branches in a frequent series from its higher side into the front and back parts of the bottom of the stomach, just as it leads others from its lower side into the upper membrane of the omentum. And this offspring of the artery,^s^ together with the branch of the portal vein extended here, ends at the middle of the bottom of the stomach. 

What remains of the right branch of the artery, after it has transmitted two remarkably thin twigs to the gallbladder,^t^ is divided into several branches^u^ and terminates at the hollow of the liver,^x^ not running very deep into the substance of the liver. The left branch,^y^ which we said was moderately thicker than the right, is also committed to the lower membrane of the omentum and its glandular body, and joins itself to the branch of the portal vein running out this way,^z^ to be divided into as many offspring as that vein. For soon this present branch of the artery offers from its higher side a shoot to the stomach^a^ where it leans on the back; this first extends one offspring on each side into the middle part of the stomach in that region which lies against the back.^b^ Then ascending upward, in the manner of the portal vein, it most fitly encircles the upper orifice of the stomach like a crown,^c^ distributing small branches to the body of the stomach and slender twigs to the end of the "stomach" <note>In this context, the esophagus</note>,^d^ where it is continued with the [actual] stomach. 

Among the remaining small branches, however, one extended to the right according to the upper parts of the stomach^e^ approaches the lower orifice of the stomach, also bringing forth twigs in its progress to the front and back parts of the stomach.^f^ Then the left branch, hastening to the spleen,^g^ diffuses an offshoot from its lower side into the lower membrane of the omentum, which shortly after its origin is split into two branches widely separated from each other, propagating a numerous offspring of arteries downward into the aforementioned membrane of the omentum and the colon. <margin>g P, P.</margin>
reaches the beginning [of the sacrum bone], it is placed over the vein <note>The vena cava</note>, and at <gloss>g</gloss> it is divided into two large trunks like an inverted Y, in this manner: λ. This change in position occurs because of the "dignity" of the artery: for since the artery is considered worthier and more noble, it was appropriate for it to be more hidden and concealed, carried deep within the body, and made resistant to bearing injuries. Indeed, lest it be easily damaged here at the start of the fleshless sacrum bone during the movements of the back, everyone is persuaded that the artery, which was previously placed below, should here be superior to the vein and should climb over it. This is done so that the vein might be placed beneath the artery like a kind of small cushion or bolster. <gloss>h</gloss> Hence also, before the veins descend into the leg with the arteries—once the vessels have already passed the sacrum bone—the veins are carried superior to the arteries; and the arteries, because they are more "noble," are hidden beneath the veins. <margin>h You will seek this, as well as the entire series of the artery, from the last figure of this book, marked i under v, v, v.</margin> Furthermore, the branches which come forth from the division of the great artery above the start of the sacrum bone correspond most exactly to the branches of the veins, if <gloss>i</gloss> you perhaps exclude the small little forks which are led downward from the lower seat of the artery where it is first <gloss>k</gloss> split in two. WHILE the branches of the "hollow vein" <note>original: "uenae cauae," the vena cava</note> that approach the base of the skull were reviewed above, it was reported that six of them are observed on each side. In the history of the distribution of the arteries, however, the count showed three of their offshoots entering the skull on each side. And indeed, the <gloss>a</gloss> first vein in that description was considered to be the offshoot which, climbing through the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae, sought the skull. The second and third <gloss>b</gloss> were branches of the internal jugular vein: <gloss>c</gloss> one, which is seen to be thicker and larger than the other offshoots of the veins sent into the skull, enters the skull through the <gloss>d</gloss> large hole <note>the jugular foramen</note> which is also prepared for the <gloss>e</gloss> sixth pair of brain nerves <note>modern classification: the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves, which Vesalius grouped differently</note>, after first spreading an <gloss>f</gloss> offshoot into the front part of the vertebrae toward the first and second vertebrae of the neck. <gloss>g</gloss> The other <gloss>h</gloss> makes use of a specific hole carved out near the hole for the third and fourth pairs of brain nerves, and enters the skull without the company of an artery. <gloss>i</gloss> I wrote that the fourth is an offspring of the external jugular, which <gloss>k</gloss> seeks the skull through its own hole, <gloss>m</gloss> where it joins the rear part of the temporal seam <note>the suture</note> in a shape imitating the letter Λ <note>the Greek letter Lambda, referring to the lambdoid suture</note>. <gloss>n</gloss> The fifth The second and third, however, were considered branches of the <gloss>t</gloss> "sleepy artery" <note>original: "soporalis arteria," the carotid artery</note>. <gloss>u</gloss> One was said to enter the skull joined to the vein through the hole of the sixth pair of brain nerves, and to derive an <gloss>x</gloss> offshoot to the front seat of the neck vertebrae. <gloss>y</gloss> But the other, appearing larger than the branch just mentioned, seeks the skull through a <gloss>z</gloss> hole proper to itself without a companion vein. And such is roughly the number of arteries and veins entering the skull on just one side. By what method and in what sequence they are mutually connected and join together, and again are separated, and run in various ways into the membranes of the brain, I shall strive to follow here: warning before all else that absolutely no vein or artery is woven into the <gloss>a</gloss> substance of the brain in the same way we know such vessels are entangled in the lungs, spleen, liver, and even most muscles.

For the vessels of the brain, contained <gloss>b</gloss> only within the membranes, lie against the brain everywhere, and are hardly ever attached to the substance itself, as will be heard more extensively in the progress of this discourse. ### BOOK III ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>
The use of the sinuses of the tough membrane of the brain. Book 9 of *On Anatomical Procedures*, section [blank].
</margin>

But in some places, this cavity approaches a triangular shape, whose three sides are equally slanted inward. These sinuses <note>The dural venous sinuses, which are venous channels found between the layers of the dura mater in the brain.</note> serve the function not only of veins, but also of arteries. However, this was hardly noticed by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–210 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium until Vesalius challenged them.</note> and the other professors of dissection, since they judged these sinuses to perform only the duty of veins. Nor did they observe, from the dissection of living subjects or the inspection of the wounded, that those sinuses pulsate in the manner of arteries. Furthermore, it seems they did not perceive that both veins and arteries empty into these sinuses alike, pouring in the material which they embrace and contain: the veins indeed pouring in the thicker blood, and the arteries the vital spirit <note>term: vital spirit (spiritus vitalis); in Renaissance physiology, a refined substance carried in the arterial blood responsible for life and heat.</note> along with the blood, diffused through the body with force. Besides these sinuses excavated into the processes of the tough membrane, the membrane <margin>g Book 7, fig. 1, D, D, D. Fig. 3, G, G. Fig. 7, around O, O. h Book 7, fig. 2, D, D, G, G. Fig. 6, H.</margin> itself possesses many others. From these (just as with those recently mentioned), numerous ducts run out into the thin membrane of the brain <note>The pia mater, the delicate innermost layer of the meninges.</note> and with it also into the ventricles of the brain; all of these represent perfectly rounded cavities in the manner of veins. However, they do not all offer an equal use to the living creature, since some perform the duty of both veins and arteries together, others only of veins, and some only of arteries. And these two features are granted to the membranes of the brain as unique, rare, and private among the <margin>What kind of sinuses belong to the brain's membranes.</margin> other parts of the body: namely, that the same cavity or duct performs the duty of both artery and vein, and meanwhile, the ducts or sinuses prepared within the bodies of the membranes can be properly considered neither vein nor artery. Rather, they exist as certain unique and altogether specific tubes or sinuses, such as one might form if they were to drive styluses lengthwise into a thick piece of leather according to its thickness, as if to construct the sinuses of veins. Therefore, as I am about to describe the series of these sinuses, tubes, cavities, veins, or arteries (if you prefer), what will prevent me from using one word or another as it seems suited to the business at hand? In the right side, then (which you shall also understand for the left, since the reason for both is the same), we said that six veins and three arteries enter the skull. But perhaps someone will think that in this description of the sinuses of the tough membrane <note>term: tough membrane (dura membrana); the dura mater, the thick outermost layer protecting the brain.</note> something has been omitted by me, because no mention has yet occurred of the region called the *torcular* <note>original: "torculari"; Latin for "wine-press." I certainly would not have passed this over, if only it were certain to me which part was so named. For in Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon was the ancient Greek physician whose anatomical theories Vesalius often challenged or clarified.</note> it is ambiguous whether the Greeks first called it the common meeting point of the first and second sinuses of the tough membrane (from which both the third and fourth proceed), or truly the end of the fourth sinus of the tough membrane, which faces the "testes" of the brain <note>term: testes of the brain (cerebri testes); the inferior colliculi, small rounded structures in the midbrain.</note> and extends into the ventricles. For Galen seems to adapt the name of "wine-press" now to this part, now to that; indeed, nothing prevents both from being called a wine-press. For that confluence into the fourth and third sinuses brings forth blood like wine from a press; just as the end of the fourth sinus dispenses blood into all the branches it emits. Thus, as far as I am concerned, you may call any seat of the sinuses a "wine-press," and establish in them the region in which the Arabs thought the blood stood outside the veins <note>A reference to medieval Arabic medical commentaries that suggested blood pooled in these areas.</note>, provided you do not disturb the sequence of the sinuses and the vessels of the brain. From this artery, therefore, and the right part of that offshoot, that plexus <note>term: plexus; a network of vessels</note>—truly very similar to a tangled and self-involved net, and perhaps for this reason first called the "reticular plexus" by the first professors of dissection—is formed in the right ventricle of the brain; the Greeks also call it the *choroeidē* <note>original: "χοροειδῆ"; the choroid plexus. Vesalius notes it is named for its resemblance to the chorion, or fetal membrane.</note>, a comparison taken from the substance of the membranes enveloping a fetus and the series of vessels running through them. Furthermore, it is named from a certain dark and reddish <note>b</note> flesh, or glandular substance, which is in a way interwoven into this plexus of the brain, and possesses something in common with <note>c</note> that substance found between the uterus and the outer covering of the fetus, which beautifully presides over the distributions of the vessels <note>d</note>. In the left ventricle of the brain, this plexus—likened to the afterbirth—is formed from the principal branch of the third artery of that side, and from the other part of that same offshoot tending there, which (as written above) belongs to the ventricles of the brain from the fourth sinus.

Concerning Galen’s reticular plexus <note>term: reticular plexus (rete mirabile); a complex network of arteries found in many hoofed mammals but not in humans.</note>, I have decided that nothing should be lied about here, because I no longer doubt that the series of the brain's vessels is clear to me. And therefore, one should be even less inclined to invent something now, because we know that Galen, misled by the dissection of the brains of oxen, described not the human brain, nor its vessels, but those of an ox—and even that quite inexactly <note>e</note>. For if you examine the series of the third artery seeking the skull in a human, you will find it just as I have now described; yet sometimes you will observe that there is only a single branch, where I said those two (extended for some distance) come together. Otherwise, if you search the artery of an ox and divide the tough membrane of the brain next to the sides of the gland receiving the phlegm, you will find something similar to Galen’s reticular plexus. But these matters belong to the seventh book, which, being consecrated to the seat of the sovereign soul, will follow the method of dissecting these vessels most clearly.

REMAINING yet in our discourse on the veins and arteries are two vessels, each of which is explained by those skilled in dissection with two names: a one they call the <term>arterial vein</term> <note>original: "uenam arterialem"; the modern pulmonary artery</note>, and b the other the <term>venous artery</term> <note>original: "arteriam uenalem"; the modern pulmonary vein</note>. These names are surely bestowed based on their use, with an added descriptor based on the substance of which they consist. Thus, the arterial vein c is the vessel said to be distributed from the higher seat of the right ventricle of the heart into the lung by a very numerous series of branches; it supplies the lung with blood elaborated in that ventricle of the heart. And yet this vessel consists not d of the body of a vein, but e of an artery. Hence, because it carries blood in the manner of veins, it obtained the name "vein"; but because it is formed with the tunics (walls) of arteries, that arterial descriptor is added to it. Furthermore, the other f vessel, emerging from the left side of the base of the left ventricle of the heart, is also divided into a scattered offspring within the lung; it serves primarily to carry air from the lung into the left ventricle of the heart, and yet it is constituted g of the body of a vein. Hence, because it serves the conveyance of air and is a "spiritual" organ <note>Vesalius uses "spiritual" in the classical sense, referring to the "vital spirit" believed to be carried in the blood after aeration</note>, it is called an "artery"; but from its substance and conformation, it is called "venous." Why these vessels differ from the [standard] vein and artery in their origin, use, and the conformation of their substance, and what sort of membranes are placed over their orifices, we shall pursue in h the sixth book, which will be dedicated to the parts of the vital soul. 

As we bring this book to a close, it should seem a wonder to no one that a prolix chapter is not added here to review the veins diffused through the body without the company of an artery, or likewise the arteries running without a companion vein. For if anyone desires an enumeration of them (as indeed all should), he will immediately see this from the tables of the veins and arteries when he compares them with one another. Indeed, the bare image of the vena cava corresponds in proportion to the delineation of the entire great artery, and we have arranged both within the same circumference. Moreover, lest anyone require my labor in this part, I place at the end of this third book the table of the *Epitome* of the present Work, expressing the veins and arteries together. This shows, and not merely in passing, which vein is distributed through the body without the company of an artery, and which artery again is without a consort vein. Truly, when I followed the series of the veins above, my discourse would have willingly broken out more than once into a treatise on <term>venesection</term> <note>The medical practice of bloodletting</note>, by which we diminish the blood. I might have described a vein now closer to this or that part, now more remote, and whether it be large or small, and its alignment—from wherever it might finally be sought—and the agreement of both straight and transverse fibers corresponding to this or that part. I would have warned in no common way that the blood flowing from a cut vein is contained within the body of the whole vein; therefore, it is not the position of the parts lying near the veins, but the duct and distribution of the veins into

...that "straightness" which is on everyone's lips must be observed: therefore, one must deal with the cutting of a vein <note>original: "uenae sectione"; venesection or bloodletting was a primary medical treatment in the 16th century</note>, and with some "uterus" <note>Vesalius uses "utero" here likely in the sense of a central cavity or source</note> that would lead out various processes here and there, and yet remain a single, continuous entity. *In order to conveniently glue the figures printed on this sheet into their proper places, and so that they may be made stronger: first, you should glue a layer of parchment <note>original: "membranam"; here referring to animal-skin parchment used to reinforce the paper for frequent lifting of the flaps</note> beneath this sheet, and then cut out each of the figures from the excess paper.*

*The **FIRST** figure, which shows the distribution of the vein lacking a pair <note>The azygos vein</note>, is to be attached to the back of the large figure <note>The main anatomical figure on the primary page</note> at the point where the trunk of the vena cava produces that vein, and where the letter **o** is seen written on both figures. The **SECOND** figure, when it has been trimmed of excess paper, will consist of two parts. The upper part represents the vein and artery of the right side as they seek their place in the abdomen beneath the upper chest bone <note>The sternum</note>. This part is to be fixed at the letter **q** where it appears in the throat of the large figure, and at the asterisk **\*** where it meets the branch at the right side marked with **ζ** <note>zeta</note> and **m** in the large figure. Furthermore, the lower part, representing the vein and artery that entwine the lower part of the abdomen, is to be joined where their roots are seen near the letter **l** at the beginning of the right leg, above the groin.*

*The **THIRD** figure, worthier than the rest, represents the distribution of the portal vein along with the arteries that accompany it, as well as a large portion of the lower membrane of the omentum <note>A fatty layer of the peritoneum that hangs over the intestines</note> and the spleen. This should be fastened to the hollow seat <note>The concave underside</note> of the liver on the larger figure, where **v**, **φ** <note>phi</note>, **ς** <note>sigma</note>, and several neighboring characters are seen on both figures.*

*The **FOURTH** figure, showing a portion of the convex <note>original: "gibbæ"; the rounded or humped top side</note> seat of the liver, will be usefully glued at a single point where the letter **A** stands between **f** and **F** on the larger figure.*

*The **FIFTH** figure, which shows the seminal veins and arteries in addition to the testes, their coverings, and the urinary passages, is to be attached where the letter **u** is found on both figures—specifically where the seminal vein first joins the artery and the urinary passages are placed beneath them.*

---

*The **SIXTH** figure—which is strong enough even if no parchment is glued beneath it—is first to be glued under the **SEVENTH**. The **SEVENTH** figure shows the front of the bladder and the penis, along with the vessels we assign to the navel <note>The umbilical vessels</note>. We have represented the lower surface of the penis in this **SIXTH** figure so that the entire composite figure arising from both of them can be fastened by the character **φ** <note>phi</note> onto the **φ** of the **FIFTH** figure, and afterwards folded like the letter **S** to resemble a limp penis.*

*The **EIGHTH** figure, containing the female bladder, the vessels of the navel, and a portion of the urinary passages, is not to be attached to the large [male] figure, but to that figure on the back of the sheet where the large one is printed, which shows the uterus, its veins and arteries, and the seminal vessels. Thus, the **EIGHTH** figure will be joined to that small [female] figure where **u** occurs and the seminal vein is joined to the artery; the connection should be made only at the urinary passages, positioned according to the location of the bladder, so that **χ** <note>chi</note> corresponds to **ω** <note>omega</note>.*

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book 4 of Vesalius's *De humani corporis fabrica*. Having completed Book 3 on the veins and arteries (the circulatory system), Vesalius now transitions to the nervous system, beginning with a definition of terms and a debate over the origin of the nerves—brain versus heart.</meta>

OF ANDREAS VESALIUS,

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK FOUR,
# PERTAINING SPECIFICALLY TO THE NERVES, AND
### presenting the figures peculiar to the Chapters to which they
### chiefly belong, at the very front.

## TO WHICH PARTS OF THE BODY THE NAME OF "NERVE"
## is attributed, what a nerve is properly called, and finally what it is,
## along with its types and use. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'T'. The internal scene of the letter depicts several putti or infants in a medical setting. One child lies horizontally as a subject, while others stand over him; one child appears to be pointing a surgical tool or stylus at the subject's head or neck area, and another child points toward a vessel on the floor.</image-desc>

<margin>
Ligaments, tendons, and the extensions of the brain and spinal cord <note>original: "dorisaliſq; medullæ" – literally the "medulla of the back," the standard term for the spinal cord in the 16th century</note> are generally called nerves.
</margin>
<margin>
*a fig. ch. 1 book 2.*
</margin>
<margin>
*b 1. fig. ch. 2 book 2 F. and throughout the seven tables of muscles.*
</margin>
<margin>
*c throughout in the 1st and 2nd figures of ch. 2 and the 2nd and 3rd figures of ch. 11.*
</margin>
IN THE THIRD book, I embraced the sequence of the distribution of the veins, which carry blood from the liver into the whole body, and of the arteries, which supply the body with vital spirit <note>In Galenic medicine, "vital spirit" was believed to be carried in the arteries to provide heat and life to the tissues</note> together with blood by the force diffused from the heart. But now it is next to follow the propagation of the nerves, which communicate animal spirit <note>Animal spirit (from the Latin "anima," meaning soul or breath) was thought to be a refined substance produced in the brain and transmitted through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation</note> from the brain to the members that require it for their duties, beginning the discourse with the general differences between nerves. For those skilled in dissection establish a triple difference of nerves (as I have also warned elsewhere): since they apply the name of "nerve," just as the common people do, to the **ligaments** connecting the bones and constituting no small portion of the muscles. Secondly, following the common custom, they include **tendons** and all the fibrous parts of the muscles under the name of "nerves." And they enumerate a third kind of nerve besides, which we have decided to undertake at present: namely, **long, round organs** <note>original: "organa"</note> that possess no internal cavity detectable by the senses, and which carry the animal spirit from the brain to the parts of the body.

<margin>
The organ specifically designated by the name of nerve.
</margin>
And these organs, the professors of dissection honor especially with the name of "nerve" without any additional description. This term has flowed down to us from the Greeks, who, based on function or duty, designated a single instrument by two names, calling it *neuron* <note>original: "νευ̃ρον"</note> from *neuein* <note>original: "νεύειν," meaning to nod or incline</note>, and *tonos* <note>original: "τόνον"</note> from *teinein* <note>original: "τείνειν," meaning to stretch</note>, because it is chiefly by the help of nerves that muscles are able both to nod and to stretch. Indeed, it is granted by everyone that no particle of the body obtains either voluntary motion (which depends upon our will) or sensation without a nerve; and if a nerve is cut, or intercepted by a snare <note>A reference to using ligatures in experimental dissection to prove nerve function</note>, or otherwise corrupted or compressed, the part to which it goes is immediately deprived of motion and sense.

<margin>
The origin of the nerves from the brain.
</margin>
However, the fact that the brain is the source and principle of the spinal cord, and that the nerves arise partly from the brain and partly from the spinal cord, was by no means known or explored by everyone. For some judged the heart to be the principle of the nerves; some, the hard or thick membrane of the brain <note>The dura mater</note>; meanwhile, no one suggested the liver or any other internal organ of that kind. But Hippocrates, Erasistratus, Herophilus, Galen, and the other chief anatomists, based on those things which are seen in the dissection <note>original: "refectione" – literally a restoring or reworking, here referring to the uncovering of anatomy</note> of bodies, most truly assert that the brain is the beginning of the nerves. Furthermore, it must also be confessed that the nerves take the animal spirit from it and derive it to those parts that require it for either some sense or for voluntary motion.

<margin>
Not from the heart.
</margin>
For it is clearly gathered from this fact that the nerves by no means lead their principle from the heart (as it seemed especially to Aristotle and not a few others), because in dissection no nerve is seen to be born from it. For absolutely no nerve is...

<sig>X</sig>
<meta>catchword: commit- (Latin: committitur, meaning "is connected" or "is joined")</meta>

<summary>Vesalius begins Book 4 by defining nerves and distinguishing them from ligaments and tendons, which were often confused in common speech. He asserts, following the great anatomists like Galen, that nerves originate in the brain and spinal cord to carry 'animal spirit,' refuting Aristotle's claim that they originate in the heart.</summary>
<keywords>nervous system, brain, spinal cord, animal spirit, vital spirit, etymology, Greek medicine, Galen, Aristotle, anatomy, voluntary motion, sensation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Book 4, Chapter 1. Vesalius is currently refuting the ancient Aristotelian view that the nerves originate in the heart, arguing instead for the brain as their source based on his own dissections.</meta>

ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE BODY

<margin>d Figure 6, Book 6 at h for the dissection.</margin>
...is committed, except for $^d$ one exceedingly slender [nerve], which I finally discovered only with the greatest effort, and which is distributed from the left nerve of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "sexti paris neruorum cerebri" – in modern anatomy, the 10th cranial nerve, or the vagus nerve</note>.

<margin>e Figure 8, g of the same [book].</margin>
<margin>f Figure 1 of the same [book].</margin>
For where that nerve is carried downward through the left side of the heart, and offers very thin little branches to the left part of the lung and also to the heart’s envelope <note>The pericardium</note>, and $^e$ forms the left recurrent nerve <note>The left recurrent laryngeal nerve</note>, it leads a tiny nerve away from itself. This tiny nerve penetrates the heart’s envelope where it is attached to the seat of the left $^f$ venous artery <note>original: "arterialis uenæ" – the pulmonary vein</note>, and is consumed into the base of the heart, near the left and posterior seat of that same venous artery.

Therefore, since a tiny nerve of this kind is provided to the heart by the sixth pair of cranial nerves—just as we shall show that tiny nerves are offered to all the other internal organs—and since the heart's tiny nerve is remarkably slender, it is readily gathered that the heart does not even give origin to the left nerve of the sixth pair. Far from it, then, that this tiny nerve could be considered the origin of all the other nerves.

Furthermore, the fibers which we know to be interwoven into the flesh of the heart are no more nerves than are the fibers of other organs, such as those of the stomach, the intestines, the veins, and the arteries.

<margin>g Figure 7, Book 6 under K, L, M. and Figure 9 G, G under E, F.</margin>
In addition to this, the $^g$ fibers which occur in the borders or ventricles of the heart without flesh <note>The chordae tendineae and valve structures</note>, because they are merely extensions of membranes, are not to be placed in the category of nerves at all. For the fibers presenting themselves in the right ventricle of the heart are considered extensions of the three membranes <note>The tricuspid valve</note> placed over the orifice of the *vena cava*.

The fibers appearing in the left ventricle of the heart are small extensions of the two membranes <note>The mitral valve</note> which the orifice of the venous artery claims as its own.

Since, therefore, such fibers of the heart are by no means to be referred to that class of nerves which carry the animal spirit <note>The "animal spirit" was thought to be the medium of sensation and voluntary movement, produced in the brain</note> to the parts of the body like certain little streams, it must also be granted that the heart cannot be considered the beginning of the nerves for the sake of those fibers—especially since nothing at all is led elsewhere outside the substance of the heart from those extensions of the membranes.

<margin>The nerve does not arise from the hard membrane of the brain.</margin>
<margin>h Figure 1, Book 7 A, A, B, B. Figure 2, H, H.</margin>
Furthermore, those who have affirmed that the origin of the nerves hangs from the $^h$ hard membrane of the brain <note>The *dura mater*</note> (among whose number was Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BC) often credited as the father of physiology</note> even until his extreme old age) have observed only the exterior part of the nerve arising from the hard membrane of the brain.

<margin>Of what parts a nerve consists.</margin>
<margin>i Figure 17, Chapter 14, Book 7 α, β, γ.</margin>
<margin>k Figure 2, Book 7 E, E. Figure 3, Θ, Θ.</margin>
For every single nerve $^i$ consists of a triple substance: namely, a middle substance very similar to the innermost marrow of trees, which undoubtedly draws its beginning from the brain, corresponding entirely to the coagulated and hardened substance of the brain; and two exterior substances: one, the same as the one closer to the innermost substance, which we have found to arise from the $^k$ thin membrane of the brain <note>The *pia mater*</note>; and the other, which we have found to arise from the hard membrane.

For not otherwise than the brain itself is clothed by those two membranes, so also the processes propagated from the brain (namely, the nerves themselves) are covered by them, and thus wrapped, they run throughout the body.

<margin>From where the animal spirit is provided to the nerves.</margin>
Thus indeed, no one who does not deny the evidence of their own eyes can deny that the beginning of the nerves hangs from the brain. And therefore one can hardly doubt whether the animal spirit, which they lead to the parts, flows into the nerves from the brain or indeed from the heart.

For some (such as Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus of Soli (c. 279–206 BC), a Stoic philosopher who argued for the heart as the seat of the soul</note> among others), even if they granted that the brain was the beginning of the nerves, they nevertheless did not establish it as the principle of sensation and voluntary motion.

<margin>l The last figure of Book 3 beautifully shows all these together in the neck.</margin>
These people are certainly more than enough refuted by a living section <note>original: "uiua ſectio" – a dissection of a living animal, or vivisection</note>, in which $^l$ all the parts pertaining to the brain from the heart are crushed, or intercepted by ligatures, or even cut through.

For this [procedure], if properly administered, as I have attempted more than once in public dissections, will certainly teach how much the brain requires the office of the heart—that is, the vital spirit—no less, clearly, than the heart requires that air which we breathe and the blood of the liver for its own duties.

Then that section will show that the [brain] provides animal spirit to the nerves no more than the liver provides vital spirit to the heart...

<meta>catchword: ...from the liver</meta>

<summary>In this text, Vesalius argues that nerves originate in the brain rather than the heart, describing the three-layered structure of nerves as extensions of brain matter and its protective membranes. He uses anatomical evidence and vivisection to prove that while the brain requires vital spirit from the heart, it is the brain alone that serves as the source of sensation and motion through the "animal spirit."</summary>

<keywords>neuroanatomy, brain, heart, vagus nerve, dura mater, pia mater, animal spirit, vital spirit, Erasistratus, Chrysippus, vivisection, nerve structure</keywords>
