<meta>This page continues Andreas Vesalius’s discussion in Book 4, Chapter 1 regarding the nature and distribution of nerves. Having argued that nerves originate in the brain rather than the heart, he now moves into a detailed classification of nerves based on their physical consistency (soft vs. hard) and their functional purpose (sensation vs. motion).</meta>

->THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK 4<-

...we know they are led from the liver <note>In the previous page, Vesalius was discussing the ancient debate over whether veins originate in the liver and nerves in the heart; he is now transitioning to his specific anatomical observations of nerves.</note>. However, because this kind of debate belongs more to the history of the heart and brain than to the nature of nerves, we will set it aside for now and proceed to the differences between nerves properly so-called. <margin>The distinction of nerves based on softness and hardness, from which many differences among nerves arise.</margin> Just as the substance of the brain and the spinal cord <note>original: "medullæ dorsalis"</note> arising from it does not maintain the same hardness in every part, so too the nerves taking their origin from these do not correspond to one another in substance, but vary greatly in hardness and softness.

<margin>
m Figures 1, 2, Chapter 2, G.
n Same figures, M.
o Figure 1, Chapter 11, from F to G.
p Figures 1, 2, Chapter 2, G, M, d.
q Figure 2, Chapter 2, R.
</margin>
On account of the substance of the origin from which the nerves emerge, the optic nerves <note>original: "uisorij nerui"</note> as well as those of the tongue are considered remarkably soft. Those that take their origin from the spinal cord where it sits in the sacrum <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note> are the hardest. Next, nerves are found to be either softer or harder due to a longer or shorter path. For the nerves of sight, taste, and hearing are soft because they creep forward over a very short distance. But by virtue of the journey and the twists in the path, a branch of the third pair of cranial nerves <note>In Vesalius's 7-pair system, the "third pair" corresponds to parts of the modern trigeminal and oculomotor nerves.</note>, coiled like the tendrils of a vine or a gourd, becomes harder. Furthermore, the passage of a nerve through a hard or soft body, and contact with that body, makes it softer or harder.

<margin>
r Figures 1, 2, Chapter 12, Book 2, E.
s Figures 1, 2, Chapter 2, M.
t Figures 1, 2, Chapter 2, c.
u Figure 2, Chapter 11, Book 1, b.
x Figure 2, Chapter 2, O.
y Same figure, arising at V and T.
</margin>
For the optic nerve is carried by a very short path through a hole carved in the bone; likewise the main portion of the third pair of cranial nerves, which is therefore hardened very little by contact with the bones, just like the optic nerve. But the small fork of the fifth pair of nerves, which creeps through the blind and winding hole of the temporal bone, and one little branch of the third pair of cranial nerves that falls from the eye-socket to the cheeks, and another likewise to the lower lip—because they travel a long way through bone—harden more through the benefit of contact with the bone than at their origins. For a similar reason, on account of the length of the journey and contact with the hard membranes, almost all nerves spread out to the muscles are seen to become harder than they were when they first emerged from their origin.

<margin>Why some nerves are rendered softer or harder than others.</margin>
All these things were devised with marvelous industry by the Creator of all things <note>original: "rerum Opifice" – the Artificer or Architect of nature.</note>. For a sensory organ needs a soft nerve: a nerve, certainly, because it is the instrument of sense and requires much <term>animal spirit</term> <note>A refined substance thought to flow through nerves to enable sensation and movement.</note> to perform its duty; but a soft one, because it must be "affected" and disposed in a certain way, and "suffer" something from the sensible object encountered from the outside <note>Vesalius uses "suffer" in the Aristotelian sense of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>. For a soft thing is more suited to receiving impressions, while a hard thing is better for action and for strength (which a nerve needs on a long path). Therefore, the sensory organs are necessarily provided with soft nerves, while other parts that must be moved are given harder nerves. Hence even the instruments of sense that are moved by the will, such as the eye and the tongue, claim two kinds of nerves for themselves: one presiding over sense, the other over motion.

<margin>
z Figure 2, Chapter 2, G; then from M, Y.
a Figure 2, Chapter 2, K; then d, u, w.
</margin>
Deservedly, then, the processes of the nerves from the brain and spinal cord do not obtain the same site of origin, nor are the same paths and passages carved out for soft and hard nerves. For the soft ones take their beginning from the soft and anterior <note>front</note> parts of the base of the brain, while the hard ones come from the posterior <note>back</note> parts and the spinal cord itself; again, the former creep out straight, while the latter go by a winding and long journey.

<margin>Nature's goal in distributing the nerves.</margin>
Furthermore, Nature seems to have had a triple goal in the distribution of the types of nerves. The first is for the sake of sensation in the sensory organs; the second is for the sake of motion to the parts which it was worthwhile to move; and the third is in all the other parts for the recognition of things that cause pain <note>original: "tristantium dignotionem" – literally, the discernment of distressing things.</note>. Unless, perhaps, it seems better to someone to make this third goal the same as the first, since it pertains to sensation.

<margin>
b See the hand, Figure 2, Chapter 11.
c Figures 14, 15, Book 5, V, T.
</margin>
Thus, in the name of sense, the largest nerves are offered to the eyes, the tongue, and the ears; as also to the inner surface of the hand and the upper orifice of the stomach, which are not ineptly considered the proper and primary organs of touch, just as the eyes are of sight and the tongue of taste. For through the hands, sensation is more exact than through...

<summary>Vesalius explains that nerves vary in texture based on their function and origin: sensory nerves are soft to receive impressions, while motor nerves are hard for durability. He notes that Nature (or the Creator) strategically places these nerves, with softer ones emerging from the front of the brain and harder ones from the rear and spinal cord.</summary>
<keywords>nerve texture, optic nerve, spinal cord, animal spirit, sensation vs. motion, cranial nerves, anatomy of the hand, stomach sensitivity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Andreas Vesalius’s classification of nerves. On the previous page, he established that nerves vary in hardness and softness based on their origin and the length of their path. He now turns to the functional reasons for these differences, specifically how nerves serve the senses and bodily movement.</meta>

->ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY<-

...another part, although many perceive it, is the recognition of touch itself. In the opening <note>original: "ore", literally "mouth"</note> of the stomach, we believe there is a sense of the lack of those things by which a living creature must be nourished, which we call hunger. In all these, as instruments of the senses, the largest nerves are inserted. For the purpose of movement, however, nerves are distributed to the muscles—the instruments of voluntary motion. Because these nerves are constructed for moving parts of the body, they receive large nerves or at least have them stretched around them. But since the sense of touch is necessarily present in every nerve, a greater power followed in the muscles and sensory organs than they needed for the recognition of touchable things. For the remaining parts, which only require the sense of touch, nerves are provided in proportion to their need. For the internal organs <term>viscera; the internal organs in the main cavities of the body</term>, such as the <margin>d Figure 2, chapter 2, q.</margin> lung, <margin>e Figure 2, chapter 2, x.</margin> liver, and <margin>f Figure 2, chapter 2, n.</margin> spleen—because they lie hidden deep within—only slender shoots of nerves are provided. In the skin, however, because it is the first to meet things encountered from the outside, many branches are distributed everywhere.

<margin>Difference based on the form of origin.</margin>
Furthermore, the appearance or form of the origin of the nerves is not seen the same everywhere. <margin>g Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, G, K.</margin> Some, and especially the softer ones, do not arise or proceed with their body divided into many shoots; among these are the optic nerves <note>original: "uisorij nerui"</note> and the second pair of brain nerves. <margin>h Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, M, Z, d.</margin> Others come forth from the brain like several small cords <term>funiculi; little ropes or bundles of fibers</term> bound together, such as the <margin>i Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, e, v; and also to be seen here in figures 9 and 14 of book 7.</margin> third, fourth, and fifth pairs of nerves. Others, at their very origin, have these shoots like cords separated from one another, each surrounded by its own portion of the thin membrane; when they exit the skull, they are all joined together and covered by a single, harder membrane. This is observed most notably in <margin>k See Figure 1, chapter 11.</margin> several nerves of the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsalis medullæ"</note>, as well as in the sixth and seventh pairs of brain nerves. For this reason, in the description of the distribution of many nerves into branches, it seems to make no difference whether you say the frequency of the aforementioned cords is loosened, or that the whole nerve is split into branches extending to different parts.

<margin>Every nerve is endowed with the sense of touch.</margin>
But I do not know with what audacity <note>original: "qua fronte", literally "with what forehead"</note> certain leaders of anatomy have dared to assert that among these shoots or cords, some serve movement while others serve sensation—as if Nature had deprived certain nerve shoots of the sense of touch. You will learn the likeness of such cords if, while eating, a piece of meat dissected from the armpit or groin of some animal is placed on the table, and in it you look at some small portion of a nerve, usually accompanying a vein and artery. You will see the end of the nerve corresponds to a thicker cord which, twisted from several smaller cords, has been divided crosswise with a duller knife.

<margin>Difference based on the cavity of nerves.</margin>
<margin>l Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, G; figure 14, book 7, B, B; figure 13, chapter 14, book 7, k.</margin>
Furthermore, I would hardly dare to seek a difference based on the cavity of the nerves, since I have never seen even the optic nerve hollowed out or perforated—even though I do not doubt that nerves, no less than veins and arteries, are called "vessels," and that the optic nerves are said to be perforated by professors of dissection <note>Vesalius is challenging the ancient Galenic view that optic nerves were hollow tubes to allow the passage of "animal spirits" for vision.</note>.

<margin>Based on the series [of distribution].</margin>
From the sequence or distribution itself, one may take a difference in this manner: some are consumed whole into a single part, such as the <margin>m Figure 2, chapter 2, M.</margin> optic nerves into the eyes; others are divided into many shoots, some offered to muscles, <margin>n same figure, X.</margin> some to the skin, <margin>o same figure, R.</margin> some to the bones, and some to a sensory organ. <margin>p Muscle table 4, r.</margin> For example, the third pair of nerves, <margin>q Figure 2, chapter 2, T, V, X.</margin> which, while it is in a way proper to the tongue, <margin>r Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, K.</margin> is also directed to certain muscles—such as the <margin>s Figures 1, 2, chapter 2, L.</margin> temporal muscle—for the sake of movement, and to the skin for the sake of sensation (namely to the lips), and also to the teeth. Others again are carried unmixed, neither meeting nor uniting with other nerves, <margin>t Figure 1, chapter 2, H.</margin> such as the second pair of the brain, which is mixed with no nerve and truly meets none, although a smaller root of the third pair attends it in its progress. But others are mixed among themselves, such as the <margin>u See these in figures 2 and 3, chapter 11, and the last figure of this book.</margin> right nerve of the first pair being mixed with the left. Others are mixed with different nerves, such as those that go to the arm; as soon as they have leaped forward from the vertebrae, they are mixed just as...

<meta>This page continues Andreas Vesalius’s discussion on the structure and categorization of nerves. On the previous page, he noted the differences in nerve texture and origin. Here, he begins the formal transition into a detailed, systematic review of the cranial and spinal nerves, emphasizing their symmetrical, paired nature.</meta>

# THE FOURTH BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>Nerves arise in pairs.</margin>
...are joined in the same way that painters are accustomed to draw the cords of hats <note>original: "galerorum funiculos"; likely referring to the braided or twisted appearance of decorative cords on headwear of the period</note>. But since I will follow these details abundantly in the specific descriptions of the nerves, it is now the right time to cover the sequence of each nerve in writing: first reviewing the pairs that arise from the brain, and then those which the spinal cord <term>dorsalis medulla; the "spinal marrow" or spinal cord</term> produces. Indeed, no nerve emerges from either the brain or the spinal cord unpaired; rather, they always hold a position in exactly the same order, one to the right and another to the left. The right and left nerves are also distributed into branches in precisely the same way, unless you exclude the sixth pair of cranial nerves, which you will hear is distributed <margin>x Compare the right nerve to the left in Figure 2, Chapter 2.</margin> somewhat differently on the right side than on the left.

In the SEVENTH BOOK, when the construction of the brain is treated, we shall teach that it is twofold: one part is anterior and superior, <gloss>a</gloss> which is called the **cerebrum**, filling almost the entire skull; <gloss>b</gloss> the other is posterior and lower, and is called by us the **small brain** <term>cerebellum</term>, being even ten times smaller than the cerebrum itself. Then we shall assert that the anterior brain, in its whole upper seat, <gloss>c</gloss> is twin—namely, right and left. However, in the lower part, where it rests on the middle of the base of the skull, we shall show it to be single and undivided; and that the **spinal cord** <term>dorsalis medulla</term> takes its origin from this, and not (as the foremost of Anatomists write) from the cerebellum; and we shall show that the cerebellum rather <gloss>d</gloss> rests upon the spinal cord, and is joined to the cord by the intervention of a thin membrane and very little of its own substance, rather than <gloss>e</gloss> being its beginning. To these points, it will be added that besides certain other sinuses and passages of the brain, two ventricles of the brain exist: <gloss>f</gloss> one indeed on the right, <gloss>g</gloss> the other...

I would like it granted to me that I may call that part of the spinal cord—which proceeds from the base of the brain under the cerebellum to the opening where it glides out of the skull—the "beginning of the spinal cord." I have already sufficiently explained what I understand by that "beginning," and I shall describe it more diffusely in the seventh book. For my part, one may give any name to that beginning or part of the brain, provided it is not ignored how it is rightly distinguished from the cerebellum. Furthermore, all the nerves born from the brain and that beginning of the spinal cord are called "pairs" or "unions" <note>original: "coniugia"</note> of nerves by the Latins, and <note>original: "συζυγίαι" (syzygiai)</note> "syzygies" <note>Greek term meaning "yoked together," used to describe how nerves emerge in pairs from the left and right sides</note> by the Greeks, because they take their origin in pairs within the cavity of the skull where the brain is contained. These are numbered as seven by the consensus of Marinus and finally Galen as well, although if we were to weigh each one accurately, even more could be counted. <margin>o 1, 2 fig. F.</margin> For the organs of <margin>How many pairs of brain nerves.</margin> smell are not called "nerves" in this kind of enumeration because they do not exit the aforementioned cavity of the skull. L, M.</margin> opinion of other anatomists would more truly be counted as <margin>q 1, 2 fig. d near a.</margin> double rather than a single pair. Then, diligent dissection has taught me that another pair, unknown to all students of dissection, arises near the root of the fifth pair. However, by no means departing from the ancient enumeration of the brain's nerves, I shall strive to explain the seven pairs in seven chapters in order; yet first, I shall subjoin certain things about the organs of smell, since even many physicians ascribe to them the first "union" of nerves, or call them by that name.

## Some things concerning THE ORGAN OF SMELL. Chapter III.

<margin>a 3, 4 fig. ch. 12 book 1 K.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' depicting several putti or small human figures in a landscape; some appear to be looking at or holding an anatomical specimen or bone.</image-desc>Various indeed are the opinions of the physicians and philosophers of our time regarding the organ of smell, and great dissension arises among them due to their lack of skill in anatomy. For you may find some who <margin>b 5 fig. ch. 6 book 1 C, D.</margin> locate the organ of smell in that cavity which we reviewed in the first book, visible in the frontal bone near the region of the eyebrows between the two layers of that bone. If these people <margin>Multiple opinions on the organ of smell.</margin> had also discovered the two remarkable sinuses which we occasionally find in the middle of the bone that resembles a wedge <note>The sphenoid bone</note>—like caves between its own layers—and had observed that somewhat marrow-like substance <note>Brain matter</note> placed in those caverns (which must be weighed here with the greatest study), they would undoubtedly have placed the organ of smell there too, in the wedge-like bone. <margin>c 1, 2 fig. C. 1: fig. book 7 1, l, 1: fig. C, C.</margin> Others, however, establish certain tips of the brain's windings and revolutions, and the tubercles of the brain protuberant toward the middle of the eyebrows at the seat of the frontal bone, as the organs of smell; and they call those tubercles, because they stand out and are reddish almost like flesh, the "mamillary processes" <note>The olfactory bulbs, which Vesalius correctly identifies here as protrusions of the brain</note> of the brain, counting one on each side (as indeed there is). <margin>d 4, 5 fig. book 7 L, L, M, M.</margin> Others again, from several passages of Galen—especially the eighth book of *On the Use of the Parts*—simply assert that the anterior ventricles of the brain are the organs of smell, just as if the anterior ventricles were the principles of this sense alone. Some indeed count two anterior ventricles of the brain, but then they devise another two, which they claim are the organs of smell.

How well these men understand this, you may learn from dissection, by inspecting the construction or shape of the right and left ventricles of the brain. You will realize in the seventh book that this shape is, by Hercules, much different than what those skilled in dissection have handed down until now. For the ventricles are by no means seen to be wide in their posterior part; rather, as they proceed toward the front, they are gradually forced into a narrow space, and there they lead out to the organs of smell. Nor do they even excrete phlegm <note>original: "pituitam"; in ancient medicine, pituita or phlegm was thought to be a waste product of the brain that drained through the nose.</note> toward the ^e site of the olfactory organs, and much less do the ^f olfactory organs themselves, like channels of the brain, lead that phlegm down to that same place, no matter how much it might abound. ^g For the present ventricles of the brain, following the length of the brain, are large at the top, and are not rendered any narrower in the anterior part; indeed, they are wider there than in the very middle. In the posterior part they are also seen to be large; but from here, descending downward through the substance of the brain like a horn and stretching forward, they are narrowed for a time until they reach that ^h part of the brain which lies over the region of the gland that receives the brain's phlegm <note>the pituitary gland</note>, and under which the larger branches of the carotid ^i arteries <note>original: "soporalium arteriarum"; literally "sleep-inducing" arteries, because pressure on them was thought to cause sleep.</note> perforate the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note> and ^k begin to ascend into the ventricles of the brain. For they enter into these narrow ends of the ventricles, which I just ^l said terminate at the base of the brain.

In this way, therefore, the ducts of the right and left ventricles of the brain are seen. From the site where I said the narrow ends of the ventricles terminate, the ^m olfactory organs arise—or at least the processes of the brain that carry the animal spirit <note>In the 16th century, "animal spirit" was believed to be a subtle fluid that traveled through nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> to the primary instrument of smell—and ^n the optic nerves <note>original: "uisorij nerui"; nerves of vision.</note> also arise there. For from here, on both sides, a white and soft substance comes forth from the brain, which in its progress is also bound to the brain by the intervention of a thin membrane <note>the pia mater</note>, until it reaches the ^o cavities of the eighth bone of the head <note>the ethmoid bone</note>, which are prepared specifically for receiving these processes. For at the posterior part of these cavities, the whitish processes of the brain depart from the brain; no longer grown together with the thin membrane, they each stretch into their own cavity: and extending even further forward, they terminate at the end of the cavities, or their anterior part, supported by the cavities and meanwhile lying very close to the brain. For even if they are no longer attached to the brain in the region of the cavities, they nevertheless always follow it and are adjacent to it. These brain processes correspond to nerves in their path, color, and shape; although meanwhile they are far softer than the nerves themselves, and a little (regarding their rounded shape) wider than they are deep. But because they do not fall outside the cavity of the skull, nor even outside the dura mater, in the manner of the other nerves, ^p Herophilus did not deign to call them by the name "nerve"; nor did Marinus, nor Galen. This is despite the fact that some anatomists have meanwhile counted them among the number of nerves, listing them as the first pair of nerves. Furthermore, in the nature of these processes—which in dogs and sheep are much larger than they happen to be in man—one must carefully consider how they are attached to the dura mater at their ends, and what holes reach from here, through the dura mater and the ends of the bones on which the processes rest, to the recently mentioned cavities of the frontal bone and the wedge-shaped bone <note>the sphenoid bone</note>. And finally, it also comes to be weighed what the true organ of smell is, by taking a certain comparison from the instrument of hearing—which is also too superficially understood by professors of dissection and philosophy. But concerning the instrument of hearing, and that of smell too, and the instruments of the other senses, [we shall speak elsewhere].

# ON THE FIRST PAIR OF NERVES
->originating from the brain. Chapter IV.<-

<margin>The origin of the first pair.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting an anatomical dissection scene. Several figures in Renaissance attire are gathered around a table; one appears to be performing a dissection or demonstration on a human head or body part.</image-desc>IN THE PLACE where we wrote that white processes, proceeding like nerves, take their beginning from the middle of the base of the brain, a single nerve arises on each side^b, easily the softest of all the nerves of the body, and thicker in circumference than the others (provided they are not mixed with various other nerves). For in the leg, and likewise in the arm^c, you may indeed find nerves thicker than this first pair, but those are composed of several nerves joining together. Each nerve of the first pair, under the base of the brain where^d it rests on the cavity in which^e the gland <note>the pituitary gland</note> sits that receives the brain's phlegm <note>original: "pituitam"; ancient physicians believed the brain purged waste fluids through this gland</note>, is carried forward somewhat obliquely, with the right nerve extended toward the left, and the left toward the right. In its progress, and soon after its origin, both join together^f, and are mixed in such a way that you cannot distinguish the right from the left by any means. Indeed, it is so much so that the question is entirely empty whether the right nerve maintains the right position in this meeting, or whether it is carried in a continuous path toward the left. Since that union of nerves <note>now known as the optic chiasm</note> is nothing other than a common body from which both nerves would be said to be born, if only the origin of that body from the substance of the brain were not investigated, and if the separate beginnings of the nerves did not appear there.
<margin>d Book 1, Chap. 12, fig. 3, M.</margin>
<margin>e Book 7, fig. 16, A.</margin>
<margin>f Fig. 1, H; Book 7, fig. 13, M.</margin>
<margin>The path of the first pair of nerves.</margin>
The nerves to be led out of the skull after the meeting are soon separated from each other: and through the openings^h carved out in their own name, they fall forward into the seats of the eyes^i outside the cavity of the skull, and^k are entirely consumed in the eyes, not indeed implanted accurately in the center of the back part of the eye: but the nerve seeking the right eye is implanted more toward the right side of its back part: while the one that belongs to the left eye enters toward the left side of the center of the back part of the eye, and (just like the nerve of the right eye) when it has entered the eye, it degenerates or is expanded into a broad tunic, closest to the vitreous humor, and surrounding only the middle seat of the eye, and very similar to the dilated substance of the brain, and therefore soft, and anything but membranous. Whence even some anatomists have not deigned to call this tunic—which is called <term>amphiblestroides</term> <note>original: "ἀμφιβληστροειδὴς"; meaning net-like, this is the retina</note> from a certain image of a net—a "tunic" at all.
<margin>g Book 7, fig. 13, N, O.</margin>
<margin>h Book 1, Chap. 12, figs. 1, 3, E.</margin>
<margin>i Easily seen in Book 1, Chap. 12, fig. 1.</margin>
<margin>The entry into the eye, and the expansion into the tunic which we compare to a net.</margin>
But whether this tunic (or whatever it has seemed fit to call it) is considered by many the principal organ of sight, I will pursue in the description of the construction of the eye. For at present, to approach these nerves or eyes more lengthily would be entirely outside the purpose: since it has sufficed here to have said that the visual nerves [optic nerves] observe that path which we have reviewed without any propagation of branches: for they claim this for themselves as something peculiar and rare (just like the meeting of the right nerve with the left soon after birth). Furthermore, among the remaining nerves of the body, these alone are said to be perforated by a passage that can be judged by the senses, and for this reason are called <term>poroi optikoi</term> <note>original: "πόροι ὀπτικοί"; optical pores or channels</note> by the Greeks. However, I can by no means assert that a passage of this kind has ever occurred to me: even though I have approached the visual nerves of dogs still living, and of other large animals, for this reason alone: and of a man whose head was still warm from decapitation, and hardly a quarter of an hour [later]...

<meta>This page continues the detailed examination of the "first pair" of nerves (the optic nerves) from page 517. Vesalius is specifically investigating whether these nerves are hollow tubes—as was commonly believed in antiquity—and the nature of their intersection, known today as the optic chiasm.</meta>

OF ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY]

Since the brain was now exposed and the nerves had been cut away, I examined them most carefully and bathed them diligently with warm water. Just as a passage <note>the "meatus" or hollow channel</note> throughout the entire length of the nerves remained completely hidden from me, so it certainly did not reveal itself at the meeting point of the nerves. Nevertheless, it would have been necessary for such a passage to be prominent there, if indeed
<margin>The reason for the meeting of the nerves.</margin>
nerves met for this reason, according to the opinion of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galen (c. 129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose anatomical theories dominated Europe for 1,300 years</note>, so that single objects would not wrongly appear double to us. Furthermore, for those who daily argue fiercely about this meeting and this passage without actually inspecting the parts, I will not begrudge adding here two things I noticed during such a meeting, so that they may have arguments for their nonsense. In **Padua**, a young man who had been hanged was brought for public dissection; a year earlier, the executioner had gouged out his right eye. Then, we obtained a woman who suffered the same punishment, whose right eye had shriveled from early childhood, while the left remained perfectly intact. In the woman, the right nerve was seen to be much thinner than the left throughout its entire length—not only outside the skull cavity, but also at its origin and at the right side of the meeting of the nerves. Besides being thin, the right nerve also appeared harder and more reddish, as was indeed seen in the young man; however, in the young man, the right nerve did not yet yield much to the left in thickness or softness. To these cases was added another, in which we saw that the visual nerves <note>optic nerves</note>, in that meeting we are discussing, did not grow together nor touch one another. Instead, the right one turned slightly to the left at the place where it was to exit the skull, and the left turned slightly to the right—as if the nerves did not meet for the purpose of uniting, but rather to pass conveniently through their own holes out of the skull. This is especially true since, proceeding along this path, they are not inserted into the middle of the back of the eye.

<margin>
In the PRESENT figure, the path of the nerves we are describing here is expressed, and A indicates a small portion of the brain.
</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing two thick, anatomical nerves (the optic nerves) curving toward one another from the top (labeled 'A') to form an 'X' shape, but notably failing to touch or cross at the center, leaving a visible gap between them.</image-desc>

I know for certain that no one burning with a desire for knowledge of Nature's works would doubt how diligently and anxiously we questioned the relatives of that man whose nerves gaped in that manner, asking whether all things always appeared double to his eyes. But we could learn nothing other than that he had never complained about his sight and always possessed excellent vision, and his relatives had never heard anything about a doubling of things seen. Indeed, **Cassius** <note>likely Cassius Iatrosophista, an ancient medical author</note> and some others, when searching for the reason why the left side of the body is afflicted by paralysis <note>original: "resolutione"</note> when the right side of the brain is wounded or otherwise injured, assert that all nerves cross in an X-shape <note>original: "decussatim"</note> at their origin—or that nerves born from the right side of the brain and spinal cord are distributed to the left region of the body, and conversely, nerves from the left are carried to the right. This I consider a most elegant fiction, dreamed up while sleeping by those "questioners of problems." For the origins of the <margin>m 1. fig. K.</margin> second pair <note>the oculomotor nerves</note> of nerves, and then the <margin>n 1. fig. M, L.</margin> third and <margin>o 1. fig. Z.</margin> fourth pairs <note>the trigeminal and trochlear nerves in Vesalius’s classification</note>, are separated from each other by the width of several fingers. I shall say nothing of other nerves, nor mention that I have occasionally seen the visual nerves of pigs not as continuous tubes, but—just like the nerves of the legs—as if they were woven together from many small cords. I will not let the conversation drift into some other longer dispute, especially with those
->professors of dissection who falsely handed down to posterity that<-
->the right brain is entirely separated from the left.<-

<meta>catchword: DE SE- (Continuing to 'On the Second Pair')</meta>

<summary>Vesalius challenges Galenic theory by reporting anatomical observations of the optic nerves, specifically noting a rare case where the nerves did not touch at the chiasm, yet the patient did not suffer from double vision. He also refutes the idea that all nerves cross (decussate) at their origin to explain contralateral paralysis.</summary>
<keywords>optic nerves, optic chiasm, dissection, Padua, anatomical variation, Galen, double vision, decussation, nerve structure</keywords>

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a group of figures performing or observing an anatomical dissection on a body laid out on a table.</image-desc>The origin of the second<sup>a</sup> pair <note>modern: the oculomotor nerve, which controls most of the eye's movement</note> does not hang from the very bottom and middle of the brain’s base<sup>b</sup> (as far as the sides are concerned) in the same way as the nerves of sight<sup>c</sup> <note>original: "uisiorum", referring to the optic nerves</note> do. Furthermore, the nerves of the present pair are much less thick than the nerves of sight, although they surpass them in hardness and differ greatly from them in function. For they take their beginning from the sides of the brain's base a little further back than the nerves of sight, because this region of the brain is somewhat harder than that from which the origin of the sight nerves is taken. And this happens with good reason: for it was necessary that the nerves of the second pair, which are to be inserted into muscle, should be harder than the nerves of sight themselves. For the right nerve (which is always to be understood for the left as well in the series of nerves, unless something is specifically added to the discourse) is carried under the side of the brain’s base toward an<sup>d</sup> opening <term>foramen<gloss>a natural hole or passage through bone</gloss></term> in the foundation of the eye socket, which it shares with several other vessels. <image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial 'T' showing a group of scholars or medical practitioners engaged in discussion or study.</image-desc>THE THIRD pair takes its beginning from a double root on each side:<sup>a</sup> one indeed is thicker, to which you might appropriately give the name of the third pair;<sup>b</sup> the other, however, is far thinner and harder, and is joined to the thicker root neither at its very origin nor even in its progress. For the beginning of this latter root is separated from the origin of the former by a considerable distance toward the rear; so much so, indeed, that one might more truly assert that this thinner root is a peculiar pair in its own right, rather than a portion of the third pair. <margin>
The origin and path of the thinner root.
</margin> But since all the leading authorities on anatomy have assigned this to the third pair <note>modern: Vesalius's "third pair" corresponds primarily to the trigeminal nerve, though his classification differs from the modern 12-pair system</note>, nothing certainly prevents me, in my zeal for clearer teaching, from also treating that thin and posterior root with the third pair. However, I must first warn the studious that in the book *On the Dissection of the Nerves* (which I would hardly consider even a fragment of a book by **Galen** <note>Claudius Galen, the 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius frequently corrects</note>), it is incorrectly taught that the third pair is softer than the second. Furthermore, in the ninth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, Galen untruthfully asserted that the third pair is only then first distributed into two trunks, or into those roots which we have decided to describe here, when it has pierced the tough membrane of the brain <note>original: "duram cerebri membranam", the dura mater</note>, as if there were only a single trunk and a single beginning for both roots. 

Therefore, this thinner root of the third pair arises from the side of the brain's base, where the spinal cord<sup>c</sup> <term>dorsalis medulla<gloss>literally "the marrow of the back," the standard Renaissance term for the spinal cord</gloss></term> begins its start from the brain itself. The<sup>g</sup> first of these runs upward into the fat covering the muscles of the eye, and passes through<sup>h</sup> a specific opening to the skin of the forehead and the<sup>i</sup> muscular substance of this region, being set in charge of the movements of the forehead skin and the upper eyelid.<sup>k</sup> The second offshoot is led downward and is soon carried into<sup>l</sup> an opening carved out privately for itself, until it glides into the forward part of the upper jaw, where it is distributed in a multiple series into the<sup>m</sup> muscles moving the upper lip and the<sup>n</sup> wing of the nose outward on its side, and finally into the lip itself and the gums of the incisor teeth.<sup>o</sup> The third offshoot,<sup>p</sup> also using a private opening, approaches the cavity of the nostrils behind the caruncle <note>the small, pink nodule at the inner corner of the eye</note> visible in the inner corner, there turning into the<sup>q</sup> lining <term>tunica<gloss>a membrane or layer of tissue</gloss></term> of the nostrils, and extending a small branch<sup>q</sup> with a thin... <margin>

...and to the membranous muscle that draws the wing of the nose inward. The **fourth branch**, which is no less thick than those already mentioned, makes its way through a hole—or rather a fissure—that can be seen on the outermost side of the eye socket between the first bone of the upper jaw and the bone resembling a wedge <note>original: "cuneum imitans os", the sphenoid bone</note>. It heads toward the internal seat of the temporal muscle, where it is entirely consumed by that muscle.

<margin>The origin of the thicker root, and the sequence of its distribution.</margin>
The **thicker root of the third pair** <note>Vesalius's "third pair" includes what we now call the trigeminal nerve (Cranial Nerve V)</note> takes its beginning from the side of the brain’s base, though further forward and deeper—or rather closer to the middle between the right and left sides—than the root just described. It tends straight downward, passing through a hole <term>foramen<gloss>a natural passage or opening through bone</gloss></term> carved for it and the fourth pair of nerves. Immediately after its exit, it spreads out a branch which is twisted like the tendril of a vine or a gourd. It gradually becomes harder and eventually admits two small branches of the fifth pair of cranial nerves (whose sequence I shall review later). Joined with these, it is inserted into the temporal muscle; it also extends small branches into the muscle which, arising from the cheekbone, we specifically call the chewing muscle <term>mansorius<gloss>the masseter muscle, essential for mastication</gloss></term>. Finally, it offers small forks to the muscles moving the cheeks, and even to the skin of the face in the cheeks. 

After this thicker root of the third pair has produced this branch twisted like a tendril, it descends a bit further and derives a fork which, creeping forward, distributes offspring in a series to the gums of the molar teeth and to the teeth themselves. Then, before this larger root of the third pair is led downward to touch the tongue, it buds off a significant branch from its back part. This is inserted into the muscle hidden in the mouth that raises the lower jaw, and it enters a hole in the lower jaw <term>mandibular foramen<gloss>the opening on the inner surface of the lower jaw bone</gloss></term> which is visible where that muscle is inserted. That branch, having slipped into the hole, is carried forward and offers individual offspring to nearly all the roots of the teeth of that side of the lower jaw. We believe that by their benefit, the teeth, more than the other bones of man, clearly feel the encounter of things that cause pain. 

However, this entire branch is not consumed by the teeth; rather, a significant portion of it exits through a hole carved in the front of the jaw, deriving many small forks to the right side of the lower lip. But the greater portion of the thicker root of the third pair of nerves, when it is joined to the base of the tongue, forms the coating of the tongue along with the nerve of the other side, creating an instrument suited for distinguishing flavors. It then also dispenses tiny forks deeper into the substance of the tongue. We believe the third pair was created by the Artificer of things <note>Vesalius's term for the Creator or Nature</note> primarily for the sake of producing these forks and the coating of the tongue; and just as the first pair serves sight and the fifth serves hearing, so we agree this third pair serves taste.

### ON THE FOURTH PAIR OF CRANIAL NERVES.
#### Chapter VII.

<margin>
a 1, 2 fig. Z thinner than M. 14 fig. book 7 K.
b 1 fig. between D, E.
c 2, 3 fig. chapter 12 book Q.

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'H' decorated with three male figures in classical robes. One figure sits on an ornate bench while two others stand before him, gesturing as if engaged in a serious medical or philosophical consultation within a grand hall.</image-desc>
THIS pair is somewhat thinner and harder than the thicker root of the third pair. It arises from the beginning of the spinal medulla <note>the brainstem/spinal cord junction</note> a little further back than the third pair. However, stretched slightly forward, it is joined to the rear seat of the third pair and slips out from the cavity of the head (or the seat of the brain) to the palate through a hole shared by both. As soon as it arrives there, it is partitioned into certain small forks and blends into the coating of the palate. Since the coating of the palate is somewhat harder than the coating of the tongue, we believe it is right that the fourth pair takes its origin further back than the third pair, and consequently that the coating of the palate is endowed with a duller sense of feeling than the coating of the tongue.

## THE FIFTH PAIR OF CEREBRAL NERVES
### Their sequence. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing several cherub-like figures engaged in an academic or anatomical discussion around a table with books and instruments.</image-desc>

The **fifth pair**$^a$ is somewhat thicker than the fourth, and appears to arise from several small shoots joined together shortly after their origin. It takes its beginning from nearly the middle of the dorsal medulla <note>The "dorsal medulla" here refers to the brainstem, specifically the pons or medulla oblongata</note>,$^b$ from that part which extends from the origin of the medulla to the region where it slips from the skull into the vertebrae and is truly called the dorsal or spinal medulla. This entire fifth pair is carried through a hole$^c$ that is exceedingly winding and specifically carved for it, until it reaches the cavity prepared for the organ of hearing. In this cavity, the fifth pair is divided in various ways; it offers certain branches spread out like a membrane$^d$ to the seats of that cavity, constituting a primary part of the organ of hearing. In addition to these branches, it leads out two small nerves, each escaping through its own private hole.$^e$ One is indeed led through a transverse hole,$^f$ which also admits a small vein$^g$ running out into the organ of hearing; and this small nerve, not far from its exit, is joined with a branch of the third pair,$^h$ twisted like the tendril of a vine.$^i$ The other small nerve creeps through a hole$^k$ that is exceedingly narrow and remarkably winding, which does not admit a bristle or a lead wire inserted into it, and for that reason is called "blind" <term>caecum<gloss>The "blind" hole refers to the stylomastoid foramen or the facial canal</gloss></term> by anatomists. This small nerve is led transversely above the muscle$^l$ that, originating from the zygomatic bone, moves the lower jaw; but where it has crept forward to the anterior side of that muscle,$^m$ it is joined to the aforementioned branch of the third pair (which is entwined in the shape of a vine tendril), to be distributed into the skin of the cheeks and the muscles of the mouth that produce movement. These, finally, are the two small nerves which I said above were joined to that branch of the third pair.

<margin>
n Figure 1, near M, it arises as L.
o Figure 1, 2, near a, it arises as d. Figure 14, book 7, L.
p Figure 3, chapter 12, book 1, H under G.
q 6th muscle table, one at A, the other at D.
</margin>
<margin>A nerve taking its beginning near the root of the fifth pair.</margin>

Furthermore, just as$^n$ near the principal root of the third pair another root arises that is ascribed to the third pair, so in a similar manner near the fifth pair of nerves, a little further inward,$^o$ another root arises. This root is much more slender than the root of the fifth pair and somewhat harder. This extends upward toward the front under the base of the brain for some distance and pierces the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note>. It falls out of the skull through its own hole,$^p$ carved beneath the hole of the second pair, and is distributed into the temporal muscle$^q$ and into that muscle which, lying hidden in the mouth, is considered (along with others) the author of the upward movements of the lower jaw. One might consider this root, with its mate, as a peculiar distinct pair. However, lest I disturb the numbering of other anatomists (who were entirely ignorant of these roots), I shall ascribe them to the fifth pair—in the same way that others before me counted the smaller or thinner root of the third pair as part of the third pair.

<margin>r Figure 2, Q, R, b, c, d.</margin>
<margin>How many nerve branches are offered to the temporal muscle.</margin>

Thus, five branches$^r$ of nerves reach the temporal muscle: the first from the more slender root of the third pair, the second from the larger root, while the third and fourth are led out from the primary nerve of the fifth pair. The fifth is that nerve which I have just now numbered with the fifth pair. Nature does not seem to have extended so many offspring of nerves to the temporal muscle in vain or by chance; for she knew that this muscle, for its size, would perform the most powerful function of all the muscles in the body. Likewise, since she was well aware of how soft those nerves were which she led from the brain, she wished them to harden as much as possible through contact with the bones and the length of their journey, by a truly great providence. For it is obvious to everyone how cleverly she made the shoot that is entwined like a vine tendril harder, because it alone is in contact with the bone for a very small space; but she did not entwine the others, because they are stretched against the bones over a long interval, and some of them are even extended through winding and coiled passages of the bones.

Vesalius explains the anatomical reasoning for the complexity of these pathways, suggesting that bone contact helps "harden" the soft nerves for their functions.</summary>

AMONG the other pairs of nerves taking their origin in the cavity of the skull, none produces such a widely scattered offspring of branches, nor is inserted into so many and various parts, as the **sixth pair**$^a$ <note>The "sixth pair" in Vesalius’s system corresponds to the modern Vagus Nerve (Cranial Nerve X), along with the Glossopharyngeal (IX) and Accessory (XI) nerves.</note> of cerebral nerves. A little lower than the fifth pair, it takes its beginning from several distinct and separate shoots, which, being joined together right from the start, form a single nerve. This nerve exits through a hole$^b$ in the skull <note>The jugular foramen.</note> that simultaneously admits the smaller branch of the soporal artery <note>original: "arteriae soporalis"; the carotid artery, so named from the Greek 'karos' (deep sleep), as compressing it was known to cause stupor.</note> and the larger branch of the internal jugular vein$^c$. Not far from its exit, this nerve spreads a branch$^d$ to the muscles occupying the back of the neck, arranged in a numerous series of offspring; the most prominent of these$^e$ are extended to the second muscle of those moving the shoulder blade <note>likely the levator scapulae or trapezius</note>. The main trunk of the sixth pair itself—clinging to the soporal artery and the internal jugular$^f$, and joined to them by the intervention of a membrane$^g$—extends all the way to the sides of the larynx, where it receives a portion from the seventh pair$^h$ <note>Vesalius’s 7th pair is the modern Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)</note> and is increased by it. Then the sixth pair, having adopted this portion, offers small branches$^i$ transversely to the muscles of the larynx. These muscles are: two$^k$ belonging only to the first cartilage of the larynx, which, arising from the stomach or the back of the throat, are inserted into the sides of that cartilage; then two$^l$ occupying the base of the third cartilage, and two$^m$ connecting the first cartilage to the second. From here, the sixth pair, accompanied by the soporal artery and internal jugular$^n$, descends to the higher seat of the chest (thorax). It soon derives a notable branch$^o$ toward the side of the first thoracic vertebra; this branch creeps along the roots of the ribs under the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note> and receives certain shoots$^q$ from the nerves$^p$ stretched into the spaces between the ribs from the dorsal medulla <note>the spinal cord</note>. When this branch, increased by shoots of this kind, has passed the diaphragm$^r$ <note>original: "septum transversum"</note>, it is distributed into the organs serving nutrition, as you will soon hear. In addition to this branch, the nerve of the sixth pair near the upper part of the chest offers small branches$^s$ to the muscle$^t$ led from the breastbone and clavicle to the mastoid process of the head <note>the sternocleidomastoid muscle</note>, which serves the movements of the head; and also to the muscle$^u$ which approaches from the breast to the bone shaped like the letter upsilon <note>the hyoid bone, often called "hyoides" or "u-shaped"</note>; and furthermore to that muscle$^x$ which is carried from here to the lowest part of the first cartilage of the larynx. This is the series of both nerves of the sixth pair before they enter deeper into the cavity of the chest. What remains to be told will be described as soon as I have inserted a figure here into the text.

<margin>The right recurrent nerve.</margin>
Therefore, when the right nerve of the sixth pair enters the cavity of the chest <term>thorax</term> and creeps between the arteries and veins in the throat, it gives off from its inner side^a^ sometimes three,^b^ sometimes two successive small branches, which constitute the recurrent nerve of the right side.^c^ For these small branches are turned back around the^d^ artery that extends into the right armpit <note>The right subclavian artery.</note> as if around the wheel of a pulley; they join together and form a single nerve running upward along the right side of the windpipe. Soon from those branches (in place of which a single one is sometimes seen) one nerve is formed which seeks the right side of the windpipe: and being attached to it by the intervention of a membrane, it hastens all the way to the right side of the larynx,^e^ resting upon the gland which—corresponding to other glands neither in color nor substance—is attached here on the right side of the base of the larynx (just as there is another on the left). As soon as the nerve touches the larynx, it is divided into several offspring to be distributed into the muscles of its own side.

g Book 3, chap. 12, fig. C, D.

<margin>The left recurrent nerve.</margin>
Which muscles those may be, I shall add after I have followed the left recurrent nerve in my discourse to the larynx.^f^ Thus, the left nerve of the sixth pair, having now entered the cavity of the chest, cannot give off branches to be reflected upward from the artery that is to be propagated into the left arm; this is because that artery tends obliquely upward into the armpit, rather than transversely <note>Crosswise.</note> like the right artery.^g^ For the reflection of any cord is by no means as safely performed on an oblique object as on a transverse one; indeed, if a cord is wound around an oblique rod, it gradually climbs upward, never keeping the same seat for its reflection.

And for that reason, the left nerve descends for a distance toward the base of the heart, until^h^ outside the wrapping of the heart <note>The pericardium.</note> it touches the trunk of the great artery^i^ <note>The aortic arch.</note> as it unfolds downward toward the spine. And here soon^k^ three, or even^l^ fewer, shoots are led out from the nerve, which, being turned back at the trunk of the artery where it deflects toward the spine, are united with each other and constitute the left recurrent nerve. This nerve, hastening upward, is attached to the left side of the windpipe by the benefit of a membrane; and as soon as it touches the larynx, it is derived into branches no less than the right nerve, all of which end in the muscles of its side which have their heads downward. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY
# BOOK IV

<margin>n. At the end of figures 11, 12, 13, chapter 21, book 2. o. Figures 8 and 9 of the same chapter, a, b.</margin>
...is led, and the little tongue <note>epiglottis</note> of the larynx is opened. Furthermore, there are two [muscles] joining the third cartilage to the first, which close the small slit or little tongue of the larynx, and alone for the most part then withstand expiration when, during evacuation, we hold our breath by force, and meanwhile strive for expiration with the other muscles as much as possible. To these, besides several others, are added the muscles of the tongue, arising from the middle of the bone resembling the letter upsilon <note>The hyoid bone, shaped like the Greek letter $\upsilon$</note>, so that they may move the tongue.

<margin>Why the recurrent nerves are believed to be made. p. Figures 1 and 2, chapter 19, book 2, D, D.</margin>
Since therefore these present muscles obtain their "heads" <note>origins</note> lower down, and were going to pull the body to be moved downward, we believe it is necessary that the "animal spirit" <note>the vital force believed to travel through nerves</note> be led in some way upward to them from the lower parts. How much industry the immense Craftsman of our body <note>God</note> exerted in the winding of these nerves (which are called by the Greeks *palindromountes* <note>original: $\alpha\lambda\iota\nu\delta\rho o\mu o\tilde{\upsilon}\nu\tau\epsilon\varsigma$, meaning "running back" or "recurrent"</note>)—although you can recognize it from the dissection itself and this succinct narration of the distribution of the nerves—nevertheless I urge you to consult Galen. In the seventh book of *On the Use of the Parts*, he celebrates true hymns to God, and requires a more attentive mind than if you were standing by at the Eleusinian and Samothracian [mysteries], or any other divine celebration, intent on those things which are done and said by the priests. For Galen rightly persuades himself that the celebration handed down there is in no part inferior to these, nor does it show less the incredible wisdom and power of God the creator of all.

<margin>The remaining course of the sixth pair in the breadth of the chest. q. Figure 2, q. r. Figure 2, r. s. Figure 6, book 6, b. t. Figure 1 of the same. u. Figure 2, f. * Figures 14 and 15, book 5, T, V.</margin>
Furthermore, the nerves of the sixth pair <note>the Vagus nerve</note>, after they have sent out the recurrent ones and now look toward the base of the heart, disperse branches of a thickness worthy of note into the tunic of the lung and the membranous envelope of the heart <note>the pericardium</note>. Likewise, from the branches entwining the left side of the heart's envelope (and taken from the left nerve of the sixth pair), a certain small fork <note>furculus</note> permeates the heart's envelope there, where it is joined to the left side of the "arterial vein" <note>the pulmonary artery</note>. And this fork is exceedingly thin, and met only by one performing a dissection most accurately; it grows onto the arterial vein itself. Stretched toward the left side, though more toward the back, it is carried to the base of the heart, where it is soon consumed into offspring as slender as hairs, and is hardly proper to the surface of the heart’s base. What now remains of the nerves of the sixth pair is carried downward to the stomach; and indeed the right one attends to its right side, the left to its left. Soon, however, as the nerves are loosely attached to the stomach by the intervention of a membrane, they each divide into two branches, wound so obliquely along the stomach that the branches of the right nerve obtain its left side in their progress, and the left branches embrace the right side.

<margin>The course of the sixth pair into the organs of nutrition. x. Table 7 of muscles, r. y. Figure 2, t. z. Figure 2, u. & Figure 15, book 5, X. a. Figure 2, x. & Figure 12, book 5, T. & Figure 15, Y. b. Figure 2, h. c. Figure 2, i, i. d. Table 7 of muscles, q. e. Figure 2, y. Then see figures 3 and 4 of book 5 in order, where the course of these nerves occurs with the vein and artery. f. Figure 2, z.</margin>
And so these four present branches permeate the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note> along with the stomach <note>here referring to the esophagus</note>, offering no small forks to the septum in the passage. But they surround the upper mouth of the stomach <note>the cardia</note> in a very scattered series, spreading branches into the front and back parts of the body of the stomach. From those branches that entwine the right side of this orifice, a somewhat notable offshoot is taken, which, approaching the lower orifice of the stomach <note>the pylorus</note> through the upper parts of the stomach along its width, diffuses certain shoots in its progress to the front and back sides of the stomach. When indeed that offshoot has passed the lower orifice, it hastens into the hollow of the liver, spread over the portal vein, to be consumed there into the tunic of the liver. The branch of the right nerve of the sixth pair, which we taught is extended before the beginnings of the recurrent nerves under the tunic lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note>, and is increased by the meeting of other nerves running through the intervals of the same [ribs], as soon as it has passed the transverse septum [diaphragm] along with the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, it begins to diffuse offshoots. Indeed, it offers the first to the lower membrane of the omentum <note>the fatty apron of the abdomen</note>, going across to the hollow of the liver. This, in the path itself, shows a branch to the lower membrane of the omentum, which, stretched downward and divided into forks, is entwined both with the omentum membrane on the right side and also with the colon...

<summary>Vesalius describes the path of the Vagus nerve and its recurrent branches, arguing that their circuitous route is a divine design to provide motor function to the larynx from below. He then details the nerve's distribution to the heart, lungs, stomach, and liver.</summary>

After this, another branch, much thicker than the upper one, is drawn out for the membrane of the omentum <note>the fatty apron covering the bowels</note>; creeping along the right side of the base of the stomach, it communicates many offshoots to the stomach and to the omentum itself. Indeed, a second offshoot of the branch of the sixth pair, stretched along the roots of the ribs on the right side, distributes to the right kidney and the fatty membrane <note>the renal capsule</note> wrapped around it. Furthermore, it spreads a third offshoot, larger than those mentioned, to the right side of the mesentery, to be scattered into the intestines joined to the mesentery here. What remains of that branch then passes into the bladder, and in women, a small amount into the base of the uterus on the right side; for the bladder and uterus also borrow their own nerves from the spinal cord where it is led into the sacrum <note>the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>. In almost the same way, the branch of the nerve of the left sixth pair is distributed, stretched out along the roots of the ribs. For it grants an offshoot to the lower membrane of the omentum, stretched crosswise into the hollow of the spleen; in its progress, before it touches the spleen, it spreads two small forks, dispersed into the lower membrane of the omentum and the colon where it is near the stomach. Then it emits another offshoot, thicker than those forks, which, creeping through the left side of the base of the stomach, derives many buds for the stomach and the upper membrane of the omentum itself (by which that very offshoot is supported). Soon also, from the offshoots entering the hollow of the spleen, thin branches approach the left side of the stomach, accompanied by those veins and arteries which we said before were reflected here from the vessels seeking the spleen. The branch stretched out along the left ribs offers a second offshoot to the mesentery of its own side and to the intestines joined to it; after this, it presents a third to the left kidney, and finally, what remains of it sometimes embraces the left side of the bladder and the base of the uterus. I believe I have noticed small forks led from the offshoots scattered in the mesentery, along with the seminal veins and arteries, all the way to the testes. Such, then, is the series of the sixth pair of cranial nerves.

### ON THE SEVENTH PAIR OF CRANIAL NERVES
->of the brain. Chapter X.<-

<margin>

The seventh and last pair of cranial nerves <note>modern Hypoglossal nerve, CN XII</note>, just as it is harder than the other pairs, so too it arises from a harder beginning. For it begins from several roots at a distance from one another from the spinal cord <note>specifically the medulla oblongata</note> where it is just about to exit the skull. From here, stretched moderately forward and with its roots uniting into one, it falls through a hole <note>the hypoglossal canal</note> carved out specifically for it. As soon as this seventh pair has slipped out of the skull, it adheres to the sixth pair and dispenses several offshoots to the muscles that take their origin from the processes imitating a stylus <note>the styloid processes</note>. Among their number is one of the third pair of muscles peculiar to the bone resembling the letter upsilon <note>the hyoid bone</note>, and that muscle which pulls the lower jaw downward <note>the digastric muscle</note>, and another proper to the tongue. From here, the seventh pair, descending all the way to the root of the tongue, is divided into many offshoots, which are entwined into the muscles of the tongue, the hyoid bone, and into all the muscles of the larynx not enumerated in the chapter above, and they preside over the movements of those muscles. But besides those offshoots, the seventh pair offers a not insignificant portion of itself to the sixth pair of cranial nerves near the root of the tongue, increasing the sixth pair with that portion.

# THE FIRST OF THREE FIGURES, WHICH
## ARE SHARED BY THE
### following chapters.

THE PRESENT figure primarily serves the two subsequent figures, which show the bare sequence of nerves emerging from the spinal cord <note>original: *dorsalis medulla*</note>. For in this figure alone, the spinal cord is drawn from that seat which takes its beginning from the base of the brain, all the way to its extreme end, proceeding from the lower part of the sacrum <note>original: *os sacrum*; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note>.

<image-desc>An anatomical woodcut of the human spinal cord and medulla oblongata, shown in isolation. The central cord is depicted with numerous nerve roots branching off bilaterally. The illustration is annotated with capital letters (A through H) on the left side and clusters of numbers (3-7, 19, 24, 30) on the right side to identify specific anatomical features and nerve pairs.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>
*The beginning of the spinal cord, originating from the base of the brain.*

<margin>B</margin>
*In this region, the spinal cord, exiting the expanse of the skull <note>original: *caluaria*</note>, enters the first vertebra of the neck; thus, that part of it still residing in the skull and leading out the posterior five pairs of the nerves of the brain <note>the lower cranial nerves</note>, is measured from A to B.*

<margin>C</margin>
*At this location, the spinal cord is no longer carried downward as a simple and, as it were, solid thing; instead, it reflects the image of many small cords <note>original: *funiculorum*; this refers to the cauda equina or "horse's tail" at the base of the spine</note> which, joined together, extend straight down.*

<margin>3, 4, 5, 6, 7</margin>
*These characters mark the roots of the nerves proceeding from the spinal cord before it slips out of the skull. These are the roots of those pairs of brain nerves <note>cranial nerves</note> indicated by each character. The numbers placed on the right side of the figure indicate thirty pairs of nerves which are produced from the spinal cord while it is already situated within the bones of the back, as we shall explain in the index of the remaining characters.*

<margin>D, 7</margin>
*Where the spinal cord, now entering the bones of the back, leads out its first pair of nerves, B is seen; this, with D on the left side and character 7 on the right, denotes the interval of the spinal cord contained by the cervical <note>neck</note> vertebrae, producing seven pairs from them.*

<margin>E, 19</margin>
*E and 19 are applied to the twelfth pair of nerves which the spinal cord, contained within the thoracic <note>chest</note> vertebrae, produces. Thus, the eleven pairs consisting between D and E, or 7 and 19, are obvious without the help of characters.*

<margin>F, 24</margin>
*We have assigned F and 24 to the fifth pair of those nerves which the spinal cord, enclosed by the lumbar <note>lower back</note> vertebrae, sends out; so that between E and F, or between 19 and 24, the remaining four pairs assigned to the lumbar vertebrae also occur.*

<margin>G, 30</margin>
*We have assigned G and 30 to the sixth pair of nerves proceeding from the spinal cord situated in the sacrum, thus showing six pairs of nerves and the part of the spinal cord related to the sacrum.*

<margin>H</margin>
*The end of the spinal cord, which proceeds unpaired from the end of the sacrum <note>the filum terminale</note>.*

<image-desc>A full-page anatomical woodcut illustrating the human nervous system. The figure is a standing male form, rendered as a network of nerves. The brain and spinal cord (medulla dorsalis) are the central axis, with nerves branching out to the head, torso, arms, and legs. The skeletal structure and musculature are omitted to showcase the complexity of the peripheral nerves and plexuses. The entire diagram is meticulously labeled with small letters (Latin and Greek) and Arabic numerals (ranging from 1 to over 80) indicating specific nerves and anatomical features described in the accompanying text of the book.</image-desc>

<note>This illustration is one of the iconic "large figures" of Vesalius’s work. It demonstrates his revolutionary approach to anatomy: by removing the "distraction" of muscles and bones, he allows the reader to trace the continuous path of a nerve from the brain down to the fingertips and toes. The "thirty pairs" mentioned in the text refer to the spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal pair), which remains the standard anatomical count today.</note>

<margin>f 2,3</margin> An offshoot of the anterior branch of the fifth pair <note>The 5th cervical nerve</note>, which, hidden among the muscles, crawls to the top of the shoulder. The characters Γ, Γ <note>Greek Gamma</note> visible in the third figure denote the offshoots of this branch offered to the muscles that lift the <term>scapula<note>The shoulder blade.</note></term>.

<header>THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK IV.</header>

->§ 1 Whenever the figures 1, 2, or 3 of Chapter 11, Book 4 appear in the inner margin throughout this entire work, they refer to the illustrations provided at the beginning of this chapter.<-

## ON THE SPINAL CORD, AND THE
### number of nerves proceeding from it. Chapter XI.

<margin>a From the three figures belonging to this and the following chapters.</margin>
<margin>The difference between the spinal cord and the marrow of the bones.</margin>
<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'D' containing a scene of several infants or putti gathered around a table, engaged in a task that appears to be a medical dissection or anatomical demonstration.</image-desc>The <term>spinal cord<note>Original: "Dorsalis medulla," literally "marrow of the back." Vesalius is distinguishing the nervous tissue of the spine from the fatty marrow found inside other bones.</note></term>, corresponding in substance to the brain from which it takes its origin, becomes more compact and harder—much like the nerves themselves—the further it recedes from the brain and extends downward. Indeed, it differs greatly from the marrow of other bones, which is exceedingly moist and almost fluid; for one might compare that bone marrow, and especially its softer substance, to fat or tallow, stored in the cavities and small spaces at the ends of bones for the sake of nourishing and lubricating them. Furthermore, this bone marrow is not covered by the wrappings of the brain or the spinal cord, nor are there arteries and veins of such noteworthy importance spread over it; nor is it white or gleaming in the same way as the substance of the spinal cord or the brain. For these reasons, it is in no way similar to the brain and the spinal cord, nor does it have any connection with the organs of sense or the muscles, whereas the spinal cord claims for itself no small connection with the muscles.

<margin>b Figures 1 and 2, chapter 2, index c.</margin>
<margin>The necessity of creating the spinal cord.</margin>
Indeed, if the <term>Creator of things<note>Original: "Opifex," a term Vesalius frequently uses to refer to the divine or natural "Architect" of the body.</note></term> had not produced this—which others have been pleased to call the "long brain"—one of two things would follow. Either all parts of the body lower than the head (which receive no offshoots from the nerves of the ᵇ sixth pair of cranial nerves) would be destitute of voluntary motion and deprived of the sense of touch; or it would have been necessary for a nerve to be derived from the brain to every single part. But if they lacked motion, then man would no longer be an animal, but would correspond to a statue of stone or clay. To stretch out a tiny nerve from the brain into every single part, however, would be the work of a craftsman who placed no value on the safety of the nerves. For it was not safe to lead a thin nerve on such a long journey, where it might be ruptured or broken; nor indeed would it be safe for any other even stronger organs, much less a vein or an artery.ᶜ

<margin>c Figure of chapter 1, book 3, index b. Figure of chapter 6, indices B, D, 1. Figure of chapter 12, index A.</margin>
For these vessels, just like the spinal cord, arise large and ample from their own origin and are divided in various ways along their progress like the trunk of a tree; and when they approach the parts of the body, they offer them shoots to communicate the material originally offered to them. Hence, it was better for the spinal cord to germinate nerves at each joint—like a river flowing from the source of the brain through the region where it passes—acting as carriers of the animal faculty or spirit, just as the Creator of things has rightly engineered.

<margin>How the spinal cord must be fortified.</margin>
<margin>d Figure of chapter 14, book 1.</margin>
<margin>By bones.</margin>
Moreover, since the spinal cord is considered a second brain for almost all parts positioned below the head, it was also necessary that it be surrounded, much like the brain, ᵈ by a hard defense that is persistent in enduring injuries—a sort of bulwark. What kind of structure this is was discussed abundantly in the first book, while I was following the structure of the vertebrae of the back.

<margin>By membranous wrappings.</margin>
<margin>e In the first figures of book 7.</margin>
Furthermore, two membranes also embrace the spinal cord, ᵉ corresponding entirely in appearance to those in which the brain is wrapped, even if they do not match in their distance from one another. For it will be explained in the seventh book that the <term>thick membrane of the brain<note>The dura mater.</note></term> gaps away from the <term>thin membrane<note>The pia mater.</note></term> in the skull for the sake of the distension and contraction of the vessels of the thin membrane and of the brain itself. However, within the boundaries of the vertebrae where the membranes surround the spinal cord, the thick membrane touches the thin one. And in this one way the membranes differ; and also in that a certain third wrapping, remarkably strong and membranous, is drawn around the outside of those two membranes that cover the spinal cord.

<header>ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY]</header>

<margin>
Why the spinal cord is single.

How many pairs of nerves are divided from the spinal cord.

Figure 1, from D to E, or from character 7 to 19.
