</margin>

...because the <term>spinal cord<note>Original: "dorsalis medulla."</note></term> is contained within vertebrae that must be moved in various ways, unlike the brain, which is embraced by bones that are almost entirely immovable. I believe it escapes no one's notice that the spinal cord was rightly made single by Nature (just as the seat of the brain from which it takes its origin is single and simple); for it would have been plainly ridiculous, and unsuitable for many actions, for a human to be created with two backs, and because a stronger spinal cord creeps through the vertebrae as a single, simple path rather than a double one. However, how vain is the reasoning of <term>Galen<note>A highly influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose anatomical theories Vesalius often challenged based on direct dissection.</note></term>, by which he teaches that the cerebellum is simple so that the spinal cord might be single, we shall explain in the seventh book. Yet, certainly even in this place, the human spinal cord must be further considered: for through the entire neck and as far as the middle of the chest, and sometimes even somewhat lower, it is carried downward simple, undivided, and still soft, merely spreading nerves from itself at intervals. But when it has crept through the middle of the chest, so that it might be rendered fit for propagating nerves that are hard and primarily serve motion, it no longer descends as a single cord, but is cut into countless offspring. This is exactly as if you were to bind many frequent and very thin little strings together, stretched straight, to some membrane; and then, through the individual openings of the vertebrae or bones of the back through which the nerves leap out, you were to distribute one or two little strings from that shared bundle until only a single little string remained, corresponding to the end of the spinal cord. Furthermore, the nerves—which the spinal cord distributes as it is led through the vertebrae and gradually grows thinner in its progress—are counted by professors of dissection as sixty, and sometimes fifty-eight, comprising now thirty, now twenty-nine pairs. For from the part of the spinal cord contained by the seven vertebrae of the neck, seven pairs leap out. From the part of the cord carried through the vertebrae of the chest, twelve pairs hang; from the five vertebrae of the loins, five; and from the <term>sacrum<note>The large, triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note></term>, six. Nevertheless, the five lower pairs of nerves of the sacrum (if it is formed of six bones) can in a certain way be called double—as usually happens with the first two pairs led out from the neck—since the nerves are led forward and backward on both sides, having barely arisen from a single root. Indeed, the end of the spinal cord proceeding from the sacrum is not considered a nerve, nor does it end in branches that would deserve the name of nerves; although I have sometimes seen it, as it falls away from the sacrum, spread into three exceedingly short shoots, when the sacrum was formed of only five bones. In dogs and other animals, the number of pairs of nerves of the spinal cord differs according to the number of bones in the back.

PROVIDED THAT the types of articulations of the first vertebrae of the neck with the <term>occipital bone<note>The bone that forms the back and base of the skull.</note></term>, and likewise of the second vertebra with the first, which were handed down previously, have not escaped your memory, you will rightly admire at present the providence of Nature. For the first and second pairs of the neck, she did not follow the manner of the other nerves of the neck or chest, but carved out a path in a certain peculiar way—since she was hindered by the articulations of the first two vertebrae—and she engineered two origins for each pair (just as in the sacrum) on both sides: extending one to the front part of the body and the other to the back. ...index, and the posterior region of the spinal cord itself, Nature carved a cavity for the articulation<gloss>b</gloss> [of the first vertebra with the head]. Here also, by carving a cavity into the <term>occipital bone<note>The bone at the very back and base of the skull.</note></term>,<gloss>c</gloss> she created a hole common to both the first neck vertebra and the occipital bone itself. This was done lest, by chance, if she had carved an entire hole into that thin vertebra (as happens in dogs, who have a larger vertebra), the bone itself—which otherwise requires great strength—might be rendered weak by many perforations. Furthermore, so that this hole might be as narrow as possible, Nature made the posterior origin of the first pair slender, distributing it only into those muscles<gloss>d</gloss> which are inserted from the first neck vertebra into the occipital bone, and into<gloss>e</gloss> those which are implanted from the occipital bone into the <term>transverse processes<note>The bony projections on either side of a vertebra.</note></term> of that vertebra. ...lest anyone should think that [the nerve] is drawn out from the breastbone, the cartilages of the ribs, or the bodies of the vertebrae. Instead, we are convinced that it resides in the middle region of the whole <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septi"</note>, which is membranous. And so, it was worthwhile for the nerves that provide movement to those fibers to creep down from above, so that they might spread their power equally into its entire seat. If Nature had instead inserted the nerves into the parts of the diaphragm that grow from the breastbone, ribs, and vertebrae, the "end" of the diaphragm would be considered its middle; however, it is an axiom among professors of Anatomy that nerves extend into the *beginnings* of muscles rather than their *ends*. For this reason, the diaphragm receives its nerves only from the cervical vertebrae <note>the neck bones</note>. For it would be the mark of an ignorant craftsman, unaware of what is most suitable in a structure, to lead nerves through such a long progression when they could have been sent from the nearest locations. Therefore, for this reason, it was necessary for the nerves to be provided to the diaphragm from the higher parts. To ensure they were not led in an unseemly way throughout their entire journey through the thorax <note>the chest cavity</note>, Nature attached them to the membranes that partition the chest <note>the mediastinum</note>, securing one nerve on the outside of each membrane.

Truly, the remainder of the anterior branch of the fifth pair of cervical nerves shows no less industry on the part of the Creator; it is primarily inserted into the muscle by whose help we raise the arm <note>the deltoid muscle</note>. For Nature, extending certain small branches from this portion to the muscles that lift the shoulder blade <note>scapula</note>, first derives a nerve from the outer side of this portion. This nerve emerges outward and, split into many offshoots, entwines the skin that covers the muscle lifting the arm. Then the remaining portion, hidden deep within, as soon as it approaches the neck of the shoulder blade, is divided into two branches of unequal size. # THE SERIES OF TWELVE PAIRS OF NERVES
## of the spinal cord, contained within the vertebrae of the thorax, Chapter XIII.

<margin>The distribution of the eighth pair of nerves of the spinal cord, or the first of the thoracic pairs.</margin>
<margin>a Figure 2, 8. b Figure 3, u. c Muscle Table 8, C; Table 14, N. d Muscle Table 9, Γ, Δ. e Table 10, Γ. f 11 14, F. g Figures 2, 3, χ, or see figure for chapter 14. h Figure 2, y. i Muscle Table 4, d.</margin>

THE FIRST pair of thoracic nerves, emerging between the seventh cervical vertebra and the first of the thorax, in the manner of the five lower cervical pairs, if compared to the higher pairs of the spinal cord's nerves, will aptly be called the eighth. Therefore, as soon as this emerges, it is divided into two unequal branches: the posterior, which is also thinner, it twists backward to the spine, hidden among the muscles attached to the vertebrae here. From this branch in its progress, sprouts are received by the root of the muscle inserted from the first rib of the thorax into the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, which tilts the neck to the side (though toward the front). Then also those muscles which are placed over the movements of the neck and head toward the back obtain sprouts from this branch of the eighth pair. But that part of its branch which touches the spine of the seventh cervical vertebra is led outward: and again departing transversely from the spine, it offers offshoots to the lower seat of that muscle, which is counted as the second and larger of those moving the scapula. Furthermore, it also provides to the muscle inserted into the base of the scapula and drawing the scapula to the back, and finally to that which we have counted as the third of those moving the human thorax. But the anterior branch of the eighth pair, far more significant than the posterior, receives no small portion of the seventh, and sometimes even more of the ninth pair meeting with it: and being entirely mixed in various ways with the neighboring pairs, if you take away a single offshoot of it, it is carried into the arm. For from its lower seat, where it has already mixed itself with the nearest pairs, it sends an offshoot forward, which, carried along the path of the first rib of the thorax as far as the top of the breastbone, dispenses sprouts in its progress to the muscle of the thorax [extending] from the collarbone into the...

Furthermore,<sup>t</sup> the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and the rest following up to the first nerve of the loins—or the twentieth pair of the entire spinal marrow—are distributed in somewhat the same sequence. For all of them, as soon as they have leaped out from the sides of the vertebrae, are split into two parts: the smaller and more slender branch is twisted backward toward the spines of the vertebrae, lying hidden among the muscles growing onto the vertebrae. These are the ones which we reported here to be in charge of the movements of the back and chest. Specifically, the fourth of the movers of the human chest,<sup>u</sup> but in dogs and monkeys the sixth; then one of the sixth pair<sup>x</sup> of those moving the back, and soon also another<sup>y</sup> of the eighth pair of those moving the back, and around the upper vertebrae of the chest,<sup>z</sup> one of the first pair and<sup>a</sup> another of the second pair of those moving the head, and<sup>b</sup> another of the third pair, and<sup>c</sup> also another of the fourth pair of the muscles moving the back specifically. For the posterior branches of the thoracic nerves are scattered into these muscles; however, they are not entirely consumed in them. Thus, when they have already reached the tips of the spinal processes, they hasten outward, emerging between the meeting point of the muscles of the right and left sides, and are afterwards distributed into the muscles which take their origin from the tips of those spines they touch. From their class (besides some recently mentioned, especially one of the first pair of muscles moving the head) are<sup>d</sup> the muscle drawing the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term> to the back and inserted into the whole base of the scapula; and<sup>e</sup> the lower part of that muscle which we enumerate as the second of those moving the scapula, and which we compare to the hoods of monks <note>the trapezius muscle, named for its resemblance to a cowl</note>, and which in this part pulls the scapula downward; soon the fifth of the craftsmen of the movement of the human chest,<sup>f</sup> and<sup>g</sup> also that which brings the arm downward to the back <note>the latissimus dorsi</note>. And besides the fact that twigs are distributed into the muscles from the posterior branches of these pairs, some also strive toward the skin spread over the back, although less frequently than the nerves extended into the skin of the arm, or chest, or neck. Moreover, the anterior branches of these present pairs<sup>h</sup> offer twigs to the branch of the sixth pair of cranial nerves<sup>i</sup> which is extended at the roots of the ribs under the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note>, and are increased by those twigs. Then the present branches, offered to the spaces between the ribs,<sup>k</sup> are accompanied by a vein and likewise<sup>l</sup> an artery, and carried in their own groove <term>sinus</term><sup>m</sup> carved into the inner and lower seat of the ribs, they hasten forward following the path of the ribs. For the branches extended to the true ribs reach as far as the breastbone; but the branches carried along the false ribs...

<margin>n Figure 2, d, g. / o then the characters of the left side of Figure 2. / o 7 Table L. / p 3 Table Δ. / q 5 Table Γ. / r 10 Table θ. / s 3 Table θ.</margin>
...do not stop along with those [ribs], but rather they creep forward into the anterior parts of the abdomen over the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. From these branches, a very scattered series of offshoots is spread into the muscles laid upon the chest, among which is the second of the muscles moving the thorax, the one that moves the arm toward the chest <note>the pectoralis major</note>, the one that brings the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term> toward the chest <note>the pectoralis minor</note>, the one that pulls the arm downward <note>the latissimus dorsi</note>, and the obliquely descending muscle of the abdomen <note>the external oblique</note>. For into these muscles, offshoots are provided from the intercostal nerves, each one reflected toward the ribs, veins, arteries, and ligaments with such industry that they perfectly follow the path of the fibers of the muscles to which they are extended. And just as offshoots are provided to these muscles laid on the chest from the intercostal nerves, so too are branches communicated to the abdominal muscles from the nerves passing over the "false" ribs, likewise following the entry of the fibers of those muscles they serve. From the offshoots entwining the muscles, small nerves are also provided to the skin of the chest—not indeed in a fixed or never-wavering sequence, but dismissively, in exactly the same way
<margin>Nerves seeking the nipple.</margin>
as the wandering branches of vessels, called "outflows" <note>original: ἀποῤῥοὰς (aporrhoas)</note> by the Greeks, are distributed. However various and inconsistent this series of nerves seeking the skin may be, Nature nevertheless—fearing that a mother might sometimes harshly deny the breast to a tender infant seeking its familiar food—wished to impart an exact sense of feeling to the nipple, so that the touch of the infant's tender lips and soft tongue would affect it with a pleasure by which humans are enticed to offer the breast more readily to be sucked and handled. And accordingly, from the nerves that creep through the fourth interval between the ribs, <margin>t Figure 2, v.</margin> offshoots are spread into the muscle by whose benefit we bring the arm toward the chest; and from those offshoots, small branches reach the nipple, which consists of a substance similar <margin>u Figure 3 of the table for chapter 49, book 2, E, E.</margin> to that from which the penis is formed <note>Vesalius is referring to the erectile nature of the nipple tissue</note>. Furthermore, just as these present branches are considered in a way peculiar to the twelfth pair of nerves, so it must be specifically ascribed to the eighteenth and nineteenth pairs <margin>x at the side of characters 18, 19.</margin> that they offer branches to the beginning of the sixth muscle moving the thigh, which we mentioned much earlier arises here from the sides of the vertebrae. <margin>y 8th muscle, Table θ.</margin>

To make the drawing clearer, I have represented all the branches that lead from the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth pairs to somewhere other than the arm as if they were cut off; whereas on the contrary, all are visible in the figure placed at the end of this book, which expresses the image of this plexus in such a way that it should by no means be a burden to look at that one also when the occasion of this plexus arises. <margin>a Figure 2, characters 5, 6, 7. b Figure 2, characters 8, 9. c Figures 2 and 3, π, ρ, τ, φ, *, ψ. From which pairs the nerves are led into the arm.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative initial letter A featuring infants or cherubs engaged in a playful yet macabre scene with medical instruments and a human skull, set within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc> Six nerves are distributed to the arm from the fifth, sixth, and seventh pairs of cervical nerves <note>nerves of the neck</note>, and then from the first and second pairs of the thorax <note>chest</note>—or rather, the eighth and ninth^b pairs contained within the vertebrae of the entire spinal cord. I shall follow the sequence of these nerves shortly, after I have added that the nerves destined for the arm, immediately from their origin at the sides of the vertebrae, are so mutually mixed and joined, and again mutually divided, and once more brought together, and finally separated, that you could by no means say which nerve of the arm depends on this or that pair. Rather, you might more truly assert that the six principal nerves take their beginning from a certain mixture, a heap of nerves, and a reticulated <term>plexus</term> <note>a network of intersecting nerves</note>. This entanglement is so elegant that artists perhaps first learned how to mix and join the small cords hanging from Cardinals’ hats by copying its form. I believe no one doubts that Nature uses this peculiar and most pleasant-to-behold artifice to make the nerves, which must be led through a very long journey, harder and more persistent in warding off injuries—especially if one also observes the entanglement of the nerves seeking the leg, and does not meanwhile rely too much on Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose works were the standard for 1,300 years</note> in the first book of *On Affected Places*.
<margin>The entanglement of the nerves entering the arm.</margin>

<margin>d Near the region of the sacrum, in Figure 2 and the last figure of this book. e Figures 2 and 3, π. f Figures 2 and 3, R. g 10th muscle table, Δ. The first nerve.</margin>
Otherwise, the first nerve entering the arm is an offshoot of the branches of that fifth pair of cervical nerves^f, which is distributed into the seat of the muscle that lifts the arm <note>the deltoid</note> arising from the spine of the shoulder blade <term>scapula</term>. This offshoot is spread only into the skin of the outer region of the arm a little below the middle of the arm’s length, and there it ends. Indeed, another slender branch^h entwines the lower skin of this region; this branch, emerging from the depths in the same manner as the aforementioned offshoot, is issued from that nerve which will be the fourth^i of the nerves of the arm. And this branch offers shoots not only to that skin, but also to the skin that embraces the outer and posterior part of the elbow joint at the shoulder <note>the humerus</note>. These present nerves, as well as all those approaching the skin, are beautifully supported by the membrane which, along with many others, I have chosen to call "fleshy" <note>the panniculus carnosus, or superficial fascia</note>. They creep forward between this membrane and the skin, and in humans, they are also immersed in much fat, binding that membrane tenaciously to the skin, yet they are as slender as hairs. Furthermore, they do not always retain the same sequence in position, number, and thickness; just as I reported before regarding the smaller vessels, neither a precise number, nor position, nor magnitude is accurately observed.
<margin>h Figure 3, character 3; last figure, g. i Figures 2 and 3, φ; last figure, c. Nerves entering the skin do not always display the same sequence.</margin>

<margin>k Figures 2 and 3, χ; last figure, S. The entry of the second nerve.</margin>
Furthermore, the other five nerves enter the arm through the armpit <term>axilla</term>, and they are spread into more branches than the first, and each is seen to be larger or thicker. The second nerve^k seeking the arm takes its beginning from the entanglement which I said the nerves entering the arm form at the sides of the vertebrae. For this reason, no one can truly ascribe this nerve to any single pair, since that "weave" is constituted not by one, but by several pairs of nerves. Otherwise, that nerve enters the arm beneath the anterior muscle of those that flex the elbow^l <note>the biceps or brachialis</note>. For where the two heads of that muscle are about to join, that nerve is first carried into the arm; at which place also the muscle bringing the arm toward the chest^m <note>the pectoralis major</note> effects its insertion along the length of the humerus. Just as also the muscle lifting the arm^n <note>the deltoid</note> is implanted there transversely into the humerus—besides the insertion which the muscle^o attempts in almost this same region, which, arising from the lower rib of the shoulder blade, pulls the arm backward. And finally, the insertion of that muscle^p also meets those dissecting in that area, by whose benefit the arm is driven downward toward the lower parts of the back <note>the latissimus dorsi</note>. The second nerve seeking the arm is therefore placed beneath the first of those flexing the elbow.

it touches the tubercle <note>the lateral epicondyle</note> of the humerus, resting upon its posterior side, where we have said Nature specifically carved a groove$^n$ <note>the radial groove</note> in this nerve's name, so that the nerve, hidden by muscles and here intended to be scattered into numerous offspring, might be carried safely. For as soon as$^o$ that nerve is led into the elbow, it puts forth a branch which, emerging from the depths, creeps forward in a wandering path under the skin all the way to the wrist <term>brachiale; the carpal bones or wrist region</term>, leading out frequent little forks in its progress, by which the skin covering the outer side of the elbow is woven together. Then the fourth nerve is split into two$^p$ trunks, hidden in the depths just like their root. One of these$^q$ is higher than the other and is extended along the radius; the other, which sits lower, is carried downward along the ulna. The higher one$^r$ reaches deep between the upper side of the muscle that extends the wrist with a double tendon <note>the extensor carpi radialis</note> and the outer or lower side of the long muscle that leads the radius into pronation <note>the brachioradialis</note>, and as it strives toward the wrist, it communicates slender little branches in its progress to both muscles by which it is attended and hidden. But when this higher branch approaches the wrist$^s$, it creeps across the transverse ligament, covering the double * tendon that extends the wrist on the outer side of the radius. Moreover, as soon as this branch of the present fourth nerve$^t$ touches the outer side of the wrist$^u$, it is divided into two offshoots: one of which is offered to the outer region of the thumb by a double fork; the other, being cut into two offspring, reaches one to the index finger (to be consumed on its outer side, also by a double fork) and grants the other to the middle finger, applying it as a simple and undivided branch to the inner side of that finger’s outer surface. The lower branch of the fourth nerve, extended toward the ulna$^x$, as it enters the elbow$^y$ at the point of bifurcation, immediately leads out frequent offspring: first, it grants a branch to the head$^z$ of the muscle that extends the index, middle, and ring fingers; second, to the head of the muscle by whose aid the little finger is extended; and third, it offers one$^a$ to the muscle extending the wrist with a simple tendon. In its very progress along the ulna$^b$, it displays offshoots$^d$ to three origins of muscles leading from this source$^c$. The first of these muscles is the shorter one seen leading the radius into pronation; next$^e$ is that which spreads a triple tendon, and connects one to the wrist bone that supports the first bone of the thumb, the second to the first bone of the thumb, and the third to the second and third bones of the thumb. Then there is the muscle which, inserted into the three bones of the thumb, leads the thumb toward the index finger by extending it. Next is the muscle by whose benefit the index, and sometimes also the middle finger, are drawn away to the side from the thumb. What remains of this branch$^f$ does not climb the wrist, and much less is it consumed in the smaller fingers; but the whole of it ends here at the root of the wrist, entwining the joint of the wrist and the ulna with several twigs. In this very manner, the fourth nerve is scattered into branches.

For, undivided$^h$ between the inner of the muscles extending the elbow <note>the triceps</note> and the posterior of those flexing the elbow <note>the brachialis</note>, it is extended, hidden along the inner side of the arm, until$^i$ it touches the inner tubercle of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle</note>. It is reflected to the posterior side of this tubercle, having here a specifically designated$^k$ groove by which it is aptly carried into the elbow. For just as the third nerve <note>the median nerve</note> was said to occupy the anterior side of the inner tubercle of the humerus, so indeed this fifth nerve sits on the posterior side of that tubercle, and is arranged in a sequence somewhat equal to the third. For from$^l$ these two present nerves$^l$, offshoots are offered to all the muscles occupying the inner side of the elbow, which borrow their origin both from the inner tubercle of the humerus and from the ulna and radius themselves. <meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Vesalius described the distribution of the third nerve (median) and fifth nerve (ulnar) as they supply the muscles of the forearm. This page continues the path of the fifth nerve into the hand and provides a practical guide for how readers can test these nerve paths on their own bodies.</meta>

->ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY<-

From here, gliding out from the depths, it is extended along the ulna into the external part of the elbow. When it reaches the external part of the wrist <term>brachialis; the carpal region</term>, it spreads branches into the external region of those fingers into which <margin>m. Character 36 of Figure 3 led out from Φ.</margin> the fourth nerve <note>the radial nerve</note> sent no offspring. Therefore, that branch of the fifth nerve <note>the ulnar nerve</note> is divided into three branches: the first of which approaches the external part of the little finger <term>minimus digitus</term> with a double fork; the second is likewise extended with a double fork to the external part of the ring finger <term>anularis digitus</term>; while the third, undivided, is entwined with the external side of the outer region of the middle finger <term>medius digitus</term>. Truly, because the fifth nerve spreads this branch extended to the external part of the hand, we have subsequently seen that the fifth nerve does not always distribute as many forks into the internal part of the hand as I have described. For more than once I have observed that the external side of the internal part of the middle finger and the internal side of the ring finger also receive forks from the third nerve <note>the median nerve</note>, with the fifth nerve then extending only two branches to the internal part of the little finger and one to the internal part of the ring finger.

You will be able to observe this described arrangement of nerves in the hand <margin>How one can experience the arrangement of nerves in the arms without dissection.</margin> quite pleasantly in yourself, provided that you compress the nerves of one hand with the thumb or by leaning your elbow against a bone, so that you block the passage of the animal spirit <note>the substance then believed to flow through nerves to produce sensation and motion</note> by the compression, and the part into which the nerves are inserted becomes numb. Indeed, this is done most conveniently near the joint of the elbow where it is not covered by many clothes, or (as in obese women) not clothed in much fat. For if you compress the fourth nerve <note>the radial nerve</note> for a while with your thumb, you will feel the external part of the thumb <term>pollex</term> and index finger, and also the internal side of the external part of the middle finger, grow numb. However, it escapes no one—unless they have listened to the arrangement of the fourth nerve with a deaf ear—that to compress the fourth nerve, one must strike the thumb forcefully between the posterior process of the ulna <note>the olecranon</note> and the external tubercle of the humerus <note>the lateral epicondyle</note>.

Now, if you intend to compress the fifth nerve, and you move your thumb forcefully to the posterior part of the internal tubercle <note>the medial epicondyle, or the "funny bone" area</note>, soon the internal and external parts of the little finger and the ring finger, and the lower part of the middle finger, will experience numbness. But if with greater effort you compress the anterior part of the internal tubercle of the humerus, <margin>That sensation can perish while motion is preserved, and vice versa.</margin> and thus obstruct the third nerve, immediately the internal parts of the thumb and index finger, and part of the middle finger, will suffer from numbness.

While you are exploring these things, consider likewise how slight a thing it is that sometimes motion perishes while sensation is still intact, and sensation is also abolished while motion remains whole. For, to remain silent about other nerves (and so as not to seek examples from more hidden things), suppose that by a wound or other affliction, the fourth nerve is cut where it reflects along the back of the humerus, or even where it begins from the reticular plexus lying at the sides of the vertebrae; or else it is so spoiled by an influx of humor <note>bodily fluids</note> or some evil of that kind that the animal spirit is not led through it. If the fifth nerve remains meanwhile unhurt (as is very easily done) and intact, will not the extension of the little finger and ring finger be lost, though their sensation is not impaired? For the fifth nerve, which supplies sensation, is unhurt; but because of the fault of the fourth nerve, the function of the muscles extending the fingers is cut off. What if by chance the fifth nerve were bruised or otherwise injured while the fourth remains intact: would not the little finger and ring finger grow numb, while their motion is not corrupted? And just as I have proposed these things concerning the fourth and fifth nerves for the sake of example, so indeed it is very easy for him from whom the arrangement of nerves and the nature of muscles do not escape to weigh and imagine how sensation is sometimes abolished while motion is uninjured, <margin>Book 1, *On the Diagnosis of Afflicted Places*.</margin> and sometimes motion is corrupted while sensation is preserved. Nor is it necessary to turn to the idea that a greater force of the animal spirit is required for motion than for sensation; and much less should the reasoning of certain anatomists be admitted, by which they imagine that certain forks of the nerves are in charge of motion only, and others in charge of sensation. As if indeed any fork of the nerves [could lack] the sense of touch...

...would be destitute of the sense of touch, and indeed any part of the body, by its essence or constitution, is not resistant to sensation, obtaining the power of touch from whatever nerve sprout creeps through it. But because these matters look elsewhere, we shall also briefly describe the path of the sixth nerve <note>original: "sexti nerui"; in Vesalius’s system, this is the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm</note> (which remains to be told). The origin of this nerve arises from the lowest seat of the "net" <note>the brachial plexus</note> already mentioned many times; it hastens through the armpit <term>axilla</term> into the arm without being hidden in the depths, but lying beneath the internal skin of the arm. It approaches the internal tubercle of the humerus <term>the inner bump of the elbow</term>, frequently producing offspring to the neighboring parts of the skin through which it creeps during its progress. At the internal tubercle of the humerus, it is divided into many branches, partly resting upon and partly lying beneath the offsets of the axillary vein stretched out under the skin. These are distributed downward in a numerous series of offsets along the ulna <note>the inner bone of the forearm</note>, led between the skin and the fleshy membrane, and ceasing before they reach the wrist <term>brachiale</term>, always extended along the lower region of the elbow or the ulna. This present nerve corresponds in thickness to the second nerve <note>the musculocutaneous nerve</note> where it approaches the elbow. However, the fifth nerve <note>the ulnar nerve</note> matches the third <note>the median nerve</note> in thickness near the elbow. In the armpit, the third is seen to be more slender than the fifth, and the second is then nearly similar to it, namely before it has mixed a portion of itself with the third. And so the fifth, third, and second nerves are somewhat thicker than the sixth at their entry into the armpit. But the fullest of all is the one I have listed as the fourth <note>the radial nerve</note>, just as the one reviewed as the first <note>the axillary nerve</note> occurs as extremely slender.

The nerves of the spinal cord <term>dorsalis medulla</term> enclosed by the lumbar vertebrae agree for the most part with the nerves of the thoracic vertebrae in this: that branches are led backward from each into the muscles attached to the vertebrae. Here, the fourth of the muscles moving the human thorax is joined to the vertebrae, then the eleventh of those moving the back, and finally the thirteenth which is spread beneath it. Offspring are offered to these muscles from the posterior branches while they are still hidden and led to the spines of the vertebrae. But when the branches proceed from the mutual connection of the muscles of both sides and from the very tips of the spines, they run out again to the sides, woven chiefly into the skin and the muscle <note>the latissimus dorsi</note> by whose help we move the arm toward the lower parts of the back. The anterior branches of these pairs are distributed into the muscles of the abdomen, and into that muscle which draws the arm toward the lower parts of the back, and even into the skin itself, as well as into the ninth muscle moving the back, and that which is numbered by me as the sixth of those moving the femur <note>the psoas major</note>. Then, from the twenty-first pair (or the second of the loins), a very small sprout is led to the testis together with the seminal artery of its side—provided that no offspring reach the testes from the branches of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>the vagus nerve</note> stretched out at the roots of the ribs and propagated into the intestines; for we sometimes observe sprouts extended to the testes from those branches as well. Furthermore, from the anterior branches of the first three pairs leaping forth from the lumbar vertebrae, sprouts are also diffused which approach the recently mentioned branches of the sixth pair <note>the sympathetic trunk</note> stretched out at the roots of the ribs, and increase them. But from the three lower pairs slipping out from the lumbar vertebrae, nerves that are certainly not the smallest approach the leg <term>crus</term>; in what sequence they are distributed in that part, I shall follow in the second chapter from this one.

We first explained in the first book how beautifully Galen's descriptions of the sacred bone <note>original: "os sacrum"; the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</note> correspond to one another, and finally how they agree with the human bone. We added that among the six bones of the human sacrum, openings <term>foramina</term> are carved in both the front and back positions; indeed, the series of human nerves differs greatly from the series found in dogs and long-tailed monkeys. And <sup>b</sup> first, one pair—in humans as well as in four-legged animals—emerges between the first bone of the sacrum and the lowest vertebra of the loins <term>the lumbar vertebrae</term>, in the same manner as the pairs of nerves exit from the lumbar vertebrae. Soon after its exit, it spreads a branch toward the back, just like the higher pairs do; this branch is distributed similarly to the posterior branches of those pairs. Specifically, from that posterior branch of the first sacral pair, a <sup>c</sup> notable offset is spread into the muscles originating from the hip bone <term>the ilium</term>, and especially into the <sup>d</sup> first of those moving the thigh. Then, substantial descendants of that offset are derived into the skin covering the buttocks. The main portion of the anterior branch of this pair is mixed with the nerves to be led down into the leg. For it is not entirely consumed by the leg, since an <sup>e</sup> offset is extended from it along the inner surface of the hip bone, offering small shoots to the abdominal muscles and likewise to that <sup>f</sup> muscle which I have listed as the seventh of those moving the thigh, which arises from the inner surface of the hip bone.

<sup>g</sup> Otherwise, the five lower pairs of sacral nerves emerge in a unique way. Before they slip out from the bone itself, they are doubled on each side: one nerve on each side from each pair emerges toward the front, and one likewise on each side toward the back. This series is seen in humans. However, in monkeys and dogs, another arrangement occurs. Just as there are only three pairs of sacral nerves in them, so also only the two lower ones fall out anteriorly and posteriorly. Then the remaining pairs (which are seen in great number in dogs and long-tailed monkeys) emerge from the sides of the tailbone <note>original: "ossis coccygis"</note>—to speak of those animals in that way—though more toward the back, in the same way that nerves emerge from the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. Meanwhile, from the human bone we call the coccyx, not a single nerve leaps out. Thus, it is not at all surprising if I, in recounting these pairs of nerves, deviate far from Galen’s opinion in his book *On Bones*. Therefore, the five lower sacral pairs primarily distribute the nerves falling out toward the back to the muscles occupying the posterior seat of the hip bone and the sacrum. Among these, on the right side, is the <sup>h</sup> eleventh muscle of those moving the back, and then the <sup>i</sup> thirteenth, besides the membrane-like beginning of the <sup>k</sup> muscle that drives the arm toward the lower parts of the back, and the <sup>*</sup> fourth of the movers of the human thorax. Likewise, the first four muscles moving the thigh, and finally the skin covering the buttocks, which itself is also gifted with several offsets from these nerves.

# THE MANNER OF DISTRIBUTION FOR THE NERVES OF THE THIGH, THE SHIN, AND THE FOOT. Chapter XVII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'R' depicting a scholar or physician seated at a lectern in a study, surrounded by books and shelves.</image-desc>
TO THE LEG, near the start of the thigh, from the lumbar vertebrae of the spinal cord and the pairs of nerves enclosed by the sacred bone [sacrum], <sup>a</sup> four nerves are presented. These proceed from a kind of net-like network <term>plexus; a branching network of vessels or nerves</term> in the same way that we previously reported the main nerves seeking the arm are born; although the entanglement of nerves in the neck is more varied than here at the loins and the sacred bone. These nerves did not obtain the same thickness, and much less an equal sequence and path. For the first and third that will be recounted are slender. However, the second is found to be thicker than those two, though it may also be thin at times. But the fourth far surpasses the thickness of those three joined together.

<margin>Series of the first nerve.</margin>
The first <sup>b</sup> takes its origin from the uppermost part of the network of nerves belonging to the leg, specifically where the anterior branch of the third lumbar pair (which is twenty-second in order in the whole spine) is mixed with the fourth lumbar pair. This nerve, resting upon the <sup>c</sup> flesh of the loins and spread under the membrane of the abdomen <term>peritoneum</term>, falls into the thigh along the outer side of the <sup>d</sup> tendon of the sixth muscle moving the thigh, which together with the <sup>e</sup> seventh muscle responsible for thigh movement stretches here above the hip bone <term>ischium</term> to the smaller process of the thigh bone <term>the lesser trochanter</term>. As soon as that nerve touches the thigh, <sup>f</sup> it brings forth a branch extended to the skin a little less than as far as the knee, which is drawn over the front part of the thigh toward its outer side. Furthermore, <sup>g</sup> the larger portion of this nerve, hiding in the depths, derives <sup>h</sup> several offshoots for the first muscle moving the shin <term>the tibia</term>, which takes its beginning from the front part of the appendix of the flank bone <term>the ilium</term>; then also to the <sup>i</sup> seventh muscle moving the shin, which arises from the root of the greater process of the thigh bone <term>the greater trochanter</term>; soon also for the ninth muscle responsible for shin movements, and with those muscles, the larger portion of this first nerve is drawn downward and terminates <sup>k</sup> higher than where the knee joint stands.

And just as that vein spreads various offspring in its progress to the skin bordering it, so indeed here also the branch of the second nerve seeking the leg, contiguous in its whole path to the front part of that vein, scatters offspring everywhere into the skin; of which <sup>p</sup> those are the principal ones which it offers to the front and lower regions of the knee toward the back of the knee <term>popliteus</term>. ### The series of the fourth nerve.
<margin>e Table 16 of the muscles, Δ. f Table 5, Φ, ε. g Figures 2, 3, character 71. Last figure 1 and also Table 10 of the muscles, 7.</margin>
The fourth nerve of the leg follows the third in its origin, but it is six times thicker, and is composed primarily of the anterior branches of the twenty-fifth and the three succeeding pairs [of spinal nerves]: it is not only the thickest of all nerves in the body, but also, since it obtains its beginning here from what is almost the end of the spinal cord, it is the hardest and likewise the strongest. For it will soon be taught that the skin situated above the knee on the posterior side of the thigh obtains branches from <margin>l Figure 2, character 74.</margin> ^l^ another offshoot of the fourth nerve. # THE FOURTH BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY
<page-num>551</page-num>

<margin>Why the fourth nerve seems to consist of several cords. *Galen*, Book 3 of *Anatomical Procedures*.</margin>

<margin>z figure character 76.</margin>

...just as if it were a single nerve, and not (as *Galen* teaches) a double one. I have described its course along the entire length of the thigh: for in humans, the whole nerve is contained within a single boundary. And if one were to strip away the membrane covering it with one's fingernails and attempt to divide it into two nerves (which is easily done if you move your hand upward from the spot where the nerve splits into two near the lower heads of the femur to the middle of the thigh), it would also be possible to divide it into many nerves by this same method. For it is nothing other than several nerves stretched out like many straight cords <term>funiculi; small cords or fibers</term> and surrounded by membranes. Therefore, by the same logic that someone might argue the fourth nerve is double, I would assert it is composed of eighteen nerves, since sometimes that many small portions or cords are found by anyone who counts them carefully. However many parts the fourth nerve consists of, in the popliteal space <note>the area behind the knee</note>, as I said before, the whole nerve is divided into two unequal trunks.

The **outer branch** <note>the common peroneal nerve</note>, which is also the thinner one, creeps toward the connection of the fibula with the tibia. It soon gives off a branch that extends under the skin along the outer side of the tibia and the outer ankle <term>malleolus</term>, all the way to the outer side of the foot and the little toe, providing thin shoots to the adjacent skin along its entire path. But the main portion of this outer trunk, passing beneath the head of the **seventh** muscle moving the foot <note>the peroneus longus</note>, also spreads a branch from deep beneath the skin, running past the middle of the tibia's length and covering the front of the tibia. The rest of this main portion descends along the outer side of the fibula, hidden between that **seventh** muscle and the **eighth** of those moving the foot <note>the peroneus brevis</note>, creeping along until those muscles end in distinct tendons and begin to turn toward the outer ankle. The **inner branch** <note>the tibial nerve</note>, which is also the thicker of the division formed by the fourth nerve behind the knee, proceeds straight downward and gives off a branch from the inner side, extending under the skin along the inner side of the tibia, slightly toward the back, to the inner ankle and then to the inner side of the foot as far as the big toe. Along its path, it sends out offshoots on both sides, just as the other branches do when running between the skin and the membrane we call "fleshy" <note>the superficial fascia</note>. Another branch of this type, though not as prominent, is sent off from the inner trunk of the fourth nerve slightly lower than the one just mentioned, spreading out in various ways into the skin covering the calf. But the trunk itself, having now fully descended into the leg and lying hidden beneath the muscles occupying the back of the tibia, produces a noteworthy offshoot at the point where the fibula first separates from the tibia near the knee, where the upper part of the membrane-like ligament <note>the interosseous membrane</note> that connects these bones throughout their length is found. For that offshoot passes through this ligament and, led to the front of the tibia, creeps downward along that ligament, hidden between the muscle that extends the big toe and the one that extends the other toes, also distributing offshoots to the muscles it touches. The remainder of it travels with the tendons of the aforementioned muscles across the transverse ligament found in the front region of the tibia near the foot. And when this offshoot reaches the top of the foot, it is distributed primarily to the muscles that pull the big toe and the three toes next to it toward the outer side. Just as this offshoot is led forward from the inner trunk of the fourth nerve, so too another (but much thinner) one is distributed toward the back, between the rear of the **fourth** of the muscles moving the foot and the front of the first two muscles...

...descending as far as the region of the muscles assigned to that same task, and being distributed there; however, the tendons of these three muscles are not fully united with one another. Furthermore, <sup>a</sup> what remains of the inner trunk of the "fourth nerve" <note>the tibial nerve, which Vesalius treats as the continuation of the sciatic</note> seeking the leg is carried downward along the posterior surface of the shin bone <term>tibia</term>, together with the <sup>b</sup> fifth muscle of those moving the foot, and the <sup>c</sup> second and <sup>d</sup> third [muscles] moving the toes of the foot. Accompanied by the tendons of those muscles, it winds around the posterior side of the inner ankle <term>medial malleolus</term> and enters the lower parts of the foot. There, it is attached to the muscles situated in the sole and is divided into small forks in such a way that nearly two branches are distributed to the lower surface of each toe. Thus, the entire fourth nerve of those approaching the leg is consumed. 

In recording this sequence (and most especially its path along the shin bone), if you notice that I have deviated significantly from the opinions <term>placitis</term> of *Galen*, I pray it may not be troublesome to weigh his description against the true dissection <term>sectio</term> of the human body. Do this so that you may learn along with me how cautiously one must agree with even the most highly approved authors. In what manner the dissection of all the nerves should be conveniently managed, I shall describe in its proper place toward the end of the three following books. For now, I shall add the finishing touch <term>colophonem; literally 'a summit' or the final stroke of a work</term> to this fourth book with a larger-scale illustration of the nerves.

-># DELINEATION OF THE NERVES,<-
->WHICH SETS FORTH THE ORIGINS OF THE SEVEN PAIRS OF NERVES THAT ARISE FROM THE BRAIN AND THE BEGINNING OF THE SPINAL CORD, AND BEAUTIFULLY REPRESENTS THE DISTRIBUTION<-
->and sequence of all the pairs that take their origin from the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsali medulla"</note> enclosed within the bones of the back.<-

### INDEX OF SYMBOLS

THE PRESENT figure displays the brain along with the cerebellum, with their origins delineated in such a manner as if they were viewed at the base, stripped from the skull; it appears as it would if someone, standing upright, bent their head as far back as possible, looking upward and backward. However, so that the Index of symbols could be beautifully applied to this sheet, we have drawn the figure as if it lacked one arm and one leg, especially since the arrangement is the same on both sides.

**A, B, C** marks the base of the brain on one side. **A** indicates the part that projects slightly toward the top of the nostrils, called by some the mammillary process <note>the olfactory bulbs</note>. **B** suggests the part of the brain entering the wide cavity of the skull, which sits at the side of the sinus where the gland that receives phlegm <note>the pituitary gland</note> is placed. **C** marks the most posterior seat of the brain.
**D, D** The cerebellum.
**E** Similarly, a process of the brain, chiefly serving the organ of smell.
**F** The origin of the left optic nerve <note>original: "nerui uisorij"</note>.
**G** The crossing of the optic nerves <note>the optic chiasm</note>.
**H** The membrane into which the optic nerve dissolves or transforms <note>the retina</note>.
**I** The second pair of cranial nerves <note>Vesalius uses a non-modern numbering; this likely refers to the oculomotor nerves</note>.
**K, k** The smaller root of the third pair.
**L** The thicker root of the third pair <note>the trigeminal nerve complex</note>.
**M** The fourth pair.
**N** The slenderer root of the fifth pair.
**O** The more prominent root of the fifth pair.
**P** The membrane into which the fifth pair primarily dissolves within the organ of hearing.
**Q, R** Offshoots of the larger root of the fifth pair, of which this one slips through a "blind" hole <note>foramen cecum</note>, and that one through another proper to itself.
**S** The sixth pair of nerves.
**T** The seventh pair of nerves of the brain. The progress of these nerves could not be drawn here, as they are most elegantly presented in the second figure placed before the second chapter of this book.
**V** The beginning of the spinal cord <note>medulla dorsalis</note> from the middle of the base of the brain.
**X** The seat of the spinal cord where it exits the skull.
**1, 2, etc.** The numbers indicate the characters of the seven cervical, twelve thoracic, five lumbar, and six sacral vertebrae, and thus the thirty pairs of nerves leaping forth from the spinal cord already contained within those vertebrae, whose sequence I have expressed in this table by my own effort <note>original: "meo marte"</note> as accurately and simply as possible. But because this space allows for only a small explanation of symbols, I will not mark every single branch of the nerves with letters.
*p* The left nerve of the transverse septum <note>the phrenic nerve of the diaphragm</note>, which you will see formed from the offshoots of the fourth, fifth, and sixth pairs without further help from symbols.

*s, s* These are the intercostal nerves, especially there where they are reflected forward with the ribs.
*t, t* Branches led toward the back, also encountered everywhere here.
*u, u* In a sequence of this kind, the nerves approach the muscles spread over the bones of the thorax.
Propagations are indicated, increasing the branch of the sixth pair of cranial nerves extended to the roots of the ribs.

*This figure follows the first in the sequence of dissection. For here, the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the thin membrane that lines the abdominal cavity</note> has been divided by a straight line from the <term>xiphoid process</term> <note>original: "mucronata cartilagine"; the small cartilaginous extension at the lower end of the breastbone</note> all the way to the pubic bone, divided in such a way that I have damaged none of the vessels of the navel. ### INDEX
#### of the characters of the Fourth Figure.

*In this figure, the <term>omentum</term> <note>a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron; original: "omentum"</note> is depicted free from the parts to which it is attached, or rather from which it takes its origin, and without being torn from any other site; its entire construction—and especially the sequence of veins, arteries, and nerves throughout it—as well as the glandular bodies <note>lymph nodes or small fat clusters</note> growing within it, are shown. Furthermore, one can see from this figure how neatly the omentum resembles a small pouch, a traveler's bag, or the smaller nets used by fishermen.*

*e,e,e The circle or orifice of the omentum, where it begins.*
*f,f,f The front surface of the upper membrane of the omentum.*
*g,g,g The front surface of the lower membrane of the omentum. However, this is not seen in its entirety like the front surface of the upper membrane; for only that part of the lower membrane is visible which lies beneath the stomach <note>original: "uentriculo"</note> and extends as far as the <term>colon</term> <note>the large intestine</note> where it stretches out from the stomach. Meanwhile, the rest of the lower membrane is still covered by the upper membrane, and will be shown in the following figure.*
*h,i,k These three characters, placed on the left side of the upper membrane of the omentum, mark its construction. For **h** marks the membranous part of the omentum, which lacks veins, arteries, and fat. **i** indicates the vessels, while **k** expresses the fat <note>original: "adeps"</note> that is attached or grows alongside the vessels. Although I have placed these characters in this part of the omentum, no one doubts that they could have been placed in any other part of it as well.*
*l The trunk of the <term>portal vein</term> <note>original: "Venæ portæ"; the main vein bringing blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note>, where it emerges from the liver and is contained and supported by the lower membrane of the omentum.*
*m The artery seeking the hollow of the liver <note>original: "iecoris cauum"</note> and the gallbladder <note>original: "bilis ueſiculam"</note>, accompanied by a nerve. This nerve is derived from a branch of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "sexti neruorum cerebri paris"; in Vesalius’s system, this refers to the vagus nerve, which modern anatomy classifies as the tenth pair</note> on the right side, which extends along the roots of the ribs on the right side and enters the hollow of the liver and the gallbladder.*
*n The beginning of the vein that primarily approaches the posterior part of the lower orifice of the stomach <note>the pylorus</note>, which has a matching artery.*
*o,o An artery, vein, and nerve, extending toward the right side of the base <note>original: "fundi"</note> of the stomach, following the beginning of the upper membrane of the omentum.*
*p,p The small branches <note>original: "ſurculi"</note> of those vessels that extend to the right side of the base of the stomach, entwining the body of the stomach.*
*q,q The offshoots <note>original: "propagines"</note> of the already mentioned vessels, which extend to the right side of the base of the stomach and are scattered into the upper membrane of the omentum.*
*r A vein and artery extending to the <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> and the beginning of the <term>jejunum</term> <note>the middle section of the small intestine</note>, frequently joined by a small nerve.*
*s The division of the portal vein into two trunks. You should consider that we have drawn the veins marked **r** and **o** higher here than in the bare figure of the portal vein because the origin of these veins varies from time to time in this manner.*
*t The right or larger trunk of the portal vein, running into the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> and thus into the intestines themselves.*
*u A vein distributed into the posterior part of the stomach, accompanied by an artery.*

# INDEX OF THE FIFTH FIGURE, AND OF ITS labels.

In the fifth figure, we have expressed the omentum in a completely different way than in the fourth figure. For here we have displayed the entire part of the colon intestine cut away from the body, which reaches from the region of the liver along the bottom of the stomach as far as the spleen, and which in humans is called by us the lower membrane of the omentum and is held toward the back. Then, along with that part of the colon, the lower membrane of the omentum is also brought before the eyes, with a large portion of the upper membrane of the omentum now pulled away and cast aside, so that the connection and fusion of the omentum to the colon intestine might be demonstrated in whatever way possible; meanwhile, the lower membrane is not coiled upon itself as in the third figure, nor contracted above the colon.

<margin>A, A, B, C, D</margin> These characters mark that portion of the omentum which, originating from the back, is placed beneath the posterior region of the stomach; it is formed in the manner of the mesentery by two membranes spread over it, which contain the part of the colon extended along the bottom of the stomach. However, B, C, and D are introduced specifically, as I will soon subjoin.

<margin>B</margin> The first vein spread from the left trunk of the <term>portal vein</term> <note>the large vein that carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver; original: "portæ uenæ"</note> into the lower membrane of the omentum, with its companion artery and usually a small nerve attached to it.

<margin>C</margin> The second vein—and a notable one—also diffused from the left trunk of the portal vein into the lower membrane of the omentum; it is presented to the colon intestine before the other veins belonging here, along with its partner artery, to which in certain places a small nerve is attached.

## INDEX OF CHARACTERS FOR THE SIXTH, SEVENTH,
## and Eighth Figures.

*The following Index of characters is common to the sixth, seventh, and eighth figures. If, however, a character is peculiar to any one of these, I will add either 6, 7, or 8 to it for the figure number; those characters to which no such little note is added, you should consider common to all three figures.*

*A 6 The pointed cartilage of the breastbone <note>the xiphoid process; original: "mucronata pectoris ossis cartilago"</note>.*
*B,B 6 The <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> together with the broken ribs, and the <term>transverse septum</term> <note>the diaphragm; original: "septo transuerso"</note> attached to it, turned backward and to the sides.*
*C 6 The primary ligament by which the human liver <note>original: "iecur"</note> is bound to the transverse septum.*
*D,D 6 The large area of the convex side of the liver.*
*E 6 A small portion of the vein inserted into the liver from the navel <note>the umbilical vein</note>.*
*F,F 6 The front part of the stomach <note>original: "ventriculi"</note>, which appears large here because this man's stomach was quite swollen with food.*
*G 6 The left side of the spleen <note>original: "lienis"</note>, or that part of it turning toward the front of the body.*
*H 7 The portion of the stomach that forms the lower orifice of the stomach, or the beginning of the intestines <note>the pylorus</note>, which we have shown tied here with a cord.*
*I,K 7 The part of the intestines extending from I to K, commonly called by us sometimes the <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> and sometimes the "intestine the length of twelve fingers."*
*L 7 The beginning of the <term>jejunum</term> <note>the middle section of the small intestine; original: "ieiuni"</note> and the site of the thin intestines where they first begin to coil into windings and rise forward.*
*M 7,8 The end of the <term>ileum</term> <note>the final section of the small intestine; original: "ilei"</note>, and thus the end of the thin intestines. Truly, I cannot guess at which point the end of the jejunum or the beginning of the ileum should be placed, since in the whole path from L in the seventh figure to M, there is no notable distinction to be found by which one might be distinguished from the other.*
*N The bulging beginning of the large intestines <note>the cecum</note>.*
*O That very thin appendage, coiled like a worm, which we call the <term>cecum</term> <note>Vesalius here uses "cecum" for the appendix; original: "caecum intestinum"</note>.*
*N, P, Q, R, S, T 6,8 The <term>colon</term> is marked with these characters, but each notes something specifically. N to P marks the path of the colon from the area of the right kidney to the hollow of the liver. From P to Q, the path of the colon is shown following the bottom of the stomach from the hollow of the liver to the region of the spleen. From Q to R is the path of the colon from the region of the spleen to the pubic bone, following the left flank. Furthermore, from R to S (seen specifically in the eighth figure), the ascent and winding of the colon is indicated, which it makes upward toward the region of the navel. From S to T marks the progress of the aforementioned ascent to the beginning of the <term>rectum</term>.*
*U,V 6,8 The depressed area of the colon along its length <note>the longitudinal bands or taeniae coli</note>.*
*X,X 6,8 The bulging half-globules on both sides of that depressed area marked U and V, which the common people call "cells" <note>the haustra or pouches of the colon</note>.*
*Y 6,8 The beginning of the rectum. Whatever lies below Y is the rectum.*
*Z 7 A portion of the duct carrying bile into the intestines <note>the common bile duct</note>.*
*a 8 The muscle encircling the end of the rectum, in charge of preventing the untimely excretion of feces <note>the anal sphincter</note>.*
*b,c 8 Two muscles that pull the rectum upward after the excretion of feces <note>the levator ani muscles</note>.*
*d 8 At this site the rectum is joined to the penis in men and the neck of the uterus <note>cervix</note> in women by the intervention of muscular substance.*
*e,f 6 Two arteries peculiar to the fetus <note>the umbilical arteries</note>.*
*g 6 This character indicates the base of the bladder, as well as the passage by which the fetus's urine is led out of its body <note>the urachus</note>, which we have shown cut off here, as we did with the previously mentioned arteries.*

### INDEX OF THE CHARACTERS FOR THE TWELFTH AND
#### thirteenth figures.

THE present Index of characters is shared in common by the twelfth and thirteenth figures. Therefore, when a character occurs that is unique to the twelfth figure, we will add a **1** to it; to those which are inscribed specifically on the thirteenth, we shall add a **2**. If, however, any character is common to both figures at once, **1 & 2** will be added to it.

**H,H 1** A portion of the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> turned back along with the ribs.
**I,K 1** The hollow [underside] of the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "iecoris"</note>.
**L 1** A small portion of the convex side <note>original: "gibbi sedis," referring to the rounded upper surface</note> of the liver.
**M 1** A section of the liver where the vein that nourishes the fetus <note>the umbilical vein</note> is first inserted.
**N,N 1** Fissures, impressions, and small bumps visible in the hollow of the liver near the origin of the <term>portal vein</term> <note>original: "venae portae"</note>. The upper (or left) **N**, which is closer to the letter **T**, indicates the place where the vein proceeding from the navel <note>umbilical vein</note> is inserted into the hollow of the liver, where the trunk of the portal vein emerges. For a passage extends from **M** all the way to the left **N**, which in a certain way freely transmits the umbilical vein through the body of the liver to that site marked **N**.
**O 1** The ligament binding the left part of the liver (which ends in a somewhat acute angle) to the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septo transverso"</note> at this point.
**φ 1** The sinus <note>depression</note> of the liver, carved out here to make room for the <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "stomachus," which in this context refers to the gullet</note> where it continues into the upper orifice of the stomach.
**P,Q 1** The stomach <note>original: "ventriculus"</note> pressed toward the left, as if out of the cavity of the peritoneum.
**R 1** The upper orifice of the stomach, or the end of the esophagus, along with the veins, arteries, and nerves surrounding that orifice.
**S 1,2** The lower orifice of the stomach <note>the pylorus</note> and the beginning of the <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> itself; in the twelfth figure, we have reflected this forward—contrary to its natural position—so that the duct of the gallbladder inserted into it (soon to be marked **c**) might come into view.
**T 1** A nerve inserted into the hollow of the liver, branched off from the nerves that wrap around the upper orifice of the stomach.
**U 2** The <term>gallbladder</term> <note>original: "bilis uesicula"</note>. This is visible in both figures: however, I have marked it with a character specifically in the thirteenth figure alone. Therefore, apply your mind here and in the following few characters first to the thirteenth and then to the twelfth, because we decided the twelfth should not be obscured by too many characters.
**X,X 2** The gallbladder ducts <note>the biliary ducts</note> stretched through the body of the liver between the branches of the portal vein and the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</note>.
**Y 2** An offshoot of the portal vein spread into the substance of the liver.
**Z 2** An offshoot of the vena cava distributed into the substance of the liver. I wished here to express, as best I could, the position of the vessels in the liver's substance: specifically, how the branches of the portal vein are placed beneath the offshoots of the vena cava, and in what manner the gallbladder ducts run through the middle of them. This is despite the fact that to those performing dissections, the offshoots of the portal vein sometimes seem continuous with the offshoots of the vena cava.
**a 2** The meeting or junction of the gallbladder ducts that are distributed through the body of the liver.
**b 2** The neck of the gallbladder, into which the duct led from the liver (marked **a**) is inserted, becoming a shared passage.
**c 1,2** The duct of the gallbladder inserted into the duodenum. In the thirteenth figure, we have represented the duodenum opened at a lower point, so that the insertion of that duct, marked **d**, would not remain hidden.

## Index of the CHARACTERS of the fourteenth and fifteenth figures.

The *CHARACTERS* to be explained in this Index are partly common to both figures, and partly peculiar to one or the other. Accordingly, we will indicate the common ones with the marks 1 and 2. To those characters peculiar to the fifteenth figure, we will add the number 1; while to the characters proper to the sixteenth figure <note>The text here says "sixteenth," though the header and context suggest the fourteenth and fifteenth figures are being compared. This may be a printer's error in the original manuscript or a reference to a figure on a subsequent page.</note>, we will add the number 2.

*A 1, 2* The part of the <term>gullet</term> <note>original: "stomachus"; in Renaissance anatomy, this term often referred to the esophagus rather than the stomach organ itself</note> belonging to the width of the mouth; it is seen here cut away from the throat.
*A, B 1, 2* From *A* to *B*, the path of the gullet is marked, descending straight over the middle position of the neck vertebrae and the four upper vertebrae of the chest.
*B, C 1, 2* From *B* to *C*, the path of the gullet extends, inclining slightly to the right side over the fifth and several following chest vertebrae.
*C, D 1, 2* From *C* to *D*, the path of the gullet is marked, climbing from the right side toward the left above the large artery <note>the aorta</note>, and reaching through the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septum transversum"</note> into the upper opening of the stomach.
*E, E 1* Two tonsils, which are located not far from the site where the gullet reaches into the cavity of the mouth.
*F, F 1, 2* A glandular body <note>likely lymph nodes or esophageal glands</note> frequently attached to the gullet, where it sits upon the body of the fifth chest vertebra.
*G 1, 2* The upper opening of the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: "ventriculus"</note>.
*H 1, 2* The lower opening of the stomach <note>the pylorus</note>.
*I 1, 2* The upper part of the stomach.
*K, K 1, 2* The lower part of the stomach, or the <term>base</term> <note>original: "fundus"</note>.
*L, L 1* The front surface of the stomach.
*M, N, O 2* The back surface of the stomach.
*P 1, 2* The <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note>, which we have represented here as cut off at the beginning of the <term>jejunum</term> <note>the second part of the small intestine</note>.
*Q 2* The passage of the gallbladder <note>the common bile duct</note>, inserted into the duodenum.
*R 2* This character is seen on the inner surface of the recently mentioned intestine, marking the insertion of that passage which I just labeled with *Q*.
*S 2* A glandular body <note>the pancreas</note> growing beneath the duodenum, supporting the vessels spread out to that intestine.

## THE TWENTIETH FIGURE, AND THE
### *Index of its characters.*

This figure follows the twelfth in the sequence of dissection: for from this one we have removed all the intestines, leaving only a portion of the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: "uentriculi"</note> to show the location of its upper orifice. A,A *A portion of the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septi transuersi"; literally the "transverse septum"</note>, wrapped in the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, and reflected upward along with several ribs.*
B,B *The concave [inner] surface of the liver.*
C *The ligament of the liver, by which its left part is bound to the diaphragm.*
D *The portion of the vein extending through the navel to the liver <note>the umbilical vein</note>, where that sinus is first indicated receiving this vein; it crawls through a private opening cut for it in the human liver to the very base of the liver, where you see the letter G placed not far from K.*
E *In this place the liver has a hollow where it gives way to the <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "stomachus"; here referring to the gullet</note> as it passes through the diaphragm to reach the higher orifice of the stomach.*

I *The trunk of the portal vein, cut off here. However, I also indicates the roots or origins of two small veins approaching the gallbladder.*

Q *The <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</note>.*
R *The <term>great artery</term> <note>the aorta</note>.*
S *The roots of the arteries branching out into the stomach, liver, spleen, <term>omentum</term> <note>fatty membrane</note>, <term>mesentery</term> <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, and finally the intestines themselves.*
T *The right kidney, still covered by its fatty tunic [capsule].*
U *The left kidney, still wrapped in its fatty tunic.*

b *The vein and artery extended into the left kidney.*

# INDEX OF THE THREE PLATES OF THE TWENTY-FIRST FIGURE, and of their characters.

<margin>$\alpha, \beta$</margin> *THE FIRST plate shows a section made along the length of the kidney through its <term>convexity</term> <note>the outer curved edge</note>, deep enough to reach into the second cavity of the kidney, though no portion of the kidney's substance has been removed. Thus, $\alpha$ indicates the anterior part of the right kidney, and $\beta$ the posterior.*
<margin>$\gamma, \gamma$</margin> *The orifices of the branches of the first cavity of the kidney, or of its <term>membranous body</term> <note>the renal pelvis and calyces</note>, where those branches join together. For here, the branches are necessarily divided by the section at their mutual junction.*
<margin>$\delta, \delta$</margin> *The body of the first cavity of the kidney, or the membranous body, in which the vein and artery of the kidney terminate.*
<margin>$\epsilon$</margin> *This small opening is the beginning of the urinary passage <note>the ureter</note>.*
<margin>$\lambda$</margin> *A part of the urinary passage.*
<margin>$\zeta, \eta$</margin> *Above the membranous body marked $\delta$ and $\delta$ lies the second cavity of the kidney: only its inner side, closest to that membranous body, appears in this section. Its parts, which extend outward to each side of the <term>septum</term> formed from the kidney's substance, making the cavity appear bipartite (divided in two), cannot be seen unless a probe is passed around beneath $\zeta$ and $\eta$. For that septum is seen in the present section divided into two parts, namely anterior and posterior; $\eta$ marks the anterior part of it, and $\zeta$ the posterior.*

*IN THE SECOND plate, all things are common with those just mentioned, except that almost the entire substance of the kidney constituting that septum (which I mentioned in the index of the first plate) has been removed in a circular fashion with a scalpel. Indeed, there was no other way to place the shape of that septum before the eyes. Here, therefore, the entire second cavity of the kidney is visible, but not as it is divided in two on its outer side, because I have removed the septum that separates this cavity on its exterior side. Thus, $\alpha, \beta, \gamma,$ and $\lambda$ mark the same things here as in the first plate. The circle <margin>$\theta, \iota$</margin> drawn in this plate between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ indicates the second cavity of the kidney. $\theta$ indicates the anterior part of the first cavity, or membranous body, which here is split into branches. $\iota$ indicates the posterior part <margin>$\varkappa$</margin> of the membranous body. Thus, $\theta$ and $\iota$ together mark the membranous body, or the first cavity of the kidney. The region of the urinary passage is marked with $\varkappa$.*

*THE THIRD plate displays all the branches of the first cavity or membranous body; for the substance of the kidney, which grows onto the highest branches of that cavity, has been completely scraped away. These things are obvious without the help of labels.*

# THE TWENTY-SECOND FIGURE OF THE FIFTH BOOK.

<image-desc>A detailed anatomical woodcut of a human male torso. The chest and abdominal walls have been opened and the ribs (a) pulled back to reveal the upper surface of the liver (b). Below the liver, the kidneys are visible, stripped of their protective fat. The large central blood vessels (the vena cava and aorta) descend toward the pelvis. The pubic bones have been separated to reveal the path of the urethra and the structure of the penis.</image-desc>

## INDEX OF THE TWENTY-SECOND FIGURE,
## and its characters.

The current figure follows the twentieth in the sequence of dissection. In this view, the ends of several ribs have been broken and turned outward and upward so that the <term>convex surface</term> <note>original: "gibbum"; the rounded upper part</note> of the liver can be seen here, just as its <term>concave surface</term> <note>original: "cauum"; the hollow underside</note> was visible in the twentieth figure. The kidneys, now stripped of their fatty membrane, also present themselves here, and the origin and path of the seminal veins and arteries are shown. Furthermore, in this figure, we have specifically depicted a small branch arising from the trunk of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein returning blood to the heart</note> which is joined with the left seminal vein. Additionally, the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> has been cut open where it provides a passage for the seminal vessels, along with the tunic arising from it that encloses the testis and the seminal vessels of its side; thus, the seminal vessels and the testes with their muscles are exposed. Moreover, the pubic bones appear so separated from each other and turned back that they gape significantly, bringing the bladder and the <term>glandular body</term> <note>the prostate</note> proper to the neck of the bladder—along with its muscle, the bodies of the penis, and their progression—under the viewer's eye. I believe no one will wonder at the fact that in this figure, we have removed the skin entirely from the right thigh and partially from the left.

*c, c The concave seat of the liver, partially visible here.*
*d The primary ligament of the liver <note>the falciform ligament</note>, located at the right side of the <term>pointed cartilage</term> <note>the xiphoid process</note>, and here largely torn away from the front of the liver.*
*e The ligament which joins the part of the liver extending to the left with the diaphragm.*
