*m* The vein and artery approaching the right kidney.

*n* The vein and also the artery leading <term>serous blood</term> <note>original: "serosum sanguinem"; the watery part of the blood that will be filtered into urine</note> to the left kidney.

*o,o* The fatty covering of the right kidney, freed from the front of the kidney.

*p,p* The fatty covering of the left kidney, also torn from the front of its kidney, and still connected to the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> from which it takes its origin.

*q,q* Both the right and left <term>passages</term> <note>the ureters</note> by which urine is carried from the kidneys into the bladder, which is marked with *q*.

*t* The seminal vein, approaching the right testis.

*u* The origin of the seminal vein approaching the right testis, which protrudes like a round bump.

*x* The seminal vein, extended toward the left testis.

*y* A small vein arising from the trunk of the <term>vena cava</term> and joined and united with the left seminal vein. Although this small vein occurs rather rarely, since the left vein is depicted without it in other figures and it obscures nothing here, it seemed best to represent it.

*α* The origin of the <term>seminal arteries</term> <note>the testicular arteries</note>.

*β* The shoots which the seminal veins give off to the peritoneum in that area, where they are connected and strive downward toward the pubic bones.

*γ* The right seminal vein and also the artery, through the peritoneum above the region of the pubic bone and the hip; and likewise the descent and ascent of the <term>vessel carrying semen</term> <note>the vas deferens</note> from the testis, which will soon be marked with *η*, *ι*, and *μ*.

*δ* The mixing of the seminal vein and artery, and the beginning of the <term>varicose body</term> <note>original: "corpus uaricum"; the pampiniform plexus, a network of veins</note> which I compare to the appearance of a <term>varix</term> <note>a swollen, twisted vein</note>.

*ε* The insertion of the varicose body into the testis.

*ζ* The testis still covered by its innermost <term>tunic</term> <note>covering layer</note>.

*η* The beginning of the vessel carrying semen away from the testis.

*ι* The site where the vessel carrying semen is reflected upward according to the lowest part of the testis, and, no longer attached to the testis itself, begins to depart.

*κ* Here the vessel carrying semen no longer shows any appearance of coiling, but is extended upward like a smooth nerve.

*υ* The bladder, the receptacle for urine.

*ξ* A <term>glandular body</term> <note>the prostate gland</note>, attached to the beginning of the neck of the bladder, and receiving the insertion of the vessels carrying semen.

*ρ* The circular muscle surrounding the neck of the bladder <note>the urinary sphincter</note>.

*ς, τ* The two bodies constituting the <term>penis</term> <note>the corpora cavernosa</note>, of which the left is freed from its origin (which is led from the left pubic bone); the right body, however, is still fastened at its origin to the right pubic bone. Furthermore, here in our figure *ς* is in view, which the penis, flaccid and limp, forms together with the bladder.

*υ* The series of veins, arteries, and nerves approaching the penis, expressed as aptly as is possible to achieve in figures of this kind.

*φ, χ* The outer of the special coverings of the testis, produced there from the peritoneum where we have written *φ*; but where *χ* is placed, that site of this covering is noted by which it is joined to the lowest part of the testis.

*ψ* The muscle of the testis <note>the cremaster muscle</note>, attached to the aforementioned covering.

*ω* The <term>seventh muscle of those moving the femur</term> <note>the thigh bone; likely referring to the obturator externus</note> offers itself to be seen here, where it is led downward over the hip bone.

*\* (asterisk)* A portion of the <term>rectum</term> <note>the straight intestine</note>, which is customary to leave in the body while the other intestines are being removed. Above this portion of the rectum, the distribution of the <term>vena cava</term> and the <term>great artery</term> around the region of the <term>sacrum</term> <note>the bone at the base of the spine</note> is also elegantly seen.

## INDEX OF THE TWENTY-THIRD FIGURE, AND OF ITS
->parts and characters.<-

The twenty-third figure, which contains many specific illustrations or plates, together with the one that immediately preceded it (and was twenty-second in the order), is primarily intended for the inspection of the male organs that serve generation. I originally intended for both of these figures to be placed before the thirteenth chapter of this book when they were first marked with characters [identifying letters]; for this reason, the system of characters is exactly the same in both. However, because I now think it better for all the figures of the present book to be placed here in succession, I will dedicate a specific index to this twenty-third figure, and I will not be reluctant to explain once more the characters that are common to this and the twenty-second figure. Furthermore, in this twenty-third figure there are two principal plates, of which we will not inappropriately call one the "right" and the other the "left." In both of these plates, we have depicted the kidneys, the bladder, and the <term>seminal organs</term> <note>the reproductive structures</note>, along with portions of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein returning blood to the heart</note> and the artery <note>the aorta</note> as they have been cut from the body. These are shown in an anterior view on the right, but in a posterior [rear] view on the left. On the right, we have also specifically opened the bladder and its <term>neck</term> <note>original: "ceruicem"; the passage at the base of the bladder leading to the urethra</note>, or the passage common to both semen and urine, whereas on the left these parts remain intact. I shall speak more extensively on this in the explanation of the characters as soon as I have described the small plates that occupy the left side and the lower section of this twenty-third figure, which are marked with capital Latin letters in this manner:

<margin>A, B</margin> In these two small plates, both showing the right testis from the front but more toward its left side, the same thing is expressed. However, the upper plate marked **A** differs from the lower one marked **B** in this: the upper shows the position of the <term>vas deferens</term> <note>original: "semen deferentis uasis"; the duct that carries sperm away from the testis</note> undisturbed, while the lower plate shows that part of the vessel (which is carried upward along the front of the testis and is no longer attached to it) reflected or pushed aside to the left from its natural place. This was done so that the insertion and attachment of the seminal vein and artery to the testis could be clearly seen. These details will now be made even clearer through the explanation of the characters common to both plates.

C *The seminal vein and artery, cut off at the point where they emerge from the large cavity of the peritoneum; there they become entwined and mixed together, beginning to form what I shall call the <term>varicose body<note>original: "corpus uaricosum"; today known as the pampiniform plexus, a network of veins in the spermatic cord that helps regulate the temperature of the testes.</note></term>. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE HUMAN BODY

We have cut the rectum away, though it remains in the body along with the entire mesentery <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place.</note>, the membranes of which we have separated from one another here in part so that the nature of the mesentery might be placed before the eyes. But the present figure was drawn primarily to show the position of the uterus and the bladder just as they occurred in this woman, with no part of the uterus moved by us. For no membrane has been torn away from the uterus here; instead, everything is seen intact, just as they meet the dissector in moderately fat women once the intestines have been removed. Indeed, women are so fatty that even those killed by long illness and who are most emaciated show no sequence of vessels unless the membranes are pulled apart from one another.

<margin>A,B,C,D</margin> *The interior surface of the front part of the peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>.*
<margin>E,E</margin> *The part of the mesentery connecting the small intestines to the back.*
<margin>F,F</margin> *One membrane of the mesentery is marked here, torn away from the other membrane which I have marked with* G *and* G. *Both membranes,*
<margin>G,G</margin> *indicate the sequence of vessels through the mesentery, and the nature of the glands placed between the distributions of the vessels.*
<margin>H,H</margin> *At this part of the mesentery, the colon was attached where it was closest to the rectum.*
<margin>I</margin> *At this part of the mesentery stood the beginning of the colon, and then the cecum <note>The pouch at the beginning of the large intestine.</note> as well.*
<margin>K</margin> *The rectum, cut at the point where the colon ends; this site is directly opposite the connection of the sacrum <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note> with the lowest lumbar vertebra.*
<margin>L</margin> *The front part of the fundus <note>The upper, rounded part</note> of the uterus, from which nothing at all is seen to be torn away.*
<margin>M</margin> *The woman’s right testis <note>original: "testis"; Vesalius, following Galenic tradition, referred to the ovaries as "female testes."</note>.*
<margin>N</margin> *The woman’s left testis <note>ovary</note>, the front part of which is here entirely exposed to the eyes, whereas only a small portion of the right testis is seen. This happens because we have drawn the right testis just as both testes are covered by the membrane that carries the woman’s seminal vessels and originates from the peritoneum; however, we have uncovered the left testis of that membrane using only our hands. For this membrane is not grown onto the front part of the testis in any way, but merely rests upon it.*
<margin>O,O</margin> *A membrane arising from the right side of the peritoneum, connecting the right testis—along with the seminal vessels of this side and those veins and arteries that entwine the higher part of the uterus—to the back; it likewise contains the uterus and finally forms the second tunic <note>layer</note> of the uterus along with the membrane of the other side <note>This describes the broad ligament of the uterus.</note>.*
<margin>P</margin> *In this recently mentioned membrane, fleshy fibers run out, forming the right muscle of the uterus.*
<margin>Q,Q</margin> *With these characters, the membrane of the left side is marked, which corresponds to that which* O,O *recently indicated.*
<margin>R,S</margin> *The front part of the neck of the uterus <note>the cervix</note>; between* R *and* S *it is still covered by that tunic which the parts of the peritoneum offer to it, which extend and lead the vessels to it and connect it to the peritoneum. Furthermore, the interval consisting between* R *and* S *signifies in a way the width of the neck of the uterus. The wrinkles visible here are those which the neck of the uterus, collapsed upon itself and not otherwise distended, reveals during dissection.*
<margin>T</margin> *The bladder, the back face of which is chiefly seen here. For in the drawing of this figure, we have directed the eye as if we wished to see primarily the posterior part of the bladder which faces the uterus in a prostrate body. For if you were to imagine the present female body to be upright (similar to the one that will follow), you would persuade yourself that the fundus of the uterus was drawn much higher than the bladder itself, contrary to how things actually are.*
<margin>U</margin> *A portion of the umbilicus <note>navel</note>, freed from the peritoneum during dissection and reflected downward here along with the vessels peculiar to the fetus.*
<margin>X</margin> *A portion of the vein seeking the liver from the umbilicus <note>The umbilical vein, which in adults becomes the round ligament of the liver.</note>.*
<margin>Y</margin> *The passage extending from the highest part of the fundus of the bladder to the umbilicus, which leads the urine of the fetus between its two coverings <note>The urachus.</note>.*
<margin>Z, and &</margin> *Reflected here along with the other vessels of the umbilicus are two arteries creeping along the sides of the bladder, which are inserted into or continuous with the branches of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> that chiefly go to the openings of the pubic bones <note>The umbilical arteries.</note>.*

# FIGURES FOR THE THIRTIETH ILLUSTRATION OF THE FIFTH BOOK
## Index of the plates and their identifying characters.

IN this thirtieth figure, which consists of four separate plates or distinct images, I have attempted to represent the membranes or coverings <term>involucra</term><note>The "involucra" are the protective layers or fetal membranes surrounding the developing child.</note> of the human fetus, which are generated anew along with the fetus within the hollow cavity and chamber of the base of the uterus.

IN the FIRST plate, we have depicted the uterus with its right horn bulging significantly, as if swollen with a male fetus. We have dissected the front part with one long incision and another transverse cut, so that when the layer of the uterus is folded back to the sides and rear, and pulled away from the outer covering of the fetus, it comes into view along with the fleshy substance growing upon it, just as the following index of characters will now set forth.
<margin>A, B, C, D</margin> The internal surface of the uterus, which, before the incision and its outward turning and folding, was covered by the fetal membranes.
<margin>E, E, E</margin> The site where the uterine veins and arteries open, and where new vessels, as it were, are generated for them. These vessels, in their various and complex groupings, have a fleshy substance woven into them, which we compare primarily to the substance of the spleen <term>placenta</term><note>Vesalius describes the placenta here; he famously compared its texture to that of the spleen.</note>, and which is also placed here to strengthen and contain the vessels.
<margin>F, F</margin> The outer covering of the fetus <term>chorion</term><note>The chorion is the outermost membrane surrounding the embryo.</note> is also largely visible here, where it is entirely membranous and the aforementioned fleshy substance does not grow upon it; thus, E, E, E together with F, F designate the outer covering of the fetus.
<margin>G</margin> Part of the neck of the uterus <term>cervix</term>, remaining after the incision.
<margin>H</margin> Veins and arteries supported by the membranes that bind and connect the uterus and its neck on both sides; these arise from the large vessels after their division above the top of the sacred bone <term>sacrum</term> and entwine the uterus in various ways.

THE SECOND plate shows the fetal membranes as they appear when the fleshy substance—which grows on the outer membrane and contains the vessels—has been pulled away from the uterus. The fetus, with its membranes otherwise intact, is freed from the uterus during dissection and placed upon a table or basin.
<margin>I, I, I</margin> The fleshy substance, similar to the flesh of the spleen, growing on the outer covering of the fetus; this was marked E, E, and E in the first plate.
<margin>K, K</margin> The outer covering of the fetus is marked here in those places where that fleshy substance we indicated with I, I, and I does not grow. Because the covering in these regions is entirely membranous and adorned only with tiny venules and arterioles for its own use, it is not surprising that it is transparent, and the form of the inner covering shines through somewhat.

IN the THIRD plate, we have opened the outer covering by a series of incisions and, having pulled it away from the inner covering, laid it to the side, so that the inner covering <term>amnion</term><note>The amnion is the innermost membrane that encloses the watery fluid around the fetus.</note>, still intact, easily comes to view with the fetus enclosed within it.
<margin>L, L, L, M</margin> The outer covering of the fetus; L, L, L mark its outer surface, while M marks the inner surface, which is otherwise closest to the inner covering of the fetus.
<margin>N</margin> The body, acting like a rope or cord <term>umbilical cord</term>, into which the veins and arteries extending from the uterus into the outer fetal membrane—and scattered through the fleshy, spleen-like substance—are finally gathered to form the umbilical vessels. Here they seek the inner covering from the outer one, where the passage <term>urachus</term><note>Vesalius is likely referring to the channel that, in some stages of development, carries fetal waste.</note> ends, pouring the fetus's urine between the outer and inner coverings.
<margin>O, O</margin> The inner covering surrounding the fetus, which is entirely membranous except for certain small veins and arteries running scattered through it. Since this covering is perfectly transparent, it displays the fetus in almost the same position it maintains within the uterus.

THE FOURTH plate also has the outer covering folded back from the inner one. However, it shows a larger portion of its internal surface than in the third plate, so that the appearance of its fleshy and spleen-like substance might be offered here. This substance, though actually residing only on the outer surface of the covering, is expressed here on the inner surface through the transparent part of the membrane. Furthermore, in this plate, the inner covering has also been divided by a long incision and pulled away from the fetus, displaying both of its surfaces. Thus, in addition to the course of the umbilical vessels running between the fetus and its membranes, the fetus itself is seen in almost the exact posture in which it mostly reclines in the womb—a position that appears beautifully balanced in all its parts and is therefore less subject to fatigue.
<margin>P, Q</margin> The outer covering surrounding the fetus; P marks its external surface, while Q marks the internal surface, which is also marked with S and S, even if those characters specifically indicate something else.
<margin>R</margin> A portion of the fleshy substance growing on the outer covering of the fetus is seen here at its external site, where we otherwise find it attached to the uterus.
<margin>S S, T</margin> On the internal surface of the outer covering, which is smooth, slippery, and membranous, the collection and series of vessels shine through in this manner. Arising from the uterine vessels, they are distributed through the fleshy substance growing on the outer covering, which is also seen here through the transparent membrane. S and S indicate almost a circle of vessels, while T indicates the final collection.

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

...as if the uterus had been opened by dissection and the fetal envelopes, undamaged in any part, had been drawn away from it and set aside here from the uterus. We also employ this figure for those things which serve to demonstrate the parts of man, so that the distinction might appear by which the fetal envelopes of the cow, buffalo, goat, deer, and indeed of horned animals—which truly demonstrate the *acetabula* <note>original: "acetabula," refers to the cup-like fleshy sockets of the ruminant placenta, now called cotyledons</note> in their uteri after conception—differ from those of the human fetus, and again from those of the dog, the pig, or any animal that brings forth many offspring at once, and from the fetal envelopes of other animals dissected by me in the meantime. For it is a wonder how much a distinction of this kind confuses the writings of authors and makes them difficult to understand, since they establish no difference between the uteri and envelopes of various animals; and since they claim all things correspond to one another, they do not specify which animal they themselves primarily dissected or described. Since the context of our discourse in the history of the parts will abundantly testify how useful such figures are, I will now only add the index of the characters for the present image.

A, A, A The outer envelope of the buffalo fetus; it is marked here in certain places where the membrane is visible, and it does not possess that substance grown upon it which is now indicated by B, B, and B.

B, B, B The sites where the outer envelope of the buffalo fetus is connected to the uterus and admits vessels; it consists of that fleshy substance which is compared to the substance of the spleen. Here it occurs in a scattered fashion, like the black spots on the skin of leopards.

C, C, C The series and meeting of veins and arteries distributed through the outer fetal envelope for the production of the umbilical vessels.

D The site toward which the veins and arteries spread through the outer envelope are more closely gathered, being nearest to the formation of the umbilical vessels themselves.

### END OF THE FIGURES AND THEIR IDENTIFYING CHARACTERS FOR THE FIFTH BOOK.

## THAT MAN, IN ORDER TO GROW AND LIVE LONGER, REQUIRED INSTRUMENTS SERVING VARIOUS TYPES OF NUTRITION; AND FINALLY, WHICH INSTRUMENTS OF NUTRITION DEALING WITH FOOD AND DRINK WERE SPECIFICALLY CONSTRUCTED. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'V' depicting several cherubic figures or putti engaged in the dissection or preparation of a large animal carcass, possibly a pig, using tools and a pulley system.</image-desc>

<margin>The primary reasons for established nutrition.</margin>
However many various reasons one might mention for the establishment of nutrition, yet that one is by no means the least which demonstrates this to be useful and necessary for the sake of the body's growth. Just as that reason also stands as primary which proposes the continuous "flow" of substance <note>The Renaissance idea that the body’s matter is constantly evaporating or wearing away</note> excited by our innate heat. Since, therefore, the entire mass of man—even after its proper growth—is in a perpetual state of flux, and since the whole would immediately evaporate and dissipate unless another similar substance took the place of that which had flowed away, the Supreme Artisan of things <note>God or Nature</note> implanted in man from the very beginning certain innate powers that always seek what is lacking and desired. For we do not learn from anyone, anywhere, how to flee, to eat, to drink, or to breathe: rather, from the start we possess faculties within us that perform all these things without a teacher. With food, we restore whatever dry substance has flowed out; with drink, we restore the moist; and thus we bring both back to their original proportion. In this same way, we preserve the balance of the airy and fiery substances through breathing and the pulsing of the arteries.

<margin>The necessity of the triple instruments of nutrition.</margin>
Furthermore, while we believe that the substance which flows away from individual parts is of the same nature as the part itself, none of the things that are drunk, eaten, or breathed in are found to be exactly of that nature. It was therefore necessary for a living being first to take these things in, then to change and "cook" them <term>concoct</term><note>The process of digestion was viewed as a form of heat-based refinement or cooking</note>, and to make them as similar as possible to the body they are to nourish and restore; and finally, the waste products <term>recrements</term><note>Waste materials such as urine, feces, or bile</note> which necessarily follow these changes...

<summary>Vesalius concludes his comparative study of fetal membranes by highlighting the differences between human and ruminant placentas, then begins Book V by explaining the physiological necessity of nutrition to counter the body's natural "evaporation."</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY]

...follow, and to expel them. And for this reason, Nature has especially established three types of instruments for nutrition within the body: some for the first purpose of receiving and processing what is consumed, and distributing it to the whole body; others for the second purpose, which serve as receptacles for waste products; and the remaining parts for the third purpose, which serve to send out these excretions, preventing them from flowing out prematurely, and expelling them at the proper time. Furthermore, the parts created by Nature for taking in, processing, and distributing air, and for expelling its waste products resulting from concoction <note>concoction: a physiological term used by early anatomists to describe the "cooking" or processing of food and humors by the body's heat</note> or alteration, will be pursued in the following book [Book VI], which is dedicated to the heart and all the organs of respiration. The present book, however, will be consecrated to the instruments of food and drink, and finally to the organs that serve generation <note>reproduction</note>, because of their proximity and connection to the seat [of the bowels].

<margin>What is to be taught in the present book, and a brief enumeration of the parts serving the nutrition produced from food and drink.</margin>

<margin>
a Figure 14, through A, B, C in L, L. or Figure 12 in P, Q.
b Figure 12, P, Q in S, and so on, or in Figures 7 & 8.
c Figure of Chapter 5, Book 3. or Figure 12, l, k, h in I, K.
d Figures 1, 2, Chapter 49, Book 2, M.
e 3rd muscle table, 4, r, s Δ, θΔ.
f 7th table, Δ.
g In X. X.
h from there into V. and again through c in S to d, Figure 13. h, Figure of Chapter 5, Book 3, T, T to a, a.
i Figure 3, d. Figure 10, O, O.
k Figure of Chapter 5, Book 3, A, A.
l Figure of Chapter 6, Book 3, A, A, d.
m Figure 25, Y, Z.
n Figure 22, q. q in v. Figure 25, d, and c in β.
o Figure 22, s. Figure 25, γ.
p Figure of Chapter 6, Book 3.
</margin>

From the mouth, therefore, through the gullet <note>original: "stomachum"; in Vesalius’s time, this term often referred to the esophagus</note>, food and drink are taken into the <gloss>a</gloss> stomach as if into a common workshop or storehouse. The stomach compresses, mixes, and concocts everything it embraces, and then pushes the concocted material into the <gloss>b</gloss> intestines. From these, the branches of the <gloss>c</gloss> portal vein suck out that which is the better part of the processed juice—suitable for making blood—along with the more liquid waste of this concoction, carrying it to the hollow of the liver. The drier waste, however, which is unfit for suction, is pushed down by the intestines; and at a person's will, it is excreted as the <gloss>d</gloss> circular muscle of the anus relaxes and the <gloss>e</gloss> abdominal muscles are compressed, with the assistance of the <gloss>f</gloss> diaphragm <note>original: "septi transversi"</note> being added at the same time.

The liver, moreover, after it has admitted that juice or cream, adds an ornament to it necessary for the generation of perfect blood, purging it of a twofold waste: namely, yellow bile, as a thinner and lighter waste, and then a dark, bilious juice <note>black bile</note>, as a muddy, earthy, and thicker waste. The former is transmitted into the <gloss>g</gloss> passage of the gallbladder and flows into the gallbladder itself; excreted from there back into the intestines, it is discharged with the harder feces. The latter, however, as we commonly believe, is transmitted through the <gloss>h</gloss> branches of the portal vein for the <gloss>i</gloss> nourishment of the spleen; and whatever the spleen is unable to process and adapt into suitable nourishment for itself, it belches into the stomach, to be subsequently moved along with the excrements of the intestines.

Therefore, the blood which is prepared in the liver for the nutrition of the human being—having laid aside those two wastes and having reserved a portion of itself in the portal vein for the nourishment of the parts through which it is digested—is now red and pure. It ascends from the <gloss>k</gloss> very narrow and numerous branches of that vein diffused through the substance of the liver to the convex <note>original: "gibbam"</note> part of the liver, into the similarly innumerable and narrow <gloss>l</gloss> offshoots of the vena cava. It is still accompanied by a thin and watery waste, which was sucked from the intestines along with the best portion of the juice prepared in the stomach; by the help of this watery waste, as if by a vehicle, it crawls through the narrowest ways with less effort. When the blood has passed through those narrow passages, the <gloss>m</gloss> kidneys diligently attract this waste to themselves and purge the blood of it, pushing it through the <gloss>n</gloss> urinary passages <note>ureters</note> into the bladder, the receptacle for this. From there, at a convenient time, once the <gloss>o</gloss> muscle of its neck <note>the sphincter</note> is relaxed, that waste or urine is returned out of the body.

The blood, however, is led to the parts of the body through the <gloss>p</gloss> vena cava, which is propagated through a most abundant series of branches. Those parts attract, assimilate, and apply to themselves whatever in the blood is familiar and suitable to each individual part; and they exclude from themselves, through their own ducts, a twofold waste that also arises in this concoction. Let these things said in general about the instruments of food and drink suffice. With what great wisdom the Creator of things <note>original: "Opifex," the Artisan/Creator</note> has created these, I shall pursue in the order in which they have been mentioned to serve nutrition. A beginning for the discourse will be timely made with the peritoneum, because it is the common wrapping of these organs.

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V. ON THE PERITONEUM. CHAPTER II.

*In showing the peritoneum, most of the figures in this fifth book are useful, and especially the first, which presents it whole in its anterior and external view. The second, however, shows its anterior part from the inner side. Those figures especially represent the posterior side of the peritoneum from the inside which have many organs dissected away from it, such as the twenty-second and twenty-fifth.*

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'L' depicting a scene of anatomical dissection. Several putti (cherub-like figures) are gathered around a human cadaver on a table; one is actively dissecting the abdomen while others observe or prepare instruments. The scene is framed within a classical architectural border.</image-desc>

<margin>Names of the peritoneum.</margin>
The Latins borrow the name of the peritoneum (which some call the membrane of the abdomen) from the Greeks. For by them, that which is stretched around no particular organs <note>Vesalius refers to its role as a general lining rather than a specific organ's casing</note> is called <term>peritonaion</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόναιον</note>, <term>peritonaios</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόναιος</note>, and <term>peritonion</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόνιον</note>. And it is not only called so in an absolute sense, but by some this entire name is given to it as the <term>peritonaeos hymen</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόναιος ὑμὴν; "the membrane stretched around"</note>, a name derived from its substance, which is primarily membranous. By some it is called <term>peritonaeos chiton</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόναιος χιτὼν; "the surrounding tunic"</note>, and by others <term>peritonaion skepasma</term> <note>original Greek: περιτόναιον σκέπασμα; "the surrounding covering"</note>, certainly from its use, by which it is wrapped around almost all the organs we will pursue in this fifth book, in the manner of a wrap or a certain tunic. The Arabs particularly name it <term>ziphac</term> and <term>zimphac</term> and <term>chamel</term> <note>Latinized versions of Arabic anatomical terms</note> by the common name for membranes.

<margin>The peritoneum is counted among the "similar" parts. a fig. cap. 1 lib. 3 inserted, & fig. cap. 2. b in the abdomen 3, 4, 5, 6, of the muscle tables.</margin>
The peritoneum is therefore counted among the number of simple and primary bodies, which we are accustomed to call <term>similar</term> <note>similar parts: a classical anatomical term for tissues that are uniform in substance throughout, like membrane, bone, or fat, as opposed to complex organs like the heart or hand</note>. For it is a membrane, with no fibers at all: unlike the <term>a</term> tunics of the veins and arteries, or the thin and membranous <term>b</term> interwoven endings of muscles. It is the widest and largest among the other simple membranes of the body.

<margin>Size and site of the peritoneum. c 3rd muscle table Γ. d 3rd table A. e 7th table from Δ in many places in the more complete figures of book 5.</margin>
For the membrane we call "fleshy," <note>the panniculus carnosus, a layer of tissue beneath the skin</note> although it may be wider than the peritoneum itself and is wrapped around the whole body like skin, is nevertheless not "simple," since it is endowed with certain fleshy fibers and is made muscular in the <term>c</term> neck and <term>d</term> forehead. Furthermore, the peritoneum lines the entire <term>e</term> cavity which is easily held to be the most capacious of all the body’s cavities, extending from the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note> down to the bone of the coccyx <note>the tailbone</note>; and it is stretched over all the organs contained in that cavity, embracing them in the manner of a receptacle: namely, the stomach, intestines, omentum <note>the fatty apron over the bowels</note>, mesentery, liver, spleen, kidneys, both bladders <note>the gallbladder and urinary bladder</note>, the uterus, and finally whatever vessels have their place between the diaphragm and the legs.

<margin>Connection. Origin. f 7th table t, u. then x, & 16th table F, G.</margin>
And while it contains these organs in its internal seat, it is grown together with the muscles on all sides of its external seat. For the peritoneum takes its beginning on both sides from the ligaments which connect the lumbar vertebrae, and those which join the sacrum to the hip bones, arising from them in the manner of a broad membrane. Soon, ascending from each side, it covers the <term>f</term> muscles of the loins, and those which, occupying the internal seat of the hip, haunch, and pubic bones, preside over the movements of the thighs: and it adheres to them with such fibers as those we see by which muscles are joined together.

<margin>g 6th table Δ. h which is seen in the 7th table, and marked with Δ.</margin>
But where the peritoneum has surpassed these muscles (which are grouped in a number of four on each side), it is stretched beneath the internal <term>g</term> transverse muscles of the abdomen and the entire <term>h</term> lower surface of the diaphragm, most tenaciously grown to them—especially to their thin, nervous parts—and in a certain way performing the role of the muscles’ own proper membrane.

<margin>Form. i 11th of the last figures of book 1, M with Θ. What its surface is like.</margin>
The peritoneum thus resembles an oblong wine-skin <note>original: "utrem", a leather bottle made from an animal hide</note> or a certain sphere, the length of which extends from the diaphragm to the lowest seat of that large cavity formed by the <term>i</term> sacrum and the bones joined to its sides. And just as wine-skins prepared from hides are usually somewhat hairy and rough on the outside, but flat and smooth on the inside: so also the peritoneum is seen to be rough and fibrous on its external part, so that it may more fitly adhere to the muscles on all sides, in exactly the same way we say membranes grown together are unequal.

The internal seat of the peritoneum, however, looking toward the viscera which it embraces, meets the dissector as exceedingly smooth and polished, and as if smeared with a watery fluid, sometimes having a wealth of fat grown to it (as is almost always the case in pigs). But you will not find this fat equally abundant in every part.

<margin>Processes arising from the peritoneum.</margin>
The anterior and superior internal region of this peritoneum^h—where it touches the stomach^i—and then also the posterior region belonging to the loins and the sacrum^l, abound with more copious fat than the sides of its internal seat^m and the part near the navel. Furthermore, this internal seat of the peritoneum extends certain portions or "processes" <note>Anatomical extensions or outgrowths</note> to the organs it contains. By these processes, it binds those organs to one another and also connects them to itself; and besides their own specific tunics <note>Membranous coverings or layers</note> (if they have any), it covers each with another wrapping or tunic. Thus it happens that those organs which are naturally provided with two specific tunics, such as the stomach and intestines,^n are assigned three; while those that possess only a single^o specific tunic, such as the uterus and both bladders <note>The urinary bladder and the gallbladder</note>,^p obtain two. But organs granted no specific tunic, like the liver and spleen,^q acquire the one that covers them from the peritoneum. In what manner and from what places the peritoneum brings forth these processes—which dilate or transform into such tunics—and how they differ from each other in thickness, will be reviewed more opportunely in the description of each organ than here.

<margin>The peritoneum is not equally thick everywhere.</margin>
Just as the internal seat of the peritoneum varies from the external, so the peritoneum does not correspond to itself in thickness and strength in every part. For where it arises from the ligaments of the vertebrae, it is thickest; then, where it lies upon the muscles of the loins, it is also seen to be thick. In the anterior part, however, which extends from the mucronate cartilage <note>The xiphoid process at the base of the sternum</note> of the breastbone down to the pubis, it is found to be thinner, more slender, and weaker. Additionally, in men, the peritoneum is thicker and stronger near the mucronate cartilage than near the seat of the pubis; but in women, it is seen to be thicker and stronger toward the pubis. Nor in women, as in men, does the peritoneum here provide a path on either side at the groins for the seminal vessels.

<margin>In which parts the peritoneum is permeable.</margin>
For in men, the peritoneum is uniquely permeable there by holes, so to speak; it offers a tunic specifically to each testicle, by which it and its seminal vessels are safely wrapped. Next, in men just as in women, where the peritoneum is drawn under the diaphragm^s <note>original: "septo"</note>, it shows three openings common with the diaphragm: the first through which it leads the vena cava; the second for the stomach <note>The esophagus</note> along with the nerves clinging to it; the third for the great artery <note>The aorta</note>, accompanied by the azygos vein <note>original: "vena coniuge experti"</note> and some branches of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>The vagus nerves</note>.

<margin>Vessels and nerves with which the peritoneum is entwined.</margin>
Furthermore, the peritoneum is perforated for the sake of the umbilical vessels^t; and in the woman, for the end of the cervix of the uterus^u; in the man, for the neck of the bladder^x; and in both, for the sake of the anus^y. Finally^z, the peritoneum provides a path for many veins, arteries, and nerves seeking the leg; then^a for those which tend upward in greatest portion into the rectus muscles of the abdomen; and^b for several others which are offered to the muscles of the back and abdomen, and to the skin, from the vessels lying upon the vertebrae of the loins—the peritoneum taking small branches for itself from these same vessels. For where it is drawn under the diaphragm, it uses the diaphragm's vessels for nutrition; at the sides, however, it also borrows many offshoots from those branches which are extended in the region of the loins in a jointed fashion from the great vein and artery. In the anterior region, the peritoneum demands offshoots above, where it faces the mucronate cartilage, from^c the vessels running out under the breastbone to the rectus muscles of the abdomen; below, however, it adopts branches from^d those vessels which are stretched upward beneath the rectus muscles. Moreover, the fact that physicians deprive the peritoneum of the sense of touch is to be laughed at rather than refuted; since, along with those organs it transmits, it also offers a path to frequent nerves from which it obtains offshoots, and that primarily from those^f which are distributed to the muscles of the abdomen. Furthermore, the peritoneum, by its own essence and constitution, is by no means foreign to receiving the sense of touch.

<header>BOOK V ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY</header>

<margin>Book 4, On the Use of the Parts</margin>
...it covers those parts we have mentioned: since many of these must be stretched and relaxed, the peritoneum is seen to be deservedly made of nervous and membranous tissue so that this may be done more easily. It is indeed strong, so that it might contain things appropriately, but thin, so that it might be less bothersome by its weight. The second use is that it separates all the things it embraces from the muscles surrounding them from the outside, lest any part of the intestines ever fall into the spaces between the muscles; for if they were to press upon the muscles or be pressed by them, the intestines would hinder the movement of the muscles, and the waste materials contained in the intestines would be more difficult to transmit downward. Galen, along with other professors of Anatomy, recounts a third use of the peritoneum: that it propels the superfluities of dry nourishment <note>feces</note> with the added help of the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note>. It is as if the peritoneum performs the same duty that we mentioned the abdominal muscles perform together with the diaphragm during the excretion of feces, and as if it were endowed with voluntary movement by which it contracts and distends itself, rather than necessarily following the movement of the transverse abdominal muscles and the diaphragm to which it is naturally joined. Indeed, the peritoneum serves that use no more than the skin, the abdominal fat, or the omentum <note>the fatty apron covering the intestines</note> itself. I wonder that the membrane lining the ribs <note>the pleura</note>, which entirely corresponds to the peritoneum in substance, use, and conformation, was not held by those authors among the number of organs that constrict the thorax; for that membrane ought to assist in compressing the thorax no less than the peritoneum assists in ejecting feces. To these follows a fourth use of the peritoneum, common to all things that the peritoneum surrounds and especially the abdominal muscles: it acts like a tightly wrapped covering to bind everything together, lest the stomach become too loose on slight occasion, or the intestines be troubled by gases. But the chief use of the peritoneum is that everything it surrounds is contained by it, and just as if individually covered by a certain skin, they are safely gathered together and remain fixed in their proper places.

THE STOMACH <note>ventriculus</note>, which like a storehouse must receive food and drink and first labor to cook <note>digest</note> and transform them, was not placed immediately after the mouth, although that site would have been suitable for taking in food ground by the teeth. For the Architect of things <note>God/Nature</note> placed the thorax and the viscera contained within it before the stomach, so that the stomach might have the outlets for its excrements in the lower regions, and these might be led away far from the senses, which hold their seat in the head. It was fitting for the thorax to be placed higher, as it must draw in air through the mouth and the holes of the nostrils and necessarily emit it again to act as the author of voice and respiration. Furthermore, lest the stomach be removed too far from the mouth—since there could be a long duct from it to the place for expelling waste, or by way of the intestines—Nature joined it as close as possible below the mouth. For it is placed immediately below the thorax and the transverse septum <note>diaphragm</note> between the liver and the spleen, and it possesses a path conveying food from the mouth to itself. This path is called the <term>oisophagon</term> <note>original: οἰσοφάγον; the esophagus</note> by the Greeks from its use, and by the common name by which they call every narrow duct placed before some larger belly in the manner of an isthmus or neck, it is also called the <term>stomachon</term> <note>original: στόμαχον; the gullet or "stomach" in the older sense</note> by them. This is the word we [find used by] Celsus and

### ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY

<margin>*The Beginning.*</margin>
Imitating Cicero, we shall use the term <term>stomachus<note>In Renaissance anatomy, "stomachus" usually refers to the esophagus (gullet), while the organ we call the stomach is termed the "ventriculus."</note></term> rather than "gullet" (as others often do, though the word also refers to the neck and the act of eating). This pathway, then, takes its start from the base of the tongue, where it is attached, and <margin>d 6th figure of the muscle tables. F. 14th figure E, E.</margin> touches the <term>tonsils<note>original: "tonsillas"</note></term> on both sides, beginning at the edge of the palate. Receiving the food that has been thrust and pushed down by the movement and agitation of the tongue, it drives the food downward by dilating the parts below what is being swallowed and contracting the parts above it. It is constructed of nervous or membranous material so that it may easily dilate and promptly collapse again; it is neatly interwoven with fibers that serve its function. Finally, like other ducts, it is rounded and is seen to be accurately smooth and slippery on the inside.

<margin>Substance, form, and layer.</margin>
* It consists of two proper <term>tunics<note>Vesalius uses "tunic" to describe the distinct layers of tissue forming the wall of an organ.</note></term>, which vary in substance, hardness, thickness, and the type of fibers. <margin>* Seek the depiction of these from the likeness of the 9th or 17th figures.</margin> The inner layer, which is continuous with the lining of the whole mouth and palate, is indeed more nervous, harder, and a little thinner, and is gifted with straight fibers that serve the "attraction" of food, much like hands. The outer layer, however, is thicker, softer, and participates almost in the nature of muscles, appearing more fleshy. It abounds only in transverse or circular fibers, which effect a more successful and sudden propulsion into the <term>ventricle<note>The stomach.</note></term> of the food already pulled in by the fibers of the inner layer. Furthermore, if the stomach ever protrudes anything during vomiting, these fibers also greatly assist in its expulsion. The esophagus required only these two differences in fibers: the straight ones to pull and the transverse ones to push. For if oblique fibers had been added, the food would linger in the esophagus with a longer delay; this would not only be useless to a person but also inconvenient and troublesome. Indeed, the esophagus, when full of food, would then be distended longer, acting as a lingering obstacle to the <term>aspera arteria<note>The trachea or windpipe; called "rough artery" because of its cartilaginous rings.</note></term>, the lungs, and the great artery <note>the aorta</note> while they are dilating.

<margin>The Course.</margin>
Nature, extending the esophagus safely through the neck and thorax to the stomach—and so as to less frequently disturb those organs I just mentioned—carries it $^e$ exactly <margin>

It creeps along next to that artery until the ninth thoracic vertebra. $^h$ As soon as it reaches that point, it is raised from the body of that vertebra and ascends higher than the artery (lest the artery perhaps be compressed by swallowed food), <margin>Book 5 of *Anatomical Procedures*, section 10. That the esophagus does not use the same opening in the diaphragm as the great artery.</margin> penetrating the nervous part of the <term>transverse septum<note>The diaphragm.</note></term> toward the left side $^i$. It does not, as Galen thought (following Hippocrates), use the same $^k$ opening as the artery sliding down to the lower parts of the body; rather, it has its own peculiar one, which we said was prepared for it and the nerves descending with it (when the diaphragm was described). Therefore, up to the beginning of the ninth thoracic vertebra, the esophagus is joined to the bodies of the vertebrae by the intervention of small membranes originating from the dorsal ligaments. From these membranes, it possesses a third tunic, which is distinguished by no fibers at all and acts as a sort of wrapping for its second tunic. The reason why the esophagus unfolds toward the right of the artery near the fifth thoracic vertebra, rather than the left, is the artery itself. The artery does not occupy the middle seat of the back like a tyrant (though it is much more worthy); <margin>q Look at the whole 10th figure of book 6 and O, P in the 6th figure of this book 6. r 22nd figure, h to g and 20th figure, R to Q.</margin> but since it takes its origin from the $^q$ left chamber of the heart, and through the rest of its course is placed beneath the <term>vena cava<note>The main vein returning blood to the heart.</note></term> toward the left $^r$, it necessarily verges to the left for the greater part of itself. Consequently, yielding a little to the esophagus, it admits it as a partner and companion of the seat of the vertebrae, so that the esophagus is less slanted and obtains a firmer seat than it could find on the left side. The esophagus stretches along the right side of the back; but, as we have said, it is carried over the artery <note>The aorta.</note> and, slanted at an obtuse angle, it seeks the left side. This is so that in approaching the stomach, it is not forced to pierce the liver (which occupies the entire right side of the lower region of the diaphragm), but instead finds that part of the diaphragm where the smaller portion of the liver is located, which offers it easy passage. <gloss>t</gloss> This is indeed the thinner portion of the whole liver, stretched here toward the left side of the diaphragm; in its posterior region, where the esophagus passes through the diaphragm, <gloss>u</gloss> a notch like a semicircle is carved out, matching the size of the esophagus (whose front side it embraces at that point). Nor should anyone believe those professors of dissection who think that the diaphragm—and especially the opening through which it transmits the esophagus—acts as a barrier to prevent food from returning from the stomach back up to the higher regions. If that were the case, it would equally prevent the descent of food into the stomach. Likewise, it is a mere fable when others contend that the esophagus is narrower here, where it continues into the stomach, than it is in the neck; they falsely believe it is gathered and constricted by black bile belched into the upper mouth of the stomach from the spleen.

Furthermore, that oblique path by which the esophagus climbs over the artery and is carried to the left <gloss>x</gloss> is also convenient for the nerves (so they are not stretched more than is proper), which you will soon hear are inserted into the stomach. Nature did not think it sufficient merely to provide the esophagus with the aforementioned fibers for the swift passage of food through such a slanted path; rather, to ensure its cavity was always moist and, as it were, lubricated, she added glands to it. In the throat, <gloss>y</gloss> some are shared by the esophagus and the larynx; these prepare the saliva and moisture for those organs to keep them from drying out, and are called <term>tonsils<note>original: "tonsillae"</note></term> in Latin. In the middle of the esophagus's path, where it lies beneath the <gloss>*</gloss> windpipe <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"</note> as it divides into two trunks toward the lungs, Nature often attaches two other glands, not just beside the esophagus, but also at its back and sides. <gloss>a</gloss> These clearly correspond to those glands which Nature placed around the beginning of the neck of the bladder in men <note>The prostate gland.</note>. And just as we shall mention in the proper place how those glands irrigate the passage for urine and genital fluid in the penis, so too the glands attached to the esophagus moisten its cavity and soak it with a certain salivary humor, lest food slide down into the stomach with greater difficulty due to dryness.

Now we shall discuss its exact position and the rest of its history. Galen asserts that the stomach is placed in the middle of the body. Many professors of dissection, borrowing from him, do not merely state this, but contend that it has obtained an exactly central seat according to <gloss>d</gloss> all differences of position, like a common workshop for all parts or some king. They are quite superficial in measuring this by the proportions of a man standing upright, or even with arms and legs fully extended as if placed within a circle. However, an equal portion of the stomach does not occupy the right and left, nor does the stomach stretch as far toward the back as toward the front, although <gloss>e</gloss> perhaps its higher orifice <note>The cardia.</note> might not undeservedly claim that for itself. For as soon as the esophagus penetrates the diaphragm in the left seat of its nervous part, it <gloss>f</gloss> becomes a continuous body with the stomach, which, touching a wide area of the diaphragm on the left side, occupies the entire empty region between the liver and the spleen. ### ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE] BODY

...stretched only under the hollow of the liver, and throughout its upper part and its right side, it is hidden by the liver. It recedes from the right side of the diaphragm by as much as the liver is thick, while in the meantime (as I was just saying) it touches a large portion of the diaphragm with its left side. Nor indeed does the spleen significantly hinder this, for it is not so much attached to the left side of the stomach, nor does it reach into the anterior parts of the body as the common crowd of physicians believes, but rather it is positioned underneath in the posterior and lower parts (though also somewhat to the side). Then, the stomach extends much further into the left side (up to the diaphragm, naturally) than into the right (where it only reaches the hollow of the liver). Indeed, its shape in humans (for I am now setting aside Galen’s considerations of dogs and monkeys) is seen to be such that its largest portion is also placed on the left, just as if it had found a larger seat there than could be properly contained, which seems suited to its functions. 

<margin>Shape of the stomach.</margin>The stomach is quite varied in form: but if one examines it cursorily, it first appears round and oblong from right to left, or somewhat cylindrical along its width. It is round because all round things are the most capacious and, meanwhile, least exposed to injury; but it is oblong because the space in which it is contained, and then its two <gloss>e</gloss> <margin>e 14, 15 fig. G, H.</margin> orifices—one by which it receives food, the other by which it pushes the processed food into the intestines—seem to require it. 

Furthermore, if the shape of the stomach is then weighed more accurately, it is seen to be much fuller and rounder on the left side, and also slightly prominent toward the lower parts; then, turning from here toward the right, it is seen to be gradually compressed into a narrow space, descending in its upper region and ascending in its lower region, so that it becomes much more slender on the right side than on the left. So too, in its upper seat, which extends from one orifice to the other, it is tighter and narrower, but in the lower part, it is wider and more ample. 

<gloss>f</gloss> <margin>f 14 figure L, L.</margin> On its anterior part, it appears uniformly convex everywhere, deformed in no part. On the posterior seat, <margin>g 15 figura M. h 15 fig. N. i 15 fig. O.</margin> it shows two bumps as it were: <gloss>g</gloss> one on the left, which is large and more prominently protruding; <gloss>h</gloss> another on the right, smaller and more flattened. And these bumps <gloss>i</gloss> are formed by a certain sinus or impression, pressed into the posterior seat of the stomach according to the length of the body. For where <margin>The two orifices of the stomach.</margin> the stomach faces the vertebrae of the back, and the descending trunks of the <gloss>k</gloss> <margin>k 22 fi. g, h. 25 fi. P, Q.</margin> vena cava and the large artery <note>The aorta.</note> stretched out upon them, and adapts itself however it can to the seat it occupies, its posterior region is somewhat pressed inward, as if toward its own cavity. Although, if the stomach is torn from the body and inflated, it does not show this kind of sinus, and appears just as convex there as in the anterior region. 

Furthermore, two orifices also pertain to the form of the stomach, <gloss>l</gloss> <margin>l 14, 15 figure G.</margin> of which one, by which food and drink were said to be taken in, is located in the highest part of the left side of the stomach for this reason: that the esophagus <note>Vesalius uses "stomachus" here to refer to the gullet/esophagus.</note> conveniently piercing the diaphragm there, could first be joined to the stomach or become a common body with it. And although we say the upper mouth of the stomach is held in its left part, it actually comes closer to its middle seat than to the left side; this appears more obvious the more the stomach is swollen. The other orifice of the stomach, transmitting food changed into a cream-like substance <note>Chyme.</note> to the intestines, is called <term>pylorus</term> <note>original: "πυλωρὸς"; literally 'gatekeeper'</note> <gloss>m</gloss> <margin>m 14, 15 fi. H. 12. fi. S.</margin> by the Greeks, and by us the "janitor" and the lower or right mouth; <gloss>m</gloss> it is located on the right side of the stomach. This is not, as the rest of the professors of dissection pass down and as those imagine who so stubbornly argue about the order of food intake, having imposed a name on this orifice from its position in a way that is not very suitable; they have never seen the crop and stomach of birds...

### ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

...and they considered the stomachs of ruminating <note>Animals that chew the cud, like cows or sheep.</note> animals in the lower region of that site, but rather in the highest part, closest to the right side of the stomach. For it was not enough that these orifices were not placed directly opposite one another (lest the food, as yet unchanged, should slip out of the stomach too quickly); rather, it was necessary for the lower exit to be planted out from the higher part of the stomach, so that the food would not escape the stomach by its own weight. Instead, only when it was fully processed and exquisitely changed into a creamy juice <note>original: "cremor"; this refers to chyle, the milky fluid of digested food.</note> would it be propelled into the intestines by the expelling strength of the stomach rather than by its own weight. This orifice of the stomach constitutes and marks the beginning of the intestines.

<margin>
n 14, 15 fig.
P. 7 figu. ab
l ad k
</margin>
For this reason, most have named the first of the intestines—which is twelve fingers in length—the "Origin" <note>original: "Exortum"; commonly known as the <term>duodenum</term>, from the Latin for "twelve each."</note>. Nor indeed does this second orifice occupy the right side of the stomach without reason, since this area is adjacent to the middle of the hollow seat of the liver. Through the benefit of its own veins, the liver seizes and "feeds" upon whatever succulent material has been prepared by the stomach, drawing it from the intestines and the stomach itself. The liver performs this more easily because the parts that first receive the creamy juice processed by the stomach are positioned closer to it. Furthermore, the orifices of the stomach vary not only in their position, but the lower one is also narrower than the upper:

<margin>The unequal size of the orifices.</margin>
This is because a person frequently swallows coarse, un-ground, hard, and large masses, for which the entrance to the stomach needed to be a wide path. Through the lower opening, by contrast, it is rare for anything large, hard, or not yet converted into juice to pass—though it is certainly not so narrow that it can only pass liquid. Indeed, many people harmlessly excrete a great many fruit pits, even very large ones, which they have frequently swallowed. Galen even tells of a certain man who carelessly swallowed a gold ring he was holding in his mouth, which was then promptly excreted.

<margin>Book on the Natural Faculties.</margin>
Nor did that "clever Spaniard" show himself ignorant of the capacity of this orifice. Last year, he stole forty large pearls <note>original: "uniones"; large, high-quality pearls often worn singly.</note>—of the kind noble matrons here wear around their necks—along with a gold cross set with five precious gems and the string that held them, from a certain courtesan named Bacchis. When she refused to give herself to him for the night unless he first counted out fifty gold pieces, and he happily agreed, she obtained from her Venetian patrician lover an elegant necklace belonging to his wife, so that she might appear more adorned and pleasing. The Spaniard, gasping for a way to pay back the little harlot, occupied her as deceitfully as he could so that she would eventually fall into a sweet sleep. Afterward, he untied the necklace and swallowed the individual pearls, the cross, and finally the string (so that nothing would hinder his theft).

### ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE HUMAN BODY

...those who are educated only by books and who invent the works of Nature according to their own whim, write that this glandular body is a muscle. They foolishly assert that it encircles the lower orifice of the stomach in a ring-like fashion, and from this, they—just like Galen in the eighth book of *On the Use of the Parts*—call this body the <term>pylorus</term><note>From the Greek πύλωρον (pylōron), meaning "gatekeeper."</note> and the gatekeeper. Furthermore (a fact those men should have noticed), <margin>Look at Figure 15 at h, k.</margin> not only in the lower orifice of the stomach but also in the upper one, the substance of the stomach is thicker and denser. The orifices possess a part that bulges inward in the shape of a circle, which corresponds entirely to the membranous and fibrous <note>original: "nervosa"; in 16th-century anatomy, this often referred to sinewy or fibrous textures rather than just nerves.</note> substance of the stomach. It is not, as one might falsely persuade oneself in Galen's name, a glandular substance. This thickness can be felt by touch while the stomach is still intact during dissection, but when opened and turned inside out, it comes into view, clearly showing the beginning of the stomach (or the end of the esophagus) and the origin of the duodenum. Indeed, at that point, the esophagus <note>original: "stomachus"; Vesalius often uses this term for the gullet/esophagus.</note> and that intestine seem to grow out of the stomach itself, appearing as entirely different parts from the stomach; yet on the outside, nothing of the sort appears, and no portion of the stomach stands out above the rest of the surface. This thicker and increased substance of the stomach, positioned so that it projects into the internal region, is created primarily so that the mouths of the stomach might be more robust and dense than the rest of its body. This prevents them from being torn or ruptured by the force of things passing through, and perhaps also so that when the mouths are constricted, they might be more quickly narrowed and closed by the inward-closing action of this bulging part. 

And truly, just as <margin>Surface of the stomach.</margin> <margin>t Figure 14.</margin> the outer surface of the stomach is smooth and flat, so too <margin>u Figure 16.</margin> is its internal cavity, provided you except the two circular protruding bumps we just mentioned. For the stomach shows nothing there except certain wrinkles (if it is found to be strongly constricted), which correspond to the cavity of the intestines and <margin>x Figure 23 in the right-hand figure.</margin> the bladder. However, the interior displays a dark color, interspersed as if with intense reddish clouds, while the exterior is almost entirely white. 

Nevertheless, sometimes in the stomachs of very obese men, a layer of fat is found—abundant but smooth and slippery—attached to the internal surface around the region of the bottom on the left side. Because of this, some writers, deluded by the <term>omasum</term><note>The third compartment of the stomach of a ruminant (like a cow).</note> of ruminating animals—which is decorated and equipped with so many cells in the internal cavity, almost like the cells of a honeycomb—have falsely written that the human stomach abounds with certain cells and continuous boundaries. 

<margin>Quantity of the stomach.</margin>
The size of the stomach is quite varied. For if it is removed from the body and inflated like a bladder, you will not wonder at all that such a great force and abundance of food can be consumed at one time. Nor is it always equally swollen in a person; but when it behaves according to its nature and uses its "constricting power," it embraces everything it contains—however small or large—from all sides, leaving no empty space. And therefore, it adapts itself according to the amount of what has been taken in, so that it can both receive and embrace a great deal (lest a person be forced to eat constantly) and, on the other hand, if only a small amount is offered, it can embrace and "cook" <note>original: "concoquat"; referring to the process of digestion, often likened to cooking by heat in ancient medicine.</note> it from all sides. 

<margin>From what layers the substance of the stomach is formed.</margin>
The substance of the stomach, which is for the most part membranous, fits this action perfectly, as it can conveniently be enlarged and dilated when use requires it, and again, when there is need, it can be drawn together and constricted. <margin>y As far as was possible, we have expressed the layers of the stomach in Figure 17.</margin> For the stomach consists of two wide and thin layers <note>original: "tunicis"; also translated as tunics or coats.</note> joined to one another, just like the esophagus, but somewhat different. The inner layer of the stomach is similarly fibrous and membranous, just like the inner layer of the esophagus, and is continuous with the inner layer of the whole esophagus, mouth, and lips, as well as the intestines. However, it differs slightly in hardness from the layer of the mouth and esophagus, because we process harder and rougher foods in the mouth before they fall into the stomach, which might otherwise bruise and scrape it...

He discusses the stomach's remarkable ability to expand and contract to fit its contents, comparing its internal texture to that of other organs and correcting anatomical misconceptions derived from animal dissection.</summary>

It is interwoven with double fibers, which also distinguishes it from the inner part of the esophagus. Indeed, the inner part of this layer, facing the cavity of the stomach, is endowed with many straight fibers. For the stomach must draw in food and drink through the esophagus, enticing them with these fibers as if with hands; when these contract, they shorten the esophagus and the stomach, so much so that 

<margin>z They show the larynx together with the esophagus in figures 2, 3, and 5 of chapter 2, book 2, where the esophagus is marked with H.</margin>

the ^z larynx rises upward as the beginning of the esophagus descends, because there is a mutual connection between the esophagus and the larynx. One can see that the inner membrane of the larynx is continuous with the inner membrane of the esophagus, and thus with the stomach. The second type of fibers in the inner layer of the stomach is the oblique type, located on the outer surface of that layer where the second layer embraces it. Just as the attraction of food and drink necessarily precedes their retention, so Nature has coordinated the straight fibers on the inside with the oblique ones. Furthermore, as the expulsion of already processed food follows retention, so also the second or outer layer of the stomach rightly possesses transverse fibers outside the oblique ones. This outer layer, thicker and softer than the inner one and less compact, abounds in transverse fibers, corresponding to the second layer of the esophagus—except that the layer of the esophagus is slightly less fleshy than this one and is also entwined with some oblique fibers. 

<margin>The outer layer of the stomach is not exceedingly fleshy at its base.</margin>

...they are first distributed through the lower membrane of the <term>omentum</term><note>A fold of fatty tissue that hangs from the stomach; Vesalius is describing how blood vessels travel through this protective "apron."</note>, and from there they are diverted into the <term>liver</term><note>original: "iecur"</note>, the <term>gallbladder</term><note>original: "bilis uesicula"</note>, the <term>spleen</term><note>original: "lien"</note>, and finally into the <term>stomach</term><note>original: "ventriculus"</note> itself. ⁱ The first vein of the stomach takes its origin from the <term>portal vein</term><note>The large vein that carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver.</note> before it splits into its two large trunks; it runs toward the lower orifice of the stomach <note>The pylorus, where the stomach meets the small intestine.</note> and the neighboring areas at its posterior side. ᵏ The artery paired with this vein is considered an offshoot of that artery which follows the path of the portal vein and enters the hollow of the liver. ˡ The second vein, which has a companion artery in every respect, is stretched under the entire lower half of the stomach, supported by the upper membrane of the omentum; from this vein, the right side of the floor of the stomach—both front and back—receives its branches. This vein frequently originates from the right region of the portal vein, where it splits into its two larger trunks. ᵐ The artery, however, arises from the one we said was diverted into the liver. ⁿ The third vein of the stomach is exceedingly thin and lacks a companion artery; it arises from the thinner left trunk of the portal vein and is dispersed in a small series of branches into the posterior part of the stomach (where the right bulge of the stomach stands out). ᵒ The fourth vein, proceeding from the same trunk as the one just mentioned, takes as its companion throughout its entire course an ᵖ artery that arises from the one seeking the spleen through the lower membrane of the omentum. This is easily the most important of all the veins reaching the stomach (as is its artery among the arteries), and it is divided into more numerous branches. It proceeds upward toward the middle of the back of the stomach, first spreading branches on both sides into many twigs across the posterior region. From there, it gradually climbs upward to the right side of the upper stomach mouth <note>The cardia, where the esophagus enters the stomach.</note>, and encircling it like a crown, it distributes several twigs downward into the body of the stomach, while sending a few thin ones upward to the end of the <term>esophagus</term><note>original: "stomachus"; here referring to the gullet.</note> where it joins the stomach. From this vein, as it circles the right side of the stomach's mouth, ᵠ a branch is produced that reaches along the higher part of the stomach all the way to its lower orifice, and in its progress downward, it also spreads offshoots at intervals for some distance. ʳ The fifth vein, not deprived of a companion artery, entwines the left side of the floor of the stomach; supported by the upper membrane of the omentum, it sends branches from its higher position into the front and back of the stomach. Its origin hangs from the larger branch of the portal vein that is to be inserted into the lowest part of the spleen; and ˢ the artery accompanying this vein sprouts from the branch of the artery approaching the spleen here. The sixth vein of the stomach would be the one that is constantly on the lips of anatomists, and which they all assert is carried from the spleen to the upper orifice of the stomach. ᵗ To tell the truth, I observe not just one, but ᵘ several veins arising—and not always in the same number—from those extended to the spleen (besides the fifth one listed above), approaching the left side of the stomach near the spleen. Among these, the principal one is usually that which takes its origin from the larger branch of the portal vein inserted into the higher part of the spleen; from this, twigs as thin as hairs rarely

<margin>The function of the stomach's veins.</margin>

reach toward the upper orifice of the stomach. Companion arteries are perpetually joined to these veins reaching the left side of the stomach, branched from those that enter the spleen. The common function of all the stomach's veins is both to bring nourishment to it and to lead the cream of the more succulent <term>chyle</term><note>original: "cremor"; the pulpy acidic fluid of partially digested food.</note> prepared by the stomach toward the hollow of the liver, just as the veins of the intestines do. However, I will admit (though timidly and almost against my own judgment, along with other professors of dissection) that the specific task of the veins I listed in the sixth place, and especially the fifth, is that if the spleen should "belch" anything into the stomach, they serve as its vehicle and

<margin>Of the arteries.</margin>

pour it into the stomach. Furthermore, the numerous arteries of the stomach refresh its <term>innate heat</term><note>A classical medical concept where the heart and blood vessels were thought to distribute a vital, life-sustaining warmth throughout the body.</note>, and it seems (if I dare say so) that some succulent material also escapes from the stomach.

For since they are soft and slender, if they were stretched in a straight path over a long way, and held the stomach (intended for receiving food) suspended from them, they would be perpetually strained by its mass and broken on the slightest occasion, unless Nature had diligently provided for them with these types of entwinements and tortuous ducts.

<margin>The function of the whole stomach.</margin> The stomach (to now approach its function) has eight faculties: four indeed common to all parts of the entire body that are nourished, and four peculiar to itself, by which it serves the whole body. But many weigh these matters too superficially, staining entire books with this question: whether the stomach is nourished by the juice it prepares for the liver, or by blood separately, or by both at once? Since, by the benefit of those faculties which the stomach acquires in common with the remaining parts, it attracts its own proper nourishment from the veins, retains it, works it out, and if there is anything superfluous to it, drives it away. In the duties, however, by which it serves the whole body, it takes in food and drink from the mouth through the esophagus by means of straight fibers; soon it retains what has been taken in by means of oblique fibers; and it embraces the whole for so long, until it, by its innate or...

Furthermore, we believe that the organs surrounding it on all sides greatly assist its transformative power by heating it, much as large hearths are accustomed to heating a cauldron. The omentum is partly stretched over and partly grows into the entire lower region of the stomach.

To this vein, where it is joined to the peritoneum and laid over the stomach, much fat is attached in its vicinity (though not equally abundant in everyone). This provides some help so that the stomach may labor more briskly in its duty of concocting food. For the liver, the spleen, and the veins and arteries stretched beneath the posterior part of the stomach contribute greatly, just as the diaphragm itself, by its untiring motion, by no means neglects the stomach. Indeed, even the heat of the heart resting upon the diaphragm <note>original: "septo"</note> is not considered useless for the more perfect functioning of the stomach.
