...however, it is not always seen extending all the way to the pubic bone covering the intestines. For a portion of it—which in humans ought to be spread over the intestines, just as it is in dogs, pigs, and monkeys—is rarely sent down beyond the region of the navel. Instead, the greatest part of it is usually found by those performing dissections to be retracted and coiled toward the left side, near the spleen. <note>original: "lienem"</note> Nevertheless, if the omentum <note>The fatty layer of tissue that hangs over the stomach and intestines like an apron; often called the "caul."</note> is grasped with the hands at its lower edge and stretched downward and toward the sides, it readily reaches the region of the pubic bone, the posterior seat of the bladder, and the flanks, completely covering the intestines. We do not observe this retraction of the omentum toward the upper regions only in those killed by hanging—lest someone should think it coils upon itself due to the shock or violent movement of the body—but it also occurs frequently in those who are suffocated by water, or who perish quietly and without bodily agitation from pleurisy, <note>original: "morbo laterali"</note> inflammation of the brain, or some similar affection, as well as in those whose thorax and abdomen are opened while still living during public executions. Indeed, in healthy men, the omentum so rarely descends to the seat of the pubic bone during dissection that some have doubted whether "ruptures" <note>original: "ramices"; a term for hernias.</note> can be produced by the descent of the omentum into the scrotum <note>original: "scortum"</note> or<margin>f Fig. 20 u; Fig. 21 p, q, r, s, t. g Fig. 25 C; Fig. 27 G.</margin><sup>f</sup> rather into the outer tunic of the testes and the seminal vessels. They also doubt whether, in very obese people, the mouth of the uterus<sup>g</sup> can be so compressed by the omentum as to prevent conception, according to the opinion of Hippocrates. But I have more than once discovered the omentum descended into that very tunic of the testes and seminal<margin>h Fig. 22 at p, p.</margin> vessels (to which the peritoneum<sup>h</sup> gives origin), and increased in size in marvelous ways beyond the ordinary constitution of the omentum elsewhere. <margin>i Everything seen in Fig. 2.</margin> For while the entire part of the omentum<sup>i</sup> resting on the intestines in a moderately fat man would hardly exceed a weight of one or one and a half pounds, I have nevertheless seen the omentum so unnaturally increased within that tunic of the testis that it weighed four or five pounds. It dragged the stomach <note>original: "ventriculum"</note> so far down from its position that, with the stomach failing in its duty and various hiccups arising, I concluded during the dissection that this weight had been the cause of death. This occurred in a certain case of pleurisy which had otherwise been well cleared, but where the wrapping of the scrotum with a support <note>original: "subligari"; a suspensory bandage for a hernia.</note> had been neglected by the patient and his attendants. Furthermore, the more accurately I investigate the nature of what we call ruptures or hernias, the more I am persuaded that all those "soft ruptures"—which the common people call "fleshy" and rightly distinguish from varicose conditions—arise from the prolapse and growth of the omentum. And just as we have often seen the omentum increase and fall into the scrotum, so too Hippocrates<sup>k</sup> undoubtedly believed that in certain women it grows so much<margin>k Fig. 24 between T & L, R, S; and Fig. 25 between β & l, x.</margin> that the mass of its growth,<sup>k</sup> collected and stored between the uterus and the bladder, could so compress and narrow the mouth of the base of the uterus <note>The cervix.</note> that it would be unable to unclose or open itself for female conception. Additionally, the width of the neck of the uterus near its base could not be so distended by the penis—especially one that is weaker or less prominent—that a path would open for the seed into the base of the uterus. Perhaps because of this mass or growth of the omentum, some were first called <term>ἐπιπλοοκομισται</term> <note>epiplookomistai; translated from Greek as "omentum-bearers."</note>, as if you were to say, "bearers of the omentum." For I hardly think all men were so named as if they possessed the largest omentum among all living creatures, as Galen handed down; for it seems to me that almost all quadrupeds are gifted with a larger omentum, which is perpetually stretched and spread everywhere over the intestines, than even well-conditioned men. The* shape of the omentum most closely resembles the image of a<margin>* This is shown especially by Fig. 4, r and s.</margin> purse, a small bag, or a traveler's scrip. <margin>The shape of the omentum.</margin> It is most like the scrip of a bird-catcher, which has a circular orifice, rising higher in its posterior part than in its anterior. For a scrip of this kind would match the shape of the omentum exactly if it consisted of a single hide, or were woven of wool, and were everywhere seamless and, so to speak, one single

<margin>A brief enumeration of the substance of the omentum.</margin>
...it is a body of such a kind. Indeed, the omentum <note>The omentum is a double-layered fold of peritoneum that hangs down from the stomach; it is often rich in fat and plays a role in immune responses.</note> is a substance consisting of a membrane not interwoven with fibers, but abundant in many veins, arteries, nerves, and—in a certain region of itself—having a naturally grown glandular body, and also much fat. But where all these things take their origin, you will understand most readily if you imagine in your mind a pouch, <note>original: "peram"</note> such as I proposed before, in which you would call one part the anterior and superior, and the other the posterior and inferior.

To the superior membrane, however, we assign that part of the circle which is led from the right side of the stomach through its bottom to the hollow seat of the spleen.

From here, both resting upon each other, they are led downward over the intestines and under the peritoneum; and if by chance the membranes in this path over the intestines are not entangled, they cover them on the anterior part and at the sides, and reach with their lower edge as far as the pubic bone. But if the membranes only cover the seat of the intestines which stays above the navel, and—as frequently happens—they lie contracted toward the left side, they offer themselves to the sight as if rolled back and gathered into coils.

<margin>The connection of the omentum with the colon.</margin>
...collected. These membranes are joined by no connections to the intestines, except for the
<margin>* Examine the fifth figure carefully here.</margin>
lower membrane, which in humans is most tenaciously * continued to the colon <note>The colon is the main part of the large intestine.</note> through the entire path of that intestine which creeps along the floor of the stomach. Nor should this be observed sluggishly, since the lower membrane of the omentum serves as a mesentery <note>The mesentery is a fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place.</note> for the colon itself where it is extended out from the stomach. For the colon, along that entire path, possesses no part of the mesentery, quite differently than in dogs and monkeys, in which the omentum is scarcely joined to the colon. However, in humans, the lower membrane of the omentum, which is spread beneath the stomach, does not only take the place of the mesentery, as we have just said; indeed, if you examine each part accurately, you will admit that the portion of the lower membrane of the omentum extended to the intestines is born, in a way, from the third tunic <note>layer</note> of the colon. And I would wish this to be weighed more diligently because it was less noticed by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the dominant medical authority whose findings Vesalius often corrected via human dissection.</note>, who attributed too much to monkeys. It certainly seems to have been most clearly seen by Herophilus and Aristotle <note>Two of the most influential ancient Greek thinkers on biology and anatomy.</note>, who did not consider the part of the omentum binding the colon to the back to be part of the omentum; instead, they recognized only that part which, arising from the floor of the stomach and the colon, covers the intestines. Although I think it better to attribute also to the omentum that part which is stretched under the stomach and contains the colon, since it is almost continuous with the rest of the omentum and provides the same uses as the lower membrane of the omentum in dogs. Meanwhile, in humans, it serves as a mesentery for the colon in abundance; and since it is constructed there under the stomach almost as a double membrane, it corresponds very much to the construction and fabric of the mesentery. Furthermore, the upper membrane of the omentum in humans is found to be so joined to the lower membrane at the region of the colon (where it extends out from the stomach) that one might not absurdly say the upper membrane of the omentum is also connected to the colon along the floor of the stomach by several ties. However, the reason why Galen claimed the omentum was joined to the colon by moderate and loose connections, and that only on the right side, was because of monkeys, which possess a nature midway between dogs and humans. For in dogs, the omentum is attached to the colon or any other intestine in no part. In monkeys, it holds a middle way, although they still approach the construction of a dog rather than a human.
<margin>Veins entwining the omentum. *Book 6 of the Anatomical Procedures.* *Book 4 on the Use of the Parts.*</margin>

None belong to the omentum from the vena cava, even where it takes its beginning under the stomach (even if Galen felt otherwise). # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...extended along the lower part of the stomach within the membrane itself. From these, innumerable branches run downward into that membrane of the omentum <note>The omentum is a fold of peritoneum connecting the stomach with other abdominal organs.</note>, not in a straight path, but in a somewhat oblique and wandering manner, much like we see the cords of nets intertwined, now coming together and now drawing apart. For this reason, the omentum is called a fishing net <note>original: "γαγγαμὸν" (gangamon)</note> and a "siglyon" <note>original: "σιγλυών" (siglyon), an ancient term for the omentum</note> by the Greeks, and is commonly called a net <note>original: "rete"</note> or a little net <note>original: "reticulum"</note>. Although perhaps the omentum was not so named because of the varied path of the vessels, but because when it is freed from the parts to which it is attached and then stretched out, it resembles a fisherman's net adapted to a single circle.<sup>a</sup>

<margin>
The artery of the omentum.
a As in figure 4.
b In figures 2, 3, 4; for the veins see figure in chapter 12, book 3, at 'm', and almost the entire series of that trunk.
</margin>
The arteries<sup>b</sup> of the omentum depend on those which are distributed to the stomach, spleen, liver, and gallbladder. For the omentum safely leads all of these just as it does the veins, and from them it acquires so many companions for its own peculiar veins that very few small branches of the veins creep through it without the companionship of an artery. Also, besides the arteries just mentioned, the lower membrane of the omentum carries a somewhat larger artery extended for some distance into the intestines.

<margin>
Nerves of the omentum.
c Figure 4, 'd'; figure in chapter 12, book 3, at 'J'.
</margin>
In this way<sup>c</sup> the omentum is also interwoven with those nerves which are implanted into the liver, spleen, and stomach from the portions of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>In Vesalius's time, the vagus nerve and others were classified as the "sixth pair."</note> extended along the roots of the ribs.

<margin>
Fat.
d These are also attached to the veins and arteries in figures 2, 3, 4. Figure 4, chapter 2, book 6, at s, s, t, u, y, z, α, β, γ, δ, ε, ζ, η, θ, ι.

Furthermore,<sup>d</sup> fat, in which the omentum abounds, is found in great quantity in obese and very stout men, in a moderate amount in the lean, and even some is found in those extremely dried out and dead from wasting <note>original: "maramos," referring to severe malnutrition or consumption</note>. This fat is always attached to the veins and arteries of the omentum; specifically, it occurs only at the sides of the vessels where there is a moderate amount, but where there is much fat, it covers the top and bottom as well,<sup>e</sup> so much so that even vessels that are otherwise slender are completely hidden by the fat. In<sup>f</sup> the spaces between the vessels, however, no fat is preserved, just as in other membranes where fat is accustomed to grow. From this it is more readily gathered that this fat is produced from the blood exuding from the veins, thickened by the coldness of the membranes, and taking on the color of the changing body.

<margin>
The glandular body of the omentum.
g Figure 4, 'n', 'o'.
</margin>
Besides the fat, which is common to both membranes of the omentum, its lower membrane, spread beneath the posterior part of the stomach, possesses a particularly<sup>g</sup> large glandular body. Because it somewhat expresses the appearance of simple flesh, it is called "beautiful flesh" <note>original: "καλλίπρεας" (kallipreas)</note> and "all flesh" <note>original: "πάγκρεας" (pankreas), the pancreas</note> by the Greeks, being redder in dogs than in humans. This body is attached to the principal branches of the portal vein, arteries, and nerves, so that their branching—supported here only by the lower membrane of the omentum—might be made more secure, and so that it might also be placed beneath the stomach like a support and a cushion.

<margin>
h Figure 4, 'd'; figure 12, 'l', 'l'.
</margin>
Clearly,<sup>h</sup> this is the substance of the body that is spread beneath the duodenum <note>The first part of the small intestine.</note>, which until now was falsely believed to close the lower orifice of the stomach <note>The pylorus.</note> so that nothing undigested might flow out.

<margin>
Uses of the omentum.
i Figure 38, table 2, E, E, F, F; table 2, l, l, K, K.
k Seen beautifully in the figure for book 7.
</margin>
And this indeed is considered by me to be the primary and greatest use of the omentum: that it safely supports the branches of the portal vein extended into the spleen, stomach, duodenum, and the lowest part of the colon, leading them intertwined within itself; and then that it sustains and protects the arteries and nerves also to be inserted into those parts I just mentioned. Finally, it serves a purpose most similar to the outer covering of the fetus in the womb<sup>i</sup> and, in the cavity of the head,<sup>k</sup> the thin membrane <note>The pia mater.</note> that wraps the brain. Furthermore, which is by no means the least thing, the omentum binds the stomach to the back, and again connects the liver and spleen to the stomach by the intervention of the vessels and nerves—to say nothing of how much separate service it provides in stabilizing the colon in a man. By chance, it also acts as a kind of wrapping and covering for the intestines, nourishing and containing their heat like a soft pad <note>original: "penicilli," a brush or pad used for applying heat or cleaning.</note>.

<margin>
The structure of the omentum corresponds to its uses.
</margin>
The structure of the omentum certainly corresponds to these uses. For it is membranous so that it may more strongly bind the veins, arteries, and nerves intertwined in it, better reflect the heat of the intestines, and be able to readily sink down and be extended with the intestines.

<summary>Vesalius describes the omentum as a net-like membrane that supports vital blood vessels and nerves while providing insulation and structural support for the stomach and intestines. He also identifies the pancreas as a glandular support structure, correcting previous misconceptions about its role in closing the stomach.</summary>

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

...might be. It is thin, however, and especially where it rests upon the intestines, so as not to weigh them down with its mass. Hence, in our Brussels dialect, it even deserves the name "feather" <note>original: "plumæ". Vesalius, a native of Brussels, often notes local terminology.</note>. Truly, that the omentum—with its heat preserved by those frequent veins and arteries—is suited to warming the intestines and the stomach (in the part where it is joined to them), I believe is manifest, even if it is not explicitly stated. However, whether it benefits them by an innate and peculiar heating nature, or whether it merely helps in the manner of a padding of flesh or rather a membrane, is not equally conceded by all; some pronounce the fat to be cold, while others declare it truly hot.

### ON THE INTESTINES. CHAPTER V.

*We have attempted to express the image of the intestines primarily in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth figures; although the third figure also serves this purpose, along with the tenth and twelfth.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting an anatomical demonstration or lecture scene where several figures are gathered around a table in a room with arched windows.</image-desc>

<margin>These are found in the figures of this and the 6th book. From H in the 1st image of the 7th figure, to D in the 8th figure.</margin>
<margin>What is included here under the name of "intestines."</margin>
I shall narrate the construction of the intestines as it suits their office and use in due course, once I have explained their position, shape, substance, and connection, as well as the veins, arteries, and nerves implanted in them, and whatever else remains for the description of their fabric. By the name of "intestines," which are called <term>entera</term> <note>original: "ἔντερα"</note> by the Greeks, we do not at present include all the viscera or organs enclosed by the membrane lining the ribs and the peritoneum; nor shall we even ascribe the esophagus and the stomach to those which will now be called intestines. Rather, the duct extending from the lower orifice of the stomach all the way to the anus <note>original: "podicem"</note>—and equaling in length about fourteen and a half Italian ells <note>An "ulna" or ell was a unit of length; 14.5 Italian ells would be roughly 9 to 10 meters.</note>—is what is now to be specifically understood by the word "intestines."

<margin>The intestines are indeed a continuous body, but are given various names for different reasons, as if they were many.</margin>
And although that duct and the intestines themselves are one continuous body, since it is nevertheless led around in various, manifold windings and coils differing in shape, and they do not possess the same nature of position, substance, and form in every part, and finally, since different parts are made contiguous to different seats, and the primary use of all of them does not seem to be equal (as if there were several intestines), they are enumerated by those skilled in dissection. First, they divide these into the<sup>c</sup> thicker <note>The large intestine.</note> and the<sup>d</sup> thinner <note>The small intestine.</note>, and from each of those they again constitute a group of three, so that there are six in total. This is done in the same way that it is established that the same continuous journey often acquires several names for various reasons. For example, in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>, the journey from the Gate of Saint James to that which is called Saint Martin’s—even if it is almost straight and does not proceed through various turns—nevertheless changes its name six times (if I remember correctly): first from Saint James, then from the Little Bridge, then from the Church of the most Blessed Virgin <note>Notre Dame Cathedral.</note>, and not much later from her bridge, then from a certain wine-shop, and finally borrowing its title from the House of Saint Martin. We see this happen much more in rivers that are not "royal" <note>Major navigable rivers.</note> and in continuous roads that proceed through many turns.

<margin>c Figure 8, d; d Figure 7.</margin>
<margin>A brief history and enumeration of the intestines.</margin>
However much the intestines vary among themselves, they are all nonetheless located between the stomach and the seat where we discharge excrement. They are endowed with a rounded shape, but are not equally capacious or circular in every part. They have a membranous substance, though it is not equally thick or thin everywhere. Furthermore, they possess two peculiar layers <note>original: "tunicas"</note> interwoven with circular fibers, and in some places longitudinal ones, receiving a third layer added to these from the peritoneum.

<margin>e Figures 14, 15, H; Figure 16, k. f Figure 7, I from H. † Figure 16, h.</margin>
<margin>The origin of the intestines from the stomach, and the position of the thin duct.</margin>
Moreover, they receive small branches of veins, arteries, and nerves, though not equally numerous everywhere, as I shall now endeavor to pursue, taking the beginning of my discourse from the very origin of the intestines. Therefore, from the lower orifice of the stomach, which consists in its higher part and nearest to its right side, the beginning of the intestines arises. At that orifice, where it is of a thicker substance...

the substance <note>The "substance" refers to the intestinal wall or the connection discussed on the preceding page.</note> protrudes inward, is continued, and as soon as it emerges from the stomach, having been turned back toward the rear parts, it proceeds straight downward <margin>g Figure 7, from I to K; Figures 14, 15, P.</margin> along the right side of the back under the posterior region of the stomach, wound into no coils at all. But when this intestine, thus hidden, <margin>h Figure 7, K, L.</margin> first reaches as far as the lower region of the stomach, lurking under the colon (which you will hear shortly is extended <margin>i Figures 6, 8, from P toward Q.</margin> this way), it soon twists to the left, and as if rising forward from on high, it is wound into frequent and <margin>k Figure 7, from L to M in a continuous path.</margin> countless turns and coils. Covered by no other intestines at all, it fills the entire space held from under the stomach down to the pubic bones and to the flanks on both sides <margin>l Figures 6, 8, N, P, Q, R, S, T.</margin>; except, finally, for that area where I shall later say the colon is led around the sides of this intestine like a circle.

Truly, of these coils or revolutions, there is no fixed number at all, nor is the same order strictly maintained, nor do they occupy the right side of the belly more than the left, except that on the right side above the ilium bone down to the pubis, they pack a larger space than on the left, because some coil of the colon <margin>m From R, S to T.</margin> claims that place on the left side for itself privately. However multiple and varied the coils of this thin intestine are seen to be, it nevertheless constantly changes <margin>n At M in Figures 7 and 8.</margin> its shape and size directly from the middle region of the right ilium and many other things (as I will add later), while nonetheless observing the same thickness and width from the lower orifice of the stomach down to that seat—unless sometimes the part of this intestine attached closest to the back under the bottom of the stomach occurs during dissection to be <margin>o This would be near L and K in Figure 7.</margin> more capacious and wider than the rest of the duct of the intestine (as happens from time to time).

<margin>Three divisions of the thin intestine. The first.</margin> Such is the course of the present intestine as seen, which changes its name three times, as if it were three separate intestines. <margin>p Figure 7, from I to K.</margin> The first part is constituted by that whole section of the intestine which, spread under the stomach, descends somewhat straight from its lower orifice to the point where the intestine first begins to be wound into coils and circles. Regarding the name of this intestine, you will find quite trivial contentions <note>original: "aniles contentions" - literally "old-womanish arguments," a common Renaissance dismissal of pedantic academic bickering.</note> among those who, neglecting the reality of the structure, argue uselessly about the word. There are those who contend that this whole part—which for the most part equals the length of twelve fingers in a man—should not be called an intestine, but an "outgrowth" <note>original Greek: ἔκφυσιν (*ekphysin*)</note> and origin, or process. Others, even if its beginning arises from the stomach, affirm it is nevertheless an intestine, and that its orifice should be called the "outgrowth," but the rest of its duct should be called the intestine, filling whole commentaries with such trifling dispute. Therefore, let us call it by the common and more succinct name, **duodenum**, or the "intestine equaling the length of twelve fingers"; since it was called by the Greeks **twelve-fingers-long** <note>original Greek: δωδεκαδάκτυλον (*dodekadaktylon*)</note>.

<margin>The second.</margin> The second intestine <margin>q Figure 7, K.</margin> begins there where it first winds into the already mentioned coils or turns; and they call it the **fasting one** <note>original Greek: νῆστιν (*nestin*)</note> or **jejunum**, because during dissection it is found to be emptier and more void than the rest of the intestines. <margin>Book 5, *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin> Others, attempting to explain its name, seem to write as if it never contains anything in itself, and that the chyme <note>original: "cremor" - the creamy fluid of digested food.</note> prepared by the stomach never passes through it, or stays in it for only a moment.

<margin>The third.</margin> The third intestine is commonly called by us during dissection, as it is by the Greeks, the **ileon** <note>original Greek: ἴлеоv (*ileon*)</note>, perhaps named from the frequent turns and coils in which it is involved. It also gave its name to the disease which, resulting from the inflammation and obstruction of this intestine—and sometimes from a kind of entanglement—tortures the sick with marvelous torments; it is everywhere called **ileus** <note>original Greek: εἰλεῶ (*eileos*)</note> and **volvulus** <note>Latin: "twisted."</note> by the Latins. This is so even though some contend that both *ileon* and *eileos* are the names not of an intestine, but of the said disease. They use a common term to call the part of the small or thin intestine we have decided to describe here simply the **thin intestine**, in the same way we know the colon is sometimes specifically granted the name of the "thick" or "full" intestine. However, whether one wishes to call this portion or interval of the intestines the "thin intestine," or for the sake of clearer speech, to call it by a specific name such as *volvulus* or *ileon*, <margin>r In Figures 7 and 8, N is joined to M.</margin> it [continues] into the beginning of the thick intestine...

<margin>Figure 17 from L to M.</margin>
...the beginning ends. However, where its actual starting point should be placed, I cannot quite determine. Indeed, it is hidden from me how much of the entire small intestine those who argue so fiercely over names <note>Vesalius is critiquing contemporary anatomists who obsessed over naming conventions without clear physical evidence.</note> wish to be included under the name "jejunum." Nor, in truth, do I observe any clear sign from the beginning of the jejunum to the end of the ileum by which I might distinguish the end of the former and the beginning of the latter. For where we say the duodenum ends and the jejunum begins, more numerous veins and arteries occur than at the boundary of the ileum near the thick intestines <note>The large intestine or colon.</note>; yet the middle parts are arranged in a middle fashion. Furthermore, the beginning of the jejunum is more reddish, while the end of the ileum is more white. To this, one might add that the beginning of the jejunum is perhaps found more empty than the end of the ileum; but in the middle of the passage, as I said before, everything is in a middle state. Therefore, I do not establish what should be considered the end of the jejunum or the beginning of the ileum. I boldly assert that nothing distinguishes the jejunum from the ileum less than that "emptiness" <note>original: *inanitione*. The word *jejunum* literally means "fasting" or "empty."</note> proposed by most anatomists. In fact, the duodenum is found no less empty than that which they call the jejunum, and for greater reasons (as I shall state later).

<margin>The form of the small intestine.</margin>
Such, then, are the passages and locations of this small intestine which changes its name three times <note>The three parts: duodenum, jejunum, and ileum.</note>. Its form is consistent throughout, being perfectly round and equally wide in every part—except occasionally (as I hinted before) where it is joined closest to the back and the jejunum begins, specifically at the <margin>Table 13, figure c in d.</margin> insertion of the vessel <note>The common bile duct.</note> that carries bile to the intestines; there, it may be observed to be wider.

<margin>Substance.</margin>
<margin>See the construction of these from Figure 9.</margin>
The substance of the entire small intestine is also the same: namely, membranous and only moderately fleshy. It consists of two tunics <note>Layers or coats.</note>, the inner of which is harder and more like a membrane, yet softer than the inner tunic of the stomach. The outer tunic is thinner and more fleshy; nevertheless, it is thin and is interwoven only with transverse or circular fibers—unless perhaps the outer layer, especially at the end of the ileum where it meets the <margin>Figures 7, 8, M.</margin> thick intestines, also acquires longitudinal fibers, though these are very few <margin>Figure 9, k, l, f ending in L, surrounding i.</margin>.

<margin>See the connection of the intestines to the mesentery in Figure 10.</margin>
In addition to these two specific tunics, a third tunic takes its origin from the membranes of the peritoneum which safely carry the vessels to the intestines. For these membranes, reaching the hollow <note>The "hollow" or "concave" side where the mesentery attaches.</note> seat of the intestines along with the vessels, are dilated and clothe the intestines in a third wrapping.

<margin>The hollow part of the intestines, as named by anatomists.</margin>
<margin>Regarding Figure 64.</margin>
That part of the intestines in their outer circle—the outer surface, really—which the vessels first touch, or which faces the mesentery, is called the "hollow" part by anatomists; the opposite side is called the "gibbous" <note>Convex or rounded.</note> part. From the part of the omentum <note>The fatty apron of the abdomen.</note>, a third tunic is extended to the duodenum, by the help of which that intestine is bound to the back. But the jejunum and ileum receive their third tunic from the mesentery, which secures them to the back.

<margin>The veins and arteries of the small intestines.</margin>
<margin>Fig. ch. 5 lib. 3. 1. Fig. ch. 12 lib. 3. q, or together Fig. 4. r. Fig. ch. 5 lib. 3. G. Fig. 12. k. then Fig. ch. 12 lib. 3. ρ Fig. ch. 12 lib. 3. λ.</margin>
<margin>As can be seen in Figures 10 and 12.</margin>
Thus, the duodenum and the beginning of the jejunum have their own specific vein and artery, led straight downward along their length, spreading many small branches into them as they proceed. The vein obtains its origin from the portal vein before it is inserted into the mesentery; the artery, however, comes from that which is offered to the liver. The jejunum and ileum receive their frequent veins and arteries from those which are extended to the mesentery from the portal vein and from the root of the artery <note>The aorta.</note> above the renal arteries. For few branches are spread into the thinner intestines from the offshoot of the artery that takes its origin from the great artery <note>The aorta.</note> after the beginnings of the seminal arteries. Nor are the vessels led along the length of the jejunum and ileum, as in the duodenum; instead, as if from the center of the mesentery, they stretch upward from the depths and reach straight forward into the intestines. There, they are implanted like a numerous growth of tree roots, with their mouths opening into the inner seat of the intestines.

# ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...they are distinguished by their respective offspring <note>original: "sobole"; here referring to the branches of the vessels or nerves</note>. The **duodenum**, however, <margin>k. Figures 11, s.</margin> if it possesses any nerves, receives them from those which approach the lower orifice of the stomach and the right side of its base. Furthermore, the duodenum specifically claims this for itself: <margin>l. Figure 13, c.</margin> that the duct carrying yellow bile to the intestines is implanted into it. <margin>m. Figure 12, i, i.</margin> This same intestine in humans—and even more so in dogs— <margin>Glands of the intestines.</margin> possesses that **glandular body** <note>Vesalius is referring to the pancreas or associated lymphatic/glandular tissue</note> which I mentioned earlier when describing the stomach; it is spread beneath it to support the vessels belonging to that intestine and to moisten its cavity with a slow-flowing humor. Although not only the duodenum, but all the remaining intestines are imbued on their internal surface with a certain slow and slippery fluid, and as **Rhazes** <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD) was a Persian physician and polymath whose works were central to medieval medicine</note> not ineptly said, they are glazed or tinned in the manner of ceramic vessels. But since most of these features are also common to the thick <note>large</note> intestines, those must now also be reviewed.

**The History of the Large Intestines.**

The **ileum** intestine, therefore, beneath the region of the right kidney, is received by a certain thick intestine which is in many ways wider than the thin intestine itself. <margin>n. Figures 7, 8, M in N.</margin> This occurs not exactly at the very beginning of that thick intestine, but into its left side near its origin. For this part swells out like a very large globe, possessing two orifices on its left side. <margin>o. Figures 7, 8, M.</margin> One is continuous with the ileum and is further from the origin; <margin>p. Figures 7, 8, O.</margin> the other is lower and closer to the origin itself. Continuous with this latter orifice in humans is the intestine which I have no doubt was called the <term>typhlon</term> <note>From the Greek *typhlos*, meaning "blind."</note> or **caecum** <note>The "blind" intestine; today we distinguish between the cecum and its appendage, the appendix.</note> by the ancient professors of dissection.

**The nature of the Caecum intestine.**

I am not unaware, meanwhile, of what most people today comment regarding the caecum intestine. They are surely deceived because it is listed somewhere by **Galen** <note>The dominant Roman-era medical authority whose work Vesalius frequently corrected through direct observation.</note> among the thicker intestines, and is described by him and others who followed him as if it were some large sack or like a second stomach. However, in humans, <margin>q. Figures 6, 7, 8, Q; Figure 10, F.</margin> that which I believe should be called the caecum is shorter than all other intestines, and much narrower and more constricted than the tightest part of any intestine. It is more similar to a thick earthworm coiled into circles than to an intestine; so much so that the caecum seems hardly worthy of being considered among the number of thick intestines, but rather as an appendage to them.

And hence it happens that our "sack-carrying" and "blind" **Rabbis** <note>original: *Rabinos*. Vesalius uses this term sarcastically to describe dogmatic academic teachers who prefer old texts over physical evidence.</note>, when they see me demonstrate this thin little portion in humans in place of the caecum, shout against me using Galen's description. They shamefully contend that the wide beginning of the colon is the "sack," or as they say, the "Orbus" and "Monoculum" <note>Medieval terms meaning "bereft" or "one-eyed," used for the cecum.</note>. Indeed, you may find some who boast that they write "paradoxes" about the caecum, bringing forward that it does not have one orifice as the Greeks said, but two very close to each other. If they have seen these, or imagined them correctly, they are simply those <margin>s. These are O and M at N in Figures 7 and 8.</margin> which occur at the swelling beginning of the colon: one hole is the end of the ileum, and the other is the beginning of what I call the caecum <note>The appendix</note>.

Truly, there is no reason why we should believe any less that this thin little portion of intestine—not attached to the mesentery but coiled upon itself and held by fibers—is the caecum intestine in humans. This remains true even though Galen attributes to it a size and use which are not seen to be present here. For he described his tailed monkeys (which lack this appendage) rather than humans; whereas the ancients, or those who actually dissected humans, undoubtedly gave this appendage the name of the "blind intestine." Furthermore, Galen’s description could perhaps be adapted to the dog, in which the caecum happens to be much larger than in humans, and in which it is almost never found empty. Indeed, we know that true dormice and squirrels possess this caecum so large that it easily matches the size of their stomach, and is observed in dissection to be swollen with feces. From this, it is clear that this thin appendage is the caecum in humans, since it is clearly equal in its duct, position, and form (though not in size) to...

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

...matches the blind intestine <note>original: "cæco intestino"; the cecum</note> of those animals, and attains a single orifice (which is why it was first called "blind"). Furthermore, Galen, that supreme admirer of Nature, if he had ever seen the human intestines, would have described this appendix, that bulging start of the colon, the unity of the ileum with it, and the shape of the colon far differently. Indeed, if a human possessed a different sort of "blind" intestine, Galen would by no means have overlooked this appendix, even though its origin in humans varies somewhat from that in dogs. For even if in both it is located at the right ileum <note>the lower right area of the abdomen</note>, the human cecum takes its beginning more from the left side of the start of the colon than the right—contrary to what is seen in dogs and what Galen attests. 

Furthermore, if I were to say—along with some who have assisted me in dissecting—that this appendix was formed by Nature in humans for the purpose Galen attributed to the blind intestine, and that because of human gluttony, the juice prepared by the stomach is pushed out of the ileum without all of it entering the cecum; and if I were to assert that this appendix hangs in us like a useless and withered thing, perhaps differently than in the "temperate" men described by Galen, one would have to resort to that trifling evasion of admitting that men were once different than they are now. This is especially true since this large start of the colon in humans abundantly fulfills the purpose of a blind intestine, and the cecum seems to be present in humans merely as a vestige.

<margin>Table 20, fig. T. Figures 6, 7, 8, N. Figures 6, 8, from N to P. Table 20, fig. H. Figures 6, 8, from P to Q. In the sixth according to F, F. The path and position of the large intestine.</margin>
Therefore, in the right ileum near the lower seat of the right kidney, there is that bulging, wide, and round beginning of the colon. From here, it stretches gradually upward toward the liver and lies somewhat beneath the hollow part of the liver, touching the gallbladder <note>original: "bilis uesiculam"</note> in humans. By this contact, the intestine here is sometimes stained with a yellow color. Then, from the right side, it is carried toward the left along the lower part of the stomach, attached to the bottom of the stomach; however, it does not climb over it, as it seemed to others, or "ride atop" the bottom of the stomach, as is commonly said.

<margin>Fig. 6, G. Table 20, fig. V. Figs. 6, 8, from Q to R. Fig. 8, from R to S and then to T. Fig. 8, from Y to a. Fig. 22, under v. Fig. 24, K under L. The large intestine is divided into the colon and rectum.</margin>
As soon as it reaches the left side of the stomach, it possesses certain lightly bent turns over the lower or forward part of the spleen. It is then carried downward over the left kidney through the left flank, descending along the side of the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> all the way to the region of the pubic bone. From here, it turns left again, ascending almost to the level of the navel, and forms a turn here (which I wish physicians would carefully consider during the agony of colicky pains and the administration of enemas). It then moves toward the beginning of the sacred bone <note>original: "ossis sacri"; the sacrum</note>, descending straight down to the anus. In men, it lies beneath the bladder; in women, however, it lies beneath the uterus, spread over the sacrum and the tailbone <note>original: "coccygis ossi"</note>. This intestine, reaching from the end of the ileum to the anus, is almost uniform in width throughout, except at the beginning where it appears much more capacious; nevertheless, it varies in shape and path. Therefore, it is subdivided as if into two intestines. Whatever hastens from the right flank over the right kidney under the hollow of the liver, then along the bottom of the stomach to the spleen, and from there is carried again over the left kidney toward the pubes—making another turn above the inner seat of the iliac bone and creeping to the start of the sacrum—is called the **colon** by both Latins and Greeks.

<margin>Fig. 8, from Y to a. Figs. 6, 8, V, V. Figs. 6, 8, X, X. The difference between the colon and the rectum.</margin>
But that part which extends from the start of the sacrum to the anus is called the **straightened** <note>original Greek: ἀπευθυσμένον / apeuthiusmenon</note> and the **chief** <note>original Greek: ἀρχὸν / archon</note> by the Greeks; the Latins call it the *longaon*, the *rectum*, and the *princeps*. For the colon in humans is not perfectly round and smooth as it is in dogs; rather, through its entire path, though it is seen to be flattened and smooth on its upper and lower sides, it bulges out on both sides in a series, as if into middle spheres or cells <note>Vesalius is describing the "haustra," the small pouches of the colon caused by the tension of the muscle bands</note>. This shape becomes less conspicuous as the colon approaches the rectum, which is seen to be exactly round, and not flattened or bulging in the manner of the colon.

Both of these, as well as the cecum, are constructed with a double layer <note>original: "tunica"</note>. Of these, just as in the thin <note>small</note> intestines, the inner layer is more nervous or membranous and harder than the outer. But the colon...

# ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY]

The colon, meanwhile, is thinner and more slender in both its layers than the rectum; and the closer the colon is to the rectum, the thicker and better nourished its layers appear. The internal layer <note>original: "tunica"; the membrane or wall</note> of both intestines is filled only with transverse and circular fibers, which are very numerous. The external layer, however, begins in the colon but also possesses a great many straight (longitudinal) fibers. These do not extend across the entire surface of the intestine, but <margin>n Figure 8, V, V.</margin> <margin>Book 4 on the Use of the Parts.</margin> ^n these straight fibers extend only along the indentations of the colon. In those places, the layers of the colon are strongest and quite thick. As Galen suggested regarding many animals, the colon is constricted on both sides by individual strong ligaments <note>These are the *taeniae coli*, the three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle that characterize the large intestine</note> that stretch from the top to the bottom along its length. By heaven, he would have attributed this to humans as well, had he not thought that human intestines corresponded to those of dogs, which lack such ligaments. Furthermore, the outer layer of the rectum is filled everywhere with very frequent straight fibers around the entire circumference of the intestine, so much so that it possesses more straight fibers than circular ones. Moreover, <margin>o Figure 9, k, k leads out from above and h.</margin> ^o the third layer of the large intestines, just like the third layer of the small intestines, hangs from the mesentery <note>the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> which provides them with vessels. However, the part of the colon attached to the bottom of the stomach <note>the transverse colon</note> receives a third layer in humans specifically from the <margin>p Figure 4, e, e, e; and Figure 5, A, A.</margin> ^p lower membrane of the omentum <note>the "fatty apron" of the abdomen</note>. Because of this membrane, this part of the colon is secured to the back, just as we know the rest of the intestines are bound to the back by the intervention of the mesentery.

<margin>Veins and arteries of the colon and rectum.</margin> Likewise, the veins and arteries of the colon and rectum—which these intestines receive in fewer numbers than the small intestines—depend on the branches of the portal vein and the great artery <note>the aorta</note>. In the entire course of the colon, which extends from the right flank <note>ilium</note> almost to the left kidney, the arteries and veins are implanted in a series, climbing upward from the depths, just as they are in the empty intestine <note>jejunum</note> and the coiled intestine <note>ileum</note>. But to the lower part of the colon, which leads from the left kidney to the rectum, and to the rectum itself, the veins and arteries are provided in the same way as they are to the <margin>q Figure 12, b; r according to H fig 10 & 11 fig u; s fig chapter 5 book 3 at d, d, e, e; t fig chapter 12 book 3 a.</margin> ^q duodenum ^r. For one notable vein, arising from the branches of the portal vein running into the mesentery, and an artery also taking its beginning from that (which is drawn from the great artery to the mesentery below the origin of the seminal vessels), extend straight along the said part of the colon and the rectum, supported by the mesentery. In their progress, they offer offshoots to the intestines in a single, orderly sequence. However, we shall deal with the veins and arteries of the intestines again in the description of the mesentery.

<margin>Nerves.</margin> These thicker intestines share nerves in common with the small ones, and both are <margin>Fat grown onto the intestines.</margin> smeared on the inside with a ^s slow and viscous fluid. On the exterior surface of the colon, where it is closest to the rectum, and on the rectum itself, certain fatty appendages <note>the *appendices epiploicae*, small pouches of peritoneum filled with fat</note> grow in great <margin>Muscles of the rectum.</margin> <margin>u Figure 8, a, b, c, d; and fig chapter 51 book 2, E, B, C, D.</margin> numbers here and there. Furthermore, the rectum ^u claims for itself specific muscles assigned to the voluntary excretion of feces; since I followed these in the second book, it is not necessary to review them here as well. <margin>The function of the intestines.</margin> Instead, we must now consider the admirable industry of Nature, who constructed the intestines first and foremost so that, by their benefit, whatever was nutritious in the food prepared by the work of the stomach might be led to the liver, the workshop of blood. Secondly, she intended that the feces and those things unfit for absorption might be properly excreted. Beyond this, we believe the intestines are useful for their moderate power of cooking and altering <note>i.e., further digestion</note>, so that what was previously prepared by the stomach might be changed a little more completely during its passage through the intestines. And truly, looking toward these goals, Nature crafted the intestines with the greatest skill. For the intestines were made in the manner we have described, especially not just for the sake of removing excrement or for digestion, but so that all that has been turned into juice <note>original: "cremore"; chyle</note> might be carried into the liver by the veins.

### ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

It is very easy to understand how the intestines were fashioned in this way. First of all, in no animal is the stomach <note>original: "uentriculus"; in this period, "ventriculus" usually refers to the stomach, though it can mean any cavity</note> constructed so as to be adjacent to the organs through which waste is expelled, even though it would not have been impossible for the stomach to extend all the way to the anus. Secondly, in most animals, the intestines are wound into many frequent coils and windings. Finally, it is established that the stomach does not send food down until it has properly "cooked" <note>original: "confecerit"; referencing the ancient theory of "concoction," where the stomach acts like a cooking pot to break down food</note> it. Therefore, the fact that the stomach is not adjacent to the seat (the anus), or at least not joined to it by a straight passage or duct, clearly demonstrates that there had to be one organ for the concoction of food and another for its return and digestion. Indeed, if they were the same, it was to be feared that the veins would frequently take up raw and unconcocted food; this food, subsequently poorly processed by the liver, would be useless and harmful to the human. 

Furthermore, the instrument of return, which does not extend in a straight line from the stomach to the anus but is seen wound in very many circles, windings, and spirals (lest the human's nourishment slip away before being sucked out), confirms what has been said. For if another "belly" <note>another chamber or stomach-like space</note> followed the stomach, and if that were a storehouse for waste just as the stomach is for concoction, a great deal of nourishment would be taken up into the liver through the frequent veins in a very short time. But as it stands, through the innumerable offspring of the veins from those various and copious windings of the intestines, whatever succulent material has been prepared by the stomach is promptly transferred into the liver. 

Otherwise, if there were only a few openings of the veins and the food (now turned into a cream <note>chyle, the milky fluid of digested food</note>) fell through continuously, digestion would be slow and long-lasting; for it is necessary that the mouths of the vessels touch the processed juice. If, however, another large "belly" were spread out beneath the first, the food would only touch a small part of that belly’s surface—namely, only that part which was directly adjacent to its walls. Thus, the main portion of the food, however much of it was in the deep or middle space of that belly, would escape the grasp and flow of the veins. But now, the narrowness of the passage, breaking the food into small particles, forces it so that almost all of it touches the tunic <note>lining</note> of the intestines, toward which the veins blink with their little mouths. 

For even if something escapes the mouths of the vessels in the passage of the first winding, it touches them during the second; and if it slides past this one, then certainly through the third, or fourth, or another of those windings which follow in frequent numbers, so that finally no food useful for nutrition escapes, or stays hidden, or falls out, when a body free from disease is governed by the law of Nature. Therefore, the windings of the intestines are provided so that whatever succulent and moist material is in the cream prepared by the stomach may be entirely distributed. 

And that is especially the duty of the small intestines. For the large intestines, although they also contribute to the distribution of juices, specifically assist in this: that we do not defecate continuously, but at long intervals. For these are placed beneath, like a sort of belly for dry excrement—just as the bladder is for urine—and the excrement is collected in them so that it can all be led out at once. Yet this is done so that some use still comes to the human even here; for if anything escaped the flow of the slender (small) intestines, since the excrement resides for a longer delay in the large intestines, their own vessels suck it out.

<margin>The reason for the construction of the intestines.</margin>
I will now also briefly add how everything I have written above concerning the construction of the intestines fits these aforementioned uses. These are conveniently located immediately next to the stomach, from which they receive food.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY]

...nearby, and so that both the branches of the portal vein and the offshoots of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> can be spread to them here by the shortest path. <margin>b 6, 8 fig. N, P, Q, R, S, T.</margin> Furthermore, the professors of dissection torment themselves quite miserably over the position of the $^b$ colon; because although it is a kind of storehouse for excrement, they see it extending to the bottom of the stomach and the hollow of the liver. From this, one professor wants the colon to be carried toward the stomach because it contains feces and lacks innate heat, so that by contact with the stomach and neighboring parts, it might take on greater power for concoction <note>The ancient theory that the stomach "cooks" food using heat</note>. Another, however, contends that the colon is led under the hollow of the liver so that bile sweating into it from the gallbladder might, by irritation, make the power of expelling waste more successful. Yet another devises something else; and meanwhile, no one notices that the colon ought not to be very close to the center of the mesentery <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, nor should it have assumed branches of the portal vein closest to the hollow of the liver, since it embraces little that is worth sucking out. <margin>c fig. cap. 5 lib. 5 G.</margin> So that the $^c$ larger or right trunk of the portal vein might be inserted into the thin <note>small</note> intestines by a shorter path, and transfer food processed in the stomach to the liver by a more direct way, the colon gives way to the thin intestines and proceeds, as it were, through places most distant from the center of the mesentery. And on this occasion, its main portion occupies the left side of the body. The rectum, however, is most conveniently placed where it can finally discharge what has been gradually stored.

<margin>The reason for the shape of the intestines.</margin> The intestines are created with a rounded shape so they may be more capacious and less exposed to the injuries they encounter. The thin intestines are narrow so that every tiny portion of food might be touched by their tunics <note>the layers of the intestinal wall</note>, and thus by their vessels. The width of the thick <note>large</note> intestines is great so they can collect much, helping us to avoid having to empty them too frequently.

<margin>Substance.</margin> They consist of a substance that easily embraces what it contains, and is again fit to be stretched by its contents. <margin>Of the tunics.</margin> <margin>d 9 fig. h and i, which are later covered by L, l k, k.</margin> $^d$ Indeed, they have a double tunic, so they are more suitable for enduring injuries without harm. For sometimes the interior one rots away during intestinal difficulties and other long-lasting ailments, while the outer one remains safe; from which some sick people even recover. <margin>e 17 fig. m.</margin> Furthermore, the interior tunic of the thin intestines is $^e$ softer than the interior tunic of the stomach, because they receive nothing rough or ground-up, as the stomach does. The outer tunic of the intestines is perhaps less fleshy than the outer tunic of the stomach, since they are organs of digestion <note>In this context, the distribution of nutrients</note> rather than concoction. Moreover, the outer tunic of the thick intestines is as much harder than the inner tunic of the thin ones as they contain harder material that is more free of juice. Since what is contained in the thin intestines is still liquid, fluid, and watery; while what is in the thick ones is hard.

<margin>The reason for the fibers.</margin> Each tunic of the intestines is allotted transverse <note>crosswise</note> fibers so they might more quickly propel what flows down into them, and thus all the juice is quickly sucked out toward the liver. But the external tunic of the rectum and colon also notably obtained longitudinal <note>straight</note> fibers, so these might act as a binding for the circular fibers, lest they perhaps move apart or be torn away while frequently pushing out hard waste. For this reason especially, many fibers of this kind are assigned to the rectum, as it embraces drier waste. Although perhaps these straight fibers are offered to it not only to gather the transverse ones, but also so they might attract waste that is otherwise not very compliant. The third tunic of the intestines is like a bulwark and bond for the second, by whose benefit the intestines are $^f$ gathered to the back through the intervention of the mesentery. <margin>f this is seen in fig. 10.</margin>

<margin>The reason for the veins and arteries.</margin> Furthermore, the veins and arteries (for I believe even these draw something out from the intestines) are not distributed to all in equal number or frequency, because the same amount of juice is not to be sucked out in all the intestines. For the closer the intestines are to the stomach in continuity, the more excellent cream <note>original: "cremor"; referring to chyle, the milky fluid of digested food</note> they contain; and accordingly, more frequent vessels are brought to the thin intestines, and fewer to the thick ones. And in this same...

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

...for this reason, fewer veins are inserted into the stomach than into the thin <note>small</note> intestines: because the food contained in the stomach is not always fully prepared and transformed. <margin>The purpose of the nerves.</margin> Just as I do not doubt that veins wrap around the stomach to offer it blood for nourishment, I also believe that these same veins—which serve to take up the chyle <note>original: "cremor"; the milky fluid of digested food</note> from the intestines and transport it to the liver—likewise serve the vital nourishment of those intestines. I consider that they bring suitable blood to them, judging that the chyle otherwise contained in the intestines contributes nothing to their own nourishment (whatever others may think). Furthermore, the intestines are endowed with nerves so they may recognize harmful humors. Indeed, if they were entirely devoid of sensation, nothing would prevent the intestine from being repeatedly corroded by yellow bile or some other biting juice before a person could even feel it. <margin>g 13 figure c to d.</margin> Now, the bile duct inserted into the duodenum stimulates the intestines by the influx of bile, greatly aiding their action <note>the movement of the gut</note> and expelling the phlegm residing in them. <margin>Reason for the insertion of the gallbladder duct. Why the jejunum intestine transmits chyle more quickly.</margin> And this is the primary reason—besides the thinness of the juice—why the jejunum intestine transmits the chyle it contains more quickly than the others. For while the bile is not yet mixed with the chyle, it flows against the sides of the intestine, stimulating it more with its sharpness and inviting it to propel its contents more swiftly. Indeed, other reasons for the emptiness of the jejunum—such as the abundance of the best juices, the frequent veins, the location closest to the liver, and above all, the path of the intestine tending straight downward, and the juice being still very liquid—all demonstrate that the duodenum ought to be more "empty" <note>the name "jejunum" means "fasting" or "empty"</note>. However, the bile flowing into it also irritates and compels it toward sudden excretion. But the nature of bile and its ducts will be treated more accurately in its proper place later.

## ON THE MESENTERY. CHAPTER VI.

*The mesentery is shown among other figures in the eleventh, then the tenth and twelfth, and quite thoroughly in the twenty-fourth.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting two men in classical dress, possibly scholars or physicians, examining an object on the ground within an ornate frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Names of the mesentery.</margin> THE BODY called *mesenterion* <note>original: μεσεντέριον</note> and *mesaraion* <note>original: μεσάραιον</note> by the Greeks was called "the milks" <note>original: "lactes"; an archaic term for the mesentery or small intestines</note> by Gaza in his translation of Aristotle’s *History of Animals*. Cicero, however, in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, not thinking it entirely correct that those Greek words referred to a specific intestine, translated or interpreted them as the "middle intestine" <note>original: "medium intestinum"</note>. But because the body to be described here should by no means be included in the number of the intestines, and because the term "milks" does not mean the same thing to everyone, and the word "median" seems not yet widely accepted, we will not inappropriately borrow the name from the Greeks. Therefore, the Mesentery—which is also specifically called the "fatty membrane," since it is more oily or fatty than all other membranous parts of the entire body—is located <margin>a As can be seen in figures 10 & 12.</margin> at the back of the intestines. <margin>Its location.</margin> It serves as a bond by which the intestines are tied to each other and to the back. To perform such a notable use conveniently, it consists of a hard and membranous substance. <margin>b 24 figure F, F one, G, G the other. Also 11 figure X, Y.</margin> For it is chiefly built <margin>Substance.</margin> from two membranes stretched against each other and lying together, taking their origin from the peritoneum. The intestines, bound by it, almost shape and vary its form. <margin>Form and origin.</margin> For just as the course of all the intestines is not without many windings, so too the shape of the mesentery is not the same throughout. Galen, perhaps noticing this, even though the mesentery is entirely continuous, nevertheless listed three mesenteries, after a fashion, in his book *On the Dissection of Veins and Arteries*.

However, the substance of the mesentery is not a membrane solely for the purpose of more firmly connecting the intestines to the back; it also exists for another great use: it safely contains all the veins<sup>h</sup> from the portal vein of the liver and the<sup>i</sup> branches running out from the great artery <term>aorta</term> to the intestines. It supports them very safely and securely so that they are not torn while a person leaps or falls. For the larger trunk of the portal vein, where the mesentery arises from the back near the region of the kidneys, is led between the two membranes of the mesentery. It has the artery as a companion, which takes its origin from the great artery <note>the aorta</note> before it distributes branches to the kidneys, so that it may be spread into the intestines. Two nerves<sup>k</sup> also reach this place, one on each side, born from those branches that extend from the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>original: "sexto neruorũ cerebri pari"; in modern anatomy, the vagus nerve is the 10th pair, but Vesalius followed an older numbering</note> to the roots of the ribs.

...provides the origin. Furthermore, I think the opinion of Herophilus <note>An ancient Greek physician (c. 335–280 BC) often called the "Father of Anatomy."</note>, cited by Galen in the fourth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, regarding the entire portal vein should be understood in the way we discussed its use: when it was proposed that the entire distribution of the portal vein does not happen just so that the juice <term>chyle</term> <note>original: "succus"; the milky fluid produced in the stomach/intestines during digestion</note> prepared by the stomach is carried into the liver, and (according to common opinion) the **melancholic juice** <note>black bile, one of the four humors of ancient medicine</note> is offered to the spleen; but also so that nourishment is supplied to many other parts.

<margin>
p 4 fig. q, q, i.

This is shown by those branches **p** of the portal vein which run in various ways through the membranes of the **omentum** <note>a fatty layer of tissue that hangs over the intestines</note> spread over the intestines, and **q** those which end in the **r** glands of the omentum and mesentery and go no further, serving only nutrition. 

The branches of the portal vein inserted into the intestines seem to me to serve both the transfer of the **cream** <term>chyle</term> into the liver and the delivery of blood suitable for nourishing the intestines. This requires one to concede a mutual transfer of materials—a point I will prove with many arguments elsewhere. So far, apart from the mentioned veins, no others pertaining to the intestines and mesentery have been encountered by me. 

Moreover, while in dogs it is easy to find the path of the vessels through the mesentery (lest I fall into trivial school disputes), on the other hand, the two membranes of the mesentery are difficult to distinguish in them. This is because a dog's mesentery is leaner than a human's; therefore, their mesenteric membranes are seen to be fused together everywhere (except where they admit vessels), as if they consisted of a single membrane. 

<margin>Fat of the mesentery.</margin>

In humans, however, the two membranes of the mesentery are very easy to find, as they are distant from each other with much fat intervening. Just as a human abounds in copious fat everywhere, so too the mesentery becomes very fatty, as blood "sweats" out from the vessels and is turned into fat by the power of the membranes. 

Besides fat, something else is added to the mesentery. For it did not seem enough to wise Nature that that frequent offspring of vessels be contained merely by the membranes of the mesentery; 

<margin>Glands.</margin>

rather, she placed and surrounded a **glandular body** at every split of the vessels, so that none of them could become weak or shaken by movement. Nature was not ignorant that anything is most vulnerable to injury where it divides into 

<margin>s 10, 11 fig. L, L. 12 fi. L.</margin>

**s** branches. And therefore, at the **s** center of the mesentery, where the first distribution of vessels occurs, a large glandular body is built, safely supporting the most significant and first divisions of the vessels. 

<margin>t 10, 11 fig. M. but especially in 24 fig. at F, F, G, G.</margin>

Through the rest of the **t** mesentery, at almost every division of the vessels, Nature also placed some **t** gland, which would provide strength and stability to the division. So much so that with those glands added, the membranes of the mesentery carry the vessels very safely toward the intestines, and bind all the intestines to the back as aptly as possible, and finally form the 

<margin>u 9 fig. l, l, k constitutes L.</margin>

**u** third tunic of the intestines. For when the membranes of the mesentery lead the vessels to the part of the intestines we call the "hollow" part, they grow to the intestines along with the vessels; and here, moving away from each other, each proceeds along its own side of the intestine and turns into the **third tunic** <note>the outer serous layer of the gut</note> of the intestine. By this means, they bind the intestines more strongly and establish a sturdier defense for the vessels.

The liver, easily the most important of the organs of nutrition, the factory of the thicker blood, and the fuel for the soul which desires food and drink and those things necessary for the nature of the body, claims for itself the highest region of the parts that serve it. For it is placed immediately under the **diaphragm** <note>original: "septu transuerso"</note>, occupying the greatest region of that lower seat. For it touches the entire right part of the diaphragm, leaving very little of that part untouched where the diaphragm grows to the eleventh and twelfth ribs, and extends the ligaments by which it is bound to the vertebrae. Moreover, the liver is stretched under the entire middle part of the diaphragm, but not in the same way under the left part: although it holds a large seat there also, namely the entire anterior part, as far as that seat where the left side begins to rest on the middle of the ribs (which I measure from their roots to their ends). Indeed, the liver reaches into the left side much further than has seemed right to our doctors. Nor does it exceed the width of the diaphragm anywhere: except that it sometimes hangs down a little lower than the **xiphoid process** <term>sword-shaped cartilage</term> <note>original: "mucronata... cartilago"; the cartilage at the base of the breastbone</note> stands, and especially when the chest is narrow. This becomes all the more manifest the larger a person's liver happens to be (as is almost always the case in children).

<margin>
Reason for the site.
</margin>
<margin>
f fig. 20. O, O, P.
</margin>
Furthermore, the human liver has the greater portion of itself extended on the right side, because of the **spleen** <note>original: "lien"</note>, which, being much lower in dignity than the liver, was to occupy the left seat. So that the body might be rendered balanced, wise Nature led the smaller part of the liver down into the left side: as birds clearly attest, in whom the liver stands equally on both sides, as it also does nearly in dogs. For in these animals, because the spleen happens to be slender and not very heavy, a large portion of the liver is carried into the left side. However, wherever the liver is led, even if it is placed under the diaphragm and within the **peritoneum** <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, it perpetually occupies that seat which is girded by the ribs: so that the site of the organs of food shows again the great providence of Nature.

<margin>
The liver is for the most part girded and protected by the ribs.
</margin>

For since the abdomen is destitute of bones because of those organs which must frequently expand and subside, Nature covered less against injuries those parts for whose sake she wished the abdomen to lack bones; but the remaining parts, not needing this expansion, she hid most safely. And so, when the peritoneum is opened during dissection, the stomach, intestines, bladder, and uterus are the first to be encountered. But the liver, spleen, kidneys, **hollow vein** <note>original: "uena caua"</note>, and **great artery** <note>original: "arteria magna"; the aorta</note> are more safely hidden away.

The shape of the liver is varied, and corresponds to the organs upon which it rests, just as if it required no peculiar shape of its own, and allowed itself to be shaped by neighboring parts like potter's clay. For the liver seems to have been pressed into that lower seat of the diaphragm like a lump of earth, and to have been formed by it there. ### THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

<margin>

<margin>
The liver possesses no unique shape of its own.
</margin>

The liver is free of inherent processes, bumps, or hollows. Just as the organs upon which the concave <note>The "hollow" or underside</note> part of the liver rests are by no means convex on their simple surfaces, so too the liver is not naturally indented on its own surface, but rather adapts to the surrounding terrain. For example, where the **duodenum** <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> extends, and where the **portal vein** <note>original: "uena portæ"; the large vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note> emerges from the liver, the liver protrudes with a certain bump to fill the empty space it finds there. Furthermore, where the **gallbladder** <note>original: "bilis uesicula"</note> grows into the concave region of the liver, a hollow is carved out to elegantly receive the body of that vesicle. In addition, the liver acquires a hollow at the part where it touches the stomach, providing a place for the stomach to pass through the **diaphragm** <note>original: "septum"</note> and join with the upper opening of the stomach <note>the esophagus</note>. Indeed, the liver obtains no specific shape of its own, but rather takes on the shape impressed upon it by neighboring parts. This is clearly shown in the dissection of dogs and goats, in whose livers a private hollow is seen to neatly admit the upper seat of the right kidney. This was rightly done by Nature, since the function of the liver requires no separate or specific shape; unlike the stomach, intestines, bladder, and many other organs of that kind, which necessarily possess a large, single cavity and are shaped as round or sometimes cylindrical as possible. Even the diaphragm, because its function is to dilate the chest, necessarily obtained the form it now holds. However, the substance of the liver and the series of veins creeping through it will easily prove to you that, for its use as the **factory of blood-making** <note>Vesalius refers to the then-current belief that the liver was the primary organ for creating blood</note>, it needed to be a large and thick organ; it matters little whether it was built round or long, convex or hollow. Therefore, the liver is exactly convex and smooth on its upper and posterior sides where it faces the diaphragm (except for the hollow prepared for the trunk of the **vena cava**), and where it embraces the stomach, it is seen to be hollow in almost every part. Again, where it rests against the back of the stomach and its right side, it is at its thickest; but where it lies over the upper opening of the stomach toward the left, it appears thin, and in humans, it gradually tapers to a sharp angle there.

<margin>

t Between H, H: figures.
u at E, Fig. 6 & at D, Fig. 10.
u Fig. 20, as if at G.

<margin>
The shape of the human liver differs from that of dogs and pigs.
</margin>

On the right side, however, the liver is observed to be somewhat round and circular. It is nowhere thinner than at its edges, and especially in its forward-facing seat. There it sometimes presents certain impressions, but all are small, except for one wide notch <note>original: "sectionis"</note> on its front part, which turns slightly toward the right side of the liver from the **xiphoid cartilage** <note>original: "mucronata pectoris ossis cartilagine"; the "sword-shaped" tip of the breastbone</note>. This notch leads deeper into the liver near where the trunk of the portal vein takes its origin. This notch is like a hole where the **umbilical vein** <note>the vein that carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus</note> is implanted in the human liver. We are describing the form of the human liver here, not that of a dog or a pig. For what the professors of dissection claim regarding the shape of the liver and its "flaps" or "fingers" (which the Greeks call **lobes** <note>original Greek: <term>λοβὸς</term> (lobos)</note>), they learned from the dissection of dogs and monkeys rather than humans. Indeed, the human liver is not divided into lobes in the manner of a pig's, and much less so in the manner of a dog's. For the human liver (much like that of an ox) is a single, continuous body in its primary substance. The liver of a dog, however, is found divided into five, sometimes six, or only four parts or lobes, connected to each other only by the intervention of veins. In pigs, the liver is divided into fewer lobes that hang only by the veins, or into four or five if one chooses to count the deep fissures as divisions. From this source arose that fiction of doctors, who claim that the stomach is embraced by the liver with five lobes like the fingers of a grasping hand. Indeed, some of the Greeks—borrowing names from I know not which "mathematical doctors," as they testify—assigned specific names to those lobes (as among...

He famously corrects the error of Galen and other anatomists who claimed the human liver has multiple lobes, clarifying that such a structure is only found in animals like dogs and pigs.</summary>
