<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 619 regarding the liver's anatomy. Having previously addressed the liver's general shape and how it adapts to surrounding organs, Vesalius now refutes the traditional Galenic and medieval belief that the human liver is divided into specific "fingers" or lobes (fibrae), a misconception stemming from the dissection of animals like dogs rather than humans.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...one may see that even Theophilus <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine writer</note>, who was surely a poor anatomist, assigns names to these parts. For since there are four lobes <note>original: "fibræ"; literally "fibers," but used historically to refer to the lobes of the liver</note> of the liver, they say, the first is called the **hearth** <note>original: "focus"</note>, because it contributes most to the "concoction" or processing of the nutritional juice, just as a hearth is used for cooking food. The second receives the name of the **table** <note>original: "mensæ"</note>, because it performs the role of a table; for the nourishment for the members of the body is set out upon it. The third is called the **knife** <note>original: "culter"</note>, for it divides and separates the humors <note>the vital fluids of the body</note> from one another; or if there is anything thicker to be distributed, it cuts and alters it. The fourth is called by the name of the **charioteer** <note>original: "aurigæ"</note>, for the natural powers govern the humors once they are fully processed and lead them directly toward a better state. Truly, these are the trifles and fictions of those who attempt to learn the human fabric through their imaginations and not through dissections—or rather from the bodies of brutes instead of men.

Meanwhile, I am well aware that in the book *On the Nature of Bones*, five lobes (or "extremities," as the translator has it) are attributed to the liver by Hippocrates. I would wonder at this greatly, were it not already more than clear to anyone even slightly practiced in anatomy—and who does not let their respect for ancient authors override the evidence of their own eyes—how many things occur in that book (and in other books related to this present argument) that are alien to the human fabric and to all truth. Such things are equally unworthy of being attributed to Hippocrates,
<margin>In the first book of *On the Use of the Parts*.</margin>
of whom Galen boldly (though I know not how truly) attests that he never erred in anatomical matters. Therefore, setting aside excessive affection for these authors, I call to witness everyone who has ever stood by me during a dissection: I have never seen a liver divided into lobes in any such fashion. Nor is there any reason for someone to 
<margin>z, z in figure 4, between H, H, where G enters. a in figure 10, between G, G.</margin>
assert that the liver consists of a double lobe because of the cleft, or rather the opening, by which the vein proceeding from the navel <note>the umbilical vein</note> is received. ### ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>How the blood-making process of the liver is completed.</margin>
Whatever moist and succulent material the stomach has prepared, the liver receives into itself. By the innate transformative power of its own substance, the liver alters this material, rendering it as similar to itself as possible, and thus generates blood. But just as in every digestion, so also in this blood-making <term>sanguificatio</term> of the liver, a twofold refuse is produced: one part is thinner, while the other is thicker. Following Galen’s comparison of this action, it is helpful to liken the juice which the veins lead into the hollow of the liver to a moist liquor that has been "pre-cooked" and previously worked upon, yet still requires a final completion by digestion. Imagine, therefore, wine recently pressed from grapes and poured into jars, which is still being worked upon by its inherent and innate heat; it is separated, cooked, and boils. That part of its waste which is heavy and earthy (which they call the dregs or feces) sinks to the bottom of the vessels, while the other part, which is light and airy, floats on top. This is called the "flower" <note>original: "flos"; the scum or foam that rises during fermentation</note>, and it floats in abundance on thinner wines, just as the most dregs reside in thicker ones. Therefore, according to the similarity of this example, the juice brought from the stomach and intestines into the veins of the liver is cooked by the transformative power of the liver and, boiling like new wine <note>original: "musti"</note>, is changed into the generation of healthy blood. In this boiling, whatever refuse is muddy and thick sinks down and is driven into the spleen <note>original: "lienem"</note> (as we commonly believe). That which is light and thin floats on the blood like foam and is drawn away by the passages of the gallbladder <note>original: "bilis uesiculę"</note> spread over the branches of the portal vein within the substance of the liver. But that moisture which exists as the watery refuse of the stomach's labor, having been taken into the liver through the veins along with the healthy juice for blood-making, does not yet purge the blood in the hollow of the liver. Instead, already performing its greatest use, it elegantly shows itself to be the "vehicle of nourishment," as Hippocrates used to call it. For the blood prepared in the hollow of the liver proceeds from the slender offshoots of the portal vein toward the branches of the vena cava <note>the "hollow vein"</note> near the hump of the liver; for its passage through those very narrow ducts, that watery liquor greatly assists in the manner of a vehicle.

<margin>The reason for the liver's own flesh or substance.</margin>
Therefore, the flesh of the liver, which is its own body, is the primary organ of blood-making. The veins dispersed throughout its entire body are considered to be in the place of hollows <note>original: "sinus"</note>, in which the material that ought to be prepared by the flesh is fittingly contained; these soon carry the prepared blood to other parts, like the liver's own little streams. Moreover, the coat <note>original: "tunica"; the vessel wall</note> of the veins distributed in the substance of the liver is far thinner than those distributed throughout the rest of the body, lest their thickness should dull the power of the liver's substance, by whose benefit the juice contained in the veins is worked upon. Thus, the liver is even nourished by the thicker blood which the thin coat of the veins transmits, drawn in by the faculty of the liver.

<margin>The reason for the arrangement of the veins.</margin>
Furthermore, so that the blood might linger longer in the liver to experience a perfect processing, and so that it might all come into contact with the substance of the liver, the Creator of things <term>Opifex</term> did not give it a single cavity like a flask, but instead distributed all those veins into an infinite series of branches and into the narrowest ducts.

<margin>The reason for the placement of the bile passages. The artery.</margin>
The passages of the bile occupy a place between both sets of veins, so that by their convenient placement, the blood might first be purged of bile before being taken into the branches of the vena cava. We believe the artery is extended only to the hollow seat of the liver so that it might ventilate and temper its heat, while the upper part of the liver, which touches the diaphragm <note>original: "septum"</note>, receives continuous motion from the diaphragm's own movement.

<margin>Of the nerves. The coat.</margin>
Truly, lest the liver should be devoid of sensation like a plant, and so that the desiring part of the soul might be less able to be moved and restrained by the rational power, Nature brought forth nerves for the liver, which the soul might use like a bridle according to her command. The coat <note>the capsule</note> of the liver is a certain envelope and covering; its ligaments indeed—lest the liver, since it is heavy, should sometimes fall down—are many and strong, committed to it.

<margin>
Whether the duct of the gallbladder inserted into the duodenum offers a branch to the stomach.
</margin>

...supported by [the liver], it hastens somewhat obliquely downward and is implanted into the duodenum <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note> not far from the beginning of the jejunum <margin>Figure 13, d</margin>. This passage carries the bile <note>original: "bilem"</note> expelled from the gallbladder into the intestines, meanwhile admitting nothing back from them—neither chyle <note>original: "cremoris," the milky fluid of digested food</note>, nor gas, nor even the very bile it just led down. This is achieved not only by its winding entry into the intestine, but also by the benefit of two small membranes <margin>Figure 15, Q, R, and Figure 7, Z</margin> which hang loosely on either side of the orifice's flank. These easily yield to the weight of the inflowing bile, yet block the way so that nothing can regurgitate into the duct; for when they are gathered together and first enter the mouth of the passage, they seal it shut. However, there is not just one single membrane assigned to this opening, like the single flap seen in bellows, or the simple little tongue found in the balls we inflate. The implantation of this duct into the intestines <margin>Figure 15, Q is distant from H</margin> is removed further from the lower orifice of the stomach <note>the pylorus</note> than the common sort of anatomists believe.

Now, I suppose you expect me to say here whether this duct, being inserted into the intestine, is entirely simple, or whether in its progress it is split into two, showing one part to the intestine and the other to the base of the stomach <term>ventriculus</term>. This is because this matter is contended most fully every day in the schools and in the books of physicians. Some affirm that this duct of the gallbladder is sometimes inserted into the intestines, yet more frequently into the base of the stomach; others assert that it is occasionally bipartite <note>divided into two parts</note>, with one portion tending toward the stomach and the other toward the intestines; still others always make this a fork, perpetually distributing one of the branches—now wider, now narrower—to the stomach. Meanwhile, all of them, however many there are, defend themselves only with a heap of authorities, not by the inspection of the things themselves.

Indeed, to say once and for all what I usually encounter during dissection, I can truly affirm that in the entire body I meet with no dissection more troublesome, nor more difficult, nor more burdensome to me than when the lower membrane of the omentum <note>the fatty apron of the abdomen</note>, the hollow region of the liver, and the neighboring organs <margin>as if preparing Figures 3 and 12</margin> must be approached, especially in a human or any animal that is overly fat. Indeed, it is so difficult that I believe any craftsman, however industrious, might easily be deceived here. I have noticed, therefore (to bring into the open what has occurred to me), that not even the smallest portion of the gallbladder duct extends to the stomach, except in one rower of the Pope's galleys. 

Just as this man varied from the structure of other men in certain other organs—especially around the ribs and muscles of the chest—so he also possessed this duct divided into two branches. The smaller and thinner of these <margin>around c. in Figures 14 and 15</margin> was inserted into the base of the stomach where the vein encircling the right region of its lower seat first joins the stomach. This man seemed to have been of a hot and dry temperament. To find out whether he had been accustomed to be troubled by bilious vomiting (which Galen <note>an influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> testifies is frequent in men of this kind), I inquired most diligently of his associates whether they had observed anything of the sort in him. They asserted, therefore, that they had never seen him vomiting, nor even nauseated in the greatest storms; but as he was most robust, they affirmed he was praised by everyone because he could blow a horn with a very long breath, and far surpassed all his fellow soldiers in reciting numbers in a deep voice and with a single breath.

<margin>
That the duct from the gallbladder does not always reach the stomach.
</margin>

But I am abundantly persuaded that a portion of this duct, which we are presently discussing, is not always led into the stomach, because during dissection, once this duct is freed from the neighboring vessels and membranes, no hole appears from which a branch of that duct might be led to the stomach. Such a hole would show itself if even the slightest branch drawn from the main duct were cut away through carelessness. For if you pierce the duct with even a needle and compress the gallbladder with your fingers, bile flows out of the duct, and it would flow out more quickly from the orifice of its branch (if Nature had fashioned one).

### THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V

If you consider it carefully, you will admit—even without a dissection—that this passage carrying bile to the intestines could not have been more suitably inserted into any other part of either the stomach or the intestines. It is placed where the duct <note>the bile duct</note> itself could be safely implanted, causing the least inconvenience to the stomach <term>ventriculus</term> and intestines, while still effectively purging that bilious waste. Indeed, those structures are guided most safely which proceed neither too far nor unaccompanied by other organs. This is exactly what happens with this duct: there was no shorter path to the stomach or any other part of the intestines than the one where it is currently implanted. Meanwhile, it is safely supported as it creeps slightly downward by the trunk of the portal vein <term>porta vena</term> <note>the large vein carrying blood from the digestive organs to the liver</note> and the lower membrane of the omentum <term>omentum</term> <note>the fatty "apron" that hangs over the intestines</note>. If it had to be inserted into the stomach, it would not be supported as conveniently by the membranes of the omentum as it is now, and it would be led further away by having to make winding turns. In the same way, if Nature had led this bilious superfluity through a long duct all the way to the end of the digestive tract (so that it would flow into the intestines there for the first time and be excreted along with the feces), it was to be feared that such a thin passage might easily rupture at any moment. 

That this material—unfit for nutrition but most suitable for the duodenum <term>duodenum</term> <note>the first part of the small intestine</note>—could not have been safely poured into the bottom of the stomach can be learned first from the nature of bile, then from the duties of the stomach and intestines, and finally from an examination of the phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; refers to the thick mucus lining the organs</note> which is necessarily preserved by both in performing their functions, and from the treatment we apply to an excess of this phlegm. For it is granted by the leading physicians that the nature of yellow bile is thin and fluid, and that it cuts through, cleanses, and purges phlegm; thus, a treatment is applied whenever it abounds too much. Furthermore, no one doubts that food must be retained until it is digested, but that the finished "cream" <note>original: "cremorem," referring to chyle, the milky fluid of digested food</note> must be led very quickly through the thin intestines. Therefore, a duct carrying bile would have been useful to the stomach for the sake of cutting through and purging that phlegm; however, because the stomach must primarily use its "retentive power," Nature by no means preferred a small benefit over a great evil. For if bile flowed into the stomach, the stomach would (as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, a dominant Greek physician of the 2nd century AD</note> rightly affirms) be perpetually irritated to excretion by the bile's sharpness. It would not perform its retentive function long enough for the food to be properly cooked; and, rejecting that bile and becoming nauseated because of it, the stomach would desire and embrace the food offered to it less than is proper. Yet, nothing at all prevented the bile from flowing into the intestines.

<margin>
The usefulness of the flow of bile into the intestines.
</margin>
For this bile cuts through, cleanses, and purges the phlegm that accumulates in great quantities in those thin passages due to the function of the intestines. Then, by irritating and "biting" the intestines, it invites and stimulates them to excrete the feces. It is finally propelled out of the body along with the excrement, causing no harm—since all things in man are dispensed by the law of Nature—but, as is clear, providing the greatest utility. Rightly, therefore, is that duct carrying bile implanted in the intestines and not the stomach; and it is not placed randomly in any part of the intestines, but almost at the end of the duodenum. This is because the duodenum is the first of the intestines, and there the bile can more quickly contribute the use it provides to the digestive tract. Meanwhile, the boundary between the duodenum and the jejunum <note>the second part of the small intestine</note> is sufficiently removed from the stomach that it rarely happens that bile climbs upward from the intestines into the stomach. Although, this is familiar to those of "bilious" natures whenever their empty stomach is tormented for a little too long (as I myself also sometimes experience). 

As for those men who lacked a gallbladder—whom Aristotle <note>the Greek philosopher</note> describes, and after him Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> along with many others, claiming they are the most robust in life—I have not yet found them. However, I believe it could easily happen that some duct carries bile from the liver to the intestines without it being first collected in a gallbladder. Indeed, I have been accustomed to wonder significantly during dissections why...

<summary>Vesalius explains the anatomical and physiological reasons why the bile duct connects to the duodenum rather than the stomach, emphasizing that bile's irritant nature would disrupt stomach digestion while aiding intestinal waste removal.</summary>
<keywords>bile duct, gallbladder, stomach, duodenum, Galen, Aristotle, digestion, yellow bile, phlegm, anatomy</keywords>

...lest bile be driven from the liver into the intestines by a too-direct path. I am not unaware, meanwhile, of that subtle anatomical invention of those who teach that bile is stored in its own gallbladder <note>vesicula</note> to protect the liver from decay. They fail to consider how many countless little bile-sacks Nature would have had to provide for the brain, spleen, lungs, and most other parts of the body to prevent them from contracting rot as well.

# CHAPTER IX. ON THE SPLEEN.

*The SPLEEN is primarily depicted in four small plates of the nineteenth figure. The first of these shows the hollow of the spleen with the portion of the omentum <term>omentum</term> <note>the fatty "apron" covering the intestines</note> attached to it; the second shows the hollow of the spleen free from the omentum; the third shows the convex side <note>the "hump" or outer curve</note> of the spleen; and the fourth displays its internal substance. Furthermore, the spleen as it remains in the body may be found in the second figure at the letter d, in the sixth figure at G, and in the twentieth at O, O, and P.*

<margin>The position of the spleen.</margin>
<margin>a Fig. 6, G; Fig. 20, O, O, P.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring several cherubs or children in an outdoor setting. They appear to be playing with or examining a large, sack-like object, a common playful motif in Vesalius’s work where children mimic anatomical or surgical tasks.</image-desc>We have already noted that the SPLEEN is located in the seat on the left side of the stomach, though situated more toward the lower and posterior <note>back</note> parts. It does not, as is commonly thought in an otherwise healthy person, protrude toward the middle or front of the abdomen; nor can it be easily felt by touch. This is despite the fact that many physicians are convinced they can determine in everyone whether it is soft or hard simply by feeling it.

<margin>Form.</margin>
<margin>b 7th muscle table, Δ.</margin>
<margin>c See figure 19.</margin>
The spleen rests against the left part of the diaphragm <term>septum transversum</term>, roughly halfway between the left side of the vertebral bodies and the cartilages of the false ribs of that side. It is walled in by the ribs as if by the safest of ramparts. Its shape corresponds to the space it occupies, much like the liver is shaped by the organs surrounding it. Where it touches the diaphragm, the spleen is slightly convex <note>gibbus</note>, just as the diaphragm is slightly hollow there. Where the stomach rests against the spleen—and because the stomach is large and bulges out like a great globe—the human spleen appears slightly hollowed out, though only on its surface. In pigs, dogs, and oxen, where the spleen is longer but narrower and stretches over a greater length of the stomach’s curve, it is more hollowed, embracing the stomach like a third of a circle. It was rightly called "long" by Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius frequently corrected</note>, who was more experienced in dissecting those animals than humans.

<margin>Book 4, On the Use of the Parts.</margin>
<margin>d Fig. 19, E.</margin>
<margin>e Fig. 19, D.</margin>
<margin>f Fig. 19, F.</margin>
<margin>g Fig. 19, G.</margin>
<margin>h Fig. 19, H, H.</margin>
A human has a thick, large, and wide spleen, but it is much shorter than in animals of that kind. It is not, however, exactly square, as someone might think if they were misled by the shape of *splenia* <note>original: "spleniorum"; these were square surgical pads or compresses named after the spleen</note>. Its length somewhat exceeds its width, and the upper part is seen to be a little wider than the lower, so that it closely resembles the image of a tongue stretched out toward the front teeth. For this reason, the spleen is called the "tongue-like organ" by some. The lower part, which extends more toward the front of the body, ends in an obtuse <note>blunt</note> angle. The upper part is compressed into an even more obtuse angle, or rather a sort of side, so that this part forms one blunt angle on both sides. The left side is slightly convex, while the right side is somewhat concave <note>simum</note> with two slight impressions. The great thickness of the spleen, which is almost equal in every part, is surpassed by its width, and even more so by its length.

<margin>The surface and color of the spleen.</margin>
The hollow of the spleen is marked by a deep line <note>the hilum</note> running straight along its length; this line is unevenly raised and curved, and it receives the vessels of the spleen (as you will soon hear). As for the rest of the spleen's surface, it is not as perfectly smooth as that of the liver or kidneys. Instead, it has certain dark, slightly protruding bumps, almost like the way the skin of those suffering severely from leprosy <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>in this period, the term referred to conditions making the skin thick, scaly, and bumpy</note> is accustomed to swelling in various places. Not only does the spleen resemble that uneven skin in its surface, but also in its color...

<summary>Vesalius describes the anatomy of the human spleen, correcting Galen's errors which were based on animal dissections. He details its location behind the stomach, its tongue-like shape, and its characteristic bumpy surface texture.</summary>

...expresses that color sufficiently. For in Paris, in the monastery of Saint Lazarus, and in many fields of upper Germany, and elsewhere too, I have seen those affected by elephantiasis <note>a term often used historically for leprosy</note> who so perfectly resembled the dark color and surface of the human spleen, as if someone had fashioned them out of a spleen. For in man, this organ is black with a certain dark and very obscure color, while in a dog it is usually redder and brighter than the liver itself. Swine and oxen, however, show a whiter spleen.

<margin>The internal organs of a human are not uselessly boiled to learn their structure.</margin>
Furthermore, this kind of difference in color occurs not only on the surface of the spleens, but also within their bodies, whether raw or cooked spleens are used for examination. For the organs of a man are sometimes not uselessly lightly boiled in water, or at least submerged in warm water for some time so that the blood might increase more intensely; for while the blood is still fluid, it often tends to stand in the way of examining the structure of the liver, spleen, and lungs perfectly <note>original: ad amussim, meaning "according to the rule" or "precisely"</note>.

<margin>The arrangement of the vessels through the body of the spleen.</margin>
Otherwise, I have sometimes thought the spleen should be condensed <note>hardened by boiling or processing</note> especially because I was intensely uncertain about its use, and I observed the veins and arteries to be dispersed in it far differently than in the liver, lungs, and kidneys. For the substance of the spleen seems to me to consist of a very thick and black blood, like a solid sponge or light pumice stone, though rare and congealed, and only interwoven with frequent fibers and filaments that are not remarkably strong. For however many veins and arteries we know for certain enter the spleen, none are observed to be dispersed through its substance in the same way as in the body of the liver and lungs, except for very few and quite slender ones; it is as if, as soon as the vessels enter the straight line of the spleen, they are spread into an innumerable offspring of branches, so thin that, lacking a cavity in a certain way, they should be called fibers rather than vessels. With these branches or fibers wound around themselves from every side, a very thick blood is spread over them, which Erasistratus <note>an ancient Greek physician and anatomist</note>

<margin>The substance of the spleen.</margin>
also called *parenchyma* <note>original: ἐπίγχυμα (epichyma), meaning "effusion" or something poured over</note> here, just as he did in the liver. Nor indeed does thin blood, by which we commonly grant the spleen is nourished because of the frequency of arteries, seem to be the sole cause of the porousness of the spleen’s substance, but rather that innumerable entanglement of fibers (for I would hardly dare call them arteries and veins). Such, then, appeared the substance of the spleen to me in healthy men. But in a certain person suffering from elephantiasis, which had not yet taken deep root, we found a more turgid and larger spleen; in the others, however, it was similar to a healthy one. In a citizen of Padua who, having been detained in prison for three years and finally dying of black jaundice <term>black jaundice</term> <note>original: nigro arquato, a severe jaundice often linked to the "black bile" of the spleen</note> amidst the greatest sorrows, was brought to public dissection, we found a spleen that was less thick and wide than usual and altogether small, and on its convex <note>outer-curved</note> part fat had grown, congealed like a very white and hard stone. The substance of the organ in this man was dry and intensely hard. He who was hanged at Montefecchio <note>original: Montisfelis</note> and brought to the Paduan schools during a shortage of bodies, exhibited such a large spleen that it yielded only slightly to the mass of the liver; it was attached to the anterior <note>front</note> part of the liver and stretched out to the front part of the stomach. The substance of his spleen corresponded perfectly to the substance of the organs of healthy people. This was a young man with very white and smooth skin, not at all melancholic <note>the "melancholic" temperament was traditionally associated with a cold, dry spleen and black bile</note> by nature, or otherwise sickly. In a French priest in the hospital at Bologna, who died from dropsy <note>original: aqua subter cutem, literally "water under the skin"</note>, I found a white but small spleen. Similarly, in Augsburg, in a weaving woman, in whose uterus I found—along with many doctors after her death—more than sixty Augsburg measures of serous water (each weighing three pounds), while no water was present around the intestines, nor was there any loose swelling in the hands or feet, nor even any defect in the organs or any other organ; except that great uterus, whose

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY

...the mouth of the stomach <note>the fundus</note> had hardened in marvelous ways, and in its entire front part it was attached to the peritoneum. And the glands of the right testicle had grown out in marvelous ways, no differently than if nine or ten goose eggs, or rather ostrich eggs, were contained within one membrane, each one filled with a fluid not unlike the white of eggs, or perhaps a little thicker. **Belloarmatus**, a distinguished legal consultant, after he had been pale for many years and judged by physicians to be suffering from a spleen ailment, died suddenly from a rupture of a small branch of the portal vein and an abscess that sent blood from the whole body into the cavity of the peritoneum. I would recount their histories more fully, except that I wish to give no detailed account here of the sick (whom I will eventually describe at length in a work on the recognition of diseases, based on my dissections, which I hope will not be regretted). ii
<meta>catchword: but</meta>

The hump of the spleen is fastened to the outer covering of the left kidney, which is abundant in fat, by means of certain fibers; this is especially true if the kidney (as not infrequently happens) lies largely beneath the spleen. And this is the account of the spleen's position, shape, and parts. Indeed, how justly the Architect of our body has distributed all things, the use and function of the spleen will teach us—a subject upon which not only the leaders of physicians, but also the most prominent philosophers, have disagreed. For **Erasistratus** <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician in the 3rd century BC</note>, persuaded by the common opinion (because it is foolishly believed that the spleen is removed from runners to avoid weight and stinging pain), testifies in a way that the spleen was made in vain. He says that Nature, fearing she might somewhere forget her art, when she was forming the liver on the right side for the newly conceived fetus, also labored at something on the left side, and placed the spleen there as a counterpart to the liver—as if she herself, once the stomach was extended a little to the left, had been unable to avoid a superfluous creation. **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher who wrote extensively on biology</note> first ascribes to the spleen a common use which he gives to all internal organs: namely, that the veins, being hanging structures, may be supported and stabilized against the body by the mass of the organs. For he says that the internal organs are cast toward the body like anchors attached to parts. Next, teaching the private use of the liver and spleen, he adds: the liver and spleen assist in the concoction <term>concoction: the "cooking" or digestion of food into nutrients</term> of food, and the spleen diverts wandering vapors and attracts them from the stomach, being able to concoct them because it is bloody in nature. To put it simply, Aristotle regards the spleen as a sort of substitute or "adulterated" liver. In the same way, the author of the book *On the Use of Respiration* (which they falsely attribute to **Galen**), besides some nonsense about veins which they think are inserted into the hump of the spleen, contends that the spleen receives the cream <term>cream: chyle, the milky fluid produced during digestion</term> perfected from the stomach and intestines through the veins of those organs, and is itself an organ for the creation of blood. To this opinion several physicians also subscribe—much as **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine," active in the 5th century BC</note> does in his fourth book *On Diseases*—affirming that when the liver is poorly affected, the spleen works to elaborate blood in the name of the liver.

<margin>†: Figure 20, V is placed beneath O, P, Q.</margin>

<margin>The use and function of the spleen.</margin>

But the use of the spleen that seems more probable to other professors of dissection teaches that it was fabricated by Nature for this purpose: to be a receptacle for the muddy and dreggy blood perfected in the liver. Just as the gallbladder is placed in charge of the thinner and lighter waste <note>original: recremento; refers to the "refuse" or byproduct of digestion</note>, so the spleen is constructed to receive the thicker and heavier waste. They say the spleen allures and sucks this to itself through the trunk of the portal vein as if it were a familiar substance; once attracted, it processes and elaborates it, rendering it fit for its own nutrition, making that blood—even if it be thick and dreggy—rare and spongy. They say that the frequent arteries inserted into the spleen assist greatly in this, strenuously aiding the exact elaboration of that blood with their heat. But that the flesh of the spleen is held to be the primary and principal worker of this action, I have no doubt is manifest, even if I do not say so. And so it is also conceded by these authors that the spleen does not process the entirety of the blood it admits from the liver and store it for its own nourishment. Rather, whatever it contains that is unfit for nutrition and cannot be adapted to its own substance is believed by them to be "vomited" back into the stomach for the sake of some great use.

<margin>What the spleen eructates into the stomach, and by what passage.</margin>

For first, everyone affirms that melancholic juice <term>melancholic juice: "black bile," one of the four humors, thought to be thick and dark</term> is eructated <note>belched or discharged</note> by the spleen into the stomach; some say this occurs through a vein extending from the spleen to the stomach, others through a specific passage of its own, and from the stomach into the intestines, where it is purged from the body along with the feces. Furthermore, some write that this vein or passage is led simply from the spleen into the stomach; others, expressing the place of insertion more boldly, add that it is implanted into the upper orifice <note>the cardia or esophageal opening</note> of the stomach. An equal dissension occurs among the leaders of dissection in assigning a use for this excrement: for some assert that this is extremely useful and friendly to the functions of the stomach, just as they claim yellow bile is a hostile and most ruinous enemy.

...but some indeed are content if they teach that this black bile <note>original: "atram hanc bilem"; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, thought to be produced by the spleen</note>, by its own flavor quality—which they admit is bitter and acidic—strengthens all functions of the stomach (which consist of a certain "embrace" <note>referring to the stomach's muscular contraction around food</note>) by astringing and collecting, and therefore prevents food from slipping out of the stomach before it is fully processed. Others, however, not content with this use alone, add to what has been said that the appetitive power of the stomach is so provoked by this waste product that they claim a vein or passage is inserted from the spleen into the upper orifice of the stomach <note>the cardia</note> specifically for the sake of this use. They are taught this by imagination alone, not by dissections. I, for my part, dare to affirm nothing concerning this belching of the spleen’s waste into the stomach, nor its use; nor does dissection clearly show me these things which, nevertheless, the professors of anatomy most boldly assert without any controversy. For first, I do not doubt that there is no passage similar to that by which bile is purged into the intestines; furthermore, the veins which are implanted into the left side of the stomach do not proceed from the <sup>u</sup> body of the spleen, but from those which are already being inserted into the spleen. Nor is any other sequence of these veins seen throughout the stomach than that of all the rest seeking the body of the stomach. Next, there is absolutely no vein here that lacks a companion artery. Lastly, if anything is carried from the spleen to the stomach, it seeks the bottom of the stomach rather than its upper orifice. <sup>x</sup> For a vein creeping along the left side of the bottom of the stomach is easily the largest of all the veins offered to the stomach from those extended to the spleen. Although neither this vein, nor any other reaching the left side of the stomach, swells with any different blood than the other veins enveloping the stomach. Indeed, it is so much so that if I did not just now fear the slanders of many—which I have experienced thus far as excessively heavy, to my no small misfortune—arguments would not fail me here with which I might disrupt the common opinion, now most persuasive to everyone, regarding the duty of the spleen. But in the meantime, it is granted to everyone that the spleen, by its own innate heat and the frequent arteries that interweave it, fosters the digestion of the stomach. As for the common belief that the spleen is the author of laughter, I conjecture this is taken from the fact that it is believed to draw thick, dreggy, and muddy blood to itself, rendering the remaining blood more agile and, so to speak, more cheerful. Furthermore, I do not believe that the heart is cooled by the benefit of the spleen for some principal use (as Aristotle judged concerning the brain), which is affirmed by the most prominent of the Arabs <note>referring to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna or Rhazes, whose works dominated European medicine before Vesalius</note>; since it does not touch the heart, and if there were any innate coldness in it, the arteries of the spleen would hardly conduct it to the heart.

THE previous discourse has already treated the **ORGANS** dedicated to purging yellow bile and the dreggy, muddy blood. This one, however, will be dedicated to those which strain the blood sent into the vena cava from the liver of its serous and watery humor <note>the liquid part of the blood or urine</note>. For after it has fulfilled its own task, and the blood no longer needs to be led through so many narrow passages, it is not fitting for all of it to be kept longer in the body, as it would be a burden to the foreign veins. To ensure that the kidneys more swiftly remove the serous humor <note>the watery part of the blood</note>—which we call urine and <term>lotium</term> <note>original: "lotium"; an archaic term for urine, often used in the context of it being a waste product or "wash"</note>—from the blood, they are both situated as close to the liver as possible. For the right kidney ^b touches the lowest portion of the liver ^c with its upper part; in dogs and goats, a cavity is even carved into the liver for it, so that it might be placed higher and fit more aptly. The left kidney, however, occupies such a high seat ^d that it is partly tucked under the spleen. Both, however, lie next to the sides of the vertebral bodies, resting upon the lower part of the <term>septum</term> <note>the diaphragm</note> ^e, where it is covered by the three lower ribs, especially in that part where they slant more steeply toward the back. This backward curvature of the ribs offers such a convenient seat for the kidneys that they are both safely walled in and, though they bulge forward, they do not occupy the space of the other nutritional organs. If Nature had not considered these things, she might perhaps have always placed a single, very large kidney (as we have occasionally seen her construct ^f in those with a greatly protruding belly or a deformed rib cage) over the bodies of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the main vein returning blood to the heart</note> and the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, which would attract the serous blood by a shorter and more direct route. For the kidneys are not, as other anatomists write, placed directly upon the muscles of the loins ^g which serve the movements of the back and thigh. Indeed, they descend no further than the ribs, even at their ^h lowest part toward the flanks, although one is always higher than the other and they are not positioned exactly opposite one another. Since the spleen descends lower than the liver, and yet each kidney strives to be near the vena cava where it is led beneath the body of the liver, we rightly see the right kidney being generally higher than the left. Indeed, not infrequently the left is observed to be higher than the right, especially in those who happen to have a smaller spleen and a larger liver; just as if the liver were depressing the right kidney downward, while the spleen allowed the left to rise higher and be tucked beneath it. Furthermore, it is clear that this varied positioning of the kidneys happened not so much for the sake of finding a fitting place, but rather so that they do not both draw serous blood from the exact same spot, and so that one, pulling in the opposite direction, does not hinder the work of the other. Nor should Galen’s reasoning regarding the position of the kidneys be approved, in which <margin>Book 5, *On the Use of the Parts*</margin> he teaches that the right is more elevated than the left so that it may draw more directly, since those things which he ascribes to the right side of the vein are no more characteristic of it than of the left side. For no one of sound mind will admit that more veins reach from the liver into the right side of the vena cava than into the left, if he has carefully examined the ^i course of that vein along the back of the liver.

For the kidney substance, like that of the liver and lungs, lacks fibers; instead, the fibers of the vessels spread through it serve beautifully for attraction, retention, and expulsion. Since...

<margin>Veins and arteries offered to the kidneys.</margin>
<margin>x</margin> Since it is necessary for the kidneys to strain the serum <note>The watery portion of the blood that becomes urine.</note> from the blood, and because the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The large central vein of the body.</note> and the great artery <note>The aorta.</note> could not conveniently grow into the bodies of the kidneys (as the liver does to the <term>vena cava</term>), <margin>u See Figure 18.</margin> remarkable branches are led from the vein and artery into the kidneys themselves. <margin>x Figure 20, d, b; Figures 22, 23, m, n.</margin> From the <term>vena cava</term>, two large branches arise—one on each side for each kidney—which do not emerge directly opposite one another. Instead, they vary in their origin according to the position of the kidneys: the right branch takes its starting point higher than the left if the right kidney is placed higher; but if the left kidney claims the higher seat, the left branch also arises from the <term>vena cava</term> higher than the right. The arrangement of the arteries is indeed the same; these are stretched out beneath the veins <margin>z Figure 22, characters 7, 8.</margin> and are carried along with them transversely to the <term>sinus</term> <note>The "sinus" or hilum is the recessed entry point on the inner side of the kidney where vessels enter and exit.</note> of the kidneys, which they bear on their inner sides. As soon as the vein and artery reach that sinus of either kidney in humans, both divide into two branches before they enter the kidney, offering one branch to the upper angle of that sinus and the other to the lower. In the progress of these vessels toward the kidneys, the arteries very rarely give off small branches, but are entirely consumed within the kidneys. <margin>a Figure 20, u.</margin> Meanwhile, from the vein of the left kidney, the <term>seminal vein</term> <note>The spermatic or ovarian vein.</note> seeking the left testis is drawn out; <margin>b Figure 20, γ at T.</margin> whereas from the vein that approaches the right kidney, a branch is scattered in numerous offspring into the fatty and membranous tunic of the kidney. The left vein sometimes mimics this when the left kidney occupies a higher seat than the right. <margin>Conformation of the kidneys in their inner seats.</margin> What sort of thing this fatty tunic of the kidneys may be, I shall explain shortly; <margin>c Lest I be too lengthy in noting this, look at the tables of Figure 21 in order.</margin> for now, I shall proceed to describe the path and distribution of the vessels through the body of the kidney, along with its cavities and the origin of the passage leading the urine from the kidney into the bladder <note>The ureter.</note>, following the continuous discussion of the vessels. And I wish I could place these things before your eyes as if I were present, demonstrating them with very little effort in a dissection of the kidney—especially since so many fables about the functions, cavities, membranes, and the vessels distributed in the kidneys have been made up until now by other professors of dissection. Galen simply says that the veins and arteries are spread through the body of the kidney; and that through the thick and hard substance of the kidneys, the blood is retained while the urine (with a portion of the bile present in the blood) is transmitted and flows out into the urinary passage extending from the kidney to the bladder. Among our own physicians, and all those who have followed Galen and strive to express these things, some approach the fabric of the kidney wrongly and lazily, and failing to observe the distribution and position of these vessels, they invent I know not what "straining membranes." Others, shunning dissection and sitting in their high chairs, like <term>Prometheis</term> <note>A reference to Prometheus, who fashioned humans out of clay; Vesalius uses this to mock professors who "create" anatomy in their minds rather than observing nature.</note> wonderfully pleasing themselves, think they have performed their duty abundantly if they fashion a "human" for their disciples out of their imagination. And hence it is that I know the leading physicians of our age have both taught and written that a triple mode can be devised by which urine is distinguished from blood in the kidneys—

...and that the artery ends there, and they pour the serous blood into it. Furthermore, they believe a membrane separating two cavities <note>original: *sinus*; refers here to the chambers of the renal pelvis.</note> is passable through such narrow and tight little holes that it transmits that watery and thin waste <note>original: *recrementum*; the byproduct of blood filtration.</note> and bile as well, while the blood, meanwhile, does not penetrate because of its thickness. Moreover, those stupid architects of the human fabric add—clearly so they can more elegantly invent a false work—that the urinary duct <note>The ureter, which carries urine to the bladder.</note> is planted out of the lower cavity and that it receives the already filtered urine. Truly, the most wise Creator <term>Opifex</term> <note>Vesalius frequently uses this term to refer to God as the "Great Craftsman" or "Architect" of nature.</note> of things did not assign such a great task to a single small membrane perforated like a sieve, nor did He build such a thing in the kidneys. Instead, the substance of the kidney, by a power innate to it, and by its own proper temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" refers to the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness that allows an organ to function.</note> and essential form, filters that serous waste from the veins and arteries led through its body, and pours it into the cavity that is received by the urinary duct. 

To see this remarkable craftsmanship, I would wish you to have at hand the kidney of a dog, or even a goat, as these are lean and not filled with fat like those of a human or even a sheep. I want you to first approach it in this way, just as I will add the dissection of the kidney to the end of this book. For after several completed dissections (provided the first one is not enough), you will find two cavities in the kidneys, formed very differently than our doctors think. 

<margin>d As I advised above, look carefully here at the tables of the 21st figure.</margin> <sup>d</sup> For the vein and artery entering the kidney degenerate into a single body, which, matching the coats of the arteries in hardness and thickness, is seen to be hollow and distributed through the body of the kidney in the manner of some vein or artery. First, it gradually widens and is divided, so to speak, into two parts: one of these we shall call the anterior <note>Front.</note>, and the other the posterior <note>Back.</note> (always mindful of the kidney's shape, which we described above) for the sake of instruction. 

The anterior part, in one series and one path, produces sometimes six, sometimes seven, or even more equally thick branches. These, moving away from each other equally according to the shape of the kidney through its anterior part, hasten toward the outer side of the kidney; they do not, however, go all the way to the external surface of that side, but remain much further inside the body of the kidney. Here, divided again into several offshoots, they mix with the posterior branches of the membrane-like body, which I shall now follow. For the posterior part of that body is distributed into branches in the same way as the anterior, heading toward the outer side of the kidney. 

When the posterior branches reach the point where the anterior ones have come, they join with the anterior ones; and each is united with the other as if they were one and the same body, and they establish a shared cavity. This elegant joining of branches is completed in the form of a semicircle, following the shape of the outer side of the kidneys. 

This membrane-like and hollow body <note>The renal pelvis and calyces.</note>, along with its branches, does not have the substance of the kidneys attached to it on all sides. For the substance of the kidney is attached to the body itself—before it is divided into branches—at the front and back, and at its inner side, but not at the outer side. However, the substance of the kidney is attached only to the front of the anterior branches, and only to the back of the posterior branches, until the branches are led to their mutual joining. Here indeed, where each is divided into more branches and the anterior join the posterior, they have the kidney substance attached on all sides. 

Nonetheless, between the branches themselves, where nothing is attached toward the inner parts of the kidney, a kind of septum <note>A dividing wall or partition.</note> proceeds, not joined to the branches, and coming forth from that kidney substance which grows together with the branches where they join. Thus, here between the anterior and posterior branches of that membrane-like body, another cavity of the kidney arises, which is in a way divided in two. For where it looks toward the outer side of the membrane-like body, where it first buds into branches, it appears to be single; but when it is carried toward the exterior parts according to the septum born from the kidney substance, it is seen to be double. For one part of it is between the septum and the branches...

...branches extend. This cavity <note>original: *sinus*; referring here to the renal pelvis</note> appears somewhat moist and entirely bloodless during dissection; however, that membranous body with all its branches—or the first cavity of the kidney, if one prefers to call it that—is always found full of blood. Humans, who are everywhere teeming with fat just like pigs, also have the second cavity filled with a somewhat hard fat and a kind of nourished, serous moisture. This fat has not only obscured the study of human kidneys for those performing dissections, but it so deceived some who attempted a more careful sectioning that they left written records claiming this fat <margin>e 22, 23 fig. q q.</margin><sup>e</sup> was a kind of "lid" for the urinary passage, placed there to oversee the excretion or straining of urine in the kidneys, acting as a sort of filter. For those who were not content with their own imaginations and dreams, but instead applied full effort alongside reason to dissection, they saw—if nothing else—at least the beginning of the urinary duct <margin>f 11 fig. n.</margin><sup>f</sup> <note>The ureter.</note>, which certainly hangs from the second cavity of the kidney, not indeed from its lower seat, but from the middle of its inner side.

<margin>The function of the kidneys.</margin>
For that duct begins from the external side of the membranous body, where it is first split into branches. Then, proceeding through the middle of that body, it emerges from the middle of the kidney through the internal side, appearing much like a vein. This, by Hercules, is the conformation of the kidneys, which demonstrates that the serous blood is drawn into that membranous body and its branches by the power of the kidney's substance and the benefit of the straight fibers of its body. This is done so that the blood may be freed from that serous humor, just as we believe blood is largely taken up and transmitted from the offshoots of the portal vein into the branches of the great hollow vein <note>The *vena cava*.</note>. Furthermore, the kidneys do not draw away the entirety of the serum; rather, so that the blood is more suited for flowing through the cavities of the veins, a portion of the serum is still led with it through the rest of the body, which we see floating atop blood that has been drawn and has already clotted. Indeed, it also becomes manifest that the substance of the kidneys filters that watery humor (and whatever bilious waste might still be mixed with it) not only from the blood contained in the hollow vein, but also from the great artery <note>The aorta.</note>, and thrusts it into that other cavity. From there, it flows down gradually through the <margin>g through q, q. in 17 figure 22, 23.</margin><sup>g</sup> urinary duct to the bladder, which is prepared like a flask <note>original: *lagena*; a large, narrow-necked bottle</note> to receive this fluid. What the structure of these ducts is, you shall hear immediately once I have added the explanation of the kidneys' tunics to the preceding points. For the kidneys have two

Where the kidneys themselves rest against it, it produces certain membranous fibers that turn into the membranous tunic that binds the kidneys themselves. This tunic is interwoven with frequent veins like the omentum <note>The fatty "apron" of the abdomen.</note>, and is abundant with much fat (as the omentum is), perhaps warming the action of the kidneys in the manner of a small brush or heater. The tunic of the right kidney obtains an offshoot from the vein reaching to the kidney itself, <margin>i 20 fig. Sometimes the arrangement of the veins entwining these tunics is the opposite. ## ON THE BLADDER, THE RECEPTACLE OF URINE,
## and the passages leading it from the kidneys into the bladder.
### Chapter XI.

*The male bladder is shown primarily in the twenty-second and twenty-third figures, which express it entirely together with the urinary passages <note>the ureters</note> as they have been drawn out, as does the fourth figure of Chapter 49, Book II. The second, third, sixth, tenth, twelfth, and twentieth figures show the upper part of the base of the bladder, still connected to the peritoneum. Moreover, the twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, and twenty-sixth figures contain the female bladder beautifully delineated, as may be sought from the indexes of those figures.*

JUST as the kidneys certainly claim for themselves a seat suitable for their functions and are safely placed, so too are the bladder and the urinary passages. For the bladder, since it is the receptacle of urine in which this is gradually strained from the kidneys (so that it need not be passed by us frequently and perpetually, but rarely and all at once), deservedly occupies that seat where it can conveniently excrete it <margin>b 1, 2 fig. ch. 49 book 2 M.</margin> when it is troubled by the quantity or quality of the urine. It was not fitting for this place to be far from <gloss>b</gloss> that from which dry excrements are emitted <note>the rectum/anus</note>. Then, other organs of nutrition, far more noble than this bladder and necessarily requiring a high position, occupied the more elevated seat: so much so, that by a certain right the bladder, no less than the rectum, is placed lower. For it stands <margin>c last fig. of book 2 g.</margin> behind <gloss>c</gloss> the pubic bone, its higher part exceeding the upper seat of that bone sometimes more, sometimes less, according as it is distended by urine. <margin>Shape of the bladder.</margin> For it is somewhat round, like an oblong sphere, and is seen to be fuller in its upper part than <margin>d 23 fig. o. q. 25 fig. γ, δ.</margin> in its lower part, which ends in <gloss>d</gloss> the neck and a narrow passage <note>the urethra</note>, and this is almost by occasion of its location. Although indeed, so that the bladder might be rendered more capacious and less exposed to injuries, a shape rounded exactly in the manner of a globe would have better suited it; nevertheless, the Creator of things <note>original: "rerum Opifex"; Vesalius’s frequent term for the divine or natural intelligence behind biological design</note> constructed it more oblong and fuller in its more prominent part: lest by chance if He had added to its width that cavity which it gains from its length, it would be pressed too much by the pubic bone and <margin>e 20 fig. o. 24 fig. K. f 4 fig. L. 25 fig. i, h, l.</margin> the <gloss>e</gloss> rectum, and additionally by the <gloss>f</gloss> uterus in women, and those organs would obstruct the distension of the bladder more than is right. Meanwhile, its upper part, exceeding the pubic bone, can be conveniently distended and dilated because of the yielding abdominal muscles. <margin>Substance of the bladder.</margin> For it was necessary that the bladder be made ample and ready to be extended, so that, as has been said, the urine would need to be passed by us less frequently. Hence it also consists of a membranous or nervous body, which can be conveniently dilated, and again, when it contains nothing, <margin>h The right figure of Figure 23 and Figure 26 propose the dissected bladder.</margin> it collapses. For <gloss>h</gloss> the bladder consists of a smooth, hard, strong, and membranous tunic, which is seen sometimes thicker, sometimes thinner, according to whether it is more heavily distended or constricted: specifically claiming this for itself, that in the highest part of its base, and where it ends in the neck, it occurs harder and thicker because of the insertions and origins of certain passages. Even boys know that this is interwoven with a triple kind of fiber; while they inflate a bladder, they rub it with their fingernails so that it may be more readily distended, tearing such fibers and sometimes adding songs <note>Vesalius describes a common childhood game in the Low Countries where animal bladders were used as toys or balloons</note>. So much so, that from the bladders which I, as is the custom among our people, used to inflate, pound, and rub with fingernails and fingers as a boy, I immediately understood what the fibers of the tunics were among the Anatomists. The outermost [fibers] are transverse, while the middle ones are oblique, obtaining their order of position according to the order of their functions. For expulsion precedes retention, and this in turn precedes attraction <note>Vesalius refers to the traditional physiological theory where organs possess specific "faculties" to attract what they need, retain it for use, and expel waste</note>. That the bladder’s tunic had to be hard and thick is proven, among other arguments, by the fact that it must often be distended to a great size, and it is frequently vexed by the sharpness <note>acrimonia</note> of urine, by ulcers from stones <term>calculis|bladder stones or kidney stones</term>, and by other evils of that kind. If it were not hard, these would easily tear, erode, and perforate it. To make this tunic even stronger, Nature uniquely wrapped it in the thick and robust covering of the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, which is considered the second tunic of the bladder. In humans, because we stand upright, the peritoneum attaches to the entire anterior base and seat of the bladder above the pubic bone; this is much different than in dogs or in Galen’s opinion <note>Vesalius frequently corrects Galen, who based much of his human anatomy on animal dissections</note>. In dogs and other four-footed animals, only a small part of the peritoneum is offered to the bladder, and its entire anterior side is not even loosely attached, but like the posterior side, it appears smooth and slippery. In humans, however, the posterior side of the bladder, which faces the rectum and the uterus, also appears smooth, slippery, and moistened with a watery fluid.

</margin>
Furthermore, since the urine of the bladder (like the bilious waste in its own gallbladder) is unfit for nutrition, Nature has very opportunely distributed veins to the bladder to nourish it, and arteries to restore its heat. First, on both sides of the neck of the bladder, she derived one vein and one artery from the branches of the hollow vein <term>vena cava|the large vein returning blood to the heart</term> and the great artery <term>aorta|the primary artery of the body</term> that approach the leg through the opening in the pubic bone. These ascend from here through the length of the bladder’s body and are dissipated into very thin, hair-like branches. Nor is the bladder lacking in nerves, which it needs most for the sensation of things pressing against it. For although the urine flows into the bladder—as bile into the smaller gallbladder—as something familiar to it, and the bladder suffers no harm from it when the urine is natural, it sometimes contains such a mixture of bilious excrement and becomes so biting and sharp that unless the bladder perceived the quality of the urine, it would be severely affected by holding it for too long. Consequently, among the other parts of the body, the bladder has obtained nerves of no small size for the sake of the sense of touch alone, receiving them from the branches of the sixth pair <note>original: "sexti paris"; in the 16th century, the vagus and sympathetic nerves were often grouped together as the "sixth pair" of cranial nerves</note> extended from the roots of the ribs, and from the lowest pairs of the spinal cord.

<margin>
The passage leading urine out of the fetus, and the peculiar fetal arteries joined to the bladder.

Just as these vessels and nerves seek the bladder, so too from the higher and middle region of its body or base arises a certain passage <term>urachus|a tube connecting the fetal bladder to the umbilical cord</term> which, formed somewhat like the tunic of a vein, travels through the navel. Joined with the other umbilical vessels, it ends between the two coverings of the fetus, carrying there the urine that is continuously accumulated while we are carried in the womb. This is done so that the urine, if discharged through the private parts and spread around the fetus's body, might not ulcerate the tender skin of the fetus with its sharpness. And just as there is no longer any use for this passage in this function once a person is born, it dries up and becomes merely a ligament of the bladder to the peritoneum. This is exactly like the two arteries entering the navel of the fetus, which are stretched on both sides of the base of the bladder and so attached that they then also beautifully connect the bladder to the peritoneum; when humans are brought into the light, these dry up like cords and are entirely useless for reviving the native heat of the fetus or for performing the duty of arteries elsewhere.

Furthermore, into the lower part of the bladder, besides its own nerves, veins, and arteries, two other passages are inserted into its cavity, formed to lead the urine down from the kidneys. Since the kidneys must necessarily be placed as close as possible to the liver, while the bladder claims a low seat for itself, it was necessary to create certain passages to carry the urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Nature constructed these very similar to the body of veins; indeed, they consist of a single tunic, slightly harder than the tunic of veins, yet with fewer [fibers] than that...

[These fibers] are more suitable, as they can be easily stretched or flattened; moreover, the oblique fibers do not at all prevent the urine from falling more quickly into the bladder. Because these channels—which the Greeks call *ereteres* <note>original: ἐρητῆρας; ureters</note>, *hedranas* <note>original: ἕδρανὰς; perhaps "seats" or "settling places"</note>, and *poroi eretikoi* <note>original: πόρους ἐρητικοὺς; excretory passages</note> based on their function—so closely resemble veins, and because they appear white unlike veins turgid with blood, they are called "white veins" by Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman medical encyclopedist</note>.

<margin>t 21 fig. E, n, λ.</margin>
Their beginning, in my view, hangs from what I call the second cavity in the body of the kidneys. Extended through the first cavity of the kidneys, they are brought out from the central seat of the kidneys. From here, stretched over the peritoneum above the muscles of the loins <note>the psoas muscles</note>, they creep downward very safely toward the bladder. 
<margin>u 7 muscul. tab. 1, 4.</margin>
For in their progress they are attached to the peritoneum, and having obtained certain fibers from it, they take on a second tunic <note>outer layer</note>, interwoven with small veins and arteries just like the peritoneum itself. Furthermore, their path is as straight as possible, since a long journey would offer no advantage here; from the cavity of the kidneys, they stretch downward and slightly inward to reach the bladder. To ensure they are not poorly supported or hanging loosely when inserted into the bladder, and to avoid an overly slanted path, 
<margin>x 2 fig. M.</margin>
they are not implanted into the highest part of the bladder, from which hangs the channel <note>the urachus</note> that carries the urine of a fetus outside the navel. 
<margin>y 23 fi. r. 25 fi. non procul ab α. 26 fig. M.</margin>
Instead, they are implanted in that seat of the bladder which is nearer to the posterior region of the peritoneum, to which the channel is securely fixed throughout its entire length. Therefore, the region of insertion is in the lower, posterior part of the bladder, a little before it ends in the neck. First, the channels are joined to the bladder, and penetrating its tunic (derived from the peritoneum) with an oblique turn, they finally open or enter into the cavity of the bladder, passing through its second tunic as well.
<margin>z 13 figur. c add d. & 15 fi. Q ad R.</margin>
<margin>The ingenious insertion of the channels that lead the urine.</margin>
This occurs in a manner very similar to how the bile duct is reported to be inserted into the duodenum <note>the first part of the small intestine</note>. Namely, loose little membranes hang on both sides of the channel’s opening, just as if the small membranes were growing there from the bladder's internal tunic. The use of these membranes corresponds to the use of the membranous processes attached to the bile duct: specifically, they yield to the urine flowing down from the channels into the bladder, but when the bladder is distended and tries to regurgitate the urine back into those same channels, the membranes are gathered together, filling the channel and blocking the passage of the urine. These present membranes perform this so conveniently that even if the bladder is filled with a great deal of air <note>original: flatu; breath or gas</note>, it can release no air at all through these channels, in nearly the same way as bellows. For through the hole that is usually placed at the back of bellows, air is drawn in; but when the bellows are compressed again, because of a small wooden flap <term>asserculum|a clack valve or check valve</term> pressed against the hole by the force of the air, no wind is exhaled through it. We also elegantly observe the same thing in the balls we inflate with breath, in the pipes of organs inflated by bellows, and in many aqueducts. However, the Creator of things <note>Vesalius frequently praises the "Opifex" or "Craftsman" (God/Nature) for the efficiency of anatomical design</note> does not use such hanging, wide, and obvious lids in the insertion of the urinary channels as we use when imitating His industry in bellows, organs, balls, and finally in the windows of dovecotes, which allow pigeons to enter by stealth but prohibit them from leaving again. Moreover, we experience in those bladders which we inflate that the oblique path of the urinary channels during insertion also restrains the return of urine, whenever we pull the remaining portions of the channels upward a bit; by straightening the channels, so to speak, we give a path to the air inflated into the bladder through its neck.

<margin>a 23 fig. d v per o ad φ. 25 fig. γ, d.</margin>

For the lowest seat of the bladder’s body or base ends in its middle in a narrow passage, which we call the *cervix* or neck of the bladder. It is extended differently in a man than in a woman, and is attached and joined to different parts in the former than in the latter, and finally provides a different use for both. ### THAT NATURE HAS PROVIDED FOR THE PROPAGATION OF THE SPECIES. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'I' depicting a classical scene: several figures appear to be engaged in an anatomical demonstration or observation of a body, with architectural elements and a tiled floor in the background.</image-desc>

AT THE BEGINNING of the books *On the Preservation of Health*, Galen beautifully concludes from the first principles of the human body that man is necessarily subject to death. Indeed, besides the fact that it is established that the human body is a mixture and a created thing, the arteries, veins, nerves, flesh, and the rest of the parts from which it is formed demonstrate abundantly that it could by no means have been made immortal and incorruptible. Therefore, when—on account of the material itself—it was not possible to produce an immortal man, the Maker of things <note>the Creator or Nature</note> devised for him what help He could toward immortality. He acted like a good founder of cities, whose heart is not only set on the present inhabitants, but who also provides a way by which the city may endure either forever or for as many years as possible. Yet no city, however fortunate, seems ever to have been established that did not eventually perish along with the passing of centuries and ages. But the works of the provident and skillful Maker of things, which are known to have already existed and endured for many thousands of years, still remain, through a certain rare art invented by Him, so that new men always succeed those who pass away, and a perpetual 
<margin>

conservation of the species is achieved. For in the beginning, He constructed men so that one [the male] might especially provide the principle of the offspring, while the other [the female], receiving it, might nourish and cherish the fetus. Thus, He added organs to the man, namely the testes <gloss>a</gloss>, which form the

BOOK V ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY.

the Creator <note>original: "Opifex"</note> coupled the mere lusts of bodies coming together and a certain peculiar power of delight with procreation for the organs serving reproduction. <margin>An appetite for use is added to the reproductive organs.</margin> Indeed, he also bestowed upon the soul itself the practice of these things, granting a certain wonderful and unspeakable appetite for their use. By this, animals are incited—even if they are foolish, or young, or entirely deprived of reason—to nevertheless provide for the succession of their species, just as if they were entirely endowed with prudence. For since the Creator was not ignorant that the substance from which he created these instruments could by no means admit perfect wisdom, he instilled in them an allure and, as it were, a bait—which was all they could receive—for the safety and preservation of the species, adding the most vehement delight to the use of those parts. And hence comes that opinion in Plato's *Timaeus*, discussing the love of generation implanted in us by God: "Wherefore the power innate in the nature of the genitals in men is disobedient and masterly, and like an animal not listening to reason, it attempts to subject all things to itself by the violence of furious lusts." The vulva and uterus in females, by the same reasoning, is an animal greedy for generating; if it should abstain from generating at the wrong time or for a long duration, it bears the delay with difficulty and is greatly indignant. I shall pass over for now the love with which animals pursue their offspring, and the temperament granted privately by Nature to the woman, so that she might not only provide nourishment to the fetus while still contained in the uterus, but also diligently and happily nourish the newborn with her breasts. How skillfully these and the remaining organs serving generation are constructed, I will now begin to describe little by little, taking the beginning of my discourse from the male organs.
