They claim it is named <term>elytron</term> <note>original Greek: ἔλυτρον, meaning a sheath or cover</note>, supposing it to be adapted from the custom of the Athenians.$^r$ The other private covering of the testis, however, embraces nothing except the body and substance of the testis with the vessels entwined within it; it corresponds exactly to the shape of the testis, or rather, it forms that shape. Indeed, it is a hard, thick, and very strong membrane, enveloping the substance of the testis, which is somewhat soft and yielding. And this is certainly to be considered the primary use of this present tunic. Furthermore, it is useful in that, through its intervention and mediation, the vessels that must be joined to the testis are attached to it. For this tunic is seen to be looser, thinner, and softer in the place where the vessels are joined to it than through the rest of its circumference. And indeed, the vein and artery carrying blood and spirit to the testis$^u$ are attached to the higher part of the tunic, and many small branches piercing this tunic here$^x$ are extended into the substance of the testis.$^y$ Besides these, many other branches, but very slender ones,$^z$ are derived downward from the seminal vein and artery into the body of that tunic; in bulls and rams, these are elegantly led out like the tendrils of a vine. On the posterior side, this tunic has all the windings of the vessel carrying the semen$^a$ very strongly attached to it along its entire length, spread over the testis; in that area, it is also pierced everywhere by thin holes that escape the sight. But through the rest of its outer surface, it is seen to be smooth and bathed in a watery fluid, connected to no part at all. On its internal surface, where this tunic contains the substance of the testis, it is grown together with that substance$^b$ everywhere. Furthermore, I know well that this was called <term>epididymis</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιδιδυμίς, literally "upon the twins," referring to its position on the testicles</note>, as if you were to say "super-geminal," by the first professors of Anatomy who called the testis <term>didymos</term> <note>original Greek: δίδυμος, meaning "twin"</note>. This is regardless of how others may trifle concerning the "head" of the testis. These people, since they were ignorant of this tunic and read <term>epididymis</term> in the ancient Greeks, imagined another small part—besides the higher part of the testis which Galen undoubtedly called the head of the testis$^c$—which, like a small testis placed upon the testis, was called its head and <term>epididymis</term>. Others, deceived by the error of these men (which other translators of the Greek greatly increased by rendering <term>epididymis</term> as "testicular vein"), but attempting dissection in the meantime, since they did not find a head of this kind, imitated certain Arabs and invented some vessel to be called by this name. They placed this vessel in the middle$^d$ between the testis and the seminal vein and artery, which are first attached to the present tunic; perhaps they so named that part of the vessel carrying the semen which is its beginning, and which in some part circularly embraces the higher region of the posterior part of the testis. But since these trifles are observed with little effort during dissection, and setting aside the dispute over names, consider this to be the second of the proper tunics of each testis, and know that it was also called <term>elytron</term> by the ancient Greeks. Now, turn your mind eagerly to the account of the vessels. Thus, to each$^e$ testis reach individual veins and likewise arteries, differing in their origin. For the vein approaching the right$^f$ testis takes its beginning from the trunk of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood back to the heart.</note>, hanging lower down than the origins of the veins extended to the kidneys. It does not start from the right side of the trunk, but from its superior or anterior$^g$ seat, declining slightly to the right, and this by a somewhat long and thickish$^h$ prominence. The vein of the left testis,$^i$ however, has its origin$^l$ from the lower seat of the vein extended to the left kidney. This is the origin of such veins as is usually seen; however, sometimes, but more rarely, you will see a small branch extended from the left side of the trunk of the vena cava$^k$, which, creeping downward to the left, is mixed with the left seminal vein. Galen testifies that the same has sometimes happened to the right seminal vein: namely, that a small branch arising from the vein of the right kidney$^l$ would extend downward and join with the vein taking its beginning from the trunk of the vena cava.$^m$ But I know not what came into the minds of the Prometheans <note>A term Vesalius uses for those who "create" or "invent" anatomy from theory rather than observation, like Prometheus fashioning man from clay.</note>, who in their dreams...

### ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE [HUMAN] BODY

Those who imagine the human body while sitting in a professor's chair <note>Vesalius is criticizing "armchair anatomists" who rely on ancient texts rather than performing their own dissections.</note> teach that the right seminal vein arises from the right renal vein, and the left from the trunk of the vena cava <note>the great central vein</note>, whenever the left kidney occupies a higher position than the right. They speak as if the right vein did not actually take its origin much lower than the renal veins, and as if, because the right renal vein was too high, the vein of the right testis had to be derived from the trunk of the vena cava. We have frequently observed that position of the kidneys, but I have seen a different origin for the right testicular vein only once, even though at that time both seminal veins were borrowing their origin from the renal veins.

The veins, extended downward from their origins along the side, are joined to their companion arteries by fibrous ties of the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>, which merge into one of their tunics. For both arteries arise from the middle<gloss>n</gloss> of the front of the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, lower than where the origin of the vein seeking the right testis is located. Indeed, the right artery, climbing over the trunk of the vena cava<gloss>o</gloss>—which I wonder has been so little noticed by professors of dissection until now—hastens obliquely downward to the right testicular vein. The left artery, approaching the vein of its own side, has more than once appeared to me to be missing, the left testicular vein being much larger than usual at those times. I have hardly ever seen it arise from the artery shared with the left kidney, although I do not deny that this can sometimes happen. However, I will by no means concede that an equal origin of the veins and arteries seeking the testes is observed as frequently as Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose work was the standard for over a millennium</note> teaches everywhere.

For just as we take in foods fit for nutrition by the mouth and process them in the stomach, and that which is processed and elaborated is carried by a long duct from the windings of the intestines into the hollow of the liver: so also the veins and arteries of the testes carry the best portion of the blood and spirits to them. Nor is this into one large cavity cut into the testes, but into very thin small vessels, formed of an equally subtle membrane, distributed through the substance of the testis in a very frequent series. This is surely so that the substance of the testis (as was said of the flesh of the liver) may impart the perfect nature of semen to the blood and spirit by its indwelling faculty. <meta>This page continues Vesalius's detailed anatomical and physiological investigation into the male reproductive system, specifically focusing on the blood supply to the testes and the structure of the vasa deferentia (the tubes that carry sperm). # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

so that [the seed] can be conveniently cast and ejaculated into the womb. To this function it contributes that the vein of the right testis arises from the trunk of the vena cava below the veins of the kidneys, so that it may offer purer and more unmixed blood to the testis. Thus, it is also highly expedient that both arteries arise similarly from the great artery <note>The aorta.</note>, so that they might lead down the thinner blood, rushing with force, and the divine soul or spirit that is within the seed, into a more refined state. Indeed, I believe there is no one now who would agree with Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BCE) who mistakenly believed that arteries contained only air (pneuma), not blood.</note> that blood is not contained in the arteries, or who would claim that the seminal arteries bring nothing but spirit to the testes. Although this was also a dogma of Aristotle’s, who falsely taught that the seminal arteries were empty of blood. 

Furthermore, Galen, along with all other anatomists, attests that the testis of the left side obtains its own vein from the vein of the left kidney, so that this vein might communicate serous <note>Watery or thin.</note> blood to the seed. By the power of the sharpness and biting nature of this blood, a stinging and titillation <note>Vesalius refers to the physical sensation of sexual arousal.</note> would be stirred up in the organ—which is entwined with many nerves—during the emission of the seed. For Galen writes that a delight of this kind occurs here, just as we know occurs from the salty and biting juices in those suffering from the itch <note>Scabies.</note>, when they itch after being warmed by fire or bedclothes, and by scratching they give place to those juices stimulating the skin. I do not consider this decree of Galen's to be very probable, since those who are urinating are not affected by an itch despite such a great abundance of serous humor, even though we know that urine is passed through a rigid and frequently warmed penis, especially in those troubled by a stone <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>. 

Moreover, those suffering from an involuntary flow of putrid seed feel an itch in the first days even with a weak and flaccid penis, with no preceding cause warming the penis. To this, we add that those who are castrated in the left testis due to a defect of a hernia <note>original: "ramicum," referring to a scrotal hernia or varicocele.</note> or other occasion, would, when copulating, be affected by neither itch nor pleasure [according to Galen's theory]; yet we hear daily from those whose hernia is treated by hand <note>Surgically.</note> that this is false. Truly, the fact that others testify that the vaporous spirit of the seed also contributes to the cause of delight does not satisfy me, since that power of piercing and stimulating cannot exist in the spirit. Thus, this delight must be referred to the specific and essential form and matter of the seed, and then to the reason of the body which is affected by sensation; for we do not perceive this delight in the entire neck of the bladder. Nor, certainly, does the seed affect other parts of the body with equal sensation as it does the womb.

<margin>
Reason for the structure of the vessel carrying semen.
</margin>
Furthermore, the attachment of the vessel carrying the seed to the testis does not occur except through very thin and narrow little openings, and that by the intervention of the innermost tunic <note>Layer of tissue.</note> of the testis. This is because it was necessary for that vessel to be hard, strong, and dense to endure the carrying, whereas the substance of the testis is loose and soft. Thus, prudent Nature here—as indeed nowhere else—has not forced two contrary essences into one, unless some bond of friendship and association was cast in between to reconcile them. For by as much as the vessel carrying the seed is surpassed in density and hardness by the innermost tunic of the testis, by so much does that tunic surpass the testes themselves—not indeed through the entire circumference by which it is wrapped around the testis, but only in that place where it has the seminal vessels attached to it. For here it exists softer than through the rest of the body and is, as I said, perforated with thin holes. For it is created for this most especially: to be a most exquisite wrapping for the substance of the testis. 

Truly, the vessel carrying the seed is wound around the testis with so many turnings and coils so that it may take up the seed from the testis more quickly and copiously, and perhaps the seed may obtain some refinement within it. That vessel is joined to the posterior part of the testis, not the anterior, so that since it now offers or contains the finished seed (while the testis only produces it), the vessel may be placed in a safer location, using the testis as a bulwark. And for the same reason, when the vessel enters the peritoneum <gloss>v</gloss> <margin>γ 23 figure at λ under fl.</margin>, it is rightly hidden under the vein and artery, so that it may more perfectly contain the seed [formed] from the blood and spirit from which the seed is prepared. The right vessel joins with the left, and both are introduced into the neck of the bladder, so that the seed of both testes [may be released] at once,

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V

and at the same time it is ejaculated into the womb. <margin>The use of the glandular body attached to the neck of the bladder.</margin> It is certain that the glandular body <note>The prostate gland.</note> (which is largest in tailed monkeys and appears externally rolled up like clouds) moistens the passage of both urine and semen in the neck of the bladder. Furthermore, it seems to serve as a support for the passages that are distributed through it from the deferent vessels, as well as for the veins, arteries, and nerves distributed to the body and neck of the bladder; and perhaps it even imparts a certain perfection to the semen and contributes to its generation. Indeed, in a man suffering from an involuntary flow of semen <note>Spermatorrhea.</note> whom we dissected at Padua, when this glandular body was divided, we saw it filled with semen no less than the testes themselves. And if the truth must be told, during dissection, in no part of the body is so great a force of semen found anywhere as in this glandular body, even though its substance varies greatly from the softness and consistency of the testes. <margin>Galen's anatomical demonstration, by which it is established that the glandular body does not preside over the preparation of semen.</margin> However, I greatly admire Galen's demonstration concerning this glandular body placed at the end of his second book *On the Semen*. Having said that those unskilled in dissection do not even know of this body, while all the skilled ones assert with one voice that semen is contained within it, he—intending to disprove their opinion—submitted this demonstration, which he regarded as frequently emphasized, true, and irrefutable. "If semen were generated in the glandular assistants (to use the words of the translator, who thus renders *parastatai adenoeideis* <note>original: "παραστάτας ἀδενωδεῖς" — literally "glandular bystanders" or "assistants," the ancient Greek term for the prostate.</note>), yet the experts who knew the glandular body said it was only contained there, then castrated animals would still desire its excretion; but they do not seem to desire this: therefore, it is clear that no semen is generated in these." Truly, if Galen's books *On Demonstration* <note>A lost work of Galen's highly prized by Renaissance scholars.</note> abound with such frequent "demonstrations"—which are not uncommon in his works (if I may dare to say so), and especially in Anatomy, where he most excelled—there is no reason why we should so greatly long for those books or envy those people in whose libraries they are preserved to be devoured by moths and beetles, offering no use of themselves. For besides the fact that such animals, like boys and eunuchs, occasionally desire sexual union in vain, by what means, I ask—even if the entire power of generating semen were in this glandular body—could they produce it once the testes were removed, since the severed testes would supply nothing to the vessel that carries semen to the glandular body? For it is more certain than certainty itself from dissection that the vessel carrying semen has no communication at all with the veins and arteries of the testes which would take up the semen without the work of the testes. Even if there were something of the sort—as I, along with most professors of anatomy, was once thoroughly persuaded, namely that the vein and artery degenerated into the nature of the vessel carrying semen, and it was formed from that vein and artery—Galen's demonstration would only hold place in those animals where a diligent castrator had removed the testis while leaving the seminal vessels unharmed (which is impossible to do). For no matter how much you strive to cut away the coils and turns of the vessel carrying semen wound around the testis from the innermost coat of the testis, you will not succeed without the part of the vessel attached to the testis appearing rough, uneven, and scraped. And if perhaps, out of a desire for this experiment, you were to divide the inner coat of the testis in some part during the castration of an animal, and leaving the coat still attached to the seminal vessels, you were to free only the substance of the testis from the coat, the pores and passages of the seminal vessels would still necessarily be broken, which we know for certain are distributed through the substance of the testis. For the sake of this procedure, and to weigh the opinion of Aristotle (who attributes no power of generating semen to the testes), I made a trial in a dog. He recovered quite well, but he seems unfit for generation, like the others whose testes have been torn out; for he, like them, has become very fat and less spirited. But to say nothing of the rest, it is a wonder that Galen did not notice, when he was weaving a demonstration of this kind, that he was moving away from Aristotle's...

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE VIRILE MEMBER, OR PENIS.
## Chapter XIV.

*The structure of the penis is shown primarily in the figures of the forty-ninth Chapter of the second book, as well as the twentieth figure of this book, and the twenty-second and twenty-third.*

<margin>
*The reason for the structure of the penis.*
</margin>
<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'A' depicting several small winged figures (putti) performing an anatomical dissection of a human form on a wooden table.</image-desc>
NATURE constructed the penis very skillfully, as its functions beautifully attest. For since she deemed it better to create two human beings who might conveniently serve generation, she adapted suitable parts to one especially for receiving the female, and to the other for its discharge. To the man, therefore, she granted a member most fit for pouring [semen] into the womb of the female, which at the time of intercourse ought to be entirely swollen, rigid, and erect for various uses. But if it were kept perpetually so tense and long, it would be a nuisance throughout life except at the time of congress, and would be as easily subject to injuries as if someone always carried their hand stretched out. Since, therefore, it had to be sometimes limp, slender, and short, and in turn tense and swollen, Nature is to be praised for fashioning a member suited to these uses. For the penis is primarily constituted by two bodies <note>the *corpora cavernosa*</note>, which find no part similar to themselves (except perhaps the nipple); these, when filled with spirit <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a refined substance in the blood that facilitated movement and function</note> and blood, can be erected, extended, and significantly swollen; and again, when the same spirit and blood are dissipated, they can be narrowed, collapse, become flaccid, and be made shorter.

<margin>
*The primary substance of the penis.*
</margin>

</margin>
<margin>
*That Galen never saw the structure of the human penis.*
</margin>
<margin>
*The site of the penis.*
</margin>
That Galen never dissected these bodies nor had a clear view of their nature will be more than enough argument for you in the sequence of his discourse in the fifteenth book *On the Use of the Parts*, once I have completed the description of the structure of the male member. Galen reviews its position at great length and elegantly, because surely this was no more hidden from him without dissection than a man's fingers or the bends at the groin and the back of the knee—places in which Galen almost believed a man differs from an ape. And just as its position comes into view without a long narrative, so too it is easily gathered how perfectly it fits the performance of the penis's duties, nor could it be more aptly placed elsewhere; so much so, indeed, that its size and shape are evident to everyone.

Two bodies primarily forming it enter into its construction, along with the common passage for semen and urine <note>the urethra</note>, and four muscles placed at the root of the penis; and finally veins, arteries, nerves, skin, and the fleshy membrane <note>the *dartos* fascia</note> placed beneath it, and the ligament connecting this skin with the fleshy membrane to the penis. Therefore, from the right pubic bone, where it is seen to be thicker and somewhat rounded at the lower seat of the joint of the pubic bones, a certain rounded body takes its very strong beginning, entirely resembling the nature of a ligament; receding somewhat upward from the bone, it touches another body on its inner side, which similarly arises from the left pubic bone. <margin>The passage common to urine and semen.</margin>
For immediately from the origin of these bodies, the urinary passage—or the neck of the bladder—is stretched beneath them. It extends with them as far as the <margin>Figure 49, chapter 2, at D.</margin> beginning of the <term>glans</term><note>The rounded head of the penis.</note> in such a way that it nowhere enters the substance of the bodies—at least until it reaches the glans, where you will soon hear how the passage is led into the substance of the bodies. Its interior substance is seen as entirely red, blackish, spongy, and filled with dark blood, almost as if a sort of net were formed from countless tiny branchings of arteries and veins closely entwined, and enclosed in a circle by that fibrous and membranous substance as if in a hide. And these two bodies of the penis retain this fibrous envelope and spongy substance individually all the way to the glans—a feature to be weighed with great care by any student of Nature’s works.

<margin>The Glans.</margin>
<margin>At D in the figures of chapter 49, book 2.</margin>
When, however, they reach that region of the penis where the glans is formed, they are brought to a point, and the fleshy substance of the glans grows over them. This glans does not merely have the passage common to urine and <term>semen</term><note>original: "feminis"; here the genitive of "semen," not "woman."</note> beneath it, as those bodies do, but actually <margin>Figure 23, q.</margin> embraces and surrounds the passage. Here, the passage is made wider than in the rest of its duct, and then narrowed again at its very end. It is as if Nature had desired there to be a delay of the semen during intercourse, and consequently a more intense delight in the glans (which she increased by providing the opportunity for friction). For this reason, those suffering from an involuntary flow of semen are frequently plagued by ulcers in this area, because of the sharpness of the putrid semen preserved in this wide space, which severely ulcerates the urinary passage. This area is significantly troubled by the biting of the flowing urine while it is being passed, no less than the part of the same passage located between the anus and the testes—which we call the <term>perineum</term>—is painfully affected in those suffering severely from that illness when the penis is rigid. This happens primarily because of the slant and bend of the passage, and additionally because of its downward position.

<margin>Figure 11, chapter 49, book 2, G.</margin>
For since the passage first bends upward here beneath the bodies of the penis, and this is the lowest point, the collection of semen which ulcerates the passage stays here no less than in the glans; consequently, it erodes this spot more than the rest of the passage. Furthermore, once the passage is eroded, it feels the "dissolution of its unity" <note>A classical way of describing the pain of a tear or wound.</note> more vehemently when it is stretched along with the penis.

<margin>Figures 22, 23, and the last figure of Book 3, f.</margin>

Although these vessels <margin>Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, chapter 49, book 2, A, B.</margin> reach the bodies of the penis, I can hardly determine by dissection the path by which they are inserted into the cavity of those bodies to deliver that dark and thick blood which the spongy <margin>Figure 20, r.</margin> substance of the bodies possesses in abundance. However, branches going to the skin covering these bodies are clearly visible even before dissection and run through it. To these nerves are added the bonds of the membrane, which connect the upper part of the bodies—where they are first led upward from the joint of the pubic bones—to that part where the penis is first covered circularly by the skin and the <term>fleshy membrane</term><note>The *dartos* fascia or similar subcutaneous tissue layer.</note>.^t The four muscles approaching the penis were described in the second book: where we recounted that two extend to the channel for urine and semen, and one extends for some distance along each of the bodies of the penis.

Thus, nothing more remains to be said about the construction of the penis, unless one wishes to praise Nature for having inserted no fat between the fleshy membrane and the skin covering the penis.^u By doing so, she established a thinner covering for the penis, better suited for being rolled, folded, and extended; this is commonly called the <term>prepuce</term><note>the foreskin</note>. This was formed primarily so that by covering the penis it would keep it smooth, moderately soft and moist, and exceptionally endowed with sensation—not indeed calloused, or dry and dull like ordinary skin. 

Therefore, if you dissect a human penis, you will not find one hollow nerve or ligament arising from the pubic bone, as Galen taught, but rather the two <term>bodies</term><note>The *corpora cavernosa*.</note> I have described. These are not empty and lacking in all moisture, as Galen writes, but consist of that spongy and, as it were, fleshy material—as Aristotle correctly suggested—and they are filled with a great deal of dark blood, like <note>original: "farciminum"</note> sausages. 

Furthermore, no other muscles extend to the passage of semen and urine than^x those two which we showed arise from the circular muscle of the rectum. Meanwhile, Galen lists two muscles along the entire length of the penis, stretched alongside the channel for urine and semen. However, it is no wonder that Galen did not properly understand the muscles of the penis, since he did not correctly weigh the origin of that "hollow and nervous" body which he placed in the penis. He asserts that it arises from the upper parts of the pubic bones^y—just as someone unskilled in dissection might judge that the penis first begins there, where it hangs down or becomes erect from the pubic bone above the scrotum, rounded and covered with skin. He did not notice (as we have written) that the nervous bodies of the penis are drawn out even lower down^z than where the lowest region of the pubic bone joint^b sits. 

The penis, once we have called upon the <term>perineum</term><note>The area between the anus and the scrotum.</note> near the anus, and throughout its entire course^a through the scrotum, and by its long attachment to the front part of the pubic bones, exists as equally thick and corpulent as it does in that rounded part emerging from the trunk of the body, which the common people call the "penis" or "rod." Nor does this occur in humans alone; in all quadrupeds, the principal portion and mass of the penis begins below the joint of the pubic bones, toward the anus—even if these animals otherwise present several common differences in the construction of the penis.

Furthermore, I marvel at the Arabs, who enumerated three channels in the penis: one dedicated to urine, a second to semen, and a third to that viscous humor which we believe is prepared by the <term>glandular body</term><note>The prostate gland.</note>^c surrounding the neck of the bladder. This humor occasionally makes the penis moist when a man intensely desires intercourse. Yet, among all these, only one channel is actually constructed. 

Truly, I easily believe that this opinion was first introduced by some Arab who, having attempted a dissection of the penis^d and noticing its structure did not agree with Galen’s decrees, thought there were three channels: the two bodies I mentioned, and the passage common to semen, urine, and the recently mentioned humor. For if you cut the penis^e crosswise and do not wipe away the dark blood that flows out from the second part, each of the bodies will certainly appear to you as an individual channel—to which a third is added,

<margin>
The womb is divided into the base and the neck.
The position of the womb, and its contact with the parts lying near it.
</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'Q' depicting two naked infants (putti) in a landscape. One infant is seated and appears to be manipulating a small object or animal on the ground, while the other stands behind, looking on or assisting. The letter 'Q' is formed by a thick, stylized border around this scene.</image-desc>

When we describe the structure of the womb, we conveniently distinguish it into the <term>fundus</term><note>The "base" or main body of the uterus, original: "fundum".</note> and the <term>cervix</term><note>The "neck" of the uterus, original: "ceruicem".</note>, or neck, just like the bladder. For although the womb is formed from both of these and one body rises from them, they differ greatly in position, shape, size, substance, the insertion of vessels, and other such things to be carefully observed in the history of the womb. Therefore, the neck of the womb ascends straight upward from the woman’s <term>pudendum</term><note>External genitals.</note> through the rear region of the pubic bones and the bladder, and along the front of the <term>rectum</term><note>Original: "recti intestini".</note>, into the cavity of the <term>peritoneum</term><note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>, until it reaches almost directly the level where the beginnings of the rectus abdominis muscles arise from the pubic bones. For there the neck of the womb ends in the base, or the base itself ends in the neck, so that even here the lower part of the base mostly remains. Furthermore, the location of the upper part of the base and its sides vary according to its size and mass. For the more the base increases with the fetus, the higher its upper part extends, even above the region of the navel; and it approaches the flanks with its sides so that I cannot circumscribe any specific position for it. In no women at all who are not pregnant, however, does the base exceed the beginning of the <term>sacrum</term><note>The "sacred bone" at the base of the spine, original: "sacri ossis".</note> joined to the lowest lumbar vertebra, nor in those do the base and neck touch anything on the posterior part except the rectum, and they hardly exceed its width; and the highest part of the base does not creep as high as the point where the rectum ends and the colon begins. Indeed, I have never noticed it to have climbed as high as the bladder, even when the bladder is completely empty, unless I grasped the womb with my hand and pulled it upward by stretching its neck. For as you allow this neck to be relaxed and coiled upon itself, or stretch it by pulling the womb upward, you greatly vary the position of the womb. For it lies so freely connected, and its neck is constructed of such substance (as you will hear in its proper place), that the base can be moved downward and upward with little effort. From this also—not to mention the <term>prolapse</term><note>A falling down or slipping of the organ, original: "procidentia".</note> of the womb—on no very great occasion in some women, especially those advanced in age and in whom the ligaments of the womb have now become looser, the mouth of the base falls down to the opening of the neck, so that it soon meets the mouth of the neck or the genitals themselves, and thus the highest part of the base descends much lower than the higher region of the bladder. Although meanwhile (as I have already warned previously), even in girls and those women who have not yet given birth, and in whom the mouth of the base is still hidden deeper and the womb is held by its ligaments, the highest part of the base, during dissection, [touches] the bladder...

Thus, because of this opening, the hymen in no way hinders the purging of menstrual blood in virgins, and also readily allows the flow of that white and raw humor <note>Vesalius refers to vaginal discharge or "leukorrhea."</note>; which Aristotle rightly pointed out sometimes happens even to very young girls. But as for the fact that the Arabs <note>Referring to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna or Rhazes.</note> wrote somewhere that five small veins reach the middle of the uterine cervix, and the mouths of the right veins are joined to the mouths of the left veins, and from these is formed what their interpreters call the *Cento* <note>original: "Centonem," meaning a patchwork garment; a medieval term for the hymen.</note>, and thus the hymen is formed—I am persuaded this was made by conjecture rather than by diligent dissection. For these Arabs certainly did not remember this membrane of ours, but imagined from the flow of blood that certain veins were found in the cervix of the uterus with their mouths joined together; which blood certainly flows most copiously in the first intercourse (which Terence <note>A Roman playwright.</note> considered most sharp), provided the girl then has a hymen that is otherwise intact and not previously damaged by any cause. Although no small veins handed down by the Arabs meet at their ends or are born together, it is nevertheless very easy to understand by reasoning that when this membrane is ruptured or torn by force, and then pulled apart and heated by continuous friction, it allows blood to flow out: no differently than the torn bond of the <term>prepuce</term><note>The frenulum of the penis.</note> in intercourse, which, if it exceeds the proper length, twists the tip of the glans downward excessively. Furthermore, as is commonly (though falsely) reported, that among certain nations the pubic bones of newborn girls are separated in some unknown way so that they might give birth more easily someday: so also I have sometimes heard from certain midwives and matrons that it is the custom for some to break a certain small membrane or film in little girls, as if it were given to women in vain, just as we see the Jews even today uncover the male glans and cut back the prepuce. And just as we know diligent midwives put their index finger into the mouth of children just born and tear the bond of the tongue <note>The lingual frenulum.</note> if it happens to reach further forward than is right and is too tight. If this is done, the hymen is then broken and damaged, and for some who are about to marry, this provides a not insignificant or rare argument for recommending their virginity—

I believe an argument can be provided for this. Thus, it happens that by this same chance, girls are sometimes born without a hymen, just as it is most certain that Jewish boys are sometimes brought into the light appearing already circumcised <note>original: "recutitos." Vesalius refers to the rare medical phenomenon of being born with a short or absent prepuce, which he compares to the natural absence of a hymen.</note>. And just as we do not doubt that certain rare head shapes have now become specific to some nations—without any compression applied by midwives and mothers—it is also well known that many unique traits occur in horse foals at the time of birth. However it may be, in virgins there is no internal connection between the surfaces of the sides of the neck of the womb, other than that which someone might say is created by the benefit of the hymen, which is otherwise perforated.

<margin>The orifice of the body of the womb.</margin>
Furthermore, the cavity of the neck of the womb <note>the vaginal canal/cervical canal</note>, throughout its entire course, is not rendered narrower in its composition in virgins nor in women already experienced in intercourse. Indeed, it is equally capable where it continues into the base <note>the *fundus*, or main body of the uterus</note>—unless it is even wider and more suited for distension there—as where it ends at the external genitalia. In the higher seat of this cavity, a notable portion of its own substance extends* out from the lowest region of the body of the womb. This portion, which resembles the glans of a penis, never touches the sides of the neck of the womb with its blunt tip and is passable via a certain hole. This is usually called the "mouth" of the womb or the body of the womb, just as we call the female* external genitalia the "mouth of the neck" <note>the vaginal opening</note>. However, while the latter is not otherwise pulled apart or gaping, and stays closed like a slit made along the length of the body or like the letter **ı** <note>the Greek iota, signifying a vertical slit</note>, the former is gifted with a transverse fissure, similar to the center of the letter **☉** <note>the astrological/chemical symbol for the Sun, indicating a circular opening with a central point</note>, though it is not always equal. For in pregnant women, it is thought to be quite wrinkled and very narrow, scarcely admitting a probe. Those who have recently given birth possess this fissure wider and less contracted or wrinkled; those who are not pregnant are in a middle state. However, I believe it is clear that whenever this orifice of the body of the womb gapes open, it is rendered circular (as is the orifice of the neck). It opens during birth, when it emits the fetus and its coverings, and when it gives way to the menstrual purgings, and then during intercourse—not always, certainly, but when, desiring the male seed, it draws it in by sucking with a natural motion. It also opens when the womb, not about to conceive, vomits back the male seed together with the female seed, or when, during a "pollution" <note>nocturnal emission or orgasm</note> or friction, it excretes the female seed. For the orifice of the body of the womb is by no means perpetually opened just because the neck of the womb is admitting the man's seed or is otherwise distended. Indeed, it would not have fallen to the judgment of an insatiable woman—who might too boldly desire love even after conception—to subject that orifice to herself. Meanwhile, consider what a great harm to the conservation of the species it would be if women did not subsequently retain the seed against their will, and with what great license they would impose upon husbands and parents, having no fear of conception, if only the orifice of the body of the womb could be opened at the woman's will, just like the orifice of the neck.

<margin>The size of the woman's womb.</margin>
We have already reviewed the size of the womb in some way when its position was explained; and surely this cannot be described more readily than the mass of the stomach. For the size of the body <note>fundus</note> varies according to the quantity of the seed or fetus contained within it, and the neck <note>cervix/vagina</note> also sometimes stays closed, folded and wrinkled, and sometimes during intercourse is drawn apart to the shape of the penis, or during birth to the shape of the fetus. And just as there is not one single width for the neck by reason of distension, so too there is no equal length. For when we lift the womb during dissection, the neck is stretched out to a wonderful length. Thus, it is no less ridiculous to describe the length or width of the neck of the womb than of the penis (for which the neck is considered a sheath <note>vagina</note>). Furthermore, the neck of the womb is made more turgid, narrower, and straighter according to the woman's desire (aside from the fact that it is tighter by nature in some). And therefore, I do not wonder that everyone who has attempted to describe its length by some number of fingers disagrees among themselves; one counting eleven fingers from the genitalia to the fold of the base, another twelve, that one more, another fewer...

He also argues that the size and length of the vagina and uterus are highly variable, critiquing contemporary attempts to provide fixed measurements.</summary>

Furthermore, the womb hangs bound by the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> in such a way that its base can move itself more or less up and down during intercourse, when it seeks generation, and can gape at the tip of the penis like a certain animal—as Plato also said <note>original: "ut & Plato dicebat." That the base of the womb is smaller in young girls than in those who have long engaged in intercourse or have at some time carried a child in the womb has also been reported by other anatomists; although in all of these, much like the rhythm of the testes, the base varies so much that I cannot specifically define its mass (just as I cannot with the bladder). Whatever the case may be, the base of the non-pregnant womb is much smaller than one unskilled in dissection would easily believe, since in width it barely exceeds two fingers, and in length it hardly ever equals the width of three fingers. Furthermore, I have read in the works of professors of dissection that a difference is placed on the size of the base of the womb on the occasion of menstrual cleansing; they teach that it is larger in one who has recently shed her entire blood. But in this regard, a difference in the womb has never presented itself to me; and concerning the collection and purging of that blood, I shall add some things below, now being about to treat the substance of the womb.

...of the stomach <note>original: "ventriculi"</note> and the intestines woven together. Yet it is not seen to be equally thick in every part. For where it forms the orifice of the base <note>the fundus, or main body of the uterus</note>, it is thickest; then in the middle region of the upper part of the base it is also quite thick, and (as I said in the description of the cavity of the base) it swells out into the cavity itself. However, where the uterus ends in obtuse angles or "horns" <note>the cornua</note>, this layer appears thinner and less compact or dense to those dissecting it than in the rest of the part. On the sides, and in the front and back regions, it is equally thick and so compact that, no matter how you dissect that layer, you can see nothing besides its own substance, without any distinction of the fibers in which it abounds, except for the noteworthy path of the veins and arteries. But in those who have already carried a fetus in the womb for some time, this inner layer displays a triple kind of fibers much more clearly than in one recently removed from a living animal or one just inflated like a bladder. It has straight fibers innermost, though these are not very numerous; the outermost are circular or transverse, exceeding the number of straight ones somewhat; but in the middle, it acquires oblique fibers, which are the most numerous and strongest. Then, in the pregnant uterus, a great abundance of veins and arteries is seen creeping through this layer,

neck of the uterus <note>the cervix</note> shares something in common with the male penis. For just as the two bodies of the penis, and especially the glans, consist of a thick covering (a substance midway between nerve and flesh) stuffed with a certain fungous and spongy substance, so too the neck of the uterus is formed of a fleshy and nervous layer, though not exceedingly thick, possessing something of that same fungous substance. By the benefit of this substance, when a woman eagerly desires sexual union, the neck of the uterus swells up in the manner of a penis, and the little hills of the private parts <note>the labia or clitoris</note> and those skin-like caruncles <note>small fleshy growths</note> protrude outward, and the cavity of the neck is narrowed to embrace the penis and is directed straight, as is sufficient for the proper emission of the male seed. neck of the bladder and the end of the rectum. Although this might perhaps increase the pleasure of intercourse for many women, and likewise be the reason why they might leave the abundance of constricting and narrowing medicines to our apothecary shops, Nature would have bestowed too much voluntary power upon the genitals and would have made the penis subject to the will <note>original: "arbitrio," or judgment</note> of the uterine neck more than is right. Furthermore, anatomists have more truly written that in the age of girlhood the neck is more delicate and softer; on the contrary, in those who are older and those who have given birth more frequently, it is rendered more calloused by the passage of time, so that they have occasionally compared it in old women to cartilage and the rough artery <note>the trachea or windpipe</note>. For by the frequent rubbing of those coming together, and the collision of parts exiting, the neck becomes calloused; and by the frequent washing with astringents and the constant flow of the menses, it is hardened no differently than we know ulcers are changed into fistulas because of a sharp humor continually flowing down. The veins and arteries inserted into the neck have almost always seemed more manifest to me in those who are not pregnant than those of the base; however, it is certain that the opposite happens in those carrying a child in the womb. But I shall now opportunely approach the sequence of the veins and arteries of the uterus, together with the structure of the seminal vessels and the nerves of the uterus.

In those carrying [a fetus], they <note>Vesalius refers to the ovaries, which were called "testes" in both sexes in the 16th century</note> occupy nearly the same position; but the more the uterus is extended, the lower they appear to be situated at its sides relative to its top. They rest upon the peritoneum at that place where the bones of the ilium are joined to the sacrum, being entirely loose, and connected to the peritoneum in no other way than by the benefit of the **seminal vessels** and **loose membranes**. These are much smaller than the testes of men, but more oblong in shape, and less round across their width; and, as if they were meant to be wider than they are deep, they are flattened at the front and back. Their external surface is uneven, and it appears filled with many unequal bumps <term>tubercula: small swellings or nodules</term>, just as if several small glands were tied together. Indeed, they do not consist of a substance that is soft and smooth with an innate moisture, like the testes of men, but rather a harder substance, not unlike the **glandular bodies** of the mesentery <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> and the lower omentum <note>the fatty apron of the abdomen</note>; and besides the small 

<margin>d 10, 11, fi. L, L. ☉ 4 fig. n, u.</margin>
<margin>The cavities of the testes, and the fluid contained within them.</margin>
plexuses of veins and arteries residing within them, they are sinuous and hollow. For the testes of women have within them, besides vessels, certain **cavities** <note>original: "sinus"</note> filled with a thin, watery fluid. If the testis is not first injured but is compressed by force, this fluid—creeping out like air from an inflated bladder—is accustomed to leap out to a surprising height during dissection, just as if from a spring. While this fluid is white, like a somewhat thick whey of milk, in healthy women, I have also found it to be a strange yellow and saffron color and a bit thicker in two girls of no common nobility. Before death, these girls were troubled by "strangulation of the uterus" <note>original: "uteri strangulatu," a historical term for a condition thought to be caused by the uterus "wandering" or "suffocating" the patient; today often associated with various gynecological or psychological distresses</note>. In them, one of the cavities of one testis protruded like a large pea, stuffed with that saffron-colored fluid, and staining the neighboring areas in the same way we see the colon intestine turned yellow by the gallbladder where it passes under the liver. And just as the color of this liquid occurs rarely, so too it smelled most foul, and it manifested something poisonous and grim. This was undoubtedly the author of those symptoms of the brain which arise daily in "strangulation of the uterus." One maiden, not yet fourteen years old, died from what seemed to be an inflammation of the lungs and frequent uterine strangulation in that disease, which had recently begun to be troublesome. The other, already reaching twenty-two years of age, after she had been remarkably pale for a year or two and had been repeatedly oppressed by those symptoms which almost commonly hold girls who, being **desperately in love**, have their menstrual purgings long suppressed, or from whom that white and raw fluid flows at long intervals; she died, I say, from "suffocation of the uterus." Since a suspicion of administered poison occurred to the parents, she was granted to me and several physicians for the requested dissection. In this, besides the great whiteness and softness of the lungs and the bloodless habit of the whole body, I found nothing faulty, even around the uterus itself, except for that yellow, strangely smelling bump on one of the testes. Therefore, there is no peculiar shape to the cavities of the female testes (lest perhaps my speech should run on too long regarding the woman whom I mentioned in passing in the chapter on the spleen, who was otherwise monstrous and sickly). They are unequal, just like the exterior surface of the testes themselves; and they are not one, but many, nor are they

Nor is it so easily pulled away from the substance of the testes during dissection, just as if it were a common and continuous body with the substance of the testis; for which reason one might rightly say that the substance itself is also membranous. Now, therefore, it becomes almost clear which parts the uterus only touches, and to which it is further bound and attached. For the front, back, and upper regions of the uterine fundus are attached to no parts they touch; but the sides are joined to the membranes leading the vessels to the uterus, and finally to^z those interwoven fleshy fibers. These form two muscles, by whose benefit the uterus is drawn upward somewhat obscurely by voluntary motion while women contract and, as it were, gather their flanks; these muscles creep forward so obliquely and, where they approach the uterus, sometimes become so thick that I once wrongly thought those muscles were the **horns of the uterus** <note>original: *uteri cornua*. Many animals have two-horned uteri; Vesalius is correcting his earlier assumption that humans shared this trait</note>, because I saw that the^a blunt angles and "nipples" of the female uterus did not very closely resemble the image of horns. Furthermore, the neck of the uterus [the cervix] is attached at the sides^b to the membranes and vessels extended to it, and through their intervention is connected to the **peritoneum** <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note> (but, just like the uterus, loosely). On the back part, in the middle of its length which is closer to the fundus,^c it rests upon the **rectum** <note>original: *recto intestino*</note> in such a way that we see the coils of the intestines lying upon one another in turn. But toward the end of the neck at the private parts, it is joined to the anus in the same way as if it and the rectum had a certain common tunic [layer], just as we do not doubt that the esophagus and the windpipe [the trachea] share a common tunic. Again, on the front side, the neck higher up and near the opening of the fundus simply has the bladder resting on it; but a little lower down, by certain fibers, it has the lowest part of the bladder and its own neck attached.^d Where this is inserted into it, it is made like a certain common body and tunic for both. So also, where the neck of the uterus ends in the private parts, a common body of both—namely the neck and the skin—is established, just as in the lips and eyelids. This skin, besides becoming hairy, has a somewhat hard fat spread beneath it, just as on the chin; in old women (even if the neck of the uterus has become calloused), this sags along with the breasts, not supporting the "little hills" [mons pubis] or the "wings" [labia] as beautifully as in younger women, who are plump with more consistent and hard fat. But since these things are obvious without the dissection of the dead, we will now try to explain what the use is of all those things described so far in this chapter.

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V

...for childbirth, no more suitable arrangement could be devised. Indeed, this [the uterus] is situated far from the face and the most noble citadel of reason <note>Vesalius refers to the head and brain</note>; furthermore, no bones hinder the uterus from being remarkably distended in that location; and also, for the one about to give birth, the exit from here to the lower parts and toward the legs is easy. Moreover, the **shape** of the fundus of the uterus <note>The "fundus" is the main, larger body of the womb</note> is nearly round, so that it might be made more capacious and less subject to injury. Then, the fundus is single and simple, because it must embrace a single fetus: <margin>Of the Shape.</margin> yet it is seen to be wider than it is deep, because it sometimes conceives even twins. It appears **small**, and more contracted than would be easily believed, in those who are not <margin>Of the Size.</margin> <margin>Chapter 27, figures A, A, B, B.</margin> pregnant, so that it might then compress other organs as little as possible, and render its cavity so narrow that it can embrace the entire seed as closely as possible, leaving no part of it untouched. And therefore <margin>Of the Substance.</margin> its substance is also established as suitable for its function, namely that it can be sufficiently contracted and gathered together when it contains nothing: and again, according to the growth of what is contained, it can be gradually unfolded into an extraordinary size. And this is seen to be not weak, nor unsuitable for being distended without tearing: but strong, and persistent in bearing injuries, with fibers that are not weak, nor interwoven by chance. <margin>Of the Fibers.</margin> But it has **straight** fibers as the innermost, because above all else it must attract the seed: and it possesses few of these, because the seed—pleasing to the womb by its temperament and its very essence, and being fluid and offered by a suitable member—glides into it more quickly. It claims for itself very many **oblique** fibers, following the straight ones in order, because the conceptus must be retained for a very long time. However, it obtains **transverse** fibers as the outermost, because the uterus most requires these only when it is about to bring into the light the fetus it has embraced long enough. We believe it happened that the uterus was content with a single and similarly thick proper tunic <note>A "tunic" is an anatomical layer or membrane</note>, and did not obtain two like the stomach—namely one more fleshy and another more nervous—because the uterus only needs to contain and embrace, and not, in the manner of the stomach, to concoct and process something other than its own nourishment. <margin>Reason for the surface and connection.</margin> The **peritoneum** <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note> extends a strong tunic to it, which will be the covering of its own proper tunic and its safest bulwark. This is smooth on its outer surface and smeared with a watery moisture, in the manner of other parts which it was better should touch each other indeed, but not grow together. For if the fundus of the uterus in those who are not pregnant grew together with the bladder lying upon it, and the rectum lying beneath it, and were bound to the parts it rests upon not by loose but by hard bonds: who will deny that the uterus could not then be conveniently distended along with the fetus, or even, during intercourse or birth, creep downward like a certain animal? <note>Vesalius is critiquing the ancient Greek idea of the "wandering womb" (the belief that the uterus moved freely like an animal inside the body), arguing its mobility is functional but limited.</note> Again, if the uterus, swollen with a fetus, remained grown fast to all the parts it then touches, in what way, I ask, would it collapse into itself to embrace seed again and form the proper narrowness? And when there is least need for its distention and size, would it not always hinder the function of the intestines? <margin>Reason for the orifice of the fundus.</margin> The **orifice of the fundus** <note>The internal opening of the cervix</note> is such that it always closes tightly, except when by natural instinct it must admit seed or provide a path for the fetus or the menses. For rightly, its opening and closing by no means depends on the woman's will, as I was also saying before. It is composed of a thicker and denser substance—and for that reason protruding into the space of the neck of the uterus [the cervix] in the manner of the glans of a penis <note>original: "penis glandis modo"</note>—than the rest of the body of the fundus, so that it may be sufficiently distended in birth: and so that in that miraculous opening, it does not run the risk of being lacerated or torn apart. <margin>Reason for the neck of the uterus.</margin> Furthermore, who is unaware that Nature uses remarkable foresight in constructing the substance of the **neck of the uterus** [the cervix]? He who sees it formed so that it can easily be directed and distended for the reception, and again, so that the uterus might not be chilled, and a space be kept empty in vain, it can be gathered and closed up in a coiled manner. Besides the fact that the neck [has] a substance for the itch of desi-

...we have said that the part is suited for itching <note>Vesalius refers here to the clitoris and surrounding structures, which he describes as being designed for sexual sensation</note>, and possesses certain furrows because of friction. Indeed, just as its convolution and inward bending provide great help so that the uterus is not affected by cold, so too the closing "hills" of the pudendum <note>The labia majora</note>, and the little fleshy cuticles <note>The labia minora and clitoris</note> filling the entrance of the cervix, are judged suitable for the same use, as well as for titillation and itching.

<margin>
Of the testes and seminal vessels of the female.
</margin>
The origin and path of the seminal vessels in women, and the very substance and formation of the testes <note>original: "testium"; in the 16th century, the ovaries were called "female testes" because they were seen as the female counterparts to the male gonads</note>, persuade me in every way that women possess seed. However, we believe it to be more humid and colder than the male seed, because the testes themselves are smaller and receive only a middle portion of the seminal artery and vein; and because we believe a woman to be colder than a man. Nor is the frequent intercourse of harlots an argument that a woman has more seed, or more of that humor which Aristotle writes was given to woman under the name of "lust," and which occurs copiously at the ends of the testes to those who dissect; for this must be measured not by the frequency of intercourse, but by the frequency and abundance of the ejection of that seed or humor (in which they are far surpassed by men). Therefore, the things we have put forward concerning the male seminal organs sufficiently demonstrate the function and use of the female vessels and testes.

<margin>
The account of the nerves, veins, and arteries.
</margin>
Likewise, the sensation they now possess clearly attests that frequent nerves were inserted into the uterus, and especially its cervix, so that they might be endowed with precise feeling. Moreover, it is beyond doubt that the veins and arteries entwining the uterus perform the common duty of veins and arteries in nourishing and refreshing the native heat, both for the uterus itself and, when a woman has conceived, for the fetus as well.

<margin>
How menstrual purgations are accumulated, and from where they flow.
</margin>
It is also established that the menstrual or lunar purifications are evacuated from the veins seeking the uterus. But how that happens, and through which veins specifically—whether of the fundus <note>The main body of the womb</note> or the cervix—and whether continuously, or now from these and now from those; perhaps if you are a diligent admirer of the works of Nature, and have not sworn your oath to the words of any single master, you also remain in doubt along with me, and even with that most learned man Joachim Roelants <note>A prominent 16th-century physician from Mechelen and friend of Vesalius</note>, the primary physician at Mechelen and a singular ornament of the Belgians. He has written to me on this matter more than once, both on account of other occasions and especially because of the sixtieth aphorism of the fifth book of Hippocrates, and Galen’s commentary on the same.

It is not that we are unaware of what the menstrual blood is, its nature, its quantity, and by what reason it abounds in a woman and how it nourishes the fetus; nor how many false things Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, whose *Natural History* contained many myths about the "toxic" nature of menstrual blood</note> and many others have handed down concerning its depravity and foul odor. Nor are we ignorant that this blood is by no means gradually accumulated in the cavity of the fundus throughout the interval of the month, only to flow forth at the period of the month when the uterus is already swelling (though it has seemed otherwise to some). For if this happened, the menstrual blood would be in no way thin and fluid, and very similar to that which drips from the nostrils or the anus; from which menstrual blood differs neither in the form of its flowing, nor in all other respects, unless perhaps it occurs more often thinner and more watery, or endowed with some other such quality. If it were saved up in the uterus, who could doubt that it would be almost clotted and would have to be brought out in chunks? Not to mention that the orifice of the fundus cannot be opened during intercourse unless the menses have been purged. Otherwise, when a woman is entered and the mouth of the fundus receives the seed, or that mouth emits seed, a way would also be provided for the menstrual blood, and it would flow out. Indeed, certain women give a great conjecture of this matter, who shortly after birth emit blood that is neither fluid nor thin, but rather large chunks of clotted blood with some serous humor—just as if you were to divide with a knife the blood drawn in a blood-letting and kept in a glass for some hours, and then cast it upon the ground. For I have sometimes seen blood flow from those women in that form, surely not otherwise than if the veins that grew in the placenta <note>original: "secundinis"</note> were still opening into the cavity of the uterus (which is then still relaxed and open, and for some time ready...

<margin>Flow of hemorrhoids; distension and branching of the portal vein</margin>
Moreover, I have observed something with interest in a certain man suffering from the affliction of hemorrhoids, which serves as a most certain proof to me that this blood accumulates in the veins and not in the cavity of the fundus. For this man was accustomed to being troubled at regular intervals—just as women are with their periods—by a flow of blood from the veins leading into the anus. When he died from "black jaundice" <note>likely referring to a form of severe jaundice or liver failure</note> and a wonderful hardness of the liver, I dissected him to investigate whether the branches of the portal vein <note>original: "portae rami"</note> or the vena cava <note>original: "cavae"</note> evacuated this blood.

<margin>f figure of chapter 5, book 3, c, c and d, d; then e, e and 11th figure n. g figure of chapter 6, book 3, y.</margin>

Furthermore, although I gather that the same thing happens in women, I have never observed it in a dissection; for so far, I have not found a non-pregnant woman who differed greatly in the thickness of her veins from other non-pregnant women. However, many women affected in various ways have come before me during dissection who might have shown something of the sort, unless the blood resides for the most part in the entire venous system of the whole body before it is purged.

In Paris <note>original: "Lutetiae"</note>, in a public dissection, I first dissected a prostitute of outstanding beauty and in the flower of her youth who had been killed by hanging. I knew this was widely confirmed, as it is commonly believed that in virgins, these purgings are drawn from the veins approaching the neck below the hymen—whatever that may eventually be. Furthermore, I read in Galen’s commentary on the recently mentioned *Aphorisms* that the blood of those carrying a fetus, which sometimes flows from them like a monthly purging, does not flow from the veins of the body <note>original: "fundi"; here referring to the main body or base of the uterus</note> of the womb, but from those of the neck. However, because it is beyond doubt that women suffering from a prolapse of the womb discharge this blood from the mouth of the body of the womb—and I myself have seen this more than once for the sake of the present dispute—and because it is necessary for the substance of the body of the womb to be thinned and its veins opened for conception, I no longer doubt that in otherwise healthy women, menstrual purgings come from the veins of the body of the womb, and not truly from the neck, even if I have not yet observed this during a dissection. 

As for what is claimed about virgins, it arises from an ignorance of the structure of the hymen. Since many people thought it was not permeable at all, and imagined some sort of mutual connection between the sides of the neck of the womb was the hymen itself, they also falsely claimed it was necessary for menstrual blood to be purged from veins leading into the neck of the womb lower than where the hymen sits. Regarding pregnant women, from whom blood perhaps flows, Galen thought it did not flow through the veins of the body of the womb because their openings are blocked by the placenta <note>original: "secundinae"</note>. But this (as we shall say more clearly in the history of the fetal membranes) is not continuous with the entire cavity of the body of the womb, and many veins reach into it to which the placenta is not attached. Thus, it is not impossible for blood to flow through the veins of the body of the womb in pregnant women, as the thickness of the womb—which sometimes caused me to hesitate and doubt during the purging of non-pregnant women—is no obstacle at all. Nor is the closure of the mouth of the womb so tight in those carrying a fetus that one must contend that blood is carried from the veins interwoven in the neck of the womb on that account, since many assert that this orifice sometimes admits semen even then. 

In the meantime, although it is very easy to conclude that blood can sometimes emanate through the veins of the neck of the womb in any woman—just as blood occasionally flows from the nostrils, the anus, the throat, and even the stomach—we have also more than once discovered through dissection that in certain women and virgins, the womb has been swollen for several years with a wonderful abundance of dark, thick water. In these women, menstrual blood otherwise flowed quite often, though not in entirely regular turns or fixed intervals and not always in the same quantity, surely from no other source than the veins entwining the neck of the womb.

### THE BODY OF THE WOMB

each would end in a point, coiled like a ram’s horn. Indeed, rather imagine here two ram’s horns having a long base and a sort of long, straight body, sharing something in common with the horns of a goat or a roe deer, however straight they may be. Then, join these bases, or oblong bodies, by their inner sides, and wrap them in a band <note>original: "fascia"</note> up to the point where the horns move apart toward the sides and narrow into a point. For horns of this kind joined together (just as we described with the two fingers) would, along the entire length where they are wrapped by the band and touch one another, express the image of the body <note>original: "fundus"; Vesalius uses this to refer to the main cavity of the uterus</note> of the womb, which I have said is like a rounded body—though it appears somewhat wide because of the compression applied to its length at the front and back. The parts of the horns that then move away from each other represent the shape of the upper part of the body, where it ends in two points led away from one another. 

The external surface of the body of the womb is entirely smooth and slippery, in the manner of membranous bodies that merely rest against each other. Along its sides and its entire length, just like the neck <note>original: "cervix"</note>, <margin>Fig. 29, H.</margin> it is joined to membranes that connect the womb to the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> and which hold the vessels reaching it. However, the very tips of the body, where they are separated from each other, are also smooth on their inner sides and are not joined to any parts; but their outer sides are continuous with the aforementioned membranes. 

The internal surface of the body corresponds exactly to the hollow shape of the aforementioned ram’s horns, and thus contains two cavities which come together at a single opening <margin>Fig. 29, s, from C to D.</margin> leading into the neck of the womb. They claim this opening as their common one, showing no long shared cavity before that opening. Thus, one must attribute two distinct chambers <note>original: "sinus"</note> to this body. These are certainly not smooth and flat, but are decorated with many yellowish tubercles <note>small bumps or nodules</note>, just as if we were looking at many peas pressed nearly halfway into flat wax and sticking there; or as if those tubercles were to be compared to those protrusions of veins which, bulging in the anus, sometimes pour out blood <note>a reference to hemorrhoids</note>. 

These tubercles in a womb that has recently conceived open up and form cavities—the sort that would arise in wax if someone had pressed halved peas into it everywhere—and they are similar to those seen on the tentacles of octopuses and squids, which we also call <term>acetabula</term> <note>original: "acetabula"; literally "vinegar cups," used here to describe the socket-like attachments (cotyledons) in the placentas of certain animals</note>. If at any time only a single fetus is contained in the womb of these animals, only one part or cavity of the womb is dilated and drawn out; but when they have conceived twins, both parts grow large, and each contains one fetus. 

The substance of this body <margin>Fig. 29, t. Because the outer coat is almost half removed, both appear; the outer is marked F, F, the inner C, D, G.</margin> is built of two coats <note>original: "tunicis"</note>: one is internal and, as it were, its own; the other is the outer coat, which is wrapped over the internal one by the membranes of the peritoneum that bind the womb and carry the vessels approaching it. However, because the entire body is not round like a bladder and does not consist of only a single cavity, the inner coat is counted as two: one is assigned to each of the "fingers" or horns of which we said the body of the womb consists—not only <margin>Fig. 29, u, above E.</margin> where the parts of the body move away from each other and sharpen into a point, but also along that entire <margin>Fig. 29, x, from D to E.</margin> area where we wrote they are held together along their length by a sort of band. Since the outer coat does not pass between the parts of the body along that length, but only grows upon them at the front, back, and along the sides, this outer coat is considered a single, simple layer—even though the peritoneum separately surrounds each of the tips of the womb, which are slanted like ram's horns and move away from each other. <meta>This page continues Vesalius’s critique of traditional anatomy. On the previous page, he began comparing the reproductive organs of various animals (cows, goats, dogs, and pigs) to the human uterus. Here, he specifically targets the widely held medieval myth of the "seven-chambered uterus" and exposes how Galen’s descriptions of uterine membranes and "horns" were based on animal dissections rather than human ones.</meta>

### THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V. 667

...supported by the books of fools, and then by the scholastic theologians, and in that most unlearned book of Albert the Great <note>original: "Alberti illius magni"; Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a philosopher whose works on nature were highly influential but often lacked anatomical accuracy.</note> regarding the secrets of men and women, and in the works of a certain most inept Michael Scot, and our own Gentile, and Nicolo, and Mondino, and even among countless other anatomists, one reads that the female uterus possesses seven cells or compartments: three indeed on the right side of the uterus, suited for receiving males; three on the left, dedicated to females; and the seventh truly existing in the middle of these, consecrated to <term>hermaphrodites<gloss>individuals with both male and female characteristics</gloss></term>. However, the cavity of the female uterus is exactly as I have described it, and shows nothing less than these kinds of compartments or pockets. Yet, it did not seem enough for some to imagine them in this way; instead, they further assert that those seven pockets (which they also call pits) contain ten wrinkled folds. Counting seven pits and seventy wrinkles, they contend that just as many fetuses can be conceived at once—having spent very little time, by Jove, in the dissection of humans, and much less even in the dissection of brutes, which usually carry several fetuses at once in the womb.

<margin>From the number of the uterine tunics, and thus the formation of the whole uterus.</margin>
But because I am convinced that Galen was by no means the author of these trifles, let us next examine his account of the uterine tunics, which testifies that a <term>vaccine<gloss>bovine or cow-like</gloss></term> uterus was described by him rather than a human one. For he writes that the inner tunic is double, but the outer one is single and simple. He does not only propose this in number, but explains it so diffusely that he says the outer tunic, which hangs from the <term>peritoneum<gloss>the lining of the abdominal cavity</gloss></term>, is simple for the reason that it is wrapped around both parts of the <term>fundus<gloss>the base or body</gloss></term> of the uterus at once, containing them just as if both were only one part. This tunic first appears double <margin>The beginning was made in figure 29.</margin> when this outer tunic is pulled away from the inner one, which is proper and peculiar to each individual part. Thus, on this occasion, a very great and noteworthy difference offers itself between the <term>caprine<gloss>goat</gloss></term> uterus and the human one. Meanwhile, Galen, in his book *On the Dissection of the Uterus*, affirms that cows and goats are similar to women regarding the uterus; therefore, in such a great and varied discrepancy of uteri, he proves more than enough that he never inspected a human uterus.

<margin>Galen is quite hesitant in the description of certain parts of the uterus and has little confidence in himself.</margin>
Furthermore, when you observe these things, you will find many more conjectures throughout Galen's descriptions with which you can corroborate this opinion of mine. It must not be passed over how hesitant and ambiguous Galen is when he notices that the writings of Herophilus <note>Herophilus (c. 335–280 BCE) was a Greek physician often called the "Father of Anatomy" because he was one of the first to perform scientific human dissections.</note> do not agree with his own cow-like uterus, and when he weighs how Praxagoras and certain others disagree with Herophilus—since they are not all recounting the history of the same animal. Finally, Galen in many places almost assents to Herophilus (whom he knew had dissected human bodies) against his own opinion, though certainly not willingly admitting that the female uterus was not described by him, even if he had never seen it.

<margin>In the explanation of the form of the uterus.</margin>
And this can be observed most beautifully—not to say anything of the form of the uterus, which Galen first proposes as round and then as something else, or of the <margin>Muscles.</margin> peculiar muscles of the uterus, which he repeatedly insists are varied and were not seen by him—when Galen mentions the <margin>Horns.</margin> <margin>n 25 fig. i, k. o 25 fi. F, f.</margin> horns of the uterus <note>original: "cornuum uteri"</note> so perplexedly that his account expresses both the obtuse angles of the female human uterus and the tips of the cow's uterus departing from one another (most similar to the points of ram's horns), and then the parts of the body of the entire canine uterus <margin>p 28 fig. F, G. q 25 fig. n, o. r 28 fi. B, B, E.</margin> in which the fetuses are placed in a row.

<margin>The acetabula <note>The "acetabula" here refer to the cotyledons or attachment points of the placenta in ruminants, which Galen mistakenly attributed to humans.</note>.</margin>
