### ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE BODY

<margin>Of the vessels carrying semen.</margin>
<margin>u* Figure 25, q from v.</margin>
<margin>x Figure 25, o, p.</margin>
<margin>y Figure 25, f, i, l, u.</margin>
<margin>z Figure 25, r, s, t, ξ. a Figure 25, γ, δ.</margin>
...provides the origin, and which he <note>Galen</note> relates as entering the uterus not in all women, but only in some. And this is certainly asserted by Galen according to the opinion of Herophilus <note>Herophilus (c. 335–280 BCE) was an early Greek anatomist in Alexandria; Galen often relied on his accounts when his own observations were lacking.</note>, such that he does not doubt these vessels in women are as described. Yet, he admits there (albeit unwillingly) that he never approached the bodies of dead women for this purpose. He adds that he has never found those vessels in other animals, except very rarely in monkeys. But I have never found these two veins and two arteries of Galen, neither in women nor in other animals. Nor do I know why Nature would have wanted vessels seeking the uterus for the sake of nutrition alone to arise so far away: since she leads both <term>seminal arteries<gloss>the gonadal arteries, which in women are the ovarian arteries</gloss></term> and the right <term>seminal vein<gloss>the right ovarian vein</gloss></term> from the trunks of the <term>vena cava<gloss>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</gloss></term> and the <term>great artery<gloss>the aorta</gloss></term> at a lower point than the veins and arteries of the kidneys. Only the left seminal vein<sup>u*</sup> borrows its beginning from the vein that is carried into the left kidney <note>The left ovarian vein typically drains into the left renal vein rather than directly into the vena cava.</note>. This is true even if Galen, in his book *On the Dissection of the Uterus* <note>original: "de Uteri sectione"</note>, incorrectly recorded that this also arises from the trunk of the vena cava below the kidneys; he assigned higher and more remote origins to other vessels (which he mentions but which remain hidden to me) than even to that vein. However, for vessels bringing material to the <term>testes<gloss>Vesalius refers to the ovaries as "female testes," following the medical terminology of the time</gloss></term>, a long path is useful,<sup>x</sup> as is argued by their varicose entanglement before the testis. Conversely, a longer course for those other vessels <note>the nutritional vessels Galen claimed</note> would be harmful and full of danger. To these points, Galen mentions certain vessels besides<sup>y</sup> those which carry semen from the testes to the peaks or "horns" of the uterus (the insertion of which he writes was unknown to Aristotle, Herophilus, and everyone who attempted dissection before him). Following Herophilus's opinion, Galen records in his book *On the Dissection of the Uterus* that certain vessels,<sup>z</sup> just as in men, approach the neck of the female<sup>a</sup> bladder and are inserted into it where a <term>glandular body<gloss>likely a reference to the paraurethral glands or an imagined female prostate</gloss></term> is present—exactly as if semen were carried into the neck of the bladder in women just as it is in men. For Galen taught that in women, semen is discharged both into the horns of the uterus and into the neck of the bladder; but how truly he taught this, let others judge. As far as I am concerned, I have found no vessels inserted from the testes into the neck of the bladder, nor any glandular body attached to the neck itself in women, just as I have found none in any of the female quadrupeds I have used for dissection. And therefore, I would think that semen is in no way drawn down into the neck of the bladder in women; likewise, women during coitus perceive neither an excretion nor any <term>pruritus<gloss>a localized itching or intense sensation</gloss></term> from their own semen in that spot. I would wish, therefore, that you seek out these vessels of Galen through diligent dissection, both in women and in other animals. Among these, the rabbit should not be neglected, since it varies elegantly in the structure of its reproductive organs from that of a dog or a pig, though it is otherwise very similar. If, however, the vessels mentioned by Galen do not eventually occur to you, consider, I pray, whether Galen perhaps described these things—which he himself had never seen—because Herophilus had passed down in passing that the insertion and sequence of seminal vessels in women and men were equal. Nonetheless, Galen, in the second book of *On Semen* <note>original: "de Semine"</note>, after a brief apology, affirms that Herophilus lied in this regard. But, lest I seem to be writing annotations against Galen here rather than describing the fabric of the human body (contrary to my purpose), I shall bring an end to this present chapter on the uterus: especially since I will find little to agree with in Galen’s views regarding the <term>acetabula<gloss>the "cotyledons" or attachment points of the placenta, which Vesalius correctly noted were different in humans vs. certain animals</gloss></term> and the coverings of the fetus in the chapters that follow.

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

### ON THE ACETABULA OF THE UTERUS. CHAPTER XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicting an anatomical dissection scene. <margin>What the *acetabula* of the uterus truly are, and what were first called by that name.</margin>
The disagreement among the ancient professors of dissection regarding the *acetabula* <note>original: *acetabulis*; literally "vinegar cups," a term used in anatomy for cup-shaped sockets or placental attachments</note> of the uterus has also reached us. For there is fierce contention in the schools about what exactly the *acetabula* of the uterus are. I myself was in doubt about this matter for a long time, until I inspected a sheep that had not long ago carried a fetus in its womb, to see what should truly be called the *acetabula* of the uterus. This animal had received the seed in one of the two "horns" <note>Vesalius refers to the *sinus*, or the horn-like extensions of the uterus found in many mammals but not humans</note> of the uterus. When dissected, it revealed a rough and uneven surface, <margin>a You will see these cavities in a sheep, goat, or cow that has recently conceived.</margin> filled with many cavities <note>original: *sinibus*</note>. These were exactly as if someone had impressed the half of a pea into each cavity, just as if one were making such a depression in wax with a pea. Therefore, when I looked at those cavities and kept in mind the passage by Galen at the end of his book *On the Dissection of the Uterus*, where he compares the *acetabula* to the hollow of the leaves of a herb which the Greeks call *kotylēdōn* <note>original: κοτυληδῶνα; likely the plant Navelwort (*Umbilicus rupestris*)</note> because of its resemblance to a vinegar cup—or rather a half-pint measure—and call it *kymbalōpia* <note>original: κυμβαλώπια</note> and *kymbalon* from the image of a cymbal, while we call it *acetabulum*, "the garden of Venus," or "the navel"; I readily concluded that these cavities of the uterus were what were first called *kotylēdōnes* by the Greeks and *acetabula* by the Latins. We apply the name *acetabulum* in the same way to the deeply carved sockets of the bones. <margin>b Book 1, chapter 29, figures 1 and 2.</margin> <margin>z g, e, f.</margin> For if you look at the *acetabulum* <gloss>the socket of the hip bone</gloss> of the hip <note>original: *coxendicis*</note> and compare it to these cavities of the uterus, you will find no parts of the body that have obtained the same name from their appearance so deservedly as that socket of the hip bone (from which the femur has just been removed) and these uterine cavities. For just as the socket of the hip appears hollow, as if a half-sphere had been pressed into it, so too are these uterine cavities formed. <margin>c Book 1, chapter 29, figures 1 and 2, i, i.</margin> Then, just as the rims <note>original: *supercilia*; literally "eyebrows"</note> of the hip socket project beyond the rest of the bone’s surface, so also in the expanse of the uterus, the rims of its own cavities swell out more prominently than the rest of the uterine surface. In addition, just as the socket of the hip bone is filled with a mucous humor, so indeed these cavities of the uterus appeared to me to be stuffed with a mucous blood. From this, in some of the cavities, a rounded and remarkably mucous little vessel seemed to grow out, in exactly the same way <margin>d Book 2, chapter 49, figure 2, P.</margin> as the round ligament <note>original: *teres ligamentum*</note> is inserted from the hip socket into the head of the femur. <margin>What were secondly called *acetabula* by the ancients.</margin> Thus, when I had inspected these cavities of the sheep's uterus—which are also very similar to the "cups" <note>original: *acetabulis*</note> found on the tentacles <note>original: *promuscidibus*</note> of octopuses and squids—I no longer hesitated as to where the name of the uterine *acetabula* was first established. However, so that I might understand how these cavities were created, I soon opened the uterus of a sheep that was not pregnant, and I found the cavity of the uterus to be rough and uneven, very different from a woman's uterus. <margin>e These are also to be sought from the uterus of a cow.</margin> For throughout its entire surface, yellowish tubercles and half-spheres occurred, exactly as if someone had glued halved peas here and there onto an otherwise flat surface. And here I first began to learn what the professors of anatomy meant when they compared the *acetabula* of the uterus to the heads of veins swelling out in the anus <note>i.e., hemorrhoids</note>, from which blood is soon to flow. For if one dissects the uterus of a cow, goat, or doe that is not pregnant, nothing will be more manifest than those protruding little heads once it is opened; and you will not doubt that those were held to be the *acetabula* by most anatomists. Perhaps this was not because they resembled true *acetabula* <gloss>cups</gloss>, or because they thought they were the true *acetabula* of the uterus, but because they had learned from the dissection of the uterus that the veins and arteries distributed between the internal and external tunics of the uterus <margin>f See Book 5, figure 29, D, G.</margin> in those horned animals—in a very manifold and tangled series—reach their ends in these little heads that swell out through the entire cavity of the uterus. Finally, once the seed has been conceived, those heads open, embrace the seed, and lead out certain vessels which, having grown from the veins and arteries reaching into the heads, are inserted into the surface of the fetus; and to those...

You will also easily reason out what the physicians meant who called not those cavities, nor the bumps, but the vessels extending from the uterus into the placenta, *acetabula* <term>acetabula: literally "vinegar cups," a term the ancients used for the cup-like sockets where the placenta attaches to the uterus</term>. <margin>Aphorism 45.</margin>
and especially in the fifth book of his *Aphorisms*, seems to have understood the name *acetabula* in this way. He perhaps took the name from the fact that these vessels extend from those uterine cavities which we first mentioned were called *acetabula*. From this, it is clear why so many completely contrary opinions of authors arise in the history of Nature's works: namely, because we trust Galen—easily the leader of those studious of dissection—too much in our knowledge of the human body's structure, and we do not undertake dissection with our own hands. Or, if we do attempt it, we happen to abstain from those animals from which Galen's doctrines might be evaluated. For in vain

There, the vessels are found in a continuous series and joined together, which extend from the uterus into that covering of the fetus. Thus, nothing reveals itself in the woman's uterus to which you could apply the name *acetabulum* on the authority of Hippocrates (if indeed we wish to assert that the structure of the human body was well known to him), unless we conjecture that he implied these vessels. But those people applied the name *acetabulum* to that flesh in order to interpret Hippocrates, just as I a little earlier twisted the name to refer to the vessels: namely, because they thought this flesh was found in women just as in horned animals (which alone possess the cavities, and thus the true *acetabula*, and those bumps from which the cavities are produced). What the *secundina* and *chorion* are.
</margin>
SINCE in this book, which has taught the construction of the organs of nutrition made from food and drink, it seemed appropriate, because of the proximity of their location, to also pursue those instruments which the boundless Architect of things <note>Vesalius frequently refers to God as the "Opifex" or "Artificer."</note> built for generation: it will certainly be next, after the discussion of the *acetabula*, to add here some things concerning the tunics or envelopes wrapping the fetuses, which are generated anew together with the fetus in the uterus, and come forth with it at birth, and follow it almost immediately. For this reason, I believe <term>the whole mass of these envelopes is called the *secundina* by the Latins</term> <note>original: *secundam, seu fecundinam*; the afterbirth</note>: just as if it were a second birth, or succeeded the fetus as it comes out into the light. But by the Greeks it is called <term>chorion</term> <note>original: *χορίον*</note>, and sometimes <term>chorema</term> <note>original: *χόρημα*</note> (as the Latins also call it *loculi* [little places]), which I take to mean the structure of the envelopes, because it is like a small box, a space, or a hollow in which the fetus is contained and embraced in the uterus. Indeed, I do not think the name *secundina*, nor *chorion*, nor *loculi*, was attributed by its namer to any one private envelope: but rather to that whole substance or structure of envelopes which, after the fetus has broken out from it and been led out as it were, succeeds it during birth. However, when those Ancients who taught anatomy to their students at home observed not just one, but several envelopes surrounding the fetus, they were not content with that common name *chorion*, and thought private names should be given to the individual envelopes. And so it happens that these two names have been preserved for us: <term>allantoeides</term> <note>original: *ἀλλαντοειδής*; sausage-like</note>, and <term>amnion</term> <note>original: *ἄμνιον*</note> or <term>amneios</term> <note>original: *ἀμνειός*; lamb-like</note>. By the former, the Ancients called the outer envelope of the fetus because of its resemblance to a certain kind of sausage; and by the latter, they named the inner envelope because of its softness and whiteness, a name taken from a lamb. However, many who after these men recommended anatomy in their books have misused those names, and easily gave proof of how much more fortunately and diligently those Ancients approached dissections than they did.

<margin>

Indeed, it is continued to the uterus only by that breadth, in the same way that a silkworm <note>original: *bombix*</note> might weave itself onto only a single and flat surface, or as a somewhat more oblong ball of wax might stick and be held in the palm of a slightly hollowed hand. <margin>

</margin>
However, the outer envelope of a canine fetus is joined to the uterus
<margin>
l Fig. 31 A, A, A.
</margin>
by a certain breadth that surrounds the middle of the envelope like a wide belt:
<margin>
k Fig. 31 B, B, B.
</margin>
just as if a silkworm had woven itself in a wider circle. In the case of a cow's fetus, the envelope is not contained by a single breadth, but many small ones occur scattered about, just as we see the skins of leopards distinguished by spots: not differently than if the individual breadths of the envelope's connections were compared to individual spots. And the connection of this envelope is almost such (to refer it to some similarity) as a silkworm manages when it first attaches itself to thin twigs surrounding it here and there. Therefore, these breadths that I am attempting to describe are nothing other than the seats and places where the outer envelope of the fetus is joined to the uterus. For when the seed has been conceived in the uterus, and is covered on all sides by a small membrane—as if in a porridge or other thicker broths that are already cooling—the veins and arteries entwining the uterus open many of their mouths into the cavity of the uterus and embrace that membrane or the seed itself. And just as if the veins and arteries of the uterus were growing, new vessels grow from these mouths, maintaining a shared cavity and continuity with them. From these new vessels, it was necessary for veins and arteries to be formed, which the fetus—now to be shaped and nourished—would use throughout the entire time it remains in the uterus, just as we know a mother's leg or arm enjoys its own veins for nourishment and its arteries especially for regulating the temperature of the "innate heat" <note>the vital heat believed in Galenic medicine to drive life</note>. Since, therefore, it would have been unskillful and entirely inconvenient for as many vessels to be inserted and implanted into the body of the fetus as were opened into the cavity of the uterus for its sake, it was certainly necessary that these frequent and otherwise slender vessels be gathered gradually into themselves, and by meeting one another, be made thicker and fewer.
<margin>

Thus, finally, from all the opening veins, almost one is formed; and from all the arteries, two arise. The arteries, however, creeping along the sides of the bladder, are continued with the branches of the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, which are soon to pass down through the pubic bones into the thighs. Furthermore, since that mutual meeting of slender vessels into thicker and larger ones, and that various series of vessels to be formed anew for the sake of the fetus between the surface of the uterus and the fetus's umbilicus, had to be supported, entwined, and woven together by some body—just as we know many distributions of vessels in the rest of the living creature are contained (whether these are seen in the mesentery, or in the thin membrane involving the brain <note>the pia mater</note>, or elsewhere)—the principal use of the outer envelope of the fetus and the reason for its connection to the uterus immediately occur to us. For it was necessary that this envelope receive the mouths of the uterine vessels and that new vessels be procreated, as it were, within it; and these, as we have said, are gathered together through that envelope so that they finally constitute the vessels of the umbilicus. But because the connection of the uterine vessels with the vessels of the envelope is weak and fragile...

[These connections] would have been strong, if Nature had added nothing to those new and tender vessels by which they might be more aptly contained and strengthened. Therefore, a certain fleshy substance was added to those connections, which I can compare to no substance in the whole body more closely than to the peculiar flesh of the spleen<sup>s</sup>. <note>Vesalius is describing the placenta. At this time, the term "placenta" (meaning "cake") was not yet the universal anatomical term; Vesalius describes its texture as similar to the spongy, vascular tissue of the spleen.</note> And just as that flesh is woven around and poured about the vessels of the spleen on all sides: so also this substance embraces and contains the vessels of the uterus opening themselves into the envelope, always appearing more abundant and thicker the closer the fetus is to birth. Moreover, this substance grows very strongly to the uterus and to the external surface of the envelope. In birth, however, or when the envelope is pulled away from the uterus in dissections at other times, it remains attached to the envelope along with the vessels woven into it. And indeed, the breadth of this substance, which always corresponds in width and position to the connections of the outer fetal envelope to the uterus, is finally that which I have attempted to describe until now, and which occurs as almost circular and unique in only one seat of the envelope in the human fetus: in a dog, however, it is also seen as unique, but it encompasses the whole envelope crosswise like a rather wide belt or band in its middle, where it is widest. <note>Vesalius correctly identifies the difference between the "discoid" placenta of humans and the "zonary" placenta of dogs.</note> In cows, however, and buffaloes, and other horned animals (as I also wrote before), small breadths offer themselves scattered through the entire surface of the envelope, not grown together with each other. <note>This refers to the "cotyledonary" placenta of ruminants.</note> Moreover, although such a distinction of breadths and connections occurs, in all animals the vessels throughout this substance and the outer envelope of the fetus—even if variously distributed—finally come together so that from the inner surface of the outer envelope, as if from a point,<sup>t</sup> one smooth and long body like a cord comes forth, embracing itself at once, containing two arteries of the umbilicus, and here [in humans] still the same number of veins. <note>Vesalius is describing the formation of the umbilical cord.</note> Just as the outer<sup>u</sup> surface of this envelope exists as unequal and in some way rough in certain places due to the connection of the vessels and the sequence of that substance: so on the contrary<sup>x</sup> the inner surface is altogether smooth and slippery, and in a way moist.

How the outer envelope obtained its name from the appearance of a sausage.

If, therefore, you imagine this envelope, having been removed from the uterus with the fetus and then, after it has been moved away from the fetus, turned inside out, so that it now embraces that fleshy substance and the thick, somewhat greenish blood that occasionally flows out from the vessels, you will easily guess how it was called *allantoides* <note>Greek: ἀλλαντοειδὲς; meaning "sausage-like." Vesalius is explaining the etymology of the allantois.</note> by the Ancients from the appearance of a sausage <note>original: *farcimen*</note>. For just as a sausage is exactly slippery, smooth, and as if membranous on the outside because of the internal surface of the intestine before it was inverted: but on the inside, because of the external surface of the intestine from which the vessels approaching it were cut away with the membranes of the mesentery, it is rough and finally stuffed with meat, or clotted blood, or any other material: so also the outer envelope of the fetus, inverted in the manner of an intestine for the construction of a sausage, then exists as entirely membranous, slippery, and smooth on the outer surface, but on the inner surface it possesses that fleshy texture similar to the substance of the spleen.

So much so, that from its brightness and softness it was called *amnios* <note>Greek: ἀμνιὸς; meaning "lamb-skin."</note> by the Ancients, and as if like a lamb, or as it pleases some, a "little cloak" <note>original: *amiculum*</note>. # ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

...extending little veins and arteries to the membrane, they then pass into the inner surface of the internal membrane and are led like a cord all the way to the fetus’s navel. This cord is quite long and decorated in several places with unequal swellings or knots; based on the number of these, superstitious midwives <note>original: "obstetrices ridiculæ." Vesalius often dismissed folk medical practices that lacked anatomical basis.</note> are known to predict the number of future children to the laboring woman. 

<margin>The passage carrying the fetus's urine between its two membranes.</margin>
Moreover, this cord, situated on the inner surface of the internal membrane, does not just contain the umbilical vein (which here is single and simple) and its two arteries; it also includes and takes up a certain passage [the urachus]. <margin>d 2 fig. M proceeding from N.</margin> This passage originates from the upper part <margin>e 22 fi. q. q.</margin> of the base of the bladder, and in its substance and shape resembles the tubes [the ureters] through which urine flows from the kidneys to the bladder. It exits through the navel and, proceeding through the aforementioned cord to the outer surface of the inner membrane, it opens there <margin>f near N 3 of the 30th table of figures.</margin>. Between this inner membrane and the internal surface of the outer membrane, it carries the fetus's urine (which is why it is called the *urachos* and *ouranos* <note>original: "οὐραχὸς & οὐρανὸς." Vesalius is linking the name of the urachus to the Greek word for urine, *ouron*.</note>). There, the urine is collected bit by bit throughout the entire pregnancy by Nature's wonderful design.

If the fetus, while still in the womb, were to discharge urine through the neck of the bladder as it does after birth, the urine would float around the fetus. Its sharpness and corrosive quality would blister the fetus's tender skin—just as the inner membrane surrounding the fetus seems specifically designed for this purpose, while the outer membrane <margin>A peculiar reservoir for fetal urine between the two membranes.</margin> is primarily built to connect and gather the vessels. However, the fetal urine is not always seen wandering and flowing haphazardly between the two fetal membranes. Instead, the passage carrying the urine through the navel ends in a membranous, extremely soft, thin, and large sac [the allantois]: which, consisting between 

<image-desc>An anatomical woodcut illustration of the membranes and bladder-like structures surrounding a fetus. Labels A, B, and C mark specific anatomical components. A indicates the outer membrane (chorion) which has been cut and pulled back; B marks the inner membrane (amnion); and C identifies a thin-walled sac (allantois) that serves as a reservoir for fetal urine.</image-desc>

<insert>IN THIS figure, we have depicted the membranous sac which expands from the duct carrying urine through the navel when the urine does not simply flow loosely between the membranes. Therefore, **A** indicates the outer fetal membrane [the chorion], cut lengthwise and pulled away from the inner membrane marked **B** [the amnion], which remains intact here. **C** marks the very soft and thin membrane that acts as a bladder to store the fetal urine within the womb.</insert>

both membranes that truly embrace the whole fetus, stores and collects urine for as long as the infant is in the womb. Not a few professors of anatomy have compared it to the shape of a sausage <note>The "allantois" takes its name from the Greek *allantoeides*, meaning "sausage-shaped."</note> (regardless of where they get the idea). It is counted among the membranes created for the fetus, such that they have named it the third (though positioned in the middle) fetal membrane. They refer to the outer membrane alone by the specific names "afterbirth" or "cells." 

<margin>Where the fetus's sweat and other excrements are collected.</margin>
Furthermore, because fetal sweat cannot be drained by a dedicated passage between the membranes or into a special sac, it accumulates between the inner membrane and the fetus itself. To prevent its potentially harmful sharpness from hurting the fetus, it turns into a thick residue. This is the same substance that is normally released through the invisible pores of the skin and sticks to our skin and clothing. We see this "muddy" or glue-like substance smeared over the fetus's skin to shield it from the effects of the sweat <note>Vesalius is describing the *vernix caseosa*, the waxy white coating on a newborn's skin.</note>. 

It appears, then, that the blood carried from the uterine veins through the umbilical cord (primarily to the fetus's liver) requires much more refinement for the proper nourishment of the fetus than the blood that nourishes the mother's own limbs. It is as if only the purest essence from the stomach and intestines is offered to the fetus. In addition to the urine, sweat, and the "muddy" residue I mentioned—all of which are kept outside the fetus while it is in the womb—one finds during dissection that a thick and varied bile, if not actual feces, collects within the fetus's own intestines... <note>Vesalius is referring to meconium, the first stool of an infant.</note>

<summary>Vesalius describes the umbilical cord and the urachus, explaining how fetal urine is channeled into a separate sac (the allantois) to protect the fetus's skin from irritation. He also identifies the vernix caseosa as a protective layer against fetal sweat and notes the presence of meconium in the fetal intestines.</summary>

# BOOK V ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

...and we see it clearly elsewhere soon after birth, when the fetus excretes it. We find that these excrements vary according to the mother’s temperament <note>The "temperament" refers to the Galenic theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which were thought to determine health.</note> and health, primarily in quantity, and somewhat in color and consistency, just as their blood happens to be more serous or thicker, or differing in some other quality from the best and most praised blood. Indeed, the sweat and urine, kept in the manner we described, when they flow out just before birth, moisten the opening of the base of the uterus and the cervix, making them more suitable for distension by softening them, and greatly aid in a easier birth; I think this is known, even if I were silent, to those who have sometimes stood by women and other animals for the sake of weighing the mysteries of Nature. 

<margin>The manner in which urine, sweat, and the membranes exit during birth.</margin>
For when during birth the mouth of the base of the uterus descends, as it were, into the vulva <note>original: "pudendum"</note>, and by a wonderful benefit of Nature is dilated, the vessels inserted from the uterus into the outer membrane of the fetus depart from it and from their own vessels from which they were born, in the same way we see ripe fruits or leaves in autumn depart and break off from their stems on the trees. Then sometimes the fetus itself, but more often brute animals with their teeth, and sometimes women themselves or midwives, break the membranes surrounding the fetus, and the aforementioned liquids flow out, and the fetus comes out into the light, still connected by the umbilical cord. Women cut this with scissors or a small knife, while brute animals generally tear it with their teeth; and the fetus itself now begins to draw breath and use the surrounding air, whereas previously in the uterus the umbilical arteries performed the duties of the fetus’s heart and lungs. 

The membranes themselves follow the fetus soon after with some flow of blood due to the departing vessels. Women generally burn these with sprinkled salt or bury them somewhere, but many brute animals devour them unless they are snatched away by those standing by. In this exit of the child, sometimes the inner membrane <note>The amnion.</note> comes out first, with the outer one still remaining in the uterus for a while, wrapped around the fetus to some extent. So much so that women privately rejoice that a **helmet** or **breastplate** (if it is a male child) or a **headband** or **tunic** (if it is female)—depending, of course, on which part of the fetus it stuck to during birth—has been given by God to that child, promising great things for that child. 

Meanwhile, that membrane is common to all children, provided someone takes the inner membrane and, just like those women with their "helmet" and "headband," cuts it away from the fetus and the external membrane, and preserves it dried like some bladder, so that it can be shown to them when they are adolescents for whatever use such a little membrane might serve. Indeed, it is a wonder how religiously women—no less than the followers of occult philosophy—think of it <note>Vesalius refers here to the "caul," a piece of membrane that can cover a newborn's head. It was historically considered a sign of good luck or psychic ability.</note>. 

In this manner, then, the fetuses have membranes, which in dogs are specific to each individual fetus, and no part of one fetus's membranes is joined with the membranes of another fetus. For they are placed in sequence, as if in some long intestine, in the dog and the pig, in both parts of the uterus, not following the reasoning—even if perhaps someone might think otherwise on the occasion of Hippocrates and Galen—that all male fetuses are in the right part of the uterus and females in the left <note>Vesalius is debunking a long-held ancient belief that sex was determined by the side of the uterus in which the fetus developed.</note>. 

<margin>How the fetus is situated in its membranes when there are several fetuses at once.</margin>
In cows, buffalo, and goats, when there is a single fetus, it is placed in only one part or one chamber of the uterus; but if there are twins, each cavity of the uterus (so to speak) embraces one fetus with its membranes. Women, however, when they have twins that are not joined or are monstrous <note>Vesalius uses "monstrous" in the early modern sense to mean congenital anomalies or conjoined twins.</note>, also contain each one in their own membranes and wrappings, and the connection of the outer membrane and that fleshy substance of both fetuses to the uterus is equal: namely, with the binding of one fetus made to one side of the uterus and the other to the other side. Thus, there is a great difference between humans, dogs, and cows in the connection of the outer fetal membrane based on the nature of the uteri. When you observe this, and compare this description of ours with Galen in his books *On Semen*, the books *On the Use of the Parts*, the book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and the book *On the Dissection of the Uterus*, where he follows the fetal membranes...

<margin>The true account of the membranes is far removed from the opinions of Galen.</margin>
...if you compare these things, it will certainly become obvious how much Galen is consistent with himself everywhere, and how consistent with the truth are the things he handed down to us regarding the membranes of the fetus—not to mention the formation of the fetus and the many disputes pertaining to this which he primarily engaged in with Aristotle. For even though it would have been within my right to set forth for myself the history of the fetal membranes, and in this to disagree far from the opinions of Galen and other professors of dissection, yet since countless things concerning the formation of the fetus hold me in doubt and uncertainty, and since I am by no means satisfied with myself for the most part in those disputes, I freely confess that I am utterly ignorant of most of them, even though I have applied myself to dissections with no small amount of diligence. This is especially true of animals; however, although I have become somewhat more experienced in anatomy, and not a few things occur to me about which I might rightly doubt, I have come across very few pregnant women. Consequently, I have judged it much better to entirely omit here the whole discourse on the formation of the fetus and the disputes closely related to it (which could not be anything but very long), and to reserve it for another place and another subject, if perhaps something worthy of being handed down should occur to me in the future from further dissections and more accurate reasoning.

## ON THE BREASTS. CHAPTER XVIII.

->*It was not possible to outline the structure of the breasts otherwise than how we have attempted to express it in the twenty-fifth figure on the right side.*<-

<margin>The location of the breasts.</margin>
The breasts, even though they are not contained in any part by the peritoneum <margin>a Not contained between A, B, C, D in figures 2 and 4.</margin>, are nonetheless recounted in the number of organs serving generation, since they nourish the fetus once it has come into the light. Therefore, we shall appropriately pursue their structure in this place as well. The location of the breasts is conspicuous to everyone: for they are placed upon the chest at the sides of the breastbone <note>the sternum</note>, layered over the lower part of the muscle that moves the arm toward the chest <margin>b Muscle table, delta [Δ].</margin> <note>the pectoralis major muscle</note>. But just as they vary greatly in shape, so too they do not always occupy the same position. For larger breasts are secured by a wider base; those that are drooping and flaccid decline from their natural place; and in some women they approach each other more closely toward the middle of the chest, while in others (which is also considered most beautiful) they move away from each other and approach more closely to the sides of the thorax. <margin>Shape.</margin> Their shape, which is almost unique to them, resembles a hemisphere; for externally they are round and protuberant, possessing a nipple (which is called <term>thēle</term> <note>original Greek: θήλη</note> by the Greeks) like a process. Internally, however, or at the back where they face the chest, they are slightly curved inward according to the protuberance of the chest, joined to it with a broad base. Furthermore, when the mass of the breasts recedes from the muscle that brings the arm to the chest, they become wider where they hang down most, rather than in the middle path, so that in most women they appear wider both at the base and at their extremity at the same time, due to the collapsing of their substance. <margin>Substance.</margin> Furthermore, the substance of which they consist is glandular, abounding in much fat, and interwoven with somewhat frequent veins, very few and altogether slender arteries, and finally several nerves. The nerves that reach into the breasts are indeed always the same and consistently similar to one another; but the veins differ greatly in thickness and the humor they contain, according to the mass of the breasts and the function they are performing at the time. Moreover, there is a far greater difference at various times in the shape, consistency, number, and location of the glandular substance of the breasts. For in many men, no such glandular substance occurs, or it is very slight and dry, as it also is in very young girls. But in young women, whose breasts are already rising into a mass with a certain itching <note>original: "pruritu", likely referring to the tingling or sensitivity of pubertal growth</note> and who eagerly desire a husband, they obtain...

[The breasts] usually acquire a compact and somewhat hard abundance, and are filled with no milky fluid (unlike what happens, of course, in those who are nursing or about to give birth), nor is their substance flaccid or sagging in the manner of what is contained in the breasts of old women. Therefore, at the center of the nipple in women, there is **c** one large gland, shaped like a small breast <term>glans<note>Latin for "acorn," used here to describe the central glandular structure</note></term>, which corresponds in substance to the unique and specific glandular body of the udders in other animals. Around this, **d** several other glands lie in a circle—almost small and similar to almonds stripped of their shells—which are joined and grown together according to the temperament of the woman, sometimes with harder fat, sometimes softer, through the intervention of veins and fibers extending from the fleshy membrane into the skin. For the entire substance of the breasts is contained like fat between the skin and that membrane; nor are the breasts attached to the muscles lying upon the ribs by any other connection than that by which that membrane clings to the muscles underlying it throughout the rest of the body—unless perhaps a few more veins intervene here, distributed from the muscles into the breasts. However much the breasts may sometimes hang soft and flaccid, the fleshy membrane never departs from the muscles for that reason; rather, that glandular substance of the breasts, along with the fat, being no longer constricted but sagging and loosened, is dissolved from the fleshy membrane. For nursing women, and those carrying a fetus in the final months, have the veins of the breasts filled with milky humor or milk, and the glandular substance itself also abounds with it; because of this, it is rendered softer and quite spongy, and not as dense and continuous. No longer preserving its tone, and with the somewhat hard fat no longer supporting it, it gradually becomes flaccid and hangs down. Although in the meantime it never reaches such a degree of thinness that it would receive into itself a hair swallowed by the woman (as is the opinion of *Aristotle*) and be troubled by the "hairy disease," called *trichiasis* <note>original Greek: "τριχίασιν"; a historical medical belief that swallowed hair could migrate through the body to the breasts</note> by the Greeks. For there is no doubt that through so many narrow passages and slender windings from the mouth to the breasts, a hair could by no means be led—even if the breasts were perhaps to embrace it if it were to stand in their veins. However, it is not entirely absurd that something similar to a hair could be produced in the breasts, just as can occur in the **e** kidneys and **f** urinary passages. The skin covering the breast matches the rest of the skin of the chest <term>thorax<note>The chest cavity</note></term>; for it grows together with the substance of the breast just as it does with the fat throughout the rest of the body, and is equally thick there. But where it turns somewhat black in a circle at the nipple, and forms a ring which is called *halos* <note>original Greek: "ἅλως"; the areola</note> by the Greeks, it grows more firmly to the primary glandular body of the breast through the intervention of many nerves and thin veins like white fibers. Furthermore, the skin here sometimes becomes thinner than elsewhere, acquiring a certain sponginess, as does the nipple itself.

### ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE [HUMAN] BODY

Professors of dissection enumerate other more principal veins than those I have just mentioned, which, accompanied by arteries, take their <gloss>l</gloss> beginning from those veins <margin>l Figure, Chapter 6, Book 3, L.</margin> that come forth from the vena cava <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</note> in the throat, and run under the breastbone <gloss>2</gloss> toward the abdomen <margin>2 Figure, Book 6, B, C.</margin> almost as far as the navel, alongside the <gloss>m</gloss> arteries themselves. <margin>m Figure, Chapter 12, Book 3, G.</margin> They distribute offshoots into the front <gloss>n</gloss> of the chest through the intervals of the rib cartilages, <margin>n Figure, Chapter 6, Book 3, M. and Muscle Table 6, f.</margin> especially involving the inner <gloss>o</gloss> part of the muscle by whose benefit we bring the arm to the chest. <margin>o Muscle Table 4.</margin> Whether these present offshoots actually permeate and penetrate that muscle, and together with their accompanying arteries are finally disseminated into the breasts, I would wish to be diligently observed during dissection. For to me, such offshoots or veins approaching the breasts are not easy to find, just as I am also unable to find arteries pertaining to this area, so much so that I would scarcely dare to attribute arteries to the breasts at all. 

However, in certain beasts where a different position of the breasts or udders occurs than in humans, branches are spread into the breasts from those <gloss>p</gloss> veins <margin>p Figure, Chapter 6, Book 3, Γ. which arises under s.</margin> which interweave the lower part of the abdomen with their branches; one of these on each side obtains its beginning from the vena cava where its principal portion is carried above the pubic bone into the groins, and first proceeds into the leg outside the cavity of the peritoneum—far indeed from the <gloss>q</gloss> origin of the veins approaching the uterus. <margin>q Figure, Chapter 6, Book 3, v. or compare Figure 25, Book 5, u with y.</margin> And indeed, in the series of these veins which are led to the abdomen both from the throat under the breastbone and upward from the groins, beasts hardly differ from humans. That distribution of vessels is seen in almost all, which we expressed in the third book, and which I would wish to be examined not just in passing, since in this Chapter, or ever elsewhere, you will deal with the relationship of the uterus with the breasts.

<margin>Where the nerves of the breasts are led from.</margin>
The nerves of the breasts depend on those which are stretched out to the muscles placed under them; nor are these derived into the breasts differently than to the rest of the skin of the thorax, except for <gloss>r</gloss> a single one, which is thicker than the others and approaches the nipple from about the fifth interval of the ribs, <margin>r Figure 2, Chapter 11, Book 4, v.</margin> offering many offshoots to it. 

<margin>The function of the breasts and the reason for their construction.</margin>
How accurately the Architect of things <note>A common Renaissance reference to God as the "Opifex rerum" or Great Workman</note> fashioned each part to be suitable for the primary function of the breasts, you will understand if you consider each part separately for its use. For the chief office of the breasts in all viviparous animals <note>Animals that give birth to live young</note> must be judged to be the preparation of food for the tender and recently born offspring. For the udders were not created primarily for this—although in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, **Aristotle** attests to it—so that they might cover the seat of the heart, and then, as if secondarily in women, or Nature somehow misusing them, to serve for the generation and containment of milk. 

Since breasts do not rise in boys, nor in any animal not yet fit for generation <note>i.e., not yet reached puberty</note>, but are held in them merely as a kind of sign without any particular body within them (by which they might be significantly distinguished from the rest of the fat between the skin and the fleshy membrane), it is certain that they are not made primarily as a defense. This is because they have nothing except the tender nipple by which they could deservedly be called defenses for the organs they lie upon. Furthermore, if any growth appears in the breasts of men, and they are held for the sake of some other benefit than merely as a sign, it happens for them for the most part after the fourteenth year, when they first begin to produce genital seed and reach puberty. Indeed, it is established that they swell for the sake of milk rather than for protection or defense, and that the breasts themselves become effeminate. For **Aristotle** himself asserts that milk is squeezed out from some men after puberty, and has come forth through frequent and much handling and sucking; and we too have seen this more than once. 

<margin>Reason for the position.</margin>
Furthermore, for man and the ape, the breasts are very conveniently placed on the chest, unlike almost all other animals, besides the fact that they do not impede the duties of the arms and hands, and man and ape claim a broad chest for themselves, not one projecting to a point like almost all other animals; a woman nursing a child abundantly...

<meta>This page continues Vesalius's discussion on the physiology of the breasts. On the previous page, he debated the vascular supply to the chest area. Here, he turns to the teleological reasons (the "why") for the placement and structure of the breasts in humans compared to other animals, and describes the erectile nature of the nipple.</meta>

# THE FIFTH BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

...abundantly indicates, and it is most easy for us to gather by various conjectures regarding that function, that no more convenient region can be devised for the breasts in a seated animal that uses its hands (to say nothing of the modes of love <note>A reference to sexual intercourse and intimacy.</note>) than the front region of the chest. For here the site is not unsuitable for the generation of milk because of the heat of the heart; and furthermore, the breasts can be considered a kind of bulwark and rampart for the heart, especially for man, who carries his chest upright and does not recline on the ground like almost all other animals. Furthermore, this present location also returns a certain reciprocal heat to the heart (though it perhaps would have been more necessary for the stomach and intestines). For the breasts, like woolen pads, or a garment, or the fat or flesh of the body itself, having been first warmed by the heart—the workshop of heat—reflect that heat back by restraining and covering it. Likewise, one easily understands that the continuous motion of the heart and chest, and the heart's unquenchable heat, contribute greatly to the generation of milk, which requires the nature of concoction <note>The process of "cooking" or refining bodily fluids into higher substances like milk or blood.</note> and alteration. Furthermore, as for the placement of breasts higher in humans and lower in other animals—according to the consensus of Aristotle, Galen, and other philosophers and physicians—due to a lack of nourishment or, as they call it, the *excrement* <note>original: "excrementi"; in early medicine, "excrement" referred to any surplus substance the body produced, such as hair, milk, or sweat, rather than just waste.</note> which was to be converted into milk, I do not believe this to be true in every respect. For first, they aim at this point: that the fetus in the womb takes in the "excrementitious" blood of the lower part of the body for nourishment, whereas the breasts primarily receive and attract the blood of the upper part for the generation of milk. Then they add that breasts are placed in the upper part in humans, but not in other animals, because in the latter, the excrement of that part is consumed by horns and manes—quite differently from women, in their opinion. As if indeed does, cows, mares, and animals of that kind lacked veins that carry blood downward from the throat under the chest, or those which are distributed to the muscles laid over the chest and the skin of the same by the vein seeking the armpit, any more than humans do; or as if in those animals, blood from the upper parts of the body could be drawn down to the womb any less than in a woman; and as if much more excrement did not perish in a woman (who is otherwise entirely hairless) in the very long hairs of the head, than in other animals in their horns and manes, and that in proportion. But truly, this reasoning of Aristotle corresponds to that by which physicians and philosophers solve many problems regarding monthly or lunar purgings—I know not whether as truly as they do it boldly.

<margin>The reason for the shape of the breasts.</margin>
Since these matters look elsewhere, we shall now approach the remaining logic of the construction of the breasts. Therefore, an externally round shape was very suitable for them, so they might be less liable to injury; but inside, on that part where they are joined to the chest, Nature rightly fashioned them flat and broad, so they might rest on a firm base. 
<margin>The logic of the construction of the nipple and its entire substance.</margin>
They also possess a tender and prominent nipple <term>papilla</term>, so that when it is placed into the narrow and tender mouth of the infant, the infant may immediately squeeze it with its soft lips, and by drawing down the lower jaw and contracting the cheeks, suck out the milk; and then, bending the tongue like a channel, propel it to the stomach without being taught by anyone. To ensure that during that flow the nipple becomes more swollen and elongated than at other times (when it is least needed), it possesses a substance similar to the penis, which is capable of both relaxing and collapsing, and again of swelling and becoming erect from sweet contact. Moreover, the nipple abounds with a more exact sense and with small branches of nerves, so that in this respect also there might be an affinity between the breasts and the genitals. For just as Nature implanted an allure and pleasure in those parts for sexual intercourse and the propagation of the species, so too did she in the breasts—and most especially in the nipples—so that the mother might more willingly offer the nipple to be tickled and stimulated by the tender and not-yet-toothed mouth of the offspring already brought into the light, and offer it to be sucked. Truly, the glandular substance of the breasts is of such a balance of temperament and form that it can convert and refine the blood, brought to it with great industry of Nature through the veins, into milk—the familiar nourishment of the child.

<summary>Vesalius explains the anatomical and evolutionary reasons for the placement of human breasts on the chest, refuting Aristotle's theories on bodily "excrement." He describes the nipple's erectile tissue and the sensory pleasure of nursing as Nature's way of ensuring the survival of the infant.</summary>

The reasoning behind the arrangement of the veins, and the sympathy of the womb with the breasts.

<margin>

<margin>
Look at the 8th muscle table, letters d, e, f; and the figure of Chapter 6, Book 3, letters l, m, r; and the figure of Chapter 12, Book 3, G, r; and the last figure of Book 3, *, q, t.
</margin>

Furthermore, in explaining the purpose of the distribution of the vessels <note>Referring to veins and arteries.</note> seeking the breasts, Galen is quite long-winded, asserting that these vessels are led from distant and remote parts in a winding path, endowed with many coils, so that the blood might be conveniently prepared for the generation of milk in those long ducts and coils. Meanwhile, I do not know what kind of special or private preparation the blood would require before it is offered to the breasts, even though I am not unmindful of the paths and ducts of the seminal vessels <note>Vesalius refers to the "seed-carrying" vessels, often comparing the refinement of blood into milk to the refinement of blood into semen.</note>. Nor was there a more direct way by which the vessels could be safely distributed to the breasts—whether in humans or in other animals—since it is well established that the trunk of the *vena cava* <term>the great vein</term> <note>original: "cauæ uenæ"</note> rightly occupies the back. Nature’s craftsmanship is also evident in how the vessels are extended to the front parts of the torso—namely the chest and abdomen—whether we look at the throat, the groin, or even those branches that spread out from the trunk of the *vena cava* and the "vein lacking a partner" <term>azygos vein</term> <note>original: "uena pari carente"</note> along the sides of the body. Yet, I do not think the arrangement of the vessels should be considered merely for the sake of the long path which the veins claim for themselves when offered to the breasts; rather, we should consider it in the context of the debates that arise daily regarding the "sympathy" <note>An ancient medical concept where distant organs affect one another through shared vessels or "spirits."</note> of the womb with the breasts. These debates concern the affinity of milk with the menstrual purgations, the abundance of both, miscarriages, and especially the mutual movement of blood, now drawn to the womb, now to the breasts. It is indeed a wonder how much Galen torments himself for the sake of such speculations. At one moment, he writes that the veins seeking the lower parts of the abdomen arise from those that go to the womb (even if he testifies otherwise elsewhere); at another, he teaches at great length how the blood that is abundant around the womb in pregnant women crawls upward through those same veins into the breasts. He speaks as if the veins seeking the abdomen from the throat beneath the breastbone, and those with which the lower part of the abdomen is interwoven, were the only paths, passages, or ducts through which the sympathy of the womb with the breasts occurred—whether through the veins proceeding under the straight muscles of the abdomen <term>rectus abdominis</term>, or through their branches spread through the skin of the abdomen. Meanwhile, I believe that such a "sympathy," whatever it may finally be, should rather be referred to the entire trunk of the *vena cava*. Indeed, when Galen zealously strives to explain the movement of blood to the upper parts, it does not seem to me to be clear by his reasoning why the blood would not flow down into the legs rather than upward through the abdominal region into the breasts—especially considering the compression of the abdomen by the pregnant womb, and given that there is no known orifice where the lower veins of the abdomen are proven to join or continue with the upper ones. But, lest this discourse on the use of the breasts grow too large, we shall now conveniently proceed to the dissection of all the organs we have described in this book.

### BOOK V ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY.

It seemed appropriate to present the anatomy of those parts described in their respective chapters; fittingly, the dissection of the veins, arteries, and nerves dedicated to those same parts must be treated here in such a way that no more complete or integrated method could have been established in the preceding books. And if, by chance, the dissection of certain veins, arteries, and nerves is not necessarily or sequentially included with the aforementioned organs, we shall append it to the end of the penultimate chapter of the seventh book. This will primarily concern the dissection of the veins, arteries, and nerves of the arm and leg. Indeed, if mention of the skin, fat, fleshy membrane, muscles, ligaments, and finally the bones happens to occur in their proper places in passing, the entire method of dissecting the body will be narrated throughout these three chapters. In fact, I shall describe them in such a way (because it can be done with a few added words for the treatment that ought to encompass it entirely) that when someone considers these chapters connected together, they may serve as a book and a rule <note>original: "instar libri ac canonis," meaning a standard or definitive guide.</note> by which students of the fabric of the human body may, by their own initiative, attempt dissections in various private homes with their companions, or seek from their teachers the sequence of parts to be cut and shown in the schools, or perceive long in advance the order which those teachers are to observe. Certainly, one order must be established when there is an abundance of bodies, and another when only a single one happens to be available for a public anatomy.

<margin>a One such as this is usually prepared for us, a part of which is expressed in the table [illustration] used at the front of this work.</margin>
<margin>What order is to be preserved in teaching and demonstrating Anatomy.</margin>

I have therefore quite often, when a supply of bodies was certainly not denied, taught anatomy in the order which I shall now set down. An elegant theater <gloss>a</gloss> <note>Vesalius refers to the temporary wooden anatomical theaters built for public demonstrations, famously depicted on the title page of the *Fabrica*.</note> having been prepared by the industry of some carpenter, which might sometimes comfortably receive over five hundred spectators, and a certain table having been constructed in its center which I judged most suitable for the business, I diligently ensured that the bones of various humans were at hand for me, some woven together <note>articulated into a skeleton</note>, others separated and placed in small boxes. I speak of the bones of children, youths, the elderly, women, and men, which through both my diligence and that of other candidates of medicine were present for me in great number and abundance in the schools of Italy, along with the bones of dogs and sometimes several monkeys and other animals. Therefore, before I arranged for an entire human cadaver to be brought into the schools, I proposed to the students the doctrine of the bones in that sequence in which I composed the first book of this our Work. Furthermore, for the sake of those still unskilled in Anatomy, before the treatment of the bones—as soon as I had prefaced certain things concerning the dignity and use of the knowledge of the human fabric as occasion allowed, and then the order in which I thought this should be learned, and other such matters, and had proposed the various methods and differences by which teachers of dissection are accustomed to divide the human body—I strove to show how it was formed from similar parts and then from instrumental parts <term>similar and instrumental parts</term> <note>Vesalius uses "similar parts" to refer to uniform tissues like bone or fat, and "instrumental parts" for complex organs like the hand or heart.</note>. To this end, I employed a dog or some lamb, which I had first mostly freed from its skin, and having opened the chest and peritoneum, and moreover the skull, I had dissected it in such a way that almost all parts of the body offered themselves to be viewed in passing, so that I might easily grasp with my hand whatever part I wished while teaching.

<margin>What the similar and instrumental parts of the body are like.</margin>

And so, when I had dealt with the constitution of the similar part from the first principles of Nature, and especially its essential form (on account of the new division and number of diseases that happen to similar parts, which has just begun to be proposed quite learnedly), I proposed the bone as the first similar part of the body, showing how it was "similar" to the senses, and expressing its use in sustaining and strengthening. To this I added the cartilage, adding the necessity of its creation, and teaching in passing those things which are treated by me in their proper place concerning the nature of cartilage. After these followed the history of the ligament, and having shown various and differing ligaments, their use and the reason for their creation were brought forward. Soon, along with the ligaments themselves, [I showed] what a membrane was and what it provided for the body...

the discourse was added, along with the demonstration of several membranes in the aforementioned dog or lamb. Thus, when the distinction between simple membranes and the coats of organs composed of fibers <term>tunicae: the layers or "coats" that make up the walls of organs like the stomach or intestines</term> was taught, I also applied a treatment of the fibers to the membranes, tearing away several coats of the intestines and pointing out the fibers within them. This was done so it would be clearly visible how certain coats, consisting of various fibers, differ from a simple membrane construction. 

Next, alongside the fibers that had to be woven together, the general account of the flesh was added, which I had previously shown in its simple form in the liver, lungs, and kidneys—those viscera <note>original: "uisceribus," referring to the internal organs</note> having been dissected frequently for the sake of demonstrating that same use. However, the ways in which flesh contains and connects fibers were made apparent in certain torn and shredded muscles, and in the dissected substance of the heart. When an account had been given of the glandular body, and then of the fat—which we see growing almost everywhere upon membranes—as well as the marrow preserved in the bones, and the humors seen even in carelessly opened eyes, as if they were similar parts <term>similar parts: in Galenic anatomy, "homogeneous" tissues like bone, fat, or nerve that are the same throughout, as opposed to "instrumental" parts like the hand</term>, I also began to review how the instrumental parts arise from those similar ones. These include, of course, the veins, arteries, and nerves, and afterwards the muscles with their tendons. Finally, I proposed the formation of the entire finger and hand, including the skin, while simultaneously demonstrating those things encountered in the large body cavities of that dog.

Therefore, after I had taught these things for the sake of the beginners, and the dog having been cast aside, I moved on to the complete discipline and knowledge of the bones and cartilages. Once that was finished, we took care to bring a human cadaver into the schools to serve for the observation of the muscles and ligaments. Indeed, we learn through no small amount of experience how diligently—and entirely according to our judgment—cadavers are now supplied for public anatomy through the care of the officials in the Italian academies and their singular love for the study of learning; even if, perhaps, those bodies are not always as well-proportioned or of the middle age we might sometimes wish for. 

Thus, after the treatment of the bones and cartilages, the instruction on the muscles, ligaments, and finally everything we pursue in the Second Book was completed on that cadaver. For the anatomy of the veins, arteries, and nerves, however, we took up another cadaver, which was also suited for showing those parts whose history is handed down in the three subsequent books. In the dissection of that cadaver, I used the order which I shall strive most of all to follow in this Chapter, in the last Chapter of the Sixth Book, and in the penultimate of the Seventh, when recounting the dissection of the vessels and the parts already mentioned. 

<margin>The order of dissection must be varied according to the availability of cadavers.</margin> However, since only one cadaver can usually be obtained for a public anatomy, I shall make mention in these Chapters of the bones, cartilages, muscles, skin, cuticle, fat, and finally the fleshy membrane <term>panniculus carnosus: a layer of tissue under the skin that Vesalius here calls the "fleshy membrane"</term>—just as I advised before—so that besides the exquisite management of those organs whose mode of dissection we have not yet handed down, the sequence may also be revealed by which anyone might, in some way, complete a total anatomy on a single cadaver. 

Therefore, as you are about to begin, having engaged studious companions rather than mere servants to assist the one cutting, you shall make a circular incision with a sharp razor <note>original: "nouacula," a surgical knife or razor</note> around the navel, deep enough to almost penetrate the skin. 

<margin>Management of the skin, cuticle, fat, and fleshy membrane in the abdomen.</margin> Then, from the middle of the length of the breastbone <note>original: "pectoris ossis," the sternum</note>, you shall effect a straight incision down to the navel, and from the lowest part of the navel you shall proceed all the way to the middle of the pubic bone, touching the root of the male member (if a male cadaver is at hand). Or, if you are dissecting the body of a woman, proceed until you have passed the seat of the pubic bone to the hills of the private parts <note>original: "pudendi colliculos," likely referring to the labia majora or mons pubis</note>, so that one single incision (keeping the navel intact) reaches from the chest all the way to the pubic bone. After this, you shall lead an incision transversely from each side of the navel all the way to the loins. Meanwhile, aim to cut only the skin; this is not so difficult to do in a human, and especially in one who is quite fat, since the thickness of the fat promptly prevents you from damaging the fleshy membrane. Once the incisions have been made in this manner, the corner of the skin, which is formed by four straight...

<margin>On the veins running through the abdominal region between the skin and the fleshy membrane.</margin>

Next, having examined the skin and the veins under it running through the abdominal region, both from the bottom upward and from the chest downward, and also the fat—if the person abounds in it (as almost everyone usually does who has not been killed by a lingering disease)—you shall separate the fat from the <term>fleshy membrane: known as the panniculus carnosus, a layer of tissue beneath the skin</term>, just as you have already freed the skin from the fat. Truly, you will never accomplish this properly unless you use a very sharp razor. If, however, a leaner body happens to be available, you will allow the fat to remain attached to the fleshy membrane. For the fat then, because it possesses a meager thickness, does not at all prevent the nature of the fleshier membrane from coming into view.

Whichever you do, whether you scrape away the fat or leave it attached to the membrane, the membrane itself is to be separated from the underlying structures using the same cuts through the membrane that I reported should be made in the skin (from the chest to the pubic bone, and from the navel to the flanks), using a blunter razor if you like, or almost entirely by the benefit of the fingers. This is so that now the entire abdomen, together with a large part of the chest, may appear uncovered of skin, fat, and fleshy membrane. 

I have often approached the procedure in the schools in this very manner; although, if anyone wishes, it is also perfectly possible to examine the skin, fat, and fleshy membrane in only one part of the abdomen, and to pull away the skin along with the fat and membrane from the rest of the abdominal site without any skill, <note>original: "laniorum ritu"</note> in the manner of butchers. But concerning the nature of these parts, and indeed their procedure, I have treated more at length in the second book; and in that same book, I taught the method by which you may best approach the abdominal muscles (which are four on each side) and bare the <term>peritoneum: the smooth, thin membrane that lines the abdominal cavity and covers the organs</term>.

<margin>The liberation of the peritoneum from the parts joined to it from the outside.</margin>

Moreover, the human peritoneum is too weak in consistency and thickness to be easily separated from the diaphragm everywhere; although, in the meantime, by the benefit of the hand alone, the peritoneum—while it is still whole—may be freed from the muscles lying beneath it all the way to the spine, and also somewhat from the fleshy site of the diaphragm, and it then clearly resembles an oblong sphere. 

Furthermore, if you wish to tear the peritoneum completely away from the diaphragm with less trouble, you will perform this most conveniently in piglets, if after (as in a human) you have separated the transverse muscle of the abdomen from the peritoneum, you strive to separate it from the lower site of the diaphragm with your fingers, using them in place of a knife. ...from the membranes of the omentum^m <note>original: *omenti*. The omentum is a fold of the peritoneum that hangs over the stomach and intestines like a fatty apron.</note> and furthermore, you will pull away the peritoneum from the convex part of the liver, and you will learn <margin>*m Just as it was shown torn apart in Figure 17, Book 1.*</margin> in what way it provides coats and wrappings to those organs. After you have carefully <margin>*n As if preparing the second figure from the first.*</margin> considered the peritoneum from the outside, with its openings, veins, arteries, and nerves,^n a cut must be made in the peritoneum with a razor or knife from the left side of the <term>mucronate cartilage: the xiphoid process or the "sword-shaped" tip of the breastbone</term> downward to the site of the navel. Care must be taken so that you do not wound any of the underlying parts by driving the knife too deep. From here, from the navel, the same cut should be attempted, slanting slightly to the left down to the region of the pubic bone (so that it deviates by some distance from the center toward the left side). Furthermore, in this left part of the peritoneum, you will make a transverse cut directly across from the navel toward the left flank, and you will fold back the upper part of that section of the peritoneum toward the ribs, and the lower part toward the hip. Now, having lifted and rolled back slightly upward, or turned to the right, the right section of the peritoneum,^o you will turn your attention to the vein reaching from the navel into the liver <margin>*o Figure 2, labels E and G.*</margin> <note>This is the umbilical vein, which becomes the round ligament of the liver after birth.</note>. You will grasp this where it is closest to the liver, and where it just begins to depart from the peritoneum, with your left hand; then, having inserted a very sharp knife between the vein and the peritoneum, you will gradually separate it from the peritoneum with transverse cuts as you approach the navel. When you have reached that point, without cutting the vein, you will lead a cut in the peritoneum from the right side of the navel to the flanks,^p folding back that part <margin>*p Figure 2, label A.*</margin> of the peritoneum, which is now free, over the ribs of the right side. However, one part of the peritoneum, which is lower on the right side, still remains attached to the navel and does not yet hang free. Therefore, so that you may free this part as well without damaging anything in the process, grasp the navel with your left hand and make a cut from its right side into this part of the peritoneum down to the pubic region, which should slant a few fingers' width to the right from the <term>commissure of the pubic bones: the pubic symphysis, or the joint where the two halves of the pelvis meet in front</term>.^q Now, when the small section of the peritoneum is turned over—which, being triangular,^r extends <margin>*q The last figures of Book 1, label s.*</margin> <margin>*r Figure 2, label N.*</margin> from the navel to the pubis and the base of the bladder^s—three cords, as it were, placed next <margin>*s Figure 2, labels M, K, L.*</margin> to each other, are seen attached to the inner side of that part of the peritoneum. These must be diligently divided from it with a very sharp knife, and afterward carefully separated from one another, lest by extending the cut too freely toward the pubic bones in a human, you wound the base of the bladder. For the human bladder, because its entire front surface is grown together with the peritoneum and covered with much fat, so deceives those unpracticed in dissection that they do not know the bladder is located here; they search for a bladder which, in humans, should occur as a free organ just as it does in oxen and dogs. When, therefore, you have considered these things without haste, you will observe that the middle cord is attached to the middle of the base of the bladder and never departs from the peritoneum. You will see the remaining two cords stretch along the sides of the bladder downward and deeper toward the^t arteries that will pass through the openings in the pubic bones into the leg—provided <margin>*t Figure of chapter 12, book 3; and it is carried between g and r.*</margin> you are not reluctant to free them from the peritoneum with a sharp knife as far as their continuation. The middle cord is the passage <note>the urachus</note> by which urine is excreted from the bladder between the two membranes enveloping the fetus while we are carried in the womb. The other two are the arteries <note>the umbilical arteries</note> by which the natural heat of the fetus is primarily refreshed. But neither these three^u bodies, nor^x that which <margin>*u Figure 2, labels M, K, L.*</margin> is inserted into the liver <note>the umbilical vein</note>, will now appear to have any cavity, but will seem clearly dead, <margin>*x Figure 2, labels F, G.*</margin> dry, nourished by much fat, and appearing just like cords. For this reason, it also escaped the notice of other leading lights of Anatomy, who asserted that these are entirely and completely abolished in humans after birth, just as happens almost always in dogs. However, after you have <margin>*Cutting of the umbilical vessels. Once you move [the peritoneum] aside, the position of the <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron</term> must be observed: namely, whether—as in dogs and pigs, and even more so in monkeys—it extends all the way to the pubic bone behind the bladder; or whether (as is frequently observed) it is found rolled toward the left side and contracted even above the middle of the intestines. If you find the latter, you will moderately lift the lower edge of the omentum with both hands and, gradually and evenly drawing it downward, stretch it over all the intestines as far as the pubic bone. In this way, you will learn how large it is, and how it can sometimes^c descend into the groin and scrotum, and^d between the bladder and the neck of the womb (the cervix). In order to see the connection of the omentum to the <term>colon: the main part of the large intestine</term> where it extends from the stomach,^e you will again lift the lower end of the omentum upward toward the breastbone with both hands. Before you free that part of the lower omental membrane which seems to grow out of the "third coat" of the colon, you should stretch the omentum as much as possible over the chest and investigate the position of the intestines with the greatest industry, using only your hands. First, before you disturb the location of any intestine, you will contemplate them with precision just as they offer themselves to be viewed^f once the omentum has been lifted.
