As soon as you have observed this accurately and not merely in passing, you will place your right hand on the <term>rectum: the final section of the large intestine</term>,^g where it begins to rest upon the <term>sacrum: the large triangular bone at the base of the spine</term>. With your left hand, you will lightly press the small intestines toward the right—not all of them, but that part which is closer to the right hand as you move up from the rectum. In this manner, with the left hand assisting the right, you will gradually move your right hand along the colon from the rectum, and^h following its path and its turns, you will reach the area of the left kidney, and from there the spleen and the <term>fundus: the base or bottom</term> of the stomach. When you have reached that point, switching the duties of your hands, the colon is to be grasped with the left hand, while with the right, the small intestines are to be pushed moderately to the left until you have passed the entire area of the stomach’s base and the liver, and have brought the colon down to the region of the right kidney (where it ends). When you reach this point, lifting the end of the colon slightly with the left hand, and having similarly observed the position and shape of the^i <term>cecum: the "blind" pouch at the beginning of the large intestine</term>, you will also place your right hand at this end of the colon. With both hands close to each other and never removed from the intestines,^k you will soon follow the path of the <term>ileum: the final section of the small intestine</term> from the colon, and then the <term>jejunum: the middle section of the small intestine</term>. This is by far the easiest thing to do until you reach the beginning of the jejunum, where it turns back under the colon and, being bound in a way to the back,^l is continued from the <term>duodenum: the first part of the small intestine immediately following the stomach</term>. Therefore, so that the entire path of the intestines may be apparent to you, you will still hold the jejunum with your right hand, but you will thrust your left hand between the liver and the right side of the stomach, searching for the beginning of the duodenum. Once you find it and descend with your left hand following its path, the beginning of the jejunum (and the part adjacent to it which you are still holding with your right hand) will also become known. If you like (and I strongly advise doing so), you can examine the position of the intestines a second time in the opposite direction: from the jejunum to the ileum, and from there to the cecum and colon, and from the colon to the rectum, making no tear in the meantime (lest you wound anything). Having weighed the position of the intestines and replaced them as best you can in their proper location, the omentum must be wrapped back over the intestines, and the position of the stomach, liver, and spleen must be examined.

For as soon as you have wounded the chest, the diaphragm, falling downward, will become remarkably slack; however much it was previously stretched or drawn upward, pulling the liver and stomach up into the breadth of the chest, and thereby making their inspection difficult.

...you will begin a very great and most laborious task. For the bile ducts, and the branches of the nerves, arteries, and veins (all of which are gathered together at the hollow of the liver by the lower membrane of the <term>omentum: a fatty layer of tissue that hangs over the intestines like an apron</term> <note>original: "omentum"</note>) must now be examined with a rather blunt knife, lest you puncture any vein with the point of a sharper blade and thus obscure everything with blood. First, a small nerve presents itself, inserted into the hollow of the liver from the lower orifice of the stomach; it hangs from the branches of the sixth pair of cranial nerves <note>In the 16th century, the vagus nerve was identified as the "sixth pair"; in modern anatomy, it is the tenth cranial nerve.</note> which approach the upper orifice of the stomach. Once you have separated this from the neighboring organs, another nerve must be divided from its connection to the membranes; one of its branches goes to the hollow of the liver, and the other to the gallbladder. An artery is attached to this nerve, following a similar distribution, and should be freed shortly after the nerve. You will find the origin of this artery, as well as that of the nerve, a little later; for now, it is enough to separate these from one another near the hollow of the liver and to learn their sequence there. Beneath the artery lie the bile ducts, which must now be freed from the portal vein: first those two which are gathered from many small shoots out of the hollow of the liver and immediately unite into a single duct, which is carried on one side into the gallbladder and on the other into the <term>duodenum: the first part of the small intestine</term>. Once you have pulled these away from the portal vein as far as the intestine and the gallbladder, you should compress the gallbladder with your thumb so that the ducts swelling with bile appear more clearly, and you may observe whether any duct reaches from this gallbladder into the stomach. If you do not find one, you should lightly pierce the duct hurrying toward the intestines with a needle, so that the flowing bile serves as proof that no passage was overlooked by your negligence. <margin>l You will also seek this from figure 11, then from 3 if you prefer with 4, or the entire series from the figures of chapter 5, book 3.</margin> Finally, the portal vein must be examined here, and as soon as you observe its boundary where it exits the liver, its branches are to be sought with a blunt knife, always taking diligent account of the arteries and nerves that accompany the vein throughout its entire sequence. <margin>How the branches of the portal vein, along with the arteries and nerves attached to them, are to be examined.</margin> First, therefore, you will approach the shoots of the portal vein which extend to the gallbladder; then that branch which, almost without the company of an artery, is distributed in a modest series of branches on the right side of the stomach near the posterior region of its lower orifice. In order that you may see it conveniently, the stomach and intestines must be <sup>o</sup> <margin>o Exactly as in Figure 3.</margin> arranged for you in that way in which they were situated when, intending to view the lower membrane of the omentum, you saw to it that the stomach was lifted upward by a companion's hand and the intestines were pressed downward. # ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY
## BOOK V, CHAPTER 13 (CONTINUED)

You will pull the intestines apart from one side to the other, rolling them now to the right and now to the left side, so that you may cursorily contemplate the nature of the **mesentery** <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place.</note> without yet cutting it. Then, with a rather blunt little knife, you will free the larger trunk of the **portal vein**, and the artery and nerve mentioned just now, from one another; and then, so that you may see their entire course and the glands interspersed between their branches, you will tear one membrane of the mesentery from the other with your fingernails. However, this should not be attempted through the entire mesentery. It will suffice for the present to have traced a few small branches of the vessels from its center all the way to the small intestines, and soon <margin>r Figure 20, k or Figure 12, Book 3, λ under ι n. s Figure 10 around H, and G near it; and Figure 12 n. or Figure 11 from R to S, then to T.</margin> to approach the other mesenteric artery, which is distributed from the **great artery** <note>The aorta.</note> after the origin of the seminal arteries. You will find this promptly if you roll the mesentery along with the intestines toward the right side, and attempt to separate the membranes of the mesentery from each other with your fingernails or a blunt knife at the point where it is attached to the colon beneath the seat of the left kidney. Here, the branches of that artery joined with the veins will immediately present themselves, showing in turn the root of their own artery. Once you have found it, follow its branching so that you may learn how it extends its branches to the **rectum** <note>The final section of the large intestine.</note> along with the vein supported by the mesentery. Do not be overly concerned if you do not now see the ends of this vein inserted into the rectum; that will be done more easily a little later. Thus, by this method of management, the positions of the omentum, intestines, stomach, liver, spleen, and mesentery—as well as the branches of the veins, arteries, and nerves extended to all of them—must be examined. Furthermore, I shall now prepare myself for the procedure by which you may conveniently see what remains to be seen in those organs and demonstrate them to others.

<margin>How the intestines are to be cut from the mesentery and removed from the body.</margin>
Therefore, you will pass a thread through a large needle curved like a semicircle—the kind used to tie up bundles of letters—and lead this through the mesentery under the <margin>t Figure 7, Book 2, N, N. u At Y and T, Figure 6, or H, Figure 11. x As was done in Figure 20 at o, or Figure 24 at K, where we also cut the remaining intestines from the mesentery. y All the way to L, Figure 7. z Figure 20, T, V. * Figure 7, Z; 13 a; 15 Q, R.</margin> rectum where it lies upon the **sacrum** <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note>. After the feces of that intestine have been squeezed upward toward the width of the colon, you will tie a ligature around the rectum. Having cut the remaining thread, you will again squeeze the feces nearest the knot upward out of the rectum; then, leaving an interval of about three fingers' breadth, you will pass the needle again under the rectum above the first knot. You will tie the rectum a second time in this way so that no excrement remains between the two <term>ligatures: threads or strings used to tie off a vessel or organ</term>. Next, you will divide the rectum between the two knots with a razor, and you will gradually cut its upper part away from the mesentery with a blunt razor (lest you accidentally wound the intestines through negligence). From there, you will free the colon, ileum, and **jejunum** <note>The middle segment of the small intestine.</note> continuously from the mesentery all the way to the beginning of the jejunum, and you will place the intestines in a basin. In this task, the connection of the colon above the fatty tunics of the kidneys must be diligently observed, along with the frequent series of vessels entwining themselves into the intestines. When you have reached the beginning of the jejunum, you will secure it with two knots just like the rectum, so that the higher knot is near the insertion of the bile duct, but does not ascend any higher.

<margin>How the tunics of the intestines are to be examined.</margin>
Once the intestines are free from the belly, you will offer them to be washed by one of the hospital servants, such as we employ here for dissection, so that if it seems useful, you may examine the <margin>a As in Figure 9.</margin> **tunics** <note>The layers or membranes of the intestinal wall.</note> and the length of the already washed parts. At Padua and Bologna, after the intestines were washed and stretched out on the lecture benches, we sometimes had them inflated like a bladder; for in this way we easily learned not only the length—which is scarcely the same in everyone, although it equals almost fourteen <term>ulnas: a measurement of length, roughly 18 to 27 inches depending on the region</term>—but also the shape and width. It is also far easiest to investigate the tunics of the intestines when they are stretched out in this manner. For the part of the mesentery nearest the intestines appears, which consists of two membranes, one upper and the other lower; if you separate these from the intestines with your fingernails, you will see that they constitute the third tunic of the intestines. You will also learn from the origin of the mesentery how this tunic hangs from the **peritoneum** <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>. Once this tunic has been pulled away from the intestines, with a blunt razor...

...you will make a longitudinal incision along the length of the intestine, taking great care not to pierce all the way into its cavity. Furthermore, you will pull apart the edges of this incision with your fingernails, and without difficulty you will free the second tunic of the intestines from the innermost one, especially if you attempt this near the **rectum**. Indeed, in the small intestines, the tunics do not come into view so easily; however, there is nothing to prevent you from examining them there as well, specifically where you have cut the intestines crosswise near the b attachments. In such a section, the tunics of the intestines—and especially the rectum—usually separate from one another. Indeed, it is now permissible to divide the intestines in whatever way and wherever it c seems best. However you choose to do it, the **ventriculus** must now be approached in the sequence of the dissection. When I must linger longer in a dissection for the d convenience of the spectators, I am forced to remove it along with the spleen, though I first carefully examine the nerves inserted into its higher orifice. In other cases, I have been accustomed to leave the stomach in place until I have finished almost all the organs contained in the thorax; in this way, the orifice of the stomach and its nerves can be more conveniently examined together with the e **stomachus** <note>In Vesalius's terminology, *stomachus* refers to the esophagus or gullet, while *ventriculus* refers to the stomach itself.</note>. <margin>*The capacity of the stomach and the examination of its tunics.*</margin>
<margin>i around G in figs. 14, 15. k as in the 4th plate of fig. 19. l as in fig. 17. m as in fig. 16. n fig. 15 R.</margin>
...that the sequence ⁱ is maintained, even if I were to say nothing, I believe no one would doubt. Furthermore, so that you may observe the substance of the spleen <note>original: "lienis"</note> ⁱ, you will make several ᵏ incisions into it: and with it compressed between two boards, you will separate its substance from the vessels inserted into it in certain places, by which method you will see some vessels alone and stripped of the flesh of the spleen. Truly, the stomach <note>original: "Ventriculum"</note> is to be washed, and then given to be inflated like a bladder, so that you may perceive its capacity, which is indeed as large as possible: and you should examine its tunics, as we instructed to be done in the intestines.¹ And afterwards ᵐ you should turn it inside out, and see the insertion of the bile duct <note>original: "bilis meatus"</note> ⁿ into the intestine, which still hangs from the stomach. Furthermore, when you have removed all these things, if any blood has flowed elsewhere and obscured those things which still remain in the belly, it must be washed out once or twice with a sponge soaked in plenty of water rather than vinegar. For if you wipe it with linen, you will cause more harm by staining it. For usually the small channels of the vessels, covered with much fat and small membranes, are found with great difficulty in a human, and more so if they are obscured by blood. Therefore, once the blood is washed away and those things which still remain in the belly are inspected in passing without dissection, you shall not yet approach the liver <note>original: "iecur"</note>: rather, for the sake of observing the origin of the <term>vena cava<note>The largest vein in the body, which returns blood from the abdomen to the heart.</note></term>, you will preserve it whole for a while, until you are about to deal with the dissection of the heart together.

<margin>*How the seminal arteries are to be observed at their origin.*</margin>
<margin>o fig. 20 h above Q. fig. 21 g, f through P. p fig. 20 h, i. fig. 25 g, h. q fig. 20 f. fig. 25 d. r fig. 20 k.</margin>
Now, however, around the region of the vertebrae in the loins, you will first attempt to tear away the small membranes—which constitute something like a second tunic for the vena cava stretched out here—all the way to the <term>sacrum<note>The triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note></term>: taking diligent care that you do not at the same time take away the right seminal ᵒ artery, which crosses the body of the vena cava, along with the membranes. For this is thin and white in the manner of a membrane, and in a human is covered with much fat. Wherefore, you will do quite conveniently if, before you approach any of those things which still remain in the belly, you search for the ᵖ seminal arteries: and then, in the management of the remaining parts, take care that they are not harmed. To perform this more accurately, you will apply your mind to the ͧ right seminal vein, which arises from the vena cava: then also to the ʳ origin of the artery which goes to the lower part of the <term>mesentery<note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note></term>. Between these two organs, partly ascending and partly descending, you will strive with a blunt knife to separate the vena cava on its left side from the <term>great artery<note>The aorta, the main artery of the body.</note></term>, having dissected the membranous fibers through whose intervention these vessels are joined. In this work, therefore, the roots of the two seminal arteries will come into view, which will show where the arteries extend, if only you diligently free them from their origin out of the small membranes in which they are involved, all the way to the seminal veins, using no force in pulling.

<margin>*The course of the vena cava and the great artery in the breadth of the peritoneum, and how they should be observed.*</margin>
<margin>s fig. 20 X, Y. t fig. 20 d, b; figs. 22, 23 m; figs. 11, 25.</margin>
When you have performed these things, and the vena cava and the great artery have been uncovered from the small membranes by which they are covered here and there so that they may come more conveniently into view, you will examine the branches which they send out in their very course through the belly, ˢ first weighing those which are presented to the fatty tunics or membranes of the kidneys: and then the ᵗ beginnings of the offshoots of the vena cava carrying the serous blood to the kidneys. When you have found these, you will uncover the offshoot of the vena cava proper to the right kidney from its own small membranes: and then, tearing the fatty membrane of that kidney with your fingernails, you will diligently examine in what way the kidney is ᵘ wrapped in it.

<margin>*Examination of the tunics of the kidneys and their whole structure.*</margin>
<margin>u Compare kidneys fig. 20 with fig. 22. x fig. 20 c, d; figs. 22, 23. y figs. 19, 25 d, c.</margin>

It will now be permissible to examine the whole nature of the kidney, or to leave the kidney until you have dissected certain other things. ʸ However you do it, now or later, the offshoots of the vena cava and the great artery must be intercepted with ligatures near the cavity of the right kidney: and then a straight incision must be made with a sharper razor along the length of the kidney on its convex side toward the cavity: and the kidney thus divided in two, it comes to be opened—

...to be cleared: and any blood that might be encountered should be washed away with a damp sponge. In this way, the nature of the kidney’s sinuses, and then the beginning of the <term>urinary passage</term> <note>The ureter, which carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.</note> in the kidney, will immediately present themselves—unless you have obtained an obese cadaver. For fat usually collects in the second sinus of the human kidney, acting as an impediment so that the nature of the sinuses is seen less completely by the one dissecting. Therefore, it will be worthwhile to first carefully examine the kidney of a dog or a goat, and from that, subsequently learn to recognize the human one. 

Therefore, having divided the kidney along its hump <note>original: "gibbum"; the convex outer margin</note> or its outer side, you will first search with your finger for the sides of the second sinus into which the urine is strained: and you will insert a stylus <note>A thin metal probe used by early anatomists to trace the path of vessels.</note> into the opening that appears in the middle of it (or rather, in the outer side of the first sinus, or the membrane of the kidney's body), which will be easily pushed forward into the urinary passage toward the bladder. 

Then, when you have observed the joining of the anterior branches of this body's membrane (or the first renal sinus) with the posterior branches—which is accomplished not far from the outer side of the kidney—so that you may discover the path of those branches, the remaining body of the first sinus, and the form and nature of the second sinus, you shall alternately close and reopen the kidney you have divided and opened by the aforementioned incision. In this way, the mutual joining of the branches just mentioned may appear more clearly. Then, you will insert a stylus into the second sinus: and when you have considered its form, you will cut away from the anterior branches of the first sinus that kidney substance which grows upon their posterior side. Furthermore, from the posterior branches, you will remove that substance which is continuous with their anterior side, so that the first sinus now appears whole. Into this, you can now insert styli to understand it even more exactly, and to marvel at how ridiculous the things produced until now by professors of Anatomy regarding the function of the kidneys have been. 

Furthermore, the tunic <note>The renal capsule.</note> investing the kidney, besides the fatty membrane, will easily be found if you pay attention to the lips of the incision made in the hump of the kidney. For that tunic usually recedes somewhat from the kidney substance there, and then is readily pulled away with the fingernails as far as the cavity <note>The renal hilum.</note> of the kidney; you can then see how this tunic arises from the additional membranes of the renal vein and artery.

Soon, with one leg of the cadaver left on the table and the other hanging down from it, you will tilt the cadaver on the table so that its <term>sacrum</term> <note>The large triangular bone at the base of the spine.</note> rests on the side of the table. Then, with the legs forcibly spread apart, you may separate the pubic bones from each other to the width of three or four fingers. You would act quite poorly if you were to remove a portion of the pubic bones; for this is done with great difficulty and, among other things, it would damage many muscles, and afterward the bones would be of no use for the preparation of a skeleton.

Therefore, once the cartilage of the pubic bones has been dissected and the bones themselves forcibly pulled apart, the<sup>u</sup> urinary passages [ureters] must first be freed from their membranes by which they are wrapped, starting from the kidneys, and led all the way to the body of the bladder. In this work, it is necessary for an assistant's hand to compress the bladder now to the right, now to the left, especially when you are investigating the path of the<sup>y</sup> <term>vena cava</term> and the <term>great artery</term> <note>The aorta.</note> in this region.

For that path must now be weighed: first the branches which the vein and artery extend to the muscles of the loins, the spine, the abdominal muscles, and the peritoneum. Furthermore, the branches of the vein and artery running out after their division over the sacrum will come into view if you always pay attention to their roots and follow their process and path with a duller knife, so as not to damage any of the branches. You will perform this with less trouble the more diligently you match our illustrations of the vessels to the work.

Examination of the origin of the peritoneum.

For in this way, you will learn the origin of the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>The serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen.</note>, and you will keep the muscles of this region, as well as the nerves seeking the leg (if perhaps you decide to approach them later), far more intact. The liver, however, as I have said before, must be preserved unharmed for as long as it takes for you to manage the heart and the organs of respiration. Meanwhile, when you remove the portion of the vena cava and the great artery located within the expanse of the peritoneum, and you no longer fear that anything will be obscured by the flow of blood, it will be permissible to open the vessels with a long section according to their course. This allows the thickness of their own substance to present itself (especially where they lead branches out to the kidneys and legs), and you may likewise weigh whether these contribute more to preventing the reflux of blood or to the strength of the vessels, as I believe. And this indeed is the method of managing the organs of nutrition and generation in a man.

...you should examine whether [the vessels] also swell together. Having neglected nothing, you will attempt a light incision with a razor along the length of the **uterus**ᶠ, taking care not to let it sink deeper than the thickness of the uterus itself. After this, you will manage two other incisions, one on each side, forming right angles with that long one. Gripping the lips of the incisions with your fingernails, pull them moderately apart from each other. You must then consider to which part of the uterus the **fetus** is chiefly attached, so that you may tear the uterine tunic away from that thick substance—which we have compared to the structure of the **spleen** <note>Vesalius refers here to the placenta, which he and his contemporaries thought resembled the texture of the spleen.</note>—by breaking the mouths of the veins and arteries that extend from the uterus into that substance. As soon as you have learned the size of this substance and its connection to the uterus during this separation, you shall remove it from the uterus along with the fetus and its membranes, placing everything together into a basin. Then, by pouring water over it, the greenish and dark blood and fluid can flow away and be washed off; much of this flows out from that substance due to the now broken and torn vessels, especially when you squeeze it and strive to break it away from the outer membrane of the fetus. For that substance must be examined with no small care, and the series of vessels through it must be observed. When you have done this, and have scraped that substance away from the outer membrane of the fetus with knives as best you can, place the fetus with its membranes upon the table. Consider the shape and substance of this outer membrane <note>The chorion.</note>. The **urine** <note>Vesalius is referring to the fluid contained in the allantois, which was thought to collect fetal urine.</note> that floats within it should be let out through a hole or an incision by which you pierce the membrane. Then, with the membrane itself torn open and turned inside out, its inner surface comes into view, and its connection with the inner and softer membrane of the fetus is revealed—a connection which is achieved only at a single point, as it were, through the **umbilical vessels**. 

Furthermore, while you are removing the outer membrane of the fetus from the inner one, and examining the place where the urine—which is collected between his two membranes for as long as the fetus is carried in the womb—is held, consider carefully whether it flows everywhere at random between the membranes, or whether the duct leading the fetus's urine through the navel is dilated into a kind of very long bladder, as we find is usually done by wise Nature. This consists of an exceedingly soft and thin membrane, beset with tiny veins, and is enclosed between the two true membranes of the fetus. It has been compared to a **sausage** <note>original: "farcimini"; this is the allantois, named from the Greek 'allos' for sausage.</note> by professors of dissection who are not of the common sort, and is recorded in the class of fetal membranes, even though it covers very little. Having weighed these matters not in passing, you will pierce the inner membrane of the fetus <note>The amnion.</note>. For that now presents itself entirely; and since it is exceedingly transparent, it readily offers for your view the fetus contained within it and the **sweat** <note>original: "sudorem"; Vesalius refers to the amniotic fluid as "sweat."</note> floating around it. It is to be divided, therefore, by a long incision. Once the fetus is extracted and the sweat let out, the membrane should be turned inside out, so that you may finally look upon its structure from every part and skillfully approach the umbilical vessels. I mean the vein, and the arteries, and the duct by which the fetus's urine is purged: these must be accurately separated from one another, and again referred back to

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK V.

However, since we rarely ever obtain pregnant women for public anatomy, we demonstrate this dissection—which specifically concerns the fetus—privately. For the schools, we routinely propose this using brute animals; just as, when following Galen, we use those animals for the entire dissection which we believe his writings primarily match. And so, for the <margin>Examination of the **acetabula**.</margin> examination of the **acetabula** <term>acetabula: literally "vinegar cups," these are the cup-like attachment points of the placenta (cotyledons) found in ruminants like sheep. Galen, following animal dissections, incorrectly assumed these were present in humans.</term>, when you handle a woman's uterus of whatever kind, a goat or a sheep that is gathered to have conceived not long ago should be prepared for the work. Once its uterus is dissected, those cavities will appear which the Ancients rightly first called by the name "acetabula" <note>original: *acetabulorum*</note>. Indeed, those small bumps from which those cavities arise should be sought in the uterus of a non-pregnant cow or goat, opened in whatever manner. The investigation of the vessels passing from the uterus into the **afterbirth** <term>afterbirth: the placenta and membranes; Vesalius uses the term *secundina*.</term>, and the flesh that grows around them, will be correctly attempted in animals that are near to giving birth, and also in women. The difference I have proposed in this part will be sought with the same approach we used for managing the pregnant woman. Thus, we have now completed the method of dissecting the parts described in this book, and we have left the body we primarily focused on in that sequence of dissection: so that for the demonstration of the remaining parts, which we have not yet fully inspected, it will by no means be useless to proceed as we

### THE INDEX OF LABELS
->*FOR THE FIRST FIGURE.*<-

*THE PRESENT figure displays as much of a person lying on their back from the left side as we judged sufficient to show the site of the thorax <note>original: "thoracis" — the chest cavity.</note>. Therefore, from the internal area and the sides of the thorax, and then from a certain region of the neck, we have first removed the skin; and then, after cutting away the muscles covering the ribs, we have freed the bones of the ribs from their cartilages together with the breastbone <note>original: "pectoris osse" — the sternum.</note>. After the rib bones were broken (as is done in the second [book/procedure]), we pulled the rib cartilages upward toward the right side so that the cavity of the thorax, and the membranes partitioning it, and the lung, and the other things might come into view, which will now be indicated in the Index of Labels.*

A,A *Indicates the cartilages of the ribs on the left side, which, along with the breastbone, have been pulled toward the right and upward.*
B,B *Intercostal muscles, occupying the intervals between the cartilages.*
C,C *The bones of the ribs separated from their cartilages.*
D,D *Intercostal muscles, filling the intervals between the bones.*
E *The **clavicle** <term>clavicle: the collarbone.</term> is seen here bare, yet still preserved in its place.*
F *The series of veins, arteries, and nerves creeping into the **axilla** <term>axilla: the armpit.</term>.*
G *The external **jugular vein** <note>original: "exterior iugularis uena"</note> which meets the dissector here immediately upon the removal of the skin.*
H,H *The membrane dividing the thoracic cavity on the left side <term>pleura: specifically referring here to the mediastinal pleura that forms the central partition of the chest.</term>, its left surface visible here; L, M, N, and O also indicate this.*
I,I *The **diaphragm** <term>diaphragm: Vesalius calls this the "septum transversum" or transverse partition.</term>, appearing here by that surface which faces the left part of the thoracic cavity.*
K *The site where the left of the membranes dividing the thorax is joined to the diaphragm.*
L *This protruding site bulges so far to the left here because of the heart. For the heart, along with its **envelope** <term>pericardium: the protective sac surrounding the heart.</term>, contained between the membranes dividing the thorax, extends much further to the left than to the right. It is primarily because of this bulge that we have depicted the present figure from the left rather than the right side.*

## THE THIRD FIGURE OF THE SIXTH BOOK.

<image-desc>Anatomical woodcut illustration of the human heart and lungs removed from the chest cavity. The lungs surround the heart, and various structures are labeled with Latin letters (A through Q) for reference in the following index.</image-desc>

## Index of the THIRD FIGURE and its characters.

Since the two preceding figures abundantly indicate the position of the heart and lung, we have drawn the present figure (as well as all subsequent ones) as if torn out from the cavity of the chest; lest, if we had added the trunk of the body to each figure, the labor would be rendered more troublesome in vain. Therefore, the third figure, the membranes dividing the chest having been removed, contains the heart contained in its own envelope <note>the pericardium</note>, together with the lung and a portion of the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note>, to which in humans the envelope of the heart is joined with great breadth.
<margin>A</margin> Here we have cut through a portion of the great vein <note>original: "uenae cauae" — the vena cava</note> ascending upward, and the great artery <note>original: "magnam arteriam" — the aorta</note>, having preserved only as much of the heart's vessels as suffices to show the origin of its envelope.
<margin>B</margin> For where I have written B here, there the envelope <note>pericardium</note> is most firmly attached to the great vein, the great artery, and the arterial vein <note>original: "uenae arteriali" — the pulmonary artery</note>, departing from those vessels just as from the heart in that whole interval that extends from B to C.
<margin>C</margin> For C indicates the site or region of the base of the heart.
<margin>D, E, F</margin> The anterior site of the heart’s envelope, reflecting the shape of the heart which is not unlike a pinecone. For D and E mark the base, while F marks the point <note>the apex</note>.

### characters.

*THE PRESENT figure shows the heart turned toward the right side in such a way as the preceding figure showed it reflected toward the left side. ### INDEX TO THE SEVENTH FIGURE, AND ITS
### characters.

*This figure shows the heart freed from the lung and the diaphragm <note>original: "septo transuerso"; literally the 'transverse septum', the historical term for the diaphragm</note>. * **A** Part of the vena cava, passing through the diaphragm.*
* **B** Part of the vena cava, seeking the throat.*

* **D, E** The orifices of the ascending and descending parts of the vena cava.*

* **G** The beginning of the coronary vein.*
* **H, H, H** The protruding circle in the orifice of the vena cava.*
* **K, L, M** Three small membranes <note>the tricuspid valve leaflets</note>, placed over the orifice of the vena cava.*
* **N, N** Fibers <note>the chordae tendineae, or 'heart strings'</note> led from the lower part of the membranes of the vena cava's orifice, downward to the sides and apex of the right ventricle.*
* **O, O** Fleshy parts <note>the trabeculae carneae</note>, which embrace the fibers just mentioned and express a rounded shape.*
* **P** Here the cavity of the right ventricle looks toward the orifice of the arterial vein <note>original: "uenae arterialis"; the pulmonary artery. Vesalius used this term because the vessel has the structure of an artery but was thought to carry 'nutritive' blood like a vein</note>.*
* **Q, R** The thickness of the substance constituting the right ventricle of the heart.*

D *The <term>pulmonary vein</term> <note>original: "Venalis arteria," or "venous artery"; so named because it has the thin wall of a vein but carries "spirituous" blood like an artery</note>.*

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE PARTS OF THE BODY WHICH THE CREATOR OF ALL THINGS FASHIONED TO REPLENISH THE AIRY SUBSTANCE, AND WHICH SERVE SPECIFICALLY THE VITAL SPIRIT. Chapter I.

<margin>*Argument of the sixth book.*</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative initial "Q" depicts an anatomical demonstration in a classical setting. A group of men, dressed in robes, are gathered around a table where a body lies. One figure appears to be pointing toward the chest or abdomen, illustrating the theme of the upcoming chapters on the internal organs of the thorax.</image-desc> HOW skillfully the Architect of our body constructed the organs of food and drink—and for the sake of their function and action, bestowed upon each its number, position, shape, connection, and finally its substance—the fifth book has explained in no superficial detail. Accordingly, the present book will opportunely encompass the instruments that restore the <term>airy substance</term> <note>original: "aeream substantiam"; the vital air or pneuma thought to be essential for life</note>—which is continually being depleted—and those that replenish the <term>innate heat</term> <note>original: "calorem innatum"; the internal biological fire that ancient physicians believed was centered in the heart</note>. Moreover, I believe it is clear to anyone that all the parts serving respiration and the pulse should be placed in this class; and I think the purpose of respiration and the pulse is also now hidden from no one (at least as far as it is granted to us to know this, given that we are ignorant of the substance of the soul). Therefore, we must not dwell for long now on explaining their use, especially since I have already discussed several matters concerning the nature and use of respiration and the pulse in the second book, where the muscles serving respiration were presented, and in the third, while the function of the arteries was being reviewed. For I did not think it necessary to undertake a complete treatment of these matters either there or here, because Galen has abundantly shown us that this requires many specialized and individual books.

<margin>*Which air is processed in respiration, and an enumeration of the functions of the heart and the parts serving it. Book 2 of "The Art of Healing, to Glaucon."*</margin> Therefore, when we inhale—provided all parts of the body are in their natural state and the quality of the innate heat (which Galen taught was the soul itself, or at least its primary instrument) has not been increased by any circumstance—we then draw in air through the nostrils by the benefit of the expanded thorax. A portion of this air is taken up toward the brain, both through the <margin>a See fig. 1, chap. 6, Book 1, A, A, B.</margin> openings in the bone [the ethmoid] described in the eighth chapter (upon which the parts of the olfactory organs primarily rest) and also—and more significantly—through the <margin>b Fig. 12, Book 7, C, D and fig. 13, L, L.</margin> passages that lead phlegm from the brain to the throat, in order to nourish the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum animalem"; the "spirit" responsible for sensation and movement, thought to be refined in the brain from the vital spirit</note> to some extent. But the more abundant portion of the air drawn through the nostrils is led from the large nasal <margin>c Fig. 3, chap. 12, Book 1, characters placed at the sides of M.</margin> openings into the throat, following the posterior seat of the <term>uvula</term> <note>original: "gargarij"; the region of the soft palate and throat</note>, being somewhat tempered by it. From here <margin>d Fig. 2, chap. 12, Book 1, u, o.</margin> it is carried into the larynx, and then through the whole <term>trachea</term> <note>original: "asperam arteriam", literally the "rough artery"</note> into its frequent branches propagated through the substance of the lung. After the air has been prepared in a way for the heart by this substance, it is drawn from the branches of the trachea by the small offshoots of the <term>pulmonary vein</term> <note>original: "uenalis arteriæ", literally "venous artery"; in Vesalius's time, this vessel (our pulmonary vein) was called an artery because it carried "spirituous" blood, but "venous" because of its thin walls</note>, which are also woven into the lung. And having been brought into the <margin>h Opened in fig. 9 and 10.</margin> left ventricle of the heart, it is mixed with the very thin and extremely hot blood that the heart contains therein. By the quality of this air, the quality of the heat contained in this <margin>f In the figure expressing the trachea, chap. 38, Book 1, and here fig. 6, Y.</margin> ventricle is ventilated; moreover, the substance of the heat (which consists of air and the exhalation of the spirituous blood) is nourished by the substance of that air. But whatever <term>soot-like waste</term> <note>original: "fuliginosum"; "smoky" or "sooty" byproducts that Galenic physiology believed were produced by the heart's "combustion"</note> is gathered from this peculiar function of the heart is sent back <margin>g Fig. 2, chap. 15, Book 3 and here fig. 6, G, and fig. 12, D.</margin> through the pulmonary vein into the lung; and being taken up by the branches of the trachea, together with the remaining air (which the offshoots of the pulmonary vein had not drawn in as being unsuitable for the heart), it is expelled once more through the trachea, the larynx, the throat, and the nostrils by the effort of the falling and contracting thorax. In this manner, indeed, the passage of air is completed in natural respiration; but in non-natural respiration, air is primarily drawn in and expelled through the mouth. We commonly call it "non-natural" respiration when we use it for the sake of a quality of innate heat other than the temperate one—as when that quality has increased in such a manner for some reason...

has increased so much that the air brought in through the nostrils does not suffice for a person: or whenever we attempt exhaling, speaking, and other things of that kind, to which respiration serves secondarily. From the substance of the air mixed in the left ventricle of the heart with the blood contained therein, the **vital spirit** <note>The "vital spirit" was believed to be a life-giving force created in the heart from air and blood.</note> is produced. From this ventricle, it is diffused into the **great artery** <note>The aorta.</note> together with the blood, which rushes in with force and heat. It is distributed through the whole body following the sequence of the arteries, and by its heat, it restores and tempers the **innate heat** <note>The internal biological fire thought to reside in the heart and limbs.</note> of each individual member, renewing what has been dispersed—not unlike how the substance of the limbs is restored by the blood brought through the veins. And just as respiration and the drawing of blood from the right ventricle of the heart into the left (however obscure this may be to us) serve the heart for the replenishment of the vital spirit and the innate heat, so by a similar logic, the matter conducted from the left ventricle of the heart through the arteries to the rest of the body restores the spirit and innate heat of the other parts. And for this reason, the use of the pulse and respiration is considered the same. For what inhalation provides for the matter stored in the left ventricle of the heart, the dilation of the arteries in the pulse provides to the remaining parts; exhalation, moreover, corresponds to the contraction of the arteries. But by which organs—constructed with the incredible and divine power of the Architect—all these things are accomplished, and by what reasoning these marvelous works of Nature are completed, I shall now strive to pursue in order. Meanwhile, I will not repeat those things which I have necessarily completed in the first book concerning the bones of the thorax, and the cartilages of the **rough artery** <note>The trachea.</note>, and in the second concerning their muscles, and in the third concerning the construction of the arteries. Therefore, just as in the preceding book we opportunely established the beginning of the discourse on the organs of food and drink from the peritoneum, so also here, we shall not without merit begin the instruments dedicated to nourishing the airy substance from the **membrane lining the ribs** <note>The pleura.</note>.

# ON THE MEMBRANE LINING THE
## ribs. Chapter II.

*SINCE the membrane lining the ribs is nothing other than a membrane, and cannot be so entirely freed from the ribs as the peritoneum can from the muscles joined to it, an image of it cannot be taken from elsewhere than from the figures expressing the internal amplitude and surface of the thorax: of which kind there occurs primarily the eighth table of muscles, and in the figures of the bones, those in which all the bones of the thorax are presented together, such as the first two of the nineteenth chapter of the first book, and the last three figures of the same book.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' set within a square frame, depicting two cherubic figures (putti) in a landscape with rocks and foliage. One cherub appears to be climbing or reaching toward a tree branch.</image-desc>

<margin>

The position of the **single membrane** or the one lining the ribs, called **hypezōkōs** <gloss>the under-girding membrane</gloss> by the Greeks, and commonly called the **pleura**, is indicated by its name. For this is stretched under all the ribs (except the twelfth, which is entirely occupied by the implantation of the **transverse septum** <note>The diaphragm.</note>) and also under the entire breastbone: and being drawn over the bodies of the vertebrae of the thorax and the upper part of the diaphragm facing the amplitude of the thorax, it acquires a shape and size corresponding to the entire cavity of the thorax. For it extends in its posterior part from the first vertebra of the thorax downward to the eleventh, in which region the part of the diaphragm that transmits the great artery is located. In its anterior part, however, it descends from the throat to the lowest seat of the breastbone, where the diaphragm originates. On the sides, indeed, it is carried from the first rib to the upper surface of the diaphragm, which we said faces the thoracic cavity, lining this entirely as well as the rest of the thoracic cavity. This membrane, therefore, just like the thoracic cavity, varies greatly in shape. For in its upper part, like the thorax, it is narrow and ends as if in a point; but in its lower part it is wider

Likewise, it is joined far more loosely to the fleshy part of the diaphragm than to the nervous <note>tendinous</note> part.

<margin>I have not illustrated these specifically anywhere, since the membrane is wrapped around the bone and should be understood from the outline of the bones.</margin>
This other membrane undergirding the ribs is the wrapping considered common to almost all bones: specifically, that membrane which we call <term>around-the-bone</term><note>original: "circumossalem"; the periosteum</note> because it surrounds the bone. For just as bones are encircled by a membrane of this kind, so too each individual rib possesses a membrane surrounding it in a circle, claiming nothing unique for itself compared to the membranes of other bones—even if Galen, meanwhile, seems to ascribe it only to the external part of the ribs, and not as something specific to each individual rib. For, being attached to the thorax on all sides, it consists of a substance that is both suitable for a wrapping and simultaneously light and flexible. Added to this is the fact that the present membrane adds effective

strength to the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note>, which is thin but strong. In the diaphragm itself, as well as in the intercostal muscles, it fully performs the role of the membrane surrounding the belly of the muscles—although the intercostal muscles also seem to be obscurely granted their own membrane, like other muscles. Furthermore, although the veins, arteries, and nerves with which this membrane is joined serve its nutrition and sensation, they are not present in such frequency primarily for its sake, but for the sake of the neighboring parts. Hence, a frequent inflammation arises in it, accompanied by great tension and <term>piercing pain</term><note>original: "punctiliq; cruciatu"</note>, just as occurs in the membranes of the brain.

The membrane that we described in the previous chapter lines and clothes the entire cavity of the chest. But the membranes which the Greeks call the *partitioners* <note>original Greek: διαφράττοντας (*diaphrattontas*)</note>, and we call the *chest-partitioning membranes* <note>original: "thoracem intersepientes"</note>, or commonly the *mediastinum*, divide that same cavity, distinguishing it into two main spaces, from which they rightly obtain their name. There are two of them in the middle of the chest, <margin>b 7th muscle table, A. & Figure 1, I, I.</margin> proceeding according to its length. For they reach from the throat to the entire length of the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: "septi transuersi"</note>, and they extend from the entire length of the breastbone to the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae. The size of the membranes is circumscribed by these boundaries, which resemble a triangle of sorts, formed by unequal and slanted sides or "ribs." For one side, which is shorter, is carried from the throat along the length of the breastbone to its <term>tip</term> <note>the xiphoid process</note> and its connection here with the diaphragm. The second side, longer than this one, proceeds from the throat along the path of the back to the eleventh thoracic vertebra. The third side, intermediate in length between the others, descends slanting from the breastbone along the length of the diaphragm to the back, joining the first two sides. These membranes vary greatly in their mutual distance and union. For along the length of the back, where they are joined to the vertebrae, they are contiguous with each other and form a very narrow cavity between them filled with membranous fibers. But where they are joined to the breastbone, in a human they are by no means contiguous, but are <margin>c Figure 6, 7 of Chapter 15, Book 1.</margin> <margin>d Figure 2, G, G are distant from I, I.</margin> distant from one another by the width of the breastbone. In the upper part, where the bone is widest and supports the collarbones and the first rib of each side, the membranes also stand quite far apart; nevertheless, they fill the entire cavity they contain between them with fibrous and membranous connections. But where the cartilage of the second rib is articulated to the breastbone—just as the <margin>e Figure 1, Chapter 15, Book 1, from D to h.</margin> breastbone has become narrower there—the right membrane is likewise less removed from the left in that spot. This separation of the membranes, gradually descending along the length of the breastbone, becomes more capacious and widens just as the bone itself does; so much so, that in a human, there arises as much distance between the membranes here as is seen in the width of the breastbone everywhere. Furthermore, where the membranes are joined to the <margin>f Figure 1, K.</margin> diaphragm, they stand furthest apart from each other, forming there a cavity as large as the width of the diaphragm’s membranous circle. <margin>g From n to l in the 7th muscle table.</margin> In humans, this cavity contains nothing at all except the <margin>h Figure 3, C, D, E, F, G. then what is held in B, B of Figure 4.</margin> envelope of the heart <note>the pericardium</note>, the heart itself, and the vena cava penetrating the diaphragm; and <margin>What is placed between the partitioning membranes.</margin> <margin>i Figures 14, 15 of Book 5, A, B, C, D. then T, V. and Figure 12 of this book, A, A.</margin> then, in the posterior and lower position, the <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "stomachum"; in this period, the term often referred to the gullet leading to the stomach</note>, rising here from the right region of the vertebral bodies and hurrying with the nerves attached to it through the diaphragm to the upper orifice of the stomach. In dogs, however, and other animals possessing a longer breastbone and a longer chest, this cavity is seen to be much more capacious and is not covered with any membranous fibers. Furthermore, its base is far distant from the tip of the heart’s envelope, quite unlike in humans. And in those said animals, it also contains a <term>lobe of the lung</term> <note>the intermediate or infracardiac lobe</note>, which, like a little cushion or a hand, supports the vena cava proceeding through here. <margin>k 7th muscle table, r.</margin> Humans lack this, since the vein is led by a shorter path in them than in those animals—although Galen, making a conjecture from monkeys and dogs, attributed this lobe even to humans. <margin>Origin.</margin> These membranes are slightly thinner than the membrane which lines the ribs <note>The pleura</note>; they arise from it at all those places where they are joined, and were created for this primary use: <margin>Use.</margin> to contain the pericardium, and thus the heart itself, in its proper place, so that it does not collapse downward or backward. For this—even if it has been little noticed by others—the dissection of both the living and the dead will show most clearly (if only you apply your mind), in whatever way you approach these membranes. Secondly, they assist in the safer passage of the vessels. And finally, from the entire volume of the chest, they create two cavities, a use which should by no means be considered the least. Since by this benefit, if one cavity of the chest is pierced by a wound and the lung in that place stops moving because of the air entering through the hole, the other cavity, still unharmed, serves the animal—as we frequently learn in wounded men and from the vivisection of brutes. Whether these organs resting in the chest cavity borrow their external tunics and coverings from these membranes or from the membrane lining the ribs, I do not think should be argued contentiously here; for clearly the same use—regarding the tunics of the vessels and their connections—should be attributed to both the partitioning membranes and the membrane lining the ribs. Furthermore, one should by no means investigate whether, besides the membranes surrounding each individual rib in a circle just like other bones, there is only one membrane lining the ribs inside the entire chest (as we described it), or whether two must be established: so that one would be the right, namely that which lines the right cavity of the chest along with the right partitioning membrane; and the other the left, which lines the chest cavity in the same way...

<margin>The number and position of the rough artery.</margin>
IN THE THIRD book, where <sup>a</sup> I described the sequence of the arteries originating from the heart, it was noted that the <sup>b</sup> artery whose history I am now undertaking was originally called "artery" by the ancients simply because it contains air. In the course of time, when the vessels that carry the vital spirit and blood rushing with force from the heart were no longer counted among the veins and were also given the name "artery," these latter vessels were called "smooth arteries," while this one was called the "rough artery" <note>original: "aspera arteria", now known as the trachea</note> because of the uneven substance of which it consists. And so, by that name, the rough artery is known to us to this day. Not only humans, but all animals that possess lungs, have only one; it extends downward from the throat like a long trunk and then spreads through the substance of the lungs in many branches. In the throat, <sup>c</sup> besides the two openings of the nostrils that lead into the space of the mouth, <sup>d</sup> two other openings correspond in the lower part of the throat. These are not side-by-side like the nostrils, but are seen one in front of the other. The rear one of these is the beginning of the <term>stomachus</term> <note>In Vesalius's time, "stomachus" referred to the esophagus or gullet</note>, the path that carries food and drink <sup>e</sup> from the mouth into the stomach. The front one is the beginning of the rough artery, which leads straight down from here without turning to the side, along the length of the neck to the fourth vertebra of the chest. Along its entire back side, it has the esophagus lying beneath it, which rests upon the bodies of the vertebrae and the first pair of muscles that move the back, without any other organ in between. Thus, the rough artery is separated from the vertebrae only by the thickness of the esophagus.

<margin>The bodies joined to it.</margin>
Furthermore, the same structures do not lie in front of the rough artery along its entire length. At its highest point, where it faces the space of the mouth, <sup>f</sup> the <term>hyoid bone</term> <note>original: "os υ", referring to the Greek letter upsilon because of the bone's shape</note> with its muscles and skin is placed before it. From here to the hollow of the throat and the higher part of the breastbone, besides the skin and the muscle beneath it formed from the fleshy membrane, a * cleft muscle is stretched over the rough artery. This muscle arises from the breastbone and is inserted into the front part of the hyoid bone. Then <sup>h</sup> two other muscles, also reaching from the breastbone to the lower part of the <term>thyroid cartilage</term> <note>original: "scutiformis cartilaginis", meaning shield-shaped</note>, lie very close to the artery here. Where it enters the chest, the beginnings of the <sup>i</sup> muscles led from the collarbones and breastbone to the <sup>k</sup> mastoid processes in the head are also placed before it like defenses. In the throat, <sup>l</sup> a gland that serves the distribution of the vessels there, and the vessels themselves, cover it beyond the breastbone. What is closest to the body of the artery in the throat is indeed glandular, and a little lower in the cavity of the chest <sup>m</sup> is a branch of the great artery <note>the aorta</note>, distributed mainly into the <sup>n</sup> <term>carotid arteries</term> <note>original: "soporalis arterias", the "sleep-inducing" arteries</note>. These, together with the <sup>o</sup> <term>vagus nerves</term> <note>original: "sexti paris cerebri nervis", the sixth pair of cranial nerves in the system Vesalius followed</note> and the <sup>p</sup> internal jugular veins, are closely associated with the sides of the rough artery. Then, at the base of the larynx on both sides, a <sup>q</sup> glandular but reddish body (which we will describe more clearly later) <sup>r</sup> is attached to it...

<margin>The form of the rough artery.</margin>
...is attached to it. As soon as the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: *aspera arteria*; the Renaissance term for the trachea or windpipe, so named to distinguish it from the "smooth" blood-carrying arteries</note> descends as far as the body of the fourth thoracic vertebra, it splits into two equal trunks. It extends one to the right lobes of the lung and the other to the left. These trunks, embraced on all sides by the substance of the lung, occupy the same position as the lung itself. For this reason, you could hardly compare the image of the rough artery more accurately to anything than to a tree stripped of its roots, whose trunk is first divided into two branches, and these in turn are spread out into innumerable offshoots. The beginning of this trunk corresponds to the <term>larynx</term> <note>the voice box</note>; the entire trunk itself corresponds to the remaining part of the rough artery extending from the larynx down to the fourth thoracic vertebra; while the branches and their countless offshoots correspond to the passages of the artery led into the lungs. Just as the start of a tree trunk growing out from the roots is seen to be varied and not of a uniform shape on all sides, so too the larynx possesses a conflicting and dissimilar shape throughout.

<margin>

Depending on whether you imagine the lid of the larynx <note>the epiglottis</note> to be depressed or erect in its upper part, it is either sharp or depressed and blunt. The front part of the larynx, as well as the sides, show the front surface of its first cartilage <note>the thyroid cartilage, commonly known as the "Adam's Apple"</note>, which bulges in the middle along its length, and from there proceeds outward at the sides obliquely toward the back. In addition to this, just as the upper part of this cartilage is far larger than the lower, so also the upper seat of the larynx is seen here to be wider than the lower.

Indeed, the lowest part of the larynx, which is formed by its second cartilage <note>the cricoid cartilage</note>, equals the size and width of the rest of the rough artery's trunk. The posterior region of the larynx is somewhat flat in its primary area, because of the notable extension of the sides of the first cartilage toward the back. Otherwise, this region would be a little less than perfectly round because of the second and third cartilages of the larynx; as indeed the lowest part of the posterior region is, because the second cartilage proceeds lower than the first. Furthermore, in the posterior area, as the third cartilage is drawn into the cavity of the larynx or extended backward, its higher peaks project more toward the inside or outside, changing the shape of the larynx. For the rest, the trunk of the rough artery (as is usually the case with the trunks of trees) is similar to itself until the distribution of the branches, though not perfectly so. For when the artery collapses and is not distended by air, it is round in its front part, but appears a little wider and flatter, being led in a circular fashion at the sides so that it becomes narrower as it proceeds toward the back. Thus, the posterior area is narrower than the front and flat, and is somewhat circularly pressed in toward its internal space. But when the artery is distended, its posterior part becomes equally as wide as the front, or even wider, and swelling toward the back, it becomes circular and round like the front. All the offshoots of the rough artery scattered into the lung maintain this same form; they are likened to the branches of trees, and running out into all parts of the lung with very frequent buds (as has already been said), they form an entire series corresponding to that image.

<margin>The nature of the artery's outer surface.</margin>
Aside from the aforementioned surface of the larynx, the external surface of the rough artery is seen to be uneven, but proceeding in an ordered series. When the artery is distended with air, it is smooth at the back like a continuous membrane, but uneven at the sides and the front region: this is because the membrane that sits between the cartilages then bulges out more than the cartilages themselves. Conversely, when it collapses and becomes loose, the cartilages protrude more than the membranous substance.

<margin>Connection of the rough artery.</margin>
Additionally, like the membranes that grow together with other parts, the outer surface of the artery is rough. In its posterior area, it is joined to the <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: *stomachus*; in this context, Vesalius refers to the gullet or esophagus, which lies directly behind the trachea</note> by several fibrous connections. The upper region of the larynx, since it shares a common tunic with the esophagus, is very strongly joined to it by the benefit of that tunic; just as the larynx is also most firmly joined to the esophagus by the muscles...

<margin>The nature of the internal surface of the rough artery.</margin> 
Moreover, although the interior surface is always uneven because of the protrusion of the cartilages, it is nevertheless smooth, and as if bathed in an oily humor, nor does it exist as rough with any fibrous expansions. And such also, as far as smoothness is concerned, <margin>h Figures 11, 12, 13, chapter 21, book 2, the indices of which you will look at.</margin><sup>h</sup> is the internal surface of the larynx: although in the meantime it is neither circular nor rounded, nor does it meet without bumps. For in the lowest part, however much it is narrowed or pulled apart, it turns out perfectly circular and open in the same way, because of the perfect circle which the second cartilage forms. But in the middle, when it is narrowed, it closes completely, not indeed in the manner of a circular orifice, but like a straight line or fissure stretched from the front parts to the back: which, if it is divided and opened, is made gradually wider from the front part to the back, until the entire interior surface of the larynx is seen as somewhat circular and rounded inside. When this fissure is narrowed and closes, and the lower part of the larynx itself necessarily remains rounded, a pit is seen on both sides of the flanks of that fissure, rising in a way higher than the surface of the fissure, whence also here a "horned" surface rises up under the fissure. But the surface of the larynx consisting above the fissure, according to how this is either opened or compressed, also differs, yet it is never entirely circular, but is narrowed more or less from the back parts to the front according to the compression of the fissure. The lower surface of the lid of the larynx <note>The epiglottis</note> is seen to be concave, but the upper is convex. 

But lest I delay longer in explaining the form of the rough artery, its substance must be approached, which for the most part is <margin>The substance of the rough artery, and by which cartilages it is constituted.</margin> membranous and cartilaginous. <margin>i If it seems good, look at the figures of chapter 38, book 2 in order.</margin><sup>i</sup> For the larynx (as was explained not superficially in the first book) consists of three cartilages. Namely, the first, which those skilled in dissections have compared to a <term>shield</term> <note>The thyroid cartilage</note>; the second, which because it lacks a name, they called <term>as if without a name</term> <note>The cricoid cartilage; *innominata* in Latin</note>; the third, which is twin, and which they judged to correspond to the orifices of vessels with which we pour water for those about to wash their hands <note>The arytenoid cartilages, named for their resemblance to a pitcher or ladle</note>. 

Then the lid of the larynx also enters into its conformation, constituted from a cartilaginous, membranous, and fatty substance (just as the upper part of the third cartilage). The remaining body of the rough artery is shaped by innumerable cartilages, each of which corresponds to a circle from which a fourth part has been cut away. For they approach closer to the figure of a perfect ring or circle than has seemed to some, reflecting the circumference of the bodies of the thoracic and lumbar <margin>k Compare figures 14 & 15, chapter 38, book 2 with the lower L, L, in the figure of chapter 14, book 1.</margin><sup>k</sup> vertebrae. These cartilages are called <term>sigmoidal</term> <note>original Greek: *σιγμοειδέας*; shaped like the Greek letter sigma, which in some ancient scripts resembled a C-shape</note> by the Greeks, and in addition called <term>bronchia</term> <note>original Greek: *βρόγχia*</note> by those to whom the entire rough artery was named <term>bronchos</term> <note>original Greek: *βρόγχος*</note>; in their small circle, they imitate the figure of an artery: however, their body is not rounded, but in a way quadrangular, meanwhile much wider than it is thick. Then they do not keep the same thickness through the whole body: for they are thicker in the middle than at the ends, by which they are gradually thinned, and degenerate as if into a membrane. Nor should anyone think, deceived by the opinion of those who handed down that the cartilages only depart from the figure of a perfect circle so that the artery would not compress the <term>stomach</term> <note>The esophagus</note> more than is fair, that they keep this form and appearance only in the trunk of the artery itself, but in the substance of the lung they are made into complete circles. <margin>l This is seen in figures 1, 2, chapter 38, book 2.</margin><sup>l</sup> Since in the substance of the lung they behave just as in the trunk, placed in the artery in a continuous series and equally distant from each other, and finally from this part presenting a certain appearance of the structure <margin>m Compare the said figures with R, R and L, L in the figure of chapter 14, book 1.</margin><sup>m</sup> of the bones of the back, in which cartilages indeed come to the bones...

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VI

<margin>*How the cartilages of the rough artery are joined together.*</margin>
<margin>n <note>original: "Quia eiusmodi mēbranarū..."</note> *Because the description of these membranes and other thin tunics is derived from the account of the whole organ, and since they are only membranes, we have not depicted them anywhere.*</margin>
...are to be compared, and the membranes occurring between them to the cartilaginous ligaments that bind the bodies of the vertebrae together. These <term>cartilages</term> <note>the rings of the trachea</note> are joined, first, by the intervention of the specific membrane of each cartilage. For just as almost all bones—and even the cartilages of the <term>larynx</term> <note>the voice box</note>—are covered by a certain membrane called the "periosteum" <note>original: *circumossalis*; literally "around the bone"</note> because it is the envelope of the bones, so too the circular cartilages of the rough artery <note>the trachea</note> are covered by a similar membrane. This membrane, extending processes from its lower and higher parts, connects the cartilages to one another through their intervention, forming as it were a membranous bond between two facing cartilages. Nor does such a bond arise only between the cartilages where they are equally distant from one another; rather, membranous processes are also led out from the ends and thinnest parts of the cartilages, binding those parts together so that the cartilages, along with the ligament formed from those processes, create what is essentially a continuous circle. To these cartilages and membranes, two other membranes are added, which are not undeservedly called "tunics" <note>layers or coats</note> based on their function.

<margin>*The outer of the two tunics of the rough artery.*</margin>
<margin>*The inner tunic.*</margin>
One of these indeed embraces the external surface of the artery on all sides, being very firmly attached to those membranous bonds of the cartilages. This tunic is thin, equal to those membranes that the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> and the membrane surrounding the ribs <note>the pleura</note> provide to the vessels attached to them. Through the intervention of this tunic, the artery is bound to neighboring parts; it especially carries most securely the <term>recurrent nerves</term> <note>the laryngeal nerves, which control the voice</note> which are in a sense proper to the artery, and it receives the small veins that entwine the larynx and the trunk of the artery. The other tunic of the artery lines the internal seat of the whole artery and contributes greatly to the strength of the connection of the cartilages to one another. It is much thicker and stronger than the outer tunic, worthy of note in many respects, and smooth on its inner surface, being as it were smeared with an oily humor <note>mucus</note>, although it does not maintain the same thickness everywhere. Since it is common to the tongue, the lips, the palate, and finally the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: *stomachus*; here referring to the esophagus or gullet</note> itself, it becomes thicker in the cavity of the larynx and is covered with fat between the cartilages and its own external surface. <margin>o *Figure 11, chapter 21, book 2.*</margin> Where the fissure of the <term>glottis</term> <note>original: *rima lingulæ*; literally "fissure of the little tongue"</note> or of the larynx closes, this tunic becomes calloused on both sides and changes its color along with its substance; for as it becomes more calloused here, as if by frequent compression while we hold our breath, so also it becomes more white and shining in that spot. In the part where the inner tunic lines the branches of the artery diffused through the substance of the lung, it is seen to be far thinner than in the larynx; in the trunk of the artery, however, it is of a medium thickness. Nevertheless, we have learned from dissection that throughout the cavity of the entire artery, this tunic is in a way interwoven with straight fibers.

<margin>*Glands attached to the root of the larynx.*</margin>
<margin>*Muscles of the larynx.*</margin>

<margin>*The use of the rough artery, and the reason for its construction and position.*</margin>
Dissection also shows individual glands attached to either side of the root of the larynx; these are large, quite spongy, and almost the color of flesh, but more blackish and covered with quite conspicuous veins. We mentioned these also in the second book when we were following the muscles of the larynx, and they need not be repeated here, lest I be too wordy. Thus the rough artery, being entirely devoid of blood, primarily serves the living creature for the passage or duct of air in respiration; secondly, it is easily the principal organ of the voice. All its construction is suited to these uses. For it leads the air, drawn in through either the nostrils or the mouth, straight from the throat into the lung, distributing it through the lung’s body in such a numerous series of branches that the substance of the lung may promptly alter it and make it fit for the duties of the heart. Then the rough artery again conveniently returns all the air useless to the heart, together with its smoky wastes <note>original: *fuliginosis recrementis*; the waste products of "cardiac combustion"</note>, through the mouth or nostrils during exhalation, just as it is currently positioned. For this function, it was certainly beneficial for it to be built like a membranous passage, which could easily fall inward when empty and be distended again when filled. Which
