<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical composition of the "rough artery" (the trachea). Having previously discussed the membranes and tunics that bind the cartilaginous rings, Vesalius now explains the functional necessity of both the flexible membranes and the rigid cartilages for the dual purposes of breathing and speech.</meta>

# ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE HUMAN BODY]

<margin>The rough artery had to be constructed from a membranous substance.</margin>
...for unless it were to be greatly filled by the <term>avoidance of a vacuum</term> <note>original: *fuga vacui*; the Aristotelian principle that nature abhors a vacuum, which Vesalius uses to explain how air rushes into the expanding lungs</note>, and in turn emptied solely by the force of compression, it must be suited to be distended and compressed. Since it is granted by everyone that the inspiration or attraction of air happens by the benefit of the dilated lung, and the dilation of the lung is considered nothing other than the distension of its vessels—not simply all of them, but primarily the branches of the <term>rough artery</term> <note>the trachea</note>—and since it is certain that expiration occurs whenever the lung is drawn back into itself, collapses, and is narrowed (and by that means expresses and drives out the air contained in its cavity, namely in the branches of the rough artery), it is easy for anyone to reason that the rough artery had to be fashioned so that it could be both distended during inspiration and compressed again during expiration. 

Indeed, for these functions, it would have been enough to construct this artery from some membranous and nervous substance, like the stomach, the esophagus, or the arteries and veins themselves; nor would it have been necessary to gift it with those cartilages in which it abounds. So much so, in fact, that the Creator of things might now seem to have granted it any cartilage in vain, as far as the attraction of air by reason of a vacuum, the distension of the rough artery from that air, and the expiration of air due to the narrowed and compressed rough artery are concerned. 

Far from showing the Creator's industry, those who imagined that all the branches of the rough artery distributed within the substance of the lung were fashioned from cartilages forming perfect circles have merely invented a fiction; they described a different construction for the artery there than the one stretched before the esophagus. They did not consider that if the rough artery were built in such a way, the lung could be neither distended nor relaxed so conveniently—or at least the branches of the rough artery could only be extended or shortened in length, but could not increase in width. 

No less are they hallucinating who assert that this artery was formed to be always open and gaping, rather than collapsing in the manner of the esophagus, so that the entry and exit of air might be freer. For besides being ignorant of the narrowing and dilation of the <term>larynx</term> <note>the voice box</note>, they have reached such a level of ignorance that they do not realize that if the rough artery and all its offshoots were always equally tense and open, the lung would never be constricted or dilated, and nothing would be attracted into the rough artery by the avoidance of a vacuum (since it would not have previously collapsed). They ought to have noticed this from <term>bellows</term> <note>original: *follibus*</note>, in which a far different mechanism is applied to the part that yields air than to the rest of the bellows' volume. For craftsmen make the latter part ready to be distended and compressed so it can be filled and emptied, but they do not do so for the nozzle, which they make rigid and, in turn, unfit to be distended or compressed. If the entire bellows were of that nature, who does not know that we would lose its entire use, and the bellows would be like a glass bottle? And such is the reason for the membranous substance constituting the artery, which demonstrates that this part had to be made membranous.

<margin>Why cartilage enters into the composition of the rough artery.</margin>
But it also abounded in cartilages so that it might become an organ not only for respiration, but also, as we have said, for the voice. For just as it would have been suitable for the rough artery to be made membranous for the sake of respiration, in the manner of the smooth arteries, so too for the voice it ought to have been fashioned wide, rigid, and hard, in the manner of pipes, flutes, and horns. Since for a voice to be produced, there must be a certain symmetry and strength between the air and the substance struck by it. Cartilage is indeed such a substance, and for the sake of sound alone, the entire artery ought to have been built like a flute from cartilage, without ligaments and membranes. But since the voice could in no way occur without inspiration and expiration, and these necessarily require compression and distension, we shall rightly praise the skill of the supreme <term>Creator</term> <note>original: *Opificis*; literally "the Artisan" or "the Maker"</note> of things, who fashioned the rough artery to be a convenient organ for both respiration and voice at the same time. Indeed, He showed such industry in the construction of the larynx...

<summary>Vesalius explains that the trachea (rough artery) is composed of both flexible membrane and rigid cartilage to serve two distinct purposes: the membrane allows for the expansion and contraction necessary for breathing, while the cartilage provides the resonance required for speech.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "rough artery" (trachea) and the larynx. Having established that the trachea requires cartilaginous rings for stability, Vesalius now moves upward to the larynx to explain how its specific shape and the opening within it allow for the complex modulation of the human voice and the protection of the airway.</meta>

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VI.

<margin>The use of the opening of the larynx.</margin>
...it shows how that opening can now be closed more, now less, so that we are able to retain our breath according to our will for many important uses. We can also make the voice now deep, now high-pitched, according to how we narrow or relax that <term>slit</term> <note>original: *rimam*; referring to the glottis, the opening between the vocal folds</note>, which is indeed the primary instrument of the voice. For this is the part we have compared to the joined pieces of reeds used by flute-players; it also corresponds to the slit found in those pipes which we blow into with our lips. In its function—though not its shape—it also matches the mouthpieces of horns and trumpets which we fit to our mouths when blowing. Furthermore, the opening of the larynx is compared to the slits in the pipes of organs, and even to the holes of those flutes which we blow into transversally. Yet, meanwhile, the craftsmanship of this opening far surpasses all such holes or slits in which sound is produced. It is so constructed that it can be relaxed now less, now more (as was said a little earlier), allowing us to produce various sounds rather than just a single one. Finally, such power is bestowed upon the chest that, by our will, we can emit now much, now little air, sufficient for breathing alone, or enough so that during exhalation the air suffices for whatever voice we wish to form.

<margin>The generation of the voice.</margin>
How necessary it was to form a perfect circle for the second cartilage of the larynx, and why the rough artery cannot be compressed here at the root of the larynx, you will observe if you carefully learn how the <margin>Table of muscles 6, figure E.</margin> voice is generated by air being driven with force from a wide path into a narrow one, and from there back into a wide one. You will see this if you examine the <term>uvula</term> <note>original: *gargareonem*; Vesalius uses the Greek term for the uvula/soft palate area</note> as the "plectrum" of the voice, the palate constructed like a round and ample space, the cavity appearing above it in the <margin>Book 2, chapter 12, figures 2, n, o. Book 1, chapter 9, figures 1, 2, r.</margin> passages of the nostrils, the hollows of the <term>fourth bone of the upper jaw</term> <note>the maxillary sinuses</note> on both sides, as well as the teeth, the tongue, and the lips. Finally, you should diligently compare the instruments of musical craftsmen and the use of those parts with these works of Nature.

<margin>The use of the lid of the larynx.</margin>
It does not seem useful here to fall into a dispute over names, contentiously fighting over the name of this slit and the "lid" of the larynx. Many writers falsely list this lid as the proper and primary organ of the voice. In reality, it contributes nothing to the voice, except perhaps for some modulation, while its main job is to prevent food and drink from falling into the larynx while swallowing (as we explained in the first book). Indeed, beyond the fact that we have observed through true dissection that it does nothing for the voice, this ought to have been known to others by reason. For no muscle has ever been described by others to move that lid, nor is it moved by any muscles except those <margin>Book 2, chapter 21, figures 2, 3, 4, K.</margin> which we mentioned were inserted into it from the <term>upsilon-shaped bone</term> <note>original: *osse υ referente*; the hyoid bone, named for its resemblance to the Greek letter upsilon</note>. Meanwhile, all the other muscles of the larynx, down to the last one, serve to dilate or narrow that slit of the glottis. You will learn with the greatest pleasure that the entire fabric of the laryngeal cartilages was built for the sake of that opening—provided you have a burning desire to know the works of Nature, and perhaps take the larynx of some brute animal into your hands to weigh the industry of craftsmen in musical instruments, which follows closely upon the works of Nature.

<margin>The reason for the arrangement of the cartilages.</margin>
That the placement of the remaining cartilages in the trunk of the rough artery is not ordinary is clear from this: the thicker and middle part of them is seen in the front, where they encounter more injuries than in the back. Furthermore, where the cartilages necessarily fail to form a perfect circle in the trunk of the artery (to allow for breathing), they conveniently face the <term>stomach</term> <note>original: *stomachum*; here meaning the esophagus</note>, so that they compress it less and do not hinder its distension during the consumption of food.

<margin>The tunics of the rough artery are aptly constructed.</margin>
Nature also did not construct the tunics of the rough artery lazily. The external one protects the cartilages like a wrapping, and by its intervention, the artery, bound and strengthened to the neighboring parts, crawls downward more securely. The internal one, however, is meant not only to connect the cartilages more firmly, but also to line them, protecting them from heavier...

<meta>This page continues the description of the internal structures of the respiratory tract, specifically focusing on the protective linings of the trachea and the lubrication provided by the glands of the larynx.</meta>

->ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE HUMAN BODY]<-

...to protect it against injuries, the outer lining has become thicker. For often some useless phlegm flows down from the head through the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: *arteria aspera*; the trachea</note>, and even some drink and food falls into it during swallowing. Furthermore, a certain sharp quality, whether of smoke, ash, coal, or some other medicinal property, is drawn in during breathing. Add to this that the pus to be coughed up in a cough is sometimes malignant and eroding; then some other humor, such as yellow bile, black bile, or salty phlegm that has undergone putrefaction within, must sometimes be carried out through the rough artery. The lining covering the cartilages prevents all these things from scraping them, so that they do not feel the erosion and alteration from these substances, which would cause them serious harm. And just as the larynx is more subject to such harmful things (being closer to the mouth), so it also possesses this lining a little thicker than the outermost branches of the artery, where the lining becomes thinner. This is so that it does not too greatly dull the power of the lung's substance which tempers the air for the heart, nor prevent the intake of air into the offshoots of the <term>venous artery</term> <note>original: *venalis arteria*; in Vesalian anatomy, this refers to the pulmonary vein</note>, and again the drawing of the heart's smoky vapors into the branches of the rough artery.

<margin>Reason for the fat and glands of the larynx.</margin> Furthermore, the fat placed between this lining and the cartilages, especially in the larynx, and also the lining itself—which is fattier here—along with the sticky humor with which it is smeared on all sides, seem to contribute to the easy passage of air. It also serves to prevent the voice from failing or the parts from drying out during great shouting and frequent movements. The glands placed on both sides of the rough artery at the root of the larynx also contribute to this. Indeed, they soak the passage with humor, not a fluid one, but one that is sticky and fatty, just as these glands themselves are thicker and denser than other glands that produce humor. Truly, we are taught daily how great the use of this humor is for the voice when we see pipes being smeared with moisturizing oil. Certainly, the glands we have mentioned are not sufficient on their own for producing such humor; rather, others lie near the larynx, the account of which we shall provide in a separate Chapter. We should also note here that this humor, continually prepared by the glands, is of no small use for that mutual rising and falling of the larynx and <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: *stomachus*; in this period, the term often referred to the gullet or esophagus</note> which occurs during swallowing and breathing. 

<margin>Reason for the mutual ascent and descent of the larynx and esophagus.</margin> In wonderful ways, the connection and continuity of the interior of the rough artery with the interior lining of the esophagus also assists this movement. For it is almost by the benefit of this connection that when the esophagus swallows food or drink, and by drawing it down pulls itself as if downward, the larynx beautifully rises. Having been drawn as if into the cavity of the mouth, and because its posterior part is solid—unlike the rest of the posterior part of the rough artery, which is membranous—it does not hinder that function of the esophagus. Likewise, during inhalation, as the rough artery moves as if to draw air in, the larynx is carried downward, and the narrowness of the throat does not prevent its <term>slit</term> <note>the glottis</note> from being conveniently opened. Hence, the larynx (which is carried upward during exhalation and when modulating the voice) descends all the more from the throat toward the collarbone the more we attempt a greater dilation of that slit. To this end, help is brought by the <gloss>x</gloss> <margin>x: 5th muscle table, P. sigma 1. 2nd figure, chapter 21, book 2.</margin> muscles which, arising from the breastbone, pull the first cartilage of the larynx downward during that function.

### ON THE UVULA [GARGAREON]. CHAPTER VI.

*In the gaping mouth, one can see the uvula without dissection, although it is marked with an E in the sixth muscle table, and an A in the seventh.*

<margin>Names of the uvula.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a cherub or putto performing a task with anatomical or laboratory instruments.</image-desc>
**THIS** small part of the body is also gifted with many names. For it is called *Gargar*, *gurgulio*, *gargareon*, *sibilus* [the whistle], and *tintinabulum* [the little bell] after the voice and its sound. Because it hangs down like a grape cluster, narrow at the top and sometimes round like a ball at the bottom (especially when it is seized by inflammation), it is called the *Uva* [the Grape] or <term>staphyle</term><note>Greek: σταφυλὴ; a cluster of grapes</note>. Then, because this part sometimes extends like a mouse's tail or a column due to an influx of humors—as is that ailment—it is called <term>kionis</term><note>Greek: κιονὶς; a little column</note> and the little column. Furthermore, because in its natural state it is seen to be wider above and narrower below, some have called it a funnel. But the names bestowed on it by occasion of sound are also adapted by many to the entire larynx, and by some to only the cover of the larynx [the epiglottis].

<margin>d Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 of chapter 21, book 2, L.</margin>
<margin>Position, shape, and substance of the uvula.</margin>
Furthermore, the position, shape, color, and almost everything pertaining to the uvula (for so that part is frequently called in our schools) will become as conspicuous as the external surface of the nails if one is not too lazy to look into the mouth of someone gaping. Hence, there is no need to linger too long over their description. To those watching, it appears as an oblong, spongy, and fleshy part hanging from the end of the palate, where the nasal openings face the throat; it is wider at the top where it continues from the palate, and sharper at the bottom like an inverted pyramid. It receives certain small veins from the vessels of the palate going into its membrane in its middle; but it does not participate much in nerves.

<margin>Use.</margin>
Furthermore, the primary use of the uvula is the modulation of the voice, and it is a great help to man for speech, as is proven by those who have this part cut away or otherwise eroded. Then, because only humans and only certain kinds of birds are seen to be gifted with this, it is not undeservedly considered hanging against the hollow palate like a kind of plectrum of the voice. Secondarily, it is believed to provide something for man in the drawing in of air, specifically so that it is not carried too cold into the lungs, since those for whom the uvula has been previ...

and are seen protruding, the lung is also made hollow. For this reason also it happens that the right part of the lung, when joined with the left, corresponds with a remarkable similarity to the hooves or claws of an ox, a deer, or another cloven-footed <term>bisulcus<note>original: *bisulci*; refers to animals with a split or "cloven" hoof</note></term> animal when their hooves are pressed together; or, one side of the lung alone reflects the appearance of a single hoof. For the entire back of the lung and its sides correspond exactly to the front and sides of the hooves. Just as hooves are separated from each other at the front by a line and an indentation, so too the back of the lung receives an impression entirely similar to this line, caused by the vertebral bodies protruding into the chest cavity. And just as this indentation slants slightly according to the length and curve of the hooves, so too the indentation on the lung follows the outward curve of the back. Furthermore, just as hooves seem closer together at the front than at the back, so too does the lung, because the membranes that separate the sections are much closer where they attach to the spine than where they meet the <term>breastbone<note>original: *pectoris ossi*; the sternum</note></term>. Then, the remaining back part and sides of the lung, because of the bending of the ribs, are seen to be rounded, just like the hooves themselves.

<margin>Figure 12 at G, H; Figure 2 at I, I; Figure 2 at N, O, P, Q.</margin>
Furthermore, the region of the lung facing the <term>diaphragm<note>original: *septum transuersum*; the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen</note></term> perfectly matches the part of the hooves that rests on the ground. For this area is seen to be slightly hollowed out, mirroring the dome-like shape of the diaphragm in this place. However, the region of the lung facing the breastbone—its front part—precisely reflects the entire back part of the hooves that does not touch the ground. Just as that part of the hoof is rounded on both sides and opens with a wide gap, so too is this region of the lung; it is shorter at its back than the front part of the hoof is long.

<margin>Figure 1 at T, V; Figure 1 at L; Figure 2 at M, M.</margin>
There is yet another indentation in the lung not yet mentioned: the place where it rests against the sides of the membranes that separate the chest cavity. Because the heart is contained there, the sides of these membranes bulge out on both sides and create a curve; the lung claims a matching hollow for itself, corresponding to the space we see between hooves where coarse hairs grow in the middle. I would have it understood that these descriptions apply to the human lung—not when it is limp and collapsed, but when it is distended as it naturally fills the chest.

<margin>As in figures 3 and 5. I have assigned individual letters to the various lobes in those figures where the lung is shown. Into how many lobes or fibers the lung is divided.</margin>
Otherwise, when it collapses and is seen clearly divided into lobes or fibers, this elegant and characteristic shape of the lung is lost. Both halves of the lung are divided into two lobes, held together in humans by membranous fibers; they are not as easy to separate during a dissection as they are in a dog. This gap between the lobes is formed by a slanted line, starting roughly at the level of the fourth thoracic vertebra and extending diagonally downward toward the front, near the tip of the breastbone; thus, the lower lobe is longer than the upper one. Nor are the parts of the lung always divided into only two lobes; sometimes they are divided into three, sometimes none at all, or two so joined that in some people there appears to be a mark of a cut rather than a true separation.

<margin>In man, no lobe of the lung supports the trunk of the vena cava.</margin>
<margin>Look for this here in the lung of some four-footed animal.</margin>
As for the lobe that supports the trunk of the <term>vena cava<note>original: *cauæ uenæ*; the primary vein that returns blood to the heart</note></term> in dogs and monkeys, as I have already said, I have never observed it in a human, and I know for certain that humans lack it. Meanwhile, I have not forgotten the passage by Galen in the seventh book of *On Anatomical Procedures*, where he says: "This fifth lobe of the lung does not escape those who perform dissection correctly," implying that this lobe was unknown to <term>Herophilus<note>A Greek physician (c. 335–280 BC) often called the father of anatomy</note></term> and <term>Marinus<note>A prominent anatomist of the 1st-2nd century AD</note></term>. Indeed it was unknown to them, since they approached the bodies of humans, whereas Galen approached only those of monkeys and dogs, in which nothing is more obvious than this lobe. Likewise, it is perfectly clear to anyone dissecting a human that it is missing, as the senses themselves indicate,

<margin>The nature of the lung's surface.</margin>
The lung is smooth everywhere on its external surface and is, as it were, moist with a viscous humor. However, in many humans, this surface is not infrequently seen to be rough in the manner of those membranes which grow together; for in these people, sometimes the right part of the lung, sometimes the left, and sometimes even both are very stubbornly bound to the sides of the <term>thorax<note>The chest cavity</note></term> by the intervention of fibrous connections. Indeed, it seems to be in some way peculiar to humans that a certain dusky color—not a bright, shining red—and a certain cloud-like smearing and inequality in color are seen in human lungs. This is not only the case in those suffocated by a noose or those who have been dead for some time, but also in those whose hearts are cut out while they are still living; although, in those who die slowly, the lungs become more intensely black and collapse. 

<margin>The connections of the lung.</margin>
In other animals, therefore, only very rarely does the lung adhere to any part of the thorax by means of membranous fibers. However, the connection which is formed by the benefit of the vessels is considered common to them just as to humans. 

<margin>Figure 16, Y. Figure 12, A.</margin>
For the <term>rough artery<note>original: *aspera arteria*; the trachea</note></term>, being bound to the back and having proceeded into the lung, binds it equally to the back in all animals; 

<margin>Figure 11, 1. Figure 22, C.</margin>
and the <term>arterial vein<note>original: *uena arterialis*; the pulmonary artery</note></term> and the <term>venous artery<note>original: *arteria uenalis*; the pulmonary vein</note></term> likewise connect it to the heart. 

<margin>Figure 26, G. Figure 12, D.</margin>

<margin>The substance of the lung.</margin>
The substance of the lung is a soft, spongy, rare, light, and airy flesh, appearing as if it were a bloody foam or foam condensed from bloody blood, and it teems with many offshoots of vessels. 

<margin>The vessels.</margin>
There are three vessels. The first is indeed the rough artery, which we mentioned is divided into two trunks near the body of the fourth thoracic vertebra; the right of these extends into the right part of the lung, as the left does into the left. First, it is cut into two branches, and these again into more, and these again divided into others, interweaving the lung with a manifold progeny. 

<margin>Figure 21, c, d. Figure 22, Book 1, Fig 11. 14 D. Figure 15, Book 3, Fig 12, C.</margin>
The second vessel is the venous artery, and the third is the arterial vein, of which we necessarily made mention in the third book along with the rest of the veins and arteries. Thus, nothing more clearly needs to be repeated about them here until we come to the construction of the heart. These vessels, in the same way as the rough artery, are distributed into the lung in such a sequence that the branches of the arterial vein attend to the posterior side of the offshoots of the rough artery, while the progeny of the venous artery attend to the anterior side. And this distribution of vessels is maintained precisely everywhere even to the external surface of the lung, always similar to itself not only in position, but also in magnitude. For just as the trunk of the rough artery inserted into the lung is much larger than the first implantations of the arterial vein and the venous artery into the lung, so also in its entire progress through the lung and in the whole series of branches, the progeny of the rough artery are larger and more open than the twigs of the veins and arteries. 

Amidst this innumerable entanglement of vessels, that flesh of the lung which we described is interwoven, and, embracing all the twigs of the vessels, it forms the lung—just as the proper substance of the liver, along with the frequent progeny of veins, constitutes the liver. 

<margin>The tunic of the lung.</margin>
Furthermore, the entire body of the lung, not otherwise than that of the liver, is covered by a certain thin and membranous <term>tunic<note>The visceral pleura</note></term>, deriving its origin from those envelopes of the vessels which are offered to the rough artery and the other two vessels of the lung by the membranes partitioning the thorax <note>The mediastinum</note>, or that membrane which lines the ribs <note>The parietal pleura</note>. 

<margin>b = Figure in chapter 2 of Book 4, and also here figure u, 6 e.</margin>
For as soon as these vessels are led into the substance of the lung, that thin tunic, departing from the proper tunics of the vessels, degenerates into the covering of the lung. 

<margin>Nerves.</margin>
Little nerves are communicated to this tunic by the <term>recurrent nerves<note>The laryngeal nerves, which branch from the vagus</note></term> from the sixth pair of nerves <note>In Vesalius's system, the "sixth pair" corresponds to the modern Vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X)</note> which constitute the nerves and are afterwards spread out into the upper orifice of the stomach. However, no nerves, or only very slender ones, are seen to be distributed into the substance of the lung for the sake of sensation...

->ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [STRUCTURE OF] THE BODY<-

<margin>
The function of the lung and the reason for its construction.
</margin>
...are distributed [throughout the lung], which does not require much [nourishment]. For the lung was created primarily for this purpose: to prepare air for the heart (which requires air most especially not only for the quality of its natural heat, but certainly for its very substance), and finally, so that the heart might have an organ placed next to it from which it could always draw air suitable for its functions. This was done so the heart would not be forced to take in whatever air immediately surrounds us, unchanged in any other way—especially since Nature willed that many animals should breathe not only for the sake of the heart, but also for the sake of the voice, which is no small necessity for the comfortable life of an animal. Indeed, that which is returned by the lung during exhalation is considered the best material for the voice. For this reason, the Creator of things constructed all the respiratory organs in such a way that we may draw in air at our own will, and expel it again now forcefully, now gently, and in varying amounts, while in the meantime the continuous and tireless movement of the heart does not depend on our will at all. However, since we have necessarily pursued these matters more extensively elsewhere, and especially in the history of the muscles of the <term>thorax<note>The chest cavity</note></term>, our discourse must now be adapted to the logic of the lung's construction. The lung, therefore, like a sort of storehouse, takes air into the branches of the <term>rough artery<note>original: *aspera arteria*; the trachea or windpipe</note></term>, so that the heart may then draw that air to itself through the offshoots of the <term>venal artery<note>original: *arteria uenalis*; the pulmonary vein, which Vesalius and his contemporaries called an "artery" because it carried "spirituous" blood, but "venal" because of its thin walls</note></term> from the branches of the rough artery, and thus from the specific substance of the lung; and conversely, that which is useless to the heart is returned by the lung through exhalation. Therefore, the use of the rough artery is hidden from no one, just as the duty of the venal artery is not unknown to many: namely, that its chief purpose is to entice air suitable for the heart into itself, and through its intervention, the heart draws that same air into its left ventricle. The <term>arterial vein<note>original: *uenalis arteria* (likely a typo in source or referring to the pulmonary artery); usually *uena arterialis* refers to the pulmonary artery, which carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs</note></term> is believed to have been made chiefly for this: to extend suitable nourishment for the lung's own substance from the right ventricle of the heart. This nourishment needed to be light, airy, and frothy, provided that the lung was meant to be easily compressed, gathered, and again distended and compliant. For this function, the venal artery is also thought to be useful to the lung; for it too brings blood most suitable for its nourishment. The lung required more of this blood than other parts of the body, both because of its softness, its continuous motion, and the abundance of heat it acquires from its proximity to the heart. Furthermore, I believe it is evident that the membrane of the lung possesses a power to alter the air (a power perhaps not common, and which I would wish physicians to weigh and investigate heavily in every way), and that it strengthens the entanglement of the branches and serves as a covering. Likewise, no one should doubt that this membrane was most rightly made thin and soft, so that it might promptly collapse with the lung and be easily dilated.

However, the base of the envelope is not continuous, but is pierced by at least five openings. First, it provides a path <gloss>c</gloss> for the <term>vena cava<note>The large vein that returns blood to the heart</note></term> where this vessel pierces the <gloss>d</gloss> <term>septum<note>The diaphragm</note></term>. The second opening is that through which the same vein seeks the throat, passing upward from the base of the heart. Furthermore, the third opening <gloss>e</gloss> transmits the <term>arterial vein<note>original: *uena arterialis*; the pulmonary artery</note></term>. The fourth <gloss>g</gloss> is prepared for the <term>great artery<note>original: *magna arteria*; the aorta</note></term>, and the fifth <gloss>h</gloss> offers a path to the <term>venous artery<note>original: *arteria uenalis*; the pulmonary vein</note></term>. This last one is in a certain way double, because the venous artery is split into two trunks before it glides out of the envelope, almost always having two openings in the envelope—although a path is also provided for the arterial vein in two places in a similar fashion.

<margin>
i Figure 5, B.
</margin>
<margin>
The origin of the heart’s envelope.
</margin>
The present envelope grows very strongly <gloss>i</gloss> onto these vessels, taking its beginning from them in a certain way. For it seems that the third tunic of the great artery and the arterial vein, and the second tunic of the vena cava and the venous artery, establish the beginning of the heart’s envelope. Indeed, in the space midway between the heart and where the envelope is joined to them, the vessels are entirely deprived of these "borrowed" tunics of theirs; a noteworthy interval exists between the base of the heart and the point where the envelope grows together with those vessels. The envelope does not touch the base of the heart any more than it touches its tip or its sides—a point which <term>Galen<note>A prominent Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries</note></term> explained far more correctly in the seventh book of *On Anatomical Procedures* than in the sixth book of *On the Use of Parts*. Moreover, these openings we have just enumerated were necessarily placed primarily at the base of the envelope because of the arrangement of the vessels passing through it, forming itself here as roundly as was possible. The rest of the body of the envelope, transmitting nothing, is continuous and corresponds to itself everywhere except in its shape, which, as we said, stretches from the base into a blunt tip in the manner of a spinning top.

<margin>
The position of the heart’s envelope.
</margin>
This base is located a little higher than the highest point of the body of the fifth thoracic vertebra, not lying entirely upon it, but only directly opposite it. For the base is halfway between the <term>breastbone<note>original: *pectoris os*; the sternum</note></term> and the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae, being equally distant from both the breastbone and the vertebrae. Likewise, the base hangs equally distant from the right and left ribs. In its progression and descent, however, the position of the envelope varies. In other animals gifted with a longer breastbone than humans, this envelope descends almost equally separated from the right and left sides, gradually extending toward the front—so much so that the rear of the base (or, if you imagine the animal lying on its back, the lower part) is seen to be lower than the tip itself. But in man, for whom the <term>Creator of things<note>original: *rerū Opifex*; God or Nature</note></term> fashioned the front part of the chest shorter, the envelope is extended so far forward and to the left that the tip reaches further downward in a certain way than the <gloss>k</gloss> part of the breastbone, to which the upper and most forward part of the transverse septum is attached; then it extends so far to the left that the right side of the tip scarcely reaches the middle of the chest.

<margin>
k Figure 2, small under s.
</margin>
<margin>
The substance of the heart’s envelope.
</margin>
The tip also proceeds so far forward that it touches the left side of the breastbone and the cartilages that are articulated to it. This envelope consists of a membranous substance, and is to be placed among the number of "similar parts" along with the rest of the membranes. For it is a simple membrane, interwoven with no fibers, yet thick and quite hard, forming a cavity in which the heart can easily be dilated and constricted. This cavity is entirely smooth, smeared with a certain thin fluid, and is completely devoid of any fat.

<margin>
Surface and connections.
</margin>
The exterior surface of the envelope also lacks fat. Although **Aristotle** thought otherwise, asserting that the heart's envelope is fatty—perhaps deceived by the membranes partitioning the chest, which grow onto this envelope and appear very fatty, especially in humans. Furthermore, this exterior surface of the envelope appears rough because of fibrous connections, just like membranes that have grown together.

<margin>

...the fibers of these membranes, filling the cavity of the membranes, are attached to the heart's envelope. Furthermore, the tip of the envelope and a significant portion of its right side are very firmly attached to the sturdy, <term>tendinous circle<note>The central tendon of the diaphragm</note></term> of the <term>transverse septum<note>The diaphragm, the muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen</note></term> over a very large area <gloss>m, n</gloss>, which is a feature unique to humans. Indeed, in monkeys, dogs, and pigs, the envelope is far removed from the septum; it is so far from being connected by a large portion of itself that it is clearer than daylight from this observation that <term>Galen<note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose work was the standard for over a thousand years; Vesalius frequently corrected his errors based on direct human dissection</note></term> either looked at human internal organs carelessly or not at all, and that he undeservedly rebuked the ancients while describing monkeys and dogs to us. Furthermore, specifically in humans, the anterior part of the tip of the envelope clings with fibrous connections to the membrane lining the ribs, in that place where the cartilages of the sixth and seventh ribs on the left side are joined to the breastbone. But the connection of the envelope <gloss>o</gloss> is also completed among the membranes that divide the chest; for the heart's envelope does not extend out from the middle of any of those, nor does it touch the lung in any part except through their intervention.

This envelope contains almost no arteries dispersed within it, nor veins, except for the very thinnest ones <gloss>p</gloss>, which mostly arise from those <gloss>q</gloss> that are distributed among the dividing membranes like in the <term>omentum<note>A fold of fatty tissue in the abdomen; Vesalius uses it here as a comparison for how vessels are distributed in membranes</note></term>. For when the envelope of the heart transmits the <term>vena cava<note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood to the heart</note></term>, it borrows almost nothing from it; since it is grown together with the septum in humans, it claims for itself the vessels it shares with the septum.

The use of the envelope and the reason for its construction.
</margin>
<margin>
r Book 4, Chapter 2, Figure r.

It also receives nerves that are very obscure <gloss>r</gloss>, and separated from those from which the running nerves have already budded <gloss>s</gloss>. As to why the heart has what is called an "envelope," I believe it is obvious to everyone: since, like a house or a small chest or a case, it most clearly embraces the heart and is seen to support it by the benefit of the dividing membranes. Furthermore, I believe no one would doubt that it is constructed from a strong membrane so that it might be both lighter and tougher at the same time.

<margin>
What kind of water is observed in the envelope.
</margin>
However, whether in humans in a natural state of health this envelope contains water—which we observe to be stored in its cavity during dissection like a <term>serous humor<note>A thin, watery fluid</note></term>—is not entirely clear to me. Although I have certainly never undertaken any dissection of a human heart in which I did not find a great quantity of such water, regardless of the type of death, whether the person had died a short or long time before. I have even noticed a greater abundance in women than in men, unless the men were of a very moist nature or otherwise abounded in serous juices. Indeed, I have generally found less water in those recently dead than in those whose dissection I had delayed for a longer time.

The man whose heart we watched being removed while alive in <term>Bologna<note>original: *Bononiæ*; likely referring to a public execution where the heart was removed immediately</note></term> also seemed to contain water in the envelope; but it was not very convenient to weigh this, however much we might have added to the <term>tragedy<note>Vesalius refers to the dramatic and somber nature of public dissections or executions</note></term>. In <term>Padua<note>original: *Patauij*</note></term>, being eager to see this water, we sometimes took care to have a heart—still beating, along with the lung and the rest of the organs, just as it had been removed from those who are cut into four parts while alive—brought immediately to the nearby apothecary’s shop, and we found some water in the envelope.

Living dogs have the cavity of the envelope and the surface of the heart moist, but in these no quantity of flowing water is observed; yet a noteworthy (even if almost always moderate) amount occurs in dogs that have been dead for some time.

In living pigs, however, more water is seen than in dogs; just as pigs that have been dead for a long time present it as being somewhat copious.

Thus, I would not want to assert anything regarding the water in the living; but I know it is false that absolutely none is contained in them (as everyone today affirms, contending that this is found in the dead because spirit is converted into water after death).

Since (as we have often warned before) membranes that are not grown together in any parts, nor clinging to each other, appear perpetually moist and slippery, like the inner surface of the eyes and eyelids. In this same way also the membranes covering the brain where they are layered over each other, and the internal surface of the membrane lining the ribs, and the surface of the <term>peritoneum<note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note></term>, and of the liver and intestines, and of the other parts merely lying against each other, but not grown together...

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'C' featuring a woodcut scene of three figures, likely students or physicians, surrounding a table where a dissection or anatomical examination is being performed.</image-desc>THE heart’s envelope <gloss>a</gloss>, which I have just described, clearly indicates the heart's own position and shape. For the heart is seen to have a pyramidal or somewhat top-like <note>original: "turbinatæ"</note> shape, corresponding roughly to a <term>pine cone<note>original: "nuci pineæ"</note></term>, as it tapers gradually from a wider <gloss>b</gloss> base to a <gloss>c</gloss> point <note>original: "mucronem"; the apex of the heart</note>—though it is a bit sharper than a pine cone and appears twisted toward the left—and it appears much longer than it is thick to those observing it. Yet, in the meantime, as far as the entire external surface or its whole mass is concerned, the human heart does not occur with an equal thickness all the way around. For its width exceeds its depth, just as if one were to claim that the heart is significantly compressed in its front and back parts and protrudes at the sides: somewhat like a <term>chestnut<note>original: "castaneæ"</note></term> that has another nut joined to it on both sides. This compression happens so notably on the right side that the heart seems to form a sharp rather than a semi-rounded surface along its entire length there. In contrast, the hearts of birds and quadrupeds are seen to be not much wider than they are deep, and they match the image of a pine cone or a top far more exactly than the human heart does. Galen would certainly never have neglected to write about this distinction if he had only approached the human heart just as he did those of monkeys and dogs. Here, carefully weighing the ingenuity of Nature—who, since a short but wide <term>thorax<note>The chest cavity</note></term> necessarily fell to man's lot, fashioned so many differences. We have shown that man differs from the structure of quadrupeds in the shortness and breadth of the breastbone, in the lobes of the lungs, in the course of the <term>vena cava<note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note></term>, and in the connection and position of the heart's envelope to the <term>transverse septum<note>The diaphragm</note></term>. And here, again, the human heart has quite appropriately turned out to be much wider and shorter in proportion than in those animals. Finally, besides a few other unusual differences, we shall teach that another position of the heart is found in man than in quadrupeds gifted with a long and narrow thorax, as soon as we have added those things to the discourse which remain to be mentioned concerning the shape of the heart. The entire outer surface of the heart, from the base to the very tip of the point, is seen to be exceedingly smooth and is not attached to any part <gloss>d</gloss>. However, the branches of the <term>coronal vein<note>original: "Coronalis uenæ"; the coronary vein</note></term> <gloss>e</gloss>, running from the base of the heart to the point along with their companion arteries, bulge a little more than the rest of the heart's surface and form a slight irregularity, since they are not embedded into the substance of the heart with their entire body. Furthermore, the fat <gloss>f</gloss>, with which the human heart is usually abundant, also adds some irregularity. The base, because of the exit of the vessels, is seen to be uneven in some way. For on its right side, the right <term>auricle<note>One of the upper chambers of the heart</note></term> is joined together with the <gloss>g</gloss> vena cava and the <gloss>h</gloss> <term>arterial vein<note>original: "arterialis uena"; the modern pulmonary artery</note></term>; while on the left...

<margin>The position of the heart.</margin>
position of the heart, about which the professors of dissection contend at great length: some of them suggesting that it is located in the left side of the chest, while others say it is in the middle, regarding the right and left. To others, indeed, it pleased them that the heart be in the middle not only regarding this difference of position, but also according to the front and back of the chest, and then also the upper and lower parts. Others again ascribe all these things to the entire mass of the heart, while others ascribe them only to the base. 
<margin>m Galen, *On the Use of the Parts*, book 10, chapter 2; and *On the Teachings of Hippocrates and Plato*, book 1, chapter 19.</margin>
Now, I think it is manifest that everyone at present calls the <gloss>m</gloss> chest <note>the thorax</note> whatever is enclosed by the ribs, the breastbone, and the twelve vertebrae of the chest; otherwise, if the entire trunk of the body were called the chest here, as Aristotle did, they would err greatly in explaining the position of the heart, although they do not otherwise come very close to a true description of the site.

Since in quadrupeds, not only the base but also nearly the apex <note>original: *mucro*; the pointed end of the heart</note> of the heart is contained in the middle, as far as the right and left are concerned. Then, according to the length of the back, the base is much closer to the first vertebra of the chest than the apex is to the twelfth. Furthermore, the base of the heart is further removed from the higher part of the breastbone than the apex is from the <gloss>n</gloss> cartilage of the breastbone 
<margin>n Figure 2, S.</margin>
compared to the image of a sword <note>the xiphoid process</note>. Thus, by this dimension, which we measure in length, the whole heart does not exactly occupy the middle seat in any animals. Regarding the front and back, in all living creatures the base of the heart is located almost in the middle of that part of the chest which it claims for itself. The apex, however, is stretched out more toward the front, though not equally in all. But the human heart, at its base, occupies exactly the middle of the right and left side, just as in other animals, and behaves similarly regarding the front and back. For it is as far distant from the breastbone as it is away from the bodies of the vertebrae. In the length of the chest, which is constituted by twelve vertebrae at the rear, it faces the body of the fifth vertebra. In the front part of the chest, however, which is bounded by the length of the breastbone, the higher part of the base claims exactly the middle position, being as far removed from the throat as it is from that part of the breastbone where the septum <note>the diaphragm</note> is inserted. From the base, the rest of the body of the heart is gradually and obliquely stretched out toward the front and toward the left side, so that the posterior part of the apex leans more forward toward the breast than the center of the base itself does, and so that even the right part of the apex, being extended more to the left than the center of the base itself, passes the middle of the breastbone toward the left; and the center of the apex itself faces the cartilages of the sixth and seventh ribs of the left side, where they are joined to the breastbone. 
<margin>The size of the heart.</margin>
By the present boundaries in which the position of the heart is understood, its size also becomes known: which indeed in man, as also the brain and liver, has turned out to be proportionally larger than in other animals. Nor is this alone peculiar to man, but it is also the case that his heart comes as close as possible to the nervous part of the transverse septum <note>the diaphragm</note> on the left side, to which the heart's envelope <note>the pericardium</note> is attached for a 
<margin>o From G to F in Figure 3.</margin>
large <gloss>o</gloss> space. This is far different than in dogs and monkeys, in which the heart is removed from the septum by a great interval: so much so that Galen's opinions on the position of the heart agree with dogs and monkeys, but truly not with men; especially when he contends that the heart is placed in the middle of the chest, contrary to the views of the Ancients. Nor is he at all mindful of what he set forth in the seventh book of *On Anatomical Procedures* concerning the summit of the heart.

# BOOK VI OF THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

->ON THE SUBSTANCE OF THE HEART.<-
->Chapter 10.<-

The substance of the heart, as far as was possible to achieve, is delineated in those figures that represent it dissected in every way: specifically the seventh figure and the four following it.

---

<margin>Flesh of the heart.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'P' depicting an anatomical scene with several figures gathered around a table where a body is being examined or prepared.</image-desc>
THE PRINCIPAL substance of the heart consists of flesh, which is slightly less red than the flesh of the muscles, and is very different from them in its hardness, density, and the type of fibers with which it is interwoven. For the flesh of the heart is far harder and denser, and as if more persistent in enduring injury; finally, it is gifted with various types of very robust fibers. Meanwhile, the flesh of a single part of the muscles possesses almost only one kind of fiber, and even that is scattered quite sparsely. Furthermore, the kinds of fibers contained in the flesh of the heart (for we are not presently dealing with the fibers of the membranes of the orifices of the <margin>a See Figure 7, N, and K, L, M; and Figure 9, G, G, and the membranes E, F.</margin> vena cava and the venous artery <note>original: *venalis arteriae*; this refers to the pulmonary vein, which was thought to carry "spirituous" blood</note>) are not as easily seen as those of the muscles. <margin>Fibers of the heart.</margin> You will find no muscle at all that does not demonstrate the differentiation of its fibers in some way as soon as it is uncovered, even without much dissection—proposing them even more accurately if it is torn apart by the nails or a knife, whether cooked or raw. Meanwhile, we arrive at the position and sequence of the very compact fibers of the heart by conjecture rather than by dissection. For in whatever way you approach the heart's flesh, whether boiled or raw, with straight, oblique, or transverse cuts, or however you please to tear it with your nails, you will hardly ever observe a noteworthy portion of the heart that can be pulled away according to only one kind of fiber. Instead, you will maintain that every part of the flesh abounds in diverse and manifold fibers (but especially transverse ones). For in the heart, it is not possible to find the layout of the fibers by the benefit of dissection as clearly as one can in the gullet, the stomach, the intestines, and even the uterus when distended for a fetus. Nevertheless, we persuade ourselves that a threefold kind of fibers has been bestowed upon the heart by Nature, both because of the various and rare entanglement of fibers we see in it (with no simple path among them), and also because of the manifest function of the heart, which we believe is performed primarily with the help of the fibers, as we are about to say. Moreover, although reason might perhaps suggest that the straight fibers (to which the faculty of attraction is attributed) are placed innermost, and then the oblique ones (which are believed to govern retention in other organs acting with natural motion), and that the transverse and circular ones (which expel) occupy the outermost seat: nevertheless, we cannot assign such a position to the fibers of the heart. Dissection itself shows that these three types of fibers are mixed together; it demonstrates now straight, now oblique, now transverse, and again straight and oblique and transverse. It is almost as if the first three differences were peculiar to the individual ventricles, while the latter were dedicated to the whole heart and both ventricles together. I call "straight fibers" in the heart those which, in a heart that has been thoroughly boiled, are seen to be drawn from its base all the way to the center of its apex <note>original: *mucronis*; the pointed end of the heart</note>, both through the septum of the heart's ventricles and through the rest of its substance. I call "transverse" those which surround the heart and the ventricles in a circular and transverse manner. I call "oblique" those which indeed embrace the heart and ventricles circularly, but proceed obliquely according to the length of the heart. These are of two types: some on the right side of the heart are nearer to the base and on the left side nearer to the apex; others on the right side look more toward the apex and on the left toward the base. And indeed, with these fibers being quite numerous in proportion to the mass of the heart (if you compare it to a muscle), and with the flesh containing and embracing them, the principal substance of the heart [is formed]...

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

the substance is established, which possesses a composition nearly identical to the substance of the bellies <note>The "belly" of a muscle is its thick, central contractile part.</note> of muscles. For just as the fibers in muscles are surrounded on all sides by flesh, so too are the fibers of the heart contained and supported by their own unique flesh. Furthermore, the combined thickness of the fibers and flesh throughout the whole heart—a detail which others have certainly noticed too little—will be explained at the appropriate time once we have described the ventricles <note>The "ventricles" are the main pumping chambers of the heart.</note> of the heart in our discourse. For the present, it will suffice to add the use of the heart's flesh and fibers, and those things which further pertain to the heart's substance; and likewise to point out that the heart's flesh appears thicker and more solid at the apex <term>mucro: the pointed bottom tip of the heart</term> than at the base. This is certainly not (as Galen believes) so that the heart would not be easily injured here during its contractions when it approaches the chest bone; rather, it is because that part of the heart is narrow, and because the convergence of the straight fibers is completed there. This convergence shows a compaction of the flesh of the apex (even if it does not otherwise differ from the rest), in exactly the same way as we often see more solid flesh at the head of a muscle or the beginning of a tendon than in the middle of the muscle's belly, where the fibers are not so compacted as in those locations, and are more separated from one another. <margin>The use of the heart's flesh.</margin> Thus, the final use of the heart's flesh corresponds with the use of muscle flesh in the strengthening of the fibers. However, we reason from the substance of other viscera that the heart's flesh, through its own peculiar and proper temperament <note>In Renaissance medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" referred to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and its essential form, assists in the principal functions of the heart, which consist primarily in the transformation of the blood and the preparation of the vital spirit; indeed, the flesh is the primary author of these functions. <margin>The use of the fibers.</margin> Moreover, the fibers of the heart serve another duty, by which the heart—for as long as the animal lives—is both dilated and contracted, and rests for a short time between contraction and dilation. Therefore, just as the heart's fibers share some commonalities in composition with the fibers of muscles, they also serve movement, but in a completely different way. For the movement of muscles is voluntary; but the movement of the heart is natural, and through the inscrutable industry of the Creator of things, it is almost tireless and unwearied, not at all subject to our will, nor depending in any part on the nerves from the brain as muscle movement does. Furthermore, the dilation of the heart—which is the pulling of the apex toward the center of the base and the stretching out of all the heart's sides—is performed by the straight fibers, which pull the apex toward the base. This is accomplished just as if you were to connect many roots of rushes or reeds in a circular series within a wicker ring, and then, gathering their tips together, you formed a kind of pyramid; and finally, if you let down a small cord from the middle of that peak through the center of the circle, which, when pulled downward, would make the pyramid shorter and much more spacious inside (the rushes, of course, being separated and moving away from each other toward the outside and the sides). From this, one might best learn the dilation of the heart: the wicker ring would respond in a way to the base of the heart, while the collection of rushes would correspond to the heart's apex; then the rushes themselves and that cord would match the straight fibers. The rushes would correspond to those fibers that exist on the sides of the heart, both front and back; while the cord would be compared to those fibers found in great frequency in the fleshy septum <margin>b Figure 8, H, H. Figure 9, K. Figure 11, I, l, m, and three times at H and G.</margin> of the heart placed between the two cavities. However, we can devise nothing that possesses a total similarity to the movement of the straight fibers. It seems easier to relate the action of the transverse or circular fibers to something. These are primarily in charge of the heart's contraction, which is the movement of the apex away from the base and a certain lengthening of the heart. This is managed by those fibers whenever the straight fibers are relaxed and the circular ones are more intensely tightened and gathered together, just as if you were now to loosen the cord previously pulled tight in that pyramid, and with your hands or another ring in the middle of the pyramid, you were to compress the rushes inward, thus diminishing its cavity while simultaneously making it taller. Now indeed, who...

<margin>The veins and arteries peculiar to the substance of the heart.</margin>
...on the other hand, it is not difficult to imagine how the oblique fibers might preside over a state of rest—that is, for a short while, as is deemed suitable for the heart's functions—so that, together with the other fibers, they may contract from all sides upon the materials contained within. This you will certainly observe most pleasantly in that procedure <note>Vesalius refers to a live dissection or "vivisection" described later in the work.</note> by which an end is placed upon the seventh book and thus the entire work. Furthermore, we commonly believe that the fibers of the heart are not merely the craftsmen of the heart's movements; we also persuade ourselves that the straight fibers lead to attraction, the transverse to expulsion, and the oblique to retention. <note>In the physiology of the time, "attraction" meant drawing in blood, "expulsion" meant pumping it out, and "retention" meant holding it during the "concoction" or processing of vital spirits.</note> Besides the flesh and fibers of the heart, we must also enumerate here the **veins** ^g which nourish its substance and the **arteries** ^h which foster the innate heat of its substance: specifically, the coronary vein itself and the two coronary arteries distributed through the heart's substance like the vessels of muscles. We have already abundantly covered the origin and sequence of the coronary vein and arteries in the third book.

<margin>The small nerve of the heart.</margin>
Therefore, having added a discussion of the heart's **small nerve** ^i to our discourse, we must proceed to the tunic <term>tunic: a covering membrane or "coat"</term> of the heart. In the fourth book, we reported that this small nerve is derived from the nerve of the **sixth pair** ^k of the brain <note>In the 16th century, the vagus nerve was classified as the sixth pair; today it is known as the tenth cranial nerve (CN X).</note>; we said then that a branch is derived from it where it forms the recurrent nerve of the left side. This branch penetrates the base of the heart's envelope <note>The pericardium.</note> and, extending to the posterior side of the left side of the **venal artery** ^l <note>original: "venæ arterialis." This refers to the pulmonary artery, which Vesalius called the "artery-like vein" because it has the structure of an artery but was thought to carry venous blood.</note>, reaches into the base of the heart (though quite obscurely).

Indeed, the tunic of the heart which we are discussing here corresponds exactly to that membrane which grows tenaciously onto the bellies of muscles—a very thin little membrane, to be sure, which cannot be fully stripped away from the muscle substance. For a membrane of this kind grows around the outermost surface of the heart; and in humans, especially toward the base of the heart, an abundance of harder fat is nourished by it. Sometimes also through the rest of the heart's surface, all the way to the **apex** <term>mucro: the pointed tip of the heart</term>, fat grows onto this membrane following the path of the veins and arteries. <margin>The tunic grown onto the heart's substance.</margin> <margin>The fat of the heart.</margin> <margin>m Figure 4, L. **I** shall now subjoin how the ventricles of the heart are formed in humans, and consequently in other animals possessing lungs, and of what number they consist, while altogether restraining my speech from the dispute between **Galen** and **Aristotle** regarding their quantity. <note>Aristotle believed the heart had three chambers, while Galen (correctly) identified two main ventricles.</note> Thus, the human heart possesses **two** remarkably large cavities within, situated according to the sides of the heart; ^a hence we rightly call ^b one the **right ventricle** or chamber, and ^b the other the **left**. Of these, the right surpasses the left in size, and both vary greatly in form. For the right, descending further down toward the apex of the heart than the left itself, ^c acquires a cavity shaped like a **crescent moon**; ^d since on its right side, and its anterior and posterior regions...

H, H</margin> It is just as if the cavity itself were the body of a crescent moon, and the outer part of the moon were defined or formed by the right side of the heart, while the inner part of that moon consisted of the septum of the heart's ventricles protruding here, as we have said. And the right ventricle of the heart maintains this shape from the base all the way to the **apex** <note>The pointed bottom tip of the heart; Latin: *mucro*.</note>, having been made narrower from the wider base along with the shape of the heart. The left ventricle begins with a wide base, <margin>Shape of the left [ventricle].</margin> and gradually ends in an arc toward the apex of the heart, possessing a cavity like a **cone** <margin>5 f. F, I, L 7 fig. K, L, M 9 f. K, L. 10 f. Q, Q.</margin>, which, as far as the whole surface is concerned, remains circular. For the septum of the heart's ventricles is seen as concave on its left side (where the right side of the left ventricle is formed), and not indeed bulging or protruding as on the right side; and it possesses a thickness and nature equal to the substance of the heart which constitutes the left side and the front and back parts of the left ventricle. Thus, it is as if the heart were constituted primarily for the sake of the left ventricle, and as if the right ventricle were formed by some thin substance of the heart growing onto the right side of the septum. <margin>k 7 fig. Q, R.</margin> For the entire substance of the heart, besides the septum of the ventricles, which constitutes the space of the right ventricle, is quite thin; but that which circularly surrounds and forms the left ventricle exceeds the substance of the right ventricle in thickness by many degrees, and is seen to be equally thick everywhere, except at the base itself: where, for the sake of the vessels protruding and opening from there, the fleshy substance of the heart is lacking in as great a space as the size of the orifices. The **surface of both ventricles** <margin>Surface of the ventricles.</margin> <margin>l This is from no figure (you will see it better than from the eleventh). m This is found in those figures where the ventricles are seen.</margin> is exceedingly uneven, and covered with many pits, as it were, impressed deeply into the fleshy substance. Nor do these exist only at the sides where the right ventricle faces the left, but (even though it has seemed otherwise to all others professing anatomy) they appear throughout the entire surface of the ventricles, not only in recently killed animals, but constantly, as long as you wish to preserve the heart itself, and never closing up even in a dried heart. However much these pits may be visible, nevertheless, none (as far as can be perceived by the senses) pass from the right ventricle into the left through the septum of these same ventricles; nor indeed do any passages, even the most obscure, occur to me by which the septum of the ventricles would be permeable, although they are described by the professors of dissection, since they have the strongest conviction that blood is taken from the right ventricle into the left. Hence also (as I will also warn more clearly elsewhere <margin>n 7 fig. O, O. 9 f. H, H. 10 f. N,</margin>) I am in no small doubt concerning this function of the heart in this part. <note>This is one of the most famous passages in the *Fabrica*. Vesalius expresses skepticism about Galen's theory that blood "sweats" through invisible pores in the septum, a key step toward the eventual discovery of the circulation of blood.</note> Furthermore, besides the unevenness which the pits form on the surfaces of the ventricles <margin>p 7 f. K, L, fi. G, G, 10 fig. M.</margin>, and which is somewhat more remarkable in the left ventricle, both acquire within themselves certain fleshy processes, as if from an unfolding, which are rounded and slender, and end in membranous fibers, continuous with the lower base <margin>q 7 f. K, L, M. 9 f. E, F.</margin> of the membranes placed in the ventricles themselves. These fleshy processes are seen especially at the apex of the ventricles, or the lower part: and I will show that they contribute to the strength of the fibers they contain when, in the second chapter from this one, I follow the nature of the membranes of the heart's orifices. For in both ventricles there are two orifices, and as many vessels occurring in the higher part of the ventricles, and thus at the base of the heart; and they differ in substance, since one is indeed venous and the other arterial. Then, in both ventricles <margin>r 7 f. C, C, C. 8 fig. C, D in the right ventricle. In the left 9 fi. C, C, C, 10 fig. A. r 7 fi. K, L, M, in the right. *Many figures are useful for observing the vessels of the heart and their orifices. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape scene with figures engaged in anatomical study or a classical allegory.</image-desc>
In the PREVIOUS Chapter, we briefly mentioned that there are four vessels of the heart and just as many orifices. In the number of vessels, there are: the **vena cava**, the **arterial vein**, the **venous artery**, and the **great artery**. All of these are provided with individual orifices looking toward the ventricles of the heart. <margin>Vena cava.</margin> The **vena cava**, therefore, is related to the right side of the heart and the right ventricle. Whether it truly takes its origin from that ventricle in humans, I have decided to address without much contentious proposing of the frivolous votes of authors; for in dissection (to say nothing of the theoretical reasons), in grown humans, I can gather nothing else than that the origin of the cava hangs from the heart, no differently than the other three vessels. And I am forced to confess the same regarding fetuses, so far as I have applied myself to their dissection—though I am not meanwhile ignorant of the opinion of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the 2nd-century physician whose work Vesalius frequently corrected via dissection</note> crying out against me everywhere. For those arguments which he brings forward concerning the principle of the vena cava in the sixth book of *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato* against the opinion of Aristotle, it would be very easy to turn all of them back against him (if only someone had proposed it). Unless, perhaps, it suited him because he had correctly declared that the liver is the "workshop of blood-making" <note>original: "sanguificationis officinam"</note>. Although even this "Achilles" <note>meaning a "strong point" or primary argument</note> would, among certain other things, disturb the principle of the venous artery. Therefore, from the right side of the right ventricle of the heart, at the lower part of its base, the **vena cava**

Furthermore, the <sup>n</sup> venous artery <note>original: *uenalis arteria*; today known as the pulmonary vein</note>—which we followed in the third book along with the arterial vein—is also called an "Artery" based on its function, because it contains or conveys air. It is <sup>o</sup> counted among the vessels of the left ventricle of the heart, and just as it acquires the substance of the veins, it also takes its origin from the softer part of that ventricle. For from the left side of the left ventricle, at the lower part of the same ventricle's base—in a manner entirely similar to how the *vena cava* arises from the right ventricle—the venous artery <sup>p</sup> emerges with a quite open and circular orifice. Immediately from its origin, or rather within the origin itself, it is <sup>q</sup> derived into two trunks: the right of these, extending under the base of the heart, is dispersed into the right side of the lung, while the left is stretched into the left part of the lung.

We shall carefully describe in the second chapter from this one how the <sup>r</sup> left auricle <note>atrium</note> of the heart is joined to the front of the venous artery’s origin. The <sup>s</sup> fourth vessel, which is still missing from our narrative and which constitutes the fourth <sup>t</sup> orifice of the heart, is considered the great artery <note>original: *magna arteria*; the aorta</note>. It takes its origin from the left ventricle in the same way the arterial vein <note>pulmonary artery</note> does from the right. <sup>u</sup> For from the right side of the highest part of the left ventricle, and from what is essentially the center of the heart's base, the great artery arises. It creeps directly <sup>x</sup> upward for some distance under the trunk of the arterial vein until, passing through the heart's covering <note>the pericardium</note>, it is split into two trunks: one seeks the upper parts of the body, the other the lower. In this way, the origins of these hard and thick vessels—namely the arterial vein and the great artery—correspond to each other so closely that the left side of the arterial vein is joined to the right side of the great artery at their very origin. Both vessels here possess a common origin and root at the most prominent part of the ventricles' septum. In certain animals, though not in man, this area becomes so hardened that Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose work was the gold standard for 1,300 years</note> affirms it is actually a bone <note>the *os cordis*, a bone found in the hearts of large cattle or deer</note>.

Moreover, <sup>y</sup> that ascent in the left ventricle of the heart toward the highest part of the septum—and thus toward the orifice of the great artery—lies hidden behind the right membrane of the venous artery's orifice during dissection. This ascent deceived Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher who believed the heart had three chambers</note> into establishing a third ventricle of the heart in that spot, reckoning it to be the origin of the great artery. This is certainly much less to be blamed than his writing that the number of the heart's ventricles varies according to the size of the animal. However, it should also be weighed significantly that Galen, in the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, asserted that the orifice of the great artery is larger than the orifice of the venous artery, when in fact the latter is seen to be far larger than the former. Nor did Galen simply compare the great artery’s orifice to that of the venous artery; he contended it was wider and larger than all other orifices of the heart. He was so spurred on by Aristotle's dogmas that he failed to notice the orifice of the *vena cava* is found to be nearly three times larger than the orifice of the great artery.
