# ON THE ELEVEN MEMBRANES OF THE FOUR
## orifices of the heart. Chapter XIII.

*THESE membranes occur in sequence in the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth figures. For the seventh figure presents three, placed over the orifice of the vena cava and marked with K, L, and M. The eighth shows three, positioned in the orifice of the arterial vein <note>original: *uena arterialis*; the pulmonary artery</note> and noted as E, F, and G. The ninth shows two from the orifice of the venous artery, indicated by E and F. Finally, the three membranes of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> are presented in the tenth figure, marked B, C, and D.*

<margin>Number of membranes.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop cap 'E' depicting several cherub-like figures in an outdoor setting; one figure appears to be reclining near a skull, while others are engaged in activities suggestive of scholarly or anatomical inquiry. The initial 'E' begins the word 'EA' (Those).</image-desc>
THOSE BODIES of the heart we call "membranes" <note>Today we call these the heart valves</note>, which are attached to the roots or origins of the heart’s vessels. In color, substance, and thickness, they are entirely like membranes, and (as far as we can gather by conjecture) they are placed there to prevent the backflow of materials. Furthermore, there are eleven of these in total: three are attached to each of the orifices of three vessels, but only two are attached to the fourth orifice.

<margin>a Figure 7, K, L, M. b Figure 7, H, H, H. c The whole body marked K, L, M in Figure 7. d Figure 7, K, L, M. e Figure 7, N. f Figure 8, H, H, H. Figure 11, I. g Figure 7, O, O.</margin>
<margin>The membrane of the cava.</margin>
The *vena cava* <sup>a</sup> possesses its own membranes, located as I shall now describe. At its beginning, which is a circle <sup>b</sup> swelling out from the substance of the heart from which it emerges, another membranous circle <sup>c</sup> is attached very closely. This second circle takes its origin from the substance of the heart in exactly the same way as the beginning of the *vena cava*. And just as the vein is carried outward from its origin away from the heart's ventricle, so too this membranous circle proceeds inward into the space of the right ventricle. Moreover, just as the *vena cava* immediately departs from the heart's substance, being attached to it only at its origin (which is very short), so also this membranous circle is attached to the heart's substance here with very little width. It departs from the heart immediately, appearing as a precise, solid, and strong membrane without excessive thickness. This membrane, led downward into the space of the heart's ventricle, is split not far from its beginning into <sup>d</sup> three processes or small membranes <note>The three leaflets of the tricuspid valve</note>. These taper from a wide base into a blunt point, differing little from the curve of a semicircle. The point of these small membranes stops a little above the middle of the length of the right ventricle; and they are attached to the substance of the heart in no other part than the circular origin of the whole membrane. However, from the entire lower surface of the three membranes (which is made somewhat thicker and stronger than the rest of their body), <sup>e</sup> certain fibers <note>The *chordae tendineae* or "heartstrings"</note> emerge in a frequent series. These, led downward through the space of the ventricle, are attached to the sides of the ventricle near its apex <sup>f</sup>. This is not only, as Galen suggests, at the septum of the heart's ventricles, but also at the rest of the circumference of the ventricle's apex (as we have already said). For every lower part of the small membranes extends fibers to that area of the ventricle's apex which is positioned directly across from it. These fibers, where they are joined to the membranes, are without flesh <note>tendinous</note>, and are not at all attached to the substance of the heart along their sides. But having been led down to the point or apex of the ventricle, they are implanted into it only by their ends, after having first been increased and supported <sup>g</sup> by a certain amount of fleshy substance <note>The papillary muscles</note>.

...and appearing exactly as if they were little fleshy rods in the ventricle of the heart. Therefore, this membrane, because of the three membranous processes drawn out from it, is counted in place of the three small membranes of the orifice of the *vena cava* <note>The "Great Vein," now known as the superior and inferior vena cava</note>. Because those processes, when they are closed and converge together, are similar in structure to the grooves of arrowheads, the Greeks called them <term>triglochinae</term> <note>original: *τριγλώχινας*; meaning three-pointed or three-pronged</note>, as if you were to say "three-furrowed." For when those three processes of that membranous circle meet one another directly at their center, they form a shape not unlike a triangular point, especially like the ones used by the Turks on their missiles; these indeed form a triangular point, but so that the long iron head might weigh less and the angles be made sharper, they file a groove between two angles. Thus the point, tapering from the base to the tip, shows three angles and as many grooves at once. You will notice this also happens here in the heart when, during dissection, you bring the tips of the three membranous processes together. Moreover, if you seek a comparison for the whole membranous body with its processes and fibers when opened, you may take it somewhat from the form of the crown which we see antiquity has carved on the heads of kings in those statues unearthed at Rome.

Furthermore, just as the venous artery <sup>h</sup> <note>original: *uenalis arteria*; the modern pulmonary vein</note> approaches the *vena cava* both in its body and in the materials to be brought to the heart, and almost in its origin; so also the membranes of the venous artery show many things in common with the membranes of the *vena cava* orifice. For at <sup>i</sup> the root of the venous artery's origin, a <sup>k</sup> membranous circle arises from the substance of the heart, which is led inward into the space of the left ventricle (just as the <sup>l</sup> venous artery is led outward), and immediately from its origin it departs from the substance of the heart, being up to this point very similar to the membranous body of the *vena cava* orifice. But when this membranous circle, or rather membrane, descends for some distance into the space of the ventricle, it is divided into <sup>m</sup> only two membranous processes. These correspond in <sup>n</sup> shape to those belonging to the orifice of the *vena cava*, but are superior in size and strength. From a wide base they end in a blunt point, reaching further into the cavity of the left ventricle than the small membranes of the *vena cava* orifice do into the right. One of these processes faces the right side of the left ventricle, the other the left side. For they gape apart from each other at the front and back. Along the entire lower seat of these (which also, like the membranes of the *vena cava* orifice, is thicker and harder), <sup>o</sup> fibers arise from them in rows, which, stretched downward, are finally continued everywhere into the substance of the heart at the breadth of the tip of the left ventricle. And as we said happens in the right ventricle, they are <sup>p</sup> augmented and stabilized by the fleshy substance of the heart. Furthermore, because the membranous circle of the venous artery is divided into only two processes, the leaders of dissection <note>The established anatomical authorities, such as Galen</note> assert that only two small membranes are set over its orifice; these you might compare not at all inaptly to a bishop's mitre <note>Vesalius is famously credited with naming the "mitral valve" here due to its resemblance to a bishop's head-covering</note>, if only you liken the part encircling the head to the membranous circle itself, and its processes to the front and back peaks of the mitre. Since only two processes are seen here, however much you imagine them converging together, you cannot call them <term>triglochinae</term> <note>three-pointed</note> with Galen, because they never reflect the image of a triangular point.

The <sup>q</sup> membranes of the arterial vein <note>original: *uena arterialis*; the modern pulmonary artery</note> do not correspond to the membranes of the aforementioned orifices in position, shape, or even strength. For from the origin of the arterial vein, these do not reach inward into the right ventricle of the heart; but they all consist in the trunk of that vessel, led outward from the orifice in such a way as the previously mentioned small membranes led inward from the orifices of their vessels. Nor is there one common circle for these; rather, there are three distinct, and not very...

<margin>The membranes of the great artery <note>The aorta</note>.</margin>
The membranes are strong, each taking its origin in the manner of a semicircle. For the orifice of the <term>arterial vein</term> <note>original: *venae arterialis*; the pulmonary artery</note>, protruding inward and somewhat into its own depth at the origin, possesses a surface of its own width divided into three semicircles that broaden outward from the heart. These, having been made thicker, protrude into the very width of the vessel, and by their swellings form three triangles in such a way that, touching each other at a point, the circles outside their surface, above and below the boundary of contact, establish angles. From these semicircular swellings, the membranes arise along their entire width, resembling the image of a half-full moon; they are attached to the vessel nowhere except at these swellings. The widest part of these membranes, which is removed further from the heart than the other parts and is the only side of the membranes not naturally fused to the vessel itself, is not seen to be straight like the diameter of a circle (which would make each membrane represent exactly the width of a half-circle). Rather, that part or side is slightly curved inward and does not rise as high outward in the middle as it does at the boundaries where it continues into the vessel on both sides. Therefore, since that side of the small membranes is bent like a half-parenthesis in this manner **(**, and the origin of the membranes and their connection to the vessels circumscribes a semicircle exactly, the Greeks called these small membranes <term>sigmoeideis</term> <note>original: *σιγμοειδεῖς*; sigma-shaped. In antiquity, the Greek letter sigma often looked like a 'C'</note> from the image of their **C**. Corresponding to these three membranes of the arterial vein, Nature has created three in the small opening of the <term>great artery</term> <note>The aorta</note>, differing from them in nothing at all except in size and strength. For the membranes of the great artery are as much larger and stronger than those of the arterial vein as the body of that vessel is surpassed in hardness and width by the body of the artery.

## ON THE AURICLES OF THE HEART. CHAPTER XIV.

->*The fourth figure presents the auricles of the heart, marked with I and K, as does the sixth figure, noted with M and F. However, the seventh figure shows the right auricle inverted at F, and the eighth at K. The ninth figure offers the left auricle inverted at I, and the tenth at L.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative capital letter 'A' depicting a scene in the wilderness. A seated man and a standing man appear to be in conversation or contemplating the landscape, which features a tree and rolling hills.</image-desc>

<margin>a Figure 4, I. Figure 5, B. b Figure 5, B to C, or rather F in the seventh figure to H near Q.</margin>
<margin>The two auricles of the heart.</margin>
<margin>The position and shape of the right auricle.</margin>
What the professors of dissection call the "auricles of the heart" are two appendages attached to its base. They are given the name of ears <note>original: *auricula*; literally "little ear"</note> because of the similarity they have with the ears properly so-called in their position, though not in their function. Thus, the right auricle is joined to the right side of the heart’s base, covering the entire anterior region where the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The great vein</note> arises along its length, so that the length of the base of the right auricle corresponds roughly to the length of this origin. The shape of the auricle resembles a pyramid in a certain way: from an oblong base, it ends in a point that is not very sharp, nor does it extend very far above the base of the heart. Indeed, the length of the base exceeds the width of the auricle itself (even when significantly distended) by almost three times; and the base of the auricle is also much longer than the distance from the base to its tip. The auricle extends from the base upward and forward, so that you could compare the form of the auricle—as far as the base and tip, and then the cavity, compression, and distention are concerned—to nothing more accurately than to the leather bumps sewn to both sides of the Turkish saddles. These are used with great effect, inflated like bladders or balls, by those about to swim their horses across a river. For the exterior surface of the auricle varies according to its fullness: when the auricle swells during the constriction of the heart and is filled up, it appears convex on all sides and smooth. But when the auricle is emptied and collapses, this surface becomes wrinkled and covered as if with folds...

But sometimes, though more rarely, the outer surface of even the distended auricle is seen to be uneven, because of fat growing upon it then. <margin>c. Figure 7, F. Figure 8, K. where the surface of the heart’s ventricles is also seen.</margin> The interior surface, however, which circumscribes the cavity of the auricle, corresponds in a way to the surface of the ventricles of the heart. For just as the latter is seen to be smooth where it leads out the vessels, but rough and full of pits in all the rest of its area: so also the former <note>the auricle</note> is smooth where it is attached to the origin of the <term>vena cava</term> <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note>; but in the rest of its extent it so abounds with pits and fibrous entanglements that it almost exceeds the surface of the heart in unevenness. And this cavity varies in its breadth according as the body of the auricle either collapses or is distended; but the pits are never entirely smoothed out. <margin>The substance of the right auricle.</margin> The substance of this auricle consists of a triple kind of fibers, and a moderate, and indeed quite hard and almost skin-like flesh embracing those fibers: so much so that the auricle corresponds to the heart’s substance in its fibers, but differs from the heart in its flesh (which, as we have said, is more <term>nervous</term> <note>original: *neruea*; here meaning sinewy or tendinous rather than relating to the nervous system</note>, skin-like, and somewhat blackish). Nor does the auricle take anything else peculiar into its constitution from this mixture of fibers with flesh, which hardly exceeds the thickness of the skin: for we do not find veins, arteries, and nerves privately inserted into it. <margin>The connection of the auricle.</margin> Moreover, the connection of the auricle is roughly as follows: the left side of its base is attached to the edge of the heart’s substance where the anterior region of the orifice of the vena cava in the right chamber of the heart stands, or more truly, the auricle comes forth from that edge. But the right side of the base is attached to the body of the vena cava along the length of its origin from the heart, and on its anterior surface, and as it were, a common body is formed with the vein. In all its remaining part, the auricle is entirely free from any connection, and just like the body of the heart, it is also contained in the <term>involucrum</term> <note>the pericardium, or the sac surrounding the heart</note> of the heart, joined to it by no fibrous connections. <margin>The left auricle of the heart.</margin> <margin>d. Figure 6, F. Figure 4, K. Figure 9, l. Figure 10, L. e. Figure 6, G. Figure 9, C,C.</margin> The left auricle of the heart possesses most things in common with the right: for it is located in the anterior region of the origin of the <term>venous artery</term> <note>original: *uenalis arteria*; the pulmonary vein, which Vesalius and his contemporaries called an "artery" because it carried "arterialized" or oxygenated blood</note> along its length. Then from its base it also ends in a point. But that point (which is considered sharper than the point of the right auricle) does not extend upwards as much as that one does, but more to the left and to the side. Furthermore, in people of more advanced age, the left [auricle] yields in size even to half the size of the right auricle: so that the very orifice of the venous artery is also seen to be far smaller than the orifice of the vena cava. As far as the external and internal surfaces are concerned, the auricles correspond to each other in some way: although the outer surface of the left always appears more wrinkled and much more uneven. Its interior surface is seen to be uneven and covered with pits, similar to the right auricle. They are also similar in substance: but the left is seen to be much harder and less compliant in constriction and distension. Furthermore, if you compare it to the right, it will appear as if withered and dried out, always more abundant in fat on the outside than the right. In their connection they entirely agree: for just as the right is attached to the vena cava and to the right side of the heart along the origin of the cava, so also the left is attached at the right side of its base to the substance of the heart where the venous artery comes forth; and at its left side, to the body of the venous artery itself. In use, as we are about to say in its proper order a little later, they differ very little from each other. For now we shall strive to set down in order the use and function of all the small parts of the heart: mentioning here as well that in fetuses and newly born animals the mass of the auricles is found to be far larger in proportion than in those of more advanced age; and moreover, in dissections of living animals, when the motion of the heart is failing, the auricles still palpitate and move for some time.

# THE FUNCTION AND USE OF THE HEART, AND OF THE 
## parts of it mentioned thus far, and also the reason for their construction. Chapter XV.

---

<margin>The heart as the seat of which soul.</margin>
<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial letter C. The scene inside the letter depicts several figures in Renaissance academic or medical attire gathered around a table in an interior setting, likely representing a scholarly discussion or an anatomical demonstration.</image-desc>THAT THE HEART is the seat of the irascible soul—or the soul that desires vengeance and honor—was agreed upon by Hippocrates, Plato, Galen, and all the Stoics and <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> alike. But in addition to these, Zeno, and Chrysippus (who sought to strengthen Zeno's dogmas), Posidonius, and the rest of the Stoic family, along with Aristotle, Theophrastus, and their followers, maintained that the heart is the principle and fountain not only of the aforementioned irascible faculty, but also of that <term>concupiscible</term> <note>The faculty of the soul associated with physical desires and appetites</note> faculty which pertains to food, drink, and sexual matters. Aristotle was accustomed to calling this the "nourishing" faculty, while others called it "natural," and still others simply "concupiscible." Furthermore, the Stoics, together with the Peripatetics, placed the power of reason—and, to put it simply, the sovereignty of the soul—in the heart, believing it to be the origin of all functions and duties in the animal. However, these thinkers occasionally conflict with one another in their decrees. For Aristotle, Theophrastus, and the rest of the Peripatetic chorus, as well as Posidonius among the Stoics, assert that the irascible, concupiscible, and rational powers are faculties of a single substance proceeding from the heart; they deny that these are distinct species or parts of the soul, nor do they distinguish between them. Chrysippus, however, by no means the least of the Stoics, forced both anger and desire into a single faculty and substance along with reason. But Galen opposes all of these men, following the opinion of the divine Hippocrates (easily the foremost among physicians) and the most eminent philosopher Plato, both in many other places and especially in the nine books he wrote *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato* <note>original: "de Hippocratis & Platonis dogmatibus"</note>. In those books, teaching that the three species or parts of the soul differ greatly from one another in their nature, he proves with the firmest demonstrations—which win belief by their own merit—that the liver is the seat of the concupiscible soul (governing food, drink, and sex), the brain is the seat of the rational and sovereign soul, and he allows that the heart is merely the workshop of the irascible soul. Furthermore, lest I perhaps stumble into some censor of heresy here, I shall abstain entirely from this dispute regarding the species of the soul and their seats. For today one finds so many judges of our most true religion (especially among our own countrymen) who, if they hear anyone—even when we are undertaking the dissection of bodies, where such things should primarily be scrutinized—muttering anything about the opinions of Plato, Aristotle, or their interpreters, or Galen, concerning the soul, they immediately claim that he is wavering in the faith and hesitating over the immortality of souls. They do not consider that it is necessary for physicians (

<margin>The physician must consider the faculties and seat of the soul.</margin>if they do not wish to approach the art rashly, nor to find and apply remedies to a diseased limb at the wrong time) to consider those faculties which govern us: how many there are in general, what the nature of each is individually, and in which member of the animal each is established and receives its nourishment. And beyond these things, they must consider—if only we could grasp it with our minds—what the substance or essence of the soul might be. As if indeed, without any impiety and without any stain upon the faith, one could not propose anything regarding the decrees of those weighty authors, or even strengthen their reasons with new ones, or refute the frivolous arguments of some; and as if it were not necessary to speak quite differently about the most holy faith (by which, through the addition of pious works, we are saved and the souls of men attain a happy eternity) than about these dogmas of the authors and the opinions supplied by weak and human reason in this matter, to be interro-

<margin>To which function all parts of the heart serve.</margin>
...should be examined. Nevertheless, for the time being, setting aside all investigation into the faculties of the soul, its functions, substance, nature, species, and their seats, we shall freely assert that the heart is the fountain of the <term>vital faculty</term> <note>The power that sustains life and movement through the body</note> and thus of the vital spirit, and that it exists as the seat and fuel of the native heat, and is the author of the pulses. We shall demonstrate that each individual part of the heart serves that use relating to heat and spirit.

As to the use of the heart's a **envelope** <note>The pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart</note> (so that we may follow these things in the same order in which we previously described their construction), the specific Chapter on the envelope has already dealt with it to some extent. Next, the **position of the heart**, mentioned before, is the safest in the thorax itself, and the most remote from all things that could bring harm to the thorax from the outside. Furthermore, the heart b sits in the middle of the lungs—which embrace it with their lobes as if with fingers—in such a way that it may manage an equal attraction of air from all parts of the lung through the c **venous artery** <note>original: "venalem arteriam"; the pulmonary vein</note>, and in turn attempt the expulsion of sooty wastes into the lung, and also provide a just d portion of blood to the lung through the venous artery and the e **arterial vein** <note>original: "venam arterialem"; the pulmonary artery</note>. In addition to these things, the heart, located not very far from the mouth (through which it was necessary for respiration to be completed), nevertheless occupies that seat of the body from which it can conveniently offer native heat and vital spirit to the whole body through the branches of the e **great artery** <note>The aorta</note>. Although, as far as the whole body is concerned, it recedes from the middle parts as much toward the upper region as it is distant from the g union of the pubic bones. For this is considered the almost exact middle of the upright body of adults; it is not, however, the navel, which Galen, in describing the position of the heart, judged to be the exact middle. Furthermore, because of its base—which had to be broad and wide due to the beginnings of the four large vessels proceeding from it—the heart was not made perfectly round; even if this were not said, I conjecture it is manifest to everyone.

<margin>
Book 2 on the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato.
The reason for the heart's shape.
h 5 fi. C, then 6 fig. I, N, G, O.

h Although Nature meanwhile wished the heart to approach a **spherical shape** (which is the most resistant of all for bearing injuries harmlessly and more capacious than all others), the heart appears entirely spherical during its greatest dilations; just as in its contractions it is seen to be oblong and drawn out in the manner of a pine nut. Nor do we say the heart is oblong for any other reason than that in the dead it is always found collapsed and elongated. For if it were observed as distended in the dead as it is in live dissections—whenever it is intensely dilated, we see it become shorter, but wider and deeper—then we would rightly judge it not to be oblong, but round, and only slightly less than a complete sphere.

<margin>The use of the heart's substance.</margin>
As for the use of the **heart's substance**, we necessarily included this in the tenth Chapter, when we were pursuing the commonalities and differences between the heart and a muscle; explaining especially then to which duty the triple kind of fibers, interwoven in the heart's substance, and then the flesh embracing and supporting these, were primarily assigned.

They attest to the great industry of Nature in the distribution of their branches, since more and larger of these are extended along the front, back, and left side of the heart than to the right, where the right ventricle of the heart is located, and where the substance of the heart occurs much l thinner than elsewhere, and for that reason stands less in need of veins and arteries.

<margin>o Visible in figures 7 and 8.</margin>
<margin>Function of the right ventricle of the heart.</margin>
duty of the heart's ventricles is believed to be of this sort.º The **right** ventricle, because it primarily contains blood and is most dedicated to the refinement of blood, is called "sanguineous" <note>original: "sanguineus"; meaning blood-filled or pertaining to blood</note>. Indeed, it is thought that this was carved into the heart by the Supreme Architect of things with remarkable justice, solely for the sake of the lung. For the lung, which is placed around the heart like a storehouse so that the heart may perpetually draw air from it, had to be made rare, spongy, light, and very compliant with the movements of the chest. Surely it could not be nourished by food suitable for such functions unless light, airy, foamy, purified blood—nothing less than dross-free—were prepared for it by another organ from that which the **great vein** <note>original: "cava"; the vena cava</note> contains, and thus led to the lung itself for appropriate nutrition. But no organ was more suitable for this task than the heart itself, the hottest organ and the one closest to the lung; nor indeed could any other serve the lung more justly in this matter. Since the heart would have to be considered far too ungrateful if it did not think to return the favor to the lung, which so kindly attracts the air (which the heart perpetually needs, unless it wishes to immediately collapse and die) on its behalf, and prepares it in the manner of a most obedient servant, having been fashioned primarily for its sake. Thus, the heart should strive by all means to repay the favor by preparing and refining suitable nourishment for the lung (since it can do so without inconvenience). Therefore, in animals gifted with a lung, the right ventricle—whenever the heart is dilated and stretched—attracts a great force of blood from the

But why this vein, among the other veins of the body, acquires the <sup>s</sup> **tunics** <note>layers or walls</note> of an **artery**, we have expressed elsewhere in passing: when we said it was made thick and strong, both because of the continuous movements of the lung and heart, and also so that the thin lung might not attract more of the blood it contains than is sufficient for nutrition (even though it needs quite a lot); then so that the lung, by its own continuous motion and heat, might further refine for itself the blood led into the arterial vein and make it more foamy. Such is the blood that is now offered to the lung from the left chamber of the heart through the **venous artery** <note>original: "arteriam uenalem"; the pulmonary vein</note>, since it has already been refined in both chambers of the heart. To this is added that the arterial vein—an organ most suitably serving nutrition alone, and which ought to rest according to the compression and dilation of the lung and move as little as possible—was made by the great providence of Nature more rigid, thick, and difficult to dilate or compress than the other veins of the body. For by this reasoning, the branches of the arterial vein less hinder the stretching and dilation of the venous artery and the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: "asperæ"; the trachea and bronchial tubes</note>; whereas, if those branches were compliant and distended on slight occasion, they would fill the great volume of the lung when it is dilated; and again, when the lung is compressed, they would readily collapse and would not prevent a great force from being exerted on the branches of the rough artery from the compression of the lung. ### ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN] BODY

<margin>
The use of the right auricle of the heart, and the reason for its construction.
</margin>
The heart draws blood into its right chamber from the great vein <note>original: "caua"; the vena cava</note>, and in a sense seizing it, absorbs it. Since the great vein itself—so that blood might seep out from it into other parts of the body for the sake of nutrition, though not as thin as that of the lung—is not composed of a body as thick and strong as an artery, the vein would certainly be in danger of rupturing during that powerful suction of the heart, had not wise Nature created the right auricle of the heart <note>The "auricle" (literally 'little ear') refers to the atrium or its appendage</note>. This auricle, following the movements of the heart and being full of blood, can pour the blood it contains into the right ventricle when the heart dilates. In a way, it rolls itself toward the ventricle to break the force of the suction, acting as a storehouse for the heart. The "skin-like" construction of the auricle corresponds to this use; it is light, yet resistant to injuries, and follows the heart’s movements. It is seen to be hollow so that it can contain material, and it is composed of fibers so that it may serve the purposes of attraction, retention, and expulsion. Nor is it lacking in the flesh that surrounds those fibers; indeed, because the substance of the auricle so closely matches the substance of the heart, it seems to show that, by an innate faculty, it contributes to a certain light preparation of the blood for the heart's ventricle.

<margin>
The use of the membranes placed over the opening of the great vein.
</margin>
Furthermore, lest the suction of blood from the great vein into the right ventricle be rendered useless when the heart dilates—that is, by the blood being pushed back out through the same opening in the manner of the Euripus <note>original: "Euripi ritu"; a reference to the Euripus Strait, famous for its reversing currents, here illustrating the risk of blood flowing back and forth without valves</note> when the heart is compressed—Nature placed three membranes <gloss>v * see figures K, L, M.</gloss> <note>These are the flaps of the tricuspid valve</note> over the opening of the great vein. These membranes admit the blood flowing into the ventricle from the great vein when the heart is dilated, but they prevent the same blood from flowing back into the vein when the heart is compressed. For when the right ventricle of the heart is distended (which happens whenever it is made shorter and increases significantly in width and depth), then those membranes, having become slack, collapse toward the sides of that ventricle and provide an entrance for the blood, the opening of the great vein having been unblocked. But when the ventricle is constricted again—or made longer and narrowed (as happens in constriction)—the fibers of the membranes and the membranes themselves are stretched because the heart's apex <note>original: "mucronem"</note> moves further away from its base. And since the apex of the ventricle is made narrower in this way, the fibers of the membranes, which are mostly attached to the apex of the ventricle, are drawn together. Consequently, they approach each other at their ends directly across the center of the opening of the great vein, closing that opening and acting as a barrier to prevent the blood from flowing back into the vein. Indeed, the blood itself, compressed by the sides of the ventricle, assists in this action. For when the blood seeks the opening of the great vein, it rushes with force against the back of the membranes, pressing them toward the center of the opening and causing them to close more tightly together. Thus, the blood stands in its own way to prevent its exit; meanwhile, it approaches the opening of the arterial vein <note>original: "venæ arterialis"; the pulmonary artery</note>, which, being open during the heart's contractions, transmits the blood toward the lung.

<margin>
The reason for the membranes of the opening of the arterial vein.
</margin>
<margin>
x * see figures E, F, G.
</margin>
But to prevent the blood from surging back again into the right ventricle when the heart dilates, three membranes placed at the opening of the arterial vein <note>These are the semilunar valves of the pulmonary artery</note> provide a safeguard. These membranes, because they take their origin from the beginning of the arterial vein and are stretched upward, ending in the cavity of the vessel and collapsing against its sides, readily allow the blood to flow into the vein during the heart's contractions. But when the blood, due to the heart's dilation, is pulled back toward the ventricle by the "flight from a vacuum" <note>an Aristotelian concept that nature abhors a vacuum, explaining suction</note>, or is even pushed toward the base of the arterial vein during the compression of the lung, it rushes toward the heart. Descending along the sides of the vein, it falls between the body of the vein and the back of the membranes, filling the space between the vessel wall and the membranes. From this, the blood necessarily pushes the membranes downward, causing them to meet at the center of the arterial vein's opening and close it. Thus, the more violently the heart pulls back blood by its dilation and the lung itself is compressed during exhalation, the more accurately the membranes block the opening of the arterial vein, preventing the blood from flowing back into the heart. Although they do not perform this so perfectly that absolutely no blood [is retracted] in the first...

<meta>The text cuts off at "retractio-", preparing to explain that the valves are not 100% leak-proof, a point Vesalius uses to discuss the movement of "spirit" or subtle matter.</meta>

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VI

<margin>

<margin>
The purpose of the left ventricle of the heart and the reason for its construction.
</margin>
...so that it does not flow back into the heart with the force of its withdrawal. The left ventricle of the heart, because it primarily contains and creates the **vital spirit** <note>In the physiology of the time, "vital spirit" was a refined substance thought to be produced in the heart from air and blood to provide life and heat to the body.</note> and embraces air, has been called "spiritual" or "airy" by professors of dissection. Just as the right ventricle draws blood from the **vena cava**, so this left ventricle draws air—which has been pulled from the lungs into the **venous artery** <note>original: "arteria uenalis"; this refers to what we now call the pulmonary vein.</note>—toward itself when the heart dilates. It uses this air to cool the innate heat, to nourish its own substance, and to produce the vital spirit, "cooking" and preparing this air so that it can be sent into the **great artery** <note>The aorta.</note> and throughout the entire body, along with the blood that is thought to sweat abundantly from the right ventricle into the left through the **septum of the ventricles** <note>original: "per uentriculorum septum copiosus resudare putatur." Vesalius is describing the then-standard Galenic view that blood passed through invisible pores in the heart's central wall, though he would famously express skepticism about these pores elsewhere.</note>. We admit that the flesh of the heart is placed in charge of these types of alterations, insofar as we are able to understand the divine fabric of man.

<margin>
The reason for the structure of the venous artery.
</margin>
Furthermore, if any **sooty residues** <note>original: "fuliginosa recrementa"; Galenic medicine taught that the heart's "burning" of spirit produced smoky waste products, similar to exhaust, which had to be exhaled.</note> are produced by this transformation of air drawn into the left ventricle and by the innate heat itself, we believe they are expelled back into the lungs through the venous artery when the heart contracts. This is the primary reason for the thinness of the construction of the venous artery's wall <margin>b Figure 1, chapter 15, book 3</margin>. For it had to continually and untiringly take in air from the branches of the **rough artery** <note>original: "aspera arteria"; the trachea and bronchi.</note> and from the lung itself; and again, by its own movements corresponding to the rhythms of the heart, it had to propel the sooty remains of the heart back into the branches of the rough artery. It certainly would have done this with great difficulty had it not possessed a body thinner and more porous than that of other arteries. For although other arteries perform the same service for the rest of the body's parts as this one does for the heart, they did not need to take in and propel so much air (which is offered to them from the heart along with blood, not through hidden passages but through the open cavities within them) as the venous artery does. Thus, it was necessary for it to be formed with a thin wall, similar to the body of a vein. Nevertheless, Nature in the meantime provided for its safety as much as possible: by preventing a long path from the left ventricle to the lung (which would have been harmful to the venous artery) <margin>c Figure 2, chapter 15, book 3, H in K, L.</margin>, she divided it immediately at its origin and distributed it into the lung with a very short course, so that being supported and entwined on all sides by the substance of the lung, it would be safer from the danger of rupturing. Then, from the thinness of the venous artery’s body (which Nature would have easily avoided unless she greatly required it), another use arises, suited for the nourishment of the lung. For this artery, being filled with thin and spirited blood, also supplies suitable blood to the lung, providing for the lung what the overly stern and rigid **arterial vein** <note>The pulmonary artery. Vesalius uses "arterial vein" because it looks like an artery but functions like a vein in the Galenic system.</note> denied it, due to the thickness of its body and its blood being less light and airy than the blood of the venous artery.

<margin>
The use of the left auricle of the heart.
</margin>
<margin>
d Figure 6, F; Figure 9, l.
</margin>
Furthermore, the **left auricle** <note>The atrium or its appendage.</note> of the heart, attached to the venous artery, performs the same duty for it and for the left chamber of the heart that we said the right auricle performs for the vena cava and the right ventricle. The left auricle is granted a cavity as much smaller as the opening of the venous artery is seen to be narrower than the opening of the vena cava. Also, air is more following (more easily moved) than blood itself; so, for this reason as well, the left auricle is rightly created smaller than the right. For since air is drawn in so promptly, there was not as much danger that the body of the venous artery would be torn away by the force of the attraction (which draws air chiefly to avoid a vacuum) as there was for the vena cava. However, the fact that the left auricle is slightly more fleshy for its size, and even thicker and fattier, and less quick to move than the right auricle, is also proof that the auricles serve the heart for a certain preparation of materials, and that the auricles themselves share a certain proportion with the chambers of the heart.

<margin>

</margin>
<margin>

</margin>

For two membranes are joined to the opening of the venous artery, and [directed] inward into the ventri-

-># ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE BODY<-

<margin>f Figure 10, B, C, D.</margin>
...led into the ventricle; indeed, when the heart is dilated, they allow air to be carried from the **venous artery** <note>original: "uenali arteria"; known today as the pulmonary vein.</note> into the ventricle. This happens because their fibers are loosened, being drawn more toward the base by the tip of the heart, and the membranes themselves collapse against the sides of the ventricle. However, when the heart constricts, these membranes act as an obstacle to prevent the air from rushing back into the venous artery, which would make the heart's labor useless. Nevertheless, I believe that since there are only two of these membranes <note>The mitral valve.</note>, they do not close their opening so perfectly as to prevent **sooty wastes** <note>original: "fuliginoſis excrementis"; contemporary theory held that "sooty" byproducts of "burning" vital spirit had to be exhaled.</note> from exiting through the venous artery during the heart's constriction. Furthermore, the membranes occupying the opening of the **great artery** <note>The aorta.</note> correspond entirely in function to those we reported finding in the opening of the arterial vein. These allow the **vital spirit**—along with the blood that rushes with force—to flow out into the great artery during the heart's contraction. But when the heart is dilated again, and the spirit and blood are pulled back toward the ventricle, they prevent its regurgitation into the ventricle, as the blood surely presses them toward the center of the great artery's opening (just as we know happens in the arterial vein).

<margin>One should not lightly agree with the common opinions of the Anatomists.</margin>
In this account of the reasoning behind the heart's construction and the use of its parts, I have largely adapted my language to the dogmas of **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–210 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note>. I have done this not because I believe these views are consistent with the truth in every respect, but because in reporting a new use and function for parts here and there, I still distrust myself; not long ago, I would not have dared to turn even a hair's breadth away from the opinion of Galen, the Prince of Physicians.

<margin>g Figure 8, H, H; Figure 10, R.</margin>
<margin>h Figure 9, I, I; Figure 11, I, I; Figure 9, M, M; Figure 10, P, Q.</margin>
For students must not lightly weigh the importance of the **septum** <note>The wall of muscle separating the left and right sides of the heart.</note> or the partition between the heart's ventricles, or the right side of the left ventricle itself. This wall is just as thick, compact, and dense as the rest of the heart's part that embraces the left ventricle. Consequently, I do not know (regardless of whatever is invented about pits in this area, and I am not unmindful of the suction of the **portal vein** from the stomach and intestines) how even the smallest amount of blood could be taken from the right ventricle into the left through the substance of that septum. This is especially puzzling since the vessels of the heart gape into the space of their ventricles with such open orifices—not to mention the true progression of the **vena cava** from the heart.

And while these things turn over in my mind, many questions simultaneously present themselves regarding the series of arteries, about which one might rightly feel ambiguous. For instance, almost no vein seeks the stomach, the intestines, or even the spleen itself without a companion artery; and almost the entire series of the portal vein takes an artery as its companion. Furthermore, such large arteries are shared with the kidneys that we can by no means assert they were produced merely to temper their heat. Still less can we claim that such great arteries were inserted into the stomach, intestines, and spleen solely for the sake of innate heat.

To this is added the fact that one must admit, by many arguments, that there are mutual ebbs and flows of materials through the veins and arteries, and that the heaviness and weight of materials do nothing at all within the veins and arteries. Moreover, the small membranes of the heart, although they serve almost the purpose already stated, do not block every return of material.

Furthermore, when the heart is cut crosswise during the dissection of living animals and the movement of the heart has completely ceased, why do the **auricles** <note>The atria, or upper chambers of the heart.</note> still move and throb? And why are they so large in fetuses and the newborn? To whom should it not be clear that they are formed for the sake of some greater benefit than merely for the strength of the vessels?

<margin>i Compare Q, R in figure 7 with M, M in figure 9.</margin>
And so also, there is a far different reason for the difference in thickness of the parts constituting the right and left ventricles (not to mention the size of the opening of the venous artery compared to the opening of the great artery) than the nature of the materials kept in the ventricles. Indeed, many other things propose themselves here on every side that call the common opinions of the Anatomists into doubt. Because it would take too long to report all of these, and because I myself...

BOOK VI OF THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY.

...having now decided to make no further innovations (since I am by no means satisfied with myself in all matters at once), I shall now bring to a close the history of the parts crafted for the restoration of the **aerial substance** <note>original: "aereae substantiae"; refers to the vital spirit or air processed by the lungs and heart.</note>. I am now about to treat the method of their **administration** <note>original: "administrandi rationem"; the standard Renaissance term for the practical procedure of dissection.</note> in the same sequence with which I completed the dissection of the organs of food, drink, and generation in the immediately preceding book.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'P' featuring a mythological or anatomical scene with multiple figures, one of whom appears to be conducting a dissection or study.</image-desc>

**P**RESENTLY, in this Chapter, in which we have decided primarily to embrace the dissection of those parts described in this book, it must now be placed in the sequence of the discourse after the final chapter of the fifth book. For these chapters, along with the penultimate chapter of the seventh book, shall be arranged in such a way that each proposes the method of administering the parts explained in their respective books. In the meantime, they shall collectively exhibit that order (since, with the addition of a few necessary words to the discourse, this can be conveniently achieved) by which one may demonstrate a complete anatomy to students in a **scarcity of bodies** <note>Vesalius often reminds readers that human cadavers were difficult to obtain, so a specific order of dissection was necessary to see everything before the body decayed.</note>, or by which they may appropriately undertake it by their own effort. Therefore, continuing the administration on the same body you used in the previous book, you will place several supports under its neck, by the help of which it may be stretched out, and the head, reclining backward and not resting on the support, may hang down toward the table.

Next, as I taught in the second book, you will strip the skin from the face and the entire anterior region of the neck. First, you will approach the muscles of the face^a^, which move the skin of the forehead and the eyelids, and the cheeks, lips, and wings of the nostrils. Among their number^b^ is also that one which I listed as the first of those moving the lips and cheeks. When you have also administered that one, you will cut away the muscle from the breastbone and clavicle, which is considered the other of the **seventh pair of those moving the head** <note>The sternocleidomastoid muscle.</note>, and is inserted into the^c^ mastoid process of the head. You will let it hang from there for now, and then apply your dissection to nearly all the muscles^d^ proper to the **bone representing the shape of the letter U** <note>original: "ossi υ imaginē referenti"; the hyoid bone.</note>. At the same time, you will free those muscles from the breastbone^e^ which, arising from it, are inserted into the first cartilage of the **larynx** <note>The sternothyroid muscles.</note>.

Then, from the breastbone, clavicle, and ribs, right up to its insertion, you will separate the muscle^f^ that brings the arm to the chest <note>The pectoralis major.</note>. Furthermore, you will remove that one^g^ from the clavicle which is numbered first among those moving the thorax; and you will also dissect away from the ribs that one^h^ which moves the **scapula** <note>The shoulder blade.</note> toward the chest. Meanwhile, observe this method: allow each muscle to remain attached at its insertion, so that they can later be examined along with the rest of the muscles that still remain to be cut in the parts to which they relate.

And it will suffice to perform this administration of the muscles on one side, while the other side is adapted for inspecting and demonstrating the veins, arteries, and nerves that creep under the skin and alongside the muscles. The sequence of these^k^, if it should happen to slip from memory, must be sought from the third and fourth books. For this discourse would grow to an immense size if I were to recount all of that now.

Now, therefore, you will strive to free the **clavicles** <note>The collarbones.</note> from the breastbone^l^ with a sharper knife, dividing the sturdy ligaments by which they are joined to the breastbone. But in the meantime, be most accurately careful lest, by thrusting the knife too deep, you wound the vessels that lie beneath this joint. And here you will examine the^m^ **cartilage** <note>The articular disc of the sternoclavicular joint.</note> which comes between the clavicle and the cavity of the breastbone, distinct from the other cartilages of the joints. It should be set aside somewhere so that you may use it later (if you see fit) in the assembly of the **skeleton**. Having freed the clavicles, you will strive to lift them with force away from the breastbone...

To more conveniently demonstrate those things that remain to be undertaken in the chest, I have been accustomed first to pluck away the membrane lining the ribs here and there with a small hook, and to use my hands to separate the lung from it if it should adhere by fibers anywhere. Furthermore, having perforated some interval of the ribs to which the lung is attached, I demonstrate in what manner a person's chest is occasionally pierced without respiration being abolished or the motion of the lung ceasing. <gloss>t</gloss>

<gloss>u</gloss> Soon, after dividing the intercostal muscles, I have been accustomed to break the ribs at about the middle of their length. This is done with little trouble if each rib is grasped firmly and separately by hand and turned outward or bent. However, since I have found that easy method of preparing a skeleton—so that the bones of the cadaver may serve for its construction—I would prefer the ribs to be kept whole, and for all the ribs to be twisted outward together by hand as much as possible. Then, after dividing the intercostal muscles to some extent, the ribs should be gradually separated from one another. In this way, the width of the chest is made sufficiently open, especially if you place a stone or some ball under the length of the back, at about the middle of the chest; by its force, the hump of the back, protruding outside the chest cavity, is pushed into the cavity of the chest, and a larger space is created between the ribs of the right and left sides.

When you see this nerve extending along with the vein originating from the throat <gloss>y</gloss>, you will break it near the septum; then you will cast it back toward the neck, so that you may later see its origin <gloss>z</gloss>.

# ON THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VI.

...[you should] move the heart with its envelope <note>the pericardium</note> from side to side, and examine the specific position and shape of that envelope. However, the inspection which I previously wished to be performed—with the breastbone slightly raised and the heart still unmoved, for the sake of the partitioning membranes <note>the mediastinum</note>—also contributes greatly to this end. The lobes of the lung must also now be handled by hand, so that their number, position, and shape may be investigated; and finally, you may learn <margin>b Figure 5, between D.</margin> that in humans, no part of the lung is placed beneath the vena cava where it stands between the diaphragm <note>original: "septum transuersum"</note> and the heart; indeed, the vein penetrates the diaphragm and the heart's envelope simultaneously and without any interval: and where the vein is led here, the envelope <margin>c Figure 3, G, F.</margin> is uniquely grown together with the diaphragm in humans with great breadth. To see this <margin>d as was done in Figure 4</margin> more accurately, the heart's envelope will be divided by a long incision, and the fluid floating within it will be wiped away with a sponge: and finally, the envelope will be cut away from the heart's vessels <margin>e Figure 6, g.</margin>, with care taken so that the beginning of the left recurrent nerve is not damaged. To examine the passage of the vena cava <margin>g drawn out from c.</margin> through the diaphragm, and its path through the chest, <margin>Examination of the distribution of the vena cava through the chest and throat.</margin> you will make an incision in the diaphragm up to the trunk of the vein: taking care <margin>f Figure for chapter 6, book 3, C.</margin> not to wound the roots of the two branches of the vena cava running into it at the same time: <margin>g Figure 5, C to B.</margin> then ascending gradually upwards, you will observe how the vena cava is joined to the right auricle <note>atrium</note> of the heart without any incision. Thus also above the base of the heart, from the right side of the vena cava <margin>h Figure 5, G; Figure for chapter 6, book 3, F.</margin> you will find the azygos vein <note>original: "uena sine coniuge", literally "the vein without a mate"</note> arising: you will learn its path better if you first lift the right part of the lung toward the left side, and afterward roll the left part onto the right side. For these things are made obvious without any incision; though with the heart and lung removed, they may be viewed even more exactly. Nor indeed should these things be looked at in passing, but the craftsmanship of Nature in the path and origin of the azygos vein must be investigated industriously: and it must be diligently observed whether, as sometimes occurs in lambs and pigs, some vein is also extended into the left side, born near the connection of the vena cava to the heart <margin>i Here look carefully at H in the figure of chapter 6, book 3, or rather the last figure of book 3 near p.</margin>. Furthermore, the distribution of the vena cava in the throat must be inquired into with a blunt knife, with which the glands <note>likely the thymus or lymph nodes</note> lying upon it are removed. Nor should you use any other artifice than to have our drawings of the veins at hand: and apply your mind with the greatest care lest you puncture any vein. When you have found the sequence of the vena cava, both jugulars and the trunk of the vein approaching the arm <margin>k Figure 2, F.</margin> and then the vena cava where it gives off the azygos vein, they shall be intercepted with ligatures: and whatever veins consist between the ligatures shall be removed from the body: and then, once the blood is washed away, the incision shall immediately be turned toward finding the branches of the aorta <note>original: "arterię magnæ"</note> and the recurrent nerves <margin>l Figure 6, I.</margin>. With the heart then taken in hand, you look at the roots of the pulmonary artery <note>original: "uenæ arterialis", literally "arterial vein"</note>, and the pulmonary vein <note>original: "arteriæ uenalis", literally "venous artery"</note>, <margin>Examination of the distribution of the great artery through the chest and throat.</margin> <margin>m Figure 6, G.</margin> and the aorta itself, where they are closest to the base of the heart <margin>n Figure 6, O.</margin>: which is very easy to do if you apply your mind to both their colors and positions. For the pulmonary artery is near the right auricle: and is seen as whitish and proceeding somewhat to the left, and stands out among the vessels of the heart. The pulmonary vein, however, is blackish like a vein: and lower than the other vessels, it lies hidden near the left auricle, and its progress offers itself with a very small interval. The aorta, indeed, occurs in the middle of the base of the heart, somewhat hidden under the pulmonary artery. As soon as you have looked at this, search for all its branches <margin>o Figure 6, R, Q, S, T, V, X.</margin>: the upper ones, and those closest to the throat, are already visible without other work, unless perhaps some remains of the gland still remain to be cut away. <margin>p Figure 6, P; Figure for chapter 12, book 3, i.</margin> The trunk, however, which is turned back toward the spine, will not appear conveniently unless the left part of the lung is lifted toward the right side. You will gradually free the nerve with a small knife: and when you have approached the thorax, you will weigh carefully the small branch of this nerve which is stretched out to the roots of the ribs, and those offshoots which it derived here to the muscles originating from the top of the breastbone <note>the sternum</note>. <margin>i Figure 6, T.</margin> As soon as you have led the nerve down to be extended to the artery of the right armpit <note>the axillary artery</note>, you will, with a very sharp knife, as studiously as possible, separate the three offshoots <margin>u Insert P at E in figure of chapter 9, book 4.</margin> <margin>x Figure 6, b.</margin> which it reflects back toward it (unless there are only two, or just one) from the neighboring small membranes. You must take care lest perhaps, by using a blunter knife, you pull the membranes while cutting them and injure the offshoots; although, on the other hand, you must also be careful not to incautiously cut away the offshoots along with the membranes with a sharp knife. <margin>y Insert Q, Q in figure of chapter 9, book 4, and Figure 6, c.</margin> Once the origins of the offshoots are found, you will free the nerve stretched out along the side of the trachea <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"</note> from the membrane to which it is joined and from the trachea itself, by making a long incision with a sharp knife between the nerve and the trachea. Having freed the nerve in this manner, you will grasp it with the tips of the fingers of your left hand, lifting it slightly from the trachea: then with your right hand, you will elevate the trunk of the sixth pair <note>The "sixth pair" in Vesalius’s system corresponds to the modern Vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X).</note> where it is stretched out toward the carotid <note>original: "soporariæ"</note> arteries. Then, by moving your hands mutually, now upward and now downward, you will investigate the reflected nature of the recurrent nerve. <margin>z Chapter 2, book 4, figure 2, q and r.</margin> In exactly the same way, after you have examined certain offshoots distributed from the right nerve of the sixth pair to the lung and the envelope of the heart <note>the pericardium</note>, <margin>a Figure 6, d from x.</margin> it is appropriate to pull away the left trunk of the sixth pair of cerebral nerves from the carotid of the left side. You should then track its offshoots, which it extends to the muscles originating from the higher seat of the breastbone and to the roots of the ribs. <margin>b Figure 6, e. c Figure 6, h.</margin> Afterward, having observed the branches it derives to the tunics of the lung, and having also accurately searched for that offshoot which it offers to the base of the heart <margin>d Figure 6, P.</margin> along the left side of the trunk of the pulmonary artery <note>original: "uenæ arterialis"</note>, the nerve of the sixth pair of this side is to be led all the way to the trunk of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> where it reflects toward the back. Here, similarly with a sharp knife, the offspring forming the recurrent nerve are to be found. <margin>e Figure 6, f. f Figure 6, g, g.</margin> When you see these, you will push a blunter probe <note>original: "stylum"</note> under that trunk of the artery toward the left side of the trachea: and with the probe lifted somewhat, you will moderately separate the trunk of the artery from the back, to which it is very firmly committed. # THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VI.

Regarding the inflammation of the lower ribs on either side, some contend that Hippocrates asserted blood should not be let; they argue that the heart draws blood so forcefully from the azygos vein <note>original: "uena sine pari," the vein that drains the thoracic wall</note> that nothing can be drawn out by bloodletting from this vein. As if indeed, now while you are dissecting, it were not perfectly clear to you that the heart—in cases of bloodletting when the eight lower intercostal spaces are inflamed—presents no obstacle, and therefore blood should indeed be let then as well. Hippocrates was not so dull that he would have thought the eight lower ribs were below the diaphragm <note>original: "septum transuerso"</note>, or remained ignorant that inflammation in this area produces tension all the way up to the collarbone. However, this discourse must be restrained, lest it wander too far from my purpose toward my personal opinion on bloodletting in cases of side-ailments <note>likely pleurisy</note>. And yet, by Hercules, I believe the truth of this matter should never be investigated more than with these present veins, rather than trying to extract it through the distorted votes of authors without a knowledge of the vessels.

Furthermore, as soon as you have inserted a probe into the vein that lacks a partner <note>the azygos vein</note>, a long and thick rod should be placed into the vena cava<sup>n</sup>. When you have pushed this rod without difficulty straight through the vena cava all the way to the lowest part of the belly, you will learn how beautifully Galen and the other teachers of dissection have hallucinated up to this point; they believed that the vena cava arose from the convex part <note>original: "gibbo"</note> of the liver as a single trunk,<sup>o</sup> and was divided into two trunks (one seeking the lower parts and the other the upper) in the same way as the great artery <note>the aorta</note>.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents you now from cutting away as much of the diaphragm from the body as you can, and reflecting the liver toward the left side so that its posterior seat comes into view. Therefore, when you have kept the rod for some time in the vena cava (having pushed it from the area where it faces the heart down to the region where the vessels are offered to the kidneys), and you have noticed that the substance of the liver does not<sup>p</sup> cover the entire posterior seat of the vena cava, you will divide the cava with a knife following the length of the rod, and you will investigate the mouths of the veins extending from the cava to the liver<sup>q</sup>. Then, having called upon those who have too stubbornly sworn by the words of Galen, the primary professor of anatomy, you will resume his individual arguments concerning the origin of the veins. You shall exhort the students not to learn to "sail from commentaries" <note>a metaphor for learning only from books rather than experience</note>, commending the unique truth, rather than authority.

# BOOK VI OF THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY

...the external surface of the azygos vein <note>original: "uenae pari carentis"; literally, the 'vein lacking a pair,' now known as the azygos vein</note> at its origin, as well as those branches which are extended from the vena cava into the liver. This is done so that the membranous thickness of the vessel’s own body may be seen there, formed for the sake of strength at the branching points of the vessels. However, I would not wish it to be overlooked that some students, when we usually discuss the movement of blood during dissection, have sometimes contended that those membranous protrusions of the vessels entirely prevent the return of blood into the trunk or stem of the vena cava. When you have also torn it away from the ribs, you will readily observe the aforementioned offsets of the veins and arteries, and the nerves extended along the ribs. By driving the point of a knife very close to the bone of any rib, you will examine the membrane that specifically wraps each individual rib. I mean that membrane which some skilled in dissection have called the "membrane lining the ribs" <note>the pleura</note>; it is the membrane corresponding to those which, because they surround bones, we commonly call "around-the-bone" <term>periosteum</term>. Indeed, some (as we mentioned in the proper place) have enumerated two membranes lining the ribs. Having completed in this manner everything enclosed by the peritoneum and the membrane lining the ribs, if you wish, you should try to replace the ribs in their places as accurately as possible.

In the manner I have described, you will use your hands to forcibly twist the parts of the jaw bone <note>the mandible</note> outward and downward, and you will open the mouth. Furthermore, you will push a probe, curved like a siphon, from the nasal openings down into the cavity of the mouth, examining the nature of the <term>uvula</term> <note>original: "gargareonis"</note>. Soon, you will lead a cut with a small knife from the root of the <term>uvula</term> all the way to the incisor teeth in the lining of the mouth, freeing it somewhat from the underlying organs just as you would with skin. In this work, the <term>third pair</term> <note>In Vesalius's system, the third pair refers to branches of the Trigeminal nerve (Cranial Nerve V)</note> of cranial nerves will present itself, where it is diverted to the tongue and the lower jaw. Then, you will see the <term>seventh pair</term> <note>likely referring to the Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) in this context</note> of cranial nerves joined with the sixth, along with the <term>carotid artery</term> <note>original: "soporiali arteria"; the "sleep-inducing" artery</note> and the internal jugular vein. If you ascend a little further, you will also see the <term>fourth pair</term> of cranial nerves, and certain branches of the third and fifth pairs extended to the temporal muscle, provided you are not reluctant to gently separate one organ from another. In addition to these, the muscles of the tongue will be found, just as we taught in the second book; in the management of these, the offshoots of the nerves running into the tongue will present themselves, along with the veins and arteries. The hidden muscles of the lower jaw are also encountered here with little effort: namely, that one which, lurking in the mouth, draws the jaw upward along with the temporal and masseter muscles; and that one which, arising from the <term>process resembling a stylus</term> <note>the styloid process</note>, is implanted into the lower jaw at the tip of the chin. Furthermore, the <term>tonsils</term> and other glands, which oversee the distribution of vessels in the throat, will beautifully present themselves to you as you attempt this procedure. The muscles of the larynx <note>the voice box</note> are to be approached exactly as we advised in the second book; their nerves must not be noticed only in passing while they are being dissected. Now, having removed the tongue together with the <term>bone resembling the shape of the letter U</term> <note>the hyoid bone, often called "upsilon-shaped" in Latin</note>, the larynx, and the beginning of the <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "stomachus"; in this era, the word often referred to the gullet</note>, you will completely free the lower jaw from the upper, not neglecting meanwhile the peculiar cartilages stored here. There is nothing to prevent you from preserving these—just like the cartilages of the collarbones that come between the joints with the breastbone—for the construction of a skeleton. In the same way, you should set aside for the same use the bone representing the letter U, the cartilages of the larynx, the wings of the nose, and the cartilages of the ears and eyelids. Now, carefully scrape the lining of the palate and the lining that girds the nostrils away from the bone, so that you may learn the mutual connection of those linings. If, however, when you were approaching the muscles that move the head and back, you did not first see the pair that acts on the back to your satisfaction, it is now very easy to do so, once those things that occupied the throat have been removed. Indeed, nothing prevents you from preserving the muscles overseeing the movements of the head and back intact for as long as it takes to remove the lower jaw and the contents of the throat in the sequence of dissection. Although all these things should be obvious to anyone from the second book, one also learns from the end of the first book which ribs must be removed from the vertebrae for the preparation of a skeleton, and which breastbone and the cartilages joined to it should be kept. Thus, nothing stands in the way of now freeing the head from the first vertebra in the proposed cadaver and learning in it those things which the following book will describe; in the penultimate chapter of which, I will recount all the remaining things that are still to be seen in our proposed cadaver.

## THE END OF THE SIXTH BOOK.

# INDEX of the FIRST FIGURE and its characters.

*THE FIRST figure of the seventh book displays the human head, prepared and separated from the neck and lower jaw in a manner suitable for showing the brain. Additionally, we have sawed away a circular portion of the skullcap <note>original: "caluariae"</note>—as much as is usually removed to view the entire cavity of the structures contained within the skull. To ensure that an image of the removed portion also appeared here, we have placed the seventh figure of the sixth chapter of Book I below the present figure; this is because that figure accurately represents the interior surface of that part of the skullcap which, before the dissection, covered and embraced everything primarily shown in this first figure. This figure places before your eyes the <term>dura mater</term> <note>Vesalius calls this the "hard membrane" (dura membrana). It is the tough, outermost layer surrounding the brain.</note> still unharmed, neither punctured nor wounded in any part. However, we have in the meantime severed the connections of this membrane which extend through the sutures of the skull to form the membrane that surrounds the skull on the outside <note>the pericranium</note>. Along with these fibers, the small vessels have also been broken; these are led through the small holes and sutures of the skull and are shared between the dura mater and the membrane covering the skull. Furthermore, of the two circles seen surrounding the figure, the lower one consists of the skin and the membrane lying beneath it, while the higher one is the skull itself. Everything contained within this circle, and marked with many characters, represents the dura mater of the brain.*

**A,A** The right side of the dura mater, or that part of the membrane surrounding the right region of the brain.
**B,B** The left side of the dura mater.
**C,C,C** The <term>third sinus</term> <note>Now known as the superior sagittal sinus, a large blood-filtering channel running along the top of the brain.</note> of the dura mater, stretched out along the length of the head, and not opened by dissection in any part here.
**D,D,D** Two ducts placed next to each other, running like veins into the dura mater along its entire side.
**E** A duct representing a vein of the dura mater, into which the "sixth vein" entering the skull is emptied.
**F,F,F** These characters indicate small veins transmitted from the dura mater through the small holes of the skull to the skin of the head and the membrane covering the skull; the more frequent and thicker of these are usually observed near the seat of the most hidden part of F.
**G,G,G** Small portions of fibers springing forth from the dura mater through the <term>coronal suture</term> <note>The joint across the top of the skull from side to side.</note> to the constitution of the membrane surrounding the skull.
**H,H** Small portions of fibers for which the <term>sagittal suture</term> <note>The joint running down the middle of the top of the skull.</note> offers a path.
**I,I** The site from which fibers are extended through the suture similar to the Greek letter Λ <note>The lambdoid suture at the back of the head.</note>.
**K** One tubercle (bump) of the dura mater, of the kind that usually grows near the unequal boundaries of the skull, often found near the union of the sagittal and coronal sutures. The head from which we drew this first figure was gifted with three tubercles of this kind, one of which we marked K, and one also appears on both sides toward the front H.
**L** The cavity of the frontal bone near the site of the eyebrows, which is opened during cutting if the frontal bone is divided with a saw not far from the eyebrows <note>The frontal sinus.</note>.

---

## INDEX of the SECOND FIGURE (which the following page will display) and its characters.

*THE SECOND figure, following the first in the sequence of dissection, shows the third sinus of the dura mater opened by a long cut made along the length of the head. Furthermore, at the sides of this third sinus, I have also made two cuts along the length of the head—one on each side of the sinus—which only penetrated the dura mater and separated the sides of the dura mater from that process of the membrane which divides the right part of the brain from the left <note>The falx cerebri</note>. Besides the three cuts already mentioned, I performed another on each side which, reaching from the region of the ear to the crown of the head, also divided only the dura mater, so that it could afterwards be properly drawn away from the <term>pia mater</term> <note>Vesalius calls this the "thin membrane" (tenuis membrana). It is the delicate, inner layer in direct contact with the brain.</note> and folded downward (as you see done here). Thus, the pia mater of the brain appears here entirely unharmed, drawn closely over the brain, and elegantly showing the sequence of its vessels in the region now laid bare.*

**A,A,A** The higher site of the process of the dura mater intervening between the right and left parts of the brain. This site, marked A and A, is the "ridge" of the third sinus of the dura mater, touching the skull, and here dissected through the middle.
**B,B** Here the cavity of the third sinus of the dura mater is in the open.
**C,C** The orifices and beginnings of vessels belonging to the pia mater from the third sinus of the dura mater. And here indeed the orifices of the vessels are in view, belonging to that part of the pia mater from the left side of this sinus which is wrapped around the left side of the brain. The orifices born from the right side, however, are not seen here: but the beginnings...

### THIRD FIGURE OF THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<image-desc>Anatomical woodcut illustration of the human brain (cerebrum) from a superior-posterior perspective, with the skull removed. In the preparation of this figure, we also had to do this: the broken starting points of those vessels are here presented to the eyes.

**F** *A channel, running like a vein into the lower part of the process of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>the <term>dura mater</term>, the tough outer layer of the brain's protection</note> which separates the right part of the brain from the left <note>this process is the <term>falx cerebri</term></note>. **G, G, G** *Offshoots of the channel already marked **F**, running upward to some extent into that same process of the hard membrane.*

**K** *The beginning of a vessel emerging from the end of the fourth sinus of the hard membrane.
