**M, M** *Cavities <note>original: *sinus*</note> visible on both sides of the callous body in the brain. These cannot be shown here any differently than we have just done, as they are narrow and mostly resemble very thin cracks.*
**N** *A portion of the process of the brain's hard membrane dividing the right and left sides; this part was attached to the <term>septum</term> or process of the eighth bone of the head <note>Vesalius refers to the <term>ethmoid bone</term> as the eighth bone; the process is the <term>crista galli</term></note>, which divides the cavities of the olfactory organs.*

# THE FOURTH FIGURE OF THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut anatomical illustration from Andreas Vesalius's "De humani corporis fabrica" depicting a superior view of a human brain dissection. The skull cap and meninges have been removed. The lateral ventricles are exposed. On the right, a large section of the left cerebral hemisphere (labeled C) has been cut away and laid open to reveal the internal structure. Various parts of the brain and ventricles are marked with uppercase letters (A-Q) for reference in the following index.</image-desc>

## INDEX OF THE FOURTH FIGURE,
### and its labels.

*In this fourth figure, we have cut away all the parts of the <term>hard and thin membranes</term> <note>the <term>dura mater</term> and <term>pia mater</term></note> which appeared in the previous figures. Then, by a series of sections, we removed the right and left portions of the brain so that the <term>ventricles</term> <note>the fluid-filled cavities within the brain</note> of the brain now begin to come into view. First, along the right side of the <term>callous body</term> <note>the <term>corpus callosum</term>, the thick bridge of fibers connecting the two hemispheres</note>, where the sinus marked with the second **M** in the third figure is located, we performed a long cut. This cut, led through the right ventricle of the brain, removed that portion of the right side of the brain which was located above the section where we divided the skull in a circle with the saw. And when we had completed the same on the left side, we placed the left part of the brain back here in such a way that it shows, to some extent, the upper seat of the left ventricle, while the callous body is still preserved in the head.*

**A, A, A** *The right part of the brain still remaining in the skull.*
**B, B, B** *The left part of the brain still remaining in the skull.*
**C, C, C** *The left portion of the brain which, having been removed from the rest of the brain by a series of cuts, here lies turned upwards.*
**D, D, D** *Lines showing partly the <term>convolutions</term> <note>the folds or gyri of the brain's surface</note> and partly the nature of the color of the brain's substance. For whatever lies outside the lines is somewhat yellowish and <term>ash-colored</term> <note>this refers to the gray matter</note>; whatever is contained within the lines is seen to be perfectly white <note>this refers to the white matter</note>. For this reason, the areas marked **E** and **F** appear yellowish, while those inscribed with **G** and **H** are entirely white, and occasionally interspersed with red spots.*
**I, I, I** *The <term>callous body</term> <note>the <term>corpus callosum</term></note>, freed by the section from the brain substance on both sides, to which it is otherwise continuous.*
**K, K** *A small portion of the callous body, still continuous with the left part of the brain that was removed.*
**L, L** *The right ventricle of the brain.*
**M, M** *The left ventricle of the brain.*
**N, N** *A portion of the upper seat of the left ventricle.*
**O, O** *The plexus of the brain, called <term>choroid</term> <note>original: χοροειδὴς, <term>choroeidēs</term></note> because of the resemblance it bears to the <term>chorion</term> <note>the membrane or afterbirth that surrounds a fetus</note>.*
**P, P** *Slender veins like spiderwebs, joined in this place to the substance of the right and left ventricles, and drawn from those vessels which construct the aforementioned plexus.*
**Q** *A small vein running from the already mentioned vessels forming the plexus into the thin membrane of the brain beneath the front seat of the callous body, presenting themselves in an irregular series (just as the vein marked **P** does) during the cutting.*

# THE FIFTH FIGURE OF THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<image-desc>An anatomical woodcut of a human brain viewed from above, with the cranial vault removed. ## INDEX OF THE FIFTH FIGURE,
### and its labels.

*The **fifth figure**, as far as the part of the brain remaining in the <term>skullcap</term> <note>Latin: calvaria</note> is concerned, does not vary in any way from the preceding figure. It has this one unique feature: here, we have first freed the <term>callous body</term> <note>the **corpus callosum**, the bridge of white matter connecting the two hemispheres</note> from the brain at its anterior <note>front</note> position; then, having lifted it, we have reflected it backwards, pulling apart the <term>septum</term> <note>the **septum pellucidum**, a thin membrane separating the left and right ventricles</note> of the right and left <term>ventricles</term> <note>the fluid-filled cavities of the brain</note>, and placing before your eyes the upper surface of the body constructed in the likeness of a <term>vault</term> <note>the **fornix**, from the Latin *testudo*, meaning a tortoise shell or an arched roof</note>.*

<margin>From A up to Q</margin>
*Therefore, **A, A, A** and **B, B, B**, and then **D, D, D**, and **E** and **F**, and **G** and **H**, indicate the same things here as they did in the fourth figure. In the same way, **L, L**, and **M, M**, and **O** and **P** and **Q** signify the same things.*

***R, R, R*** *marks the lower surface of the callous body. For it has been moved from its seat and turned back toward the rear.*

***S, T, U*** *The upper surface of the body constructed like a <term>vault</term> <note>the **fornix**</note> or arch, and its triangular boundary, which we measure from **S** to **T**, and from **T** to **U**, and from **U** to **S**.*

***X, X*** *The lower part of the <term>septum</term> <note>the **septum pellucidum**</note> that comes between the right and left ventricles, which is continuous with the body representing the vault.*

***Y, Y*** *The upper part of the already mentioned septum, which is continuous with the callous body. For this septum could not be depicted in any other way than as it has just been torn apart. Another figure was also prepared, in which two hands (as I was accustomed to do in the second book) slightly raised the callous body—not yet freed from its anterior seat—so that the "mirror" or septum might be presented to the eyes while still intact. However, since the matter did not turn out as elegantly in the drawing as it did in the actual <term>dissection</term> <note>Latin: sectione</note>, I rejected that figure so as not to clutter the page in vain.*

## INDEX TO THE SIXTH FIGURE,
## *and its labels.*

*This **sixth figure**, regarding the portion of the brain left in the <term>skullcap</term> <note>Latin: calvaria</note>, also corresponds to the fourth figure. It differs from the fifth figure in this way: we have now freed the <term>vaulted body</term> <note>the **fornix**; from the Latin *testudo*, referring to an arched roof or tortoise shell</note> from the brain substance at its forward position, reflecting it upward and backward so that its lower surface comes into view. This also allows one to see that vessel which, originating from the fourth sinus of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>the **dura mater**</note>, is carried under the vaulted body we just described; it finally forms a significant part of the <term>plexuses</term> <note>the **choroid plexuses**, networks of blood vessels</note> which the ancients compared to the appearance of the <term>afterbirth</term> <note>Latin: secundae; the fetal membranes or placenta</note>.*

*A, A, A The vaulted body <note>the fornix</note> as just described; here its lower surface is visible, which forms the upper seat of the **third ventricle**.*
*B, B The portion of the vaulted body in the right ventricle, taking its origin here from the brain substance.*
*C The portion of the body resembling a vault in form and function, which arises from the left ventricle of the brain.*
*D, D The right ventricle of the brain.*
*E, E The left ventricle of the brain.*
*F An artery passing through the lower and rear part of the right ventricle, coming from a branch of the right <term>sleep-inducing artery</term> <note>the **carotid artery**; the name stems from the ancient belief that compressing these arteries induced sleep</note> which pierces the hard membrane of the brain and climbs here into the right ventricle.*
*G An artery climbing into the left ventricle of the brain.*
*H A vessel taking its origin from the fourth sinus of the hard membrane of the brain, and hastening under the vault-like body into the common cavity of the right and left ventricles (or the **third ventricle**); in its entire course, it is entwined in wonderful ways.*
*I The division of the vessel marked **H** into two portions.*
*K The other portion of the division of the vessel marked **H**, seeking the right ventricle of the brain.*

### INDEX TO THE SEVENTH FIGURE,
### *and its labels.*

The present figure varies greatly from the three immediately preceding it. For in this figure, that brain substance which we had still left in the sequence of dissection in those earlier figures is now seen as a removed part—specifically the part that formed the seat of the right and left ventricles so visible in those images. Furthermore, the entire portion of the brain that was still resting upon the <term>cerebellum</term> <note>the "little brain" at the back of the head</note> has also been cast back here, as has the process of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>the **dura mater**; specifically referring here to the **tentorium cerebelli**</note> that comes between the cerebellum and the cerebrum. Additionally, we have opened the sinuses of the hard membrane located here in this figure, as well as the vessel reaching from the fourth sinus of the hard membrane into the ventricles of the brain, which has been raised out of the third ventricle of the brain and from the plexuses similar to the <term>afterbirth</term>... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "libus" suggests the next page continues describing the plexuses being "freed" (liberatis) from their attachments.</note>

# BOOK VII ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

...having torn it away, we have reflected it toward the rear: so that the site of the third ventricle of the brain—the common cavity of the right and left ventricles—might come better into view, together with the passages of that cavity.

**A, A** The right part of the brain substance still remaining in the skull.
**B, B** The left part of the brain substance still preserved in the skull.
**C, C, C** The lines occurring here and there correspond to those which the three preceding figures similarly showed. But because this kind of diversity in the brain's substance exists only where the brain is closest to the <term>thin membrane</term> <note>the **pia mater**, the delicate innermost layer surrounding the brain</note>, the preceding figures showed it only on the sides. This figure, however, since it has such a large portion of the brain removed that the visible surface at the base is not far from the thin membrane, also shows this difference in the color of the brain's substance; and the lines just mentioned are seen at the base. Thus, the area intercepted by the lines and marked **D, D, D** is yellowish and somewhat pale; whereas what lies outside the lines, marked **E, E, E**, is white and completely bright.
**F** A portion of the <term>soporific artery</term> <note>original: *arteria soporalis*; the **internal carotid artery**, so named because pressure on it was thought to induce sleep or stupor</note>, creeping upward along the lower and narrower part of the right ventricle toward the <term>afterbirth-like</term> <note>original: *secundinas imitantis*; the **choroid plexus**</note> construction. Furthermore, if you consider where this **F** is placed here, and where it occurs in the sixth figure, you will readily observe how the right ventricle of the brain (just like the left) is narrowed like a horn from its posterior seat and is led downward into the anterior parts through the brain's substance. For here, where we have removed more of the brain's substance than in the sixth figure, the portion of the artery marked **F** turns more forward than the **F** in the sixth figure, also suggesting that part of the artery where it already ascends the posterior seat of the ventricle. And this is shown more clearly by **F** and **G** of the subsequent figure, in which I have removed even more brain substance in the name of showing the path of this ventricle than in this one, which is seventh in order.
**G** A portion of the soporific artery creeping upward along the lower and posterior seat of the left ventricle.
**H** The lowest seat of the third ventricle: which, so that it might be more aptly perceived, we have depicted as somewhat distended.
**I** A passage sloping straight down from the third ventricle of the brain, reaching and carrying the brain's <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *pituita*; the **cerebrospinal fluid**, which ancient and Renaissance doctors believed was a waste product filtered through the pituitary gland</note> to the <term>basin</term> <note>the **infundibulum** and **sella turcica**</note> prepared to receive it.
**K** A passage from the third ventricle of the brain between the <term>testes and buttocks</term> <note>original: *testes natesque*; the **corpora quadrigemina** (superior and inferior colliculi)</note> of the brain, reaching into the cavity common to the cerebellum and the <term>dorsal marrow</term> <note>the **spinal cord**</note>.
**L** A gland not unlike a pine nut <note>the **pineal gland**</note>, and the support for the vessels seeking the brain from the <term>fourth sinus</term> of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>the **dura mater**</note>.
**M, N** This part of the brain, still covered by the thin membrane, we call the "testes" and "buttocks" of the brain.
**O, O, O** The process or portion of the brain's hard membrane placed between the cerebellum and the brain <note>the **tentorium cerebelli**</note>. The vessel ducts, like veins, that approach this or run through it, arise partly from the first and second sinuses of the hard membrane, and partly from the fourth.
**P, P** The right or first sinus of the brain's hard membrane <note>the **right transverse sinus**</note>.
**Q, Q** The left or second sinus of the brain's hard membrane <note>the **left transverse sinus**</note>.
**R** The meeting point of the first and second sinuses of the hard membrane, which some of the Greeks called the <note>original: ληνὸν (*lēnon*); which is a **wine press** (*torcular*)</note> <note>the **confluence of sinuses**, still known as the *torcular Herophili*</note>.
**S** The beginning of the third sinus of the hard membrane.
**T** The fourth sinus of the hard membrane <note>the **straight sinus**</note>, opened here by dissection just like the others.
**V** A vessel stretching from the fourth sinus of the hard membrane into the ventricles of the brain <note>the **great cerebral vein** or Vein of Galen</note>, here reflected backward from its place.
**X, X** In this place the cerebellum, not covered by the hard membrane of the brain, presents itself.
**Y** Ducts, in the manner of veins, reaching from the fourth sinus of the hard membrane into the thin membrane, where the cerebellum and the "testes" of the brain itself are clothed.
**Z, Z** The site of the hard membrane where it is attached to the <term>hardest bone of all the bones of the body</term> <note>the **petrous part of the temporal bone**</note>, which contains the organ of hearing within it. We have uncovered this region of the skull by removing the brain that lay upon it.

->Index of its characters.<-

<margin>A through H.</margin> *The eighth figure differs from the seventh in this: that here we have cut away still more of the brain, and have divided the <term>testes of the brain</term> <note>original: *cerebri testes*; these are the **inferior colliculi**, part of the midbrain</note> with a long incision so that the passage extending from the third ventricle into the fourth might be encountered. Additionally, the portion of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>the **dura mater**</note> covering the cerebellum is seen here dissected and reflected toward the rear. Since the present figure has many things in common with the seventh, in this figure* **A A**, *and* **B B**, *and* **C C**, *and* **D D**, *and* **E E**, *and* **F** *&* **G** *&* **H** *indicate the same as they did in the seventh. However, the arteries marked* **F** *&* **G** *turn forward so much more here than in the seventh, because more of the brain was removed toward the base in the seventh than in the sixth.*

<margin>I</margin> *A passage descending straight down, carrying the <term>pituita</term> <note>original: *pituitam*; in the 16th century, "pituita" or phlegm was thought to be a waste product of the brain that drained through this area</note> of the brain to the <term>basin</term> <note>original: *peluim*; the **infundibulum**, shaped like a funnel or basin</note>.*

<margin>K</margin> *A passage prepared for leading away the pituita, which is sometimes drawn from that passage which extends from the third ventricle between the "testes" into the fourth ventricle.*

<margin>L</margin> *Lest **L** should be hidden entirely in shadow—or if it were placed in its proper location and the shadow had to be carved away to make the name visible—the drawing would be entirely ruined; therefore, I have repositioned this **L** at the front part of the cerebellum to mark the opening and passage which is carried from the third ventricle of the brain into the fourth <note>the **cerebral aqueduct**, or Aqueduct of Sylvius</note>.*

<margin>M</margin> *Here we have still left the gland which, showing the shape of a pine nut <note>original: *pineæ nucis formam*; the **pineal gland**</note>, is made to be a support for the vessels extending from the fourth sinus of the hard membrane into the ventricles of the brain.*

<margin>N,O,P,Q</margin> *By these four characters, that body is indicated which was a single unit before dissection, and was marked **M** & **N** in the seventh figure; here, however, it appears divided and spread apart by the sequence of the incision. **N** & **O** indicate the seats of that body to which the name "testes" <note>the **inferior colliculi**</note> is applied. **P** & **Q**, moreover, suggest those seats which we generally call the "buttocks" <note>original: *nates*; the **superior colliculi**. Together with the testes, these form the **corpora quadrigemina**</note>.*

<margin>R,R,R</margin> *The cerebellum, still covered by the <term>thin membrane</term> <note>the **pia mater**</note>.*

<margin>S,S,S</margin> *Vessels, entwining the thin membrane of the cerebellum in the manner of veins.*

## INDEX OF THE NINTH FIGURE, AND its characters.

*In this figure, the same portion of the brain is preserved as in the eighth. However, the present figure is placed entirely on its face, and has that process of the hard membrane cut away which separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum. Then, the cerebellum is here pulled by hands downward out of its seat in the skull, and hangs down moderately turned inward, so that its region (otherwise adjacent to the skull) might be subjected to the eyes, and the cavity of the <term>dorsal medulla</term> <note>original: *dorsalis medullæ*; here referring to the **brainstem** or **medulla oblongata**</note> might be seen, constituting the other part of the <term>fourth ventricle</term>. In addition to this, besides the paths of certain veins and nerves, the first and second <term>sinuses of the hard membrane</term> <note>the **dural venous sinuses**</note> are also expressed here, opened exactly.*
*A, A The portion of the cerebrum still remaining in the expanse of the skull, and here still preserved in its seat.*
*B, C, D By these three characters, the cerebellum is indicated, reflected downward from its seat, still enveloped in the thin membrane, and joined to the dorsal medulla. But **B** specifically indicates the right seat of the cerebellum, corresponding to the sinus of the skull marked **P**. **D** indeed marks the left, which sits in that seat of the skull upon which I will write **R**. **C**, however, marks the middle part of the cerebellum, not unlike a worm <note>the **cerebellar vermis**</note>, and establishing at its boundaries those processes which we compare to the image of worms <note>the **vermicular processes**</note>.*
*E The posterior boundary of the middle part of the cerebellum, which will be counted as the posterior of the <term>worm-like processes</term> <note>original: *uermiformium processuum*</note>.*
*F, G, H The part of the dorsal medulla still consisting within the skull. And **F** and **G** indicate the seats of this part or dorsal medulla to which the cerebellum is joined. **H** indeed signifies the seat of the dorsal medulla proceeding out from the expanse of the skull <note>leading toward the spinal canal</note>.*

I *The depression of the <term>dorsal medulla</term> <note>original: *Dorsalis medullae sinus*; referring here to the brainstem</note>, which is not unlike the nib of the pen we use for writing, and which forms the central cavity of the ventricle common to the brainstem and the brain.*
K *Vessels or ducts very similar to veins, extending to the cerebellum from those vessels that drain into the first and second sinuses of the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>original: *durae membranae*; the **dura mater**</note>. Just as these ducts are quite numerous, they are also not always arranged in a consistent sequence.*
L *And here also, a duct similar to a vein is extended into the <term>thin membrane</term> <note>original: *tenuem cerebelli membranam*; the **pia mater**</note> of the cerebellum, from those vessels which interweave the hard membrane of the brain in this region.*
M *The fifth pair of cranial nerves.*
N *The sixth pair of cranial nerves.*
O *The seventh pair of cranial nerves. And here one may see from how many filaments these last two pairs of cranial nerves derive their origin from the beginning of the brainstem, and by no means from the cerebellum.*
P, Q, R *The sinuses of the occipital bone, which correspond to the shape of the cerebellum. For the part marked **B** on the cerebellum matches **P**; **C** matches **Q**; and **D** matches **R**.*
S, S, S *The right or first sinus of the hard membrane, here opened with the tip of a knife.*

## INDEX OF CHARACTERS FOR THE TENTH FIGURE.

*In this figure, we have represented that portion of the brain which brings forth the beginning of the brainstem; then, the cerebellum has been removed from the brainstem at this visible part; and the <term>testes</term> and <term>nates</term> of the brain <note>the superior and inferior colliculi</note>, and the gland resembling the likeness of a pine nut <note>the pineal gland</note>, and finally that cavity of the brainstem which, with the cavity of the cerebellum, forms the fourth ventricle of the brain, are likewise represented here.*

A, A *The part of the brain producing the brainstem, here cut away from the rest of the brain.*
B *The passage tending from the third ventricle of the brain into the fourth, beneath the "nates" of the brain <note>the **cerebral aqueduct**</note>; I have marked its end, where it reaches the fourth ventricle, with*
C *a mark.*
D *The gland of the brain, likened by the professors of dissection to the image of a pine nut <note>the **pineal gland**</note>.*
E, F, G, H *With these characters, the "testes" and "nates" of the brain are indicated. For the leaders of dissection, by means of the line visible between **E** and **F**, and between **G** and **H**, seem to have distinguished the upper swellings marked **E** and **G** from the lower ones marked **F** and **H**. They called the upper ones "testes" <note>testicles</note> because the gland <note>pineal</note> rests upon them like a penis; and the lower ones "nates" <note>buttocks</note> because the end of the passage reaching from the third ventricle to the fourth could be compared to an anus.*
I, K *The two sites where the beginning of the brainstem grows into the cerebellum <note>the cerebellar peduncles</note>.*
L, M, N, O *The cavity of the beginning of the brainstem, forming the other part of the fourth ventricle, and likened to the cavity of a pen <note>original: *calami*; the **calamus scriptorius**</note> which we dip in ink when writing. For the site marked **L** corresponds to that part of the pen’s cavity closest to the writer’s index finger. **M** and **N** can be likened to those angles which exist at the sides of the pen’s cavity. **O**, however, expresses the tip with which we form characters.*
P *The brainstem is cut through here, where it proceeds into the vertebrae and exits the skull.*

### Index of the Eleventh Figure and its Characters.

In this figure, the <term>cerebellum</term> <note>the "little brain" located at the back of the skull, responsible for coordination</note> lies overturned and torn away from the skull and even from the <term>dorsal medulla</term> <note>original: *dorsali medulla*; here referring to the brainstem where it meets the spinal cord</note>, showing its lower surface which faces the spinal marrow. Accordingly, it shows those regions where it is continuous with the spinal marrow, and moreover, the cavity which forms the other portion of the <term>fourth ventricle</term> <note>a chamber for cerebrospinal fluid</note> shared by the cerebellum and the spinal marrow. Furthermore, at the lower part of the present figure, we have depicted the ends of the middle part of the cerebellum as if they were cut out from some other cerebellum, so that the nature of the processes resembling the image of a <term>worm</term> <note>original: *uermis*; the central part of the cerebellum</note> might be more accurately observed.

<margin>A</margin> The right part of the cerebellum, free from the <term>thin membrane</term> <note>original: *tenui membrana*; the **pia mater**, the innermost layer of the meninges</note> which clothes the cerebellum; indeed, the entire cerebellum appears here stripped of that membrane.
<margin>B</margin> The left part of the cerebellum.
<margin>C, c</margin> The middle part of the cerebellum; **C** marks the anterior region of this part, while **c** marks the posterior.
<margin>D, d</margin> The boundaries and ends of the middle part of the cerebellum; **D** indicates the anterior end, and **d** indicates the posterior.
<margin>E</margin> The cavity of the cerebellum which, together with the cavity of the spinal marrow, constitutes the fourth ventricle.
<margin>G, G</margin> In these places, the cerebellum is attached to the spinal marrow.
<margin>H</margin> The anterior end of the middle part of the cerebellum, expressed here as if it had been cut away from another cerebellum.
<margin>I</margin> The posterior end of the middle part of the cerebellum, cut out from some cerebellum.

## INDEX OF THE TWELFTH FIGURE, AND its characters.

*In this figure, the head is depicted from the left side, with the right side slightly raised. We have torn the <term>cerebellum</term> <note>the "little brain" at the back of the skull</note> out of the cavity of the skull, leaving only that portion of the <term>cerebrum</term> <note>the main, larger part of the brain</note> which was still preserved in the eighth and ninth figures. ## THE EIGHTEENTH FIGURE OF THE SEVENTH BOOK.

<image-desc>A small anatomical woodcut illustration labeled with letters A through F. It depicts the infundibulum (labeled B) descending into the pituitary gland (labeled A), with various outlet ducts (C, D, E, F) shown around the base.</image-desc>

*In this small figure, we have depicted the upright <term>basin</term> <note>original: *peluis*; the **infundibulum**, a funnel-like structure</note>, or cup, by which the brain’s <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *pituita*; Vesalius refers to the waste fluids early medicine believed were filtered by the brain</note> drips down into the gland placed beneath it. And then we have depicted here four ducts, carrying the phlegm from the gland through the holes nearest to the gland. Let **A**, then, indicate the gland into which the phlegm is instilled. **B** the basin, through which it is brought here. **C**, **D**, **E**, and **F** the passages prepared for the easier exit of the phlegm lying down here. Furthermore, besides these figures of the seventh book, which look especially to the knowledge of those structures contained in the cavity of the skull, two figures added near the end of the first Chapter of the fourth book also apply here; they express the delineation of the seven pairs of brain nerves. Since, however, we necessarily included a rather lengthy index for them in that place, it would be entirely out of place to repeat them here as well. Moreover, the figures expressing the construction of the eye—even though they refer to the seventh book—I shall nevertheless place before the fourteenth Chapter, which will be dedicated to the fabric of the eyes, since they serve no other Chapter but that one.*

### THE BRAIN IS CONSTRUCTED FOR THE SAKE OF THE SOVEREIGN SOUL, just as it is for the senses and for movement that depends on our will. Chapter I.

<margin>
What the fifth and sixth books treated.
</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'I'. The woodcut depicts three figures in a landscape setting with trees and hills in the background, appearing to be in discussion or observation.</image-desc>IN THE TWO immediately preceding books, we addressed as best we could the instruments serving nutrition. For the former <note>Book V</note> described the organs of food and drink (in whose principal organ <note>the liver</note> we said the <term>concupiscible soul</term> <note>the part of the soul associated with desires and vegetable growth</note> resides). The latter <note>Book VI</note>, however, reviewed those parts to which the duty of refreshing the airy substance and of increasing and recreating the innate heat is entrusted: in whose primary organ <note>the heart</note> we suggested the power of the <term>irascible soul</term> <note>the part of the soul associated with passions and vital heat</note> is implanted. In this, we do not so far agree with the opinions of the <term>Stoics and Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Zeno and Aristotle, who believed the heart was the center of all functions</note> as to grant that the sovereignty of the soul is located in the heart, or that the nerves take their origin from it.

<margin>
The argument of the seventh book.
</margin>
Wherefore, since the source of sense and voluntary movement, and of the <term>sovereign soul</term> <note>original: *principis animae*; the **rational soul**</note> (by whose benefit we imagine, reason, and remember) still remains to be reviewed, the present book will be opportunely consecrated to it, for the purpose of treating the brain and all its parts together with the organs of the senses.

<margin>
A brief enumeration of the functions and parts of the brain.
</margin>
Just as, therefore, the power of the vital soul is implanted in the substance of the heart, and the faculty of the natural soul in the proper flesh of the liver; and as the liver produces the thicker blood and the <term>natural spirit</term>, and the heart produces the blood rushing through the body with force together with the <term>vital spirit</term>, and just as these organs exhibit their materials to all parts of the body through the channels dedicated to them: so also the brain, in its own seats and in organs appropriately serving its duty, prepares the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>the "spirit" of the *anima* or soul, thought to be the medium for thought and nerve signals</note>—by far the clearest and thinnest, and of a quality almost more than a body. The brain partly uses this spirit for the divine operations of the sovereign soul, and partly distributes it continuously to the instruments of the senses and movement through the nerves, as if through little cords, never depriving them of the spirit, which is considered the chief author of the function of those instruments—no less certainly than the liver and heart [supply] no [parts of the body...]

The nerves, therefore, perform for the brain what the <sup>a</sup> **great artery** <note>The aorta</note> does for the heart and the <sup>b</sup> **hollow vein** <note>The vena cava</note> for the liver: they lead the spirit, prepared by the brain, to those instruments to which it must be commanded, and they are considered the diligent attendants and messengers of the brain. Furthermore, the material for the **animal spirit** <note>original: *animalis spiritus*; in Galenic medicine, this was the "soul-spirit" responsible for sensation and voluntary motion</note> is supplied by the **vital spirit** <note>The spirit produced in the heart and carried in the arteries</note>, which is abundant in the numerous series of <sup>d</sup> **arteries** reaching the <sup>d</sup> **dura mater** <note>The "hard membrane" protecting the brain</note> and the <sup>e</sup> **thin membrane** <note>The pia mater, or "tender membrane"</note> that enwrap the brain. Added to this is the air which, as we have said much earlier, is drawn toward the brain during breathing, both through the small holes specifically carved for odors in the <sup>f</sup> **eighth bone of the head** <note>The ethmoid bone</note>, and especially through those <sup>g</sup> **passages of the cavity** that face the palate and throat. And indeed, wherever the air finds an entrance, it insinuates itself into the <sup>h</sup> **right**, <sup>i</sup> **left**, and <sup>k</sup> **middle ventricles** <note>Cavities within the brain</note> of the brain.

Moreover, although the **vital spirit** is found in great abundance in <sup>l</sup> all the vessels and sinuses of the brain’s membranes, it is carried in the greatest amount into the right and left ventricles of the brain by the principal <sup>m</sup> **branches of the arteries** that extend to the sides of the <sup>n</sup> **gland** <note>The pituitary gland</note> that receives the brain’s phlegm. For from these, <sup>o</sup> significant offshoots, supported by the processes of the thin membrane, enter through the lowest floors of the right and left ventricles, finally proceeding through the whole length of the ventricles into their breadth. 

But besides these arteries, from the <sup>p</sup> **fourth sinus** of the dura mater, a <sup>q</sup> **certain vessel** passes under the <sup>r</sup> **vault-like body** <note>original: *corpore teſtudinis*; the fornix</note> (which reflects the image of an arch built like a chamber) into the anterior parts of the brain through the common cavity of the right and left ventricles. After various windings, this vessel is finally split into <sup>s</sup> **two portions**, one spreading to the right ventricle and the other to the left, and being mixed with the arteries of that place, it forms the <sup>t</sup> **network** <note>Vesalius refers here to the choroid plexus, though he compares it to the *rete mirabile* found in animals</note> which is best compared to the substance of fetal membranes.

Thus, from the air entering the brain, and from that vital spirit which is more and more adapted for the brain’s uses by its frequent turnings, the **animal spirit** is elaborated by the power of the brain in the right and left ventricles and in their common cavity, the **third ventricle**. A portion of this spirit is carried from that <sup>u</sup> **ventricle** of the brain through a long passage extending between the <sup>x</sup> **bodies of the brain** (which are likened to **buttocks** and **testicles**) <note>The corpora quadrigemina of the midbrain, historically called the *nates* and *testes*</note> into the **ventricle of the cerebellum**, which is formed partly by the sinus of the cerebellum and partly by the cavity at the beginning of the **dorsal marrow** <note>The spinal cord</note>. From this ventricle, a significant portion of the animal spirit is distributed into the <sup>y</sup> **dorsal marrow**, and thus into the nerves propagated from it. From the <sup>z</sup> **remaining ventricles** of the brain, however, the spirit is dispensed into the nerves taking their origin closest to them, and so into the organs of the senses and of voluntary motion.

In the meantime, we do not dispute very anxiously whether that spirit is directed through some passages in the nerves (as the vital spirit is through the arteries), or whether it is directed like light to a pillar along the sides of the body of the nerve, or whether the power of the brain reaches the parts merely by the continuity of the nerves. And truly, thus far I can attain the functions of the brain in the dissections of living animals with considerable probability and in a certain way, truth. But how the brain performs its office in **imagination**, **reasoning**, **thought**, and **memory** (or however else you wish to subdivide or enumerate the powers of the **sovereign soul**, following the dogmas of I know not whom), I do not understand according to my own satisfaction.

<margin>The construction of the brain in brutes does not differ from that of man.</margin>

Furthermore, I do not think anything more should be investigated by the anatomist on the occasion of the theologians, who take away all the power of reason and almost the entire faculty of the soul we call "sovereign" from **brute animals**. This is because, in the construction of the brain, the **monkey**, **dog**, **horse**, **cat**, and all the quadrupeds I have seen so far, and even all **birds** and many types of **fish**, correspond to man in almost every part. No difference occurs to the dissector that would suggest otherwise concerning man...

<summary>Vesalius explains how vital spirit from the heart is refined into animal spirit within the brain's ventricles and then distributed via the nerves. He concludes by noting that because the brain anatomy of humans and animals is nearly identical, anatomy alone cannot explain higher cognitive functions or the unique nature of the human soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Vesalius’s critique of traditional medieval and Scholastic theories of brain function. While the previous page discussed the distribution of animal spirits through the nerves, he now contrasts the actual physical size and structure of the brain with the speculative "cell doctrine" (the idea that different mental faculties live in specific cavities) taught by theologians like Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus.</meta>

->ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE FABRIC [OF THE HUMAN BODY]<-

### AS IF-

how the functions of the human brain must be established compared to those of animals—unless, perhaps, someone might rightly say that the mass of the brain fell most largely to man, who is surely the most perfect animal we know, and that his brain is found to be larger than even three brains of oxen. Furthermore, according to the proportion of the body, a large brain likewise falls to the monkey, and then the dog, just as if animals excelled in brain mass only to the extent that they are seen to be endowed more openly or closely with the powers of the **sovereign soul** <note>original: *principis animae*; referring to the highest part of the soul responsible for reason and sensation</note>. Truly, the more I examine the nature of the heart, liver, testes, and the organs serving them—whose functions (to say nothing of generation and corruption) we do not doubt that we certainly hold in common with many animals—and the less I persuade myself that anything should be decided concerning the duties of the sovereign soul other than what our most holy and true religion teaches, the more I am truly astonished by what I read among the **Scholastic theologians** <note>Medieval philosophers and theologians who integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine</note> and common philosophers.

<margin>The opinion of Thomas, Scotus, Albert, and their troop of writers regarding the ventricles of the brain.</margin>

They teach that the human brain is gifted with three ventricles <note>The hollow cavities or "cells" within the brain</note>. The first of these, bordering the forehead, is called the ventricle of **common sense** <note>original: *sensus communis*; the faculty that integrates data from all five senses</note>, because from this ventricle the nerves of the five senses are carried to their instruments, and because, by the benefit of these nerves, smells, colors, tastes, sounds, and tactile qualities reach it. Consequently, those men believe the chief duty of the first ventricle is to receive the objects of the five senses and transmit them by a certain passage into the second ventricle, placed in the middle of the head, so that the latter can imagine, reason, and think about those objects. For they attribute thought or reason to the second ventricle, and they consecrate the third (which claims the back of the head for itself) to memory. Indeed, they assert that into this second ventricle are conveniently deposited all those things which it has decided should be committed to memory after reasoning abundantly upon them. They further suggest that the third ventricle carves these things into itself—either more quickly or slowly depending on whether it is wetter or drier—as if into wax or, conversely, as if into a harder stone. They claim it preserves these things for a shorter or longer interval of time according to the ease or difficulty of the "sculpting." Furthermore, they teach that this third ventricle does not retain or carve these things for itself, but for the sake of the second ventricle; namely, so that whenever the second ventricle decides to reason about something entrusted to the bosom of memory, the third might quickly send whatever it is back into the second ventricle, holding it out to be processed as if in a **workshop of reason**. Such are the fictions of men who never look into the craftsmanship of God, the Maker of things, in the fabric of bodies, and who arrogantly claim for themselves free opinions on all sides—fictions devised, truly, not without grave impiety. How far they wander in describing the construction of the brain, the following discourse will show, using the same method I employed in the fifth and sixth books. After this brief description of the brain, I shall explain its individual parts separately, together with all the instruments of the senses.

# ON THE TOUGH MEMBRANE SURROUNDING THE
## brain, and the small membrane encircling the skullcap beneath the skin.
### Chapter II.

*The **tough membrane** <note>original: *dura membrana*; now known as the dura mater</note> of the brain appears in many figures. In the first, its entire external surface is shown, standing above the cut where we usually divide the **skullcap** <note>original: *calvaria*; the top part of the skull</note> to show the brain. The second figure demonstrates that part of the membrane from the internal view, just as it was also pulled away in the series of dissections in the ninth, twelfth, thirteenth, and even more in the fourteenth figures. Furthermore, the third figure shows the process of the membrane drawn down between the right and left parts of the brain at D, D. The seventh figure at O, O, O, shows that which is spread beneath the cerebellum. In those figures, the **sinuses** <note>Venous channels</note> of the tough membrane also occur, as most excellently seen in the figure for Chapter 14 of Book III. Moreover, we have nowhere separately depicted the membrane wrapped around the outside of the skullcap, since it is thin and surrounded on all sides by bone, and must be understood entirely from the outline of the bone.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' depicts several cherubs or putti gathered around a table, actively engaged in the medical examination or dissection of a human head.</image-desc>

**JUST AS** we have already reviewed how the entire cavity of the body’s trunk, visible below the <gloss>a</gloss> **transverse septum** <note>The diaphragm</note>, is contained by the <gloss>b</gloss> **peritoneum**, which embraces the organs placed within it like a sack; and just as we mentioned that the <gloss>c</gloss> membrane lining the ribs <note>The pleura</note> surrounds everything located in the thorax: so too the entire cavity of the <gloss>c</gloss> **skull** <note>original: *calvaria*</note> adapted for receiving the brain is lined with a certain <gloss>d</gloss> membrane. Because of its thickness—which exceeds all other membranes, not only of the brain but of the whole body—we call it the "thick" membrane, and because of its remarkable hardness, the "hard" membrane <note>original: *dura*; the dura mater</note>, as well as the "skin-like" membrane. This is seen as a single, continuous membrane, no less than the peritoneum and the membrane lining the ribs, so that a knowledge of the bones elegantly teaches the location, the form of its external surface, and its size. For we have written that no bone of the skull swells out into the <gloss>e</gloss> cranial cavity for any private use to which this membrane does not yield, allowing itself to be pressed inward by it. Conversely, we have related that there is no <gloss>f</gloss> **sinus** <note>A cavity or channel</note> in that cavity which this membrane does not fill, except for the sinus of the <gloss>g</gloss> **wedge-shaped bone** <note>The sphenoid bone</note> where the <gloss>h</gloss> **gland receiving the brain's phlegm** <note>The pituitary gland</note> sits, and those <gloss>i</gloss> sinuses which yield to the principal branches of the <term>soporary arteries</term> <note>original: *soporariae arteriae*; the carotid arteries, named from the Greek 'karos' meaning deep sleep, as compressing them was thought to cause sleep</note> running out to the sides of that gland, and which are considered suited for the <gloss>k</gloss> drainage of phlegm. For in the region of these sinuses, the hard membrane departs from the skull, and between the membrane and the skull sit that gland and the said branches of the arteries. Meanwhile, throughout the rest of the cranial cavity, the membrane is adjacent to the bones most closely and without any intervening body, and is joined to them in almost the same way that muscles lying against each other are usually stuck and connected together. However, by that kind of connection, the membrane is more firmly attached to the bones at the base of the head than at the sides, the crown, the forehead, and the back of the head. Furthermore, it grows most tenaciously to all the sharper <gloss>l</gloss> bone processes described in the cranial cavity, as well as to the circles of the <gloss>m</gloss> cranial foramina <note>The holes in the skull through which nerves and vessels pass</note> visible in this cavity, just as if it took its origin from them.

To these, it also connects to the **sutures** <note>The seams where the skull bones meet</note> of the skull, but with a connection not as strong as that which it exerts toward the bone processes; this is because that connection happens only like a simple line, and not with a noteworthy width like the latter. But meanwhile, the hard membrane not only grows to the sutures, but also transmits thin and <gloss>n</gloss> membranous fibers through them toward the exterior of the head. When these are pulled away from the upper part of the skull by <gloss>o</gloss> those dissecting, they swell out on the hard membrane like a <gloss>p</gloss> simple line, showing its surface to be rough and reflecting the position of the sutures upon it. Moreover, besides the fibers, certain <gloss>q</gloss> **tubercles** <note>Likely the arachnoid granulations</note> on the crown near the junction of the **sagittal suture** with the <gloss>p</gloss> **coronal suture**, protruding unevenly from time to time and occupying matching <gloss>q</gloss> pits in the skull into which they strongly grow, make the external surface of the hard membrane even less even. Hence, these must be weighed not in passing or through a lattice-window <note>i.e., not superficially</note>, lest through lack of caution in the administration of **cauteries** <note>Burning the skin or bone for medical treatment</note> and in contusions of the head, we perforate the skull. For if no account is taken of these tubercles, we might puncture the membrane along with the bone, causing no small evil; because in these places, as also in the regions of the sutures, the membrane departs from the bone with difficulty, and is not significantly removed from the external surface of the skull. Furthermore, certain <gloss>r</gloss> small veins increase the connection of the membrane to the skull and the roughness of its exterior surface; these pass through the sutures of the skull and certain small holes, partly from the hard membrane to the coverings of the skull, and partly from those coverings to the hard membrane. Furthermore, this membrane is not adjacent to the bones of the skull in this manner throughout its entire body, but <gloss>s</gloss> it insinuates a large portion of itself between the cerebrum and the cerebellum. This portion, covering the entire upper seat of the cerebellum, divides the region of the cerebrum lying upon the cerebellum from it, and, as it were, lifts it up <note>This describes the tentorium cerebelli</note>.

Furthermore, from the middle seat of this portion of the hard membrane <note>The dura mater</note>, where the right part of the brain faces the left, and following the whole length of the <sup>t</sup> third sinus <note>The superior sagittal sinus, a major blood channel</note> of the hard membrane (which we reviewed with its other <sup>u</sup> vessels in the third book), another portion or process of the hard membrane is extended, dividing the right side of the brain from the left. This process somewhat resembles the <sup>x</sup> shape of a reaping sickle <note>The *falx cerebri*</note>: for its posterior part, which is continuous with that portion of the hard membrane covering the cerebellum, corresponds to the base of the sickle. The <sup>y</sup> anterior part, however, which originates at the <sup>z</sup> septum of the olfactory organs, can be compared to the point of the sickle. For that process of the hard membrane, led forward from the posterior part of the head, is gradually narrowed in the manner of a sickle. Then, the part of this process continuous with the third sinus of the hard membrane—not <sup>a</sup> unlike the back of a sickle—is encountered by those performing dissections. Indeed, it curves outward and is seen to be thicker because of the presence of the third sinus of the hard membrane. However, the part of the <sup>b</sup> process facing the callous body of the brain <note>The *corpus callosum*</note> is slanted inward, reflecting the form of a sickle's edge. These processes of the harder membrane vary in thickness and hardness from the rest of its body in only one place. For where the process covering the cerebellum <sup>c</sup> is closest to the origins of the brain, it becomes nearly three times thicker and harder than in other places, turning almost cartilaginous; so much so, indeed, that <sup>d</sup> dogs possess a bone in this location covering the upper region of the cerebellum and supporting the brain so that it does not press upon the cerebellum.

But meanwhile, neither of these processes is doubled (even though Galen, considering the matter too little, taught otherwise), but each is simple, just as the membrane itself is where it is applied to the sides of the brain or the skull. For although the third sinus of the hard membrane, <sup>e</sup> dissected lengthwise with a scalpel, shows at first glance that the <sup>f</sup> membrane process intervening between both parts of the brain is twofold, and consists as if of a doubled membrane, this is nevertheless seen only because of the presence of the sinus. For however much you strive to separate the lower angle of the third sinus, you will never subdivide the membrane into two parts outside the width of the sinus. Furthermore, just as the third sinus in this process of the hard membrane imposes a false image on the one dissecting, so too in the <sup>g</sup> process separating the cerebellum from the brain, the <sup>h</sup> first, <sup>i</sup> second, and <sup>k</sup> fourth sinuses of the hard membrane present a false image of doubling.

The surface of these processes of the hard membrane matches in appearance the rest of the interior surface of the whole membrane. Furthermore, this interior surface is bathed by a watery fluid far more than the exterior, and it appears much whiter; and since it lacks all fibers by which it might be attached to another part, it is seen to be more exceedingly slippery and clean than the exterior surface.

Nature, taking precaution against this, produced the cavity of the hard membrane to be somewhat larger than the mass of the brain with its thin membrane, <sup>n</sup> just as the covering of the heart <note>The pericardium</note> is seen to be significantly larger than the heart itself.

<margin>The openings.</margin>

<margin>The use of the hard membrane and the reason for its construction.</margin>

<margin>The creation and use of the membrane surrounding the skull on the outside.</margin>

...to explain the number, position, and nature of the <sup>o</sup> sinuses <note>Large blood-collecting channels</note> and vessels of the hard membrane <note>The dura mater</note>. However, since I attempted this in no passing way in the third book along with the rest of the veins and arteries of the whole body, I shall not without reason spare these pages here. Even in the description of the openings of the hard membrane, which must now be added, I will pass over those holes—or rather paths and ducts—by which the hard membrane receives veins and arteries into its cavities and sinuses for their use, and from those boundaries brings forth not a few vessels here and there. Furthermore, a <sup>p</sup> significant number of true openings through which the hard membrane of the brain is passable occur in that place where it is <sup>q</sup> joined to the eighth bone of the head <note>The ethmoid bone, located at the roof of the nose</note>. For just as that bone is granted many small <sup>r</sup> holes for the sake of odors, so likewise the hard membrane that is spread over it is perforated in the manner of a <sup>term</sup> cribriform <gloss>sieve-like</gloss> plate. Next, it provides a path for the seven pairs of brain nerves <note>Vesalius followed the ancient system of 7 pairs of cranial nerves, whereas modern anatomy identifies 12</note> such that it displays eight openings on each side for their sake. Of these, the <sup>s</sup> first transmits one of the nerves of the first pair; the <sup>t</sup> second opening sends out one nerve of the second pair. The <sup>u</sup> third, however, leads down the smaller root of the third pair, which in the hard membrane (even if it happens otherwise in the skull <sup>x</sup>) does not fall forward with the second pair. Through the <sup>x</sup> fourth opening, the principal root of the third pair is led with the fourth pair. The <sup>y</sup> fifth is prepared for a small nerve that arises near the root of the fifth pair and is numbered by us with the fifth pair. The <sup>z</sup> sixth opening yields to the principal portion of the fifth pair. The <sup>a</sup> seventh is carved out for the sake of the sixth pair, and the <sup>b</sup> eighth for the seventh pair. In addition to these, the hard membrane is pierced by <sup>c</sup> one unpaired and circular true opening, which provides a path for the <sup>d</sup> funnel <note>The infundibulum of the pituitary gland</note> of the brain that receives phlegm. Moreover, next to the sides of this opening, <sup>e</sup> another opening is seen on both sides, transmitting the largest branch of the arteries seeking the brain <note>The internal carotid arteries</note>. Additionally, the hard membrane dismisses the dorsal marrow <note>The spinal cord</note> through a <sup>f</sup> very large and likewise unpaired opening <note>The foramen magnum</note>; for this marrow, just as for the nerves passing through it, the membrane provides a process and covers it like a certain wrapping, so much so that the hard membrane contains the nerves and the dorsal marrow in almost the same way as the brain, and becomes a covering and a coat for them. Indeed, the hard membrane is also specially constructed so that it may receive all the veins seeking the skull and all the <sup>g</sup> arteries (if <sup>h</sup> you only remove two branches) into certain suitable boundaries, and take their material into its sinuses. It leads them out so that, through offshoots drawn from those boundaries in the manner of veins, they may be most conveniently carried into the thin membrane <note>The pia mater</note>. Thus the hard membrane imitates a <sup>term</sup> flask <gloss>lagena</gloss>, from which the thin membrane and then the brain itself draw material that has been sent toward the head in the veins and arteries. Furthermore, the offshoots derived from the third sinus of the hard membrane on both sides in an innumerable series into the thin membrane support the brain, suspended so that it does not collapse downward and its ventricles are not compressed; thus the hard membrane becomes both a wrapping and a support for the brain. To this end, the fibers creeping out from the hard membrane through the <sup>term</sup> sutures <gloss>the seams of the skull</gloss> are also of great service; they fasten it to the skull (which otherwise could not be sufficiently joined to the very hard bone) and ensure it does not slip downward, dragged by the weight of the brain. And certainly, Nature would not have provided this unless she had devised a peculiar artifice outside the skull, which craftsmen imitate daily whenever they bend back the points of nails when they fasten two boards together, so that if one board is pulled, the nail is not easily plucked from the other. For Nature herself sent these fibers through ducts that fasten them not only by being bent back but also by their slanted path; she then dilated and increased those that were sent through, and mixed them all together into one, so that they degenerate into a certain thin membrane. Because this covers the skull, it is called the **pericranium** [περικράνιον] <note>literally "around the skull"</note> by the Greeks. Nevertheless, this is not attached to the skull entirely without the mediation of another body; for beneath it there still sits another thin membrane, common to almost all other bones...

# ANDREAS VESALII, ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

<margin>k Where you see C and D under figure 15, the whole 16th figure.</margin>
...which surrounds the bones, called the <term>periosteum</term> <note>original: *perionsteon*; a dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</note>. Among the other sites of the bones deprived of this membrane, there is the internal cavity of the skull, adapted for receiving the brain: to which nowhere, where it touches the hard membrane <note>the dura mater</note>, does a small membrane of this kind arise, so much so that even as much of this cavity as the hard membrane does not grow together with, is also girded by this small membrane common to other bones. That site is seen ^k where the gland of the hard membrane that receives the pituitary of the brain and the largest branches of the arteries seeking the brain are placed underneath.

### ON THE THIN MEMBRANE ENVELOPING THE
### BRAIN. Chapter III.

->*The thin membrane covering the brain occurs in the second figure, but it is shown torn away in the third. And it is also seen wrapped around the cerebellum in the eighth.*<-

<margin>Number of the thin membrane.</margin>
<margin>a You should seek this from the figures following each other in the series of dissection, as 2, 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'T' depicting several figures in classical or academic attire, possibly engaged in a medical discussion or a dissection, surrounding a central table or block.</image-desc>
The thin membrane of the brain <note>the pia mater</note>, just like the hard one, is only one and continuous with itself: for you would find no portion of its nature—whether at the cerebellum, or at either part of the brain, or in the very ventricles and windings of the brain, or to say it once, in the entire cavity which the hard membrane constitutes—that is not a portion of the one thin membrane. This is in the same way that in the skin of an animal already removed from the body, we say the parts which covered the ears, feet, and tail are continuous with the rest of the skin.

<margin>Position.</margin>
<margin>b Figure 2: L, L.</margin>
The position of the thin membrane must be understood from knowledge of the brain and cerebellum. For no ^a small portion of the outer surface of the brain, the cerebellum, the spinal cord, and the nerves is seen which the thin membrane does not cover very closely and without any other substance coming between, provided you ^b except the upper surface of the callosum corpus <note>the corpus callosum; the bridge of nerve fibers connecting the two hemispheres</note>, which alone is not contained by a membrane of this kind, though it is hard in its own way. Furthermore, all the windings of the brain and cerebellum, into which the thin membrane inserts its parts or processes from every side, show its position, as indeed do its shape and size.

<margin>Exterior surface.</margin>
<margin>c Figure 3: C, C, C. and here and there on the surface of figure 11. d in figure 4. G in 8 & 9.</margin>
This membrane is smeared on its outer ^c surface as if with a watery fluid, swelling out according to the prominences of the parts it surrounds. For it hardly varies in thickness anywhere else, always showing the image of a very thin membrane ^d blocked by innumerable paths of vessels.

<margin>The purpose and reason for its construction.</margin>
<margin>e Especially part of Figure 10, Book 5 and the whole of Figure 11.</margin>
<margin>f Figure 2, Book 5: c, c, c.</margin>
Indeed, the Architect of things ^e created it primarily for the sake of the vessels, namely so that, like the mesentery <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> and the lower membrane of the omentum, it might safely lead and support those vessels. Moreover, it is the wrapping of the brain and cerebellum which most closely contains and strengthens their substance, not unlike how ^f cheese molds support and shape milk that has just recently curdled. For these uses, the Architect of things produced this membrane as especially suitable. For it is so soft, thin, and yielding that it most fittingly inserts itself into all the windings and folds even to the deepest parts: and it can safely lead whatever vessels the brain requires. Furthermore, it is seen to be so light that by its weight it in no way exerts force on the brain: and yet meanwhile it is so strong and tough that it is not torn apart when pulled upward by the hard membrane of the brain. Rather, it elegantly sustains that force of suspension brought about by the frequent, numerous, and continuous ^g series of vessels; it is called <term>choroid</term> <note>original: *χοροειδὴς*; meaning 'like the chorion' or fetal membrane</note> by many because it embraces the vessels of the brain like the ^h wrappings of a fetus.

<margin>Why the thin membrane is also called choroid.</margin>
<margin>g Figure in Chapter 14, Book 3: S, S, T, T, T. & Figure 1 of this book.</margin>
<margin>h Expressed in Figure 30, Book 5.</margin>
<margin>i Figure 6: H, M, N.</margin>
<margin>k 2nd table, Figure 30, Book 5: I, I, l.</margin>
Although meanwhile the ^i plexus <note>the choroid plexus, a network of blood vessels</note> in the right and left ventricles of the brain, and also placed in a large part in the middle of their cavity, is also given that name, not so much because it contains various branches of veins and arteries as if in some small membrane, but because it moreover shows a certain fleshy substance born around the vessels, and similar to that ^k flesh which is seen in the outer wrapping of the fetus...

<summary>Vesalius describes the pia mater (the "thin membrane"), emphasizing its role in supporting blood vessels and shaping the soft substance of the brain, famously comparing it to a cheese mold.</summary>

# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY BOOK VII.

<sig>XX 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: now the cere-</meta>

<margin>Book 5 on the Use of the Parts.</margin>
...I have written that it is born from the wrapping and is suitable for supporting and embracing the vessels. So much so, that for the sake of its substance, that network <note>the choroid plexus</note> was likened to the thin membrane of the "afterbirth" <note>the chorion or fetal membrane</note> by those whom Galen almost rebukes when he says he wonders why some do not want all parts of the thin membrane to be called *choroid* <note>original Greek: χoρoειδεῖς; meaning "like the chorion"</note>. Indeed, if we accurately weigh the difference between the substance of the thin membrane and that network, and if the true composition of the fetal wrappings is not hidden from us, we shall not lightly cherish the diligence of those authors whose reasoning Galen writes was unknown to him.

# ON THE NUMBER, POSITION, SHAPE, WRAPPINGS,
### and substance of the cerebrum and cerebellum. Chapter IV.

<margin>Number of the brain.</margin>
Professors of dissection are accustomed to divide the whole * brain into <sup>a</sup> the anterior part, which they call the **cerebrum**, and <sup>b</sup> the posterior part, which they call the **cerebellum** <note>literally "the little brain"</note>; then they divide the anterior part into <sup>c</sup> right and <sup>e</sup> left. This is not because the whole brain is completely divided and not continuous with itself in at least some part, but because, just as a single hand is divided into fingers, so too the brain is seen to be separated into different parts. Just as we previously reported concerning the thin membrane of the brain, <sup>f</sup> so also the right part of the brain and the left, and with these the cerebellum, and the spinal marrow <note>original: *dorsalis medulla*; includes the medulla oblongata and spinal cord</note>, and all the nerves to a man—furthermore, even the <sup>g</sup> "buttocks" and "testicles" of the brain <note>the superior and inferior colliculi, parts of the midbrain</note>, then the <sup>h</sup> **corpus callosum**, and <sup>i</sup> that which is shaped like a **vault** <note>original: *testudinis*; the fornix</note>; moreover, the <sup>k</sup> **septum** of the right and left ventricles, and the <sup>l</sup> **worm-like processes** <note>the vermis</note> of the cerebellum, and whatever else is of this kind, exist as mutually continuous parts and are composed of the same substance, varying only slightly in hardness and color. Furthermore, all the things I just reviewed differ from one another in position, use, shape, size, and other factors to be weighed in the construction of parts, so much so that they have shamefully deceived many reading the writings of the Ancients, as if they were various and disconnected parts. Therefore, although the cerebrum is thoroughly dissected into two parts throughout its entire seat <sup>m</sup> where it lies upon the cerebellum and <sup>n</sup> where it faces the forehead, and though this same section is led quite deeply through the whole length of the brain in its higher region, it is nevertheless not seen to be entirely divided in its middle near the <sup>o</sup> base. For as great as the <sup>p</sup> length of the corpus callosum is, so great also is the seat according to the length of the brain where its right part is continuous with its left. And so, either by the intervention of this body, and of <sup>q</sup> that which is built like a vault <note>the fornix</note>, and of the <sup>r</sup> septum of the right and left ventricles, the two parts of the brain are continuous with each other above the <sup>s</sup> common cavity of those ventricles, or the third ventricle. Furthermore, that they are continuous at the base is shown both by the region where they are joined with great and fertile length and depth, and by the "testicles" and "buttocks" of the brain, and most of all by the <sup>t</sup> beginning of the spinal marrow arising from the middle of the brain's base, which is large and thick, and just like those two parts of the brain, is continuous and one in this place. Next, even if the right and left parts of the brain, where they cover the cerebellum, are no less continuous with the cerebellum, nevertheless the lower seat of the cerebellum is <sup>u</sup> continuous in two places with the already mentioned beginning of the spinal marrow, which I shall describe separately just like all the parts enumerated a little earlier. For I have chosen to include what has now preceded so that no one, about to dissect the brain, may think that I, along with many others, am hallucinating regarding the number of the brain. Onwards then...

...now I shall opportunely approach the position of the cerebrum <note>the large brain</note> and cerebellum <note>the small brain</note>, which is revealed by their membranes, and the internal capacity or cavity of the skull. For whatever part of that cavity is not occupied by the two membranes of the brain, the pituitary gland <note>original: "glande pituita"; the gland that receives brain secretions</note>, and certain branches of the largest arteries entering the skull, is entirely filled by the cerebrum and cerebellum. The cerebellum is ten or eleven times smaller than the cerebrum, and together with the beginning of the spinal cord <note>original: "dorsalis medullae"; literally "dorsal marrow"</note>, it claims that seat of the cranial cavity which is circumscribed at the back by the z prominences that project into the cranial cavity for the sake of the hearing organs, and then by the two b boundaries of the occipital bone <note>the bone at the base of the skull</note>, which are carved into the skull's cavity so that the bone yields to the right and left c edges of the thick membrane <note>the dura mater</note>. The cerebellum does not exceed any part of this circular boundary. In humans, it does not extend so far into the back of the head that the hindmost part of the cerebrum does not incline further back than the cerebellum itself, filling what we call the occiput <note>the back of the skull</note>. Indeed, the hindmost and highest part of the human cerebellum scarcely rises to the point where the lower region of the occipital part—free from the origins and insertions of muscles d—resides. Thus, there is no fleshless region of the occipital bone that you can grasp with your fingers that the cerebellum actually fills, even though many anatomists describe its position as if the cerebellum occupied the entire protruding region of the back of the head (from whose bulge the common people measure the power of memory and intellect). On the contrary, its highest portion reaches only to the middle e region of that interval which extends from the posterior f opening that transmits the spinal cord to the higher g seat of the suture resembling the letter Lambda [Λ] <note>the lambdoid suture, named for its shape like the Greek letter L</note>. Meanwhile, many others, deceived by their oxen, donkeys, and sheep, have taught that the cerebellum climbs all the way to that upper point. In those animals, the cerebellum appears rounded and pointed in its upper region, but in humans, it is somewhat flat and depressed, projecting very little in its center, much like the human cerebrum.

Therefore, the seat of the skull dedicated to the cerebellum teaches us its position, boundary, shape, and size. For the cerebellum, just like its seat, is wider than it is long or deep. In its lower region, and especially near its posterior parts, it expresses the image of a wide sphere; in the middle of this, there is a sharp and not very wide h impression, which is created by the i protrusion resembling a very thick line on the occipital bone, significantly increasing the strength of that bone.

Furthermore, in the front part k where the cerebellum extends toward the nates <note>literally "buttocks"; refers to the corpora quadrigemina of the midbrain</note> of the cerebrum, it is carried as if to a point, accurately reflecting the shape of its seat on all sides. As for the rest, the shape and size of the cerebrum are shown by the remaining cavity of the skull not filled by the cerebellum. Hence, the cerebrum is also very uneven and varied at its l base. m Where it rests upon the seats of the eyes and the boundaries of the olfactory organs, it bulges forward into those n cavities; but on both sides of these cavities, it is compressed as if with a flat surface o because of the prominence of the bones bulging into the skull for the sake of the eyes. Then it fills two large p cavities seen at the sides of the q hollows of the wedge-shaped bone <note>the sphenoid bone</note>, where the gland that receives the brain's phlegm <note>the pituitary gland</note> is supported. From this, the cerebrum here claims for itself the shape of the bone in which it is contained, like a clod of earth, and establishes on both sides of its base a r protrusion like a half-sphere. In the middle of these protrusions, the cerebrum is seen to be s impressed, due to the processes of the wedge-shaped bone produced here around the sides of the cavity containing that gland.

And so also on the sides, and the front, and the back, and the upper...
