# THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VII
<page-num>781</page-num>

<margin>The cerebrum and cerebellum hardly possess a form of their own.</margin>
The upper part of the brain neatly reflects the shape of the skull’s cavity. There, it becomes like an oblong sphere, flattened on both sides toward the front because of the cavity for the temples; it turns rounded and is much wider in the back than in the front. To put it simply, it is shaped as if it and the cerebellum required no specific form of their own; it would be more than enough for them if their substance—collected in a great mass and in whatever manner possible to contain the sinuses or ventricles suited for their functions—were simply placed in the head. <margin>4th muscle plate, r.</margin> For the sinuses and protrusions of the skull's base show this, as do the visible impressions in the temples made for the sake of the temporal muscles (to say nothing of the various shapes of human heads). Therefore, the cavity of the skull shows the image of the brain’s external surface, to which the section dividing the brain and its countless windings and turns are also related. For the entire seat of the brain is divided by that section; just as the feet of cloven-hoofed animals are split into two hooves by its aid, a large part of the brain's outer surface is accounted for. <margin>u Seen whole in Figure 3.</margin> <margin>x Figure 3: C, C, C.</margin> <margin>The section dividing what we call the right part of the brain from the left, and the brain's convolutions.</margin> However, this does not significantly disrupt the brain's shape, since the right part lies against the left. Nor do the parts divided by that straight line gape apart from each other more than the thickness of the hard membrane <note>original: "durae membranae"; the dura mater</note> and the doubled thin membrane <note>original: "tenuis"; the pia mater</note> allows. For in man (unlike in the sheep), <margin>y Figure 3: D, D, D.</margin> a portion or process of the hard membrane occupies this section, separating the two parts of the brain like a partition. Then the thin membrane individually surrounds and enwraps each part of the brain. Furthermore, the gyri <note>the ridges or "folds" of the brain</note> and windings of the brain—which the <margin>z Figure 7: l, i, s.</margin> Ancients beautifully compared to the convolutions of the small intestines—are found with the same frequency everywhere across the entire surface of the brain. These windings are truly numerous recesses <term>sinus<gloss>hollows or channels</gloss></term> penetrating deeply into the brain's substance, and in appearance, they are indeed very similar to the coils of the small intestines. I do not think they can be compared more aptly to anything than to these, or even to the clouds that untrained students of painters or boys in school are accustomed to draw. Although one should not labor too much in searching for comparisons, since man shares these windings appearing in the brain's substance with asses, oxen, and other animals I have seen so far. Unless perhaps someone decided to draw a distinction from the fact that Nature has implanted these gyri deeper in man to the same degree that the brain substance itself is seen to be more abundant. Furthermore, in reviewing their use, not only physicians but also <margin>The use of the brain's convolutions.</margin> <margin>Book 8, On the Use of the Parts.</term> philosophers torment themselves, contending whether humans understand by virtue of them. Just as Galen, fighting against the opinion of Erasistratus <note>Erasistratus was a Greek anatomist who believed brain complexity determined intelligence; Galen disagreed</note>, judged that they contribute nothing to understanding, in this manner:

> <margin>“</margin> "Since even asses have a brain folded in many ways, though it would be more fitting for them—
> <margin>“</margin> as far as the coarseness of their character is concerned—to have obtained a brain that was
> <margin>“</margin> simple in every way and not at all varied. One should rather believe that a good
> <margin>“</margin> temperament of the substance of the thinking body (whatever this may be) follows
> <margin>“</margin> wisdom, and not a variety of composition."

But Galen here, being true to himself just when we most require his effort, pulls back his speech as if with a bridle; when he should have explained the use of the windings, he turns it elsewhere, thinking it enough if he indicates they do not preside over intelligence. We certainly do not deny this, but meanwhile Galen should have added that they were created for no other reason than the nourishment of the brain's substance. For the substance of the brain, continuous without any network of membranous fibers, was by no means firm enough for arteries and veins to be distributed through it as in other parts of the body; and it is so large and thick that veins and arteries running only on its surface would by no means suffice to nourish it and refresh its innate heat. Foreseeing this, Nature [created] those winding folds everywhere...

<summary>Vesalius describes the shape of the brain as being molded by the skull and details the structure of the cerebral hemispheres and gyri. He argues against the idea that the complexity of brain folds determines intelligence, suggesting instead that they serve to allow blood vessels to nourish the brain's deep tissue.</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY]
<page-num>782</page-num>

<margin>The reason for the sectioning of the brain.</margin>
<margin>Figure 2: E, E, E.</margin>
<margin>Figure 3: A, A, B, B.</margin>
...impressed into the substance of the brain, so that into these folds the thin membrane <note>the pia mater</note>, filled with numerous vessels, might wind itself, thus most suitably providing nourishment to the brain’s substance. It was also primarily for the sake of this nourishment that the brain was divided into two parts, so that the thin membrane could wrap itself into the middle of it; and there, drawn into folds, it might nourish the brain substance with the material contained in its vessels. Indeed, without such a division of the brain and these very deep windings, that part of the brain where the right side faces the left could not have been nourished.

<margin>The reason for and appearance of the cerebellum's folds.</margin>
<margin>Seen in Figure 11.</margin>
<margin>Figure 11: E.</margin>
<margin>Figure 5: R, R, R; Figure 9: A, B, C; and Figure 11: A, B, C, D, e, d.</margin>
<margin>Figure 9: C; or Figure 11: C, D, c, d.</margin>
<margin>Figure 11: C, D, e, d; then H, I.</margin>
<margin>At A, B.</margin>
<margin>Figure 11: G, G.</margin>
<margin>That Galen inappropriately assigned the reason for the unity of the cerebellum.</margin>
<margin>Figure 1, chapter 1, book 4.</margin>
The convolutions of the cerebellum also support this view. They do not penetrate nearly as deeply as those of the cerebrum, but are slightly less than superficial; however, they are very frequent and are seen to be drawn in a continuous series. They are superficial because only a small part needs nourishment, and because the cerebellum would easily be punctured by deeper turns all the way to its ventricle. They are frequent, however, so that their number may somewhat compensate for that shallow penetration. Furthermore, the series of these folds is in a way triple, and their shape does not match the convolutions of the brain at all. For the cerebellum appears to be formed of three parts because of its convolutions and that impression which it receives from the prominence of the occipital bone in its posterior seat: one right, another left, and a third in the middle. The right and left parts of the cerebellum resemble two spheres placed against each other, in the empty space of which—where the spheres do not touch—the third part of the cerebellum is placed. This part expresses the image of a woodworm or a cheese-maggot <note>original: "ligni caſei ue uermem"; this is the "vermis" of the cerebellum</note> because of its convolutions, which are drawn transversely and equidistant to each other along the length of the cerebellum. We shall show in its proper place that the ends of this part, reflected toward the lower seat of the cerebellum, form the worm-like processes of the brain. Furthermore, the right and left parts of the cerebellum, in the upper seat of the cerebellum, also possess parallel convolutions drawn according to the width of the cerebellum; these, extended downward, are gathered as if into a center, stretching toward the seat of the cerebellum that is joined to the beginning of the spinal cord <note>original: "dorſalis medullæ", referring to the brainstem and spinal cord</note>. Therefore, these three parts of the cerebellum are by no means distinct from each other, but are continuous with one another to constitute a single body, namely the cerebellum itself. Galen teaches that this was constructed by Nature as a single unit—rather than being doubled like the cerebrum—because it would not have been fitting for a man to have two backs, nor as many spinal cords. He argues as if a single spinal cord could not have been produced from the cerebrum (which he asserts is necessarily divided as if into two parts and is not continuous in substance), and therefore the cerebellum had to be created as a single body to provide a suitable origin for a single spinal cord.

<margin>The beginning of the spinal cord.</margin>
<margin>Figure 1, chapter 8, book 4: D.</margin>
<margin>Figure 10: L, M, N, O.</margin>
<margin>Figure 11: E.</margin>
<margin>G, G in Figure 11 are joined to Figure 10 and K in Figure 10.</margin>
<margin>This is clear in Figure 9: E.</margin>
<margin>This is clear at L in Figure 8.</margin>
But by Hercules! The brain is seen to be a single unit in the middle of its base, and not divided as it is in its upper part, and it produces a single spinal cord. In the upper part of this cord, immediately from its origin, Nature carved out cavities, which we shall say constitute the middle of the width of the fourth ventricle of the brain. For the cerebellum supplies the rest of the width of that ventricle; it is attached to the spinal cord on both sides only at the sides of the cavities of the spinal cord, as if by two circular implantations, becoming a continuous body with it. For neither the middle part of the posterior seat of the cerebellum, nor that of the anterior seat, is continuous or innate with the spinal cord; rather, the posterior part of the cerebellum is joined to the spinal cord only by the intervention of a thin membrane, and the middle part of the anterior seat does not even touch the spinal cord. Believe me, it is exactly as if Nature had created the cerebellum so that it might better adapt and protect the vital spirit transmitted from the borders of the cerebrum to the spinal cord.

<margin>In book 8, On the Use of the Parts.</margin>

For from the cerebellum—however much you may be concerned with assigning the difference in its hardness from the cerebrum and weighing the reason why it is divided from the cerebrum—you will find that absolutely no branch of even the smallest nerve takes its origin. And truly, there is no difference in hardness in the brain between the part that faces the forehead and the part that...

### BOOK VII ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY
<page-num>783</page-num>

...difference; nor is it especially noteworthy that the cerebellum, when seen freed from the thin membrane <note>the pia mater</note>, differs in hardness from the cerebrum. But just as the base of the brain, from which the <term>dorsal medulla<gloss>the spinal cord</gloss></term> takes its origin, is seen to be harder than all other parts of the brain and even the cerebellum itself: so too the dorsal medulla gradually becomes harder from its beginning, corresponding neither in color nor in hardness to the cerebellum situated above it. For the cerebellum is more yellow or ash-gray <note>original: cinericium</note>, interspersed with very few whitening lines, and is white only on the surface of its <margin>Figure 11, E.</margin> cavities. Truly, the entire beginning of the dorsal medulla, which is produced under the cerebellum while still in the head, is extremely white, as is the base of the brain that provides its origin; this part is entirely devoid of all the convolutions and windings in which the cerebellum abounds. Furthermore, what the substance of all these might be can be learned quite well even at the table from the brains of calves, hares, or some bird. It is, however, a substance with its own 

<margin>The color and substance of the cerebrum, cerebellum, and dorsal medulla.</margin>
peculiar and proper essential form, such as you will find no similar example of in the whole body, suited for the functions innate to the brain—surely no less than the substance of the heart, the lung, the liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the testes, and even the muscles themselves are deemed most fit for the duties they oversee. The substance of the brain, which some have called the "marrow of the head" and others "white marrow," <margin>The difference between the brain substance and bone marrow.</margin> differs from bone marrow both in many other accidental qualities and because it cannot be melted; nor is it consumed or diminished in times of starvation or other occasions, as is the rest of the body's fat. <margin>a This is clear from the difference of the brain substance in Figures 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. b Figure 3, C, c.</margin> This substance is not entirely white, but whatever <margin>b</margin> is closest to the convolutions is yellowish or ash-colored, always at an equal distance from the surface of the winding. For however great the depth of the convolution is, the color we described is observed in the brain substance at that same interval from the innermost part of the convolution—as if that color in the substance, as far as color is concerned, doubled the convolutions. However, whatever part of the brain is not colored in this way is seen to be entirely white and bright. But as there are very many convolutions of the cerebellum, so also almost the whole of it, as I warned a little while ago, appears yellow. Therefore, in whatever part you uncover the substance of the cerebrum or cerebellum from the thin membrane which most closely contains it, you will find this substance to be yellowish and as if smeared with a watery humor, and never entwined with veins—even if sometimes red and, as it were, bloody points are observed in the substance of the brain, especially in those who suffered from <term>phrenitis<gloss>an acute inflammation of the brain or delirium</gloss></term> before death, and those who perished by hanging. Truly, points of that kind do not represent the appearance of a vein. <margin>How the nutrition of the brain substance is provided for.</margin> For the brain assumes nourishment from no vessel other than those which, supported by the thin membrane, surround it. So that frequent vessels might be spread over it from every side, the brain was chiefly divided into as many parts as we have said—although those divisions, as well as the windings, also help considerably in supporting the soft substance of the brain so that it does not collapse, and in propping it up equally. <margin>Galen, Book 8, On the Use of the Parts.</margin> For I grant little weight to Galen’s reason <note>Galen was the primary medical authority for 1,300 years before Vesalius</note> as to why the brain is divided or, as he says, "twin." For he says that the brain is twin on this occasion: so that just as we preserve one eye when the other is damaged, or one testis when the other is cut out, so also if the right ventricle of the brain were injured, the left might still perform its duty. Indeed, this reasoning of Galen's might perhaps have some place in accounting for the number of ventricles, but not in explaining the division of the brain, since it is not divided or "twinned" except above the ventricles. For the body we must call "callous" <note>the corpus callosum</note>, which demonstrates the continuity of the parts of the brain, consists at the highest seat of the right and left ventricles. Furthermore, now will be the opportune time to approach the history of that callous body and the ventricles of the brain, and so to follow the internal surface of the brain and those parts of it which remain to be more fully described.

## ON THE CALLOUS BODY OF THE BRAIN, AND the septum of the right and left ventricles of the brain. Chapter V.

*THE upper surface of the callous body <note>The corpus callosum, the thick bundle of nerve fibers connecting the two brain hemispheres.</note>, which is not divided in any part, is elegantly displayed in the third figure by the characters L, L. Furthermore, this surface, shown where it is free from the brain substance at the sides, is shown in the fourth figure at l, l, l. The lower surface of the callous body is offered for inspection in the fifth figure at R, R, R, where the septum to be discussed in this Chapter is also seen at X, X, and then Y, Y.*

<margin>The site and name of the callous body.</margin>
<margin>a 3rd fig. L, L.</margin>
<margin>b 5th fig. R, R, R.</margin>
<margin>c 5th fig. S, T, V. 6th fig. A, A, A, A.</margin>
<margin>d As was done in the 3rd fig.</margin>
A LITTLE earlier, I reported that the entire substance of the cerebrum and cerebellum is surrounded on the outside by a thin membrane <note>The pia mater</note>, and that the part facing this membrane is yellowish and almost ash-colored. But a certain<sup>a</sup> part of the brain presents itself on its outer surface which is not wrapped in this thin membrane. Rather, in the manner of the innermost substance of the brain, it is bright and white on its outer surface, and harder than the rest of the brain substance residing at the surface. For this reason, the most ancient of the Greeks called this part <term>tyloeidē <gloss>callus-like</gloss></term> <note>original: τυλοειδῆ</note>: following them in my sequence of discourse, I have always called that part the callous body <note>The corpus callosum</note>. Furthermore, by some of the Greeks it is also called <term>psalidoeidē <gloss>vault-like</gloss></term> <note>original: ψαλιδοειδῆ</note> because of its shape—since<sup>b</sup> on its lower side it is curved in the manner of two arches—and because of its use, as it provides support. However, I shall review another<sup>c</sup> body in the brain <note>The fornix</note> that is gifted with this name by more authors, and more deservedly so. Otherwise, the callous body sits in the middle of the brain, whether you look at the right and left sides of the cerebrum, the middle of the base of the brain in its lower part, or the highest region of the brain at the crown, and even if you attend in some way to the front and back. For the hindmost part of the callous body is a little closer to the front of the brain than its front part is to the back. It comes into the view of those dissecting when the right part of the brain is gently separated from the left with the hands.<sup>d</sup> For whatever appears to unite and join the parts of the brain when it is thus pulled apart is seen to be white and bright; and this is the callous body itself—long, indeed, but narrow. This body, on the surface which first comes into view when the brain is pulled apart, is seen to be convex <note>Vesalius uses "gibbosum," meaning humped or protuberant.</note>: in much the same way as the crown of the head protrudes above the highest part of the forehead and the back of the head, and above the sides of the head.

<margin>The beginning of the callous body, or its continuity with the rest of the brain substance.</margin>
Just as the brain separated in the manner I described shows the upper surface of the callous body to be remarkably smooth and even: so also it indicates that this body is a part held in common with the brain, and that it does not arise from the surface of the brain substance (which is softer and yellowish), but from the deeper substance which is seen to be harder and white.

<margin>Sinuses encountered at the sides of the callous body.</margin>
<margin>e At M in the 3rd fig.</margin>
<margin>f If that body is reflected upward and backward; and so it is seen here at R, R, R.</margin>
<margin>g On both sides together at Y, Y in the figure, by which characters the tubercle is marked.</margin>
<margin>h In the 5th fig. it is torn apart, and one part is marked X, X, the other Y, Y.</margin>
Individual<sup>e</sup> sinuses <note>Grooves or channels</note> are observed on both sides at the edges of the callous body along its length, carved into the brain substance like a deep line; these open up further along with the upper surface of the callous body the more forcefully you separate the brain, as if you were about to drive it upward into the sides.<sup>f</sup> However, the interior or lower surface of it does not meet those dissecting unless the right and left ventricles of the brain are opened. Although this surface is curved in a certain way along the length of the callous body, and is not convex like the upper surface, it is nevertheless not seen to be simple. For along its length,<sup>g</sup> two hollowed-out surfaces like the fourth part of a circle are drawn, and in the middle of them a certain tubercle <note>A small rounded projection or ridge</note> is seen stretched out like a line, just as if you were to imagine two quarters of a circle joined at one end in the middle of the callous body, but at the other end extended upward to the sides. This tubercle, projecting downward and gradually thinning out, finally forms the septum<sup>h</sup> of the right and left ventricles of the brain <note>The septum pellucidum</note>: and the entire internal surface of the callous body is as large a portion of the right and left ventricles as the whole surface is. Indeed, the right portion of the surface faces the right ventricle, and the left faces the left.

Furthermore, the septum <note>The septum lucidum, the thin membrane separating the brain’s lateral ventricles.</note> of the right and left ventricles consists of the same substance as the brain, but in the middle (with respect to its upper and lower parts) it is so thin that when we perform a dissection in bright light, or bring a candle to only one side, its brilliance shines through as if through glass or a mirror-stone <note>original: "specularem lapidem"; likely a reference to mica or selenite, used for windows before glass was common</note>. However, you might more fittingly compare this region of the septum to a moist host—of the kind priests are accustomed to use for the Mass—than to those hard stones. In the upper part, where the septum is joined to the entire length of the callous body <note>the corpus callosum</note>, and in the lower part where it is united to the upper region of that part of the brain which we shall say is most similar to a vaulted arch <note>the fornix</note>, the substance is thicker than in the middle. For the lower part of the septum produces the vaulted body <note>the fornix; literally "tortoise-shell body"</note> from its upper region, just as the upper part of the septum arises and is produced from the lower region of the callous body. The callous body, together with the septum, is interwoven with no veins, nor even with the thin membrane <note>the pia mater</note> or any other part, but it takes its nourishment from the neighboring areas.

<margin>
The use of the callous body and the septum.
</margin>
Indeed, this portion of the brain is not so large or thick that it requires its own vessels, although meanwhile it provides a great use to the living creature. For by its intervention, the right part of the brain is continued with the left; then it produces the septum of the right and left ventricles of the brain,

Furthermore, two <insert>k</insert> sinuses <note>grooves or channels</note> are carved into the substance of the brain like a deep line at the upper surface of the callous body; beyond the fact that the outermost and superficial part of the brain is unsuited for producing the callous body (which ought to arise from the deeper and therefore harder substance), these are believed to serve the drainage of phlegm <note>original: "pituitae"; in Vesalius’s time, this was thought to be a waste product of the brain</note> from the upper parts of the brain. Receiving this fluid, they allow it to flow forward over the humped surface of the callous body. But we shall deal with the passages that purge phlegm in their proper place; for now, the ventricles will be discussed at the appropriate time.

## ON THE VENTRICLES OF THE BRAIN.
### Chapter VI.

*THE right ventricle of the brain is shown in the fourth and fifth figures at L, L, and in the sixth at D, D. TO THE NUMBER of ventricles of the brain is added that one which is common to the cerebellum and the dorsal marrow <note>the spinal cord</note>, and it is also called the fourth ventricle. In the right <insert>c</insert> part of the brain, therefore, the right ventricle is situated along its length, removed from the forehead at the front as much as it is removed from the back of the head at the rear; and it is separated from the external surface of the brain in those places by as much as the right, or outer, part of the ventricle itself...

The side is distant from the surface of the brain, bordering its own side of the skull. But the internal side of the right ventricle, along the length of the $^d$ callous body <term>corpus callosum: the thick band of nerve fibers connecting the two hemispheres</term>, is very close to the internal side of the left ventricle. No other space separates the two than a $^e$ certain thin portion of the brain’s membrane—thin enough to be called a membrane—which we have named the septum. However, where the ventricles are located in that part of the brain which is entirely divided, such as the part resting upon the cerebellum and the part closest to the forehead, there their sides are separated from each other to the greatest extent. For besides the membranes of the brain entering this section, much of the brain's substance also separates the ventricles, and for this reason, a certain $^f$ slant in the path of the ventricles' sides presents itself. Furthermore, the $^g$ anterior part of the ventricle is blunt and round, and not—even though everyone else seems to write otherwise to me—ending in a point toward the $^h$ organs of smell or the $^i$ optic nerves. Nor does it extend any duct or passage from itself in this part, except that on the internal side, as I will soon describe more fully, it slopes down to reach the $^k$ third ventricle. However, the $^l$ posterior region of the ventricle, facing the back of the head <note>occiput</note>, is indeed blunt and round, and gradually descending into the brain substance toward the front, it narrows for a while $^m$ in the manner of a horn until it reaches the place where the origin of the olfactory organs and optic nerves is located, and where the largest branches of the $^n$ carotid <note>original: "soporalium"; ancient physicians believed these arteries caused sleep or stupor</note> arteries are carried into the brain. Moreover, this $^o$ duct by no means ends with its tip in the olfactory organ or optic nerve of its side. Much less does it pierce that olfactory organ with any continuity; rather, it $^p$ terminates in one of the brain's convolutions there at the base of the brain. It admits into itself the largest $^q$ artery seeking the brain, along with a process of the thin brain membrane <note>the pia mater</note> supporting it, and it carries a portion of the phlegm <note>original: "pituitæ"; the ancients believed the brain produced waste fluid or phlegm that drained through these structures</note> collected in it to the $^r$ funnel <term>infundibulum: a funnel-shaped passage</term> and the bowl <term>cyathus: literally a "cup," referring to the region of the pituitary gland</term>, which you will hear receives and transfers the phlegm in this place.

In saying these things, I do not doubt that countless dogmas of Galen cry out against me—dogmas which variously teach that the olfactory organs are the anterior ventricles of the brain, and that these same ventricles, having gradually become thin, end with their tip in the optic nerves. And what is most alien to the truth, he attests that these anterior ventricles of the brain lead phlegm through the hollow olfactory organs, as if through a channel, toward the $^s$ sieve-like bone <term>os cribri: the ethmoid bone, which has many small holes like a sieve</term> or toward the upper part of the nose, which is perforated like a sponge. Many such things are better learned through dissection than through any lengthy dispute. The entire surface of the ventricle is seen to be slippery and smeared with a watery fluid, and during dissection, it is occasionally found filled with the same.

An account of the common cavity of the right and left ventricles, or the third ventricle.

Next, the upper $^u$ part of the entire $^t$ duct of the ventricle traveling along the length of the brain is devoid of all unevenness. But a certain $^y$ cavity <note>sinus</note> makes its $^x$ lower part uneven, creeping forward obliquely from the outer side of the posterior part of the ventricle toward the common cavity of the ventricles, ready for the easier downward flow of phlegm. Then that $^z$ part of the ventricle which creeps downward from the posterior seat of the ventricle contributes to the unevenness. For that bend of the ventricle, together with that cavity, is the reason why a $^a$ little mountain <note>original: "monticulus"; Vesalius is describing the hippocampus or a similar structure on the floor of the lateral ventricle</note> swells out in the anterior and posterior regions of the lower seat of the ventricle; it is carried sloping from the right side to the left side, and toward the common cavity of the ventricles. For the lower parts of the right and left ventricles, which are seen to be $^b$ continuous throughout the whole length of the callous body, incline downward toward the middle and that common cavity of both, and do not stand out like the upper parts. 

<margin>
c Figure 6 under H, I. Figure 7, 8, H. 
d Figure 5, S, T, V. Figure 6, A, A, A.
</margin>
And indeed, the $^c$ common cavity of the ventricles <note>the third ventricle</note> is nothing other than the descent and meeting-point of the lower parts of the right and left ventricles under the $^d$ body compared to the image of a vaulted arch <term>testudinis: literally "tortoise shell," referring here to the fornix</term>, which expresses in its lower part an oblong valley of two neighboring mountains, or forms an acute angle throughout its length.

<summary>Vesalius describes the shape and path of the lateral ventricles of the brain, specifically refuting Galen's claim that they connect directly to the olfactory and optic nerves. He explains how these cavities slope downward to meet under the fornix, forming the third ventricle.</summary>

Passages led out from the third ventricle.

On its upper surface, in the likeness of a body imitating a **vault** <note>original: "testudinem"; referring to the arched structure of the fornix</note>, that cavity is seen to be circular or rounded according to its hollow. What sort of body that is will be explained in the following chapter; for now, as we have only undertaken a discussion of the ventricles—of which we have already reviewed two, namely the right and the left—we shall now proceed to the **third ventricle**. This is the common cavity of both lateral ventricles, and it leads out two passages from itself. One of these, from its lower seat, where it expresses a sharp angle throughout its length in the manner of a valley, stretches straight down toward the $^f$ **funnel** <term>cyathus: literally "cup," referring here to the infundibulum which drains into the pituitary gland</term> of the brain that receives the **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"; ancient and Renaissance doctors believed the brain produced waste fluids called phlegm or pituita</note>. The $^i$ other passage, which is further back, must be considered a significant part of the third ventricle. Sloping down between the $^i$ **testes and nates** <term>corpora quadrigemina: four bumps on the brainstem which Vesalius calls "testicles" and "buttocks" based on their shape</term> of the brain and over the beginning of the dorsal marrow <note>the brainstem/spinal cord</note>, it reaches backward to the fourth ventricle. The beginning of this passage is not seen to be perfectly circular, but in a certain way triangular. Indeed, in its lower part, it preserves the sharp angle of the cavity from which it emerges; but in the upper part of the passage, which is seen closest to the gland presiding over the division of the vessels seeking the third ventricle, a transverse line connects the sides of that angle, and with them constitutes two other angles. Such is the $^i$ orifice of this passage, by which it looks toward the fourth ventricle beneath the "buttocks" of the brain. From the lower angle of this passage, where it first begins to pass between the "testes" of the brain, $^k$ another passage is rarely led out; this one, extended downward and forward through the substance of the brain, finally ends at the extremity of that passage which we said was led straight down from the lower seat of the third ventricle to terminate in the funnel. You will hear that both of these passages carry the brain's phlegm into that funnel.

The "testes" and "nates" of the brain are continuous with the beginning of the dorsal marrow, and they lead that passage of the third ventricle along with the start of the dorsal marrow in such a balanced way that the upper seat of the passage is carved into them, while the lower seat is $^n$ carved into the dorsal marrow. After that passage has passed the "nates," the portion of it seen carved into the dorsal marrow begins to widen and $^p$ forms a sinus that reaches nearly to that $^q$ place on the dorsal marrow where it exits the skull.

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC OF THE] BODY

<margin>
What is contained within each ventricle.
</margin>
...nor does the posterior part of the cerebellum attach to the **spinal marrow** <note>original: "dorsali medullæ"; referring to the brainstem and spinal cord</note>, although this ventricle is, in a way, enclosed in both its anterior and posterior parts by the thin membrane of the brain <note>the pia mater</note>. In the <margin>z 7 fi. X, X next to M N.</margin> anterior part, the thin membrane—which connects the cerebellum to the brain and to the **buttocks of the brain** <term>nates: refers to the superior colliculi of the corpora quadrigemina</term>—wraps around the ventricle. But <margin>a 9 fi. as if you were connecting E to H.</margin> a portion of the thin membrane obstructs its posterior seat, binding the cerebellum to the spinal marrow at that same spot. During dissection, the fourth ventricle is observed to contain nothing within itself except for a **watery humor** <note>original: "aqueum humorem"; what we now call cerebrospinal fluid</note>, which is common to the other ventricles as well; the same is true of the passage extending from the third ventricle of the brain into the fourth. However, the right and left ventricles, besides this kind of humor, also <margin>b 4, 5 fi. O, O. 6 figure M, N.</margin> contain a certain **plexus** <note>the choroid plexus</note> within them, which those skilled in dissection <margin>c fig. 30 book 5.</margin> compare to the **afterbirth** <note>original: "secundinis"; the placenta</note> or the coverings of a fetus. The third ventricle <margin>d 6 fi. H, I.</margin> leads down that venous vessel which we taught in the third book is propagated from the fourth sinus of the **hard membrane** <note>original: "duræ membranæ"; the dura mater</note>, being folded in many ways for the sake of forming that plexus. Furthermore, the anterior part of these ventricles sometimes receives extremely slender venules from that vessel <margin>e 7 fi. V led out from T.</margin>, which are very similar to those <margin>f 4 fig. P. 6 fi. O, O. f 18 fi. chap. 14 ", 4.</margin> we see adorning the adherent tunic of the eye <note>the conjunctiva</note>. These types of venules are more easily attached to the surface of the ventricles because the substance of the brain is harder and more **callous** <note>tough or thickened</note> on the surface of the ventricles than elsewhere.

<margin>
The first three ventricles of the brain are not lined by a thin membrane.
</margin>
Moreover, I am amazed that **Galen** <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician whose work dominated medicine for 1,300 years</note>, and all others who produced anything in anatomy after him, wrote that the surface of the first three ventricles of the brain is girded and covered by a thin membrane, just as the brain itself is. This is not the case; absolutely no surface of any ventricle or passage is wrapped in a thin membrane. For I ask, who, diligently examining the parts of the human fabric and not merely devoted to the writings of others, will not see from this very fact that Galen imagined many things—especially in his books *On the Use of the Parts*? For he believed the substance of the brain to be so soft that the ventricles themselves would have collapsed if they were not lined inside by a thin membrane. Then, attributing a harder substance to the cerebellum, he persuaded himself that its ventricle could be maintained without the benefit of a membrane to serve as a support. I truly believe that when Galen was writing those books, he had read in **Herophilus, Andreas, or Marinus** <note>famous ancient anatomists</note>, or someone else, that processes or parts of the thin membrane extend into the three ventricles of the brain, but not likewise into the fourth ventricle. By those words, they did not mean that the ventricles were lined by some membrane like the **peritoneum** <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> or the membrane lining the ribs; rather, they understood "parts of the thin membrane" to be the vessels leading into the ventricles, from which the plexuses—formed like the afterbirth—are constructed. No such part <margin>g 8 fig. M, N, H, I.</margin> extends into the fourth ventricle.

<margin>
The use of the ventricles.
</margin>
Furthermore, besides the fact that the ventricles are in no way lined with membranes, such membranes would be an obstacle; they would prevent the substance of the brain, being hindered by a gap, from transforming the material offered to its ventricles into **animal spirits**. Now, the present chapter would indeed require me to review the entire use of the ventricles; however, almost everything I have dared to bring forward and commit to writing, I reviewed at the beginning of this book, where the use of the brain had to be narrated in passing. For I have decided to attribute nothing else to the ventricles at present than that they are cavities and sinuses in which the air attracted through inspiration, and the **vital spirit** <note>believed to be produced in the heart and carried by arteries</note> transmitted to them from the heart, are transformed into **animal spirit** <term>spiritus animalis: the "gas" or essence believed to power thought and movement</term> by the power of the brain's unique matter and form. This spirit is afterwards distributed through the nerves to the organs of sense and motion, so that those organs—by the benefit of this spirit and by a construction suited to their duties—may perform their peculiar office: by which muscles move, the eye sees, the organs of smell perceive odors, the organs of hearing perceive sounds, the tongue distinguishes tastes, and finally, almost every part to which a nerve extends judges tactile qualities.

<summary>Vesalius argues that the brain's ventricles are not lined with membranes, contrary to Galen's teachings, and defines them as the site where "vital spirits" are converted into "animal spirits" to power the senses and movement.</summary>
<keywords>ventricles, choroid plexus, animal spirits, Galen, cerebellum, anatomy of the brain, sensation and motion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Vesalius’s critique of the traditional localization of the soul's "faculties" (such as logic or memory) within specific chambers of the brain. He transitions from a philosophical and theological discussion into a technical anatomical description of the fornix.</meta>

# THE SEVENTH BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY

...judges. Therefore, I am by no means afraid to assign this use to the ventricles in the generation of the animal **spirit** <term>spiritus: the vital breath or "pneuma" believed to flow through the nerves</term>. However, I believe nothing should be described regarding the seats of the faculties of the **sovereign soul** <note>original: "principis animæ"; referring to the "rational soul" or the highest part of the mind</note> in the brain. For indeed, all those with whom we live deny the principal powers of the sovereign soul to monkeys, dogs, horses, and animals of that kind—as well as to birds and fish—and, to remain silent about the rest, they attribute the faculty of reasoning to man alone. This faculty they grant to all men equally, as far as I can gather from them.

Yet, meanwhile, in the course of dissection, we observe that man is surpassed by many animals in no cavity [of the brain]; not only is the number [of ventricles] the same, but all other things (provided you look at the mass and the temperament perhaps according to their proper integrity) are most similar to one another. It may be permitted, therefore, for the sake of those men, that I abstain from inquiring into any other use of the ventricles. I will not even recall here the opinion of **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose works dominated medicine for over a millennium</note>, who, in his third book on the *Teachings of Hippocrates and Plato*, teaches that the middle ventricle is the most important, but in his books on the *Use of the Parts*, he teaches it is the last.

And therefore, singing hymns to God, the Creator of all things, let us give thanks that He has bestowed upon us a **rational soul** <note>original: "rationalem animam"</note>, which we have in common with the angels—as **Plato** <note>the Greek philosopher</note>, not unmindful of the poorly handled philosophers, also suggested. By its benefit, provided that faith is present, we shall enjoy that eternal happiness, when it will no longer be necessary to inquire into the seat and substance of the soul by the restoration of bodies, nor by our reason, which is still buried in this bodily bond and depends on the good health and constitution of the body. For He who is true wisdom will teach us, as we will no longer consist of this generative and perishable body, but of His own spiritual body, as similar to Him as possible.

THE body constructed in the manner of an **arch** <term>fornix: an arched structure in the brain, which Vesalius likens to a vault or "fornix" in architecture</term> or a **tortoise shell** <term>testudo: another architectural term for a vaulted ceiling</term> is placed among the number of those parts of the brain by whose intervention we cannot deny that the right part of the brain is continuous with the left. It is, therefore, a single structure, placed in the middle of the brain, and common to both parts of the brain equally. For from the posterior seat of the right and left ventricles, where they reflect downward into the anterior parts, this body^c arises immediately at that very reflection. It is endowed with a substance entirely similar to the substance of the ventricles of the brain, except that it is a little whiter than the substance of the ventricles and^b harder, in the manner of the **callous body** <term>corpus callosum: the thick band of nerve fibers connecting the two brain hemispheres</term>, and it is nowhere covered by the thin membrane of the brain.

The part of this body^c which the right ventricle leads out is continuous with that whose beginning hangs from the left; and together both parts produce a certain wide body, which immediately from its origin departs from the rest of the substance of the brain's ventricles. Gradually tapering into a sharp point^d, it is carried forward, reaching as far as that place in the brain where the anterior part of the third ventricle^e ends. There, indeed, by a certain sharp angle, this body is again united to the substance of the brain. Throughout its entire course, it reflects a triangular shape consisting of unequal sides. Its^f first side, which is also the shortest, extends from the posterior seat of the right ventricle to the posterior seat of the left. The^g second consists in the right ventricle, extending from its posterior seat toward the inner parts as far as the anterior part of the third ventricle. The^h third, placed in the left ventricle, corresponds in length to the second side. And thus, that body is gifted with a single surface on its lower seat^i, which is most similar to a triangular **vault or arch** <note>original: "testudini fornicíue"; referring to its vaulted shape</note>. Hence, this body is named from this image...

# ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VII.

<margin>g Figure 12, Book 5; Figure 1, i; Figure 15, S.</margin>...he entirely denies that it opens; he does not attribute the same use to this gland as to the glandular body which is born under the right orifice of the stomach <note>The pylorus</note> at the duodenum, and which he believed presided over the construction of that stomach orifice. But just as we showed in its own place that it was not built for the sake of that duty, so also here we testify with Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> that the present gland of the brain <term>pineal gland: a small endocrine gland in the brain, which Vesalius calls the conarium</term> by no means blocks the passage we mentioned. This is especially true because it does not touch the passage in such a way that it could close before its orifice. Rather, I believe it was made so that—just as <margin>h Figure 6, H.</margin> many other small glands of the body do—it might serve as a support for the vessel <note>The great cerebral vein or a branch of the choroid plexus</note> which approaches the **third ventricle of the brain** and is immediately divided from its origin into frequent branches woven together by a thin membrane. Supported by this present gland, the vessel does not immediately obstruct the beginning of the said passage upon its entry into the brain's cavity by leaning too closely upon it, which would prevent the **animal spirit** <term>animal spirit: a hypothetical substance thought by early anatomists to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves</term> from being carried from the third ventricle of the brain into the fourth.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a group of scholars or medical students gathered around a table or desk in a Renaissance-style room.</image-desc>ABOVE, when the form of the cerebellum was explained, we hinted at what sort the worm-like processes of the cerebellum are. For we were saying that, in a certain way, ^a one part of the cerebellum is led from the front to the back, as if in a circle, and is tangled with such convolutions that it most aptly shows the image of a worm born in wood. Therefore, the two tips or processes of this part—of which ^b this one faces the front seat of the ventricle common to the cerebellum and the spinal marrow, while ^c that one faces the back—were called *skōlēkoeideis* <note>original: "σκωληκοειδεῖς", meaning worm-shaped or vermiform</note> by the Greeks from the similarity just mentioned. 

But I do not quite know why Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the ancient authority whose anatomical works Vesalius both respects and corrects</note> taught that a worm-like process was set over the lower ^d orifice of the passage belonging to the third ventricle and leading into the fourth ^e, and explained the duty of only one process or tip, as it were. Although it is also not clear to me which of them he indicated—namely, the anterior or the posterior. For if he means the former, even if its point were extended, it could by no means reach the orifice of the passage: since it would then be directed more backward, occupying the ^f common ventricle of the cerebellum and spinal marrow rather than that orifice of the third ventricle's passage. 

But the posterior process or tip, which extends forward from the back parts, besides the fact that its point seems to blend more into the substance of the cerebellum's sinus than the former, nor does it protrude like that one, could in no way be extended as far as the posterior orifice of the third ventricle's passage. But why do I mention these things? Since I think no one should doubt that this passage must never be closed, given that we are unable to discover any use for obstruction (whatever we might imagine for ourselves); meanwhile, it is beneficial for that passage to be perpetually open so that the **animal spirit** <term>animal spirit: a hypothetical substance thought by early physicians to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves</term> may flow continuously into the spinal marrow. 

Nor do I believe there is anyone—unless perhaps taught by Albert, Thomas, Scotus <note>Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, and Duns Scotus: medieval Scholastic philosophers who attempted to map cognitive functions like memory and reason to specific parts of the brain</note>, and the theologians of that class—who would persuade himself that one of the "worms" (for the use of both cannot be equal in the closing of one orifice) was set over this passage to allow **phantasms** <note>mental images or perceptions</note> to enter the seat of memory (which they imagine to be in the cerebellum); and again to transmit "thieves," so to speak, bound in the prison of memory, into the middle ventricle (which they say is the seat of reason). For then God, the craftsman of things, would have bestowed such worm-like processes in vain upon dogs, sheep, and animals of that kind, to whom those [theologians] ascribe no power of reasoning. 

But from where, I ask, would this movement, depending on its own will, happen to this process (whoever he may be)? Then, if perhaps some motion were to be assigned to it by reason of some peculiar essential form or temperament, it still could not be extended and contracted in the manner of a worm, since the convolutions—for the sake of which these processes are compared to worms—do not surround them in a circle like the rings of worms; and since nothing else occurs by which those processes might steady themselves by leaning back, except where they are continuous with the substance of the cerebellum according to their own path. However it may be, it is enough for me at present to have indicated the location and construction of these processes; meanwhile, I attribute no movement or other duty to them than to the rest of the substance of the cerebellum. Indeed, if it were permitted to imagine anything, it would be [the duty] not of just one process, which Galen seems only sometimes to have known, but of
two,

Another passage, which I have observed very rarely and which Galen also seems to have overlooked in the ninth book of his *On Anatomical Procedures*, appears to dissectors as much narrower than the one already mentioned. It proceeds from that passage which reaches from the third ventricle into the fourth through the "testes" and "nates" <note>Anatomical terms for the colliculi, small rounded structures in the midbrain</note> of the brain. For as soon as that passage begins to go under the "testes" of the brain, from its anterior or lower seat, this second passage serving to purge the phlegm is led out. At the sides of this opening, the thin membrane <note>the pia mater</note>, which here also wraps the base of the brain, leads out from itself a circular portion or process. Its substance is entirely similar to the rest of the thin membrane, except that it is interwoven with quite slender, though frequent, veins. The beginning of this process accurately resembles the uppermost region of a funnel <note>original: "infundibuli"</note> used to pour wine into narrow-mouthed flasks. It is wide and circular, and then from its origin it is gradually narrowed in the manner of a funnel, until it finally ends in a narrow and oblong tube, much like a funnel. This tube, stretching downward, descends through a hole specifically carved for it in the thick membrane <note>the dura mater</note> of the brain, ending with its tip at the gland where the brain’s phlegm is received. Thus, this entire membranous body should be considered very similar to a funnel in both form and function, which is why it is called the *choane* <note>Greek: χοάνη, meaning "funnel"</note> by the Greeks. Although it is also called the *pyelos* <note>Greek: πύελος, meaning "trough" or "basin"</note> from the shape of a cup or the basin in which we wash in baths (which the upper part of this body neatly resembles). Nevertheless, elsewhere by those who assign names, the lower part of this body, not unlike the tube of a funnel, seems to be called *choane*, while the remaining upper part—which gradually narrows toward the bottom and sits largely beneath the optic nerves where they meet—is called *pyelos*. Again, I see this entire membranous body called *pyelos* by some, and the gland into which the phlegm drips, the *choanisko* <note>Greek: χοανίσκῳ, meaning a "small funnel" or a "casting mold"</note>, as if it were some form into which something is poured.

Truly, if the ancients, who taught their children anatomy, had not attributed that name to that gland, they would seem to have left it as the only part among all those placed in the cavity of the skull unworthy of a private name. This gland is located beneath the thick membrane of the brain, in a cavity carved for it in the bone that resembles a wedge <note>the sphenoid bone</note>, the shape of which it also expresses in some way. For it is flattened, convex on its lower part, and concave on the upper, tucked into a certain cavity. Furthermore, viewed around its circumference, it is not perfectly circular, but rather almost entirely square. It consists of glandular substance, but a substance far harder and more compact than that of the other glands of the body. On every side it is covered by a thin membrane, which either arises from the end of the funnel where it is attached to the gland's cavity, or else from the membrane that lines the entire skull at that spot where the thick membrane of the brain recedes and stands apart from the bones of the skull. By the intervention of the membrane covering the skull there, the gland is fixed to the bone, and it also adheres to two notable branches of the carotid <note>original: "soporaliū", literally "sleep-inducing" arteries, because the ancients believed compressing them caused stupor</note> arteries, which creep along its sides. Indeed, it is as if this gland were formed for the sake of those branches, providing them the same use that other glands serve in strengthening and supporting the distributions and divisions of vessels.

...indeed it descends further toward the back, and is led through an uneven and rough opening or fissure, which is found at the front and sides of the opening that transmits the more prominent branch of the <term>soporary artery</term> <note>original: "soporalis arteriae"; the carotid artery, so named because ancient physicians believed it caused sleep (sopor) when compressed</note> into the cavity of the skull. And all these serve to evacuate the brain's <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; in Galenic medicine, this was one of the four humors, often viewed here as a waste product of the brain's metabolic activity</note>. Indeed, the two channels which we said were carved into the brain substance carry that fluid from the brain's ventricles and allow it to flow down to the <term>infundibulum</term> <note>Latin for "funnel"; the stalk connecting the hypothalamus to the pituitary gland</note>. The infundibulum itself is built wide and broad at its upper part, not only for the purpose of these channels (which eventually end in a single orifice), but also so that it might contain those ends of the right and left ventricles of the brain, which we mentioned end here between the brain's convolutions after turning downward and forward from the back of the ventricles; for these also lead down the phlegm from their own area and extend it into the infundibulum.

<margin>
u 3rd figure, L, L.
x 23rd figure, M, M.
</margin>
Furthermore, the infundibulum is of such width that if any phlegm were collected over the <term>corpus callosum</term> <note>the "tough body"; the thick bundle of nerve fibers connecting the two cerebral hemispheres</note> and those sinuses which we reported were visible at the sides of the corpus callosum in its upper seat, that fluid would fall into the infundibulum by the help of the <term>thin membrane</term> <note>original: "tenuis membranae"; the pia mater, the innermost layer of the meninges</note>. For whether such fluid descends from the front of the corpus callosum (which protrudes like an arch) or from the back, it can flow down to the thin membrane covering the base of the brain, and from here gradually slip into the width of the infundibulum.

<margin>
Phlegm is not strained through the wedge-shaped bone by a long delay and tiny holes.
</margin>
The infundibulum, receiving the phlegm from all these ducts, is narrowed so that it may eventually lead it through a single opening in the <term>hard membrane</term> <note>original: "dura membrana"; the dura mater, the tough outermost layer of the brain's coverings</note> specifically open for it, and allow it to flow harmlessly into the center of that gland <note>the pituitary gland</note>. The gland, sustaining the force of the flow by some familiarity of its substance, and as far as I can conjecture, perhaps protecting the bone from harm, admits this phlegm and gradually allows it to flow down from its sides in every direction without dripping, through all the openings carved here in the base of the skull for the veins, arteries, and nerves themselves. For I cannot agree here with Galen in the ninth book of *On the Use of the Parts*—in which he treats most seriously the purging of the brain's excrements—where he claims the base of the head is cavernous and built like a <term>pumice stone</term> <note>Galen believed the sphenoid bone was porous to filter phlegm</note>, covered by no continuous scale; and that by this means, as if through a sponge, the phlegm is filtered out through a long delay and some rare and peculiar artifice of Nature. Nor would I agree that it flows straight down through the otherwise necessarily open holes (which would no longer be preserved), as I wrote at length in the first book when I followed the structure of the <term>wedge-shaped bone</term> <note>original: "ossis cunei"; the sphenoid bone</note>. I wrote this extensively because of certain people who pretend I am unwilling to see that cavernous bone structure covered in many holes like a sponge, and because of others who, by transposing or changing the word for "sieve" or "strainer" for the word "wedge" in a single place, conclude that Galen judged the passage of phlegm through the bones and the entire composition of the bones in the same way I do.

a 13th figure, D, G and D, G.
Phlegm is not purged according to nature by any excretion through the seat of the olfactory organs or the eighth bone of the head.
b 6th figure, D, D, and E, E.
</margin>
And so the phlegm settles both into the palate through those openings facing the palate, and indeed a significant portion flows through the opening of the second pair of nerves <note>the optic nerves</note> to the root of the eye sockets, and from there through a large opening (along with many other openings unknown to other anatomists) into the width of the nostrils. But I do not doubt that someone will wonder here why I have not yet described, as Galen did especially in the eighth and ninth books of *On the Use of the Parts*, any channels leading the phlegm to the cavities of the olfactory organs. This happened for no other reason than that I believe no phlegm at all is purged through these cavities or the eighth bone of the head <note>the ethmoid bone</note>; and I wonder greatly that Galen wrote that the phlegm (in whatever way it exceeds the anterior ventricles of the brain) is led to the nose through those thin processes, like nerves, which we attribute to the organ of smell. For there is no channel at all in them, nor are they of such thickness in humans as to carry a channel for phlegm.

<summary>Vesalius describes how waste fluid (phlegm) flows from the brain's ventricles through the infundibulum to the pituitary gland, eventually draining through nerve and vessel openings. He famously disputes Galen's theory that the sphenoid bone acts as a porous filter and rejects the idea that waste is purged through the olfactory nerves.</summary>

# ANDREAS VESALIUS, ON THE [FABRIC] OF THE [HUMAN] BODY. 796

...were led down, they could contain. Add to this that no duct for the phlegm to the cavities of the organs of smell can be imagined, unless perhaps the anterior region of the *corpus callosum* <note>the thick band of nerve fibers connecting the two brain hemispheres</note>, which is able to release the phlegm flowing into it into that breadth of the cavities of the organs of smell: as perhaps happens, if ever the brain is troubled by entirely too much phlegm. <margin>Lower c, figure 3, book 3.</margin> From where also an entirely unnatural flow of phlegm through the nostrils is then completed, and itching, heat, pain, and damage to the sense of smell, and many symptoms of that kind arise: just as we experience daily in those "distillations" <note>runny noses or catarrh</note> that reach the top of the nostrils, which we call "heaviness" <note>original: *grauedines*; a common term for head colds</note>. So indeed, that if we weigh each thing precisely, it must be confessed that when a person is formed according to the law of nature, no phlegm flows down through the cavities or holes of the olfactory organs, which are perforated like a sieve or sponge; and if by chance it does flow down, we will grant that this flow is far more contrary to nature than when the holes carved at the sides of the <term>gland of the brain</term> <note>the pituitary gland</note> that receives the phlegm do not fully lead away the whole phlegm, and this falls downward toward the <margin>d Where it is led, H of the 9th figure.</margin> hole prepared for transmitting the spinal cord <note>original: *dorsali medullae*</note>; and slipping along with the spinal cord, it flows into the back, and then according to the path of the nerves, now into the arms, now into the legs, now into the muscles of the loins, now elsewhere. I will be silent for now on how gravely Nature would have to be accused, who would have made such open and wide ducts for purging the phlegm in the brain and its membranes while it is still thin and watery, and yet would have produced such twisted, narrow, and <margin>e Figure 8, chapter 6, book 1, characters A, B, A.</margin> bent passages in the eighth bone of the head, or even in the <term>cuneiform bone</term> <note>the sphenoid bone, located at the base of the skull</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a putto or small child in a classical or pastoral setting.</image-desc>HOW MUCH has been attributed to Galen (the undisputed leader of the professors of dissection) by the physicians who followed him, sometimes beyond reason, is attested to by that blessed and marvelous <term>reticular plexus</term> <note>the *rete mirabile*, a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain found in some animals but not humans</note>, which he mentions everywhere in his books, and which physicians have nothing more frequently in their mouths: describing it according to Galen's opinion, even if they have never seen it. For nothing is less formed from the <term>soporary arteries</term> <note>the carotid arteries, so named because ancient physicians believed compressing them caused sleep or "sopor"</note> than a reticular plexus of the kind Galen describes. Much less do the arteries enter the hole in the skull that he himself describes, or are they entirely consumed into some plexus. First, for example, the entire right <margin>a</margin> soporary artery (and the case is the same for both) seeking the skull, does not enter through a single undivided hole as Galen records; but when it has ascended to the base of the skull, it sends off a notable branch of its own to the <margin>b</margin> hole carved out for the <margin>c</margin> nerve of the sixth pair of brain nerves, which is drained together with the large <margin>d</margin> companion vein into the right, or first, sinus of the <term>dura mater</term> <note>the tough outermost membrane of the brain</note>. Secondly, the soporary artery by no means occupies a <margin>e</margin> common hole with the <margin>f</margin> third pair of nerves; but the Creator of things used far greater ingenuity than Galen supposed. For He designed an oblique <margin>g</margin> hole proceeding for a long way in the bone for the main branch of the soporary artery. In its path, He perhaps wished that to happen for which Galen contends a plexus was formed. For so that the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>the life-force carried in the blood from the heart</note> might be refined in many turns and windings of the artery, and rendered fit material for creating <term>animal spirit</term> <note>the higher spirit responsible for thought and movement, which Galen believed was produced at the base of the brain</note>, Galen said that the artery, as soon as it entered the cavity of the skull, was <margin>h</margin> diffused into countless branches, which are so placed upon or mixed with one another that they form a plexus...

<meta>catchword: ...to form</meta>

...they seem to form something similar to it, such as we see occurring in a gathered fishing net: or like that plexus <note>a network of vessels or nerves</note> which would arise from many nets lying upon one another in turn. And he <note>Galen</note> asserts that this entanglement is formed between the bone and the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note>; yet in the meantime, a small portion of the hard membrane, which surrounds the bone, lies beneath the plexus. Then, just as that plexus begins to be folded together from one vessel—or, if Galen imagines the right joined to the left, from two—so he also testifies that the offshoots of this plexus, after a long series of successive branches, are gradually gathered together and finally end again in two vessels, seeking the ventricles of the brain, and corresponding in size to those vessels which were said to form the plexus at the beginning. But how far these things are from all truth, and how much they prove Nature's sluggishness <note>Vesalius is being ironic; he implies that nature is never "sluggish" or inefficient, and therefore Galen's complex and nonexistent structure makes no sense</note>, only he perceives who has learned the true course of that branch of the <term>soporal artery</term> <note>original: *arteria soporalis*; now known as the internal carotid artery. It was called "soporal" because it was believed that compressing it caused sleep or "sopor"</note> which we said penetrates the skull through that oblong hole of the bone. And, to pass over many things, he should likewise weigh how impossible it is for vessels of equal size to seek the brain as those which first reach the skull, since such remarkable ^i branches are dispersed from those vessels to the sides of the hard membrane, and through the holes of the second pair of brain nerves <note>the optic nerves</note> to the eyes and to the breadth of the nostrils, before they reach the thin membrane of the brain <note>the pia mater</note>. Furthermore, as to what the true series of these vessels or soporal arteries is, I have already attempted to describe it so truly and precisely in the third book—where I followed the vessels of the brain no less than the remaining veins and arteries of the whole body—that this place in no way requires a retelling of that series.

And for that reason, I must not linger here on the explanation of ^k that plexus which the brains of other animals show to be entirely in common with the human brain—and indeed the same—in the forward ventricles of the brain. It is formed by those arteries which enter the lowest ^l seats of the right and left ventricles, where they extend downward toward the front, and even nearly to the middle of the ^m base of the brain. Then, from that ^n vessel which is extended from the fourth ^o sinus of the hard membrane into the third ventricle of the brain, it is surely wound in a very varied way, as is the whole plexus, presenting the appearance of a membrane interwoven with innumerable vessels—now coming together and now again divided—and so covered with a certain fleshy substance that the Ancients, comparing this rare composition of membrane, vessels, and flesh to the ^q wrappings of a fetus, rightly called this plexus <term>chorioid</term> <note>original: χοροειδῆ (*chorioide*); from the Greek *chorion*, the outer membrane surrounding a fetus, which the vascular network resembles</note>, just as we have warned before. Whether they also likened this same plexus to nets folded and rolled up together—appearing red, just as the large nets of fishermen often do after being washed in a decoction of oak bark—and called it a <term>net-like plexus</term> <note>original: δικτυοειδὲς πλέγμα (*diktyoeides plegma*)</note>, must be gathered from the image of the plexus, which is red in the said manner and presents the figure of a folded net; for no part of the plexus is moved when it is encountered in the ventricles of the brain during dissection. If, however, it is then spread out and, as it were, unfolded, you could compare nothing so much to a drawn-out net as the said series of vessels in the plexus. Nevertheless, I wish to have no dispute over names, since I have only mentioned the plexuses in passing so that I might not seem to have overlooked anything in the construction of the brain in this book. While writing the third chapter of the fourth book <note>where Vesalius describes the cranial nerves</note>—and following the sequence of the nerves as was necessary—I considered the construction of the organ of smell. I thought that I would teach more extensively and accurately about the instrument of smell here than I had done in that chapter, where I chose only to describe its bare construction. But since nothing more certain has occurred to me so far, despite my very diligent inquiry into the nature of the organ of smell, I wish the present chapter to be considered in common with that one. For besides <margin>a</margin> those two brain processes <note>the olfactory bulbs</note>, which are not unlike nerves and reach into the <margin>b</margin> cavities of the eighth bone of the head <note>the ethmoid bone, located between the eyes</note>, and the <margin>c</margin> sinuses of the frontal bone, and the substance contained within them, and the <margin>d</margin> openings in the hard membrane of the brain <note>the dura mater</note> and the bones, I could review absolutely nothing else here. For I do not wish in this place to treat anything concerning odors, the medium of this sense, or its temperament <note>the "balance of humors" or qualities</note>; I do this so that my effort, which has already grown beyond expectation, does not increase too much and even into the infinite.

*A The crystalline humor.* <note>The lens of the eye, which Vesalius, following ancient tradition, believed was the primary organ of sight and located in the center of the eye.</note>
*B The tunic drawn over the front part of the crystalline humor, extremely thin and transparent, like the skin of an onion.* <note>The lens capsule.</note>

*F The portion of the thin membrane of the brain <note>the pia mater</note> which covers the visual nerve.*
*G The uveal tunic, into which the thin membrane covering the visual nerve transforms and expands.* <note>The uvea, including the choroid and iris; named 'uveal' because its dark color and shape reminded early anatomists of a grape skin.</note>
*H In this place the uveal tunic is compressed toward the back, and does not touch the corneal tunic drawn over it.*
*I The pupil, or the opening through which the uvea is passable.*
*K The tunic taking its beginning from the uvea, corresponding to the appearance of the 'cilia' or the hairs of the eyelids, and likewise the boundary between the vitreous humor and the aqueous humor.* <note>The ciliary body; 'cilia' is Latin for eyelashes, describing the fringed appearance of this structure.</note>

<margin>Position of the eyes.</margin>
<margin>How the construction of the eye is to be described.</margin>
**W**hen we investigated the nature of the head's structure in the first book, we described the position of the eyes. In the second book, we necessarily discussed their number and the muscles that move them, as well as the nature of the eyelids. At present, however, as we prepare to describe the fabric of the eye—which is round in the manner of a sphere—it would be perfectly valid to begin either from the center or from its outermost circumference. This is just as if one were to approach the construction of an egg, moving from its yolk to the white, then to the thin membrane covering the white, and finally to the shell or crust; or if one were to describe it from the shell to the thin membrane, then to the white, and from there to the yolk. It is in exactly the same way that we might recount the parts of the world, either from the earth to the water, air, fire, the heaven of the moon, and so on up to the outermost heaven, or from that heaven toward the center of the world. For the fabric of the eye, as far as its construction is concerned, can be compared to both the world and an egg. So that it may be taught more precisely and later remain more firmly in the memory, we shall discuss it conveniently first from the center to the outermost surface, and afterwards from the surface back to the center.

and the whole of
Figs. 2 and 3.

Center of the eye.
Crystalline or Glacial humor.
</margin>
The center of the eye is the humor which the Greeks call <term>crystalloides</term> <note>original: "κρυσταλλοειδῆ"; crystalline-like</note>, just as we also call it the <term>glacial humor</term> <note>ice-like</note>, surely from the resemblance it bears to the clearest ice and the most perfect crystal—not indeed in its consistency or hardness, but in its color, or rather its light. For this humor is most transparent, like the finest crystal. If it is removed and placed upon something, much like a piece of glass, it magnifies everything beneath it, acting like those magnifying lenses that bulge out on both sides. Its consistency is such that when it is freed from the other parts of the eye during dissection, it does not flow away like a liquid or fluid, but maintains its shape like a somewhat soft wax. Although it appears round, it does not represent a perfectly round globe; rather, it expresses the appearance of a globe that has been compressed at the front and back. It is as if you had taken a perfectly round wooden globe and sawed out a thick disc from the middle along parallel lines, and then glued the two remaining parts of the globe back together. Thus, this humor protrudes less at the front and back than it does at the sides, top, and bottom, somewhat in the likeness of a <term>lentil</term> <note>a "lens" shape, from which our modern word derives</note>. For this reason, I believe this humor was also called <term>phakoides</term> <note>original: "φακοειδῆ"; lentil-shaped</note> by the Greeks.

<margin>Consistency of the Humor</margin>

<margin>

</margin>
<margin>A little tunic, transparent like the skin of an onion, born upon the front seat of the crystalline humor.</margin>
Its surface is smooth and remarkably slippery. Upon its entire front seat<small><sup>b</sup></small> a little tunic is born, like the thinnest skin of an onion (such as we find between the thicker layers of an onion); it is thin, perfectly clear, and transparent. However, this little tunic is tougher than those onion skins. It does not touch the back seat of the crystalline humor at any part<small><sup>c</sup></small>, but ends there where the humor is seen at its widest<small><sup>d</sup></small>, and where its largest circle would consist if you imagined it wrapped in many parallel circles. No private name seems to have been given to this tunic, unless perhaps the Greeks called it <term>arachnoides</term> <note>original: "ἀραχνοειδῆ"; spiderweb-like</note> from the image of continuous spiderwebs. For it corresponds in thinness to those spiderwebs, though not at all in strength or hardness. During dissection, as I have already said, I compare it to the thinnest membranes of onions; I would even compare it to horn <note>the cornea</note> if only horn could be divided into layers and made as thin, transparent, and smooth as this tunic is when used for lanterns. Indeed, its substance differs nothing from the substance of horn. Let this, then, be the second body described by us in the construction of the eye; and since it covers only the front seat of the center, or crystalline humor, it should be considered as only a semi-globe in the fabric of the eye.

<margin>

d Fig. 3, R.
</margin>

<margin>Vitreous humor. <gloss>hyaloid</gloss> <note>original: "ὑαλοειδής"</note></margin>
Furthermore, the back seat of the crystalline humor is contained in another, <term>vitreous humor</term><small><sup>e</sup></small> <note>glassy</note>, which in color or clarity is like common white glass that has already cooled.
