matches it in clarity: yet it is not quite as clear as the **crystalline humor**, or the most perfect crystal. In its consistency, however, it is seen to be much softer than the crystalline humor; and once removed from the eye, it by no means retains its boundary or shape. Nevertheless, it does not flow away like water, but rather holds together in the same manner as glass melted in a furnace, which we see clinging to the iron tubes used by craftsmen to draw it from the furnace for blowing and shaping. In consistency, this humor matches such glass; but not in color, since, as I said before, the humor is similar in clarity to glass that has cooled, whereas molten and liquefied glass appears most similar to glowing iron. Therefore, since the present humor corresponds in consistency to molten glass, but in clarity to glass already cooled and shaped, it is deservedly called *hyaloeides* <note>original: $\text{\dot{\upsilon}\alpha\lambda\omicron\epsilon\iota\delta\acute{\eta}\varsigma}$, meaning "glass-like"</note> by the Greeks, and by us, the **vitreous humor**. This humor, exceeding the mass of the crystalline humor by many measures, resembles a half-sphere when it is still situated in the eye; its flat surface faces the front of the eye, while the round or convex part extends toward the back.

<margin>f Fig. 4, s.</margin>
In the middle of the front area, or flat surface, a $^f$ pit is impressed, as large as the posterior part of the crystalline humor. For that part is set into the vitreous humor just as if you were looking at a sphere floating in water, whose middle part is completely submerged in the water while the other part is visible above the water. And just as nothing comes between such a sphere and the water, so too nothing at all comes between the crystalline and the vitreous humors; nor are these humors joined together in any other way than you might imagine a ball embraced within a somewhat firm porridge <note>Vesalius uses "duriuscula pulte" to describe a thick, semi-solid texture, emphasizing that the two humors are held together by physical contact and pressure rather than a membrane.</note>.

<margin>
g Fig. 1, K.
h Figs. 11 & 12.
h Fig. 12, h, b; joined at i.
</margin>
Furthermore, you will hear in its proper place that the remaining region of the front area of the vitreous humor, which is not occupied by the crystalline humor, is covered by a $^g$ certain tunic. This will be compared to the $^h$ eyelashes or the hairs of the eyelids, and it will be taught that it is $^i$ attached in a circle, only as thick as a line (so to speak), to the crystalline humor where it is at its widest.

<margin>The wrapping of the eye, loosened from the substance of the optic nerve, and compared to a net [the retina].</margin>
<margin>

Now, however, I must describe the $^l$ wrapping by which the posterior seat of the vitreous humor is closely contained. Thus, the **optic nerve** <note>Vesalius calls this the "neruus uiforius" or "seeing nerve."</note>, accompanied by the thin and hard membranes of the brain <note>The pia mater and dura mater.</note> and several veins and arteries, is carried to the posterior part of the eye. Inserted there slightly toward the outer side of the eye, its substance dissolves into the wrapping I am about to describe. The thin membrane surrounding the substance of the nerve degenerates into $^k$ another tunic of the eye, which will be called the **uvea**; and the hard membrane also $^m$ ends in another, which will be called the **dura** <note>The sclera.</note>; and the veins and arteries likewise enter into the construction of the eye (as I shall describe in order). Therefore, as soon as the substance of the optic nerve is plunged into the eye, having been rendered softer, it expands into a certain wide wrapping. This is spread over the posterior seat of the vitreous humor and reaches forward not much beyond the middle of the eye. It is interwoven with extremely slender and obscure little veins and likewise arteries, which are extended to it from the root of this tunic and the place where the nerve first expands. Galen, in the tenth book of *On the Use of the Parts*, suggests that this wrapping is not considered worthy of the name "tunic" by many—perhaps because it is not a membrane in the manner of other tunics, but is soft, and like some mucus falling from the nostrils. For when this wrapping is gathered into one mass by those dissecting it and hangs from its root, it resembles mucus or brain substance diluted with some water; for it is not seen to be as solid and thick as brain substance. However it may be, whether it should be called a tunic or not, it is certain that Galen also called this wrapping a tunic in his books *On the Opinions of Hippocrates and Plato*, and likewise in the eighth book of *On the Use of the Parts*. Nor do I know what name could be more aptly given to it than "wrapping" or "tunic," since, as we have said, it is spread closely over the entire posterior seat of the vitreous humor and covers it—just as we might say a thin egg-film contains the egg white when we hold in our hands half of an egg broken from the other part and still filled. For this wrapping is, in shape, halved... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "dimidiato" (halved).</note>

is only to be compared to half an eggshell, or to a smaller fisherman’s net that is fitted to a single pole, which rises from a wide base into a blunt point like a half-sphere. I believe it was from the likeness of this kind of net that the Greeks called this wrapping the *amphiblestroides* <note>original: $\text{\dot{\alpha}\mu\phi\acute{\iota}\beta\lambda\eta\sigma\tau\rho\omicron\epsilon\iota\delta\grave{\epsilon}\varsigma}$, meaning "net-like." Today we call this the **retina**.</note>. For it resembles the shape of a net, though not its weave, since it is continuous on all sides—unless perhaps one were to argue that the little veins and arteries interwoven within it in various ways are like a net. Thus far, I have reviewed four parts of the eye: namely, two humors and the same number of <margin>net-like</margin> tunics. And so, I shall now deservedly move on to the layer produced by the thin membrane <note>the **pia mater**, the delicate inner membrane covering the brain</note> that accompanies the substance of the optic nerve.

As soon as this membrane enters the eye along with the nerve, it transforms into a tunic, occupying not only the posterior seat of the eye (in the same manner as the tunic arising from the nerve substance) but also covering the anterior seat. In the entire back of the eye, it closely invests the tunic born from the nerve substance; <margin>The **uveal tunic**, prepared from the thin membrane of the brain.</margin> <margin>n Figure G drawn from F, and nearly all of Figures 14 and 15.</margin> nothing at all lies between them where they touch, nor are they joined to each other by any bond other than by lying against one another. However, where the tunic arising from the thin membrane is stretched over the anterior seat of the eye, its inner surface touches and surrounds the humor on all sides, which we will soon call the **aqueous** or **albuminous humor**. <margin>o Figure 1 O, O, Figure 7 Y, and Figure 8 b.</margin> On the other hand, the outer surface of this tunic is covered by that tunic which I shall say arises from the hard membrane <note>the **dura mater**, the tough outer membrane of the brain; this refers to the **sclera** and **cornea**</note> that clothes the optic nerve. <margin>p Figure 1 M arising from L, or Figures 16 and 17.</margin> In the meantime, it happens specifically to this tunic (which the thin membrane produces) that it is not perfectly round like an exact sphere; for in the anterior region, it is somewhat compressed inward, showing a flat surface in one part rather than a convex and round one. <margin>q Figure 1 H, Figure 14 m, Figure 15 q, q.</margin>

When this tunic reaches that region of the front of the eye where the largest circle of the eye is drawn—which we call the **iris**, or by which the white of the eye is distinguished from the "black"—and when that part of the tunic born from the hard membrane of the brain consists of what we compare to **horn** <note>the **cornea**</note> in its clarity and substance, this inner tunic, I say, departs from the one created by the hard membrane. <margin>r Figures 16, 17 x; Figures 18, 19 $\text{\delta}$.</margin> It no longer touches it, but is compressed backward in that area where it was to be drawn under the part we liken to horn—as if it were required to be wrapped and girded equally closely on all sides by the tunic produced by the hard membrane. <margin>s Figure 1 N.</margin>

Nor is this tunic (generated from the thin membrane of the brain) gifted only with this compression; rather, in the middle of this compression, it is pierced by a certain hole, <margin>t Figure 1 I, Figure 14 m, Figure 15 r.</margin> which forms the smaller circle visible in the eye, and is called the **pupil** by us. <margin>The **pupil**.</margin> Thus, this tunic is very similar to the skin of a grape from which the stem that held it has been pulled out; <margin>u Figures 16, 17 y; Figures 18, 19 u.</margin> especially if you imagine the grape has collapsed a little and (as often happens) has been emptied when you pulled out the stem. For the whole skin of the grape corresponds to this tunic; that collapsing resembles the compression which this tunic claims for itself in its front part; while the hole where the stem was fixed is compared to the pupil itself. From this likeness, the Greeks call the present tunic *rhagoeides* <note>original: $\text{\rho\alpha\gamma\omicron\epsilon\iota\delta\tilde{\eta}}$, meaning "grape-like"</note> and *rhoga* <note>original: $\text{\rho\tilde{\omega}\gamma\alpha}$, a grape</note>, while we call it the **uvea** <note>from *uva*, the Latin word for grape</note>. <margin>The **choroid**.</margin> Since it is formed from the thin membrane of the brain, which is also called *choroeides* <note>meaning "membrane-like"</note>, the Greeks also named this tunic the **choroid**. Because the uveal tunic is covered everywhere by the one generated by the hard membrane of the brain, <margin>x Figure 15 p, p; Figure 16 u, u.</margin> little branches of veins and arteries reach from the latter into the uvea. These make the uvea so rough that in its outer surface, it also approaches the inner surface of a grape skin, which contains those fibers by which the flesh and seeds of the grape are supported.

Furthermore, since many branches of vessels (as we have already said) are produced from the tunic created by the hard membrane and are distributed into the uvea, the uvea is also joined to that tunic by the intervention of those branches. But where the uvea...

<margin>The colors of the uveal tunic</margin>
The tunic departs from that [inner membrane] following the circle of the iris and is pressed inward; the uveal tunic <note>The **uveal tunic** here refers to the choroid and the iris. Vesalius is describing how the iris separates from the outer layers to form the colored part of the eye.</note> is strongly attached to it throughout the entire circuit and varies in color. For the uvea is always black and slightly moist on its entire surface where it is closely surrounded by the hard tunic <note>The **sclera**.</note>; however, in the anterior part where it is compressed, it is tinted in various ways, and it always expresses that color which is found in the iris of the eye—the larger circle—in healthy people. It is for the sake of this color that we say eyes are black, or grey-blue, or blue-green. 

<margin>The color of the eyes does not vary due to the abundance of humors or spirits.</margin>
For this color in no way arises from the abundance, lack, or thinness of the eye’s humors, nor from the contraction or dilation of the pupil, nor from the depth or thinness of the eye, nor should it be attributed to any similar cause. Although this will perhaps seem a great paradox to those who stuff entire books with theories on the colors of the eyes, I would have it proved in no other way than this: the color that happens to each person (no matter how varied it is, or how it differs between the two eyes, or even sometimes within a single eye) always appears the same in the uvea itself—whether you examine it in an intact eye, or when the humors have flowed out halfway or entirely, or when the uveal tunic itself has been freed and torn away from the neighboring parts by dissection. So much so, that I believe one should discuss eye colors no differently than one discusses the black, brown, and white skin given to men even in the womb, or red, blonde, and black hair. Indeed, we see a similar pattern observed between skin and eye color among various nations. 

Furthermore, the internal surface of the uvea is distinguished by different colors, which are nevertheless the same in all humans. In the posterior part of the eye, where this tunic first arises, it is whitish; soon it becomes green, and then blue, in the manner of a rainbow. The internal surface possesses these colors in the posterior part of the eye, but in the anterior part of the eye, the whole surface is intensely black. It is not as smooth here as it is seen in the posterior part; this happens to it primarily because of the processes <note>The **ciliary processes**, which look like small ridges or pleats.</note> which it leads out from itself in this area, <margin>y Figure 1, K.</margin> <margin>and Figures 11, 12.</margin> which are to constitute the tunic that is spread over the anterior seat of the vitreous humor <margin>z Figure 1, K between C and O; and Figure 8, c between a and b.</margin> and acts as <insert>z</insert> an interstice between the vitreous humor and that which we shall call the aqueous humor.

<margin>The tunic compared to eyelashes and the hairs of the eyelids.</margin>
Thus, this tunic is endowed only with flat surfaces, not concave or convex ones. Indeed, you would create it if you were to cut out a circle from the thinnest spider’s web, as large as the anterior seat of the vitreous humor, and then cut another small circle within this circle to make a hole as wide as the crystalline humor <note>The **lens**.</note>. For you could compare the present tunic to such a circle, if you imagined it arising in a ring from the uveal tunic and joining with the crystalline humor at its own opening. But this tunic almost exceeds the spider’s web in thinness, and it consists of such processes arising from the uvea that it remarkably mirrors the form of black cilia, or the hairs of the eyelids. Whether it should be called a "tunic" or something else, I do not care much; as long as I explain in what seat it is placed, to what it is joined, and what its appearance and substance are. Nor does any name occur to me that I might more aptly give it than "tunic"—or, if you prefer, an "interstice" or "septum" placed between the vitreous humor and that which we shall call the white or aqueous humor.

<margin>The hard tunic of the eye, drawn out from the hard membrane of the brain.</margin>
Now it would be timely <margin>a Figure M drawn from L; and almost all of 16, 17.</margin> to include in our discourse the hard tunic of the eye, which we believe arises and is unraveled from the hard membrane of the brain <note>The **dura mater**.</note> that invests the optic nerve. For as soon as this membrane <margin>b Figure 16, f.</margin> is flattened against the posterior seat of the eye, it dilates; and becoming thicker and harder than the dura mater of the brain itself, it is wrapped around the eye in a circle on all sides, reaching into the anterior as well as the posterior parts. Yet, meanwhile, it is not similar to itself everywhere, nor is it given a single name. <margin>Hardness <note>original: $\text{\sigma\kappa\lambda\eta\rho\acute{\omicron}\tau\eta\varsigma}$ (sklerotes)</note></margin> For where it constitutes the posterior seat of the eye and reaches in the anterior seat as far as <margin>c Figures 18, 19.</margin> the larger circle of the eye, it is thick and hard (whence it is also called <insert>d</insert> "hardness") <margin>d Figure 1, N; Figures 16, 17, x and y together.</margin> and then, in the manner of the dura mater of the brain, it is opaque and not at all transparent. In that seat...

In the place where the dark part of the eye is located, this tunic changes into the appearance of horn, which, being perfectly polished, is used in place of glass for a lantern. This part of the present tunic does not only resemble horn in its transparency—which it even exceeds—but also in its substance: for this part of the tunic is hard in the manner of horn, and like horn, it can be divided into layers and scraped, just as if it were composed of several plates or scales packed together. And for this reason, from its resemblance to horn, it is called <margin>horn-like <note>original: *keratoeides*</note></margin> **horn-like** by the Greeks, but we call it the **cornea**. However, it seems that most of the Greeks did not call only this part of the hard tunic by that name, but also the entire tunic (since it is remarkably hard in the manner of horn).

It is also very firmly attached to it in a circular fashion along the larger circle of the eye, or the iris. Furthermore, in the place where this tunic is seen to be transparent like horn, the uvea itself does not touch it; as long as the eye is healthy, it is separated from the uvea by a notable interval where the uvea is compressed in its forward position.

<margin>
Aqueous humor.
water-like <note>original: *hydatoeides*</note>
</margin>
This interval, and the entire space consisting between the front of the crystalline humor <note>The lens.</note> and the pupil, is filled by that humor which remains to be described and is considered a true humor. For it is thin and fluid like water, encountered by those who dissect or treat cataracts <note>Vesalius refers to the "couching" of cataracts, a common surgery in his time.</note>, and it is seen to be remarkably transparent like water. For this reason, it is called **water-like** by the Greeks and **aqueous** by us. Although many, comparing this to the fluid of an egg white, call it the **albugineous** humor, I believe the Greeks did not compare this humor to egg white because it is by no means as thick; rather, it is much closer to that fluid which we see sweating out of fresh, whole eggs placed over a fire. This humor supports the part of the uveal tunic that is not in contact with the cornea in a healthy eye and (as I said) is contained in its front and back parts. When it stays within the eye, enclosed by its surrounding boundaries, it forms a half-sphere like the vitreous humor; its posterior part, which consists of a flat surface, has a depression as large as the part of the crystalline humor that bulges forward. The anterior site of this aqueous humor, however, is convex and round like a half-sphere, following the shape of the eye.

Furthermore, the external surface of the hard tunic <note>The sclera.</note>, in the entire area where it is transparent and truly the cornea, is very smooth and slippery; but in the other areas, it is seen to be so rough and uneven, just as membranes grown together are roughened by mutual contact.

The adhering or white tunic of the eye.

Then, onto the anterior part of the hard tunic as far as the iris, another tunic grows, which remains to be mentioned. It is called **on-grown** by the Greeks and **adhering** <note>The conjunctiva.</note> by the Latins because, being grown onto or attached to the eye, it holds it and joins it to the neighboring parts; it is also called the **white** [of the eye] because of the color it possesses. This membrane, drawn over only the anterior site of the eye as far as the iris, is thin and is continuous with the membrane that lines the inner site of the eyelids; it is counted among the parts of the eye, just as the eyelids themselves can be added to these parts if it seems right to anyone.

Furthermore, if anyone now wishes to approach the construction of the eye from the outermost to the innermost parts, it is now very easy to follow them in reverse order, and then to discuss the humors and tunics separately. I have followed the description of the eye in the way I am accustomed to use in the schools. But just as I have been used to demonstrating the fabric of the eye so studiously that no one among the spectators should miss anything in it, so too in explaining the *use* of its parts I here become completely silent. This is because I do not satisfy myself regarding the primary instrument of sight, and I am persuaded that in this area I cannot offer anything that is sound in every respect. It is not that I am unable to mention or even write at length here that the crystalline humor is the principal instrument of sight, and that the vitreous humor is produced so that the crystalline may be nourished, and that the rest of the parts of the eye were formed for its sake—as Galen pursues extensively in the tenth book of *On the Use of the Parts*—but rather because it is not certain to me how sight occurs. Since the explanation for the rest of the eye's construction depends on this, and because I have thought that I should eventually write something privately concerning these types of controversies among philosophers and physicians, this current labor has now reached its proper bulk.

---

# ON THE INSTRUMENT OF HEARING.
## Chapter XV.

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'Q' showing several figures gathered around a table engaged in a dissection or anatomical examination, including a figure holding a skull.</image-desc>
<margin>a All these are shown in the figure for chapter 8 of book 1.</margin>
THOSE things which were just now to be told concerning the fabric of the organ of hearing, I have already explained in the first book in such a way that, if nothing had been mentioned there, I would treat them now. For in the eighth chapter of that book, I reviewed <gloss>a</gloss> the cavity carved and prepared in the temporal bone for the sake of the organ of hearing, and then the openings, membranes, and small bones of that cavity. In the thirty-sixth chapter, however, I followed the construction of the cartilage of the ear and its other parts, as it occurred to me then and as it now occupies my mind. For I can weave nothing more certain here concerning hearing and the perception of sound than I did there; unless, indeed, I am now even more in doubt than when I was telling those things, and satisfy myself far less. I cannot wonder enough that everyone writes so prolifically about hearing and its objects without even a superficial knowledge of the organ itself; from which, however, the principal demonstrations for this discussion ought to have been sought.

THAT THE TONGUE is the instrument of taste is granted by all physicians and philosophers alike. In that part of the tongue which we see through the gaping mouth without any cutting, we have reviewed its appearance along with its coverings or tunics. In the fourth book,<sup>c</sup> not neglecting its nerves—of which<sup>d</sup> one was counted as a principal portion of the larger root of the third pair of nerves <note>original: "tertij neruorum coniugij." ### ON THE INSTRUMENT OF TOUCH.
### Chapter XVII.

<margin>What is to be performed in the following chapters, now that the description of the parts of the body is finished.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting several putti or cherubs engaged in an anatomical or surgical scene, appearing to handle a human head or torso for study.</image-desc>
I believe I also completed the description of the instrument of touch at the beginning of the fourth book, when I asserted that no nerve is not endowed with the sense of touch as it is distributed through the body. There, I narrated Nature's aims in the distribution of nerves as much as that place required, and addressed the opinion of those who taught that one little portion of the same nerve presides over sensation while another over motion without sensation. And so, with the description of the parts of the whole human fabric completed to the best of my ability, it now remains to write down the method of dissection for all the parts we have undertaken in the present book. Furthermore, if the method of dissecting any part handed down in other books was not expressed, I will also add that in order at the end of this book, and finally propose some things regarding the dissection of living animals <term>vivisection|the practice of performing operations on live animals for the purpose of scientific research, which Vesalius used to demonstrate functions like breathing and heartbeat</term>.

## THE METHOD OF ADMINISTERING THE BRAIN, AND ALL THE ORGANS HANDED DOWN IN THE PRESENT BOOK, TOGETHER WITH THE EXAMINATION OF THE VEINS, ARTERIES, AND FINALLY THE NERVES CRAWLING THROUGH THE ARMS AND LEGS. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>How to prepare the head for the inspection of the brain.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting putti working with a body part, possibly preparing it for dissection or transport.</image-desc>
PROVIDED that you have already approached the muscles occupying the neck and the nerves springing from the cervical spinal medulla <note>the spinal cord</note> in a body that has so far served for inspecting the organs of nutrition and the vital faculty <note>the internal organs of the abdomen and chest</note>, I now advise that the head be removed from the rest of the body, just as I reviewed at the end of the previous book. For you will handle it much more conveniently and with less trouble once it is removed. Hence, the heads of decapitated men are also very well suited for this use; especially because they are scarcely well dead, but meanwhile (which is inconvenient primarily for the inspection of vessels) they are for the most part bloodless, obtained immediately after the punishment has been carried out through the help of judges and officials who are not too difficult.

<margin>
a Just as figure 7 of chapter 6 in book 2 was removed from figure 6 of the same chapter, and as the 1st figure of this book is prepared.
How the skull is to be opened for the anatomy of the brain.
</margin>
Whatever head is obtained, you will make a circular cut<sup>a</sup> in the skin of the head down to the bone with a razor or knife, which will be timely started at the width of a thumb higher than the eyebrows. From here it will be led through the temples to the most prominent and rear-most seat of the occiput <note>the back of the skull</note>, and from there back through the temples to the forehead. Then with a saw, such as we are accustomed to use for removing limbs in gangrene, or another sought from the makers of ivory combs, you will divide the skull <term>calvaria|the upper part of the skull, or skullcap</term> along that line; taking careful care that the saw does not descend deeper than the bone. In this work it will be helpful if the hair of the head has not yet been shaved, nor the ears cut off; so that with lighter effort, with your other hand,

When you have divided the skull in a circle, run the blunt tip of a small knife along the cut to examine whether any part of the bone remains to be divided, so that you may also divide it with the saw. Furthermore, lest you make the end of the cut higher or lower than its beginning, nothing prevents you from tightly wrapping a string dipped in some color around the skull—in the manner of those who saw beams into planks—so that the color marks a circular line on the skull to guide your saw. It is best to wrap this string around the bone after you have already cut the skin in a circle; indeed, the cut in the skin cannot guide your hand, since its sides, while the head is being held firmly, are pulled apart here and there as the skin naturally recedes. 

When the skull has been divided in this manner, if you have the head free from the neck and lower jaw, you should place its base upon the table; if it seems necessary, place a stone or something similar on either side so it does not fall over. But if the head is still attached to the rest of the body by whatever method of dissection you are using, you should place enough square stones or a block of wood under the neck and the back of the head <note>original: "occipitio"</note> so that the head is tilted forward and elevated, as if it were resting on its base, rising up toward you. Additionally, into the cut made through the skull, first place the back of a stronger knife transversely at the forehead; by moving it slightly up and down, you will pry the cut open to some extent. The same must be done at the back of the head and the temples, until you judge that the upper part of the skull is free from the hard membrane of the brain <note>the *dura mater*</note>. Then, by grasping the hair at the crown of the head, the bone will follow the pulling hand.

<margin>Examination of the skin, fat, fleshy membrane, and then the covering of the skull and the membrane still underlying it.</margin>
Once the bone is removed, you will easily pull away the skin along with the fat and the fleshy membrane <note>the *galea aponeurotica*</note> using only your hands. Next, with the tip of a small knife, you will search for what the Greeks call the <term>περικράνιον</term> <note>pericranium; the fibrous membrane covering the skull</note>, which in this location is the <term>περίοστιον</term> <note>periosteum; the layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</note>. You will also look for <margin>b 1st figure F, F.</margin> the small veins proceeding from the skin of the crown into the skull toward the hard membrane of the brain, or from that membrane into the skin.

<margin>The amplitude of the hard membrane, how it is to be examined.</margin>
Now, the hard membrane of the brain <note>the *dura mater*</note> must be perforated in some part with a knife; and with a reed, a pipe, or a syringe <note>original: "syphone"</note> such as we use for drawing out urine inserted into the hole, the sides of the cut must be compressed against it with your fingers. Then, by inflating the syringe, you may learn how much larger the hard membrane is than the mass of the brain. It will be sufficient to make a hole of this kind on only one side, for the abundant air that is blown in distends and inflates the hard membrane of the brain everywhere. But if, while you were dividing the skull with the saw, you carelessly cut the hard membrane anywhere, that cut should also be conveniently pinched while the membrane is being inflated so that it does not let the air through. 

When the membrane has been released and has collapsed after you have pulled out the syringe, <margin>c From the first figure you will make the second.</margin> you will thrust the tip of a sharper knife into its third sinus <note>the superior sagittal sinus, a large vein-like channel</note>, which runs through the whole length of the head in the highest part of that membrane. With a long cut, you will divide the whole sinus as far as you can; and once the sinus is stretched open, you will inspect its shape and <margin>d 2nd figure C, C & D, D.</margin> the orifices of the branches which sprout from both its sides and from its lower part.

<margin>Detection of the thin membrane.</margin>
Furthermore, to strip the brain of its hard membrane, you will perforate it near the frontal bone to the right side of that third sinus. Then, with a probe inserted into the hole, you will lead a continuous cut with the knife toward the right side of the sinus all the way to the occipital bone. Next, you will again perforate the hard membrane with the tip of a knife near the ear, where it is closest to the bone; from here, you will proceed by cutting straight upward into the cut made along the length of the head. Finally, at the crown of the head, you will lift the two corners where the cuts meet with your fingernails, and pulling them downward, reflect them away from the brain. Take care of the branches which reach into the thin membrane of the brain <note>the *pia mater*</note> from the third sinus of the hard membrane and <margin>e 2nd figure G, G.</margin> from those vessels with which the right side of the hard membrane is entwined. When you have observed this, you will divide those "testes" and "nates" with a small knife along the <gloss>a</gloss> probe, so that the passage extended from the third ventricle to the cerebellum becomes visible. Let the passage be observed a little more accurately, which sometimes reaches from the brain to the basin <note>original: *pelvim*; the infundibulum or pituitary stalk</note> and leads the phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; ancient doctors believed the brain purged waste fluids through this structure</note> down to that point. You can now tear away the thin membrane of the cerebellum with a small hook and examine the <gloss>b</gloss> vein which extends from its ducts into the posterior and lower seat of the anterior ventricles. Indeed, you will find this very easily, provided you search for it near the connection of the front part of the cerebellum with the brain, which occurs primarily through the intervention of this vein. To recognize the <gloss>c</gloss> union of the cerebellum with the dorsal medulla <note>original: *dorsali medulla*; the brainstem and spinal cord</note>, the head must be reclined as if on its <gloss>d</gloss> face, and with a hand placed between the cerebellum and the hard membrane <note>the dura mater</note> joined to the bone of the back of the head, the cerebellum should be pulled forward and downward until the whole structure falls away, freed from the dorsal medulla.

In that procedure, nothing will prevent you from seeing the <gloss>e</gloss> small veins or ducts from the beginnings of the first and second sinuses of the hard membrane, or the <gloss>f</gloss> veins and arteries creeping through the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae, reaching into the cerebellum. You will also see the origin of the dorsal medulla from the brain itself, its shape, and the cavity which, together with the cavity of the cerebellum, forms the <gloss>g</gloss> fourth ventricle. Then, with the cerebellum turned <gloss>h</gloss> face down, you will look at its own cavity, and the parts and seats where it was joined to the dorsal medulla, and especially the beautiful image of its own coils and windings. From these, you will be led as if by the hand to the two <gloss>h</gloss> peaks of the coils which resemble worms <note>original: *vermibus*; the cerebellar vermis</note>, appearing as the ends of the revolutions drawn through the middle of the cerebellum along its length.

<margin>
*Of the worm-like processes.*

And this will appear most clearly if, by a long section on both sides along that length drawn to the sides of those revolutions, you free them from the rest of the substance of the cerebellum and spread the excised parts out on the table. For in this way, a single worm will appear to you, very similar to those which are accustomed to fall from willow trees in the springtime, or to silkworms before they enclose themselves in a cocoon—and even more so when they have already been enclosed for some time but have not yet gnawed through the cocoon. But if you do not remove all those middle revolutions of the cerebellum at once, but only cut out the ends, you can demonstrate two worm-like processes of the cerebellum: one being the anterior, and the other the posterior.

Furthermore, the image of the worm-like processes themselves should be examined not only when they have been excised in this manner, but their use should also be weighed with particular study when the cerebellum is torn away from the beginning of the dorsal medulla.

<summary>In this page, Vesalius provides a step-by-step guide to dissecting the cranial nerves and the pituitary gland. Most significantly, he explicitly debunks Galen's claim that humans possess a "rete mirabile" (reticular plexus), noting that this structure is found in animals like sheep but is absent in human anatomy.</summary>

# THE STRUCTURE OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VII
<center>815</center>

<margin>

Once you are satisfied with this view, nothing truly prevents you from approaching the other side as well, or even using the skulls of beasts, such as the ox and sheep, for this work, since the organ of hearing in those animals does not differ much from the human structure. Furthermore, if you do not think the bones must be preserved, I would suggest that you break away the frontal bone where it looks toward the eyebrows in various places, in order to accurately examine <gloss>p</gloss> that sinus <note>the frontal sinus</note> which it contains. The same must also be done in the bone that mimics a wedge <note>the sphenoid bone</note>, so that its <gloss>q</gloss> frequently appearing cavities, and what lies hidden within them, may also be seen.

<margin>
Examination of the muscles in the body at hand that have not yet been dissected.
</margin>
Otherwise, the management of several muscles now remains (provided you are going to complete the entire anatomy in one body), for which the other side will suffice for viewing. You will therefore approach the muscles moving the elbow, and those which move the radius, the wrist, and the fingers; then those moving the shin, and those considered the authors of the movements of the thigh; finally, you will cut away the workers of the movements of the foot and fingers together with their ligaments, just as I have commemorated much earlier in the second book. For I would consider it entirely beside the point if I were to treat those muscles, and the method of managing them, here again even in passing.

<margin>
Examination of the VEINS and nerves of the arm.
</margin>
As for what pertains to the veins, arteries, and nerves of the arm and leg, since the management of these alone has not yet been described, I shall now approach it. First, therefore, you will draw a transformation in the skin from the top of the shoulder all the way to the nail of the thumb, so lightly that you do not wound the <term>fleshy membrane</term> <note>original: *carnosa membrana*; the superficial fascia or subcutaneous layer</note>. Then, having separated the lips of the incision from one another, with all zeal and patience for the labor, you will remove the skin from the fleshy membrane in such a way that you allow all the fat to adhere to the membrane. Observe studiously that you do not allow any vein or small nerve to remain connected to the skin. And if by chance you have through negligence divided any branch extended toward the skin, and have separated it for some distance from the fleshy membrane along with the skin, cut it away diligently from the skin and lay it back over the fleshy membrane just as it was creeping along; then resume taking away the skin as you began, leaving no bit of skin anywhere, neither on the upper arm, nor the elbow, nor the hand.

...while the back parts of the inner bump of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle</note> are carried into the elbow) by the extended portion of the ulna, which scatters a branch below the middle of the ulna’s length. This branch, having turned back toward the outer parts of the elbow, offers small forks to the outer side of the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger; you will find this with little effort, as it is led almost on the surface. You will find the rest of the progress of the fifth and third nerves, however, if <insert>u</insert> you divide the transverse ligament <note>the flexor retinaculum of the wrist</note> placed in the internal seat of the wrist, and then with a small knife trace the series of the vein, the artery, and those nerves all the way to the tips of the fingers.

Furthermore, before you investigate the nerves and vessels of the leg, you will also diligently observe the distribution <insert>x</insert> of the nerves leaping out from the sides of the thoracic vertebrae. You will find this opportunely only when—having carefully read their distribution in these our commentaries—you have a very clear view of the dissection of the muscles, which you need here no less than you needed an absolute knowledge of the bones before the management of the muscles. Therefore, when you have come to the lumbar vertebrae, you shall lead the section from the groin all the way to the big toe of the foot, just as in the arm, dividing the skin down to the fleshy membrane <note>original: *carnea membrana*; this refers to the subcutaneous fascia and its associated layers</note>. Then, you should remove the entire skin of the thigh, the tibia, and the foot—leaving the fleshy membrane unharmed and the veins, arteries, and nerves running between it and the skin—as conveniently as possible. 

Soon <insert>y</insert> you should seek the origins and roots of the four nerves seeking the leg, following the nerves leaping forth from the lumbar vertebrae and the sacred bone <note>the sacrum</note> according to their series. Once the order of the section has been led to the leg in this manner for its four nerves, you will weigh the offshoot <insert>z</insert> of the first nerve extended into the fleshy membrane on the outer side of the thigh. Then you will find the offshoot <insert>a</insert> of the second nerve on the anterior side of the thigh, usually diffused to the fleshy membrane. Here <insert>b</insert> you will also observe a vein extended through the inner parts of the thigh and tibia all the way to the top of the foot, along with the offshoot of the second nerve. You will find the offshoot <insert>c</insert> of the third nerve offered to the fleshy membrane if you apply your mind to the groin. 

However, so that the branch <insert>d</insert> of the fourth nerve diffused into the fleshy membrane may be encountered, <insert>e</insert> you shall first free the first muscle moving the thigh <note>the gluteus maximus</note> from the ilium, the sacrum, and the coccyx all the way to its insertion; soon you will see the trunk of the fourth nerve and that branch. Once this is found, you will also seek the branch <insert>f</insert> of the fourth nerve diffused into the fleshy membrane near the popliteus <note>the back of the knee</note> and the lower parts of the thigh, and then you will track the branches of the fourth nerve in the fleshy membrane, brought forth in many ways to the skin of the tibia together with the veins. 

And soon, having returned to the groin, you will seek with a knife through the muscles the series of the first nerve hidden within the muscles; you will do this also in the second and third—although with the third, the offshoots <insert>g</insert> of the artery and vein must also be found, which glide down into the thigh through the foramen of the pubic bone <note>the obturator foramen</note>. You will gradually find the more notable vein and artery seeking the thigh by dissecting and setting aside the muscles; having observed their branches, you will follow their progress where they are turned back along the thigh bone and go to the popliteus along with the fourth nerve. Where you find these three—namely, the vein, artery, and nerve—you will investigate how they are divided in the popliteus, and with the muscles and ligaments variously dissected, you will learn their entire series. In this work, you will easily experience by use itself how much you will be helped by diligent reading of our descriptions (repeated more than once) and by the ready application of the images to the restoration itself. 

Furthermore, if it seems good to form a skeleton from the bones that remain for you from the present body, or otherwise to preserve them for the study and inspection of bones, you shall use our method for preparing bones and cartilages which we handed down at the end of the first book; and thus you will apply the finishing touch <note>original: *colophonem*; the final piece or completion of a work</note> to the entire dissection of the dead.

# SOME NOTES BY ANDREAS VESALIUS ON THE DISSECTION OF LIVING BODIES. Chapter XIX.
<center>818</center>

->AND. VESALII, DE CORPORIS DE VIVORVM SECTIONE NONNVLla. Caput XIX.<-

<margin>What is learned from the dissection of the dead, and what from the living.</margin>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'P' depicting several men performing a dissection on a human body lying on a table in an architectural setting.</image-desc>

**Just as the dissection of the dead** most accurately teaches the number, position, shape, property of substance, and composition of each part, so too does the dissection of a living creature clearly show the function itself at times, and at other times provides very convenient reasoning for its discovery. For this reason, students are rightly practiced first on dead animals, so that later, when they are ready to investigate the action and use of the parts, they may promptly approach a living animal. Moreover, since there are very many small parts of the body dedicated to different actions and uses, no one should doubt that the dissections of the living are likewise manifold.

<margin>How the use of bones and cartilages is to be seen in a living creature.</margin>

Indeed, regarding the bones—to treat each thing in order—we seek from the anatomy of the living whether these are the best support and foundation of the body, and whether they are all grown together and stabilized. For when we see some bone of a living creature broken, we observe the entire limb subject to the fracture collapse and no longer be supported. Because this happens frequently by accident, we do not greatly require the dissection of living subjects to investigate the use of bones. We learn by similar reasoning that cartilages also strengthen certain parts when they are broken; but in the dissection of some joint, we see what the cartilage provides, even if we do not perform this on a living creature.

<margin>
The use of ligaments.
a. 4th muscle table, character a.
b. 4th muscle table, character β; 5th table, character θ.
c. 2nd muscle table, characters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
</margin>

And so too, the use of the ligament binding the bones together is seen in the dead as well, just as is the use of ligaments covering the tendons transversely. For while we divide the <insert>a</insert> transverse ligament <note>original: "transversum ligamentum"; the flexor retinaculum of the wrist</note> placed in the internal part of the wrist, and we pull the <insert>b</insert> muscle that flexes the second or third joints of the fingers toward its origin, we see that this was done specifically so that it might hold the tendons in place, preventing them from rising out of their seat. Although this can also be seen in a living dog if you briefly free the skin from the elbow and hand, and with a knife divide the transverse ligament in the wrist and <insert>c</insert> others located on the outer side of the ulna and radius at the wrist. For soon, when the dog flexes and extends its fingers by its own impulse, you will see the tendons lifted from their boundaries.

<margin>How the use and function of the muscles are observed.</margin>

In this procedure, you will also observe the action of the muscles, when you see them contract and thicken where they are most fleshy, and then stretch out and become thin again, according as they draw a part to themselves when contracted, or when relaxed and led out, they allow it to be pulled in the opposite direction by another muscle, or otherwise do not exercise their contraction. Nor is this to be observed only here in the elbow; rather, the skin should be removed higher up from the same dog, so that the entire arm and the <term>axilla</term> <note>the armpit area</note> are bared, and the nerves creeping through the armpit into the arm appear. From these, you should catch one with a snare <note>a surgical loop or ligature used to isolate a vessel or nerve</note>, once you have recognized that its path belongs to certain muscles.

<margin>
The use of the nerve in the muscles.
d. Figures 2 and 3, characters c, d; Book 4, character τ, and the last figure of that book, character T.
e. Figures 2 and 3, characters c, d; Book 4, asterisk (*), and the last figure, character m.
</margin>

But since the number and distribution of a dog's nerves do not entirely agree with a human's, I would advise that when you are about to undertake this dissection on a living dog, you also have a dead one at hand, in which you have learned the sequence of nerves running through the arm and elbow, and thus have found some nerve that is distributed into certain muscles. These will usually be the ones where, in humans, the <insert>d</insert> third nerve is carried into the elbow along the front part of the elbow joint, while the other—the <insert>e</insert> fifth nerve—hastens into the elbow along the back region of the inner bump of the humerus <note>the medial epicondyle of the upper arm bone</note>. Nerves of this kind are observed in the dog as well, and if they are tied somewhere before they reach the elbow joint, the movement of the muscles flexing the fingers and the wrist is abolished. Hence, if you also intercept that nerve with a cord, which in humans...

<header>BOOK VII OF THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY.</header>

<margin>Figure f, in the 2nd and 3rd figures of chapter 11, and the 4th line of figure 4, and the last figure e.</margin>
is counted by me as the fourth <gloss>f</gloss>, and it extends along the shoulder to its outer bump; if this is cut, the motion of the muscles that extend the wrist and fingers will also be destroyed. It is useful to intercept such nerves with loops <note>original: "laqueis" — these were fine cords or ligatures used to temporarily stop nerve function</note>, so that by loosening them now in this nerve, now in that one, you may observe the motion of the muscles being restored. Now, if you make a long incision in a muscle shaped like a mouse <note>The Latin word "musculus" literally means "little mouse," referring to how a muscle looks like a mouse running under the skin when it contracts.</note> (of which many occur here in the elbow), penetrating the entire belly of the muscle, you will weigh the fact that the motion of that muscle is not lost because of this cut. However, when you make a transverse cut across the belly, you will see the motion of the muscle abolished in proportion to the depth of the cut. But when you divide the belly entirely, you will observe the muscle retracting and bunching up, one part toward its insertion and the other toward its origin. Furthermore, if you cut the tendon of any other muscle, you will see the muscle recoil toward its origin. Likewise, if you divide the head of the muscle, it will contract toward its insertion. If you cut away both the insertion and the head together, the muscle will bunch into a ball at its belly and at the place where it is most fleshy. Thus, the function of the muscles will be obvious to you as you perform these actions. If you decide to investigate the function of a specific nerve or a particular muscle individually, you should approach that nerve and muscle as I have already instructed you to do in the arm and elbow. Nor is there any reason for me to recount here at length how it is appropriate to bind dogs or animals of that kind for these procedures, since anyone, through their own industry, will perform all these things most correctly, provided they have been precisely trained in the dissection of the dead. Thus, nothing more remains to be said about the live sectioning of nerves and muscles, although I will add a few new things regarding the recurrent nerves <note>The recurrent laryngeal nerves, which control the voice; Vesalius famously demonstrated that cutting these causes an animal to lose its bark/cry.</note> a little later when the opportunity arises.

But if one decided to probe the duty of the spinal cord,

<margin>

Spinal cord.
</margin>
to see how, when it is damaged, the parts below the injury lose sensation and motion, <gloss>h</gloss> he may bind a dog to a plank or a trunk in such a way that it extends its back and neck. Then, with a larger knife, several spines of the vertebrae can be cut away, and finally the spinal cord can be exposed in that place where one thinks it should be cut. For nothing is easier than to see then that the motion and sensation of the parts below the cut are abolished. Furthermore, in investigating the use of the veins,

<margin>Of the Veins.</margin>
there is also scarcely a need for the dissection of the living; for we learn enough from the dead that they carry blood through the whole body, and that any part in which a significant vein is cut in a wound is not nourished. Likewise, in the case of the arteries, we scarcely require

<margin>k Figure of chapter 12, book 3, letter ρ.</margin>
the dissection of the living, although one may <gloss>k</gloss> expose an artery proceeding into the groin and intercept it with a ligature, and observe that the part of the artery held below the ligature no longer pulses. And thus, it is observed with little trouble that blood is naturally contained in the arteries whenever we open an artery in living creatures. 

<margin>Of the Arteries.</margin>
However, so that we may be more certain that the power of pulsing does not reside in the artery itself, nor that the material contained in the arteries exists as the maker of the pulses, but rather that this virtue depends on the heart—besides the fact that we see an artery intercepted by a ligature no longer pulsing below the ligature—one may make a long cut in the artery of the groin or thigh and take a small tube made of a reed, as thick as the capacity of the artery. Then, insert it into the cut so that the upper part of the tube reaches higher into the cavity of the artery than the upper site of the cut, and likewise the lower part of the tube is pushed down further than the lower part of the cut itself. And then [tighten] the ligature of the artery...

...is wrapped around the artery, so that it cinches the body of the artery over a small tube <note>original: "canalem" — a cannula or hollow reed used in this experiment to prove the pulse is a force from the heart, not the vessel wall</note>. For when this is done, blood and spirit indeed flow through the artery all the way to the foot, but the entire part of the artery placed over the tube no longer pulses. However, when the bond is loosened, the part of the artery following the tube shows the pulse no less than the upper part. We shall see later how much force is led from the heart through the arteries to the brain; for now, we greatly admire Galen’s living demonstration <note>vivisection</note> in this regard, by which he urges that all things common to the brain and heart should be cut away. So, it is no wonder that the brain continues to perform its function in that procedure longer than Galen thought could conveniently happen. For in this dissection, the animal continues to breathe for a very long time and moves in other ways. If, however, it runs and thus requires much spirit, it collapses not long after—even though the brain still receives the substance of the animal spirit from those arteries which I mentioned seek the skull through the transverse processes of the neck vertebrae. </margin>
dedicated to each book. And since we have now reached the fifth [book], we shall now begin a discourse on the organs of nutrition, whose function we almost always learn even in the dissection of the dead. We see that the <term>peritoneum</term> <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> is the wrapping for all the organs enclosed within it; that the <term>omentum</term> <note>a fatty layer of tissue hanging over the intestines</note>, as well as the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, best serve the guidance and distribution of the vessels; and that the stomach prepares food and drink, which are brought here through the esophagus. Nevertheless, nothing prevents one from approaching living dogs that have taken food either a little or a long time before, and thus also examining the function of the intestines. But the office of the liver, as also that of the spleen, the kidneys, or the bladder, we can hardly observe better in the dissection of the living than in the dead—unless someone wishes to cut out the spleen from a living dog, as I have occasionally done, and kept the dog alive for several days. And thus I also once cut out a kidney; but the care of the wound is more troublesome than the knowledge gained from it is pleasant. This is unless someone approaches these dissections not so much for the sake of knowing the organs, but rather to exercise the hand and learn how to aptly sew abdominal wounds; which must also be studiously attempted in the intestines, so that one may become accustomed to suturing wounded 
<margin>Of the organs of generation.</margin>
intestines and replacing them in the abdomen when they have fallen out. Furthermore, we observe vivisections of the instruments serving generation almost daily in the treatment of hernias and in animals that are castrated. # THE SEVENTH BOOK ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY.

...you have pierced [the membranes] and freed its head from them, you will soon see it [the fetus] as if reviving and elegantly breathing. And once you have investigated this in one fetus, you shall approach another: which you will not free from the uterus, but instead, having opened the uterus according to the procedure already described, you will turn it inside out for a moment and reflect the lips of the incision outward, until the lowest part of the membranes or the "seat" of the next fetus appears. You should uncover this from the uterus up to the region where it is joined to the outer fetal membrane, and where that ample flesh, similar in substance to the spleen <note>Vesalius is describing the placenta, which he compares to the spleen due to its dark, spongy appearance</note>, is found; this flesh interweaves the vessels extending from the uterus into the outer fetal membrane. In this procedure, that connection of vessels must be preserved entire, and the rest of the outer membrane must be uncovered from the uterus, so that through the transparent fetal membranes, you may see the arteries distributed through them and entering the umbilical cord, pulsing at the same rhythm as the mother's uterine arteries. You will see the naked fetus attempting and struggling to breathe; then, once the membranes are broken and pierced, you will watch the fetus breathe and the pulse of the membranes and umbilical arteries perish, while the uterine arteries still pulse along with the remaining arteries outside the uterus.

<margin>An examination of the use of the heart and its subordinate parts.</margin>
In the functions of the heart and the lung, we have weighed many things: namely, the movement of the lung, and whether the windpipe <note>original: "aspera arteria" — the trachea</note> takes in any portion of what is drunk; then the dilation and constriction of the heart, and whether the rhythm of the heart’s pulse and the arteries is the same; likewise how the pulmonary vein <note>original: "venalis arteria" — literally the 'venous artery', the historical term for the vessel carrying oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart</note> is distended and compressed, and how an animal may still live even when its heart has been cut out.

<margin>Reference to Table 2, Figure 6, G, G, and I, I.</margin>
In observing these things, we would greatly require an animal endowed with a broad breastbone <note>the sternum</note> and possessing membranes that partition the chest <note>the mediastinum</note> which are so far apart that, by dividing the breastbone along its length, we could lead the incision between those membranes all the way to the heart, without piercing the cavities of the chest in which the lungs are contained. But since no such animal occurs besides man and the tailless ape, in dogs and pigs—and those animals of which we have a plentiful supply—the incisions must be approached in such a way that you may behold all the aforementioned things. It is evident that the lung follows the motion of the chest from this: when an incision is made in any interval between the ribs <note>the intercostal space</note> leading to the cavity of the chest, the part of the lung on the injured side collapses and is no longer distended with the chest, while the remaining part of the lung still follows the chest’s motion. This part will also soon collapse if you perform an incision into the chest cavity on the other side as well; thus the animal, even if it moves its chest for some time, will die no less than if it had been suffocated. 

However, in this procedure, it must be observed that you lead the incision as close as possible to the upper part of any rib, lest by directing the incision toward the lower part, you pierce the vessels stretched out there <note>the intercostal arteries and veins, which run along the bottom groove of each rib</note>. For then blood would flow out from there, which, by the grace of the air let in and out through the wound, would be made foamy and deceive you into thinking it was the lung. Indeed, to those who dissect incautiously, such foam seems to be the lung, and they believe that the lung is still being distended by its own innate power for some time. But so that you may see the natural following of the lung with the chest, you will dissect the cartilages of two or three of the middle ribs on one side; and with incisions led through the intervals of those ribs, you will reflect each rib outward and break them, so that you may establish a convenient opening through which you can see the uninjured lung. Since the membranes partitioning the chest <note>the pleura</note> in dogs are very transparent, it is quite easy to see through them the part of the lung still following the motion of the chest, and even to consider, once those membranes are lightly pierced, how that part of the lung also collapses.

<margin>Reference to Table 6, Figure 6, G.</margin>
Before you pierce them, however, it will be useful to grasp with your hands the branches of the pulmonary vein in that part of the lung which has already collapsed, and to free the substance of the lung from them for some distance, so that you may learn whether they move just like the heart.

<margin>Reference to Table 3, Figure 6, D, E, F.</margin>
For the motion of the heart is also visible to you here, especially if you divide the heart's envelope <note>the pericardium</note> and uncover the heart from it on that side where this procedure...

<margin>As prepared in Book 6, Figure 2.</margin>
...you attempt this procedure. It will be useful to try this on the left side, so that the right part of the lung may still move, and you can conveniently grasp the entire trunk of the vein-like artery <note>original: "arteriae uenalis"; Vesalius refers here to the pulmonary vein, which was thought to carry "vital spirits" and air like an artery</note> with your hand. In this kind of procedure, you will also not unprofitably grasp the base of the heart, and with a single cord, you will intercept the vessels coming out of it all at once and quite quickly, and then you will cut out the heart below the cord; once the ligatures binding the animal are loosened, you will let it run. For we have seen dogs, and especially cats, run for some distance even when affected in this way. Furthermore, you will see the motion of the heart, as well as the arteries, more correctly if, as soon as you have bound the dog to the board, you make an incision from the throat through the costal cartilages where they continue into the bones, using a very sharp knife on both sides; and soon from the end of one incision across to the end of the other, you will make a third incision down to the cavity of the peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. Once the breastbone [sternum] is raised along with the cartilages attached to it, and the transverse septum <note>The diaphragm</note> is freed from them, you will reflect the breastbone upward toward the animal's head. Then, having divided the heart's covering [pericardium], you will grasp the heart with one hand, and with the other, you will hold the great artery [aorta] extending along the back. However, you will perform all these things better in that vivisection which I am accustomed to show in the schools among others, as it is more comprehensive.

<margin>
Examination of the brain's functions.
</margin>
And for this reason, as soon as I have added a few things about the brain, I will describe this procedure more at length, so that it may be attempted by others with less trouble. In the examination of the brain itself and its parts, very little indeed is to be seen in vivisection, since here—whether we wish it or not, perhaps for the sake of our theologians—we must deny memory, reason, and thought to brute animals, even though their construction is the same as man's. <note>Vesalius is likely being ironic here, noting that while animals have the same brain structures as humans, religious doctrine of his time insisted only humans possessed a rational soul.</note> And so the student of anatomy, well-versed in the dissection of the dead and infected by no heresy, understands well how poorly I would be advised if I were to establish anything regarding the vivisection of the brain—something I would otherwise do most gladly. Yet, as far as sensation and motion are concerned, it can be seen that both perish when the brain is removed. And here the same method of investigation is to be followed as we prescribed in the procedure for the nerves. Whether the brain actually "feels" must be investigated in man: who, when it is cut or pressed, might indicate whether he is affected by pain, or whether he senses that by which the brain is altered; as is possible to experience daily in head wounds. Again, I think no one doubts that a dog's skull can be broken and either the right or left ventricle of the brain opened, and how the animal loses motion, and receives it again once the ventricle is closed.

<margin>
The vivisection which is usually employed as the colophon <note>The final, crowning touch or climax</note> to anatomical speculation in the schools.
</margin>
Furthermore, the dissection which I promised to describe a little earlier should be attempted on a pregnant dog or sow; although it is more convenient to use a sow for the sake of the voice. For a dog, having been tied up for some time, no matter how you affect it, eventually neither barks nor howls; and thus you sometimes cannot examine the loss or weakening of the voice. First, therefore, you will bind the animal so that it lies on its back, presenting the front of the neck and the free trunk of the body, to the board <note>original: "asser"</note> as strongly as possible according to your industry and the abundance of your equipment.

<margin>

And if I loosen the ligatures, it is beautifully heard how powerful an exhalation the animal attempts without a voice, once the recurrent nerves have been divided with a knife. ON THE FABRIC OF THE HUMAN BODY, BOOK VII.

<margin>
An investigation of whether the pulse of the heart and the arteries is equal.
f Figure 2, Book 6, B, C, D, E.
</margin>
...so that you may then once again examine with great precision the heart, the arteries, and the fetuses contained in the womb, for as long as you see fit. Thus far, the flow of blood has caused little harm to the animal, provided that an assistant blocks those f vessels which creep under the breastbone <note>original: "pectoris osse"; likely the internal mammary vessels</note> and holds the breastbone itself reflected upward toward the neck, so that because of the slant of the vessels, they pour out nothing further. This also occurs in the vessels stretched along each rib when the broken ribs are turned downward; and you yourself, while performing the sectioning, should strive to close the vessels for as long as they are slanted. But so that life may be restored to the animal in a certain way, an opening must be attempted in the trunk of the windpipe <note>original: "asperæ arteriæ"; the trachea</note>, into which a tube made of a reed or cane is placed; this is then inflated so that the lung rises and the animal, in its way, draws in air. For with a light inflation in this living animal, the lung swells as much as the cavity of the chest was, and the heart assumes its strength once more, beautifully varying the different types of its motion. Therefore, having inflated the lung once and then again, you can examine the motion of the heart by sight and touch as much as you please, and you can grasp the trunk of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> where it is laid out along the back, either in the chest cavity or at the vertebrae of the loins, and watch them both together: nothing will occur more clearly to you than the rhythm of the pulses of the heart and the arteries. Having observed this for a while, the lung must be inflated again; by this artifice—than which I have found none more pleasing to me in Anatomy—a great knowledge of the differences in pulses is to be gained. For when the lung collapses and remains flaccid for a long time, an undulating, "ant-like" <note>original: "formicans"; a term for a very weak, small pulse</note>, and "worm-like" <note>original: "uermicularis"; a pulse that feels like a crawling worm</note> motion or pulse of the heart and arteries is seen. But when the lung is inflated, the pulse becomes large and swift again, and presents marvelous inequalities. To put it simply, this procedure is of such a kind that it is the one I most often use to present the nature of all pulses to candidates of medicine. However, in the examination of these,

When this is subsequently separated from the uterus, I remove the fetus with its coverings, and having broken the outer covering, I show through the very transparent inner covering how the fetus attempts to breathe, and how beautifully it draws air once the inner covering is also broken. Soon, I uncover the next fetus as much as I can, without detaching the uterus from the outer covering at any part, so that the nature of the vessels of this fetus may be examined, just as I previously instructed that the live dissection of fetuses should be performed. Then, if before the dissection we gave the animal a drink stained with some color, and it had ingested various foods in succession, I investigate what kind of liquid occurs in the branches of the lung’s windpipe, and what the sequence of foods is in the stomach. With this dissection, I add the crowning touch <note>original: "colophonem"; the finishing stroke</note> to the whole of anatomical speculation in our schools, just as I now place the end to this, my history of the Fabric of the Human Body.

All are **ternions** <note>gatherings of three folded sheets, making six leaves</note>: except for **X**, which is a **half-ternion**; and **bb**, **Aa**, which are **quaternions** <note>gatherings of four folded sheets</note>. Likewise, **bb** is made a quaternion because of the **figure of the nerves** that must be sewn in before the beginning of Book V.

->HOUSE OF JOHANNES OPORINUS, IN THE YE-<-
->*ar of Salvation obtained through CHRIST 1555.*<-
->*In the month of August.*<-
